# Patrologia Latina, Volume 17

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

The complete, uniform, convenient, economical, and universal library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age down to the time of Innocent III; the chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries, and furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything written by each Father on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each biblical book and in which passages of their works they did so.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and readily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which, for the first time in our library, gathers together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

## FIRST SERIES

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

An edition more complete than all others, which may be regarded as their standard; revised and corrected from Vatican, Gallican, Belgian, and other manuscript codices, as well as from ancient editions, especially the Benedictine edition; continuously elucidated by notes and variant readings placed beneath the text; and further enriched with various minor works which the learned Benedictines either omitted or did not even mention.

## Part One

Containing Works Admitted by the Benedictines in Their Edition

## [On the Forty-Two Stations]

[Col. 0009]

## Prefatory Notice Concerning the Following Book

[Col. 0009] The Roman editors were the first to publish this treatise. But they refrained from informing us on what authority they did so, whether they relied upon one manuscript or several, and again whether these had been written by an ancient or a recent hand. We have nowhere discovered even a single manuscript of it; nevertheless, this little work itself supplies evidence by which its spurious attribution may be detected. For, to say nothing of the difference in style and the divergence in the treatment of the subject, one finds Josephus repeatedly cited in it, with his own words attributed to him—something that no one will deny to be foreign to Ambrose’s practice.

But what removes every reason for doubt is that the author of this treatise not only imitated, to some extent, the commentaries of Origen and Jerome, but also frequently appropriated Jerome’s very words and copied passages from Origen taken from Rufinus’s translation, which at that time had scarcely been published. We shall indicate all these matters in the margins.

As for the author of this work, we might perhaps offer more certain information if at this point we were not compelled to rely upon a single Roman edition, whose reliability may be shown to be exceedingly weak by the treatise alone *On the Trinity and the Resurrection of the Dead*. Nevertheless, the work itself, in the form in which it has come down to us, provides reasons from which we may reasonably suspect that it consists of sermons delivered to the people, and perhaps even that its author was a monk.

Nor would we be unwilling to adopt the view that, if he did not live in the times of Bede and Rabanus, he at least followed their method. For when they undertook to write on the same subject, they repeatedly transcribed Jerome—or rather the author whose sermons appear at the beginning of the Appendix to the fifth volume of Augustine’s works, and who is known to have borrowed a great deal from Origen—often word for word.

## A Treatise on the Forty-Two Stations of the Children of Israel (G, S)

[Col. 0009] 1 The Book of Numbers, which is now under discussion, is one of the five books of Moses. It is called by this name because, by God’s command, it contains the number and census of the able-bodied men of the Israelite people who went out from Egypt. For God spoke thus to Moses:

“Take the total of the whole congregation of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, according to their ancestral houses, everyone fit to go forth to battle in Israel.”

Therefore, since the Lord commanded that men twenty years old and upward, fit for battle, should be numbered, it is clear that he understood perfect men. From this total women, because of the impediment of feminine weakness; slaves, as degenerate in life and morals; and Egyptians, as foreigners and barbarians, are excluded (Origen, *Homily 1 on Numbers*, from Rufinus’s translation).

Only Israelites are numbered, and not all of them, but only those distinguished by strength and valor. For thus it is written:

“The census of the children of Israel, with their army, from twenty years old and upward, everyone fit to go forth to battle in Israel,” and so forth (Num. I, 45).

Nor is this without a mystery. For while a childish and unstable understanding, or feminine and enervated sluggishness, remains in us, or while we display Egyptian and barbarian ways, we are not worthy to be numbered by God’s holy reckoning.

Then, in the same book, the journeys, departures, and stations of the children of Israel are recorded—from the borders of Egypt to the time and place where Moses died—by God’s command. For he says:

“And Moses wrote down their departures and their stations, according to the word of the Lord” (ibid. 44).

Moses was not commanded by the Lord to write this without reason, but for our instruction. The Apostle says:

“All these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction” (1 Cor. X, 11),

[Col. 0010] so that, as we read and discern how many dangers threaten us on this journey to the land of the living, how many ambushes of enemies, how many struggles of spiritual warfare, and how many dangers of seas and rivers, of the world and of pleasures (Origen, *Homily 27 on Numbers*, from Rufinus’s translation), we may undertake our journey neither sluggishly nor carelessly, lest, as the day declines, we fail halfway along the road, overwhelmed by the darkness of night.

For at night the firstborn of Egypt are struck down by the destroyer (Exod. XII, 29); at night the soul of the rich miser is demanded by demons (Luke XII, 20). But, girding ourselves wisely for the journey and preparing ourselves bravely for battle, let us pass from virtue to virtue, and let the Lord our God go before us, in front of us, defeating our enemies, carrying us as a mother carries her child, and leading us by day with a cloud and by night with fire, so that, having at last overcome all the difficulties of the journey and the attacks of hostile powers, we may complete our departure gloriously.

[Col. 0010B] The stations of the children of Israel are counted as forty-two in number. Through the numerical relation of the ten, the four, and the two that they contain, they teach us many mysteries. Since I wish to explain this to you, brothers, look attentively, I beg you, and fix it in your memory, lest you be found despisers of the word, and lest your soul become a road where the seeds cast upon it do not germinate; for, he says, “the birds of the air will come and carry them away.” Receive these things, then, and store them in your hearts.

The number ten is mystical and is commended by Moses in no ordinary way. For to it he refers first fruits, offerings, and vows. He says:

“Every tenth of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the tree, belongs to the Lord; and every tenth of cattle and sheep, everything that passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to the Lord” (Lev. XXVII, 30 ff.).

Finally, when Jacob was setting out on his journey to Mesopotamia, to Laban his uncle, he promised God, who had appeared to him on the way, saying:

“Of everything that you give me, I will give you a tenth” (Gen. XXVIII, 22).

For this reason Noah, who is the first man pronounced righteous in the Old Scripture, is introduced as the tenth from the first-created man—not to indicate the lifespan of those then living or to prescribe a number of human beings, but so that it might clearly be taught that, just as ten is the most perfect of the numbers that follow unity, so tranquility in the soul is truly the completion of the activities of life.

For three multiplied by itself completes nine, and, according to the divine oracles, signifies quarrels, dissensions, and wars, as is evident in the case of the four and five kings who were at variance and fought one another. Unity, however, coming after nine, completes ten and signifies peace and friendship.

When nine kings were fighting, the wise Abraham, arriving as if a tenth, brought, by God’s favor, tranquility in place of storm, peace in place of war, and victory in place of death. Hence he also paid tithes to Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High God.

The number ten, therefore, is perfect and signifies unity.

The number four is also mystical and is commended in Scripture. For prophetic speech declares that on the fourth day the beautiful light, which reveals itself and all other things, together with the parents of light—the sun and moon—and the brilliant choir of stars, which by their rising and setting mark night and day, months and years, were created.

[Col. 0011C] The roots of the world are counted as four: earth, water, fire, and air. 3 The annual changes of the seasons are likewise four: winter, summer, spring, and autumn.

Finally, offerings of the fruits of the earth to God are forbidden before the fourth year. Thus it is written:

“For three years its fruit shall be unclean for you; you shall not eat of it. But in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy and praiseworthy to the Lord” (Lev. XIX, 23–24).

Nor is this without reason. For the tetrad contains everything: point, line, surface, and solidity—the measures of all things. It also contains the principal musical harmonies. Moreover, the sides of a square must be equal. Equality is the mother of justice, which is the guide and teacher of the other virtues.

[Col. 0011D] The number four, therefore, suggests justice.

Finally, the number two is not without its own mystery. We read that the widow was commended by the Lord with exceptional praise because she put two small coins into the treasury (Luke XXI, 2). The Samaritan spent two coins for the care of the wounded man (Luke X, 35). The Savior Christ spent two days among the Samaritans (John IV, 43). For the twofold charity—namely, toward God and toward one’s neighbor—is signified:

“On these two,” says the Lord, “hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 40).

Thus Moses records forty-two stations of the children of Israel from the borders of Egypt to the land of promise. In the same way Saint Matthew, describing the generation of Christ, counts forty-two generations. [Col. 0012A] For he says:

“From Abraham to David, fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ, fourteen generations” (Matt. I, 17).

He wished to show that the true Israelite, who hastens to pass from the Egypt of this age to heaven, the true land of the living, through so many dangers of every kind and temptations from enemies, must be armed with peace through the number ten, with justice through the number four, and with charity through the number two.

With peace, because it is written: “God has called us to peace” (1 Cor. VI). With justice, because the same Apostle says: “Stand clothed with the breastplate of justice” (Eph. VI, 14). With charity, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. IV, 8).

Christ, therefore, reaches the Virgin; Israel, the Jordan; and the Christian, heaven, through an equal number of stations. But now let us consider Israel’s departures one by one.

## First Station, RAMESSES

The order of the departures and the distinction of the stations of the children of Israel as they went out from Egypt toward the land promised to their fathers are exceedingly necessary to know for those who strive to walk after God and aspire to progress in virtue, because of the mysteries contained in them (Origen, *Homily 27*, from Rufinus’s translation).

For the things that were physically accomplished among the people of the fathers do not merely show us a history and sequence of events; understood spiritually, they are especially beneficial for our instruction. The Apostle had this in mind when he said in his Letter to the Romans:

“Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. XV, 4).

And to Timothy:

“All Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, and for training in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. III, 16).

We therefore read that, after all Egypt had been struck by such great plagues, at the time appointed by the heavenly oracle for them to depart into the wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord God, the children of Israel left the land of Goshen, which they had received as a dwelling place, and first gathered in the city of Ramesses. There they halted and there they fixed their first station.

Ramesses is a city of Egypt fortified by the Hebrews when Pharaoh raged against them and oppressed them with clay, bricks, and straw. For thus it is written:

“And they built fortified cities for Pharaoh, Pithom, Ramesses, and On” (Exod. I, 11).

It is situated at the farthest borders of that kingdom, as is recorded in the Book of Exodus (Exod. XII, 37).

In this station the people of the fathers, after slaughtering the lamb and smearing its blood on the thresholds and both doorposts of their houses, escaped the plague of the destroyer. In this station Egypt saw its firstborn slain. In this station, at the word of God, the people gathered unleavened flour and silver and golden vessels borrowed from the Egyptians.

Brothers, each of these things that have been mentioned is filled with mysteries and contributes to our instruction.

First, Ramesses is interpreted by some to mean “turbulent commotion,” which signifies repentance. For through repentance a turbulent commotion takes place in the sinner, so that the oldness of sin may be abolished and the newness of grace introduced; so that the old man may be crucified and the new man rise again; so that, once the former way of life in the flesh has finally been put aside, the newness of the spirit may be introduced.

Repentance, therefore, produces a great commotion and disturbance. Hence the prophet says:

“After I came to know, I groaned” (Jer. XXXI).

Whoever therefore desires to set out for the homeland of the eternal inheritance promised by God, and approaches the Lord God in order to offer himself as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to the Father, must first approach Ramesses—that is, the commotion produced by repentance—and fix his station there.

Ahab fixed his station there when, after tearing his garment, putting on sackcloth, fasting, sleeping in sackcloth, and walking with his head bowed, he humbled himself [Col. 0013B] (1 Kings XXI, 27). The king of Nineveh fixed his station there when, rising from his throne, he removed his robe, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes (Jon. III, 6). The Corinthians fixed their station there when they were grieved according to God; this grief, as the Apostle writes, produces repentance leading to steadfast salvation (2 Cor. VII, 10).

Then what else does the slaughter of the lamb signify but the passion of Christ, who, as the Prophet says, “was led like an innocent lamb to be sacrificed” (Jer. XI, 19)? When his blood is poured out upon the doorposts of our houses, we are delivered from the Destroyer, because through Christ’s passion, shared with us by the sacraments, we are delivered from him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews (Heb. II, 14).

Therefore in another place he says:

“Christ suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Heb. XIII, 12).

In this station also the firstborn of Egypt are extinguished—that is, the perverse passions of the flesh and the evil desires that wage war against the soul. The Egyptians are extinguished when you do not perform works of darkness; the Egyptians are extinguished when you live not carnally but spiritually; the Egyptians are extinguished when you drive impure and filthy thoughts from your heart or do not admit them at all.

Therefore, when he asks, “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” the Apostle answers: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24–25).

In this station flour, silver, and gold are accumulated. Flour, from which bread is made, is the teaching of Christ, because Christ is bread, as John says: “I am the living bread” (John VI, 51). Silver signifies the divine utterance:

“The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7).

Gold is the good mind, which is rightly compared with gold. For just as gold surpasses the other metals, so a good mind is superior in a human being to the other parts of human substance.

Three things, therefore, are heaped up in Ramesses: flour, silver, and gold—teaching, utterance, and a good mind—in which the wise person’s wealth consists.

But meanwhile let us consider the precious exchange. The children of Israel gave straw, which is consumed in unquenchable fire, and received flour, in which that wise woman hid the leaven. They gave clay, which is destroyed, because it is written: “I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets” (Ps. XVII, 43), and they received silver, which is the word of the righteous. For it is written: “Silver tested by fire is the tongue of the righteous” (Prov. X, 20).

They gave bricks, which fall, because it is written: “The bricks have fallen,” and they received gold (Isa. IX, 10), which is the good mind with which we serve the law of God.

A good exchange indeed! Hence the Apostle says: “You are already full; you have already become rich” (1 Cor. IV, 8).

Let us acquire these riches for ourselves, with which we may fill the intelligible treasures of our souls. But the Lord himself gives us grace so that we may be able to seize them from the Egyptians. Therefore the Apostle rightly says to the Hebrews: “It is good to establish the heart by grace” (Heb. XIII, 9).

A good station, then, is Ramesses.

## Second Station, SUCCOTH

[Col. 0014B] The second departure of the children of Israel was to Succoth. There, leaving Egypt behind and setting up their tents, they established their second station. Hence he says:

“And the children of Israel departed from Ramesses and camped at Succoth” (Num. XXXIII, 3).

The intention of the holy prophet Moses, who at God’s command described the progress of the people from Egypt to the Jordan, was not to record every place at which they happened to turn aside during the whole journey, but only those in which certain mysteries occurred.

Succoth is a city in the mountains, outside the land of Egypt but neighboring it, as is read in the Book of Joshua (Josh. XIII, 7). Finally, Succoth is interpreted as “tents.”

Thus when Jacob separated from Esau, who met him as he returned from Mesopotamia, Scripture says:

“He returned to the tents” (Gen. XXXIII, 17).

Another translation has: “He returned to Succoth.” It then adds:

“And Jacob made houses for himself, and made tents for his livestock; for this reason he called the name of that place Tents.”

Another translation says there: “He called the name of that place Succoth,” that is, tents.

In this station also they baked flour. For it is said in the Book of Exodus:

“And they made from the flour unleavened cakes baked under the ashes” (Exod. XII, 39).

For it had not been leavened, since the Egyptians had driven them out.

In this station, moreover, the number of years that Israel spent in Egypt is calculated. For he says:

“Now the dwelling of the children of Israel, which they dwelt in, they and their fathers, in the land of Egypt,” and so forth (ibid. 40).

Finally, in this station they are commanded to preserve a perpetual memorial among themselves of this liberation from Egypt. Moses said to the people:

“Remember this day, on which you came out of Egypt, from the house of slavery; for by a strong hand the Lord brought you out from this place” (Exod. XIII, 3).

Finally, in this station the feast of unleavened bread and the rite of eating unleavened bread are prescribed. For he says:

“For six days you shall eat unleavened bread; but on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the Lord. No leavened bread shall appear there” (ibid. 6).

So much for the literal meaning.

As for the mysteries, we say that the departure of the children of Israel to Succoth, which is interpreted as “tents,” signifies that whoever has had his station at Ramesses—that is, in the commotion of repentance—must proceed to Succoth, that is, to tents, as though walking by means of reflection.

For just as one who is traveling toward another place and has no permanent home dwells in tents, so what else is dwelling in tents than living as a pilgrim? The Apostle testifies to this when speaking of the fathers in the Letter to the Hebrews. He says:

“Confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth” (Heb. XI, 13).

And, recognizing himself as a stranger on earth, let him say with the Prophet:

“I am a sojourner upon the earth” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13).

Let him also consider the Apostle’s saying:

“We do not have here a lasting city” (Heb. XIII, 14).

Finally, let him recognize that as long as he is in the body he is away from the Lord. Therefore let him reject the things that are in the world, because they are the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.

Let him follow the Apostle’s counsel:

“Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle,” things which all perish through use; but let him long for the dwelling that is from heaven, always striving to please God (Col. II, 21 ff.).

The baking of the unleavened cakes teaches that, once the leaven of the ancient wickedness of the philosophers and the malice of the Jews has been purged out, one should feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Let each of us keep continually in mind the Lord’s command:

“Look and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. XVI, 6),

and let him not forget the Apostle’s warning:

“See that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Col. II, 8).

Then in Succoth the number of the years during which the people were in Egypt is calculated, because the penitent is told that he ought, like the swallow to cry out and like the dove to meditate upon his years in the bitterness of his soul (Isa. XXXVIII, 14), and not to be without fear concerning the forgiveness of sin (Ecclus. V, 5), but to grieve and say with the Prophet:

“My sin is always before me” (Ps. L, 5).

He must not look back by desiring his former vanities, like Lot’s wife and like the dog returning to its vomit. Rather, just as he gave himself over to uncleanness and iniquity, so let him present his members to serve justice for sanctification. To the extent that he glorified himself and lived in luxury, let him correct his errors and punish himself, experiencing torment and mourning.

Finally, the feast and perpetual solemnity of unleavened bread are prescribed—that is, perseverance in meditation and works is commanded—because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Hence the Apostle says: “Persevere in discipline, children.”

The departure, therefore, from Ramesses to Succoth is a departure toward better things.

## Third Station, ETHAM

The third station is Etham. [Col. 0015D] For after departing from Succoth, the children of Israel came to Etham; there, setting up their tents, they completed their third halt. He says:

“And departing from Succoth, they camped at Etham” (Num. XXXIII, 5).

Etham is a region between Egypt and the wilderness in which the town of Petra is located. Samson dwelt in a cave there when he was being harassed by the Philistines:

“And he sat,” it says, “in the cave of Petra of Etham,” a place that was very strongly fortified, as Josephus testifies (*Antiquities*, book 10).

This region was at the beginning of the wilderness. Hence he says: “And it is part of the desert.”

The prophet David mentions this region, saying:

“You dried up the rivers of Etham” (Ps. LXXIII, 15).

In this station the Lord first appeared at night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, showing the people the way to the land of their inheritance:

“And the pillar of cloud did not fail by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, before all the people” (Exod. XIII, 22).

But because Etham means “strength,” when Rehoboam prepared to defend himself against Jeroboam, he “built fortified cities, Etham and Tekoa” (2 Chron. XI, 6)—that is, cities of strength—we are taught that when someone has resolved in Succoth, amid the pilgrimage of this life, to persevere in meditation and the practice of good works to the end, he ascends to Etham, that is, to strength, because the Lord himself gives power and strength to his people.

Hence the Apostle said:

“I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus” (Phil. IV, 13).

Indeed, through cloud and fire he opens the way for him and becomes the guide of his journey, until he sees the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.

Let us therefore ascend also to Etham, so that we may resist the devil, strong in faith.

## Fourth Station, PIHAHIROTH

The fourth station is called Pi-hahiroth. Hence what follows says:

“And departing from Etham, they camped at Pi-hahiroth, which is opposite Baal-zephon and opposite Migdol” (Num. XXXIII, 7).

Pi-hahiroth is called Pihairoth in another translation. It is a village and suburb of Migdol, toward the Red Sea, as is recorded in the Book of Exodus.

In this station Pharaoh became indignant that Israel was abandoning Egypt. He gathered a large army and pursued them, saying:

“What have we done, that we released the children of Israel, so that they would not serve us?” (Exod. XIV, 2 ff.).

The text adds:

“So Pharaoh harnessed his chariots,” and so forth (ibid. 5).

As for the moral meaning, Pi-hahiroth, interpreted as “mouth of nobles” (Jerome, Letter 127), shows that, having assumed strength at Etham, we ascend to Pi-hahiroth because we are ennobled in the Lord.

The fact that Pi-hahiroth is a village is not without mystery: it teaches that the smallest things must first be taken up. For the proper order is to proceed from small things to great ones:

“Immoderate prosperity at the beginning has always been as dangerous as adversity” (Origen, *Homily 27 on Numbers*, from Rufinus’s translation).

Just as we proceed through a suburb to a city, so we ascend from the lowest things to the highest.

Finally, Baal-zephon, which is interpreted as “Lord of the North,” signifies the devil, because, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, he said:

“I will sit on a lofty mountain, above the high mountains toward the north” (Isa. XIV, 13).

Pi-hahiroth, therefore, is opposite Baal-zephon—that is, opposite the devil, who always stands ready to oppose those journeying toward Jerusalem, which is in heaven.

Hence the Apostle said:

“Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil” (Eph. VI, 13).

The same thing is signified by Pharaoh pursuing the people.

## Fifth Station, MARAH

Marah is the fifth station. Thus he says:

“And departing from Pi-hahiroth, they passed through the midst of the sea into the desert, and traveled for three days through the desert, and camped at Marah.”

Marah is a place in the desert of Shur, called by this name because of the bitterness of its waters. For thus it is written in the Book of Exodus:

“They came to Marah, but they could not drink the waters of Marah” (Exod. XV, 23).

For they were bitter; therefore the name of that place was called Bitterness.

Three things must be considered concerning this station: the departure, the station itself, and the action.

The departure: on this journey the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea on dry ground. For Scripture says:

“But the children of Israel went on dry land through the midst of the sea; and the water was a wall for them on their right and on their left. Pharaoh, however, with his army, was drowned in the raging waters” (Exod. XIV, 22).

For thus it is written of him:

“And the water returned and covered the chariots and the riders, and the whole army of Pharaoh who had entered the sea after them; not one of them was left” (ibid. 28).

The station itself: they found bitter waters, and, feeling their bitterness, they could not drink them, although they were suffering from great thirst.

The action: at the Lord’s command Moses touched the waters with a piece of wood; and those that had previously been bitter were changed into sweetness and became drinkable, so that they could quench their thirst.

By these things we are first taught that Pharaoh with his army meets those who hasten toward grace—that is, the devil with a power so great that, as it is written, nothing like it has been made on earth (Rev. XX, 9); nevertheless, just as Pharaoh with his army is drowned in the raging waters, so too the devil is cast into the lake of fire and sulfur.

Therefore we must not be terrified on this account and abandon the journey.

Then, in the station, bitter waters are tasted, because even while we remain in grace, many bitter tribulations still endure. Hence the Apostle John said:

“I, John, your brother and sharer in tribulation” (Rev. I, 9).

Indeed, the Apostle Paul said:

“If you are without discipline, you are illegitimate and not sons” (Heb. XII, 8).

Finally, in the action, just as the Lord is present by his word so that the waters may become sweet, so he grants us his presence in tribulations, as the Prophet says:

“I am with him in tribulation, so that afflictions may become mild” (Ps. XC, 15).

Hence the prophet Isaiah proclaims:

“If you pass through the waters, I am with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you; and if you pass through fire, you will not be burned” (Isa. XLIII, 2).

Therefore for Stephen the stones of the torrent became sweetness, and for Laurence the coals became refreshment.

The Apostle rightly says, then:

“We glory in tribulations” (Rom. V, 3).

## The Sixth Station, ELIM

The sixth station is called Elim: for, departing from Marah, the children of Israel came to Elim; there they halted, and there they pitched their tents. [Col. 0017D] Hence he says: “And they departed from Marah and came to Elim.” In Elim there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; and they encamped there beside the waters (Num. 33:9). The same is read in the Book of Exodus.

But what a beautiful order, and what a blessed progress in virtue, which always strives toward better things: from darkness to light, from hardships to happiness. Behold, after the savagery of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, after the dangers of the sea and the wilderness, after the burning thirst of three days and the bitterness of Marah, the children of Israel finally came to the palms; they came to the springs. By this we are instructed that those weighed down by hardships are eventually received by joyful and pleasant places, since one reaches rest only through labor, and joys only through sorrows.

[Col. 0018A] The people came to the palms, but first they endured very many hardships from the Egyptians. They came to the springs, but first they suffered three days’ thirst and the bitterness of the waters. Yet even here the journey is not finished, nor is this the final rest from labor, because still more difficult things await. But God, the dispenser of all things, who orders everything gently, inserts certain refreshment even into the journey itself, so that the soul, restored by them and recovering its strength, may return more readily to the labors that remain (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, from Rufinus’s version).

Finally, it must be observed that Elim is interpreted as “rams.” Rams, however, are leaders of sheep. Therefore the twelve springs and the seventy palms signify the leaders of the Christian flock: namely, the twelve Apostles, concerning whom Luke writes: “He chose twelve of them, whom he also named Apostles” (Luke 6:13), and the seventy disciples whom Saint Luke elsewhere mentions, saying: “The Lord also appointed seventy others and sent them two by two before his face” (Luke 10:1). [Col. 0018B] The Apostle distinguishes these groups when speaking of the Lord’s appearances after his resurrection. For he says to the Corinthians: “He was seen by Cephas, and after that by the eleven, and then he was seen by all the Apostles” (1 Cor. 15:1). Yet all of them are leaders and teachers of the Lord’s flock. Therefore it is written concerning them: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

Let us therefore draw and drink from springs of this kind, so abundant; let us also pluck and eat joyfully from the solid fruits of these palms of victory, so that, refreshed by such food and drink, we may be found stronger for completing the remaining stations [Col. 0018C] (Jerome, Letter 127).

## The Seventh Station, THE RED SEA

The seventh station is beside the Red Sea. For, after crossing the Red Sea and traversing the stations of Marah and Elim, a certain gulf of that same sea again confronted the children of Israel (Jerome, Letter 127). And because they landed there and erected their tents, they are now said to have encamped beside the sea. For he says: “And they departed from Elim and encamped beside the Red Sea” (Num. 33:10). [Col. 0018D]

But observe that they see the sea, yet do not enter it. It was sufficient to enter and cross it only once, since that sea was a figure of our baptism (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, from Rufinus’s version), as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “Our fathers were all baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:2). Their baptism, however, was in figure, whereas ours is in reality. And since baptism must not be repeated, as it is written, “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5), just as it was necessary to be baptized once, so it was sufficient to enter the sea once.

Now, therefore, as the people journey toward the promised inheritance, the sea again confronts them, so that, seeing it and gazing upon its waves, they may proceed more cautiously, lest something worse befall them.

## The Eighth Station, THE WILDERNESS OF SIN

The eighth station is the wilderness of Sin. Therefore he says: “And they departed from the Red Sea and encamped in the wilderness of Sin” (Num. 33:11). It must be observed, however, that this whole wilderness, from the Red Sea to Mount Sinai, is called Sin (Jerome, Letter 127). In it the children of Israel had five stations: [Col. 0019A] namely, the Red Sea, as mentioned above; this one of which we are speaking; and the three that follow.

This station, however, is a particular one, although it is called by the common name “the wilderness of Sin,” taken from the name of the entire wilderness—just as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province.

But because Sin is interpreted as “bush,” it signifies to us that, just as in the eighth station we come to Sin, that is, to the bush, where the liberation of the children of Israel from Egyptian slavery was enacted, so in the resurrection, which is understood through the eighth, we shall come to the bush, where our liberation from the slavery of corruption will be enacted. We await this, as the Apostle says: “And we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of sons, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23). And elsewhere: “We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20). [Col. 0019B]

Then we shall see the bush burning and not being consumed, because the body of our humanity will die but will not be destroyed; rather, it will rise to greater glory. The Apostle says: “It is sown in dishonor; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power” (1 Cor. 15:43).

Let us therefore pray God that we may be able to come to the eighth station—or rather, that it itself may soon come to us.

## The Ninth Station, DEPHCA

The ninth station is called Dephca. It is counted as the third among the stations of the wilderness of Sin. For, departing from the station which is called by the common name “the wilderness,” the children of Israel came to this one. Therefore he adds: “And they departed from the wilderness of Sin and encamped at Dephca” (Num. 33:12). [Col. 0019C]

This station is not found in Exodus; only the departure from the wilderness to Rephidim is recorded. Thus this station and the one that follows are passed over in silence, because that was not the place where Moses was making a detailed, station-by-station account of the journeys.

Finally, Dephca is interpreted as “health” (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, from Rufinus’s version). Perfect health of the soul is that by which it cannot sin, just as perfect health of the body is that by which it cannot become ill. This does not occur except in the resurrection. Then, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Praise and joy shall seize their head; sorrow, mourning, and groaning shall flee away” (Isa. 51:11).

You see, therefore, the order of the journeys. The children of Israel reach Dephca from the eighth station; and we attain perfect health of soul and body from the resurrection, as the Apostle John testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: “God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more; neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Rev. 21:4). [Col. 0019D]

But because the soul’s sickness is sin—for the Prophet said, “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5)—the sickness of our soul is pride, anger, and greed. Therefore let each one of us, bending the knees of heart and body, pray to our Lord Jesus Christ, who heals all our infirmities, and say with the prophet: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” (Jer. 17:14). Let him also say with David: “Heal me, Lord, for all my bones are troubled” (Ps. 6:3).

## The Tenth Station, HALUS

The tenth station is Halus, to which the children of Israel departed from Dephca. Therefore he says: “And they departed from Dephca and encamped at Halus” (Num. 33:13). [Col. 0020A]

In Exodus this station too is not named distinctly; rather, it is included among the stations from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim. For when he says, “And the whole congregation of the children of Israel departed from the wilderness of Sin by their encampments, according to the word of the Lord” (Exod. 17:1), he indicates that there were several encampments and resting places.

Three things occur at this station. First, the people of God behold glory, for it is written in Exodus: “The glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud” (Exod. 16:10). Then they are fed with meat: “In the evening,” as it is written there, “the quail came up and covered the camp” (ibid., 13). Third, they are fed with manna from heaven. Thus Moses addresses the people: “This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat” (ibid., 15)—that is, the word which the Lord established. [Col. 0020B]

By these things we are warned that the one who rests in the tenth station, that is, in observance of the Law—for the number ten signifies the Law, which consists in ten words, as it is written, “Moses wrote these ten words on the tablets of the covenant” (Exod. 34:28)—beholds the glory of God.

Therefore, when the Prophet asks who will dwell in God’s tabernacle and who will rest upon his holy mountain, the answer is that it is the diligent observer of the Law: “He who walks without blemish and does justice, who speaks truth in his heart,” and so forth (Ps. 14:2ff.).

He is also nourished by meat and heavenly manna, that is, by the precious body of our Lord Jesus Christ. His body is true flesh, as the Apostle John says: “My flesh is truly food,” and true manna, not in figure but in reality: “I am,” he says, “the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:35). It is true flesh because of his true humanity; it is living bread because of his divinity. Therefore, when we eat Christ’s body, we share in both his divinity and his humanity, as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 11:24ff.). [Col. 0020C]

These greater benefits are rightly bestowed at this place, for Halus is interpreted as “labor.” For one who labors, it is fitting that the glory of the Lord should appear, so that he may endure his labors more eagerly through the vision of the reward. It is also fitting that food should be supplied, so that, refreshed by it, he may pursue the journey he has begun with greater strength.

## The Eleventh Station, RAPHIDIM

The eleventh station is reached at Rephidim. There the people, exhausted by the arduous journey, received refreshment. Therefore it follows: “And they departed from Halus and encamped at Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink” (Num. 33:14). [Col. 0020D]

The same station is also recorded in Exodus: “And they encamped,” it says, “at Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink” (Exod. 17:1).

This station is especially adorned by the distinction of three miraculous works.

First, there was the miraculous bringing forth of water from the rock. The people, wearied by the roughness of the mountains and the length of the road, were burning with intense thirst. When they came to Rephidim and saw that the place was dry and without water, they began to grow angry and riot against Moses (ibid., 7). Hence the place was called “the place of quarrelling” in Scripture. [Col. 0021A]

But Moses took the staff and struck the rock at the Lord’s command. When it had been struck, it poured forth such an abundant supply of water that the people and the animals could quench all their thirst. The prophet David, astonished at this, burst into these words: “For he struck the rock, and the waters flowed, and the torrents overflowed” (Ps. 77:20).

Second, there was the memorable victory over the Amalekites. While the people were stationed there, the Amalekite tribes began to oppose and harass them and to attack them with a powerful army. But Moses, considering that the people’s strength had already been broken by the weariness of the long journey and that they were not sufficiently fit to repel the enemy’s boldness, resolved to have recourse to divine assistance.

[Col. 0021B] Leaving with Joshua both resistance to the enemy and the entire conduct of the war, he withdrew to a hill to pray to God. O the wondrous power of prayer! While Moses stretched out his hands toward heaven, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Israel was overcome. Aaron and Hur, however, supported his hands until sunset, and Joshua obtained the victory, as Scripture says: “He routed Amalek and his entire people with the edge of the sword” (Exod. 17:13).

Third, there was Jethro’s prudent counsel concerning the administration of public affairs. Seeing that his son-in-law Moses was occupied with hearing the people’s cases for longer than was proper and was spending all his time on them from morning until evening, Jethro advised him to appoint judges, tribunes, and other officials for war and peace, who would judge the people, hear cases, settle disputes, and briefly resolve all minor matters, reserving only serious affairs for Moses’ judgment. Moses agreed with him. Therefore it is written: “Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did everything that he said” (Exod. 18:24). [Col. 0021C]

And because Rephidim is interpreted as “praise of judgment,” it is fitting that at its station the rock should provide water: for Christ, the rock, provides the water of grace to one who keeps judgment. It is written: “Blessed are those who keep judgment” (Ps. 105:3)! Amalek is defeated because the devil is condemned by judgment. Right administration of the people is taught because it is written: “A wise judge instructs his people” (Eccl. 10:27). This is the one who judges all things and is himself judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:15).

## The Twelfth Station, THE WILDERNESS OF SINAI

The twelfth station was in the wilderness of Sinai. Therefore he adds: “And they departed from Rephidim and encamped in the wilderness of Sinai” (Num. 33:15). [Col. 0021D]

This station is exceedingly famous. There God descended in fire upon the mountain, and Moses, having purified the people according to God’s command, ascended to the summit of the mountain, spoke with God, and received the precepts of the Decalogue.

There the pattern for the construction of the Tabernacle was displayed; there the multiplicity of sacrifices, the distinction of vessels, the vestments of the high priest, and the ceremonies of priests and Levites were prescribed. There the number of the people and of the Levites was recorded, together with the distribution of the people among their individual tribes. The offerings of the leaders were also described at this station.

[Col. 0022A] There too two silver trumpets were ordered to be made for moving the camps. There it was commanded that those who were unclean through contact with a dead person and had been unable to celebrate the Passover in the first month should assemble in the second month; and those who lived far away or had been unclean were ordered to celebrate the Passover in the second month.

This is understood as a figure of the people of the nations. Although they had fornicated with demons and appeared unclean in soul, they were commanded to be purified through a wholesome confession of faith in a second birth, as though in a second month.

At this station the Nazirites were also commanded not to drink wine or strong drink, nor vinegar made from wine or strong drink; they were not to eat fresh grapes, nor even raisins (Num. 6:2ff.). The same is commanded in Proverbs: “Princes who are wrathful must not drink wine, lest when they have drunk they forget wisdom” (Prov. 31:4–5).

[Col. 0022B] What, then, is signified by the name “Nazirites” except the life of those who abstain and practice continence? For them luxury is forbidden in wine, and every earthly pleasure in strong drink. Strong drink is made from different kinds of ingredients, just as pleasure arises from a varied mixture of vices.

Thus those are said to drink wine who pretend to possess certain shadows and images of virtues in order to deceive people. Those feed on raisins who, for the sake of human eyes, stain themselves with the appearance of abstinence in order to receive glory from human beings. Those drink vinegar who, after a holy way of life, relapse into former vices and delight in the corruption of their former wickedness.

God therefore commanded that those who have assumed the title of holiness should be free from every vice and should not seek any such disturbance as overturns the state of the mind.

[Col. 0022C] At this station lepers, those with seminal discharges, and the unclean are separated from the camps: lepers in doctrine, those with seminal discharges in thought, and the unclean in deed—that is, heretics, schismatics, and the lustful. These, like contagious and diseased people, are expelled from the camps, lest through the contagion of their unbelief or their conduct they pollute the lives of the innocent.

Finally, from the age of twenty years and upward, the people who were found fit for battle were numbered. But why from the age of twenty, unless because at that age battles against the individual vices arise? They are therefore chosen for battle, so that they may engage in conflict against lust and not be overcome by luxury.

Here too the Levites were commanded to serve in the Tabernacle from the age of twenty-five, and from the age of fifty they were appointed guardians of the vessels. What is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth emerges, except the battles of the vices themselves against each person? And what by the fiftieth year, in which even the earth rests according to the law of the Jubilee, except eternal rest, represented by the conquest of the mind’s warfare? What are the vessels of the Tabernacle except the souls of the faithful?

[Col. 0022D] Therefore the Levites serve in the Tabernacle from the age of twenty-five and become guardians of the vessels from the age of fifty, so that those who still admit, through the consent of pleasure, the struggles of attacking vices may not presume to take responsibility for others. But when they have subdued the battles of temptation, when they are reasonably considered secure in their own profound tranquility, then they may be assigned to guard souls.

[Col. 0023A] Yet who can completely overcome these battles, when Paul says: “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (2 Cor. 11:2)? But it is one thing to endure battles bravely and another to be enfeebled and conquered by battles. In the former virtue is exercised, lest anyone become elated; in the latter it is utterly extinguished, lest it continue.

Then the Law commanded all the Levites to shave all the hair of their flesh (Num. 8:7), because those who are taken up into divine service ought to appear pure before the eyes of God from every thought of the flesh, lest the mind bring forth illicit thoughts and render the soul’s beautiful appearance deformed, as though by overgrown hair.

[Col. 0023B] After this they were also commanded to make two trumpets, at whose blast the people would be moved to battle. For thus it is written concerning them to Moses: “Make two trumpets for yourself, of beaten silver” (Num. 10:2); and shortly afterward: “When the short blast sounds, the camps shall move” (ibid., 5).

Through the two trumpets the army is led, because through the two Testaments—or through the two commandments of love—the people are called to the battle of faith. They are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of preachers may shine with the brilliance of eloquence and not confuse the minds of their hearers through any obscurity of their own. They are commanded to be beaten because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations.

It is rightly said: “When the short blast sounds, the camps shall move,” because when a subtler and more minute word of preaching is expounded, the minds of the hearers are stirred more ardently against the battles of temptation.

From this point the children of Israel move forward from Mount Sinai and pass into the Graves of Lust.

## The Thirteenth Station, THE GRAVES OF LUST

The thirteenth station is in the Graves of Lust. Therefore he says: “And they departed from the wilderness of Sinai and encamped in the Graves of Lust” (Num. 33:16). [Col. 0023C]

This station received its name from the event that occurred there. For the people, weary of manna, craved meat, fish, melons, and the other stimulants of appetite that had been available among the Egyptians, and they raised a tumult against Moses.

Therefore the Lord, becoming angry, sent an innumerable multitude of quail flying close to the ground, with which they could satisfy their appetite. But Scripture says: “The meat was still between their teeth” (Num. 11:33)—that is, before it had been digested, the Lord struck the people with a very great plague. “And from this,” it says, “the name of that place was called the Graves of Lust, because there they buried the people who had desired” (ibid., 34).

[Col. 0023D] From this we are taught that those who have abandoned worldly conduct and rejected the Egyptian pots—that is, the boiling passions of carnal desires—must not murmur against the heavenly bread, nor desire the poisonous things of the Egyptians, which are great quantities of meat, but must seek the simple food of manna, that is, a pure and heavenly life.

Otherwise, if after the commandments, the angelic food, and the manna of heavenly life—or of heavenly doctrine—we should again desire the Egyptian meats, which are the carnal pleasures of this world, and the former desires of vices, we shall immediately be struck and tormented by the Lord’s anger. Our desires will be turned into tombs, so that we become whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people outwardly but within are full of every impurity. [Col. 0024A]

At this station, by God’s command, Moses chose seventy elders from among the people to assist him in governing the nation. “They shall bear with you,” he says, “the burden of the people, and you shall not bear it alone” (Exod. 11:22). The Spirit afterward descended upon them, and they prophesied.

This happened as a figure, because on the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit poured himself upon the Apostles, so that they might be wise for founding the Church and strong for governing it. “Pay attention,” as it is read in the Acts of the Apostles, “to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God” (Acts 20:28).

Thus the gift of heavenly power that formerly existed in Moses and the Prophets appeared visibly upon the Apostles.

## The Fourteenth Station, ASEROTH

The fourteenth station is completed at Aseroth. For he adds: “And they departed from the Graves of Lust and encamped at Aseroth” (Num. 33:17). [Col. 0024B] Concerning the same station we read elsewhere: “The people departed from the Graves of Lust to Aseroth” (Num. 11:34).

Here Aaron and his sister Miriam, because Moses had taken an Ethiopian woman as his foreign wife, spoke against him with considerable insolence. Therefore she was immediately covered with the contagion of leprosy and was excluded from the company of others until the time of her healing.

This clearly prefigured a new mystery: namely, that the priestly people of the fathers would rise up, out of zeal for Christ our Savior, against the Church gathered from the nations. Because of the impure jealousy of its unbelief, it would not be admitted into the tabernacles of God until the appointed time had become clear, when the fullness of the nations had been completed, as the Apostle wrote to the Romans (Rom. 11:25). [Col. 0024C]

Only then will it be able to recover its former health, when the grace of the sevenfold Spirit has interceded for its pardon.

But because Aseroth is interpreted as “blessedness,” it is rightly reached from the Graves of Lust, since unless someone buries the desires of the flesh, he cannot attain eternal blessedness. Therefore the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50).

## The Fifteenth Station, RETHMA

The fifteenth station is called Rethma. Therefore it follows: “And they departed from Aseroth and encamped at Rethma” (Num. 33:18). [Col. 0024D]

But elsewhere we read: “After this the people departed from Aseroth and encamped in the wilderness of Paran” (Num. 13:1). Therefore, lest the passages of Scripture appear to contradict one another, it must be observed that from this point to Ezion-geber all the stations—eighteen in number, all of them, extending to the thirty-second—are included under the name “the wilderness of Paran.”

This station is therefore elsewhere called Paran, the common name of the wilderness shared with many others, but Rethma by its proper name.

Scripture commends Paran in another passage, saying: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran, covered with shadow” (Hab. 3:2).

In this wilderness Moses, by God’s command, sent twelve men to explore the land. They brought back a cluster of grapes, pomegranates, and figs from the land (Num. 13:4). [Col. 0025A] In this wilderness Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, together with their families, were swallowed by the opening of the earth because of their rebellion. In this wilderness Aaron the priest, standing between the living and the dead, appeased the angered God by offering incense and restrained the plague. In this wilderness Aaron’s dry staff, placed in the Tabernacle, both budded and flowered by a miracle. Many other events also occurred there, as is read in the Book of Numbers, though they were not distributed among the individual stations.

Through these things we are taught mystically that the men sent to explore the fertile land, and those who caused the people to despair of the Lord’s promised inheritance, prefigured the scribes and Pharisees.

Just as the former were sent by Moses to examine carefully the fertility of the soil and encourage the people to obtain it, so the latter were established through the Law and the Prophets to contemplate, by investigating the Scriptures, the coming of the Lord, through which they might attain eternal life. [Col. 0025B] But just as the former withdrew the people from hope of possessing the inheritance—or the people themselves, through their report, alienated themselves from God’s promise—so the latter used deceptions to dissuade the people from believing in Christ the Lord.

Therefore it is said to them: “Woe to you who have taken away the key of knowledge! You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11:52).

The cluster of grapes that they brought back is Christ. Therefore in the Song of Songs the Church says concerning Christ: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus for me in the vineyards of Engaddi” (Song 1:13).

The pomegranate, because of its redness, is the blood of Christ. Hence Isaiah says: “Why are your garments red, and your robes like those of one coming from Bosra?” (Isa. 63:1). [Col. 0025C]

The fig, because of its sweetness, is the evangelical Law. Therefore he says: “My yoke is sweet” (Matt. 11:30).

What else are signified by Dathan and Abiram except those who introduce heresies and schisms into the Church? Disregarding the authority of the priest, they separate themselves from him and from the Church of God, imagining other churches, another altar, and other customs, like Apollinaris, Novatian, and others like them. Rejecting God’s ordinance, they attempt to establish their own vanities.

When the heretics and schismatics have finally been swallowed by the abyss of the earth, Aaron the priest—that is, Christ the Lord, the priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek—is established as mediator to appease God, because he possesses an everlasting priesthood and always lives to intercede for us (Heb. 7:24). [Col. 0025D]

Aaron’s dry staff, which afterward budded by a miracle, is the flesh of Christ. The prophet calls Christ a staff: “A staff shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11:1). This dry staff flowered because, having died, it rose again.

## The Sixteenth Station, REMON-PHARES

The sixteenth station is called Remon-phares. For it follows: “And they departed from Rethma and encamped at Remon-phares” (Num. 33:19). [Col. 0026A]

This is the second station in the wilderness of Paran. In our language it is interpreted as “lofty division.” For when someone has dwelt at Rethma, which means “the mouth of the seer”—that is, when he has attained perfect understanding of things—he comes to Remon-phares, that is, to the lofty division by which he can separate heavenly things from earthly things and exalted things from those below.

And not without reason. For when understanding has been strengthened and knowledge of things has increased, judgment is poured in, by which eternal things are distinguished from temporal and perpetual things from those that pass away. Therefore it is said through the Prophet: “If you bring forth the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19).

## The Seventeenth Station, LEBNA

The seventeenth station is at Lebna. Therefore he adds: “And they departed from Remon-phares and encamped at Lebna” (Num. 33:20). [Col. 0026B]

By this station we are taught mystically that, on the journey of this life, we must be washed in body and pure in heart, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “Let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Heb. 10:22).

The interpretation of the word Lebna itself indicates this. In Latin, Lebna means the same as “whitening.” But it is not the whitening of which it is said blamefully, “a whitened wall” and “whitened tombs” (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, from Rufinus’s version). It is the whitening for which the Prophet prays, saying: “You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. 50:9), and which the Lord promises through the prophet: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I shall make them white as snow; and though they be like crimson, I shall make them white like wool” (Isa. 1:18).

This whitening arises powerfully from the brightness of judgment at Remon-phares and from the clarity of visions at Rethma, where the true Israelite completes his stations.

## The Eighteenth Station, RESSA

The eighteenth station is reached at Ressa. Therefore he adds: “And they departed from Lebna and encamped at Ressa” (Num. 33:21). [Col. 0026C]

Through this station we are taught mystically that, however much someone may seem to have progressed and however great the advances he may have achieved, temptations nevertheless do not abandon him.

The Apostle Paul had already progressed so far that he had been caught up even to the third heaven and had heard ineffable secrets; nevertheless, he felt himself still oppressed by extraordinary temptations. Therefore he complained: “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7).

The Apostle James nevertheless testifies that such temptations are praiseworthy, saying: “Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations” (James 1:2), for these are applied to a person as a kind of safeguard.

Just as meat, however excellent, is spoiled unless it is sprinkled with salt, so the soul, however perfect, becomes lax unless it is salted with continual temptations [Col. 0026D] (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers, from Rufinus’s version). This is because Ressa is interpreted as “praiseworthy temptation.”

## The Nineteenth Station, CALATHA

The nineteenth station is called Calatha. The children of Israel reached it after departing from Ressa. Therefore it follows: “And they departed from Ressa and encamped at Calatha” (Num. 33:22).

Calatha means “staff” in Latin and signifies dominion. Compare: “A staff of equity; the staff of your kingdom” (Ps. 46:7). [Col. 0027A]

Calatha rightly follows Ressa, because when the soul has overcome temptations at Ressa, it becomes so strong that it ascends to Calatha—that is, it acquires dominion not only over its lower powers but also over the whole world.

The Apostle had ascended to this point when he said: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Let us therefore encamp at this station also, so that, crucifying the flesh with its vices and desires and putting its deeds to death, we may say with the Apostle: “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God” (Gal. 2:20).

## The Twentieth Station, ARSAPHAR

The twentieth station is at Arsaphar. Therefore he says: “And they departed from Calatha and encamped at Arsaphar” (Num. 33:23). [Col. 0027B]

This is a courageous station. For it invites us to difficult things, namely to battles—very harsh battles—and against the strongest and most savage enemies. Concerning them the Apostle said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness,” and so forth (Eph. 6:12).

The same Apostle felt himself oppressed by them and subjected to their force; therefore he said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

This is because Arsaphar means “the blast of a trumpet,” or “trumpeting,” which is a sign of war.

And not without reason. For when the soul sees itself armed with so many and such great virtues in the higher stations, it cannot restrain itself from advancing into the midst of things and offering itself for battle—or rather, from presenting itself as ready for battle. The blast of the trumpets also challenges the others, together with the Prophet, who says: “Take up arms; bring out the shields for battle; saddle the horses; mount the riders; polish the spears” (Jer. 46:4). Indeed, another prophet says: “Proclaim this among the nations: consecrate a war; rouse the warriors; let the men of war draw near” (Joel 3:9).

[Col. 0027C] The fathers undertook and conquered this war, as the Apostle reports to the Hebrews: “They stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the force of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, and became strong in war” (Heb. 11:33).

This station, therefore, is full of strength and spirit.

## The Twenty-First Station, ARADA

The twenty-first station is Arada. Therefore he says: “And they departed from Arsaphar and encamped at Arada” (Num. 33:24). [Col. 0027D]

This station too must be recalled with extended praises. For Arada indicates one who has been made fit.

The order is beautiful, but the stages of those making progress must be observed, and the sequence of their advances examined. For when the soul has overcome temptations, it dares to trample its lower powers; and when it sees that it possesses dominion over them, it insults the opposing powers. It not only ceases to fear their strength but challenges them to battle.

Now, secure in victory, it ascends to Arada—that is, it glories in the Lord that it has been made fit—and says with the Apostle: “Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us fit ministers of the new covenant” (2 Cor. 4:5–6).

Let us therefore pray God that we too may reach Arada and be able to remain stationed there.

## The Twenty-Second Station, MACELOTH

The twenty-second station is called Maceloth. Therefore he adds: “And they departed from Arada and encamped at Maceloth” (Num. 33:25). [Col. 0028A]

Maceloth is interpreted as “from the beginning.” By this it is indicated that one who strives toward perfection, or feels that he has attained it in some measure, ought to look toward the beginning of all things, from which everything depends, and refer everything to it, never departing from it (Origen, place cited above).

God is the beginning and the end, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “I am the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” (Rev. 1:8).

Therefore everything must be referred back to God. The Prophet recognized him as the beginning when he said: “Are you not from the beginning, Lord my God, my Holy One?” (Hab. 1:12). The Apostle recognized him when he said: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3:14).

### Twenty-Third Station, THAATH

The twenty-third station is Thaath; hence it follows: “And setting out from Maccloth, they encamped at Thaath” (Num. XXXIII, 26). But since Thaath means in Latin long-suffering or endurance, it indicates to us that whoever strives to advance in the way of God and to benefit others must suffer much and bear much with equanimity. Therefore it is said to the apostles: “By your endurance you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19).

The Apostle invites us to endurance by setting before us the example of our fathers who went before us, and of Christ. For he says: “Therefore, since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses laid upon us, let us lay aside every burden and the sin that clings closely, and let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith” (Heb. XII, 1). For our Lord Jesus Christ gave us many examples of gentleness toward human beings and of endurance of evils, as they are clearly recounted in the Gospels, so that we might follow in his footsteps, as the apostle Peter says (I Pet. II, 21).

### Twenty-Fourth Station, THARE

The twenty-fourth station is called Thare; for it follows: “And setting out from Thaath, they encamped at Thare” (Num. XXXIII, 27). Thare is interpreted in Latin as “stupor,” and in Greek as ἔκστασις (*ekstasis*), which is a kind of intense astonishment arising from the sight of difficult and extraordinary things. For when things that are unusual and impossible according to nature present themselves to human sight, the senses fail in investigating their cause, reason succumbs, and the mind is struck with wonder. Daniel expressed this more clearly, saying: “I was stupefied at the vision, and there was no understanding in me” (Dan. VIII, 27).

Thus, when the people saw that the paralytic who had been carried by four men rose at the Lord’s mere command, took up the bed on which he had lain, and went away to his own house, they were astonished, because this surpassed human ability. Therefore Saint Luke says: “And astonishment seized them all” (Luke V, 26). The prophet Jeremiah, speaking of this, says: “Stupor and terrible things have been done in the land” (Jer. V, 30).

And because many splendid and astonishing works were performed at these stations, the causes of which the human mind cannot comprehend by reason, one finally arrives at Thare, that is, at stupor—for this is its interpretation. Hence it is written: “And they were all astonished at the greatness of God” (Luke IX, 44).

### Twenty-Fifth Station, METCHA

The twenty-fifth station is made at Metcha; therefore it says: “And setting out from Thare, they encamped at Metcha” (Num. XXXIII, 28). Metcha is called in Latin “new death.”

To understand what “new death” is, we must observe that Scripture speaks of three kinds of death. One is the death of the body, by which, to use the Apostle’s words, “our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved” and the soul departs from the tabernacle of the body. Concerning this the Apostle writes: “It is appointed for human beings once to die” (II Cor. V, 1). Abraham and the prophets died this death; by this death we shall all die, and, like water poured out upon the ground, we shall not be gathered again.

Another death is that of the soul, by which the soul, corrupted by the contagion of sin, dies—not in its substance, which cannot die, but with respect to God’s life-giving grace. For when God departs because of the guilt of sin, the soul loses its spiritual life. Hence the Apostle says: “She who lives in pleasure is dead” (I Tim. V, 6). It is said to die through sin because “the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4). It dies to the Lord not through a weakness of nature, but through the guilt of sin; this is not a departure from life, but a fall into error.

The third is the death of sin, by which the desire of the flesh dies so that the mind may live to God. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Our old self was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. VI, 6). And rightly so: just as a dead person is no longer subject to sin, so one reborn through grace ought no longer to serve sin. Of this death the Apostle speaks, saying: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Coloss. III, 3). Rebuking those who are dead in this way, the same Apostle says: “If you have died with Christ to the elements of the world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to decrees?” (Coloss. II, 20).

Thus one death is natural, another penal, and the third spiritual. This last is signified by Metcha, which is called “new death,” because it renews the old person and makes a new creature, as the Apostle says: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V, 17). Let us therefore also make our station here, so that, dead to sins, we may live perpetually to righteousness.

### Twenty-Sixth Station, ESMONA

The twenty-sixth station is called Esmona; for it says: “And setting out from Metcha, they encamped at Esmona” (Num. XXXIII, 29). Esmona is called in Latin “acceleration,” which suitably applies to this station. For when the soul, through the preceding station of death to sin, has escaped into a new creation, it cannot remain stationary in mind or grow sluggish in idleness; rather, it strives to advance farther and hasten its journey.

Speed is especially appropriate for travelers. For this reason the people of the fathers are commanded to eat the Passover hurriedly and in haste. Hence the apostles were commanded: “Greet no one on the way” (Luke X, 5). Likewise, in the Book of Kings, Elisha is said to have instructed Gehazi: “Gird up your loins,” he said, “take my staff in your hand, and go; and if you meet anyone, do not bless him, and if anyone blesses you, do not answer him” (IV Kings IV, 29). For the work of God requires even urgent haste. “Cursed,” says the prophet, “is the one who performs the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII, 10).

Therefore that disciple who ran ahead of Peter more quickly to the tomb (John XX, 4) is greatly commended. In the way of God there must also be rapid progress, so that no opportunity is left for the devil, who always stands at the right hand to oppose the saints, to obstruct the journey begun.

Therefore let us who, through Metcha, have died to sins and live to righteousness not merely follow on toward the prize of the heavenly calling; let us run on to Esmona, hastening toward the contest set before us. For the shepherds came in haste and found the child Jesus (Luke II, 16).

### Twenty-Seventh Station, MOSEROTH

The twenty-seventh station is called Moseroth; for it says: “And setting out from Esmona, they encamped at Moseroth” (Num. [Col. 0030B] XXXIII, 30). Moseroth now suitably follows; for it signifies disciplines. Thus whoever has taken up haste at Esmona should now wisely summon it for acquiring disciplines. Let it be as the apostle James teaches: “Let every person be quick to hear” (James I, 19).

God is the author of this discipline. For it is said through the prophet: “Who has ascended into heaven and taken hold of it and brought it down from the clouds? Who has crossed over the sea and found it and will bring it for chosen gold? There is no one who knows its way, nor anyone who considers its paths; but the one who knows all things knows it and discovered it by his prudence” (Baruch III, 29 ff.). Therefore it must be sought from him, as the apostle James says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all generously” (James I, 5).

This discipline reveals God and his works. “She is,” says Solomon, “the teacher of the discipline of God and the chooser of his works; her guardianship is the rod of correction.” For it is written: “Stripes and reproofs give wisdom” (Prov. XXIX, 15).

It is read in Numbers that a certain man was caught gathering wood on the sabbath, was ordered to be brought before Moses and the elders, and was finally punished by death at God’s command, being stoned: “Let the man die by death; let the whole congregation stone him with stones outside the camp” (Num. XV, 35). Some think that this happened at this station. Hence the Apostle also said: “Reprove the sinner before all, so that the others may have fear” (I Tim. V, 20).

Let us therefore maintain our station at Moseroth—that is, let us be held within the discipline of God by the mortification of corrections.

### Twenty-Eighth Station, BANEJACHAM

The twenty-eighth station is completed at Banejacham; for he says: “And setting out from Moseroth, they encamped at Banejacham” (Num. XXXIII, 31). Whoever has his station in the discipline of God must diligently devote all study and effort so that not even the smallest thing from the law of God is violated or lost; and, as the Savior says, so that not one iota or one stroke may pass from the Law (Matt. V, 18).

For he must continually retain in mind that saying of the Gospel: “I tell you, you will not come out from there until you have paid even the last farthing” (Matt. X, 26). For just as a debt of interest is not discharged before the entire principal, down to the very smallest coin, has been paid in full by whatever method of payment may be used, so the punishment for sin is not dissolved except by the compensation of charity and the other virtues, or by strict satisfaction.

Sin is not washed away, brothers, unless the guilty person is exercised by punishments long enough to pay the penalties of the error committed. The apostle James said: “Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James II, 10).

That sentence of God written in the Law must also be weighed: “I am the Lord your God, a jealous God” (Exod. XX, 5). The law of God must therefore be examined with the utmost exactness and preserved with the greatest diligence possible, lest we somehow fall away from it. This present station teaches us this: Banejacham signifies “straining through” or “filtering.” Whoever filters the law of God carefully observes it, lest even the smallest syllable or stroke slip away through negligence.

### Twenty-Ninth Station, GADGAD

The twenty-ninth station is at Mount Gadgad; for it says: “And setting out from Banejacham, they encamped at Mount Gadgad” (Num. XXXIII, 32). Temptation is the soul’s faithful guard, strength, and increase of virtue. For if the soul of the righteous did not sometimes feel itself pressed by temptations, it would not remain in vigilance; rather, flowing away as though overwhelmed by an abundance of graces, it would become lax.

This teaching is clearly found in the holy Moses. When the people saw the lamps and the smoking mountain and heard the voices, and fled in terror from the Lord, Moses said: “Have confidence, for God has come to test you, so that his fear may be in you and you may not sin” (Exod. X, 20).

It is also called strength, because the soul, recognizing that it is surrounded by many temptations, proceeds more cautiously and asks the Lord for greater strength, saying with the Prophet: “Have mercy on me, O God, for many are those who fight against me” (Ps. LV, 2).

It is called an increase of virtue because the soul, exercised by temptations, emerges purer.
