Therefore Solomon says in Proverbs: “As silver and gold are tested in the furnace, so chosen hearts are tested by the Lord” (Prov. XVII, 3). The holy apostle James likewise testifies that the soul advances through temptations, saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation; for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James I, 12).

Temptations, therefore, are not to be fled but sought. Hence the prophet David says: “Test me, O Lord, and try me” (Ps. XXV, 2). As those advancing in the way of the Lord proceed, temptations are more frequently brought upon them, so that they may walk more cautiously and fruitfully. This station suggests this to us, for Gadgad means “temptation.”

Therefore, lest the traveler be dissipated or fall through the abundance of such great virtues acquired at the earlier stations, this station follows the preceding one.

### Thirtieth Station, JETHEBATHA

The thirtieth station is celebrated at Jethebatha; hence it follows: “And setting out from Mount Gadgad, they encamped at Jethebatha” (Num. XXXIII, 33). Through the experience of temptations, the virtue of the righteous, as was said at the preceding station, shines forth more conspicuously and clearly. Hence the apostle Peter also says: “You will rejoice now, if it is necessary that you be distressed by various temptations, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold that is tested by fire, may be found genuine” (I Pet. I, 6).

Through this he also acquires greater grace. Therefore it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “When virtue has been tested, it reproves the foolish” (Wis. I, 3). Through it, virtue hidden amid a perverse nation also comes forth and shines. Therefore the apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19).

More sincere goodness emerges from temptations, like purer silver from a furnace of fire. For Scripture says: “Silver is tested in fire, and acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Eccles. II, 5). Since, therefore, goodness emerges from temptation purer, as from a furnace, Jethebatha, which is interpreted as “goodness,” rightly follows now.

### Thirty-First Station, EBRONA

The thirty-first station is made at Ebrona; therefore it says: “And setting out from Jethebatha, they encamped at Ebrona” (Num. XXXIII, 34). Although the righteous person may have attained even perfect goodness in this life, he nevertheless does not settle in mind or remain content with his present state. Rather, passing through all things, he strives with ardent desire toward better things.

Hence the prophet David said: “I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. IV, 5). There he will rest; there all his desire will be fulfilled. Therefore in another place the same prophet said: “I shall be satisfied, Lord, when your glory appears to me” (Ps. XVI, 15).

In this life there is not rest but perpetual passage. Therefore the bridegroom in the Song of Songs is compared, because of the swiftness of his course, to a gazelle and a young stag (Song II, 9); hence he leaps upon the mountains and bounds over the hills.

This is what this station teaches us, because Ebrona means “passage”: although you have reached goodness through the preceding station, all things must nevertheless be passed beyond. You must proceed to better things until you come to that good which is supreme, which satisfies every desire, and in which you ought to remain forever (Origen, cited above).

### Thirty-Second Station, ASIONGABER

The thirty-second station is called Asiongaber, where the children of Israel arrived; hence it follows: “And setting out from Ebrona, they encamped at Asiongaber” (Num. XXXIII, 35). This is the final station of the children of Israel in the desert of Paran. For, as we said above, that wilderness, encompassing many stations, extends this far. Asiongaber is interpreted as “the counsels of a man.”

And this fits the intention perfectly, since the person who has completed so many stations, penetrated so many recesses of the virtues, felt so many breathings of the charisms, and exercised himself in so many practices of perfection has ceased to be a child in understanding, has reached the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, and has grown into a perfect man.

Therefore he has acquired the counsels of a man, so that with the Apostle he may say: “When I became a man, I put away the things of a child” (I Cor. XIII, 11). Indeed, he has acquired a profound counsel, because Solomon says in Proverbs: “A deep water is counsel in the heart of a man” (Prov. XX, 5).

Concerning this counsel the wise man said: “Do nothing without counsel, and when you act, you will not regret it” (Eccles. XXXII, 24). This is not the counsel about which the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: “Woe to the apostate children! Thus says the Lord: You have made a plan not through me and made an alliance not through my Spirit” (Isa. XXX, 1).

Rather, it is the counsel of which the wise man says: “The knowledge of the wise will abound like a flood, and his counsel is like a pure fountain of life, which preserves from evil” (Eccles. XXI, 16); for good counsel will guard you, and holy thought will preserve you.

Let us therefore proceed here without hesitation and joyfully raise our tents here, so that we may confess to God with all our heart, as David did “in the council of the righteous and in the congregation” (Ps. CX, 1).

### Thirty-Third Station, SIN

The thirty-third station is in the desert of Sin; therefore it adds: “And setting out from Asiongaber, they encamped in the desert of Sin” (Num. XXXIII, 36). An eighth station is also called by this same name above; for it says: “And setting out from the Red Sea, they encamped in the desert of Sin.”

But it must be noted that this place is different from the former one. Therefore it is added below: “From the desert of Sin, this is Kadesh” (Num. XX, 1). And elsewhere, while the people were staying at this station, Moses sent messengers to the king of Edom: “And now we are,” he said, “in Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory” (ibid., 14).

The prophet David mentions this place, saying: “The Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh” (Ps. XXVIII, 8). Here Mary, the sister of Moses, completed her days, and died and was buried, as was read above. Josephus also describes this, saying: “Then, accordingly, the end of life overtook his sister Miriam, when she had completed the fortieth year from the time he had left Egypt; and they buried her publicly with great splendor” (Book IV of the *Antiquities*, chap. 4).

Finally, here the people suffer from a lack of water; therefore they grow angry and murmur against Moses. At God’s command, he struck the rock with the wondrous staff, and abundant water flowed from it; thus, when everyone had drunk, the desire caused by thirst was removed.

### Thirty-Fourth Station, HOR

The thirty-fourth station is at Mount Hor; for it says: “And setting out from the desert of Sin—that is, Kadesh—they encamped at Mount Hor, near the land of Edom” (Num. XXXIII, 37).

While the children of Israel were staying at Kadesh in the desert of Sin, Moses sent envoys to the king of the Idumeans, asking him to grant passage through his territory for him and his people. He assured him, however, that they would not demand even water from him without payment. But he did not consent to the request or grant passage; rather, he replied: “You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will come out to meet you in war” (Num. XX, 18).

Therefore, according to God’s command, as recorded in Deuteronomy, the people turned away from him. They departed from Kadesh and reached Mount Hor, and had the station that we read of there (ibid., 27 ff.).

There, in accordance with the Lord’s command, Aaron ascended Mount Hor with Moses his brother and Eleazar his son. There Moses, by the word of God, stripped Aaron of his priestly garments and immediately clothed Eleazar, his son, to whom the priesthood fell on account of his age, while the whole people looked on in amazement at what was taking place. There Aaron died and was gathered to his people, and his son Eleazar was declared priest in place of his father Aaron. This station is therefore memorable.

### Thirty-Fifth Station, SALMONA

The thirty-fifth station is at Salmona; for it follows: “And setting out from Mount Hor, they encamped at Salmona” (Num. XXXIII, 38). After leaving Mount Hor, the people did not continue along the direct road on which they had begun, but, circling around the land of Edom, took the road toward the Red Sea, so that, according to the word of the Lord, they would not attack their brothers in war or harm them at all. For he said: “Do not wage war against them” (Deut. II, 5).

Wearied, therefore, by so many winding roads and tired of the manna, they spoke, it says, against God and Moses. Consequently the angry Lord sent venomous and deadly serpents among the people, whose bites killed them, and a very great number of the people perished.

The Apostle also mentions them, saying: “Nor let us put Christ to the test, as some of them did, and were destroyed by serpents” (I Cor. X, 9). Then, when Moses prayed that the serpents might be destroyed, God answered him: “Make for yourself a bronze serpent and place it as a sign; and everyone who has been bitten, when he looks at it, shall live” (Num. XXI, 8). Moses did as the Lord commanded, and the people were freed from the plague.

Since Salmona, however, is interpreted as “shadow,” this event is rightly applied to the station. For the serpent hung upon the wood was a type and shadow of Christ hanging upon the cross for our salvation, as he himself explains in the Gospel, saying: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III, 14).

Let us therefore frequent this station, so that we may look upon Christ hanging upon the cross for the salvation of the world, for he is saving.

### Thirty-Sixth Station, PHINON

The thirty-sixth station is called Phinon; for it says: “And setting out from Salmona, they encamped at Phinon” (Num. XXXIII, 42).

The moderation of the tongue is among the things that are no less necessary to a human being than they are difficult. The holy apostle James enumerates these matters at length, saying: “If anyone does not stumble in speech, that person is perfect, able to bridle the whole body as well” (James III, 2).

Behold, we put bridles into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, and we turn their whole bodies about. Behold also the ships: although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a small rudder wherever the impulse of the one directing it wishes. So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. Behold how small a fire sets ablaze how great a forest. The tongue also is a fire, the whole universe of iniquity (Eccles. XXVIII, 28–29); and the other things that the holy Apostle explains to you are relevant to this subject.

If so many evils threaten human beings from the tongue, who would dare say that it does not need restraint? Therefore the Wise Man gives this command, saying: “Surround your possession with thorns, and make doors and bars for your mouth; melt down your silver and your gold, and make a balance for your words, and make a door and a bar for your mouth” (ibid., 12).

But when a balance, door, and bar did not readily present themselves to him as images for the tongue, the same Wise Man said: “Who will set a guard over my mouth and a seal upon my lips?” (Eccles. XXII, 33). The prophet David, recognizing that these gifts are granted by the Lord, prayed to the Lord in these words: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. CXL, 3).

Moderation of the tongue has its place at this station. For Phinon is interpreted as “restraint of the mouth.” Let us therefore also take care to maintain our station here, so that we may know what, when, how, and to whom it is fitting to speak; and so that our mouth may meditate wisdom and our tongue speak judgment (Ps. XXXVI, 30).

### Thirty-Seventh Station, OBOTH

The thirty-seventh station is called Oboth, where the children of Israel finally arrived; therefore it follows: “And setting out from Phinon, they encamped at Oboth” (Num. XXXIII, 43). Concerning this station it is also read elsewhere: “And the children of Israel set out and encamped at Oboth” (Num. XXI, 11).

It must be understood, however, that the greater and more destructive temptations by which the soul is attacked in this life are, by universal agreement, considered to be the illusions of demons and the tricks of magicians and diviners. For through evil spells and magical arts these sorcerers claim to accomplish things possible only to the divine nature, so that they may remove the worship of divinity from human hearts. Thus they dare continually to resist its power.

But when their vanities had finally been exposed and their arts overthrown, divine power always prevailed. The magicians dared to resist Moses before Pharaoh and claimed that their staffs had become dragons. But finally the staff of Moses, transformed by God’s providence and power into a serpent, sprang upon the magicians’ dragons and immediately devoured them (Exod. VII, 10 ff.). For the things done through Moses were accomplished neither by error nor by tricks but by truth; therefore they endured through wondrous power.

It is also read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XIII, 8 ff.) that while the apostle Paul was preaching before the proconsul Sergius, who wished to hear the word of God, Elymas the magician resisted, seeking, it says, to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Finally, when he was rebuked by the Apostle, he was made blind, so that, it says, he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand.

Therefore the Law especially commands that dealings with such people be avoided. For it says: “The soul that follows ventriloquists or enchanters, prostituting itself after them, I will set my face against that soul and destroy it from among its people” (Lev. XX, 6).

This station is cultivated for the destruction of magicians, for Oboth is interpreted as “magicians.” Let us therefore also approach Oboth and raise our tents there, so that, dwelling under the protection of the God of heaven, we may not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, or the attack and demon of noonday (Ps. XC, 2, 6).

### Thirty-Eighth Station, JEABARIM

The thirty-eighth station is called Jeabarim; for it is written: “And setting out from Oboth, they encamped at Jeabarim, in the region beyond, at the borders of Moab” (Num. XXXIII, 44). Concerning this station it is read more clearly elsewhere: “And setting out from Oboth,” it says, “they encamped at Jeabarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the rising of the sun” (Num. XXI, 11).

For this reason we must remember that the Idumeans, as we said above, hostilely refused to grant the children of Israel passage through their land. Therefore, turning away from them, they were forced to go around the borders of the Moabites. Hence it is said that they came to the borders of Moab toward the east.

Jeabarim means “a heap of stones of those who pass over,” which is the Church of the righteous. For the righteous are “stones that pass over.” They are called stones because of their firmness; concerning them the apostle Peter writes: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II, 5).

Firmness is rightly attributed to the righteous because they neither waver nor are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Hence in the Gospel they are compared to a house founded upon solid rock, against which the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and it did not fall (Matt. VII, 2).

They are also called those who pass over because, according to the Apostle, they confess that they are “guests and strangers upon the earth” (Heb. I, 13). Finally, the Church is rightly called a heap of stones because she is “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III, 15).

Let us therefore also maintain our station at Jeabarim, so that, according to the apostle Paul, we may hold fast the hope set before us, like a safe and firm anchor of the soul, reaching into the interior of the veil (Heb. VI, 19); and so that, according to the apostle Peter, knowing these things beforehand, we may beware lest, carried away by the error of the wicked, we fall from our own steadfastness (II Pet. III, 17).

### Thirty-Ninth Station, DIBONGAD

The thirty-ninth station is at Dibongad; for it is written: “And setting out from Jeabarim, they encamped at Dibongad” (Num. XXXIII, 45). But concerning this station something very different seems to be read elsewhere. For it is written: “And setting out from Oboth, they encamped at Jeabarim, in the wilderness that is opposite Moab, toward the rising of the sun. From there they departed and encamped in the valley of Zared; [the remaining words are uncertain in the source]” (Num. XXI, 11).

If, therefore, they encamped in the valley of Zared (Origen, cited above), you will ask: How did they encamp at Dibongad? The answer is that in the former passage the place is expressed generally, whereas here it is expressed specifically. Dibongad is situated near the valley of Zared, which lies between the boundaries of the Amorites and the Moabites.

Mystically, however, Dibongad signifies “an apiary of temptations.” We are taught by this that although the righteous person may be near perfection or even supreme perfection, temptations are nevertheless not absent from him. This is a precaution of divine providence, lest we take occasion from successful circumstances to depart from the right path.

Hence Job said: “Blessed is the person whom the Lord corrects; do not reject the chastening of the Almighty” (Job V, 17). And although, while we are in the flesh, temptations appear bitter to us, they nevertheless contribute wonderfully to our future life, as the Apostle says: “All discipline for the present seems not to be joyful but sorrowful; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Heb. XII, 11).

Let us therefore draw near and hasten to enter this station, knowing that we are sometimes corrected by the Lord so that we may not be condemned with the world (I Cor. XI, 32). Let us also maintain a sure hope that God will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but will provide a way out along with the temptation, so that we may be able to endure it (I Cor. X, 13).

### Fortieth Station, ELMON DEBLATHAIM

The fortieth station is made by the children of Israel at Elmon Deblathaim; for it is written: “And setting out from Dibongad, they encamped at Elmon Deblathaim” (Num. XXXIII, 46). Since the expression Elmon Deblathaim is twofold, it likewise indicates two things, namely, contempt for figs—that is, contempt for earthly sweetness. For figs display sweetness. Hence the prophet Jeremiah saw “good figs, very good” (Jer. XXIV, 3).

And our Savior, hungry and having left behind the bitterness of the scribes and Pharisees, approached a fig tree, so that he might find at least some sweetness among the common people. When he found nothing but leaves, he cursed it, saying: “May no fruit ever come from you” (Matt. XXI, 19).

Contempt for earthly pleasures is therefore supremely necessary for one hastening toward heaven. For unless we disregard the allurements of pleasure and the things that seem delightful on earth, we cannot raise ourselves to heavenly things. Therefore the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Think on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Coloss. III, 2). Indeed, to set one’s mind on earthly things is shameful. Thus the Apostle writes: “Their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. III, 19).

But since our citizenship is in heaven, we who have risen with Christ (ibid., 20), having trampled the allurements of the world with complete gladness of heart, let us enter the tents of this station, seeking the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Coloss. III, 1). Let us strive, whether absent or present, to please the Lord our God.

### Forty-First Station, ABARIM

The forty-first station is made by the children of Israel in the mountains of Abarim; for it follows: “And setting out from Elmon Deblathaim, they encamped upon the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo” (Num. XXXIII, 47).

But what is read elsewhere concerning this station seems very different. For it says: “They encamped in the valley of Zared; from there they departed and encamped beyond the Arnon, in the wilderness that extends from the borders of the Amorites” (Num. II, 12–13). From these words it appears that the children of Israel did not have their station after Elmon in the mountains of Abarim, but in the wilderness beyond the Arnon.

There is no contradiction, however, because Abarim is in the wilderness beyond the Arnon. What Scripture expressed elsewhere under a common name, it expresses here under a proper name. Hence it adds: “For the Arnon is at the borders of Moab, between the Amorites; and there is Mount Abarim, at whose foot, beside the Amorites, the river Arnon flows.”

Mount Abarim is said to be beyond the Arnon not with reference to the crossing of the Hebrews, but with reference to the location of the Holy Land, as is Moses’ custom in this description. For in the Book of Deuteronomy it is read: “These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness toward the west” (Deut. I, 1). Moses, however, did not cross the Jordan at all. Therefore “this side” referred to the route of the Hebrews, while “beyond” referred to the location of the Holy Land.

At this station Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, asking him to grant him and his people passage through his territory without doing any harm whatsoever to his people: “We will pass through your land; we will not turn aside into a field or a vineyard, nor will we drink water from a well; we will go by the king’s highway” (Num. XXI, 22).

But Sihon absolutely refused and answered harshly. Rather, having armed a strong army, he immediately came down to the river Arnon, where Israel was to pass, to block the road and resist the attack. But by divine power it came to pass that, after the king had been killed in battle, the Hebrews struck down the Amorite people with the sword and devastated and depopulated their lands.

Meanwhile Og, king of Bashan, armed enormous forces to bring aid to his friend the Amorite, and advanced to attack Israel in hostility. But Israel, fighting with heavenly assistance, killed the king himself in battle, destroyed his entire army, and finally subdued all their land. Thus, with a notable victory, they carried away great stores of wealth. Josephus recorded all these events in extensive detail (Book IV of the *Antiquities*, chap. 4).

## The Forty-Second Station, at the Jordan

The forty-second station is located in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan. Therefore he says: “And they set out from the borders of Abarim and came to the western region of Moab, above the Jordan, near Jericho; and there they encamped by the Jordan, between Bethsimon and Belsachin, in the western part of Moab” (Num. 33:48). Elsewhere Scripture also mentions this same station, saying: “And the children of Israel departed and encamped in the western part of Moab, by the Jordan, near Jericho” (Num. 22:1).

Finally, this is the last station described by Moses, by the word of God, in the long and arduous journey of the children of Israel. Although many things were said and done there worthy of remembrance, we shall relate only a few. First, when Balak, king of the Moabites, saw the children of Israel advancing with such increase and their affairs prospering with such favorable success, he conceived great fear for his own affairs, as is evident from what he said beforehand to the people of Midian. For he said: “Now this assembly will lick up all those who are around us, just as a calf licks up the green things of the field” (ibid., 4).

Therefore, since he did not dare to attack them openly with weapons, he resolved, lest they should at least become more powerful, to resort to secret arts. Accordingly, he summoned the magician Balaam and asked him to curse and destroy the people by his imprecations and magical arts. Yet, because divine providence opposed him, he was never able to obtain this from Balaam, either by persuasion or by gifts. On the contrary, when the Lord opened the magician’s mouth, he blessed the people and foretold their happy fortunes: “How beautiful,” he said, “are your tents, Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel, like valleys shaded by trees, like gardens beside a river, and like tents that the Lord has pitched” (Num. 24:5); and later: “May those who bless you be blessed, and may those who curse you be cursed”; likewise: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise up from Israel” (ibid., 17).

Then, because the people, through their love for the women of Midian, had abandoned the true God and turned to idols, Phinehas, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, burning with zeal for the Lord of hosts, before iniquity, left unchecked, could rage more violently, publicly killed with a drawn dagger a Hebrew man and a Midianite woman who had been caught in fornication and brought before Moses. Stirred by his example, many others seized their weapons and rose up against the fornicators; and twenty-four thousand people were killed on that day. Thus, when the fornicators had been slain, God was reconciled with the people: “And the plague,” he says, “ceased from the children of Israel” (Num. 25:8).

Moreover, since the land of the Canaanites, which the children of Israel were moving toward by the word of God in order to possess it, was already close at hand, and they were now almost grasping the borders of the holy land after wandering for more than forty years; and since it was granted to them to seize it only by armed force, after the enemy’s strength had been broken, the priest Eleazar therefore resolved, at God’s command, to make a new census of the people fit for war. In it, apart from the tribe of Levi, which had been set apart for the special worship of God, and apart from the women, six hundred and one thousand seven hundred and thirty men, twenty years old and above and prepared for war, were counted, as Scripture says.

Moses and Eleazar the priest also arranged in due order, at this station, many other matters pertaining to religion and the worship of God, as well as to the administration of the commonwealth in war and peace (Num. 26:51). Since recounting these would prolong our reading excessively, or because we have often set them out elsewhere, we now judge that they should be omitted.

Nevertheless, we have not thought that the following should be passed over in silence: Moses, recognizing that his final day was at last approaching by the word of God, declared Joshua son of Nun to be his successor and the leader of the people by God’s command; he also prescribed the blessings and curses (Deut. 34:1 ff.) that those who observed or transgressed the divine law would incur, and foretold what would individually befall each tribe. Then he climbed Mount Nebo. From there he surveyed with his eyes and considered in his mind the broad and excellent region of the Canaanites—the land indeed flowing with milk and honey—which had been repeatedly promised by oracles to the fathers, and which lay opposite Mount Nebo; and, to use the words of the Apostle (Heb. 11:13), “he greeted it from afar.”

When this had been accomplished, the Lord said to him: “I have shown this land to your eyes, but you shall not enter it” (Deut. 34:4). Immediately thereafter, by the word of God, he died and was buried in the valley; and no one knows his tomb to this day.

This was the end of Moses and of the stations of the people, which had been listed in order at God’s command. Some mystical matters would now remain to be explained, were we not to find that we have scattered most of them throughout the present treatise and explained others elsewhere.

Finally, we have judged this worth observing: the whole of this journey is recalled here, and this entire course is proposed for completion, so that, when at last we reach the Jordan, the river of God, we may be watered by the streams of divine wisdom; and, purified in every respect, may at last, through God’s mercy, enter the land of promise and be able to say with the Apostle: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; and the crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge, the Lord, will render on that day to those who love his coming” (2 Tim. 4:7–8), may be laid up for us through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong all honor, glory, and perpetuity forever and ever. Amen.

[**Commentaries on the Thirteen Epistles of Paul.**]

## [Column 0039]

## NOTICE PREFATORY TO THE FOLLOWING COMMENTARIES

[Column 0039C] As much as people in former centuries unanimously conspired to attribute the following work to Saint Ambrose, so unanimously at the present time learned men, wherever they are heard, wish to take it away from him. For as early as the ninth century Hincmar (Treatise on the Divorce of Lothair, etc.), the Church of Lyons (*Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. IV, part II), the Third Council of Aachen (A.D. 862, canon 8), Amalarius, Prudentius, Haymo, and several other authors of the same period brought forward many passages from these very Commentaries under Ambrose’s name.

Rabanus, a contemporary of Hincmar, in his *Exposition of the Pauline Epistles*, compiled from the Fathers, cites many passages in the first five epistles as genuinely Ambrosian, although they are in fact found in these Commentaries of ours. Sedulius likewise transferred some passages into his exposition of the earlier epistles of Paul, once attributing them to Ambrose by name. Lanfranc, too, in his *Compilation*, attributes to the holy Doctor those fragments that he borrowed from this work. Finally, this work was accepted as Ambrosian by Gratian, Peter Lombard, Ivo of Chartres, and countless others.

Nevertheless, when that universal opinion did not seem sufficiently certain to Erasmus, Turrianus, and others, after a more thorough examination they all subsequently rejected it by common consent.

For this reason, we might seem to be doing again what has already been done if we lingered at length in proving a matter so thoroughly established. We shall not, however, remain silent about the fact that the style of the work differs so greatly from Ambrose’s that it is plainly astonishing that the difference was detected so late. Nor is the disagreement between the doctrines of the two authors any less significant. For in Ambrosiaster there occur not only certain extraordinary opinions, differing immensely from the views of the true Ambrose, but even in affirming doctrines that are especially Catholic the two do not sufficiently agree. In refuting the arguments that the Arians used to make, Ambrosiaster employs answers which, when set aside, leave the holy Doctor proposing something altogether different.

Moreover, it would be useless to point out what is obvious to everyone: namely, that this writer was entirely foreign to the Greek language. What if we add that it is not entirely clear whether Ambrose ever composed commentaries on Paul at all? Yet even if the holy man did publish such an exposition, it is at least highly credible that it had already perished by the time of Cassiodorus. This may be inferred from the following words of Cassiodorus: “It is also said,” he writes, “that blessed Ambrose left behind a codex of all the epistles of Saint Paul, fully supplied with a most pleasing exposition; yet I have not so far been able to find it,” etc. (*On the Institution of Divine Literature*, chap. 8).

The entire difficulty, then, lies in discovering the true parent of this work. Some have preferred to regard its author as a compiler who, cutting up scraps from Chrysostom and Jerome, fashioned a patchwork from them. Others maintain that the prologues prefixed to the individual expositions were the work of an incompetent assembler who stole many fragments chiefly from Jerome. Yet, when we compared the works of those same Fathers, we detected no such thing at all.

On the contrary, we frequently observed that this author disagrees with their opinions, offers different explanations, sometimes cites the Apostolic text in a manner unlike theirs, and, finally, that wherever he agrees with them, this occurred because it is impossible for those who write commentaries on the same book to differ everywhere. We shall not, however, deny that our author appears to have borrowed certain things from Jerome; but we do not think that for this reason he should be regarded as a compiler in the sense they intend.

Among those who have attempted to identify the author of these Commentaries, those who attributed them to Remigius labored in vain. For both in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* and in quite a few manuscripts, works of Remigius are found that are entirely different from ours. Nor were there lacking those who argued that this commentary was the work either of Julian or of some other Pelagian. There were likewise writers who thought that its author should be freed from that charge; and if anything occurs in it that might favor those heretics, they attributed it to the fact that, since he wrote before their heresy arose, he had spoken less cautiously and thoughtfully.

The final and more common opinion is that Hilary, a deacon of the Roman Church who had adhered to the Luciferian schism and was attacked by Jerome in such harsh language (*Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, near the end), is the true author of this work. Since there are also those who oppose this view, it must be considered more carefully.

We shall first observe that scarcely any genuine work of Ambrose has more copies from every period surviving over the last eight hundred years than this Ambrosiaster. Yet some of those copies differ from the others to a considerable degree. Indeed, in the library at Corbie there is one work contained in two volumes, superior to any other we have been able to see, whether one considers its antiquity or the elegance of its script.

Since it contains commentaries on all Paul’s epistles, except the one entitled “To the Hebrews,” under Ambrose’s name, it agrees with other written and printed codices only in the first three epistles, while differing in the rest. Rabanus Maurus, proceeding further in his Commentary compiled from the Fathers, attributes to Ambrose everything he cites from Ambrosiaster on the first five epistles. But whatever he inserts under the title of the holy Doctor in the remaining epistles is found only in the Corbie codex.

Ivo of Chartres also cites several words from the prologue to the exposition of the Epistle to Philemon (*Decretum*, part XVI, chap. 84) which are found nowhere except in Rabanus and in the Corbie codex.

Whoever carefully considers all this will cease to wonder that many things are missing from our Author which Lanfranc brings forward as taken from Ambrose’s Commentaries on the Apostle. He will easily perceive that the name of Ambrose was assigned by the antiquaries to various expositions of Paul’s epistles.

It should additionally be noted that those same scribes exercised great license, at least in the first three epistles. For it is probable that long fragments were often inserted there by them which are not found in the more ancient manuscripts, as will be noted in the various readings. From this one may draw a strong conjecture against the integrity and authenticity of this work; and it becomes clear that it is not a matter for hasty judgment to affirm whether it is the labor of one author or of several.

If, however, we deny that it belongs to several authors, we shall also seem obliged to admit that it belongs to an ancient commentator. For what he says about the Church, whose ruler today is Damasus (*On the First Epistle to Timothy*, chap. 3), must either be attributed to an interpolator—and indeed it does not reflect the usage of those times, nor is it necessary to the sense—or it will become clear that the same author wrote his Commentaries before the year 384, when that pope died.

This may also be confirmed by his testimony that the Marcionites still survived, although, he says, “they have almost disappeared” (ibid., chap. 4). It is certainly established from Epiphanius (*Against Heresies*, 42) and Theodoret (*Book I of the Fables of the Heretics*, chap. 24) that these heretics were extinguished only very late. Yet it is also established that in several places they readily passed over to the party of the Manichaeans, who are mentioned more frequently here.

It should also be observed in passing that this work mentions a certain law promulgated against them by Domitian (*On the Second Epistle to Timothy*, chap. 3), which is found only in the *Collection of Mosaic and Roman Laws*. The antiquity of the author is further indicated by the fact that he does not omit the Patricians (*On the First Epistle to Timothy*, chap. 4), whom Philaster and Augustine mention among those who survived, although they did not continue beyond the fifth century.

Moreover, none of the other heretics whom he attacks—of whom there are very many—is mentioned as even slightly more recent. Since he applies himself more frequently and laboriously to refuting the Donatists, Novatians, Arians, and Photinians than to the others, this is undoubtedly evidence that the later heretics, such as the Nestorians and those of subsequent times, had not yet emerged; rather, the heresies of those whom we have just named were then still flourishing.

Add to this that the writer sometimes cites the Apostle’s text from a different version than the one we now use, and that the testimonies of the Old Testament are taken from the version of the Seventy Elders. The same conclusion follows from the fact that among ecclesiastical authors he uses passages only from Tertullian, Cyprian, and Victorinus, the last of whom was equal in antiquity to Damasus.

Finally, the same period may likewise be established from the fact that, in the baptism of the sick and in quite a few other matters, he accurately represents the ecclesiastical discipline of those times.

[Column 0043] Everything we have mentioned seems to support the opinion of those who maintain that these Commentaries were published by Hilary. They were led to this view by Augustine’s testimony, when he writes against the Pelagians: “For Saint Hilary also understood what is written, ‘In whom all sinned.’ He says: ‘In whom,’ that is, in Adam,” followed by the rest, which may be read word for word in this work (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, chap. 4).

Yet, they say, these things can apply only to Hilary the Deacon, who himself indicates that he was a contemporary of Damasus. It was objected to them that this author vigorously attacks those who rebaptize, although Hilary was himself charged with the same offense; and, moreover, that Augustine would never have bestowed the title “saint” upon this Hilary, whom he knew to have withdrawn from the Church after creating a schism.

They reply that Hilary did not believe that all heretics should be rebaptized, but only the Arians; and that he indicated by this distinction that he had been led to that opinion for no other reason than that these heretics, holding an incorrect view of the Trinity, also used an invalid form in baptism. Thus nothing prevented him from attacking heretics who rebaptized Catholics.

They think that they satisfy the second objection if they deny that the aforementioned title of honor proves that Saint Augustine meant Hilary the Luciferian. Rather, they say, it should be inferred from it either that the deacon never separated from the universal Church, since he preserved peace and communion with its head, blessed Damasus, or that he was eventually reconciled with the Catholics before his death.

Jerome, however, is plainly opposed to this response. He speaks of Hilary not as someone separated from only a few bishops or for only a time, but as one separated from the entire Catholic community throughout the whole course of his life (*Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, near the end).

This opinion is also contradicted by the fact that Hilary, as a deacon of the Roman Church, would not have spoken of that Church as a stranger or outsider. For how could he have written of his own Church: “Now there ought to be seven deacons and several presbyters, so that there may be two in each church” (*On the Epistle to Timothy*, chap. 3)? For when, under Diocletian, there were already forty basilicas in the City, it would have been necessary to ordain not merely several presbyters, but at least eighty.

There is no doubt that these very considerations led Petavius to attribute the same Commentaries to Hilary, but to someone other than the Luciferian—whoever he may have been. Indeed, even if we did not have Hilary, bishop of Pavia under Damasus, famous for holiness and zeal against the Arians, to whom those writings might perhaps be attributed, many writings still survive whose authors are known only by name and whom we would otherwise entirely ignore, had it not happened by chance that someone else once mentioned them.

Yet although these considerations cannot altogether be denied, Augustine, against the Pelagians, who were fiercely attacking the doctrine of original sin, would not have used the testimony of an author who, although he seems in some places to acknowledge that doctrine, sometimes nevertheless displays the opposite view; an author whom very serious and reputable theologians judge to favor the Pelagians openly, and whom the learned Jesuit Justinian, at least in one passage, explicitly declares to be Semipelagian (*Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, chap. 14).

What if we add the other errors that are discovered throughout these same Commentaries? Certainly their author cannot be defended without admitting that he agreed with Origen that it lies within the will of demons to turn back from error (from Estius’s *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, chap. 3).

There is also the notorious and well-known fault that he insists that a husband is always permitted, after divorcing his wife on account of adultery, to take another wife (*On the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, chap. 7), while he denies that a wife separated from an adulterous husband may enter into marriage with another man.

Nor are the following teachings sufficiently sound: that a woman was made in the image of God (*On the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, chaps. 11 and 14, and *On the Epistle to the Colossians*, chap. 3); that bishops hold a rank superior to presbyters (*On the Epistle to the Ephesians*, chap. 4); or that the author denies that different ordinations were established. From time to time he also transmits certain other views less compatible with the common understanding of Catholics.

Furthermore, even if many things seem to favor assigning this work the same antiquity as Damasus, there are also other features from which it may be assigned to a much later period. To say nothing here of the fact that Jerome, in his *Ecclesiastical Authors*, recognizes no Latin commentator on Paul’s Epistles except Victorinus, it is entirely plausible that many passages in these books were transferred from Augustine, Chrysostom, and Jerome. Indeed, it is worth observing that they may also have been taken from that very commentator whose work, published at the end of Jerome’s writings, is said by many to belong to Pelagius.

For since quite a few passages are read in identical words in both commentaries, and therefore it is beyond doubt that one borrowed from the other, we consider it less probable that the Pseudo-Jerome commentator, who is so brief and concise, borrowed certain passages from Ambrosiaster than that the reverse occurred.

In addition, it may be added that this author proves with no less care that Christ the Lord is not the Son of God by adoption than if he had written after the errors of Felix and Elipandus (*On the Epistle to the Philippians*, chap. 2).

If to these differences of period one adds some differences of wording and thought in the expositions of the various epistles on the same subject, as well as the inequality of the manner of argument—sometimes extremely expansive, sometimes extremely compressed—there may perhaps be someone who disagrees that all these Commentaries are by the same hand, or at least who asserts that they should be attributed to some compiler of this kind: one who, while extracting from various works, many of which had perished, preserved certain indications of the period of each and also added some features belonging to his own age.

Yet, however great the difficulty in assigning an antiquity either to the Author or to the Work, the handwritten volumes of these Commentaries, as well as the writers from whom passages are cited or extracted, make it clear that they cannot in any way be assigned to a period later than the eighth century.

Perhaps some will wish to know our opinion concerning the author of the *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, whom many, following the Louvain theologians—who relegated those books to the appendix of the works of Saint Augustine (*vol. III, part I*)—have considered to be the same as Ambrosiaster.

Yet what we have argued thus far sufficiently shows that it is not an easy matter to decide this question. Very many passages indeed appear in both works in the same words and with the same cited passages of Scripture. But nothing can be inferred from this except that these passages were copied from one work into the other. Nevertheless, it is more probable that the author of the *Questions*, if indeed they have a single author, was the compiler of this work, since he is much more expansive in his treatment and has added to Ambrosiaster’s errors several that are peculiar to himself.

Since, however, the work cannot be denied to possess usefulness, and since it has held a place among Ambrose’s writings up to this edition, with passages cited under his name occurring everywhere, we admitted it into this Appendix all the more willingly because a greater number of manuscripts were available, with whose help it could be produced in a much more accurate form.

Among other corrections, we restored a substantial fragment at the end of the Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians and at the beginning of the following one. Some writer had repaired the loss from a strip of the commentary of the Pseudo-Jerome.

It remains only to advise the reader that we have omitted the Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Neither Amerbach nor Erasmus recognized it in the more ancient manuscripts. When it was later admitted by those who undertook the task of editing Ambrose’s works, it failed to deceive men of more discerning judgment, so that it was not believed to belong to the same author to whom the preceding works are attributed, and even less to our Doctor.

In reality, it is nothing other than a poorly organized compilation from several Fathers. Since a fuller version was published among the works of Rabanus Maurus, where the authors of the individual fragments can be read alongside them, we saw no reason to receive it into our edition.

# COMMENTARIES ON THE THIRTEEN EPISTLES OF BLESSED PAUL

## [Column 0045]

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS (C, S)

### PROLOGUE

[Column 0045A]

25 In order that there may be a fuller knowledge of things, their beginnings must first be sought. For then the explanation of their cause can more easily be made clear if their origin is learned. Since we have shown the manner and circumstances in which the epistle was delivered, what we say may appear true.

It is therefore established that in the time of the Apostles Jews lived in Rome because they were subject to Roman rule. Those among them who had believed taught the Romans that, while professing Christ, they should keep the Law. The Romans, however, having heard the report of Christ’s miracles, were readily inclined to believe,

[Note: The Roman edition in the margin and in the main text reads: “They were inclined to believe; but, having been badly instructed, they immediately corrected themselves and remained in that position, being prudent.” The Roman edition, however, also reverses the final two clauses.]

being prudent. Nor were they without reason prudent, since, having been badly instructed, they were immediately corrected and remained steadfast in it.

[Note: Several editions and manuscripts read: “These, then, believing from among the Jews and holding an improper view of Christ, said that the Law must be observed, as though there were not complete salvation in Christ. Therefore he denies that they had obtained spiritual grace. These are the people who had also subverted the Galatians, so that, withdrawing from the Apostle’s tradition, they might Judaize.”]

These, then, as may be understood, having believed in Christ from among the Jews, did not accept that God was God from God, thinking that this was opposed to the one God. Therefore he denies that they had obtained the spiritual grace of God, and consequently that they lacked confirmation.

These are the people who had also subverted the Galatians, so that they might withdraw from the Apostles’ tradition. The Apostle therefore became angry with them because, although well instructed, they had been easily led astray.

He ought not to have been angry with the Romans, but rather to praise their faith, because they had received the faith of Christ without seeing any remarkable miracles or any of the Apostles, albeit in a Jewish manner of observance, in words more than in understanding. For the mystery of Christ’s cross had not been explained to them.

[Note: The same manuscripts and editions read: “Seeing miracles, they received the faith of Christ, although with a corrupted understanding; for they had not heard.” The Roman edition reads: “They had plainly heard the mystery,” and so forth.]

Therefore, when certain people who had rightly believed arrived from Judea, questions arose about whether meat should or should not be eaten, and whether the hope that is in Christ was sufficient, or whether the Law also had to be observed.

[Note: The cited manuscripts and editions read: “When those who had rightly believed arrived from Judea in the city of Rome, such as Priscilla and Aquila …” The editions, together with Florentinus, Vindobonensis, and Colbertinus alone, contain the following: “and whether the hope … and whether the Law should be observed.”]

[Column 0046B] He therefore writes to the Romans in four ways, arguing from the beginning against the human race by natural reasoning.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For they are the head of all nations, so that the others may learn in them, accusing from the beginning the human race partly by natural reasoning and partly through the Law.” The manuscripts agree with our text, except that some retain “partly through the Law,” while others omit it.]

For they are the head of all nations, so that the others and all the Gentiles may learn through them.

The first method is that by which he shows what he is, what he was, and whose he is; by this means he also strikes down the heresies.

The second method is that by which he reproves them because, contrary to the reasoning of nature, they did not submit to the one God, and because they committed dishonorable and shameful acts among themselves, on account of which they were despised by God; this is so that believers may rejoice.

The third method is that they despised the Law that had been given; hence he places the Jews before the Greeks.

The fourth method is that by which he teaches that the Jews had deviated from the Law and the promise of God in the matter of Christ, and had become like the Gentiles, so that both groups needed the mercy of God, placing their hope of salvation not in the Law but through faith in Christ Jesus.

[Note: Carnotensis and four other manuscripts read: “had deviated from the Law and the prophets in the matter of Christ.” The remaining manuscripts and the editions read as in the text.]

This is why he applies every effort to remove them from the Law, because “the Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16), and to establish them solely in faith in Christ. He also vindicates the Gospel as if against the Law,

[Note: Codex Pratensis and Codex Gemblacensis read: “so that the Gospel may prevail over it.”]

not destroying the Law but giving Christianity precedence.

[Note: All the editions read: “He shows … so that when he came”; most manuscripts, however, read as in the text.]

For he asserts that Christ was promised in such a way that, once he had been preached, the Law would cease—not the whole Law, because the Law has been abridged: an abbreviated form of the Law was made that would give salvation in summary. For many things had been handed down to the ancients because of the hardness of their hearts, things that were burdensome; God’s mercy abridged them through Christ by granting forgiveness of past sins.

Therefore, whoever wishes to remain under the Law is ungrateful toward God’s mercy. For Moses had said: “Thus you shall make the children of Israel fear” (Lev. 15:31),

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “Thus you shall cause the children of Israel to do.”]

so that wherever they turned they would have the Law, and would never be entirely free from anxiety.

Therefore, in order to teach that the hope of life and salvation must be placed in Christ without the Law, and to show that the Lord himself is Lord of all, he begins as follows:

## CHAPTER ONE

### (Verse 1) Paul, servant of Christ Jesus

Among our ancient people names were formed according to a particular rationale, as Isaac was named on account of laughter and Jacob on account of the heel. In the same way, this man was called Saul on account of unrest. After he believed, however, he says that he is Paul,

[Note: The same edition reads: “He was called Paul from Saul, that is, changed.” Other editions and manuscripts agree with us, except that for “changed” Codex Michaelianus reads “diminished,” which is not inappropriate.]

that is, changed.

Since, according to the meaning mentioned above, Saul is interpreted as “unrest” or “temptation,” when he came to the faith of Christ he says that he is Paul, that is, as though he had been made peaceful, humble, or small from being a tempter; for our faith is peace.

Previously he had brought temptations upon God’s servants out of the unrest of Judaism; afterward he himself suffered temptations because of the hope that, through his former love of Judaism, he had denied.

[Note: The Gill edition in the margin and the Roman edition in the text, together with some manuscripts, read: “from zeal for the Law,” that is, “from unrest,” and so forth.]

By declaring himself a servant of Christ Jesus, he shows that he has been stripped of the Law. For this reason he used both names, namely, Jesus Christ, so that he might signify the person both of God and of man, because he is Lord in both respects, as the Apostle Peter also testifies, saying: “This one,” he says, “is Lord of all.”

Since, therefore, he is both Lord and God, David says: “For the Lord himself is God” (Ps. 99:3). The heresies deny this. For Marcion, out of hatred for the Law, seems to deny that Christ and his body exist, while professing Jesus. The Jews, however, and Photinus, out of zeal for the Law, deny that Jesus is God.

[Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, together with the manuscripts, read as here. The Gill and Roman editions, however, read: “For whenever Scripture says …” In the others, “Paul” or “the Apostle” is correctly understood.]

For whenever he says either “Jesus” or “Christ,” he sometimes signifies God and sometimes man, as in this passage, among others: “And there is one Lord,” he says, “Jesus, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6), which certainly pertains to the Son of God, insofar as he is God.

Elsewhere he says: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2:52), which certainly pertains to man.

### Called an apostle

Because he knew and confessed God, he became worthy, as a servant, and showed that he had been promoted by saying: “Called an apostle,” that is, sent by the Lord to carry out his affairs.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “First a servant, then he shows himself.”]

By this he shows that he possesses merit before God, since he serves not the Law but Christ. For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath (Matt. 12:8).

### Set apart for the Gospel of God

The Gospel of God is God’s good news, by which sinners are summoned to forgiveness.

Since the Apostle held the position of teacher in Judaism, being a Pharisee, he therefore says that he was set apart from preaching Judaism for the Gospel of God, so that, disregarding the Law, he might preach Christ, who granted to those who believe in him what the Law could not: justification.

[Note: The Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, omits everything from the words “justified” through “Therefore, if the Law of God,” and continues with “had slain.” We restored this passage from several manuscripts and ancient editions. The same Roman edition again omits the entire passage beginning with “Therefore, if the Law of God” and ending with “and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” Gill restored it to the text from various readings, and we retained it on the authority of those readings and of the Corbie manuscript.]

But this is not against the Law; rather, it is on behalf of the Law. For the Law itself says that this would happen, as the prophet Isaiah says: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns captivity away from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”

Therefore, if the Law of God was given through Moses, and the preaching of the new Law is also God’s, why does he say that he has been transferred from the Law given by God into the Gospel of God? It is like someone who advances from the second rank to the first, and from something good to something better.

For the Law was given by God for the correction of discipline. The Gospel of God, however, is that through which the mystery of God is revealed—a mystery hidden for ages in God—which is Christ.

To this all are invited, and they receive double gifts (*apophoreta*): they receive the remission of sins and become children of God, so that they can no longer die the second death.

This is why the Lord says in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

### (Verse 2) Which he had promised beforehand

In order to prove that the hope of faith in Christ is valid and complete,

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “and that the faith is whole and complete.”]

he says that his Gospel had previously been promised by God. And, in order to show that Christ was a trustworthy guarantor of life, he demonstrates that testimony had been given to him before he came, with the Apostle Peter bearing corresponding witness: “For no other name,” he says, “has been given under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

Through his prophets. To signify more clearly that Christ’s coming would be salutary, he also identified the persons through whom he had marked out the promise, so that from them it might be seen how true and magnificent the promise was. For no one announces an insignificant matter through great forerunners.

In the holy Scriptures. He added this to reinforce the true testimony, in order to give believers greater confidence and to commend the Law; for the Scriptures are holy, since they condemn vices. In them, too, the mystery of the one God and of the incarnation of the Son of God for human salvation is contained, with signs and wonders as witnesses.

**(Verse 3.) Of his Son.** Since God was promising his own proper Son to the world, it was fitting that he should promise him through illustrious men, so that from them it might be known how powerful he was who was being proclaimed; and so that he might record his future coming in the holy Scriptures, and so that what had been proclaimed by the holy Scriptures could not appear false.

**Who was made his Son from the seed of David according to the flesh.** He says that the one who was the Son of God according to the Holy Spirit—that is, according to God (for God is spirit, and without doubt is holy)—was made, according to the flesh, [Note: Some manuscripts: “the Son of God from Mary.”] the Son of God from the seed of David, in accordance with the passage: “And the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). Thus Christ Jesus is now one Son of God and man, [Note: The words “so that, just as he is true … from flesh and soul …” from various readings of Gill’s edition were admitted into the text by the Roman edition, but the words “so that, if perfect” were omitted. We have restored them from the same readings of Gill and from the Corbie and Reims manuscripts.] so that, just as he was true God, he might also be true man. But he will not be true man unless he is from flesh and soul, so that he may be perfect.

For he who was eternally the Son of God was unknown to creation. But when he wished to be manifested for human salvation, he had to become visible and corporeal, because he also wished to make himself known through his power and to wash humanity from sins in the flesh, after conquering death. And therefore he is made from the seed of David, so that, just as he had been born as king from God before the ages, so also according to the flesh he might receive royal origin from a king, having been made by the work of the Holy Spirit from a Virgin—that is, born—so that, with reverence reserved for him, he might thereby be recognized as more than human, since his birth differed from human birth according to the law, just as had been foretold by the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb” (Isaiah 7:14). Thus, when the event appeared new and worthy of praise, a certain providence of God concerning the future visitation of the human race might be recognized.

**(Verse 4.) Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.** By saying “the Son of God,” he signified God the Father; by adding “the spirit of sanctification,” he revealed the mystery of the Trinity. This one, therefore, who, having been incarnate, was hidden as to what he was, [Note: Some manuscripts: “who indeed was incarnate and was hidden.”] was then predestined to be manifested as the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification, when he rose from the dead, as it is written in the eighty-fourth psalm: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12).

Every doubt and distrust was trampled down and suppressed by his resurrection. Indeed, while he was still placed upon the cross, the centurion, seeing the mighty deeds, confessed him to be the Son of God (Matthew 27:54). For even the disciples doubted at his death, when Cleopas said at Emmaus: “We were hoping that he was the one who was beginning to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). And the Lord himself said: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28); and again: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32)—that is, “then I will be recognized as Lord of all.”

He did not, therefore, say “by the resurrection of Jesus Christ,” but “by the resurrection of the dead,” because Christ’s resurrection grants a general resurrection. For this appears to be the greater power and victory in Christ: that, though dead, he should work by the power by which he had also worked while alive. By this deed it became clear that he had mocked death in order to redeem us; hence he calls him our Lord.

**(Verse 5.) Through whom we received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all the nations for his name.** After the Son of God had been manifested in power through the resurrection, he gave grace, justifying sinners, [Note: Some manuscripts: “and strengthened the apostles.”] and appointed apostles, among whom he declares himself to be a companion, so that apostleship, together with grace, might be a gift of God, not like the apostles of the Jews.

From God the Father, therefore, through Christ the Lord, they received this power: in the Lord’s place, by signs, to make the Lord’s teaching acceptable; so that, when the faithless Jews saw the crowds admiring in his servants the power over which they had been envious in the Savior, they might be tormented all the more. For power is the witness of teaching, so that, because what is preached is incredible to the world, it might be made credible by deeds. [Note: The Roman edition: “Therefore he sends the apostles, that they might preach.”]

He therefore calls the apostles “sent,” so that they might preach faith to all the nations, in order that they might obey and be saved; so that the gift of God might be seen to have been granted not only to the Jews but also to all the nations; and so that this might be God’s will: that in Christ and through Christ he should show mercy to all, with his representatives preaching, namely: “For his name,” as he says elsewhere: “For whom we are ambassadors” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

**(Verse 6.) Among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ.** That is: while we are carrying out an embassy among all the nations for the name of Jesus Christ, you too are among those who have been called. For God’s gift has been sent to all, so that when they hear that they have been called along with the others, they may know that they ought not to live under the Law, since the other nations received the law of Christ without the law of Moses.

**(Verse 7.) To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as holy.** Although he is writing to the Romans, he indicates that he is writing to those who are in the love of God. Who are these, unless those who rightly think about the Son of God? These are holy and are called; for those who live under the Law understand Christ wrongly, and they do injury to God the Father when they doubt whether perfect hope of salvation is in Christ. Therefore they are neither holy nor called.

**Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.** He says that grace and peace are with those who believe rightly. It is grace because they have been absolved from sins; peace, because from being enemies they have been reconciled to the Creator, as the Lord says: “Into whatever house you enter, and they receive you, say: ‘Peace to this house’” (Luke 10:5). And to teach that without Christ there is no peace and no hope, he added that grace and peace are not only from God the Father but also from Christ Jesus. [Col. 0051C] He calls God “our Father” because of our origin, since all things are from him; but he calls Christ “Lord,” because, having been redeemed by his blood, we have become sons of God.

**(Verse 8.) First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.** Having finished his preface, he first declares his joy, as the Apostle of the nations, that although the Romans ruled the world, they had submitted themselves to the Christian faith, which appears humble and foolish to the wise of this age. [Note: The Roman edition alone: “appears foolish to the wisdom of this age.”]

Since there were many things about the Romans over which he could rejoice—[Note: The same edition: “of moral discipline”; the old edition and several manuscripts: “of teaching”; some: “memorable for discipline.” But the reading should altogether be, with the Carnuntine manuscript, “memorable for teaching,” unless one prefers, with the Vatican manuscript, “memorable for teaching,” singular, as in the text.] for they were notable for their teaching and eager for good works, and more zealous to do good than to speak, which is not far removed from divine religion—nevertheless, he says that he rejoices first of all because their faith was spreading everywhere. [Note: The Reims manuscript inserts: “For it appeared a remarkable thing that the lords of the nations should bow to the promise of the Jews.”]

Although their faith had not been handed down according to the rule of the truth delivered by its authors, he nevertheless congratulates them because, when the name of Christ had been added, they had begun to venerate what came from the one God, knowing that they could make progress. Through this he also shows his love for them, since he rejoices in their good beginning and urges them toward progress.

He therefore says that he gives thanks only to his God, [Col. 0052A] because they did not yet fully belong to him; for all fatherhood is from him (Ephesians 3:15). But because the whole arrangement of our salvation is indeed from God, yet through Christ, not through the Law or through any prophet, he says that he gives thanks to God, but through Christ, because the fame of their faith was bringing progress to many; thus he refers this very thing to God’s providence through Christ.

For either those who had believed were rejoicing because they had been strengthened, while the others rejoiced because they saw their leaders made their brothers; [Note: So the old edition and many manuscripts; but Gill’s edition in the margin and the Roman edition in the text, together with other manuscripts, read: “because they saw their leaders made their brothers in faith …” from the better reading.] or certainly those who had not believed could believe by the example of these people. For an inferior person readily does what he has seen a superior person do.

**(Verse 9.) For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always make mention of you in my prayers.** To persuade them of his love, he calls God as witness—God whom he serves and to whom he also makes petition for them—not by serving under the Law, but in the gospel of his Son. That is, not in what Moses, a servant, handed down, but in what the most beloved Son taught. For as far as a servant is from the master, so far is the gospel from the Law—not because the Law is evil, but because the gospel is better. He therefore serves God in the gospel of his Son, to show that it is God’s will that people believe in Christ.

**Whom I also serve. How?** “In my spirit,” he says—not in handmade circumcision, nor in new moons, nor in Sabbaths, nor in the distinction of foods, but in the spirit, that is, in the mind. Since God is spirit, he ought to be served in spirit, or rather in the soul; for one who serves him in the soul serves him from faith.

The Lord also said this to the Samaritan woman, who thought that God wished to be worshiped on the mountain, saying: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit” (John 4:23–24). Therefore those who worship must worship in spirit and truth; and it is not a place that commends prayer, but a devout mind.

This is to worship in truth: in spirit, to worship God who is spirit, and Christ, one from whom all things exist and one through whom all things exist (1 Corinthians 8:6). The Father seeks such worshipers. He therefore earnestly asks that he may remember them in his prayers, so that he may sow love in them; for he creates in them a longing for himself. Who would not love someone whom he hears remembering him? If they had gladly received teaching from those who had not been sent, under the name of Christ but with adulterated words, how much more would they desire to hear from one whom they knew to be an apostle, whose words were accompanied by power!

**(Verse 10.) Asking whether, at last, I might somehow have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come to you.** He reveals the intention of his prayer for them. He says that he asks God to come to the City for their progress, with God’s will, whose gift he proclaims. For progress is present when what must be done is done with God’s will.

He therefore prays that, for whatever reason, an opportunity might now be granted for him to come to the City, since he was occupied with preaching elsewhere; and he considers the journey prosperous if he comes by God’s will, because God’s will is provident. A prosperous journey, therefore, is one in which the labor of traveling is not undertaken in vain.

He asks that God fulfill these things by calling them to his grace. He speaks from the eagerness of his soul; for he desires them, knowing that his coming would benefit both them and himself, as he says elsewhere: “What is our joy and crown? Is it not you at the coming of the Lord?” (1 Thessalonians 2:19). For the Apostle’s fruit is greater if he wins many.

Moreover, there is greater joy if the powerful of the world are converted to God, because the more formidable the enemies, the more necessary their reconciliation. Thus an opportunity was given according to his desire, so that he was compelled to appeal to Caesar and was directed to the city of Rome for another reason, by God’s will, in order to fulfill the purpose of his desire. Finally, when he was in the shipwreck, the Lord stood beside him and said: “Do not be afraid, Paul; for just as you testified about me in Jerusalem, so also must you testify in Rome” (Acts 27:24).

**(Verse 11.) For I long to see you, so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift for strengthening you.** This strengthening requires three persons: God, who grants assent; the Apostle, who administers; and the people, who receive. He now reveals the desire of his will and what his intention was toward them. When he says, “So that I may impart to you a spiritual gift,” he indicates that they had acquired a carnal understanding, because under the name of Christ they had not obtained what Christ had taught, but what had been handed down by the Jews.

He therefore longs to come quickly, so that he may draw them away from this tradition and hand on to them a spiritual gift, in order to win them for God, making them participants in spiritual grace, so that they might be perfect in their confession and faith.

From this it may be understood that earlier he had not praised their faith, but their readiness and disposition toward Christ. For, while professing themselves Christians, they were living simply under the Law, just as it had been handed down to them. The mercy of God was given for this purpose, [Note: Some manuscripts: “so that the burdens of the Law might cease, because …”] that the Law might cease, as I have often already said; for God, taking human weakness into account, decided to save the human race by adding faith alone to the natural law.

**[Col. 0053D]** Yet what does it mean that, although he corrects them in writing and draws them away from a carnal understanding, he declares his presence necessary in order to impart spiritual grace to them, when the things he writes are spiritual? It means that otherwise words stated for one purpose are often seized for another, as happens among heretics. Therefore he desires to be present so that he may hand over the gospel teaching to them in the sense in which he writes it, lest, under the authority of his letters, error should not be removed but strengthened; for when present he could persuade them by power of what he could not persuade them of by words, so that his arrival might benefit them more.

**(Verse 12.) That is, that we may be mutually comforted among you by each other’s faith, yours and mine.** He says that he will be comforted with them if they grasp spiritual things. Although he rejoices with them over their faith, he nevertheless grieves because they were not receiving the right faith. Such was the Apostle’s disposition that he grieved over the faults of others as though they were his own.

“Therefore,” he says, “let us be comforted by one and the same faith,” so that their consolation might be one when they became of one faith in Christ; and so that the administration of spiritual grace, with the Apostle preaching the gospel, might produce this result.

**(Verse 13.) I do not think you are unaware, brothers, that I have often planned to come to you, but have been prevented until now.** He reveals his intention and desire, which he does not doubt they know through those brothers who came to the City from Jerusalem or the neighboring cities on account of their religion, such as Aquila and Priscilla, who made his desire known to the Romans.

Since he had often wished to come but had been prevented, it happened that he wrote the letter, lest, being held for a long time in an evil practice, they should not easily be corrected. He calls them brothers not only because they had been reborn, but also because among them there were at least a few who thought rightly. Hence he said: “Called as holy” (Romans 1:7).

But what does “called as holy” mean? If they are already holy, how are they called in order to be made holy? This pertains to God’s foreknowledge, because those whom God knows will be holy are already holy in his sight, and remain called.

He nevertheless says that he was prevented up to the time when the letter was given, by God, certainly, who, knowing that they were still unprepared, directed the Apostle to other cities that were already capable of receiving the truth. Although they were living under the name of the Savior, they were prevented by carnal vices from being worthy to learn spiritual things.

Finally, when Paul and Silas wished at one point to go into Bithynia, they were prevented by the Holy Spirit (Acts 16:7). Why, unless he knew that the proper disposition was still lacking? But among the Corinthians the Apostle is instructed when the Lord says: “Speak, and do not be silent, because I have many people in this city” (Acts 18:9–10).

He therefore does not say that he was prevented without reason; rather, he distinguishes the causes of the delays and exhorts these people to prepare themselves. When they heard that spiritual grace would be imparted to them, they were to make themselves worthy to receive it by abstaining from carnal vices.

**So that I may have some fruit among you as also among the other nations.** He declares that he is eager to come to them for the sake of their common benefit, so that they too may obtain the salvation of spiritual grace, confirming the profession of their faith; so that he may have fruit with God from his ministry, by which he urges them toward right faith through the example of the other nations. For a person becomes more ready to accept something handed down to him if he sees many others agreeing with it.
