**(Verse 14.) I am a debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish.** He says that he is a debtor to those whom he mentions because he was sent for this purpose: to preach to all. Through this he also signifies that all people are debtors; for confessing God the Creator, from whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, is both an owed honor and the salvation of the one who confesses him.

He uses “Greeks” for gentiles, but for those who are called Romans, whether by birth or by adoption. He calls “barbarians” those who are not Romans, whose origin is opposed to theirs, [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, together with many manuscripts, read “and are not gentiles.” The editions of Gill and Rome, with the Miché and Vallombrosa manuscripts, more correctly exclude the negation.] and who are gentiles.

He calls “wise” those who, educated in worldly disciplines, are called wise in this age, whether they are observers of the stars, or students of measures, numbers, grammar, rhetoric, or music. He shows all these people that such things are of no benefit and that they are not truly wise unless they believe in Christ.

He calls “foolish” those who follow simplicity and are unskilled in these matters. He testifies that he was sent to preach to all of them. He says nothing about the Jews, because he is the teacher of the nations. Thus he professes himself a debtor, because he received the teaching for the purpose of handing it on; and when he hands it on, he wins others.

**(Verse 15.) Thus, as far as I am concerned, I am ready to evangelize you also who are in Rome.** Although he says that he was sent to preach to all the nations, he nevertheless declares himself ready to deliver the gospel of God’s grace to the Romans, among whom the capital and seat of the Roman empire is located. For the welfare or repose of the members depends upon the head not being disturbed. He therefore desires the peace of the Romans, so that Satan may not boast greatly and so that his work may bear more abundant fruit.

**(Verse 16.) For I am not ashamed of the gospel; for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.** By saying this, he touches those from whom they had received an incorrect faith, although the apostles’ teaching was commended by power. Because what was preached seemed incredible, the signs and wonders performed by the apostles served as testimony; one ought not, therefore, to distrust what they said, since such power was present in them. For no one doubts that words yield to power, and therefore, since their opponents had no miracles [Note: The Florentine and Vindobonense manuscripts: “no power had appeared”; the Corbie manuscript: “there was no force of power.”] and their preaching lacked the power of God, he says that he is not ashamed of the gospel of God, whereas they are ashamed.

For what they had handed down was coming under criticism and was not confirmed by any testimony, and it differed from apostolic teaching. [Note: The old edition and several manuscripts: “what he had handed down to them”; the Roman edition, together with the Prat and Gembloux manuscripts, more suitably reads: “what they had handed down,” as in the text.]

It is therefore the power of God that invites people to faith and grants salvation to everyone who believes, while forgiving sins and justifying, so that one marked with the mystery of the cross cannot be held by the second death. For the preaching of Christ’s cross [Note: The Miché manuscript and some Paris editions: “is the judgment.”] is an indication that death has been conquered, as the apostle John says: “For the Son of God came for this purpose, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:9), so that no believer might be held by death, because he bears the sign that death has been conquered.

**To the Jew first, and to the Greek.** That is, to the one who is from the race of Abraham and to the one who is from the nations; for in Greek usage the term signifies a gentile, while “Jew” signifies one who is descended from Abraham.

The Jews began to be called by this name from the time of Judas Maccabaeus, who, in the cause of the disaster, resisted the sacrileges of the nations, gathered the people through trust in God, and defended his race. He was one of the sons of Aaron.

Although, therefore, he places the Jew first because of the patriarchs, he nevertheless says that the Jew likewise needs the gift of the gospel of Christ. If even the Jew is not justified except through faith in Christ Jesus, what need is there to be under the Law?

**(Verse 17.) For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith.** He says this because in the one who believes—whether Jew or Greek—the righteousness of God is revealed (Habakkuk 2:4). He calls it “the righteousness of God” because God freely justifies the ungodly through faith, without works of the Law, as he says elsewhere: “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the Law, but that which is from faith” (Philippians 3:9).

He says that the righteousness that comes from God through faith is revealed in the gospel, while God grants a person the faith by which he may be justified. For the truth and righteousness of God are shown in the one who believes and confesses: it is God’s righteousness because he gave what he promised. Therefore the believer, thinking that he has obtained what God promised through his prophets, proves God to be just and bears witness to his righteousness. [Note: The Gembloux and Prat manuscripts: “that this had been established.” Below, where the old edition and manuscripts read “what he promised concerning himself,” the Roman edition alone reads “what he promises.”]

**From faith to faith.** What else is “from faith to faith” except that there is God’s faithfulness in what he promised concerning himself, and human faith in the one who believes the one making the promise? Thus the righteousness of God is revealed from the faithfulness of God who promises to the faith of the human being who believes.

In the believer, God appears just; in the one who does not believe, he appears unjust, for the one who does not believe that God gave what he promised denies that God is truthful. He says this against the Jews, who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised.

**As it is written: “But the just shall live by faith”** (Habakkuk 2:4). For this reason he turns to the example of the prophet Habakkuk, in order to declare that it was shown long ago that the just person lives by faith, not by the Law—that is, that a human being is not justified before God by the Law but by faith. For life from faith is not this present life but the future one, because the just person lives by faith, but with God.

**(Verse 18.) For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness.** Just as the righteousness of God is revealed in the one who believes, as I mentioned above, so ungodliness and unrighteousness are revealed in the one who does not believe.

From the very structure of heaven God appears angry with them. For he created such beautiful stars so that from them it might be recognized how great and how admirable their creator is, and so that he alone might be worshiped. Hence it is written in the psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands” (Psalm 18:2).

By the natural law, therefore, he makes the human race guilty. They could have grasped this through the law of nature, since the structure of the world bears witness that God alone, its author, is to be loved, as Moses handed down in writing (Deuteronomy 6:5). But they became impious by not worshiping the Creator, and unrighteousness appears in them when, although they see, they conceal themselves from the truth, [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, with quite a few manuscripts, read: “not making one God”; Gill’s and Rome’s editions, with the remaining manuscripts, read: “not confessing one God.”] not confessing the one God.

**(Verse 19.) Because what can be known of God is manifest among them.** Knowledge of God is manifest from the structure of the world. For, so that God, who is invisible by nature, might also be known through visible things, a work was made by him that would manifest its maker through its visibility, so that the unknown might be known through what is evident. Thus it was to be believed that the one who made this work, which is impossible for others, is God of all.

**For God manifested it to them,** that is, he made a work by which he could be known through faith. [Note: So the old edition and manuscripts, except that they read “faith is recognized in them,” while the others read “recognized through faith.” The Roman edition presents the passage thus: “God manifested himself to them when he made a work by which he could be known. For his invisible things …”]

**[Col. 0057B] (Verse 20.) For his invisible attributes, understood and seen through the things that have been made, are perceived from the creation of the world.** The meaning is the same as that which he repeats, in order to teach more fully that, although the power and majesty of God cannot themselves be seen by the eyes of creation, they are perceived by understanding through the work of the world. [Note: Gill’s and Rome’s editions, with some manuscripts: “through a work”; manuscripts: “through works, the structure of the world”; Amerbach and Gill, with the remaining codices: “through the work”; several manuscripts: “through the works of the world.”]

By this reasoning, therefore, he makes guilty those who lived without the Law, both without the law of nature and without that of Moses. For by their habit of sinning they buried the law of nature and forgot its memory; and they were unwilling to receive the Law that had been given for their reform, so that they might become liable to condemnation in two ways.

**And also his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse.** So that ungodliness might have no possible excuse, he added that God’s power and eternal divinity were also known by human beings. Yet they had been dulled by a kind of stupor so as not to honor the God whom they knew both to exist and to work for their benefit. For no one doubts that the things produced for human use as the year unfolds were ordained by him.

His eternal power, therefore, is Christ, through whom he established the things that did not exist and through whom they remain. Although his person was not recognized long ago, his works were nevertheless manifest. His divinity is shown because the elements of the world persist in the work ordained by him.

**So that they are without excuse.** For a person who is convicted as guilty in many ways cannot be excused.

**(Verse 21.) Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks.** They were by no means ignorant, since they acknowledged that there is one beginning from which all things received their origin—heavenly, earthly, and underworld things—and that this one being had naturally assigned properties and functions to all things. Yet, knowing these things, they did not give thanks. He speaks of those who came before, in order to correct those who are present and those who will come.

**But they became futile in their thoughts.** [Note: Some manuscripts and Gill’s edition, with various readings: “This truly is vanity: that, knowing the truth, they should think that something else ought to be worshiped which they knew was not true; thus, concealing themselves from him, they worshiped idols. And their foolish heart was darkened …”] They became futile. Although they saw the world arranged with marvelous beauty by the one whom they recognized as its maker, they concealed themselves from him.

**And their foolish heart was darkened.** A cloud of error covered their hearts. Although, from the beautiful things he made, they ought to have honored the Creator more greatly, they became dull, abandoning him and saying that the visible things alone were sufficient for their worship.

**(Verse 22.) For, claiming to be wise, they became fools.** They consider themselves wise because they think they have investigated the principles of nature, examining the courses of the stars and the qualities of the elements, while scorning their Lord. Therefore they are fools. For if these things are to be praised, how much more their Creator!

Yet, ashamed of their neglect of God, they commonly make use of a miserable excuse, saying that one can go to God through these beings just as one reaches a king through attendants. Come now: is anyone so insane or so forgetful of his salvation that he would assign the honor due to a king to an attendant, when anyone found doing such a thing would rightly be condemned as guilty of treason?

These people do not think themselves guilty when they transfer the honor of God’s name to a creature and, abandoning the Lord, worship fellow servants, as though something greater were being reserved for God. One goes to a king through tribunes or attendants because the king is a human being and does not know to whom he ought to entrust the government. But to win the favor of God, from whom nothing is hidden—for he knows the merits of all—there is no need of an advocate, but of a devout mind. Wherever such a person speaks to him, he will answer.

**(Verse 23.) And they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man.** Their hearts were so blinded that they changed the majesty of the invisible God, whom they had recognized from the things he made, not by ascribing it to human beings, but—what is worse and an inexcusable crime—into the likeness of human beings. Thus the form of corruptible man, that is, an image of man, is called God by them; although they do not dare to honor living people with this name, they receive images of the dead into the glory of God. [Note: The old edition and almost all manuscripts: “What misery … among whom the dead can do more than the living, and the dead are preferred to the living.” The Roman edition, with some manuscripts, has the reading followed in the text.]

What dullness, what folly, to call these people wise for their own condemnation—people among whom an image has more power than the reality, and the dead are preferred to the living! For, turning away from the living God, they favor the dead, among whose number they themselves are, as it is written in the Wisdom of Solomon: “A mortal fashions a dead thing with wicked hands” (Wisdom 15:27).

**[Col. 0059A] And of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents.** [Note: So the old edition and manuscripts, except that some omit “to.” The Roman edition changed the passage thus: “By adding these things he increased their dullness, so that …”]

By adding these things he increased the punishment of their dullness, so that such people might go beyond folly and vanity. For they diminished the majesty and glory of God so greatly that they gave honor due to God to the likeness of things that are least and small. The Babylonians were the first to call God the image of a certain Bel, a dead man who is said once to have ruled over them. They also worshiped a serpent-dragon, which Daniel, the man of God, killed (Daniel 14:26), and of which they possessed an image.

The Egyptians, however, worshiped a four-footed animal that they called Apis, in the likeness of a cow. This evil was imitated by Jeroboam (2 Kings 12:28), who set up cows in Samaria for the Jews to sacrifice to. They also worshiped birds, because the pagans kept sacred ravens or crows (*Coracina sacra*). [Note: The Corbie manuscript: “Jeroboam, imitating him, established cows both in Dan and in Bethel”; the other manuscripts and editions agree with our text, except that in many manuscripts “establishing” or “he established” is read in place of “established.” Below, instead of “sacred rites of the crow” or “of the raven,” some manuscripts have, in Latin, “sacred rites of the raven.”]

The Egyptians worshiped images of all the things I have mentioned, as well as others that it is not now necessary to name. These things were done by people who considered themselves wise in the world. For, although they recognized the invisible God, they did not honor him by doing these things, nor were they able to be wise even in regard to visible things.

For it is difficult to be prudent in greater matters and not to be wise in lesser ones. [Note: So the old edition and by far the majority of manuscripts; some others read: “In greater matters he is imprudent; in lesser matters he is wise”; the Roman edition alone: “In lesser matters he is prudent; in greater matters he is not wise,” an unsuitable sense.]

**(Verse 24.) Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves.** Because, he says, they deified images and likenesses of things to the injury of God the Creator, they were handed over to be mocked. They were handed over not so that they might do what they did not want, but so that they might carry out what they desired.

And this too is God’s goodness. For it would have been fitting to subject them so that they might do what they did not want and be tormented, since even what is good becomes bitter and evil if it is done against one’s will. These people, however, turning away from God, were handed over to the devil.

To hand over means to permit, not to incite or implant, so that the things they had conceived in their desires might be completed in action with the devil’s assistance; for they could not have such a good thought.

Therefore they were handed over to impurity, so that they might dishonor their bodies in themselves. In recalling what has already been said, he also indicates the evils of the present time: for they are still being handed over, so that they dishonor their bodies. People of that origin still exist who are said to dishonor their bodies with one another. Although the crime lies in the soul’s thought, the bodies are said to be dishonored; why else, unless the stain upon the body is evidence of sin in the soul? For when the body is defiled, no one doubts that the sin belongs to the soul.

**(Verse 25.)** They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

“They exchanged the truth of God for a lie”: that is, they gave the name of God, who is true, to those who are not gods. Taking away from stones, wood, and other metals what they really are, they give them what they are not; and this is to change the truth into falsehood. For they are no longer called stone or wood, but God. This is to serve the creature rather than the Creator. They do not deny God, but serve the creature; and by this they are not excused but rather accused, because, though they recognize God, they do not honor him.

[Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Remiremont, Colbert [Col. 0059D], and Gill present what follows, with various readings, as follows: “They give them what they are not, so that the truth of God becomes a lie, when a stone is called God; when a crafted object strikes the true God; so that, because they suppose false and true to have a common name, the true God is regarded in the same way as the false. This is to change the true into the false. Thus they served the creature rather than the Creator. For some do not deny God, but serve the creature; and, in order that they might appear to worship these things worthily, they placed upon them the honor due to God, so that the worship of these things might be an insult to God. Therefore this contributes to their punishment, because, although they recognized …”]

Who is blessed forever. Amen—that is, truly so. God is called “blessed forever” because God remains; but he grants the gods of the nations honor only for the duration of their impiety. Therefore that honor is not true. In God, however, truth remains. Elsewhere he assigns this blessing to the Son of God, saying among other things: “From them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 9:5). Or both statements refer to Christ; or he said of the Son the same things that he said of the Father.

**(Verse 26.)** Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural intercourse for intercourse that is contrary to nature.

He testifies that, because God was angry on account of idolatry, this came upon the human race: that a woman should desire a woman for shameful intercourse. Some interpret this differently, failing to perceive the force of the statement. For what does it mean to exchange natural intercourse for intercourse that is contrary to nature, [Col. 0060D] unless it means to use, once the permitted use has been set aside, some other use, so that one and the same bodily part of each person of either sex is put to a different use from that which has been permitted?

[Note: Thus the old edition and more manuscripts; the Roman edition differs only in altering the opening words to: “unless it means to use natural and permitted intercourse in another way.” Some manuscripts abbreviate the whole passage as follows: “unless, once the permitted use has been removed, she presents herself for intercourse in another way.”]

For if it is the bodily part they suppose, how have they exchanged the use of nature, when nature has not granted such a use? He had already said above that they were handed over to impurity, but he had not yet shown the character of the deed of impurity itself; therefore he now explains it:

**(Verse 27.)** Likewise, the males too, abandoning natural intercourse with the female, burned with desire for one another, males committing shameful acts with males.

Now he has made clear how what he previously said about women is to be understood. When he added, “Likewise the males,” saying that “they burned with desire for one another,” he openly displayed the sin of the women. Indeed, he did not say of the men that they exchanged natural intercourse with one another, because such intercourse has not been granted to that bodily part; rather, he said this of the women. And what wonder is it, since even today such women are found, so that just as this was invented by men, so also that has been invented by women? Indeed, women accuse one another, and men likewise. It is therefore clear that those who had already exchanged the truth of God for a lie also exchanged natural intercourse for intercourse by which they were dishonored, becoming liable to the second death through the deed.

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “abandoning natural female intercourse, they were inflamed with desire for one another.”]

For Satan cannot give another law; he has nothing of his own. He turns what has been permitted and lawful into another order, so that, when things are done differently from how they were permitted, they become sin.

[Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads: “And receiving reciprocal recompense …” It explains this as: “He calls this reciprocal recompense …”; some others and the editions read: “And recompense”; but the reading found in the context is best of all.]

And receiving in themselves the recompense that was due for their error. He says that this recompense is the result of their contempt for God—that is, shame and defilement; for this is the first cause of the sin. What is worse, what is more destructive, than this sin?

[Note: The same codex reads: “What is worse than this sin, which, with the devil deceiving him, kills the human being who has become subject to it? And just as …”]

For as idolatry is an utterly impious and most serious offense, so its recompense is a dreadful and most filthy passion.

**(Verse 28.)** And just as they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper.

Because of the errors of images, they were handed over to perform shameful acts with one another, as has already been said. And because they supposed that these acts would go unpunished, judging God unconcerned and therefore to be disregarded, this was added: that, becoming ever more and more dull-witted, they would grow readier to admit every evil, believing that God would not punish deeds which they themselves could not doubt were displeasing to human beings. He now lists all the evils added to them, so that, even in this way, they might turn back to natural understanding and recognize that these things had come upon them because God was angry.

**[Col. 0062A] (Verses 29–30.)** “Filled,” he says, “with every kind of iniquity.” Here he has spoken summarily and then sets out the members of iniquity:

“Malice, sexual immorality,” he says, “greed, wickedness; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insulting, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil.”

He called malice the head of iniquity, and assigned fornication and greed as its works. Fornication includes adultery; if he had said “adultery,” he might have seemed to excuse fornication, as do the Roman laws. Therefore he named the lesser offense, so that the greater might be understood as something that could not be believed to go unpunished.

[Note: The old edition and several manuscripts read: “could not be believed.” They continue: “And the remaining things, which are evident: greed, wickedness, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity, whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insulting, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents. What arrogance!” The manuscript of Corbie adds after “disobedient to parents”: “foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy; although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them. The head of iniquity,” and the rest as above. We have retained in the Roman edition the various readings from Gill that have now been incorporated into the text.]

Then he added “wickedness,” whose inclination produces envy and murder, strife and deceit. After this he added “malignity,” which gives birth to whispering and slander. And because these things cannot fail to displease God, he said: “hateful to God.” And because they do not please human beings either, he said: “insulting, proud, arrogant, inventors”—that is, authors—“of evil.”

Evil, therefore, does not always exist. These people, however, having become imitators of their father the devil, invented the evil of idolatry, through which all vices were born in the world, along with the greatest destruction. For although the devil, whom Scripture testifies to have sinned from the beginning (1 John 3:8), is devoted to tyrannical presumption, he nevertheless did not dare openly to claim this by saying, “I am God.” Indeed, among other things he said to the Lord: “All these things have been handed over to me” (Luke 4:6); he did not say: “They come from me,” or “They are mine.” And in the Book of Job he demands that power be granted to him.

[Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads “requests.” And in the prophet Zechariah he thinks himself to be contradicting the priest, not claiming power for himself. Therefore …]

For this reason these people are worse: they attribute divinity not only to the elements but also to crafted objects.

**(Verse 31.)** Disobedient to parents.

How great was the arrogance with which they were seized, [Col. 0062C] that they did not even recognize as worthy of honor their parents, whom they had as the authors of their birth and who rejoiced that they had been born! Yet they despised those through whom they had begun to exist. This is to be without understanding and without affection—though they did have natural affection toward them, but not the affection of God.

[Note: The variants in Gill, together with those in the manuscripts of Corbie and Remiremont, largely agree at the end of the chapter. The sequence we present is nevertheless preferable and more correct: “So that they did not even recognize that their parents were to be honored; therefore he called them foolish and disorderly, as having affection neither for God nor for human beings. Hence they were also without mercy. For if someone is cruel toward his own, how much more toward strangers! Thus, having become rebellious in all these matters, and knowing the justice of God, they did not wish to take to heart that those who do such things are worthy of death; nor did they wish to realize that even those who, though they do not perform them, consent to those who do them are not exempt from death. Since the latter neither shudder at nor rebuke them, the former advance into worse things. For when someone sees himself honored by those who are not such, he grows in wickedness and boasts that he is such a person; therefore it is fitting that both groups be punished with the same penalty. Yet every conscience knows that God’s justice has been entrusted to the world; for they secretly do what ought to be punished. How, then, can they believe that these things will go unpunished, which they do not dare to do publicly?” The manuscripts of Thuanus and Corbie agree with this as far as “they did not wish to take to heart”; the rest they present as in the text.]

Although these people recognized God’s justice through the law of nature—for they knew that these things displeased God, but did not wish to take that knowledge to heart—[Col. 0063A] “because those who do such things are worthy of death,” they knew God’s justice so thoroughly that they did not deny that all the things they did were deserving of punishment and death. And not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them. For consent is participation.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and old edition, except that they preface the passage with: “Foolish, disorderly, without affection, without mercy.” Since these words occur in the manuscripts of Florence, Corbie, Vindobonensis, and the Roman edition, we have removed them. We have nevertheless retained “So thoroughly … worthy of death,” though these words are absent from those three codices and, in the Roman edition, after other material has been cut, are placed after the same scriptural text, following “Who, having known the justice of God.”]

**(Verse 32.)** Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death; and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.

All these evils form the body of sinners, into whose power they have been delivered, so that they do what deserves punishment. For this cause of evils began among the Sodomites through an offense against God, as was said above, and has extended its branches through almost every part of the world, proclaiming the wrath of God as the cause of idolatry. Idolatry is the first element of error and impiety, which he condemns first, so that, once this has been corrected, the vices of conduct may easily be corrected as well. For when the seed of malice has been removed, the fruits of wickedness will wither; a tree whose roots have been cut off does not produce fruit.

[Note: Some manuscripts add to “roots” the words: “Concerning those who do these things and contradict them”; one has: “Woe to them,” and so on. Likewise, below, after “consent to those who do them,” they append: “Concerning those who consent to those who do them”—one manuscript reading: “Woe to those who consent to those who do them.” These headings, however, were carelessly transferred by scribes from the margins into the text.]

36 For this reason Moses too recorded what happened at Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24 and following), and did not conceal their destruction, so that he might instill fear and thereby prevent this offense. Therefore this vice and pollution of a dishonored life is not admitted by one who holds God in his mind.

There are some who do not consider themselves guilty if they do not perform the evil deeds themselves but consent to those who do them. To consent is to remain silent when one is able to rebuke, or, when hearing such stories, to flatter the speaker. For the impure and malicious person, knowing that what he does is not unknown and that he is not avoided, but is even honored, boasts that he may perhaps be such a person; nor can he be put to shame in these matters when he sees that those who are not such favor and indulge him. In this way they become those who provide fuel for the offenses of others; and therefore it is right that they be held guilty of the same crime.

There are again others who not only do evil but also consent to those who do it, so that they not only commit evil themselves but also approve those who commit it. Their wickedness is therefore doubled. For those who do evil yet oppose those who do it are not equally wicked; knowing the deeds to be criminal, they do not defend them.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For, while doing wicked deeds, they condemn them.”]

But those are utterly wicked who both do evil and consent to those who do it, so that they neither fear God but desire evils to increase. For this reason they do not punish such things, in order to persuade others that they need not be avoided.

**CHAPTER II**

**(Verse 1.)** Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge.

Since he showed that the person who does evil and the person who consents to those who do it are worthy of death, lest the one who does evil but does not consent to those who do it should think that he could excuse himself, he teaches that such a person will also be inexcusable. For it is not just that he should be granted impunity, since through hypocrisy he presents himself as not being such a person, while he is found to be worse. He deceives others so that, although he ought to be punished, he may appear worthy of honor.

**(Verse 2.)** We know, however, that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things.

That is, we do not doubt that God will judge such people according to truth, since we ourselves judge them. For if they displease us, how much more will they displease God, who is more just and is jealous for his work? Therefore, when he says that God will judge them according to truth, he inspires terror: the very one whom these faithless people call unconcerned will judge the wicked according to truth—that is, he will most truly repay each person according to his measure and will spare no one.

**(Verse 3.)** Do you suppose this, O human being who judges those who do such things and yet does them yourself, that you will escape God’s judgment?

[Note: The manuscript of Corbie reads: “He does not wish him to hope for impunity in this matter, because it is unjust that those to whom the examination and authority to judge such evils or sexual offenses have been given should escape, when they themselves are such people. For even if,” he says, “there is presently no one to judge you, you will nevertheless not escape God’s judgment in the future.”]

That is: because the authority to judge such evils and sexual offenses has been entrusted to you, do you suppose that, although you commit the same things and there is presently no one to judge you, you will escape God’s judgment? Certainly not. For even if you have escaped God’s judgment in this world—since all authority and judgment come from him—you will not escape it in the future. God himself will judge, and before him flattery and partiality cease.

Or, if anyone thinks it just that such a person should be free from punishment, let him say so. But if it is just that he should not escape, let him believe that God will judge, so that what he judges to be just may be true and be fulfilled, and so that he may confess that God, the Creator of the world, wisely and attentively examines the merits of his work. For if he made it and then neglects it, he is called a bad craftsman, because by what he neglects he shows that the things he made were not good. But since it cannot be denied that he made good things—for it is unworthy and implausible that the good should have made evil—he must necessarily be said to care for them. It will be an insult and an accusation against him if he is presented as neglecting the good things he made, especially since life itself is sustained by his will and providence through the ministry of the elements, as the Lord himself says: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). Therefore, will the one who provides such care not preserve what he has made, rewarding those who love him and condemning those who despise him?

**(Verse 4.)** Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?

He says this so that no one may now suppose that he has escaped because God’s goodness allows him to remain in sin for a long time, nor may he despise God’s patience as though God did not care about human affairs. Rather, let him understand that God delays judgment because judgment has not been promised for this life, so that in the life to come he may repent of not having believed that God would judge.

[Note: The manuscripts of Remiremont, Corbie, Thuanus, and Corbie read: “He did not believe that, in order to display the terror of his future judgment and to show that his patience must not be despised, he said: ‘I have been silent; shall I always be silent?’ Such a person, therefore, placed in judgment, will repent without benefit, seeing God’s judgment, whose future reality he denied; nor will he have the shame to plead for mercy, because he thought God’s long-suffering goodness worthy of ridicule. It is necessary …”]

Placed in punishment, he will repent without benefit, because he did not believe in God’s judgment, which he now sees to be true. For the person whom the long-suffering of God’s patience did not reform must necessarily be corrected more harshly—or rather, be tormented by everlasting punishments. He speaks with the utmost severity, knowing that a malicious mind cannot easily be recalled from vices except by fear.

**(Verses 5–6.)** But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works.

Hoping that his sins will go unpunished, the sinner not only persists, remaining unconverted and intractable, but sins even more harshly, secure in the belief that no vengeance will come. He has an impenitent heart and does not know that he is storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. For the person whom God’s long patience has not reformed—who not only refused to correct himself but, adding further contempt, increased his sins—must necessarily be punished with a more severe penalty, indeed tormented by everlasting flames.

The day of wrath is the day for sinners on which they will be punished.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Therefore wrath belongs to those who have fallen, because …” In the following verse, the manuscripts of Remiremont and Corbie read: “For what is now denied as future will be made manifest, so that even against their will they may acknowledge God’s just judgment, seeing that each person is repaid according to his works. To those indeed who according to patience …”]

Wrath belongs to them because they will experience punishment on the day of the revelation of God’s just judgment. For what is now denied as future will be revealed—that is, recognized—and therefore, when what is believed not to exist is displayed, it is revealed. It is displayed to those who deny it, although it is manifest to believers, so that even against their will they may confess God’s just judgment, when he repays each person according to his works. Will they not admit that these things are justly done when they see evil deeds avenged in turn?

[Col. 0065C] **(Verse 7.)** To those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption—eternal life.

Since God’s judgment has been proclaimed just, he has also declared what will be granted to the good. He speaks of those who know that God’s patience is prolonged partly for correction and partly for the greater punishment of those who do not correct themselves; repenting of their former deeds, they live well, relying on the confidence of faith, so that, by remaining here too long, they do not suffer the loss of the life that has been promised.

Therefore he will give them glory and honor. And lest this seem insufficiently great in comparison with the present life, since even here some appear glorious and honored, he added: “And incorruption,” so that another glory and another honor might be understood, when incorruption accompanies them as well. In the present life, honor and glory are frequently lost, because both the one who gives and what is given, as well as the one who receives, are corruptible. On the day of God’s judgment, however, incorruptible honor and glory will be given, so that they may be entirely eternal; for their very substance will be glorified through a certain transformation of their merits.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “the whole eternal life.” It is better in others to omit “life.” Some codices likewise have “will glory” instead of “will be glorified.”]

Those, then, seek eternal life who are not merely people of a good profession but also of a good life.

**(Verse 8.)** But to those who are contentious and who distrust the truth but obey iniquity: wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress—that is, repeated distress.

Distrusting the future judgment of God through Christ, and therefore despising his patience as well, they contend in order to nullify that judgment, although it is true and steadfast. They believe in iniquity; for it is iniquity to deny what God foretold would happen.

He therefore assigned three other things appropriate to unbelief, saying: “Wrath and indignation, and distress.” Wrath does not belong to the one who judges but to the one who is judged, when he is found guilty. God is said to become angry so that he may be believed to be about to avenge; for God’s nature is free from such passions. And so that he might be believed not only to become angry but also to avenge, he added: “And indignation.” By adding indignation to wrath, he signifies that God will avenge the injury done to him. Distresses are the sufferings by which the condemned person, confined by the sentence, will be tormented in punishment.

**(Verse 9.)** Tribulation and distress upon every soul of the human being who does evil.

In this expression he signifies not only deeds but also the profession of faithlessness. He is speaking of the unbeliever; and therefore he said “upon the soul,” so that you may understand spiritual rather than bodily punishment, because the soul will be confined by invisible punishments.

The Jew first, and the Greek.

He always places the Jew first because of the privilege of the fathers, so that he may either be crowned first or condemned first. The believer is more honored on account of Abraham, whereas the unbeliever must be treated more severely because he rejected the gift promised to the fathers.

**(Verse 10.)** But glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, for the Jew first and for the Greek.

Just as he assigned three punishments to unbelievers, so he assigned three magnificent rewards to the faithful, so that they might possess a double honor, as sons of God; that glory might correspond to transformation; and peace, because those who live well will be at rest in the future, disturbed by no turmoil. For every person who abstains from what is opposed to him has peace before the Judge.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “so that they may possess what is genuine,” or “genuine honor.” Immediately afterward, where the old edition and manuscripts read: “glory for transformation, but peace because …,” some have: “peace and honor because …”; the Roman edition restored: “glory in transformation, but peace because …”]

**(Verse 11.)** For there is no partiality with God.

Since he showed that neither the Jew nor the Greek is despised by God, provided that he believes in Christ, but that the righteousness of faith is credited to both, so likewise unbelievers are equally guilty. Circumcision without faith will be more harmful, and uncircumcision through faith will be beneficial. Thus he teaches that God is not partial. He does not follow the privilege of ancestry by receiving the unbeliever because of his fathers, nor does he reject the believer because of the unworthiness of his parents; rather, he either rewards or condemns each person according to his own merit.

**(Verse 12.)** For whoever sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law.

How can anyone sin without the law, when all of us alike are subject to the natural law? He is speaking of the law of Moses, to which the Jews are subject while they do not believe; and the Gentiles also, but they have long since refused to attach themselves to it. Unbelieving Gentiles are therefore guilty in two ways: they neither assented to the law given through Moses nor received the grace of Christ; therefore it is fitting that they perish.

Accordingly, just as the one who sins without the Law will perish, so also the one who keeps the Law without the Law will be justified. For the person who naturally keeps righteousness is a guardian of the law. Since the law is not imposed on the righteous but on the unrighteous (1 Timothy 1:9), the one who does not sin is a friend of the law. Only faith is lacking to him, through which he may become perfect; for abstaining from what is opposed to God will benefit him nothing unless he receives faith in God, so that he may be just in both respects: the former is a righteousness belonging to time, the latter to eternity.

And whoever sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “will be judged.” Just as Gentiles who keep the law of nature will nevertheless perish unless they receive the faith of Christ—for confessing the one God is a greater matter than abstaining from other sins, since the former concerns God and the latter concerns us—so Jews living under the Law will be judged when accused by the Law, because they do not receive Christ promised in the Law. And, if you ask, the pain is greater for the Gentiles; for it is worse to lose a promise than not to receive what one did not hope for.]

Because the Jews have the Law, in which salvation was promised to them, and because they did not believe or receive the promise, they will be judged by the Law under which they lived. It will itself accuse them, and they will pay the penalty. For the case of the Jews is almost more serious in their own regard than that of the Gentiles. Just as believers are preferred, so when they distrust, they are found to be worse. The one who loses what he possessed is more displeasing than the one who could not obtain what he never hoped for.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “The former did not enter the kingdom.”]

The former did not enter the royal palace; the latter was sent outside.

**(Verse 13.)** For it is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law will be justified.

He says this because those who merely hear the Law are not righteous, but those who believe in Christ, whom the same Law promised. This is what it means to do the Law. Anyone who does not believe the Law does not do the Law, since he does not receive the one to whom the Law bears witness. But the person who does not appear to belong to the Law because he is uncircumcised in the flesh, yet believes in Christ, is said to have done the Law. And the one who says that he is in the Law—that is, the Jew—is a hearer of the Law, not a doer, because he does not believe in Christ written about in the Law, as Philip said to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, whom Moses and the prophets wrote about in the Law” (John 1:45).

[Note: The manuscript of Corbie and some others read: “Because he does not transfer what is said into his mind, he does not become a doer of the Law but a hearer; for he does not believe …”]

39 **(Verse 14.)** For when Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do the things of the Law …

In another place he calls Christians “Gentiles”: “For I speak to you Gentiles” (Colossians 2:16). They are uncircumcised and do not observe new moons, the Sabbath, or the dietary law, yet, guided by nature, they believe in God and Christ—that is, in the Father and the Son. For this is what it means to keep the Law: to acknowledge the God of the Law. The first part of wisdom is to fear God the Father, from whom all things are; and the Lord Jesus, his Son, through whom all things are. Nature itself therefore recognizes its Creator by its own judgment, not through the Law but through natural reason; for the work perceives the craftsman within itself.

**(Verse 15.)** They show that the work of the Law is written in their hearts, although they do not have the Law; they are a law to themselves.

The meaning is the same: because, guided by nature, they believe, they show the work of the Law not through the letter but through conscience. The work of the Law is faith. When they display it to God through their words, they show by natural judgment that they themselves are a law to themselves, because they freely do what the Law commands when they believe in Christ.

Their conscience also bears witness to them.

With their inner conscience as witness, they believe, because they are conscious that what they believe is fitting for them. It is fitting for a creature to believe in and worship its Creator; nor is it absurd that a servant should recognize his Lord.

**(Verse 16.)** Their thoughts alternately accusing or even defending one another on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Since he said that the unbelieving Jews would be judged through the Law—for the Law will accuse them, since it promised them Christ, whom they refused to receive when he came—and that the Gentiles, who certainly do not have the Law, will be judged through conscience if they refuse to believe, the meaning is as follows.

First, believing Gentiles will be the accusers of unbelieving Gentiles, just as the Lord says concerning his disciples to the unbelieving Jews: “They will be your judges” (Matthew 12:27). The faith of the apostles, who were themselves Jews but believed while the others distrusted, will judge the Jews’ faithlessness.

Then the Gentiles will be accused by their own thoughts if, having been moved to recognize the Creator’s faith and power, they refuse to believe. Or, if they fail to consider these matters because of some stupefaction and therefore do not believe the Lord’s words and deeds, they may defend themselves by their conscience on the day of judgment, claiming that they did not think they ought to believe; and they will be judged not as malicious but as ignorant. Nevertheless, they will not be without punishment, because such ignorance is not permitted.

By “Gentiles” he signifies both believers and unbelievers. Above he speaks of believing Gentiles; afterward he also speaks of those Gentiles who do not believe. Thus, just as believers are praised through their conscience, so unbelievers are accused through their conscience. Although the one who did not believe may seem to himself not to be guilty because he was unable to consider the matter within himself, he is nevertheless convicted by reason, because he did not persuade himself that this was true, even though he had seen it confirmed by signs of power and had seen many follow it.

I think the passage may also be understood in this way, if it is believed that he spoke throughout about believing Gentiles, because he says: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Corinthians 5:12); and: “Whoever has not believed,” he says, “has already been judged” (John 3:18); and: “The wicked do not rise in the judgment” (Psalm 1:5). For those who sin without the Law will also perish without the Law; consequently, they will not be able to stand before the tribunal of Christ and give an account, because, once raised, they will be led to Gehenna.

Those whom he says will accuse or defend one another through their thoughts on the day of God’s judgment are Christians who dissent from the Catholic truth, holding different views about Christ or about the meaning of the Law within the Church’s tradition—whether Cataphrygians, Novatians, Donatists, or other heretics. Their thoughts will accuse one another on the day of judgment. If someone understood the Catholic doctrine to be true but refused to follow it lest he appear corrected, being ashamed to depart from what he had held for a long time, he will be accused on the day of judgment by his own thought.

For there are two thoughts in a person that accuse one another: a good one and an evil one. The good thought accuses the evil because it resisted the truth; the evil thought in turn accuses the good because it did not follow what it recognized. Thus the person who thought that the Catholic Church was good and true, yet remained in heresy or schism, is made guilty.

But his thoughts will defend one another if he has always thought that what he followed was useful. For he will say: “I always thought in my mind that what I followed was useful; this was my faith.” His case will be lighter, although he must still be corrected, because his conscience will not accuse him on the day of judgment.

In this way the hidden things of human beings will be judged on the day of God’s judgment through Jesus Christ our Lord.

**(Verse 17.)** But if you are called a Jew. The designation “Jew” derives from the prerogative of their ancestors, since they are called Israelites. Yet, if we wish to comprehend everything that pertains to the matter, we must recognize that the designation “Jew” is signified in a threefold way. First, because they are children of Abraham, who, through the merit of his faith, was appointed father of all the nations. Second, because of Jacob, who was called Israel for the sake of increasing faith; for the dignity begun in the father is ennobled in his children. Third, not principally because of Judah, but because of Christ: since he arose from Judah according to the flesh, they are called Jews, because in Judah was signified what was to come in Christ. For it is said: “Judah shall be your leader” (Judg. XX, 18), and: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX, 8). This praise is not shown to have been given to Judah, but to Christ, whom all those daily praise whom he has deigned to call his brothers. For he himself said to the women: “Go and tell my brothers that I am going before you into Galilee” (Matt. XXVIII, 7). Who indeed would not praise him, by whose beneficence he lives? Thus the Apostle wished everything to be understood under this signification, which is later in number but more perfect in merit: namely, that the Jews, not understanding this, defend for themselves the name of the carnal Judah.

[Note: Thus read most manuscripts; but some others, together with the old edition, read “to be denoted by a threefold kind”; the Roman edition reads: “… derived.”]

**(Verse 18.)** And you rest upon the Law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve what is more useful, being instructed by the Law. He does not wish it to appear a very great thing if a Jew believes, since he is instructed by the Law; but it is exceedingly dangerous if he does not believe, for he has the Law as his guide. Yet the merit of the Fathers causes the believer to be preferred; for although someone may flourish by himself, he is nevertheless ashamed in his own people.

**(Verses 19, 20.)** And you are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light for those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, possessing in the Law the embodiment of knowledge and truth. These things are true, because the instruction of the Law is to educate the ignorant and subject the profane to God; or, through the promise made in the Law, to summon the impious from the worship of idolatry to confidence in a better hope. Therefore the teacher of the Law rightly glories in these things, because he hands down the embodiment of truth. But if he does not receive the one whom the Law promised, he glories in the Law in vain, doing it an injury while rejecting Christ, who was promised in the Law. He will then no longer be an instructor of the foolish, or a teacher of infants, or a light for those who are in darkness, but the guide of all these toward destruction.

**(Verse 21.)** Therefore, you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? That is: you who accuse the Gentiles of being without the Law and without God do not accuse yourself. For, by distrusting Christ promised in the Law, you are found in the very things which you condemn.

**(Verse 22.)** You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? For you do what you preach ought not to be done. While you steal Christ’s faith through a false interpretation, you deny our Christ, who was promised in the Law.

[Note: The Roman edition adds: “That is, when you deny Christ promised in the Law, you steal away his faith through a bad interpretation; for you do what you preach ought not to be done.”]

You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? (II Cor. II, 17). You adulterate the Law when you remove Christ’s truth and substitute a lie. Hence he says elsewhere: “Adulterers of the word of God.”

[Col. 0070D] You who abominate idols, do you commit sacrilege? You are sacrilegious when you deny Christ, whom the Law and the prophetic word signify to be God. For Isaiah says: “Because in you is God, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it: God of Israel, the Savior” (Isa. XLV, 14). Surely the Jews were not speaking of God the Father when they said, “For you are God, and we did not know it,” since the whole Law proclaims the authority of God the Father, from whom all things are? But because the Son of God had indeed always appeared, although it was hidden who he was, when he is recognized after the resurrection it is said to him in confession: “For you are God, and we did not know it.” He who in the Law was thought to be merely an angel and the commander of the Lord’s army is, once understood to be the Son of God, addressed with thanksgiving: “For you are God, and we did not know it.” Through this, therefore, he signifies that it was he who had indeed appeared to the patriarchs as God and was afterward incarnate, but had not been understood by everyone.

[Note: After the word “patriarchs,” the Roman edition had deleted “into God.” Where the same edition, along with the old edition and several manuscripts, reads “understood by men,” many manuscripts more correctly read “understood by everyone.”]

**(Verse 23.)** You who glory in the Law dishonor God through transgressing the Law. You are a transgressor of the Law when you pass over the meaning of the Law, which concerns Christ’s incarnation and divinity; and you dishonor God when you do not receive his testimony concerning his Son. For he himself said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III, 17).

[Col. 0071B] **(Verse 24.)** For “the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written” (Isa. LII, 5). The prophet Isaiah said this because the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles when they failed to understand that the Jews, handed over to them because of their offenses, had been punished; instead, they gave glory to their idols, as though they had conquered the God of the Jews through the Jews. In the same way, in the time of the Apostles the name of God was blasphemed in Christ, because by denying Christ to be God the Jews blasphemed the Father also, as the Lord says: “Whoever receives me does not receive me, but him who sent me” (Luke IX, 48). Therefore it was blasphemed among the Gentiles because, when the Gentiles were believing, the Jews strove to persuade them that Christ, as God, ought not to be believed; so that the Gentiles’ blasphemy proceeded from the Jews, or from the adherents of Photinus.

**(Verse 25.)** Circumcision indeed profits, if you observe the Law. One might argue conversely: If circumcision profits, why is it set aside? But it profits only if you observe the Law. Circumcision must therefore be retained, and, in order that it may profit, the Law must be kept. What, then, prohibited what it showed could profit if the Law were observed? It therefore appears to have been wrongly prohibited, since it is said not to be displeasing in itself but to be frustrated through another’s negligence.

But if you are a transgressor of the Law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. This is what he says: if the Law has not been kept, a Jew becomes a Gentile. Yet he used “circumcision” for the ancestral status of Abraham, because circumcision came from Abraham; for he could not build up what he had destroyed. He says this to teach that belonging by descent to Abraham profits only if the Law is observed—that is, if one believes in Christ, who was promised to Abraham—because those justified through faith possess their own merit and are exalted by the honor of the Fathers. For all salvation in the Law concerns Christ. Therefore the one who believes in Christ keeps the Law; but if he does not believe, he is a transgressor of the Law, because he does not receive Christ, whom the Law proclaimed as coming for justification, although the Law itself could not give justification. Nor will it profit him to be called a son of Abraham, because, according to merit, he is a son of Abraham who follows the faith through which Abraham became worthy of God. Hence he says: “Your circumcision has become uncircumcision”—that is, you have become like a Gentile because you do not believe in him who, in the sign of circumcision, was promised to Abraham as a son.

[Note: The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “who was promised to Abraham in the sign of circumcision.”]

**(Verse 26.)** Therefore, if uncircumcision keeps the ordinances of the Law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? The righteousness of the Law is Christian faith, as he says elsewhere: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). It is therefore evident that if a Gentile believes in Christ, he becomes a son of Abraham, who is the father of faith.

**(Verse 27.)** And uncircumcision, which is so by nature, fulfilling the Law, will judge you who, through the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the Law. The believing Gentile, guided by nature, believes in Christ and condemns the Jew, to whom the Law had promised Christ but who refused to believe in him when he came. How great, then, is the glory of which the Gentile is worthy, who through nature alone recognized the author, as the Apostle Peter says: “But you killed the author of life” (Acts III, 15). So much more must the Jew be punished, who recognized Christ as author neither through nature nor through the Law.

**(Verses 28, 29.)** For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter. His praise is not from human beings but from God.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “It is not obscure that circumcision of the flesh has no praise.”]

It is clear that he denies circumcision of the flesh praise before God—for Abraham was not justified because he was circumcised, but because he believed; only afterward was he circumcised—and that he affirms circumcision of the heart to be praiseworthy before God. To circumcise the heart is to cut away error and recognize the Creator. And because circumcision of the heart was to come, Moses was the first to say: “Circumcise the hardness of your heart” (Deut. X, 16). Jeremiah likewise says: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Jer. IV, 4). He said this to the Jews who followed idols; for there is a veil around the heart, which the person who turns to God circumcises. Faith removes the cloud of error and grants perfect knowledge of God in the mystery of the Trinity, which had been unknown throughout the ages.

The praise of this circumcision, therefore, comes from God and is hidden from human beings; for it is the merit of the heart that God regards, not of the flesh. The praise of the Jews, however, comes from human beings, for they glory in the circumcision of the flesh because it comes from the Fathers.

[Note: The same edition, together with one or two manuscripts, adds: “Hence, among other things, he says in another Epistle…”]

Hence, among other things, he says: “And their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. III, 19)—that is, those who consider circumcision of the flesh a glory. For the person who glories in the flesh sets his mind on earthly things; but the person who glories in the Spirit has praise from God, for he is believed through the Spirit, not through the flesh.

## CHAPTER III

**(Verses 1 and 2.)** What advantage, then, has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them. Although there are many things that pertain to the honor and merit of Abraham’s offspring, he mentions this one thing openly: that their greatest praise is that they were judged worthy to receive the Law, through which they might learn to distinguish right from wrong. Once this has been established, the nature of the other matters can be understood.

But since he shows that testimony of ancestry profits carnal Jews—that is, unbelievers—nothing, lest he seem to have treated all Jews, including believers, as though they were alike, he teaches that it is greatly beneficial to believing Jews because they are children of Abraham. To them the oracles of God were entrusted: they receive the Law, which had grown obsolete because of human sins, as though it had been possible to sin against God with impunity, restored through the merit of the Fathers; and they are called the people of God. Egypt, too, is struck with various plagues because of the injuries it inflicted upon them; they are fed with heavenly bread; they are a terror to all the nations, as Rahab the prostitute bears witness: to them Christ the Savior was also promised for sanctification (Josh. II, 9 ff.). Therefore he says that the Jew has much advantage in every way, because they are children of Abraham; for they are preferred to the nations—but those who believe.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “that is, both believing and unbelieving.” Other editions and manuscripts rightly have the text as here, since it includes believers as well.]

**(Verse 3.)** For what if some of them did not believe? Will their unbelief abolish the faithfulness of God? Certainly not.

[Note: The Roman edition adds: “Certainly not, as though he were saying: Because some did not wish to believe what God promised the faithful…” It does not read “since…” as in some versions. Gill, among various readings, has: “He says this because believing Jews are not to be prejudiced, so that they should be considered unworthy to receive what God promised to the others who distrusted him, since the promise was made in such a way that his gift would benefit those who believe.”]

He does not say that, because some Jews did not wish to believe what God promised to the children of Abraham, the other Jews would therefore be prejudiced, so that they would be considered unworthy to receive what God promised the faithful; for the promise was made in such a way that it would benefit those who believe. Therefore God, not angered by the faithlessness of those Jews, will give the other believers the eternal life that he promised would come through faith in Christ, because those who did not believe made themselves unworthy, without prejudicing the others. By these statements he commends believing Jews, since the fact that many of them did not wish to believe does them no harm.

**(Verse 4.)** For God is truthful, but every human being is a liar, as it is written: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L, 6).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and several others, as well as Dionysius according to Gill, add “as it is written.” They continue: “Therefore, because God is truthful, he gives what he promised; but it belongs to human beings to deceive, since time and the weakness of nature make them changeable, because they do not possess foreknowledge. God, however, before whom nothing is future, remains immutable, as he says: ‘I am, and I will not change.’ He therefore calls every human being a liar, and this is true; for a nature that is deceived may not improperly be called lying. Thus a person is sometimes a liar deliberately, sometimes through error. This, therefore, is not to be expected of God, who is both truthful and benevolent, so that he may fulfill what he promised. He confirms this also by a prophetic oracle, saying, as it is written: ‘So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.’ To this verse the Dionysian and Remigian codices append: ‘God promised to be just, and the prophetic word testifies by its words; nor is his faithfulness diminished by anyone’s faithlessness, but by giving he prevails. The faithless deny this because they do not believe that he will give. He will therefore give what he is judged not to give, so that by doing what they deny he will do, he may prevail. Then impiety will be conquered, since, by refusing to believe, it denies that what God promised is true. It will see the resurrection accomplished, which it denied, and will know that faithlessness has been defeated by God’s promise and truth. This is why God is truthful and every human being a liar, namely, the one who denies what is to come. For Christ also…’”]

To confirm what he said above—that God is faithful in his promise and every human being is a liar—he added a prophetic example from the fiftieth psalm, in which he marked both that God is justified by his words and that human beings are liars because of unbelief. Both statements are read in the Book of Psalms: God is just and truthful, and every human being is a liar (Ps. LXXXV, 15). He calls a person a liar when he does not believe what God promised; for by denying that God will give what he promised, he is a liar. And while he himself is a liar, he declares God a liar for many reasons when he does not believe his promises.

Thus he calls every person a liar who distrusts God’s promises. This applies especially to the Jews, whose case the Apostle is treating here. Although they saw Christ, they denied that he was the one whom God had promised, and therefore they are pronounced liars. God, however, is truthful: he sent Christ as he promised, and thus he prevails when he is judged, because he will give what people deny he will give. For when he is not believed, he is judged a liar. But when he gives what he is judged not to be going to give, he prevails, showing himself truthful and showing the other, who does not believe his words, to be a liar.

That person will see the Son of God in majesty whom he denies; he will also see the resurrection of the flesh and will know that faithlessness has been defeated by God’s promise and truth.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “and will know that the promise and truth of God are true.”]

For Christ also prevailed when he was judged: he was unjustly killed and made the devil guilty—the devil whom he had already conquered by not sinning—so that, defeated a second time, he would lose those whom he held.

[Note: Two manuscripts add: “in the underworld,” that is, “because every human being is a liar, but God alone is truthful.”]

**(Verses 5 and 6.)** But if our injustice commends God’s justice, what shall we say? Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath? I speak according to human reasoning. Certainly not.

The Apostle says this according to the meaning of the prophet David. When David had sinned in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (II Kings II, 4), knowing that a promise cannot be given to sinners, he pleaded that the justification of God’s words might prevail over the judgment by which those who sin are judged (Ps. L, 6), and that repentance might restore him by sanctifying him, so that he might receive what God promised to give the righteous.

Accordingly, he added: “But if our injustice commends God’s justice,” and so forth. That is: if, because we are sinners, God is justified, will he be unjust if he punishes? For if our injustice benefited him, he would undoubtedly be unjust if he condemned sinners, because our injustice would make God just if, while we sinned, he gave us what he promised the saints.

[Note: Some manuscripts add: “And it is true, if indeed our iniquity benefits him. But because it is dangerous to say this, God is not unjust if he judges; for our injustice does not benefit him by making him just when we sin—that is, by causing him to rejoice in our sins, through which he alone would appear just. But he says, ‘Certainly not; I speak according to human reasoning,’ that is, this reasoning applies to human beings, not to God, because it is not possible for God to be unjust, but it is possible for a human being. Nor does our injustice make God just if, while we sin, he gives us what he promised the saints.”]

Although we are sinners, we are nevertheless restored through repentance, so that we are no longer sinners but, having been cleansed, deserve to receive the promise. The meaning of the words of the prophet David is therefore not what the malicious interpretation of wicked people asserts when he says: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done what is evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (ibid.). It is not that human sins and evil acts benefit God’s justification, that he may appear good through our evils and that our injustice may show him to be just.

Since, therefore, God is not unjust when he inflicts wrath, he is not now justified by our sins. For if he were justified by our sins, he would be unjust if he punished. But because he is not unjust when he punishes, it is clear that our injustice does not commend God’s justice. If it did commend it, he would not punish, because he is just.

Accordingly, he added: “I speak according to human reasoning.” “Certainly not”—that is, far be it from us to call God unjust, because this applies to human beings, whom we know both to err and to be deceived and to deceive. God, however, remains immutable and cannot fail to love what he has made.

Otherwise, how will God judge the world? This is true, because it would not have been just for God to judge the world if its sins benefited him, so that, while sinners obtained pardon at his will, God might appear good; and if they did not sin, he would not appear just, since, if they did not sin, he would have no one to whom he could grant pardon and would not be good.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that, if they did not sin, since he would have nothing to forgive, he would not be good.”]

**(Verse 7.)** For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? It is clear that if human beings’ lie benefits God’s glory, so that he alone appears truthful, then those who sin ought not to be called sinners, since they would appear to sin not by their own will but under his impulse. Far be it from us to say this.

**(Verse 8.)** And why not—as we are slanderously accused, and as some claim that we say—let us do evil so that good may come? [Note: Some manuscripts add: “This is the point from which the Apostle raised the question. By perverse people…”]

He now makes clear the reason why he discusses these matters so carefully and reverently. Perverse people were objecting to this, as though the meaning of those who preached the remission of sins were that people should do evil so that good might come—in other words, that they should sin so that God might appear good by forgiving them, according to what was said above. He calls this blasphemy and rejects it as contrary to the meaning of divine teaching. Faith does not teach that one ought to sin, especially since it proclaims that God will judge; rather, it counsels those who have sinned so that, having recovered salvation and living under God’s Law, they may no longer sin.

[Col. 0076A] Therefore he added: “Their condemnation is just.” That is, the condemnation of these people who, out of jealous envy, interpret what was said above about us in this way is just.

These were the claims made by the Jews in order to discredit apostolic teaching: they said that when the Apostles preached the remission of sins, they supplied an incentive to sin, so that people, as though secure because of the promise of remission, might sin readily. Yet it is clear that after receiving faith it is dangerous to sin, and that this is what is preached to believers.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “secure because of the promise.” Below, instead of “and that this is preached,” the Roman edition has “and that this is what they preach.”]

**(Verse 9.)** What then? Are we superior to them? Not at all. For we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin.

That is: why do we still delay by speaking at greater length? After giving our reasons, we have shown that both Jews and Greeks are guilty, and therefore that the Law is observed in vain.

First he showed that the Greeks are guilty according to the law of nature, and also because they did not receive the Law of Moses; hence their case is especially bad and exceedingly grave. Then he also showed that the Jews are guilty, although they appear to live under God’s Law and rightly defend the dignity of their ancestors, especially because they despised the promise made to the Fathers, rendering God’s grace void. To confirm this, he added a prophetic example from the thirteenth psalm, saying:

**(Verse 10.)** “As it is written: There is no one who is righteous” (Ps. XIII, 4 ff.). He began with their injustice in order to enumerate their evil works, and then added worse things, so that he might show that no hope could be seen in them unless they implored the mercy of Christ, who forgives sins.

[Col. 0076C] **(Verses 11 and 12.)** Then he added: “There is no one who understands.” This is true, because if a person made an effort to understand, he would not be unjust.

“There is no one who seeks God.” This too is not hidden, because if a person understood what would benefit him, he would seek God. It is not like King Asa of Judah, who, after receiving many benefits from God, became so depraved that, when he suffered from a disease of the feet, he did not seek God even though a prophet was present.
