“They have all turned aside; together they have become useless” (III Kings XV, 23). No one doubts that all who do not seek God turn aside so as to seek help from vanity. An idol is vanity; therefore they become useless.

“There is no one who does good, not even one.” Since they neglected God and became useless, they certainly cannot do good; for, having already been corrupted, they advance toward worse things.

**(Verse 13.)** “Their throat is an open grave.” Having already been enslaved to evils, they wished, if possible, to devour the good, so that their throat might be open against the good just as a grave is open to receive corpses.

[Col. 0077A] “They dealt deceitfully with their tongues.” Those who had become accustomed to such evil works were deceitful in what they said.

“The poison of asps is under their lips.” He says this because the words of such people are traps. They speak for the purpose of deceiving; and just as poison is poured through the lips of a serpent, so deceit and trickery come through their lips.

**(Verse 14.)** “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.” It is clear that the wicked always bring curses and bitter words against the good, breaking out into their abuse and defamation.

**(Verse 15.)** “Their feet are swift to shed blood.” He said this about the killing of the prophets, whom they killed eagerly: sluggish when it came to good, swift when it came to murder.

[Col. 0077B] **(Verse 16.)** “Destruction and misery are in their ways.” Since they were swift to do evil, he declares their road, or their walk, to be troubled and miserable.

“And they have not known the way of peace.”

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and Dionysius, according to Gill, read: “They have not known the way of peace, choosing the way of enmity, by which one goes to the second death, rather than the path by which one proceeds to eternal life. It is called peace because it will have no disturbance. Although they had God favorable to them, they despised him, unwilling to know that people of good will will have this rest with God.”]

The way of peace is smooth and undisturbed; for every good life is tranquil, and modest actions are themselves peaceful, and through them one goes to God. Those people, however, unwilling to know these things, chose the way of tribulation, through which one goes to Gehenna.

**(Verse 17.)** “There is no fear of God before their eyes.” Since such people are without understanding, they do not possess the fear of God. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” Solomon says (Prov. I, 7). He did not say that they do not have the fear of God, but: “There is not,” he says, “the fear of God before their eyes.” Because they see their very wicked deeds and are not horrified by them, they are said not to have the fear of God before their eyes.

The prophet Jeremiah also signifies all these people when he says, among other things: “Then they all rose up against the prophet of the Lord, wishing to kill him.” And he continues: “But all the people did not permit it” (Jer. XXVI, 8, 16). He therefore calls them all, but evil people; and he calls these all, but good people. For when he says, “They have all turned aside,” he does not mean the entire people absolutely, but this portion of the people, just as the prophet mentioned also reports: “In whom all the evil people had hidden themselves.” There are always two peoples within one population.

This is therefore the people whom the Lord rebukes under the name of Jerusalem, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets” (Matt. XXIII, 37). And elsewhere: “An evil and adulterous generation,” and: “Brood of vipers” (ibid. XII, 39). The prophet Isaiah also complains of such people, saying: “Woe to the sinful nation, the evil seed” (Isa. I, 4)! Through their evil will, while they produce evil fruits, they are an evil seed.

And because, if they wish, they can be converted, the Apostle’s voice proves this in another Epistle, saying: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the others” (Eph. II, 3).

**(Verse 18.)** We know, however, that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are under the Law. It is clear that the Law rebukes those who first did not believe their leader Moses, nor obeyed their fathers the prophets, whom they persecuted and killed, nor their kinsmen according to the flesh, the Apostles, whose blood they shed—always impious and rebellious against God—so that they might be condemned by the Law whose authority they thought ought to be despised.

For just as there is one cause underlying all evil, so there is also one cause underlying all good. In these people, therefore, the evil of all who are like them is condemned. These statements concern the confusion of the Jews, who produced testimony from the Law for themselves and for their ancestors.

[Note: The Corbie, Remigian, and Thuanean manuscripts read “one name in evil.”]

**(Verse 19.)** So that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God. He says this because, once the Jews have been confined by sins, the whole world becomes subject to God. No one doubts that the pagans are overwhelmed by offenses and impieties, and therefore the whole world is prostrated before God so that it may attain forgiveness.

[Note: The same Corbie manuscript reads: “so that it may pertain to forgiveness; for the whole world consisted of Jews and Gentiles, whom he proves to be subject to sins, since the promise was made to them.”]

The whole world consisted of Jews and Gentiles, from whom the faithful have been separated. Therefore, when he proves that the Jews who received the Law from God and to whom the promise was made are subject to sins, there is no doubt that all the Greeks are guilty of death. Hence he says: “Let every mouth be stopped, and let the whole world become subject to God,” since all who have been proved guilty need God’s mercy, both Jews and Greeks.

**(Verse 20.)** For no flesh will be justified before God by works of the Law. He does not assert that people are not justified before God because they have not observed the Law of righteousness in its commandments, but because they did not wish to believe the sacrament of God’s mystery, which is in Christ.

Through this God determined to justify a person—not through the Law—because the Law justifies for a time, but not before God. Therefore those who observe the Law in its temporal sphere are righteous, but not before God, because they do not possess the faith through which people are justified before God. Faith is greater than the Law, because the Law pertains to us, while faith pertains to God. Therefore the Law has a temporal righteousness, whereas faith has an eternal one.

When he says “all flesh,” he means every human being, just as the prophet Isaiah says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isa. XL, 5)—that is, every human being shall see the Christ of God, in whom the salvation of all is contained. They are called “flesh” because they are subject to sins. Just as righteousness makes people spiritual, so sins make them carnal; thus a person receives his name from his conduct.

For through the Law comes knowledge of sin, but through faith its abolition; therefore faith must be followed. What Law is this through which he says that sin became known, and in what way did it become known? We see that the ancients were not ignorant of sin, since Joseph was sent to prison, although through false accusation (Gen. XXXIX, 20), and Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker were imprisoned because of an offense (Gen. XL, 3). How, then, were sins hidden?

There is indeed a threefold Law. The first part concerns the mystery of God’s divinity; the second corresponds to the natural law, which forbids sin; the third concerns works, namely the Sabbath, the new moon, circumcision, and so forth. This, then, is the natural law, partly restored through Moses and partly reinforced by his authority for the restraint of vices; it made sin known—not because sin was hidden, as I have said:

[Note: The same codices read: “but he showed that God’s future judgment would come, so that no sinner might be free from punishment, lest perhaps…” This is what the Law shows: sin would be reckoned before God.]

Rather, it showed that the sins being committed would not remain unpunished before God, lest someone who escaped for a time be thought to have mocked the Law. This is what the Law shows.

**(Verse 21.)** But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, although it has testimony from the Law and the prophets. It is clear that the righteousness of God appeared apart from the Law—but apart from the Law of the Sabbath, circumcision, the new moon, and punishment—yet not apart from the mystery of God’s divinity, since the righteousness of God proceeds from that mystery.

For when those whom the Law held guilty were forgiven by God’s righteousness, he did this without the Law, since he granted forgiveness to those whom the Law was going to punish. And lest this be thought to have been done contrary to the Law, he added that the righteousness of God has testimony from the Law and the prophets. That is, the Law itself, in another respect, had long before declared that this would happen, because the one who would save human beings was to come (Isa. XIX, 20), although it had not been granted to the Law to forgive sins.

It is called the righteousness of God, although it appears to be mercy, because it has its origin in a promise. When God’s promise is fulfilled, it is called God’s righteousness. It is righteousness because what was promised has been given; and when it receives those who flee to it, it is called righteousness, because not to receive one who flees to it would be iniquity.

**(Verse 22.)** But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ. What else is meant by “through faith in Jesus Christ” except that the righteousness of God itself is the manifestation of Christ? Through faith in the preaching of Jesus Christ, the gift long ago promised by God is recognized and received.

For all, and upon all, who believe—that is, upon all believing Jews and Greeks—the true righteousness of God is bestowed.

**(Verse 23.)** For there is no distinction, since all have sinned and lack the glory of God. Because he had said that the righteousness of God is upon all believing Jews and Greeks, he added this to prove it: “For all have sinned.”

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “the righteousness, that is, grace.” They add: “And to prove it he said: ‘For all have sinned,’ both Jews and Greeks, to show that the Law profited nothing.”]

This must be understood universally, so that both Jews and Greeks are included. Hence he says, “There is no distinction.” He includes everyone here, even priests, to show that the Law without faith profited nothing. For the Law was given in such a way that faith would be present in the Law, awaiting the salvation that was to come. Therefore Christ’s death benefited everyone: while in this world he taught what must be believed and observed, and from the underworld he rescued everyone.

**(Verse 24.)** Justified freely by his grace. They were justified freely because, doing nothing and offering no repayment, they were justified by faith alone, through God’s gift.

Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. He testifies that God’s grace is in Christ, because by God’s will we were redeemed by Christ so that, having been set free, we might be justified. Thus he also says to the Galatians: “Christ redeemed us” (Gal. III, 13), offering himself for us.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, offering himself for us and becoming a curse for us. For he thought that he could retain Christ, like a hawk [retains] a bird.”]

He surrendered himself to the raging devil, although the devil did not know what he was doing. Thinking that he could retain Christ, the devil seized him as though he were a hawk seizing a bird; but because he could not endure Christ’s power, he lost along with him all those whom he held.

**(Verse 25.)** Whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith. He says that in Christ God determined—that is, ordained—that he would be favorable to the human race if they believed.

In his blood. For this reason, in his blood, because by his death we have been set free; so that he might both show him to be dead and, through his suffering, condemn death.

**(Verse 26.)** For the demonstration of his righteousness—that is, so that he might make his promise public, by which he was to free us from sins [Col. 0080B], just as he had promised beforehand; and when he fulfilled it, he showed himself to be righteous.

Because of the preceding sins, in the patience of God. God, knowing the purpose of his goodness, by which he determined to assist sinners—both those who are among the inhabitants above and those who were being held in hell—waited for both groups for a very long time, setting aside the sentence by which it seems just that all should be condemned. He wished to show us what he had long ago decreed: to free the human race through Christ, just as he promised through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). And lest it perhaps seem that he had promised this gift to the Jews alone, he says through Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer among all nations” [Col. 0080C] (Isaiah 56:7). Although the promise was made through Judaism, God, foreknowing that the wicked Jews would reject his gift, promised to admit the nations to receive his grace; provoked to jealousy by them, the wicked Jews would be driven to anger and tormented.

In this time—that is, in our time, when God gave what he had long ago promised to give at the time when he gave it. So that he might be just, justifying the one who is from the faith of Jesus Christ. He rightly says this, because, in order to be just, he gave what he had promised; and what he promised was to justify those who believe in Christ. He says in Habakkuk: “But the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4), so that, while he possesses faith in God and in Christ, he may be righteous.

**(Verse 27.)** Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? By that of works? No, but by the law of faith. [Col. 0080D] Having supplied the reasoning, he speaks to those who act under the law: they boast without cause, flattering themselves about the law and about their descent from Abraham, while they see that no one is justified before God except through faith.

**(Verse 28.)** For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. He says that a Gentile is regarded as justified when he believes and performs none of the works of the law—that is, without circumcision, new-moon observances, or keeping the Sabbath.

[Col. 0081A] **(Verse 29.)** Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of the nations? Indeed, of the nations also. Without doubt, there is one God of all. For the Jews cannot claim for themselves alone that their God is not also the God of the nations, since they acknowledge that all have their origin from one Adam and that no foreigner wishing to approach the law is forbidden. Indeed, some came out with them into the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0081D] The Roman edition reads: “into the wilderness of Egypt,” where they are commanded to be received.] from among the Egyptians, whom they are commanded to receive (Exodus 12:28 and following), provided only that they be circumcised and eat unleavened bread or the Passover together with them. Likewise, the fact that Cornelius, a Gentile who had not become Jewish, received the gift of God, and that he had been justified, is confirmed by divine testimony (Acts 10:31).

**(Verse 30.)** Since indeed there is one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. [Col. 0081B] By “circumcision” he signifies the Jews, because they were justified by faith in the promise, believing that this was the Christ whom God had promised in the law. By “uncircumcision,” however, he signifies the Gentiles, who are justified before God through faith in Christ. For he justified Gentiles and Jews alike in no other way than by their believing; because there is one God of all, he justified all by one method. What benefit, then, is there in circumcision of the flesh, or what harm in uncircumcision, when faith alone confers dignity and merit?

**(Verse 31.)** Do we then nullify the law through faith? Certainly not; rather, we establish the law. The law is certainly not destroyed through faith but fulfilled; its standing is strengthened when faith testifies that what it said would happen has arrived. He says this on account of the Jews, who think that faith in Christ is hostile to the law [Col. 0081C], not understanding the meaning of the law. Faith does not therefore nullify the law when it now teaches that the law ought to cease; for it asserts that the law was rightly given in its own time, but that it ought no longer to be practiced. Indeed, the law itself says that, when the promise had been fulfilled, the law ought to cease. For the angel Gabriel showed the prophet Daniel, who desired to know this matter (Daniel 9:25), among other things, that when Christ came, the chrism—that is, the royal anointing, which signifies power—would cease. “And judgment,” he says, “will no longer exist,” which is the law, “and my sacrifice will be taken away.” He says “my” so that it might be understood that the former offering would cease.

Opening up this meaning, the Savior says: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). And because, when the law of Moses ceased, God was going to give better commandments, the prophet Jeremiah proclaimed, saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will conclude a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers” (Jeremiah 31:31). This applies to those who received the Christ who came according to the promise. Therefore the Savior says: “I have not come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them” [Col. 0082A] (Matthew 5:17). And because the house of God was going to exist not only in Jerusalem but also in other places, the prophet Zechariah says: “I will place Jerusalem among all the nations” (Zechariah 12:2)—that is, the Church.

## CHAPTER IV

**(Verse 1.)** What, then, shall we say that Abraham our father found according to the flesh? After he had shown that no one could be justified before God through works of the law, he added that Abraham, too, could not have merited anything according to the flesh. By “flesh” he signified circumcision, because Abraham sought nothing through circumcision. He was justified before he was circumcised.

**(Verse 2.)** For if Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but not before God. This is the position being proposed. [Col. 0082B] For Abraham certainly has glory before God, but through faith, by which he was justified; because no one is justified by works of the law so as to have glory before God. And because those who keep the law, whether the law of Moses or the natural law, are justified for the present, he says: “If Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but [Col. 0082D] not before God”—but before the world, so that he may not appear liable under the law presently in force. Before God, however, the faithful person has grace. For what does he say, and so forth? [Note: The Corbie manuscript and Remigius read: “For Abraham indeed has glory before God, but through faith, by which he was justified; because no one is justified by works of the law so as to have glory before God. And because those who keep the law are justified for the present, he says: ‘If Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but not before God,’ but before the world, so that he may not appear liable under the law presently in force. Before God, however, the faithful person has grace. For what does he say, and so forth.”]

For Abraham was justified through faith, which no one doubts; therefore he has glory before God. But because those who keep the law, whether of Moses or the natural law, are justified for the present, so that they may not be liable in the present judgment, he therefore says: If Abraham was justified by works of the law, he does not have glory before God; because, he says, “the one who does the law will live by it”—that is, he will not die as one liable to condemnation. Yet from this he will not have merit before God, but because of faith.

**(Verse 3.)** For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). He made clear that Abraham has glory before God not because he was circumcised or because he abstained from iniquity, but because he believed God; for this reason also he was justified, and he will receive the reward of his praise in the future.

[Col. 0082C] **(Verse 4.)** Now to the one who works, the reward is not counted according to grace but according to debt. It is clear that for the person subject to the law of works—that is, to the law of Moses—or to the natural law, merit is not counted as a reward so that he may have glory before God. For he is a debtor bound to perform the law, because necessity has been imposed through the law: whether he wishes or not, he must perform the law so that he will not be condemned, as he says elsewhere: “Those who despise it acquire condemnation for themselves,” because they are liable at present (Romans 13:2).

But believing or not believing is a matter of the will. [Note: The Corbie, Thuane, and Remigius manuscripts read: “It is a matter of the will, because it is not extorted but persuaded. Therefore it contributes to merit: he believes what he does not know, but hopes for it.”] For no one can be compelled to accept what is not manifest, but one is invited; it is not extorted but persuaded. Therefore the person who assents ought to be rewarded, as was Abraham, who believed what he had not seen.

[Col. 0082D] **(Verse 5.)** But to the one who does not work—that is, to the one liable because of sins, who does not perform what the law commands—but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness. He says this because, apart from works of the law, the faith of the ungodly—that is, of the Gentile—who believes in Christ is counted as righteousness, just as Abraham’s was. How, then, do the Jews think that they are justified through works of the law with Abraham’s justification, when they see that Abraham was justified not through works of the law but by faith alone? Therefore the law is not necessary when the ungodly person is justified before God by faith alone.

According to the purpose of God’s grace. He says that God decreed that, once the law had ceased, the grace of God would require faith alone for salvation. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Faith alone would contribute to salvation through the grace of God.”]

**(Verse 6.)** As David also says. He strengthens this very point by the example of the prophet. The blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without works. He calls those blessed concerning whom God decreed that they should be justified before God without labor [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “and without any entreaty.”] or any observance, by faith alone. He therefore proclaims the blessedness of the time in which Christ was born, just as the Lord himself says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear, and they did not hear it” (Matthew 13:13).

**(Verses 7 and 8.)** “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the person to whom the Lord has not counted sin” (Psalm 31:1 and following). Clearly blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered without labor or any work, no works of repentance being required of them except that they believe. This person, too, is blessed, to whom the Lord has not counted sin. To forgive, to cover, and not to count are one method and one meaning; everything is obtained and granted in the same way.

Some, however, think that these statements have a threefold meaning, because the prophet used different words and descended from the plural number to the singular. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “For when he wishes to enumerate, through the names of sins, the abundance of God’s grace, since sins have different names…”] When he wishes to enumerate the abundance of God’s grace through the names of sins, since sins have different names [Col. 0083C], he speaks at greater length; nevertheless, the words have one form and one meaning, because when he covers, he forgives, and when he forgives, he does not count the sin. He speaks at length in praise of God’s grace [Note: The same edition, the Roman edition together with certain manuscripts, reads: “so that he might enlarge God’s gift.”] so that he may enlarge the grace.

He made three degrees because of the variety of sins. The first degree is iniquity or impiety, when the Creator is not acknowledged; the second consists in the deeds of serious sins; the third in those of lesser sins. Yet he teaches that all of these are obliterated in baptism. By these three degrees he signified the body of every sin.

How, then, can this apply to the person of penitents when he says, “Blessed are those whose sins have been covered,” when it is established that penitents acquire remission of sins through labor and groaning [Col. 0083D]? Or how does what he says, “Blessed is the person to whom the Lord has not counted sin,” accord with martyrdom, when we know that the glory of martyrdom is acquired through sufferings and hardships?

The prophet, foreseeing the blessed time at the Savior’s coming, calls those blessed whose sins are forgiven, covered, and not counted through the bath of baptism, without labor or any work. Yet the Apostle, on account of the fullness of the times, and because there is more grace in the apostles than there was in the prophets, proclaims greater things that we obtain through the gift of baptism [Col. 0084A]. He declares that we receive not only remission of sins but also justification and adoption as children of God, so that this blessedness may possess complete security and glory.

**(Verse 9.)** Does this blessedness, then, remain only in circumcision, or also in uncircumcision? That is, has this blessedness been granted only to Abraham’s sons, or also to those who are uncircumcised? For if, at that time, the nations were not forbidden to approach the law and the promise given to Abraham, how could they be forbidden in the time of Christ when they were coming to grace [Note: Some manuscripts read: “coming to glory.” Immediately afterward, the Roman edition alone reads: “when the grace of God invited more fully”], when God fully encouraged them by grace?

For we say—that is, if we speak according to the meaning of the law [Col. 0084B]—that Abraham’s faith was counted as righteousness. He begins at the origin, so as to exclude every evasion of sophistry; for the person who is excluded from the beginning has no point from which to begin raising a question.

**(Verses 10 and 11.)** How, then, was it counted? When he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of the faith that he had in uncircumcision, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might also be counted to them (Genesis 17:10–11).

When Abraham was in uncircumcision, he believed God. What did he believe? That he would have offspring—that is, a son—in whom all the nations would be justified through faith while uncircumcised, just as Abraham was justified. For he received circumcision as the sign of the righteousness of faith: believing that he would have a son, he received a sign of what he had believed, so that it might be seen that, because he believed, he had been justified.

Circumcision, therefore, possesses no dignity in itself but is merely a sign. Abraham’s sons received that sign so that they might be known to be the sons of the one who, believing God, had received this sign; they were to be imitators of their father’s faith and believe in Jesus, who was promised to Abraham and whose symbolic figure was Isaac. For all the nations are not blessed in Isaac but in Christ: “For there is no other name given under heaven by which we must be saved,” says the apostle Peter (Acts 4:12).

**(Verse 12.)** And that he might be the father of circumcision not only to those who are from circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised [Col. 0084D]. He says this because Abraham, believing, first became the father of circumcision—but of the heart, not only of those who descend from his ancestry but also of those among the nations who believe in the same way. According to the flesh he is the father of the Jews, but according to faith he is the father of all believers.

**(Verse 13.)** For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. It is clear that neither had the law yet been given [Col. 0085A] nor did circumcision yet exist when the promise was made to the believing Abraham and to his offspring, which is Christ [Note: The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read: “because he was to wash away the sins of all.”], who would wash away human sins. Hence John the Baptist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:19).

Therefore he became heir of the world not through the merit of keeping the law but through faith. The heir of the world is the heir of the earth, which he obtained in his descendants. Christ, however, is the heir of the nations, as David sings: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2:8); for we shall die and live with him.

**(Verse 14.)** For if those who are from the law are heirs—that is, if those who are from the law or under the law are heirs by virtue of the law—faith has been emptied and the promise abolished (Romans 14:8). It is clear that if the inheritance comes through the law, the promise made to Abraham through faith has been rendered void. But the promise was not made through the law; rather, the inheritance comes through the righteousness of faith. The Apostle has shown what evil there is in hoping for an inheritance from the law.

**(Verse 15.)** For the law produces wrath. To show completely that a person cannot be justified before God through the law, nor could the promise have been made through the law, he says: “The law produces wrath.” For it was given for this purpose: to make transgressors liable. Faith, however, is a gift of God’s mercy, so that those made liable through the law may obtain forgiveness; therefore faith produces joy.

He is not speaking against the law but placing faith before it, because those who could not be saved through the law are saved through faith by God’s grace. The law, therefore, is not wrath, but it produces wrath—that is, punishment—for the sinner, since it does not pardon but exacts vengeance. Punishment is generated by wrath, and wrath arises from sin. For this reason he wishes the law to be left behind, so that people may flee to faith, which forgives transgressions and thus saves.

For where there is no law, there is no transgression. He says this because, once those liable have been removed from the power of the law and pardon has been granted, there is no transgression; for those who had been sinners through transgressing the law have been justified. The law of works therefore ceases—that is, the observance of Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, distinctions among foods, [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “or blood that must be expiated by the law of death.” Remigius and the Thuane manuscript read: “the blood of a weasel [must be] expiated.”] and the observance concerning a dead animal or the blood of a weasel [the reading is uncertain].

**(Verse 16.)** Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all offspring. The promise cannot be firm for all offspring—that is, for every person from every nation—unless it comes through faith; for the origin of the promise is from faith, not from the law. Those who are under the law are liable, but a promise cannot be given to those who are liable. Therefore they must first be purified through faith, so that they may become worthy to be called children of God and so that the promise may be firm.

For if they call themselves children of God while they are liable—that is, under the law—the claim is not firm, because the children of God are free from sin. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “If, then, those who are under the law must be instructed”; others: “If, then, those who are as though under the law must be instructed” [Col. 0086D], “so that they may be under the law.”] If, then, those who are under the law must be rescued from under the law [Col. 0086A] in order to deserve to receive the promise, how much more must those who are not under the law be rescued? It is therefore not advantageous for anyone to place himself under the law, so that he may be able to find the cure for his wound by a shorter route.

Not only for the one who is from the law, but also for the one who is from the faith of Abraham. This is what he said above: “For all offspring,” both Jews, who certainly came from the law, and Gentiles, who follow the faith Abraham possessed so that he might be righteous. Abraham believed without the law; therefore he is joined more closely to the Gentiles, so that the promise may be firm for those who believe in the one in whom he himself believed.

**(Verse 17.)** Who is the father of us all, as it is written: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Genesis 17:4). By the example of the Law, he confirmed that Abraham is the father of all—but of those who believe—and that the promise is firm if one departs from the law for the sake of faith; for the promise of the kingdom of heaven is assigned to the righteous, not to sinners. Those who are under the law are under sin, because all have sinned; and no one can both be under the law and obtain grace, as he also says to the Galatians: “You have been separated from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen from grace” (Galatians 5:4).

Before the God in whom you believed. In order to teach that there is one God of all, he addresses the Gentiles, saying that Abraham believed in that very God and was justified before him [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “and was justified before him, so that the nations too may believe”], in whom the Gentiles also believe, so that they may be justified and there may be no distinction between Jew and Greek in faith. For, with circumcision and uncircumcision removed, they become one in Christ; Abraham too believed while uncircumcised and was justified.

[Col. 0086C] Who gives life to the dead and calls things that do not exist as though they did. By saying this, he invites the nations to Abraham’s faith. For while Abraham was uncircumcised, believing in God, whose faith is now proclaimed in Christ, he was brought to life together with his wife. Although they were worn out by age, the elderly pair became youthful again, so that he did not doubt that he would have a son by Sarah, whom he knew to be barren and in whom the natural flow of menstruation had already ceased.

Through this, they should not be concerned either about uncircumcision or circumcision, but should be ready with regard to faith, confident because they believe in the one who gives life to the dead, and because there is no other who possesses this power. When he wills something to exist that does not exist, it immediately comes into being by his will.

Therefore, although Abraham was not yet a father, he was called the father of many nations, and he believed, confident in God’s power. And so that it might be believed that the same God was the Father of Christ, the God in whom Abraham believed, a sign of this kind was given in Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:13), when the promise was fulfilled in the world as Christ approached, just as a sign of the same kind had been given to Abraham and Sarah when the promise was confirmed. In a similar manner, bodies dead from old age brought forth holy John, just as Isaac had been born.

**(Verse 18.)** Who against hope believed in hope (Genesis [Col. 0087A] 15:5). It is clear that, although Abraham had no hope of begetting a child, he believed God, possessing faith that he would beget a child against hope, while knowing that God could do all things.

So that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said: “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15). In Genesis, after showing him the stars of heaven, he said: “So shall your offspring be”; and by believing this, Abraham was justified. He believed what appears impossible to the world, since it does not fall within the course of nature that the aged should beget children and that their offspring should multiply in such abundance that it could not be counted.

Therefore faith is precious, because it believes that something will happen contrary to what one knows or sees. By this hope he consoles himself, because it is God who promises; and it is right to think more highly of him than human weakness can grasp.

[Col. 0087B] **(Verses 19–22.)** And he did not grow weak in faith, nor did he consider his own body, already dead, since he was now almost one hundred years old, or Sarah’s womb, already dead. Yet he did not waver in disbelief regarding God’s promise; rather, he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that he was able also to do what he had promised. Therefore it was counted to him as righteousness.

He proclaims Abraham worthy of praise for this: knowing that he himself was incapable, he strengthened his weakness through faith, so that he would believe that, through God, he could do what he knew could not happen according to the world’s laws. Great, therefore, is the merit before God of the person who believed God against his own knowledge, not doubting that God, as God, could do what he knew could not happen according to the world’s order.

He is fully convinced that God exists beyond the world’s order; for no one should be said to exist within that which he created. Therefore such a person deserves to be rewarded by God, because he attributes more to his Creator than his own understanding can grasp. This would have no value if everyone thought the same; but the disbelief of many commends the faith of believers before God.

He therefore urges the nations to this firmness of faith [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “to this dignity of faith”], so that they may receive God’s promise and grace without any hesitation, confident in Abraham’s example. For praise increases for the believer if what is incredible and appears foolish to the world is believed; because [Note: Some manuscripts read: “the more foolish what is believed is thought to be”] the more impossible what is believed is thought to be, the more honorable the believer will be. Yet it would truly be foolish to believe this if it were said to happen without God.

For this reason Abraham’s faith is all the more praiseworthy than that of others, because it was not drawn on by any prodigies of signs. Since the world is governed by a definite law and power and is directed according to an order established by God, [Note: The Roman edition reads: “But people, intent on the order of the flesh…”] people, devoted through love of the flesh to the world’s order, neglected God, its maker. To remove error and demonstrate that he is Lord of all, God wished it to be proclaimed that he could do and had done what is impossible for the world. Thus those who believed this, while those puffed up by the world’s reasoning and neglectful of God were condemned, would be saved as a distinct people, devoted to God’s lordship.

**(Verses 23–25.)** It was not written for his sake alone, that it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:4), but also for our sake, to whom it will be counted when we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was handed over because of our sins and rose because of our justification.

He says that a pattern was given in Abraham for Jews and Gentiles, so that, following his example, we might believe in God, in Christ, and in the Holy Spirit, and so that righteousness might be counted to us. Although there is a difference in what is now believed [Note: Several older editions and many manuscripts read: “what is not believed”; some: “what he does not believe.” The Roman edition’s “what is believed,” or the Michæan manuscript’s “what is now believed,” is preferable], faith nevertheless possesses one gift.

This, then, is what we obtain when we believe. For by believing that Christ is the Son of God, we are adopted by God as sons [Col. 0088B]; for he could give believers nothing greater than to be called children of God, while unbelievers are rejected. We are called children of God, whereas they are not even worthy to be called servants.

In keeping with his infinite magnificence, God gave those who love him something worthy of his majesty, not something proportionate to what human beings deserve; for in a gift, the greatness of the giver is considered more than that of the recipient. He receives greater praise when, through Christ, he bestows great gifts on the small—Christ, who for our sake allowed himself to be killed so that, once pardon had been granted, he might rescue us from the second death, that is, from the punishment of hell.

And he rose [Note: Thus read the majority of the manuscripts, the older and better ones; certain others and all the editions read: “and all [this was done] for the joy of triumph”; one reads: “above all, for the joy of triumph”], so that, through the joy of the triumph over death, he might grant us the grace of justification, making us worthy to be called children of God.

Before the Passion, those who were baptized received only remission of sins, through the zeal of which Satan killed the Savior. After the resurrection, however, all were justified—both those who had been baptized earlier and those baptized later—through the form of faith in the Trinity that had been given, and through receiving the Holy Spirit, who is the sign of believers that they are children of God.

And, so that this might contribute to the full measure of our justification, in rising he granted authority to his commands, so that [Note: All editions and certain manuscripts read: “so that he might make us imitators of them through this confidence, by which we might be justified and increase our merits, through which, having attained glory, we might appear resplendent in the kingdom of God; because, having been justified, and finally…” The reading followed in the text is much more suitable according to other manuscripts.] by imitating them we might increase our merits, through which, having attained glory, we might appear resplendent in the kingdom of God, with this confidence that, having been justified, we cannot be held by death.

For through the Savior’s Passion, death was conquered. Death, which had previously ruled as the cause of sin, does not dare to retain those whom it has justified.

## CHAPTER V

**(Verse 1.)** Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus [Col. 0088D] Christ. Faith, not the law, enables us to have peace with God; for faith reconciles us to God by removing the sins that had made us God’s enemies. And because the Lord Jesus is the minister of this grace, through him we have been reconciled to God. Faith is greater than the law: the law is for our sake, but faith is of God; the law belongs to present discipline, whereas faith belongs to everlasting salvation. [Col. 0089A] But the person who does not think rightly about Christ will not be able to attain the rewards of faith, because he does not hold the truth of faith.

**(Verse 2.)** Through whom we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand and boast in the hope of the glory of the children of God. It is clear that through Christ we have access to God’s grace. He is the mediator of God and human beings; by raising us up through his teaching, he caused us to hope for the gift of God’s grace while standing in his faith. We stand because previously we lay prostrate; by believing, we have been raised up, boasting in the hope of the splendor that God promised us.

**(Verse 3.)** And not only this, but we also boast in our tribulations. Since “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21), he therefore teaches that we should boast in them as well. Tribulation added to hope increases the reward; for tribulation is an indicator of fixed hope, bearing witness toward the crown. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed will you be when they persecute you and say every evil thing against you on account of God’s righteousness. Rejoice and exult, for behold, your reward is abundant in heaven” (Matthew 5:11).

To despise present things and things that give pleasure, and not to yield under pressure because of hope for the future, is a great merit before God. Therefore we should boast in tribulations, because a person believes that he will receive so much more the stronger he sees himself to be in tribulation.

Knowing that tribulation produces endurance. This is how tribulation produces endurance: if the tribulation itself does not undergo the movement of weakness or doubt.

**(Verse 4.)** And endurance produces proven character. It is clear that endurance, if it is such as we have described, will be seen to be a firm test.

And proven character produces hope. Hope is rightly spoken of in one who appears to have been tested; for he will be known to be worthy to receive a reward in the kingdom of God.

**(Verse 5.)** And hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Hope does not disappoint, even when we are judged foolish and dull-minded by unbelievers because we believe what lacks worldly rationality; for we possess within us the pledge of God’s love, the Holy Spirit given to us.

The Holy Spirit given to the apostles and to us proves that God’s promise is faithful. He enabled the unlearned to speak in different languages with interpretations, to confirm hope, and also to commend God’s love in us (Acts 2:4). Since those who are beloved cannot be deceived, he made us secure concerning the promise: both because it is God who promised and because he promised to those whom he wishes to hold dear.

For human words cannot establish the rational basis of our faith except by the testimony of works of power. When these works are silent, they cry out, and faith is shown to be reasonable, to the confusion of the world’s wise [Col. 0090A], who with bold words wage war against heavenly things with earthly weapons and against spiritual things with carnal ones, yet are not ashamed to call themselves wise.

For just as the dubious origin of a foreigner is unpersuasive in a foreign land, so the truth of our faith is a foreigner on earth. And because its nature cannot be explained in words, it is commended by the testimony of power, which is the greater reality.

(Verses 6 and 7.) For why did Christ, when we were still sinners, according to time die for the ungodly? For scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person. If Christ gave himself over to death for a time for unbelievers and enemies of God—for he died for a time, since he rose again on the third day—how much more, when we believe in him, will he fortify us with his aid? For he died for us in order to acquire both life and glory for us. Therefore, if he died for enemies, it must be understood how much he provides for friends.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] The Roman edition reads: “For while he seemed to die among human beings, he was among the dead, etc.” The old editions and manuscripts do not differ among themselves, except that in some copies *irreverentes* (“irreverent”) is read, and *reverenter* (“reverently”) in others.]

Among human beings, then—that is, according to time—he seemed to die; for among the dead he was judging irreverent and wicked spirits for the salvation of souls. There are times in the world, where the sun rises and sets, where the moon waxes and wanes, and where day and night do not remain in their fixed condition; for whatever is subject to time and age is always changeable.

[Note: [Col. 0089D] The Roman edition reads “and wanes.” Below, instead of *mutabilis* (“changeable”), some manuscripts have *mortalis* (“mortal”).]

To this time, therefore, Christ died, when he departed from the body. But where there is neither time nor age, there he was found not only alive but also victorious. Hence he wished to commend the Savior’s love toward us when he says: “Scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; but Christ died for the ungodly.” For if someone scarcely dies for a righteous person, how can it happen that someone would die for the ungodly? And if someone might perhaps dare to die for one good person—or perhaps might not dare, since he indicates that both are difficult—how can it be imagined that anyone would dare to die for the ungodliness of many?

Indeed, if someone perhaps dares to die for a righteous or good person, drawn either by a certain compassion or by affection for that person’s good works, in the case of the ungodly there is not only nothing to persuade him to die, but also nothing to move him to tears. Yet Christ died for the ungodliness of the people, and even for those who were not his own,

[Note: [Col. 0090D] The Corbie and Remigius manuscripts add *non sui*, “not his own,” here, as follows: “just as one might reluctantly allow his credit to be pledged for cunning or dilatory debtors.”]

in order to make credible everything in which the world disbelieves. Thus he established two grades: the righteous and the good. Although the righteous must also be called good, he nevertheless set out the categories themselves, signifying the righteous by practice, but the good by nature—one who is called innocent through simplicity.

Therefore, although, insofar as this passage is concerned, the righteous is of better merit than the good, he says, “Perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person,” because the case of innocence is more pitiable; he indicates that someone might perhaps be compelled to do this. Indeed, parents wish to die for good children—not to mention wives for good husbands.

If, however, we wish to set the good and the righteous against one another, sometimes we find the righteous to be better, and sometimes the good to be preferable. For if, according to the law of God, the righteous person is better than the good person—but only than one who has not yet labored upon himself so as to increase himself through good works—the righteous person will improve the goodness of his nature through practice.

If, however, the righteous person is righteous according to the world, the good person is preferred to him because of innocence, since righteousness of this kind is not without severity.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] All editions and many manuscripts read “righteousness without impiety”; several others, more appropriately, read “righteousness without severity,” and some of these add “nor is severity free from wickedness.”]

Thus every nature is good, while righteousness is the fitting fruit of nature according to God’s law; and therefore righteousness is goodness, from which the righteous are always called both righteous and good. Yet the good are not always righteous, because they are called good not on account of their works but on account of their innocence. For perfect righteousness is goodness when it fulfills through action the goodness of its nature.

(Verses 8.) But God commends his love in us.

[Col. 0091B] He commends his love in this way: while he is still benevolent toward his enemies, he sends one who will save them, although they certainly do not deserve it.

(Verses 9.) For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now justified in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him.

He says this because, if God permitted his Son to be killed for sinners, what will he do for those who have been justified, except preserve them from wrath—that is, keep them safe from the devil’s deception—so that they may be secure on the day of judgment, when vengeance begins to devastate the faithless? Since the goodness of God wishes no one to perish, he gave a most worthy death,

[Note: [Col. 0091D] “He would heap punishment upon the ungrateful” is absent from all manuscripts, although it is found in every edition.]

so that, for those who understand God’s grace toward them, it might increase dignity and glory, while it would heap punishment upon the ungrateful. The ungrateful are those who, when God calls, dissent, rejecting God’s grace in order to remain in their chosen error and wickedness.

(Verses 10.) For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life.

It is clear that if God handed over his Son to death in order to reconcile us to himself, how much more will he save those who have been reconciled through his life? For one who benefits his enemies cannot fail to love his friends.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] The Roman edition, drawing on various readings, restores the following: “For surely one who benefits enemies cannot possibly fail to love friends.” These words are also found in the Vindobonensis, Thuaneus, and Remigius manuscripts.]

If the Savior’s death benefited us while we were still ungodly, how much more will his life benefit those who have been justified, when he rises from the dead? For just as his death rescued us from the devil, so also his life will free us from the judgment of God on the day of judgment.

(Verses 11.) And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

[Col. 0091D] He teaches that we must give thanks to God not only for the salvation and security we have received, but also glory in God through Christ Jesus,

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Some manuscripts read: “who deigned, through his Son as mediator, to call us his friends from among the ungodly,” etc.]

who deigned to call us his friends from among the ungodly and enemies, so that we might rejoice that we have obtained every benefit through Christ. Since through him we have come to know God, let us glory in him and render him an honor equal to that rendered to God the Father, with Christ himself as a suitable witness proclaiming: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23).

After explaining the providence of God the Father and the gift he gave through Christ, by which he made the person of the Son pleasing to us—since through one Christ we have been redeemed by one God the Father—he added:

(Verses 12.) Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.

Since above he demonstrated, according to the order of truth, the grace of God given through Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0092D] So read the old edition and all the manuscripts. The Roman edition, on the contrary, reads: “now he declares the order of the one God the Father himself,” etc.]

he now declares the order of the one God the Father through his one Son, Christ. For just as Adam, one man—that is, Eve, for she too is Adam—sinned in all, so one Christ, the Son of God, conquered sin in all.

And because he has shown God’s purpose toward the human race, in order to show the very beginnings of sin he began with Adam, who first sinned, so that he might teach that the providence of the one God restored through one person what had fallen and been dragged into death through one person. This one, therefore, is the one through whom we were saved; and by his own will we owe him the reverence that we owe God the Father.

For he himself says elsewhere: “Whoever serves Christ in these matters pleases God” (Romans 14:18), although it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13). If, then, he says that one must serve God alone, and he commands that Christ be served, Christ is in the unity of God, neither a different nor another God. Since the law says that one must serve God alone, it plainly proclaims that whoever serves Christ jointly pleases God.

[Note: [Col. 0092D] All editions read: “The law reminds us that one who serves Christ is said to please God.” The very numerous manuscripts, however, agree with the reading given in the text.]

Thus, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, so also through one Christ came the condemnation and death of sin, bringing eternal life, as he explains below.

“In whom,” that is, in Adam, “all sinned.” Therefore he said “in whom,” although he is speaking about a woman, because he did not refer to the individual sex but to the human race. It is therefore clear that all sinned in Adam as in a mass; for he himself was corrupted through sin, and all whom he fathered were born under sin.

Thus all are sinners because we are all from him. For he lost God’s benefit when he transgressed, becoming unworthy to eat from the tree of life, so that he would die. Death is the dissolution of the body, when the soul is separated from the body.

There is also another death, called the second death, in Gehenna. We do not suffer this because of Adam’s sin, but acquire it through our own sins on that account. From it the good are free, although they were in the underworld,

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Some manuscripts read: “but in the upper region, as if in free purity”; several others read: “but in the upper regions, as if free,” and Vall. adds, “[where] they were held,” which is not inappropriate. Nevertheless, the remaining manuscripts and all editions read more suitably: “but in the higher region, as if in a place of freedom,” where “custody” is to be understood.]

but in the higher region, as if in a place of freedom, since they could not ascend to heaven. For they were held by the sentence pronounced against Adam, a written bond that was erased by Christ’s death in the decrees (Colossians 2:14).

The sentence of the decree was that the body of one man should be dissolved upon the earth, while the soul, held by the bonds of the underworld, should suffer destruction.

(Verses 13.) For until the law, sin was in this world; but sin was not reckoned when there was no law.

He says, as I mentioned above, that all sinned in Adam, and that sin was not reckoned until the law was given. For people thought that they sinned with impunity before God, though not before human beings. Nor had the natural law entirely grown numb, since they did not fail to understand that what they did not wish to suffer themselves they ought not to do to others.

Indeed, sin was so far from being unknown among human beings that when Jacob’s father-in-law Laban searched for his idols among Jacob’s possessions, he judged the person with whom the theft was found worthy of death (Genesis 31:30 and following). Joseph, although falsely accused, was nevertheless shut up in prison as though guilty (Genesis 39:20). Pharaoh’s baker and cupbearer likewise suffered punishment for an offense (Genesis 40:3). Moses, after killing an Egyptian, was terrified by the law.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] Some manuscripts read: “terrified, he fled.”]

How, then, was sin not reckoned when there was no law? Or how was it punished unless the law was known?

The natural law always exists and was never unknown. But people thought that it had authority only for a time, and that it did not make them guilty before God. For they did not know that God would judge the human race, and therefore sin was not reckoned, as though sin were not known to God, thereby asserting that God was unconcerned.

[Note: [Col. 0093D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “as though sin did not exist.” Several others agree with us: “as though sin were not known.” The Corbie manuscript alone reads: “For if sin were not known to God, they would assert that God was unconcerned.”]

But when the law was given through Moses, it was revealed that God cares for human affairs, and that those who do evil will not escape with impunity merely because, for whatever reason, they escape punishment in the present.

For if people, with justice or nature as their teacher, judged that sins committed among themselves should not go unpunished, how much more ought they not to have failed to understand that God, whom they knew to be the creator of the world, would call these matters to account?

Indeed, since Sodom and Gomorrah were sentenced to perish by fire (Genesis 19:24)—a fact that oblivion had covered—Moses made it known by writing it down, in order to establish that God would be judge.

But when, having neglected God, people began to accept fabricated objects in God’s honor,

[Col. 0093D] their minds corrupted,

[Note: [Col. 0094D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “having corrupted the law of the natural mind, which is first,” etc.]

they trampled upon the first part of the natural law. For the natural law has three parts.

The first is that the Creator, once known, must be honored, and that his splendor and majesty must not be assigned to any creature.

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Several manuscripts read: “must not be assigned to anyone except the Son.”]

The second part is moral: that one should live well, with moderation governing one’s conduct. For it is fitting that a person who knows the Creator restrain his life by the law, lest his knowledge prove fruitless.

The third part is instructional: that knowledge of God the Creator and an example of moral conduct be handed on to others, so that they may learn

[Note: [Col. 0094D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “how the Creator is rightly honored.”]

how merit is assigned before the Creator. This is true and Christian wisdom.

(Verses 14.) But death reigned from Adam to Moses.

Since sin was not reckoned before the law was given through Moses, as I said, death reigned through the very presumption of impunity, knowing that those people were devoted to it.

Death therefore reigned with the security of its dominion both over those who escaped for a time and over those who even in this life paid penalties for their evil deeds. For it saw that all belonged to it, because “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

Thinking that sin could be committed with impunity, they sinned all the more, especially in those matters that the world nourished as though they were lawful. Satan rejoiced in this, confident that, because of Adam’s situation, the human being abandoned by God was in his possession.

Death therefore reigned over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is the type of the one who was to come; we shall demonstrate this in what follows.

It is therefore clear that death did not reign over everyone, because not everyone sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—that is, not everyone sinned after despising God. Who are those who sinned after despising God, except those who neglected the Creator and served the creature, establishing gods for themselves to worship, to the injury of God?

[Note: [Col. 0094D] “Therefore the devil rejoiced that they had become imitators of him” was missing from all editions; we have restored it from nearly all the manuscripts.]

For this reason the devil rejoiced in them,

[Col. 0094C] because he saw that they had become his imitators. Terah, the father of Abraham, Nahor, and Laban each claimed personal gods for himself.

Adam’s sin is not far removed from idolatry. For he transgressed, thinking that he would become a god. He judged that what the devil suggested would benefit him more than what God commanded, setting the devil in God’s place; and therefore he was subjected to the devil.

These people likewise, having transgressed against God while serving the creature, sin in a similar manner, though not in the same manner, since likeness ordinarily contains some unlikeness. For it cannot be said that those who received the command not to eat from the tree, as Adam did (Genesis 2:16), sinned in the same way; they sinned not by transgressing God, but within the natural law.

Whoever understood—whether through inherited teaching or natural indication—and revered God, assigning the honor of his name and majesty to no one, if he sinned, sinned under God, not against God, whom he recognized as judge. Therefore death did not reign over such a person.

But, as I said, it reigned over those who under the appearance of idols served the devil. Because the law had not been promulgated with authority, they could not anticipate God as judge.

For the greater part of the world did not know that God would be judge. Very few were those over whom death did not reign. Those over whom it did reign, after this death—which is called the first—were excluded from the second death, for future punishment and destruction.

But those over whom it did not reign, because they had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, were preserved in hope for the Savior’s coming, in a state of freedom.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] Some manuscripts read: “for the Savior’s coming for liberation.” Others, together with the edition, differ among themselves: many manuscripts and the old edition read *adventu* (“by the coming”), while the remaining manuscripts read more suitably *adventui* (“for the coming”). The Roman edition alone has *adventus* (“the coming”).]

Thus it is read concerning Abraham: although he was in the underworld, he was nevertheless separated by a great interval, so that there was a great chasm between the righteous and sinners (Luke 16:26).

If there was a great chasm between the righteous and sinners,

[Note: [Col. 0095D] Gill’s edition and the Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, read: “how much more would there be refreshment for the pious and righteous?” The old edition and the remaining manuscripts read: “how much more, so that there would be refreshment for the righteous.”]

how much more was there a distinction among the ungodly, so that the righteous would have refreshment, sinners anguish, and the ungodly burning, so that before the judgment it would not be hidden what each person deserved?

[Col. 0095B] Accordingly, death reigned over them because it saw that the works of its cunning had benefited them toward punishment, as enemies. For it was not hidden from Satan that the human being had been made in the world for the purpose of proclaiming the dominion of the one God, which Satan transgressed.

And if the Greek text does not express the matter so cautiously—for it is written in this way: that death also reigned over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression—it seems to encompass everything here. Since death, that is, dissolution, was brought about through the envy of the devil, it says that death reigned even over those who did not sin, because they die, which is Satan’s desire.

But if this were true, it would not have been appropriate to say, “Death reigned from Adam to Moses,” if it reigns over all from the beginning to the end. Or perhaps he established stages, so that it reigned from Adam to Moses, from Moses to Christ, and from Christ to the end. But what usefulness would this expression have, since he is not shown to have spoken even in this way?

For he said: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses,” because the law had not been revealed, so that once the law had been given, people might live under its authority, knowing what they should avoid, lest death reign over them.

Therefore, can it be said that death reigned over the person who, before the law, followed by the guidance of nature what the law later commanded? Consider what is written concerning him: “Sin was not reckoned when there was no law.” And he added: “But death reigned from Adam to Moses”—that is, during the very time when there was no law.

It follows that, since death reigned before the law was given, it is said to have reigned over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, as we mentioned above. For just as, after the law was given, death reigned over those who served idols or fornication, despising the lawgiver, so before the law, death certainly did not reign over those who anticipated the meaning of the law and honored its author.

For this reason it is said to have reigned: because knowledge of the one God had vanished from the earth. Finally, the law began in this way: “I am,” he says, “the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods besides me, and you shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness” (Exodus 20:2).

The law was therefore given so that death would not reign, and so that, with former sins abolished, the human race might obey the one God. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it” (Romans 6:12).

By these words he shows that even now death reigns if the law is despised. For what is the reign of death except that its will is done, while it commands to the destruction of the one who obeys it? The will of that dominion is the root of idolatry.

And yet this is imposed upon us from Greek manuscripts as though the Greek manuscripts themselves did not differ from one another. This is the work of a contentious spirit. Since one cannot use one’s own authority to win a victory, one adulterates the words of the law, asserting one’s own meaning as though it were the words of the law, so that authority rather than reason appears to prescribe.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] The Roman edition reads: “Furthermore, it is established by certain Latin copies once translated from ancient Greek manuscripts, which the simplicity of earlier times preserved and has preserved incorrupt. But after, when minds had departed from concord and heretics began to disturb them with questions, many things were changed,” etc. The old edition and the manuscripts agree with us, except that the same edition and a few manuscripts read *dissidentibus* (“disagreeing”) instead of *discedentibus* (“having departed”), less appropriately.]

Furthermore, it is established that certain Latin copies were once translated from ancient Greek manuscripts, which the simplicity of the times preserved and proves to have been uncorrupted. But after minds had departed from concord and heretics had begun to trouble them with questions, many things were changed to suit human understanding, so that the letters would contain what seemed right to human beings. Hence the Greeks themselves also possess different manuscripts.

I consider this to be true when reason, history, and authority are all observed. For even today Latin manuscripts are criticized in which the passages are found as the ancients set them down—Tertullian, Victorinus, and Cyprian.

The kingdom of death therefore first began to be destroyed in Judea, because “God is known in Judea” (Psalm 75:2). Now, however, it is being destroyed daily among all nations, while to a great extent children of the devil become children of God.

Thus death did not reign over everyone, but over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, as I mentioned above. Adam is the type of the one to come because even then God decreed in the mystery that through one Christ he would repair what had become sin through one Adam,

[Note: [Col. 0096D] So read most manuscripts. Several others, and all editions, read: “what had been transgressed.” The Corbie manuscript, however, reads: “sin had increased through transgression.”]

as it is said in the Apocalypse of the Apostle John: “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8).

Finally, he added:

(Verses 15.) But the gift is not like the trespass.

Since he said that one Adam is the type of one Christ, lest anyone think that he meant Adam’s causation to be of the same kind as Christ’s, he therefore says: “But the gift is not like the trespass,” because Adam is a type of Christ only in this respect: what one person sinned, one person corrected.

For if many died through the trespass of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for many. That is, if many died through the trespass of one, imitating his transgression, much more did the grace and gift of God abound for those who flee to it.

More people receive grace than died through Adam’s trespass. Therefore it is clear that he did not refer to the death that is common to all, because absolutely everyone dies, yet not everyone receives grace. Nor is it signified that death reigned over everyone, but over those who died through Adam’s trespass—that is, those whom he says sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “whom he asserts sinned in the transgression resembling Adam’s.”]

These are the ones of whom he says that many died through one person’s trespass, while the grace of God abounded for many. For the grace of God abounded both among those who are said to have died through Adam’s trespass, by sinning in the same way, and among those who did not sin in this likeness of Adam’s transgression.

Because of the ancestral sin, by God’s sentence they were in the underworld; but the grace of God abounded in the Savior’s descent, granting forgiveness to all and raising them triumphantly to heaven.

(Verses 16.) And the gift is not like what came through one sin. For judgment came from one trespass to condemnation, but the gift came from many trespasses to justification.

The difference is plain. Those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression were condemned because of Adam’s one sin; but the grace of God through Christ justified human beings not from one trespass but from many, granting them remission of sins.

He says this to magnify the mercy of God and Christ: although many are held by Adam’s trespass under the second death in the lower underworld, the gift of God’s grace, although it would have been just to punish them, not only forgives them but justifies them.

(Verses 17.) For if, through the trespass of one, death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift and of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

It must be observed that the meaning is one and does not differ at all. For he says that death reigned, not that it reigns, because those who understood God’s judgment through the law were removed from its dominion.

It reigned because, before the law was revealed, the fear of God was absent from the earth. The superior meaning, therefore, is this: since death reigned from Adam to Moses over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, much more will grace reign through the abundance of God’s gift unto life through one Jesus Christ.

For if death reigned, why should grace not reign all the more, since it justifies many more than those over whom death reigned? How much more, then, must grace be believed to reign, since it bestows life through Christ?

(Verses 18.) Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings.

That is, just as through the trespass of one person all deserved condemnation by sinning in the same way, so through the righteousness of one person all who believe will be justified.

If some think that this condemnation is universal, they will likewise have to accept justification as universal. But this is not true, because not everyone believes.

(Verses 19.) For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be made righteous.

Those whom above he called “all,” he here signifies as “many” and “the greater number.” Many followed Adam’s trespass by transgressing, but not all; and many will be made righteous through faith in Christ, but not all.

Therefore death did not reign over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

[Col. 0098B] (Verses 20.) But the law entered alongside, so that the trespass might abound.

One might argue the contrary: “Then the law ought not to have been given, lest sins increase. For if there was less sin before the law, there was no need for the law.”

The law was plainly necessary, so that it might show that sins believed to be committed with impunity were reckoned before God, and so that afterward people might know what they ought to avoid. Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “The law was given for help” (Isaiah 8:20).

For since the seeds of righteousness are in a certain way implanted in nature itself, the law was added so that, by its authority and instruction, natural ability might advance toward producing the fruit of righteousness.

Just as natural endowment perishes unless it has nourishment by which it may be sustained and grow,

[Note: [Col. 0098D] The same Corbie manuscript reads: “unless birth grows warm.”]

so the natural ability for righteousness, unless it has something to look toward and revere, does not easily advance but becomes sick and yields to the sins that come upon it.

For it is weighed down by the habit of sinning, so that it does not grow into fruitfulness, and thus it is extinguished. The law was therefore providentially given for help, as the prophet testifies.

But the people, following their old habit, multiplied their sins. Through the very practice of sinning they began to sin more than they had sinned before. Thus it came about that, when the law was given, sins were not diminished but increased.

The Apostle shows what resulted from the giving of the law, not what the law itself did. How could sins increase through any fault of the law, when the law threatened punishment lest people sin? Yet it is said to have entered so that sin might abound.

The explanation is true: the law entered as though it would be beneficial, and it entered humbly. Later, however, it began to exercise dominion over those whom it had commanded not to sin, while they continued to sin.

The law began to show the abundance of sins, since the things it had forbidden were being committed more frequently than they had been before.

[Note: [Col. 0098D] Certain Paris editions read: “Therefore, for this world, etc.”]

Thus the law was given so that the trespass might abound. For in commending the faith through which sins are certainly erased, the Apostle said that the law made sin abound, as I said above, because it was not given so that sins would be abolished but so that they would abound: it showed sinners both before the law and, after the law, held everyone guilty.

But where sin abounded, grace abounded beyond measure.
