It is clear that when sin abounded, grace abounded beyond measure: when God’s gift came from the promise and covered the sins of all,

[Note: [Col. 0099D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “covered their sins.” Immediately afterward, the Amerbach edition and not a few manuscripts read *profecisse doceat* (“teaches that it has advanced”), whereas Erasmus and later editions, together with other manuscripts, have the more suitable *profecisse doleat* (“grieves that it has advanced”).]

so that the devil’s envy might grieve that it had accomplished nothing.

For when the law had been given for the benefit of humanity, the devil brought it about, by persuading people to do what was unlawful, that what had been given for their benefit should work in the opposite direction. Since the commandments were despised,

[Note: [Col. 0099D] The old edition reads: “so that not benefit from the law, but the commendation of God’s grace, would proceed to judgment for punishment.” The manuscripts and the Roman edition agree with our reading, except that some of them have “and punishment” instead of “for punishment.”]

the result was not benefit from the law but judgment leading to punishment.

Then the just and merciful God, in order to empty the devil’s glory—which he had sought from the human being he had conquered—decreed that his Son would come and forgive all sins, so that the joy produced by the gift of grace would be greater than the grief produced by sin.

The joy of God’s gift also benefits those over whom Satan could not triumph. For this reason grace abounded beyond measure over the sin that Satan had persuaded people to commit.

[Col. 0099B] (Verses 21.) So that, just as sin reigned unto death, grace might also reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Sin reigned when it saw its work advancing in sinners toward death, in which it gloried.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Some manuscripts read: “In the same way grace also reigns, and makes them disobedient to itself, while those to whom it has shown mercy conduct themselves rightly, destined to become heirs through Christ, just as through Adam they had been subject to destruction. What then shall we say?”]

In the same way grace also reigns through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. Just as sin began through Adam and reigned, so grace reigns through Christ.

Grace reigns through righteousness if, having received the remission of sins, we follow righteousness. Then, when grace sees that it has fruit in the good whom it has redeemed, it reigns unto eternal life, knowing that we will become eternal.

Grace therefore abounds beyond measure, because sin reigned for a time, while grace reigns forever. For the kingdom belongs to God, with grace reigning, just as the devil’s kingdom existed with sin reigning.

Nevertheless, he refers everything to Christ, so that all the grace of God may be learned from Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] The Roman edition alone reads: “may be said to come from Christ.”]

He therefore responds to the preceding meaning by saying:

## CHAPTER VI

(Verses 1.) What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means.

That is: Must we continually sin so that God’s gift may abound by covering our sins, and so that, always hoping for the remission of sins because God is merciful, we may prefer Christ’s grace?

Certainly not. God has had mercy on us through Christ for this very purpose: that, no longer sinning, we might cause both our merit and God’s grace to reign in us.

For he removes the reign of God’s grace and hands himself over to sin who returns to the old person—that is, to the practice of his former life. We received mercy for two reasons: so that the devil’s reign might be excluded, and so that God’s dominion might be proclaimed to those who were ignorant of it, thereby acquiring dignity for us through this very act.

(Verses 2.) For we who have died to sin, how shall we still live in it?

He says this because, while we were living in sin, we were dead before God. For the person who sins lives to sin, just as the person who does not sin lives to God.

When God’s grace came through Christ, and through faith the spiritual washing regenerated us, we began to live to God and to be dead to sin, which is the devil. Yet to die to sin means to be freed from sin and to become a servant of God.

Therefore, having died to sin, let us not return to our former evils, lest we live to sin again and, dying to God and losing our dignity, incur the punishment we escaped.

(Verses 3.) Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

He says this so that we may know that, having been baptized, we must no longer sin, because when we are baptized, we die together with Christ.

This is what it means to be baptized into his death: there all our sins die, so that, renewed and having laid aside death, we may appear to rise again into life, reborn.

Just as Christ, having died to sin, rose again, so we too may have the hope of resurrection through baptism. Baptism, therefore, is the death of sin, so that another birth may follow—one that, while the bodily structure remains, renews the human being in mind, burying the oldness of every evil act.

(Vers. 4.) For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the power of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. In saying this, he also signifies what comes first: that Christ raised his body from the dead, for he himself is the power of God the Father, as he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But, he says, “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21); and he rose into a new life, which now knows no death. It is called “new” because it was given by Christ, namely, Christian discipline. We, however, were buried with Christ through baptism (Col. 2:12), so that thereafter we might follow this life in which Christ rose. Baptism, therefore, is the pledge and image of resurrection, so that, remaining now in Christ’s commandments, we may not turn back again to what has passed. For whoever dies no longer sins: death is the end of sin. It is therefore celebrated through water, so that, just as water washes away bodily dirt, so we too may believe that through baptism we have been spiritually cleansed and renewed from every sin, so that what is incorporeal may be washed invisibly.

[Col. 0100D] (Vers. 5.) For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be in the likeness of his resurrection. He says that we can rise happily if we have been planted in the likeness of his death—that is, if, laying aside all vices in baptism and being transferred into a new life, we thereafter do not sin. Through this we shall likewise be like his resurrection; for the likeness of death will produce a corresponding resurrection. The apostle John recalls this in his letter, saying: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2)—that is, we shall rise immortal and glorious. Nor will this likeness mean that there is no difference at all; it will be likeness in the glory of the body, not in the nature of divinity.

(Vers. 6 and 7.) Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we might no longer serve sin. He joins together and repeats many things in order to teach the baptized that they must no longer sin—especially so that they may not return to idolatry, the gravest crime and the source of every error, and thus lose the grace received from God through Christ. He therefore calls the past deeds the “old man,” because just as a “new man” is called new through faith and a pure life, so the “old man” is characterized by unbelief and evil deeds.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “The new man through Christ,” that is, one who has his faith and practices a pure life, is called new, and so forth.]

He calls these deeds crucified—that is, dead—so that the body of sin might be destroyed, which means all crimes. For he calls all sins together a “body,” which he says is destroyed through a good life and the catholic faith.

(Vers. 8.) But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with him (Gal. 5:24). It is clear that those who have crucified the flesh—that is, the world with its vices and desires—die to the world and die together with Christ, and are likewise fashioned for eternal and saving life, so that they may deserve to become like Christ in glory. But the flesh, that is, the body, is crucified when its desires are trampled underfoot.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “which remain in it”; for sins are created from transgression, and so forth.]

These desires began through the transgression of the first man, while sin remains in the flesh; for in the flesh the devil is crucified, since he is the one who deceives through the flesh. “Flesh,” therefore, sometimes means the world, that is, the elements; sometimes the human body; and sometimes the soul itself when it follows bodily vices.

(Vers. 9 and 10.) Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and that death will no longer rule over him. For the death that he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life that he lives, he lives to God. He displays the security of eternity in the resurrection of the Savior—a destiny reached if one strives after the better life. Whoever lives to God by doing good truly lives, because he possesses eternal life.

(Vers. 11.) So you too must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. He speaks in this way to teach that one cannot die to sin and live to God in any other way than by placing all hope in Christ. He calls him “our Lord” so that nothing belonging to the Law may contribute to the attainment of salvation in the age to come, when one lives to God only through Christ.

(Vers. 12.) Therefore, do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires. The body is mortal because of the cause of Adam’s transgression; through faith in Christ it is believed to become immortal. To reach this promise, he says that sin must not be obeyed, so that it may not reign in our mortal body. It reigns when it commands. But if it does not reign, this body will not appear to be mortal, because it is held in the hope of eternity. He did not call the body mortal because of dissolution, but because of the punishment of Gehenna; the one who is to be sent into Gehenna is called mortal. For those who obey sin do not escape the second death of hell.

[Note: The old edition, together with not a few manuscripts, reads “the death of hell”; Gill in the margin and the Roman edition in the text, with some manuscripts, read “the second death”; but the manuscripts Gem., Prat., Mich., Vall., Thuan., and Remig. read “the second death of hell.”]

The Savior has delivered believers in him from this death. By saying “mortal body,” therefore, he signified the whole human being, because those who obey sin are called mortal. For he says: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:4), that is, the whole person; no one will be judged without a body.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “No one will be judged without cause in the body.”]

[Col. 0102B] (Vers. 13.) Nor present your members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. He shows that the devil attacks us with our own darts; for our sins give him an opportunity, so that, when God abandons us, he may receive power to mock and kill us. Therefore we must restrain our members from every work of unrighteousness, so that, when our enemy is found unarmed, he may be subjected. He did not say, “Present your bodies,” but “your members”; for error is committed through the ministering members, not through the whole body.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “For through the members, as sins dictate, the ministry is led astray, or it is armed by its ministers.”]

But present yourselves to God as those who are alive from the dead. He signifies death as ignorance and unbelief together with an evil life, because life consists in knowing God through Christ. Since no one comes into life without a parent, and since all things have come from God into life through Christ, the one who does not know God to be the parent of all things through Christ is not said to possess life. He is regarded as though he did not exist, for he denies his own existence when he thinks he exists without God as his parent. Thus ignorance and a shameful life are death. These vices acquire death for him—not the death common to all, but the death of Gehenna, as I mentioned above—so that knowledge of God the Father and holy conduct may be life, not this life subject to decay, but that of the age to come, which is called eternal. Therefore, he says, present yourselves to God, for through knowing him you have advanced toward salvation, so that, renouncing a dishonorable life, you may be alive from the dead.

61 And your members as weapons of righteousness for God. He wishes us to govern our conduct with such great restraint that our deeds, advancing God’s righteousness, may provide him with weapons for defending us, not the righteousness of the world. For the world’s righteousness is without faith in Christ, and without that faith there is not life but death. When we provide God with weapons through good works, we make ourselves worthy to be helped by that righteousness, because God’s righteousness rejects the unworthy. For wherever God’s righteousness is, there the Holy Spirit dwells to assist our weakness. Just as we provide weapons to sin when we act badly, so we provide them to righteousness when we conduct ourselves rightly, guarding our members from every disgrace.

(Vers. 14.) For sin will no longer rule over you, since you are not under the Law but under grace. If we walk according to the commandments he gives, he says that sin cannot rule over us; for it rules those who sin.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “For it rules those who sin, because every sinner is a slave of sin, and must be under the Law.”]

When we walk as he commands, we are not under the Law. If we do not sin, we are not under the Law but under grace. But if we sin, we turn back under the Law, and sin will begin to rule over us, because “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). He must therefore be under the Law so long as he does not receive forgiveness; for sin, by the authority of the Law, makes the sinner guilty. Accordingly, the one to whom forgiveness has been given, who guards himself so that he may not sin thereafter, is neither ruled by sin nor under the Law. The authority of the Law ceases in the case of one who has been freed from sin; for those whom the Law holds guilty have been handed over to it by sin. Therefore, the one stripped of sins cannot be under the Law.

(Vers. 15.) What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the Law but under grace? By no means. Since the Law is from God, and therefore this objection might perhaps be raised, he himself proposed it: “If the Law is from God,” he says, “why should we not be under the Law?”

[Note: One edition alone reads: “He raised the objection against himself.” Below, where this same reading is found in some manuscripts and in Gill’s margin, “This he clears up” is given; the old edition, together with other manuscripts, has: “This he recognizes.”]

He clears this up and teaches that, in accordance with the will of God, who is the author of the Law, we have been freed by Christ from being under the Law. Although the Law was rightly given—for it was given both to show before God those who had sinned before the Law and to inspire fear, so that sin would not thereafter be committed—yet, because the human race could not restrain itself from sins through the weakness of its own frailty, it became liable to the death of hell. God, moved by the compassion of his mercy, by which he has always helped the human race, provided through Christ a means by which a remedy might be given to those who had already despaired. Having received forgiveness of sins, freed from the Law that held them liable, relieved and restored, and with God’s help through faith,

[Note: All editions read this way; but, by contrast, all manuscripts unanimously omit the words “through faith.”]

they might resist the vices by which they had previously been overcome. Therefore we did not sin as though we were despising God’s Law; rather, through Christ we followed the providence of God himself.

(Vers. 16.) Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness? Now, lest we profess one thing but do another, and, while we are called servants of God, be found by our deeds to be servants of the devil, he warns and declares that we are servants of the one whose will we fulfill through our works. It is of no small harm to confess God as Lord while serving the devil by our deeds. For God formerly marked and condemned this, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24).

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “And elsewhere it is said.”]

And it is said in the Law: “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7).

(Vers. 17 and 18.) But thanks be to God that, although you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over. By believing in Christ, we have become slaves of righteousness. For we are called servants of the one whom we obey. Since it is right to obey Christ—for he himself is righteousness, and what he commands is just—he therefore says that we have become servants of righteousness from the heart, not from the Law; from free will, not from fear, so that our profession may proceed from the judgment of the mind.

By nature we have been led to faith, not by the Law. In this pattern of teaching we have been formed by the command of God, who fashioned nature. For in nature we possess the capacity to know from whom, through whom, and in whom we were created. The pattern of teaching, therefore, is that into which the Creator has handed us naturally; that is what he said above: “They are a law to themselves” (Rom. 2:14), since they see that what they believe belongs to their nature. Thus what the Law and the prophets proclaimed to the Jews about Christ, the Gentiles confess from the heart.

[Note: All manuscripts read this way, whereas all editions read “confess from the heart”; the Amerbach edition has “confess.”]

For this reason he gives thanks to the Lord: although we were slaves of sin, we obeyed from the heart, believing in Christ, so that we might serve God not through the Law of Moses but through the law of nature.

(Vers. 19.) I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. By mentioning the weakness of the flesh, he indicates that he requires less from human beings than is appropriate in the worship of God. Hence what follows:

For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to iniquity, leading to iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to sanctification. In order to remove from us the occasion of fearing to approach the faith, since it might seem to us unbearable and harsh, he commanded us to serve God by the same measure by which we had previously served the devil. Yet God ought certainly to be served more zealously than the devil, since the one produces salvation and the other condemnation. Nevertheless, the spiritual physician does not demand more from us, lest, while fleeing commandments as though they were burdensome and considering our weakness, we should remain in death. Hence the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you . . . for it is gentle, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29).

(Vers. 20 and 21.) For when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. It is clear that whoever is free from God is a slave of sin; for when he sins, he withdraws from God and comes under sin. What, then, are the fruits of sin, in which we lived while learning the good life, except that we are confounded because we formerly lived shamefully?

[Note: All editions read “in which, while learning”; all manuscripts more suitably read “in which we lived, while learning”; one has “renouncing,” but this gives a faulty sense.]

And not only this: the judgment of the pagans is also shameful and disgraceful, especially that which arose in Phrygia, in which, unless a filthy person takes part, the mute sacrament remains silent and the religious observance grows numb!

[Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read: “Unless filth takes part”; the Roman edition and a few manuscripts read: “Unless filth is involved”; but many other manuscripts read as in the text. Again, instead of “the mute sacrament,” as found in the editions and some manuscripts, other codices read “the moved sacrament,” and others “the spurious sacrament.”]

Behold a freedom full of stains and bound by filth, whose work earns a shameful reward. Its end is death. By “end” he means the outcome of life and deeds, to which either death or life succeeds. But in this passage death is twofold, for one passes from death to death.

(Vers. 22.) But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification, and the end is eternal life. This means that, if we become eager for good deeds after receiving forgiveness of sins, we shall acquire holiness; and our end—that is, our outcome—will be everlasting life. For from this death, which he called the end, we shall pass to life, which has no end.

[Col. 0105B] (Vers. 23.) For the wages of sin is death. He calls death the profit of sin,

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “because sin is death”; the other manuscripts, more suitably, read: “because death comes through sin.”]

because death comes through sin. Accordingly, those who thereafter abstain from sins receive eternal life as their wages, because those who do not sin are strangers to the second death.

But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Just as those who follow sin acquire death, so those who follow the grace of God—that is, the faith of Christ, which grants forgiveness of sins—will have eternal life. Thus they may rejoice that they are released for a time, knowing that they will attain this life, which is free from every weariness and has no succession. Holy Simeon desired this and asked to be released from here (Luke 2:29), so that he might go in peace—that is, into the life that suffers no disturbance. And he testifies that this gift was given to us by God through Christ our Lord, so that we may give thanks to God the Father through no other than his Son.

CAPUT VII.

CHAPTER VII

(Vers. 1.) Or do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the Law? To strengthen their minds in divine teaching, he uses the example of human law, so that once again he may persuade them of heavenly things through earthly ones. God is likewise known from the creation of the world, because everything belongs to one author. Although things are diverse, they are nevertheless similar to one another in some respect. The Romans therefore know the Law, because they are not barbarians; but they have grasped natural righteousness partly from themselves and partly from the Greeks. For laws were brought to the Romans from Athens, just as they were brought to the Greeks from the Hebrews. Before Moses, the Law was not unknown, but it had neither order nor authority.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read this way. But many others have the following: “Partly from the Greeks and partly from the Hebrews; although the Law was not unknown before Moses, there was neither order nor authority; for the order of the Law was brought to the Romans from Athens.” Some others read: “Partly from the Greeks, just as the Greeks did from the Hebrews; for although before Moses . . . . for the laws were brought to the Romans from Athens.”]

He therefore says that he is speaking to those who know the Law:

For the Law rules over a person for as long as he lives.

It is not hidden that the entire life of a human being is subject to the law of nature, which was given to the world. This is the general Law. But now he introduces another, particular law—although it too is general, but because it is not accepted by everyone it becomes particular—through which he wishes to prove his assertion. He wants to convey the truth gradually. Thus he says:

(Vers. 2.) For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law of her husband as long as her husband lives. This law comes from the Gospel, not from Moses, nor from earthly righteousness. Learning some things under the guidance of nature and others from the Law of Moses, they were made perfect through the Gospel of Christ. By the following example he more clearly persuades us that Christianity has been stripped of the law of works, not of every law, and that it is no longer advantageous to be under the Law, lest returning under the Law should nullify the grace of God. For the grace of God freed the human being from the Law so that he might serve God in the spirit—that is, in the mind.

Just as a woman, when her husband has died, is freed from the law of her husband but not from the law of nature, so those who have been freed by the grace of God from the Law under which they were held guilty are no longer subject to it. The Law has died for them, so that, joined to Christianity, they may not be adulterers.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Freed from the Law, they will not be under it, from which they were held guilty; nor is it any longer advantageous to be under the Law, so that, as death . . . .”]

For if the Law lives among them, they are adulterers, and it will profit them nothing to be called Christians, because they will remain liable to punishment. The adulterer will not belong to the Law but to the Gospel: when the Law has died, one is joined to the Gospel, but afterward returns to the Law.

[Note: The same codices read: “For the Law is said to have died when its authority ceases. But if he has died . . . .”]

The Law is said to have died when the one whom it held guilty is unknown to it, because the authority of the Law has ceased.

(Vers. 3.) Therefore, if her husband has died, she is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is joined to another man. Those who have been removed from the Law, received forgiveness of sins, and joined to the Gospel are not adulterers against the Law, because the Law has died for them. But if, while observing the Law, they think they are approaching the Gospel, they will be guilty and adulterers, because they have joined themselves to the faith while the Law remains alive, and so will be adulterers in both relationships.

(Vers. 4.) Therefore, my brothers, you too have been put to death to the Law through the body of Christ. Since our Savior allowed his body to be crucified by the devil, knowing that it would be for us and against him, he therefore says that we were saved through the body of Christ. To die to the Law is to live to God, because the Law rules over sinners. Whoever is forgiven his sins dies to the Law—that is, he is freed from the Law.

Thus we obtain this benefit through the body of Christ. For by handing over his body, the Savior conquered death and condemned sin. The devil sinned in him when he killed the innocent one who knew no sin at all. While he was defending the human being as his own because of sin, he was found guilty in the very one whom he accused. As a result, all who believe in Christ are rescued from the Law, sin having been removed.

[Note: The Carn manuscript reads: “Because sin, having been bound . . . from which he was bound.”]

For sin, which is the devil, has been conquered through the body of Christ and no longer has authority over those who belong to him by whom it was conquered. Since Christ did not sin but was killed as though he were guilty, he conquered sin through sin; that is, he condemned the devil by the very sin that the devil committed against him. He also erased the bond that had been decreed because of Adam’s sin (Col. 2:14), when he rose from the underworld, giving believers in him this pattern: they could not be held by the second death.

Accordingly, we have died to the Law through the body of Christ. Whoever has not died to the Law is guilty, and whoever is guilty cannot escape the second death.

So that you may belong to another, to him who rose from the dead, so that we may bear fruit for God. He says this because we died to the Law for the purpose that thereafter we might belong solely to Christ as his servants; and this will be to bear fruit for God. Whoever remains in God’s grace is acquired by God and made worthy of the promised resurrection.

(Vers. 5.) For when we were in the flesh. Although he is in the flesh—that is, in the body—he denies that he is “in the flesh,” because the one who follows something forbidden by the Law is said to be in the flesh. Being in the flesh is therefore understood in many ways. Every unbeliever is in the flesh, that is, carnal; the Christian who lives under the Law is in the flesh; the person who places hope in human beings is in the flesh; the one who misunderstands Christ is in the flesh; and any Christian who leads a luxurious life is in the flesh.

In this passage, however, we should understand being in the flesh in this way: before faith we were in the flesh. We lived under sin; that is, following carnal perceptions, we were subject to vices and sins. The perception of the flesh means not believing spiritual things: that a virgin gave birth without intercourse with a man, that a human being is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, and that the soul, released from its union with the flesh, will rise again in the flesh. Whoever doubts these things is in the flesh. Hence:

The vices of sins, he says, which are revealed through the Law, were at work in our members so that they might bear fruit for death. It is clear that the one who does not believe acts under sin and is dragged captive into admitting vices, so that he may produce fruit for the second death. For death makes a profit when sin is committed.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “When sin is committed in the members.” “He rightly says that vices are at work,” and so forth.]

He nevertheless says that vices are at work in the members, not in the body, so that he would not provide an opportunity for those who treat the body wrongly. The tongue is accused in abusive speech, the hand is reproved in theft, and the ears are condemned in one who pretends not to hear; and likewise in other matters. Although these things come forth from the heart,

[Note: The words “as the Lord testifies in the Gospel” were absent from all editions and some manuscripts, but have been restored from several others.]

as the Lord testifies in the Gospel (Matt. 15:18), they are nevertheless carried out through the service of the members in deeds. This discussion concerns Jews and those who are called Christians but wish to live under the Law, so that, learning that they are carnal, they may withdraw from the Law.

He does not demonstrate that the vices of sins, which he says rule over those living in the flesh, are produced by the Law; rather, he demonstrates that they are revealed by the Law. The Law is the indicator of sin, not its mother; it makes sinners guilty.

(Vers. 6.) But now we have been released from the Law of death, in which we were held. We have been released from the Law when we received forgiveness of sins; for it no longer has power over us. It rules over unbelievers and sinners. It is called the Law of death because it punishes the guilty and puts sinners to death. It is therefore not evil but just. Although what the Law inflicts is evil for those who suffer it, the Law itself is not evil, because it justly brings wrath. Thus it is not evil toward sinners but just; toward the good, however, it is spiritual.

Who could doubt that it is spiritual to forbid sin? But since it could not save a human being by forgiving sins, the law of faith was given, which would free believers from the domination of the Law, so that those whom the Law held guilty for death might restore themselves to life. For the Law is the Law of death precisely for those upon whom it brings wrath because of sin.

[Col. 0108B] So that we may serve in newness of spirit and not in the oldness of the letter. Here he is thought to be touching upon the Law, which he certainly makes inferior by comparison with the law of faith; nevertheless, he does not judge it hostile. For this is why he says that we have been rescued from the Law of death: so that we may serve the law of faith, which has brought us saving protection that the old Law could not provide. Otherwise we would seem to make the benefit of grace void by serving the old Law.

The old Law is not a name for crime, but for time or age; it has grown old because it has ceased. The Law of the spirit is the law of faith itself, because faith is in the soul. It is not learned through works but believed in the heart. The mind itself understands that what it believes belongs to its nature; it is not seen with the eyes or touched with the hands. The gifts that are hoped for are not visible or earthly but spiritual.

The old Law was therefore formed on tablets of stone, whereas the law of the spirit is written spiritually on the tablets of the heart, so that it may be eternal.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “But the letters . . . are completed . . . restrained from evil error.”]

The letter of the old Law is consumed by age. There is also another interpretation of the law of the spirit: the earlier Law restrained people from evil deeds, but this Law, when it says that one must not sin even in the heart, is called the law of the spirit because it makes the whole person spiritual.

(Vers. 7.) What then shall we say? Is the Law sin? By no means. Since he calls it the Law of death, rejoices that we have been rescued from it, and denies that we serve God in it, someone might think that he was asserting that it is unjust. He dispels this suspicion when he says: “By no means.”

But I did not know sin except through the Law. The Law, therefore, is not sin but the indicator of sin. It revealed both sins that had lain hidden and the fact that they would not go unpunished before God. Once this had been discovered, the human being became guilty; and for that reason he does not seem to give thanks to the Law. For who willingly welcomes someone who announces that punishment threatens him?

But he gives thanks to the law of faith, because the one who was made guilty through the Law of Moses has been reconciled to God through the law of faith. Yet the former Law is also just and good, for it is good to reveal impending danger. But he gives greater thanks to the one through whom he has been rescued from danger and lives.

65 For I would not have known desire unless the Law had said in Exodus: “You shall not desire” (Exod. 20:17). He did not distinguish this desire from sin but joined them together, signifying that, although there had not even been a suspicion that this was forbidden before God, “I came to know,” he says, “that it was sin.” Speaking in his own person, he treats a general case. The Law therefore forbids desire, which, because it brings pleasure, was not thought to be sin. The matter seemed simple: to desire something belonging to one’s neighbor. But the Law disclosed that this was sin. For worldly people think that nothing is so unpunished and peaceful as pleasure.

(Vers. 8.) Therefore, taking an opportunity through the commandment, sin worked in me every desire. By saying “every desire,” he signifies all sins. Above he mentioned desire in relation to the Law; now, adding the remaining vices, he says that every desire was produced in the human being through the impulse of the devil, whom he signifies as sin. Thus the Law that had been given for the human being’s benefit came to be turned against him.

For when the devil saw that help had been provided through the Law for the human being—whom he rejoiced to hold in his own condition, both because of Adam’s sin and because of his own—he understood that this had been done against him.

[Note: The old editions differ from the Roman edition only in placing the words in another order. Most manuscripts, however, read: “Whom he was pleased to regard as belonging to him by his condition” (some read “his own”) because of Adam’s sin. Others, although corrupt, come closer to the editions; the reading retained here is the one found in the editions.]

When he saw the human being placed under the Law, he was certain that the human being had been removed from his dominion; for the human being had learned how to escape the punishment of hell. From this the devil’s anger against the human being was inflamed, so that he might overturn the Law for him, inducing him to commit what was forbidden, offend God again, and fall once more under the devil’s power. He began not to command but subtly to deceive, because, when the Law had been given, the devil had lost his dominion, knowing that thereafter the human being belonged to God’s judgment.

For without the Law sin was dead. This must be understood in two ways: you should know that the devil is signified in sin, and also sin itself, which is called sin.

[Note: The Roman edition adds: “And this very thing that is called sin.” The devil was said to be dead.]

The devil is said to have been dead because before the Law he had ceased from deceiving the human being, but was as though at rest; for he was secure in his possession of him. He said that sin was dead because it was thought not to be counted before God. Thus, for the human being, it was dead, as though sin could be committed with impunity. For sin was not hidden, as I said above; rather, it was unknown that God would judge.

When the Law was given, sin was revealed to have come back to life. Why did it come back to life, unless because it had lived previously and afterward, through human negligence, was considered dead even while it lived? Sin was thought not to be counted, although it was counted. Thus, what was alive was regarded as dead.

(Vers. 9.) But I was once alive without the Law. What does “without the Law” mean, since the Law has always existed, as I mentioned above, unless that the human being lived without fear of God, secure in the belief that God would not judge human deeds?

But when the commandment came, sin came back to life. He therefore said that sin came back to life in order to signify that it had lived previously. Later, through human negligence, it was considered dead while it lived, just as a false report often arises concerning foreigners.

[Note: Many manuscripts add after “foreigners” the words “not true,” but this is less skillful.]

This therefore signifies that, in the beginning, it was not hidden that sin was counted before God—that is, that it was alive. But when the habit of sinning had obliterated this fact, sin was considered dead, so that the crime was thought to perish together with the person. When the Law was given or restored, sin came back to life among those among whom it had been considered dead; for they began to know that sin was counted against them.

[Col. 0110B] (Vers. 10.) I, however, died. The human being died because he saw himself guilty before God, whereas previously he had thought that he would not be held liable for the things he committed.

And the commandment that had been given for life was found by me to be for death. It is true that the Law was given for life. But when it made the human being guilty not only for past sins but also for future sins, the Law given for life became, as it were, for death.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “The Law given for life was found to be for death,” and so forth.]

But, as I said, this was for the sinner; for those who obey, it contributes to life.

(Vers. 11.) For sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Here understand “sin” as the devil, who is the author of sin. Through the Law he found an opportunity to satisfy his cruelty through the death of the human being. Since the Law threatened sinners,

[Note: The old edition, together with many manuscripts, reads: “The Law ruled”; the Roman edition, together with other manuscripts, reads: “The Law threatened.”]

the human being, at the devil’s instigation, continually committed what was forbidden, offended God, and incurred the vengeance of the Law, so that he was condemned by the very Law that had been given for his benefit. Because the Law had been given against the devil’s will, envy against the human being was inflamed in him, so that he might stain the human being more deeply with sinful pleasures and prevent him from escaping his grasp.

(Vers. 12.) Therefore the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good. So that no suspicion hostile to the Law might remain, he commends it in such a way that he declares it not only just but also holy and good. The Gospel saying demonstrates that “commandment” means the Law. For it says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17).

[Col. 0110D] (Vers. 13.) Did then what is good become death for me? By no means. Truly, by no means; for how could what is proven to be good be understood as death?

But sin, in order that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through what was good. He says that the devil received an opportunity through what was good to work evil against man, when he seduced him to death. For, in order that the things done wickedly before the Law might, through the enticement of desire, be shown to be sins and thereafter avoided, the Law was given and made manifest in writing. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “the Law was given, formed in letters on stones.”] [Col. 0111A] Then Satan was inflamed—through what was good, to be sure; for he saw that provision was being made for man—and suggested to him what was unlawful, so that instead of life from the Law, death might come to him.

This must indeed be attributed to human negligence, which so weakened the strength of its nature through the desire to sin that it could not restrain the suggestions of the adversary. Yet the enemy, whom he signifies by sin, in order that he might appear to be an enemy, received through the Law an opportunity to work death against man. For when he suggested what was unlawful to him, he showed himself to be an enemy. Although he had also procured death for man before the Law—apart from Adam’s first offense—after the Law he devised greater punishments for him in the underworld, where the second death [Col. 0111B] is. For it is a lesser crime to have sinned before the Law was made manifest than after the Law.

So that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure (Gen. XV, 16). What does “beyond measure” mean? It is as though a limit had been assigned to those who offend, even though sinning is not permitted. But these are the words of God, who says: “The sins of the Amorites have not yet been completed” (ibid.). By this He shows that there is a certain measure of offenses; when sinners have filled it, they are judged utterly unworthy of life. Thus also, because Pharaoh had filled up this measure, [Note: Some manuscripts read: “because he had filled this righteous measure.” Not sufficiently correct.] God’s powers and signs were displayed against him, through which the others, terrified, might devote themselves to the benefits of life, so that life might be learned from one who was dead.

But the Apostle is treating another measure: for in order to show that sin under the Law was greater than it had been [Col. 0111C] before the Law, he signifies that, after the Law, through the envy and cunning of Satan, an additional and greater measure of sins had grown beyond that former measure of sins, so that God’s provision became contrary to man, although he ought by fear of the Law not to have sinned at all. Therefore, in order to overcome the devil’s envy and to make His provision effective for man, God changed the order of things, sending the Savior Christ, [Note: Some manuscripts read “who would both crush the devil and liberate man.”] who would both conquer the devil and confirm God’s decrees concerning man.

**(Verse 14.) For we know that the Law is spiritual.** Since he is speaking to those who know the Law, he says: “We know that the Law is spiritual”; for they would not have submitted themselves to the Law unless they recognized it as spiritual. He calls the Law of Moses spiritual, the Law given on tablets. Because it forbids sin, it is spiritual, especially since it forbids the worship of visible and material things. These remarks belong to the commendation of the Law, lest anyone should perhaps think it deserving of blame because it exercised severity against sinners.

**But I am carnal, sold under sin.** He calls a man carnal when he sins. “Sold under sin”: this means that he derives his origin from Adam, who sinned first, and becomes subject to sin through his own offense, as the prophet Isaiah says: “You were sold,” he says, “because of your sins” [Col. 0112A] (Isa. L, 1). For Adam first sold himself, and therefore all his offspring were subjected to sin.

Consequently, man is weak in keeping the precepts of the Law unless he is fortified by divine assistance. Hence he says: “The Law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin”—that is, the Law is firm and just and free from blame, whereas man is fragile and subjected to paternal or personal [Note: Thus some manuscripts, followed by the edition of Gill; other manuscripts and editions read: “and subjected to paternal offense.”] offense, so that he cannot exercise his own power with regard to obedience to the Law.

Therefore one must flee to God’s mercy in order to escape the severity of the Law and, freed from offenses, thereafter resist the enemy with God’s favor. For what does it mean to be subject to sin except to have a body corrupted by the fault of the soul, into which sin inserts itself and drives man, as a captive, to offenses, so that he does its will? Hence, among other things, the Lord says: “The devil comes and takes away what has been sown in their heart, so that they may not be saved” (Luke VIII, 12).

Accordingly, the same Apostle says in another epistle: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12)—and these are plainly Satan’s satellites. For before man’s transgression, before he gave himself over to death, they had no power to approach man’s inner self and implant hostile thoughts. Hence, through his cunning, he contrived to circumvent man by conversation through the serpent (Gen. III, 1).

But after he had circumvented and subdued him, he received power over him, so that he might strike the inner man, joining himself to his mind, with the result that man cannot recognize what in his thought belongs to himself and what belongs to the devil unless he turns to the Law. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “But his first act of cunning was that man should be circumvented …”; this reading is followed by several manuscripts.]

**(Verse 15.) For I do not understand what I do.** He does not understand what he does because he sees that, through the Law, he knows one thing but does another. “For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” Being subject to sin, he does what he does not want.

**(Verse 16.) But if I do what I hate, I agree with the Law.** He proves that the Law rightly forbids, since he confesses that he does unwillingly what the Law forbids. He says that what the Law commands is in accord with his nature, because he declares that what he does contrary to it is hateful to him.

**(Verse 17.) But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.** Since, through the Law, he sees that what he does is forbidden, and agrees that it ought not to be done, he declares that there is another power at whose prompting these things are done—namely, sin. He always calls it “sin,” although it is known to be the devil together with his angels, because these things would not have come about unless the first man had sinned. Therefore it is sin that does all these things. [Note: The Roman edition alone adds “so that it may be understood that it is the devil,” and so forth.]

**(Verse 18.) For I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh.** He does not say, as some think, that the flesh is evil, but that what dwells in the flesh is not good, but sin. How does sin dwell in the flesh, since it is not a substance [Col. 0113A] [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “but a privation of good.”] but the transgression of what is good? Because the body of the first man was corrupted through sin so that it could be dissolved. The corruption caused by sin remains in the body through the condition resulting from the offense, maintaining the force of the divine sentence pronounced upon Adam, which is [Note: All editions read “the sign of the devil … Adam sinned”; all manuscripts agree with the reading in the text.] the sign of the devil, at whose prompting he sinned.

Therefore, because the cause of what happened remains, sin is said to dwell in the flesh. The devil approaches the flesh as though it were his own law and remains, as it were, in sin as sin, because the flesh is now of sin, so that it may deceive man through evil suggestions and prevent him from doing what the Law commands.

**For the desire to do good is present in me.** He asserts that what the Law commands is so good that he says it naturally pleases him and that he wishes to do it. **But I do not find the power to accomplish the good.** What the Law commands pleases him, therefore, and there is a will to do it; but the power and strength to fulfill it are lacking, because he is so pressed by the power of sin that he cannot go where he wishes, nor is he able to resist it, since another is lord of his power.

For man is now weighed down by the habit of sinning and more easily succumbs to sin than to the Law, although he knows that the Law teaches what is good. Even if he wishes to do good, habit presses upon him, with the enemy assisting.

**(Verse 19.) For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I do.** He repeats this frequently in order to make it clear. This, then, is what was said above: that, as a captive, through the causes mentioned earlier, he is compelled to do what sin wants. [Note: The Roman edition, with some manuscripts, reads “he is compelled to do the sin he does not want.” This is not at all a bad reading; nevertheless, the reading of the other editions and manuscripts must not be abandoned: “sin” here is in the nominative case and has the same meaning as “the devil.”]

**(Verse 20.) But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.** This is what he mentioned above: pressed down and subjected to sin, he accomplishes not his own will but that of sin. [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “That is, the devil, whom he mentioned above.” A few verses later the same manuscript reads “through fault and desire” instead of “through fault and negligence.”]

But because he says that man sins unwillingly, should he therefore appear free from guilt, since he does what he does not want under the pressure of a powerful force? Certainly not; these things began through his own fault and negligence. For since he gave himself over to sin by his consent, sin rightly exercises dominion over him: it first persuades him, [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads “so that, once vice has been overcome, it may already rule”; several others read “so that vice may already rule.”] so that, once he has been overcome, it may rule.

But the Apostle explains these matters in order to place God’s grace first: he shows from what great evils God has liberated man, what destruction he derives from Adam, and what benefits he has obtained through Christ, so that he might demonstrate that even the Law could not help the one whom it could not save.

**(Verse 21.) I find, therefore, this law: when I wish to do good, evil is present in me.** He asserts that the Law of Moses agrees with his will against the sin dwelling in the flesh, which compels him to do something other than what both the man and the Law desire.

**(Verse 22.) For I delight in the Law of God according to the inner man.** He says that the mind takes pleasure in what is handed down by the Law; this is the inner man. For sin does not dwell in the mind but in the flesh, which derives from the origin of sinful flesh, and through transmission all flesh becomes sinful.

For if the soul too were derived by transmission and sin dwelt in it— [Note: Some manuscripts read: “and itself dwelt in it.” Sin is not permitted to dwell in the mind because of the free choice of the will. “Therefore in the flesh …”] —the soul of Adam sinned more than his body; but the sin of the soul corrupted the body. Sin therefore dwells in the flesh as though at the doors of the soul, so that it may not allow the soul to go where it wishes. But if it dwelt in the soul, man would never know himself. Now, however, he knows himself and delights in the Law of God. [Note: The same manuscripts read: “If it dwelt there, it would disturb him so that he would not know himself at all.”]

**(Verse 23.) But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.** He mentions two laws, of which he says that he sees one in his members—that is, in the outer man, who is flesh or body. [Col. 0114B] This is the hostile law, the one that fights against the mind, dragging it captive into the condition of sin, lest, when it enters farther, it find an advocate.

The other is the law of the mind, which is the Law of Moses, or the natural law that is in the mind. It is oppressed by the violence of sin, through its own negligence, because, while it loves vices, it subjects itself to sin so that it may be held captive by the very habit. For habit rules man.

He names four laws: first, the spiritual law, which is also natural, which was reformed through Moses and established with authority; this is the Law of God. Next, the law of the mind, agreeing with the Law of God. Third, the law of sin, which he says dwells in the members as a result of the transgression of the first man. Fourth, the law that is seen in the members when it suggests evil and then withdraws.

But these laws appear to be repeated four times, although there are two—that is, good and evil. For the law of the mind is itself the spiritual law, whether the law of Moses, which is called the Law of God. The law of sin is the same as the law that he says is seen in the members, which contradicts the law of our mind.

**(Verses 24, 25.) Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.** He calls man wretched because he is born under sin. Is the man who has entered into this inheritance of transgression, carrying sin—an enemy—with him, [Note: All editions read “having a guest with him”; all manuscripts read “having an enemy with him.”] through which Satan has access to him, not truly wretched? Adam constructed steps by which the despoiler might climb to his sons, unless the most merciful Lord, moved by compassion, had given His grace through Christ, [Note: Thus the majority of the better manuscripts; others and the editions read “so that, as it was revealed …,” which is not sufficiently correct.] so that the human race, raised up through the remission of sins received, might thereafter recover its senses, with sin restrained and condemned.

For, freed from evils and purified, man can resist the adversary with the power received against him, while being assisted by God. Here he introduces a third and superior law of faith, which he also calls grace. Yet it derives its origin from the spiritual law, because through it man has been liberated. Since Moses gave the Law, and the Lord also gave it, there are said to be two, although one is understood insofar as its meaning and providence are concerned. The former initiates salvation; the latter brings it to completion.

But I am not speaking of that part of the Law which concerns new moons, circumcision, and foods; I mean the part that pertains to God’s mystery and discipline. Thus, through the grace of God, man has been liberated through Christ from this body of death. He calls “death” the death which, as he showed above, was devised through sin for the destruction of man in the underworld and is called the second death. The body of death, however, is all sins; for many sins form one body, each like a member, devised by one author, from which man, rescued by the grace of God through baptism, has escaped the death mentioned above.

For he would not say that, while placed in a bodily body, he had been rescued from that very body. Rather, he called “body” that which, as he indicated above, is destroyed through baptism and observance of the Law. And when he says “from the body of death,” he shows that there is another body that is not of death.

**Therefore I myself serve the Law of God with my mind.** When he says “the Law of God,” he also signifies the Law of Moses [Note: The Roman edition alone adds “and of Christ.” The Corbie, Thuane, and Remigian manuscripts gather the following passage much more briefly as follows: “I who have been delivered from the flesh of death according to the foregoing meaning serve the Law of God with my mind or soul. For now the mind is free …”] and of Christ. **But with the flesh, the law of sin.** “I myself”—that is, I who have been liberated from the body of death—am in the body. How has he been liberated from the body of death unless he has been liberated from all evils? For the remission of sins removes all sins.

Liberated, therefore, from the body of death by the grace of God through Christ, he serves the Law of God with his mind [Col. 0115C] or soul, but with the flesh he serves the law of sin—that is, the devil, who, through the flesh subjected to him, introduces evil suggestions into the soul.

Since man is twofold, composed of flesh and soul, [Note: The Roman edition reads “composed of flesh and soul.”] he says that he serves the Law of God with his mind, because the soul is devoted to God and, having recovered control of itself, can resist the sin that operates through the flesh. For because the flesh was corrupted and subjected to death, although it had been made such that through companionship and union with the soul it would not die, it received desires and transfers them as a kind of burden to the soul, so that the soul too is weighed down. But what rejects that death? The death of the grace of God. [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “transfers to the mind a kind of honor” (some manuscripts: “once”); the others, and the Roman edition, have the reading in the text, except that the Roman edition prefers “so that it might also merit.” Immediately afterward the Roman edition reads: “But because the grace of God rejected that death, he says …” instead of “But what rejects that death? The grace of God.” The manuscripts read as in the text, except that they have “who” where, following the old edition, we have retained “what.” The death itself is the death of Christ, the grace of God.]

**With my mind I serve the Law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin, as has been said.** For now the mind is free and, having been restored to a good habit, can, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit, despise evil suggestions; authority has been restored to it, by which it dares to resist the enemy.

For one who is no longer subject to him cannot be searched out against his will. [Note: All editions read “to be examined in vices”; all manuscripts read “to be examined unwillingly.”] But the flesh, because it has no judgment and is incapable of discernment—for its nature is brutish—cannot close the entrance to the enemy, preventing him from entering when he comes and suggesting what is contrary to the soul. Hence he says: “With the flesh I serve the law of sin.”

Since one man consists of flesh and soul, in that part by which he understands he serves God; in the other, by which he is foolish, he serves the law of sin. If man had remained in the condition in which he was made, the enemy would not have had power to approach his flesh and whisper what was contrary to the soul.

But so that the whole man might not be completely restored by the grace of Christ to his former condition, the sentence pronounced upon Adam stood in the way (Gen. III, 17); for it would have been unjust to annul a sentence rightly pronounced. Therefore, while the sentence remained, God’s providence found a remedy, so that the salvation which man had lost through his own fault might be restored to him; [Note: Some manuscripts read “so that he might believe that he had been reborn here.” Further below, where all manuscripts and the old edition read “lest the first origin …,” the Roman edition had substituted “so that the first …” and so forth.] so that, once healed, he might believe that his adversary, defeated by the power of Christ, would not dare to claim man for himself, the sentence of the first death having been pierced through, and the race of Adam having been united, lest he be restored to the workmanship of his first origin, now remaining wholly immortal.

## CHAPTER VIII

**(Verses 1, 2.) Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh.** It is true that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, serving the Law [Note: The Corbie manuscript and some others read “there will be no condemnation for those who are Christians.” In the following verse, however, the Roman edition, with some manuscripts, reads “serving in devotion of mind.”] of God attentively.

**For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has liberated me from the law of sin and death.** He demands security for man through the grace of God, so that he need not fear the devil’s suggestions, provided that he rejects them. For they will do man no harm at the second death, because the law of faith—that is, of the Spirit—has liberated man from the second death, sin having been condemned.

The fact that sin remains in the flesh no longer harms man, provided that he resists it, remembering God’s assistance. Indeed, the one who crushes the counsels of sin remaining in the flesh is to be crowned; for great skill is required to avoid the ambushes of an enemy within one’s own household.

The law of the Spirit of life, therefore, is itself the law of faith. The Law of Moses too is spiritual, because it forbids sin; yet it is not a law of life, because it cannot remit sins to those liable to death [Note: All editions read “so that it may give life to the dead”; nearly all written manuscripts read “to those who are going to die.”], so as to give life to those who are going to die.

But this law, because it both does not desire sin and recalls man from death, is called the law of the Spirit of life. It does not consist in the letter but in the Spirit, because it is believed with the heart, and what is believed is spirit. Thus this Law in Christ Jesus—that is, through faith in Christ—liberates the believer from the law of sin and death.

The law of sin is the law which he says dwells in the members and strives to persuade them to what is contrary. The law of death is the Law of Moses, because it puts sinners to death. For in another epistle, among other things, he says concerning the authority of the Law: “If the ministry of death, formed in stones, was in glory” (II Cor. III, 7).

It is therefore not surprising that the Law is called both spiritual and a law of death, since the Gospel is likewise so called. For elsewhere, among other things, he says: “To some an odor of life unto life, to others an odor of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 16).

For those whom the reputation of virtues, or the sight or hearing of deeds, attracted to faith, the Gospel was an odor of life. But for those whose understanding was inflamed by the power of these deeds to oppose them, the preaching of faith was an odor of death. [Note: Not a few manuscripts read “the transgression of faith.”]

Although faith is one, therefore, it produces diversity among men, just as the sun, although one, melts wax but hardens mud. In whatever manner someone has received the fragrance of faith in his mind, so will he progress through it.

But someone may say: If faith produces the same result as the Law, why is it not also called, in part, a law of death? For it puts unbelievers to death. But this is not so. Faith was given to justify those who flee to it, so that it might remit the sins of those whom the Law holds guilty, and so that those who act under faith might be free from sin; for those who act under the Law are held liable.

Those, therefore, who do not obey faith are not killed by faith but by the Law, because those who do not approach faith remain guilty under the Law. Accordingly, all who receive the words of faith with an evil disposition remain in death.

Let us now see what difference there is between calling it the spiritual law and calling it the law of the Spirit. It is called the spiritual law because it gives commandments through which one does not sin, since the one who does not sin is called spiritual, [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “an imitator of those above, that is, of the heavenly beings”; the Roman edition reads “an imitator of the heavenly spirits”; the other manuscripts agree with the text.] an imitator of those above, that is, of the heavenly beings.

But it is called the law of the Spirit because God, whose faith it is, is spirit. There, therefore, are words; here, realities. There are the things belonging to God; here, God Himself.

**(Verse 3.) For what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God did: sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin He condemned sin in the flesh.** He says this in order to make those who have been baptized secure, because they have been liberated from sin.

“For what was impossible,” he says, “for the Law.” For whom was it impossible? For us, certainly. It was impossible for us to fulfill the commandment of the Law because we were subject to sin. For this reason God sent His Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.

This is the likeness of flesh: although it is the same flesh as ours, it was not formed and born in the womb in the same manner as our flesh. It was sanctified in the womb and born without sin, and He Himself did not sin in it. For this reason a virgin womb was chosen for the Lord’s birth, so that the Lord’s flesh might differ from our flesh in holiness. The cause is similar, but not the quality of the sinful substance.

Therefore he said “similar,” because, although it was from the same substance of flesh, [Note: Some manuscripts read “it did not have the same birth; for it was purified …”] it did not have the same birth, since the Lord’s body was not subjected to sin. The Lord’s flesh was purified by the Holy Spirit so that He might be born in a body such as Adam’s was before sin, [Note: Thus the old edition and many manuscripts; the Roman edition reads “with the sentence pronounced upon Adam nevertheless remaining.” These words are omitted in not a few manuscripts.] with only the sentence pronounced upon Adam remaining.

Therefore, when God sent Christ, He condemned sin on account of sin—that is, He condemned sin by means of its own sin. For when Christ was crucified by sin, which is Satan, sin sinned in the flesh of the Savior’s body. By this deed God condemned sin in the flesh, precisely where it had sinned, as He also says in another epistle: “Triumphing over them in it” (Col. II, 15)—that is, in Christ.

For it is customary to say of anyone who has been condemned: “For what offense was he condemned?” The answer is, for example, “For murder.” So too sin was condemned in the flesh—that is, in the sin it committed in the flesh.

Thus Satan, made guilty by this sin, lost dominion over the souls he had retained, so that he would no longer dare to hold in the second death those marked with the sign of the cross, in which he had been defeated. For this reason the Apostle discusses these things for our security.

**(Verse 4.) So that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.** He says that sin was condemned so that the justification of the Law given through Moses might be fulfilled in us. For, having been removed from the condition of the Law, we have become its friends; and those who are justified are friends of the Law.

But how is its justification fulfilled in us except when the remission of all sins is granted, so that, once sins have been removed, the person may appear justified, serving the Law of God with his mind? This is what it means not to walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit: the devotion of the mind, which is spirit, does not consent to the desire of sin, because through the flesh it sows [Note: The old edition, with some manuscripts, reads “the desires of the soul, which is sin.” If sin has been condemned, how can it be present? “It was condemned both by the Savior and in three ways …” The Roman edition reads “the desires of the soul, while it is present. If it has been condemned … It was condemned by the Savior in three ways …” Many and better manuscripts agree with the text; the Corbie manuscript supplies, instead of “it was condemned by the Savior,” the reading “especially because it was threefold …”] the desires of the soul, which is sin.

If sin has been condemned by the Savior, how can it be present? It was condemned by the Savior, and condemned in three ways. First, He condemned sin in the first place by not sinning, dissociating Himself from sin. Then sin is said to have been condemned on the cross, because it sinned. Hence its authority as sin was taken away, by which it held men in the underworld because of Adam’s offense, so that thereafter it would not dare to hold those who bear the sign of the cross.

Third, He condemned sin by making offenses invalid through the remission of sins. For when the sinner ought to have been condemned because of the sin committed, Christ, by forgiving him, condemned sin in him. Thus, if we too do not sin according to the example of the Savior, we condemn sin.

**(Verse 5.) For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh.** He says this because whoever obeys the suggestion made through the flesh sets his mind on the things of the flesh. What follows seems pleasant to him, as he desires, contrary to what is right, the practice and judgment of the flesh’s error. For worldly error is signified by the flesh in every respect. [Note: Thus the old edition and many manuscripts; the Roman edition, with Gill in the margin and some manuscripts, reads “it seems pleasant to him”; some manuscripts read “it seems vain to him.”]

**But those who are according to the Spirit perceive the things that are of the Spirit.** [Note: The Florentine and Corbie manuscripts read “understand.” They are those who, having overcome error, have trampled underfoot the desires of the flesh; who, having set aside the world—though the Corbie manuscript reads “having set aside the flesh”—do not fight while walking in the flesh; and whose glory is not from men but from God. Remaining, therefore, in these spiritual works, which are of the Spirit of God, in whose commandments they walk, they set their minds on spiritual things. It is clear that … The Corbie manuscript, omitting the following text as well, connects the word “perceive” immediately with “For the mind of the flesh …”]

It is clear that whoever restrains himself from the desires of the flesh lives according to the law of the mind. For it seems useful to him to set his mind on what agrees with the Law.

**(Verse 6.) For the mind of the flesh is death.** [Note: Gill, in various readings, and some manuscripts read: “For the mind of the flesh is death for this reason, because it is a grave sin; for death comes through such sin. For the mind …”] The mind of the flesh is sin, which generates death. It is called “mind” for this reason, although the matter is foolish: to worldly men, errors conceived from visible things, whether in thought or action and contrary to the Law of God, appear to be wisdom, especially because all their industry and cunning are directed toward sinning.

They seem to themselves to be wise if they take greater care over this, although nothing is more foolish than sinning. There is also another mind of the flesh, which, puffed up with worldly reasoning, denies that anything can happen which lacks the world’s rationale. Hence it mocks the Virgin’s birth and the resurrection of the flesh.

**But the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.** This truly is wisdom, which acquires life and peace. For by following spiritual things and despising the allurements of the present life, one will have eternal life with peace—that is, without disturbance—where there is neither disturbance nor punishment. [Note: Thus a large number of written manuscripts; some, however, and all editions read “where there is disturbance, there is also punishment.”]

**(Verse 7.) For the mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the Law of God, nor indeed can it be.** He did not say that the flesh is hostile, but the mind of the flesh—that is, not the substance, but either evil actions, thought, or assertion arising from error.

The mind of the flesh is, first of all, the philosophical speculation about the stars invented by men, and then the enjoyment of visible things. These are hostile to God, because they equate the Lord of the elements and the maker of the world with the things He made, asserting that nothing can happen beyond what the order of the world contains.

Therefore they deny that God caused a Virgin to give birth or that the bodies of the dead should rise, because, they say, it is foolish for God to have done more than man’s understanding allows. [Note: The Corbie manuscript adds the word “man” after “than what he understands,” and consequently reads “and therefore he did not do it.”]

O wise men of the world, who think that God ought not to act otherwise than the creature fashioned by Him acts, so that He Himself may be thought similar to creatures! Thus they have been blinded, lest they see what an insult they offer to God. For, while condemning the work that He graciously undertook to make for the proclamation of His praise, they declare it incredible and foolish. [Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read: “and therefore this zeal cannot be subject to the Law of God in the matter in which it is exercised”; some manuscripts read “in the matter in which it has been exercised.” The Roman edition, with various readings in Gill and some manuscripts, agrees with the text, except that at the end the Roman edition and Gill read “so that the nations may oppose God.”]

Therefore this mind of the flesh cannot be subject to the Law of God, for they sharpen their zeal for this purpose: to oppose God’s deeds.

**(Verses 8, 9.) Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.** The wise men of the world are in the flesh because they devote themselves to worldly wisdom, through which they oppose the Law of God. Whatever is contrary to the Law of God is carnal, because it is from the world; for the whole world is flesh. Everything visible is assigned to the flesh; indeed, the elements are akin to the flesh, or rather they are the flesh. Therefore whoever obeys worldly things is in the flesh. [Note: Thus the Roman edition, with various readings in Gill, the Corbie manuscript, and several others. The old edition and the remaining manuscripts read: “because, looking toward the world, they resist spiritual wisdom, since the whole world is flesh.”]

**But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit.** Those placed in the flesh are said not to be in the flesh if, agreeing with the Apostle John, they do not love worldly things. For a man’s judgment, as it were, fashions his nature, so that he is called what he thinks.

**If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.** He says this ambiguously because, having been brought under the Law, their faith was not yet perfect; but he saw in them hope of perfection. Hence at times he speaks to them as perfect, at times as those who are to become perfect—that is, at times he praises them, at times he admonishes them. If, according to what was mentioned above, they live according to the law of nature, they are said to be in the Spirit, because the Spirit of God cannot dwell in one who follows carnal things. [Note: The Roman edition alone adds “if they live according to the Law, not in the Spirit …”]

**But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Him.** [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “The Spirit of God he now calls the Spirit of Christ, because …” We have restored the passage from several better manuscripts.]

The one whom he previously called the Spirit of God he now calls the Spirit of Christ, because everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son. This, then, is what he says: whoever is subject to the errors mentioned above does not belong to Christ; he does not have His Spirit, which he had received in order to be a son of God.

The Holy Spirit abandons a man for two reasons: when he possesses either a carnal understanding or carnal actions. Therefore, through these admonitions, he urges them toward good conduct. For although men are raised up by God’s goodness, those called sons of God are burdened if they do not live in this way, lest they appear unworthy of the name granted to them. [Note: Thus most manuscripts; others and the editions omit “which he admonishes,” and some, as well as the old edition, read “compels” instead of “urges.” Immediately afterward, where the editions and some manuscripts read “men,” some manuscripts read “they will not, however, be called sons of God unless they live in this way, lest they appear sufficiently unworthy of the name granted to them.” The Roman edition reads “lest they appear altogether unworthy of the name granted to them.” Frequent manuscripts agree with our text, except that instead of “are burdened,” many read “are honored.” The latter yields an absurd meaning.]

(Verse 10.) “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of justification.” [Note: [Col. 0121D] Quite a few manuscripts read: “but the spirit lives.”] He asserts that the body of those whom the Holy Spirit abandons is dead because of sin, and that the suffering of their death does not reach this one—that is, the Spirit.
