[Note: [Col. 0121D] All printed editions have “that is, the Spirit, lest anyone of them be able to attain through their suffering”; Erasmus and subsequent editors deleted *lest*, but nearly all manuscripts agree with us.] For the Spirit of God does not know how to sin; he is given for justification, so that by his help he may justify. Therefore, since he does not know how to sin, he is life; for he cannot die, since death comes through sin. Consequently, the sinner harms himself, not the Spirit whom he has received. Nor will the Spirit be the cause, since he wishes to justify.

The sign of justification [Col. 0121B] in a person is this: by what dwells within him he appears to have been justified and to be a son of God. For the Holy Spirit cannot dwell in a feigned person or in a body subjected to sins, as Solomon says (Wisdom 1:4): “But if anyone again lives carnally, abandoned by the Holy Spirit, he will die in his injustice.”

By saying “body,” he signifies the whole person dead because of sin, just as the prophet too, under the term “soul,” signifies the whole person, taking the part for the whole. For he says: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4). Surely without the body? Here he used “body” for the whole person; the other used “soul.” Another prophet, by saying “flesh,” signified the whole person; for he says: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40:5).

And because the Holy Spirit is given to the baptized, he is also said to be the spirit of that person. Therefore he called the remaining part of the human being “body” in comparison with him, because the soul, while it sins, is called flesh; for this is called what follows, as I have often already said. In the same way, when the Lord did not wish it to be understood that his divinity feared anything in his Passion, but that he displayed the sorrow of a human being, he said: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41), so that by “spirit” he might signify God, and by “flesh” the human being.

73 (Verse 11.) “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you.” He treats the same point in the same way: for he said “bodies,” by which he signifies human beings. And because above he said that, on account of sin, the body dies with the second death, here again he promised that, on account of a good life, mortal bodies would be given life—that is, the whole person.

(Verses 12.) “Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.” The meaning is right and clear: we ought not to obey the invention of Adam, who acted carnally, who, by sinning first, left death to us by hereditary title. Rather, we ought to serve the law of Christ, who redeemed us from the death mentioned above by a spiritual principle. We are debtors to him, for he justified us, washed clean through the washing of the Spirit from the stains of carnal vices, and made us children of God.

Previously, being placed in the flesh, we lived according to Adam’s example, subjected to sins; but now, having been set free, we ought to render obedience to the Redeemer. This obedience certainly benefits not him, who needs nothing, but obtains eternal life for us. For he loves us so much that he counts as his own what benefits us.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] Thus the Roman edition, with several manuscripts and Gill in his various readings; the old edition, however, with the other manuscripts: “which he promised us.”]

(Verses 13.) “For if you live according to the flesh, you will die.” Nothing is truer: if we live according to Adam, we will die. For Adam, transgressing, sold himself to sin, having been assigned to the flesh. Every sin is flesh; therefore the vices and offenses that arise externally from the senses—that is, from hearing, sight, touch, smell, or taste—are assigned to the flesh. Every thought that looks outward falls into sin; for the sin of the first human being also arose outwardly.

To live according to the flesh, therefore, is death; for every act of the flesh is outside the Law.

“But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” He wants the body to be governed by the law of the soul. Hence he shows that, if the deeds and counsels of the flesh, which are contrived at the instigation of the powers of this world, are restrained under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, so that they do not receive the power to act, life is granted. They are said to be put to death if they cease; for they do not exist if they cease, because there is no sin if it is not committed.

[Col. 0122C] (Verse 14.) “For whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.” He says that those are led by the Spirit of God in whose actions the counsels of the rulers and powers of this world are not seen. For in those in whom they are seen, they are not sons of God but of the devil, because “whoever is born of God does not sin,” as the apostle John says (1 John 3:9). This is what distinguishes the children of God from those of the devil. Hence the Lord said to the Jews, who were doing evil and plotting murder: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44).

(Verses 15.) “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear.” He says this because, having received the Holy Spirit, we have been stripped of fear of evil deeds, so that henceforth we do nothing of that kind by which we would again become afraid.

[Note: [Col. 0122D] The words “For formerly we were under fear” are not found in the manuscripts; nevertheless they occur in all printed editions.]

For formerly we were under fear, because, once the Law had been given, all were constituted guilty. He therefore called the Law the spirit of fear, because it placed human beings in fear on account of sin. But the law of faith, which is signified in the spirit of adoption, is the law of security, because it removes us from fear while granting forgiveness of sins, and by this has made us secure. Thus it is called the spirit “not of fear according to this world.”

“But you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” [Col. 0123A] Having been freed from fear by the grace of God, we received the spirit of adoption as sons, so that, considering what we were and what we have obtained by God’s gift, we might order our lives with great care, lest the name of God the Father suffer insult in us and, like ingrates, we fall again into all the things from which we escaped.

For we have obtained such grace that we dare say to God: “Abba,” that is, “Father.” Therefore he admonishes us lest the confidence we have received be turned into recklessness. For if we present a life unlike the voice by which we say, “Abba, Father,” we insult God by calling him Father. For this reason, in his goodness, he granted us what is above our nature, so that what we are unworthy of by our substance we might deserve by our works.

(Verses 16.) “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God.” When we act well, and the Holy Spirit thereby remains in us, the Spirit of God bears witness to this voice and to our mind, by which we cry out in prayer, “Abba,” that is, “Father.” He bears witness by remaining in us that we do not say “Abba, Father” recklessly. Let us present a life worthy of this voice; and this is the testimony of sons, if through the Spirit the paternal sign is seen in them.

(Verses 17.) “But if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs of Christ.” Since God the Father can in no way be called dead, while Christ, his Son, is said to have died because of the Incarnation, how is one who died said to be heir of the one who always lives, when heirs are surely heirs only of the dead?

But this belongs to his humanity, not to his divinity. For with God what is called inheritance among us is a gift of the Father transferred to obedient sons, so that the living may be heir of the living by his own merit, not through the necessity of the deceased. Hence the Lord in the Gospel, using not merely a human but also a divine mode of reasoning, signified that he had divided his living substance among the living, although he did so in a parable (Luke 15:12); for the parable is not composed by an absurd line of reasoning.

Therefore, to make us ready to obey God the Father, he exhorts us with this hope, saying that we will be heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ. Since the hope of reward is great, we should be all the more devoted to God’s affairs, setting aside care for worldly things. What it means to be a co-heir of the Son of God we are taught by the apostle John; among other things he says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2).

“If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified together.” He explains how we can become co-heirs of Christ, saying: “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified together.” Let us therefore see what it means to suffer with him. To suffer with him is to endure persecutions for the hope of future things, and to crucify the flesh with its vices and desires—that is, to despise the pleasures and pageants of the world. When all these things have died in a person, he crucifies the world, believing in the life of the future age, in which he hopes to become a co-heir of Christ.

(Verses 18.) “I consider, therefore, that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” This exhortation belongs to what was said above. Through it he shows that the things unbelievers can inflict here are small in comparison with the gift decreed for the future age.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] The words “he commands us” were absent from all printed editions and from some manuscripts, but have been restored from several others.]

For this reason he commands us to be ready for every kind of destruction, because great rewards have been promised in return, so that the mind may console itself in tribulation and grow through hope. For we know that some, indeed many, endure harsh and difficult labors for present gains that will profit them only briefly, and sometimes cannot reach the things toward which they strive, since life itself is fragile and uncertain.

[Col. 0124B] Sailors expose themselves to such storms and tempests for what advantages, when they know that in them death is more before their eyes than life? Soldiers, with hope of a present reward, do not hesitate to rise against swords, although victory is uncertain. How much more, then, must one suffer for Christ, whose benefits have also been extended to us: who promises magnificent things in place of small things, heavenly things in place of earthly things, and everlasting rewards with glory in place of temporal ones!

[Note: [Col. 0123D] The words “heavenly things in place of earthly things,” taken from the Florentine and Vindobonensian manuscripts, are here admitted into the text for the first time.]

We are said to suffer for Christ when what we suffer does not benefit him, but because he seeks an opportunity to reward us, he commands this. For, being a good and generous giver, he seeks a reason by which he may give either to the unworthy or to the bashful. Finally, so that these very destructions can be endured, he himself supplies the strength.

[Col. 0124C] (Verse 19.) “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God.” Since he said that the sufferings of the present time are unworthy of comparison with the glory that is to come, he added that creation awaits this: that the number of the sons of God destined for life may be completed. Then creation itself will finally be able [Note: [Col. 0123D] So all printed editions and several manuscripts read; others, however, read: “to be freed from the slavery of corruption and to cease from servitude”; some have “[lacuna] and it would cease in vice”; finally, the Corbie manuscript reads: “to be freed from the duty of servitude and to rest.” Thuanus adds: “in leisure.”] “to be freed from the slavery of corruption and to cease from vice.”

(Verses 20.) “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly.” Creation, placed under the power of the Lord and Creator, was not willingly subjected to vanity; for what it has been subjected to will not benefit it but us. What, then, is its subjection to vanity except that what it produces is perishable? It works to produce corruptible fruits; corruption itself, therefore, is vanity. For everything born in the world is weak, perishable, [Col. 0124D] and corruptible, and therefore vain. They are vain because they cannot maintain their condition; for all things, disfigured by continual change, return confusedly into themselves, into nature.

75 Solomon says the same about these things, because “all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). David does not disagree with him when he says: “Yet every living human being is vanity” (Psalm 38:6). Is it not vanity to eat and drink and care for the things of the world? Yet this very vanity is useful; for it benefits human beings born into the world, so that, trained through these things in their bodies, they may learn the mystery of the Creator. In comparison with eternal things they are vain; but in themselves they are good, since they are necessary.

(Verses 21.) “But because of him who subjected it in hope.” He immediately explains what this hope is, saying: “For creation itself will also be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God.” Since creation cannot oppose its Creator, it was subjected for his sake, not without hope. For, placed in labor, it has this consolation: that it will have rest when all whom God knows will believe have believed; for their sake also he subjected it.

(Verses 22.) “For we know that the whole of creation groans and is in labor pains until now.” To be in labor pains is to suffer. The meaning is that all creation groans and suffers through daily labor until now. “Until now” means for as long as it is read. For the elements themselves perform their appointed tasks with anxiety: the sun and moon complete the spaces assigned to them not without labor, and the spirit of living creatures is constrained with a great groan to perform its services. We see them groaning and being forced unwillingly into labor.

All these things therefore await rest, so that they may be freed from servile work. But if this were a servitude that benefited God by winning his favor, creation would rejoice, not suffer. But because it was subjected to the slavery of corruption for our sake, it suffers. For it sees its works perish every day; every day its work rises and sets.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] Some manuscripts read: “dies and kills.” Below, where we read “knowing that,” the Amerbach edition and all the manuscripts have “knowing that it advances toward its liberation.” Yet this author happened to speak incongruously here, and not in this passage alone.]

It rightly suffers, therefore, since its activity does not pertain to eternity, [Col. 0125C] but to corruption. As far as can be understood, it is sufficiently concerned for our salvation, knowing that it will advance more quickly toward its own liberation if we recognize our Creator more quickly. Knowing this, let us present ourselves as worthy with every care and diligence, so that we may also be an example to others, moved not only by compassion for ourselves but also for the sake of that creation which, suffering injuries day and night, groans. We are accustomed to keep more watchfully alert in the causes of others.

(Verses 23.) “And not only it, but we ourselves, who have the receptacle of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting the redemption of our body.” After worldly creation, he added that we too await this and groan to God, so that all of us destined for life may be freed from here. For Christians this world is an open sea.

Just as the sea is stirred by adverse storms, surges, and creates a tempest for sailors, so the age, stirred by the conspiracy of unbelievers, disturbs the minds of the faithful. And the enemy does this with such variety that it is not known what must first be avoided.

[Note: [Col. 0125D] Three manuscripts add after the word “unknown”: “for the source from which tribulation arises does not fail.” As for the fact that the Roman edition substitutes “storm” for “power,” this not only conflicts with the authority of all the other manuscripts, but also with the proper meaning: “power” here is opposed to private individuals, as the passage clearly shows.]

For if the power ceases to be against us, he agitates the minds of private individuals. If these too are restrained, he kindles a fire through household members; [Col. 0126A] and if this [Note: [Col. 0126D] So the Amerbach and Erasmus editions and most manuscripts read; other manuscripts have partly “if this has been subdued” and partly “if this has been put to sleep,” which Gill and the Roman edition preferred.] is suppressed, by his art he creates discord among blood relatives themselves, so that, when a house is struck at its four corners, he may cause its ruin on some side.

For this reason Christians must flee from here with one purpose. They ought to follow the example of the holy Simeon, who, knowing that war was being waged here against unbelief, asked to be dismissed in peace (Luke 2:29). This is what we pray for individually on behalf of all, that the kingdom of God may come (Matthew 6:10). Then there will be the liberation of our body—that is, of all Christians. For by “body” he signified everyone, because we are members of one another.

The Apostle, as a spiritual man, has a good understanding of us when he says that we groan to be freed from here, just as Simeon also groaned. But I see that we are held by the attraction of the world. Thus, through the things said above, he shows how great is the force that creation suffers for our sake. When we, for whom its service is beneficial and who have the Spirit of God as our helper, groan to be freed from here and to obtain the promised rewards, how much more does creation groan, which neither has the Holy Spirit as helper nor labors for its own cause?

Added to this is that creation sees the things which it produces through its labor, so that they may benefit the nourishment of God’s servants, unlawfully sacrificed to idols. Hence it suffers more and desires to be freed more quickly, 76 knowing that this contributes to the injury of the Creator.

(Verses 24.) “For in hope we were saved.” He says this because, by hoping for what God promised in Christ, we have acquired merit so that we might be freed. Therefore we have been freed in hope, because what will be is no different from what we believe.

“But hope that is seen is not hope.” It is clear that what is seen is not hope, but what is not seen. Consequently, believers are to receive rewards, because they hope for what they do not see.

(Verses 25.) “For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.” There is no doubt that what is not seen is hoped for, for future things are awaited. This expectation is patience, which merits much from God: as one awaits the kingdom of God from day to day, one desires its coming and does not doubt because it is delayed.

(Verses 26.) “Likewise the Spirit also helps the weakness of our prayer.” Since above he mentioned that we groan and pray for liberation, and since, being placed in suffering, we either want things spoken of as far in the future to happen immediately or want to be quickly removed from the circumstances through which we attain merit, we seem to pray with a feeble prayer when its effect is denied us.

For it is weak to ask contrary to reason. Therefore he shows that this weakness is helped by the Holy Spirit given to us. He helps because he does not allow things to happen that are either requested before they ought to be requested or are contrary to what is right.

“For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought.” He made clear that the weakness of our prayer signifies ignorance: we are mistaken when we think that what we ask is beneficial, although it is not. Finally, when the same Apostle prayed three times that temptations might cease for him because they were frequent, the Lord said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9); that is, a person acquires merit by being found patient in tribulations. He therefore learned that what he was asking was against him.

Sometimes a request is also proud and foolish, as was the request of the two apostles James and John. When they asked for something inappropriate and excessive, they were told: “You do not know what you are asking” (Matthew 20:22).

[Col. 0127B] “But the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings.” The Spirit of the Lord is said to plead for us not in human speech but according to his own nature. For when what is from God speaks to God, it must speak in the manner in which the one from whom it is speaks. No one speaks to a fellow citizen in another language.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The Roman edition reads: “He speaks in another language … may cover us with his coming.”]

The Spirit given to us pours himself over our prayers, so that by his movement he may cover our ignorance and lack of foresight, and ask from God for us those things that benefit us.

(Verses 27.) “But he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God.” It is clear that God, to whom nothing is hidden or concealed, knows the prayer of every spirit—how much more that of the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance! He speaks not through the impulse of air, nor like the angels or the rest of creation, but in the manner appropriate to his divinity.

He therefore speaks to God when he seems silent to us, because he also sees when he is not seen, and asks for those things which he knows please God and benefit us. The same Spirit interposes on our behalf when he knows that through ignorance, not through boastfulness, we are asking for things contrary to our good.

(Verses 28.) “But we know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called saints according to his purpose.” He says this because, even if those who love God have prayed without understanding, it will not harm them. For God, knowing the purpose of their hearts [Note: [Col. 0127D] So all manuscripts and the old edition read; the Roman edition instead has “and weakness.”] and their negligence, does not charge them with asking for things adverse to them, but grants those things that ought to be given to those who love God.

[Col. 0127D] Hence the Lord also says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:32). Those, therefore, are called according to his purpose whom God, knowing beforehand that they would become suitable for him, foresaw as believers before they believed.

[Col. 0128A] (Verses 29.) “For those whom he foreknew.” Those whom he foreknew as destined to be devoted to him, he chose to receive the promised rewards, so that those who seem to believe but do not remain in the faith they began might be denied as chosen by God. For those whom God chooses remain with him.

There is also one who is chosen for a time, such as Saul and Judas—not by foreknowledge, but by present righteousness.

“To be conformed to the image of his Son.” He says this because they are predestined for the future age so that they may become like the Son of God, as I have already mentioned above.

“So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” Rightly “firstborn,” because he was not made before all creation but was born. Following his example, God was pleased to adopt human beings as sons.

Christ is also firstborn in regeneration. He is also firstborn [Note: [Col. 0127D] The Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, reads “from the dead, when, having conquered death, he ascended into heaven.”] from the dead, whose nature is unknown. And he is firstborn after ascending into heaven in victory.

He is therefore called our firstborn brother in all things, because he graciously consented to be born as a human being. Yet he is the Lord, because he is our God, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “This is our God, [Note: [Col. 0127D] We have restored to the text from several manuscripts the words “and no other is reckoned beside him,” or, as some manuscripts read, “no other will be esteemed,” which had been omitted. Below, in some manuscripts, one reads partly: “to call is to consider the human being to be God’s, to call”; partly: “what does it mean to call a human being?” Others read: “To call is to consider him as believing,” and so forth. In some, the passage is omitted. We have retained the reading of all the better printed editions and manuscripts.] and no other is reckoned beside him” (Baruch 3:36).

(Verses 30.) “And those whom he predestined, he also called.” To call is to help one who is considering faith, or to pierce with compunction one whom he knows will listen. “And those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

He says the same as above: those whom God foreknew to be suitable for him remain believers, since it cannot happen otherwise than that those whom God foreknew he also justified. Consequently, he also glorified them, so that they may become like the Son of God.

As for the others whom God did not foreknow, he does not care for them in this grace, because he did not foreknow [Note: [Col. 0128D] Most manuscripts restore: “that they would become suitable.”] that they would become suitable. But if they believe, or are chosen for a time because they seem good, so that justice may not appear to be despised, they do not remain in order to be glorified—just as Judas Iscariot, or those seventy-two who, after suffering offense, departed from the Savior, although they had been chosen (John 6:71).

(Verses 31.) “What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?” It is clear: since God bears witness on our behalf, who would dare accuse us, when he himself who is judge foreknew us and judged us suitable?

(Verses 32.) “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” In order to make us secure through faith, he exhorts us in this way, showing that God, as one who foreknew, delivered his Son to death for us before we became believers from among the ungodly.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Amerbach and Erasmus, together with several manuscripts, read: “so that God, who foreknew, before we were …”]

“How will he not also, with him, freely give us all things?” He says that God determined long ago to reward those who believe in Christ. If he granted us what is greater and most important—namely, that he delivered his true and most beloved Son for us while we were still ungodly—why should it not be believed that he will do for us believers what is less? The rewards are already prepared for believers. For it is less to grant us all things with him than to deliver him to death for our sake.

(Verses 33.) “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” It is clear that no one dares or is able to challenge God’s judgment and foreknowledge concerning us. For who could disapprove what God approves, when no one is equal to God?

“God, who justifies” (Isaiah 50:8). This is found in the prophet Isaiah, which he presents here as his own, because there is no one else who can accuse what God approves. Or perhaps God himself might accuse us—but he cannot accuse what he justifies.

(Verses 34.) “And who will condemn? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again—and is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.” He denies that God, since he justifies us, accuses us; and that Christ can condemn us, because he loves us with such affection that he died for us and, having risen, always pleads our cause with the Father.

His petition cannot be disregarded, because he is at the right hand of God—that is, in the honor that belongs to God—so that, secure concerning God the Father and Christ his Son, who will judge, we may rejoice in faith.

Hence comes what he says to the apostle Peter: “Behold, Satan demanded to sift you as wheat; but I prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). In this way the Savior intercedes for us; [Note: [Col. 0129D] Some manuscripts read: “for he knows the power”; one reads: “ignorance.”] for, knowing [Col. 0129C] the shamelessness and arrogance of our adversary, when he stirs himself against us if we do not agree with him, the Savior intercedes for us, lest he violently presume anything against us, so that his insolence may be restrained.

For this reason, however, the Son is said to intercede, although he himself does everything and is equal to God the Father. And because God is said to be one, lest the Father and Son be thought to be a single person or a union without distinction, Scripture speaks in this way to distinguish the persons, while presenting the Son as not unequal and giving precedence to the Father because he is Father and because all things are from him.

(Verses 35.) “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” That is, who will be able to turn us away from love for Christ, who has granted us benefits so great and innumerable? “Tribulation?” But it does not, because no torments overcome the love of a steadfast Christian. For the love of one who loves is increased if he is prevented from loving the one whose benefits he has experienced. For, while they think that they are sowing in his merits, the benefits recalled stir them up. [Note: [Col. 0129D] All printed editions and some manuscripts read: “sowing his undeserved benefits, he recalls”; the other manuscripts, which are also the better ones, read as we do in the text, except that some omit the word “recalled,” and nearly all write “undeserved” with an absurd meaning. But “we sow in the merits of Christ,” because he first loved us and gave himself for us.]

(Verses 36–37.) “Or distress? Or persecution? Or hunger? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer because of him who loved us.” This is written in the forty-third Psalm.

It is therefore clear that all these things which he enumerates—destructions, tribulations, pressures, and death—cannot be set against or compared with the love of Christ which he has sown in us. His benefits are far greater than all those things that seem adverse.

If we die for him, which seems the most serious of these things, he too died for us—but he died to benefit us, whereas our death does not benefit him but us. We lose temporal life so that eternal life may be repaid to us. And what wonder is it if servants die for a good Lord, when the Lord died for his servants, even though they were evil? [Col. 0130B] His benefits therefore prevail and encourage the mind to persevere for the sake of him who loved us.

(Verses 38–39.) “For I am confident that neither death”—this confidence comes from Christ’s promise, by which he promised to help the faith devoted to him in tribulation—“nor life, nor angel, nor power, nor height, nor depth, nor things present, nor things to come, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

These are all the things that the devil brings against us to lead us away. He mentions them in order to fortify us, so that, if they come, confident in hope and in Christ’s assistance and armed with faith, we may resist them.

For what if death is inflicted? Is it not the greatest gain to find an opportunity by which one may go more quickly into the promised kingdom? Nor, if the present life is promised to us and fortified by honor, should it turn us away from the hope of Christ’s benefit, since we know that he will benefit us not only in the future but also in the present.

Nor, if an angel should appear to us in order to deceive us, [Note: [Col. 0130D] Some manuscripts read: “suborned by the deceptions of his deceitful father.”] suborned by the deceptions of his father, the devil, ought he to prevail against us, since we know that nothing should be placed before Christ, the Angel of the great counsel (Isaiah 9:6).

Nor, if a power is performed by someone, as is said to have been performed by Simon Magus, who is said to have flown upward in the air in order to scandalize Christ’s people, should it diminish our faith, since we know that the Savior, received by a ministering cloud, ascended above all the heavens (Acts 1:9).

Nor, if he should show himself to us in the height of heaven, of which the apostle John says: “Do you not know the height of Satan?” (Revelation 2:24), should this remove us from devotion to the Lord Jesus, whom we know descended from heaven to join earthly things with spiritual things.

Nor, if through the phantasm by which he plans to deceive us he should show us a depth terrifying in its horror, by which we might perhaps be frightened and fall before him, is it fitting even then for us to break faith with Christ, whom we know descended for our sake into the depths of the earth and, by pressing death down, freed the human race.

Nor, if he promises us future things, as he promised Eve (Genesis 3:4), will we give him our assent, separated from Christ, whom we believe and know to be God in power and nature.

Nor, if by the art and subtlety of his cunning he fashions another creature for a time, as Jannes and Jambres fashioned one before Pharaoh, [Note: [Col. 0131D] All printed editions and some manuscripts read “and grandeur”; the others, including the older manuscripts, read “and subtlety.” A little later Erasmus and subsequent editions, together with one or two manuscripts, had restored “it is fitting”; here we have restored “it is unfitting” with Amerbach and most manuscripts.] is it fitting that through these things he should recall us from God the true Creator, whom we know to have created through Christ his Son a creature destined to exist forever (2 Timothy 3:8).

Some think that by “another creature” he meant idols, but this is not true, because he ought to have signified the creature which Satan appears to fashion with the wonder of deception. For who among the faithful could be deceived by these things, from which he has withdrawn after the error was revealed?

79 But he devises and fabricates these things by which he might even deceive the elect. Therefore there is nothing that can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus. For God has shown us his love in Christ by delivering him up for us.

CHAPTER IX.

(Vv. 1–3.) I speak the truth in Christ Jesus—I do not lie—my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit: I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself could wish to be accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites.

Since above he appears to speak against the Jews, who think that they are justified by the Law, he now wishes to show his desire and affection toward them. With his conscience bearing witness, he says that he speaks in Christ [Col. 0131C] Jesus and in the Holy Spirit, so that his faith may not be rejected as though he were their enemy. Therefore he gives Christ and the Holy Spirit, who know nothing that is hidden, as witnesses—witnesses whose testimony cannot be rejected and who bear witness to the Apostle by commending him through the power of the signs they performed through him.

Because Christ’s protection is so great, because he has shown an exceptional love toward the human race, and because by his glorious favor he has promised immortal rewards, he grieves for his own race according to the flesh, since by their unbelief they have deprived themselves of this perpetual and saving benefit. Therefore, he says, “I could wish,” not “I wish,” because he knows that it cannot happen that so honorable a member, with no preceding fault, should be cut off from the Christian body [Note: The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads “from the body of Christ.”] Nevertheless, he shows his affection [Col. 0131D] and love toward his own race.

(V. 4.) To whom belongs the adoption as sons. He proves that he is right to grieve when he proclaims the praise of their race, because, although they had once been adopted as sons, they rendered ineffective the affection and grace of God the Father. He added still more, in order to cause others also to grieve for them, saying:

(V. 5.) And the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.

He enumerates so many praises of the nobility and dignity of the Jewish race and of its promises that he moves everyone to grieve for them, because, by not receiving the Savior, they lost the prerogative of their fathers and the merit of the promise. They became worse than the Gentiles, whom they had previously abhorred because they were without God; for it is a greater evil to have lost dignity than never to have possessed it. Meanwhile, concerning the Savior he says:

“Who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.” Since no mention is made of the name of the Father and the subject is Christ, the statement cannot be deferred lest he be called God. Frequently, because of the confession of one God, when Scripture speaks of God the Father and joins the Son to God, it calls the Father “God” and the Son “Lord.” But if anyone does not think that “who is God” is said of Christ, let him identify the person of whom it was said; for in this passage no mention has been made of God the Father.

But what is surprising if in this passage he openly called Christ God over all, when elsewhere in the Epistle he confirmed this meaning in words of the same kind, saying: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 10)? These are all the things over which Christ is God. For there are no others apart from these, so that Christ should not be God over all; nor can every creature bend the knee except to God.

Finally, when the Apostle John, in ignorance, wished to worship an angel as God, he heard from him: “Do not do this, for I am your fellow servant. Worship God” (Apoc. XIX, 10). Nor would the Lord have allowed himself to be worshiped unless he were God; otherwise he would have to be accused of usurpation and sin—which is impossible—since, rebuking the devil, he shows that the Lord God must be worshiped and that he alone must be served (Matt. IV, 10).

Therefore nothing is prejudiced against God the Father when Christ is worshiped as God; for although it is said that one must serve God alone, Christ also is served. For he says elsewhere: “Whoever serves Christ in these matters is pleasing to God” (John X, 4). What then remains except that the Father is God and the Son is God, and nevertheless both are believed to be one God? For whether one worships the Father or the Son, one is said to worship one God; and whether one serves the Father or the Son, service is rendered to one God [Note: Several manuscripts read: “and to serve the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, one God … he worships the Father and the Holy Spirit … he serves the Son and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. The other manuscripts and editions agree with our text, except that the Roman edition, instead of “and to serve the Father,” reads “and if the Father is served”; and after “therefore there is no distinction” it adds “in these matters.” Finally, below, instead of “confession,” it substitutes, with the manuscripts of Tours, “profession.”]

Therefore there is no distinction [Col. 0132D], because whoever worships the Son also worships the Father, and whoever serves the Father serves the Son. And in order to show that this confession of the deity was made without flattery, he placed “Amen” at the conclusion—that is, “truly”—so that he might show Christ, God over all, truly blessed forever.

(V. 6.) But the word of God has not failed. The word of God has not failed when he said: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Gen. XXI, 12). That is, what God said would happen has happened: those were not to be called Abraham’s offspring who were his children according to the flesh, but those who received the faith through which Isaac was born—a faith renewed in the time of Christ, no longer particular but universal. Thus what Abraham believed concerning Isaac, they were to believe concerning God and Christ, because the Son of God was born for the salvation and redemption of the human race [Note: Gill and the Roman edition, together with the manuscript of Tours, read “for the restoration of the human race.”]

(V. 7.) Nor are all those who are from Israel Israelites; nor, because they are Abraham’s offspring, are they all children. Rather, “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” [Note: Thus the manuscripts and the older editions, except that Gill omits “That is.” The Roman edition, adding—as it usually does—the following verse of Scripture and repeating part of the preceding one, adds this: “He wishes it to be understood that not all who are Abraham’s children are worthy to be children of the promise, that is, those whom he foreknew,” and so forth.]

This is what he wishes to be understood: they are not all worthy simply because they are Abraham’s children; rather, those are worthy who are children of the promise, that is, those whom God foreknew would receive his promise, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles. These are worthy to be called Israelites—that is, “seeing God”—because they believe.

Certainly all these are Abraham’s children through Isaac, since the entire offspring of the Jewish race comes from Abraham through Isaac. [Note: “But because … which was made in Isaac” is absent from a very large number of manuscripts.] But, as I said, those are truly Abraham’s children who follow the promise made in Isaac. Consequently, the other children must not be called Abraham’s children; for Abraham, by believing, received Isaac because he believed God. In this the mystery of the future faith was signified: those would be Isaac’s brothers who possessed the same faith in which Isaac was born. Isaac was born as a type of the Savior from the promise, so that whoever believed Christ Jesus to have been promised to Abraham [Col. 0133C] would be Abraham’s son and Isaac’s brother.

Therefore it was said to Abraham: “In your offspring all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18). This was certainly not fulfilled in Isaac, but in the one who was promised to Abraham in Isaac—namely, Christ—in whom all the nations that believe are blessed. The other Jews, then, are children according to the flesh, while they are deprived of the promise; nor can they be counted worthy by reason of Abraham if they do not follow the faith through which Abraham became worthy.

(V. 8.) That is, not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and certain manuscripts read “in the offspring.” It is clear that they cannot be called children of God, for these are …; Gill and the Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, read “in the offspring”; the Roman edition reads “into the offspring.” It says: “He speaks of children of the flesh and children of God. These indeed …” We have restored the passage from the majority of the best manuscripts.]

It is clear that the children of the flesh cannot be called children of God. They were born from the desire of the flesh, whereas these were born spiritually from faith, according to what was promised to Abraham. Thus those are counted as offspring who believe.

(V. 9.) For the word of the promise is this: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.”

This is found in Genesis, and it was prefigured in Christ, so that Christ, who was to come, might be promised as the son of Abraham, and the word of the promise might be fulfilled in him, so that all the nations of the earth might be blessed in Christ. For when the promise was made to Abraham and he heard, “In your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,” Christ was certainly promised to him through the descent of Isaac, in whom we see this fulfilled.

(V. 10.) And not only this—that is, Sarah—but Rebecca also, having conceived by one intercourse with Isaac our father [Note: The Roman edition and the manuscript of Tours had removed from this point the words “that is, Sarah.” Likewise, below, the Roman edition alone had omitted “This is found in Malachi”; yet these words are found in all the manuscripts and editions.]

He therefore says that not only Sarah, in a symbolic sense, bore Isaac, but also Rebecca, the wife of Isaac. But the case of Isaac differs from that of Jacob and Esau, because Isaac was born as a figure of the Savior, whereas Jacob and Esau represent two peoples—that is, believers and unbelievers—so that, although they are from one source, they are nevertheless different.

In each case a race is signified, so that those are said to be of one race who are united in the cause of faith or of unbelief. One is signified in many, not by physical descent but by a common cause. For the sons of Jacob must also be said to come from Esau, and the sons of Esau must be reckoned as coming from Jacob. Nor, because Jacob is praised, should all born from him rightly be called his children; nor, because Esau is displeasing, are all from his origin reprobate. We see that some born from Jacob’s line became unbelievers, and that some from Esau’s became faithful and dear to God.

That many from Jacob were unbelievers is beyond doubt, for all the Jews who do not believe—or who believe—have their origin from him. And that there are good and faithful people from Esau is proved by Job, who was the fifth from Abraham, that is, a grandson of Esau.

(Vv. 11–13.) For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, it was said—not from works but from the one who calls—that “the elder shall serve the younger,” as it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

This is found in Malachi. He demands that God’s foreknowledge be considered in these matters, because nothing can happen other than what God knows will happen. Knowing what each of them would become, he said: “This one, who will be the younger, will be worthy; the elder will be unworthy.” By his foreknowledge he chose one and rejected the other. In the one whom he chose, God’s purpose remains, because nothing else can happen than what he knew and purposed concerning him—that he should be worthy of salvation. Similarly, in the one whom he rejected, the purpose he had formed concerning him remains, because he would be unworthy.

He did this as one who foreknew, not as one who shows partiality; for he condemns no one before he sins, and crowns no one before he conquers. This pertains to the case of the Jews, who defend their prerogative on the grounds that they are Abraham’s children. The Apostle, however, consoles himself: since he had said that he had continual sorrow in his heart because of the unbelief of those whose adoption as sons, establishment of the Law, and Christ were theirs, as he himself says, “Salvation is from the Jews” (John IV, 22), he examined the Law and found that not all who are from Israel would believe; nor, merely because they are called Abraham’s children, are all to be called Abraham’s children, as I mentioned above.

Thus he diminishes his own sorrow, finding that it had long been foretold that not all would believe [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, together with many manuscripts, read “so that only these should grieve.” The other editions and manuscripts, however, more correctly read as in the text.] so that he might grieve only for those who suffer in unbelief through envy. Nevertheless, they can believe, as he makes clear in what follows.

There is not much reason to grieve for those unbelievers who had been foretold, because they were not predestined to life; for God’s foreknowledge had long ago determined that they would not be saved. Who would mourn for one who is long regarded as dead? But when the Gentiles, who had previously been without God, entered in and received the salvation that the Jews had lost, sorrow is stirred up again. Yet because they themselves are the cause of their destruction, it is quieted once more.

Thus God, foreknowing that they would have an evil will, did not count them among the good, even though the Savior says to the seventy-two disciples whom he had chosen in a second group and who later withdrew from him: “Your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). This was said on account of justice, because it is just that each person should receive according to his merit. Since they were good, they were chosen for ministry, and their names were written in heaven on account of justice, as I said; but according to foreknowledge they were numbered among the wicked.

For God judges according to justice, not according to foreknowledge. Hence he also said to Moses: “If anyone sins against me, I will blot him out of my book” (Exod. XXXII, 34), so that according to the justice of the Judge he appears to be blotted out when he sins, whereas according to foreknowledge he had never been in the book of life.

For this reason the Apostle John also says concerning such people: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II, 20). There is no partiality in God’s foreknowledge. Foreknowledge is that by which he has determined what each person’s future will be, and in what he will remain, through which he will either be condemned or crowned.

Indeed, those whom he knows will remain in goodness are frequently evil beforehand, and those whom he knows will remain evil are sometimes good beforehand. Therefore complaint ceases, because God is not one who shows partiality (Acts X, 34).

Saul and Judas Iscariot were both good beforehand. Scripture says of Saul: “He was a good man, and there was no one better than he among the sons of Israel” (I Sam. IX, 2). And concerning Judas Iscariot the Apostle Peter says: “He received his share in this ministry” (Acts I, 17), that is, in the apostolate [Note: Thus read the edition of Amerbach, Erasmus, and many manuscripts. In the other editions and manuscripts we do not find “in the performance of signs and wonders” [Col. 0136D].], in the performance of signs and wonders.

How, then, could he have received a saving ministry unless he had been good? In his appointment there was a judgment of God that he was worthy at the time when he was chosen, just as were the seventy-two mentioned above (Matt. XVII, 5). This is why Judas, after committing every evil deed, was moved to repentance and ended his life by hanging himself.

For no good can be completely erased in anyone, since nature cannot be changed, but the will can—though not in every respect, because something remains in nature that bears witness to the Creator.

(V. 14.) What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not.

Because he loves one and hates the other, he adds: “Is there injustice with God?” (Exod. XXXIII, 19.) Certainly not; God is just. He knows what he is doing, and his judgment must not be retracted. This is found in the prophet Malachi: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 3).

Here he is speaking about judgment. Previously he spoke about foreknowledge, saying that the elder would serve the younger. In the same way, through foreknowledge he condemned Pharaoh (Gen. XXV, 23), knowing that he would not reform, but chose the Apostle Paul, who was persecuting him (Acts IX, 3), foreknowing that he would become good. He therefore anticipated him before the appointed time because he was necessary, while he condemned Pharaoh before the future judgment, so that it might be believed that he would judge.

(V. 15.) For he says to Moses: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

Therefore, “I will have mercy,” he says, “on him on whom I will have mercy”—that is, I will have mercy on the one whom I foreknew I would make the object of mercy, knowing that he would turn and remain with me. “And I will show compassion to him on whom I show compassion”—that is, I will give mercy to the one whom I foreknew would return to me with a right heart after his error.

This means giving to the one to whom it should be given and not giving to the one to whom it should not be given: calling the one whom he knows will obey, but not calling the one whom he knows will not obey [Col. 0136C]. To call, however, is not to contend but to prick the heart so that it may receive the faith [Note: All the editions and several manuscripts read “to call, however, is to pierce the heart”; many other good manuscripts agree with our text.]

(V. 16.) Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.

Rightly so, because what is requested should depend not on the will of the one who asks but on the judgment of the giver. Whether something should be given must be weighed by the judgment of the giver. For when Saul sinned and asked forgiveness, he did not receive it (I Sam. XV, 24); whereas David, after sinning and asking to be forgiven, obtained pardon (II Sam. XII, 8).

The judgment of God, who gives and does not give, must therefore be followed, because he who wishes all to be saved does not judge unjustly, while justice remains. For he who examines the heart knows whether the one asking seeks in such a frame of mind that he deserves to receive.

Although it is dangerous to scrutinize God’s judgment, we should nevertheless, for the sake of those who doubt, explain it so that their minds may obtain healing and they may not think God’s judgment unjust, saying: “He calls one and neglects the other.” By supposing this, they think that the condemned can be excused. Let us prove the matter by facts rather than words. Where there are examples of actual events, no one dares complain or offer any excuse.

There were two men, David and Saul. Let us examine their histories and see what each was found to be after God’s judgment, so that, if Saul is proved to have acted well after he did not receive mercy, we may—God forbid—judge God’s decision unjust; or if David, after receiving mercy, is found to have despised God, whether he remained in the condition in which he obtained mercy. To put it briefly, both endured the necessity of kingship.

How great was David’s necessity when his own son wished to deprive him of the kingdom! In that distress he traveled weeping and barefoot, fleeing as king and leader of God’s people, humbled to such an extent that he did not answer even when his servant cursed him to his face. Through patience he sought to make God favorable to him, trusting that God would preserve his kingdom for him (II Sam. XV, 16).

Saul, however, was not found in such distress; for civil war is a greater evil than foreign war. Moreover, after he had been refused once and again, although he was unworthy, he did not persevere in prayer so as to acquire merit by which he might become worthy. Instead, impatient and indignant at God’s judgment, he sought help from idols that he had previously condemned as worthless.

Behold, the justice of God’s foreknowledge is manifest even to those who do not wish to acknowledge it.

(V. 17.) For Scripture says to Pharaoh (Exod. IX, 16): “For this very purpose I have preserved you, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

Other manuscripts read: “For this purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you.” Whether one reads “preserved” or “raised up,” the meaning is the same. For he says that when Pharaoh—a name for kings among the Egyptians, just as among the Romans kings are called Augusti— [Col. 0137C] was guilty of such great evils that he was unworthy of life [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts have this reading. The older edition and certain manuscripts instead read: “Therefore, when this Pharaoh was guilty of such great evils that he ought not to live, and would never become good, lest he should think either that he was … or that God was powerless …” The Roman edition cut off the first three words.]

This Pharaoh persisted in his evils and refused to reform, thinking either that he deserved to live or that God, whom he often supposed he could deceive, was powerless to inflict vengeance. He heard from God: “For this purpose I have preserved you, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.” Thus the other nations would learn that there is no other God besides this one, who belonged to the Jews and became the God of Christians.

Nevertheless, they too were Christians, and we are now Jews because of Judah, from whom Christ descended according to the flesh. For the Jews of old, by hoping for Christ the Redeemer who was to come, were Christians. Rahab the prostitute says to the spies sent by Joshua the son of Nun, who was formerly called Auxes: “We have heard of the mighty deeds and plagues that your God performed in Egypt, and we have been greatly terrified; for they fear before your presence” (Josh. II, 9) [Col. 0137D].

Therefore Pharaoh was preserved for this purpose, so that many signs and plagues might be displayed against him as though he were already dead [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Therefore Pharaoh was preserved, as though already dead, for this purpose, so that … might be displayed in him. He was raised up …”]. He is said to have been raised up because, although he was dead before God, he received a short period in which he might appear to live. Thus, through his punishment and the various kinds of torments inflicted on him even unto death, all who were without God might be terrified and, with the greatest amazement, confess that this alone was God, from whom such acts of vengeance proceeded.

In the same way, ancient physicians, when dealing with people worthy of death or already condemned to death, investigated how the hidden conditions revealed in a dying person might benefit the living. By exposing what lay concealed in the person, they learned the causes of the illness, so that the punishment of the dying might contribute to the salvation of the living.

(V. 18.) Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.

You will say to me—he speaks in the person of an objector, who seems to think that God, neglecting justice, favors one person, accepting one of two equal persons and rejecting the other: that is, pricking one so that he believes and hardening the other so that he does not believe. He answers this objection with authority, while preserving justice, in accordance with the foreknowledge mentioned above:

(V. 19.) Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?

First, he says that no one can resist him, for he is more powerful than all. Then he says that God is the Father of all, and therefore wishes evil to no one. For he wishes the things he has made to remain unharmed. Nor is it fitting that the one whose benevolence is so great should be unjust: he not only caused things that did not exist to exist, but also granted them eternal life and glory, so that his work might possess something resembling his majesty. Since he is therefore so provident and good, there should be no doubt that he is just.

(V. 20.) O man, who are you to answer back to God?

He says that it is a great indignity and presumption for a human being to answer God in adversity; for the unjust to answer the just, the evil the good, the ignorant the perfect, the weak the most powerful, the corruptible the incorruptible, the mortal the immortal, the wicked servant the master, and the creature the Creator.

Does the molded object say to the one who molded it, “Why did you make me like this?” (Isa. XLV, 9.) This comes from the prophet Isaiah, but here he presents it as his own in order to show that a work cannot complain against its maker. For it is in the power of the maker to form whatever kind of creature he wishes.

(V. 21.) Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

It is clear that some vessels are made for honor, being necessary for honorable uses, while others are made for dishonor, serving as kitchen utensils. Yet they are of one substance; they differ in honor according to the will of the craftsman.

So too God, although we all come from one and the same lump in substance and are all sinners, has mercy on one and looks down upon another—not without justice. In the potter there is only will; in God, however, will is joined with justice, for he knows on whom he ought to have mercy, as I mentioned above.

(V. 22.) But what if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction?

The meaning is the same: through the will and long-suffering of God—that is, his patience—the unbelievers are prepared for punishment. They were awaited for a long time, but they did not wish to convert. Therefore they were awaited so that they might perish without excuse. For God knew that they would not believe.

(V. 23.) And in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.

God’s patience and long-suffering are the same qualities that, just as they prepare the wicked for destruction, prepare the good for the crown. The good are those in whom there is the hope of faith.

He sustains everyone, knowing the outcome of each. Thus it is patience that prepares for glory those who are corrected from evil or who persevere in goodness. The riches of glory are the manifold dignity prepared for believers.

But those who turn from good to evil and persist in the evil they have begun, he prepares for destruction. This is what it means to make his power known through great patience: he is thought not to intend vengeance because he delays for a long time. When he begins to exact vengeance, his power will appear; for although he could exact vengeance immediately, he endured for a long time so that the unbelievers could not complain when they were condemned.

To prepare each person means to foreknow what will happen.

(V. 24.) Those whom he also called—us—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.

Those whom he called he prepared for glory, whether they were near or far away, knowing that they would remain in the faith.

(Vv. 25–26.) As he says in Hosea: “I will call the one who was not my people, ‘my people,’ and the one who was not beloved, ‘beloved.’ And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

It is clear that this was foretold concerning the Gentiles, who previously were not God’s people. Later, receiving mercy to the shame of the Jews, they were called God’s people. Those who had not previously been beloved were adopted as sons and became beloved after the Jews had been rejected, so that in the place where they had not been called God’s people, they might be called sons of the living God.

Previously they were nowhere called sons of God except in Judea—that is, in Jerusalem, where the house of God was—as he says in the seventy-fifth Psalm: “God is known in Judea” (Ps. LXXV, 2). Later, in the prophecy of Zechariah, he says: “I will set Jerusalem among all the nations” (Zech. XII, 2), because sons of God and the house of God, which is the Church, were to exist everywhere.

For this reason the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI, 43).

(V. 27.) Isaiah, however, cries out concerning Israel.

He says this because Isaiah cries out for those who believe in Christ [Col. 0139D] (Isa. X, 22). These are the true Israelites, as the Lord says to Nathanael: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John I, 47).

“Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

When the Jews departed from the merit and promise of the fathers by refusing to receive it, those who persist by believing in the faith promised to the fathers are the remnant, having become faithful. Those depart from the Law who do not believe in the one whom the Law promised alone to be sufficient for salvation. Therefore they must necessarily be regarded as apostates, since, by not receiving Christ, they are guilty of violating the Law.

Thus, from the greatest multitude he says that only the believers will be saved, those whom God foreknew.

(V. 28.) For he will complete and abbreviate the word in righteousness, because the Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth.

He promises that those whom he calls the remnant will be saved through the word that the Lord, defining it justly, has abbreviated upon the earth. For it is fitting that the creature should obtain salvation in the name alone of the Lord the Creator—that is, through faith. When all the new moons, the Sabbath, circumcision, the law of foods, and animal offerings were removed, faith alone was established for salvation.

This faith is an abbreviation drawn from the Law, because what is contained in faith is found in the Law as the principal element of the Law, when the Savior says: “For Moses wrote about me” (John V, 46).

Thus, with the Law abbreviated, the remnant of the Jews are saved. The others, however, cannot be saved, because they are rejected by God’s decree through which he determined to save the human race.

(Vv. 29–30.) And as Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9).

This offspring, which alone was left and preserved from all others for the restoration of the human race, is Christ and his teaching, as he himself says: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke VIII, 11).

This offspring, promised to us long ago, he left for redemption after removing the things that were a burden of the Law, so that, forgiveness of sins having been granted, we might not be punished by the Law as Sodom perished [Note: All the editions read “so that we might not perish by the Law”; all the manuscripts read “so that we might not be punished,” and so forth.]

He therefore says that the Savior was left to us as a support for life, which the Law could not provide. God had determined from the beginning that he should be born. Because he alone was found without sin, he defeated the enemy of the human race and erased the sins of all.

This is also found in the Apocalypse of John: “No one,” he says, “was found worthy, either in heaven or on earth, to open the book and its seals, except the Savior, who conquered death” (Apoc. V, 3).

This, then, is the offspring that God preserved after having promised it long ago, so that it might bear fruit when the sins of all—both Jews and Gentiles—had reached their fullness. Its fruit is the forgiveness of sins. For unless Christ had been preserved—whom he calls “offspring” because through him the human race was restored—the descendants of Abraham would have perished, since they were overwhelmed by sins and the Law could not benefit them.

Therefore he teaches that we must follow the one who brought assistance for life.

What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that comes from faith.

There is a righteousness in the Law, which was entrusted to the world and forbids sin. Therefore he does not say that the Gentiles attained this righteousness, which is recognized through nature as its teacher, but the righteousness that comes from faith in Christ. For to God this is true and enduring righteousness, if it is acknowledged.

What is as just as acknowledging God the Father, from whom all things are, and Christ his Son, through whom all things are (I Cor. VIII, 6)? The first righteousness, therefore, is to acknowledge the Creator; next is to keep what he commanded.

The Gentiles, then, who previously did not seek righteousness—that is, the Law, which bore witness to the Creator—found, when Christ came, a righteousness surpassing that of the scribes and Pharisees. They had not previously pursued what was lesser, but afterward attained what was greater. The Jews, however, who had been placed in the Law and ought to have made greater progress, became worse.

(V. 31.) But Israel, pursuing the Law of righteousness, did not attain the Law of righteousness.

The perfection of the Law is faith. The Gentiles, by apprehending faith, appear to fulfill the whole Law. But the Jews, refusing to believe in the Savior through envy and claiming the righteousness commanded in the Law—that is, the Sabbath, circumcision, and so forth [Col. 0141B]—did not attain the Law; that is, they did not perfect the Law. Those who do not perfect the Law are guilty according to the Law.

For the one fulfills the Law who comes from the Law of Moses to the faith of Christ.

(V. 32.) Why? Because it was not from faith but as though from works.

For, rejecting the faith which, as I have said, is the perfection of the Law, they said that they were justified by the works of the Law—that is, by the Sabbath, new moons, circumcision, and so forth—forgetful of the Scripture that says: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. II, 4).

The righteousness of the Law is so called because these things were given to the Jews by God’s just judgment on account of the hardness of their hearts. Thus, if someone accidentally stepped on a dead weasel or touched some corpse, or if a mouse fell into a vessel, it was called unclean (Lev. XI, 29). They observed these matters with great care, so that whatever cause they encountered, they became unclean.

If the blood of a weasel stained the pavement, it had to be cleansed with no small care, and one had to abstain from better foods. The Sabbath and circumcision likewise had their own righteousness in their proper time, because they were given as figures.

The Lord showed this through the prophet Ezekiel, saying among other things: “Therefore I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. XX, 25), because they were irreverent and unfaithful. But at Christ’s coming, because he was about to give the saving gift, he proclaimed through Jeremiah: “I will give them a new covenant, not like the one I gave their fathers” (Jer. XXXI, 32).

He calls this covenant the Law, which they did not attain, as I mentioned above. For when the believing Jews wished to impose this burden of observance upon the Gentiles who had believed, the Apostle Peter said: “Why are you placing a yoke upon the neck of the brothers that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts XV, 10).

From Christ’s time the forgiveness promised in the Law was given. For the prophet Isaiah says: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob. And this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isa. LIX, 20). That is, the new covenant promised by God in Christ.

(Vers. 33.) They stumbled over the stone of stumbling, as it is written: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” This is found in Isaiah (Isa. 8:14; 28:6). It has been established by the testimony of many that Christ is signified by the rock or stone. For the prophet Daniel calls this the stone which, cut from the mountain without hands, struck and shattered all the kingdoms and filled the whole earth—something plainly said of Christ (Dan. 2:34). And in the Law the rock from which waters flowed is also called Christ. “But the rock,” he says, “was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). The apostle Peter likewise says, among other things, to the Jews: “This is the stone which was rejected by you builders” (Acts 4:11). Therefore, the offense placed in Zion is Christ. Zion, moreover, means “height,” or the city of Jerusalem itself, which, because of its knowledge of God, was rightly called exalted. In it the Savior, placed there as a preacher by God his Father, became an offense to the Jews, while proclaiming himself the Son of God, born of a woman through the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Many manuscripts, and not inferior ones, read “has been called,” with the Apostle himself bearing witness: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.”]

Because of his body they suffered scandal, and they said: “Are not his mother and brothers among us? How then does he say, ‘Because I have come down from heaven’?” (John 6:42). They did not want to compare his words with his deeds, so as to recognize accordingly that what he said about having come down from heaven was not absurd—as though it were merely the body that was acting, and not the hidden God, who nevertheless revealed himself through his works in the body. Therefore, this rock is a scandal and an offense to the Jews; and without doubt this rock is understood to be the Savior’s body. It was cut without hands because he was formed from a virgin by the Holy Spirit without a man.

## CHAPTER X

(Vers. 1, 2.) “Brothers, the desire of my heart and my supplication to God for them is for salvation; for I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.”

Because he says that he wants to remove them from the Law, since they believe that it is a veil for the Jews—

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “he wants to remove the Jews,” because, since the Law is a veil for them, he might otherwise appear to be doing this out of hatred of Judaism.]

—and so that he would not seem to do this out of hatred of Judaism, he demonstrates his affection toward them and grants the Law considerable importance. Yet he teaches that the time for observing the Law has now passed; and thus he testifies that he wishes to provide for them, provided that they listen to him and recognize that he is not their enemy—especially since he bears witness to their nobility and ancestral tradition.

(Vers. 3.) “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God.”

He says that through ignorance they did not believe in Christ. Although they had zeal for God, they did not know his will and purpose; they were acting against the God whom they claimed to defend. He is speaking of those who did not receive Christ through malice and envy, but through error. To them the apostle Peter also says: “I know, brothers, that you acted in ignorance in doing this evil, as did your rulers” (Acts 3:17). For, not knowing that this was the Christ whom God had promised, they said that another was still to be expected. They placed before him their own righteousnesses, which they possessed from the Law—him who is God’s righteousness through faith.

(Vers. 4.) “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

He says this because whoever believes in Christ possesses the perfection of the Law. Since no one was justified from the Law, because no one fulfilled the Law except one who hoped in the promised Christ—

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “in the promised Christ … which would convey the perfection of the Law.” The older editions and manuscripts agree among themselves, except that in them and in some manuscripts one finds “believed the perfection,” which should perhaps be read “into perfection,” or at least, with the manuscripts we follow, in the same sense, “for perfection.” In addition, several manuscripts, with two intervening words, read: “faith to satisfy throughout the whole Law and the prophets.”]

—faith was established, which would yield to the perfection of the Law, so that, with everything else set aside, faith might satisfy for the whole Law and the prophets.

(Vers. 5.) “For Moses writes of the righteousness that is from the Law: ‘The person who does these things will live by them’” (Lev. 18:5).

He says this because the righteousness of the Law of Moses did not make them guilty for the time being, provided it was observed; that is, they lived by doing the Law, for they were debtors.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “This was said in Numbers and in the prophet Ezekiel. What follows, etc.” But this was said in Numbers and Leviticus.]

(Vers. 6, 7.) “But the righteousness that is from faith speaks in this way: ‘Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven?’” (Deut. 30:12).

This was said in Deuteronomy, but here the Apostle interprets it concerning Christ, saying: “That is, to bring Christ down. Or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ That is, to bring Christ back from the dead.” This is peculiar to the Apostle. Thus he says that this righteousness belongs to faith, provided there is no doubt concerning the hope that is in Christ; so that one who distrusts does not say, “Who could ascend into heaven?” For he suffered for this reason: having stripped the underworld by the power of the Father, and conquered death by rising again, he ascended into heaven with the souls he had rescued.

Everyone who, upon seeing the Savior in the underworld, hoped for salvation from him was set free, as the apostle Peter bears witness. For he says that “the gospel was preached even to the dead” (1 Pet. 4:6). Whoever, therefore, does not doubt these things in his heart is justified by faith. But fear brings justification from the Law: one fears the Law because one sees that it inflicts punishment on sinners. Therefore the righteousness of the Law is not great, nor does it confer merit before God, but only for the present. Faith, however, although it is regarded as folly by unbelievers, has a reward with God, from whom one hopes for what is not seen.

(Vers. 8.) “But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart’” (Deut. 30:14).

This is written in Deuteronomy, because what is said to us so that we may believe is not far from our mind or mouth. Although it is not seen by the eyes, what we believe is nevertheless not contrary to the nature of souls or to the manner of speech. For in that very nature are implanted, as it were, seeds which, cultivated through hearing and the will, bear witness to the Creator as fruit.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “cultivated, they would signify the testimony,” which is not entirely correct.]

(Vers. 9, 10.) “This is the word of faith that we preach.”

He speaks of no work of the Law, but says that only faith is to be given in the cause of Christ. “For if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

Here he has made clear all that he said above: this is the rule of faith—to believe that the Lord is Jesus, and not to be ashamed to profess that God, raising him from the dead, brought him into heaven with his body, whence he had come to be incarnate.
