Otherwise one incurs the judgment expressed in the Gospel: “Many,” he says, “of the rulers believed in Jesus, but they did not confess him openly because of the Jews. For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John 12:42).

(Vers. 11.) “For Scripture says through Isaiah: ‘Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame’” (Isa. 28:16).

When the examination of all things begins on the day of judgment, and all false inventions or doctrines are brought to shame, then those who believe in Christ will rejoice, seeing it openly demonstrated to all that what they believed was true and what was thought foolish was wise. Among all others, they will see themselves alone as glorious and wise, though they had been considered contemptible and foolish. For there is true approval where there are reward and condemnation.

(Vers. 12.) “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.”

He says generally that all will either be put to shame because of unbelief or exalted because of faith, since without Christ there is no salvation with God—indeed, there is punishment or death. The Jews cannot be commended by the prerogative of the Fathers; nor can the giving of the Law commend them, since they did not receive the merit and promise of the Fathers. The Gentiles, moreover, have no testimony by which they may be commended according to the flesh, unless they believe in Christ.

“For the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him.”

It is clear that this applies to everyone, whether Jews or Greeks, because without calling upon the Lord Christ no one lives before God. Since, therefore, he is Lord of all, in agreement with the apostle Peter, who says, “This is the Lord of all,” yet he is rich only toward those who call upon him, because they will receive the reward. He is not rich toward the faithless, because they do not share in his blessings; nor will they receive what they did not believe he would give.

Yet he did not say that God is rich toward those who believe, but toward those who call upon him, so that, after the mind has believed, it does not cease to ask for what it has always been taught to ask from God,

[Note: Thus read the majority and better manuscripts. Others, as do all the editions, read: “because in the Gospel of Luke he says, on account of the adversary …”]

as it is written in the Gospel according to Luke, because the adversary is subtle and crafty and one must always pray: “But to those who believe, forgiveness of sins alone is given.” It follows that the person devoted to prayer is delivered from evil and can obtain what God has promised to those who watch with their whole heart (Luke 18:1 ff.).

(Vers. 13.) “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “This was said in Joel.” But although the cited passage is found in that prophet at 2:22, it is preferable to present the author’s words with their blemishes rather than to correct them without the authority of manuscripts.]

This is said in Micah. For the same God who appeared to Moses says: “The Lord is my name” (Exod. 6:3). This is the Son of God, who for that reason was also called both Angel and God, so that he would not be thought to be the one from whom all things come, but the one through whom all things come. Thus his being called God refers to the fact that the Father and the Son are one; his being called Angel refers to the fact that he was sent by the Father as the messenger of the promised salvation. He is said to have been sent so that he would not be believed to be the Father himself, but one begotten by him.

Therefore, “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.” Moses also spoke in this sense: “Whoever,” he says, “does not listen to that prophet will be exterminated from the people” (Deut. 18:18–19). If he is the Lord of all, he is called upon by servants. And because this is true, he added:

(Vers. 14.) “How then will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?”

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “Certainly they do not believe in Christ.”]

Certainly the Jews themselves do not believe in Christ, whom he called Lord. This follows what I said above: one must first believe, so that there may be confidence in asking. “Or how will they believe in him whom they have not heard?” It is obvious that no one can believe one to whom obedience is denied. “How, moreover, will they hear without a preacher?” This too is not obscure, because whoever resists the preacher does not receive his author.

(Vers. 15.) “Or how will they preach unless they are sent?”

This question likewise admits of no difficulty, because they will not be true apostles unless they are sent by Christ, nor will they be able to preach without an author; for no signs of miraculous powers bear witness to them.

“As it is written: ‘How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!’”

The prophet Nahum says this (Nah. 1:15). By mentioning feet, he signifies the coming of the apostles as they traversed the world, and their proclamation that the kingdom of God was approaching.

[Note: The Corbie manuscripts read: “And the kingdom of God is the coming of those who preach.”]

For their arrival enlightened human beings, showing the way by which one travels in peace to God—a way that John the Baptist had first come to prepare. This is the peace toward which those who believe in Christ hasten. Accordingly, holy Simeon, because there is discord in the world, rejoiced at the Savior’s birth: “Now, Lord,” he said, “let your servant depart in peace” (Luke 2:29), because the kingdom of God is peace. For when all discord has been cut away, everyone will bend the knee to the one God. Accordingly, the heavenly Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace”; she is our mother.

(Vers. 16.) “But not all obey the Gospel.”

This is true, because although the world is illumined by the splendor of the Lord’s teaching, there are nevertheless those who resist and call the light darkness. Their mental vision has been so dulled by error that they do not receive even the radiance of the true light. The Gospel accuses them, saying: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5).

“For Isaiah says: ‘Lord, who has believed our report?’” (Isa. 53:1).

That is: Who has believed what we heard from you and proclaim? He confirmed by the prophetic example that the Jews are contradictors of evangelical truth. The Law rebukes the Jews, because what was found among the ancients is found now as well. He does not touch upon the number of those who do not receive faith.

(Vers. 17, 18.) “Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”

It is clear that unless something is said, it can neither be heard nor believed. “But I ask: Have they not heard?” That is: They heard, but they refused to believe. Although faith comes from hearing, there are nevertheless those who do not believe when they hear. They hear and do not understand, because their hearts have been blinded by malice.

“And indeed, their sound has gone out through the whole earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

He testifies that the preaching of God was heard by the Jews to such an extent that he even declares the inhabited world to have been filled with the divine announcement. For the very structure of the world proclaims the Creator. What the Psalmist said of creation (Ps. 18:5), the Apostle says here of the evangelists, because the preaching of Christ’s name was heard everywhere and reached every place. For where the presence of a human preacher was lacking, the sound and report nevertheless arrived, just as the report of the miracles performed in Egypt had reached all the nations, as Rahab the prostitute bears witness. Since it reached every place, the Jews could not fail to hear the apostolic preaching, so that none of them might be excused from the charge of unbelief.

(Vers. 19.) “But I ask: Did Israel not know?”

That is: Did it not know? Having already accused the people of Israel of unbelief through the testimonies cited above, he seemed, in grief, to be complaining about all Israelites. He does not deny that Israel knew and obtained what had been promised to it in the Law; rather, he speaks of the one who is Israel more in spirit than in flesh, whom God had also foreknown as destined to believe. For all heard, but not all believed. Therefore:

“Moses is the first to say,” in the song of Deuteronomy: “I will provoke you to jealousy by a non-nation; I will send you into anger by a foolish nation” (Deut. 32:21).

These are the words of one who is indignant, because the Jews were always found to be unbelieving.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “They were found among the Jews and all evil people …”]

He assigns one generation and one cause to all the wicked: while rebuking those who were present, he touches there upon those yet to come, to whom this applies. For all these have one condemnation if they persist in unbelief.

Thus jealousy arose in them from envy, when they saw a nation that formerly, because it had been without God, was brutish in understanding, calling its God the one who had been the Jews’ God, and attaining the gift promised to them. Because of this, they were stretched out in anger, suffering jealousy, so that they might pay the price of their malice and unbelief. Nothing consumes a person so much as jealousy. God therefore appointed it as the avenger of unbelief, because it is a grave sin. For those who are continually cast into anger are tormented whenever they hear that the Law and the prophets belong to us who believe in Christ.

(Vers. 20.) “Isaiah dares to say: ‘I was found by those who were not seeking me, and I appeared to those who did not ask for me’” (Isa. 65:1).

Because above he used Moses’ words concerning the exclusion of the Jews, he now adds this example from the prophet Isaiah, so that through Isaiah’s further statement he might teach more clearly that God, after expelling the Jews, freely offered his grace to the Gentiles, to the reproach and death of the Jews. For the prophet Isaiah testifies to this in the person of Christ.

(Vers. 21.) “But to Israel he says: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands toward a people who did not believe and who contradicted me’” (ibid., 2).

Here he means carnal Israel, that is, the children of Abraham, but not according to faith. For true and spiritual Israel is the one who sees God by believing. “All day long” means always; for they were always rebuked. Therefore they are reproved as unbelieving, so that they may know that they themselves are the cause of their destruction.

This may also be understood of the Savior, who, with his hands extended on the cross, charged those who were killing him with their sin. That event cries out against the Jews’ wicked deed. Isaiah dared to say of those who had been God’s enemies that they would become his friends, and that those who were called Israelites, because they were disobedient, would be rejected as enemies.

## CHAPTER XI

(Vers. 1.) “I ask, therefore: Has God rejected his inheritance? Certainly not.”

Because he had shown the people of Israel to be unbelieving, he now makes clear, lest anyone think that he had called all Israel unbelieving, that God had not rejected his inheritance, which he had foreknown—that is, the children of Abraham, whom he knew would be faithful to him.

[Note: The Corbie manuscripts read: “which he promised to Abraham. For neither would he …”]

For he would not promise them the kingdom if he knew that none of them would believe. Therefore, according to the Law, the Lord’s inheritance is the children of Abraham—but those who believe.

“For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.”

By his own example he teaches that part of Israel has been saved, the part God foreknew would be saved, or that may still be saved; while he assigns another part of Israel to destruction because of its continual unbelief.

(Vers. 2.) “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.”

This is what the Savior says: “Father, those whom you gave me I have guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition” (John 17:12). Likewise, of those whom God foreknew would believe, none was rejected from the promise, because it happened as God foreknew it would.

(Vers. 3, 4.) “Or do you not know what Scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he pleads against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars; and I alone am left, and they seek my life’” (1 Kings 19:10).

“But what does the divine response say to him? ‘I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal’” (ibid., 12).

These things are clear. For he shows that not only Elijah remained, devoted to God and refusing to worship idols, but also many others who remained in the faith of God, just as not a few Jews believed. The history agrees with this, because many were hidden in caves (1 Kings 18:4) on account of Ahab, king of Samaria, and his wife Jezebel, who, believing the false prophets, persecuted the prophets of God and encouraged the people to idolatry.

(Vers. 5.) “So then, at the present time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.”

That is, he says, even now these have remained in the promise of the Law, while many whom God had foreknown have departed. Those who received Christ as the one promised in the Law stood within the Law; those who did not receive him departed from the Law. Therefore believers are called the remnant—that is, those who remain in the Law.

(Vers. 6.) “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works.”

It is clear that grace is the gift of God, not a wage owed for works, but granted freely through mercy.

“Otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

This is true: if it is a wage, it is not grace. But because it is not a wage, it is undoubtedly grace, since granting pardon to sinners is nothing other than grace; and it is offered even to those who do not seek it, so that they may believe.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “It is nothing other than grace for those who do not seek it … Therefore grace is twofold, and this is fitting for God: that someone may abound in mercy and that he may seek …” The older editions and manuscripts read as we have in the text.]

Grace is therefore twofold, because this is fitting for God, who abounds in mercy: both to seek those whom he may freely heal.

(Vers. 7.) “What then? What Israel sought, it did not obtain; but the election obtained it.”

The carnal Israelites are those who, thinking they could be justified by works of the Law, did not attain righteousness through faith before God. Therefore, since all are guilty through the Law—for “cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them” (Deut. 27:26)—

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “to do them. Although even if they remained in all the Scriptures—which is scarcely possible—they would not be justified before God, because ‘the righteous person lives by faith.’ He is righteous before God only for the present.”]

those who believed they were justified by faith obtained the election, so that, having been justified, they might become children of God, remembering the Scripture that says: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4)—that is, not by the Law.

(Vers. 8, 9, 10.) “But the rest were blinded, as it is written”—the following passage is found in Isaiah—“God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, to this very day” (Isa. 6:9).

[Note: This following passage is found in Isaiah. The Roman edition deleted it, although it is found in the other editions and in many more manuscripts.]

“And David says: ‘Let their table become a snare, a trap, a stumbling block, and a recompense for them. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and keep their back always bent’” (Ps. 68:23–24).

He curses the table of the wicked because the innocent are commonly deceived there. Through deceit they are invited to a banquet so that they may be killed. Thus Ammon, David’s son, was deceived by his brother Absalom (2 Sam. 13:27); the wicked Holofernes thought he could deceive the holy Judith through a banquet (Jdt. 12:1); and at the table of the wicked Herod, evil men raged against the head of John the prophet (Mark 6:28).

The two prophets have one meaning concerning such people, who from the beginning of the faith have been found resistant and hostile to good people. Some of them, however, were corrected and reformed, although late; others, remaining in obstinacy, did not escape the sentence’s severity, but remained bent forever—that is, blinded—so that thereafter they could not look upon the way of truth, which they had scorned through malice, turning away from it, or reach the grace of salvation.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “disdaining grace and refusing to attain it.” Below, however, that edition, together with Gill, adds after “and be saved”: “which he knowingly and deliberately rejected.”]

For whoever understood and refused to believe ought to receive what he desires, so that thereafter he may be unable to receive faith and be saved. The examples of the prophets cited above therefore contain a twofold meaning, for they were decreed and written in two ways.

There are two kinds of people included here. One is blinded forever because of its own malice, so that it may not be saved. Such people are of the worst will, to the point that, although they understand, they say that they do not know what they hear. Thus they said concerning the Savior: “What does he mean? We do not know what he is saying. Why do you listen to him? He has a demon and is insane” (John 10:20).

But another group, which truly is Israel, contradicted them: “These words do not belong to one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” While they envied the Savior, they did not want to appear to understand what they were hearing, so that, since he seemed not to be understood by the teachers of the Law and Pharisees, he might be thought to be speaking absurd things outside the Law; and this might also turn others away from faith.

Therefore they hear from the Savior: “You have the key of knowledge, and you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter” (Luke 11:52). For who would not follow the counsel and judgment of the teachers of the Law and Pharisees—not in trivial matters but in matters of somewhat greater importance—when they appeared to be defenders of the Law?

Accordingly, they said to those who were truly Israelites: “Has any of the rulers believed in him?”

[Note: The Roman edition adds to the words “of the rulers”: “or of the Pharisees.”]

Thus they seemed rightly not to have believed if they had made many accomplices in their conspiracy, because what is defended by only a few is usually thought not to have been approved. Therefore they were blinded so that thereafter they could not believe and be saved.

They were thus assisted in accordance with their own will: since they knowingly called the truth false, thereafter they would not understand what was true, so that they would regard the truth as false, as they desired.

[Note: Amerbach’s edition, together with the manuscripts, reads thus. Erasmus and Gill do not differ from it except that, after “they would have,” they add “but false.” The Roman edition altered the passage as follows: “They would not understand the truth that they had, but the falsehood that they desired.”]

The second kind consists of those who, while pursuing the righteousnesses of the Law, do not receive the righteousness of Christ. They do this no longer out of the envy of an evil will, but are temporarily blinded through error, while zealously imitating the tradition of their ancestors. They ought to learn from Christ’s miracles that the one whose magnificent power is evident in his deeds cannot deceive, and compare his preaching with the new testament promised through the prophets, and then profess that he is the one who was promised. Instead, they were found neglectful toward God and compliant with human beings.

Therefore they are blinded so that, when they join themselves to the promise through the very jealousy with which they envy the Gentiles, they may return to the faith of God.

(Vers. 11.) “I ask, therefore: Did they stumble so as to fall? Certainly not.”

He says what I mentioned above: they did not disbelieve in such a way that they would never believe again. That is, they were not blinded because of their wickedness so completely that they could not be healed, just as we read that the devil fell, when the prophet Isaiah says: “How Lucifer fell from heaven” (Isa. 14:12), signifying a fall and apostasy. Therefore he does not say that they stumbled so as to fall, but that, because of their stumbling, they were dulled for a time.

“But through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to provoke them to jealousy.”

This is what he said: salvation was given to the Gentiles because of their sin. Since the Jews rejected the gift of God, it was transferred to the Gentiles, so that the Jews, inflamed by the jealousy of rivalry, might be converted,

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “to the Christ promised to Abraham. But if …”]

jealous for the promise made to the Fathers.

(Vers. 12.) “But if their transgression is the wealth of the world, and their diminution the wealth of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness!”

It is clear that if their transgression benefited the world, since through their loss it has more good people—for the Gentiles are far more numerous than the Jews—and if their diminution, that is, the loss of the promise, has become the wealth of the Gentiles through the fact that they have gained eternal life, how much more will their fullness accomplish!

It is evident that the world will be richer in good people if those who were blinded are also converted; for the world will be saved in large part. By “world” he means human beings, as it was said concerning the Savior: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19).

(Vers. 13, 14.) “For I say to you Gentiles: Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them.”

He shows the Gentiles with what affection he loves the Jews. For he honors his ministry, by which he is the apostle of the Gentiles, if, because of his affection for his own people, he deliberately also wins the Jews to faith. His ministry will be more honorable if he wins to life even those to whom he was not sent. For it will be a source of the highest praise to the Fathers if he finds as brothers those who had perished.

(Vers. 15.) “For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be, except life from the dead?”

He says this because, if the Gentiles were reconciled to God through the unbelieving Jews, to the increase of the world in the faith of Christ, what and how great will the fullness of salvation be in this respect if the Jews are accepted into the faith of Christ, except that the world in human beings may be brought to life from the dead?

Therefore, since this is progress, he says that effort must be made so that they may believe, because the dullness of their blindness is removed when the time of their punished transgression has been completed, so that they may recover the free choice of their will.

(Vers. 16.) “And if the first portion is holy, so is the whole lump.”

It is clear that what is of one substance is one. Therefore the first portion cannot be holy while the lump is unclean; for the first portion comes from the lump.

[Note: “For the first portion comes from the lump” was omitted in most manuscripts. In the following verse, instead of “whose fathers already are,” quite a few manuscripts read “whose equals already are.”]

Accordingly, he shows that those whose fathers have already attained faith cannot be called unworthy of faith. For if one part of the Jews believed, why should it not be said that another part also can believe?

(Vers. 17.) “And if the root is holy, so are the branches.”

Changing only the wording, he repeats the same point in order to reinforce the meaning by two examples. “But if some of the branches have been broken off”—that is, if some of them did not believe and were cut off from the promise—“while you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted among them and became a participant in the root and the richness of the olive.”

This signifies that, while many Jews did not believe, the Gentiles were grafted through faith into the hope of the promise, to the grief of the Jews. But this was not according to the law of agriculture, because a good shoot is grafted into a bad tree; these, however, though they were in a bad root, were grafted into a good tree. Therefore he says that the wild olive was grafted in, so that the shoot might bear the fruit of the root after becoming its companion.

(Vers. 18.) “Do not boast against the branches.”

That is, do not rejoice in their unbelief. For it displeases God if someone exults in another’s misfortunes, as Solomon says (Prov. 24). They were not cast away for the sake of the Gentiles so that the Gentiles might rejoice; rather, because they did not believe, they gave occasion for the Gentiles to be preached to.

“But if you boast, you do not carry the root; the root carries you.”

That is, if you exalt yourself over those whose root you have been grafted into, and insult the race that received you so that you might become good from being bad, you will not stand if you destroy the very thing by which you stand.

(Vers. 19.) “You will say, then: ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’”

He speaks in the person of a believing Gentile, who thinks he should rejoice at the fall of the unbelieving Jews, saying: “Their rejection made room for the Gentiles.”

But they were not rejected by God so that the Gentiles might enter. Rather, they made themselves rejected by scorning God’s gift; hence they also gave the Gentiles an opportunity for salvation. He wishes to restrain this arrogance, so that one may rejoice in salvation rather than insult another’s misery; for the person who rejoices in another’s misfortunes is easily deceived.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “The person who insults one who is sinning is deceived.”]

[Col. 0151D] (Vers. 20.) “Well”—that is, you speak correctly—“you were grafted in because the branches were broken off.” But they were broken off through unbelief; that is, not because of you, but because of their own fault. When they disbelieved, you were called to salvation in order to provoke them to jealousy. Therefore you ought to give thanks for God’s gift through Christ, not insult them; rather, you ought to ask that, if their evil brought you salvation, they too may return to their origin. Then you will please the God who had mercy on you; for he called you precisely so that, through your rivalry, he might bring them back to grace.

But you stand by faith. Since the Jews fell through unbelief, he says that these stand by faith; for although previously they lay fallen because of faithlessness, they began to stand by believing. Do not be proud, but fear. That is: Do not be arrogant, but beware lest you too stumble.

(Vers. 21.) “For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either.”

This is true. If he blinded those who, by the prerogative of the Fathers,

[Note: The great majority of manuscripts read thus. The editions, however, read “who were worthy,” and some manuscripts likewise have “who were worthy”; in another place, where all the editions and some manuscripts read “adopted by God as sons,” or, somewhat better in some, “having been adopted,” the remaining manuscripts most correctly read “to be adopted.”]

were worthy to be adopted as sons of God, and to whom the promise had also been made, because of unbelief, what will he do to these if they doubt or exalt themselves, who have been raised up by no distinction? Indeed, although they possessed no dignity, they have been honored.

(Vers. 22.) “See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off.”

He bears witness that God is good toward the Gentiles. Although they followed idols and were certainly worthy of death, he awaited them in his patience, and, while they were not yet seeking him, freely called them and forgave their sins.

Toward the Jews, however, he is severe; for he blinded them because they scorned God’s gift. Here he refers to those Jews who, because of their malice, have been blinded forever; hence he says that they fell. But those whom he mentioned above he says stumbled, yet did not fall, because he shows that they were blinded only for a time. Accordingly, God was severe toward those who were apostate, so that they might remain blinded forever.

(Vers. 23.) But they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again. He shows that God’s justice does not remain in severity toward those whom he blinded [Note: [Col. 0152D] Some manuscripts read: “for a time,” and “not even toward those who do not wish to believe, if they do believe,” because he did not cut off the Jews in such a way, etc.] for a time; for he did not cut them off in such a way that he could not graft them in again if they should repent—he who said through the prophet: “Those who return to me I will replant” (Jerem. XXIV, 6). Thus, knowing this, Gentile Christians should not insult the Jews, being certain that God’s mercy is reserved for them as for those who have fallen.

(Vers. 24.) For if you were cut from the naturally wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more will these—who are grafted in according to nature—be grafted into their own olive tree! [Col. 0152D] [Note: [Col. 0152D] Erasmus and later editions read “the olive tree.” The Roman edition reads “the olive faith . . . . we understand; but the wild olive . . . . . signifies unbelief”; Amerbach, however, and the manuscripts preserve our reading, except that some have “and by nature it is unfruitful,” while others have “and it is of an unfruitful nature”; immediately afterward Amerbach, with a few manuscripts, reads “signifies unbelief.”]

Let us understand the olive tree as faith, through which Abraham was justified; but since the wild olive tree is wild and naturally unfruitful, it signifies unbelief. Therefore, if those who had always been enemies of God have been converted and grafted into the faith of Abraham, although they are not of his stock, how much more should the Jews, if they believe after their distrust, be restored to their ancestral nature and grafted again into their own promise!

(Vers. 25, 26.) For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation: a hardening in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved. It is not obscure that a hardening was given to those Jews for a time because of their blindness [Note: [Col. 0153D] Thus Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts; Gill and the Roman edition, with some manuscripts, read: “a hardening was given to the Jews.”]—those who, while zealous for the Law, did not see that the gift promised by God had come, the gift proclaimed by Christ. For they were blinded by zeal, thinking that the law of works ought never to cease; hence they were zealous for the Sabbath. By this offense they were hardened in part, so that they might be tormented because of their unbelief when they saw the Gentiles joyfully professing that they had obtained Abraham’s promise. Yet, when the abundance of the Gentiles had been admitted, the darkness would be wiped away from the eyes of their minds, so that they might be able to believe; and the one who prevents the spirit of remorse from entering their hearts, the one who grants them blindness, would restore to them the free choice of the will. For their unbelief did not arise from malice but from error; they would be corrected and afterward saved.

As it is written. To prove that the gift had been reserved for them by God, he sets forth below an example from the prophet Isaiah, in order to teach that by this grace—through which the Jews who believe have been freed—we too can be freed, because it has not been emptied but always abounds. He therefore says:

(Vers. 27.) “He will come from Zion, the one who will deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isa. LIX, 28).

The meaning of this example remains always, as long as there are those who believe. For this is the Lord Jesus, who was promised as coming from heaven for the liberation of the human race. He himself forgives the sins of those who turn to him every day. Nor does he immediately condemn those who do not believe, but waits, knowing that they can advance toward the knowledge of God.

(Vers. 28.) According to the Gospel, they are indeed enemies for your sake. Because of their unbelief, they are enemies of the Gospel, so that their error and offense might open the way for the Gentiles to enter the faith before the appointed time, as I mentioned above. For the word of God first had to be preached everywhere to all the Jews; only then was it necessary that the Gentiles also believe. But because they did not believe, the kingdom was taken from them and given to the Gentiles. Therefore he warns that they must not be insulted, since their offense benefited the Gentiles; it is rather the one whose sin harmed someone who ought to be insulted. Their unbelief is not to be celebrated but lamented, if they delay in being converted, so that just as the Gentiles rejoiced at their sin because they were saved, so they may rejoice at their conversion, since through their occasion they received God’s grace more quickly.

But according to the election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. Although the Jews sinned gravely by rejecting God’s gift and are worthy of death, nevertheless, because they are the sons of good men, through whose privilege and merit they received very many benefits from God, they will be received with joy when they return to the faith, because in them love awakens the memory of the fathers.

(Vers. 29.) For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. This is true, because God’s grace in baptism does not require groaning, weeping, or any work, but only a confession from the heart. For although they had sinned gravely by not receiving God’s promise, and although grave sins obtain forgiveness only through weeping and groaning, they should not therefore think that they can no longer receive mercy because they were not seen to grieve. He shows that such grief is not required at the beginning of faith; for God’s gift freely grants the forgiveness of sins in baptism.

[Col. 0154B] (Vers. 30, 31.) For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their distrust, so they too now have not believed through your mercy, in order that they themselves also may obtain mercy. He recalls the unbelief of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0153D] The Roman edition reads: “so that, covered with shame . . . . but might delight them, so that they might acknowledge God’s promise.” The Codex Corbeiensis abbreviates the following passage as follows: “For because you,” he says, “were Gentiles . . . . now, however, you have obtained mercy,” etc.] so that they would not, in their very shame, vaunt themselves by insulting the Jews who had not believed, but might encourage them to acknowledge God’s promise. “For,” he says, “you Gentiles, although the oracles of God had been entrusted to these people, were disobedient; now, however, you have received mercy, not through your own merit but for their reproach. Why, then, should these people not rather be converted and receive mercy, since they formerly lived within God’s Law and to them the promise was made?”

(Vers. 32.) For God has shut up all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all. The Gentiles, moreover, had lived in ungodliness and ignorance from ancient times, since they were without God. For this reason the Law was revealed in writing, by which they could be restrained from rushing headlong. And because, through the cunning of the adversary, they began to pile up sins [Note: [Col. 0154D] The Codex Corbeiensis reads: “so that by the prohibition.” After an interval of not many words, the Roman edition reads: “providing salvation for humanity, he decreed that what was sin without the Law could also be erased without the Law, and he established faith alone,” etc.], so that through prohibition a person might be made all the more guilty, God, in the clemency of his goodness, always providing for humanity, decreed that what had been sin without the Law could also be erased in the Law. He therefore decreed that faith alone should be established, through which the sins of all might be abolished, so that, since there was no hope for all humanity through the Law, they might be saved by God’s mercy. This is what it means that he shut up all in unbelief: the gift decreed by God would come at the time when all were afflicted by distrust, so that the grace of the gift might be all the more welcome. Therefore, let no one boast; for it is wretched to be proud when one has been forgiven.

(Vers. 33.) O the depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! He bears witness, with every expression of praise and thanksgiving, to God as exalted and immeasurable in the riches of his wisdom and knowledge; for his plan and judgment are incomprehensible. Since he knew from the beginning the ways of life and works of human beings—because the human race could be saved neither by justice alone in its severity nor attain progress in merits by mercy alone [Note: [Col. 0155D] The Codex Corbeiensis and the Codex Thuaneus read: “unto perfect merit.”]—he decreed at each time what was to be preached, while nevertheless first allowing each person to follow his own judgment, since justice is recognized under the guidance of nature itself. And because the authority of natural justice had grown dull through the habit of sinning, the Law was given, so that the human race might be restrained by fear of the revealed Law. But because they did not restrain themselves and were held guilty by the Law, mercy was proclaimed, which would save those fleeing to it, but would blind those who rejected it for a time. At the same time it invited the Gentiles to their promise, who earlier had refused to follow the justice of God given through Moses, so that, while they envied the salvation of these people, they might by that very zeal be reformed toward the origin of the Savior’s root, promised in the Law. This is the depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God, who by his manifold providence acquired both Jews and Gentiles for life.

(Vers. 34, 35.) “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him?” (Isa. XL, 13.) This is written in Isaiah. It is clear that God alone is the one who knows every plan, and that he alone is in need of no one, because all things are from him. Therefore his plan is neither comprehended nor measured by anyone, because those below cannot know the mind of the one above [Note: [Col. 0155D] All editions and a few manuscripts read: “because the lower things are of the higher”; some read: “because the lower are of the higher”; many others read as in the text.]. Finally, it seemed impossible to believing Jews that God’s plan and will could extend to the redemption of the Gentiles. In the same way, it seemed difficult and incredible to the Gentiles that the Jews who had not believed could be converted, or that, if they believed, they could be received so as to be saved. Among the other elements of God’s plan, this is one that remained hidden and could not be comprehended.

(Vers. 36.) For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory. He has declared why God’s mind and plan cannot be investigated: “For from him,” he says, “and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory.” By these words he disclosed the mind that had been hidden from the world. Since God is the creator of all things—for he made what did not exist, so that it might exist—all things are therefore from him. And since they are from him, they began to exist through his Son, who is of the same substance; what is the work of the Son is also the work of the Father. Since, therefore, he works through the Son, all things are through him. And since what is from God exists through God, after being reborn in the Holy Spirit all things are in him, because the Holy Spirit too is from God the Father; hence he knows what is in God. Therefore the Father is also in the Holy Spirit, because what is from God the Father cannot be other than what God the Father is.

And therefore, to him be glory, because from him, through him, and [Col. 0156A] in him are all things. [Note: [Col. 0155D] The Roman edition reads: “Therefore, because from him . . . . all things came to be,” etc.] Accordingly, those things that began to exist from him, through him, and in him cannot know his mind and plan. But he knows all things, because all things are in him. He has disclosed the mystery of God, which earlier he said ought not to remain unknown to them.

CHAPTER XII

(Vers. 1–3.) “I therefore appeal to you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service. And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is—what is good, pleasing, and perfect.”

By the mercy of God [Note: [Col. 0155D] The Codex Thuaneus, Gill, and the Roman edition read “he urges them”; the final words alone read: “after the treatment of the Law and faith, believing toward the good,” etc. The older edition and the manuscripts differ only in this: where “nature” appears, Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read “by nature.”] he exhorts them, through which the human race is saved. After discussing the Law and faith, he exhorts the Jewish and Gentile peoples to lead a good life; for through this hope of faith is obtained. This admonition, then, is that they should remember that they have received mercy and be vigilant in their service to the one from whom it was given to them, through whom they were freely justified from ungodliness. They should know that this is a living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice to God: if we keep our bodies undefiled, unlike worldly people who pursue pleasures. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thess. IV, 3). Bodies subjected to sins are not considered living but dead; for they are under the despair of the promised life. For this reason we are washed from sins by God’s gift, so that thereafter, leading a pure life, we may call forth God’s love toward us and not render his work of grace ineffectual.

Among the ancients, a sacrifice was therefore killed when it was offered, to signify that human beings, because of sin, were subject to death. But now, because human beings have been purified through God’s gift and freed from the second death, they ought to offer a living sacrifice, so that it may be a sign of eternal life. For then bodies were sacrificed on behalf of bodies [Note: [Col. 0156D] The Roman edition reads: “not bodies to be sacrificed on behalf of bodies, but vices,” etc.]; now, however, it is not bodies but the vices of the body that must be put to death. In order that we may be able to produce the effect of our service, while preserving justice let us guard modesty; for modesty accomplishes nothing and cannot appear rational if justice is neglected. This will be to become conformed to spiritual realities: renewed in spirit and faith, to know what pleases God and that nothing else is good and perfect.

For I say, through the grace given to me, to everyone among you: do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly, according to the measure of faith that God has assigned to each one. 95 He clearly shows that we ought to think only what does not exceed the limits of justice, so that it may be useful not only to ourselves but harmful to no one. For this is prudence: to benefit some rather than harm them, and to be content with the lot that God has measured out, and with each person’s measure of faith [Note: [Col. 0156D] The old edition and a large number of manuscripts read “according to merit and faith”; the Roman edition reads more suitably “according to the merits of faith”; some manuscripts read as in the text.]. No one should claim for himself what he sees has not been granted to him. This is not to think more highly, because the whole cannot be granted to one person. For if someone leads a good life, he should not therefore claim for himself the prudence of teaching; nor, because he possesses knowledge of the Law, should he claim for himself the services of the Levites. He therefore exhorts and teaches through the grace given to him. This grace is understood as knowledge of the Lord’s teaching, through which he teaches that one must pursue humility and justice.

(Vers. 4, 5.) For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members of one another. By the example of the body he teaches that no individual can do everything, because we are members of one another [Note: [Col. 0157D] The Roman edition alone reads: “lest one be a member of another,” etc.], so that one may not be without need of another. Therefore we ought to care for one another, and one member ought not to obstruct another, because we need one another’s services. This will be to love Christ: if the members exhort one another to fulfill the measure by which the body may be perfected in Christ.

(Vers. 6.) Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us [Note: [Col. 0157D] Some manuscripts add the word “different” to “us”; others have “differences.”]. Now he enumerates the functions assigned to the members according to the merit of faith, so that when one member sees what function has been assigned to it, it may not complain against another to whom it sees that something else has been entrusted [Note: [Col. 0157D] The old edition and a few manuscripts read “but may heap together.” In the following passage Amerbach and Erasmus, with some manuscripts, read “according to the operation of faith.” Neither reading is satisfactory.], but may rejoice with it, so that the body of the Church may be perfect.

Or prophecy, according to the proportion of faith. He begins with prophecy, which is the first proof that our faith is rational. Indeed, after receiving the Spirit, believers prophesied. This gift is therefore given according to the measure of the recipient—that is, as much as the situation for which it is given requires.

(Vers. 7.) Or service, in serving. For providing service to the brotherhood, the minister is strengthened as much as he believes that he ought to serve, lest by laboring beyond faith in his service he be wearied in vain; for each person receives what he strives for from the heart.

Or the one who teaches, in teaching. Likewise, he says that the teacher is assisted in teaching, so that to the extent that his faith is directed toward teaching, to that extent he may be inspired to hand on heavenly instruction.

(Vers. 8.) Or the one who exhorts, in exhorting. In the same way, this person too is prepared by the help of the Spirit in the very activity toward which he strives [Note: [Col. 0157D] Some manuscripts read “in which he shows”; several others “in which he stretches himself”; the remaining manuscripts and all editions “in which he strives.”], so that he may have grace when he urges others on. For he challenges brothers to goodness or unbelievers to faith.

The one who gives, with simplicity. He says that for the person who gives with a good disposition, assistance is always supplied, with the Spirit ensuring that the one who gives simply does not lack, as Solomon says: “The one who gives to the poor will not be in need” (Prov. XXVIII, 27). He gives simply who does not do this in pretense, so that praise may be given to him by human beings, but so that he may receive merit from God for this very act.

The one who presides, with diligence. The person who undertakes the care of presiding over the brothers is to receive vigilance and authority according to his faith, so that he may prosper in the task for which he is diligent and have fruit in those over whom he presides.

The one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. The person who shows mercy with a joyful spirit, rather than as though something were being wrested from him unwillingly, is likewise, according to his understanding, established and strengthened by God, so that he may suffer no weakness in this matter, knowing what Solomon said: “While you have the opportunity, do good” (Prov. III, 27). But this must be understood in many ways, for under one word there is a multiplicity of meanings concerning mercy [Note: [Col. 0157D] Some manuscripts read: “For under one word there is a manifold understanding.” This is not at all unreasonable.]. For if he said above, “The one who gives, with simplicity,” what need was there to repeat it, unless he intended by the single name of mercy to signify many good works? To forgive those who sin is mercy; to bring help to one who is in some need or oppression is mercy; to clothe the naked, to break bread for the hungry, to take in an exposed child, to cover a corpse [Note: [Col. 0158D] The Roman edition reads: “and to perform such things.” This is not unsuitable.], and to perform other works are mercy. Therefore, if he performs these things diligently and without weariness, he will have the reward of this work both in the present and in the future. Every act of mercy, then, ought to be performed both simply and joyfully, so that simplicity may exclude hypocrisy, while joy, resting on future hope, may testify to the test.

(Vers. 9.) Love without pretense. [Note: [Col. 0158D] The old edition and some manuscripts read: “For this merit, he who meditates”; the Roman edition removed the word “merit”; we have restored the passage from several better manuscripts.] The Spirit assists the mind that meditates on loving a brother for this reason: because it knows that this pleases God the Creator, so that it may not do this in the flattery of the present life, but may fulfill it through acts of service because it seeks this with a devoted mind. For they hear the Lord say: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII, 34).

(Vers. 10, 11.) Hating evil, clinging to good, being kindly disposed to one another in brotherly love, anticipating one another in showing honor. He does not say that it is a great thing merely to avoid evil unless one also clings to good; the former is done from fear, the latter from love. Nor is someone said to be kind or to possess brotherly love if they do not anticipate one another with mutual services [Note: [Col. 0158D] The Codices Pratensis, Gemblacensis, Michaelinus, and Vallensis correct the passage in this way; previously the editions and manuscripts had: “nor is the honor of brotherhood kind if it is not”; Gill in the margin and the Roman edition in the text, with one or two manuscripts, read “the love of brotherhood.”].

[Col. 0158D] Not sluggish in diligence. This is what the prophet Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the one who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jerem. XLVIII, 10). The person who is sluggish in divine conduct is without hope; therefore he adds:

Fervent in spirit. That is, in the exercise of divine work or of the Law, do not be lukewarm, as it is said in the Apocalypse of John: “Because you are lukewarm,” he says, “I will vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III, 16). For daily meditation removes sleepiness and makes a person watchful. The works of the Lord are those he commands to be done for the benefit of the Church, that is, of the brothers.

Serving the time. In Greek it is said to read as follows: “Serving God,” which does not fit the passage itself. For what need was there to insert here a summary of all devotion, when he is mentioning one by one the members who pertain to God’s service and ministry? In all the things he enumerates, full service is rendered to the Lord. Elsewhere he explains what it means to serve the time, when he says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” [Col. 0159B] (Eph. V, 16). But because he had said, “Fervent in spirit,” lest they understand this in such a way that they should indiscriminately and inopportunely introduce religious language at an unfriendly time, thereby perhaps provoking scandal, he immediately added: “Serving the time,” so that they might speak of the faith of religion modestly and honorably, at suitable places, to suitable persons, and at a suitable time. For even in this time of peace there are some who so dread the words of God that, when they hear them, they blaspheme the way of Christ with great anger. Paul himself also served the time when he did what he did not wish to do: unwillingly he circumcised Timothy, and, with his head shaved, he was purified according to the Law and went up to the temple, so that he might calm the madness of the Jews.

(Vers. 12.) Rejoicing in hope. After saying, “Serving the time,” he added, “Rejoicing in hope,” so that if, because of the wickedness of the time, it should not be permitted to speak publicly about the faith but one must remain in fear, one might rejoice in hope; for this sadness produces joy.

Patient in tribulation. This is what it means to rejoice in hope: to be patient in tribulation. For the joy of hope enables one to endure tribulation, knowing that the things promised in return are far greater.

Devoting yourselves to prayer. Prayer is greatly necessary, because in order that tribulation may be endured one must persist in prayers.

(Vers. 13.) Sharing in the remembrances of the saints. It is clear that the person who wants his prayers to be heard ought to be zealous for the life of the saints. For when he imitates them, he shares in them; thus to remember and share with them means to imitate their deeds. And if they need financial assistance, one must share with them, as he says elsewhere: “Concerning the collections that are made for the saints” (1 Cor. XVI, 1); and to the Galatians: “That we should remember the poor” (Gal. II, 10).

Pursuing hospitality. The imitator and lover of the saints pursues hospitality by the examples of the holy Abraham and the just man Lot.

Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse. In order to make Christians new in every respect, he wishes to remove from them even this custom, which is common to all, lest, stirred by an angry spirit, they first readily wish to curse; but rather, having conquered their anger, they should bless [Note: [Col. 0159D] Some manuscripts read: “and the Lord’s discipline may be praiseworthy.”], so that the Lord’s discipline may be praised.

97 (Vers. 15.) Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. This is what he says elsewhere: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer together; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice together” (1 Cor. XII, 26). When someone offers faithful consolation to another in need, he lifts that person’s spirit and secures merit for himself before God, because he loves a member of Christ’s body. And if he grieves together with an unbeliever, he more strongly moves that person toward advancement in the Lord’s discipline [Note: [Col. 0159D] The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads “moves him toward affection”; some manuscripts read “toward effect,” etc.].

(Vers. 16.) Having the same understanding toward one another. This is what was said: that one ought to share in a brother’s tribulation, as he also says in another epistle: “Keeping watch over yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI, 1, 2).

Not being wise in lofty things. To think lofty thoughts is pride; for the devil too, when he thought lofty thoughts, apostatized. If there is exaltation in the mind, and someone, perhaps presuming on the soundness of his conduct, does not grieve for his brother but reproaches him as though he were a sinner, this is pride; when it places itself above another, it gives offense. The Lord also condemns this when he says: “First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Luke VI, 42). For exaltation itself is sin; and even if someone were not a sinner—which is impossible—he becomes a sinner by being proud. Finally, Solomon says: “God resists the proud” (Prov. III, 34).

[Col. 0160C] But agreeing with the humble. This means that, having laid aside pride, one should make another’s cause his own and his own cause as another’s, so that he may have grace with God, because “the one who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, 11).

Do not be wise in your own estimation (Isa. V, 21). This is written in the prophet Isaiah, and here he presents it as his own, so that justice may be held in common, rather than one person being just toward himself and unjust toward everyone else.

(Vers. 17.) Repaying no one evil for evil. This is what the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. V, 20). For the commandment in the Law was: “You shall love your neighbor, and you shall hate your enemy” (Lev. XIX, 18). This, as it seems, is justice; but in order that the justice of Christians may abound, they are taught not to repay evil for evil, so that they may be perfect and a reward may be repaid to them at God’s judgment. For the imitator of heavenly justice appears to surpass justice itself when, in order to be better, he does not do what is permitted. The justice of the world, therefore, granted to him by God [Note: [Col. 0160D] The Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “granted to him for a time, makes him innocent.”], makes him innocent; but heavenly justice makes him perfect, so that he may have merit before God.

Providing what is good not only before God but also before all human beings. To provide means to keep future good things before one’s eyes, so that one may do what, once done, will not incur blame but rather bring praise, whether before God or before human beings. No one should think that, because things permitted by God are not displeasing to him, it does not matter if they become a stumbling block to a brother. He warns that one ought to do what is displeasing neither to God nor to one’s brother. Even if something is permitted but scandalizes a brother, it does not please God, because God commands that one strive for salvation. Thus good things are provided before God and human beings when permitted things are done in such a way that they do not cause scandal.

(Vers. 18.) If possible, so far as it depends on you, living in peace with all human beings. He wishes all who preserve divine justice to be peaceable [Note: [Col. 0161D] Thus all editions, with some manuscripts; many other manuscripts read: “who seem to preserve divine justice. If someone,” etc. In the following verse, instead of “enemy,” the Roman edition substituted “one who is not peaceable.”]. Let anyone who rejects this peace see to it that he is an enemy to such a man, whether because he does not wish to be reproved by him or because he envies his good qualities. Nevertheless, as far as the other person is concerned, he does not disagree with those who act well. For the one who, abandoning the will of the Law, follows his own right is the one who is not peaceable, although David says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable” (Ps. CXIX, 7). But this was necessary because of the power of the persons involved, so that by humble services he might overcome one whom pride so exalts that he despises the commandments of the Law. It can happen that, out of fear of God, a person presents himself as peaceable toward one who hates peace. For when he does not wish to repay evil in kind, he is peaceable; that is, he conquers evil with good, so that by humble services he may overcome one whom the commandments of the Law do not overcome.

Therefore, he says, “if possible, so far as it depends on you,” so that those who act well may appear to live in peace. If the other person is not a lover of peace, you nevertheless wish to be peaceable as far as it depends on you. But if someone is irreverent and blasphemous, and you cannot live in peace with him, this will certainly not be counted against you; for the apostle John did not even permit those who deny that Christ came in the flesh to be greeted (2 John VII). We, then, are ready, if possible, to live in peace with everyone; but when others resist, it will be impossible—not because of us—provided, nevertheless, that no complaint against us is brought [Note: [Col. 0161D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “if only no complaint against us is brought”; the remaining manuscripts read “with us.” In the following passage, instead of “defending,” the Roman edition, though without any suitable sense, preferred “vindicating.”]. For the one who harms no one plainly appears to be peaceable.

(Vers. 19.) Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. In order that the bonds of peace may be preserved, he advises that one refrain from anger, especially since sin is usually committed through anger, when someone, moved by fury, exacts more than the case of the offense requires, or brings harm upon himself by wishing to carry out heavier sins through an unsuitable act of vengeance. For he makes weak the person whom he could have had corrected and sound. Hence Solomon also says: “Do not be excessively righteous”; for, he says, there is one who perishes in his own righteousness (Eccles. VII, 17). By wishing to answer each sin with punishment, a person may find death in vengeance, both for himself and for the one whom he afflicts with blows; for people often fall into wrongdoing through punishments. He forbids not only fitting vengeance against those subject to us, but also vengeance against equals and superiors—that is, if perhaps a brother sins against us, we should not seek revenge but forgive, reserving the matter for God’s judgment. Otherwise, while we are held by anger, the enemy may find a place in which to suggest and persuade us to do what is against us.

For it is written. To give stronger force to his exhortation, he confirms it by the example of the Law, saying: “For it is written [Note: [Col. 0162D] The Roman edition reads: “he had pierced,” in Proverbs. These words are in fact found in Deuteronomy.], ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Deut. XXXII, 35). If we do not at all do what he teaches, he shows that God is being despised by us. Thus, if vengeance is left to God, there is progress in two ways: when a person conquers anger, he becomes perfect, and the matter will be judged by God.

[Col. 0162B] (Vers. 20.) “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Prov. XXV, 21). He shows that vengeance should not merely be reserved for God, but that benefits should also be bestowed upon enemies, so that we may truly show that we do not have enemies because of our own merits, while we strive to overcome them through services and thereby make them cease from enmity [Note: [Col. 0162D] The Codex Corbeiensis and some others read: “so that they may cease from iniquity.”]. If they persist in enmity because of the wickedness of their minds, our services will contribute to their punishment; or, certainly, touched by the assiduity of our services, they will revive like dead coals. Therefore, in order to make us so perfect that we acquire not only ourselves but also others for life, the Lord, through Solomon, not only forbids us to repay enemies in kind but also urges us to invite them to friendship through kindness.

(Vers. 21.) Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good. This is the Apostle’s interpretation as he exhorts us not to repay enemies in kind, as was said. It will greatly benefit us if we yield to malice; for the one who appears for a time to be conquered by evil is the one who conquers it. Indeed, the Savior conquered evil in this way, by not resisting; malice acts against itself, and while it is being conquered it thinks that it is conquering. For this is what the enemy seeks: to draw us away from our purpose and to look for an opportunity by which we may sin. Therefore, if, when provoked by him, we do not repay him in kind, we conquer him with good. For this reason we do not resist: so that we may preserve good while neglecting justice [Note: [Col. 0162D] The same Codex Corbeiensis reads: “so that we may preserve good for repayment, neglecting justice.”], because justice compels us to repay.

CHAPTER XIII

[Col. 0162D] (Vers. 1.) Let every person be subject to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God. Because he commanded that the law of heavenly justice be followed, lest he seem to disregard this present law, he commends it as well; for unless it is observed, the other cannot be preserved. For this law is like a pedagogue, instructing children so that they may be able to follow the path of the more excellent justice. For mercy cannot be imputed to anyone unless that person possesses justice.

[Col. 0163A] In order, therefore, to confirm the right and fear belonging to natural law, he testifies that God is its author and that those who administer it possess God’s ordinance. Therefore he added:

Those authorities that exist have been ordained by God, so that no one may think that they are to be despised as merely human inventions. For they see that divine right has been assigned to human authorities. Therefore the person is subject to authority [Note: [Col. 0163D] Some manuscripts and Gill in the margin read: “who restrains himself through the terror of the Law.”], who restrains himself through fear of God from the things that authority forbids.

(Vers. 2.) Therefore, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. This is directed against those who are powerful through their strength, or who do not believe that they can be discovered by anyone and therefore think that they can mock the law. He shows them that the law belongs to God and that those who for a time escape by some means will not evade God’s judgment. But those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves. It is clear that each person will be justified or condemned by his works. For those who sin after hearing the Law are without excuse.

(Vers. 3.) For those who rule are not a terror to good works but to evil works. [Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read: “they are not for the fear of good work, but of evil.”] He calls these rulers kings, who are established to correct conduct and prohibit wrongdoing, bearing the image of God, so that the rest may be subject to one. But do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it. Praise arises from authority when someone is found innocent.

(Vers. 4.) For he is God’s minister for your good. It is clear that rulers were appointed for this reason: so that evil might not be done. But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not carry the sword without reason. This means that he threatens for the purpose of taking vengeance if he is despised. For he is God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. Since God has established a future judgment and wills no one to perish, he has appointed rulers in this age, so that, by interposing fear, they may be like tutors for everyone, instructing them in what they should observe lest they fall under the punishment of the future judgment.

(Vers. 5.) [Note: Several manuscripts read: “Therefore be subject of necessity.”] Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. He rightly says that they must be subject not only because of wrath—that is, present vengeance; for wrath produces punishment—but also because of the future judgment. For if they escape here, punishment awaits them there, where they themselves will be punished while conscience accuses them.

(Vers. 6.) For this is also why you pay taxes; for they are God’s ministers, serving precisely for this purpose. He therefore says that taxes, or what are called fiscal payments, are to be paid so that they may demonstrate subjection, through which people may know that they are not free but act under an authority that comes from God. For they are subject to their ruler, who acts in God’s place, just as they are subject to God, as the prophet Daniel says: “For the kingdom is God’s, and he will give it to whomever he wishes” (Dan. IV, 14). Hence the Lord also says: “Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s” (Matt. XXII, 21). They must therefore be subject to him as to God; and the proof of this subjection is that they pay him taxes.

(Vers. 7.) Therefore render to all what is owed. He wishes what is owed to be rendered by everyone, because the powerful also owe something to those beneath them, so that they may respond to their merits. To whom tax is owed, tax; to whom revenue is owed, revenue. First he commands that what is owed to royal authority be paid, because in these matters the claim or necessity is greater. To whom fear is owed, fear. Fear is to be shown to authority, because fear restrains sin; then also to a parent or an earthly master, so that he may give thanks in the Christian son or servant. To whom honor is owed, honor. This honor may also be shown to those who appear exalted in the world, so that, when they see the humility of Christ’s servants, they may praise rather than condemn evangelical discipline.

(Vers. 8, 9.) Owe nothing to anyone, except to love one another. He wishes us to maintain peace, if possible, with everyone, but love with the brethren, and even this with honor preserved. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “with the brethren; and this will be to owe no one anything: to render to each person the duty appropriate to his station. For the one who loves,” and so forth.] He calls them debtors for this reason: toward a person worthy of honor, whether present or future, it is fitting and obligatory to bow. One bows to the person from whom one has received honor; therefore he is called a debtor. For if you do not do this toward your ruler, you are proud; someone must be honored either on account of merit or on account of age.

For whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law. Whoever loves his neighbor fulfills the Law given through Moses; for the commandment of the new Law is also to love enemies. “For you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet” (Matt. V, 43). Moses received this in writing from God for the restoration of the natural law. And if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”; this is written in Leviticus (Lev. XIX, 5). Thus, while the commandments mentioned above remain, he indicates that the Law is fulfilled in love, as though he said: even if there are other commandments that he has now omitted, love nevertheless satisfies on behalf of all the commandments. For if the human race had loved one another from the beginning, there would be no injustice on earth; the beginning of injustice is discord. Therefore, the love of iniquity is iniquity; for what is evil to the wicked is good to the good.

(Vers. 10.) Love of one’s neighbor does not do evil; for love is the fullness of the Law. It does not do evil because love is good, and that love which is the perfection of the Law cannot sin. [Note: Gill and the Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts, read: “nor can one sin through it . . . . . . reaches the evangelical [sense].” Amerbach and Erasmus, with a few manuscripts, read: “nor can one sin; it [Erasmus: ‘to sin’] can reach the evangelical [sense]”; many other manuscripts have the reading found in the text.] He wishes to arrive, through the words of the Law, at the evangelical meaning. For this reason he recalls what is supreme in the Law, so that he may join the Gospel to it, showing that both have one author’s meaning. But because something had to be added in the time of Christ, he commanded that not only neighbors but also enemies be loved. Hence what follows: “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Matt. V, 43), so that justice consists in loving one’s neighbor, while abundant and perfect justice consists also in loving enemies. But what else is it to love an enemy than to wish that he cease from hatred and to seek nothing harsh against him? This is to love him: to wish for him those things through which he may have God favorable toward him. This is heavenly justice; this makes one like God the Father, who bestows yearly gifts even on those who do not worship him. The Lord also, while hanging on the cross, pleads for his enemies (Luke XXIII, 35), in order to demonstrate the fullness of the justice he had taught.

(Vers. 11.) And knowing this time, that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep. He says that the time has come when we ought to advance toward merit. This means rising from sleep: doing good as in the daytime, that is, openly; for unlawful acts are done at night, that is, in secret. Since we have now been placed in manifestation, that is, in the knowledge of God, and recognize what we ought to follow, we must strive, by living purely, to reach the promised reward after shaking off sleep, that is, ignorance or negligence. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “which is the innocence of God.”]

For our salvation is now nearer than when we believed. It is clear that, after the washing, those who live well and devote themselves to love are not far from the merit of the promised resurrection. For the good life of a Christian is a sign of future salvation. [Note: Quite a few manuscripts add after “sign”: “of future salvation.” “When, therefore, each person is baptized, it pertains to forgiveness, not to the crown; but afterward, walking in newness of life, he is near to eternal life.” Some also add: “for he signified it.”]

(Vers. 12.) The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. He signified the old human being by the night, who has been renewed through baptism. He says that this has passed like night, while the day has drawn near, by whose light truth has appeared to us, so that we might know what we ought to do. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “has drawn near, that is, the Sun of righteousness, by whose,” and so forth.] Previously, when we were ignorant of Christ, we were in darkness; but once we learned, light arose in us, for we passed from falsehood to truth.

Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light. The works of darkness are a carnal life, driven by worldly enticements; this is worthy of darkness, as the Lord says: “Take him away; and, after binding his hands and feet, cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. XXII, 13). [Note: So the old edition and some manuscripts, and the Roman edition does not depart from them except that it reads “the vices of the flesh.” Other fairly numerous manuscripts read: “carnal vices, which are driven by worldly enticements”; these things are worthy of darkness.] But putting on the weapons of light means good deeds. For just as evil acts are assigned to darkness because they are done secretly by those who do evil, so those who do good act openly, because they are not afraid but rejoice. Good deeds, therefore, are the weapons of light, attacking the darkness, which consists in the vices of the flesh.

[Col. 0166A] (Vers. 13.) Let us walk honorably as in the day. This is true: since no one sins publicly, let us act as people act publicly; for nothing is so public as truth.

Not in revelries and drunkenness. Revelries are extravagant banquets, celebrated either by everyone contributing or customarily offered in turn by table-companions, so that no one there is ashamed to say or do anything dishonorable, because each person presumes that the banquet belongs to him. People are usually restrained by shame at another’s table; but here they meet so that disgraceful things may be done there amid an abundance of wine, and various pleasures of lust may be aroused. Therefore he commands that such banquets be avoided. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “there an abundance of wine is amassed.”]

Not in bedrooms and indecencies. After the extravagant banquet and drunkenness he added what follows, namely, shameful intercourse; for this is the fruit of such licentiousness. [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and not a few manuscripts read: “this kind of this licentiousness”; Gill and the Roman edition, with other manuscripts, read: “for this is the fruit of this licentiousness”; the Roman edition has “of licentiousness.”]

Not in strife and rivalry. He rightly warns that they should be restrained from these things, because every strife and jealousy produces enmity, which he calls darkness, since those who engage in them cannot attain the reward of light.

But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires. He forbids care for the flesh, that is, pleasure, so that whatever is prohibited by the Law may not be desired, or at least, once desired, may be overcome. For these are the works of the flesh, and those who have stripped themselves of them should put on the Lord Jesus Christ; that is, having been renewed through Christ, they should restrain themselves from these evils. For the person who has separated himself from every error and disgrace has put on Christ, lest he be found without a new garment at the wedding feast and, shamefully cast out, be consigned to darkness (Matt. XXII, 11). [Note: So the more numerous and better manuscripts; others, as well as the editions, read: “lest he be found at the wedding feast”; the Roman edition reads: “at the heavenly wedding feast, without his garment, shamefully cast out,” and so forth.] Otherwise, they have not put on Jesus Christ the Lord, over whose new garment they put on old rags; for, having stripped off the old human being, one must remain in newness of life. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “one must walk in newness of life.”]

## CHAPTER XIV

(Vers. 1.) But receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes over thoughts. Since there were people from the Jews who had brought the Romans to the name of Christ with the Law mixed in, as I mentioned at the beginning of the epistle, [Note: The Roman edition likewise reads: “to faith in Christ.”] it therefore seemed to some that they ought not to eat meat that had been prohibited, while to others who followed Christ without the Law it seemed permissible to eat contrary to the Law.
