Consequently, disputes arose among them. The Apostle, concerned for harmony and salvation, removes these disputes by divine reasoning, showing that neither does eating benefit one before God nor does not eating harm one. He calls weak the person who fears to eat because the Jews were forbidden to do so. He therefore wishes this person to be left to his own judgment, lest, having suffered offense, he withdraw in mental disturbance from love, which is, as it were, the mother of souls; for Christians ought to be peaceful and tranquil.

(Vers. 2.) For one person believes that he may eat everything. Trusting in his reading, this person does not doubt that everything given for human use may be eaten. For he reads in Genesis that everything God created was very good (Gen. I, 31); therefore nothing should be rejected. Neither Enoch, who first pleased God, nor Noah, who alone was found righteous in the flood, nor Abraham, that friend of God, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, righteous men and friends of God, among whom Lot also was found, nor the other righteous figures are reported to have abstained from these things.

But the one who is weak should eat vegetables. Therefore, since he thinks this way and eats vegetables, he must not be persuaded to eat meat, lest he eat with scruple and appear to sin because he is not keeping his own resolve.

(Vers. 3.) Therefore let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. Since eating or not eating is a matter of choice, no dispute should arise from it. For everything was made for this purpose: to be subject to the will, since it has been subjected to human dominion.

For God has received him. He has been received by God when he was called to grace.

(Vers. 4.) Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. It is clear that a servant ought not to judge the will of a fellow servant to whom the law has not been delivered in this matter; for God is the judge of the conscience with which he eats or does not eat, since he is God’s servant.

But he will stand, for God is able to make him stand. “He will stand,” he says, before his own master, because he will be neither guilty if he eats nor blameworthy if he does not eat, provided that he does this out of devotion and does not avoid it as something contrary.

(Vers. 5.) For one person judges one day to be different from another; that is, someone is pleased to eat on specified days. For there are some who have decreed that meat should not be eaten on Wednesday; there are some who do so on Saturdays; and there are others who eat from Easter until Pentecost. [Note: The Carnutian manuscript and several others read: “who [do so] on Tuesday.” A little later, instead of “do not eat until Pentecost,” the Corbie manuscript reads: “do not eat until the fiftieth day.”]

But another judges every day alike. He judges every day alike who never eats. Let each person abound in his own understanding; that is, let each person be left to his own judgment.

[Col. 0167D] (Vers. 6.) The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord. This is true, because the person who always abstains thinks that he is pleasing God. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord. He eats for the Lord because he gives thanks to the Creator. And the one who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. He gives thanks when he acknowledges that God’s creature is good and was created good. [Note: All editions and the majority of manuscripts read: “and good as created”; but several others read better: “and created good.” Immediately afterward, where the old edition and many manuscripts read “but he pretends to withdraw from it, not to condemn it,” the Roman edition reads: “. . . to be condemned on account of it”; other manuscripts, more suitably, have the reading found in the text.]

(Vers. 7.) For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. Someone would live for himself if he did not act under the Law. But the person governed by the restraint of the Law certainly does not live for himself, but for God, who gave the Law so that he might live according to God’s will. And the one who dies likewise dies for God, by whose judgment he will either be crowned or condemned.

(Vers. 8.) [Note: This text is absent from a great many manuscripts. Below also, where the old edition and several manuscripts read “Christ both lived and died,” the Roman edition, together with more manuscripts, omits “both lived”—τὸ “and lived.”] For whether we live, we live for the Lord; or whether we die, we die for the Lord. The meaning is the same. Therefore, whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord. It is true that we all belong to the Lord as servants by condition and by the dominion of the Redeemer, and that each person is dealt with according to his merit.

(Vers. 9.) For it was for this that Christ died and rose again: so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. Through Christ the Lord the creature was made, and through sin it was alienated from its author and made captive. God the Father, lest his work perish, sent his Son from heaven to earth and taught it what it should do in order to escape the hands of pirates. For this reason he also allowed himself to be killed by his enemies, so that, descending to the underworld, he might, because he had been killed though innocent, make sin liable, and release those whom sin held in the underworld. Since, therefore, he showed the living the way of salvation and offered himself for them, while he liberated the dead from the underworld, he is Lord of both the living and the dead; for from those who were lost he re-formed them once more for himself as servants.

[Col. 0168C] (Vers. 10.) But why do you judge your brother for not eating? Or why do you despise your brother for eating? [Note: The words “for not eating,” and below “for eating,” have been suppressed in the Roman edition.] For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. He teaches that one ought not to judge in this matter, both because it is not contained in the Law and because we await God as judge.

(Vers. 11.) For it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to God” (Isa. XLV, 24). This is written in Isaiah, because every tongue will confess God in the faith of Christ. [Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “For the one who was killed rose again.”] Since the one who was killed rose again and will be judge, he rightly says: “As I live, says the Lord”; and not only do I live, but I will also judge, and my enemies will be astonished at me and bend the knee, recognizing me as God from God. [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “and my enemies will confess me”; some read “in me”; the remaining manuscripts, which are also the better ones, support our reading.]

[Col. 0168D] (Vers. 12.) Therefore each of us will give an account of himself to God. Since, he says, each of us will give an account for himself, let us not condemn one another in this matter, which has been discussed above.

[Col. 0169A] (Vers. 13.) Therefore let us no longer judge one another; that is, knowing this, let us cease from discord. But judge this rather: that you should not place a stumbling-block or an offense before your brother. He urges judgment in what is beneficial, which can also be defended by the authority of the Law; but no offense should be caused to any of the brethren, whether he eats meat or does not eat it. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “what he betrays.”]

(Vers. 14.) I know and am confident in the Lord that nothing is common through him. It is clear that, through the benefit of the Savior, all things are clean. He has rescued people from under the yoke of the Law and justified them, restoring them to the condition of their former freedom, so that they are worthy to use the whole of creation, as the holy people of old did. But those who are still under the Law may not use or eat what the Law prohibits, because they despise the indulgence that has been granted. They are not unclean according to their nature, but become unclean when they are eaten contrary to the commandment. Finally, the Law says: “They shall be unclean for you,” and so forth (Lev. XI, 4).

And plainly, for the person who considers something common, it is common. Whether he is a Christian from the Jews or a faithful Gentile, if he thinks that something of this kind must be avoided, he is the one whom he called weak above; for he is weak through doubt. For such a person, what he thinks ought not to be eaten is unclean; and since he does not act from superstition but from fear, he must be left to his own judgment. [Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read: “the one whom Scripture calls weak.”]

(Vers. 15.) For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. In another epistle he says: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI, 13). Since no one is pleasing or displeasing to God because of food, he therefore urges us to pursue the love by which God deigned to free us; for he says: “But God, because of his exceedingly great love, had mercy on us” (Eph. II, 4). Therefore the person who remembers this benefit cultivates love and places nothing before it, but he sets aside the greatest things, knowing that they do not prepare a promise for him before God. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “because of his love, with which he loved us, he had mercy on us.”]

Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. The value of a brother’s salvation is known from Christ’s death. Therefore the person who knows what it cost ought to strengthen him, not scandalize him, making him scrupulous over something trivial. Someone who perhaps had been eating simply and confidently, with a clear conscience, may begin to hesitate whether meat ought to be eaten or not. But when controversies arise, he will begin, in his disturbance, to sin against God’s creature, and it will become an insult to the Creator, which will lead to the destruction of the doubter.

(Vers. 16.) Therefore let our good not be blasphemed. This means that the Lord’s teaching, since it is good and salvific, must not be blasphemed over something trivial. It is blasphemed when there is doubt about God’s creature. It may also be understood in this way: our good is blasphemed because someone who has good works, if he is reproached in some other minor matter, obscures that good of his, and his good will begin to be blasphemed through his evil, as it is written in Ezekiel: “The righteousness of the righteous will not benefit him if he goes astray” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12). Such is the case if someone who is otherwise handsome should happen to have some blemish on his forehead or a flattened nose, by which his appearance is disfigured. Therefore he urges the pursuit of those things that do not remove the favor attached to one’s other good qualities. [Note: By far the most manuscripts have this reading; several others, as well as the editions, read: “If someone who is handsome happens to have something new,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 17.) For the kingdom of God is not food and drink. It is clear that no one pleases or displeases God because of food. Rather, it is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. He says that those enter the kingdom of God who pursue righteousness while possessing the Christian peace that the Lord gave, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). From this peace joy in the Holy Spirit arises. Dispute, however, does not have joy but anger; therefore the Holy Spirit does not look upon it there, because he rejoices only in the peaceful. For just as he is saddened by us, so he also rejoices in us.

(Vers. 18.) For the one who serves Christ in this is pleasing to God and approved by human beings. Since Christ redeemed us, he says: “The one who serves Christ in this,” as Redeemer, is pleasing to God. Why? Because God himself sent Christ to redeem the human race, as the Lord himself says: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John V, 23). Therefore the person who pleases God is approved by human beings. How? He has received a gift by which he may appear worthy of God. [Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “is pleasing to Christ—that is, whoever causes no one to stumble—he fittingly obeys the Redeemer.”]

(Vers. 19.) Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace and let us guard one another’s edification. Since dispute produces discord, he teaches us to conceal ourselves from the controversy over eating or not eating, so that we may be peaceful. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “so that we may be able to be peaceful, free from the contention over eating.”] He urges us to follow the way of edification, so that in peace we may discuss those things through which we may build one another up, turning away from what is fruitless and more harmful. Discussion can be beneficial, for it stimulates the mind, provided that the desire to win is rejected; for that is what produces quarrels.

(Vers. 20.) Do not destroy the work of God because of food. A human being is God’s work by creation, and again is God’s work when he is re-formed through regeneration. Food too is God’s work, but the human being was not made for food; food was made for the human being. There is therefore a great difference. For this reason he says: do not destroy this work of God, which is noble, for the sake of what is most insignificant. This means to care about your brother’s salvation rather than about food, so as not to distress your brother. For the person who again provokes into sin through dispute a brother freed from sin makes God’s benefit void, destroying in that brother the works of Christ, which he performed to free the human being from sin.

All things indeed are clean. It is true and clear that all things are clean, since Genesis says that everything God made was very good. But it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense (Gen. I, 31). Since all things are by nature good and clean, they nevertheless become unclean for those who doubt; and it will be a stumbling-block to the person who, although doubting, eats with an unclean conscience. For he does what he considers useless for himself. Therefore no one should be contradicted concerning what he follows in this matter.

(Vers. 21.) It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine. Since he was speaking only about meat, he added drink as well, in order to encourage those who abstain from these things by reminding them that it is permitted both to eat meat and to drink wine. So that they would not be distressed by those who use these things, he gave them the comfort of breathing freely, so that they might rest in their own choice and the dispute through which discord arises might cease. For when they learn that eating meat and drinking wine is good, and conversely that not eating meat and not drinking wine is also good, no one quarrels. Creation was given for use to those who wish to use it; nevertheless, no necessity has been imposed either on the willing or on the unwilling.

Nor [anything] by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened. He says the same thing: no dispute should be made with a brother who has established for himself a weak conscience concerning eating, lest, being disturbed, he stumble, not knowing what he should hold.

(Vers. 22.) You have faith; keep it to yourself before God. This means: you who sit secure because God’s creature is good need not judge another, because it is more important for you to have peace with your brother; this is useful before God. In food there is usefulness for the flesh, but in peace there is usefulness for both flesh and soul. Therefore one must cease from such dispute, so that each person may remain in the resolve of his own heart. [Note: Erasmus and the subsequent editions, with one or two manuscripts, read: “you who eat, being secure . . . . . . it is good, not necessary,” and so forth. Amerbach, with the remaining manuscripts, has the reading found in the text.]

Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. He judges each person to be condemned by his own judgment when he does what he says he ought not to do; and he calls blessed the person who does nothing other than what he proves useful for himself.

(Vers. 23.) But the one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned. This is true: the person who judges that something must not be eaten and yet eats is condemned; for he condemns himself when he does what he asserts to be useless for himself. Because it is not from faith. The person who says that it ought not to be eaten and yet eats certainly does not eat from faith.

But everything that is not from faith is sin. He rightly calls sin what is done otherwise than it has been approved. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “than it has been judged.” “Therefore everything that pertains to conscience, if it is done otherwise than one knows it ought to be done, he says is sin. But we ought—” All the other manuscripts and editions agree with us, except that instead of “they had been introduced,” the Carnutian manuscript reads “they had been taught.”] Since the Romans had been instructed in the Law, as I mentioned at the beginning of the epistle, but when people who believed more correctly arrived, questions arose about eating and not eating meat, and the party that said it should be eaten and not condemned seemed better because all things are very good, he calls weak those who said it should not be eaten, whether they were Jews or Gentiles, and he leaves them to the resolve of their own hearts. For not eating does not harm, nor does eating benefit one before God; otherwise, being bound by some rule, they might sin by eating with scruple.

## CHAPTER XV

(Vers. 1.) But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak. He rightly says “ought,” because teachers must strengthen the weak and instruct the unlearned with gentleness, lest, when provoked and wishing to contend so as not to appear humble, they make worse progress. [Note: Thus the majority of manuscripts; several others and Amerbach differ only in reading “and still less humble”; Erasmus and the subsequent editions, with a few manuscripts, read: “lest, when provoked, they wish to contend, and lest, while they seem humble,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 2.) And not to please ourselves; that is, we must not claim what benefits and pleases us, but also what benefits our brother, because we ought to care for one another. Let each person please his neighbor for the good, unto edification. He now distinguishes the persons concerned: he urges these people, while devoting themselves to love, to please their neighbors for what is useful. This is edification, as he says elsewhere: “I please everyone in all things” (I Cor. X, 13).

(Vers. 3.) For Christ also did not please himself, but, as it is written: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.” He says that the Savior did not please himself but God the Father, because he says: “For I did not descend from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John VI, 38). And because, while saying these things, he was killed by the Jews who contradicted him as though he were a sinner, the Psalmist makes him speak to God the Father, saying: “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me” (Ps. LXVIII, 10). This means: while I was doing your will, they said that I was sinning against you; by not receiving me, whom you sent, they reproached you. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “because the Jews sinned against God.”] For when the Jews sinned against God by not receiving Christ whom he sent, they also killed him as though he were sinning against God. Thus the sins of those who sinned against God fell upon Christ; for the innocent was killed by sinners as a blasphemer, as it is written in the Gospel (Mark XV, 28).

(Vers. 4–6.) For whatever was written was written for our strengthening, so that through the patience and exhortation of the Scriptures we might have hope. [Note: Thus the old edition and not a few manuscripts; the others read: “for our instruction”; the Roman edition: “for our discipline.”] It is clear that whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through this exhortation we might advance toward hope, not distrusting the promises even if they are delayed.

[Col. 0172D] But may the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same understanding toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. As though sent for salvation, the Apostle follows the people with a good prayer, wishing that God grant them one understanding of wisdom according to Jesus Christ, so that they may think according to Christ’s teaching. Then they will be able to preserve love, following the example of the Lord who says: “No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends and brothers” (John XV, 13). In this way they may praise God the Father in Christ with one mouth and one confession, if they exhort one another according to Christ’s understanding, so that without ceasing they may praise God for all the things he made through Christ and, after they had fallen through error, deigned through the same Christ to raise and restore them again, granting a double benefit: mercy and knowledge. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “mercy and work.”] [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read: “no one has greater love than this”; the Roman edition reads: “love”; the remaining manuscripts have the reading found in the text.] [Note: Some manuscripts read: “let them praise God, who made all things through Christ, and after they had fallen through error,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 7.) Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received you, for the honor of God (Isa. LVI, 4). We were received by Christ when he took on our weaknesses and bore our infirmities, so that, following this example, we might strengthen one another’s weaknesses through patience, lest the honorable name of God, which has been taken upon us, be made void. For we are called children of God through the grace of Christ.

(Vers. 8.) For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, in order to confirm the promises made to the fathers. He commends the origin of the Jews. By “circumcision” he signifies the sons of Abraham, to whom Christ was sent and among whom he ministered the grace promised to the fathers. Hence the Savior says: “I am among you” (Luke XXII, 27), not to be ministered to but to minister, so that the truth of the promise made to the fathers might be established. Circumcision of the flesh was given to Abraham as a figure of circumcision of the heart, which the prophet later signified would come, saying: “Circumcise the hardness of your heart” (Jer. IV, 4). [Note: So the old edition and many manuscripts, from which the Roman edition differs only in substituting “his” for “this”; other manuscripts prefer: “Therefore Christ is the minister of this promised circumcision.”] Christ is the minister of the promised circumcision expressed in these words, that is, its preacher. Then he said to the apostles, so that they might minister circumcision of the heart to those circumcised in the flesh: “Just as you sent me into this world, so I also sent them into this world” (John VI, 58). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “Circumcision of the heart occurs if the error approaching the heart is cut away like decay, so that, when truth has been revealed, it may be able to recognize that God the Father, the Creator, is the Father of Jesus Christ, through whom he created all things.”] Circumcision of the heart consists in removing the cloud of error and recognizing God the Father as Creator, and his Son Christ, through whom he created all things, so that the truth of God might be fulfilled. For he had promised that he would give mercy, and he had promised it to the fathers of the Jews. For he had said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18). And to David he said: “I will place upon your throne one from the fruit of your womb” (Ps. CXXXI, 11), and: “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. XXIV, 17).

(Vers. 9.) But the Gentiles are to honor God for his mercy. Since no promise had been made to them, they were received into salvation as though unworthy, through mercy alone, so that they might honor God through confession; for unbelievers dishonor him.

As it is written: “For this reason I will acknowledge you among the nations, and sing to your name.” He proves by prophetic example—for it is written in the seventeenth Psalm—that the nations were to be admitted to the grace of God in order to receive salvation (Ps. 17:50). For this is the voice of Christ, who foretold that his preaching would bear the fruit of the confession of God’s sacrament among the nations. Therefore, on this account, the Son gives thanks to the Father for the obedience of the nations. Hence he says in the Gospel: “I acknowledge you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones; for it was pleasing in your sight” (Matt. 11:25). This confession, therefore, is of the one God in the Trinity, from which joy arises, so that after the true confession he may joyfully sing of the mercy and gift of God.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “with the confession of the sacrament.” But below, where all editions and some manuscripts read, “the Son effects the obedience of the nations,” many other manuscripts read, “the Son effects [it] for the Father,” and so forth.]

**(Verses 10–11.)** And again he says: “Rejoice, nations, with his people.” This is in the Song of Deuteronomy (Deut. 32:43).

[Note: This was removed by the Romans from the Song of Deuteronomy.]

And again: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and magnify him, all peoples.” In this passage from the hundred and sixteenth Psalm he shows that God formerly decreed, through the intervention of his mercy, to make Jews and nations harmonious, so that the Gentiles, having obtained grace, might become companions of the Jews—who themselves had formerly been called his people by God’s gift.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “because they too … had been called”; the old edition and manuscripts, “who themselves … had been named”; several manuscripts, “they had been named.”]

But the Jews were already noble, whereas these others were ignoble; through mercy they were ennobled, so that all together might rejoice in the knowledge of the truth. While the nations praise him, let all peoples magnify God—the twelve tribes, the one God—who increased the number of his people by adding the nations.

[Col. 0174C]

Finally, when the Jews disputed with the apostle Peter on account of Cornelius, after he had given them an account, they yielded, magnifying the Lord and saying: “Perhaps God has granted repentance also to the nations, so that they may obtain life” (Acts 11:18).

**(Verse 12.)** And again Isaiah says: “There shall be the root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope” (Isa. 11:10).

In order to give the nations greater confidence and an unquestionable hope, he confirms by many testimonies that this was God’s decree: that all nations should be blessed in Christ. Thus the arrogance of the unbelieving Jews would not grieve them or make the souls of believing Gentiles doubtful, as though they were promising themselves hope in vain, since the faith of the Jews, received by Abraham from God, is handed down. In this way they might grow in joy and security.

Why, however, is Christ said to come from the root of Jesse, and not from the root of the righteous man Boaz, or from the root of Obed? It is because he is called David’s son on account of the kingdom: just as, being born from God, he was born as king, so also, according to the flesh, he was to arise from David the king. Therefore Jesse’s root is the tree of David, which produced fruit through the branch that is Mary the virgin, who bore Christ.

**(Verses 13–14.)** “May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit. I myself, brothers, am also confident concerning you, that you too are full of love and filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another.”

These words are exhortatory. Through praise he urges them toward better understanding and conduct. For one who sees himself being praised deliberately strives to make true the things that are said.

[Note: The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads, “Therefore he did not say,” while the rest continue, “He did not say that they should teach one another, but that they should admonish one another.” After the words “it escapes the mind,” Gill and the Roman edition add, “or is treated negligently,” a reading found nowhere else except in the Codex Thuaneus.]

Therefore he did not say that they should teach one another, but that they should admonish one another. For what is already known is what is customarily admonished about when, at times, it slips from the mind. The remaining matters are not obscure and do not require explanation.

[Col. 0175B]

**(Verses 15–16.)** “But I have written to you somewhat boldly, brothers, as reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God, so that I might be a minister of Christ Jesus among the nations, sanctifying the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the nations may be acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit.”

He does not indicate that he wrote rashly. Rather, by saying that authority was given him through God’s grace, he declares that he dares to write to all the nations, both admonishing and confirming their purpose in Christ. He shows his concern in the ministry of the Gospel, as a teacher of the nations, so that their sacrifice may become acceptable for the purpose of sanctification in the Holy Spirit. For whatever is offered with undivided faith and a sober mind is purified by the Holy Spirit.

**(Verses 17–19.)** “Therefore I have glory in Christ before God. For I do not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through me for the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, through the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Holy Spirit.”

He says that he has glory before God through Christ Jesus.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “with God in Christ Jesus.”]

For by believing in and serving Christ Jesus with a pure conscience, he acquired merit before God the Father, to such an extent that he says that nothing is lacking that Christ did not accomplish through him for the exhortation of the nations. Christ gave signs and wonders through his hands, so that his preaching might be commended by divine power.

This is why he shows that he has glory in Christ before God. For by serving Christ he has glory before God, to such an extent that he does not lack any manifestation of divine power that has not been granted to him by God. Rather, because he was found to be a suitable steward, he professes that he has obtained everything that could advance the conversion of the nations through the power of signs.

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read this way; the others read, “which he says for this reason, so that he might show that he was able to do nothing less,” and so forth.]

This serves to prove that he was no less capable than the other apostles who had been with the Lord, and that God worked no fewer manifestations of power among the nations through him. In this way the nations would grow, seeing that they had obtained the same grace that the Jews had obtained—those Jews who claimed the prerogative of the patriarchs.

**(Verse 20.)** “Thus I have fulfilled the Gospel of God and of his Son Christ from Jerusalem and its surrounding regions as far as Illyricum.”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “But there I endeavored to preach.”]

Thus I preached the Gospel, not where Christ had already been named, lest I build upon another’s foundation. He does not say without reason that he endeavors to preach where Christ had not been named. For he knew that the pseudo-apostles were presenting Christ differently from what was proper. They went about for this purpose: under the name of Christ, to subject the people to other doctrines. Correcting this afterward was a work of the greatest difficulty. Therefore he wished to forestall them, so that he might deliver to his hearers the words of an unimpaired preaching,

[Note: The Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts, reads, “and so that, in a straight line …”; the Codex Corbeiensis reads, “so that the foundation might remain whole and unharmed upon another surface”; the remaining manuscripts and editions read as in the text.]

and so that an ordered surface along a straight line might preserve intact the strength of the foundation.

[Col. 0176B]

And because he had been appointed teacher of the nations, he ought carefully to ensure that he taught there where Christ had not been announced; both to establish his authority and to obtain the full fruit of his labors from what he had planted.

This is why the Church occupied all those places.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “that he might occupy the Churches.” The others more appropriately read, “that he might occupy the Church.” Again, certain manuscripts, quibbling over the subtlety of malice, prefer “the subtlety of malignity.”]

For afterward heresies, maliciously employing subtlety, tried under the name of Christ to corrupt the meaning of the Law and the faith. He gave warning of this by the testimony of the Law, saying:

**(Verse 21.)** “But as it is written: ‘Those to whom nothing was announced about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.’” This is found in Isaiah (Isa. 52:15).

Therefore, so that this understanding might be true and inviolable concerning the true Son of God, he says that he always hastened to imbue the nations with evangelical truth:

**(Verses 22–24.)** “For this reason I was hindered very much from coming to you. But now, having no further place in these regions, and having had for many years a desire to come to you, when I begin my journey to Spain I shall see you, and I shall be sent on from you to there, if first I have enjoyed your presence for a little while.”

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read, “and be sent on by you”; the Roman edition, “and be sent on”; the Florentine and Vindobonense codices, “and be escorted.”]

He recalls what he mentioned at the beginning of the letter, saying: “I have often proposed to come to you, and have been hindered until now” (Rom. 1:13). Now he explains the reason why he was hindered: although he wished to come, he had to do something else that was pressing, namely, to exclude the perverse inventions of the pseudo-apostles. Finally, after preaching throughout all the surrounding regions, he says that he now has leisure to come to Rome, which he had long desired.

He therefore corrects the Romans for the time being by letter, since they had been introduced to the Law. But those who had not yet heard the preaching would more profitably be taught by his presence, so that, having been founded upon the right faith, they would be less likely to receive something else.

[Note: The Codex Corbeiensis reads, “would discover something else.”]

Nevertheless, he promised that he would come at the time when he was going to Spain, because Christ had not been preached there, so that he might occupy their minds. And because the pseudo-apostles found it difficult to travel to them, there was no harm if he went later.

**(Verses 25–26.)** “But now I am departing for Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have approved making some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem.”

Beforehand, however, he says that he will go to minister to the saints in Jerusalem. Through this he wishes the Romans to know that such works must be attended to. For those who live by mercy and have been justified before God ought to devote themselves to it.

[Note: The Codices Thuaneus, Florentinus, and Vindobonensis read, “they ought to show themselves pious toward the brothers.”]

**(Verse 27.)** “For they are their debtors. Since the nations have become participants in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to minister to them in material things.”

He calls them debtors to the believing Jews, so that just as they have become participants in their spiritual blessings, so also they may share in their bodily necessities. In this way the believing Gentiles, rejoicing with the Jews, may praise God’s providence for their salvation through their ministry.

These people, devoting themselves wholly to divine service and caring nothing for worldly matters, provided believers with an example of good conduct. Indeed, the Apostle wishes us to be so humane in showing mercy that he calls us debtors with regard to giving alms and practicing good works with a willing heart. For one who hopes for mercy from God ought himself to be merciful, so that he may prove that he rightly hopes for it: if a human being shows mercy, how much more does God!

This is the repayment, or reward: that those who receive mercy should show mercy. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful” (Matt. 5:7), “for God will have mercy on them.”

[Col. 0177C]

**(Verses 28–29.)** “When, therefore, I have completed this and delivered this fruit to them, I shall depart through you to Spain. For I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of Christ.”

Confident, therefore, in God’s arrangement and grace, he promised that he would come in the abundance of the blessing that he preaches as Christ’s. This blessing is the power of signs, by which they were confirmed.

**(Verses 30–31.)** “I beseech you, therefore, brothers, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit, to share my concern in prayers for me to the Lord, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea.”

He then prays that he may be helped by their prayers, so that he may escape the hands of the unbelieving Jews—not because he himself is less worthy, but because he follows the proper order, namely, that the Church should pray for its ruler.

[Col. 0177D]

For many insignificant people, when they gather together with one mind, become powerful; and it is impossible that the prayers of many should not obtain their request.

[Note: The Codex Corbeiensis reads, “it is impossible to despise them.”]

If, therefore, they too desire to see the Apostle, let them pray with greater earnestness, so that, after he has been delivered from there, they may receive him with the joy of love.

**(Verse 32.)** “So that the ministry of my gifts may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem; so that I may come to you with joy through the will of Jesus Christ and be refreshed with you.”

He says that this too should be prayed for: that the ministry of his gifts may be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, and that he may show himself to be doing everything according to God’s will. Since his spirit is devoted to carrying the gifts, he also wishes their disposition to correspond to God’s judgment concerning him, so that, recognizing his love toward them, they may give thanks to God with him in unity.

For this is a great advancement for him: that those made joyful through his ministry should praise God.

**(Verse 33.)** “May the God of peace be with all of you. Amen.”

Christ is the God of peace, who says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:17). He wishes Christ to be with them, knowing that the Lord said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

He therefore desires them to be such that the Lord Christ Jesus may be with them. Having removed all discord arising from human error, Christ gave and showed them what is true, so that they might remain peaceful in that very truth.

# CHAPTER XVI

**(Verses 1–2.)** “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is a minister of the Church at Cenchreae, so that you may receive her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you. For she herself also assisted many, and me as well.”

He commends Phoebe, who is coming, as a sister common to them,

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “that is, one to be loved.”]

that is, one belonging to the Law. To commend her appropriately, he says that she is a minister of the Church at Cenchreae. Because she had assisted many, he says that she ought to be assisted worthily on account of her journey.

To persuade them to receive her without delay and assist her in her need, if she should arrive, he also testifies that she had assisted him. Thus, the more exalted her status was in comparison with the others, the more he shows that the service owed to her should be rendered through love.

**(Verses 3–6.)** “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life. Not only I give thanks to them, but also all the Churches of the nations—and their household Church.”

They were Jews who became believers and companions in the Apostle’s labor. They believed so rightly that they themselves also exhorted others to the right faith. Indeed, although Apollos was well trained in the Scriptures, he was more carefully instructed by them in the way of the Lord. Therefore he calls them companions in his labor, but in Christ Jesus, for they were his fellow workers in the Gospel of God.

[Note: The Florentine and Vindobonense manuscripts read, “Aquila is the husband of Prisca.” This is incorrect.]

Aquila was Prisca’s husband. It is clear that they did not come to Rome without purpose; they were especially devoted to God. For the sake of confirming the Romans, all those whom he greets seem to have been of this kind.

Thus he says that not only he, but also all the Churches of the nations, give them thanks. He also touches upon the Romans, so that they may obey those whom they hear laboring for the advancement of the nations and the exhortation of faith in Christ.

He praises them so highly that they did not refuse to suffer dangers for him. They did not shrink from enduring the hostility of both Jews and false brothers, provided that they could assist the Apostle through service and love.

The false brothers were those who believed in Christ but nevertheless said that the Law had to be observed. They thought that Christ was insufficient for the full effect of salvation. The Apostle refuted this, and therefore suffered persecutions from them.

He also greets their household servants, whom he calls a Church because they were disciples of holy men in matters of faith.

“Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the firstfruits of Asia in Christ.” He does not conceal Epaenetus’s present dignity, in order to show

[Note: All editions read, “and to believe that men of rank also believe”; other manuscripts read, “and to believe these men worthy,” or “to believe these more worthy”; others, “and to believe men of rank,” while the Codices Corbeiensis and Thuaneus add, “and inclined toward faith.”]

that men of rank also believe, and to invite the leading Romans to faith—or at least so that the humble might grow.

“Greet Mary, who labored much among you.” By naming Mary he reminds them that she labored diligently for their exhortation, so that they may give thanks to her.

[Col. 0179B]

**(Verse 7.)** “Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles and who were in Christ before me.”

He calls them relatives both according to the flesh and according to the spirit, just as the angel said to Mary: “Behold, Elizabeth your relative,” and so forth (Luke 1:36). He declares by his testimony that they also served the earlier apostles and suffered captivity together with him for the sake of the faith. For this reason they deserve fuller honor.

**(Verse 8.)** “Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in Christ.”

[Note: Amerbach’s edition, with one or two manuscripts, reads “Ampliadus”; Gill and Erasmus, with several other manuscripts, “Ampliandus”; the Roman edition alone, “Amplius”; a large number of manuscripts, “Ampliatus”; some add “most beloved.”]

He greets him as a friend, but as a friend in the Lord—not, however, as one who had shared his labor or captivity.

**(Verse 9.)** “Greet Urbanus, my fellow worker in Christ.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Urbanus, a participant in our work.”]

He says that this man was not only his assistant but also a companion of the others in the exhortation of belief.

“And my beloved Stachys.” Although he calls Stachys beloved, he nevertheless subordinates him to Urbanus, a participant in the work of the Gospel.

**(Verse 10.)** “Greet Apelles, approved in Christ.”

He does not greet Apelles as his own friend or as a participant in his work, but because he had been tested by temptations and found faithful in Christ.

**(Verse 11.)** “Greet those who are of the household of Aristobulus.”

This Aristobulus is understood to have been a gatherer of brothers in Christ. He approves his action in such a way that he identifies those whom Aristobulus gathered as worthy of his greeting.

“Greet Herodion, our relative.” By calling him merely a relative, he shows him to be devoted to the love of rebirth, but he does not indicate his vigilance.

[Note: The old edition and several manuscripts read, “You see for what reason”; after a few intervening words, the Roman edition alone reads, “Narcissus was carrying out the office of presbyter abroad.”]

“Greet those who are of the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord.”

Narcissus is said at that time to have been a presbyter, as is read in other codices. Since he was not present, you see for what reason he greets as holy those who were of his household in the Lord. This Narcissus, however, was carrying out the office of presbyter abroad, strengthening believers by his exhortations. Since the Apostle did not know the merits of those who had been with him, he said: “Greet those who are of the household of Narcissus in the Lord”—that is, greet in my name those among them whom you know to be worthy of my greeting, those who have placed their hope in the Lord.

**(Verse 12.)** “Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord.” He declares these women worthy of equal honor in Christ.

“Greet Persis, the most beloved, who labored much in the Lord.” She seems to be placed before those mentioned above because she labored much in the Lord. This labor consists in exhortation, in the ministry of the saints, in distress, and in poverty for Christ’s sake. For they left their homes when driven into exile and became objects of reproach to unbelievers.

**(Verse 13.)** “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine.”

He placed this Rufus before his mother because of his election to administer God’s grace, in which a woman has no place. He had been chosen—that is, promoted by the Lord—to carry out his affairs. Yet he had a mother so holy that the Apostle also called her his own mother.

**(Verse 14.)** “Greet Asyncletus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.”

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read “Asyncletus”; some others, “Asyndetus”; the Roman edition, “Asyncritus.”]

He greets these together because he knew that they were harmonious in Christ, that is, joined in Christian friendship. He also greets the brothers who were with them, whose names he omitted.

**(Verse 15.)** “Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus,

[Note: Gill and the Roman edition, with certain manuscripts, add, “and his sister and Olympias.”]

and his sister Olympias, and all the saints who are with them.”

All these are understood to have been united in spirit. He greets them together for this reason, and their merit is discerned from those who were with them. He calls them saints so that it may appear that he rightly greets them.

**(Verse 16.)** “Greet one another with a holy kiss.”

He commands all to whom he writes and whom he names to greet one another with a holy kiss, that is, in the peace of Christ—not in carnal desire, but in the Holy Spirit—so that the kisses may be religious, not carnal.

“All the Churches of Christ greet you.”

From this it is understood that there is a Church that is not Christ’s. Hence David also calls the conspiracy of the wicked “the assembly of evildoers” (Ps. 26:5). He therefore says that the Churches of all those places greet them, so that they may grow in faith.

He refers this back to the preceding meaning, in order to show that Christ is the one in whom salvation exists, and that this is the people who are faithful to him and by whose will every creature lives.

[Col. 0180D]

He is the author of life, as the apostle Peter says (Acts 3:15), not the Law, in which some of them thought that they ought to hope.

[Col. 0181A]

**(Verses 17–19.)** “I beseech you, brothers, to watch those who create dissensions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and to avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly; and through seductive and flattering speech they deceive the hearts of the innocent. For your obedience has been proclaimed everywhere.”

Here he burst forth against the persons of the pseudo-apostles, whom throughout the letter he had warned them to avoid, as he does now. Yet without naming them, he suppressed their tradition.

These men compelled believers to Judaize, so that they might make God’s benefit toward them void, as I mentioned above. For by composing genealogical arguments, they adapted discourses to commend their tradition, through which they deceived the hearts of the simple.

[Col. 0181B]

“For your obedience,” he says, “has been proclaimed everywhere.” This is what he says at the beginning of the letter (Rom. 1:8): “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” He means that he is confident of their obedience.

For it was unbelievable

[Note: All editions read this way; almost all manuscripts, however, read, “that they would not submit themselves.”]

that after knowing the truth they would submit themselves to something foolish, as though they were wise.

“Therefore I rejoice in you.” This meaning too comes from the preceding part of the letter. He rejoices because the Romans, who seem to possess sovereignty, have subjected themselves to Christian faith.

“I wish you to advance, so that you may be instructed in what is good but inexperienced in what is evil.” One instructed in what is good is one who does good works; those inexperienced in evil are people who are ignorant of evil deeds, that is, who do not know the practice of wickedness.

**(Verse 20.)** “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet”—that is, shortly.

He says this concerning his coming, because his arrival would crush the devil on account of the fact that these people were going to receive spiritual grace. Satan envies this, because he wishes human beings to remain in error. The remaining matters are intended to be distinguished, although they belong to one confession.

“May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.” He now wishes the grace that he promised them at his coming to be with them. For if they deserve to receive it, it is already with them in hope.

**(Verse 21.)** “Timothy, my fellow laborer, and Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my relatives, greet you.”

Timothy was his companion in labor, almost a fellow bishop, who governed the Church with great concern. He was exposed to the hostility of the Jews to such an extent that at the beginning he was circumcised because of the Jews’ scandal, so that, since his mother was Jewish, he could not be a teacher while uncircumcised.

He calls the others his relatives partly on account of their lineage and partly on account of their faith.

**(Verse 22.)** “I, Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.”

Tertius is a name, not a number. He was the secretary of the letter, to whom Paul allowed the privilege of greeting the Roman people in his own name—the people to whom he was writing—so that they might greet the others whom he names. At that time there were still few rulers of the Churches in the various places.

**(Verse 23.)** “Gaius, my host, and the whole Church greet you.”

[Col. 0182A]

This is, I think, the Gaius to whom the apostle John writes (3 John 1), rejoicing in his love, which he showed to the brotherhood by providing them with the expenses necessary for them.

Although above he says, “All the Churches of Christ greet you,” he repeats here: “The whole Church greets you.” I do not think that this repetition is pointless; such a great and accommodating man would not insert anything superfluous.

But because he says, “All the Churches of Christ greet you,” that is, all the saints—as he says elsewhere, “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh” (Gal. 5:24)—he now adds that these people too greet them, those who follow after the others.

[Note: The Codex Thuaneus reads, “so that it may be said twice”; the Florentine, “so that from these words he may signify the whole people.”]

In this way he signifies the blessed people of the Church, because in every Church there are two peoples. He may also have named the Churches of two provinces, so that he first referred to all the Churches of one place and then to those of another, or else to the Churches of Jews and Gentiles.

**(Verse 24.)** “Erastus, the steward of the city, and Quartus, the brother, greet you.”

The steward of the city is like a curator or administrator who governed the city under the direction of justice, especially by regulating prices.

He lists all these people by name in his greeting to the Romans so that they would know what kind of people, and how many of them, rejoiced together with them in their good beginning.

**(Verses 25–27.)** “To him who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept silent in eternal times, but is now manifested through the prophetic Scriptures according to the command of the eternal God, made known for the obedience of faith among all the nations, to the only wise God through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

He gives glory to God the Father, from whom all things exist, so that, because he is powerful, he may deign to complete the Romans’ undertaking by confirming their minds in the faith for the advancement of the Gospel. He also gives glory for the revelation of the mystery hidden throughout the ages but manifested through Christ, or in Christ (Eph. 3:9).

For the sacrament that had always lain hidden in God was disclosed in the times of Christ, because God is not solitary: the Paraclete also has been with him from eternity.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “the Word and the Paraclete.”]

In this truth he decreed that every creature should be saved through knowledge. The truth of this sacrament had indeed been indicated beforehand by the prophets through certain figures, and it was known only to the wise God. He wished the nations to share in this grace, which had been hidden from the human race.

He alone, therefore, is wise, because all wisdom comes from him, as Solomon says: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him” (Eccles. 1:1).

This Wisdom is Christ, because it comes from him and was always with him. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Therefore nothing is complete without Christ, because all things exist through him. When he is acknowledged, praise is given to God the Father through him, because he is understood through Christ, as through his Wisdom, in whom he saved those who believe.

Glory, therefore, belongs to the Father through the Son—that is, glory belongs to both in the Holy Spirit, because both possess one glory.

[Col. 0183A]

**(Verse 28.)** “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “The glory of our Lord,” and so forth.]

In the conclusion he places Christ, through whom we were made and through whose grace we were again restored, so that he may remain fixed in our minds. For if we remember his benefits, he will always protect us, as he said: “And behold,” he says, “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Amen.

[Note: The manuscripts Remigiensis, Michaelianus, and Colbertinus append here a lengthy section belonging to the final chapter of the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians. This matter will have to be discussed in its proper place.]

[Col. 0183]

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Note: The old edition reads “Preface”; the Roman edition, “Introduction”; some manuscripts, “Argument”; many others, “Prologue.”]

# PROLOGUE

[Col. 0183B]

Admonished by the Lord’s command, the Apostle remained at Corinth for one year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. Hence he deals with them with great confidence and affection, sometimes admonishing, sometimes reproving, and sometimes flattering them as children.

There are many reasons why he writes to them. The first is that, dissenting from one another in the manner of heretics and devoted to human beings, they wanted to be called Paulinians, Petrians, and Apollonians, rather than Christians. The Apostle strongly reproves this. Yet there were some among them who dissented from these groups and were devoted to Christ alone.

The second reason is that they had begun to delight in eloquence and earthly philosophy, so that under the name of Christ they might be imbued with teachings contrary to the faith.

The third is that they had become puffed up because the Apostle was not going to them.

The fourth concerns the fornicator whom they allowed to remain among them.

The fifth is that he might remind them of the earlier letter that he had written before this one, which is called the First.

The sixth is that they had begun to inflict injuries and frauds upon one another and to seek the judgments of unbelievers rather than those of the faithful.

The seventh reason is where he indicates that he has the right to receive support, but refrains from it, lest he become an example for the rapacious pseudo-apostles.

The eighth is that he might answer their letter, for they had begun to be disturbed by heretics concerning marriages.

The ninth is where he declares that each person ought to remain in the condition in which he believed.

The tenth concerns virgins, since no command had been given to him about them.

There are also the remaining reasons, which will become apparent in the body of the work.

# CHAPTER I

[Col. 0183D]

**(Verse 1.)** “Paul, called an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God.”

He began differently in the letter to the Romans because the situation was different. To these people he writes that he is an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, because everything he did, he did by the will of the Son of God, who said to him: “Go, I will send you far away to the nations” (Acts 22:21).

By this he was called an Apostle—that is, sent to the nations by the will of God. Through this he also touches upon those whom Christ had neither sent nor authorized to say what they claimed.

He frequently names God and Christ for this reason: to show that Christ is God, but not the Father himself; rather, that Christ is the Son and that God is the Father,

[Note: The old edition and several manuscripts read this way. The Roman edition differs only in preferring “not by union.” Other manuscripts read partly, “not into union, because when he is extended he is called the Son”; some are defective: “[...] the Son is called.”]

not a union, when he is shown to be called the Son.

For many sects had arisen that asserted the Gospel of Christ according to the inclination of their own understanding,

[Note: The Codex Corbeiensis reads, “according to the inclination of his own will.”]

and branches of these, now dry, still exist. Their advocates were overthrowing the Churches. For this reason the Apostle sets forth everything contrary to the heresies and asserts that he is a true preacher because he was sent by Christ according to the will of God.

**(Verse 2.)** “And Sosthenes, the brother.”

He also commends Sosthenes by associating him with himself.

“To the Church of God that is at Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus.”

He writes to the Church because individual rulers had not yet been appointed over the Churches. Although he censures them in many respects, he says: “Sanctified in Christ Jesus.”

He says this because they had been regenerated and sanctified in Christ. Later, however, they began to conduct themselves badly. Thus he shows that the whole Church had been sanctified in Christ, but that certain members had been turned away from the tradition of truth by the perverse teaching of the pseudo-apostles.

Called to be holy. That is, you have been called so that you may be holy—which means that you must not depart from the rule of sanctification. Together with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in every place that is theirs and ours. That is, he joins true Jews and Gentiles together, because salvation is from the Jews; so that in every place where there are Gentiles who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and where the Jews mentioned above are found, all are likewise one. For the pseudo-apostles, who preached the name of Christ according to the wisdom of the world—that is, with philosophy mixed in—rejected the ancient Law and the prophets. For they denied that Christ had truly been crucified, claiming only that he had appeared to be crucified, as did Marcion and Manichaeus. Hence the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified” (I Cor. I, 23). Nor did they acknowledge the resurrection of the flesh, which the prophet Isaiah proclaims, saying: “Those who are in the tombs shall rise” (Isa. XXVI, 19).

**(Verse 3.)** Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Lest, because he had said, “those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” he should seem to have passed over the name or gift of the Father and thereby perhaps provide suspicion or an occasion for the doctrine of unity, he teaches that Christ is rightly invoked, but that all grace belongs to the Father; thus he both shows that the two are one through divinity and gives precedence to the Father’s authority.

**(Verse 4.)** I give thanks to my God always for you. Although he is writing to everyone in the Church, he expresses himself in such a way—sometimes reproving, sometimes praising—that each person, when the letter is read, may understand what is said for him and what is said against him. For he writes to two peoples within one populace, so that when he reproves those who conduct themselves badly, they may know that these things have been written about them; likewise, when he praises, the one who remains in the rule of faith may know that these words are addressed to him. And so he says:

I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus. He says that grace was given by God in Christ Jesus, and that this grace was given in Christ Jesus because God established that whoever believes in Christ should be saved without works: by faith alone, freely, he receives the forgiveness of sins.

**(Verse 5.)** Because in every respect you have been enriched in him, in all speech and in all knowledge. This signifies that, having received grace and the knowledge of spiritual teaching in the word of the truth, they have continued to possess it; and for this reason he gives thanks to God concerning them.

**(Verse 6.)** Just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you. The testimony of Christ was confirmed in them because, strengthened in faith, they hoped for nothing from human beings; all their hope was in Christ, and they were captivated by no enticements of pleasure.

**(Verse 7.)** So that you lack no grace in anything, while awaiting the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is clear that the one who awaits the day of judgment is watchful and concerned. He speaks of the future judgment of God, in which our Lord will be revealed both to the faithful and to the unfaithful, so that the unbelievers may recognize and know that what they refused to believe was true, and perish; while the faithful may rejoice, finding more good than they had expected.

**(Verse 8.)** He will also confirm you to the end, blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Confident in their hope, he is secure in spirit concerning them, because they will remain undefiled until the future judgment. For those who, amid so many dangers of opinion and disturbances caused by diversity, could not be changed at all plainly show that they will remain in the same state. While he praises these people, he invites those who had been corrupted by the error of the pseudo-apostles to repentance: by proclaiming the faith of the former, he calls the latter to repentance.

**(Verse 9.)** God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. Who could doubt the promises and faithfulness of God, since it will not be otherwise than he has said—that we, believing in Christ, have been adopted as his sons? He grants us what we believe: because we believe that Christ is the Son of God, we begin to be this ourselves, remaining in the same dignity, just as Christ remains whom we believe to be the Son of God. Fellowship is brotherhood; thus, just as he shows that God’s faith will remain unimpaired for us in this matter, so we must not be found doubting and faithless, but persevering in adoption.

**(Verse 10.)** But I appeal to you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing. He now entreats them all to think alike—specifically, to hold the belief in which they were reborn and called sons of God. He speaks now to the whole Church, so that those who had begun to disagree might return to the faith they had begun, which they saw being praised in those who persevered in it.

And let there be no schisms among you, but be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge. He wants them to be perfect in the same understanding that he had handed down to them, so that they would not disagree. He summons them to follow the example of those whom he praised above, so that they may think and defend the same thing.

**(Verse 11.)** For it has been reported to me about you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. Although they had been overturned, he nevertheless calls them brothers, just as God also says through the prophet Isaiah to those who were with him, instructing them to say to those who believed the false prophets: “You shall be our brothers” (Isa. LXVI, 5), so that by this they would not dissent from them as though they were brothers.

As for what he says, “by those who belong to Chloe,” some think that these were people who remained and bore fruit in the faith of God. Others think it refers to a place, as if one were to say, “by those who are in Antioch.” Others think that she was a woman devoted to God, with whom many worshipers of God lived, whose faith was not to be denied; so that what they reported about the Corinthians would be true—namely, that there were quarrels among them.

He said that there were quarrels among them in order to show the diversity of their minds concerning the Lord’s discipline. He then added what that diversity was, saying:

**(Verse 12.)** I mean this: each of you says, “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos,” or “I belong to Cephas,” or “I belong to Christ.” He points out the error but does not disclose the names of its authors; for they did not remain in one place but went about to overthrow the simple. The men whom he names were undoubtedly good teachers, but under their appearance he attacks false apostles. If he denies that one should glory in these men, how much more does he deny it in evil teachers, whose perverse doctrine he indicates below! Yet among them he designates those who persevered in saying that they belonged to Christ and not to a human being—the very people whom he praises above.

**(Verse 13.)** Is Christ divided? He says that Christ is divided because human beings have divided his glory among themselves. Thus heretics do not shrink from being called Photinians, Arians, Cataphrygians, Novatians, Donatists, or Manichaeans; so the Corinthians too had begun to be subjected to the names of various heretics, appearing to honor human beings in place of Christ. By receiving different teachings about Christ, they divide Christ. For one accepts Christ as merely human, another confesses him as pure God without a human being or body, another says that Christ was foretold through the prophets, while another denies that the prophets spoke about Christ. Since Christ is one, God and human, these people, each claiming a different aspect of him for himself, divide Christ. And because they establish many churches under their own names, he added:

Was Paul crucified for you? He began with himself, so that he would not seem to reject the persons of others merely in order to commend his own. For if Christ, he says, died for us, how do we attribute his grace and benefit to human beings, to his injury?

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? If, he says, we are baptized as believers in Christ so that we may be justified in his name, why do we make human beings the authors of this faith for ourselves, forgetful of the faith we began?

**(Verses 14–16.)** I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Caius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. I also baptized the household of Stephana; as for the rest, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

He gives thanks to God because he did not baptize many of them, lest, since error had begun under this matter, the error should spread widely under his name, reproving through this both those who baptized and those who were baptized, because they attributed the grace of baptism to human beings, to the injury of the Savior, while those people concealed the matter for the sake of glory. For they were like the Novatians and Donatists of today, who claim baptism for themselves and reject those baptized by us, while those baptized by them glory in the persons of their baptizers. Finally, having repudiated the name of Christ, they glory in being called Novatians and Donatists.

Crispus and Caius, then, are Corinthians whom he names as witnesses, because they were baptized by the Apostle in such a way that they asserted that no glory should be granted to him on this account. The household of Stephana, however, are the first fruits of Achaia, as he indicates in the final part of the letter; he bears witness to them because they had appointed themselves for the service of the saints.

**(Verse 17.)** For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize. Since evangelizing is greater than baptizing, he says that he was not sent to baptize but to evangelize, because in a bishop lies the dignity of all ordinations; for he is the head of the other members. By this he also humbles those whom they greatly valued because they had been baptized by them (Acts X, 48), so that they might know from this that baptizing is not a great thing, since not everyone who baptizes is also capable of evangelizing. For the solemn words are those spoken in baptism. Thus the Apostle Peter ordered the believing Cornelius and his household to be baptized, and, while ministers were present, did not consider himself worthy to perform this work; if they had been absent, he himself would have done it, compelled by necessity.

He shows how much better he is than those whom they revered, and yet he did not allow this to be attributed to his own name, knowing that it is dangerous to claim God’s glory for a human name; for this is a kind of idolatry.

Not in the wisdom of the Word, lest the cross of Christ be emptied. Because Christian preaching does not need the pomp and ornament of speech, uneducated fishermen were chosen to evangelize, so that the truth of the teaching might commend itself by its own power. It was not to appear acceptable through human cleverness and the craft of human wisdom, but through truth, as with teachings invented by human beings, in which neither reason nor power is sought, but only the arrangement of words. Thus the person who wants to adorn faith in Christ with words seeks his own glory. He obscures faith with the splendor of words, so that he, rather than faith, may be praised.

The pseudo-apostles did the same. So that they would not appear foolish to the wise of the world, they preached Christ in human wisdom in two ways: they devoted themselves to eloquence, and they avoided those things that the world judges foolish in us. Thus they neither taught that the Son of God had become incarnate and been born of a Virgin, nor that there would be a resurrection of the flesh, because the wisdom and reasoning of the world judge these things foolish. Therefore the Apostle says that he does not preach Christ in human wisdom, lest, he says, the cross of Christ be emptied; for whoever announces Christ in human wisdom denies the truth of the preaching, as I mentioned above.

**(Verse 18.)** For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. It is clear that those for whom the cross of Christ is foolishness are in perdition, for they have not been rescued from the death of hell.

**(Verse 19.)** But to those who are being saved it is the power of God. It is not obscure that for those who believe it is the power of God. They believe that the cross of Christ is not weakness but power, understanding that death was conquered on the cross. Those who bear its sign are saved, because they cannot be held by death.

For it is written in Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (Isa. XXIX, 14). He destroys the wisdom of the wise when he does what that wisdom denies can be done; and he rejects the understanding of the prudent when he proves that God, whom they call unconcerned, undertook the things they consider foolish, so that the Son of God, incarnate and born of a Virgin, might be crucified for human salvation. The fact itself truly bears witness to this through power, not words.

**(Verse 20.)** Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? With these words he attacks both Jews and Gentiles. For the scribes and teachers of the Law among the Jews consider it foolish to believe that God has a Son. In the same way, the Gentiles assign this to ridicule. But the Jews distrust it because it was not so openly signified in the Law; the Gentiles reject it because the reasoning of the world does not admit it. For that reasoning says that nothing can happen without mixture and judges the doctrine foolish.

Yet the investigator of this age is the one who governs the world by the constellations and determines, through calculations, that risings and settings occur according to the twelve signs, thinking that absolutely nothing can happen without their movement.

Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish? The wisdom of this world has been made foolish: for although it thought itself wise, it was found to be foolish. What it judged impossible has been shown to be possible, since it considered God unconcerned. Is anything more foolish than this assertion—that God is said to have made the world but not to care for it? Why did he make it, if what he made does not belong to him?

But because they see some people enjoying the world happily while others are oppressed, the good despised and the malicious prospering, they therefore believed that God was unconcerned. Someone who calls God unconcerned does not deny that he is malicious or unjust; for either he is going to judge the world and is unjust, since he disregards the good and permits evil to occur. If, therefore, setting aside their hatred of the divine law, they should observe carefully, they can see that this matter is settled by us, since we await God’s judgment, in which those crushed down by force will be exalted and the violent will be humbled; for with God there is no partiality (Rom. II, 11).

**(Verse 21.)** For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. The world—that is, human beings—did not know God in his wisdom, because they attributed his unique majesty to fabrications or to the elements, disregarding him and thinking through the wisdom of the flesh that those things which are seen ought to be worshiped. Therefore God was pleased to establish a preaching that would appear foolish to them, so that those who believed what they distrusted might be saved, while they were condemned. This, then, is the reversal by which, according to God’s plan, falsehood is condemned by the truth.

**(Verse 22.)** For Jews demand signs, and Greeks seek wisdom. The Jews demand signs because they do not doubt that such things could happen, but ask whether they have happened. They know that Aaron’s staff, though dry, blossomed and produced fruit (Num. XVII, 8), and that Jonah was swallowed by a sea creature, remained in its belly for three days and three nights, and was cast out alive (Jonah II, 1). Yet they especially seek to see something like what Moses saw: God in the fire. Hence they say, “We know that God spoke to Moses” (John IX, 29), although it is a greater thing that the dead and stinking Lazarus came forth alive from the tomb on the fourth day (John XI, 44). The Greeks, however, seek wisdom because they refuse to hear anything except what is possible according to the reasoning of the world.

**(Verse 23.)** But we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles. He is a stumbling block to the Jews when they hear Christ claiming to be the Son of God and abolishing the Sabbath. To the Gentiles he is foolishness because they hear preached things that, since they do not conform to worldly reasoning, appear senseless—such as the birth from a Virgin and the resurrection of the dead.

**(Verse 25.)** But to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Persuaded by power, which is more effective than words, those who believe in Christ understand—first the Jews who were seeking a sign—that Christ is the power of God; and the Greeks likewise see that Christ is the wisdom of God. They recognize that the worldly wisdom which they previously thought to be prudence is the greatest foolishness.

He is therefore the power of God because through him God the Father made all things; and he is wisdom because through him God is known. For God could not be known except through one who was from him, since “no one knows or has seen the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27).

Because what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings.
