He says “the foolishness of God” not because it is truly foolish, but because human beings consider it foolish when it does not conform to worldly reasoning, although it is spiritual reason. Thus it is recognized as wiser than human beings, because spiritual things possess greater wisdom than bodily things. For spiritual things do not come through bodily things; rather, bodily things are sustained through spiritual things. Therefore bodily things are subject to spiritual things.

And what is weak of God is stronger than human beings. Without doubt, heavenly things conquer earthly things. Consequently, God’s weakness is not weakness, because Christ’s weakness is a great victory. He conquered when he appeared to be conquered, as he says in the fiftieth psalm: “And you will conquer when you are judged” (Ps. L, 6). For the one who is unjustly killed proves victorious, making the one by whom he is killed guilty.

**(Verse 26.)** For consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are noble. It is clear that there are few who are more puffed up by the world’s reasoning than instructed by it—that is, those who observe and distinguish the movements of the stars. He also calls these people powerful according to the flesh, just as he calls them wise. They are powerful because they assert that the passion of Christ’s cross is weak; for iniquity is powerful and seems to prevail for a time. They are also noble, through whom they assign antiquity as the origin of their superstition, calling us recent or novel.

God therefore did not choose this assertion, which exists among the few.

**(Verse 27.)** But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise. The foolish things of the world are that a Virgin gave birth and that the Son of God was crucified. For the world considers it foolish to believe this. Therefore God chose those who believe what the world judges foolish, in order to confound it. The wise are confounded when they see that the many confess what the few deny; for it is not doubtful that the opinions of the many are preferred to the opinions of the few.

And God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong. The meaning is the same. What the few think weak is affirmed by many to be power, to the shame of those who consider themselves wise in the world and distrust the hope. For more believe than do not believe, to their shame. They see the things of Christ called weak commanding demons and performing miracles.

To the world, however, the insults and suffering of the Savior are weak, since it does not know that these things lead to power. For he permitted himself to suffer these things in order to conquer death. To suffer unjustly while being able to resist but unwilling to do so is the glory of the one who suffers and the condemnation of the one who kills.

**(Verse 28.)** And God chose the ignoble things of this world and the despised, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are. He therefore chose the ignoble and despised things—not because they truly are ignoble and despised, but because they are judged so by the world. By choosing them, God destroys the things that truly are ignoble and despised, because those who judge are themselves more deserving of judgment and condemnation.

Their assertion was produced by error and did not exist from the beginning; our discipline, however, is from the beginning. Their doctrine is destroyed because it is asserted in bare words, without testimony, whereas ours is proved not by words alone but also by the testimony of power.

**(Verse 29.)** So that no flesh may glory in his presence. That is, so that the wisdom of the flesh may be put to shame in its error before God, the judge. For the mind of the flesh is to distrust the power of God to bring forth a Virgin’s child, and so forth, because the reasoning of the world—which is akin to the flesh—does not accept this.

**(Verse 30.)** For from him you are in Christ Jesus. “From him”—that is, from God, who is almighty—we are in the faith of Christ. For God’s purpose is that through Christ we should learn his truth and mercy. Truth is the mystery of the Trinity; mercy, however, is shown in that, when we were captives, he redeemed us.

**(Verse 31.)** Who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. To strengthen believers, he says that Christ acted by the will of God in all that he did, so that we may know that through Christ we have truly learned wisdom, been sanctified, justified, and redeemed by God; for no one redeems anything except what had been his own.

Whether, then, we have been redeemed; or sanctified—that is, cleansed from the work of the flesh and the uncleanness of idols; or justified—for it is just to worship the Creator while despising all else; or made wise because we have learned that worldly people are ignorant—all of this is God’s benefit through Christ. Our redemption, however, consists in this: Christ offered himself to the devil who desired him, in order to remove the contradiction of sin in himself and thus rescue his captives.

So that, as it is written: “Let the one who glories glory in the Lord.” This is written in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. IX, 24). What the prophet says is fitting: let us glory in God, because the one who glories in the Lord cannot be put to shame; his works and majesty are evident in his deeds. Therefore, he says, let those who do not send rain and did not make heaven and earth be put to shame in their idols. Likewise, let those who glory in human beings be put to shame, since they certainly know that such people possess no power. Hence Scripture also says: “Vain is hope in a human being” (Jer. XVII, 5).

For the wise are confounded when, etc.” [Col. 0191D] The same Corbie manuscript reads: “What they consider weak is asserted by many to be power, to their shame. ## CHAPTER II

**(Verses 1–2.)** And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not with superiority of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the mystery of God. For I judged that I should know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

Since above he gradually set forth the form of our discipline, he now proves that he handed it on to them in no other way than the one he described. In the humility of speech and the foolishness of preaching, as it appears to the world, he spoke to them of the mystery of Christ.

He calls it a mystery because what was incarnate had been hidden from the ages with God: God the Word. The heretics whom they gloried in were such because they commended their perverse doctrine through eloquence and, pursuing the wisdom of the world, emptied the cross of Christ, being ashamed to be called foolish by the world. Thus they neither preached that Christ had been born of a Virgin nor taught that he had truly been crucified, because it seems foolish to confess that the Son of God was born as a human being and crucified.

The Apostle John also identifies them when he says: “Whoever denies that Christ came in the flesh is the antichrist; and whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either” (I John II, 23–24). For they said that the Father himself had been called the Son; from these people Marcion derived his error.

The things he rebukes appear obscure because he does not make them explicit but wants them to be understood from the fact that the wisdom of the world—which is hostile to religion—is involved. What he censures is to be learned from his judgment, so that whatever our teaching is ridiculed for as foolish may be shown to be precisely what he rebukes in the Corinthians. For he mentions the body itself, so that from it the order of its members may be discerned. To the Corinthians, however, these matters were clear, because they were not ignorant of the reasons for which they were being reproved.

[Editorial apparatus and source pagination: [Col. 0192C–D], [Col. 0193A–D], [Col. 0194A–D], [Col. 0195A–D]; source page numbers: 117–119. [Col. 0192D] Several manuscripts read, “proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ.” [Col. 0192D] The Corbie codex reads, “the Word of God … who also, apart from eloquence …” [Col. 0192D] All editions and some manuscripts read, “they said.” From these Marcion derived the error which the Apostle rebukes: “the things he rebukes appear veiled.” Most manuscripts more correctly support the reading printed in the text; for the words “which he rebukes” refer to the Apostle. Below, where editions and part of the manuscripts read, “because wisdom, etc.,” another part reads, “because he attacks the wisdom of the world.” [Col. 0193D] All editions and several manuscripts read, “and hostile to Jews and Gentiles”; a larger number read, “and [he] shows that, in order not to acquire human favor, he was unwilling to please human wisdom.” [Col. 0193D–0194D] Several manuscripts read, “But in a demonstration of the Spirit and of the power of God.” The Roman edition then has: “That is, because things weak in words but strong in power, foolish things … so that by words [he might show] folly … founded upon reason.” [Col. 0194D] The Corbie codex reads, “in the world, concerning those things which he was going to do.” [Col. 0194D] The same codex reads: “After the temptations which the devil dared to inflict upon the Lord, the evangelist says: ‘The devil departed until a time.’” [Col. 0195D] All manuscripts except the Thuanus and Laudianus, where, as in all editions, one reads “as [it is written],” read: “in the prophet Isaiah, in different words.”]

**(Verse 3.)** And I was with you in weakness, fear, and much trembling. Preaching Christ in the foolishness of human wisdom, he provoked hatred and persecutions against himself, as though he were announcing something vain and hostile to Jews and Gentiles.

**(Verse 4.)** And my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom. He shows that he did not seek to please human wisdom in order to gain human favor, nor did he devote himself to the art of words; rather, he showed faithfulness to the author, who did not want his teaching to be made acceptable by the ornament of human tradition or by the clamor of words, but by the things themselves, because things come before words.

But in a demonstration of the Spirit and of the power of God. Because things that are weak in words but strong according to power may appear, when adorned, to be wise things to foolish people, God did not want his preaching to be commended by the testimony of words but by power. Thus, once the foolishness of the word had been indicated, he would demonstrate by deeds that it was wisdom founded upon spiritual reason.

**(Verses 5–6.)** So that your faith might not be in the wisdom of human beings but in the power of God. Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—that is, among those who acknowledge the cross of Christ as wisdom through the testimony of its power. For they are wise and perfect who possess faith not more in words than in realities.

Yet wisdom not of this age. He rightly says that it is wisdom not of this age but of the future age, in which God’s truth will appear to those who deny it. This age, because of the weakness of its earthly thought, cannot comprehend this reasoning.

Nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed. It is clear that this is not the wisdom of the rulers of this world, because they are destroyed by it. Christianity cut away the errors that they introduced—idolatry, greed, and the other vices—as the Apostle John says (I John III, 8): “For this reason the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil.”

**(Verse 7.)** But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden. He testifies that he was sent to reveal a hidden meaning that neither rulers nor powers knew and that the world had not heard. Hence it is considered foolish because it is unknown; yet it is rational and saving, as its power bears witness, before which all human reasoning gives way.

The wisdom of God was therefore hidden because it consists not in words but in power; it is not possible through human reasoning but believable through the efficacy of the Spirit.

Which God predestined before the ages for our glory. Its truth as wisdom, and the fact that it was always with God, are declared to such an extent that it is said to have been predestined before the ages for our glory—for the glory of us who believe. God, foreknowing the errors that would arise in the world he was going to make, decreed this for the confusion of those who were going to make foolishness into wisdom for themselves, but for our glory, since we were going to believe and do believe.

**(Verse 8.)** Which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. The rulers of this age should not be understood merely as the human rulers of the Jews and Romans, but also as those rulers and powers mentioned above, to whom this statement truly applies—those against whom our struggle is with spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places—for Christ was crucified by their counsel and will (Eph. VI, 12).

Finally, after the temptations that the devil dared to bring upon the Lord, the evangelist says that the devil departed “until an opportune time” (Luke IV, 13). The Lord himself also says: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John XIV, 30).

The rulers of this age therefore crucified the Lord of glory through ignorance. For how can the rulers of the Jews be understood as the rulers of this age, since they were subject to Roman rule? Nor did the Roman rulers crucify Christ, since Pilate said: “I find no cause of death in him” (John XIX, 4). Hence he also washed his hands, saying to the Jews: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you will see to it” (Matt. XXVII, 24).

These rulers, then, crucified Christ the Lord, whom he openly triumphed over in himself (Col. II, 15). Yet the evangelist Mark says of the demons: “For they knew that he himself was Jesus” (Mark I, 34). They did indeed know that he was Jesus, but they knew him as the one promised in the Law; they did not know his mystery, by which he is the Son of God.

The Apostle Peter also said this to the Jewish people: “I know, brothers, that you acted in ignorance in doing this evil, as did your rulers” (Acts III, 17)—but not the rulers of the age. If servants killed the Lord through ignorance, then sin ought not to be attributed to them. Yet it is not permitted to be ignorant of this. Although they did not know that he was the Lord, they were nevertheless not ignorant that they were committing an impious deed.

The Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, although he does not know death. But because the Word became flesh—that is, the Son of God became incarnate and became human—the death was attributed to him. For the Jews did not persecute flesh as such, but the one who worked through the flesh. Thus, although the Lord of glory is untouched by death, insofar as the Jews’ desire and that of the rulers of this age are concerned, they killed the Lord in the flesh.

**(Verse 9.)** But as it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him.” This is written in the *Apocalypse of Elijah*, among the apocrypha. By this example he speaks of an unexpected event, something that not only would not enter human understanding but would also be hidden from the heavenly powers—namely, the Son of God becoming incarnate. Thus he confirms what he said above: if the rulers of this age did not understand that God had become human, how much less did human beings understand it?

But although the words caused offense or scandal, faith ought not to have been denied because of the powers and signs. Power ought to have been preferred to human weakness and ignorance, and what appeared impossible to human reason ought to have been believed. Therefore he prepared this gift for those who love God—that is, for those who believe.

(Vers. 10.) But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit. And because the rulers of the age were ignorant of this, God revealed it through his Spirit to those who believe, since the things of God cannot be learned without the Spirit of God [Col. 0195B]. For he says that this mystery was not disclosed only to human beings, but also to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms who crucified the Lord, so that, when it is proclaimed on earth, those who are in the corporeal heavens—that is, who dwell beneath the elements of the firmament—may learn it. He therefore is the apostle who is unique in this respect, because no one else was able to explain the mystery of the Trinity in such a way; hence by divine judgment he was also repeatedly called “the vessel of election” (Acts IX, 15).

For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God. Since this Spirit is from God, he knows everything. He says “the deep things of God” because the Spirit knows all his power and foreknowledge—something utterly impossible for a creature [Col. 0195C].

(Vers. 11.) [Note: [Col. 0195D] The Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “For who among human beings knows the hidden things of a human being”; but the oldest edition and the very numerous manuscripts read as in the text.]

For who among human beings knows the things that belong to a human being, except the human spirit that is in him? It is clear that no one can know our thoughts except our own mind, which he called “spirit.” Accordingly, in the Gospel he says among other things: “And her spirit returned to her” (Luke VIII, 55).

So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. This Spirit of God taught us what he knows naturally, without being taught; and he taught us about the mystery of Christ, because he is not only the Spirit of God but also of Christ.

(Vers. 12.) Now we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God. From this we know that we have received the Spirit who is from God: the spirit of the world cannot know the things that have been communicated to us by him. Yet the spirit of the world is the spirit by which those who are without God are seized in frenzy; for it is the more powerful among worldly spirits. Hence it is accustomed to divine worldly things by conjectures, and they call it the “python.” It is the spirit that is deceived and deceives through probabilities; it is [Col. 0196A] the one who spoke through the Sibyl, following our understanding and desiring to have a place among the heavenly beings.

So that we may know the things granted to us by God. Since the Spirit of God has been given to us, we know the things granted to us by God. We could not know these things if we had the spirit of the world, because the spirit of the world cannot know them. [Note: [Col. 0195D] Thus read the oldest edition and by far the greater number of manuscripts. The Roman edition, with some others, reads: “The spirit of the world cannot know the things that belong to God.”]

For no one knows the mind of God except the one who is from God, the Spirit of God; for inferior beings cannot know the counsel of those above them, nor can a creature discern the will of its Creator.

(Vers. 13–14.) And these are the things we speak. This makes it clear that we know what has been granted to us by God, because we also speak these things, so that others may learn them through spiritual instruction. For the things divinely communicated to preachers—that is, to the apostles—were to be handed on to the peoples, and the rulers of this age were to learn what evil they had committed [Col. 0196B].

[Note: [Col. 0196D] The Roman edition, together with one or two manuscripts, reads: “Not in the persuasion of human wisdom, but in the manifestation of the Spirit … nor is it apprehended through literary studies.” The other editions and manuscripts agree among themselves, except that for “studies of literature” several manuscripts and the oldest edition read “studies of literary learning,” perhaps meaning “through letters and study.”]

Not in instruction consisting of words of human wisdom, but in instruction of the Spirit. For the words of human wisdom do not perceive this meaning, nor is it grasped through literary studies; rather, it is conceived through faith by spiritual reasoning, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 9). It is learned more through the natural law than through the course of the stars and the calculations of the signs marked out in the firmament. In the end, believers see that what they believe accords not with human words but with their own nature; for the work recognizes its maker. Therefore the Gospel speaks spiritual things to our minds, awakening them to knowledge of their Creator.

[Col. 0196C] Comparing spiritual things with spiritual. This means transmitting to those who reject worldly wisdom the spiritual efficacy contained in the mystery of faith, to enlighten the understanding of well-disposed people. For those who believe what the wisdom of the world judges foolish are spiritual.

[Note: [Col. 0196D] The Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “For the natural person does not know the things of the Spirit of God, and they are foolishness to him.” The oldest edition and the remaining manuscripts agree with our text.]

But the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God and does not know them; for they are foolishness to him. Like cattle, 120 he presses his understanding down toward the earth, and therefore grasps only what he sees; nor does he think that anything can happen except in the manner he knows. Thus he judges foolish whatever he hears in a form different from what he knows, since he believes that nothing can happen without material composition. Hence he laughs when he hears that God begot the Son, whom he knows to be simple and incorporeal; that a Virgin gave birth; and that bodies, once dissolved, are restored to life. Yet these things contribute all the more to God’s praise, so that one may believe him to have done what cannot be investigated by reason—for it is God who did it. Human weakness considers foolish whatever its knowledge cannot encompass, although it ought rather to regard this as foolish, and as wise that which, because it is said to have been done by God, cannot be comprehended [Col. 0197A].

And he cannot know, because it is judged spiritually. Following human tradition, while they deny faith in the one God, they think, puffed up by fleshly reasoning, that what has been done spiritually cannot happen; and thus, marked as reprobate, they have been condemned spiritually.

(Vers. 15.) But the spiritual person judges all things, and is himself judged by no one. Because the true reasoning of spiritual people is the reasoning of believers—for a person is called by what he believes—they judge everything. Their example will be the standard by which unbelief is judged; but they themselves will be judged by no one. For who could condemn one who speaks the truth? Since it is evident that all the enemies of faith hold falsehoods as truths, their accusation has already been nullified and condemned by the judgment of truth; for, as the Lord says, “Whoever has not believed has already been judged” (John III, 18) [Col. 0197B].

(Vers. 16.) “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Who has instructed him?” (Isaiah XL, 13.) The mind of God is that he commanded these things to be done spiritually, through which the wisdom of the world would be proved foolish, since it denies that what has been done could be done. No one has known this mind and found fault with it, as though God’s plan needed correction; for whoever has known it praises God’s power, whereas the one who denies that he can do all things does not even believe that he made the world. What great thing is it, then, to believe that he begot from himself, when no one doubts that he made all things from nothing? Indeed, the Savior says: “With God all things are possible” [Col. 0197C] (Matthew XIX, 26).

But we have the mind of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0197D] Thus read the majority and the better manuscripts; they differ from the oldest edition only in having “that is, of divine knowledge.” The Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “Since we who believe have the mind of that same divine knowledge.”]

He says this because, as believers, we are participants in that same divine judgment.

## CHAPTER III

(Vers. 1.) And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal. He now speaks to those who, because they were still serving the pleasures of the age, were carnal. Although they had already been baptized and had received the Holy Spirit, because immediately after baptism they had returned to the old person whom they had renounced, they are called carnal. For the Holy Spirit remains in the one into whom he has poured himself if that person remains in the resolve of renewal; otherwise he departs, yet in such a way that, if the person reforms himself, he returns to him. For he is always ready for what is good and cherishes repentance [Col. 0197D].

As little children in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. Although they had been reborn in Christ, it was nevertheless not fitting to entrust spiritual matters to them. Having received faith, which is like a spiritual seed, they had produced no fruit worthy of God, so as to deserve to learn the words of perfection; rather, like little children, they devoted themselves to the perceptions of imperfection. The apostle, however, a divine man and spiritual physician, gave each person what accorded with his strength [Col. 0198A], lest anyone, through imperfection and inexperience, should suffer scandal concerning spiritual matters.

(Vers. 2.) For you were not yet able. He openly shows that they ought not to have heard what is to be said to the mature.

Nor are you able even now, for you are still carnal. Here he strongly rebukes the rashness of those who complained that they had not previously heard spiritual things, although they were still unworthy to hear them. For the pseudo-apostles indiscriminately instructed everyone in one and the same manner, distinguishing no person, so that they might become acceptable through the commendation of hypocrisy. Yet it is clear that our Lord and author, Christ, spoke one way to the crowds and another way to the disciples, and that there was even a distinction among the apostles themselves. For he showed his glory on the mountain to three disciples, telling them to keep silent about what they had seen until he had risen from the dead (Matthew XVII, 9) [Col. 0198B].

121 (Vers. 3.) For while there are jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways? He shows the cause of their unworthiness: one who hopes for help from a human being is carnal. But one who, rejecting humanity, hopes in God is spiritual, because God is spirit.

(Vers. 4.) For when one says, “I am of Paul,” and another, “I am of Apollo,” are you not human? Just as those who glory in God and hope for every grace from him are called gods, adopted by God, so those who glory in a human being are called both human and carnal, convicted by God’s judgment, which says: “I said, You are gods; but you shall die like human beings” (Psalm LXXXI, 6). He therefore begins with his own person, lest it be thought that he was attacking their persons out of envy. He shows that this is a great error and an insult to God: when God is preached, glory is given to human beings. What, then, is less different from paganism, while something is still hoped for from human beings?

(Vers. 5.) What, then, is Apollo? And what is Paul? Ministers of him in whom you have believed. Since they are ministers, hope should not be placed in them but in God, whose ministers they are. Thanksgiving is due to the one whose gift it is; these men, however, are servants, who must administer even unwillingly. Was Moses not compelled to go to Pharaoh? Was Jonah not sent unwillingly to preach to the Ninevites? And was Ananias, despite his objections, not sent to lay his hands on Saul [Col. 0198D]?

And to each one as the Lord gave: that is, as he willed and knew, he distributed the duties of ministry to each person.

(Vers. 6.) I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. To plant is to evangelize and draw people to faith; to water is to baptize with the prescribed words. But to forgive sins and give the Spirit belongs to God alone. If, then, God gives the effect of salvation, there is no human glory in this matter (Acts II, 4). For we know that the Holy Spirit has also been given by God without the laying on of hands [Col. 0199A] (Acts X, 4), and that an unbaptized person has obtained the remission of sins. Was this person not invisibly baptized when he received the gift of baptism?

(Vers. 7.) Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. Even planted things commonly die, and watered things do not reach the fruitfulness intended unless God gives vigorous life. Thus, as far as honoring God is concerned, a human being is nothing; but as far as ministry is concerned, he is necessary, so that he may be honored as a servant, not so that anything may be hoped for from him to God’s injury.

(Vers. 8.) For the one who plants and the one who waters are one. They are one [Note: [Col. 0199D] Some manuscripts read: “because both are necessary.”] because both are hired servants, although their duties are different. But each will receive his own reward according to his labor. Although they are one, because the one who evangelizes is greater than the one who baptizes, he therefore distinguished their rewards. This also pertains to the sincerity of teaching, so that the one who hands on the teaching inviolate may be worthy of the greater reward.

(Vers. 9.) For we are [Note: [Col. 0199D] Thus read the oldest edition and by far the greater number of manuscripts; the Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “fellow workers in the work.”] participants in God’s work; you are God’s cultivation, God’s building. This refers to the persons of the apostles, whom it is clear are God’s assistants, because they are Christ’s deputies.

(Vers. 10.) According to the grace of God given to me, as a wise architect I laid a foundation. He says that grace was given to him so that he might be worthy to preach the Gospel, thereby showing that this too belongs to God, not to a human being [Col. 0199C]. According to this grace, therefore, he says that he laid the foundation as a wise architect. A wise architect is one who places the foundation according to the discipline of the author—that is, one who evangelizes according to the Savior’s tradition.

But another builds upon it. The superstructure consists of what, after the apostles’ preaching, is handed on by later teachers, whether bad or good.

But let each one take care how he builds upon it [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “how he builds upon it. Although their duties are different, it is necessary that the superstructure …”], that is, so that the superstructure agrees with the foundation. If it is crooked and worthless, it may cause a collapse while the foundation remains intact. For if someone teaches badly, the name of Christ, which is the foundation, remains; but the bad teaching will perish, as the Lord says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matthew XV, 13) [Col. 0199D].

(Vers. 11.) For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which 122 is Christ Jesus. No one can lay another foundation because, although there are certain heretics, they nevertheless teach only under the name of Christ. They cannot commend their inventions of error in any other way than by preaching them with the Savior’s name inserted, so that the dignity of the name makes contrary and absurd things acceptable [Col. 0200A].

(Vers. 12.) But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones. Precious stones are those that fire does not destroy. He set forth three splendid kinds found in the world, by which he signified good teaching: wood, hay, straw—three other kinds, but worthless ones. In these, corrupt and empty teaching is represented [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read “is discerned.”] Whatever anyone’s work is, it will become evident.

(Vers. 13.) The one who does this work will be revealed; for the day will disclose it, because it will be revealed in fire. That is, bad teaching will appear to everyone in the fire; for now it deceives some people. And the fire will test what sort of work each person’s work is. Since the examination will take place through fire, if it finds nothing in someone that can be burned, it shows that he was a good teacher. For bad and adulterated teaching is signified by wood, hay, and straw precisely to show that it is fuel for the fire [Col. 0200B].

(Vers. 14.) If anyone’s work that he has built upon remains, he will receive a reward. When no impurity of perverse teaching has been found in it, he will be like good gold; like the three brothers in the furnace of fire (Daniel III, 23), he will receive eternal life with glory as his reward. For just as gold, silver, and stones are not consumed by fire, so a good teacher will remain incorruptible.

(Vers. 15.) If anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss. The work said to burn is bad teaching, which will perish. For all evils will perish, like the way of the wicked, since they are not substances but perverse assertions. To suffer loss means to endure punishments [Col. 0200C]. For who, placed in punishment, does not suffer loss?

But he himself will be saved, yet as through fire. He said that the person would be saved because the substance of which he consists will not perish, just as the bad teaching will perish, since it is an accidental cause. He therefore said, “yet as through fire,” so that this salvation would not be without punishment. He did not say, “He will be saved through fire,” as though he might be saved by merit, unburned by the fire and tested through it; rather, by saying, “yet as through fire,” he shows that he will indeed be saved but will suffer the punishments of fire. He will be purified through fire and thus saved, and will not, like the faithless, be tortured forever in eternal fire. Thus, in some respect, it is worthwhile to have believed in Christ. For the one who sees that he defended falsehood as truth must always be ashamed; and in the same way he will always have confidence in God who, having rejected falsehood, followed truth and, having spurned ungodliness, submitted to piety. [Note: [Col. 0200D] The Roman edition reads “outside the Catholic” in the masculine; the other editions and manuscripts read it in the feminine, with “Church” to be supplied. The Corbie manuscript alone explicitly gives it in this form: “For whatever is outside the Catholic Church is impious and deadly.”] Whatever is outside the Catholic Church, therefore, is contrary.

(Vers. 16.) Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? He says that we are God’s temple, so that we may know that God dwells in us; for he must dwell in his own temple. And because he says that the Spirit of God dwells in us, he indicates that the Spirit is to be understood as God [Col. 0201A].

(Vers. 17.) If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him, for God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are. He prefaced this so as to prick those who, living shamefully and violating their bodies, had corrupted themselves—especially the man who had his father’s wife—so that he might already be guilty before his case came into the open. Accordingly, in a similar, indeed identical, manner, when he judges his case, he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?” (I Corinthians VI, 19). [Note: [Col. 0201D] Thus read the oldest edition and the manuscripts; the Roman edition altered it as follows: “Here he calls it God’s temple, but below, the temple …”]

Above he called it God’s temple; here, however, he calls it the temple of the Holy Spirit. Who could doubt here that he indicated the Holy Spirit to be God?

[Col. 0201B] (Vers. 18.) Let no one deceive himself; that is, let no one think that his own judgment or human counsel can benefit him. He returns to the preceding meaning: If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may become wise. He says this because if anyone understands the salvation that has been promised and the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him become foolish—that is, let him flee the wisdom of the world, so that the world may judge him foolish—and then he will be prudent. For the one who is foolish to the age is prudent before God, while he believes that God 123 did what the reasoning of the world cannot comprehend, as I mentioned above. But the pseudo-apostles, wishing to appear wise in the world, preached that God did not have a Son, that there was no true incarnation, and that the flesh could not rise again [Col. 0201C].

(Vers. 19.) For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God because God does what the world denies can be done. He proves its wisdom foolish, and, since they say there are many gods while faith proves there is one, they will be confounded in their own prudence, as power bears witness.

(Vers. 20.) For it is written: [Note: [Col. 0201D] The Roman edition reads: “I will seize the wise … their wisdom has seized them.”] He rebukes the wise in their craftiness. And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.” This is found in the ninety-third Psalm. The meaning is the same: knowing that their thoughts were futile, he proved them foolish, rebuked their wisdom, and showed that what they called false was true, while what they thought true was false.

(Vers. 21.) Therefore let no one glory in a human being. Since human thoughts and plans are imprudent and weak, he teaches that one should not glory in a human being but in God, whose plan cannot be overturned. For whatever human beings think wisely without God is foolish.

(Vers. 22.) For everything is yours, whether Paul or Apollo [Note: [Col. 0201D] Some manuscripts read: “whether Cephas, who is Peter.”] or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things to come: everything is yours, but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s. Elsewhere he says concerning the same meaning: “We are your servants for Jesus’ sake” (II Corinthians IV, 5). He used “servants” for “ministers,” so that they would not [Note: [Col. 0202D] The Roman edition reads “claim individual persons for themselves.” Below it reads “because we should accommodate ourselves to what is better.”] claim individual persons for themselves, while they made use of everything, just as the Lord also says: “I am among you not as one who is served, but as one who serves” (Luke XXII, 27).

For the world is certainly ours, but so that we may understand it according to God’s will and place its appointed courses within God’s will. The present life has also been granted to us, but so that we may pass it in moderation and for God’s glory. Death is ours, so that we may willingly die for Christ in hope of the future promise. Things present are ours, so that we may use them in such a way as not to give offense. Things future are ours, so that, believing in the future, we may entrust ourselves more fully to it, since it is better [Col. 0202A].

(Vers. 23.) But you are Christ’s: just as these things have been granted and subjected to us by our judgment, so we too should be subjected to Christ, since through him we began to exist, both in our first origin and in regeneration [Col. 0202B]. Christ, however, is God’s. Christ is the proper Son of his Father, doing his will, so that we too may do Christ’s will. If, then, we are Christ’s servants, why should we, to his injury, hope for anything from human beings?

## CHAPTER IV

(Vers. 1.) Let a person regard us in this way—as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. He indicated this because some of the Corinthians thought too little of him. But he wanted a person to think of him as did God, who had chosen him. Therefore he calls them ministers of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries. Since he was understood to rely neither on a din of words nor on human wisdom, he ought to administer the mystery of Christ, in which power, not words, shone forth; through which not a human being but God would appear glorious. For, as a companion of fishermen, he preached Christ in no other way than they did. When, therefore, he proves himself a minister of Christ and of God’s mysteries, he marks the pseudo-apostles and denies that what they hand on belongs to Christ, by showing that they disagree with the apostolic tradition.

(Vers. 2.) Here, moreover, it is required among stewards that someone be found faithful. What he says pertains not only to the person of the pseudo-apostles but also to the others who, having received a stewardship, hesitated to rebuke bad opinions or conduct consistently, whether out of embarrassment, fear, or concern for their own commendation. He was so steadfast that he did not spare even his own life, provided that he carried everything out faithfully [Note: [Col. 0202D] The same Roman edition reads “completed everything.” Shortly afterward it reads “he rebukes, he says ‘the least.’”]

[Col. 0202D] (Vers. 3.) But it is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day. He says that it is wretched for him to be judged by those whom he rebuked for such great vices, since he knew that he should not even be judged by the just. Or “by a human day,” that is, because he did not believe that he should be judged by the laws accepted by the world. Having surpassed human justice, he devoted himself to heavenly justice, as the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of God” [Col. 0203A] (Matthew V, 20). When, therefore, he says “a human 124 day,” he also signifies a divine day, on which Christ will judge. For just as legal experts or pontiffs, whom they call priests, have appointed particular days on which judgment is held, so the Lord’s day has also been fixed, on which he will judge the world.

(Vers. 4.) But neither do I judge myself; for I am conscious of nothing against myself. It is clear that, having a pure conscience, he was not anxious about himself. But I am not thereby justified. Now he humbles himself and speaks as a human being who is unaware that he might incur guilt. But the one who judges me is the Lord. He speaks rightly: although he has humbled himself, he has nevertheless ascribed very great power to the Lord Christ, because Christ can reveal what is hidden from a human being when he judges secret things—not to make him guilty, but prudent [Col. 0203B]. [Note: [Col. 0203D] The oldest edition and not a few manuscripts read: “Although he is human, one whom nothing can remain hidden from unless something escapes him.” The Roman edition, with Gill’s marginal note and some manuscripts, emended the passage quite suitably as follows: “For who is a human being from whom something does not remain hidden?” But the Corbie manuscript supplied the true reading, as we have it in the text.]

For although he is holy, he is still a human being, and it cannot happen that nothing remains hidden from him. At times we think something useful that is useless; nor do we have every member or aspect of human conduct fully described. We have been openly prohibited from the things that are serious. Yet certain circumstances arising from various causes commonly deceive us, so that we think what is not useful to be useful. This is a minor matter, since the intention remains free.

(Vers. 5.) Therefore do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes. He warns them not to judge when they themselves are to be judged, and thus to incur a double sin, as the Lord says: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matthew VII, 1). Instead, await the day of God’s judgment, to learn whether they are faithful and good. For it is an insult to a judge if judgment or a sentence proceeds from a servant before the judge has conducted his inquiry [Col. 0203C].

He will also illumine the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God. He says this because on the day of judgment nothing will be hidden of what has been done or thought. Sincerity and hypocrisy will appear there, so that one who was held in contempt may perhaps be shown worthy, while one who was thought to be something may be found reprobate. [Note: [Col. 0204D] Some manuscripts read: “For everything will be known.”] Everything will be exposed on the day of judgment, and then the one who has acted or thought well will receive praise. Here, however, it is uncertain whether the person who is praised is worthy, as he says elsewhere: “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (II Corinthians X, 17)—and nothing is hidden from God.

[Col. 0203D] (Vers. 6.) Now, brothers, I have applied these things to myself and Apollo for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to go beyond what is written, so that no one may be puffed up in favor of one person against another. He applied these matters to himself and Apollo, while under his own person and that of Apollo he set aside the glory and perverse traditions of the pseudo-apostles, indicating them collectively rather than individually, lest greater discord arise among the people. For no one who hears his own name criticized, or the name of the person he favors, is content to remain silent; but if the name is left unmentioned, someone who hears the words, even if he understands that they are spoken about him, pretends not to notice. Under this heading, therefore, he nullified their persons when he said: “I planted, Apollo watered,” and so forth (I Corinthians III, 6), so that through these examples they might learn that nothing should be attributed to human beings [Col. 0204A].

(Vers. 7.) For who makes you different? That is, there are some who say that those who received more in baptism or in teaching have attained more than the rest. He speaks to those who thought that people baptized by others were somehow superior. They were seduced by the eloquence of such people, so that, through a kind of cosmetic coloring, they considered what was perverse to be right. For there was such great discord among the people that there were many factions devoted to different parties. The apostle therefore adapted all his statements to every party without revealing names, so that when the letter was read each party might receive what was said as directed to itself, hearing what it recognized as applying to its own case [Col. 0204B].

For what do you have that you did not receive? He says that the person in question received no greater good from others than he had received from the apostle, and therefore complained without cause; whatever they had, they had received from the apostle. He appears to speak to one person because he is addressing one section of the people.

But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? The apostle’s detractors acted in this way through inexperience: while hearing the same things they had already learned from the apostle, they set him aside and gloried in the teaching of these others. Commended for their eloquence, they turned the glory of preaching toward themselves. The apostle, however, wanted himself to appear contemptible, provided that he made God’s glory acceptable.

[Col. 0204C] (Vers. 8.) Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us. This is irony, as they say, for these are the words 125 of someone who is angry, not of someone confirming their status. Although he rebukes them for such great vices, he says that they reign; for this is how they thought, glorying in the things handed on by the pseudo-apostles [Col. 0204D].

And I wish that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you. Like a loving father, he wishes good even for ungrateful children. For how could they reign without the apostles? Whatever has not been handed on by the apostles is full of crimes. The proper order would have been to say, “So that you may reign with us”; but because he had first said, “I wish that you did reign,” he could not express it otherwise than, “So that we too might reign with you.” To reign is to be secure in the hope and promises of Christ and to rejoice in the adversities that occur for Christ’s name, for they bring gain, not loss. Hence he says elsewhere: “When I am weak, then I am powerful” (II Corinthians XII, 10).

(Vers. 9.) For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as though destined for death. He applies this to his own person because he was always in distress and suffered persecutions and pressures beyond the others, just as Enoch and Elijah will suffer. They will be apostles at the end of time [Note: [Col. 0204D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “who will be appointed as apostles in retribution.” They must be sent before the Antichrist.] They must be sent before Christ to prepare God’s people and fortify all the Churches to resist the Antichrist. Scripture in the Apocalypse also testifies that they will suffer persecutions and be killed. The apostle therefore compared their time with his own when he said, “as though destined for death” (Revelation XI, 8 and following), for they will come for the purpose of being killed [Col. 0205A].

Because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. Enoch and Elijah will be a spectacle to such an extent that their bodies will be thrown into the street in the sight of the entire unbelieving people. In the same way the apostles became a spectacle, because they were publicly mocked and exposed to the insults and death that they suffered. He spoke of the world, angels, and human beings because the angels too are evil, as David says in the seventy-seventh Psalm: “He troubled them through evil angels.” And there are evil and unbelieving human beings; the insults suffered by the apostles are entertainment for them. The world is called unbelief because it follows visible things [Col. 0205B].

(Vers. 10.) We are fools for Christ’s sake. It is true that those who love Christ are fools in the eyes of the world. But you are wise in Christ. One who is judged wise in Christ by the faithless does not rightly confess Christ. Thus Marcion, because he denies the Son of God and that God could become incarnate, is wise to the world; and Photinus, because he does not acknowledge Christ as God by virtue of his birth, appears wise to worldly people.

We are weak. We are weak because, preaching Christ without flattery and with what appears foolish to worldly people, we were subjected to insults. But you are strong [Col. 0205C]. They are strong because they professed Christ in such a way as not to offend human beings, so that they might remain secure.

You are noble. One who does not confess that Christ was promised to Abraham and preached from the beginning is noble in opposition to Christ, because he assigns the antiquity of Christ’s promise to others. But we are ignoble. The person who confesses from the beginning that Christ is what the world denies is ignoble to the world. Thus he confirms all the things stated above that he appears to deny, and denies what he appears to confirm. These are the words of an angry person, who confesses by denying and denies by confessing.

(Vers. 11–12.) Up to this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten, homeless and laboring, working with our own hands. For preaching Christ openly and according to the true faith, without any flattery, and rebuking the deeds of an evil life, they found no favor with human beings. They were beaten—that is, treated with insults—and they were homeless because they were driven away, lest by remaining long in one place they teach more people. They therefore also worked with their hands, because not only did they find no favor with human beings, but it was also disgraceful to receive anything from those who devoted themselves to error, as he says in the hundred and fortieth Psalm: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head” (Psalm CXL, 5). For one who accepts from someone who gives precisely so as not to be rebuked loses the freedom to rebuke and commits sin [Col. 0205D].

[Col. 0206A] (Vers. 13.) We are cursed, and we bless: those who treated them badly, they encouraged toward what was good. We suffer persecution and endure it, because we did not resist those who persecuted us. We are blasphemed, and we entreat: those who blasphemed them, they asked to allow them to give an account.

126 We have become like the refuse of this world, [Note: [Col. 0205] Roman edition: “like purifying offerings up to the present.”] the offscouring of all things until now. By resisting no one, repaying no one evil for evil, but always submitting himself, he became contemptible and despised, so that through patience he might recall them to what is good. “Until now,” that is, even until the present among the Corinthians, for whom he suffered the evils mentioned above. And because he saw that his humility was accomplishing nothing in these matters, moved by grief he complains that such submission and insults had been able to produce no result, but—what is worse—that they had actually advanced matters in the direction of evil.

(Vers. 14.) I am not writing these things to shame you: that is, I am not writing them to make you blush, but so that you may correct yourselves. But I admonish you as my most beloved children. He continues to make himself a suppliant, lest, after being reproved and provoked to anger, they should reject his admonitions. He acts like a healing physician who, cutting away diseased matter, softens the pain he has inflicted with hope and gentle words, so that the sick person may allow himself to be treated.

(Vers. 15.) For though you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel. By these words he shows that no one could love them with the affection with which he loved them. For who would place another’s children before his own in love? [Col. 0206C] Consequently, they ought not to despise the admonitions of one who had also suffered such great evils on their behalf.

(Vers. 16.) Therefore I beseech you: become imitators of me. O the goodwill of the holy Apostle, who begs his children to imitate their father—that is, who willingly asks the sick to accept medicine! Yet he wants them to be his imitators in these matters: just as he had suffered many deadly things from unbelievers for their salvation and had not yielded, provided only that he might evangelize to them the gift of God’s grace day and night, so they too, remaining in his faith and teaching, should not accept the wicked fabrications of the false apostles, [Note: [Col. 0205] All editions: “but should persevere”; all manuscripts: “but should resist.”] but should resist them, disregarding insults and slanders, so that they might preserve an unimpaired affection for their spiritual father.

[Col. 0206D] (Vers. 17.) For this reason I sent Timothy to you, who is my most beloved and faithful son in the Lord. In the person of this Timothy he exhorts them in the same matter. He calls Timothy his most beloved and faithful son in the Lord so that they might learn from him what they were doing wrong; for when he bears witness to Timothy, he reproves them.

He will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every Church. Through this man, whom he confirms as a faithful son in the Lord, he wants them to return to the rule of the truth he had handed down, so that, reminded by his words and by the examples of his works, they might come to their senses, recognizing that they had not been taught wrongly by the Apostle, since they would learn that all the Churches held the same things.

(Vers. 18.) As though I were not coming to you, some have become inflated. Certain Corinthians were indignant because he was not going to them—not out of longing, but through pride, as though he considered them unworthy; whereas the Apostle’s chief concern was rather to make the unworthy worthy. He therefore had the intention of going, but the matters he was dealing with were more important.

(Vers. 19.) But I shall come to you soon, if the Lord permits. [Note: [Col. 0207D] Corbie manuscript: “He promises in pious admonition,” etc.] After admonishing them, he promises that he will go to them, but only if the Lord permits. Since God knows more than a human being, if He knew that the journey would be worthwhile, He would permit it; and if Paul did not go, this would show that the Lord had not allowed it, evidently because of their unworthiness.

[Col. 0207B] And I shall find out not the speech of those who are inflated, but their power. He puts them to shame, because although they behaved deceitfully, they were indignant as though they were worthy to be visited by the Apostle.

(Vers. 20.) For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. Just as the kingdom of God is commended not by verbal splendor but by the power of signs, so these men should show themselves worthy to be visited by the Apostle not through bare words but through the power of spiritual works.

(Vers. 21.) What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness? He introduces words of terror so that those who were inflated, having been put to shame, might be humbled; and so that, if they truly desired the Apostle’s presence, they might prepare themselves to receive him—that is, cleanse themselves [Note: [Col. 0207D] Some manuscripts: “from every wound of sin.”] from every stain of crime—so that, when he came to them, he might rejoice as among his most beloved children.

CHAPTER V

(Vers. 1.) It is commonly reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles. To show how grave this sin was, he said that it was not even admitted by those who do not know God; and thus he showed with what punishment the man should be struck who, subject to eternal and divine justice, had committed a crime of such enormity. [Note: [Col. 0207D] Several manuscripts: “who is subject to earthly and divine justice.”]

So that someone has his father’s wife.. He disclosed the kind of crime previously mentioned, so that he might make not only that man openly liable to death but also demonstrate that those who associated with him were not free from guilt. For in a matter where sin is difficult, it makes the offender more guilty.

[Col. 0207D] (Vers. 2.) And you are inflated, and have not rather mourned. He humbles their pride so greatly that he makes them not merely complainants but rather suppliants. For they themselves were also participants, since they allowed a man guilty of such an enormous crime to associate with them without correction. They should all, with one accord, have cast him out if he refused to amend himself. But if someone has no authority to expel one whom he knows to be guilty, or is unable to prove the charge, he is free from guilt; and a judge cannot condemn without an accuser, for the Lord also did not cast out Judas, although he was a thief, because he had not been accused.

So that the one who committed this deed might be removed from among you. Once this deed was known, he should have been expelled from the assembly of the brethren. For everyone knew his crime and did not reprove him; he openly kept his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter there was no need for witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.

(Vers. 3–5.) For I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit—that is, absent in person but present in the authority of the Spirit, who is absent nowhere—have already judged as though present the man who committed this deed: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you and my spirit are assembled with the power of our Lord Jesus, [Col. 0208B] to hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.. Since every pleasure of the flesh is from the devil, when a person gives himself over to this pleasure, he is handed over to Satan. For the flesh has this in its nature: that it should perish. Therefore, when the soul joins itself to its desire and weakens its spiritual strength, it too suffers destruction at the same time. Thus, if the man reproved here for the fornication he had committed were ashamed at having been expelled, he would not perish, since repentance would follow.

[Note: [Col. 0207D] Some manuscripts read: “For by the consent of all and by the presence of the Spirit, through whose embassy he ordered . . . from the Church”; other manuscripts and editions agree among themselves, except that the old editions prefer “for” instead of “not,” and, like the Roman edition, omit “only,” which we have restored from several manuscripts.] It was not merely by the consent of all and by the presence of the Spirit, but by the power of the Lord Jesus—that is, by the judgment of the one whose embassy the Apostle was carrying out—that he decided that the man should be expelled from the Church. When he is expelled, he is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. Both soul and body perish when things contrary to the law are done; but in this case the destruction of the flesh is assigned to the man in a particular sense. For although all sins produce a carnal person, this desire is especially a desire of the flesh: through it, the soul, stained by filth, hands itself over with the body to hell. When the soul has been overcome and stained by filth, through the lust of the flesh it becomes flesh, just as a body rightly governed is also called spiritual. Yet it is the mind that, whether overcome by allurements, makes the whole person carnal, or, remaining in the vigor of its own nature, gives mastery to the flesh, so that it may be called spiritual.

So that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ. He hands the aforesaid contaminated man over to Satan so that the spirit of the people of the Church may be saved on the day of judgment. For unless he had been expelled, the spirit of the Church would not be saved on the day of judgment. He was harming everyone by the cause of his contamination, so that on the day of the Lord, found naked of the Holy Spirit, they might hear from the Lord the Judge: “Depart from me; I do not know you” (Matt. 7:23). As he says to the Romans: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9); and in another epistle: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. 4:30). For if He is grieved, He departs, and the person will not be saved—not, of course, for His own sake, since He is incapable of suffering, [Col. 0209A] but for our sake, since He has been given to us so that through Him we might be proved to be children of God. A thing that is lost is not safe—not safe, that is, for itself, since wherever it may be, it must exist, but for the one from whom it is lost.

(Vers. 6.) [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts almost unanimously have this reading; all editions, however, read: “Your boasting is not good,” that is, “it is evil.”] Is your boasting good? That is, it is not good. They were rejoicing when they ought rather to have been grieving over a brother who was sinning so grievously, just as Samuel grieved when Saul sinned. Evil teachers either concealed this crime or reproved it negligently, as Eli the priest did with his sons when they sinned against God (1 Sam. 2:23), [Note: [Col. 0209D] Remigius and Laon manuscripts: “lest he should be harsh, he did not reprove them.”] lest they should be harsh toward men.

Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? So also the sin of one person, when it is known but not reproved, contaminates many—indeed, all who know it and do not avoid it, or who, although they can reprove it, conceal it. A person does not seem to himself to be sinning when no one reproves or avoids him.

128 (Vers. 7.) Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump. This must be understood in two ways, since there is also the leaven of human teaching, as the Savior says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. 16:11), that is, of their doctrine. Thus this was said both in order to avoid evil teaching and with reference to the present matter, because, when the fornicator was expelled, the old leaven was expelled. It is called old because it is the sin of ancient error. The new composition, however, is the teaching of Christ.

Since you are unleavened. “Unleavened” was said with reference to the flour that was not fermented when the children of Israel were expelled from Egypt, so that leaven might signify antiquity and unleavened bread novelty. For after the old errors of the Egyptians had been cast off, they were introduced into the new law; so the Corinthians, after the errors of the pagans, were introduced into the Gospel of Christ. He therefore urges them to live according to the profession they had received from the Apostle under the name of Christ, now as worshipers of a new life; and this is what it means to be unleavened.

Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. According to the Law, he teaches that the newness of the Passover consists in its meaning, and that Christ was therefore slain so that from him a new proclamation might produce a new way of life; since we celebrate the meaning of the Passover, we must not follow the old life. Passover, therefore, is a sacrifice, not a passing-over, as some think. First comes the Passover, and then the passing-over, because the example of the Savior comes first and then the sign of salvation. For there was no sign before the cross. After the lamb had been slain in the evening, the children of Israel celebrated the Passover in Egypt and marked the doorposts with its blood, so that when the Angel passed through at night he would not touch those places that had been smeared with the lamb’s blood (Exod. 12:28).

(Vers. 8.) Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven. That is, let us possess the joy of renewal and flee from former things, casting every impurity away from ourselves, since impurity is corruption. For just as leaven corrupts the whole lump, so an evil life corrupts the whole person. Therefore, so that we might guard ourselves not only from a shameful life but also from the pursuit of iniquity, he added:

[Col. 0210A] Nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. That is, sincerity should produce a clean life, while truth should exclude every form of deceit.

(Vers. 9, 10.) I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators. He indicates that he had previously written to them, admonishing them not to join themselves to people of evil conduct. And because they seemed perhaps not to have understood what he had written, he now explains in this letter what he meant, saying: Certainly not with the fornicators of this world. Rather, I wrote that you should withdraw from brothers of this kind.

Or with the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. He therefore reproves their understanding, since they perhaps thought that he had forbidden association with unbelievers who were fornicators, greedy, rapacious, or idol-serving, but not with brothers; and for that reason they did not mind having among them the man who had his father’s wife. If, then, you associate with such people, he says, it would be better for you to die. For it is an advantage for those who do evil to die sooner than to remain longer in sins. [Note: [Col. 0210D] Corbie manuscript: “for those who do not amend their ways, if they die sooner,” etc.]

(Vers. 11.) But now I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother among you if he is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious; with such a person not even to eat. He forbids eating with a brother, but he did not forbid it with an unbeliever, since he says: “If anyone of the faithful invites you to dinner, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you” (Luke [Col. 0210C] 10:8). Therefore he says:

(Vers. 12.) For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? It is true that a bishop cannot judge unbelievers. But with a brother in whom these vices are found, he teaches that one should not only refrain from sharing the sacraments but also not eat ordinary food with him, so that he may be ashamed when he is avoided and may correct himself.

(Vers. 13.) Are you not to judge those who are inside? A person judges when he distinguishes which brother he should associate with, whom he should reprove, and whom he should avoid. But those who are outside, God will judge. Above he said: “Do not judge before the time” (1 Cor. 4:5); here he does not forbid it. Above, however, he principally forbade judging a ruler on the basis of suspicion about things unknown, because it belongs to God alone to judge hidden matters. Here he even commands that a brother examine his brother [Col. 0210D] (2 Cor. 13:5), just as he says elsewhere: “Test yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves” (2 Cor. 13:5). Those who are outside will be condemned on the day of judgment, because the Lord said: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). For a person in whom there is no hope is to be regarded as dead.

Remove evil from among yourselves.. He still admonishes them to distinguish themselves from evil both in deeds and in people.

CHAPTER VI

(Vers. 1.) Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? He signifies the unrighteous in two ways: those who do not believe, and those who frequently interpret the laws believed to have been given by God to the world with flattery, assigning their authority to idols. For this reason they are unrighteous. And because the law is more truly present in the Church, where the Lord of the law is feared, he says that it is better to conduct a case before God’s ministers; for out of fear of God they more readily deliver a true judgment according to the law.

(Vers. 2.) Or do you not know that the saints will judge this world? The Apostle says nothing idly. He said “this world” in order to indicate another as well, since the Apostle John also says: “Do not love this world” (1 John 2:15), and the Lord says in the Gospel: “God so loved the world,” and so forth (John 3:16). This world, then, is in error; it is not that higher world in whose likeness this one was made. Hence man was placed here and made in the image of God, so that just as everything in the higher world comes from one God, so in this world all people might have their origin from one man. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he dispersed the children of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32:8). What could be clearer than that this world is, for a definite reason, an image of the higher one? There is also a lower Jerusalem and a higher one, which the same Apostle calls our mother (Gal. 4:26). There is a lower paradise, in which man was placed and received the command both to work there and to guard it (Gen. 2:8). There is also that heavenly paradise in which the Apostle, having been caught up, heard ineffable words [Col. 0211C] (2 Cor. 12:2). The saints, therefore, will judge this world, because through the example of their faith the world’s unbelief will be condemned.

And if the world is judged in us. This world will then be judged in us if the work of faithless people is not found in us. Are such people, then, unworthy even to judge the smallest matters? That is, those who are going to judge the world itself are certainly not unworthy to judge the things that belong to the world.

(Vers. 3.) Do you not know that we shall judge angels? He added something greater by saying, “We shall judge angels,” that is, spiritual powers, which he states elsewhere dwell in heavenly places. Angels will be judged by us according to the same principle by which the world will be judged.

(Vers. 4, 5.) If, then, you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church. Secular lawsuits are those pertaining to the body or to bodily matters. And because it ought not to be done in this way, he added: [Note: [Col. 0211D] Some editions and manuscripts: “to your shame”; other, more numerous and better manuscripts: “to your reverence.” In the following verse, instead of “divine affairs,” only the Corbie manuscript reads “divine judgments.”] I say this to your reverence. Since above he mentioned a case but did not specify what kind, there are also divine affairs, as the same Apostle says: “A helper in my affair” (Rom. 16:2). And perhaps they thought that secular lawsuits, since he had forbidden them to be conducted before unbelievers, might nevertheless be heard or settled in the Church by persons of any kind, as they had heard. To their shame he says: Appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church. For there are also wooden vessels in the Church. He meant that such men were so intractable and thoughtless that they might perhaps choose unskilled men from among the brothers as judges. The Apostle said this from experience, for he knew how lukewarm and heedless they had been found in other matters.

Is there therefore no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? Since, then, there are wise brothers, he says, let some of them be chosen to judge, whose judgment [Note: [Col. 0211D] Some manuscripts have this reading, as does the old edition; the Roman edition reads “let the world imitate”; more manuscripts read “the world deserves to be examined”; the Corbie manuscript reads “the world will be examined by their judgment.” Below, where the old edition and not a few manuscripts have “according to evangelical law,” other codices read “according to his Gospel.”] the world might admire. For it is a great disgrace if, among those who are said to have known God, no one is found who can examine a case according to evangelical law. He says that a brother should be chosen as judge because their ruler of the Church had not yet been ordained.

(Vers. 6.) But brother goes to court against brother, and that before unbelievers. It is clear that by unbelievers he means either arbitrators who are requested, as usually happens, or a public judge to whom one might say: “Today is a day of sacred observance; judgment cannot be given.”

130 (Vers. 7.) Now, indeed, there is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits among yourselves. He signifies that it is a sin for brother to litigate against brother, when they ought to take care that they be at peace as kinsmen, especially since our faith strives for peace. Although a Christian ought not to litigate, nevertheless, if something serious has occurred that cannot be disregarded, he should bring the case to the Church, lest he suffer both present loss and perhaps offense.

(Vers. 8.) Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather suffer fraud? [Note: [Col. 0212D] Roman edition and some manuscripts: “Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?”] But you commit injustice and commit fraud—and this against your brothers. He now reproves those whose injustice gives rise to quarrels, because they are guilty not only through the fraud they have committed but also share in the offense of those who, compelled by their injustice or fraud, ask unbelievers to judge. Although they ought not to pursue the fraud or injuries inflicted upon them, they not only seek revenge but themselves commit fraud and inflict injuries, thus offering their brothers examples worthy of punishment. And what would such a person be thought likely to do to others, when he does not spare his own?

(Vers. 9, 10.) Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? By saying this he shows that they were not unaware that they were sinning, and therefore that they deserved a more serious punishment. [Note: [Col. 0212D] Certain editions of Paris: “For if the merciless are guilty.”] For if the merciless are guilty before God, how much more the unrighteous? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idol-servants, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God. He did not mention these things because they were ignorant of them, since he had stayed among them for a year and six months, teaching the Gospel of God, but he admonished them in order to restore in them reverence for the Law and the merit required for the kingdoms of heaven (Acts 18:11).

(Vers. 11.) And this indeed you were.. Lest he seem to ascribe this to everyone—or, if he were silent, certainly make everyone free from these crimes, since he would appear to have prohibited them without exposing their crimes—he therefore says: “And such were some of you.” And lest he provoke them to anger, he added: “But you were washed,” so that, recognizing that they had been made guilty by their crimes, they might immediately breathe again when they heard: “But you were washed.” Some people are accustomed to feel shame and correct themselves when they hear good things said about them.

But you were sanctified; but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. They are understood to have received all these benefits of purity in baptism, which is the foundation of evangelical truth. [Col. 0213B] There, after laying aside all sins, the believer is washed and justified in the name of the Lord, and through the Spirit of our God is adopted as a son by God. Through this he reminds them how great and of what kind is the grace they obtained through the true tradition; afterward, however, by thinking contrary to this rule of faith under the impulse of evil teachers, they stripped themselves of these benefits. He therefore seeks to recall them to the true and original judgment, so that they might recover what they had obtained.

(Vers. 12.) [Note: [Col. 0213D] The exposition of this verse is omitted at this point in not a few manuscripts, but is placed on the following page; consequently other material is again transposed.] All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. Some think that the Apostle said “All things are lawful for me” because of the freedom of the will that has been granted, so that it would be lawful to fornicate, although it would not be expedient. But how can what is forbidden be lawful? Or if all things are lawful, nothing can be called unlawful. Yet it is lawful, but it is not expedient.
