Those who say this whisper rather than assert it, either forgetful or negligent. For John the Baptist says to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18). But perhaps John was lacking in human eloquence, having been inspired in the womb; for if this were the case, he ought to have said: “It is lawful for you, but it is not expedient.” The Lord likewise says to the Canaanite woman: “It is not lawful to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15:26). And again the Lord says to the Jews: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry—how he entered the house of God and took the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat,” and so forth (Mark 2:25). Therefore everything that is forbidden is unlawful; [Note: [Col. 0213D] “And everything . . . is forbidden” has been restored to the text from the Vallombrosa manuscript and several others.] and everything that is unlawful is forbidden. But sometimes, when some circumstance intervenes, something is lawful, although it is not expedient.

All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. He says that all things are lawful for him—namely, those things that were also lawful for his fellow Apostles and that the natural law contains, not the law of Moses. For Moses prohibited many things because of the hardness of heart of the unbelieving and stiff-necked people (Matt. 19:8). Yet, if one considers the matter at hand, the Apostle had another meaning when he said these things. He introduced them in advance because he was about to treat this subject, just as he did in the case of the man who had committed incest. He sets out the premise, indicating what he would treat afterward. Finally, he immediately returns to the preceding meaning, having briefly dealt with the matter for the moment. He said this because it was lawful for him to receive support from them. But since he knew that the false apostles were looking for an opportunity to receive, he did not wish to accept anything from them, lest the vigor of evangelical truth should grow weak through concern for the belly. For if he accepted from those whom he reproved for such great vices, he would bend the authority of the teaching office granted to him by the Lord. A person cannot firmly reprove someone from whom he accepts something, especially when the giver is eager to give for the purpose of humbling the one set over him. Hence he also says: “But I will not be brought under the power of anyone.”

(Vers. 13.) Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other. The destruction of the belly occurs when its function of eating ceases; the destruction of food will occur when birth has come to an end. The false apostles, however, who traveled around not for the sake of religion but for profit, did not want to be harsh toward sinners.

But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord. He now returns to the preceding meaning: and the Lord is for the body. What is the Lord for the body? It is understood that He will grant immortality to the body when it has been raised. For the body dedicated to God will be rewarded with a spiritual gift according to the merit of its guide, that is, the mind.

(Vers. 14.) But God both raised up the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. The meaning is the same; he wished to strengthen it by the example of the Lord’s resurrection. For the power of God is Christ, through whom He will raise us and the Lord himself. He said this because the Lord himself raised his own body, just as the Lord himself also says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He said this about the temple of his body (John 2:19).

(Vers. 15.) Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Our bodies are members of Christ, but in the new man who was created according to God, because he is the head of the Church. Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not (Eph. 4:24). He says, “Certainly not,” because members that cling to a prostitute cease to be members of Christ.

(Vers. 16.) Or do you not know that the one who clings to a prostitute becomes one body? He says this because whoever mixes himself with contamination becomes one with that with which he mixes himself. For fornication makes both into one, so that they are one in the stain just as they are one by nature. “The two shall be one flesh,” he says (Gen. 2:24). It is clear that, since the woman is from the man, both are one flesh.

(Vers. 17.) But the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit. For in those who act well, the Spirit of God is shared by God and human beings.

(Vers. 18.) Flee fornication. [Note: [Col. 0214D] This section is absent from our manuscripts, but appears in all the editions.] He rightly warns that fornication must be fled, since through it the children of God become children of the devil. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body. For although the other sins are generated through the body, they do not bind and subject the soul to the fleshly desire in the same way that the use of lust makes the soul intermingle with the body itself, acting in the deed of carnal fornication. The soul is so closely attached to the body that at that very moment a person is unable to think of or attend to anything else, because the very immersion and absorption of lust and carnal desire takes the mind captive and subjects it. Therefore what follows is:

But the one who commits fornication sins against his own body. He shows that this is a most serious sin, because through it the whole body is destroyed; in other sins only a part is destroyed, not the whole. For the whole body is man and woman, since woman is a part of man. Whoever commits any other sin sins outside himself; [Col. 0215B] but the fornicator sins against his own flesh. Suppose that he ends his life by hanging or cuts himself with a sword: he does not seem to sin against his body but against his soul, to which he does violence. Fornication, however, is a bodily offense that affects both body and soul. For the soul does not desire to sin against the flesh without the desire of the flesh, since the flesh also has its own movement, although it can do nothing without the soul. Therefore, because he sins against the flesh that comes from himself—he refers to its origin—he is said to sin against his own body, so that he may cease from fornication as though sparing himself.

According to Novatian, however, the fornicator does not seem to sin against his own body but against Christ’s body. For he interprets this differently, saying that even the one who commits fornication sins against the Holy Spirit, because of the reason for which he has been cut off from the Church. This cannot be established in any way. The body of Christ is not one or two Christians, but all of them, while individuals are members. How, then, does the fornicator sin against the body of Christ, when he does not contaminate everyone? If it were as Novatian thinks, all other sins would be outside God, and fornication alone would be a sin against God. Even one who goes to idols would not sin against God, nor would one who denies Him during persecution, since, according to him, every sin that a person commits is outside the body of Christ. But if he wishes to interpret this in another way and deny that any sin is outside the body of Christ, he will be forced to say that whoever commits any sin sins against God and against the Holy Spirit, so that a thief, a perjurer, and a liar would also be said to sin against the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0215D] And what then is the meaning of the Lord’s statement: “All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven people, but whoever has sinned against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:31)? It is plainly evident that, apart from the other sins, there is another sin that is called sin against the Holy Spirit.

Some again think that the fornicator is said to sin against his own body for this reason: he is a member of the Church, and by contaminating himself he sins against the Church, of which he is a member. Thus, when a member of the Church commits fornication, it should be said to him that he sins not against himself but against the Church. Yet the Apostle says that the fornicator, because he sins against his own portion, sins against his own body.

(Vers. 19.) Or do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God? Above he called us the temple of God (1 Cor. 3:16); here he calls us the temple of the Holy Spirit, because in substance the Spirit is what God is. He said this so that we might keep our bodies undefiled, so that the Holy Spirit might be able to dwell there.

(Vers. 20.) And you are not your own, for you were bought at a great price. It is clear that one who has been bought does not belong to himself, but to the one by whom he was bought, so that he should do not his own will but that person’s. And because we were bought at a costly price, we ought to serve our Lord with greater devotion, lest, being offended, He return us to the death from which He redeemed us. For at how great a price did He purchase us, that He should give his blood for us?

[Col. 0216B] Glorify and bear God in your body. To glorify and bear God in the body means to walk according to his law; for through his law he himself is seen in us. To bear God, however, means to display the image of God in good deeds.

CHAPTER VII

(Vers. 1.) Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. Agitated by the distorted opinions of the false apostles, who taught hypocritically that marriage should be despised so that they might appear purer than others, they asked the Apostle about these matters by letter. Since they were not pleased with this opinion, they passed over the other matters and asked only about this one. To them, however, he replied that it is indeed good not to touch a woman, although they were not asserting this to him simply.

(Vers. 2.) Nevertheless, because of fornication—that is, so that nothing contrary to the law should be admitted, since sometimes what the law does not prohibit is avoided—let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Those who seek a shortcut are accustomed to fall into error. For how could it happen that these men would abstain from their wives, when he found them involved in such great vices? Therefore he does not permit it, lest, while abstaining from what is lawful, they presume to do what is forbidden, as the Manichaeans do.

(Vers. 3, 4.) Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. They are mutually subject to one another in this matter, so that, since they are one body, their will also may be one according to the law of nature.. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman. He means that neither the man nor the woman is permitted to give his or her body to someone else. In this matter they are mutually indebted to one another, so that no occasion for sin may be given.

(Vers. 5.) Do not defraud one another. He says this [Note: [Col. 0215D] Roman edition: “so that they may come together.”], so that they may come together in the marital relationship, lest disagreement produce fornication. Except by mutual consent for a time—that is, so that by agreement they abstain for the sake of prayers of thanksgiving. So that you may devote yourselves to prayer. Although one must pray without ceasing—for this meditation must be practiced every day—nevertheless he commands them to persist in prayer and to devote themselves to this, setting aside periods for winning the Lord’s favor; for in order that he may have mercy, he must be entreated with greater purity. Although marriages are pure, one must nevertheless abstain even from what is permitted, so that prayer may more easily achieve its effect. For those who wished to be sanctified under the Law also abstained, among other things, from raisins at the Lord’s command, so that they might become holier (Num. 6:4). For when someone does not even touch what has been permitted, he shows that he wishes to receive what he asks for.

And return again to the same thing. Since [Note: [Col. 0217D] Codex Laudensis: “Advice is given to married couples that after the days of prayer they should return to the Lord himself, abstaining from their wives, so that they may be able to receive the Lord’s body more worthily.”] he gives married couples the advice that after the days of prayer they ought to return to natural intercourse: Let Satan not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. He warns them to abstain for the intervening days, lest an opportunity be given to the devil, as the apostle Peter says: “Behold, the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). If a wife is taken for the sake of having children, the time allowed for intercourse itself does not seem extensive; for both feast days and days of procession, and the very process of conception and childbirth according to the Law, show that intercourse ought to cease at such times.

133

(Vers. 6, 7.) But I say this by way of concession, not by command. It is clear that he gives this advice in order to exclude fornication, not to close the way to those striving toward a better life. I wished all people to be as I myself am. Thus, insofar as concerns a benevolent and solicitous teacher, he wished all people, if it were possible, to be like himself. What sort of person he was, he immediately shows in what follows: But each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that. That is, each person has God’s gift according to his own desire, so that, if he wishes, by God’s will he may attain the ability. Therefore no one ought to be forced, lest, having been prohibited from what is permitted, he admit what is illicit; rather, let each person choose for himself what he will follow.

(Vers. 8.) But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I do. He would not say, “It is good for the unmarried to be as I am,” unless he were physically chaste. Nor would he say, “I wished all people to be as I am,” if he had a wife; for if he had had a wife and said this, he would not have wished them to be virgins. But far be that from us; for from childhood he served in such a way that he had no inclination toward this matter—for he had been anticipated by the grace of God while still a young man. After saying that each person has his own gift from God, he showed in what respect it is better to be more inclined toward one way: for each person is helped in that which he appears to desire eagerly in his mind.

(Vers. 9.) But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry. [Note: [Col. 0217D] The old edition and very many manuscripts: “he wishes them to imitate those people”; the Roman edition: “he wishes himself …” We think, not unreasonably, that the true reading is the one we have restored from Codex Vallensis.] In this matter he wants them to strive so that they may exercise self-control. But if, driven by the flesh, they see that they cannot persevere, because they are not sufficiently ready in this very matter to be helped by God—for God helps the one whom he sees striving with all his strength—then let them marry if they fear burning. Perhaps afterward they will be able to attain this; for when the obstacle has been removed, the will recovers itself with stronger strength.

For it is better to marry than to burn. He did not say, “For it is better to marry than to burn,” as though burning were good and therefore marriage better; rather, he followed customary usage. We commonly say, “It is better to make a profit than to suffer a loss.” To burn, however, means to be driven or overcome by desires; for when the will consents to the heat of the flesh, it burns. To endure desires without being overcome by them belongs to a distinguished and perfect man.

(Vers. 10, 11.) But to those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord. After speaking to the unmarried and to widows, he addresses those who are joined in marriage [Col. 0218B] with the Lord’s own word: A wife must not depart from her husband; but if she has departed, she must remain unmarried. This is the Apostle’s advice: if she has departed because of her husband’s evil conduct, she should now remain unmarried. Or else she should be reconciled to her husband. If, he says, she cannot exercise self-control because she does not wish to struggle against the flesh, let her be reconciled to her husband. A woman is not permitted to marry if she has dismissed her husband on account of fornication, apostasy, [Note: [Col. 0217D] Roman edition: “or if, impelled by wantonness, he seeks to invert the use [Col. 0218D] of a wife”; old edition and manuscripts: as in the text, except that elsewhere it reads “illicitly,” elsewhere “illicit.”] or if, impelled by illicit wantonness, he seeks to invert the use of a wife; for the inferior party does not altogether use the law by which the superior party does. Yet if the husband has apostatized, or seeks to invert the use of a wife, the woman may neither marry another [Note: [Col. 0218D] Codex Corbeiensis: “nor return to him on account of fornication.” But the passage below, “And therefore he did not add,” through verse 12, is absent from one Codex Remigiensis; Peter Lombard, Book IV, distinction 35, contends that it was added.] nor return to him. And a husband must not dismiss his wife. “Except on account of fornication” is understood. Therefore he did not add, as he did concerning the woman, “but if she has departed, let her remain so,” because a man is permitted to take a wife if he has dismissed a sinful wife: for the man is not bound by the law in the same way as the woman, since the man is the head of the woman.

(Vers. 12.) For to the others I say—not the Lord. He said this to show what the Lord commanded with his own mouth and what he entrusted to this authority, since the Lord also speaks through him. For he says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Cor. 13:3).

134

(Vers. 13.) If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not leave her husband. He said this because in those earliest times, when both parties were certainly Gentiles, it happened that one of them came to believe; and because the unbelievers detested the worship of God, while believers likewise detested the contamination of their former error, he commands that if they were content to live with those who had not been changed, the faithful should also be content to remain with them.

(Vers. 14.) For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through the believing husband. [Note: [Col. 0219D] So the old edition and most manuscripts, from which the Roman edition does not differ, except that it prefers “not to have for protection”; but Codex Corbeiensis reads: “In the brother they have the benefit,” and so forth.] He shows that they have the benefit of good will, because they do not abhor the name of Christ; and this pertains to the protection of the household, in which the sign of the cross is made, by which death was conquered—for this is sanctification.

Otherwise your children would be unclean. Their children would be unclean [Note: [Col. 0219D] Codex Corbeiensis: “if they dismissed their wife, unwilling to have her with them.” And below: “because this also concerns licit marriages.”] if they dismissed their wives, though wishing to live with them, and joined themselves to others; for they would be adulterers and consequently their children would be illegitimate; therefore they would be unclean. But now they are holy. They are holy because they have been born from licit marriages and because, for the greater part, they have been born under the worship of the Creator. For just as [Note: [Col. 0219D] Some manuscripts: “whatever is done through the preaching of idols.”] whatever is done through the dedication of idols is unclean, so whatever is done under confession of God the Creator is holy.

[Col. 0219B] (Vers. 15.) But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. He preserves the purpose of religion by commanding that Christians not abandon their marriages; but if an unbeliever departs out of hatred for God, the believer will not be guilty of dissolving the marriage. For the cause of God is greater than that of marriage.

(28, q. 2, c. “Si infidelis.”) For the brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such a case. That is, marital reverence is not owed to one who abhors the author of marriage; for a marriage that exists without devotion to God is not valid. Consequently, it is not a sin for the person who is abandoned for God’s sake to join himself or herself to another. The insult to the Creator dissolves the right of marriage with regard to the person who has been abandoned, so that he or she will not be accused when joined to another. The departing unbeliever, however, is known to sin both against God and against marriage, because he or she did not wish to maintain the marriage under devotion to God. Therefore fidelity to the marriage need not be kept with such a person, because that person departed in order not to hear that the Christian God is the author of marriage. For if Esdras (3 Esd. 9 and following) caused unbelieving wives or husbands to be dismissed so that God might become propitious and not be angry if they took others from their own people, and if they were not commanded that, after dismissing these, they should not take others at all, how much more, if an unbeliever has departed, will the believer have free choice, if he or she wishes to marry a person of his or her own law? For a marriage contracted outside God’s decree ought not to be counted as a marriage; but when the person later recognizes this and grieves that he or she has sinned, the person corrects the fault in order to merit forgiveness. But if both come to believe, they confirm the marriage through knowledge of God.

But God has called us to peace. This is true, because one ought not to quarrel with the person who departs; for that person departs out of hatred for God and consequently is not worthy to be held in esteem. [Col. 0219D]

(Vers. 16.) For what do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? He says this because perhaps those who do not abhor the name of Christ may come to believe. [Note: [Col. 0220D] Roman edition: “those who now abhor it”; all other editions and manuscripts: “those who do not abhor it,” to which Codex Corbeiensis adds “may come to believe.”]

(Vers. 17.) Except that each person should live as God has apportioned. The Lord apportioned to each person when he or she would be saved—that is, he knows when a person can believe, and he bears with that person. Here also he teaches that such people must be awaited and that one ought not to be scandalized by them, because their hope must be preserved; but if they themselves depart, one must overlook it in their case.

Let each person walk as God has called him. That is, if the believer is joined in marriage, let neither husband nor wife abandon the marriage; rather, let the person remain as he or she is, whether Jew or Greek.

As I teach in all the churches. He says this to show that he does not hand this teaching down to them differently from the others, so that, when they hear that the rest are being taught this faith, they may more readily accept it. For a person is easily inclined if he sees a companion agreeing.

(Vers. 18.) Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not acquire the foreskin. This means what he said: let him walk as he was called, so that a Jew who has become a Christian does not think himself perhaps unworthy because he does not have the foreskin, thereby giving glory to the foreskin. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. He says this so that a Gentile who has been called does not think that he ought to be circumcised because he hears that the sons of Abraham are preferred. For they are not preferred because they are circumcised, but because of the merit of Abraham, whose children they are in both cases if they believe; if they do not, they will be worse than Gentiles. For it is worse to have been something and no longer be it than never to have been it.

(Vers. 19.) Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. It is clear that neither harms nor benefits. But the observance of God’s commandments—that is, faith—makes God favorable, if it is approved by good works.

[Col. 0220C] (Vers. 20, 21.) Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called. This confirms what he said above. Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned; but if you can become free, make better use of it. He encourages the person who serves well, out of fear of God, an earthly master to make himself worthy of freedom, lest, on hearing “Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned,” he become more negligent concerning good actions toward his earthly master, the teaching of Christ be blasphemed, and the person who serves well in earthly matters fail to win God’s favor, though he is storing up merit for himself with God. For the Lord said: “The one who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

(Vers. 22.) For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Having been rescued from sins, which truly prove people to be slaves, he becomes a freedman; for the one who acts foolishly is altogether a slave. Thus the ancients also held, calling all wise people free and all foolish people slaves. Hence Solomon says: “The free will serve a wise slave” (Prov. 7:2). Therefore the person who believes, even if he is temporarily a slave, becomes the Lord’s freedman because he acts wisely in believing in Christ. If sins make people slaves—as Ham, the son of Noah, was made a slave because of sin and folly—then when someone receives forgiveness of sins, he becomes a freedman.

Likewise, the one who was called while free is Christ’s slave. It is an advance from being free to becoming Christ’s slave; for he was free from God, which is the greatest crime. Therefore, having lost that bitter and harmful freedom, he has received a condition that benefits him, as the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you, for it is gentle, and my burden, for it is light” (Matt. 11:29). Thus he cut away pride and established unity, so that neither the slave, out of shame at his condition, would think himself despised, nor the free person, puffed up by mental elation, would place himself above the slave.

(Vers. 23.) You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. This is true, because we were bought at so great a price that no one could have redeemed us except Christ, who is rich over all. Therefore the person who is bought at a price ought to serve more, so that he may in some measure repay the buyer. Bought by God—that is, by Christ—they ought not to be slaves of human beings. The slaves of human beings are those who subject themselves to human superstitions. Yet the Apostle recalls what he reproved at the beginning of the letter, because they were saying: “I belong to Paul”; and another: “I belong to Apollos” (1 Cor. 1:12). Nevertheless, he added the qualification that Christ must be confessed as God, when he showed that they should be called slaves of Christ, not slaves of a human being.

(Vers. 24.) Let each brother remain with God in the condition in which he was called. This is what he said above, and in order to commend it fully he repeats it.

(Vers. 25.) Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord. He responds here to what they had written, as he said above: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me,” and so forth (chap. 7:1). But I give an opinion, as one who has received mercy from the Lord so as to be faithful. He denies that he received a command concerning virgins, because the author of marriage could not command something opposed to marriage without condemning his own former act. But he says, “I give an opinion,” not something displeasing or disguised by flattery; for he received grace for this purpose, so that he might be competent to give saving advice.

(Vers. 26.) I therefore think this is good because of the present necessity, because it is best for a person to be so. He says that it is good to remain a virgin. And in order to show this more decisively, he says “because of the present necessity,” since, between what is good and what is best, nothing so distinguished and useful is recognized as virginity. For he teaches that virginity is more highly commended not only before God but also in the present life, since it does not know the necessities of time endured by marriage, nor the sorrows of childbirth, nor the bereavements of children. Thus, to encourage people to desire this state, he teaches that those who love it gain an advantage amid the afflictions of the present necessity, so that, when they learn that it holds a better place not only with God but also in the present life, they may pursue it with every effort. For there is only one thing with which it struggles: to overcome the inclination of the flesh; in all other respects it is free. [Col. 0222A] Since the flesh, in its origin and nature, makes its use seem pleasant and its inclination sweet, it is no small glory to overcome this.

(Vers. 27.) Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. These are counsels of remedy; for he says that no one ought to be released from his wife except on account of fornication. Often those who dismiss their wives, under the guise of self-restraint, deceive others when their resolve grows cold. But if he wishes to live better while remaining with his wife, let him exhort her so that they may live more purely, without scandal.

Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. Knowing that this is more pleasing to God and free from necessity, let him not seek a wife, provided that he also abstains from other things. Otherwise, what benefit is there in suppressing the desire of the flesh—that is, in rejecting what is permitted—only to become subject to what is illicit?

(Vers. 28.) But if you take a wife, you have not sinned. He certainly does not sin, because he does what has been permitted. But if he rejects it, he stores up merit and a crown for himself. For it is a sign of great endurance not to touch what has not been prohibited. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. She does not sin, because before God she is free in this matter.

Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh. That is, even though they are free from sin, in this life they will nevertheless have tribulations: the groans of the womb, the feeding of children, food, clothing, dowries, illness, household preparations, the needs of a wife, and the domination of a husband.

But I spare you. He spares them when he directs them instead toward those things that exclude the tribulations of the flesh and the anxieties just mentioned. He may also be understood to spare them when he permits and does not oppose those who wish to marry, while showing that it is burdensome.

(Vers. 29.) This, therefore, I say, brothers: the time has been shortened, and it remains. By saying that the time has been shortened and that little remains, he indicated that the end of the world is near, although he knew that time still remained. But he ought not to write otherwise on account of those who will read these words when very little time remains, lest, because the day of judgment is always thought to be far away, it either not be feared or be considered false. Yet when the end is still far away, saying that it is near is highly beneficial; for it instills fear in people so that they may lead a better life. Indeed, how anxious in the present are those who have business before judges when the day of proceedings is said to be approaching? This is what he expresses here, as he says elsewhere: “deceivers, yet truthful” (2 Cor. 6:8). [Note: [Col. 0221] Everything from these words, although he knew it, through the following discussion of those who have wives, was omitted in Codex Corbeiensis.]

So let those who have wives live as though they had none. Since the end of the world is near, they ought not to be anxious about begetting children or devoted to intercourse itself; rather, being more inclined and vigilant in divine works and practiced in care for the Law, they should resist while battle is imminent. For there will be pressures such as have never existed, and many will fall into the devil’s snare. In short, none of us wishes these things to occur in our own time, fearing the pressures foretold by the Savior (Matt. 24:15 and following). [Note: [Col. 0223D] Some manuscripts: “the pressures proclaimed by the Savior.” In the following verse, where the text reads “let us advise” and others, Codex Corbeiensis has “let us console, and console others.”] Therefore, just as we wish for ourselves, let us advise others, so that we may abstain from begetting many children, devoting ourselves more fully to prayer and the service of God, foreseeing the day of judgment. Thus neither may we be unprepared through the hindrances of present necessity, nor may they encounter what we fear. Therefore he also wishes the faithful to abstain from what is permitted, so that they may appear not only innocent but also glorious; for passing over what is permitted is the greatest virtue, and not desiring what is prohibited is not far from virtue. [Note: [Col. 0223D] After the words “the end is not far away,” Codex Vallensis adds “by virtue.” In Codex Corbeiensis, from these same words backward to “Therefore he also wishes them to abstain from what is permitted,” nothing is found.]

(Vers. 30.) And let those who weep live as though they did not weep; for, knowing that the end of the world is near and that consolation will soon come to those who perhaps suffer for the justice of God, they should console themselves among one another with this hope. And let those who rejoice live as though they did not rejoice; for those who rejoice in the present should know that mourning will soon come—namely, to those who rejoice in the world and are uncertain about God’s judgment. And let those who buy live as though they did not possess; for those who buy, believing that little time remains for the world, should act in such a way that they do not devote all their care to a possession that will soon perish; rather, let them care for their souls, which they know to be eternal.

137

(Vers. 31.) And let those who use this world live as though they did not use it—that is, let them not presume upon this use, because it will quickly perish when the world collapses. For the form of this world is passing away. Since he said that the world will come to an end, he showed that its form is passing away. This is the end: not that its substance passes away, but its form. Therefore, if the form of the world will perish, there is no doubt that everything in the world will perish. It is passing away because the world grows old day by day. [Note: [Col. 0223D] Instead of “its passing away,” and below “therefore it is passing away,” some manuscripts [Col. 0224D] offer “its perishing … therefore it will perish.” But there is also a lacuna in Codex Corbeiensis at this point.]

(Vers. 32.) I want you to be without anxiety. For when worldly anxiety has been diminished, one watches more attentively over the things of God. How we can be without anxiety he shows by saying: The unmarried man thinks about the things of the Lord. Once the anxiety of marriage—which alone in the world is more burdensome than other things—has been cut away, the mind is trained to win God’s favor, provided that the mind frees itself from these troubles with the intention of serving God more fully.

(Vers. 33.) But the married man is anxious about the things of this world, how he may please his wife. Concern for a wife and children is thought concerning the world; for among other things, people sometimes admit actions deserving punishment so as not to offend them, as Zerubbabel, one of the three chamberlains of Artaxerxes, reports (1 Esd. 4:13). For it is a great bitterness in a household when the wife is sad. He is therefore said to be divided, because he cannot both persist in divine matters and do his wife’s will.

The woman and the virgin are divided. They are divided not in nature but in conduct, because we read in Numbers that women were called virgins (Num. 31:9). The concern of a woman, therefore, is one thing, and that of a virgin another. Yet when “woman” is said, it is uncertain what is meant unless an explanation follows; when “virgin” is said, the meaning is clear. Here the Apostle placed the virgin after the woman in order to indicate a woman who is not a virgin. By this he wished to show that the virgin is free from the weariness and labors endured by a woman joined to a husband.

(Vers. 34.) For the unmarried woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy both in body and in spirit—that is, in mind. For while, in hope of heavenly things, she does not take upon herself the anxiety of a husband and children, she thinks about the Lord and how she may preserve her purpose devoted to God, provided that, while her body is pure, her mind casts away earthly concerns and applies itself to heavenly things. For it is the mind that either sanctifies or pollutes the body. What benefit is there in having a pure body and a polluted soul, when the body is honored or condemned according to the soul’s merit? But the married woman thinks about the things of this world, how she may please her husband. Bound by marital law, she is anxious about how to fulfill the right of marital duty, being subject to worldly necessities. [Note: [Col. 0224D] Codex Corbeiensis: “But if, in a pure body, the mind thinks about earthly things, it pollutes the body. But the married woman …”]

(Vers. 35.) I say this for your own benefit, not to cast a snare over you, but for what is honorable. Since some people think that what is more useful or better is harsh and burdensome because of the habit of temporal life, after giving his reasoning he encourages them, with the affection of charity, simply to accept that what he says is more useful and more honorable. It is honorable because it is holy and pure; it is useful because it is more worthy before God and lighter in the world.

What, then, shall we say? If virgins think about God, while women joined to husbands think about the world, what hope remains for married women before God? If this is so, their salvation is doubtful. For we see virgins thinking about the world, and women joined in marriage devoting themselves to the works of the Lord. Such virgins will not have their chastity credited to them by God, whereas such marriages will have a reward before God, because, though bound by earthly and fleshly ties, they have devoted themselves to earning some immortal reward in the future. But those virgins will not only have their virginity fail to be credited to them; they will also be subjected to punishment, because, under the cover of a better hope, they have occupied their life and conduct with worldly care and anxiety and made themselves sluggish in carrying out God’s works, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the one who performs God’s works negligently” [Col. 0224D] (Jer. 48:10). These are the people of whom he says in another letter: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). [Note: [Col. 0224D] So all editions and most manuscripts; some others, however, read “the appearance of truth.”]

The Apostle is speaking to those who desire to obey heavenly commandments with extraordinary devotion, showing and teaching by what shortcut one goes more quickly to God. For the person who wishes to remain a virgin in order to win God’s favor, knowing what reward he or she can receive by abstaining from what is permitted in order to become better, at the same time despises all the hindrances of the flesh, not unaware that these hold back the runner’s progress as though with the weight of fetters.

(Vers. 36.) But if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably toward his virgin, if she is beyond puberty, and if it ought to be so, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries. [Note: [Col. 0225D] Roman edition, with a few manuscripts: “if he thinks that he appears dishonorable.”] Since above he had encouraged the preservation of virginity and self-restraint with such reasoning that marriages almost seemed, by comparison, useless and to be rejected, now, lest he be thought to deny marriage, he shows that a virgin does not sin if she marries. Yet she is undertaking a task of the greatest labor and one that has no reward before God, just as it has no punishment; for he wishes Christians to be better in every respect. Therefore, if a woman has a desire for marriage and is already mature for intercourse, it is better for her to marry publicly according to the permitted law than to do that dishonorably in secret and bring shame upon herself.

(Vers. 37.) But the one who stands firm in his heart, having no necessity but having authority over his own will, and having decided this in his heart—to preserve his virgin—does well. He says this so that the man who has a virgin, whose mind is not inclined toward marriage, may preserve her and not impose upon her the incentive to marry when he sees that she has no desire to marry. If benefits are to be bestowed, how much more must they not be taken away?

(Vers. 38.) Therefore, the one who gives his virgin in marriage also does well. He does well because what he does is permitted. And the one who does not give her in marriage does better. He does better because he stores up merit for her before God and frees her from worldly anxiety.

(Vers. 39.) A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. He pursues this point in order to teach that even if a woman has been expelled by her husband, she does not have permission to marry. [Note: [Col. 0225D] So the old edition and most manuscripts; the Roman edition, with several other manuscripts, reads: “But if he has fallen asleep.”] But if her husband has died, she is free. This too pertains to the causes mentioned above: to show how blessed the virgin is, since she is subject to no one except God alone. She seems to conquer natural subjection when she raises up what nature has humbled. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord—that is, let her marry the person she considers suitable, because unwilling marriages usually have bad outcomes. “Only in the Lord” means that she should marry without suspicion of dishonor and should marry a man of her own religion. This is what it means to marry in the Lord.

[Col. 0225D] (Vers. 40.) But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice. When above he says “let her marry,” he is speaking according to natural law, although first marriages are from God, while second marriages are permitted. Indeed, first marriages are solemnly celebrated under God’s blessing; second marriages, however, lack glory even in the present life, though they are permitted because of lack of self-control and because younger widows commonly fall into misconduct. [Col. 0226A] Consequently, he permits second marriages. But because it is better for her to exercise self-control, so that she may be more worthy in the future, he gives the special advice, on spiritual grounds, that she exercise self-control. [Note: [Col. 0225D] Some manuscripts: “younger women commonly fall into opposing conduct.” Here too, everything between the words “Indeed, first marriages” and “he permits second marriages” is omitted in Codex Corbeiensis.] For I think that I too have the Spirit of God. Thus, in order to show that his advice is valid and foresighted, he commends it with humble wording but profound understanding. [Note: [Col. 0226D] Roman edition omits the words “that she exercise self-control” and continues: “For I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”]

## CHAPTER VIII

(Vers. 1.) Concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all possess knowledge. He is now about to speak of knowledge. He does not immediately say what this knowledge is, but shows it in what follows by saying that an idol is nothing.

Knowledge puffs up. It is clear that the person who possesses knowledge glories in that very fact, whether outwardly because he is wise or inwardly before himself. For this is the kind of knowledge that makes a person glory in himself; therefore it puffs him up. But charity builds up. Thus knowledge is great and useful to itself only if it is humbled by charity, so that it may grow more greatly. Love moderates it, so that it is not too unmixed and does not intoxicate the knower and make him exalt himself. For just as unmixed wine deranges the mind unless it is diluted with water, so knowledge makes a person proud unless it is tempered. Everything by itself is unpleasant and harmful; for neither is bread eaten well by itself, nor are other foods agreeable without mixture, [Note: [Col. 0226D] Some manuscripts: “but not harmful”; not sufficiently correctly.] but harmful. Therefore charity builds up.

Although charity may be called by one name, it consists of many things; for it cannot exist without patience, nor without humility, nor without simplicity of heart. These people, then, were puffed up through knowledge [Note: [Col. 0226D] Codex Corbeiensis: “who, against the salvation of ignorant brothers, ate the meat sacrificed to an idol.”] because an idol is nothing. Knowing that it was permitted to eat meat, and because an idol is nothing, they ate sacrificial meat, believing that the person who ate it was not defiled. They were a scandal to their brothers because they did not keep charity before their eyes; for it was more important to despise the meat than to cause scandal to their brothers. Their knowledge was destroying the souls of their ignorant brothers, who thought that some divine power existed there by the idol, when they saw more knowledgeable brothers taking part there and not recoiling. Therefore he says: “Charity builds up,” so that, while seeking the salvation of their brothers, they would not use their knowledge there according to its rules and thus cause them scandal.

(Vers. 2.) But if anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know. He shows that these very people who glory in knowledge have not known in the manner in which they ought to know. Since they do not pursue charity, which is the mother of all good things, they do not know as they ought. Therefore, if knowledge is to be able to bear fruit, it must subject itself to charity.

(Vers. 3.) But if anyone loves God, this person is known by him. The person loves God who moderates knowledge for the sake of charity, so that it may benefit his brother, for whom Christ died.

(Vers. 4.) [Note: [Col. 0226D] Some editions and manuscripts: “Therefore concerning foods sacrificed to idols,” [Col. 0227D] (Roman edition: “to idols”) “the food of those who sacrifice”; the Roman edition: “food offered in sacrifice,” and so forth. We have followed the other, more numerous and better manuscripts.] Therefore, concerning foods sacrificed to idols. [Col. 0227A] He now treats the matter itself, in order to show by reasoning that knowledge, when charity is despised, not only fails to advance but also does harm. We know that an idol is nothing and that there is no God but one. This is true; for among Christians there is one God.

(Vers. 5.) For although there are those who are called gods and lords, whether in heaven or on earth. The pagans call the sun, moon, and other stars heavenly gods; on earth they call Apollo, Aesculapius, Hercules, and Minerva gods and lords.

(Vers. 6.) Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are in him. For everything that exists, wherever it exists, is from him. But when he says, “And we are in him,” he distinguishes us from the others, who, although they are from him, are not in him because they still do not believe. And there is one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, and we are through him. For everything was created from the Father indeed, but through the Son. But when he says, “And we are through him,” he signifies that we have been re-formed through the one through whom we had been created, in the knowledge of God. For although we were made through him along with the others, after the dullness of mind and ignorance, through him we recognized the mystery of the one God. Thus he called the Father one God and his Son Jesus one Lord, so that, since God cannot fail to be Lord, the Lord likewise might be understood to be God; and he demonstrated that God and Lord are one, while preserving the order of one principle.

(Vers. 7.) But not everyone possesses knowledge. That is, not all believers know the mystery of the one God; therefore some of those who believe think that there is some divine power in idols.

For some still eat with a conscience attached to the idol, as though it had been sacrificed to an image. For some of the common people still ate sacrificial food with veneration for the image, as though some divinity were present there. And since the conscience of others is weak, it is defiled. The conscience is polluted if it is weak with regard to God.

**(Verse 8.)** “Food, however, does not commend us to God.” This is true, because we shall not therefore please God if we eat everything, nor shall we offend him if we abstain from certain things. For neither shall we abound if we eat, nor shall we lack if we do not eat. If sacrificial food is rejected, what can be eaten will certainly not be lacking; but if it is taken, it will not abound to such an extent that nothing further is needed. Therefore it must be rejected, because one can live without it and it is a scandal to the brothers.

**(Verse 9.)** “But take care lest this liberty of yours somehow become an offense to the weak.” That is: lest, because you say that you are permitted to eat meat from a sacrifice, you cause offense by what you know—that an idol is nothing—to brothers who do not yet know that an idol is nothing.

**(Verse 10.)** “For if someone sees you who possess knowledge reclining at table in an idol’s shrine, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat what has been sacrificed to images?” He said this because, when someone sees a knowledgeable brother invited to an idol’s shrine and reclining there to eat sacrificial meats, he supposes that some grace is present there and begins himself also to eat sacrificial meats—not with that understanding by which the other, through his knowledge, knows that the idol is nothing, but with the understanding by which he supposes that a divinity is present there, since he sees the knowledgeable brother eating there and showing no horror.

**140 (Verse 11.)** “And the weak brother will perish through your knowledge, the brother for whom Christ died?” The weak person will perish if he eats sacrificial food against faith in the one God. These are, as it were, the words of someone angry and showing what evil knowledge can produce if it is not tempered by charity.

“Through your knowledge”: that is, your knowledge kills him when he sees you doing what he understands differently. And you will become the occasion of death to the brother whom Christ permitted himself to be crucified in order to redeem. Thus he teaches that, for the sake of charity, one must sometimes conceal one’s knowledge, because the brother’s salvation is without doubt more important than food: it is permitted, certainly, but it is not beneficial. This is what it means to have come to know as one ought.

[Note: The old edition and very many excellent manuscripts read “the weak brother will perish through your knowledge” once and again, that is, in both places. The Roman edition, together with certain manuscripts, reads “in your conscience.”]

[Note: The Roman edition and some manuscripts read, “by your action you kill him . . . conscience must sometimes be disregarded”; the remaining editions and manuscripts agree with one another, except that in some places the reading is “you kill,” and in others “he kills.”]

**(Verse 12.)** “But when you sin in this way against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.” For when they are not zealous for the charity by which Christ freed us, they sin in Christ, not against Christ; for to sin against Christ is to deny Christ, whereas to sin in Christ means to sin against those things that belong to Christ. Just as one who is under the Law is said to sin against the Law, so those who are under Christ are said to sin against Christ.

**(Verse 13.)** “Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble.” He teaches that one must be so devoted to charity that things permitted are treated as forbidden, lest they harm one’s brother. For how great an evil it is not to transgress through what is forbidden, yet to give offense through what is permitted—to observe the Law in forbidden matters but not to keep it in permitted matters, when these are eaten without consideration! The Law permitted what it permitted in such a way that there should nevertheless be a limit for them to observe. Certainly, it is permitted to have a wife, but if she has committed fornication, she must be cast off; so also it is permitted to eat meat, but if it has been offered to idols, it must be rejected.

# CHAPTER IX

**(Verse 1.)** “Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” Although he seems to deny it, he is affirming it, for he speaks angrily. He proves himself to be an apostle because he was sent to the Gentiles, since the Lord said to him: “I will send you to the Gentiles” (Acts 22:21). He also shows himself to be free because he desired nothing from anyone and did not teach by flattery. He saw Jesus our Lord while praying in the temple at Jerusalem (Acts 22:18). “Are you not my work in the Lord?” They are his work because he himself planted them in the Lord, evangelizing the word of God among them for a year and six months.

**(Verse 2.)** “Even if I am not an apostle to others, nevertheless I am one to you.” For believing Jews who nonetheless continued to observe the Law denied that he was an apostle. He was already teaching that circumcision ought not to be practiced and that the Sabbath ought not to be observed. But while the other apostles, because of the scandal it might cause, refrained from addressing this matter, he seemed to teach otherwise. Therefore they denied that he was an apostle; for he was an apostle to those who had seen signs of power in him.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “He was denied by everyone . . . who saw signs of power in him.”]

“For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.” For while he preached this, they turned from idols to faith in the one God.

**(Verse 3.)** “My defense before those who examine me is this.” He now begins to plead the case that he introduced above when he said: “All things are permitted to me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Food is for the belly, and the belly for food” (1 Cor. 6:12). Thus he begins this case by saying: “My defense before those who examine me is this.” And he adds what that defense is:

**(Verses 4–5.)** “Do we not have the right to eat and drink? This is what he had said: ‘All things are permitted to me.’ Do we not have the right to take along a woman, as also the other apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?” He added “Cephas” because, although he was first among the apostles, he did not refuse the expenses offered to him. Cephas is Simon Peter himself. Women, desirous of the Lord’s teaching and eager for virtue, followed the apostles, supplying them with expenses and services, just as they also followed the Savior, ministering to him from their own means.

**(Verse 6.)** “Or are Barnabas and I alone without the right to do this?” That is: we have the right to do it, but we do not wish to. He says “to do” instead of “to receive,” in order to speak more honorably. And to confirm this he supplies examples, saying:

**(Verses 7–8.)** “Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock of sheep and does not receive milk from the flock? Am I speaking these things merely according to human judgment?” That is: am I following a merely human opinion? “Does not the Law also say the same?” He taught that the testimonies mentioned above agree with divine instruction, so that he might show that he does not refuse to receive expenses from them without reason, since so many examples show that payment is both to be given and received.

**(Verse 9.)** “For it is written in the Law (Deut. 25:4): ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ Does God care about oxen?” For the moment let us settle this briefly. In the prophet Jonah it is written: “Should I not spare the city in which more than one hundred and twenty thousand people and many animals live?” (Jonah 4:11). And the Psalmist says: “You will save humans and beasts” (Ps. 35:7). How, then, does God not care about oxen and cattle? Rather, he does not care about oxen and cattle for their own sake, but for us, for whose sake they were made; therefore he cares about us, not about them.

**(Verse 10.)** “Or,” he says, “does he say this rather for our sake? For it was written for our sake.” Through a figure, everything that is said is transferred to us. “For the one who plows and threshes in hope ought to receive the fruit of his hope.” This is true, because one labors in this hope, in order to obtain the fruit.

**(Verse 11.)** “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” He does not say that it is a great matter, nor that it is an equal exchange, if, while evangelizing the kingdom of God and nourishing the Church with heavenly food, they should receive bodily sustenance—if, while handing on eternal things, they should obtain temporal things.

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “As though he were saying, ‘It is not a great matter,’ and so forth.”]

**(Verse 12.)** “If others share in your authority, do we not rather?” For if those who are not your fathers through the Gospel and do not have the same affection for you have the right to receive, how much more do we? “And ‘your apostles’ is understood,” because Barnabas also was an apostle.

“But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure everything, so that we may place no obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ.” He revealed a meaning long concealed. For he showed that, although it was permitted, he did not wish to receive expenses lest the vigor of evangelical authority grow slack. The pseudo-apostles flattered those who were sinning, wishing to receive payments, so that they did not seem to themselves to be sinning when they submitted to them. But because this practice was contrary to evangelical discipline, he does not wish to receive, so that he may rebuke freely and not be found among their number. To preserve the authority of the Christian rule, he made permitted things forbidden, because they were giving offense through their permissiveness.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “when they were subject to them . . . made lawful what permission allowed.”]

**(Verse 13.)** “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuaries live from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share in the altar?” By “sanctuaries” he signifies the law of the Gentiles, but by “altar” that of the Jews. For the Lord decreed through Moses (Deut. 18:3) that the priests should take a portion of the things that had been offered.

**(Verse 14.)** “So also the Lord Jesus ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.” Therefore God did not follow the pattern of the Gentiles through Moses; rather, natural reason itself has it that one should live from the place where one labors. He therefore assigned this principle to nature itself and to human society. Nevertheless, by adding these points to complete the argument, he makes the case weightier, so that what he commends by so many testimonies may not appear trivial or objectionable; yet he does not wish it to benefit himself, lest the freedom of his rebuke be weakened.

[Note: The Corbie codex reads: “nature itself and human society decreed it.” A little later the same manuscript, together with several others, reads: “nor is it idle, that such great things . . .”]

**(Verse 15.)** “But I have used none of these things.” After demonstrating in many ways that it is permitted to receive payment, he nevertheless says that he has no need of it; for, as I mentioned above, it is harmful to receive from those who are sinning. “Nor have I written these things so that this should be done in my case; for it is better for me to die.” “No one will deprive me of my glory.” He calls it his glory if the severity of the Gospel remains; and he chose rather to die than to violate the rights of the Gospel, knowing that this would benefit him more for future salvation. For he refuses to accept the service owed to him by them, lest through this they gain confidence to sin.

[Note: More and better manuscripts read: “for it is better for me to die”; others, including the editions, read: “rather to die than for anyone to empty my glory.”]

**(Verse 16.)** “For if I evangelize, there is no glory for me.” The old edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “there is no grace for me.” “For necessity is laid upon me.” As the Lord says: “When you have done all that I command you, say: ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10). “Woe to me,” he says, “if I do not preach the Gospel.” A servant sent by his master does, even unwillingly, what has been commanded him; otherwise he must necessarily be bound over to blows. Indeed, Moses was sent unwillingly to Pharaoh (Exod. 4:14), and Jonah was compelled to preach to the Ninevites (Jonah 1:3).

**142 (Verse 17.)** “For if I do this willingly, I have a reward.” It is clear that no one receives payment for something he does unwillingly. If he acts voluntarily, he is worthy of a reward, because he consents to his master; and what is done willingly is done better. “But if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” This too is clear: one who does something without devotion does it not willingly but from necessity. Since it is not within his own power, he unwillingly does what has been commanded him.

[Note: All the editions read: “it is not of his own will”; but almost all the manuscripts instead read: “it is not within his own power,” and so forth. Again, where, together with the old edition and many manuscripts, we restored “I shall make the Gospel effective,” the Roman edition, following one or two manuscripts, had changed it to “I shall preach the Gospel.”]

**(Verse 18.)** “What, then, is my reward? That, while announcing the Gospel, I may make the Gospel free of charge; so that I may not misuse my authority in the Gospel.” Suppressing the boastfulness of his words, he glories and wishes it to be understood how great a reward he deserves, because he does not use his authority in the Gospel, rejecting the expenses offered to him lest he weaken the force of his preaching. This is the meaning of “it is permitted, but it is not beneficial” for the salvation of the brothers, so that they may be corrected. He wants to be an example to the others: when they see that something is not beneficial, they should not use even what is permitted. Otherwise, they will become liable through what is permitted.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “they become liable through wrongdoing.”]

**(Verse 19.)** “For although I am free from all, I made myself the servant of all, so that I might win the more.” He is free from all because he has not handed the Gospel over to anyone through flattery, nor desired anything from anyone except the salvation of that person, nor accepted larger payments from anyone for enjoying luxuries as the reward of hypocrisy. But he says that he made himself the servant of all by presenting himself, through humility, as like all those weak in understanding, so that through patience he might strengthen them for future salvation, comforting the spirits of those who were either sinning or following divine things more slowly, so that they would not bear being rebuked harshly.

[Note: Several manuscripts add: “nor did he desire anything belonging to anyone for the sake of salvation.”]

**(Verse 20.)** “And to the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might win the Jews.” He seems to have pretended in order to become all things to all people, as flatterers commonly do, but this is not so. For, as a divine man and spiritual physician who knows the causes and wounds of all, he comforts and sympathizes with them with great care; for we have certain things in common with all human beings. Thus he became as a Jew to the Jews because, on account of their scandal, he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), and, after purification, went up to the temple, lest through him they should receive an occasion for blasphemy (Acts 21:26). He therefore did something that ought already to have ceased, but he did it according to the Law. He also agreed with them that the Law and the prophets were from God, and showed from them that this Christ was the one who had been promised, so that his agreement might have its intended effect.

[Note: The old edition and quite a few manuscripts read: “It does not seem that he pretended”; the Roman edition and other codices more correctly remove the negation.]

**(Verse 21.)** “To those who are under the Law, as though I were under the Law—although I myself am not under the Law—so that I might win those who are under the Law.” Those who are under the Law are understood to be the Samaritans, for they accept the Law alone, that is, the five books of Moses. They are descended from the Persians and Assyrians, whom the king of the Assyrians, after taking the children of Israel into captivity, placed to inhabit the regions of Samaria (2 Kings 17:6). Therefore they also worship fire in the Persian manner. To these, then, while the Apostle did not deny that the Law was from God, he became as though under the Law. But from it he gently taught them to understand Christ, just as that Samaritan woman said to the Lord: “I know that the Messiah is coming” (John 4:25), having been taught through the Law.

[Note: The Amerbach, Erasmus, and Roman editions, together with part of the manuscripts, read: “he gently taught them to understand Christ.” Gill and other manuscripts instead have “to send the Word to them”; one codex has “the Word.”]

“To those who are without the Law, as though I were without the Law—although I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of Christ—so that I might win those who are without the Law.” He says this because, since he is in the law of Christ, he is in the law of God; for what belongs to Christ belongs to God, and what belongs to God belongs to Christ, as he says: “All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine” (John 17:10). He became as one without the Law in order to win those who were without the Law. For while agreeing with them—that is, with the Gentiles—that the world and the things in it were made by God, that the soul is immortal, and that we have our origin from him—for thus he says in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 17:28): “And as some of you have said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring’”—he became as one without the Law. Through this he introduced to them that Christ himself was the one whom God had chosen beforehand to judge the world, and that he himself was the one through whom God made all things.

**(Verse 22.)** “I became weak to the weak, so that I might win the weak.” He became weak by abstaining from what was permitted for the sake of weak brothers, lest he generate a scandal for them. “I became all things to all, so that I might save all.” This was the action of a prudent and spiritual man: becoming all things to all, yet not exceeding the purpose of religion. For wherever he yielded, he yielded in order to make progress; nor did he do anything other than what the Law commanded.

[Note: Some manuscripts add: “This was truly prudent.”]

**(Verse 23.)** “But I do everything for the sake of the Gospel, so that I may become a participant in it.” That is: I do all the things mentioned above so that I may become a participant in the will of the Gospel, which it possesses regarding human salvation.

**(Verse 24.)** “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” He now wishes to explain something else. By this example he shows how great is the benefit of our law, in which the prize is promised not to one person but to all. “Run in such a way that you may obtain it.” He wishes them to run eagerly toward the promise, because it is great.

**(Verse 25.)** “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things.” They abstain from all those things that the same discipline teaches must be avoided, since they know that only one will be crowned. How much more must we observe such discipline, since salvation is promised to all! “And they do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.” Here too the gift is greatly different. Therefore we ought to be more diligent, since a spiritual crown is reserved for us, not woven of earthly and withering flowers, but adorned with eternal jewels in the form of a royal diadem.

**(Verse 26.)** “Thus I run, not as though toward uncertainty.” He declares that he runs with great hope, knowing what has been promised. “Thus I fight, not as one striking the air.” That is: I contend not chiefly with words, but with realities.

“But I chastise my body and subject it to slavery.” To chastise the body is to afflict it by fasts and to give it those things that contribute to life, not to luxury.

[Note: The old edition and most manuscripts read: “to treat it by fasts”; the Roman edition, more correctly, together with other manuscripts, reads: “to afflict it.”] It is subjected to slavery when it does not carry out its own will but the will of the spirit. “Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified.” He shows that he restrains his body so that he too may be found worthy of the reward he preaches to others, lest, while caring for others, he himself remain wounded. He therefore affirms the certainty of his hope in preaching when he shows by his actions that he pursues what he teaches. For one who acts differently from what he preaches makes his hearers suspicious, so that they doubt the promises. By his own example, therefore, he urges them to practice not merely in words but in deeds.

# CHAPTER X

**(Verses 1–2.)** “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (Exod. 13:21; 14:22). By the example of the Jews, who offended through their own negligence (Num. 9:22), he wants us to be vigilant.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “were done for our care.”] Therefore he says that they were under the cloud, because everything that happened was done as a figure of us, so that they possessed an image of our truth. For, covered by the cloud and protected from their enemies, they are said to have been baptized when they were delivered from death. For when the Egyptians died in the sea and these people, under Moses’ leadership, passed through safely, they were rescued from death; this is what baptism accomplishes. Their former evils were not counted against them; rather, having been purified through the sea and the cloud, they were prepared to receive the Law and the figure of our future sacrament.

**(Verses 3–4.)** “And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” He calls the manna and the water that flowed from the rock (Exod. 16:15; 17:6) spiritual because they were not prepared according to the laws of the world, but were created for a time by the power of God without the mixture of the elements, possessing within themselves a figure of the future mystery that we now receive in remembrance of Christ the Lord. Therefore it was also called the bread of angels, because it was created by the power by which angels subsist; this signified that the one who would feed spiritually was going to come from heaven. Hence manna first came from heaven on the Lord’s Day, to the satiety of the people. Yet the rock that followed is said to signify Christ. For whenever human assistance failed them, Christ was present; therefore he followed them, so that whenever they failed, he might come to their aid. For it was not the rock that gave the water, but Christ.

**(Verse 5.)** “But God was not well pleased with most of them.” He said this because they did not understand the benefit they had received. For they were struck down in the desert (Num. 26:65). It is fitting that one who has obtained great things but distrusts in small matters should not only fail to attain these things but also lose the things already received. Since he therefore exhorted them above to better things, he now also says that he labors so as to be found worthy of attaining the promise. Now, in order to restrain and persuade them through the terror of this example, he says that the Jews at that time received the gift and grace of God in a manner similar to us; and because they were negligent and doubting regarding God’s promise, they were struck down in the desert. He showed that he afflicted himself for this reason, so that he would not be found among their number. Accordingly, we must labor to become his imitators.

[Note: The same Corbie manuscript reads: “should not despise it, but should also strive to labor so as to be found worthy of attaining the promise”; not a few passages are omitted there.]

**(Verses 6–7.)** “Now these things happened as a figure of us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they also desired them.” This is the meaning and reasoning that I mentioned above. “Nor should we become worshipers of images, as some of them did.” He now touches upon those who, reclining at table in an idol’s shrine, thought it was not a sin. As it is written (Exod. 32:6): “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”—certainly before the idol—so that those who feasted in an idol’s shrine might not consider themselves free from guilt. For when Moses was on the mountain with God, an image of a calf was made, after an offering had been made for its dedication; then “the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” This is indulgence and luxury, because, always devoted to pleasure, they were found faithless in the things of God.

[Note: The Corbie codex alone reads: “and therefore he destroys it”; but the same codex, together with certain others, reads: “lest we fall into the luxury of the idol.”]

Therefore he instructs us not to fall into this distrust through consenting to indulgence in an idol’s shrine.

**(Verse 8.)** “Nor let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day” (Num. 25:1). This was repaid to them when they defiled themselves with the women of Midian. For the wrath of God arose against them, but it was quieted through the zeal of Phinehas the priest, who possessed zeal for God, so that more would not die.

**(Verse 9.)** “Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him, and perished by serpents.” Those who detracted from God are said to have tested Christ, because it was Christ who spoke to Moses. Finally, he warns us not to be found in the same situation, lest we be handed over to the devil, whose serpents bear his figure.

**(Verse 10.)** “Nor murmur, as some of them murmured” (Num. 14:1). To murmur is, according to the meaning of the passage, to complain falsely to one another about those set over them and their rulers, since murmuring can also arise from a just cause. “And they perished by the destroyer.” That is: they yielded their place to Judas, anticipating him, because, after betraying Christ, he was destroyed from the number of the apostles by God the judge. Through these examples he calls us to a more disciplined life, so that, if we obey his warnings, we may deserve a reward, but if we disobey, a more severe punishment. For it is not doubtful that those who sin will be subjected to greater torments when the punishments of sinners have been related for this purpose: so that they might not sin.

**(Verse 11.)** “Now all these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” We are the ends of the ages, because these things are known to have happened then with regard to their recompense so that they might be an example for us, who were to exist in faith in Christ at the end of the age. They were carried out for our benefit, so that, if we remain in the fear of God through terror of these events, we may receive the glory promised to them. Otherwise, their punishment will be doubled for us, because greater knowledge of the Law makes a person more guilty.

**(Verse 12.)** “Therefore, whoever thinks that he stands must take care lest he fall.” He says this to those who, presuming upon their knowledge that everything is permitted to be eaten, were a stumbling block to weak brothers; and who, thinking that they were making progress through the teaching of the pseudo-apostles, had become worse, while they judged the Apostle even though they themselves were guilty. He therefore cuts off their pride, lest they be tested through it as the Jews were tested and perished.

**(Verse 13.)** “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.” Thus those who detract from the Apostle appear to be testing the Lord, because when they once detracted from Moses and doubted him, they are said to have tested God. Everything that has not been proved is tested; therefore he warns them with fear in order to tear away this temptation. But he urges that a human temptation should seize them. For a human temptation is to distrust a human being because of hope in God, since hope in a human being is vain. Thus, in necessity or distress, one should not despair of God by seeking human assistance, as the Jews, doubting God, sought the aid of idols. This is human assistance, because the gods of the pagans are earthly, and human error invented their worship. To suffer, therefore, for Christ is a human temptation, through which one makes progress before God.
