“But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure.” He calls God faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, because God promised that he would give heavenly kingdoms to those who love him; and he must give them, because he is faithful. Therefore, when you are afflicted for his sake, he will be present and will not allow so much to be inflicted that it cannot be endured. Rather, he will cause the temptation either to cease quickly or, if it lasts a long time, will give the strength to endure. Otherwise he would not give what he promised, because the one who suffers would be overcome. For a human being is subject to weakness, and there will be no one to receive it.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “who may rescue.”]

But because God is faithful, who made the promise, he comes to the aid of the sufferer so that he may fulfill what he promised. Finally, the Lord wishes the days to be shortened so that the elect may be saved and be able to obtain the kingdom of God (Matt. 24:22). How, nevertheless, is one helped by God if he is permitted to be tempted only as much as he can bear? He is plainly helped by this: he is not permitted to have more imposed upon him than he is known to be able to bear. Thus one who is known to be unable to endure more than three days is not permitted to suffer on the fourth day.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “How, nevertheless, is one helped by God if he is permitted to be tempted only as much as he is known to be able to bear?” The entire passage from “How, nevertheless” through “Therefore, beloved” is omitted in the Corbie manuscript.]

**(Verse 14.)** “Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols.” He again urges them to withdraw from every association with idolatry, so that not only hope but also the mind may be removed from it, lest through this temptation against God arise. No one who is constantly in an idol’s shrine hopes for nothing from it; for to hope for something from it is to doubt God, just as Saul, after abandoning God, who had become angry with him because of his offense, turned to idolatry, hoping for something from it (1 Sam. 28:12 and following). This harmed him in the present life and prepared avenging Gehenna for him in the future.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “let no one in an idol’s shrine hope for anything from it.” The old edition and the manuscripts differ only in that they have “also hope,” while some of them read “from God” instead of “from it.”]

**(Verse 15.)** “As prudent people, judge what I say.” He supplies examples so that he may persuade them more easily, because examples commonly persuade those whom words alone do not satisfy.

**(Verses 16–17.)** “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not participation in the blood of the Lord? The bread that we break, is it not participation in the body of the Lord? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread and of the one cup.” Since we are one—members of one another—he says that we ought to have one mind, so that one faith may have one understanding and one practice.

**(Verse 18.)** “Consider Israel according to the flesh.” That is: learn, you who see God, how matters of the flesh stand, namely, idolatry. “Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?” For just as, receiving from the one bread and the one cup, we are participants and sharers in the Lord’s body, so those who eat sacrifices are participants in the altar of error.

**(Verses 19–20.)** “What, then, am I saying? That something sacrificed to an image is something?” Not that the image is something, but that what they sacrifice they sacrifice to demons. The image itself is truly nothing, because it appears to be the likeness of a dead thing; but under the covering of images the devil is worshiped.

“I do not want you to become participants in demons.” He showed them that what appears in the idol is merely what is visible, but that there is a hidden mystery of iniquity, which Satan devised in order to corrupt faith in the one God. Hence the Apostle John also says in his letter: “For this reason the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil” (John 3:9).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “which is seen in the idol.”]

**(Verse 21.)** “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons.” As the Lord also says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6:24). For one who drinks the cup of demons insults the cup of the Lord; and when he shares in the table of demons, he opposes the table of the Lord—that is, the altar—and crucifies the Lord’s body. For this reason Christ was crucified, to destroy the works of the devil.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Christ was crucified because he destroyed the works of the devil.”]

Therefore whoever does the works of the devil resists Christ.

**(Verse 22.)** “Or are we provoking the Lord Jesus to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?” It rarely happens that a humble person is jealous of someone powerful, for he knows that it does not belong to him to envy one in whom he can see superiority; one envies an equal or someone nearly equal. Therefore the Apostle said that human beings cannot be jealous of the Lord Jesus, because they know him to be Lord. Otherwise it would seem that the one of whom they are jealous is not worthy to be called Lord, since they begrudge him being Lord. For Satan invented idolatry out of jealousy, so that human beings, by denying God the Lord, might serve images as gods and lords.

“All things are permitted to me, but not all things are beneficial.” He says that all things are permitted according to the law of nature, for all things are clean. The subject was foods, and meat sacrificed to idols. For how can things that are prohibited and forbidden be said to be permitted, when here he indicates that even things granted to us are sometimes not beneficial? As the Apostle Peter says: “If this is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not beneficial to marry” (Matt. 19:10).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “as the apostles say.”]

**(Verse 23.)** “All things are permitted to me, but not all things build up.” The meaning is the same: it is permitted to eat everything, but what has been sacrificed to idols does not build up, because it causes a brother to stumble, as was said above. Therefore one must sometimes abstain from permitted things, so that they may be beneficial. This is why, although it was permitted, he did not wish to receive expenses from them, knowing that it was not beneficial.

**(Verse 24.)**

[Note: The Apostle’s text and the exposition of it are restored here from the Corbie codex, since they are absent from the others, as well as from all the editions.]

“No one should seek his own advantage, but that of the other.” It is true that, while each person reclines in an idol’s shrine, he satisfies his own desire and places a stumbling block before the brother whose conscience is weak. Therefore we must act promptly for the charity of our Lord Jesus Christ, preferring to restrain our own will in matters necessary to our neighbor’s salvation, just as the same Apostle, the vessel of election and spiritual physician, says: “Not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many.”

**(Verses 25–26.)** “Eat everything sold in the market, asking no questions for the sake of conscience; for ‘the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness’” (Ps. 23:1). To show that everything is clean, he strengthened this with the example of the twenty-third psalm, because what belongs to the Lord cannot be unclean. And since above he said concerning foods, “All things are permitted,” he immediately added: “Eat everything sold in the market, asking no questions for the sake of conscience.” He added this so that conscience might be free. Although something may be polluted accidentally—that is, by an idol’s offering—when the buyer does not know this, he suffers no scruple and is innocent before God.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “discerning nothing.”]

**(Verse 27.)** “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you go, eat everything set before you, asking no questions.” That is: eat simply whatever is set before you, without asking where it came from.

(Verses 28–29.) But if someone says, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” do not eat it, for the sake of the one who pointed it out, and for the sake of conscience. By “conscience,” however, I mean not your own, but the other person’s. He is speaking to the perfect, who, scorning idolatry, can be certain that it makes no difference to eat from a sacrifice, since what is eaten under the name of God the Creator cannot defile. But because the other person, who serves idols, will boast when he sees you eating what has been sacrificed, as though you revered the idols, it therefore ought not to be eaten. For in his own conscience he will rejoice, [Col. 0238C] because he sees you eagerly desiring what has been sacrificed to idols.

“For why should my liberty be judged by another’s conscience?” He says this because, although his conscience is free from devotion to an idol, what need is there for him to be thought to eat what has been sacrificed to idols for the sake of reverence? For he is judged not to differ from the one who worships idols when he does not shrink from what has been offered to an image.

(Vers. 30.) “If, then, I partake of grace, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks?” That is: if I share in the grace of God, because I eat in his name, why should anyone suppose that I am devoted to an idol, since I do not shrink from what has been offered to an idol—that is, why am I blasphemed? He therefore blasphemes me, and the other rejoices in his idol; while he supposes me to be a participant, he has an occasion to persist in error, and a bad example is given to the brothers. For if the Law commanded that the sacred groves, altars, inscriptions, and the idols themselves be destroyed, see whether it is not a sin not only to fail to do these things, but also to take part in banquets of this kind. Therefore it is not fitting to eat what has been sacrificed.

[Note: The same Codex Corbeiensis: “not only to do these things, but also it is not expedient to eat what has been sacrificed.”]

(Vers. 31.) “Therefore, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” By what follows he has shown that eating in an idol’s temple, whatever one’s conscience may be, is hostile to God; for these things are dedicated to the devil to the dishonor of the one God. To eat and drink and do anything for the glory of God means that a banquet is held with moderation under invocation of the Creator. Something is done for the glory of God when God is praised in the actions and conduct of a Christian, or when the procreation of children is hoped for from God.

(Vers. 32.) “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks, and to the Church of God.” Thus he teaches that our conduct should be regulated so that no one suffers scandal through it. An offense is given to Jews when they see a Christian—who says that he accepts the Law and the prophets—not shrink from idols, which they abominate. To Greeks, that is, to Gentiles, this is an offense: if, in the practices in which they remain, they are not only not reproved, but become even more eager because the vows they make to their idols are not avoided. An offense is given to the Church of God when it sees some of its own number cling to things that are hostile to God.

(Vers. 33.) “Just as I please everyone in everything, seeking not my own advantage but that of many, so that they may be saved.” To please everyone in everything means to act without giving offense to anyone, for the sake of their benefit, so that what is useful may be useful both to them and to him.

## CHAPTER XI

(Vers. 1.) “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.” What he says is human: we are to be his imitators, since he has been granted to us by God as a teacher. For if he is an imitator of God, why should we not be imitators of a human being? Because just as God the Father sent Christ as teacher and author of life, so Christ sent the apostles as our teachers, so that we might be their imitators, since we cannot be Christ’s directly. For the Lord says to the Father: “Just as you sent me into this world, so I also sent them into this world” (John XVII, 18). And because they were worthy imitators of him, he added: “And for their sake I sanctify myself” (ibid., 19).

(Vers. 2.) “I praise you, brothers, because you remember me in everything, and just as I have handed on my traditions everywhere, you hold to them.” After criticizing their morals and conduct, he now wishes to correct their traditions. He therefore does not affirm this but reproves them, because, although he was their apostle, they were forgetful of his traditions; nor did they follow what they had not yet learned from his teaching, [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “but they were following the tradition of other Churches.”] but followed the tradition of other Churches. [Col. 0239D] Accordingly, as though he were giving them the tradition anew, he says:

(Vers. 3.) “I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ.” He referred this to authority: man is from God, but through Christ. “The head of woman is man.” Although woman too is through Christ, she was nevertheless made from man and is therefore subject to man. “The head of Christ is God.” It is fitting that the Father be called the head of the Son, as his begetter. Yet Christ is the head of man in one way, man is the head of woman in another, and God is the head of Christ in another. God is the head of Christ because Christ was begotten from him or by him. Man is the head of woman because she was formed from his rib by God’s power (Gen. II, 21). Christ is the head of man because man, when he did not yet exist, was created through him. Thus one word has different meanings, because the persons and the substances differ.

(Vers. 4.) “Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head.” By “praying” he means making supplication; by “prophesying,” declaring in symbolic speech, after prayer, that the Lord’s coming will take place.

(Verses 5–7.) “But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head, for it is one and the same thing as if she were shaven. If a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn; but if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God.”

Although man and woman have one substance, woman is nevertheless presented as subordinate because man is the head of woman; thus he is superior by cause and reason, not by substance. Woman, therefore, is inferior to man, for she is his portion; the origin of woman is man, since she is from him. Accordingly, woman appears bound to man, so that she may be subject to his authority. He says that the honor and dignity of man prevent him from covering his head; for it is unfitting that the image of God should be concealed. It ought not to be hidden, since the glory of God is seen in man.

“But woman is the glory of man.” There is a great difference between the glory of God and the glory of man; for man was made in the image of God, not woman. This image of God is in man because the one God made one human being, so that, just as all things come from one God, all human beings might also come from one human being. Thus the invisible God would have the image of one visible human being on earth, so that the one God, seen in one human being, might preserve the authority of one principle, to the confusion of the devil, who, neglecting the one God, wished to usurp dominion and divinity for himself. The prophet Ezekiel signifies this (Ezek. XVIII, 16), and the Apostle likewise says: “So that he takes his seat in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (II Thess. II, 4).

(Verses 8–10.) “For man is not from woman, but woman from man; and indeed man was not created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man. Therefore a woman ought to have authority over her head, also because of the angels.” By “authority” he signifies the veil; by “angels” he means bishops, as is taught in the Apocalypse of John (Apoc. II, 1 ff.). And since they are certainly human beings, they are reproved for not correcting the people, while what is right in them is praised. Woman, therefore, [33rd question, distinction 5, chapter “Mulier”] ought to cover her head because she is not the image of God, but is to be shown as subject. And because transgression began through her, she ought to bear this sign: in the Church, out of reverence for the bishop, she should not have her head free, but covered with a veil; nor should she have the authority to speak, because the bishop bears the person of Christ. Thus, as before a judge, so before the bishop, since he is the Lord’s vicar, she ought to be seen as subject because of the origin of guilt.

[Note: Gratian in the Decree: “because of original sin.”]

[Col. 0241A] (Vers. 11.) “Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord.” It is “in the Lord” because God made both from one and made them one; for they are one flesh and one body in the Lord—that is, according to the Lord who created them. In the end, those who do not believe that woman was taken from man believe the origin of humanity to be without the Lord, or not according to the Lord.

(Vers. 12.) “For just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman.” He confirmed what he had said: both are one in nature, and the origin of woman is man, as we read that it was accomplished by the Lord the Creator in Genesis. “But all things are from God” (Gen. II, 22). After explaining each point step by step, so as to subject everything to God while preserving one principle, he says: “But all things are from God,” so that neither woman might be saddened because of her subjection, nor man, as though exalted, become proud.

(Vers. 13.) “Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled?” This is why earlier he reproves them ironically, saying: “I praise you because you remember everything of mine, and just as I hand on my traditions everywhere, you hold to them” (above, vers. 2). Since the rule of the tradition was that women should be veiled in the Church, they instead allowed them to be unveiled in the Church. Therefore he now attempts to persuade them of the truth not by the authority of the tradition—which they had neglected—but by nature itself, saying:

(Verses 14–15.) “Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears his hair long, it is a disgrace to him? But if a woman wears her hair long, it is a glory to her, because her hair has been given to her as a veil.” He spoke this according to the Law, for it forbids a man to wear his hair long. He wants this to be regarded as naturally honorable and almost as a decree: that a veiled woman should be satisfied and give thanks to God. Thus hair is an indication of the veil, so that nature may be joined to the will. In the end, no woman, even when unveiled, approaches authority.

(Vers. 16.) “But if anyone seems contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.” After giving his reasoning, he brings in authority to defeat the contentious: neither Judaism had this custom, and therefore he says, “Neither we nor the Church of God,” meaning that neither Moses nor the Savior handed it down in this way.

(Vers. 17.) “But in giving this instruction I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.” Just as he corrects their conduct piecemeal through reproof, so also their traditions—not praising them, certainly, but censuring them.

(Verses 18–19.) “For first of all.” [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “For where there is dissension, we shall speak first.” It indicates the kind of sin from which the errors arose, since where there is dissension nothing is right.] By saying “first,” he indicates the kind of sin from which the errors he censures arose; for where there is dissension, nothing is right. “When you come together in the Church, I hear that there are dissensions among you, and to some extent I believe it. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.” Knowing that some had been corrupted in mind by the devil’s cunning, he says: “There must be heresies.” He certainly did not will or desire this, [Note: All editions and some manuscripts: “but because they will exist, he said it would happen”; other manuscripts: “but because he knew”; some: “he knows that it will happen,” said it.] but because he knew it would happen, he said so, just as the Lord also says: “It is necessary that scandals come” (Matt. XVIII, 7). And: “It is necessary for the Son of Man to suffer” (Luke IX, 22), since he foreknew that Judas would be a betrayer.

When he says “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you,” he refers to those who persevere in the tradition they received and are examples of the testing of evangelical discipline, to the condemnation of the others. These are the ones he refers to at the beginning of the epistle, because they said, “But we belong to Christ,” while others said, “I belong to Paul,” or “I to Apollos” (I Cor. I, 12).

(Verses 20–22.) “When you come together, then, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand while eating; and one is hungry, while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?”

He censures those who came together in the Church in such a way that, when they offered their gifts and the presbyters arrived—for at that time rulers had not yet been appointed for the Churches in every place—they claimed for themselves everything they had offered, thus causing schism. Dissensions had been sown among them by false apostles, so that they were jealous over their offerings. Although the offerings of all were blessed with one and the same prayer, those who had not offered, as commonly happens, or who had nothing with which to offer, were overcome with shame and confusion and took no part; and the others acted so quickly that those who arrived later found nothing to eat.

Therefore, he says, if you come together in such a way that each takes his own portion, this should be done at home, not in the Church, where people gather for the sake of unity [Note: Codex Laud: “and for the sake of the mystery,”] and the mystery, not for dissension and the belly. The offering should belong to the whole people, because all are signified in the one bread. Since we are one, it is necessary for all of us to partake of one bread.

“What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.” Once the error has been exposed and reproved, he makes clear that they should correct it thereafter and recognize as true what they themselves had learned long before, in the beginning. He repeats the form given by the Savior for such a matter, saying:

(Verses 23–25.) “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat. This is my body, which is broken for you.’ [Note: Roman edition: “which will be handed over for you.”] Do this in remembrance of me. In the same way also the cup, after supper, saying: ‘This cup is the new Testament in my blood. Do this, whenever you drink, in remembrance of me.’”

He showed them that the mystery of the Eucharist was celebrated during the meal but was not itself a meal. It is a spiritual medicine which, tasted with reverence, purifies the one devoted to it. It is the remembrance of our redemption, so that, remembering the Redeemer, we may deserve to receive greater things from him.

(Vers. 26.) “For as often as you eat this bread and drink from the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.” Since we have been freed by the Lord’s death, by remembering this in eating and drinking the flesh and blood offered for us, [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “signifying that we have also obtained the new Testament in these things, which is...”] we signify that we have obtained the new Testament in these things. This is the new law, which commits the one who obeys it to the heavenly kingdoms.

For Moses too, having taken the blood of a calf in a basin, sprinkled the children of Israel, saying: “This is the Testament which God established for you” (Exod. XXIV, 8). This was a figure of the Testament which the Lord, through the prophets, called new, so that what Moses handed down might be old. The Testament, therefore, was established by blood, because the blood is the witness of the divine benefit.

As a type of this, we receive the mystical cup of blood for the protection of our body and soul [Note: Some manuscripts: “for protection”; one: “for sprinkling.”] because the Lord’s blood redeemed our blood—that is, it saved the whole human being. The Savior’s flesh was poured out for the salvation of the body, but his blood for our soul, as Moses had earlier prefigured. For he says: “The flesh is offered for your body, but the blood for your soul” (Lev. XVII, 11). Therefore blood is not to be eaten.

If, then, among the ancients there was an image of the truth that has now appeared and been revealed in the Savior’s coming, how can it seem to heretics that the old is contrary to the new, when the two themselves bear mutual witness to one another?

[Col. 0243C] (Vers. 27.) “Therefore, whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily of the Lord will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” He says that the person is unworthy of the Lord who celebrates the mystery in a manner different from what the Lord handed down. For one cannot be devoted who presumes to act otherwise than it was given by its author. Therefore he warns that, according to the order handed down, the mind of the one approaching the Lord’s Eucharist must be devout, since judgment will come, and each person will have to give an account on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ according to the manner in which he approaches. Those who approach without the discipline of tradition and conduct are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

What does it mean to be guilty except to suffer the penalties of the Lord’s death? [Note: Roman edition: “For he was killed by those who render his benefit void.”] He was killed for those who nullify his benefit.

[Col. 0243D] (Verses 28–29.) “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.” He teaches that one must approach communion with a devout mind and with fear, [Note: Ivo of Chartres: “so that all may know ... let them approach.”] so that the mind may know that it owes reverence to the one whose body it approaches to receive.

This is what he ought to judge within himself: that the one whose blood he drinks in the mystery is the Lord, and that this blood is the witness of God’s benefit. If we receive him with discipline, we will not be unworthy of the body and blood of the Lord; [Col. 0244A] for we will appear to give thanks to the Redeemer. [Note: Several manuscripts: “for grace will be seen.”]

(Vers. 30.) “That is why many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep.” To prove the truth that there will be an examination of those who receive the Lord’s body, he already displays here an image of judgment upon those who had received the Lord’s body carelessly: they were seized by fevers and illnesses, and many died. The others were to learn from these cases and, frightened by the example of a few, reform themselves, knowing that it is not without punishment to receive the Lord’s body negligently; and that the one whom punishment has postponed here will be treated more severely because he despised the example.

(Verses 31–32.) “But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. Yet when we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.” He says that if we corrected our own errors, we would not be judged by the Lord. And because we are chastised, this is nevertheless for our benefit, so that we may be corrected by that very fear. For the correction of all is found in a few. We must not be condemned with the world—that is, with unbelievers. For there is no difference between an unbeliever and one who approaches the Lord’s table carelessly.

(Verses 33–34.) “Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home.” He says that they should wait for one another so that the offering of many may be celebrated together and all may be served. If anyone is impatient, let him feed himself at home with earthly bread. “So that you may not come together for judgment”—that is, so that you may not conduct the mystery reprehensibly and with offense.

[Col. 0244C] “As for the remaining matters, I will arrange them when I come.” He shows that what concerns the order of salvation must first be dealt with, and he has already explained how both sexes should assemble in the Church. If there is error in these matters, it is no slight sin. The remaining matters that pertain to the building up of the Church he promises to arrange by his presence.

## CHAPTER XII

(Verses 1–2.) “Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were Gentiles, you went after mute images, however you were led.” As he is about to hand on instruction concerning spiritual gifts, he recalls an example from their former conduct, so that, just as they had been the image of idols—worshiping images and being led by the will of demons—so, worshiping God, they may be an image of the Lord’s law, walking as pleases the Lord.

The form of each law ought to be seen in the profession and conduct of its worshiper. For the one in whose faith and conduct the truth of the Gospel shines is himself the form and image of God’s law.

(Vers. 3.) “Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” Because they were ignorant of the order of spiritual gifts, they gave glory to human beings rather than to God through the individual gifts, failing to understand that this gift was administered through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0245A] [Note: Codex Val.: “that this gift is administered to God.”]

And because the one who calls Jesus Lord does not say this without the Holy Spirit—for he has grace in that very confession of his faith, for the glory of Christ’s name—it is not without the gift of God to call Jesus Lord. Accordingly, he shows them that in everything praise and grace belong to God. Just as the image of idols is present in their ministers, having its own order through individual ranks, yet is wholly a human creation, so in the Lord’s law there are ranks of gifts according to the offices of the Church. These were not granted because of human merits, but as members contributing to the building up of the Church, possessing glory in and of themselves, as is also the case with human offices.

For offices are like schools: those placed in them receive dignity, so that the honor of the position makes a person glorious, not his own praise. Therefore he says: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’” The voice that says “Anathema to Jesus” is uttered through human error [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “approved through error.”]; for whatever is false comes from a human being.

“And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” The very expression by which Jesus is signified as Lord does not flow from human flattery—as idols too are called gods—but is poured forth through the truth of the Holy Spirit. Whatever is said truly by anyone is said by the Holy Spirit.

Thus, so that they would not suppose that human favor belonged to the Christian rule, and consequently refuse to allow themselves to be reproved, as happens with images [Note: Gill edition: “for a human being brought this about...”]—for a human being devised that one who is not God should be called God, and consequently the priests are subject to those images—he shows them that there is no human benefit in calling Jesus Lord, [Col. 0245C] but rather a gift of God, who deigned to reveal his mystery to human beings. Indeed, the very profession obtains remission of sins, just as the dedication of idols intensifies guilt. [Note: Several manuscripts: “the very confession”; Codex Corbeiensis: “the very promise.”]

He therefore teaches them that, by saying “Lord Jesus,” they do not confer a benefit upon religion but receive one, lest, after the manner of idol worship, they should think that grace belongs to human beings in the Lord’s law, while one who is not God is called God. Finally, because they did not understand that the gift of God was present in faith, each had chosen individual human beings for himself to follow, saying: “I am of Paul, but I am of Apollos” (I Cor. I, 12). Thus he humbles their pride, so that they may allow themselves to be reproved, as I said.

(Vers. 4.) “But there are divisions of graces.” He does not want this attributed to human merits, but to the grace of God, for the honor of his name. Just as the one who says “Lord Jesus” speaks in the Holy Spirit, whatever his status may be, so also the person placed in the position of an ecclesiastical office has grace, whatever his status may be—not his own grace, but that of the office, effective through the Holy Spirit. Hence, near the beginning, he says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 7).

(Verses 5–6.) “And there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are divisions of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all.” Through the same Spirit he says that different gifts are bestowed. “But the same Lord.” He now joins Christ to the Holy Spirit. “And it is the same God who works all things in all.” He insists that this must not be attributed to human beings as though it were their own, but asserted as belonging solely to God. He even calls the gift of the Holy Spirit and the grace of the Lord Jesus the work of one God, so that grace and gift may not be divided because of the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but the one work of their undivided unity [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “the nature of the unity and the one work of the three.”] and nature may be understood, so that all glory and divinity may be referred to one.

The divisions of graces are assigned to the offices of the Church, not to human merits. For if the Holy Spirit is the same Lord, and the same Lord is God, and the three are one God—since the glory, power, and nature of the Holy Spirit are God’s, and the Lord Jesus is the same in nature as God—the one Holy Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and the Father are God. Each individually is the one God, and the three are the one God.

Finally, when one acts, the three are said to act, so that the mystery of the Trinity may be contained within the nature and power of the one God, although it is immeasurable.

(Vers. 7.) “But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” That is, he receives a gift so that, governing his life by divine bonds, he may be useful both to himself and to others, while he displays an example of good conduct.

(Vers. 8.) “For to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom.” That is, prudence is given to him not from letters, but from the radiant fire of the Holy Spirit, so that he may have an enlightened heart and be prudent, discerning what must be avoided and what must be pursued. “To another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit”—that is, so that he may possess knowledge of divine things. “To another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit”—that is, so that he may grant healing to the weak or sick.

(Verses 9–10.) “To another, faith in the same Spirit.” He says this so that, overcoming constrained embarrassment, he may receive the ability to profess and defend the faith. “To another, the working of powers.” He signifies that power is given for casting out demons or performing signs. “To another, prophecy”—that is, so that, filled with the Holy Spirit, he may speak of future things. “To another, the discernment of spirits.” He says this so that he may understand and judge whether what is said is of the Holy Spirit or of the worldly spirit. “To another, kinds of tongues,” [Note: Codices Gemblacensis and Vallumbrosanus: “tongues, namely, of those who receive through the majesty of the Holy Spirit the grace to understand the speech of different languages.”] “to another, the interpretation of speech.” To interpret means that, through the gift of God, he faithfully explains the words of those who speak in tongues or through written texts.

(Vers. 11.) “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills.” What above he attributed to the three persons, he now professes to be carried out through the one Holy Spirit. Since they are one in nature and power, what one works, the three work. Yet there is one God, whose grace is distributed to each as he wills—not according to human merits, but rather for the building up of his Church. Thus all the things that the world attempts to imitate but cannot accomplish because it is carnal may be seen in the Church, which is the house of God, granted through the offices, gifts, and teaching of individuals by the Holy Spirit, as a proof of the truth in those who are contemptible to the world.

(Verses 12–13.) “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the one body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free; and we were all given to drink of one Spirit.”

By this he teaches that no person who appears despised is to be disregarded, nor anyone who appears perfect to be preferred; nor is the glory owed to God alone to be attributed to human beings, since one and the same God is glorified in all. For we all have one baptism and one and the same Holy Spirit. He says this because of the matter mentioned above: some were boasting, while they despised others as though they were contemptible.

(Vers. 14.) “For the body is not one member but many.” By saying this, he shows that the unity of the body includes varieties of offices, and that this diversity does not conflict with unity of power. The unity of the body consists not in singularity but in many members, so that they may provide one another with what they owe.

(Vers. 15.) “If the foot should say, ‘Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body,’ is it for that reason not of the body?” That is, someone who appears weak among the brothers cannot be denied to belong to the body merely because he is not powerful.

(Vers. 16.) “And if the ear should say, ‘Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body,’ is it for that reason not of the body?” He says that a person who is somewhat inferior must not be considered unnecessary to the body merely because he is not among the foremost.

(Vers. 17.) “If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing? If the whole body were hearing, where would be the sense of smell?” That is, if everyone had one and the same office and function, how would the body’s remaining needs be fulfilled, since it is clear that many offices are needed for the body’s governance?

(Vers. 18.) “But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body, as he willed.” He says that God, whose will is provident and rational, fitted the members to the body, so that nothing might be lacking to it, but that it might be complete with its many members. [Note: All editions, with some manuscripts: “so that nothing might be lacking in the many members”; many manuscripts omit “complete”; Codex Corbeiensis most appropriately supplies the reading from which we have restored the passage.]

(Vers. 19.) “But if they were all one member, where would the body be?” It is clear that if all had possessed one dignity, they would not be called members, nor would there be a body. Therefore they are governed together through the various functions of the members; for all could not be one member. They are many because they differ from one another in dignity.

(Vers. 20.) “But now there are many members, yet one body.” He says that although the many members need one another, they do not differ in the unity of nature, even though they are diverse. This diversity comes together into one so that the body’s usefulness may be fulfilled. The same is true of the things of which the world itself consists: although they differ not only in functions but also in natures, they nevertheless contribute to the perfection of one world, and from all of them arises a certain harmony in the fruits that benefit human use.

(Vers. 21.) “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you.’” That is, the superior cannot say to the inferior, “I do not need you,” because the eye sees, but the hands are what perform the work. “Nor again can the head say to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me.’” That is, one greater in rank and dignity cannot exist without one who is humble, because the humble can do something the exalted cannot. Iron can do what gold cannot; and therefore the feet confer honor upon the head.

(Vers. 22.) “But much more, the members of the body that seem to be weaker are more necessary.” It is clear that even if someone is exalted in dignity, if the subordinate who makes him glorious through his services is absent, the dignity itself will be contemptible; for it is the office through which dignity is established. It is like an emperor lacking an army. Although the emperor may be great, he nevertheless needs an army; for it is a member of his body, with tribunes, counts, and commanders before it. The soldiers are inferior to all these, but they are more necessary, like the members of the body which, although they appear inferior, are more useful. Without eyes, the hand works, and the walking foot seeks food.

(Vers. 23.) “And the members of the body that we think less honorable, upon these we bestow more abundant honor.” The meaning is similar: those who are thought to be without dignity are found to possess something that we praise, just as in the less valuable members we find something that pleases us more than what we find in the others. With what honor are hands worthy to be regarded, since we hold whatever we wish with them? Or feet, with which we go wherever we wish? Therefore we too add honor to them; for example, because the feet are humble and without dignity, we adorn them with shoes.

“And those members of us that are unpresentable have greater honor.” It is clear that our private parts, which seem shameful, conceal themselves with propriety because they avoid public view, lest through irreverence they become repulsive. In the same way, some of the brothers, though poor and disgraceful in dress, are nevertheless not without grace, through which they are members of our body. For they commonly walk wearing a shabby little garment girded about them and barefoot. Although they appear contemptible, they are more worthy of honor because they commonly lead a purer life. What appears despised to human beings is often judged beautiful by God.

(Vers. 24.) “But our presentable members have no need of this.” It is clear that the head, the face, and the hands do not need anything added to adorn them. So too with brothers in whom the zeal for knowledge and the propriety of conduct flourish: there is nothing for us to add, since the honor due to them is rendered. The despised or humble, however, need encouragement, through which some honor may be added to them so that they may become useful. Otherwise, through the very contempt shown toward them, they will become more negligent concerning themselves, even though they are the ones who most need to make progress.

(Vers. 25.) “But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there may be no schism in the body, but that the members may care for one another.” [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “so that there may be no separation.”]

He says that God has so ordered the human body that all its members are necessary. Accordingly, they care for one another, because one cannot exist without the other. What is thought to be inferior is more necessary, just as has been set forth and discussed concerning the brothers: no one ought to be despised as useless.

(Vers. 26.) And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. There is no doubt that this concerns the members of the bodily flesh; for if the eye, foot, or hand is seized by some weakness of illness, the whole body suffers with it. [Note: Codex Vall., “so it is fitting for us also, not improperly.”] Thus he teaches us also to grieve with our brothers if anything of this kind, or any necessity, should arise. Or if one member is glorified, let all the members rejoice with it. It is clear that the head, or the other members, are glad if the feet are well cared for or sound. So we too ought to become cheerful if we see some brother worshiping God and increased in uprightness of conduct—that is, sound in judgment.

(Vers. 27.) But you are the body of Christ, and members individually. He plainly shows that he treated our situation by means of the analogy of the bodily members, because we cannot all do the same things, but each of us has a gift according to the measure of faith and the grace granted to us.

(Vers. 28.) And God has appointed some in the Church: first, apostles. Thus, in the Church he appointed the apostles as the head, for they are Christ’s ambassadors, as the same Apostle says: “For which we are ambassadors” (II Cor. 5:20). These are bishops, as the apostle Peter confirms when, among other things, he says concerning Judas: “Let another receive his bishopric” (Acts 1:20).

Second, prophets. Let us understand prophets in two senses: those who speak of future events and those who reveal the Scriptures. Although the apostles too are prophets, since the first rank contains all the subordinate functions. Thus even the most wicked Caiaphas prophesied because he was high priest (John 11:51)—on account, certainly, of his office, not his personal merit. Nevertheless, there were prophets specifically who interpreted the Scriptures and spoke of future events (Acts 21:11), as Agabus did. He prophesied the disasters and imprisonment that awaited this Apostle at Jerusalem, and foretold the famine that occurred under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Therefore, although an apostle is greater, he sometimes nevertheless needs prophets. And because all things come from one God the Father, he ordained that individual bishops should preside over individual Churches.

Third, teachers. He calls those teachers who, in the Church, instructed children in retaining letters [that is, literary learning] and readings, according to the custom of the Synagogue, because their tradition has passed over to us. [Note: Roman edition, “and in retaining traditions.”] In the fourth place he says:

Then powers, then gifts of healings. For someone may not be a bishop and yet possess within himself the gift of miraculous healings. Helps, administrations: so that in divine matters he may be vigilant in understanding; nevertheless, in certain matters that he is not permitted to fulfill, he should receive from another what he does not possess, since everything cannot be granted to one person. There are also administrators who serve as an example to people through spiritual restraints. Varieties of tongues: so that it may be a gift of God to know many languages. [Note: “Interpretation of utterances” is absent in some manuscripts, and in fact is also absent from the Greek and Syriac copies of the Bible. In the following verse the Roman edition restored “so as to interpret utterances,” while other manuscripts have “so as to interpret languages,” and so forth.] Interpretation of utterances: so that God may bestow on someone the grace to possess skill in interpreting languages. [p. 154]

(Vers. 29.) Are all apostles? It is true, because in the Church there is one bishop. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “There is one Christ. Are all …”] Are all prophets? It is not doubtful that prophecy is not granted to everyone. Are all teachers? He is a teacher to whom it is granted to instruct others.

(Vers. 30.) Do all possess powers? Someone may possess power when God grants him the ability to cast out demons. Do all possess gifts of healings? How can it be that everyone should possess gifts of healings? Do all speak in tongues? Certainly not, except the one who receives the gift for this purpose. Do all interpret? [Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads, “Do they interpret?” This too is not doubtful, because no one can interpret unless the Lord grants him his grace. “But desire the spiritual gifts,” and so forth.] He can interpret utterances to whom God grants it. These words should be inserted in the sense stated above. For he has explained, by giving the reason, that everyone possesses different gifts and that the whole is not granted to anyone, using the example of the members. By the example of the bodily body he suggests the spiritual body; and thus God must be blessed in all things, and glory must be given in his name, whose grace it is. We find the same principle even in physical matters: although gold is better than silver, silver is nevertheless more useful in practice; and although bronze is necessary, iron is needed more, for almost nothing is made without iron, even though it is inferior. And after this:

(Vers. 31.) Desire the better gifts. He immediately completes this in what follows: “And I will show you a still more excellent way.” He gradually leads them toward what is more useful, showing them that the grace of all the gifts mentioned above, which appear in human beings—whether of speaking, healing, or prophesying—does not belong to human merit but to the glorification of God. Therefore he now says that he will show them a clearer way, by which one goes to heaven, which places merit with God. Since the things mentioned above do not always pertain to merit, the Savior says: “Many will say to me on that day,” that is, the day of judgment, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?” (Matt. 7:22). And because this does not pertain to merit but consists in the services of the Church, for the confusion of the Gentiles and the public declaration of God’s glory, the Lord says to them: “Depart from me; I do not know you, workers of iniquity” (ibid., 27). Secure because God’s activity was seen in them, they were negligent concerning themselves. For when the seventy-two disciples rejoiced because the demons had been subjected to them, the Savior said: “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you; but rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Why, unless it is because they were subjected to the name of God, not to human merit? And why does this not now happen, so that people possess the grace of God? It was necessary for this to occur at the beginning, so that the foundations of faith might receive firmness. Now, however, it is not necessary, because one people leads another to faith when their good works and simple preaching are seen.

## CHAPTER XIII

(Vers. 1.) If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I am like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. It certainly seems a great gift to speak in various tongues; but something greater is involved if someone can even know the language of angels—that is, if he can possess spiritual knowledge of the angelic movement. Yet he shows in what follows that this is not to be attributed to merit but to the glory of God, saying that such a person is like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. For just as bronze resounds when struck by another and a cymbal rings, so the one who speaks in tongues has the activity and movement of the Holy Spirit, enabling him to speak. [Note: Codex Corbeiensis adds, “and movement,” without which he shows that one cannot speak usefully.] As the Savior says elsewhere: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). Balaam’s donkey also spoke with a human tongue to Balaam son of Beor, in order to declare the majesty of God (Num. 22:28); and infant children burst forth in praise of God, to the confusion of the Jews (Matt. 21:16). The Savior also showed that not only these but even stones could cry out for the condemnation of the faithless and the glory of God (Luke 19:40). And in the very beginnings, as confirmation of the faith, those who were baptized spoke in tongues (Acts 10:46).

(Vers. 2.) And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, but do not have love, it [p. 155] profits me nothing. Truly it profits nothing; prophecy is given for the glory of God, as the prophet David says: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. 113:1). Balaam also prophesied (Num. 23:8 ff.), although he was not a prophet but a diviner; and Caiaphas prophesied (John 11:51), not by merit but by the dignity of the priestly office; and Saul prophesied (I Sam. 19:23), although he had already been filled with an evil spirit because of his disobedience, but for God’s purpose, so that he could not seize David, whom he also wished to kill.

And if I know all mysteries: it profited Judas nothing to have been with the apostles and to have learned the mysteries when, as an enemy of love, he betrayed the Savior (Ezek. 28:13 ff.). [Note: Codex Corbeiensis adds, “when he handed over the Savior, the victim of love,” and so forth.] The prophet Ezekiel also shows that the devil knew the heavenly mysteries when, speaking in an admonishing voice, he testifies that the devil had been in paradise with God and had possessed precious stones. The same Apostle signified by these stones the mysteries of divine teaching (I Cor. 3:12). Yet this profited him nothing, because, forgetful of love, he burst into pride.

And if I have all knowledge. Knowledge profits me nothing if love is absent. Thus it profited the scribes and Pharisees nothing, as the Savior says: “You have the key of knowledge, and you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow others to enter” (Luke 11:52). For by corrupting love through envy, they reduced its knowledge to nothing. Tertullian and Novatian too possessed no small degree of knowledge; but because through zeal they lost the bonds of love, they turned to schism and created heresies to their own destruction.

And if I have all faith, so that I move mountains. To perform miracles or cast out demons through faith is the power and glory of God; nor does this contribute to merit unless one is zealous for upright conduct, as I mentioned above.

(Vers. 3.) And if I distribute all my possessions. It is clear that even if all one’s possessions are spent, this profits nothing when love is neglected, because love is the head of religion; and whoever does not have the head does not have life. And if I hand over my body so that I may burn, it profits me nothing. Without love it profits nothing, because love is the foundation of religion. Whatever, therefore, is done without love is transitory.

(Vers. 4–8.) Love is patient; it is kind. Love does not envy, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, is not ambitious, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never falls away.

He taught such great praises of love that he seemed, not undeservedly, to place it before all other things, and to show that those who devote themselves to other commandments while failing to obey this one labor in vain. Hence the apostle John says: “Love is God” (I John 4:8), so that whoever does not have love may know that he does not have God. Therefore in another epistle the same Apostle Paul says: “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love, had mercy on us” (Eph. 2:4). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “because of his mercy.”] Whoever, therefore, does not have love is ungrateful for God’s mercy, because he does not love the means by which he was saved. [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “So that they might consequently understand.”] Thus they were to learn that those who placed food before brotherly love were committing a grave offense. For love is useful both in the present and remains with God forever.

(Vers. 9, 10.) Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished. For we know in part and prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be abolished. He said that all the gifts of the charisms would be abolished because they cannot comprehend as much as truth itself contains. Nor can we grasp or express the fullness of truth. For how could a human tongue encompass everything that belongs to God? Therefore our imperfection will be destroyed; what is true will not be abolished. Rather, when what is lacking is added to the imperfect, the imperfection will be destroyed. [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts add “the imperfection that is lacking will be destroyed.” The Roman edition more appropriately reads, “what is lacking will be added; the imperfection will be destroyed.” Nevertheless, most manuscripts are to be preferred, and these are the ones we follow here.] The destruction of imperfection occurs when what is imperfect is brought to completion in the truth.

(Vers. 11.) When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I abolished the things that belonged to childhood. He says this because the saints, when they depart from this world, must find more than they now imagine, as the apostle John said concerning the Savior: “Then we shall see him as he is” (I John 3:2). In comparison with the future life, therefore, we are children in this life; for just as this life is imperfect, so also is our knowledge.

(Vers. 12.) Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. It is clear that now we see images through faith, but then the [p. 156] realities themselves. Now I know in part; but then I shall know, just as I am known—that is, I shall see what has been promised, just as I am seen; that is, I shall be present with the Lord, where Christ is.

(Vers. 13.) But now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; and the greatest of these is love. Love is rightly the greatest, because love made it possible for faith to be preached and for hope of the future life to exist, as I mentioned above. Hence the apostle John says: “By this we know his love, because he laid down his life for us” (I John 3:16). Love is therefore rightly the greatest, since through it the human race has been restored.

## CHAPTER XIV

(Vers. 1.) Pursue love; desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy. After love, he urges them to devote themselves especially to prophecy. For although the spiritual ranks he enumerates are great, this one is nevertheless better because it advances the usefulness of the Church, so that all may learn the meaning of the divine law. For whatever someone devotes his mind to, in that very thing he receives a gift, as Solomon says: “To know the law is the understanding of the good” (Prov. 9:33). Knowledge supported by love is not puffed up but gentle, benefiting everyone for the common good. [Note: Codex Laudunensis reads, “the zeal for prophesying, preaching, and teaching.”]

(Vers. 2.) For the one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God; no one hears him, yet in the spirit he speaks mysteries. This is what he means: the one who speaks in an unknown tongue speaks to God, because God knows everything; human beings, however, do not know it, and therefore there is no benefit from it. In the spirit he speaks mysteries, not with the understanding, because he does not know what he is saying.

(Vers. 3.) But the one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation. He is edified when he learns the solution of questions. He is exhorted when he develops the desire to prophesy; and he is consoled because in hope he sees contempt for discipline. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “because he sees contempt for discipline,” and so forth.] Knowledge of the law strengthens the mind and urges it toward the progress of a better hope.

(Vers. 4.) The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but the one who prophesies edifies the Church. By knowing alone what he says, he perhaps edifies only himself; but the one who prophesies edifies the entire people, since everyone understands what he says. He calls the prophets interpreters of the Scriptures. For just as a prophet foretells future events that are unknown, so this person is said to prophesy when he reveals the meaning of the Scriptures, which is hidden from many.

(Vers. 5.) Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but especially that you may prophesy. He could not prohibit speaking in tongues, since above he says that this gift is of the Holy Spirit; but he therefore urges a greater devotion to prophecy because it is more useful. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue, unless he interprets. If he can interpret, he will not be lesser, because he edifies the Church; and what benefits everyone is greater. He speaks in tongues through the gift of God, and also interprets, as did those twelve in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2:4).

(Vers. 6.) But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you unless I speak to you either by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by teaching? All these expressions signify one thing: no one can teach unless he is understood.

(Vers. 7, 8.) Nevertheless, lifeless things that give sound, whether a flute or a lyre, if they do not produce distinctions of sound, how will it be known what is played on the flute or what is played on the lyre? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? Because examples persuade more easily than words, he commends by examples the point that those who cannot interpret should not speak in tongues in the Church. Why should someone speak whom no one understands?

(Vers. 9.) So also you, unless you give through the tongue a speech that has meaning, how will it be known what you are saying? For you will be speaking into the air—that is, accomplishing nothing. For there are, so to speak, many kinds of languages in this world, and nothing is without a voice. “There are many kinds of languages,” he says, but they have their own meanings of sounds, so that they may be understood.

(Vers. 10, 11.) Therefore, if I do not know the force of the sound, I shall be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, and the one who speaks will be a barbarian to me. He certainly does not urge them to pursue the situation in which they appear as barbarians to one another through an unknown language. Rather, because the matter concerns harmony, they must strive for this: that through unanimity of understanding they may rejoice together in a common joy.

(Vers. 12.) [p. 157] So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek the edification of the Church, so that you may prophesy. [Note: Codex Vallensis reads, “seek the Church’s zeal in the prophets.”] Since it is beneficial to explain the Scriptures—for the mind is stirred and rejoices when it grasps something from the Scriptures, and the more eager it becomes in this respect, the more it abandons vices—he urges them to direct their zeal toward this.

(Vers. 13.) Therefore let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. He instructs the person who desires to speak in tongues that he ought to pray to receive the gift of interpretation, so that his zeal may benefit the others.

(Vers. 14.) For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is without fruit. It is clear that our mind is ignorant if our tongue speaks a language it does not know, as Latin speakers often sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words while nevertheless not knowing what they are saying. But the spirit that is given in baptism knows what our mind is praying when it speaks or pleads in a tongue unknown to it; the mind, however—that is, the soul—is without fruit. For what fruit can the one who does not know what he is saying possess?

(Vers. 15.) What then? I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing a psalm with the spirit; I will sing a psalm also with the mind. He means that when someone speaks in a language he knows, he prays both with the spirit and with the mind. For not only does his spirit—which, as I have said, is given in baptism—know what is being prayed, [Note: The same Codex Vallensis reads, “but the mind, which is the soul,” and so forth.] but his soul likewise does not fail to understand the psalm.

(Vers. 16.) Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit—that is, if you speak the praise of God in a tongue unknown to those listening—how will one who occupies the place of the unlearned person say “Amen” over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying? [Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads, “over your eucharist.”] The uneducated hearer, hearing what he does not understand, does not know the end of the prayer and does not respond “Amen,” that is, “True,” so that the blessing may be confirmed. For those who respond “Amen” complete the confirmation of the prayer, so that all that has been said may be confirmed in the minds of the hearers by the testimony of truth.

(Vers. 17.) For indeed you give thanks well. He speaks of the person who says what he himself understands, because he knows what he is saying. But the other is not edified. If you certainly come together for the edification of the Church, those things should be said which the hearers understand. For what benefit is it for someone to speak in a tongue that he alone knows, so that the one who hears gains nothing? Therefore he ought to be silent in the Church, so that those who benefit the hearers may speak.

(Vers. 18.) I thank my God that I speak in the tongue of all of you. Since above he said that speaking in tongues is a gift of the Holy Spirit, he therefore refers to God the fact that he spoke in all their tongues. And lest he appear to say this out of rivalry or envy, he shows that he speaks in all these tongues, but that this is not very beneficial.

(Vers. 19.) But in the Church, he says, I would rather speak five words by means of the Law, [Note: The Roman edition reads, “to speak through my understanding, so that …”] so that I may edify others, than ten thousand words in a tongue. He says that it is more useful to speak a few words in clear speech, which everyone understands, than to give a lengthy speech in obscurity. These people were Hebrews, who sometimes used the Syriac language and more often Hebrew in their discourses or offerings, to enhance their reputation. For they gloried in being called Hebrews on account of Abraham’s merit, which the same Apostle considered worthless, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). [Note: Some, imitating these people, preferred to speak in the Church to the people in a language unknown to themselves rather than in their own. The passage has been restored from Codex Corbeiensis.] Certain people, imitating them, preferred to speak in the Church to the people in a language unknown to themselves rather than in their own.

(Vers. 20.) Brothers, do not become children in your understanding; but be children in malice, so that you may be mature in understanding. He wants them to be mature, [Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads, “so that they may do what,” and so forth. Below, most manuscripts read, “For this is the mature understanding,” instead of what appears in other manuscripts and all the editions: “mature in understanding.”] so that they may know what is necessary for the instruction of the Church; so that, turning away from malice and errors, they may devote themselves to the things that benefit their brothers. For this is mature in understanding: to act so as to benefit someone, especially a brother.

(Vers. 21.) For it is written in the Law: “Because in other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord” (Isa. 28:11). The Lord said this concerning those whom he foreknew would not believe even the Savior. To speak in other tongues and with other lips means to preach the New Testament, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31). That is, he would speak in a changed manner, different from the way the words of the old Law had been formulated: they would hear that the Sabbath was abolished, that new moons were annulled, that circumcision had ceased, that sacrifices were changed, that foods formerly [p. 158] forbidden were permitted to be eaten, and that Christ, God from God, was preached. This is to speak in other tongues and with other lips; yet even so the faithless refused to obey God.

It may also be understood in this way: since many of the Jews were malicious, and therefore it was not fitting for the Gospel to be spoken to them openly in revelation, he spoke to them in parables. Though they understood that it was not revealed to them because they were evil, even so they did not correct themselves, so that by the explanation they might make themselves worthy to hear the words of God. Hence the disciples say to the Lord: “Lord, why do you speak to them in parables?” (Matt. 13:10). And the Lord says: “Because it has been given to you to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to them it has not been given, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (ibid., 11). They were unworthy to receive salvation; and although they perceived that this had happened according to their merits, even so they did not turn and satisfy God.

(Vers. 22.) Therefore tongues are for a sign. That is, by the veil of an unknown tongue the words of God have been obscured, so that they would not be seen by the faithless. When unknown tongues are heard, it is a sign that this was done because of faithlessness, so that the hearer would not understand. They are not for those who believe, but for those who do not believe. This is what he said: tongues are useful for concealing meanings from unbelievers. But prophecy is not for unbelievers, but for those who believe. That is, it is not fitting for the faithful to hear tongues they do not understand, but for unbelievers who are not worthy to understand, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Go and say to this people: You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand,” and so forth.

(Vers. 23.) If the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and unbelievers or unlearned persons enter, will they not say that you are insane? It is clear that if everyone speaks in different tongues, a kind of disorderly tumult arises among the people, as though they were suffering from madness. [Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads, “in the gathering of the people.”]

(Vers. 24, 25.) But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all; the secrets of his heart become manifest, and then, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you. For when he understands and is understood, hears God praised and Christ worshiped, he sees clearly that the religion is true and worthy of reverence. He sees nothing fabricated and nothing done in darkness, as among the pagans, whose eyes are veiled lest, seeing what they call sacred rites, they perceive themselves to be deceived by various vanities. Every imposture seeks darkness and presents false things as true. Therefore among us there is nothing crafty and nothing hidden under a veil; rather, one God is simply praised, from whom all things come, and one Lord Jesus, through whom all things exist (I Cor. 8:6). For if there is no one who understands, or by whom he himself may be examined, he can say that it is some kind of deception and vanity, and that tongues are sung for this reason: because it would be shameful if the matter were disclosed. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “if there is no one whom he understands.”]

(Vers. 26.) What then, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a song—that is, he expresses the praise of God through a song. He has a teaching—that is, he possesses an exposition of meanings through spiritual wisdom. He has a revelation—that is, the prophecy of hidden things is present in him, so that it may reach everyone’s understanding, with the Holy Spirit’s favor. He has a tongue: so that he would not grieve those who were able to speak in tongues, he permitted them to speak in tongues, but only in such a way that interpretation would follow. Therefore he says: “He has an interpretation,” so that if an interpreter were present, an opportunity would be given for speaking in tongues. [Note: Codex Geminianus reads, “has a psalm.” Codex Corbeiensis reads, “he has an exposition through natural prudence.”]

Let everything be done for edification. This is the conclusion: nothing should be done in the Church without purpose. They should work especially toward this, that the unlearned too may make progress, so that no part of the body may be darkened through ignorance. Therefore he wants them all to come prepared with different spiritual gifts, so that, vigilant through the very eagerness of their minds and exhorting one another, they may desire the better gifts for the enlightenment of their brothers.

(Vers. 27.) If someone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two, or at most three, and separately, with one interpreting. That is, no more than two or three should speak in tongues, and they should speak individually, not all at once, lest they appear insane. Therefore he says “at most three,” so that those speaking in tongues and their interpreters would not occupy the entire day and leave the prophets no time to expound the Scriptures, since they are the illuminators of the whole Church. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “to distinguish the Scriptures.”]

(Vers. 28.) But if there is no interpreter, let him be silent in the Church; but let him speak to himself and to God. That is, let him pray silently within himself, or speak to God, who hears all things that are mute. In the Church, the person who benefits everyone ought to speak.

(Vers. 29.) [p. 159] Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine or question. He maintained the same order when he said, “Let two or three speak,” individually, as above. He permitted the others to question them about matters that perhaps become doubtful or that someone cannot grasp, since people have different abilities, so that these matters may be clarified through more lucid discussion.

(Vers. 30.) But if something is revealed to another person sitting there, let the first be silent. That is, let the superior yield to the inferior, so that, if he can, the latter may speak; and let the former not take offense, because the gift may also be given to the other, so that he may speak about what was not granted to the superior, although he appeared inferior. For just as the whole cannot be granted to one person, even if he is superior, so no one, however inferior, can be left entirely without a gift, so that no one may be empty of the grace of God.

(Vers. 31.) For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be exhorted. This is the tradition of the Synagogue, which he wants us to follow. For although he writes to Christians who have been made from the Gentiles, not from the Jews, he wants them to sit and discuss: the elders, according to their dignity, on chairs; those who follow, on benches; and the last, on the floor upon mats. If something is revealed to any of them, he commands that an opportunity to speak be given and that they not be despised, because they are members of the body.

(Vers. 32.) And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets. Since there is one and the same Spirit, who pours himself out according to the proportion and quality of the circumstances both upon prophets who speak of future events and upon those who reveal the Scriptures, he said, “He is subject to the prophets,” in order to kindle their abilities with the hope that the Spirit assists good efforts. He comes to the aid of the best desire in proclaiming the works of God, so that he may fulfill the will of a good intention. For the same thing is said concerning the Savior: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. 10:4). That is, to be subject also means to follow; for he followed so that, when human support failed, he might be present to provide assistance. So the Spirit is also said to be subject, because he assists good efforts when he inspires them; for the one who completes another’s undertaking appears to be subject to that other. [Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads, “for carrying out the works of God.”]

(Vers. 33.) For he is not the author of dissension but of peace. Since he is the author of peace, as the Savior says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:17), no one should prevent another from speaking, nor should anyone resist the speaker out of a desire to contradict, lest discord arise in the body. Those who are called in peace ought to devote themselves to patience, lest the rights of peace be dissolved. “As I teach in all the Churches of the saints.” By saying this he urges them to do what he has commanded, since he testifies that he preaches the same thing to the Churches of the saints.

(Vers. 34.) [Note: This and the following section are relegated to the end of the chapter in quite a few manuscripts.] Let your women be silent in the Church. Now he gives what he had omitted. Above he commanded that women be forbidden to speak in the Church; here he shows that they are to be quiet and modest, so that it may be worthwhile that they are veiled (I Cor. 11:5). For if the man is the image of God, not the woman, and she is subject to the man by the law of nature, how much more ought she to be subject in the Church, out of reverence for the one who is the ambassador of him who is also the head of the man! They are not permitted to speak [Note: The Roman edition reads, “but to be subject”], but are to be in silence, as the Law also says. What does the Law say? “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3:16). This is the specific law.
