Hence Sarah called Abraham, her husband, “lord.” [Col. 0259B] Accordingly, they are commanded to be silent, lest the judgment of the law mentioned above be weakened. Remembering this, Sarah was subject to her husband, as it is said (Gen. 2:24). Although she is one flesh with him, she is commanded to be subject for two reasons: because she comes from the man and because sin entered through her.

(Vers. 35.) But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home; for it is shameful for women to speak in the Church. It is shameful because it is contrary to discipline for them to presume to speak about the Law in the house of God, where he commanded them to be subject to their husbands, when they know that men have primacy there and that it is more appropriate for them to devote themselves to prayer in the house of God while restraining their tongues. Let them open their ears, so that they may hear how the mercy of God conquered death through Christ—the death that had reigned through them. For if they dare to speak in the Church, it is disgraceful, because they are veiled for the very purpose of appearing humbled. But they show themselves shameless, which is also a reproach to their husbands; for in the insolence of women, husbands too are marked with blame.

(Vers. 36.) Or did the word of God come forth from you, or did it come to you alone? These are the words of one rebuking them. They were so puffed up that they seemed to imagine that this salvation had been promised to them alone, and that through their example the other nations would be called to faith, or that there were no others who could receive the grace of God when the apostles preached. For they [p. 160] behaved as though they were conferring a benefit rather than receiving one by approaching the faith. Hence he says: “Or did the word of God come to you alone?” Anyone who wishes to buy something that he knows is not sought by others approaches the purchase with a certain disdain, as though he were conferring a benefit on the seller. Therefore the Apostle rebukes this attitude in the Corinthians, who displayed themselves in such a way through the arrogance of their vanity, as though, if they themselves did not obey the words of faith, no one else would believe. Thus he says to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of this life should be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it, judging yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

(Vers. 37.) If anyone is thought to be a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I am writing to you are the Lord’s [Col. 0260A] commandments. In saying this he touches upon the false apostles mentioned above, by whom they had been led astray; for, to satisfy human desires, they taught earthly things rather than divine ones. Therefore he says here that he is handing on nothing of his own, but the Lord’s; [Note: [Col. 0260D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “so that those whom they have won over by persuasion may give glory not to men but to God.”] so that those whom he persuades may appear to have been won for God, not for men. With this confidence he preaches boldly and steadfastly, having a clear conscience, because he desires to please not men but God. Hence he does not flatter sinners so that they may increase in sin, but admonishes them to cease.

(Vers. 38.) But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored. Rightly so: for whoever does not know that what the Apostle says belongs to the Lord will himself be ignored by the Lord on the day of judgment, when the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12).

(Vers. 39.) Therefore, brothers, be zealous to prophesy [Col. 0260B]. Although he reproves these people, and in many matters censures and corrects them because they had departed from his tradition, he nevertheless calls them brothers, because Isaiah says to the people of the Lord: “Say to those who do not walk rightly in my ways: ‘You are our brothers’” (Isa. LXVI, 5). Thus, in order to console them after his rebukes, he calls them brothers and urges them to zeal for prophecy, so that through continual discussion and explanation of the divine law they might become better instructed and learn that the preaching of the pseudo-apostles was perverse.

And do not forbid speaking in tongues. This too is on account of charity: those who are able to speak in tongues should not be forbidden if an interpreter is present, lest dissension arise.

(Vers. 40.) But let everything be done decently and according to order—that is, according to the order stated above. What is done decently is done [Note: [Col. 0260D] The same Corbie manuscript reads: “when accompanied by prayer.”] with peace and [Col. 0260C] discipline.

## CHAPTER XV

(Vers. 1, 2.) Now I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, through which you will also be saved, which I also announced to you in speech: you must hold fast to it, unless perhaps you believed without purpose. He shows them that if, in the matter now under discussion, they have been led astray from his tradition, they have lost what they believed; for all the hope of believers rests on this understanding: that the dead will rise. When he says, “in which you also stand,” he is speaking to those who were firm in the faith of this tradition. He speaks indiscriminately, so that those who are firm in the faith may rejoice, while those who waver may grieve that they are being corrected and may reform.

(Vers. 3.) For I delivered to you first of all that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures [Col. 0260D]. He is recalling the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which foretold the Lord’s future passion. The prophet Isaiah says: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7). And among other things: “For his life shall be taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death” (ibid., 8). These things are recognized as having been fulfilled in Christ. But since the wording appears to signify past time, this is not a contradiction; for with God, who knows all things beforehand, nothing is future. Therefore he speaks of what will be future for us as though it had already happened [Col. 0261A]. Indeed, in the Apocalypse of the apostle John it is said: “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. XIII, 8). Since it will not happen otherwise than God knows, it is said to have happened; for it happens for us, not for God, since with God there is nothing that can be called future. And in the Psalm he says: “The Lord has reigned from the wood” (Ps. XCV, 10). Moses likewise signified his cross, saying: “Then you will see your life hanging before your eyes, and you will not believe” (Deut. XXVIII, 66). For this reason, in the same matter, the significance of future time is sometimes also employed, lest the wicked defend that the passage was not spoken of Christ if everything were signified as though it belonged to the past.

(Vers. 4.) And that he was buried. No one doubts that a dead man was buried, as the prophet Isaiah says: “And I will give the wicked for his burial” (Isa. LIII, 9).

And that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures. Everything is enclosed within faith; therefore the Lord’s resurrection on the third day was described under the person of the people as something that would take place. For the prophet Hosea says: [Note: [Col. 0261D] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “After two days he will heal us, and on the third day we shall rise.”] “After two days he will heal us, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight” (Hos. VI, 3). No believer denies that all have risen in Christ, just as all have died in Adam. In a similar way, in the Psalm, under the person of a man, he also signifies Christ, saying: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet; you have crowned him with glory and honor” (Ps. VIII, 8).

(Vers. 5.) And that he was seen by Cephas—that is, by Peter. This is also what the disciples said to Cleopas and his companion, as appears in the Gospel according to Luke (κατὰ Λουκᾶν, “according to Luke”), that he appeared to Peter alone [Col. 0261C]. Afterwards, to the eleven (Luke XXIV, 34). This too is contained in the Gospel.

(Vers. 6.) Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once. He speaks this on his own authority. Of these, most remain until now, while some have fallen asleep. He says that, after the resurrection, many of those to whom the Lord appeared were still in the body.

(Vers. 7.) Then he appeared to James. He appeared to James individually, just as he did to Peter. I think this happened so that, through manifold appearances, he might strengthen belief in the resurrection. Afterwards, to all the apostles. He was seen again by all the apostles on the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, as the evangelist Matthew reports (Matt. XXVIII, 16). Earlier, in Jerusalem, eight days after his resurrection—that is, on the Lord’s Day—he entered to the disciples through closed doors, so that Thomas’s mind might be strengthened, as the apostle John says (John XX, 26). The mountain, then, is understood to be the place where he gave them commandments.

(Vers. 8.) And last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. He appeared to him first in heaven, and afterwards, while he was praying in the temple (Acts IX, 4; XXII, 17). He called himself “untimely born” because, born in Christ outside the proper time, he received the apostleship after Christ had already been received into heaven in the flesh.

[Col. 0262A] (Vers. 9, 10.) For I am the least of all [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Corbie manuscript adds: “the apostles.” Thus he calls himself the least of the apostles with respect to his calling, not with respect to grace; but he gives glory and honor to God, who chose him.] the apostles. He humbles himself and attributes the matter to the difference of time; for he is later in time, not inferior in dignity. But because he had also been a persecutor, he lowers himself, saying: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” But by the grace of God I am what I am. He gives glory to God, who chose him, and does not defend his own dignity; rather, he says that he is unworthy. Hence he truly deserves more, knowing that the Lord said: [Note: [Col. 0262D] Several manuscripts read: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.”] “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 10).

And his grace toward me was not in vain. He says this because, although he had persecuted the Church, he did not receive lesser grace in the apostleship. But I labored more than all of them. He adds this to the argument because he was not merely not made inferior, but was afflicted even more [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “because of his conscience.”] on account of the steadfastness with which he flourished [Col. 0262B] in Christ; and, not bearing this unwillingly, he became more worthy. Yet it was not I, but the grace of God with me. Lest he be thought to have exalted himself boastfully, he immediately humbles himself by attributing this very thing not chiefly to himself but to the grace of God, so that he always refers all glory back to God, from whom he is rightly to receive exaltation.

(Vers. 11.) Whether, then, it was I or they, so we preach, and so you believed. This is what he indicated above: that he received no lesser grace in preaching than the other apostles, but one and the same grace. Thus he all the more reproves the Corinthians’ faithlessness, because, although this belief had been made manifest among all the churches, they had departed from the faith and hope he had set forth, saying:

(Vers. 12, 13, 14.) Now if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not risen. But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and your faith is also void. These teachings had been handed down by false apostles, who asserted that Christ had neither been born, nor suffered in the flesh, nor risen again. The apostle John also marks them out as denying that Christ had come in the flesh. Hence he says: “Whoever denies that Christ has come in the flesh is the Antichrist; and whoever denies the Son does not have the Father” (1 John IV, 3). These men went about overturning the faith of certain people, lest they be judged foolish by the wise men of the world; for worldly wise men consider it foolish when they hear of the resurrection of the dead. If, he says, it is true that Christ has not risen, then we are false preachers and your faith is empty. For they believed this when the Apostle preached: that the dead would rise; and drawn by this hope, they came to the faith. He asserts that this will be to their detriment if they have believed something that will not happen; and it is shameful for anyone to admit that he believed what is false. Thus he both brings shame upon them and declares their labors fruitless, if what they heard from the false [Col. 0263A] apostles is true—namely, that the dead will not rise. No one, of course, willingly hears this said of himself; and so, seeing that it is directed against them, they might return to their first faith.

(Vers. 15.) We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. Whoever asserts that God raised Christ from the dead is a false witness if it did not happen; nevertheless, he proclaims God’s power—not, certainly, as an enemy, since he attributes so astonishing a deed to God’s power. But if it is true that he raised Christ from the dead, [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Corbie manuscripts read: “What should be said of this man?”] what should be said of the man who is both a false witness against God and declares his work to be foolishness?

(Vers. 16, 17.) For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ been raised. But if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; for you are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. He terrifies them, so that, since no one wishes evil upon himself, they may grieve that they have begun to believe what is against them. For who would not want to hear that his sins have been forgiven?

(Vers. 18.) Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. He adds this to increase their terror, because they do not wish to regard the death of their loved ones [Note: [Col. 0263D] The same Corbie manuscript reads: “They wish to consider it the loss of those dear to them.” Then, where all the editions and most manuscripts read, “For those who did not fear, under this hope …,” the Vallombrosan manuscript more appropriately reads as we have in the text.] as destruction. For those who departed from this world in this hope—or who did not fear being killed because they believed, following Christ’s example, that they would rise—and if this is not true, have perished. He says this to them because, out of love for their dead, they do not wish to hear it, so that he may remove from them what previously, through error, they wanted to hear.

(Vers. 19.) If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all people [Col. 0263C]. It is clear that we hope in Christ both in this present life and in the future one. For Christ does not abandon his servants here either, [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Vallombrosan manuscript reads: “but gives them glory.”] but gives them grace, and in the future they will be in eternal glory. But if there were no hope of the future life, we would be more pitiable than all people, as he says. For what purpose are fasts, vigils, departures from the world, a pure life, justice, mercy, and death, if there will be no reward for these things in the future? Unbelievers at least enjoy this life.

(Vers. 20, 21.) But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also came through a man. In saying this he touches upon the false prophets who denied that Christ had been born and therefore denied that the flesh had risen; for whoever was not born cannot die. He proves Christ to have risen from the dead by showing that he was a man, so that it is beyond doubt that a man was raised by God from the dead. Thus, because death was brought about through man’s sin, Christ’s righteousness earned the resurrection of the dead.

(Vers. 22.) For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ [Col. 0264A]. He says this because, just as Adam, by sinning, brought about death [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Roman edition reads: “and held it fast, so that all from his origin might be dissolved.”] and held all who came from his origin for dissolution, so Christ, who did not sin and therefore conquered death—for whoever does not sin conquers death, since death comes from sin—obtained life, that is, resurrection, for all who belong to his body. Although, therefore, he granted a general resurrection, so that just as all—whether righteous or unrighteous—die in Adam, so also all—both believers and unbelievers—might rise in Christ, although unbelievers rise for punishment, they nevertheless appear to be made alive because they will receive their bodies, no longer to die but to suffer punishment in them without end. This is what they did not wish to believe.

(Vers. 23.) But each in his own order. He now wishes to explain the order of the resurrection, lest they think it fictitious because it has not yet happened to the rest. He explains to them the orders and the times: when it has happened and when it will happen that the dead rise. Christ the firstfruits. As the Acts of the Apostles testifies, it is written in Moses (Acts XXVI, 23): “If Christ is subject to suffering, if he is the first to rise from the dead,” and so forth. He therefore rose first, [Note: [Col. 0264D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “so that the resurrection might be made firm for those who believe in him.”] so that he might become a pattern for those who believe in him. Then those who belong to Christ, who believed in his coming. This is to be understood in two ways, because at his second coming the saints will rise, according to the faith of John’s Apocalypse (Rev. XX, 12), just as at his first coming, when he rose, many bodies of saints also rose (Matt. XXVII, 52), as a testimony to death’s defeat and despoiling. Thus, under one expression, he encompasses the Lord’s two comings [Col. 0264C].

(Vers. 24, 25, 26.) Then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has brought to nothing every principality, every authority, every power, and every dominion. For he must reign until he places all his enemies beneath his feet; for he has subjected all things beneath his feet. And last of all, death, the enemy, will be destroyed. He says this because, once the kingdom has been handed over, the end of the world will come, when the resurrection has been completed. Some, terrified by the harshness of the statement, turn away from its proper meaning while wishing to understand it piously. For they shudder when they hear the words, “when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father,” thinking that, if the handing over of the kingdom is understood according to the wording, the kingdom would remain empty; as though, if he hands it over, he himself would no longer possess it. It would be as though the Father, handing everything over to the Son, had emptied himself. [Note: [Col. 0264D] All editions and manuscripts except one read: “thinking that by this handing over of the kingdom … an empty thing would remain.” The Corbie manuscript gives the excellent reading adopted in the text.] For the Lord himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matt. XI, 27); and later: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3). Behold: while the Son reigns, the Father also reigns. How, then, would the Son be thought to empty himself by handing over the kingdom, when the angel says to Mary: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke I, 32)? Daniel likewise says of this same kingdom, among other things: “The God of heaven will raise up another kingdom, which shall never be destroyed; and this kingdom shall be eternal” (Dan. II, 44). Let no one, therefore, doubt that the Son will reign forever with the Father. This handing over of the kingdom means that, when all things have been subjected to the Son and they have worshiped him as God, after death has been destroyed, the Son will show them that he is not the one from whom all things derive, but the one through whom all things derive. This will be handing over the kingdom to God and the Father: showing that he himself is the one from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named (Eph. III, 15). Then there will be the end. The destruction of death, however, is the resurrection of the dead.

[Col. 0265B] (Vers. 27, 28.) But when he says, “All things have been subjected to him,” it is plainly excepted that one who subjected all things to him. And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all. This is the same meaning that he is now opening up, to make clear what it means for the Son to hand over the kingdom to God and the Father. He adds this to the meaning because, when the Father handed the kingdom over to the Son, he was not subjected to him, as the Son subjected himself to the Father; for it is incongruous that the Father should be subjected to the Son. The Father therefore subjected all things to the Son, so that the Son might be honored in the same way as the Father is honored. When, therefore, all things have confessed Christ to be God and have been placed beneath his feet, then Christ the Lord himself will also be subjected to God the Father: “so that God may be all in all.” He says this because, when the pride of all principalities, authorities, and dominions has been crushed and they have worshiped Christ as God, then Christ also [Note: [Col. 0265D] The same edition reads: “on account of the Father’s unique authority,” and so forth. In the second verse the Corbie manuscript reads: “the sublimity and ineffability,” and so forth.] on account of the Father’s unique authority will show that he is indeed God, but from God, so that the authority of one sublime and ineffable source may remain. This is the Son’s subjection to the Father; this is God being all in all: when every creature learns that Christ is its head, and that Christ’s head is God the Father, then God the Father is all in all (Phil. II, 10, 11). That is, every creature will hold one understanding, and every tongue of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth will confess with one voice that there is one God, from whom all things are. If he had said, “so that God may be in all,” it would be understood that he is indeed in all, but through affection or a common understanding; yet not that the things themselves come from him. But when he said, “all in all,” he signified both that they come from him and that he is in them: from him, because they were created by him; in them, because in the confession of all there is one God. Nevertheless, the Son is not subjected to the Father in the same way that creation is subjected to the Son.

(Vers. 29.) Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why are they also baptized for them? He wishes to show the resurrection of the dead to be so certain and firm that he gives as an example those who were so confident about the future resurrection that they were even baptized for the dead, if death had perhaps overtaken someone: [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “fearing that he might either suffer evil or …”] fearing that the one who had not been baptized might either suffer harm or not rise, a living person was baptized in the name of the dead. Hence he adds: “Why are they also baptized for them?” By this example he does not prove that their practice was correct, but demonstrates their fixed faith in the resurrection.

164 (Vers. 30, 31.) Why are we also in danger every hour? Daily I die, by the glory that I have in the Lord. By saying, “Why are we also in danger?” he distinguishes the persons, showing that those who were baptized for the dead were not Catholics. Accordingly, above he said: “Why are they baptized for them?” Are we perhaps also baptized for them? For Jephthah, although he was found faithful in a matter that could not be made acceptable, when he offered his daughter according to the vow he had foolishly made (Judg. XI, 39), [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Laudian manuscripts read: “although it cannot be credited to him as a matter of rest,” while the Corbie manuscript reads: “although it cannot be made acceptable in other respects.”] is not therefore commended for the deed itself; rather, his perseverance in faith is put forward as an example. He recalls the dangers and labors of preachers, saying: “Why are we also in danger?” The implied answer is: unless we hope for the future resurrection, as he mentioned above. Secure that true life will follow this death, they do not fear the dangers inflicted by unbelievers because of their zeal for those whom they grieve to have lost because they believed. Thus he shows his concern for their salvation, on account of the glory promised by the Lord, as it is also said in the Law: “Raise your voice like a trumpet; if they hear you, you will gain their souls” (Ezek. XXXIII, 5). The Apostle was always hastening toward this, ever concerned that his glory before God might increase through the salvation he had won for many.

(Vers. 32.) If, according to human judgment, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantage is it to me if the dead do not rise? This means: if, according to human understanding—which, seeing that it does not fall within the nature of things for flesh once dissolved to be restored to life, scarcely believes that the dead will rise—I did not fear being handed over to beasts and dying, I have gained nothing. But this is not the case, because, certain of the promised life, he not only did not fear but willingly allowed himself to be handed over to beasts, as he says among other things in the Acts of the Apostles: “For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts XXI, 13).

“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” This was said by the prophet Isaiah concerning those who, as though nothing would exist after death, devoted themselves only to their bellies like animals (Isa. XXII, 13), as did those who were corrupting the Corinthians.

(Vers. 33.) Do not be deceived: “bad conversations corrupt good morals.” He signifies that a good purpose can be overturned through association with wicked people [Note: [Col. 0266D] The Roman edition reads: “that the good purpose can be overthrown.”]; for constant evil conversation corrupts the mind, and therefore such people must be avoided. Whoever wishes to preserve the faith he has received must especially, at the very beginning, avoid those who oppose it, so that he may fulfill what he has judged beneficial.

(Vers. 34.) Be watchful, be righteous, and do not sin. He urges vigilance, lest they be caught by a perverse understanding and, having been drawn away from the faith, become corrupted by refusing to believe in the resurrection of the dead. He commands them to be righteous, so that they may cultivate not merely earthly justice but heavenly justice as well; for earthly justice does not create merit, just as its absence does not create guilt. For what great thing is it not to take what belongs to another, [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Corbie manuscript adds: “since this is not done recklessly.”] since this is a matter of fear? But it is a great thing to give from one’s own possessions to someone who has nothing; this is true justice. And in order that they might not sin, he adds this. Thus he wished it to be understood that he had commanded not the observance of temporal justice but of divine justice; for whoever observes heavenly justice is undoubtedly [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Laudian and Vallombrosan manuscripts read: “in this present life.”] perfect in this present life.

For some have ignorance of God; I speak this to your shame. Those who had ignorance of God, [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Roman edition reads: “who lived among them.”] who were living among them, said that it was foolish to believe that the dead would rise. Therefore he brings shame upon them as though they were unintelligent; for they believed those who, possessing ignorance of God, taught against God’s decrees.

(Vers. 35.) But someone will say: How do the dead rise? With what kind of body will they come? He said that those whose corrupted opinions he has expressed in the words “How do the dead rise? With what kind of body will they come?” possess ignorance of God. To them he appropriately responds, saying:

[Col. 0267C] (Vers. 36.) Fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it first dies. He is not dealing with the natural man by the authority of the Law, as though he were persuading him through examples which, if he accepted them, would keep him from error; rather, he argues by physical reasoning, which the man uses to flatter himself so that he will not believe that dissolved and dead bodies rise again. He shows that dead things are restored to life again, and in greater abundance, so that human error may be confounded.

(Vers. 37, 38.) And what do you sow? You do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of one of the other kinds. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each seed its own body. If, therefore, a bare grain is sown and, by God’s command, clothed, as it were, through the service of the elements, it rises with much increase [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “its own body is sown”; immediately afterward the Laudian manuscript reads: “for the service of the elements,” while another reading has: “for the service of the elect.”] useful to human life, why should it not be credible that, by God’s power, what is dead can rise, with its substance improved but not multiplied in number? What, then, is the unbeliever asking when he asks in what body the dead will rise, [Note: [Col. 0267D] The old edition and manuscripts differ here: some read “proclaim,” while others read “display.” The Roman edition has: “when they proclaim examples of resurrection as evidence for this faith in an improved substance, not a lost one.”] when examples precede to establish faith in a resurrection that improves the substance rather than destroys it? It will receive its own body, in which Adam was created, according to the examples given above.

[Col. 0268A] (Vers. 39.) Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one flesh of human beings, another of animals, another flesh of birds, and another of fish. Since all flesh comes from the same mass, whence and how is there such great diversity among them, so that one material produces different kinds? Let the sophists of the world and the investigators of the stars speak now, if they are able to comprehend what lies outside themselves, when they do not know what is within themselves. Indeed, all the philosophers of the world, who refused to humble their minds before the law of God so as to receive its faith, have always confused one another with their empty arguments, asserting diverse and contradictory things; [Note: [Col. 0268D] The Laudian manuscript reads: “because in none of these was the sign of truth attested …”] for in none of them was a sign of truth recognized that, placed before their words, might commend their teaching, as God also determined for our discipline: it is not proved by words but by power, [Col. 0268B] against which words cannot prevail. Just as, therefore, flesh of different animals comes from one material, so human beings, though of one flesh, will differ in dignity at the resurrection, so that each person will appear as his merit has been, since even here we see a diversity of bodies.

(Vers. 40.) There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but one is the glory of the heavenly and another of the earthly. The heavenly bodies are those of the resurrected; the earthly bodies are those before they die or rise. Thus, because Christ is heavenly, the bodies are called heavenly from him; but because Adam is earthly, the bodies are earthly from him.

(Vers. 41.) [Note: [Col. 0268D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “One glory of the sun, another glory of the moon … it differs in glory.”] There is one brightness of the sun, another brightness of the moon, and another brightness of the stars; for star differs from star [Col. 0268C] in brightness. He uses a comparison within one nature to explain substances that are not identical, because just as the sun, moon, and stars, although of one nature, nevertheless have different brightness, so human beings, although of one kind, will nevertheless differ in glory according to merit. Their dignity will correspond to the brightness of the sun—those who possess the hundredfold number, who, in order to become perfect, were imitators of the first degree, of whom it is said: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43). Those are to be compared with the brightness of the moon who have acquired the sixtyfold number through good works, so that they possess the merit of the second degree. The merits of those who have attained the dignity of the third degree through righteous labors, acquiring the thirtyfold number, are to be compared with the brighter stars. Those who follow—stars that are midway between the bright and the dim—are to be identified with sinful people who did not wish to attain the honor of any degree among the three. But the resurrection of the faithless resembles the dark stars, the very last of all; for because they followed error, they are to be compared with stars that lead people into error, as the apostle Jude says in his Epistle (Jude I, 13). Unbelief cannot have a bright resurrection [Col. 0269A], because just as a coal covered with its own ash is darkened, so these, surrounded by the darkness of the error of their faithlessness, will lack light.

(Vers. 42.) So also is the resurrection of the dead. He gives examples so that there may be no doubt that the dead will rise in the future; once the reasoning has been accepted, no one should hesitate. It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. To sow is to bury, so that the body may decay; to rise in incorruption means that, once raised, it can no longer decay, but possesses the splendor of immortality.

(Vers. 43.) It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in dishonor because, when it is placed in a foul place, it becomes putrid and teems with worms; but it will rise in glory because, once raised, it will be luminous and will suffer no injury from filth. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in [Col. 0269B] power. It is sown in weakness because it is immobile and unable to move; but it will rise in power, 166 because it will then be wholly unified and vigorous.

(Vers. 44.) It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body. If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual one. The body is animal while it is sustained by food so that it may live; it is spiritual when it will need none of these things, having been transformed into life. All the foregoing statements are enclosed within this meaning: [Note: [Col. 0269D] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “For the animal body cannot always have the Holy Spirit here; but then, that is, at the resurrection, it will remain always among the saints. It will rise a spiritual body, able to go to meet Christ.” These words can readily be recognized as having been patched together from the commentary of Pseudo-Jerome on this passage. Yet the words from this point through the words at the beginning of the commentary on the following epistle—“It is manifest because of what we suffer”—are found in most manuscripts and all editions of Ambrosius, from whom Rhabanus Maurus also transferred something into his Exposition of Paul’s Epistles under the name of our Doctor. The same words, except for the prologue, are found verbatim in those spurious Commentaries of Jerome. From this it may readily be inferred that, in some old manuscript of our Commentary, a leaf was lost or displaced, and that the scribes wished to repair the damage from Pseudo-Jerome. This is confirmed by the fact that the Corbie exemplar contains everything else, but passages that agree much more appropriately with the style of the writer called Ambrosiaster. Add that in three other manuscripts, at the end of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, there is a fragment of an exposition of the final verses of this epistle attributed to Ambrose, in the same words as those found in the Corbie manuscript. We have therefore judged that the reading of the Corbie manuscript should be accepted.] For nothing else is contained in the foregoing than that the animal body dies and will rise a spiritual body, which will neither eat nor drink, nor grow weak, nor be naturally foul or filthy.

(Vers. 45.) The first man Adam was made a living soul. This is said in Genesis (Gen. II, 7), because, having received the breath of God’s spirit, man was made a living soul [Col. 0269C]. For the function of the spirit is to animate the body, yet in such a way that it does not possess continuous life unless it uses the assistance of food and drink. But the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. This means that he who had previously been made a soul was made spirit through the resurrection, so that he could no longer die, since he would become wholly alive.

(Vers. 46.) But the spiritual did not come first; for the animal came from Adam, while the spiritual comes through Christ and the resurrection of the dead.

(Vers. 47, 48.) The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. The first man, Adam, is from the earth and is temporal, and death follows him. The second man, Christ, is from heaven; having risen, he does not know death [Col. 0269D]. As is the earthly one, so are the earthly: that is, because the earthly man is mortal, the earthly are also mortal. Adam sinned and thereby found death, so that all who come from him are mortal. And as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly: that is, because Christ did not sin and, conquering death, is heavenly, so also are those who believe in him. Although unbelievers too will be spiritual, they will be spiritual in the likeness of spiritual wickedness, so that they will be dark. He is speaking now of the saints, who will rise to glory; for just as those who do not believe have already been judged, those who believe are already called heavenly (John III, 18).

(Vers. 49.) Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly one, let us also bear the image of this heavenly one. That is, just as through Adam’s sin we bore the form of mortality and became slaves of sin, so let us also bear the form of life through the righteousness of the Savior, becoming servants of righteousness, not of the world but of God, while doing those things that are worthy of immortality.

### (Verse 50)

But this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God. By “flesh” he wants perfidy to be understood, and by “blood,” a shameful and licentious life, because this desire is generated by the heat of the blood. Thus he showed that not only the unbeliever is unworthy of resurrection, but also the one who obeys the desires and vices of the flesh. He therefore warns and instructs us by what manner we may deserve to attain the kingdom of heaven.

Nor will corruption possess incorruption. He says this because corruption and the wantonness of life must necessarily suffer punishment. For he has called suffering “corruption”; yet it is certainly established that all human beings will rise immortal.

[Col. 0270C] (Verse 51.) Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all indeed rise—that is, both believers and unbelievers. But we shall not all be changed. Here he indicates the merit of each person, namely, what each one’s condition will be in the resurrection.

(Verses 52.) In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye—that is, quickly, without any delay—at the last trumpet. It is called “last” because the final battle is waged against the demons, the principalities, the powers, and the devil himself. This will happen after the thousand years during which the Savior will reign here, once the Antichrist has been destroyed, when Satan will be released from his prison to deceive the nations Gog and Magog, who are demons, so that they may fight against the camp of the saints; for temporal human beings could not fight against eternal beings. The Apostle John also says: “I saw Michael and his angels fighting in heaven against the dragon and his angels,” who is the devil and [Col. 0271A] Satan (Rev. 20:7). Therefore he says here “the last trumpet,” because he has not fought against him only once: for there was also a battle against him in the Antichrist, through the false prophets who performed signs and wonders before him; and he himself was victorious. Finally, in this place he will be fought against for the last time, so that he may now be sent into Gehenna. The Savior also says among other things: “Now the prince of this world will be cast down” (John 12:31). And thus he has frequently been defeated, as the prophet Isaiah says: “How has Lucifer fallen from heaven, who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12).

For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. When sinners and the ungodly rise, the saints will be changed in glory, so that the flesh may become spiritual together with glory, like lead if it were made into gold. For the saints will rise at the Lord’s coming, just as he said above [Col. 0271B] (verse 23): “Christ the beginning; afterward those who are Christ’s at his coming,” as is contained in the Apocalypse. For sinners are not Christ’s, those to whom the Lord says: “I do not know you” (Ps. 1:5). For it is also written in the first Psalm: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous” (Matt. 7:23). There is nothing to be required from the ungodly; rather, they will rise for this purpose: that they may perish, seeing that what they refused to believe was true. To perish, however, is to be alienated from God, as he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “For whoever sinned outside the law will also perish without the law, and whoever sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom. 2:12). Consequently, sinners will judge; for they are unworthy to rise with the saints, as he says: “Nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

[Col. 0271C] (Verse 53.) For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality. Above he said, “and the dead will rise incorruptible,” that is, they will be immortal, though not free from suffering. For those whom he mentions will suffer punishments according to the character of their sins, until they depart from there once their debt has been paid; but the ungodly will be tortured by eternal punishment. For he says: “The one who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). Hence the prophet Isaiah also says: “Their fire shall not be quenched, and their worm shall not die” (Isa. 65:24).

At the Lord’s coming, however, both the saints will rise and those who are found alive will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, undergoing death as though it were sleep. For in that very rapture they will experience both death and resurrection, as the same Apostle writes to the Thessalonians (2 Thess. 4:6 and following). [Col. 0271D] For at the time of the Antichrist, the remaining Gentiles will either be apostates or guilty, or they will be in hiding or subjected to punishment; the Lord Jesus, at his coming, will kill them together with their leader, the Antichrist, by the breath of his mouth (2 Thess. 2:8)—that is, at his command they will be burned by fire through the angels of his power.

(Verses 54–55.) But when this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying will come to pass that is written: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” For after the resurrection of the ungodly and sinners, death will be swallowed up in victory. These are the words of one who insults, saying: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your goad, O death?” The resurrection of the dead is the victory over defeated death. Death, however, is the devil, who is insulted; and he is called contentious because, through pride, although he was unequal in strength, he resisted. When he is overcome and killed and his spoils are taken from him, the one who fought against him heaps reproach upon him.

(Verses 56.) The sting of death is sin. “Sting” signifies authority, because through sin death received authority; as though, if sin did not exist, the devil would have been powerless and death would not exist. But the power of sin is the law. Therefore the law is the power of sin, because sin would not be imputed if the law did not exist.

(Verses 57.) But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. He says that the Savior’s triumph has benefited us; for what the Savior accomplished, he certainly did not accomplish for himself but for us. [Col. 0272B] Therefore it is our victory. For this reason he became human while remaining God: so that, by conquering the devil while committing no sin, he might acquire victory for us, who were held in death because of sin. Thus, when the devil was defeated through the killing of Christ, who had committed no sin, he lost all those whom he held on account of sin. But when he insulted the human being, he became liable to judgment, and thus the written bond—that is, the sentence by which the human race was held for death—was erased, so that the human race might be rescued and souls brought into heaven. They were not taken from him by power, but by justice, by God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

(Verses 58.) Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Having set forth everything necessary for ordering the Church’s teaching, and having shown what must be avoided and what must be followed, he now urges them to remain fixed in the good and always ready and abundant in works that bear fruit before the Lord. For through what has been explained they will thereafter receive from the Lord the reward of good work, so that they may not be overturned by corrupt conversations.

## CHAPTER XV

(Verses 1–2.) Concerning the collections that are made for the saints: just as I ordered the churches of Galatia, so also you must do. On the first day of the week, let each of you set something aside privately, storing up whatever he wishes, so that collections may not be made when I come. He commands that the collection be made on the Lord’s day, just as he had arranged in the other churches, so that on the day on which the Lord rose, his people might gather for the praise and glory of God, death having been conquered. At that time they were to gather funds for the ministry of the saints who, because of the Lord’s name, were suffering oppression from the zeal of Gentiles or Jews who did not allow them to preach the grace of God under the name of Christ, so that they might receive relief from those on whose account they were suffering. Therefore he commands the people to be gathered every Sunday and to contribute to God’s gifts as each person wishes, and to store this up privately, as though in a treasury, so that when the Apostle came it might be found prepared for necessary uses; for what is collected little by little is not burdensome and is found to amount to much.

(Verses 3.) When I come, I will send by letter those whom you approve to carry your gift to Jerusalem. This consolation had a twofold benefit, as it still does: it benefited both the saints mentioned above and the poor established in the Church, which also now benefits the needs of the elders and the needy. He says that he will send by letter those whom they select as suitable for administering the gift. The letters provide testimony on behalf of those sent, so that they may be received with favor.

(Verses 4.) And if it should be worthy, they too will go with me. He says that, if the collection is large, they can also go with him; for it is fitting, and necessary as well, that if he goes, he should carry a great amount with him for the relief of the saints. This is what he signifies when he says to the Romans: “For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Rom. 15:27). For they were from the Jews, concerning whom the Lord says that salvation is from the Jews; and in Jerusalem they were greatly hated by the unbelieving Jews.

(Verses 5–6.) I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia; but I may remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever I go. After all his instruction, he promised them his coming in order to make them glad, and thereby strengthened all his admonitions with which he corrected them. Whoever hears that the one from whom he received the law is coming will be more watchful, lest he be ashamed when he arrives.

(Verses 7.) For I do not wish to see you now merely in passing. Knowing that he had many things to do with them, he does not wish to see them in passing; and, so that they might not be saddened, he promises to remain with them for a long time, because he does everything with foresight. For I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits. “If the Lord permits”: for the Lord permits him to remain with them if they show themselves worthy by correcting the vices that he reproves in them.

(Verses 8–9.) But I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost; for a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries. He explains why he had remained in Ephesus: there he had found hearts thirsting for the grace of God, into which he might pour the mystery of Christ. But because the devil is always restless and jealous of those who desire God, he added: “And there are many adversaries.” For the more suitable they were found to be for the faith, the more there were those who were jealous of them, contradicting and resisting the Lord’s teaching.

(Verses 10–12.) If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you; for he is working the Lord’s work, as I also am. Therefore let no one despise him. Although Timothy preached what he had received from the Apostle and was a suitable evangelist, nevertheless, because he did not possess the same authority, he commends him, lest perhaps he should not be received as he deserved by those among the people who dissented, and his arrival should accomplish nothing for their salvation. For the Gentiles too might be stirred up to sedition and disagreement among the people, taking the opportunity to attack Timothy. Therefore, he says, let no one despise him, because he performs the Lord’s work as I do—that is, so that he might be received with the authority that I possess as an apostle. For he himself was a bishop.

Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me; for I am expecting him with the brothers. He recalls Timothy’s great merit, instructing them not only to honor him among themselves but showing that they must send him on his way with due respect as an apostle of the Lord, since he himself was also awaiting him with the brothers for the sake of Christ’s Gospel.

Concerning our brother Apollos, I inform you that I urged him very much to come to you with the brothers, but it was certainly not his wish to come now. He will come when the opportunity is suitable. By saying this, he shows that he had satisfied their will or request by presenting them with his own desire, while excusing Apollos. He did not explain why Apollos would not go to them at that time; nevertheless, he did not excuse him altogether but merely postponed his coming. It may also be understood in this way: by mentioning Apollos, he touches upon their situation, indicating that Apollos did not wish to go to them because they were divided, so that, upon hearing this, they might strive for peace. For this reason he said of Timothy: “See that he is without fear among you,” because some who had been sent had not been well received; and consequently Apollos would come when they were in agreement.

(Verses 13–14.) Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strengthened. Let everything you do be done in charity. “Be watchful,” he says, lest they be deceived in the faith. “Act manfully”: that is, he urges them to be strong concerning what had been entrusted to them, not like children who do not know what they should follow. “Be strengthened,” so that they may be robust both in word and in deed; for profession and good works make people perfect. He urges that these same things be done in charity, because what is done with charity possesses the fear and zeal of God. Whatever is done while offending a brother bears no fruit.

Some people must be provoked to what is good, not saddened—for example, if you discourage another from showing mercy, or if you are inhumane, or criticize others, or eat something while insulting someone who abstains from it, thereby causing him scruple. Everything must be done in such a way that it is an exhortation to better things, not an insult; and then there is peace. Hence the Lord says: “By this it is known whether you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35). But where there is contention and dissension, there is no love.

(Verses 15–16.) I urge you, brothers—you know the household of Stephanas and Fortunatus—that they are the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have appointed themselves for the ministry of the saints. You too should submit to such people, and to every fellow worker and laborer. The Corinthians are Achaeans; therefore he speaks to them about these people, through whom he urges them toward this kind of work, since they are from among them. For this is something great in Christians: having trampled avarice underfoot, they distribute from their labors to those who have nothing, becoming imitators of God the Father, who is rich in mercy. When he says, “You should submit to such people,” he urges them still more strongly, so that, having become rivals in this work, they themselves may have others submitting to them.

(Verses 17–18.) I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking on your part. For they refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge such people. The contribution that, as he says, is made for the saints is one thing, and repaying those who serve the Gospel is another, just as the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). He shows that the household of Stephanas was devoted in both respects: in the ministry of the saints and toward those who served the churches, so that they benefited the Apostle together with the brothers Fortunatus and Achaicus, and so that those who belonged to them might also benefit. Hence he says: “For they refreshed both my spirit and yours.”

And although the Apostle denies that he will accept anything from them—for he says, “This boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia”—how did they refresh both my spirit and yours? But I believe that his spirit was refreshed in those whom they had benefited; for he says that what benefits those whom he wished to benefit was given to him. “Therefore acknowledge such people”: that is, imitate them.

[Col. 0275B] (Verse 19.) The churches of Asia greet you. Through the greeting of these people he urges them to become like them, since they belong to the same province. Aquila and Priscilla greet you in the Lord, together with the church in their household. He mentions two churches, the public and the domestic: he calls “public” the one to which everyone comes, and “domestic” the one gathered through friendship. Wherever the presbyters celebrate the solemn rites, it is called a church.

(Verses 20.) All the brothers greet you. He lifts their spirits when he shows that all these people remember them. Greet one another with a holy kiss. [Col. 0276A] The holy kiss is a sign of peace, by which he teaches them to cling to one another after discord has been removed.

(Verses 21.) The greeting is by the hand of Paul. He shows that he signed this letter himself, and he added what the words of the subscription are, saying:

(Verses 22.) If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema. Maranatha, which is interpreted: If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, who has come, let him be cut off. For *Maranatha* signifies “the Lord has come.” This is directed against the Jews who said that Jesus had not come; therefore they are accursed by the Lord who has come.

(Verses 23–24.) The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. He placed such a subscription because those who devoted themselves to dissension did not love the Lord Jesus, since they said: “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I indeed to Cephas” (1 Cor. 1:12). For the one who loves Christ does not give glory to human beings, because there is no hope in human beings. “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you”—with the implicit addition, “who love the Lord Jesus.” And because they did not love one another, he therefore says: “My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus,” so that they might learn to love one another with the same love by which they were loved by the Apostle—not with carnal affection, but in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 0275]

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF BLESSED PAUL TO THE CORINTHIANS

169 [Note: [Col. 0275D] This prologue is not found in the Corbie manuscript, as we have already observed. Nevertheless, since it is found in all the others and in all editions, and does not appear in the Commentary of Pseudo-Hieronymus, we have decided that it should be retained.]

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0275C]

The Apostle writes the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, the principal reason for which is this. In the first letter he had chiefly rebuked their teachers for the sins of certain people, and they had been greatly saddened. Now he consoles them, setting before them his own example and teaching that they ought not to take offense at having been rebuked for the salvation of others, since he himself is daily exposed to dangers and death for the salvation of others.

## CHAPTER ONE

(Verses 1.) Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ. Now secure concerning them, he confidently proclaims himself an apostle of the Lord. In the first epistle, he says that he was called an apostle, but that this was not accepted by those who had been led away from his tradition. By the will of God. To establish the validity of his apostleship, he says that he became an apostle by the will of the Lord Christ. For the Lord says to the Jews: “I always do what is pleasing to him,” that is, to God the Father (John 8:29). And Timothy, a brother. When he writes this—with the one through whom he had sent the first letter to them, that is, with Timothy—he shows them that he had heard from Timothy about their good will, by which they had submitted themselves to correction. To the church that is in Corinth, with all the saints who are in Achaia. Now he joins these people to the saints of the other churches, so that they may know that they have made progress.

[Col. 0276C] 170 (Verse 2.) Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Since the gift of God and of Christ is one, he therefore wishes them to be participants in the grace of God, which is also Christ’s.

(Verses 3.) Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. In every epistle, whenever he is about to speak of God the Father and his gift, he always transmits the order of the mystery. The Father of mercies and God of all consolation. He began with this very idea, for it provides much relief to those who had been saddened because of correction. When they hear that the Lord is not only the Father of all origin but also the Father of mercies, they are raised up by hope and made certain that they were corrected for this purpose: so that, having been converted, they might find God’s mercy. Why did he call him the Father of mercies, unless so that he might be recognized as regenerating and reforming penitents again through mercy, so that there might be not merely pardon but restoration to their former condition? Therefore he says “of mercies” because of the various sins, so that he might console those saddened on account of their offenses—that is, so that he might not deny hope to those who had been converted.

(Verses 4.) Who consoles us in all our distress. This is what he said: “the God of all consolation,” who is present in every distress, so that we too may console those who are in every distress through the exhortation with which we are exhorted by God. He introduced two kinds of consolation: one by which those who suffer distress unjustly for the name of Christ are consoled, so that they may be delivered; the other received by those who are saddened because of their sins, when hope is promised to them if they correct themselves, by those who, having been consoled by the Lord, have been rescued from distress.

(Verses 5.) For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds. It is clear that the one for whom we suffer is himself present with us, [Note: [Col. 0277D] Several manuscripts read: “consoling us through deliverance.”] consoling us through deliverance and rescuing us from distress through the intervention of his majesty.

(Verses 6–7.) [Note: [Col. 0277D] In these Pauline verses, whenever *exhortatione* and *exhortationem* are read in the manuscripts and early editions, the Roman edition has, correspondingly, substituted *consolatione* and *consolationem*.]

But whether we suffer distress for your exhortation and salvation, or whether we receive exhortation for your exhortation, which works through the endurance of the same sufferings that we ourselves also suffer, so that our hope for you may be certain—for we know that just as you are partners in sufferings, so also you will be partners in consolation. [Note: [Col. 0277D] For “for you,” the Roman edition adds: “or whether we receive consolation for your consolation and salvation, because …”] He speaks generally: because, on account of believers, they were suffering persecutions from unbelievers, being subjected to insults and killings, so likewise they would again be delivered by God’s help for the consolation of believers, lest, having suffered scandal, they should fall away from the faith. For the injuries inflicted upon the apostles were trials for believers, as it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. 13:7). Although the faithful believe in what is to come, during the very beginnings of distress such things cause scandal to the inexperienced; for they think the promise empty if they see the preacher oppressed by force. But if a believer is already firm, he suffers together with his teacher, trusting in future hope, so that he may be consoled together with the one with whom [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “and he suffers together.” They suffered for the sake of the faith, so that they would not bear their errors more heavily if they were corrected. “For we do not wish …”] he also suffers.

[Col. 0277C] (Verses 8.) For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning the distress that came upon us in Asia, because we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we even despaired of living. He therefore indicates that the sufferings of their distress had been inflicted almost to the point of death, so that he might show what evils they endured for the sake of their salvation, and so that they would not bear more heavily the correction of their errors by those who endured such hardships for them. [Note: [Col. 0277D] The same manuscript reads: “because they endured the evils of their salvation from those who inflicted such harsh things, on their behalf.”] For what physician does not rebuke a patient who treats himself carelessly, lest the care of his medicine remain without effect?

(Verses 9.) Indeed, we ourselves received within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we would not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead. He signifies that such insolence of wickedness had risen up against the preachers of the faith that they had death before their eyes. Finally, having been rescued from that very distress, they say that they had been raised from the dead. For they had been afflicted in such a way that they despaired of their present life. But because God does not deny his protection to those placed in necessity, especially to his own, he rescued them when they were despairing of themselves but trusting in God. For they acknowledged that they were failing under excessive distress unless God were present.

(Verses 10–11.) He delivered us from such great deaths, and he delivers us; in him we have hoped that he will also deliver us, with your prayer coming to our aid, so that the gift bestowed upon us through many persons may be celebrated through many in thanksgiving on our behalf. He says this because the grace of God, for the sake of many, [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “was bestowed upon the apostles”; Vall. reads: “the Apostle was consoled.”] consoled the apostles—that is, for the sake of all believers, on whose account the distresses were also inflicted upon them. Therefore, because it is for the sake of all, let everyone give thanks to God when the trial ceases; or, when it arises, let everyone entreat him together.

(Verses 12.) For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience. He says this because they relied upon their conscience, which was pure from all [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “pretense, presenting an undivided faith to God in preaching; therefore, concerning God’s help …”] pretense; therefore they did not lose confidence in God’s help. For we have conducted ourselves in this world in simplicity and sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God—and more abundantly among you. This is the glory of conscience that he mentioned: simplicity and sincerity. And because these things come from the teaching of God, he added: “Not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God,” so that he might show that he had presented a free conscience not to human wisdom but to evangelical preaching. [Note: [Col. 0278D] Gill, in the margin, and the Roman edition in the body, together with certain manuscripts, read: “he repeats the past.”] He reopens matters already dealt with; for this signifies what he rebuked in the first epistle: preaching adapted to human opinion and outward appearance (1 Cor. 2:4). He accuses its preachers of fleshly wisdom in two ways: they preached according to the world’s understanding, so as not easily to offend people; and they did this for profit, pursuing their own fleshly gains. Hence the Apostle never wished to accept expenses from the Corinthians, lest he give them an occasion, since in this matter he would appear like them. This is why he says: “We conducted ourselves more abundantly among you in simplicity,” [Col. 0278C] because, although he had accepted from others, he did not wish to accept from them, [Note: [Col. 0278D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “lest they abandon the authority of one who rebuked them.”] lest he lose his authority to rebuke them.

(Verses 13.) For we are not writing anything else to you but what you have read and understand. He says that he is writing things that they would not merely see in letters but would also have recognized as evident in his actions, so that he might prove that he fulfills by his deeds what he says, by which the mind and purpose of each person are learned.

(Verses 14.) But I hope that you will understand fully to the end, just as you have already understood in part, that we are your glory, just as you also are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. He hopes that they will make progress because they had already begun to become better, having recognized the Apostle’s affection toward them, and they gloried in him as children [Note: [Col. 0278D] Two manuscripts read: “in a most illustrious father.” This is by no means incorrect.] in a most beloved father. Hence the Apostle also testifies that his glory is seen in obedient children, and that it ought to be seen when it is beneficial—that is, on the day of God’s judgment. By saying this, he urges perseverance.

(Verses 15–16.) In this confidence I had intended to come to you first, [Note: [Col. 0279D] The Roman edition reads: “so that you might have a full grace, and that I might pass through you …”] so that you might have a second grace, and to pass through you into Macedonia, and again to come to you from Macedonia, and to be sent on my way by you into Judea. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Several manuscripts: “This confidence has been corrected …”] This confidence arose from their reformed life; for he now signifies that he longs to see those whom previously it had been unworthy to see. They would therefore have received a full grace from his arrival, because a letter is an image, whereas presence is reality. Thus it is not without purpose that he had wished to go and did not go; for he wants it understood that there were some among them on whose account he did not fulfill his intention, so that, through the work undertaken, they might be purified.

(Verses 17.) Therefore, when I formed this intention, did I act frivolously? Or do I form my intentions according to the flesh, so that with me there is “Yes, yes” and “No, no”? Since he had said, “I intended to come to you,” [Note: [Col. 0279D] The Roman edition reads: “and I did not come”; the old edition, with several manuscripts: “and I did not go”; the other manuscripts: “and he did not go.”] and did not go, he therefore asks whether he had acted frivolously, since someone who says something and does not do it seems to act frivolously. Therefore, lest they think this of the Apostle, he clears it up: he did not act frivolously but deliberately, so as not to fulfill what he had planned.

Or do I form my intentions, he says, according to the flesh? For the one who thinks according to the flesh does not fulfill what he plans when he either defers to more powerful persons or is overcome by profits or displays—things that the Apostle always rejected. But the spiritual person does not fulfill a plan when he considers something more prudently for the salvation of the soul. Thus the Apostle did not fulfill what he had wished so that through this very act they might become better, knowing that he had postponed his coming because some among them had not yet purified themselves from sins.

“Let there be with me,” he says, “‘Yes, yes’; ‘No, no.’” This means that he did nothing other than what he knew ought to be done, because usefulness must be placed before will. This is the spiritual meaning. The carnal meaning, however, is changed in such a way [Note: [Col. 0279D] Two manuscripts read: “so that he places pleasure before usefulness.”] that it places will before usefulness.

(Verses 18.) But God is faithful, because our word to you is not “Yes and No.” This is what he also says to the Galatians: “If I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I show myself to be a transgressor” (Gal. 2:18). Therefore he declares the preaching of God to be faithful; [Note: [Col. 0279D] The Vallis manuscript reads: “lest flatterers do this.”] for flatterers do that. Frequently, so as not to offend people, they omit what is true.

(Verses 19.) For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not “Yes and No,” but “Yes” was in him. As far as suitable preachers are concerned, this ought to be the case: there should be with them “Yes, yes” and “No, no,” so that they do nothing other than what they know to be useful. Because we frequently desire something other than what is useful, the Apostle placed usefulness before his own will, so that his will would not prevail and he would not go to them.

For in Christ Jesus there was not “Yes and No,” but “Yes” was in him, because he never desired anything other than what is useful. His will is always joined to usefulness; nor was he changed so as to do unwillingly, like a human being, what is useful, or so as to waver concerning something and change his will.

(Verses 20.) For however many the promises of God are, they are in him; and through him is the “Amen” to God for glory through us. It is clear that truth is always in God—that is, the “Amen”—made manifest through Christ and afterward preached through the apostles for the glory of God, with the power of signs bearing witness that what God promised through Christ our Lord is true. For the glory of God consists in the fact that all things are said to be from him, through him, and [Col. 0280B] in him. [Note: [Col. 0280D] Several manuscripts, Amerbach’s edition in the body, and Gill in the margin read: “are learned to exist.”]

(Verses 21–22.) Now the one who confirms us with you in Christ is the Lord, and the one who anointed us is God, who also sealed us and gave us the Spirit as a pledge in our hearts. He says that Christ confirms the nations in the faith promised to the Jews, because he is the one who made both one (Eph. 2:14)—that is, circumcision and uncircumcision—making peace in one new human being.

The Lord therefore confirms us, and God is the one who anointed us, that is, who bestowed royal honor, as the Apostle Peter says: “For we are,” he says (1 Pet. 2:9), “a royal race,” through spiritual anointing, whose type was present in the kings of the Jews. He also sealed us by giving us his Spirit as a pledge, so that we might not doubt his promises. For if he has entrusted his Spirit even to mortal human beings, there is no doubt that he will add it to immortal beings for glory.

Nevertheless, he speaks of one work of the Father and the Son, since he says both that Christ confirms and that God confirms. Whomever the Son confirms, the Father also confirms; and when the Father gives the Spirit, the Son also gives it, because the Holy Spirit belongs to both, as he says to the Romans: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). Therefore, because he has spoken of human perfection, he has mentioned the Trinity in this passage; for the whole fullness of perfection consists in the Trinity.

But I call God as witness upon my soul: it was to spare you that I did not yet come to Corinth. Now he makes clear the reason why, although he had wished to go to them, he postponed it: so that he might go when he found nearly all of them already corrected. For now he is speaking to those who seemed to wish to correct themselves but were not making the effort to accomplish this. Since it was therefore necessary to rebuke them, [Note: [Col. 0280D] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “he turned toward them”; the Roman edition: “he turned away from them”; most manuscripts: “he turned toward others.” But below, where all editions and a large number of manuscripts read “that they were unworthy,” the Corbie manuscript reads “that they were worthy.”] he turned his journey toward others, so as not to sadden many; and this was his way of sparing them. To impress this upon their minds, he calls God as witness, lest they think that they were unworthy and despised by him. Once they learned this, they would correct themselves so as to deserve his presence.

Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy; for you stand firm in faith. [Note: [Col. 0281D] The Corbie manuscript reads: “for you stand by faith.” But he says that they resist God by their will, not that we lord it over them, and so forth. There is also a lacuna here in the Carnutian manuscript.] Since faith is a matter not of necessity but of will, he therefore says: “Not that we lord it over your faith.” Domination belongs to necessity. “But we are helpers,” he says, “of your joy”: that is, just as there is sadness in an evil work, so there is joy in correction. “We are helpers of this joy,” he says, because, when they wish to correct themselves, they offer admonitions, so that they may accomplish what they have begun to desire.

## CHAPTER II
(Vers. 1.) But I resolved this within myself: not to come to you again in sorrow. It is clear that he did not wish to go lest, perhaps, while correcting a few, he should grieve many and himself also be grieved; for all the members of one body share in the sorrow of one.

[Col. 0281B] (Vers. 2.) For if I grieve you, who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me? He says this because he does not wish to grieve them; but since they had devoted themselves to sins, they necessarily had to be grieved, against the Apostle’s will—yet in such a way that thereafter, having become obedient, they might gladden those who were grieving along with them. Thus the one who had grieved them by correcting them would be made glad by them when they were corrected.

(Vers. 3.) And for this very reason I wrote this, so that when I came I might not have sorrow from those by whom I ought to have been gladdened, being confident that my joy is the joy of you all. He says that he wrote these things for this reason: that when he came later, there might be no cause for grief, since the vices had been removed, but that he might rejoice with them as with dearly beloved children. For, since he was afflicted by tribulations from unbelievers, he would certainly rejoice because of those who had believed. The Apostle’s joy [Col. 0281C] is the purification of the people. He rejoices for this reason: that there is no reproach in those with whom he ought together to rejoice.

(Vers. 4.) For out of great pressure and anguish of heart I wrote to you, with many tears—not so that you might be grieved, but so that you might know the abundant love that I have for you. It is evident that when someone corrects another with this disposition—so that he grieves over the other’s sins more than the sinner himself—he does not correct him in order to grieve him, but to show with what love he loves him. [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “When he corrects him, he shows him with what love he loves him. For he who…”] Whoever does not correct with this disposition grieves his brother; for he insults the brother who does not grieve together with him.
