(Vers. 5.) 174 But if anyone has caused grief, he has caused grief not to me, but in part, so that I may not burden you all. All those whom he here calls “in part” are holy; for there are two parts among the people, as I mentioned in the First Epistle. These, then, belong to the part of the holy, whom he indicates to have been grieved by the brother’s error, just as he himself was. By saying this, however, he burdened the sinner, or the one who had sinned. For the one in whose offense many suffer becomes more guilty; and therefore he says:

(Vers. 6–7.) Sufficient for such a person is this rebuke inflicted by the majority. The one who sees that his offense is abhorred by many will certainly suffer great pain. So that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest somehow such a person be swallowed up by excessive [Col. 0282A] grief. [Note: Several manuscripts: “Help the afflicted man because of his own sin.”]

He commands that the man afflicted because of his own sin be helped, because repentance, if it comes from a true heart—that is, if the person, once corrected, immediately grieves inwardly—bears fruit at once. Accordingly, the Book of Kings records that when Ahab had been reproved by the prophet, he was moved in heart and immediately merited pardon (1 Kings 21:20). David likewise, in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, when reproved and recognizing that he had sinned, had his offense blotted out (2 Sam. 12:13).

So also the Apostle commands that the man who had committed incest by having his father’s wife, after being rebuked and rejected, should be recalled when grieving. Otherwise, seeing himself rejected and grieved for a long time, he might despair of himself and turn his mind to enjoying the world, as though he no longer had a place with God. This is to be swallowed up by greater grief: when a person, despairing of himself, turns to committing sins, by which, weighed down, he is swallowed up by the second death. For this is true repentance: to cease from sin. In this way he proves that he grieves for himself—if thereafter he desists.

(Vers. 8–9.) Therefore I entreat you to confirm your love toward him. For I wrote for this purpose, to test whether you are obedient in everything. As can be understood, he shows that they have become obedient in other matters; for they had corrected what pertained to ecclesiastical order. Therefore he also wishes them to be obedient in this matter: to strengthen the brother in love by receiving him into communion.

(Vers. 10.) But to whomever you forgive anything, I forgive it also. It is clear that he himself does what he commands to be done; nor can he refuse what he writes while entreating them to do it, although he had the authority to command. In the First Epistle he had exposed the man’s grave offense [Note: Codex Laudensis: “so that they might shudder at it”], so that all might abhor him. Now, since he wishes him to be received, he asks that, with their minds still embittered against him, it not be difficult for them to have ecclesial communion with him. For they did not possess as much foresight as the Apostle, so as immediately to understand that what the Apostle said ought to be done in this particular case. Therefore he entreats them to forgive him, signifying that God has forgiven him, since the Apostle did nothing without the Spirit of God.

For whatever I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have forgiven it for your sake in the person of Christ. By saying this, he places a burden upon them: if the teacher forgave the sin of those who asked him, and forgave whomever they wished, how much more ought the disciples to obey their teacher? And to show that the forgiveness he granted was ratified before God, he says that he forgave in the person of Christ—that is, he credited it to Christ, whose ambassador he was—so that the Apostle’s act might be Christ’s act, just as he said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18). If, then, Christ forgave this man for whom they had asked through the Apostle, how much more was this man already forgiven, for whom the Apostle himself urges them to grant forgiveness? [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “How much more this man, for whom the Apostle had asked, that they should forgive him, etc.”]

(Vers. 11.) So that we may not be possessed by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his schemes. He says what I mentioned above: consolation ought to follow the brother who weeps over his offense, lest, being grieved for a long time and despised by the love of the Church, he should begin to despair of himself. Then the subtle devil, who is always lying in wait, seeing that his mind has become degraded [Note: The same Codex Corbeiensis: “might kindle him with a base disposition and suggest, etc.”], may approach and suggest that he enjoy at least present things, since he has been cast down from hope of the future reward. Thus the brother, possessed by the devil, would perish, although repentance had been given to him for this purpose: that, having turned back, he might restore himself, as the prophet Ezekiel says: “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. 18:23). And again: “Let them turn back,” he says, “and I will replant them” (ibid., 6).

(Vers. 12–13.) When I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened for me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit because I did not find Titus my brother; but, taking leave of them, I departed for Macedonia. He indicates that he went to Troas to preach the Gospel of Christ to them, and that, when he had begun preaching, there were people who received the word of faith. But because Titus’ companionship was lacking, the labor caused by the tumult of the opposition was unbearable. For although some of them had opened their hearts to receive the word of God, [Note: Some manuscripts: “nevertheless, because of the recklessness of the unbelievers”] there was a considerable insolence among the unbelievers, rising up against the Apostle out of zeal for those who believed. These two tasks could not be fulfilled by one person: both to instruct the faithful and to resist the unbelievers. Therefore, taking leave of those who had received him, he departed for Macedonia.

(Vers. 14.) But thanks be to God, who always triumphs through us in Christ Jesus. This means that God triumphs in Christ through the apostles, making them victors in the faith of Christ, so that unbelief is trampled down and faith possesses the trophy, while unbelievers become believers and the malicious do not succeed in persecuting those who believe.

(Vers. 15.) And through us manifests the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. The fragrance of the knowledge of God is in Christ and through Christ. He said “fragrance” for this reason: just as certain things, though not seen, are nevertheless recognized by their smell, and one understands that something unseen is present in a particular place, so also God, because he is invisible, wished to be understood through Christ. Thus the preaching of Christ—which, being invisible, reaches the ears just as a scent reaches the nostrils—might make known God the Father [Note: Older editions and Codex Corbeiensis: “might make known the Creator to creation”] and his only-begotten Son.

The apostles, acting as ambassadors in this matter, as the Lord says to God, the Son to the Father, “As you sent me into this world, so I also send them into this world” (John 17:18), were to manifest the fragrance of the knowledge of God and Christ through signs and wonders. The truth of this preaching concerning God and Christ is proved by the testimony of its power. It is represented by fragrance because, although God is not seen, through this power—which works invisibly—he is understood to be present in the apostles, so that the truth of the teaching may be manifested.

Whoever rightly proclaims Christ is a good fragrance to God, worthy of praise in the one who believes and not blameworthy in the one who does not believe. But whoever does not rightly proclaim Christ is a bad fragrance to God, both among those who are faithful and among those who distrust; for he will be guilty on behalf of both. The one who distrusts seems not to believe because what he hears is perverse; and the one who believes believes wrongly.

The Apostle therefore spoke according to the reasoning of the Law: just as in the Law the one who offered sacrifices with good intention was a good and acceptable fragrance to God, so now the power of preaching provides God with the burning fragrance of teaching. For this reason God made the apostles secure by his assistance [Note: Codex Laudensis: “God wholly supplied the apostles with assistance, so that they might pour forth the word, etc.”], so that they might pour the words of his knowledge into receptive ears, whether of Jews or Gentiles, adding to them the mystery of the birth of the Lord Jesus according to the will of God and his Father, in the unity of saving faith, for the salvation of believers and the destruction of those who distrust.

(Vers. 16.) To some, indeed, we are the fragrance of death leading to death. He says this because to unbelievers the preaching of Christ’s cross is a fragrance of death. For when they hear the word of God, they receive it as though it were a pestilence from which death arises; and it is necessary that it happen to them according to their faith. But to others, a fragrance of life leading to life. This is true, because to the faithful the word heard from God is a messenger of eternal salvation, and according to their faith it will happen to them. Therefore, whether among those who are perishing or among those who are being saved, the apostles were the good fragrance of Christ to God, because they preached sincerely [Col. 0284C] and without flattery.

Those who did not believe were tying the noose for themselves, while these others were free, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Preach; if they listen to you, you will gain their souls. But if they do not, let them see to themselves; you, nevertheless, will be free from their destruction” (Ezek. 3:19).

(Vers. 17.) And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not like the many who adulterate the word of God, but in sincerity, as from God and before God, we speak in Christ. This verse touches upon the pseudo-apostles, who, having corrupted the teaching, adulterated the words of God by a faulty interpretation, removing the divine meaning and substituting a human one. Some of them, zealous for Jewish tradition, did not teach rightly concerning Christ; therefore he calls them less competent. The apostles, however, preached sincerely, speaking in Christ as from God, that is, as God had given it, before God, with God himself as witness. They did not seek their own glory, but God’s. To speak in Christ means to proclaim his honor and power.

176 **CHAPTER III**

(Vers. 1.) Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Since he censures the pseudo-apostles, exposing their wicked inventions, and testifies that he himself is a true preacher, he appears to be commending himself again, as in the First Epistle. And lest he seem to do this through some worldly cunning for the sake of profit, he added: Do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you or from you? By saying this, he clears his own intention and once again censures the pseudo-apostles, whom he shows to travel around the churches for the sake of their own honor and gain, to take away salvation rather than to bestow it.

They belonged to those of whom the Lord says: “You devour widows’ houses while praying long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater judgment” (Matt. 23:14). For these men seized both their possessions and their souls. The Apostle, however, did not touch their possessions, and through the truth of his teaching saved their souls. Therefore he commended himself not carnally but spiritually, for the advancement of their salvation, so that they might believe of him [Col. 0285B] what he was. For whoever thinks wrongly about a good man sins; and consequently this commendation benefits them all the more. [Note: The following words are lacking in Codex Corbeiensis: “so that they might believe this about him … it benefits them all the more.”]

(Vers. 2.) You are our letter, written in our hearts. The Apostle’s letter is an indication of salvation. Therefore he rightly says that the salvation of the Corinthians was in the heart of the Apostle and of those who were with him; for they were always thinking about their salvation. Since, then, they are in the hearts of the Apostle and of those who were with him, they are letters written in their hearts, because whoever always remembers someone has that person written in his mind.

(Vers. 3.) Which is known and read by all people, since you are manifestly a letter of Christ, ministered by us. It is clear that when Christians are called a letter of Christ, they indicate the salvation that God gave in Christ to all people, with the apostles as the writers; for while they teach, they write.

Written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God. Since the things promised are eternal, they are said to be written by the Spirit of God, who is eternal. Temporal things, however, are written with ink, which fades and destroys memory.

Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts. He now attacks the old Law, which, having first been given on tablets of stone, was abolished when Moses broke the tablets beneath the mountain (Exod. 32:19). The new Law is written in the mind—that is, in the heart—not by a pen but by the Spirit. Since faith is eternal, it is written by the Spirit so that it may remain. The old commandments, however, will cease when the world comes to an end. Therefore, just as one law differs from another, so the ministers of that Law differ from the ministers of the Law of faith.

[Col. 0285D] (Vers. 4.) Now we have such confidence through Christ toward God. He reveals how great the dignity of the apostles is when he says: “We have such confidence toward God through Christ.” He shows that the ancients did not have this confidence toward God, because their administration was lesser.

(Vers. 5–6.) Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to consider anything as coming from ourselves, as though it were from us; but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament—not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Although he exalts the apostolic dignity, he nevertheless breaks forth in praise of God [Col. 0286A], attributing this not to human merits but to the grace of the one who deigned to establish, for the life of humanity, a saving proclamation. Through the forgiveness of sins given by Jesus Christ our Lord, this proclamation was to save those whom the old Law held guilty.

The letters were given to Moses for this purpose: that, according to the law of nature, they might kill those who despised the Law. But the Spirit—that is, the law of faith, which is not written but held within the mind—gives life to those condemned to death, provided that they turn back, so that, having been justified, they do not sin thereafter.

The Law was therefore rightly given, so that there might be fear of sinning. But because the human race is fragile, the mercy of God was given in the preaching entrusted to the apostles, so that, with sins forgiven, those who believe in Christ might escape death. This is the preaching of the New Testament, which God had promised through the prophets.

[Col. 0286B] (Vers. 7–8.) Now if the administration of death, formed in letters on stones, was in glory—so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, which is being brought to an end—how will the administration of the Spirit not be even more in glory? It is clear [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “that its glory is greater”] that the grace of the law of faith is greater than that of the law of Moses.

Although the law of Moses was given for the sake of helping, when it was despised it became a law of death. Therefore, since it could not provide for sinners, the law of faith came, which would save them—not merely forgiving them but also justifying them.

There is therefore a great difference between one law and the other. At that time, those stained by sin could not gaze upon the face of Moses as he descended from the mountain with the Law received on tablets, because his face had become glorious and could not be looked upon by sinners [Col. 0286C], who were worthy of death (Exod. 34:30). This glory is now brought to an end through the law of the Spirit, when, having received forgiveness of sins and been made righteous, people become worthy and able to behold the glory of God, just as Peter, John, and James saw the glory of Christ on the mountain (Matt. 17:2).

(Vers. 9.) For if there is glory in the administration of condemnation, much more will the administration of righteousness abound in glory. He says this because the gift of God’s righteousness through the faith of Christ is greater than that of the old Law. For there is greater glory in salvation than in death. Although condemnation is just, it contributes more to praise when God shows mercy, so that the guilty person may be able to correct himself.

(Vers. 10.) For what was glorified in this respect has not been made glorious, because of the surpassing glory. It is clear that what appeared glorious in the face of Moses was not made glorious [Col. 0286D] (Exod. 34:29). For since the glory of his face benefited no one, but rather caused harm, it bore no fruit of glory—not because of any fault of his own, but because of sinners. Nevertheless, in this respect it is not glory.

The greater glory is that which abounds in grace, so that people, purified by God’s gift and having their darkness wiped away, may be able to see the glory of Christ.

(Vers. 11.) For if what is being brought to an end was in glory, much more will what remains be in glory. He does not deny that there was glory in the Law or in the face of Moses, but it did not remain, because it existed in Moses as something future, not as the truth itself. Therefore, when the Savior came, the figure ceased, because the truth appeared, remaining forever. Thus, to the extent that an image differs from the truth, so much does the glory of Moses’ face differ from the glory of Christ.

For this reason he said above: “Because of the surpassing glory.” The former glory was as great as was appropriate for a servant to receive; but the latter is as great as that of his begetter, because the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:11). [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “For just as during the night … when Christ appeared in glory.”] Just as the stars are glorious in the evening, but when the sun rises their brightness is brought to an end, so the glory of Moses is brought to an end when the glory of Christ appears.

(Vers. 12.) Therefore, since we have such hope, let us use great confidence. He says that we have hope of seeing glory—not such as there was in the face of Moses, but the glory that the three apostles saw on the mountain when the Lord revealed himself (Matt. 17:2).

From this we ought to infer [Col. 0287B] how much divine mercy has bestowed upon us and how greatly it has deigned to enrich us with the gift of a grace higher than that which had been given to the Jews. For the Jews, when the glory of Moses’ face was lesser, could not gaze upon it; but we believe that we shall see not the glory of Moses, which is inferior, but the surpassing glory of the Savior. The Jews, therefore, did not merit to see the glory of the servant; but we shall see the glory of our common Lord.

Therefore we too ought, insofar as we can, to return something in response to God’s goodwill, so that we may be more ardent in love for the one who has given us confidence—washing us from our sins—in order that we may see the glory of God. Now, then, it is necessary that the confidence prepared by good works grow within us; for we shall see only as much as we believe.

[Col. 0287C] (Vers. 13.) And not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon the end of what was being brought to an end. Since, by the grace of God, we have been made worthy to see the glory of Christ, he therefore says: “And not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon it” (Exod. 34:33).

He placed the veil because they could not endure the splendor of his face on account of sin. Once that sin has been removed, the power to see the glory of God is granted to the end, because the glory is not revealed so long as they remain with the Law; but when they turn to the grace of faith, it is brought to an end. For when dignity comes through faith, indignity is brought to an end.

(Vers. 14.) But their minds were hardened until the present day. He says that they remain hardened for as long as they do not believe. This hardness has come upon them because of unbelief. Therefore, when they turn to faith, the sharpness of the mind is restored, so that they may see the splendor of the divine light.

[Note: Roman edition alone: “This very hardness in the reading, etc.”]

This same veil remains in the reading of the Old Testament so long as it is not revealed, because it is brought to an end in Christ. He says that this hardness remains in the reading of Exodus for as long as they do not believe. For it is not revealed unless they believe. In Christ it is brought to an end—that is, through the faith of Christ the veil is removed. Once the offense has been removed, they begin to see what, while sin stood in the way, they could not see.

[Col. 0288A] 178 (Vers. 15.) But to this present day, whenever Moses is read (Exod. 34:33), a veil lies over their heart. It is clear that when this part of the Law is read, the judgment of those who are under the Law is being recited.

(Vers. 16.) But whenever he turns to the Lord, the veil will be removed. To turn to the Lord means to believe in Christ, so that, recognizing the Lord, a person may merit to receive forgiveness. This is the removal of the veil: the nullification of the sentence by which he was held guilty under the Law.

(Vers. 17.) Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Since God is Spirit, through Christ he gave the law of the Spirit—not written in letters, but impressed upon souls through faith. It does not teach visible things, but urges belief in invisible things; it is grasped spiritually by the mind, not perceived by the eye. This law gives freedom, asking only faith, so that, because a person believes what he does not see, he may merit to be rescued from bondage.

(Vers. 18.) Therefore we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being formed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. By “we all” he means all who have obtained freedom through the gift of God’s grace. Beholding the glory of the Lord through faith, we are transformed into the same image for which we hope—that is, so that, when this life has passed, we may be found like the image of Christ’s glory, as the apostle John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2).

From glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord—that is, [Col. 0288C] [Note: Some manuscripts: “having been raised up by the benefit of God from the glory of Moses”] having been raised, through God’s gift, from the glory of Moses, which because of guilt we were unable to see, we are transformed into the glory that we believe is given to us by the Spirit of the Lord.

The amount of glory will be as much as it is fitting for God to give through his Spirit. For this reason he said: “As by the Spirit of the Lord,” to show that such glory is given as corresponds to the majesty of the giver. The glory of Moses was neither so great nor everlasting; he received glory according to the measure of the Law. Likewise, according to the measure of the law of faith, in which the Spirit of God is present, glory will be given to believers. For God has granted so much to the faithful that he gives them his Spirit [Note: Several manuscripts: “as the pledge of that grace”], the pledge of the glory that he promised.

**CHAPTER IV**

(Vers. 1.) Therefore, since we have this ministry, just as we have received mercy, let us not fail. He says that we possess such hope in this ministry that we do not fail amid pressures, strengthened by faith in the promises. Hence above he said: “Let us use great confidence” (2 Cor. 3:12). For those who trust in what has been promised endure whatever adversity occurs. He attributes this not to human merits but to the mercy of God, which first washes a person, then justifies him, adopting him as a son for God, so that he may grant him a glory like the glory of God’s own Son.

[Col. 0289A] (Vers. 2.) But we renounce the hidden things of shame. He teaches that, if a person is to be worthy of that glory, all shameful and polluted things that can be done or conceived must be removed, so that they may be expelled not only from conduct but also from thought. These are the words of one who invites them. Speaking in his own person and that of his companions, he urges them toward a better life because of the vices mentioned above, [Note: Roman edition: “which he often reproves in these epistles”] which he has frequently censured in these letters.

These hidden things of shame may also be the things they perversely devise for preaching in order to deceive. Hence he adds: Not walking in cunning or adulterating the word of God. For the one who, with a deceitful mind, fabricates a teaching in order to deceive simple hearts contributes to its shame and disfigurement; he will be found shameful on the day of God’s judgment. For the cunning of an evil mind adulterates the words of God in order to accomplish what it desires and to twist their meaning. To adulterate is to wish to exclude the true meaning by means of a false one.

But by the manifestation of the truth, commending ourselves to every human conscience before God. He says this because in evangelical preaching [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “he makes no one suspicious”] he made himself suspect to no one, adding still more when he says: “Before God,” so that he might prove this to be manifest not only to human beings but also to God, from whom nothing is hidden. He therefore calls upon God as witness [Note: Several manuscripts: “so that he himself might be believed”], so that he too may be believed, because he preaches as it was given by the Author. God is witness in this way: by causing signs and wonders to be performed through his hands.

(Vers. 3.) But even if our Gospel is still veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing. This is true, because unbelievers do not see the splendor of God’s power, being blinded by unbelief. For a veil lies over their heart, and the hardness of unbelief, especially among the Jews [Col. 0289C].

(Vers. 4.) In them the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers [Note: Codex Vallensis alone: “has blinded the minds of unbelievers with respect to the faith of Christ.” And, with some manuscripts: “the light of the glory of Christ”], so that they do not see the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. He calls the god of worldly people the one who blinds their minds, because they are malicious toward the faith of Christ, so that they may not see the truth of the Gospel of the glory of Christ. Thus he grants them what they want. For since they are malicious and, although they understand the truth, say that it is false, they are thereby assisted in being unable to believe [Note: Most manuscripts: “what they want”; other manuscripts and editions more correctly: “what they do not want”] what they do not wish to believe.

Although Christ is the image of God, they assert that he is merely corporeal. Abandoning his deeds, they speak only of the flesh. Concerning them Isaiah said: “He has blinded their eyes, so that they may not see, and their ears, so that they may not hear, to this present day” (Isa. 6:10).

[Col. 0289D] (Vers. 5.) For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus our Lord. This means that we do not proclaim our own glory, lest anyone say that we preach the Gospel for our own sake, perhaps so that it might benefit us for a time. Rather, we proclaim Jesus our Lord, submitting ourselves to his power and majesty.

When, therefore, we burden no one, assault no one, and confess Christ [Col. 0290A] our Lord, why should we be judged arrogant, as though we preached for our own advantage, so that we might appear glorious? But we are your servants for Jesus’ sake. He proves himself so completely to be Christ’s servant that, at Christ’s command, he testifies that he is their minister in preaching, so that, for their benefit, he and his companions may be subject in the ministry of the Gospel.

By calling himself a servant, he means a minister; but he spoke humbly in this way to show truly that he does not preach the Gospel for his own glory [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “but through the love of Christ”], but for the glory of our Lord, whom he obeys and serves, just as the Lord himself says: “I am among you not as one who is served, but as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). He does this not because of the merit of those whom he serves, but because of the Lord’s command.

(Vers. 6.) For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus. He says that it happened through God’s mercy that we—who had been unbelieving in ignorance, that is, in darkness—might give light to the other nations through us [Col. 0290B]. How greatly does he still humble himself, preferring the glory of God alone and of Christ? He is illuminated so that they may have knowledge of the glory of God through Christ.

For this reason he says “the knowledge of the glory of God”—that is, not of God alone, but also of Christ, who is his glory. He signifies that not only God himself is to be known, but also his works, mercy, and providence, by which he created and saved the human race, having appeared in Christ through the glory of his power.

(Vers. 7.) [Note: The same Roman edition: “But we have this treasure … so that the excellence may be … The treasure signifies the mystery, etc.”] But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may be God’s and not from us. By the treasure he signifies the mystery of God in Christ, which is revealed to believers but is covered by a certain veil for unbelievers. For just as a treasure is kept hidden, so the mystery of God is hidden within a person—that is, in the human heart.

He therefore says that this treasure has been given by God in mind and body, so that the excellence of God’s power may appear through human preachers alone. Thus every tongue may be reconciled to its Creator, not for the honor of human beings but of God, who reveals himself through human beings. Although they were humble and unskilled, they received from God the power both to speak great things and to perform them. [Note: Codex Corbeiensis: “By calling them earthen vessels, he signifies the weakness of human nature, because no one can do anything, etc.”]

By calling them earthen vessels, therefore, he signifies the weakness of human nature, which can do nothing unless it receives power from God. God proclaims himself through these weak things for his own praise, so that glory may be given to him, not to the human being formed from clay.

(Vers. 8.) We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed. Now he shows why they were competent preachers: because God was always present with them in their need. Therefore he says: We have suffered pressure, but have not been crushed. That is, God did not permit us to be oppressed so greatly [Col. 0291A] that we should believe.

We have suffered want, but have not been abandoned. That is, when we were placed in poverty, God the shepherd was present with us.

(Vers. 9.) We have suffered persecution, but have not been forsaken. It is true [Note: The same Codex Corbeiensis: “God comforted them”], because God cared for them, so that their enemies might not satisfy their hostility against them. We have been cast down, but have not perished. That is, struck down by blows, but, because God stood in the way, not killed. Whether imprisoned or bound, they escaped the hands of their enemies through God’s help.

Accordingly, when Paul and Silas were imprisoned, already beaten, and their feet had been fastened in the stocks, they sang a hymn joyfully to God, having become stronger than those who had not been beaten.

(Vers. 10.) Always carrying in our body the death of the Lord Jesus [180], so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our body. There is no doubt that Christ is killed in the martyrs, and that in those who suffer for the faith—whether exile or death, imprisonment, or blows [Col. 0291B] [Note: Roman edition: “They suffer or undergo exile”; the remaining editions and manuscripts: “they suffer or undergo departures,” that is, death, slaughter, etc.]—the sufferings of Christ are present, so that his life may also be openly manifested in their bodies.

For these sufferings reveal the merit that leads to the future life promised by Christ. Hence he says elsewhere: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12:10). And again: “Through tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22).

(Vers. 11.) [Note: The same Roman edition: “For we who live are always …” And below: “that is, we do not fear death.”] For we who live are always being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. What he says is clear: we do not refuse to be handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, although we are able to live, so that the life by which Christ rose from the dead may be bestowed upon our mortal flesh—that is, we do not fear dying because of the resurrection that has been promised.

(Vers. 12.) Thus death is at work in us, but life in you. He says this because they were subjected to death for the sake of the Corinthians’ salvation. For while preaching to the Gentiles, they stirred up hostility against themselves from both Jews and Gentiles, even to the point of death.

(Vers. 13.) But since we have the same spirit of faith—that is, the common spirit by which faith is strengthened, [Note: [Col. 0291D] The Laud manuscript: “the Spirit which we possess with firm faith”; [Col. 0292D] “with you.”] we have it with you. For this reason he suffered such great evils on their behalf, so that they might be joined to one another in faith. As it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (Ps. 115:1). He gave this example from Psalm 115 in order to show that he was ready to endure everything because he believed in the future resurrection. Thus, secure concerning the future life, he has no concern for the present life; [Col. 0291D] [Note: The old edition and several manuscripts: “he has no concern for the present life.”] for this is believed: that the blessed life may then be hoped for if this life is despised. Secure, therefore, because what he believed is true, he dares to preach it, so that he may make others share in his hope.

Knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus [Note: [Col. 0292D] The Roman edition: “will also raise us through Jesus.”] will also raise us with Jesus and establish us with you. He says that he labors for the sake of faith in this hope, because the resurrection of the Lord Jesus goes before as an example, showing what those who believe will become; for just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. Adam is the pattern of death, the cause of sin; Christ, however, is the pattern of life because of righteousness, since he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. And because he called these people participants in the common faith, he says that, once raised, he will establish them with you, so that those of one faith may be in one house of peace. For when they understand that he suffers deadly things on their behalf, they too are concerned about the sufferings of these men, as though suffering with them; together they will also share in the promised life, so that, having been saddened together, they may rejoice together. He speaks in this way because of those who denied the resurrection, whom he also rebukes in the First Epistle.

(Vers. 14, 15.) For everything is for your sake, [Note: [Col. 0292D] The same Roman edition: “so that the abundant gift.”] so that abundant grace, through the thanksgiving of many, may abound to the glory of God. God did not wish anyone to be alienated from his gift. And because not everyone embraces the word of faith, the Apostle, knowing God’s will, did not fear suffering persecutions and dangers, provided only that he preached faithfully to all, so that more might believe; so that God’s abundant gift might not be diminished, to God’s insult, by the thanksgiving of only a few, but might benefit many and overflow through the thanksgiving of many to the glory of God. How worthy of honor, then, is the man who always subjected his soul to death, lest God’s gift produce an effect far different from that for which it was given! Is it not a great insult to one who prepares a sumptuous dinner and invites many, if only a few are present at the feast?

[Col. 0292C] (Vers. 16.) Therefore we do not lose heart. It is clear that this belongs to the preceding thought. In order to show his devotion to God’s affairs as still more earnest, he added these words, by which he proves that in no way does he fail to accomplish what is pleasing to God, while remaining secure concerning the promised resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0292D] The Roman edition: “And although our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man,” etc.] And although our outward man is being corrupted, the inward man is nevertheless renewed day by day. Through pressures, blows, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness, the flesh is corrupted; but the soul is renewed by hope of the future reward, because it is purified by continual tribulations. It advances through pressure; it does not perish. Thus, as temptations increase, it daily gains in merit; for this corruption also benefits the body, leading to immortality through the merit of the soul.

(Vers. 17.) For this momentary and light affliction of ours, which is in the present, produces for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure in sublimity. He calls the tribulations of the present time, which are inflicted because of faith, momentary and light because they are temporary; yet for those who endure them they produce an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure and in the highest degree. For great reward is given for small labors, and in exchange for light tribulation the sublimity of everlasting glory will be reckoned beyond all measure.

[Col. 0293A] (Vers. 18.) We do not contemplate what is seen, but what is not seen; for what is seen is temporary, while what is not seen is eternal. He declares that, possessing a desire for heavenly and spiritual things, he despises these present and earthly things, because in comparison with spiritual realities they are nothing. For these things stand in relation to heavenly things as a figure does to reality: the figure passes away, but the reality remains. Therefore the righteous do not fear leaving this world; rather, they rejoice.

CHAPTER V

(Vers. 1.) We know that if our earthly house, this dwelling, is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens. With this confidence he says that one should not fear being dissolved from the body by the violence of unbelievers or by the lot [Col. 0293B] of life, because an eternal dwelling of this kind has been prepared in heaven for such people, so that, expelled from the temporal and earthly dwelling, they may be received into an everlasting house. Hence this too ought to be desired, if it can happen; but since this ought not to be desired lest another perish through your glory, [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Roman edition: “which is already heavenly.”] nevertheless, if it should happen, it must be borne willingly.

For he called this flesh an earthly house because it is mortal. Thus, if we are dissolved from it, we shall find an eternal house built in the heavens. This house signifies the immortal body in which we shall always exist after rising; its form has already been revealed in heaven in the body of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Vallian manuscript: “if nevertheless he should kill.”]

(Vers. 2, 3.) For in this dwelling of ours we groan, longing to put on over it that which is from heaven, if indeed, once clothed, we shall not be found naked. Therefore he says that we groan in prayers, so that the glory promised from heaven may clothe us after we rise. Thus they persist in prayer, desiring this, lest, once risen and having received the body, they be found naked—that is, strangers to the promised glory. For this is what must happen: once the soul has been clothed with the body, it must also be clothed, by God’s judgment, with the glory that consists in transformation into brightness.

[Note: [Col. 0293D] The section from “For death is from the earth” through “For when we are” is entirely absent from the Corbie manuscripts.] For death is from the earth, but resurrection is from heaven, provided that it is transformed into glory. Other manuscripts read as follows: “If indeed, having been stripped, we shall not be found naked”; that is, if, when we leave the body, we shall be clothed with Christ; [Note: [Col. 0293D] Several manuscripts: “Whoever is baptized puts on Christ.”] for whoever is baptized in Christ puts on Christ (Gal. 3:27). Therefore, if we remain in the form of baptism and in its tradition, when stripped of the body we are not found naked, because Christ dwells in the inward man. [Col. 0293D] When we are seen to have put him on, or to have the Holy Spirit given to us, we shall be worthy to be clothed over with the promised heavenly glory. For the promised brightness will fall upon the one in whom it sees the sign of adoption.

(Vers. 4.) [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Roman edition: “For while we are in this body, we groan.”] For while we are in this body—that is, the mortal body—we groan under a burden, because we do not wish to be unclothed, [Col. 0294A] but to be clothed over, so that this mortal nature may be swallowed up by life. The meaning is the same: he says that we are burdened by the sufferings of the body, [Note: [Col. 0293D] The Corbie manuscript: “And even in death to direct petitions to God, so that the body itself may not be alienated from us, but so that we may always be clothed with immortality, so that it may no longer be able to die or be entangled in sufferings—that is, so that it may be swallowed up by life. But who brings this to completion,” etc.] and by the storms of the world itself, and that we should direct petitions to God, lest we be changed by being overcome and become unworthy; but rather, when our departure occurs, may we be found clothed in the Holy Spirit, who in substance is Christ. Then we shall be able to be clothed over with the promised glory, if, having been stripped of the body, we have not been stripped of the Holy Spirit. Thus mortality is swallowed up by life: that is, when we rise, we are clothed over with immortality together with glory, so that we can no longer die or be entangled in sufferings. This is what it means to be swallowed up by life; for one who rises in order to be driven into punishments ought not to be said to have been swallowed up by life.

(Vers. 5.) Now the one who brings us to this very state [Col. 0294B] is God, who has also given us the Spirit as a pledge. [Note: [Col. 0294D] The same Corbie manuscript: “What we ask for is this: not that we be stripped of the body forever, but that, once it has been received on the day of God’s judgment, we may be clothed over with immortality together with glory. He is said to confess God because he promised,” etc.] What we ask for while groaning—that is, not that we may deserve to be stripped, but that we may deserve to be clothed over, in accordance with the preceding interpretation—he says that God will bring to completion on the day of judgment, because he has promised and is faithful, giving the Spirit as a pledge that this matter will be fulfilled. For the Spirit is the seal of our adoption.

(Vers. 6, 7.) Therefore, always confident and knowing that while dwelling in this body we are away from the Lord—for we walk by faith, not by sight. It is clear that by faith we are with the Lord, not by presence; and thus we are away from him not in faith, but in sight. Why, then, since he says the same thing in the Acts of the Apostles—“For in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)—does he say here that we are away from the Lord? If he is everywhere, how, placed here, are we away from the Lord? Without doubt he is everywhere; indeed, all things are in God. But because God’s dwelling is in heaven and he is always seen there, we are said to be away from him here, where he is not seen. For when we do not see him, although he is present, we are absent from him.

(Vers. 8.) Therefore we are confident and agree that we would rather be away from the body and present with God. He rightly says “we are confident”; for, possessing confidence in God’s promise, [Note: [Col. 0294D] The Roman edition: “And knowing that it is much more advantageous to be there than in the body.”] and knowing that it is far more advantageous to be there than in this world, they agree and desire to depart from the body, so that they may rest beneath the altar of God until the day of the resurrection.

(Vers. 9.) And therefore we strive, whether present or away, to be pleasing to him. He says that this must be done, and that one must persist in good works, so that, whether we are still placed in this life or are present before Christ’s tribunal, we may please him. Therefore, if discipline is maintained, we shall please him both here and there; for whoever pleases him here will not displease him there.

(Vers. 10.) For we must all be revealed before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to him according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Therefore, if, when Christ judges, each of us will receive the deeds done in the body, he will certainly not be judged good or evil without the body. And he did not say “the deeds of the flesh,” because the vices of the flesh are always to be punished, but “the deeds of the body,” which sometimes acts spiritually and sometimes carnally. [Note: [Col. 0295D] The same edition: “Each will be judged good or evil according to the deeds of the body.”]

(Vers. 11.) Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but we are manifest to God. Since, then, God’s judgment is to come through Christ in order to distinguish the works of each person, the Apostle says that he persuades them toward sound understanding and life, so that his hearers may be secure concerning the future punishment, and so that he himself may glory, having the fruit of his labors in them. For through the perverse speech of some, the day of God’s judgment is brought into doubt: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

“We persuade people,” he says, so that they may believe and take precautions lest they fall into punishment and repent only then, [Note: [Col. 0295D] The Laud manuscript: “when repentance has no fruit.”] when repentance has no fruit. “But we are manifest to God”: for he preached what God had commanded, and God is said to know what is good. Indeed, to those who do evil he says: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). But I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences.

Their purity was manifest to the Corinthians, because they had never been caught in flattery, their preaching had not displeased the holy, nor had they secretly tried to extract anything from anyone, as is customary, so that they might appear simple before the crowds but inwardly be impostors. Therefore he appeals to their conscience, so that they themselves might be witnesses to the truth of these men.

[Col. 0295C] (Vers. 12.) We are not commending ourselves to you again. Since above, while affirming the truth of his preaching, he seemed to praise himself, he now indicates the same thing: that he is not saying this for his own praise, but for their glory, so that they may rejoice that they have learned sound preaching from those who announce it.

But we give you an occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have something to say against those who glory in appearance and not in heart. He says this because many, through arrogance, gloried in themselves on account of the apostles, claiming that they had been taught by those who had always been with the Lord. Therefore he says here that he gives them a defense by which they too might glory against such people, because he was an apostle from whom these men also had learned. Hence elsewhere he says: “I have done nothing less than those who are very apostles” (2 Cor. 12:11). He says this under compulsion, lest his silence harm them.

Therefore the one who glories in his heart restrains pride, knowing that God gives grace to the humble but resists the proud (Jas. 4:6); for the mind of the proud produces no fruit worthy of God.

(Vers. 13.) For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are of sound mind, it is for you. He says this, [Note: [Col. 0295D] The Roman edition: “Because if he is thought to have spoken loftily or insanely … it must be forgiven. For all pride is regarded as a kind of insanity. But if he is understood not to have spoken proudly … it must be left to God. For charity,” etc.] because if he is thought to have spoken boastfully or arrogantly—since he seemed to praise himself—this must be forgiven by God. But if he is understood not to have spoken proudly, but to have spoken for the glory of his hearers, he says that it benefits the Corinthians. His words are sound for his hearers if they are understood as they were spoken; but if they are thought to have been spoken boastfully, they must be forgiven by God as something like madness, since all pride is regarded as a kind of irrationality.

(Vers. 14.) For the love of Christ urges us, having judged this: that if one died for all, then all died. Since Christ, loving the human race, gave himself over to death in order to redeem them, the apostles, in order to repay him in some measure, exhort people to his service. And in order to draw them, they must testify that they themselves preach the truth, since others teach wicked things; nor must they conceal their own merit, so that they may point out the punishment of evil teachers.

They did not act, therefore, from mental arrogance, but so that Christ’s gift might be understood by all and that, faithfully devoted to him, they might return thanks. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Because of Christ, from these words through “Therefore all died,” there is a gap in the Corbie manuscript; the other manuscripts and editions largely agree among themselves, except for a transposition made in the Roman edition: “… they are silent, so that the apostles’ praise might be recognized, not for the sake of boasting … lest it appear fruitless. For through the merit,” etc.] Because of Christ’s love, therefore, they do not remain silent about how great and how many his gifts are toward those who love him—not for the sake of boasting, but to invite their hearers to devotion to him, lest Christ’s death appear fruitless, not so that the apostles’ praise might be recognized. For through the merit and glory of the apostles, Christ’s grace and God’s beneficence are recognized.

(Vers. 15.) Therefore all died, and Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them. Since all must die because of Adam, Christ died for all in order to free them from the second death. Therefore those who live in the body, knowing that Christ died for them, must be subject to him and confess him as Lord. For since his death benefits them, his resurrection bears witness to it. Thus the person does not live for himself who is ready to do the will of his Lord.

(Vers. 16.) Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way. It is true that, when Christ rose from the dead, carnal birth in him ceased, bodily weakness ceased, and the suffering of death also ceased. [Note: [Col. 0296D] The Corbie manuscript: “the suffering of death.” This is not said on Christ’s account, as though the lot of human weakness touched him, but on our account, for whom an example was given: if we follow the footsteps of the one who died for us, then likewise, when we rise at the promised time after the departure from this life, every weakness and corruption will cease. Therefore he says, “from now on we know according to the flesh,” because in Christ’s resurrection the general pattern of incorruption and brightness was given, so that it might be known that this would come to all who obey Christ. Therefore, if any …] Until the cross there was a suspicion of weakness in Christ; afterward, however, what had not been believed appeared, just as he himself says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John 8:28).

The Apostle recalls this in order to show with what devotion Christ must be served. For the salvation of human beings he not only did not disdain to be born as a human being, but also willed to be subjected to insults and to die, so that, understanding how precious his death is, they might serve him more earnestly—not as though they were repaying a debt to a human being, but to God, since each person’s service must be rendered according to his standing and merits.

(Vers. 17.) Therefore, if there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. It is clear that through Christ all things have been renewed, if they recognize his dignity. For he becomes new to those for whom he previously seemed to be merely human when he is understood to be God. Thus, when weakness has departed, his divinity is acknowledged; and when the old error has ceased—the error that, by introducing belief in many gods, had led the human race away from faith in the one true God—all things return to the profession of simplicity, worshiping one God in the Trinity.

(Vers. 18.) But all things are from God. Although Christ redeemed us, all things are nevertheless from God, because all fatherhood is from him (Eph. 3:15). Therefore the person of the Father must necessarily be placed first.

(Vers. 19, 20, 21.) He reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation on behalf of Christ. Therefore we act as ambassadors, as though God were exhorting through us: we entreat you, on behalf of Christ, to be reconciled to God.

He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. Almighty God, the Father of Christ—when all things that he had made through Christ had become subject to ruin through error and had forgotten their creator— [Note: [Col. 0297D] Thus the old edition and the manuscripts; the Roman edition differs only slightly, preferring: “Christ the Lord … was pleased to send … and to become flesh in the appearance of a human being.” The Corbie manuscript gives the passage as follows: “Christ our Lord was pleased to come from the sacred dwellings to earthly things, made according to the flesh in the appearance of a human being, so that he might be a pattern,” etc.] was pleased for Christ our Lord to come from the sacred dwellings to earthly things, and to become flesh in the appearance of a human being, so that he might be a pattern for human beings of how they should make God their creator favorable to themselves.

Therefore God was in Christ. How? As in a deputy or ambassador, as he was in the prophets, or in some other way? Can it be understood that he was in the Son in the same way as he was in the prophets? For the Son is naturally the ambassador of God the Father. Hence he says: “Because the Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 10:11). For the Father is understood to be in the Son because they have one substance. [Note: [Col. 0297D] The old edition and one or two manuscripts: “was naturally born of God the Father”; the Roman edition: “is naturally of God the Father”; but nearly all the manuscripts support the reading given here.] [Note: [Col. 0298D] Some manuscripts: “For truth is there.”]

There is unity where there is no difference; and therefore they are mutually in one another, because their image and likeness are one. Thus, whoever sees the Son is said to have seen the Father, just as the Lord himself says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 10:9). Therefore it is rightly said: “God was in Christ,” that is, the Father was in the Son, reconciling the world to himself and not counting their trespasses against them. For creation sinned against God and did not repent so as to return to him. God, unwilling that his work should perish, sent his Son, through whom he had created us, so that, after the forgiveness of sins had been preached to them, he might reconcile them to himself through the very one through whom he had created us.

[Note: [Col. 0298D] The Corbie manuscript: “He created us, placing in us the word of reconciliation. On behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” It says that God commissioned the apostles through Christ so that, after Christ had returned triumphantly to heaven, they might proclaim among the nations the gift of God’s grace in his place, so that God might preach through the apostles just as through Christ.] Whether, then, through the Son or through servants, God exhorts the people, because all the whole matter must be referred to him, by whose will and providence Christ was incarnate for the redemption and salvation of human beings. When he wished to return to the Father, he entrusted to the disciples the dispensation he had received from the Father.

[Col. 0298B] Entreating you, on behalf of Christ, to be reconciled to God. This is what I said: he gave the apostles as deputies on behalf of Christ, so that they might preach reconciliation to God in his place.

(Vers. 22.) He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us. He says that God the Father made his Son Christ sin—him, namely, who knew no sin, that is, who had not sinned. For, having become flesh, he was not changed but became sin by being incarnate, just as one who becomes a prefect does not lose what he was, but assumes what he was not. Christ, therefore, became human because of sin, although neither that condition nor the dignity of being born as a human being touched him. But because all flesh is under sin, when he became flesh he also became sin.

And because he was offered for sins, he is not improperly said to have been made sin, since in the Law the victim that was offered for sins was also called “sin.” [Col. 0298C] So that we might become the righteousness of God through him who knew no sin, as Isaiah says: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Isa. 53:9). He was killed as though he were a sinner, so that sinners might be justified before God in Christ.

Satan was jealous of the Savior, seeing him teach human beings how to make God favorable to them by renouncing the devil. For this reason he killed him, unaware of what would come against himself. For after the cross Christ descended to the underworld and, having conquered death—for the one who knew no sin could not be held by death— [Note: [Col. 0298D] The Corbie manuscript: “through sin it grew in the underworld.”] death, through sin, emptied the underworld, so that the death of the righteous might benefit sinners; so that from then on death would be unable to hold those who bear the sign of the cross.

CHAPTER VI

(Vers. 1.) But as fellow workers, we also exhort you not to receive God’s grace in vain. The Apostle strives in two ways to care for human salvation: so that he might remain devoted to God’s providence and render the service of charity to human beings. [Note: [Col. 0299D] The Roman edition: “to take care”; the old edition, together with many manuscripts: “to submit care”; but other manuscripts more correctly: “to undertake care.” In the following verse the same Roman edition has “might show charity,” whereas the others, together with all the manuscripts, read “might show the service of charity.”]

(Vers. 2.) “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 59:8). This is written in the prophet Isaiah. He teaches that God’s grace was predestined for the time of Christ; for God determined to pour out his mercy in such a way [Note: [Col. 0299D] All editions: “so that he might grant help to those invoking Christ’s name”; some manuscripts: “so that he might grant help by the name”; others: “so that he might grant help to those asking in the name of Christ.”] that he would grant help to those who asked in the name of Christ.

(Vers. 3.) Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. We give no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed. He says that the time has come in which sinners can advance toward pardon; he says that the time has come in which medicine can be infused into mortal diseases. Therefore he is anxious about the salvation of the sick, lest through some negligence the grace of his good will [Note: [Col. 0299D] The manuscripts and editions differ here only in that the editions and some manuscripts read “would lack the effect of his good will,” whereas more manuscripts do not have the conjunction. The Corbie manuscript reads “would attain the effect of good will,” where it is clear that a negation is needed.] should fail to achieve its effect.

By his faith and vigilance, therefore, he removes every cause of offense from the negligent, lest their sluggishness perhaps create an occasion of offense for the disciples. Thus they show themselves free, because they preach what is salutary simply and with complete earnestness. Hence he adds: “So that our ministry may not be blamed.” Their ministry would indeed be blamed if they did not give, by their own works, examples of the things they taught in words, so that others might do them.

(Vers. 4.) But in everything let us commend ourselves as ministers of God. The ministers of God teach without flattery, so that they may please the one whose ministers they are—not like the false apostles, who, knowing that they had not been sent by God, pursued present advantage. [Note: [Col. 0300D] The Corbie manuscript: “they hated present quarrels,” which is absurd. That manuscript, together with the other manuscripts and editions, has “if he had abused patience,” where the Roman edition reads “had patience”; but among authors the words “to use” and “to abuse” often have the same meaning.]

In great patience. Patience is what saves human beings. If he had not exercised patience, how could he have saved the Corinthians, whom after his preaching he found entangled in such great moral vices and in the errors of various sects? By his patience he gradually recalls them to true doctrine.

In pressures. He endured pressures, knowing what had been promised by God for them.

In necessities. Necessity also consisted in teaching while placed under pressure, because he had been sent by the Lord.

In hardships. Constricted by hope of the future, he did not yield to the opposition of the faithless.

(Vers. 5.) In beatings. Frequently beaten by Jews and Gentiles, he did not remain silent about Christ’s grace.

In prisons. Often sent to prison, he disregarded his own safety and preached God’s gift even there.

In disturbances. He was so devoted to God that not even disturbance [Col. 0299D] diminished the confidence he had in God.

In labors. He did not cease laboring with his own hands, so that he might not be a burden to anyone, certain that this benefited him before God.

In sleepless nights. He was so concerned about the ministry entrusted to him that he did not cease even at night.

In fastings. Sometimes he endured voluntary fasts, and sometimes fasts required by necessity because of poverty; and he gave thanks to God, who fed him spiritually. He was content for this reason, so that he would not be bent toward the concern of the stomach.

(Vers. 6.) In purity. By defending purity, whether of body or of the Gospel, he made not a few enemies.

In knowledge. [Note: [Col. 0300D] The Roman edition had omitted “of the Law and the Gospel,” which is found in all the others and in the manuscripts.] By affirming his knowledge of the Law and the Gospel—not in human wisdom or pretense—he showed himself to God as a faithful steward of Christ.

In long-suffering. He was great-hearted in bearing the weaknesses of the brethren and in despising this world. Hence elsewhere he says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

In kindness. He was kind, because just as he rebuked, so also he encouraged; after correction he consoled them with gentle exhortation.

In the Holy Spirit. “The Holy Spirit flees deceit” (Wis. 1:5). Since he taught sincerely, he conveyed God’s gift in the Holy Spirit.

In unfeigned love. [Note: [Col. 0300D] Gratian, at the cited passage in the margin: “Love is feigned when it abandons people in adversity.”] Love is feigned in those who abandon their brothers in necessity. Therefore, since he always made the necessities of the brethren his own, he was sincere in love (*De Poenitentia*, distinction 2, chapter “Ficta charitas”). For he sympathized with everyone, as he says elsewhere: “Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). This is true love: when, setting aside one’s own advantage, one cares for the person whom one professes to love. This is what the Apostle always did.

(Vers. 7.) In the word of truth. The word of truth was in his teaching, because he handed on nothing other than what he had received from the Lord.

In the power of God. God’s power was in him, proving him a suitable minister through signs and wonders.

With the weapons of righteousness at the right hand and at the left. [Col. 0300C] He signifies that he was free before believers and unbelievers. For the weapons of righteousness destroy iniquity.

(Vers. 8.) Through glory and dishonor. To those who regarded the Gospel of God as glorious, he openly declares that he was an upright and faithful preacher. Likewise, to those who considered the words of divine teaching dishonorable and deformed, he showed himself a faithful minister of God, since he was neither frightened nor ashamed to speak to them the things they dreaded hearing.

Through evil report and good report. He showed himself an upright steward of God even to those who formed a good opinion of the faith and to those who formed a bad one, since he did not fear this hostility but remained steadfast.

As deceivers, and yet truthful. Unbelievers called them deceivers; believers, on the contrary, declared them truthful and sincere. 186 He did not yield to this hatred in such a way as to spread a disguise over the truth.

As unknown, and yet recognized. They were unknown to the wicked but known to the good, for the good recognized the truth in them.

(Vers. 9.) As dying, and behold, we live. Those who hated them thought every day that they would not escape the threats of wickedness; but these men, because they taught with God’s favor, were protected by Christ’s help from present and future death.

As tested, but not handed over to death. They seemed to be tested when they were treated in such a way that they appeared likely to yield; and because they were not conquered, they were not delivered over to death. For the person who does not remain in the faith is delivered over to death—not this death, but the future one. This may also be understood of present death: God allowed them to be tested so that they might increase in merit through pressures, but he did not permit them to be killed.

(Vers. 10.) As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. It is true, [Note: [Col. 0301D] The Corbie manuscript: “because they magnified their joy through sorrow.”] because this sorrow produces joy, and those who saddened them with insults increased their joy.

As poor, yet enriching many. As far as the present life is concerned, they appeared poor; but they bestowed spiritual riches on believers: needy on earth, rich in heaven.

As having nothing, yet possessing everything. This was glorious in the apostles: without the anxiety and title of possession, they possessed not only the things contained in estates, but also the very owners of those things. For everything had to be placed at their feet because of their virtues, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4:35).

(Vers. 11.) Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians. He says this because of liberty and a pure conscience; for a mind conscious of evil trembles to speak, loses its meaning, and errs in its words.

Our heart is enlarged. The hearts of those who rejoice in themselves with the confidence of a good way of life are enlarged, [Note: [Col. 0301D] Some manuscripts: “or, certain of the hope of the future,” etc.] or certainly of those who, in tribulation, are not constricted by hope of a future reward. For just as in this life no return is received unless labor has gone before, so also in divine matters, unless deadly things go before, reward will not follow.

(Vers. 12, 13.) You are not constricted in us, but you are constricted in your own inward parts, having the same recompense of reward. He says this because it was not the teachers’ fault if the disciples went astray by despising the vigor of the teaching. Each person will receive a reward according to his works; for, as far as the teachers are concerned, they did not remain silent, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Raise your voice and speak to the people. If they listen to you, you will win them; if not, you will save your own soul” (Ezek. 3:19).

(Vers. 14.) As I speak to children, be enlarged also yourselves, and do not be yoked together with unbelievers. He exhorts them toward good conduct and hope, so that, confident and cleansing their consciences, they may be able to rejoice in themselves, possessing the confidence of a pure mind like their teachers and separating themselves from the society of unbelievers in evil works. By acting well and hoping for the future, therefore, he wishes them to be enlarged in spirit; [Note: [Col. 0301D] All editions and certain manuscripts: “For whoever works labors, and does not believe in the future”; the other manuscripts more suitably omit “works.” Of these, only the Corbie manuscript adds: “His spirit is constricted by despair.”] for whoever labors without believing in the future, like an unbeliever, has a narrow spirit because of despair concerning what is to come.

**(Verses 15–16.)** [Note: The Roman edition reads: “What participation does righteousness have…”] For what partnership does righteousness have with iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what share does the believer have with the unbeliever? Or what accord does the temple of God have with idols? It is clear that the things he lists are opposites; and therefore he teaches that one must flee from them, since the Lord says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

For the Law proclaims righteousness, so that iniquity may be avoided; it displays the light, which is truth, so that one may withdraw from ignorance, which is darkness; it announces Christ in the mystery of God, so that one may depart from the devil, who wishes to lie that he is God; it promises eternal life to believers, so that, stripped of unbelief, they may be alien to every error of unbelievers; it forbade idols to be worshiped, because they are enemies of the temple of God. For you are the temple of the living God. Nothing is so hostile to a human being as idols, because they compel him to withdraw from faith in the one God.

**(Verses 17–18.)** As God said (Leviticus 26:12): “For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people. Therefore come out from their midst and separate yourselves, says the Lord (Isaiah 52:11), and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord almighty.”

For the present, let us explain the sense of the first cause, so that we may make clear whose words these are when he says: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.” These are Christ’s words. For this is what Jeremiah also testified among other things, saying: “Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:38). For he dwelt among us, as the apostle John says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

And because he is our God, Jeremiah says again: “This is our God” (Baruch 3:36). And that we are his people is beyond doubt, for the Church is Christ’s. Therefore he wishes us to be separated from every defilement, so that he may receive us as sons, as he says: “Little children, I am with you only a little while longer” (John 13:33).

And because he is almighty, I think there should be no doubt about it. For if, as he himself says, “whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5:19), this means that the Son can do everything the Father can do. If the Father cannot do something, neither can the Son. But the Son is a reliable witness, since he says of the Father: “With God all things are possible” (Matthew 19:26).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “He himself says that whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does; that is, the Son can do everything the Father can do. The Son is a reliable witness that the Father can do everything . . . . Through this testimony of the prophet . . . . and he showed that Jesus, our Lord from ancient times, etc.”]

By this testimony he has also exhorted us to a pure life, and he has shown that our Lord Jesus had long ago been predestined to be our Lord and to receive us in the affection of his love.

## CHAPTER VII

**(Verse 1.)** Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh, perfecting holiness of spirit in the fear of God. What he says is clear; nevertheless, “defilement of flesh” must be understood in many ways. For this reason he did not say, “from the defilement of flesh,” but “from every defilement,” so that we might flee every carnal vice; for everything the Law forbids is carnal.

We perfect the holiness of spirit if, in the fear of God, we follow what is right, so that, abstaining from sins under the name of Christ, we may be holy. Those who appear to restrain themselves from vices without professing Christ are sanctified according to the world, not according to the Spirit of God; for according to God those are clean who are believers, whereas all the rest, whatever they may be, are unclean. Whatever is without Christ is unclean, as he says to Titus: “To the unbelieving nothing is clean, for their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15).

**(Verse 2.)** Make room for us. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “We have corrupted no one.”]

He wishes them to consider what he says, so that, taking these words into their hearts, they may recognize that what he says is true; and, rejecting those whom he is touching upon, may turn their entire attention toward those whom they see loving them with genuine affection. For the false apostles were harming them, corrupting their understanding, and burdening their purses through the serpentine cunning of their deception.

**(Verse 3.)** I do not say this for your condemnation. That is, I am not rejecting you, but admonishing you so that you may correct yourselves; for whoever condemns someone does not forgive him. For I have already told you that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

From what he has already said, he wants them to understand the spirit in which he speaks to them. Those whom he wishes to have as participants both in present sufferings for Christ and in future life, he certainly does not reject; rather, he exhorts them to make themselves worthy of that participation.

**(Verse 4.)** Great is my confidence in you; great is my boasting about you. I am filled with consolation; I overflow with joy in all our affliction. This confidence arises from the rebuke in the first letter. Because they did not receive it harshly, they gave him confidence to admonish them; for they appeared willing to correct themselves, and therefore he boasts.

He declares that his own spirit has also been consoled on their account, so much so that he calls God to witness that he overflows with joy in all his affliction. Seeing that there is hope in those for whom he suffers distress, he rejoices when he is afflicted, certain that he will receive from God a reward for the salvation he has brought about in them.

**(Verse 5.)** For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest. [Note: The Corbie manuscripts read: “our flesh.” Does “flesh” make sense, since flesh cannot suffer without a mind? But by “flesh” he signified the whole human being, just as the Savior says: “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Since the Holy Spirit was also in them, he could not say, “Our spirit had no rest,” because the spirit is incapable of suffering. But in comparison with it he called the whole human being “flesh,” just as stars are dark in comparison with the sun’s brightness, because the spirit was joyful, knowing that they were making progress through tribulation. “But afflicted in every way,” etc.]

He recalls the pressures and beatings they endured for the sake of believers, so that he might stir them more strongly to love. “Our flesh had no rest,” he says, so that they might sympathize with them, certain that they were giving their lives for the salvation of the faithful even unto death. Before one tribulation and bodily injury had subsided, another came, so that there was no rest for the sufferer.

Since all flesh is irrational in its perception, he therefore indicates that it had no rest and has no rest in suffering. But the soul, although it itself suffered in the body, nevertheless had rest in this respect: it hoped that God would grant a reward for these tribulations inflicted by unbelievers because of the faith. Indeed, in the midst of the very pressure they were singing hymns to God.
