**(Acts 16:9 and following.)** But we were afflicted in every way. According to the historical account, when the Lord called them, they entered Macedonia. When not a few had believed and they had found the consolation of the woman Lydia, who believed together with all her household, the following then occurred: he drove the pythonic spirit—that is, a divine spirit—from a servant girl belonging to certain people. When they saw that they had lost a considerable profit, which the girl had brought them by fortune-telling, they stirred up a riot against Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the magistrates. After inflicting many blows on them, the magistrates sent them into the innermost part of the prison, so that their feet were fastened in stocks. This is the pressure they suffered in Macedonia. Hence he says: “Our flesh had no rest.”

Outside, conflicts; inside, fears. The conflicts concerned the body while it was being beaten; the fears concerned the mind. Fear exists where there is understanding; but this fear was on account of those who had believed, lest they should be scandalized by his suffering. For what did he have to fear for himself, since he was suffering? Moreover, in the Acts of the Apostles he says that he was ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 21:13).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “signified.” It may also be understood in this way: “Outside, conflicts”—that is, in public there was dissension by unbelievers against believers, while the noise announcing that matter, etc.]

It therefore appears that he signified the whole human being afflicted in the flesh, so that it should not at all be understood that the spirit, which is given to a human being in order that he may endure, could be afflicted, since it is incapable of suffering. Rather, the whole human being is said to be afflicted in the flesh in respect of both body and soul, but in respect of the spirit he is incapable of suffering.

It may also be understood in this way: “Outside, conflicts”—that is, in public, unbelievers were fighting against believers, resisting the truth while filled with fury. News of this generated fear inside, where the Apostle was. For what person would not fear such distress? But because he was more intent upon the things of God, he overcame this fear by hope.

[Col. 0304D] **(Verse 6.)** But God, who consoles the lowly, consoled us by the arrival of Titus. Since God does not forget his own but always gives them consolation in tribulation, he hastened Titus’s arrival, so that he might bring relief to those placed in the heat of suffering. For it is a great consolation for one who is suffering to have someone suffering with him.

**(Verse 7.)** And not only, he says, by his arrival, but also by the consolation with which he himself was consoled among you. He adds still more to the consolation, indicating that he had heard from Titus of their ready willingness to convert, so much so that Titus, who had been grieved by their disobedience, received consolation from their repentance.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “their conversions with ready willingness”; others: “their willingness was ready.”]

The Apostle shows how great his affection for them was, since he did not count the innermost prison, the pain of the beatings, the laceration of his body, or the stocks in which his feet had been confined. Rather, when he heard of their correction, he rejoiced, becoming forgetful of his sufferings and giving thanks to God for their salvation, regarding it as though it were the repayment of his tribulations.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “He shows how great an affection the Apostle had for them!”]

He reported to us your longing. Titus reported that they desired to correct themselves. For, learning what is promised to those who live well, they were stirred to desire these things. Your weeping. When rebuked, they wept, grieving because they had sinned and refusing to make excuses; hence the Apostle boasts of them. Your zeal for me. Learning of the Apostle’s love for them, they began to defend him against his adversaries.

**(Verse 8.)** So that I rejoiced all the more; therefore, even if I grieved you by the letter, I do not regret it. It is clear that he should not regret what produced such an outcome, since in the first letter he had rebuked their errors rather severely. “I do not regret,” he says, “having written more harshly, because the situation demanded it.”

**(Verse 9.)** [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Even if I had regretted it, seeing that …” He means: “Even if I had regretted it because of love, since I grieved you, now I rejoice, because consolation follows upon joy.”]

And even if I regretted it, I see that that letter, although it grieved you for a time, now makes me rejoice. He means this: “Even if I regretted it,” he says, “because of love, since I grieved you, consolation would follow upon joy, because it benefited you that I grieved you.”

Not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance; for you were grieved according to God. Therefore he says that he rejoiced, because they were grieved with shame, not with anger. Whoever, when rebuked, feels shame promises to correct himself; but whoever becomes angry shows that he will become worse. So that you might suffer no loss through us. “Everything we do,” he says, “has its effect in you; even the fact that we grieved you is for your sake.”

**(Verse 10.)** For godly grief produces repentance leading to lasting salvation. It is clear that the person who is grieved because he has sinned is grieved according to God; he is sorrowful because he has done what God hates. This pertains to the stability of salvation.

But worldly grief produces death. He means that just as grief according to God produces life—for one repents and hopes for God’s mercy—so grief according to the world produces death. The exposed sinner is sad as one destined for punishment, having no one from whom to hope for mercy; and even if, for the moment, there is no one to avenge the matter, he will nevertheless be unable to escape God’s judgment.

[Col. 0306A] **(Verse 11.)** See what earnestness this very godly grief has produced in you. It is true that the person who repents is anxious not to sin again.

But an excuse. Properly so, because repentance has not an excuse but a confession.

[Note: The Corbie manuscripts read: “But indignation.” The person who confesses when rebuked is not indignant. “But fear,” etc.]

But fear. He shows the fear in the sinner who, because of his offense, asks forgiveness.

But longing. The person who knows that sin has disfigured him longs to be restored.

But zeal. The person who understands that he is being rebuked for his own sake begins to experience zeal for accomplishing good works.

But vengeance. It is necessary that someone avenge the person whose affection toward himself he feels; and he takes vengeance on himself when he afflicts himself on account of the offense.

In everything you have shown yourselves to be pure in that matter. Since they appear to have considered everything that pertains to progress toward a better hope, they strive to show themselves upright in every duty of human conduct, possessing the zeal of the Apostle and their teacher.

[Note: The same Corbie manuscript reads: “They strive to see him as the guide of faith, insofar as they can.”]

**(Verse 12.)** Therefore, even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who acted unjustly. He calls the one who committed incest “the one who acted unjustly.” He also touches upon those whom he indicates in the first letter to have inflicted injury and fraud upon their brothers.

Nor was it on account of the one who was treated unjustly (1 Corinthians 6:7). These were treated unjustly because they suffered things contrary to what was due from their brothers. This is the sense he recalls at the beginning of the letter, where he says: “If you have forgiven anyone anything, I also have forgiven him” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

For he shows that he wrote that forgiveness should be granted not so much for the sake of those who had sinned as for the sake of the Church; because when one person acts wickedly, many are put to shame, and when one person suffers insult or fraud, many are indignant, since if one member suffers anything, all the members suffer with it.

But so that our concern for you might be made manifest before God. By correcting the unjust, sanctifying the polluted, and reconciling them to the Church, he demonstrates that he has concern for the whole people, in accordance with what I mentioned above.

**(Verse 13.)** Therefore we received consolation. He says that he received consolation and, consequently, that he also gave consolation. He received it when he learned that those whom he had rebuked wished to correct themselves and reform themselves through repentance; and he gives it when he restores them to the Church, lest, being grieved for too long, they should despair of themselves and turn toward a public and disastrous life.

But in our consolation we rejoiced all the more over the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “we were filled with joy over the consolation of Titus.”]

When Titus heard from those rebuked in the first letter that they wished to correct themselves, he received consolation. But when he learned that they were suffering grief over their error, his consolation increased and he was filled with joy, because their willingness had begun to be confirmed in action, with Titus as a reliable witness joyfully reporting it.

[Col. 0307A] **(Verse 14.)** For whatever I have boasted about you, I have not been put to shame. Before Titus went to the Corinthians, he had heard from them—that is, from the Apostle and those who were with him—that the Corinthians had a good will to correct their vices. Therefore, when Titus returned and reported the same things, the Apostle was certainly not put to shame but was made glad, because Titus had found them no differently from what he had heard about them.

But just as we have spoken everything to you in truth, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true. The Apostle writes these things exulting in spirit and rejoicing in them, so that he proves the effectiveness of their conduct to be as true as his own preaching to them.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “to those who were making progress only in the correction … if those things that are rebuked begin to be corrected.”]

For the truth of the one who rebukes becomes manifest precisely when those who are rebuked begin to correct themselves; for when the rebuked are changed, they bear witness to the one who rebuked them.

**(Verse 15.)** And his affection for you is all the more abundant. He says that Titus’s mind and affection are directed toward them, because he saw their progress; for the mind of a holy person is directed toward every good thing.

As he remembers the obedience of all of you, how you received him with fear and trembling. The Corinthians knew that Titus had been sent to them by the Apostle, by whom they had already been rebuked for such great vices; therefore they were frightened at his arrival. And because they had begun to correct their way of life, they were anxious to obey his commands, so that, when he returned, he might soften the Apostle’s attitude toward them. For this reason he indicates that they had honored Titus, since in Titus they revered the Apostle.

**(Verse 16.)** I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you. He rejoiced not only in their good will but also in the good works by which they were correcting what they had done wrong. Therefore, he says, “in everything I have confidence in you.”

## CHAPTER VIII

**(Verses 1–2.)** We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that amid much testing through affliction their joy has overflowed. Because the Macedonians received the word of faith with devoted hearts, he therefore says that grace was given to them by God, so that they would not be scandalized by the tribulation of Paul and Silas, which I mentioned above (Chapter 7, verse 5), but would receive it with exultation of mind, confident in the promised hope, and show themselves approved through their sufferings.

And that their profound poverty overflowed in the riches of their simplicity. He praises their devotion, because, although their material resources were meager, their spirit proved rich in service to the saints. For they acted with a pure conscience, seeking to please not human beings but God.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “although they had retained their possessions.” Read instead: “although they were of modest means,” etc.]

**(Verse 3.)** For I bear them witness that according to their means, and beyond their means, they were willing of their own accord. They gave to the ministry what was worthy and pleasing to God, who knew their means. And because they had given themselves to God with their whole heart, they wished to offer more than their means allowed.

**(Verse 4.)** With many entreaties they begged that they might be received into the grace and fellowship of service to the saints. He praises them for having offered so simply and devoutly a ministry that was beyond their means, so that they begged with tears to be allowed to offer it, as though in this way they might compel others to accept what did not seem acceptable to receive, since it exceeded the resources of their possessions and might later cause poverty to persuade them to regret their good work.

But because they showed themselves to be such that, already setting aside present things with pure hearts, they strengthened themselves through the confidence of faith in future promises, it seemed right to accept their offering, lest the grace of their good heart fail to bear fruit.

**(Verse 5.)** And not as we had hoped; rather, they first gave themselves to God, and then to us by the will of God. Therefore, he says, their offering ought to have been accepted, because, after first correcting their former errors and the vices of their life and conduct, they devoted themselves to God beyond what had been expected.

[Note: The Corbie manuscripts read: “They were absent from these actions, first correcting,” etc.]

It appeared that they were acting with such simplicity that the one to whom the offering was made need not fear accepting it. For they were not offering it with the intention of purchasing the favor of their superiors, so that they might tolerate their vices and not rebuke them, since gifts blind the eyes and bend the force of authority.

Thus, by giving themselves to God while correcting their vices, and then to their brothers while offering funds, they ought to have grieved that they had wished to be perfect almost before they had begun. By this example, therefore, he invites the Corinthians, so that, strengthened by this exhortation, they might diligently complete in spirit what they had begun.

[Col. 0308C] **(Verse 6.)** So that we urged Titus that, just as he began, so he might also complete this grace among you. Because he knew that Titus’s affection toward them was sincere, and that they were obedient to him, he indicates that through Titus he could more easily exhort them to this work: just as in other matters his exhortation had borne fruit among them, so it might also bear fruit in this grace, making them ready for service to the saints. Since they were already correcting their vices, they were to gain the fruit of this generosity. Those who give for the purpose of avoiding rebuke will gain no fruit from the matter.

**(Verse 7.)** But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, every earnest concern, and also in the love that comes from us and is among you—see that you abound all the more in this grace also.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and in that which comes from you toward us.” Some manuscripts read: “that which comes from you in us,” as in this passage, etc.]

He exhorts them so that he may boast about them before the other churches. For this is the proof of their correction: whether they are ready for service to the saints.

**(Verse 8.)** I do not speak according to a command, but by the concern shown by others, and in order to test the genuineness of your love. It is clear that he is not commanding but exhorting them to send funds to those suffering want and relieve their distress, showing their good will to God and to human beings; for this they will undoubtedly receive a reward.

**(Verse 9.)** For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that for your sake he became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might become rich. He says that Christ became poor because God deigned to be born as a human being, humbling the power of his majesty so that he might acquire for human beings the riches of divinity, so that, as the apostle Peter says, they might become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4).

He therefore became human so that he might take the human being into God, as it is written: “I said, You are gods” (Psalm 81:6). In this way he exhorts them to become poor by giving, so that their poverty may benefit them just as Christ’s poverty benefited us. Christ became poor for our sake, not for his own; we are to become poor so that it may benefit us.

**(Verses 10–11.)** And in this I give an opinion, for this is useful for you, who began not only to do but also to desire it from the previous year. Now, therefore, complete the doing as well, so that just as the willingness to desire is ready in you, so also the completion may be according to what you have.

He says this so that their willingness may appear in action, if it is genuine, according to their means: let each one give as much as his spirit can and wishes, so that his conscience may be clean—not in pretense, to please human beings while receiving no reward from God.

**(Verse 12.)** For if the willingness is ready, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. Since the Corinthians are being urged toward this work of service, they are instructed not to give more than they can, lest, offering more than they can afford under compulsion rather than voluntarily, they should appear burdened and destined to receive no reward; for whoever does something under compulsion has no reward.

The churches of Macedonia offered voluntarily and with entreaties, demonstrating that they were doing this with their whole will, so that they offered more than they could. For this reason it was acceptable. The more they offered, the more they will receive.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “They will receive. For if the willingness is ready, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.” The meaning itself is that if someone gives as much as he wishes and can, it is acceptable. For he appears to do this deliberately and therefore to have a reward for the matter.]

For if someone gives as much as he wishes or can, it is acceptable; he appears to do this deliberately. Therefore let him give as much as his spirit can and wishes, so that he may receive a reward for this matter.

**(Verses 13–14.)** For this is not so that there may be relief for others and distress for you. It is true that one should give in such a way that it does not bring poverty upon those who give.

But from equality at the present time. He says that each person should, for the present, share with the saints as much as he has; for no more is demanded than he ought to retain for himself. For he says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). Hence Zacchaeus says: “Behold, I give half of my possessions to the poor” (Luke 19:8).

So that your abundance may become a provision for their want, and their abundance may become a provision for your want. This is what he means: because, for a time, the saints are suffering want, having abandoned everything in the world and devoted themselves solely to divine works, so that they might persist in teaching and prayer for the benefit of many, those who have believed and who devote themselves to crafts or commerce, or who at least possess ancestral resources, should minister to the needs of the saints.

And again, in the place where the saints are rich and these others are in want, the saints should share with them, as though repaying in turn the service they received, just as the Lord says: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

So that equality may result, as it is written. This is equality: because these people now minister to the saints, they will receive repayment from them in the future. For they make the saints their debtors.

**(Verse 15.)** The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little. This is read in Exodus (Exodus 16:18). For the saints possess more in the hope of the future age, and more than those who appear rich in the present age; nevertheless, there both groups will be made equal. Just as the poverty of the saints is sustained by the benefit of these people, so by the benefit of the saints those who are rich here will become rich in the future age, in which they appear poor.

For they have not given themselves wholly to God, so as to be poor here and rich there; rather, because they are rich here, they are poor there, and they will be enriched through the support of the saints, who, although placed here, are already in heaven in their minds. For it is no ordinary merit to minister from righteous labors to the saints.

**(Verses 16–17.)** But thanks be to God, who gave Titus this very concern for you in his heart, for he indeed received consolation. God, who is just, knowing that the Corinthians wished to make progress, inflamed Titus’s affection toward them, so that through his exhortation he might bring their willingness to completion in good action. Seeing their progress, he was consoled and rejoiced in them.

And being even more concerned, he went to you voluntarily. That is, seeing them making progress in good actions, he became more concerned for their affection, so much so that he went voluntarily to those from whom he had previously excused himself even when asked, because of their vices.

**(Verses 18–19.)** We sent with him our brother, whose praise in the Gospel is spread through all the churches. Not only that, but he was also appointed by the churches as our companion in this grace that is administered by us, for the glory of the Lord and our earnest concern.

[Note: The same edition reads: “for the glory of the Lord and your readiness.”]

They commend this man because he was unknown to the Corinthians, so that they might understand how highly regarded they already were, since such men were sent to them. Thus they might rejoice with them, increasing them in faith’s work, which the deputies of Christ diligently carried out for the glory of God the Creator of heaven and earth, so that he might be recognized in them.

**(Verse 20.)** We are avoiding this, lest anyone reproach us in this abundance that is administered by us. Since the matter concerned the ministry, he added this, lest he be judged negligent in caring for the poor or the saints if he performed it too sluggishly.

For the apostles had agreed among themselves concerning this matter that they should remember the poor, as he indicates in Galatians. Since the Apostle was blameless in everything (Galatians 2:10), he indicates that he is taking care beforehand that he not be judged negligent in this cause, so that, once this work was completed, his concern and foresight might appear in every respect.

**(Verse 21.)** For we provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings. He provides what is good before God by teaching that what God commands concerning the ministry to the saints or the poor should be done. Before human beings he provides what is good because he sends to this work men whose integrity will not cause scandal among them but will move them to act, lest the Apostle’s good teaching fall into disrepute through his ministers’ lack of foresight.

**(Verses 22–23.)** We also sent with them our brother, whom we have often tested in many matters as being earnest, but now much more earnest, with great confidence in you—whether concerning Titus, who is my companion and helper among you, or concerning our brothers, the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.

He calls Titus his companion because Titus too was a bishop, to whom he gave as a minister a man known in all the churches of that province. To these he adds a third brother, approved in many good works and earnest.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Through Titus’s report.”]

By Titus’s report—who related the good will of the Corinthians and of the other men sent with him, whom he calls the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ—he shows that he had become more eager to see them and exhort them to service to the saints. For he gained confidence after hearing that the Corinthians had become better. Therefore he hastened to them, certain that they would obey by doing good works.

[Col. 0311C] **(Verse 24.)** Therefore, demonstrate before them, in the presence of the churches, the proof of your love and of our exultation on your behalf. He admonishes them to show their love in the persons whom he sends, so that the good things they had heard about them might prove true.

For they showed that they had progressed through the Apostle’s admonitions if they received those sent by him with honor, so that the other churches might recognize that the good things that had begun to be said about them were true. He therefore stirs their minds, because a person who is thought well of usually makes himself better.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “He ought to show himself better.”]

## CHAPTER IX

**(Verses 1–2.)** For concerning the service that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you among the Macedonians. These are also words intended to encourage them. He says that it is superfluous for him to write about the service performed for the saints, so that he may appear to think well of them; for it is superfluous to remind someone whom you know will act.

But in order to show his diligence, it is necessary for him to write, both to make them more ready and to reveal what he proclaims about them to others. For things that seem superfluous often produce greater concern. The Lord himself, though he had no doubt about the apostle Peter’s love for him, nevertheless asked him three times: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:17). This threefold repetition appears almost superfluous, but it is useful for perfecting the admonition, so that he may know that he must attend with great diligence to what is frequently entrusted to him.

For Achaia has been ready since the previous year. After Macedonia, Achaia—that is, the churches of the province of Achaia, though not all of them, since the Corinthians too are Achaeans—had prepared themselves, moved by the example of the Macedonians, to minister to the saints.

By saying this he further exhorts the Corinthians, stating that they had been ready since the previous year but were now awaiting the distribution of their service according to each person’s need.

And your zeal has stirred up many. After saying that Achaia was ready after Macedonia, he then urges the Corinthians also to become ready according to their promise. The other churches, having heard that the Corinthians had first been entangled in many errors but afterward corrected themselves and became people of good will, were stirred by the Corinthians’ example to undertake the good work.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “with the affections of good will.”]

For if those who behaved badly after receiving the faith had begun to possess this willingness, how much more should those in whom such vices had not been found possess it.

**(Verse 3.)** But I sent the brothers, so that our boasting, by which we prefer you, might not prove empty in this matter, and so that, as I said, you might be ready. He is referring to the brothers mentioned above—that is, Titus and the assistants whom he added to him—who would exhort them more earnestly to fulfill their promise concerning service to the saints. They were to encourage them not only by letter but also face to face through frequent admonitions, lest the Apostle’s exultation, in which he boasted of the splendor of their spirit, should be emptied of meaning.

By recalling this so often, therefore, he shows his concern for them, unwilling that they should be put to shame.

[Col. 0312C] **(Verse 4.)** Lest, when the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—and, not to say, all of you—should be put to shame in this matter. It is clear that, if what he testified concerning them is not found to be true, he himself will be ashamed, and they themselves will be even more confounded, since, merely because the Apostle had stood as their witness, they did not strive to do what would make his testimony true, or to act for the sake of so great a man’s reputation.

**(Verse 5.)** Therefore I considered it necessary to ask the brothers to go ahead to you and prepare your promised [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Roman edition reads, “this blessing of yours”; but it should be understood as “to have this blessing prepared, as though,” etc.] blessing, so that it might be ready as a blessing and not as an exaction. To make his concern still more evident, he says that he asked the brothers, through whom they might be reminded to fulfill what they had promised but were not fulfilling. Although above he says that Titus went voluntarily—that is, that nothing had been extorted from him, but that as soon as he heard, he willingly embraced the task, so that he might appear to have gone to them voluntarily because of the hope he had in them—now he does not indicate that he asked these men to go because they were unwilling; rather, he demonstrates his affection for them by asking those who were already willing to go, so that without any delay what both they desired and he requested might be accomplished. His purpose, therefore, is that they should be faithful to their promise, and that they should understand his admonition as arising from his regard for their reputation, not as an attempt to impose upon them, but so that they might offer only as much as they would not later regret.

[Col. 0313A] **(Verses 6, 7.)** But I say this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. By “the sparing man” he means the miser, from whom a contribution must be extorted; for he regrets having promised. He infers this from their delay, since they had promised long ago and had been deliberating for a long time. Such a sparing man has a small harvest, because he sows with hesitation; for he does not know that what he is doing is beneficial. But whoever sows with blessing will also reap from blessing. He sows with blessing who does this with good will and in hope of future recompense. Let each one give according to the purpose of his heart, not out of sadness or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver. He teaches them that this will benefit them in the future if it is done with a joyful spirit. From among those who contribute, God chooses the one to whom recompense is to be given—the person who acts with a devoted heart, as though storing up treasure with God—because the one who gives unwillingly, out of present shame, lest he be found disgraceful in comparison with others who contribute, receives no reward.

**(Verse 8.)** God is able to make every grace abound in you. [The number 194 appears in the edition.] He wishes that God’s power may be present with them, so that just as, in correcting their vices and establishing the truth of the teaching, He pricks their hearts, so also in this matter He may favor their undertaking, so that by God’s grace they may abound in every good work. So that, always having all sufficiency in all things, you may abound in every good work. He says and wishes that, in every matter, they may always be sufficient for themselves by God’s will and may lack none of the things necessary for salvation. If, therefore, they choose sufficiency alone, they will be able to abound in God’s work; for by retaining for themselves what is sufficient, they must expend the rest for the use of the saints [Col. 0313C] or of the poor. This will be to abound in every good work.

Although what a poor person gives may be small, it nevertheless abounds, because it is done with right judgment; for the question is not only how much is given, but from how much it is given and with what intention. Thus that widow in the Gospel (Luke 21:3) was praised for giving little, while those who contributed much were not praised. Her little was much, because she gave more than she was able to give; whereas the rich gave less, although they could give more. Consequently, the small offering of the woman who gave beyond her means was found to be greater than the rich men’s large offerings, because they gave from what they had in abundance. Whoever, therefore, gives as much as he can does rightly; yet he has that widow before him, because she gave all that she possessed.

[Col. 0313D] **(Verse 9.)** As it is written: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” This is written in Psalm 111, and by this example he adds to their concern for the poor, so that they may abound in every good work. For if the righteousness of the one who gives generously to the poor endures forever, how much more that of the one who ministers to the saints? The poor may be understood as those who are publicly needy. [Note: [Col. 0313D] All editions and certain manuscripts read, “who are publicans and needy”; other manuscripts more correctly read, “who are publicly needy,” etc.] The saints, however, are distinguished from them, because they are servants of God, devoted to prayers and fasts and leading a pure life, like Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:37), who did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers day and night and setting aside every worldly concern.

This mercy, therefore, is called righteousness, because the one who gives knows that God has given everything in common to all: His sun rises upon everyone, He rains upon everyone, and He gave the earth to everyone. For this reason he shares with those who do not possess an abundance of the earth, lest they appear to have been deprived of God’s benefits. [Note: [Col. 0313D] Some manuscripts read: “This, then, is the one who … and this man’s righteousness endures not only for a time.”] He is therefore righteous who does not keep for himself alone what he knows was given to all; and he is righteous not only in this age but also forever, because in the world to come he will possess this righteousness with him perpetually.

**(Verses 10, 11.)** He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruit of your righteousness, so that you may be enriched in every way for all generosity. Everything belongs to God, and seeds and growing things increase and multiply by God’s will for human use. Therefore God, who gives these things, also commands that they be shared with those in need. Consequently, the one who gives according to God’s will cannot fail, by God’s will, to be increased by such growth for the enlargement of the fruit of righteousness; for to the giver He adds, so that he may have more from which to give. [Note: [Col. 0313D] Cod. Vall. adds, “so that he may have more to give to the needy,” etc.]

This is righteousness: because God gives, a person should in turn give from what he has to the one who lacks. For God wishes these people to be ministers to those who choose what is better, despise the abundance of the present age, and devote themselves entirely to God’s affairs. According to each person’s good will, God supplies help. For the saints, who wish to possess nothing here except food and clothing, God has appointed those who wish to have these things as their protectors, so that the person who ministers to them well and simply may, by God’s will, be increased, having always something from which to give, enriched both for the present and for the future.

The one who sows once will reap twice, provided that, if he provides for future hopes, he does not want to keep them subject to himself but rather bends himself toward them; for he will receive from God the reward for this deed. If he wishes to humble them for himself in the present, he loses hope for the future; for here he receives the reward of his work, since he does not act simply, as the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:16).

[Col. 0314D] **(Verses 12, 13.)** [Note: [Col. 0314D] The old edition and some manuscripts read, “if anyone works”; the Roman edition, together with the remaining manuscripts, reads, “which works.” In the following verse, however, the Codex Carnotensis alone has “the ministry of the sacrifice.”]

Which, through us, produces thanksgiving to God. For the ministry of this service not only supplies what is lacking to the saints, but will also abound through the thanksgiving of many to God. Through the testing of this ministry, they glorify God in the submission expressed by your confession of the Gospel of Christ and in the simplicity of your sharing with them, while they themselves pray for you and long to see you because of the superabundant grace of God in you.

[Col. 0315A] But thanks be to God for His indescribable gift. He says this because whoever performs through the stewards of God’s gift this work—which elicits thanksgiving to God from those who receive the necessary support in the name of Christ, not being subjected to beggary but to God, from whose gifts they know they are nourished—not only receives thanksgiving from them, but also from the remaining brothers, who give thanks to God for them and commend their deed to the Lord. Thus, although they give to a few, they are commended to God through the prayers of many.

Testing their minds in this work, they glorify the Lord in them; strengthened by hope in Him, they obey the Gospel of Christ with a submissive mind, not wishing those who minister to them to be humbled so that they may provide what is necessary for the saints. This will be the simplicity of giving thanks for their sharing, as they commend themselves to the prayers and desires of those whom they assist. For who would not desire to see with his own eyes those who, for God’s name, are subjected to their needs? Thus God’s gifts are so called: the person who ministers with them gives to God, because what is given is credited to the One who commands it to be done. [Note: [Col. 0315D] The Roman edition reads, “But thanks be to God for His ineffable gift. For the gift of God is,” etc.]

Giving thanks to God for these things and for His ineffable gift. For it is God’s gift that stirs people to good work; the promised hope urges them on to the ministry described above.

## CHAPTER X

**(Verse 1.)** Now I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the gentleness and modesty of Christ—I who am humble in appearance when among you, but when absent am confident toward you. This is what he now says: that when absent he is such as he is when present. For he was not humble in appearance through flattery or submission to anyone or anything; rather, he guarded his firmness so carefully that at times he even abstained from what was lawful, lest he be bent. Hence he says in another letter: “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both one and the other” (1 Corinthians 6:13).

He therefore appeals to them while absent and invokes the modesty of Christ, lest, when present, he should be found harsher in the case of those men than he is in the letter. Those who had not yet corrected themselves were to moderate the Apostle’s severity by composing themselves; then, finding them restrained, he would rejoice in them with his severity diminished. By “confidence,” therefore, he signifies the confidence of severity, which perhaps they thought he possessed only in the letter, but not when present in person, since in the first letter he appears severe and exceedingly strict. For this reason he warns them not to expect him to use the same severity when present.

**(Verse 2.)** But I ask that, when present, I may not have to act boldly with the confidence with which I am thought bold against certain people who suppose that we walk according to the flesh. The meaning is the same, and he repeats it in order to make it clear. He prays that he may find them such as he wishes, so that he will not be forced to become angry but may rest with them. [Note: [Col. 0315D] Some manuscripts read, “he said that this was the confidence given,” etc.]

Here, therefore, he has explained what he indicated above and makes still more fully manifest in what follows: that this is the confidence which he here called boldness—the authority given to him by Christ, whose representative he is—so that he may punish those who, acting under Christ’s name, do not obey, in order that they may correct the matters for which they are reproved. He is speaking of those who, by refusing the spiritual matters proclaimed by the Apostle, regarded him as though he were speaking about carnal things that ought not to be received. Therefore he says: “Who suppose that we walk according to the flesh”; for whoever despises spiritual things supposes that they are carnal. [Note: [Col. 0315D] The Codex Corbeiensis reads, “he thinks that carnal things please him.”]

**(Verse 3.)** For although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. That is, although we are placed in the body, we live spiritually; for the person who does what pleases God lives spiritually. The one who obeys the desires of the flesh wages war according to the flesh; for every error is called flesh. But the person who obeys Christ in faith and discipline wages war for Christ.

**(Verse 4.)** For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God. They are powerful because they are incorruptible; for all carnal things are corruptible. They are called weapons because they resist vices and bear the sign of their commander, Christ, who is the enemy of vices. Just as a commander vindicates his kingdom through his soldiers, so the Savior, through us His servants, defends the confession and discipline of the one God.

**(Verse 5.)** For the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. The spiritual weapons are faith in the incorruptible proclamation. Through these, God conquers the principalities and powers who, seeking to usurp sovereignty for themselves, are known to exalt themselves against the faith of Christ, inserting themselves into human thoughts so as to draw people away from God’s dominion. The truth of faith destroys these thoughts.

By “strongholds,” therefore, he means the principalities and powers and the spiritual forces of wickedness that exalt themselves and arm the minds of unbelievers to contradict Christ. Against these the law of God fights, scattering their counsels. And taking captive every [Note: [Col. 0315D] The Roman edition reads, “every understanding into obedience to Christ. It takes the understanding captive.” Immediately afterward, however, Cod. Vall. reads, “while he contradicts, while he conquers reason.”] understanding and leading it into the obedience of Christ. It takes the understanding captive when it conquers by reason the one who contradicts, and brings it, humbled and gentle, to the faith of Christ against which it had previously fought.

**(Verse 6.)** And being ready to punish every disobedience when your obedience has been fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0316D] The old edition and not a few manuscripts read, “when our obedience has been fulfilled.” The Codex Corbeiensis has: “It is clear that the one who punishes disobedience condemns it through obedience.”] It is clear that he punishes disobedience: when he condemns it through obedience, he destroys it, bringing those who resist to faith, so that their unbelief may be condemned by the very people whom it had defended.

**(Verse 7.)** Look at what is before your eyes. He now wants them to consider what is apparent—that is, what he is about to say—for they are able to judge things that are open and plain. He therefore says: If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: that just as he belongs to Christ, so also do we. [Note: [Col. 0316D] The Roman edition reads, “is confident that he is a servant of Christ.”]

He is speaking to those whose pride he touches—those who, presumptuously inflating their minds, thought less of the Apostle than was fitting, as though they did not need his instructions. He admonishes them that, if they were confident about themselves because they were servants of Christ, they certainly ought not to doubt the Apostle; rather, although he was their equal, they should think similarly about him, and indeed ought even more to prefer to themselves the teacher of the Gentiles.

Here he teaches them humility by making himself equal to them, although he was a chosen vessel and teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. He therefore wants them to consider what is plainly visible: that no believer would esteem himself more highly than the Apostle; how much less should anyone esteem him less highly than himself? He affirms and teaches this so that they might not lose the merit of a good life through mental arrogance. For whoever knows that he is something should humble himself, so that he may become greater.

**(Verse 8.)** For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for building you up and not for destroying you, I shall not be put to shame. He now indicates that, although above he humbled himself by comparing himself with them, if he should raise himself up he would not be ashamed, because he received from the Lord the authority to preach, in order to save those who obey, not to destroy them. If, then, the one who was sent by the Lord humbles himself and compares himself with inferiors, how much more should those who had no testimony to their credit refrain from comparing themselves with, not to say preferring themselves to, their superiors?

**(Verse 9.)** This is so that we may not appear to be frightening you through letters. The person who may be seen as frightening others through letters is one who possesses neither any authority nor confidence to rebuke when present; when absent, he dares to do so because when present he is afraid.

**(Verses 10, 11.)** For his letters, they say, are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible. Let such a person consider that, whatever we are in speech through our letters when absent, such also are we in action when present. Thus he proves that he is not one person when absent and another when present, because he was not presumptuous. He had received authority from the Lord; for the person to whom authority has not been given may dare when absent, but when present he suffers shame. The Apostle, therefore, is not ashamed when he rebukes, because he acts with the confidence of authority. He says these things because of those who preached without being sent, flattering others because they wished to commend themselves.

[Col. 0317D] **(Verse 12.)** For we do not dare to join or compare ourselves with certain people who commend themselves. [Note: [Col. 0317D] The Roman edition reads, “we do not dare to compare or liken ourselves.”] These are the people who commend themselves, who, having received no authority, wish to dominate, claiming authority for their own name. For the person who is sent does not claim authority for himself, but for the one by whom he is sent; by this he also shows himself to have been chosen by the Lord as a steward. Thus he does not join or compare himself with those who preach without being sent, since he presumes nothing beyond what has been granted. [Note: [Col. 0317D] Several manuscripts read, “presumes nothing beyond the agreement.”]

[Col. 0318A] **(Verse 13.)** But we will not boast beyond measure, measuring ourselves by ourselves and comparing ourselves with ourselves, but according to the measure of the rule that God has assigned to us—the measure extending even to you. He says that he uses as much authority as has been granted by the Author, and does not go beyond its measure. Therefore, he says, our boasting will not be arrogant, since we do not overstep the limit of the authority given. He uses “glory” for the authority with which he exercised correction over sinners, so that he might save them. Yet he says that he does not boast of it in an exalted display of power, but for their edification.

For he shows the authority of which, if he wished to boast, he would not be ashamed, because it had been given to him by the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0317D] The same Roman edition reads, “if he should exalt himself, why should he be ashamed?” One manuscript reads, “if he should correct himself.”] But he uses it in such a way that he boasts only in the progress of believers, steadfastly rebuking those who are vicious, so that he may glory in their salvation and so that the authority given may contribute to salvation, not to arrogance.

He therefore testifies in two ways that he does not boast beyond measure: first, because he acts according to the authority given, as he said; and second, because he claims no authority beyond the reach of his preaching. He was confident concerning those whom he himself had founded in the faith of Christ. For he says that it was assigned to each person to whom he was directed in preaching, so that individuals might have their own cities whose faith they could glory in. By God’s will this Apostle was summoned to preach to the Macedonians, and by the Lord he was instructed to evangelize the Corinthians. He therefore speaks boldly to those whom he himself founded and to whom he reached by God’s will; he does not speak to others with the same confidence, because they were within another’s rule—that is, within the portion of another Evangelist.

**(Verse 14.)** For we are not extending ourselves beyond our measure, as though we had not reached you; that is, [Note: [Col. 0318D] The old edition, together with certain manuscripts, reads: “not as though, having not been sent, we had come to you in preaching, but as appointed by God, who sent us to you. To extend oneself beyond measure,” etc.] we are not extending ourselves in preaching as though we had not reached you; rather, being appointed and sent by God, we reached you. To extend oneself beyond measure means to extend beyond what has been granted, but we have not done so, because God gave a measure for His evangelists to observe, and he testifies that he observes it.

He makes this clear so that they may know that he was sent to them by God, and consequently ought to obey his admonitions, lest, by despising him, they should appear to resist the God by whom he was sent.

**(Verse 15.)** For we have reached even to you in the Gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others. Here it becomes more evident what he is saying: that he himself had founded them. Therefore he speaks to them with such confidence; they had not been brought to faith through another’s labor, as he says in another letter: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). The person who glories in his own labor, therefore, does not boast beyond measure.

But having hope that, as your faith grows, we shall be magnified among you. Because he hopes for the fruit of the faith he had sought, he declares that he does not carry out this work negligently, lest he yield to weariness and troubles. For he believes that he will be magnified before God if his hearers increase in faith, as the Lord says: “Father, just as you sent me into this world, I also sent them into this world, and for their sake I sanctify myself” (John 17:18). He says this because the obedience of disciples is the teacher’s testimony. Hence he says:

**(Verse 16.)** So that we may be magnified among you according to our rule in abundance, and that we may evangelize in regions beyond you. Rejoicing in their faith, he declares that he will necessarily preach beyond them in order to increase the glory of his preaching, where the Gospel had not yet been preached. So that we may not glory in what has been prepared according to another’s rule. It is clear that a prudent man neither trusts in nor hopes for things that depend upon the labors of others. [Note: [Col. 0319D] The Codex Corbeiensis reads, “in which the labor of others is evident.”]

Therefore the Apostle also does not dare to glory in those who believed when others preached to them, lest he appear to glory in another’s labor. Rather, he relies on preaching to those to whom the Gospel had not been announced, so that he may seek glory through his own labor. [Note: [Col. 0319D] All editions and several manuscripts read, “may seek it for his own labor”; the Codex Corbeiensis, “may acquire it for his own labor”; the rest, “may seek it through his own labor.”]

**(Verse 17.)** But whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord. By this statement he signified that the confidence and glory itself must be given to the Lord, whose grace it is. Thus whoever trusts in evangelical authority should trust with God as its author, so that all profit from the divine undertaking may accrue to the Lord. But whoever does not receive authority from God cannot glory in the Lord, because he seeks his own glory.

**(Verse 18.)** For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. It is true that the Lord commends and approves the person whom He considers worthy and sends to preach His gift; but the one whom He does not send He does not commend. The person who preaches without being sent commends himself, and consequently is not suitable, but presumptuous and rejected.

## CHAPTER XI

**(Verse 1.)** I wish that you would bear with a little of my foolishness! But indeed, bear with me. As he begins to speak truthfully about himself, he calls himself foolish, because this seems to contribute to his praise. For it was said: “Let your neighbor praise you, and not your own lips” (Proverbs 27:2). But here he is compelled by grief because those who ought to have thought more highly of him than of others were thinking of him unworthily.

**(Verse 2.)** For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I prepared you as a chaste virgin to be presented to one man, Christ. What he is about to say, he shows that he will say out of love for them, so that it may contribute not so much to his own praise as to their progress: that they may learn how to favor their father in the Gospel. For the dishonor of a father is the disparagement of his children, and the praise of children is the glory of their father (Ecclesiasticus 3:13).

He therefore wants them to be virgins in faith, and for this reason he is zealous against those who corrupt their faith, so that he may present them undefiled to Christ the Judge on the day of judgment. This is why we also read in the Apocalypse of John: “These are the ones,” he says, “who have not been defiled with women; for they remained virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever He goes” (Apocalypse XV, 4).

By “women” he signified error, because error began through a woman, just as he also calls Jezebel a woman because of Ahab’s wife, who killed the prophets of God out of zeal for Baal (1 Kings 18:40); by this he means idolatry, through which morals and the truth of faith are corrupted. For if you understand “women” literally and suppose that they are called virgins because they preserved their bodies undefiled, you exclude the saints from this glory, because all the Apostles except John and Paul had wives. Consider whether it would be fitting to accuse the Apostle Peter, who was first among the Apostles, and how much more this would apply to the others.

**(Verse 3.)** But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the purity that is in Christ Jesus. [Note: [Col. 0319D] Some manuscripts read, “may be corrupted by the purity of God.”] He shows why he is compelled to testify truthfully about himself. He declares that glory has been given to him not in order to praise himself, but to expose those who, under Christ’s name, preached against Christ, and by whom the Corinthians were being led astray. This truth would benefit them more than it would him.

His purpose was that they should not listen to the deceivers, whom he compared with the devil because of the cunning of their wickedness, since they tried to corrupt the hearts of the faithful away from the truth of Christ. Fearing this, he is always concerned for them, lest they be violated.

**(Verse 4.)** For if the one who comes preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or if you receive another Spirit whom you did not receive, or another Gospel which you did not accept, you rightly tolerate it. [Note: [Col. 0319D] The Codex Corbeiensis correctly reads, “you would rightly tolerate it.” It does not mean that it would be right to receive another Christ, another Spirit, or another proclamation, especially since he says to the Galatians: “If anyone should preach to you,” etc.]

Why does he say, “You rightly tolerate it,” if another Christ had been preached to them, or if another Spirit or another Gospel had been handed down to them, when he says to the Galatians: “If anyone announces to you anything other than what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9)? If it was wrong for the Galatians to receive anything other than what had been handed down by the Apostles, how would it have been right for the Corinthians if another Christ had been preached to them?

But the Apostle knew that no other Christ than the one who was crucified was ever preached. Therefore he says, “You would rightly tolerate it,” if some superior Christ had been preached to you by those who come. To the Galatians, however, he said that anyone should be accursed if they heard something else—not something greater, but something contrary. But, he says, if those who come preach Christ Himself, the one whom we announce, and this Gospel, what reason is there for us to be considered inferior, when nothing more is learned from them?

Above he speaks of the pseudo-apostles, corrupters of the faith; here, however, he speaks of true preachers, because the Corinthian people were wavering amid various errors. Some favored the pseudo-apostles; others favored those from whom, through carefully composed words, they heard the same things they had heard from the Apostle; while others favored the Apostles because they had been with the Lord, disparaging their own Apostle Paul because he had not seen the Lord in the flesh.

**(Verse 5.)** For I consider that I was in no way inferior to those who are regarded as eminent apostles. He does not wish God’s grace to appear inferior in him, since he taught in the same way and did the same things as the Apostles who appeared more prominent, because they had begun teaching earlier and had been with the Lord. For this reason they were thought to possess greater authority. [Note: [Col. 0321D] The Roman edition reads, “who appeared to be superior.”]

Yet this Apostle’s election was approved by a remarkable testimony, and he labored more than the others; he saw the Lord while praying in the temple, and spoke with Him. [Note: [Col. 0321D] The old edition and several manuscripts read, “since his election is accompanied by testimony, and even more,” etc.]

**(Verse 6.)** But even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge. [The number 199 appears in the edition.] This does not refer to the Apostles, because they were not eloquent, being uneducated, though they were full of the Holy Spirit. Rather, he touches upon those whom the Corinthians preferred because of their polished speech, although in religion what is necessary is the force of speech, not sweet sound. [Note: [Col. 0321D] “Not sweet sound. In all things, however.” Thus Cod. Corb., in which everything between these words is omitted.]

How, then, does he humble himself by saying that he is unskilled in speech? And what of Festus’s statement: “Paul, Paul, much learning is driving you mad” (Acts 26:24)? By saying this, he did not intend it to be understood that he did not know how to speak, but that he was addressing those who wished to be commended not by faith but by eloquence.

Nevertheless, he called himself unskilled in the matter that involved no fault. But in the matter [Note: [Col. 0322D] The Roman edition and some manuscripts read this way; the old edition, together with many more manuscripts, reads, “which is not without fault and acquires salvation”; the Laudian manuscript more correctly reads, with the negative removed, “which is without fault,” etc.] by which salvation is acquired, and whose ignorance is not without guilt, he did not pronounce himself unskilled. For the person who is unskilled in speech is not guilty before God; but the person who lacks the knowledge of God is guilty of ignorance, because it is not permissible to be ignorant, especially of what pertains to salvation.

Therefore the Apostle, rejecting eloquence, acted so that faith might be acceptable as witnessed by virtue; not so that eloquence might commend faith, but so that virtue—before which eloquence yields—might commend it.

In all things I have been made manifest to you. He says that he is manifest to the Corinthians in all things, because they knew that he also possessed skill in speaking. Knowing this, some nevertheless favored others in the very respect in which they knew him not to be inferior. He therefore speaks with indignation, because this was worse: although they knew that he lacked nothing, they humbled him in comparison with the others, even though they had seen that through him not only was the preaching fulfilled, but apostolic signs and wonders were also performed.

**(Verse 7.)** Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the Gospel of God to you without charge? Because they were inflated by the fact that he had refused to accept support from them, and for this reason they preferred others to him, he asks whether he had sinned because he humbled himself and judged himself unworthy to receive anything. They were angry with him for this, although it was not a matter of sin but of glory.

Thus he humbled himself when he did not demand what was owed to him. It was owed to him that he should receive support from those to whom he preached the Gospel of God, just as the Lord established when He said: “The worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). But for their benefit he refused it.

He refused the support offered for two reasons: first, so that he would not be found similar to the pseudo-apostles, who preached not for the glory of God but for their own advantage, seeking an opportunity to plunder them; for when one person does not accept, another cannot demand very much. Second, he refused it so that the force of evangelical authority would not grow weak; for the person who accepts from sinners loses the authority to rebuke them.

Thus they are exalted when he does not accept from them for the purpose of their correction, so that, being raised from death, they may be brought to life.

**(Verse 8.)** I robbed other churches by accepting support for your service. And when I was with you and was in need, I was not burdensome to anyone. He presses the charge against them, showing that he not only refused to accept from them but also accepted from others and ministered to them. To show that this was substantial and not insignificant, he says: “I robbed other churches for your service.” He therefore signifies that he spent no small amount on them. For when he says, “I robbed,” he signifies that much was received and given, not extorted. Hence he adds: “Having accepted support.” For support is what a soldier receives for expenses in place of pay.

He therefore brought shame upon them, since he certainly did not refuse through deceit, given that he himself ministered to them; and he did so so that, through this ministry, they might more easily fulfill what they had promised, knowing that they were debtors. Their ministry should no longer seem especially glorious, but rather a debt, lest they boast about it for that reason.

**(Verse 9.)** And when I was with you and was in need, I was not burdensome to anyone. He wished to benefit them to such an extent that he consoled his own poverty for the sake of their salvation. He endured poverty contentedly so that they would suffer no scandal. For the person who gives thinks that he is exalted and no longer permits himself to be rebuked. [Note: [Col. 0322D] Cod. Vall. reads, “and for this reason he allows himself to be rebuked.”]

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. He always received from the Macedonians because they had first corrected their vices. Just as he ought not to accept from the Corinthians, lest it become a stumbling block to them, so he ought to accept from the Macedonians, lest those who sowed well lose their fruit.

**(Verse 10.)** And in everything I have kept and will keep myself free from burdening you. He says that he will always continue in this course, so that they may correct themselves, because of the pseudo-apostles who were seeking an opportunity to plunder them.

[The number 200 appears in the edition.] The truth of Christ is in me: this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. He urges all Achaia to minister to the saints, but he himself does not permit them to minister to him, lest he fail to fulfill the glory he has begun. For it is glory to abstain from what is lawful, especially for the salvation of others. In the regions of Achaia, therefore, he did not wish to make use of support; elsewhere he did. And under the testimony of Christ he promises even more strongly that he will remain in this practice, lest at any time he accept from the regions of Achaia.

**(Verse 11.)** Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. Having given the reason, he also calls upon God’s knowledge as a witness to the love he had for them. He did not refuse to accept because he did not love them, but rather because he loved them more, so that this very refusal might benefit them, as I have said.

(Vers. 12.) But what I am doing—and will continue to do—is intended to cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity, so that in the matter of which they boast they may be found to be like us. The boast of the false apostles consisted in receiving money. Therefore the Apostle rejected this practice, lest he appear like them; for unless the Apostle had avoided this, a greater opportunity would have been given them to receive, or rather to extort, since they could have pointed to the example set by the Apostle in this matter.

(Vers. 13.) For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. They are deceitful because they preached Christ for the sake of avarice, not with a religious mind and not as men sent, usurping for themselves the name “apostle.”

(Vers. 14.) And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is clear that Satan frequently deceives many people by presenting himself to them as though he were an angel of God, in order to mislead them. Hence Jesus son of Nave, being concerned, asked who it was that had appeared to him (Joshua, LI, 3). And the Apostles, terrified in the boat, thought that it was a phantom. Therefore, when the Lord said, “Do not be afraid; it is I” (Matt. XIV, 7), the Apostle Peter, not readily believing him, said, “If it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (ibid., 28), so that, if he firmly placed his foot upon the waters, he would know that the one appearing was truly not a phantom.

(Vers. 15.) It is therefore no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. The ministers of righteousness are the Apostles, whose associates these men falsely claimed to be in order to deceive their hearers. Their end will be according to their works. Without doubt, men of this kind will be judged according to the wickedness of their minds, because they pretend to be ministers of God not for God’s sake but for the sake of their own belly. Yet he says that their end will be according to their works: just as the works and care devoted to the belly perish, so they too are to be understood as perishing.

(Vers. 16.) I say again, let no one think me foolish; otherwise, receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. Above (chap. II, verse 1) he had already said, “Would that you could bear with a little of my folly”; now he repeats it. For he frequently sets forth something which he will pursue only later, after many intervening matters. What, therefore, he proposed above, he now begins to explain. Since he is about to speak the truth, he calls himself a fool, because what he is saying appears to contribute to his praise. “So that I too,” he says, “may boast a little.” He calls it “a little” because the qualification lies in the words, not in the meaning. He is not truly speaking these things for his own glory; rather, he wishes to show them that those whom they consider glorious possess nothing more than he does. Accordingly, if they are thought glorious, “then I too,” he says. He calls this the speech of a fool so that, while pursuing something to his own praise, he may show that he is compelled to speak in this way. For he is grieved that they should consider those men exalted, though this point had been disregarded [reading uncertain], although they had nothing more than he did.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “they should consider them exalted in this conception, because they have nothing,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 17.) What I am saying, I am not saying according to God. He is not speaking according to the Lord, because these things belong to the swelling of the flesh, and glory does not arise before God from self-inflation; for before God humility is glorious. But he speaks as though in folly, in this matter of boasting. He did not call it complete folly, but folly in part, for it is true. Yet because self-exaltation is a vicious thing, although what is said is true, it is nevertheless like folly for anyone to praise himself. Complete folly, however, is for someone to praise himself falsely: the former is proud because of the truth, the latter foolish because of falsehood. Yet the substance of the boasting in this matter is carnal, because, like the flower of hay, this glory withers.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “if someone praises himself falsely.” Again, a little later, some manuscripts read, “it is carnality,” where others, as well as all the editions, read, “it is carnal.”]

(Vers. 18.) Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. He says this because certain Jews who had believed presumed upon the claim that they were sons of Abraham. This is to boast according to the flesh: to claim for oneself the nobility of the flesh. For they defend the privilege of their lineage on the ground that those who believe in God are called his sons: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 20). “If, then, this is glory,” he says, “I too will boast, because I too am a son of Abraham.” But being a son of Abraham is of no benefit before God, because it is faith that saves, not descent from the lineage of Abraham. Therefore this is the glory of the flesh, as when someone is called the noble son of a man.

(Vers. 19, 20.) For you gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise. He calls those who gloried in the circumcision of the flesh fools; and because they were tolerated by the Corinthians so that they might appear glorious, the Apostle also wishes to be tolerated by them, so that he might show himself to be what they were, while nevertheless not boasting according to God on this account. Hence he calls this glory folly. For he says that he boasts according to the flesh, but he confesses that this is foolish, both to empty this glory of its force and to show that he was compelled to break into praise of the flesh. This, therefore, is irony. For how are they wise, when they are so often reproved? Is not the Apostle’s folly wiser than their wisdom? He, being wise, tolerates the imprudent; by his patience he bears with them so that they may make progress, lest by provoking or rejecting them he make them worse—or at least, if he cannot make progress in them, he preserves his own restraint.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “who bear with them by their wisdom.”]

There is none of this in the Corinthians. How, then, do they gladly tolerate the imprudent, when they themselves are wise—unless the words are not to be understood as they sound? The matter lies in the meaning and in the manner of pronunciation: the same words do not have the same meaning when pronounced differently, so that he sometimes confirms and sometimes denies what he says.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “who, by their wisdom, tolerated the foolish,” and so forth.]

For you tolerate it if someone reduces you to slavery. This is true, because they were being reduced to slavery, not through wisdom but through folly, so that they might serve the false apostles. If someone devours you. Nor is this false, because they were content to have their possessions devoured by false teachers. If someone takes hold of you. “To take” means to seize someone by deceit; therefore he indicates that these people are being captured by deceitful teachers and endure what is not expedient.

[Note: The old edition and the manuscripts, except the Corbie manuscript, read, “and endure what is not expedient.” The Corbie manuscript reads, “and to do what is not expedient.” The Roman edition alone reads, “but to bear what is not expedient.”]

If someone exalts himself. Exaltation is pride. He therefore touches upon those who were proud, wrongly censuring the Apostle, and who did not find these things displeasing. If someone strikes you in the face. Someone is struck in the face when an insult is inflicted upon his mouth. Here he signifies those who, because they were of the lineage of Abraham, taunted them for being uncircumcised, preferring themselves and humiliating them.

(Vers. 21.) I say this according to dishonor. By “dishonor” he means what he said above: “And I will boast according to the flesh” (II Cor. XI, 18). He does not say that this belongs to praise, because he was not weak in the matter in which those whom he covertly rebukes were boasting. Hence he added: “As though we had been weak in this respect.” It is clear that he was not weak in this glory in which the believing Jews whom the Corinthians tolerated were preferring themselves—as though the Apostle were unlike them in this matter, since he too was of the seed of Abraham.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “in which they were preferring themselves to the Jews, because they too were of the seed of Abraham, but they were not boasting on that account.”]

[Col. 0326D] Finally he says: “In whatever anyone dares,” and so forth.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “they were not inferior in this glory of the flesh”; the Laud manuscript reads, “the glory of Christ.”]

Accordingly, he was not weak in this glory of the flesh. Those who had attached themselves to the lineage of Abraham were judged weak. For, as though weak in the matter in which they preferred themselves because they were Israelites, they wish to be tolerated in this very respect. In order to show that he was not unlike them or weak in this glory of the flesh, when he speaks of his own case he introduces the person of Barnabas, his companion. Hence in the First Epistle he says: “Or are Barnabas and I alone without authority to work?” (I Cor. IX, 6.) They were therefore not inferior in the glory in which the Jews boasted, but they did not boast on that account.

[Col. 0325D] Finally he says: “In whatever anyone dares.”

To folly, I say, I dare also. That is, he was not weak in the glory in which the Israelites boasted, nor indeed was he to be considered wise in this matter; for the wise do not wish to prefer themselves. Thus he says that he dares to be foolish in the matter in which those who boast that they are sons of Abraham dare, in order to empty their glory. He declares himself imprudent, lest they should appear wise or noble in this respect.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that they might show that they were unlike and weak”; others, “so that he might show that he was unlike and weak”; the remaining manuscripts and the editions read as in the text.]

[Col. 0326A] (Vers. 22.) Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham? So am I. In these matters he shows himself equal to those whom he indicated above, in order to demonstrate the falsity of the disparagement by which they judged him unworthy.

(Vers. 23.) Are they ministers of Christ?—I speak as a fool—I am more. In speaking the truth about himself, he declares himself a fool, so that it may be understood that he burst forth into his own praise under compulsion. For one who voluntarily recounts things that contribute to his praise does not call himself imprudent. He therefore shows what makes him more truly a minister of Christ than the other preachers.

Having found this opportunity, he touches upon the persons of all, even the Apostles, grieving that he was judged inferior in the grace of God, although he performed the same works as the other Apostles and endured greater dangers for the sake of the faith. Hence in another Epistle he says: “I labored more than all of them” (I Cor. XV, 10).

In labors more abundant. He says “in more labors” because they too labored, but not as much. For from morning until the fifth hour he sought his livelihood with his hands, and from then until the tenth hour he debated publicly, laboring so greatly that he might persuade those who contradicted him. In prisons more abundantly. It is clear that he was sent to prison more frequently than they were. In beatings beyond measure. He says “beyond measure” because they exceeded what was necessary. They too were beaten, but not so much. In deaths often. This is true, because he endured dangers more frequently than the others.

[Col. 0326C] (Vers. 24.) Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one. He says this because he was scourged five times by the Jews according to the law of Moses, receiving thirty-nine blows, as it is written in Deuteronomy (Deut. XXV, 3). What happened on five occasions he here reports in summary.

(Vers. 25.) Three times I was beaten with rods. He suffered this at the hands of the Gentiles. Once I was stoned. He was stoned by the Jews in a city of Lycaonia (Acts XIV, 18).
