Three times I suffered shipwreck. Since he is said to have been sailing constantly, it was readily possible for him to suffer shipwreck three times amid adverse storms. A night and a day I was in the deep of the sea. This happened when he was sent to Rome after appealing to Caesar (Acts XXV, 12). At that time, in despair of life on the open sea—that is, in the depths of the sea—he was facing death. For this is what is written in that passage: “So that we despaired even of living” (II Cor. I, 8).

(Vers. 26.) Frequently on journeys. He now recounts other dangers, so that he may show that, in the flesh, he was harassed for Christ both on land and sea. “In dangers,” he says, “from rivers.” If he is recounting the dangers of journeys, why does he say “dangers from rivers”? But when he traveled in winter, since the rains are naturally constant, he encountered danger from rivers overflowing their banks.

In dangers from robbers. When the devil could not kill him in the city, he stirred up robbers against him on the road, although he carried nothing that robbers might desire.

In dangers from my own people. He means the persecutions of the Jews, who were his brothers according to the flesh. For they grieved because he had abandoned the Law and turned to the Gospel of Christ.

[Note: Thus the Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, reads: “because he had abandoned the Law”; the old edition, together with other manuscripts, reads: “because he had rejected the Law”; the Corbie manuscript reads: “because he acted contrary to the Law.”]

In dangers from the Gentiles. He suffered persecutions from the Gentiles because of the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and the preaching of the one God.

In dangers in the city. The danger in the city was so great that he escaped through a window from the hands of those lying in wait for him (II Cor. XI, 33).

In dangers in the wilderness. This danger was arranged by the Jews when, having laid an ambush, they wanted to kill him on the road (Acts XXVII, 43).

In dangers at sea. He has already said above: “Three times I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I was in the deep of the sea.” What other danger at sea was there? It was the danger that occurred when, at sea—that is, on the ship—the soldiers had decided to kill all the prisoners, lest anyone swim away and escape. The centurion prevented this danger from being carried out, lest Paul be killed, so that he might bring him alive to Rome.

In dangers from false brothers. These are the false brothers of whom he says to the Galatians: “Because of the false brothers who slipped in, who entered secretly to spy out our freedom which we have in Christ Jesus” (Gal. II, 4). Some of these were Christians and some were Jews, perfect in neither respect. Out of zeal for the Law they stirred up hostility against the Apostle because, when Christ had been preached, he said that the Law had already come to an end. Finally, because of their persistent pressure, he was compelled to circumcise Timothy. A false Christian, therefore, is one who persecutes a Christian out of zeal for the Law; and this is a false brother.

For if these men were merely Jews, and he calls them false brothers because of Judaism, what need was there to repeat the point? He has already said above: “In dangers from my own people.” But according to the flesh they are not false brothers; in Christ they are false, because they are not Christians with their whole mind (II Tim. I, 4). There were also other false brothers, such as Demas and Hermogenes (II Tim. IV, 9).

(Vers. 27.) In labor and hardship.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “in labor and distress.” Here it adds “distress” in order to show that their labor was severe.]

It is true that there can be labor without hardship; but here he added “and hardship” in order to show that the labor itself was destructive. In many sleepless nights. His vigils were numerous; some were voluntary, others necessary. For when he was placed under pressure, he necessarily had to remain awake while seeking God’s help; and he taught not only by day but also by night, as he says in the Acts of the Apostles.

In hunger and thirst (Acts XX, 31). Since he was frequently driven away by persecuting Jews, he necessarily suffered hunger and thirst through deprivation. In frequent fastings. He fasted often so that he might deserve to be protected by God’s help; for one fasts when, although one has food to eat, one abstains.

[Note: Not a few manuscripts read, “who abstains although he has what he can eat.”]

In cold and nakedness. He endured cold and nakedness when he suffered shipwreck. Finally, he says: “They kindled a fire and refreshed us because of the rain that was falling and the cold,” the barbarians on the island of Malta (Acts XXVIII, 2).

(Vers. 28.) Besides those external things, my daily burden is my concern for all the churches. This concern, which he calls daily, arises from the practice of handing on the tradition, so that every day he might instruct the people entrusted to him. The things he mentioned above, however, were imposed from outside, necessity compelling him. For the day is given for work and the night for rest; but because necessity pressed him to assist everyone, he taught even at night. He did not hesitate to afflict himself, lest the grace of God should be idle.

[Note: Thus most manuscripts read. Others, as well as the old edition, read “from the practice of detraction”; the Vatican manuscript reads “from the practice of drawing away”; the Roman edition reads “from the practice of administration.”]

(Vers. 29.) Who is weak, and I am not weak? He says that he sympathizes with everyone and grieves with them, with that concern by which he provides medicine for the wound. He pursues this point in order to show with what care he protects and governs the Church entrusted to him, and therefore that he ought in no respect to be judged inferior to the other Apostles, since, as he has made clear, he labored more than all of them.

[Note: The Amerbach edition, together with some manuscripts, reads, “according to what he made clear.”]

For he endured greater hostility among the Jews than the other Apostles, because, after persecuting the Church, he was suddenly changed and became its defender, testifying and affirming that he had heard Christ—whom he had previously regarded as a dead man—speaking with him from heaven (Acts IX, 6 and following). Many necessarily followed his testimony, knowing that he had not become its defender from being its persecutor without reason. For this reason the Jews were tormented and continually sought to kill him.

Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed? To be scandalized, in this passage, means to suffer the desire of the flesh. And because people are sometimes scandalized even unwillingly, being enticed by a form or bodily beauty or by the heat of their own flesh, the Apostle, considering the necessity of human nature, says that he is inflamed, so that he may care for such people by sympathizing with their weakness. He does not condemn them, but admonishes them in humble language, so that, in hope of the promised reward, they may resist the goads of the flesh; lest any of those who hear him, overcome by the desires of the flesh and despairing of themselves, should think that God will no longer accept them if they reform, and, remaining in the same state, perish.

(Vers. 30.) If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness. He says that if a Christian must boast, he must boast in the humility by which he grows before God. Hence elsewhere he says: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Cor. XII, 10)—that is, when I humble myself for the salvation of my brothers, then I am exalted. This is the matter in which one should boast, not in fleshly descent, in the fact that someone is of the seed of Abraham.

(Vers. 31.) The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. He calls God as witness, so that what he says may readily be believed, especially by those who did not honor him as a true apostle.

(Vers. 32, 33.) In Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and through a window I was let down in a basket through the wall, and I escaped his hands.

CHAPTER XII

(Vers. 1.) If it is necessary to boast—but there is no need for me.

[Note: Thus the majority of the more authoritative manuscripts; the others and the old edition do not depart from this, except that they prefer “it is not expedient for me” to “there is no need for me.” The Roman edition, rejecting this same text and placing it after the later words “if human assistance should fail,” begins chapter 12 there.]

The governor of Damascus, seeing the Jews laying ambushes for the Apostle, wanted by his authority to carry out their evil design, so that he himself might seize him if possible, both to please the Jews and to appear diligent in the duty entrusted to him, if he should hear that someone was disturbing the peace and should kill him for the sake of restoring tranquility.

This happened at the very beginning, when the Jews were inflamed against him after the Lord appeared to him on the road as he was going to Damascus. They saw that the man who had come to bring believers in Christ, bound, to Jerusalem was now preaching the sect that he had come to condemn (Acts IX, 2 and following). And so it happened that he escaped, being lowered by the disciples through a window in a basket along the wall.

Some say that this was an unworthy thing, because he was not delivered by God’s help. But when what could be accomplished by human beings was available, why was it necessary for him to be delivered by divine aid, since God’s help is necessary when human assistance fails?

After this event he says that it was not expedient for him to boast, because the joy of the present life is fragile. For if he had not escaped, he would have achieved martyrdom. But since the command is given to flee during persecution (Matt. X, 23), he deliberately escaped; for no one ought to wait until sin is committed against him. Therefore he says that he should boast because he escaped; but, he says, it is not expedient because of pride, since one grows through humility, and God’s help benefits the meek, not the haughty. Moreover, because he boasts that he escaped the death inflicted for the sake of faith, he indicates that suffering for Christ might seem pointless; therefore it is not expedient to boast.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads, “it seems to signify something pointless.”]

(Vers. 2.) But I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. He is now about to show to what height he was taken, so that it may consequently be understood how great and how extraordinary were the things shown and said to him, lest, as it seemed to some, he should be thought inferior to the other Apostles.

“I know,” he says, “a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body, I do not know; or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—such a man was caught up to the third heaven.” He confirmed both possibilities, because he did not deny that either could occur: he could have been caught up without the body or in the body. Perhaps some may think it insignificant if a man of Christ was caught up to the third heaven, since the moon is said to be in the third sphere.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “since the moon is said to be in the fourth sphere.”]

But that is not the case, because he is understood to have been caught up beyond all the stars of the world. Therefore what he relates is magnificent and wondrous: for he signifies that he himself was caught up above the firmament, numerically into the third heaven among the spiritual heavens.

(Vers. 3, 4, 5.) And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words, which it is not permitted a human being to utter. On behalf of such a man I will boast.

He says that he was caught up twice: first from here to the third heaven, and then into heavenly paradise, where the Lord said to the thief that he would be with him in paradise, as he said (Luke XXIII, 43), the paradise of the Father—there where the city of God, Jerusalem our mother, is also said to be. What wonder, then, if after the resurrection the body, once purified and made refined, is believed to become immortal in the heavens (Gal. IV, 26), when the Apostle does not doubt that a still mortal body could have been raised into the heavens and taken into the heavenly paradise of God the Father?

For the sake of such a man—that is, one so worthy of God that he experienced this—he says that he boasts; and he does not want to say openly that he is speaking of himself, lest he seem to praise himself. The Apostle John likewise, although it was known that he was speaking of himself, said: “This is the disciple whom Jesus loved, who also reclined at supper upon his breast” (John XXI, 20), lest he seem to speak of himself boastfully.

But on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses. Thus he does not boast of himself, since he does not openly declare that he is speaking of himself. “In my weaknesses,” he says, “I will boast.” For to recount the pressures of suffering and the weaknesses of distress does not appear glorious but mournful.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “but weak.”]

Therefore he says that he boasts in these things, knowing nevertheless that they lead to the attainment of heavenly rewards.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “the reward of heavenly things.”]

For what could be so glorious in the future for a Christian as to recount the dangers inflicted upon him for Christ?

(Vers. 6.) For even if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would speak the truth. He says that if he were to declare the merit he possesses before God, he would not be imprudent, for he would be speaking the truth. Therefore, if someone speaks of the merits that were shown to him, he is certainly not a fool; but if he remains silent, he is also prudent.

Now he states why he does not boast openly, saying: But I refrain, lest anyone think more of me than what he sees in me or hears from me. He therefore shows the reason why he does not boast openly: “Lest anyone,” he says, “think that I extend my glory beyond what the limit of my merits permits.” He signifies those who opposed him on account of the Law, as I mentioned above. Certainly, it is good not to conceal the glory of one’s merits, so that believers may be encouraged.

205 (Vers. 7.) And lest I should be exalted by the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, lest I should be exalted.

[Note: After the words “to buffet me,” the Roman edition reads, “he had struck me down, lest I should be exalted.”]

He testifies that God provides for those who have good merits, when he permits the good to be humbled by temptations, not only so that they may not be deprived of the fruits of their labors, but also so that these may be increased for the accumulation of their eternal possession. This remedy, therefore, was given to the Apostle: pressed by insults, he could not be exalted in spirit because of the greatness of the revelations, since an idle heart necessarily had to become exalted in the things he had seen.

(Vers. 8, 9.) For this reason I thrice besought the Lord that it might depart from me; and he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “is perfected in weakness.” It has “the thorns which the devil treacherously…”; the old edition and the manuscripts support us here, except that some, together with the codex, have “thorns,” while several manuscripts have “treacherous” or “treacherous minds.”]

He testifies that he begged the Lord three times that the thorns of the devil—which he treacherously drives into the minds of people in order to harm them, inciting them against the servants of God—might cease, but that he did not obtain this. He does not say this because he was despised, but because, without knowing it, he was asking for something contrary to his own good: that the temptations through which he was becoming more perfect should cease.

Hence he says to the Romans: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. VIII, 27). Therefore he says that this answer was given to him, so that God’s grace might be sufficient for him, by which either strength to endure was added or the time of distress was shortened, so that his devotion, not being broken by the weakness of the distress that befell him, might appear proven.

Therefore I will most gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “so that he may display himself in me,” and so forth.]

It is clear that he teaches that one should boast when one is humbled by insults. The power to endure is supplied by Christ, so that the insults which previously seemed harsh and therefore contemptible might afterward be willingly accepted, being softened by Christ’s help. Thus he says that he is willing to be beaten, provided that Christ heals him, knowing that Christ’s medicine adds more to salvation than weakness takes away from health.

[Col. 0331C] (Vers. 10.) Therefore I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in insults; for when I am weak, then I am strong. This is true, because the Christian conquers when he is thought to be losing, and faithlessness loses when it rejoices that it has conquered. He therefore applauds when he is insulted and rises when he is pressed down.

(Vers. 11.) I have become a fool; you compelled me. He says that he was compelled in order to show what he was. And certainly the one who has spoken the truth about himself is not a fool; but he lowers himself in order to show that he did not display his merits voluntarily.

For I ought to have been commended by you. It is clear that they ought to have borne witness on his behalf against his detractors, among whom he established the Church and displayed the wonders of the signs of his apostleship. Since he was silent, they should have defended the one whom they had as a father in the Gospel of Christ.

For I was inferior in nothing to those very great apostles. “Very great” means “exceedingly great,” as some thought; for they were what the Apostle Paul was as well. He therefore says that he is not inferior either in preaching or in performing signs to the Apostles who preceded him—not in dignity, but in time.

For if precedence is to be determined by time, John began to preach before Christ, and it was not Christ who baptized John, but John who baptized Christ. Does God judge in this way? Finally, Andrew followed the Savior before Peter, and yet it was not Andrew but Peter who received the primacy. Why, then, did some not regard him as an apostle, when by the grace of God he could do the same things as the Apostles?

Therefore he grieves and, being compelled, shows what he has received from the Lord’s favor.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “for recognition of the Lord,” and so forth.]

This is why he was displeasing to those who did not consider him an apostle: out of zeal for the ancestral Law, they rejected his preaching as though he were an enemy of the Mosaic tradition, because he said that the Law had already come to an end. They favored the other Apostles more and humbled him in comparison with them, because the others did not assert anything against the Law with equal firmness.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “Therefore he was displeasing to them, and he was not considered an apostle; these men were humiliating him because they rejected apostolic preaching.” It then continues: “And if I am nothing,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 12.) And although I am nothing, nevertheless the signs of an apostle were performed among you with all perseverance, with signs and wonders and mighty works. He humbles himself in order to raise himself up. Nevertheless, he mentions perseverance first, because he bore with them for a long time as with impatient invalids, so that, after the medicine of signs and mighty works had been applied, he might heal the wounds of their error.

(Vers. 13.) For what is there in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong.

Even now he commends himself through humility; for he shows that they had nothing less than the other churches, but rather more. He preached the Gospel of God to them freely, something granted to no other churches, since the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X, 7).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “If I am worthy of insult because of a good work, forgive me—that is, pardon me.”]

“If, then, I am worthy of insult because of a good work,” he says, “forgive me.” For every fool is an accuser of what is good. Thus, in order to show them to be inexperienced, he asks pardon from them for an act on account of which he deserves praise.

[Note: The same Corbie manuscript reads: “He exalts himself through humility; for he shows that they had nothing less, and then exposes their faithlessness when they rejoice that they have conquered. He applauds when they insult him,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 14.) Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I will not burden you. Lest anyone think that he had done this at the beginning merely to commend himself, and that afterward he wanted to receive the reward of evangelical preaching, he shows that he remains constant in this intention, lest his conduct later appear to have been corrected and provide his detractors with something to criticize.

For I do not seek what is yours, but you. He shows that he does not wish to receive from them in order to gain them themselves, so that, recognizing that he places them before money, they might at last understand his affection for them. For children ought not to store up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children. He signifies that he is their father, as he says in the First Epistle: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (I Cor. IV, 15).

Carnal parents, however, are the ones who store up treasure for their children; for spiritual parents it is right to receive from their children the expenses necessary to sustain the present life. It is not a great thing for those who hand on spiritual things to receive carnal things. Here he proves to such an extent that he does not wish to receive from them that he transfers the principle concerning a carnal father to a spiritual one: not only does he refuse to receive from them, but, if it can be done, he himself wishes to give to them, as I have already said above.

“I robbed other churches, receiving support for serving you” (II Cor. XI, 8). By saying this he touches them, so that they may understand how great he is and what they deserve who neglected the care of so great an Apostle.

(Vers. 15.) But I will most gladly spend and spend more, and myself be spent for your souls. Now he openly shows the affection and love that he had for them. He says that he is ready not only to spend what is his for them, and to spend it even more generously, but also to die for the salvation of their souls, just as the Apostle John says: “Following the example of the Savior, we too ought to lay down our souls for our brothers” (I John III, 16).

Though I love you exceedingly, am I loved less? He urges them to love, because they ought to love him more, especially since through him they learned the way of salvation, and through him they were acquired for God, having been made faithful from faithless and purified from defiled.

(Vers. 16.) But be that as it may: I did not burden you, yet, being crafty, I caught you by deceit. He does not conceal any of the objections that could be brought against him, so that he may clear himself in every respect. For he did nothing among them by deception, but in simplicity, looking after himself in one way and them in two ways: both by providing for them before God and by not seeking their money here, being satisfied with what God had promised him in the future.

Perhaps they suspected that he had despised them because what they offered was small, so that he might obtain greater things—so that, considering his own merits, he rejected not money itself but judged the amount unworthy of him and despised it.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and editions, except the Corbie manuscript, which reads, “not considering the money”; the Roman edition reads, “but judging the gift unworthy,” and so forth.]

(Vers. 17.) Did I perhaps defraud you through any of those whom I sent to you? This is what he means: those whom he sent did not inform them of this, so that, if they wished to keep the Apostle at peace with them, they might offer an amount worthy of his person; and that he had refused to accept because less than what was fitting had been offered. Thus, through the Apostle’s cunning, they might understand that what he had done was done not out of contempt but out of greed.

(Vers. 18.) I urged Titus, and I sent the brother with him. Was Titus greedy toward you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same footsteps? It is clear that, since nothing of this kind was said or done by those whom he sent, their single judgment is approved as good, with suspicion of greed excluded.

(Vers. 19.) Do you think once again that we are defending ourselves before you? This is what he means: for a long time you have doubted us, thinking that we do not act toward you straightforwardly.

[Note: The Laud manuscript reads: “You doubt us, thinking that I am defending myself,” and so forth.]

For the pseudo-apostles were harassing them, asserting that, because they themselves wished to plunder them, the Apostle was acting in this evasive way, as though he might thereby receive more. Before God, in Christ, we speak; and everything, beloved, is for your edification. He desires them to think well and truly of him, and therefore satisfies them both by reasoning and by testimony: he does not prove himself to be such a person for his own advantage, but for their edification, so that he might in this way stir up their love toward him, while neither burdening their resources nor weakening the authority of his power in reproving faults. For without doubt it benefits the one who is corrected that he should amend, if a superior refuses what is offered for the very purpose of being able to rebuke freely.

(Vers. 20.) For I fear that, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and that I may be found by you such as you do not wish. Since not all those whom he had rebuked in his first epistle had yet corrected themselves in the vices for which they had been censured, he now wishes to appear to be going to them with authority, so that they may be frightened into correction and he may find them such as he wishes. He says this so that they may present themselves in such a way as to be in harmony with the Apostle, so that they may rejoice in one another. For he finds someone not as he wishes when that person makes himself such as to be at odds with him.

Lest there be among you contentions, jealousies, animosities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, swellings, seditions. He now recalls the errors that he censured in the preceding epistle, when, showing partiality toward persons and preferring one to another, they were at odds among themselves.

(Vers. 21.) Lest, when I come again, God should humble me before you, and I should mourn for many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed. He gives this warning so that he may not find them such as he had found them previously, with various vices of unclean acts—or rather, of terms; for every act is without accusation, but the name of disorder makes it a crime.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “because every good work is without accusation.”]

For something is unlawful when it is done otherwise than it has been permitted. He therefore says that he will be humbled by their sins, because, as a merciful father, he begins to mourn the sins of his children. For what father does not rejoice when his children act well? So likewise he must mourn again if they conduct themselves wickedly.

[Note: The same Corbie manuscript reads: “if they are perverted.”]

He therefore admonishes them that, if any of those who had committed fornication in the past, or some other uncleanness or shamelessness, have not repented—as he indicates that some have not—they should now repent,

[Note: The old edition, with many manuscripts, reads: “whom he indicates have repented.”] so that, when he came, he might be with them without sorrow. For when he says, “And I should mourn for many of those who sinned before and have not repented,” he proves that some of them had repented and some had not. This is contrary to Novatian, who says that fornicators cannot complete their repentance and be received into communion. Here he proves that they did complete it and consequently were received into the peace of the Church. He therefore identifies three forms of sin when he names fornication, shamelessness, and uncleanness.

# CHAPTER XIII

(Vers. 1.) This is the third time I am coming to you. Earlier he said that he was prepared; now he indicates that he is actually coming. “In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.” He said this according to the Law (Deut. 19:15), so that someone might be either acquitted or condemned by two or three witnesses. In the same way he warns them that, at the Apostle’s third coming, they should be found acquitted.

(Vers. 2.) I told you before, and I tell you beforehand, as though present for the second time, and now absent I write to those who sinned before and to all the others, that if I come again I will not spare. He indicates that he had formerly told them, while present, to correct themselves, so that they would not be reproved with shame; and now, while absent, he again declares the same thing, so that after the second reproof, if they do not amend, they should not be spared.

(Vers. 3.) Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me? They seek proof of Christ speaking in the Apostle, since they do not obey his commands, wishing to test whether he dares to exercise judgment, so that it may thereby be understood that the authority of his office is firm and credible, and that he is to be feared thereafter.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “that the faith of his authority exists.” In the following verse the Roman edition had restored “he contends with the teacher,” and some Paris manuscripts, “he contends with the teacher”; but the older edition and the manuscripts have the better reading found in the text. It should be understood as “to be corrected,” as though the sense were “to be reproved and chastised.”]

For whoever despises the teacher seeks to be corrected. He who is not weak among you, but is powerful in you. Christ is powerful in them, because they saw the dead raised in his name, demons driven out, paralytics restored, the deaf hearing, speech returned to the mute, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. All these things belong to power, not weakness. Indeed, for this reason they were drawn to the faith.

(Vers. 4.) For although he was crucified through our weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. It is true that Christ was crucified on account of our sins, so that, by destroying death, he might free from it those who believe in him. He therefore allowed himself to become weak for our sake, in order to conquer death for us. Descending into the underworld, he who knew no sin at all, and having been slain as though he were a sinner, erased Adam’s bond, so that thereafter the dead, under his name, would not be held by death but would have confidence to go to heaven. Therefore, slain because of our weakness, he rose again by the power of the Father, in order to prove to the disciples that what he had taught was true, displaying the example in himself.

For we are weak in him. This refers to the persons of the apostles, who, while preaching him—that is, Christ—were made weak when they were insulted, imprisoned, and beaten. But we shall live with him through the power of God toward you. It is clear that, if they were made weak by unbelievers in the presence of believers, this weakness was not weakness but progress, because through it the faithful become stronger while they are made weak.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “Therefore, death inflicted by unbelievers upon such men …”]

The death inflicted by unbelievers is therefore life toward believers; for by the power of God they will rise so that they may live with Christ.

(Vers. 5.) Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves. He commands the brothers to examine one another, for they become more conscientious if they compare themselves with one another. He therefore wished this testing to be understood as examination, because every examination is a testing, though not every testing is an examination. If God is said to test, it is an examination;

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “But if the devil tests, he overthrows.”]

but if the devil is said to test, it is temptation, because he strives to overthrow. A human being, too, sometimes tests in order to examine and sometimes in order to entrap. Do you not recognize yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you, unless you are rejected? He says this because, if they do not know how to examine one another, they do not recognize that Jesus Christ is in them; and this is what it means to be rejected: not to know the faith of one’s religion and profession. For whoever holds the understanding of his faith in his heart knows that Christ Jesus is in him.

(Vers. 6.) But I hope that you will recognize that we are not rejected. He challenges them to knowledge of the faith and of a righteous life. For when they begin to know the certain authority and merit of their apostle before God, they will also be able to be concerned about themselves.

(Vers. 7.) But I pray to God that you do no evil—not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, while we may be as though rejected. He prays for them with the same disposition with which he always prays, namely, that they refrain from evil. “Not that we,” he says, “may appear approved,” that is, not that we may appear to possess authority while you are sinning, but that you may do what is good, while we may be as though rejected.

What does this mean? Is the Apostle praying that he be rejected? Certainly not. Rather, he prays that, when they act well, he may be humbled and appear as though rejected because he does not dare to rebuke them. Those who judge sinners appear approved by God, through the authority granted to them. If, therefore, there are no sinners for them to judge, their authority ceases, and they appear as though rejected.

(Vers. 8.) For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. He says this because power was not given against the truth, so that they might rebuke one who lives well, but for the truth, so that they might punish one who is hostile to the Law. Therefore, their power will cease if they do what is good. Hence he also says to the Romans: “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. 13:3). When, therefore, a person does good and does not fear, authority has been emptied of its force in his case. This is what it means to be as though rejected, because that by which authority is proved has ceased in him.

(Vers. 9.) For we rejoice when we are weak, while you are strong. To be weak means not to exercise authority. He wishes them to be strong, so that, by acting well, they may conquer their vices and prevent punishment or correction from being directed against them. This is also what we pray for: your perfection. He asks in prayer that they may be perfected in this, and that, perfected in the virtue of a good life and in incorrupt faith, they may not sin.

(Vers. 10.) For this reason I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I may not act harshly. It is clear that he admonishes them while absent so that he may find them more corrected, and so that, when he is there, he will not rebuke them with shame, causing the one who sins to be ashamed in the brotherly assembly.

According to the authority that the Lord gave me for edification and not for destruction. This is the authority that above he wishes to remain inactive if they act well; otherwise he will exercise it so that those who are reproved may be edified, not that sinners may be destroyed. For those who are rebuked so that they may be corrected are not destroyed but built up for life.

(Vers. 11.) Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfected; receive consolation; think the same thing; live in peace; and the God of peace and love will be with you. This joy will arise from their amendment, from which perfection also will be able to proceed. But first there will be consolation, so that, in hope of future things, they may abandon present pleasure.

Think the same thing. He says this because of their former discord, so that now they may have one mind. Live in peace. If they are harmonious, they will have peace. “And the God of peace and love,” he says, “will be with you.” Christ is the God of peace, who said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). He is also the God of love, for he says again: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. And by this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have the love with which I loved you for one another” (John 13:34).

Yet the peace of God is one thing and the peace of the world another, because the wicked and the impure also have peace, but it is for condemnation.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “and the spurious have peace”; certain other manuscripts more suitably read “and the filthy,” that is, the shameless, soft, and so forth.]

The peace of Christ, however, is free from sins. It flees faithlessness, rejects deceit, and resists evil deeds. It is pleasing and friendly to God but hostile to the devil. Whoever has this peace will also have love, and their God, for perpetual protection.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. This greeting is ecclesiastical, because these kisses are not carnal but spiritual; through the embrace of bodies they join souls, not by the desire of the flesh but of the spirit. All the saints greet you. He urges them toward holiness, so that they too may dare to return the greeting of the saints; for this reason they are greeted by the saints, so that they may imitate them.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen. Here there is a summation of the Trinity and a unity of power, because it is the perfection of the whole of salvation. The love of God sent us the Savior Jesus, by whose grace we have been saved. The fellowship of the Holy Spirit enables us to possess this grace of salvation; for he protects those who are loved by God and saved by Christ’s grace, so that the perfection of the three may be the completion of the human being in salvation.

[Col. 0337]

# ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE GALATIANS

209 PROLOGUE

[Col. 0337C]

Everyone who believes in Christ and observes the Law of works misunderstands Christ. So too do the Symmachians, who trace their origin to the Pharisees. Although they preserve the whole Law, they call themselves Christians and, after the manner of Photinus, define Christ not as God and man but as man only. For if they understood Christ to be God, they would expect nothing from the Law of works—that is, from new moons, the Sabbath, circumcision, and the distinction of foods; for whoever worships God and the Lord of the Law is above the Law, nor can one who agrees with the lawgiver be judged by the Law.

In the end, the Law was not given for those who worshiped God, but for those who both believed and acted wickedly, in contempt of the Creator. Hence he says to Timothy: “For the Law was not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and those who behave wickedly” (1 Tim. 1:9). And Moses says: “You shall make the children of Israel fear” (Lev. 15:31).

Hence the Galatians—or those who were subverting them—still having hearts covered by the cloud of error, do not perceive the meaning of the prophet Isaiah, who among other things says: “For he will finish the word and shorten it in righteousness; because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Isa. 10:23).

[Col. 0338C]

If they understood these statements, they would withdraw from the Law, knowing that from the preaching of John the Baptist the Law had already ceased, so that faith alone might suffice for salvation, having been abbreviated from the Law. For in the Law there is contained, concerning God the Father, Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit, what had been predestined in time and manifested in preaching.

Now, if the Israelites were circumcised as a sign, so that thereby they might appear to be sons of Abraham according to the flesh, circumcision ought rightly to cease, because believers have the sign of death conquered, by which they are recognized as sons of Abraham, but according to faith. For the one who would come and conquer death was promised to Abraham. Indeed, Abraham was waiting for him; sensing in the spirit that he had been born, he rejoiced, knowing that he would soon be brought into heaven.

Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “Abraham desired to see my day; and he saw it, and rejoiced” (John 8:56). At the time when the children of Israel were still together in the wilderness, before they were near the Gentiles, they were not circumcised. But when they were about to mingle with the Gentiles, they were circumcised by Jesus son of Nave from the rock (Josh. 5:3), which signifies Christ, because, he says, “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “They were circumcised with knives of stone … so that it might be signified through Christ,” and so forth.]

This signified that through Christ there would be a future circumcision of the heart, as Moses and the prophet Jeremiah had said: “Circumcise yourselves for God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Deut. 10:16; Jer. 4:4). When the darkness had been cut away through the forgiveness received for sins, they would become worthy to see the glory of God, which those placed under the Law had been unable to see because of sin.

Therefore, in order both to signify that Christ is God and to assert that he had not learned from a human being the things he taught, he begins as follows:

# CHAPTER ONE

(Vers. 1.) Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead. He testifies that he was not chosen and sent by human beings to preach, as were certain men who were chosen by the apostles and sent to strengthen the churches; nor like others who were sent by the Jews to disturb the churches, whom he calls pseudo-apostles. Rather, he says that he was sent by the Son of God, whom in this context he seems for that reason to deny to be a man: because he gave commands as God, not as man.

And the one who chose him chose him by divine judgment.

[Note: The Vallian manuscript reads: “And because he chose him by divine judgment.”]

Through this he indicates that he is a suitable and steadfast preacher, because the one whom God chooses is certainly much better than the one whom a human being chooses. “Nor,” he says, “through a man,” as they supposed concerning Christ, who compelled these people to be circumcised, but through the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, through the one who is God and man.

He immediately makes this clear when he says, “And God the Father, who raised him from the dead.” By this statement he condemned two heresies, that of Manichaeus and that of Photinus. Manichaeus denies that Christ is man, though he does not deny that he was crucified; Photinus does not concede that Christ is God, and yet he does not dare deny that Christ himself—that is, his body—raised him from the dead.

Thus, when Manichaeus does not deny that Christ was crucified, he appears foolishly unwilling to acknowledge him as man; and Photinus, by a kind of impiety, denies God while confessing that he raised himself from the dead. For he read that the Lord said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19).

Therefore, by raising himself from the dead, he indicates that he raised his body from the dead; nevertheless, he is also said to have been raised by his Father, because all the power of the Son is from the Father, so that the deeds of the Son are the deeds of the Father, from whom all things exist.

(Vers. 2.) And all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia. After commending his own authority, he further strengthens his case, so that he might show that all those who were with him were moved against them. Although his authority would have been sufficient to prevent him from being refuted, nevertheless, in order to aggravate their offense, by which they had fallen away from their original faith, he indicates that many who were with him were aroused to denounce their error. For someone can easily understand that he is in error if he sees himself reproved by many.

[Col. 0340A]

(Vers. 3.) Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He shows that the human race has been raised up by the benefit of both the Father and the Son. Nor does he signify that the Son is lesser when he calls him our Lord, or that the Father is greater because he calls him our God; for the Father will not be true God unless he is also Lord, nor will the Son be true Lord unless he is also God.

If, therefore, the grace of the Father and the Son toward us is one, what does it mean, he says, that you, thinking less of the Son, make the Law equal to him, so that you serve partly Christ and partly the Law, when you have read the Lord saying: “For the Son of man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Luke 6:5)?

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Thinking less concerning the Son of man.”]

By this they may see how great an insult they inflict upon the Lord when they compare the Lord with a maidservant.

[Col. 0340B]

(Vers. 4.) Who gave himself for our sins. He plainly shows that the Law is of no benefit, when he says that Christ offered himself to suffer for us, in order to justify us, whom the Law held as guilty, so that, freed from the Law through faith in Christ, we would no longer be sinners but, justified by a second birth, would be called sons of God.

For when the human race was held under the power of the devil, the Savior offered himself to the willing devil, so that, mocking him by the power of his strength—for he wished to receive the one whom he could not retain—he might take from him those whom the devil held subject by an evil right.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “When the human race was held in the dominion of the devil”; others, “in the condition of the devil,” and some, “in servitude.”]

Thus, after stripping the underworld, he carried a trophy of souls to the Father, from whom all things exist—something the Law certainly could not do. Although the Law had been given for our benefit, when we sinned it was turned against us and became hostile; it began to kill rather than to give life.

Christ, however, by forgiving sins, not only gave us life but also joined us to himself, so that we might be called sons of God through faith. What a great error it is, therefore, after grace to return beneath the Law; that is, after receiving freedom, to wish to serve, like one rescued from the sword who, forgetful of the benefit, sells himself again to the gladiator-trainer. For the purchaser is accused by the slave who abandons him and returns again to his former master.

In order to free us from the present evil age. He says this because the Lord gave himself over to death for the purpose of freeing us from the error of the age, that is, from the understanding of this age, which, growing old through the progress of time, hastens toward its end. Having been made strangers to it, we are to become participants in the future age, which knows no setting, in the knowledge of the one God.

The evil of the present age consists in this: it does not offer fitting reverence to God the Creator and to Christ the Restorer, while human error invents many gods for itself, or while believers fail to preserve for Christ the honor that is his due.

[Col. 0340D]

(Vers. 5.) According to the will of God and our Father, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen. So that what he says—that Christ freed us—may be firm and full of authority, he adds that the Father did this with his will.

(Vers. 6.) I marvel that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from him who called you by the grace of Christ to another gospel. The gospel is good news, and therefore the Old Law too is a gospel, apart from the Law of works.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “Having accepted the Law of works.” This is incorrect.]

But the gospel is especially that in which what was promised has been fulfilled, through which sinners are summoned to forgiveness. He therefore says that he marvels because, falling away from the greatest and best benefit, they have enslaved themselves to the Law of works, so that they might lose what they had attained and, falling swiftly from the freedom they had received, plunge into servitude.

Usually someone gradually passes from evil to good; these people, however, were easily led from good to the works of the flesh, which are burdensome. It rarely happens that someone flees from joy into destruction; hence he marvels at their stupidity, that, placed in security, they have subjected themselves to useless labor.

It is like a mad sailor standing in port, safe from the storm, who launches his ship into the open sea so that it may be tossed by various tempests. So these people, through folly, subjected themselves so that they might suffer the pains of the cut-off shameful member, and accept the yoke of the Law’s servitude, with no hope of this outcome proclaimed.

They had therefore been called to a different gospel from that preached by those who had subverted them—not, however, a gospel different from the one proclaimed by the apostles, although the pseudo-apostles asserted that it was different, out of hostility toward the Apostle who had instructed them.

In order to ensnare the Galatians through this deception, it was necessary for them to say that the Apostle’s gospel was different from what the Savior’s reason taught, while claiming that their own was true because it was preached in agreement with the ancient Law. These are the men who disputed this matter with Paul and Barnabas, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 15:2). They taught believers from the Gentiles that unless they were circumcised according to the custom of Moses and became Jews, they could not be saved.

(Vers. 7.) Which is not another gospel, except that there are some who are troubling you and wish to pervert the gospel of Christ. It is clear that they were doing this in order to pervert the gospel of Christ, altering its traditions so that they might be Jews under Christ’s name. This is to turn the gospel of Christ into the Law.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “And they wish to change it.” Below it reads: “So that they might change the gospel.”]

(Vers. 8, 9.) But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what we preached, let him be accursed. As we said before, and now I say again: If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be accursed. No one should be surprised that the Apostle, who softened the harshness of human conduct, was so agitated; for he is indignant against the enemies of Christian discipline for the sake of the Galatians’ salvation.

This indignation shows that it is no slight sin, after receiving the faith, to turn back to the Law. He asserts the gospel that he had preached to them to be so firm and true that he teaches that even the apostles themselves should not be heard if, perhaps, they preached something different, although their reputation as apostles of Christ had spread everywhere.

Or, if the devil, pretending to be an angel of God so that he might easily be heard, were to appear from heaven preaching against these things, he would be recognized as an adversary and treated as an abomination. If, therefore, he commanded that the apostles of Christ—whose illustrious reputation rested upon the performance of signs and wonders—and an angel from heaven, whom a spiritual rationale might commend, should be accursed if they taught anything other than what they had learned from the Apostle Paul, how much more should those be rejected whom no testimony can commend for seduction?

He repeats his declaration in order to confirm them in the original tradition; for a repeated law makes the negligent more attentive.

(Vers. 10.) For am I now satisfying human beings, or God? This means: Am I satisfying human beings by persuading you to return to the grace of Christ, or God? Certainly not human beings, but God, so that through this satisfaction they may return to God, whom they had despised.

He immediately adds: Or do I seek to please human beings? If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ. He therefore indicates that those by whom they had been subverted sought to please not God but human beings through the subversion of the Galatians, just as he himself had formerly done when he persecuted the Church in order to uphold the traditions of his fathers.

In order that they might be praised by the Jews, they said, according to the Jews’ will, that the Law had to be observed, lest, if they preached the true gospel of Christ, they should make the Jews their enemies. But the Apostle Paul, who taught that God should be pleased with complete devotion, did not fear offending human beings, provided that he commended the glory of God. For, putting all present things after future things, he commended himself to hope, as a worthy servant of Christ.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “He commended himself by appearances.”]

Those cannot be worthy servants who, under the Lord’s name, pursue their own profits.

But perhaps someone might object: Therefore those who preached the Law, which is said to have been given by God, were serving human beings. How, then, can the Law be called suitable if its preaching is said to have been adjusted according to human wishes?

Before the Lord’s coming, the Law was preached according to God’s will, for its appointed time required that it be observed. But when the Lord promised in the Law had come, the Law ought to have ceased, according to the previously announced judgment of the prophets. Hence the Lord says: “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). For it was not fitting that, when the Lord was present, the authority of the Law should continue to be observed.

Therefore, if anyone thereafter thinks that the Law must be observed, he no longer obeys the Lord’s will but resists it; for he satisfies those like himself.

(Vers. 11, 12.) I make known to you, brothers, that the gospel preached by me is not according to man. For I neither received it from a human being nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. Now he opens the beginning of the epistle. He wishes to reveal its very meaning: that he had not learned from a human being the things he taught, lest there be doubt concerning them.

Nor was his preaching fashioned according to human judgment, so as to appear unworthy of divine authority. Rather, he says that he learned it from the Son of God through revelation, when the Son was already in heaven after the resurrection, as I have mentioned above. He testifies that the things he learned accord with the will and majesty of the one from whom he learned them.

The things that, when observed, establish merit before God are spiritual. Those things are carnal which, when observed in their proper time, produced neither merit nor demerit before God. Failure to observe them was harmful, because those who had not performed the Law were under a curse, while those who had performed it were not justified before God, since “the righteous person lives by faith.” They were commanded to be observed so that they might be a burden, not so that they might confer dignity.

(Vers. 13.) For you have heard of my former conduct in Judaism: how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it; and I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. He briefly recalls his former purpose, by which he had previously flourished according to the flesh while opposing the Church; but he says that he abandoned this in order to become a servant of Christ.

He indicates that he had been more devoted than they in defending the Law, not for the sake of human favor but because he thought this useful before God. Through ignorance, while pleasing human beings, he thought that he was serving God and had a clear conscience. He did not know that it was no longer time to uphold the Law.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “the time for observing the Law,” and so forth.]

He followed the teaching of his fathers, who were established either in error or in malice, and with every effort and fervor of mind he acted so that, through zeal for the Law, he might appear superior to all his contemporaries. Thus he raged against the discipline of Christ so fiercely that he spared no one who had obtained the covenant of faith.

But when he learned through God’s revelation that this labor was futile and, indeed, opposed to God, he records that he abandoned it and submitted himself to the grace of faith, so that it might be profitable to him before God.

If, therefore, this man, who was an Israelite and held the dignity of a teacher among the Jews, instructed by Gamaliel, a most prudent man, and associated with men of the highest quality of life, abandoned the Law, how much more should those who were outside the Law not have subjected themselves to it? And if he rejoices that he had emerged from beneath the yoke of servitude, why did they bind their freedom with the chains of the Law?

(Vers. 15, 16.) But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not consult flesh and blood. While he had confidence in the Law, unaware that the time for observing the Law had passed, and was striving with complete eagerness, thinking that he was acting according to God’s will by resisting the gospel of Christ, God saw that his zeal was good but that he lacked knowledge. It pleased God to call him to his grace, knowing that this man was already suitable for preaching the gospel of his Son among the Gentiles.

For if, in a small matter, he was so swift and faithful in the boldness of his conscience, without anyone’s flattery, how much more steadfast would he be in preaching God’s gift, in hope of the promised reward?

Therefore, through God’s foreknowledge, he was separated from his mother’s womb—that is, before he was born, or as soon as he was born, God knew that he would become good.

As he says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you,” and so forth (Jer. 1:5). So too, knowing what the Apostle Paul would become, God went before him and called him before his conversion, because he was necessary.

Indeed, he immediately undertook the administration of God’s gift, putting aside every carnal concern. For he neither sought anyone’s counsel nor referred to anyone what he was about to do; instead, he immediately preached Christ, because he is the Son of God. For just as those who will become evil are often good at first, so those who will become good are also often evil at first.

(Vers. 17.) Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and again I returned to Damascus. He says that he was not under any necessity, imposed by God, to go to the apostles who preceded him in order to learn something from them, because God had revealed through his Son how he should teach.

He says this to show that nothing should be held except what he teaches, and that people should not be believed but God, from whom he testifies that he learned. Consequently, those who had led them into the Law were false teachers, because what they taught had not been handed down by God.

From Damascus, therefore, he went to Arabia to preach, where there were none of the apostles, so that he himself might establish churches there,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “lest the pseudo-apostles, slipping in, should sow Judaism.”]

and from there he returned again to Damascus, in order to visit those to whom he had first preached the gospel of God’s grace.

(Vers. 18.) Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days. It was fitting that he should desire to see Peter, because Peter was first among the apostles, to whom the Savior had entrusted the care of the churches.

He did not go in order to learn anything from him, because he had already learned from the author himself, from whom Peter too had been instructed; rather, he went because of the affection of the apostolate and so that Peter might know that the same permission had been granted to Paul that Peter himself had received.

When he came to him, he was received as a guest and remained with him fifteen days, as a fellow apostle of one mind with him. He makes these things known in order to show that he had been in harmony with the apostles and had disagreed with them in nothing, contrary to what the pseudo-apostles whispered about him, seeking to discredit him among the churches of the Gentiles and to implant their own evils in the minds of the simpler believers by claiming that their teaching agreed with that of the senior apostles.

[Col. 0344D] (Verse 19.) “Again I returned to Damascus, but I saw no other of the apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.” He saw James at Jerusalem, because James had been appointed bishop there by the apostles. He himself had previously been an unbeliever, as the Evangelist says: “For even his brothers did not yet believe in him” (John 7:5). This James was the son of Joseph, and for that reason he was called the brother of the Lord, because Joseph, his father, was also called the father of the Lord. For thus Mary says to Jesus in Luke’s Gospel: “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I, grieving and sorrowful, were seeking you” (Luke 2:42). And in the Gospel of John [Col. 0345A] Philip says to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets” (John 1:45). Thus, then, the Lord was called the brother of James and the others in the same way in which he was also called the son of Joseph. For certain men, led by madness, impiously contend that these true brothers of the Lord were born of Mary, although they do not say that Joseph was called his true father. For if these were truly his brothers, Joseph would also be his true father, since the one who called Joseph his father likewise called James and the others his brothers.

(Verses 20.) “Now, concerning the things I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie.” Since he is about to speak for the commendation of his authority, he calls God as witness that what he is going to say is true, lest it seem to have been fabricated; [Col. 0345B] for it would not suit his character to invent anything. But when he commends himself, he wishes these people to advance; for this commendation benefits them, so that they may know that the things spoken by him are altogether true.

(Verses 21–24.) “Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that were in Christ; they only heard that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy; and they glorified God in me.” He says this because, while he was defending Judaism against the faith, just as those men were doing by whom the Galatians had been overthrown, he was chosen by God and taught to depart from Judaism and preach the new Law. Thus Jewish believers rejoiced in him—those whom he had formerly persecuted—and gave thanks to God, who had made a defender out of a persecutor. In this way the Galatians were to recognize that they had been deceived, so that, under the name of Christ, they might profess themselves Jews, circumcising the flesh of their foreskin, although the law of Christ commands something different from Judaism. There circumcision is of the flesh; here, of the heart. There one serves under the elements, observing new moons and the Sabbath; here, one serves God alone in the spirit, because belief is a matter of the heart. There, human condition is the cause of sin; here, freedom comes through the forgiveness of sins. There is therefore a great difference between them.

## CHAPTER II

(Verses 1–2.) “Then after fourteen years I again went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up according to revelation, [Note: [Col. 0345D] The Roman edition reads, ‘and I conferred with them about the Gospel.’] and I set before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or should have run, in vain.”

Since his reputation had for a long time been spreading among all the Jews, but he was not recognized by face, for he was continually travelling among the Gentiles to establish and strengthen the Church with his customary steadfastness, the Jews, because of the matter of the Law, formed an unfavorable opinion of him, as though he disagreed with the preaching of the other apostles. Hence many were troubled, so that the Gentiles too might be disturbed, fearing that he was leading them into something different from what the apostles who had been with the Lord had handed down. Indeed, it was on this very occasion that the Galatians were subverted by the Jews, who said that Peter taught something different from Paul. Therefore, warned by a revelation of the Lord, he went up to Jerusalem with witnesses to his preaching, Barnabas and Titus—one a Jew and the other a Gentile—so that, if anyone had taken offense at him, their testimony might remove it, as he disclosed to them the meaning of his preaching.

With the apostles he conferred privately, so that they might know that he did not disagree with the evangelical rule—that is, lest they think that he was running or had run in vain, as certain Jewish believers supposed. For he could not have learned anything from them, since he had been instructed by God. But for the sake of concord and peace, this was done by God’s will, so that the doubt or suspicion might be removed from the brethren [Col. 0346B] and his fellow apostles, and so that it might benefit the Gentiles, who would learn that his Gospel agreed with that of the apostles.

Furthermore, [Note: [Col. 0345D] The old edition reads, “when they had learned the Law”; the Roman edition, “when they had learned with the Law”; other manuscripts read better, “when they had given the Law.” Below, only the Roman edition reads, “they should abstain,” that is, from blood, fornication, and meat sacrificed to idols.] when they had given the Law, they instructed that those who believed from among the Gentiles were not to be troubled, but were to observe only these things: that they abstain from blood, fornication, and idolatry (Acts 21:25).

Now let the Greek sophists, who claim expertise and assert that they naturally excel through subtlety of intellect, say what things were handed down for the Gentiles to observe. Were these things unknown to them, or were they things they already knew? But how can anyone learn what he already knows? Therefore, the Gentiles were shown that those things were unlawful which they thought permissible. Consequently, they were certainly not prohibited from murder when they were commanded to abstain from blood. But they received what Noah had learned from God: that they should refrain from eating blood together with flesh (Genesis 9:4).

For how could it happen that men trained in Roman laws, whose authority in the observance of commands is so great, did not know that murder must not be committed, when Roman laws punish adulterers, murderers, false witnesses, thieves, sorcerers, and perpetrators of the other kinds of evil? In the end, these three commands are found to have been given by the apostles and elders, although Roman laws do not know them: that they abstain from idolatry, from blood—as Noah did—and from fornication. The Greek sophists, not understanding these things, although knowing that one must abstain from blood, corrupted Scripture by adding a fourth command, namely, that one must also abstain from what has been strangled. I think that now, by God’s will, they will understand this, since what they added had already been stated above.

[Col. 0346D] (Verse 3.) “But not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised.” He means, “At that very time when I was in Jerusalem, Titus, who was with me, was not compelled to be circumcised.” Although we were among the apostles and those who had believed from the Jews, no one compelled him—that is, Titus—to be circumcised. The implied argument is: Why are you being circumcised, when Titus was not compelled to be circumcised by the apostles, who seemed to be something, but was accepted uncircumcised?

[Col. 0347A] (Verses 4–5.) “But because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might subject us to slavery, we yielded in submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you.” [Note: [Col. 0347D] Quite a few manuscripts consistently read here and below, “secretly brought in.”]

Because Titus was a Greek, just as the Galatians were, Paul denies that he was circumcised. By saying this, he rebukes those who allowed themselves to be circumcised although they were Greeks. But lest anyone object that he himself had circumcised Timothy, he now explains why he did what he denied ought to be done, saying: “But because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might subject us to slavery, we yielded in submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you” (Acts 16:3).

The Greeks, on the contrary, say: “We did not yield even for an hour.” They say that this suits the case, because, they argue, the one who prohibited the act ought not to have said that he had done it, lest he prove that it ought to be done. But the divine man, the apostle, knowing that this could be brought against him, himself brings it forward in order to forestall his slanderers; and he gives the reasons that compelled him to do what he did not wish to do.

“Because of the false brothers secretly brought in,” he says. He calls them secretly brought in because they entered deceitfully, presenting themselves as brothers although they were enemies. “Who slipped in”—that is, they entered with humility, feigning friendship. “To spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might subject us to slavery.” To spy out means to enter in such a way that one pretends one thing while seeking another. Their purpose was to accuse our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus. Freedom in Christ Jesus consists in not being subjected to the Law. “So that they might subject us to slavery”: that is, they entered deceitfully and treacherously for this purpose, to subject our freedom to slavery, compelling us to submit to the law of circumcision.

“We yielded in submission for an hour”: that is, for an hour we submitted ourselves to slavery, humbling ourselves before the Law, so that, after Timothy had been circumcised, the deceit and scandal of the Jews might cease. For, as can be understood, they were ready to stir up tumult and sedition. The occasion was this: Timothy was Jewish on his mother’s side but Greek on his father’s, and therefore, according to the Law, he had not been circumcised as an infant.

The apostle wished to take him with him and ordain him bishop, as he did—for, he says, “all those who were there bore good witness to him” (Acts 16:2)—but he fell into an ambush laid by the Jews. They were watching to see whether he would receive as uncircumcised the son of a Jewish woman, preparing a sedition. For if he maintained that the Greeks ought not to be circumcised, as the letter sent by the apostles on this matter had commanded (Acts 15:23 and following), he nevertheless did not forbid the sons of Israel to be circumcised, because the apostles had indicated nothing about them in that same letter. The Jewish believers were all the more enraged on the authority of that letter, because the letter itself did not prohibit Jews from circumcising their sons.

“Then,” he says (Acts 16:3), “taking him, he circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places.” [Col. 0348A] They had no scandal concerning the Gentiles; therefore Titus was not compelled to be circumcised. He yielded, then, for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among the Gentiles, since they did not subject themselves to circumcision.

Among the Jews, however, there was no truth of the Gospel, because believers were circumcising their sons. For in Christ Jesus neither foreskin nor circumcision has any power, but faith working through love (Galatians 6:15).

Not only the historical account but also the text indicates that he yielded. Above he says that Titus, although he was a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised; then he adds: “But because of the false brothers secretly brought in.” What can this mean except that he yielded for an hour because of the false brothers secretly brought in? Otherwise, how would the words or the meaning follow?

Certainly, he denies that Titus was compelled to be circumcised. “But because of the false brothers secretly brought in”—what does this mean except that he yielded? If he did not yield because of the false brothers secretly brought in, then he did not yield voluntarily; for he indicated that he would yield if this were the case. But if he did not yield because of the false brothers secretly brought in, what benefit did these false brothers provide, since he did not do what ought not to have been done?

Therefore, if this is the meaning, they benefited the apostle, because on their account he did not yield when he had been about to yield. Why, then, are they called spies if they did not want him to do what he was going to do, but because of them he did not do it? If he was not going to do it, then undoubtedly he did it because of them; there is no other possibility. The text indicates that he yielded, and history cries out that he did so. How could he deny that he yielded for an hour when it is proved that, because of the Jews, he circumcised Timothy—which is to yield for an hour—and that, compelled by them, he purified himself and went up into the temple (Acts 21)?

He could have said that he did not yield even for an hour only if he had never been found to yield. Either, although he was going to yield, he did not yield because of the false brothers; or, although he was not going to yield, he yielded because of the false brothers. Choose one of these two alternatives. The false brothers are those who, while believing, practiced Judaism.

(Verses 6.) “But from those who are considered to be something—whatever they once were makes no difference to me; God does not accept a person’s appearance.” He signifies that the apostles had formerly been simple and inexperienced men, possessing no distinction in the Law, but that this was not an impediment. For who could accuse one whom God excuses? The question is not what someone once was, but what he is now. For past things [Note: [Col. 0348D] The Vallensis Codex reads, “they neither condemn nor judge.”] are neither condemned nor vindicated.

Nevertheless, he wishes it to be understood that he was also learned in the Law and distinguished in life; and therefore he was an outstanding minister in the administration of the Gospel. “For those who were considered to be something contributed nothing to me.” He says that he received nothing from the apostles, but from God. For the one who gave the unlearned understanding of Christian discipline, he says, also deemed me worthy, although I was learned in the Law, to receive an understanding of this kind of reasoning.

How, then, could he have learned from them, when God found him learned and made him more learned through the grace of Christ?

[Col. 0349A] (Verses 7–8.) “But, on the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the Gospel of the uncircumcision, just as Peter had been entrusted with that of the circumcision—for he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me for the Gentiles—”

He names Peter alone and compares himself with him, because Peter had received the primacy for founding the Church; Paul likewise had been chosen to have the primacy in founding the churches of the Gentiles. Yet this was so arranged that Peter also preached to the Gentiles if occasion required, and Paul to the Jews. Both are found to have done both things, but full authority in preaching Judaism is recognized as having been given to Peter, while Paul’s complete authority is found in preaching to the Gentiles.

Therefore he calls himself the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth (2 Timothy 1:11); for each received an administration according to his abilities. It was more difficult to attract and persuade those who were far from God to faith than those who were near.

(Verses 9–10.) “And when they recognized the grace of God that had been given to me, Peter and James and John, who were considered to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcision; only that we should remember the poor, which I was also diligent to do.”

The apostles who were more distinguished than the others—whom he calls pillars on account of their steadfastness, and who had always been with the Lord in private places and had been worthy to behold his glory on the mountain (Matthew 17:2)—are said by him to have approved the gift that he received from God, so that he might be worthy to hold the primacy in preaching to the Gentiles, just as Peter held it in preaching to the circumcision.

Just as he gives Peter distinguished men among the apostles as companions, so he joins Barnabas to himself, who was attached to him by divine judgment. Yet he claims for himself alone the grace of the primacy granted by God, just as it was granted to Peter alone among the apostles (Acts 13:2).
