Thus the apostles of the circumcision extended their right hands to the apostles of the Gentiles, demonstrating the concord of their fellowship, so that both, knowing that they had received from the Lord the spirit of perfection in the administration of the Gospel, might show that they did not disagree with one another in anything.

They agreed among themselves only on this: that they should command those to whom they preached to remember the poor—something about which they had received no instruction by the Lord’s command or gift, since it was easy to learn from the Law—so that they might cultivate the mercy through which they had been redeemed by God.

For this reason he sets forth these things that took place between himself and the apostles: so that the Galatians may know that what they had received from him was true and approved.

(Verses 11.) “But when Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.” After the concord of their fellowship and the honor of the primacy that, through the grace of God, they had mutually shown one another, the apostles now appear to disagree because of negligence or error—not in a personal matter, but in their concern for the Church.

“I opposed him to his face.” What does this mean except that I contradicted him in his presence? And why does he add, “because he stood condemned”? He was condemned, of course, by evangelical truth, which this action opposed. For who would dare resist Peter, the first apostle, to whom the Lord had given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, unless he were another of equal standing, who, confident in his own election and knowing himself not inferior, should steadfastly reject what Peter had done without counsel?

(Verses 12–13.) “For before certain people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews joined him in this pretense, so that even Barnabas was led along with them in their pretense.”

All these Jews who joined Peter and Barnabas in this pretense were sincere. But because of the scandal of those who were coming from James—for they were zealous for the Law and honored both the Law and Christ on equal terms, which is contrary to the discipline of faith—they did not mingle with the Gentiles in their presence.

They feared the force of the audacity of those who were zealous for the Law. If this had been the only issue, it would not have been blameworthy; but where the error lay, he shows in what follows. Peter himself had yielded to the hostility and audacity of the Jews, fearing that through something easy to do a scandal might arise that would be difficult to settle. For he also purified himself according to the Law under compulsion (Acts 21:26), and he circumcised Timothy against his will (Acts 16:3).

(Verses 14.) “But when I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all: If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to practice Judaism?”

He attacks Peter alone so that the others might learn from the one who was first. Now he discloses the reason for his rebuke. There would have been no error if, in the presence of the Jews, Peter had withdrawn from the Gentiles out of fear of causing scandal. But the whole reason for the rebuke was this: when the Jews came from James, Peter not only separated himself from those with whom he had lived as a Gentile, but also compelled them to practice Judaism because of his fear of those men, so that the Gentiles would not know which course was true.

They knew that Peter himself had not lived among them as a Jew. But afterward, hearing from him that they had to follow the pattern of the Jews, they naturally hesitated over what was true. If it was true that they ought to practice Judaism, they regarded Peter as a transgressor because he had lived as a Gentile. But if the other course was better and true—that they should live simply—the Gentiles were being overthrown by his weakness, since, after the good had been taken away from them, a burdensome and ineffective way of life was being handed down.

When the apostle Paul yielded for an hour, he did not persuade others to do the same; rather, he loudly declared that he was doing something superfluous and empty because of the fury of the Jews. He would not have submitted to this matter unless an occasion had arisen in which the audacity of many Jews could boast against him.

Timothy was the son of a Jewish woman but had a Greek father (Acts 16:1); consequently, as an infant he had not been circumcised according to the Law. The Jews were lying in wait, watching to see whether Paul would take with him uncircumcised the one who had been born a Jew. They considered this unlawful for the Jewish race and were looking for an opportunity by which they might hold him as a destroyer of the Law. For this reason he yielded for an hour to their fury.

[Col. 0351A] (Verses 15–16.) “We are Jews by nature and not sinners from among the Gentiles. Yet, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the Law.”

By a clear argument he shows that they had been deceived into observing the Law, in which no one is justified before God. For even those who are Jews by nature, wishing to be justified, abandon the Law and take refuge in faith in Christ.

“For by works of the Law no flesh is justified.” He says that no human being is justified by works of the Law. For whoever is righteous is justified by faith, as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints were.

(Verses 17.) “But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? Certainly not.” How can Christ be a minister of sin, when he forgives sins? Therefore he says, “Certainly not.” But if, while wishing to be justified through faith in Christ, we serve the Law, we confess ourselves to be under sin, because faith draws a person away from the Law so that he may be righteous.

Therefore, if we give ourselves to the Law, we are found to be sinners, because those who are under the Law are under a curse.

(Verses 18.) “For if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor.” The meaning is clear: one who comes to Christ abandons the Law; for from being a slave he becomes free. But if he returns again to the Law, he becomes his own accuser, because he condemns his own action.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] Thus the Amerbach edition and several manuscripts; Erasmus and the editions that follow him, together with some manuscripts, read: “for he who approaches … from a slave he becomes free.”]

(Verses 19.) “For through the Law I died to the Law, so that I might live to God.” He says this because, through the law of faith, he died to the law of Moses. One dies to the Law when one is freed from it; and he lives to God, whose servant he becomes after being purchased by Christ.

“I have been crucified with Christ.” He is crucified with Christ who, imitating Christ’s footsteps, is not seized by any desire of the world, so that, living to God, he may appear dead to the world. For whoever does not do the things of the world or of error is dead to the world.

(Verses 20.) “But I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me.” There is no ambiguity: in the one who is freed from death through faith, Christ lives. For while he gives forgiveness of sins to one who deserved death, he himself lives in that person; the person has been rescued from death by Christ’s protection.

“And the life that I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I am not ungrateful for the grace of God.”

Because the future life has been promised to Christians, the person who now lives in this life, fortified by God’s help, lives in faith in the promised life. In the present life he contemplates its image, possessing, as it were, a pledge of the future life that has been obtained for us through God’s will by the love of Christ.

Therefore, he is not ungrateful to Christ who perseveres in faith in him, knowing that he possesses no one’s benefit except Christ’s, and that it would be an insult to Christ if he compared him with another whose help he could not have.

(Verses 21.) “For if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing.” Nothing could be clearer. If a person could have been justified through the Law, Christ ought not to have died. But because the Law could neither grant forgiveness of sins nor, after conquering the second death, strip the captives whom the cause of sin held captive, Christ died in order to provide what the Law could not. Therefore he did not die for nothing; his death is the justification of sinners.

## CHAPTER III

(Verses 1.) “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?” These are the words of one who is angry and astonished, because they had been so corrupted that they did not even recognize that they had been deceived. [Note: [Col. 0352D] The latest Paris editions say, “He used a proverb.” This is not objectionable if it rests on the authority of some manuscripts.]

He uses an introductory saying, for everyone who is bewitched passes from good to evil. So these people had passed from freedom and security to slavery and anxiety.

“Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed and crucified among you.” It is evident that, in the eyes of fools, Christ appears as one publicly proscribed—that is, stripped or condemned. In the eyes and understanding of the wise, however, he appears not only not to have been condemned, but to have condemned death itself by his cross. For the Lord’s passion is our life and the destruction of death.

But because these people had begun to think unworthily after being transferred to the Law, he complains that Christ appeared condemned in their minds. Therefore he adds: “Crucified among you.” That is, he was crucified in your understanding, as though he were merely a human being; for wherever there is no complete hope, he is regarded as a human being.

For this reason they did not think that complete salvation existed in Christ, because they placed the Law on an equal footing with him. But in those who understand Christ rightly, Christ lives in them; in Photinus he was crucified. For Christ is truly dead in the one in whom Christ is said to have been crucified, since this is presented as an accusation against him.

(Verses 2.) “I wish to learn only this from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law or by hearing with faith? Are you so lacking in understanding?”

He continues to speak with indignation. He is deeply grieved over their error, because he saw that the structure he had built among them through the Gospel had been destroyed. He was not moved in this way by the Corinthians. Although he calls them carnal (1 Corinthians 3:2), they had not been so bereft of understanding as to allow themselves to be circumcised.

Therefore the Galatians are called foolish and lacking in understanding, because they were unable even to care for the pain of their own flesh. A person is usually led only as far as something that delights him or does not cause pain.

[Col. 0352D] 219 The words are therefore those of one asking a question, and the question itself partly confirms the answer, when he says: “I wish to learn only this from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?”

He asks them about what they both gloried in and could not deny: that they had received the Holy Spirit through faith, not through the Law. Thus, coming to their senses, they might recognize that the gift of God in which they gloried had not been received through a work of the Law, but through believing in Christ; and so, at least for this reason, becoming grateful to Christ, they might abandon the Law, which they had learned was of no benefit to them.

He puts forward what at that time could not be denied: that the Spirit of God was present in believers. For the purpose of commending the beginnings of faith, this gift of God was manifested to human beings, just as it happened at the very beginning among the apostles and the other disciples, and also among the twelve men who—because they had not been baptized but polluted in an adulterous baptism under the name of John’s baptism [Note: [Col. 0353D] The Laudensis Codex reads, “in a second baptism.”]—were commanded by the apostle Paul to be baptized in the name of the Trinity. When Paul laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them and supplied speech in various languages together with their interpretation, so that no one would dare deny that the Holy Spirit was in them.

For this reason he calls the Galatians lacking in understanding: although they knew and were conscious of this fact, they degraded themselves by subjecting themselves to the care of the flesh.

(Verses 3.) “Having begun with the Spirit, are you now being brought to completion by the flesh?” He says this because, although the ascent of faith proceeds from lower things to the highest, these people had instead fallen from the highest things to the lowest. For having become spiritual through faith, they turned to the Law and lost the grace of the Spirit that they had obtained. “Completion” signifies destruction—that is, the destruction of faith.

(Verses 4–5.) “Have you suffered so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?” He indicates that they suffered many things for the faith at the hands of unbelievers. At that time those who believed were a reproach to others, whether household members or outsiders; for they were pointed out with a finger as though guilty of treason against the majesty of the state.

In the same way, the Galatians suffered many things at the hands of madmen, yet they had lost the reward of those sufferings by placing themselves under the Law. But by adding, “if indeed it was in vain,” he shows that he hopes they can be restored.

“Therefore, the one who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you, does he do this by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?” The meaning is the same, but he adds the signs of power, which testify to faith as a sure and reasonable hope.

No power accompanies the Law that might draw people toward its hope, because things that are seen are not hoped for; they are temporary, like the law of works, as we showed above.

(Verses 6.) As it is written (Genesis 15:6): “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” By the example of Abraham, who is the father of faith, he shows that righteousness is not reckoned from works of the Law, but through faith. For Abraham was justified by believing. Therefore, the Galatians had foolishly and imprudently subjected themselves to the Law, which was not given for justification.

(Verses 7.) “Know, then, that those who are from faith—these are sons of Abraham.” It is true that believers are sons of Abraham. For if Abraham was the first to be justified by faith, all who believe after him are his sons, whether they come from the Jews or from the Gentiles.

(Verses 8.) “And Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the Gospel beforehand to Abraham: ‘In you all the nations shall be blessed’” (Genesis 12:3). He says this because Abraham is a model of all believers, so that those who believe may be blessed in him. For by following his faith they become participants in the same blessing.

(Verses 9–10.) “Therefore those who are from faith are blessed with faithful Abraham; but as many as are from works of the Law are under a curse.” It is clear that the faithful are blessed with the faithful, just as the unfaithful are punished with the unfaithful. For those who live under the Law are under a curse, because they are transgressors of the Law.

(Deuteronomy 27:26.) “For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.’” This is written in Deuteronomy, because if anyone transgressed any provision of the Law, he was considered accursed. There are so many commandments that it is impossible to observe them all. Hence the apostle Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why do you place upon the brethren a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). These things were given to a negligent and arrogant [Note: [Col. 0354D] The same Laudensis Codex reads, “these things were spoken to the people.”] people, so that they might have the Law throughout their entire way of life.

[Col. 0354B] (Verses 12.) “Now that no one is justified by the Law before God is evident, because ‘the righteous person lives by faith’” (Habakkuk 2:4). Thus he teaches that one must withdraw from the Law, lest the righteousness sought through faith perish.

“The Law, however, is not from faith, but ‘the one who does these things will live by them’” (Ezekiel 20:21). The Law is not from faith because it commands nothing that must be believed. All its provisions are evident, so that the person who observes the Law may live; otherwise he must be punished, because he has committed what he knew ought to be avoided.

An objection can be raised from the opposite direction: If no one is justified by the Law, why is the one who transgresses some provision of the Law cursed? It is true that no one is justified by the Law before God, but he is justified before the world, so that he may be secure in the present life. But if he wishes to be justified before God, so that this may contribute to his merit on the day of judgment, he must follow the faith of God; otherwise, although secure here, he will be guilty in the future.

The Law is therefore beneficial, but only the Law written on tablets; for the other provisions, as he said, were given to be a burden.

(Verses 13.) “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us.” Because no one could fulfill the Law, all were liable to the curse of the Law, so that it might exact vengeance from them. But Christ, born as a human being and offered by the Father for us, redeemed us from the devil.

For he willingly offered him to death on behalf of those who were subject to the curse of the Law, and in this way made him a curse, just as in the Law the victim offered for sins was called “sin.” Therefore, because he was offered on behalf of the accursed, he became a curse. He also became a curse to the Jews, when he was killed as though he were a sinner.

[Col. 0354D] For this reason he did not say, “Having been made accursed for us,” but “having become a curse.” The one who was offered to death because of his own sin became accursed; for he died on account of his own case. But if one looks more closely, one will see that Christ became the curse of those by whom he was killed. For the cross of the Savior is the sin and curse of the Jews.

“For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’” (Deuteronomy 21:15). Moses said this in Deuteronomy concerning those condemned to death, so that it would be enough for those hung on a tree to remain there until evening and then be taken down for burial.

“Cursed is everyone,” he says, “who hangs on a tree,” so that this would be sufficient for one condemned to death, because he died suspended on a tree. If he remained suspended longer, his death would carry a greater disgrace than it ought, and it would become a stain upon his race if his death were made public for too long.

Therefore the innocent Savior, suspended on a tree, is not accursed, but is the curse of those by whom he was suspended. Yet, as far as the Jews are concerned, when they handed him over to Pilate to be killed as though he were a sinner, they made him a curse, so that he might be killed as though he were guilty, although he was innocent, because according to the Law one condemned to death is accursed.

For when they saw many people gathering around his teaching, they were jealous and said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19). Therefore he is said to have been killed for us, and for us in two ways. When they thought he ought to be killed so that he would not teach, they accomplished nothing, because his teaching increased and he abolished death through his passion.

For descending to the underworld, he freed the human race. For this reason also he allowed himself to be killed, knowing that it was for us and against the devil.

### (Verse 14.) So that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles through Christ Jesus—[Note: Roman edition: “and that we might receive the promise of the Spirit.”]—and that we might receive the blessing of the Spirit through faith.

He says this because, when the Jews were reproached and cursed while flattering themselves on account of the righteousness of the Law, and after killing the Savior [Note: Older edition, with several manuscripts: “as though he were guilty of violating the Sabbath”] as though he were a violator of the Sabbath, the blessing promised to Abraham passed to the Gentiles through faith in Christ Jesus. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:43).

### (Verse 15.) Brothers, I speak in human terms.

[Col. 0355C] He says this because he wishes to commend the reasoning of the divine promise by the example of a human legal case. No one annuls or adds provisions to a human testament once it has been confirmed. It is true that a properly executed testament of a deceased person cannot be rescinded.

### (Verse 16.) The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.

He does not say, “and to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though to one: “and to your seed,” which is Christ. This is what is written in Genesis to Abraham: “And in your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). This was certainly fulfilled in Christ, in whose name all the nations are blessed through faith. Therefore the promise was established not in many but in one, who is Christ.

By this argument the Apostle designates as guilty of falsifying the testament those who, believing in Christ, nevertheless hope for something from the Law as well, so that salvation would be promised not only in Christ but also in the Law. Therefore he proves that the promise of blessing was made in Christ alone.

### (Verse 17.) This is what I mean: a testament confirmed by God in Christ—[Note: Roman edition: “The Law, which was given afterward, does not annul it, so as to cancel the promise.”]—the Law, which came 430 years afterward, does not invalidate it so as to cancel the promise.

He teaches that the promise of blessing was established in Christ alone, in order to show that the Law was given 430 years later. For after the promise had been established, the Law was subsequently given—not, of course, to weaken the promise, but to signify what was to come and when it would come.

For if the inheritance comes from the Law, it no longer comes from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through a promise. [Note: Roman edition: “They defend two things that are contradictory to one another.”]

The Jews defend two contradictory positions. For it cannot in any way or by any reasoning be persuaded to them that the promise made to Abraham was nullified by the Law—and rightly so. Yet, through reckless presumption, they defend another position opposed to this, thinking that justification cannot come about without the works of the Law, even though they know that Abraham, who is the pattern of this matter, was justified without the works of the Law, by faith alone.

[Note: Codex Vall.: “But blinded by a certain rivalry.”]

But blinded by a kind of rivalry, they do not understand or consider that if justification comes through the Law, the promise is excluded; and if the promise is excluded, Abraham’s faith will unquestionably be frustrated. Yet the Jews cannot even bear to hear this, knowing that the promise to Abraham comes through faith. This promise justifies through faith, not through the Law, just as Abraham too was justified by faith.

Therefore the heirs of Abraham’s promise are those who succeed him by embracing the faith in which Abraham was blessed and justified. The testimony of Abraham’s promise is therefore called a testament, so that after his death his heirs might be heirs in the promise, having become his children through faith. This process continued until Christ, who had been promised to Abraham, so that after Christ’s death believers might, through the testament of Christ’s blood, become heirs of Abraham’s faith. Thus the gift promised to Abraham was bestowed upon his children in Christ, although Abraham himself also received this gift in the place where he was found.

### (Verse 19.) [Note: Roman edition: “Why then the Law? It was added because of transgressions … ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Why then the Law, etc.”]

Why then was the Law of works established until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made?

The Law of works—that is, the Law given through Moses—was placed between the beginning of the promise and the seed to whom the promise was made, that is, between Abraham and the Savior. It was therefore given long after the promise had been made, so that by this very distinction the Law might be seen to be one thing and the promise another; and so that it might instruct the people of God, separated from the Gentiles, under the fear of God, making them worthy to receive the promise, which is Christ.

It is called the Law of works because it teaches what is to be done bodily at God’s command concerning sacrifices, firstborn children, tithes, and other such matters.

Ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.

By “angels” he means messengers of God, namely Moses, Joshua the son of Nun, and the other prophets up to John the Baptist, concerning whom God says: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Mal. 3:1). Through these men, therefore, the Law was ordered and arranged by God in the hand—that is, under the authority—of the Savior. For he himself is the mediator, or reconciler, of God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5), so that he may save those whom he wills from among those who received the Law through the angels mentioned above. For he himself says: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21).

### (Verse 20.) Now a mediator is not of one party.

Without doubt, a mediator—that is, an arbiter—is not of one party but of two. When two peoples were fighting against each other, always divided and hostile because of their differing doctrines, the Savior came as their arbiter, removing from both peoples the matters over which they disagreed, so that they might be at peace.

He therefore took away from the Gentiles the multitude of gods and the service of the elements, which was a stumbling block to the Hebrews. He also took away from the Jews the works of the Law—that is, new moons, circumcision, observance of the Sabbath, distinctions among foods, and the other practices detested by the Gentiles. Thus those who had previously been enemies became peaceful.

If these things are so, why do the Galatians, through dullness of mind, [Col. 0357B] corrupt this arbitration by turning to Judaism?

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts: “corrupt this arbiter”; other manuscripts read more elegantly, as in the text.]

They nullify the Savior’s judgment when, after peace has been made, they submit themselves, as though repenting of that peace, to the things that had previously been hostile to peace. According to the Galatians’ understanding, therefore, Christ is not an arbiter, since, by bringing the two peoples under the Law, they have made them one; and no one is the arbiter of a single people.

He pursues this same meaning in his letter to the Ephesians, saying: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one and, in his flesh, broke down the dividing wall of hostility, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in decrees, that he might create in himself one new man from the two, making peace” (Eph. 2:14).

If he makes peace in one new man, he took away from both whatever caused their disagreement; and by giving them his Law he established for them what would make them peaceful. The Galatians have overturned this by turning to Judaism.

But God is one. He says this lest, by preaching Christ as God, he should be thought to have preached, contrary to the Law and the prophets, as God alongside the one God him whom he calls the arbiter.

[Note: Roman edition: “whom he appointed as arbiter, he was thought to have preached.”]

He therefore teaches that this arbiter is to be understood through the assumption of flesh, as he says to Timothy: “The arbiter of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (2 Tim. 5:2). But insofar as he is God, he is not separated from the Father but is one with the Father. Whether Father or Son, there is one God; for “God” is the name of nature and power, and the very relation of the names teaches that this nature remains undivided in the Father and the Son.

### (Verse 21.) Is the Law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not.

[Col. 0357D] Certainly not, because the Law is not hostile to the promise, especially since it confirms it. For Moses first says: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. 18:15). The Apostle Peter proves in the Acts of the Apostles that this was spoken about Christ.

For if a Law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly come from the Law (Acts 3:22). He calls this the righteousness that is counted as righteousness before God, namely, the righteousness of faith. For the Law too possessed a kind of righteousness, but one for the present age, not one that justified before God. It could not remit sins so as to make the sinful righteous; but it was given to inspire fear, urging people toward a good life and punishing the irreverent. Therefore the Law was not given to give life, but to condemn.

### (Verse 22.) But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.

He gives the same meaning in his letter to the Romans, saying: “God confined everything under sin, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32). He means what I mentioned above: the Law was given so that sinners would know themselves to be guilty before God. Once their sins had been made manifest, they were confined, so that they could not excuse themselves but would seek mercy; and so that, when the one promised to Abraham came, he might demand from them the faith that Abraham possessed, in order that they might obtain both the remission of their evils and justification.

God had made this known through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns ungodliness away from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isa. 59:20).

### (Verse 23.) Before faith came, we were kept under the Law, confined for the faith that was about to be revealed.

This is what he says: before the Savior came, we lived under the guardianship of the Law, so that we would not sin and would be worthy when the promise came. In this hope the Law kept us safe, so that it might present us—that is, the Jews—to the coming Christ.

### (Verse 24.) Therefore the Law was our pedagogue in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith.

The meaning is the same: we were under the care of the Law until Christ came, who would justify us when we believed.

### (Verses 25–26.) But when faith has come, we are no longer under a pedagogue; for you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.

One who acts under a pedagogue is not his own master; for a child, being small and prone to sin, is kept under the care of a pedagogue. But when Christ came, who makes those who were like minors into adults, we were freed from the pedagogue’s authority. Through the washing away of sins we became sons of God, although we had been slaves of sin.

### (Verse 27.) For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

He says this because believers, when they are transformed, put on Christ; when they are called by the name of what they believe.

### (Verse 28.) There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

He declares that there is no distinction among believers, so that no one is prejudged on the basis of what he was before he believed; for the same gift has been decreed for all these conditions. With God there is no partiality between persons, except according to character and life, so that people of one faith are distinguished by their merits, not by their persons.

### (Verse 29.) If therefore you are all one in Christ Jesus, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.

[Note: Roman edition: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise.”]

All believers are Abraham’s seed, because Abraham is the father of all believers. And if they are children, they are necessarily also heirs of his promise, so that through faith they may obtain what was promised to Abraham and become participants in his justification in the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER IV

### (Verses 1–2.) I mean that as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of everything; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father.

It is true that fathers have established the law and determined up to what age a child must remain subject before reaching maturity. Thus, as long as he is a child, he cannot use his freedom or rule as an heir; rather, in his condition under guardians or stewards, he is almost like a slave.

By this example he proves that those who were under the Law were children with regard to merit and did not possess freedom, because they were subject to the condition of the Law on account of sin.

### (Verse 3.) So also, when we were children, we were subject to the elements of this world.

By “elements” he means new moons and the Sabbath. New moons are lunar days, which the Jews observe; the Sabbath is a day of rest.

Before the promise came—that is, before the gift of God’s grace, purifying and justifying believers—we were imperfect and childish under the Law of God, subject to fellow servants as to pedagogues. Our freedom was held captive because of sin.

The Jews, however, did not hope for anything from the elements, as the pagans did; rather, they worshiped God the Creator in the creature.

### (Verses 4–5.) But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

The fullness of time is the completion of the period appointed by God the Father, when he would send his Son. Born of a Virgin, he was born as a human being and subjected himself to the Law until the time of baptism, so that he might provide the pattern by which sinners, washed clean and freed from the yoke of the Law through God’s gracious favor, would be adopted as his sons, as he had promised to those redeemed by the blood of his Son.

It was necessary for the Savior to be born under the Law, as a son of Abraham according to the flesh, so that, appearing circumcised, he might be shown to be the one promised to Abraham, who would come to justify the Gentiles through faith, bearing the sign of the one to whom he had been promised.

Therefore no one else needed to be circumcised; for the sign continued until the one who had been promised to restore the faith in which Abraham was justified while uncircumcised had come, so that believers would have no need of circumcision.

Abraham, however, was circumcised because he believed that he would have a son in whom all the nations would be blessed. Thus the sign continued until the promised one came.

If people had believed what Abraham believed, circumcision would not have continued, lest the objection be raised: If Abraham believed and was circumcised, why are believers not circumcised?

### (Verse 6.) And because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.”

He began with those to whom he is writing, saying: “Because you are sons of God”; and then he includes the Jews when he says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.”

When he said that the Gentiles who believe in Christ, who had previously been enemies, are sons of God, there was no doubt that believing Jews were also called sons of God, since it is clear that they had long ago been called by this name.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts: “For they had formerly received the name as an image.”]

For they had long ago received the name, as it were, in an image, so that it might later be confirmed through Christ; for without the Spirit it was incomplete. This is what he also says to the Romans: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are sons of God” (Rom. 8:16).

To prove that we had been adopted by God as sons, he gave us his Spirit, who displays the Father’s mark upon his children. Since in our weakness and unworthiness we would not dare to say this, he prompts us to dare to say “Abba,” which means “Father.”

[Col. 0360B] In the past, this was not granted even to the Jews to say.

### (Verse 7.) Therefore you are no longer a slave but a son.

He is not a slave because he has been removed from the power of the Law and made a companion of the blessing of God’s own Son.

And if a son, then also an heir through God.

There is no doubt that someone adopts a son for the purpose of leaving him as an heir. But an inheritance comes from someone’s death. How, then, are mortals called heirs of one who always lives? Scripture speaks according to our custom, so that we may understand. To show that the Father will give his children a share of his goods, it calls the things he will give an inheritance.

### (Verse 8.) But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods.

Since previously they sinned through ignorance while serving idols, he indicates that these things were unknown to them, as Abimelech says to God in Genesis: “Lord,” he says, “will you destroy an ignorant nation?” (Gen. 20:4).

### (Verse 9.) But now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God—how can you turn back again to weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved again?

He notes the gravity of their offense, because after coming to know God they had begun to follow the practices of the pagans. He adds even more: “It is not that they came to know God, but rather that they were known by God.”

For although they were not seeking God, he called them to his grace. Yet these ungrateful people had begun to turn back to the things they had worshiped when they did not know God, venerating weak and beggarly elements rather than Christ with their whole mind, in whom all divinity dwells.

He calls the elements weak and beggarly because they are imperfect; for in governing the world they need one another. In Christ, however, salvation is perfect.

### (Verse 10.) You observe days, months, seasons, and years.

Now he explains which elements he meant. The sun makes the day; the course of the moon makes the months. The seasons are spring, summer, autumn, and winter; these four, completing their proper cycle, make the year.

Those observe days who say, for example: “One must not set out tomorrow; nothing should be begun the day after tomorrow.” In this way they are accustomed to be deceived even more.

Those observe months who scrutinize the course of the moon, saying, for example: “On the seventh moon one must not make tools; on the ninth moon one ought not to bring a purchased slave home.” Through these practices misfortunes more easily occur.

They observe seasons when they say: “Today is the beginning of spring; it is a festival; the day after tomorrow is the Vulcanalia.” They say such things as: “It is tomorrow; one may not leave the house.”

They observe years when they say: “The Kalends of January are the new year,” as though the year were not completed each day. They use this superstition to recall that Janus was two-faced, a practice that ought to be far from the servants of God.

For if God is loved with the whole heart, then, with him propitious, there should be no fear or suspicion concerning such matters. Whatever is done simply in devotion to God can turn out well.

### (Verse 11.) [Note: Roman edition: “I fear that I have labored in vain.”] I fear for you, that I may have labored in vain among you.

The Galatians had been subverted in two ways: after God’s grace, they had turned not only to the Law but also to their former errors. Once led astray or overthrown, they had easily inclined toward the observance of days and months in connection with the Law; for the observance of the Sabbath and of new moons had drawn them to these practices.

Therefore he says: “I fear that I may have labored in vain among you.” For he saw them advancing toward worse things, so that they might even withdraw completely from Christ.

### (Verse 12.) Become as I am, because I also became as you are.

He says this so that they may make an effort to correct these matters. It is not impossible for them to be as he is, because he too was what they were—that is, a human being. Although he had been in error, persecuting the Church, he was corrected and converted.

Brothers, I beg you, you have done me no wrong.

He now deals with them more gently and begins to recall their good qualities.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “and their good works.” This is incorrect. Below, where all editions and a few manuscripts read “pressed for a long time, they would become harsher, embittered,” other manuscripts read more appropriately, as in the text.]

After the severe reprimands, he mentions their good works so that, on hearing their good qualities, they might be encouraged and deliberately reform themselves, lest, pressed too long by harsher rebukes, they become embittered.

He nevertheless says that they had done him no harm; their offense harmed them, for the Apostle had fulfilled the ministry entrusted to him, preaching to them with all diligence, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “You,” he says, “preach. If they listen to you, you will gain them; if not, you will save your own soul” (Ezek. 3:21).

### (Verses 13–14.) You know that it was because of weakness of the flesh that I first preached the gospel to you, and you did not despise or reject your trial in my flesh.

He recalls to their memory the time when he first preached the Gospel of God to them. At that time the Apostle was being treated outrageously and weakened by beatings. One who is humbled and does not resist for the sake of the Gospel of God appears weak.

In this he praises their steadfastness, because they were not drawn away from the faith. The Apostle’s injuries were a trial for the Galatians, in which they were found firm and did not doubt the faith.

They could have taken offense and said: “What power or hope is there in this faith, when its minister is being so humiliated?”

[Note: Laudun manuscript: “They could have presented a stumbling block and said: ‘When the Lord’s servant knows that he…’”]

But because they had already filled their minds with hope for the future, they did not fear present outcomes for the name of Christ. They were certain that the dignity of our faith is found not on earth but in heaven, and that great rewards are repaid for these tribulations.

He brings shame upon them because, after these praiseworthy beginnings, they had been deceived so that they appeared blameworthy.

But you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

He praises this especially in them: his afflictions had not disfigured him in their eyes but had commended him to them, since they knew that he suffered ruinous treatment for the sake of those who believe.

Just as they received the Apostle as an angel of God, believing that what he preached was God’s gift, so they showed him honor as though they were honoring the Lord Jesus himself, the author of that gift.

### (Verse 15.) [Note: Roman edition: “What then has become of your blessedness?”] What then had become of your blessedness?

He says that they had been blessed among the other Churches because the Apostles were not broken by insults but grew in faith.

For I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.

He shows that their devotion had been so complete that they had not merely received him well but had also been found strong in faith. What contributes even more to their praise is that they offered almost all their possessions to him to be expended.

For this reason he grieves all the more: such great love had been overturned by perverse teaching.

### (Verse 16.) Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?

He says this because, he declares, it cannot be that he should be their enemy, since he had experienced such great devotion from them. But because no one wishes to be reproved when he is in error, he appears to them to be an enemy, although he is rightly correcting them.

### (Verse 17.) They are zealous for you, but not rightly; rather, they want to exclude you so that you may be zealous for them.

He indicates that the envy of the Jews had subverted them. Seeing them prosper so greatly in the Gospel and possess such love for the Apostle, the Jews acted in every way to deceive them.

They were enemies of the Apostles on account of the Law, wishing, while the Savior’s name remained, to make the Galatians Jews. They rejoiced in their overthrow, for they could not tolerate the Gentiles who were uncircumcised hearing that the grace promised to them had been given.

Therefore they wanted the Galatians to become their imitators, so that they might be circumcised according to their custom.

### (Verse 18.) [Note: Roman edition: “Zealously pursue better gifts, always for what is good.”] But pursue better gifts; pursue what is good always, and not only when I am present with you.

The better gifts are spiritual gifts, which, when imitated, will have effect before God. These are the spiritual goods that he wants them always to imitate, not temporarily, as they had done before, or only while he was present; afterward they were to turn to something else. He wants them henceforth to persevere in what is good.

### (Verse 19.) My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.

He had first begotten them through faith in baptism. But because they were found to have been born as though by miscarriage, deformed and weak,

[Note: Some manuscripts: “as though born by miscarriage.”]

he now reforms them into Christ with the pain of his counsel. Having conceived faith but paying no attention at all to the meaning of faith, they are said not to have Christ formed in their minds. For if they had understood God’s grace in Christ, they would not, after believing, have been led over into Judaism.

### (Verse 20.) I wish I were present with you now and could change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.

[Note: Roman edition: “He wishes to deal with them while present.”]

He wants to rebuke them in person, so that he may change his tone from praise to blame, in order that they may be put to shame in two ways: by their error and by the shame of the Apostle, which he suffered among those whom he had preferred to others.

### (Verses 21–22.) Tell me, you who want to be under the Law, do you not read the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.

[Col. 0363B] This is found in Genesis. Since Sarah could not bear children—for she was barren—she offered her slave woman Hagar to her husband Abraham as a concubine, so that she might adopt whatever child she bore. Thus Ishmael was born from Hagar.

Afterward, by God’s command, a son was promised to Abraham from his wife Sarah, who was barren; she bore Isaac to Abraham. Then Abraham began to have two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.

### (Verses 23–24.) But the one born from the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one born from the free woman was born through the promise. These things are said allegorically.

Ishmael, who was born from the slave woman Hagar, was born according to the flesh, because he was born according to ordinary custom. Isaac, however, was born through the promise, not according to ordinary custom but through God’s providence and power, since Sarah was both old and barren.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit “through the promise.”]

Isaac was born as a type of Christ. Therefore he asserts that these things were spoken allegorically, so that the persons of Ishmael and Isaac might signify one thing through another.

Ishmael signifies the origin of the Jews, or of those who are slaves of sin; Isaac signifies Christians, because they are born in freedom. For the one who receives remission of sins becomes free.

For these are the two Testaments.

Moses took the blood of a calf in a bowl and sprinkled the people, saying: “This is the blood of the Testament that God has established for you” (Exod. 24:8).

This is what he said: “One is from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar.” For the Law was given on Mount Sinai. When Moses recited it to the people, he called the book the Testament, and then sprinkled the people with blood, as I have said.

This Law held sinners guilty, and they began to be slaves of sin, becoming children of Hagar, as of a slave woman.

### (Verse 25.) Now Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which is joined to the Jerusalem that now exists, for it is in slavery with her children.

He says that Hagar signifies the earthly Jerusalem, that is, the Synagogue, which generates for slavery; for those whom it generates are under sin.

### (Verse 26.) But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

The one whom he calls our mother is the rule of the Lord’s mystery, through which we are reborn into freedom, just as she herself is free.

Therefore she is also called heavenly, because heaven is her dwelling. Those whom she generates will be with her there, as the Lord says: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be where I am, and that they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

She is also life, because those who are reborn through her by believing are granted immortality. For this is what has been said about the Lord: that what was made in him is life. Just as the Father has life, so he also gave the Son life, and life was the light of human beings (John 5:26).

This life and light is the mother of the faithful. In Isaiah this is stated, as follows:

### (Verse 27.) For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not suffer the pains of childbirth; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. 54:2).

He says that the earthly Jerusalem has a husband because she generates according to the flesh. But he calls the heavenly Jerusalem, which he says is our mother, barren because she does not give birth according to the flesh and does not suffer labor pains—that is, she does not labor.

She does, however, generate spiritually and without suffering, crying out in joy. Once deserted—for by whom, if not by Adam, who abandoned life and pursued death?—she now has more children than the one who has a husband, that is, than the one who generates carnally.

For Christians are far more numerous than Jews, as it is said in the Apocalypse: “And I saw a great multitude that no one could number, from every tribe and nation” (Rev. 7:9).

### (Verse 28.) But you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.

This means that they are not children of the flesh but of God, because Isaac was born as a type of the Son of God.

He wants them to understand that, after becoming children of God, they turned aside and became children of the flesh; but if they repent, they are children of God.

### (Verse 29.) But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now.

Not only was Ishmael born according to the flesh, but Esau was as well, since he too was born as a type of the Jewish people. Concerning him it is written in the prophet Malachi: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” (Mal. 1:3).

He persecuted Jacob, who was born as a figure of the Christian people and was called Israel, that is, “a man seeing God” (Gen. 27:41).

Similarly, this signified that the Jews, through envy, persecuted Christians. For this reason they deliberately overthrew the Galatians through carnal cunning.

### (Verse 30.) But what does Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

These are Sarah’s words. She bears the type of the heavenly Jerusalem, which generates Isaac through the promise, so that, once the son of the slave woman—that is, the Jewish people—has been cast out and rejected because of unbelief—for they are slaves of sin, since remission of sins has not been granted to them—the son of the free woman, that is, the new people of the kingdom of heaven, may be heir of that Jerusalem above.

### (Verse 31.) Therefore we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom with which Christ has set us free.

We were therefore children of the slave woman while we were subject to sins; but after receiving remission of sins from Christ, we have been set free.

## CHAPTER V

### (Verse 1.) Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery.

He urges them to stand firm in the grace they have received, lest by returning to former things they lose the gift of freedom they had obtained.

### (Verse 2.) Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will benefit you nothing.

Now he does not conceal the force of his evident truth and authority, saying: “Behold, I, Paul, tell you”—that is, I, the teacher of the Gentiles, whose work you are in Christ, openly tell you—“that Christ will benefit you nothing if you are circumcised.”

For the Lord himself says: “The Law and the prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of heaven is preached” (Luke 16:16).

Before the new preaching began, therefore, circumcision was necessary. But now, with the law of faith taking its place, the things commanded by the unformed truth must be followed, because the old and the new should not be mixed, according to the authority of the Lord who preached. For he says: “No one sews a patch of new cloth onto an old garment; for it tears the garment, and the rent becomes worse” (Matt. 9:16).

Therefore circumcision added to a believer will not only benefit him nothing but will also harm him. For it is a greater evil to become a slave from being free than to be born a slave.

### (Verse 3.) I testify again to every person who circumcises himself that he is obligated to keep the whole Law.

Some people can observe the Law to some extent without being circumcised. For many Romans in Judea observed the Law while uncircumcised.

Thus the Apostle Paul says to King Agrippa of Judea: “I know, King Agrippa, that you believe the prophets; I know that you believe” (Acts 26:27).

And the centurion whose servant was dying sent to Jesus and asked him to come and heal his servant. The Jews, bearing witness on his behalf, said to Jesus: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him; for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us” (Luke 7:4–5).

Nevertheless, no circumcised person fails to observe the whole Law; he is obligated because the Law was given to the circumcised. He said this because they showed themselves so foolish that they deserved to bear all the burdens of the Law.

### (Verse 4.) You have been severed from Christ.

Those for whom Christ is of no benefit have been severed from Christ; for they had been full of his grace, and when it departed they were emptied.

He speaks to those who, after receiving the gift of God’s grace, preferred to be circumcised.

For you who glory in the Law have fallen away from grace.

[Note: Thus read by the majority and the better manuscripts; some, however, and all editions read: “You who seek justification in the Law.”]

The righteousness of the Law consists in observing the things that were given. Therefore whoever wishes to be justified in these things after faith loses grace, because the gift of God came for this purpose: that, when the burdens of the Law had ceased, it might justify believers before God.

(Verses 5–6.) But we, through the Spirit and by faith, await the hope of righteousness; for in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any force nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love. What he says is clear: the hope of justification is in faith through the Spirit, not through the works of the Law; for in faith God is served spiritually, with devotion of mind and purity of heart. Hence the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). Accordingly, neither uncircumcision nor circumcision has any force; only faith working through love is necessary for justification. Faith must be strengthened by brotherly love, so that the believer may be perfect. Finally, when the scribe asked what the first commandment was, the Savior replied: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments,” he says, “the whole Law and the prophets depend” (Matthew 22:37ff.). All the other commandments, therefore, are imperfect, since perfection is contained in these two commandments.

(Verses 7.) You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth? He testifies that their exercise in the work of faith had been good, but that the wickedness of evil men had detained them, so that they did not complete their course through effective perseverance. Therefore he urges them to come to their senses and henceforth to believe none of those who, by persuading them that the works of the Law had to be observed, prevented them from obeying the truth of the Gospel.

(Verses 8.) This persuasion is not from him who calls you, namely, God. It is true that the Jews were doing these things according to human counsel, in order to place them under the yoke of the Law—not according to the judgment of God, who was calling them through his Apostle to grace.

(Verses 9.) A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. He says this because, although they add even a small amount of the Law to faith, they violate faith, so that it may neither bear fruit nor be acceptable. He added this lest they perhaps think that they retained the grace of faith intact if they observed a few precepts of the Law. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “to possess the grace of God.”]

[Col. 0336C] (Verse 10.) I am confident in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise. He says that he trusts in them with this hope: they had entered the path of error not willingly, but after being deceived. Therefore, having shown them the true road, he is confident that they can easily return. But whoever is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be. Just as the one who converts an erring person is to be rewarded—as the Apostle James says in his epistle: “Whoever brings a sinner back will save his soul from death” [Note: Some manuscripts restore “from death.”] “and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:20)—so also whoever forces one walking on the right road to turn onto a byway incurs condemnation, whoever he may be. He adds this on account of those who might claim merit for themselves because they were sons of Abraham according to the flesh. Indeed, they say to Jesus: “We are sons of Abraham” (John 8:33).

(Verses 11.) But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still suffering persecution? What he says is clear: for this reason he was regarded as an enemy by the Jews, and they did not cease persecuting him, because he taught that circumcision no longer remained in force. Finally, when the Jews compelled him and repeatedly brought false accusations against him, seeing the judge to be biased, he was forced to appeal to Caesar. Therefore the offense of the cross has been removed (Acts 25:11). The preaching of the cross was an offense to the Jews because it abolished the Sabbath and circumcision. If he had admitted circumcision, there would have been no offense, and the Jews would have been at peace with us. For they said concerning the Savior: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9:16).

(Verses 12.) I wish that those who are unsettling you would even mutilate themselves! This is like what he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed” (1 Corinthians 16:22). These too belong to that diseased flock, and he joins them to its sentence, so that they may be cut off [Note: Some manuscripts read “from the mind of the Lord”; one, “from the commandments of the Lord”; the remaining manuscripts and editions, “from the mercy of God”] from the mercy of the Lord, since they have stripped the Galatians of God’s grace. And he curses them not only spiritually but also bodily: since they were compelling the Galatians to be circumcised, they themselves should be mutilated, so that the pain of the body might be increased for them.

(Verses 13.) For you were called to freedom, brothers. They were called to freedom because, although they were subject to sins, they received the grace of God, their offenses were forgiven, and they were set free. [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “receiving the grace of God, with their offenses forgiven,” and below the Roman edition alone reads “and into the dominion of the Law.”] Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. He says this lest the opportunity of the flesh deprive them of the freedom they have received; for this reason they wanted to have them circumcised, so that they might enter into subjection to the Law. Therefore he warns them not to give an opportunity for this by consenting to them. But through the love of the Spirit serve one another. He urges them to possess love not through an affection of the flesh but through the love of the Spirit, so that they may be subject to one another.

(Verses 14.) For the whole Law is fulfilled in you in one saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). This is written in Leviticus, as was said above: the perfection of salvation is accomplished through love, because, as the Apostle John says, whoever does not love his brother does not love God (1 John 4:20).

(Verses 15.) But if you bite and accuse one another [Note: The Roman edition reads “bite and devour one another”], take care that you are not consumed by one another. It is clear that dissension among brothers is hostile to love. Therefore he urges them to be peaceful and to advance in goodness. Contentions produce quarrels, whose fruit is the destruction of life.

(Verses 16.) But I say: walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desire of the flesh. After forbidding them the law of works, which contains carnal precepts, he now commands them to restrain themselves from the vices of the flesh. For the one who walks by the Spirit is the one who flees sins.

(Verses 17.) For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “so that you do not do whatever you wish”]. He sets forth two laws, as he also does in the Epistle to the Romans (7:23), which are opposed to one another: one of God and the other of sin. The latter is signified in the flesh because it delights in visible things and is desirous of sins, so that, with these forces opposing one another, the inner man does not do what he wishes. The divine law presses down and drives away the law of sin, advising a person to preserve the vigor of his nature, lest he be captured by enticements. The other, on the contrary, acting in ambush, provokes a person with blandishments so that he may despise the commandment of the divine law. When a person has consented to the law of God, the law of sin resists, persuading him not to do what the divine law commands. Conversely, the law of God recalls the person, so that he may not do what the law of sin suggests. A person does not regard this as absurd, for he knows that it accords with his nature to do what the law of God commands. Indeed, he rejoices when he does these things; but when he performs what the law of sin suggests, he sees himself as shameful and shudders afterward. Therefore the precepts of the law of the Spirit must be observed, and carnal things must be fled, for conscience itself accuses a person if he consents to it, knowing that the things suggested by the Law of sin are objects of horror.

(Verses 18.) But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law. This is not obscure: whoever has the Holy Spirit as his guide does not go astray. For the law rules over those who go astray, as he says elsewhere: “The law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Timothy 1:9). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “But if you are led by the Spirit of God.”]

(Verses 19–21.) The works of the flesh are manifest: adultery, fornication, impurity, obscenity, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, contentions, pretenses, anger, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I also warned you, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “contentions, jealousies, angers.”] All these things and those like them are members of the law of sin, which the Apostle calls works of the flesh, because these errors are from the world, and the flesh is from it as well. For all sins arise externally from the side of the flesh, not from the side of the Spirit; therefore they are not improperly called works of the flesh.

[Col. 0368C] (Verses 22–24.) But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, hope, gentleness, self-control, chastity, and goodness; against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. He did not say, “The works of the Spirit are love,” but “the fruit of the Spirit”; for the law of the Spirit produces the things he mentioned above, so that through them the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven may be sought. Those devoted to Christ he calls “christs,” that is, anointed ones. They crucify the flesh—that is, the world—when they condemn the things from which errors arise. Following this same meaning, the Apostle John says: “Do not love this world, nor the things that are in this world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything that is in this world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes” (1 John 2:15). Whoever, therefore, does not desire the world and what is in the world crucifies the flesh. These vices—idolatry, sorceries, heresies, envies, enmities, anger, and the like—must not be attributed to the human body; rather, they are called carnal because they belong to the side of the world, as I mentioned above. Meanwhile, he has set down no more than ten things signifying the fruit of the Spirit, so that he may appear to have comprehended everything in them according to the tablets of God’s Testament, in which no more than ten words of the commandments were handed down.

(Verses 25–26.) If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not pursue empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another. He says this because, if we live well and honorably, we ought also to have good conduct. For this is to live by the Spirit: to possess an undefiled life. We walk by the Spirit if we strive for peace, for peace produces love. Empty glory consists in wishing to win where there is no prize, so that someone develops a zeal for contention and rivalry, knowing that these generate disagreements and quarrels. “The servant of the Lord,” he says, “must not quarrel” (2 Timothy 2:24). Such conduct dries up the fruit of a good life, destroying the promised hope of chaste behavior. A good and chaste life must be adorned with good conduct and enriched with goodwill.

CHAPTER VI

(Verses 1–2.) Brothers, even if someone has been overtaken by some offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted; bear one another’s burdens. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads “even if he has been overtaken”; it agrees with the old edition and some manuscripts in reading “humble such a person,” while the remaining manuscripts have the more suitable “restore such a person.”] He now addresses those who were stronger, lest, inflated by their good life, they think that someone who had perhaps been ensnared by sin should be despised and rejected. Therefore he counsels them concerning this. They should be urged to reform themselves with gentleness, because, if they are rebuked too harshly and authoritatively, they will not allow themselves to be corrected; instead, they will begin to defend themselves, lest they appear shameful, and they will begin to become worse. Remove a person from contention and boldness, and you will have him submissive; humility is accustomed even to bend the proud. And so that this might be done with complete gentleness of spirit, he added: “Lest you also be tempted,” so that for this reason alone he would not despise the sinner, knowing that he too could sin. And thus you will fulfill the law of Christ, for the law of Christ wishes all to be saved. Accordingly, whoever counsels a sinning brother to return to his former purpose fulfills the will of Christ.

(Verses 3–4.) For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another. This is true, and no one is unaware of it: if we consider our actions and our mind, we put ourselves before no one and do not easily judge anyone. Whoever exalts himself as though he were something is in error, for he does not know that growth comes from humility. He does not keep before his eyes the words and deeds of the Savior, who, although he is Lord of all, humbled himself (Philippians 2:8), in order to give us an example of what we ought to follow if we wish to grow. If we exalt ourselves, we will be brought low; this is what the ignorance of an inflated heart does, so that a person may appear more commendable in the eyes of men. For by despising and scorning sinners, he strives to appear righteous, like that Pharisee whom the Lord censures (Luke 18:10). Is the one who desires present glory not truly ignorant? Is the one who wishes to obtain the reward of righteousness in the present not truly despairing of future things? Why? Because he is not righteous in his deed but falsely pretends to righteousness. Whoever wishes to be righteous places another before himself, so that he may truly be righteous. For each person knows his own evils better than another’s.

(Verses 5.) For each person will carry his own burden. Finally, he wished to make this known to the proud: no one is defiled by another’s sin, provided that he dissents from it. Thus no one should be afraid to join himself to a sinner or to receive one who approaches him, so that he may gain him.

(Verses 6.) Let the one who is catechized [Note: The Roman edition omitted this parenthesis.] in the word—that is, the one who hears the word of God—share in all good things with the one who catechizes him. He says this so that those who hear may share in all good things with their teachers. But if the teachers act otherwise than they teach, one should not share with them in those matters but dissent from them, so that the Law may be your guide more than a human being. The teacher will harm himself, not you, because you observe what he has taught.

(Verses 7.) Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. No one doubts that deception cannot be practiced against God, but that each person receives from him what he deserves.

(Verses 8.) For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. Whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh. Here he signifies the carnal vices that are ordinarily admitted in the flesh, so that whoever has corrupted his flesh may know that he will become subject to corruption. The one who presumes upon what is forbidden corrupts the body. But whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit. A Christian consists of spirit and flesh; for, in comparison with the Holy Spirit, a human being is flesh. When, therefore, he gives assent to the Spirit, restraining himself from the things that oppose it, he sows spiritually, so that he may be able to reap eternal life. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “For by the testimony of the Spirit he will receive immortality.”] He receives the testimony of the Spirit and immortality as his reward. For just as the one who corrupts himself by dishonoring his body will belong not to eternity but to corruption, so also the one who keeps himself undefiled will obtain eternal life. For this is eternal life: to live without punishment and to possess glory. If, in the present, the person who is in anxiety denies that he is living, how much more will the one who is alienated from God suffer torturing fire! [Note: Some manuscripts read: “he will suffer a consuming fire.”]

(Verses 9.) Let us not grow weary in doing good, for at the proper time we shall reap without weariness. He says this because the one who is strong in sowing will also be strong in reaping—that is, he will receive according to what he does. Therefore he urges us to be ready to do good and not to become weary, confident that we shall receive great things in exchange for small things, and eternal things in exchange for earthly things, at the time God promised.

(Verses 10.) Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone. The Gentiles have time for doing evil; for how can people without God do good? Christians, however, once they have become such, have time to do good to all people, so that, after receiving faith, their good work may advance toward the promised reward. Time is granted to life for this reason: so that we may now conduct ourselves justly, giving an example to the Gentiles. And especially to those who are of the household of faith. It is true that we ought to be more ready and inclined toward goodness with respect to our brothers, because we are members of one another. We should therefore devote ourselves to what is beneficial, not to circumcision, which is now an empty matter.

(Verses 11.) Know with what sort of letters I have written to you with my own hand. [Note: The manuscript of Vallicelliana reads: “Observe with what sort of letters I have written,” and so forth.] He gives authority to his epistle. When he says, “I have written with my own hand,” he wishes these words to be obeyed. For where there is an autograph hand, it cannot be said to be false. Otherwise, they might make excuses concerning the epistle, claiming either that it was false or that it was not the Apostle’s, unwilling to be reproved.

[Col. 0371B] (Verses 12.) All who wish to please in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. To please in the flesh means to please human beings. In order to live with the Jews—whom he calls false apostles—favorably or without hostility, they preached Christ in such a way that they also taught that the Law had to be observed. The Apostle, however, never feared this; he consistently did not keep silent about what is true, providing for both himself and those whom he taught. Finally, he says: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 21:13).

(Verses 13.) For even those who are circumcised do not keep the Law; but they wish you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh. This is like what was said to the Apostle Peter: “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Galatians 2:14). So also these men, although they themselves did not keep the Law and lived unjustly, were zealous for circumcision, so that they might appear to be defenders and lovers of the Law. Yet it is clear that the one who defends and keeps the Law is the person who carries out its righteous requirements and does not neglect the commandment given for life [uncertain reading in the source: “per inens datum”]. Such, therefore, was the excuse of the Galatians. He says this so that, at least in this way, they may understand that they were being mocked as fools and dullards, whose sufferings were occasions of glory for those men. [Note: The Vallicelliana codex reads “calamity”; some others read “disaster.” Thus their exultation was over the Galatians’ sufferings.]

(Verses 14.) But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “But may it not happen to me to boast.”] Just as the false apostles, through hypocrisy, avoided tribulations endured for the name of Christ as though they were useless, being ashamed of them, so the Apostle gloried in them, knowing that great reward would result from them. So did his fellow apostles, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Then, having been beaten, the apostles went out from the council, rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ” (Acts 5:4). Whoever has all his hope in Christ glories in his cross. For that person the world too has been crucified, being certain that the love of Christ’s cross is life, while love of the world produces death. Thus they have died to one another: the world to the Apostle and the Apostle to the world, since the Apostle desires nothing of the world and the world has nothing of its own that it recognizes in the Apostle, just as the Lord says: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30).

(Verses 15–16.) For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision is anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And upon all who follow this rule there will be peace and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. Our regeneration is the new creation; it is this that gives growth to those who persevere. For upon these is the peace of God. Whoever is at peace with God fears the hostility of no one; he is safe under the protection and mercy of God, which was promised and remains upon the Israel of God, not upon the Israel of man. The unbelieving Jews are Israelites according to the flesh. He therefore signified two groups upon whom the peace and mercy of God remain: believing Jews and faithful Gentiles.

(Verses 17.) Henceforth let no one cause me trouble.
