He did not wish to be troubled any longer, lest he perhaps be compelled to write again; instead, he now wishes them to become more corrected, so that, with their errors cut away, he might have rest after so many annoyances. But if they should show themselves more stubborn and inflexible in being converted, they should withdraw from him, so that he might devote his labor and effectiveness to those from whom he could hope for reward or gain. For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body. He says this in anger, because he saw that the sufferings he endured for the sake of believers were ineffective among them. For with steadfastness and faith in his teaching he did not fear suffering blows and chains for Christ; rather, out of love for believers he endured having the scars of wounds in his body, so that he might preach to them no less faithfully, as did the false apostles who had deceived the Galatians. Therefore he does not want anyone who is not devoted to this cause to trouble him. For these marks—that is, the scars of wounds—are the testimonies of believers, who suffer because they are worthy of the future promise. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “For with great steadfastness,” and so forth.]

(Verses 18.) The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. He does not speak of the grace of the Law, but says that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ is with the spirit of those whom he calls spiritual brothers; for not all of them had been completely overthrown.

[Col. 0371]

IN THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE EPHESIANS

231 PROLOGUE

[Col. 0371D]

The Apostle did not establish the Ephesians in the faith but strengthened them, having suffered many evils for them at the hands of the faithless, as he says: “If, speaking humanly, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantage is it to me if the dead are not raised?” (1 Corinthians 15:32). And because he foresees that his struggle will not be without the effect of their progress [Note: The old edition reads “not without the effect of progress”; the Roman edition, “progress”; manuscripts have lacunae before “perfection”], he rejoices in them and urges them by his writing toward better things concerning his confinement in the city of Rome. For when he came from Jerusalem in custody under bail, he is understood to have lived outside the camp in his own rented lodging (Acts 28:16).

CHAPTER I

(Verses 1.) Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to all the saints who are in Ephesus and the faithful in Christ Jesus. [Note: After introducing the first two verses of the Apostle in this way, the Roman edition resumes: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ. As usual he writes … he testifies … by the will … To all the saints who are … in Christ Jesus. He writes not only to the faithful.”] He writes in his customary manner, testifying that he is an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. He writes not only to the faithful but also to the saints, so that they may then truly be faithful if they are holy in Christ Jesus. For a good life is then beneficial and is considered holy if it is possessed under the name of Christ; otherwise it will be defilement, because it advances to the injury of the Creator.

(Verses 2.) Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He says that the grace of God is with the saints and the faithful, calling God our Father because all things were both created and restored by him. He calls Christ our Lord because he redeemed us, offering himself for us.

(Verses 3.) Blessed is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing—that is, not with a worldly blessing but with a heavenly blessing, not with a corruptible blessing but with an eternal one. For the glory of Christians is not on earth but in heaven, and it is in Christ. Every gift of God’s grace is in Christ; therefore, if anyone thinks that he can be blessed by God while despising Christ, he should know that he is in error. God is blessed in one way, and human beings in another. The name of blessing is indeed one, but it must be understood according to the merit of the person. For God is said to make, and human beings also make; but God makes by a mere command and without suffering, whereas human beings accomplish things with their hand, effort, labor, and sweat. God, then, is blessed when he is exalted with worthy praises; but God blesses human beings by imparting to them the gift of his grace, not according to their merits but according to his mercy. Therefore he said, “who blessed us with a spiritual blessing,” to show that a perfect blessing is given from heaven to those who believe in Christ, so that they may be full of heavenly glory and raised above the powers of the heavens. “For where I am,” he says, “there my servant will also be” (John 12:26).

[Col. 0373D] (Verses 4.) Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love. God, who foreknows all things, knows those who would believe in Christ, as he says to the Romans: “Those whom he foreknew, he also called” (Romans 8:29)—not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. Those, therefore, whom God is said to call persevere in faith. These are the ones he chose in Christ before the world, so that they might be undefiled before God in love; that is, so that the love of God might make their conduct holy. For no one obeys another better than the one who obeys out of love.

(Verses 5.) He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself. He says that God decreed that those who believe in Christ should be adopted by God as sons, so that Christ, the true Son of God, might be their head.

(Verses 6.) According to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of his glory. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “According to the good pleasure … of the glory of his grace”; the old edition and the manuscripts agree among themselves, except that some of the latter read “of his love” instead of “of his glory.”] He says that God had this good pleasure: that the grace given to human beings should advance to the praise of his glory, so that our salvation might be the glory of God. By this grace he has favored us in his beloved Son. God gave us grace because we believed in his Son Christ; for, loving his only-begotten Son, he bestows divine gifts upon those who love him.

(Verses 7.) In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. He demands a twofold grace: for he both redeemed us by his blood and did not reckon our sins against us; that is, he both redeemed us and set us free.

(Verses 8.) According to the riches of his grace, which he made abound in us in all wisdom and prudence. He adds to grace, because after the benefits mentioned above there comes the gift of wisdom and prudence concerning spiritual matters.

(Verses 9–10.) Making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, restoring all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth. This pleased God, whose plan cannot be revoked: to reveal in Christ the mystery of his will at the time when he wished it to be disclosed for the knowledge of creation. His will was this: that he should then become favorable to all who were in error, whether in heaven or on earth, when he manifested Christ as this gift for believers, so that their sins might not be counted against them when they received the faith of Christ. Thus all creation in heaven and on earth, while learning the knowledge of Christ, is restored to that for which it was created. For when it is instructed in faith in the one God, having recognized the mystery of the Savior, it is restored from the error into which it had begun to fall, holding firmly that its Creator is one God and Lord. This is why John also says in the Apocalypse: “I saw Michael and his angels in heaven fighting against the dragon and his army” (Revelation 12:7). This opposition arises partly from error and partly from the presumption of usurped tyranny.

(Verses 11–12.) In him we have also received an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of God, who created all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who first hoped in Christ might be for the praise of his glory. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “In him we also were appointed by lot.”] This is what he says: the dispensation of preaching was decreed by God for those from the Jews who believed in Christ. Therefore no one from the Gentiles was chosen for the apostolate; for it was fitting that preachers should be chosen from those who had first hoped for the salvation that had been promised to them in Christ.

(Verses 13–14.) In him you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, and believed, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the acquired possession, to the praise of his glory. It is to the praise of God’s glory when many are acquired for the faith, just as it is to the glory of a physician if he cures many. Therefore it pertains to the glory of God that he called the Gentiles, so that they might obtain the healing of their salvation through the faith promised to the Jews, having the sign of redemption and the future inheritance: the Holy Spirit given after baptism. For those who have been redeemed have been designated as heirs, if they persevere in regeneration, so that the first faith may obtain forgiveness, while holy conduct persevering with faith may merit the crown. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “when many come together for the faith.”]

(Verses 15–16.) For this reason I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers. Since, in accordance with God’s decree by which he established that the Gentiles should become participants in the promise of the Jews, the Ephesians heard the word of God, received the faith of Christ, and loved all the saints as the Lord commanded, he gives thanks to God for their conversion and love. God was pleased to unite the Gentiles bodily with the Jews.

(Verses 17–19.) May the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your heart enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints. It is clear that he says he prays for them so that they may know the hope of their faith in the heavenly reward. For when they fully know what fruit belongs to believers, they will become more eager to cultivate their religion. They already appear destined for such progress: if they are so devoted before they know the glory of the promise, they will necessarily become more eager when they come to know it. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “when they have come to know its splendor. Nevertheless …”] Yet he calls God the Father of glory and the God of Christ, although God is the true Father of Christ and the God of creation. The Lord himself also says the same: “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). He is therefore the Father of all glory, because from him come all glory, power, and dignity. He is also the Father of Christ, but in another way, because Christ is his true Son and the God of all; yet God is not the God of Christ in the same way. He is the God of Christ because Christ is God from God; but he is the God of the others as the cause of fear, as he himself says through the prophet Malachi: “If I am God, where is my fear?” (Malachi 1:6).

(Verses 20–21.) And what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and seating him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every Principality, Power, Virtue, and Dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He declares that the example of the salvation and glory of believers consists in the resurrection of the Savior, so that from it the faithful may know what has been promised to them. In a similar way they will one day be raised above the heavens with Christ, as he himself says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me and may see my glory” (John 17:24). This is said on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, so that even as a human being he may be said to be above all the heavens and, seated at the right hand of God, above every creature, possessing the name of God by nature, not by adoption, so that those who crucified him may know that he is the Son of God. The honor that the Father gave him through generation was manifested when, having been born as a human being and having suffered, he conquered death and rose, ascending to where he had descended, above all the heavens. Hence it is said: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). Because the Father gave all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), he is said to sit at the right hand of God as judge. Finally, he himself says to the disciples: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and I will do it” (John 16:24). Hence he says to the Jews: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:64). From the time when he was made known, people began to approach him and make requests of him as judge.

(Verses 22–23.) “And he subjected all things under his feet,” and “gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and his fullness, who is filled completely in all things.” He says that the Father subjected every creature to the Son, so that, because he made all things through him (John 1:3), he himself might be the head and Lord of all. He subjected all things to him when he begot him before all things, so that through him he might make what did not exist.

By saying “the whole Church,” he comprehensively embraces everything that is in heaven and on earth, so that its members may be made into the new man, while they confess that this is the one through whom they were made by God. For the members are subjected to him as their head, from whom they derive their origin, so that he may be “all in all.” When they have returned to the confession of the one God, bowing the knee to Christ, he is fulfilled in all things, so that he may be all things, because they are from him; and consequently he is in them, since they subsist by his power. For when they depart from God, they appear to empty him. Hence he says elsewhere: “So that all things may grow into the increase of God” (Colossians 2:19).

## CHAPTER II

(Verses 1–2.) “And you, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world.” He calls them dead because they follow the errors of the world. Whatever departs from the confession of the one God is considered dead, because it does not remain in the root from which it derives its origin.

“According to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief.” By “the prince of the power” he means the devil, who corrupted the understanding of the world, so that people might depart from the one God and adopt the opinion of many gods, making them accomplices in his conspiracy, since they are found in the same impiety, denying the one God. He therefore calls this prince of error the spirit “of the air” in order to show that he usurped this region to exercise dominion. For air is one thing and a prince another; but because he rules in the world, or in the air, he is called the spirit of the air.

(Verses 3.) “Among whom we too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of its thoughts; and we were by nature children of wrath, as also the others.”

[Note: [Col. 0377D] The old edition and not a few manuscripts read “the pleasures of the flesh.” But we have already noted more than once that it is customary among ancient writers to confuse *voluntas* (“will”) and *voluptas* (“pleasure”) with one another.]

He indicates their infidelity when he mentions the desires of the flesh. For the will of the flesh is to delight in visible things, so that it calls gods those elements which God appointed as the governing principles of the world, although this name is owed to the one God, from whom all things come. Just as he has no partner among these in power, so he has no companion in name.

This name is not denied to Christ, however, because just as their nature is common, so also will their name be. Yet there is this difference between the Father and the Son: the Father received this from no one, whereas the Son received everything belonging to the Father through generation, so that in power, substance, and name the Son differs in nothing from the Father. Hence he says: “All things that the Father has are mine, and mine are the Father’s” (John 16:15).

It is therefore neither unworthy nor contradictory for Christ also to be called God, but to be called God from God the Father, so that the authority of the one God may be preserved. For if anyone thinks that something else is meant when he speaks of “the will of the flesh,” let him remember that the Apostle also lived a pure life, since he conducted himself blamelessly according to the righteousness of the Law. But because he persecuted the faith of Christ, he says, “we once lived in the desires of our flesh.” For every sin is called “flesh,” especially infidelity, which is the mother of every crime. Good works and chastity will benefit no one if he is faithless; for infidelity stains them all.

This is why he added: “And we were by nature children of wrath, as also the others.” When an evil will is added to nature, nature becomes a nature of wrath—that is, one subject to vengeance—not because its substance has been changed, but because of its evil will. For that which follows is attributed to nature. Hence he says in Isaiah: “A wicked seed” (Isaiah 1:4). And to show how wicked the seed is, he adds: “For you have abandoned the Lord,” he says, “and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger.” Thus nature that abandons God is called a wicked seed. For to degenerate is to depart from one’s author; and when it offers a bad example to others, it is a bad seed, since it produces the worst fruits. But if it returns to its Author, nature will be good, according to the Apostle, who, changed when he recognized his Creator, was called a vessel of election (Acts 9:15).

(Verses 4.) “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us.”

These are the true riches of mercies: that mercy should be freely granted to those who were not seeking it, as Isaiah says: “I became manifest to those who were not asking for me” (Isaiah 65:1). For this is to abound in mercy: that it should be given even to those who do not request it. This, however, is God’s love toward us: because he made us, he does not wish us to perish. For he loves his own work. He made it for this reason: that he might love what he had made; no one hates his own labor.

(Verses 5.) “And when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ.”

Separated from God, we were dead; but by his grace he recalled us—that is, he made us alive in Christ. Because he made us through him, he again re-formed us through him and in him, that is, so that we might be his members. He himself is our head; and, by God’s providence, we have him as the author of our life, as the Apostle Peter says: “But you killed the Author of life” (Acts 3:15).

(Verses 6.) “By whose grace you have been saved.”

To this gift he adds the Gentiles also, signifying that we have been saved by the grace of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] The Roman edition alone reads: “that we have all been saved,” and so forth.]

(Verses 7.) “And he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.”

This says what I mentioned above: that the saints, including those from the Gentiles, will be there where Christ is, since he is their head.

(Verses 8.) “So that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus.”

This signifies that in the future age the immortal gift of God will appear in the reward of the faithful: “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). These are the surpassing riches: that believers should receive as much as the mind cannot investigate.

(Verses 9–10.) “For by grace you have been saved through faith.” The grace of faith has been given so that believers may be saved. “And this is not from yourselves; for it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.”

It is true that every thanksgiving for our salvation must be referred to God, who grants us his mercy, so that he might recall those who were wandering to life, even though they were not seeking the true way.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] Some manuscripts read: “recalling all who were wandering to the faith.”]

Therefore, we must not glory in ourselves, but in God, who regenerated us through a heavenly birth by the faith of Christ, so that, trained in the good works which God ordained for us who have already been reborn, we might deserve to receive the promised rewards.

(Verses 11–12.) “Remembering that you were once Gentiles in the flesh, who are called the uncircumcision by that which is called the circumcision, made in the flesh by human hands; for at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants and without hope of their promise, and without God in this world.”

He admonishes the Gentiles to remember what they once were. For they were carnal and without hope, having no share in the Jews’ promise in Christ. Christ had been promised to the Jews, not to the Gentiles, so that they might give more abundant thanks to God through Christ, who in his mercy made them, though carnal, participants in spiritual things.

He nevertheless says “circumcision made in the flesh by human hands” in order to signify another circumcision, one not made by human hands, but spiritual.

(Verses 13.) “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ.”

He continues to commend God’s gift and grace, to whom he always wishes us to render thanks as though we were his debtors. He therefore recalls that we were brought near to God by the blood of Christ, in order to show how great God’s affection toward us is: he permitted his Son to die for us. Thus, if we remain steadfast in his faith, we must not yield to any destruction inflicted upon us for his sake, knowing that he deserves more from us than anything enemies can inflict. For although he is Lord and needs nothing, he offered himself for us, so that it might benefit not him but us.

Even if it did not benefit us, we might perhaps be compelled to die for him, the Lord of his servants. How much more, then, when not only his death but also our own death produces an effect beneficial to us!

(Verses 14.) “For he is our peace, who made both one and, by breaking down the middle wall of the barrier, the hostility in his flesh.”

The Savior’s passion made peace between circumcision and uncircumcision. The hostility, which was like a wall standing in the middle and separating circumcision from uncircumcision and uncircumcision from circumcision, was broken down by the Savior. He gave the law that neither the Jew, presuming upon circumcision, should reject the Gentile, nor the Gentile, trusting in uncircumcision—that is, in paganism—abominate the Jew. Rather, both, having been renewed, should follow the faith of the one God in Christ.

Everything the Savior taught he confirmed when he rose from the dead. Yet by the wall that stood in the middle, dividing the Law of works from the Gentiles, he signified a barrier or hedge—that is, not a stable or strong wall. For neither was Gentilism a firm reality, since it had been invented by human beings, nor were circumcision, new moons, the observance of foods and sacrifices, or Sabbaths stable and fixed. They were given in such a way that they would cease when Christ came.

Although God gave these things, he gave them only for a time; whereas the preaching of faith is firm and has no successor.

(Verses 15.) “By abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace.”

This is what I summarized above: he abolished the Law that had been given to the Jews in circumcision, new moons, foods, sacrifices, and the Sabbath—that is, he ordered it now to cease—because these things were a burden, and thus he made peace.

Hence the Apostle Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why do you impose a yoke upon the neck of the brothers which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

(Verses 16.) “So that he might present and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross.”

Having removed the hostility, Christ first reconciled the peoples to one another by his death, and then made them peaceful before God the Father. Thus human beings, who shared one nature but had been made diverse through error, might become members of one new body, whose head is Christ.

(Verses 17–18.) “Destroying the hostility in himself, he came and preached peace to you who were far away, and peace to those who were near; for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.”

The meaning is the same. He destroyed the hostility in himself when he died for all, both Jews and Gentiles. The Savior’s death benefits everyone. Rising from the dead, he condemned the death that held everyone and showed what hope those who believed in him possessed.

From this he commanded the preaching by which all were to be summoned to God the Father in the unity of the Spirit, discord having been torn apart. Thus both Jews—who are called “near” because the promise was made to their fathers—and Gentiles—who are called “far away” because they did not receive the Law given through Moses—were to accept the faith of Christ, once the former ritual had been removed, and thereby become one.

(Verses 19.) “Therefore you are no longer strangers and resident aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.”

[Note: [Col. 0379D] The Roman edition reads: “you are not strangers and foreigners.”]

He admonishes them to remember God’s benefits: although they had been far from knowledge and fear of God, they were joined to him by his mercy, so that they might become participants with those who were near to God, having been made fellow citizens of the sons of God.

Just as any nation of Romans that desired to follow the Roman peace was received after offering gifts, so that its members might become Roman citizens—as happened with the people of Tarsus in Cilicia, from which the Apostle says that he is a Roman citizen (Acts 22:26)—so also anyone who joins himself to the Christian faith becomes a fellow citizen with the saints and a member of God’s household.

(Verses 20.) “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.”

This means that they have been placed upon the New and Old Testaments. What the apostles preached, the prophets foretold, although he says to the Corinthians: “God placed in the Church first apostles, second prophets” (1 Corinthians 12:28).

But those are different prophets. There he is discussing the ordering of the Church; here, however, he is discussing the foundation of the Church. The prophets arranged the structure, but the apostles laid the foundations.

Hence the Lord says to Peter: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18)—that is, upon this confession of the catholic faith I will establish the faithful for life. David also arranged the house of God and marked out the place where it would be built; Solomon, however, founded it.

237 (Verses 21–22.) “In him the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you too are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.”

This is the meaning of the Lord’s saying: “Upon this rock I will build my Church.” The Savior received two peoples into himself and made them one in the Lord, just as the cornerstone holds together two walls, made firm in the unity of the house. For the faithful are the surfaces of God’s temple, living in the Spirit, so that they may become heirs of the heavenly dwelling.

## CHAPTER III

(Verses 1.) “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus for you, brothers.”

Having shown what the arrangement of divine mercy toward the salvation of the Gentiles had been before the world existed, he now declares that, by God’s providence and with Christ sending him, he carries out the embassy of this gift.

For after his resurrection the Lord sent his apostles to preach in his place (Matthew 28:19), directing this man toward the conversion of the Gentiles. For he said to him: “Go, I will send you far away to the Gentiles” (Acts 22:21).

Thus he uses the Lord’s own word when he says: “Peace to you who are far away, and to those who are near.”

(Verses 2–4.) “If indeed you have heard of the dispensation of God’s grace that was given to me for you.”

He wants them to know that, by God’s judgment, he was sent by Christ to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of God’s grace.

“According to the revelation, the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote before briefly, so that, when you read, you may understand my prudence in the mystery of Christ.”

He indicates that the revelation of God’s mystery was shown to him. He had mentioned writing about it briefly before—that is, moderately, in accordance with the capacity of those who could grasp the Apostle’s understanding of Christ’s mystery.

(Verses 5–6.) “Which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his saints and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and participants in his promise in Christ Jesus.”

[Note: [Col. 0381D] The Roman edition adds after “in Christ Jesus”: “through the Gospel.” But the following verse begins: “of which I was made a minister,” and so forth.]

He asserts that this was shown by God in Christ’s time, although it had been hidden: namely, that the Gentiles would become participants in the grace promised in the Law. He says that it was shown to holy preachers and prophets—that is, to the apostles and interpreters of the Law—not to the ancient prophets.

Although Gentiles had previously been admitted to the Law, they were ordered to be circumcised. The prophets knew that the Gentiles would become participants in the good of God—for they indicated this in many places—but what remained hidden was that they would become participants in God’s grace without circumcision, Sabbaths, new moons, and other such observances; that they would receive the faith of Christ and be saved without the Law.

This is what he says: that in the Spirit the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and participants in his promise in Christ. For whoever worships God in the Spirit has no need of the work of the Law.

(Verses 7.) “Of which I was made a minister through his Gospel, according to the gift of God’s grace that was given to me according to the operation of his power.”

Through the preaching of his ministry he declares that the gift which God had ordained for the Gentiles was made known according to the operation of his power. For the operation of his power is that he raised Christ from the dead, conquering the death in which he saved all.

The dispensation of his Gospel, however, is this: through it the will of God was recognized, because he decreed to save the Gentiles without the works of the Law.

(Verses 8.) “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given.”

He humbles himself when he calls himself the least, knowing that humility brings progress. For he says that such great grace was given to him that he was granted the gift which had previously been unknown throughout the ages, so that he might reveal it to the Gentiles.

How, then, can he appear to be the least of all the saints, when even before he was baptized he was called a vessel of election?

[Note: [Col. 0381D] The same Roman edition reads: “that I might preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches,” and so forth.]

“That I might preach among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ” (Acts 9:15).

He proves himself chosen to preach God’s gift in the incomprehensible riches of Christ, which Christ graciously determined to bestow upon the Gentiles, who had already been without hope, so that they might be saved through faith without works.

It is clear that no one sends an outstanding and very great gift through an unworthy person. Yet, while showing how much he deserves from God, he humbles himself so that his merit may increase.

(Verses 9.) “And to enlighten all concerning the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.”

He says that he was sent to teach the Gentiles the mystery in two ways: the mystery that was in God, from whom all things come, so that through him they might learn and understand that Christ has always been in God and with God, and that God had determined to save the Gentiles without circumcision and the other commandments of the Law.

The Jews were found unworthy to have so great and such a teacher. For the Jews believed in Christ in such a way that they nevertheless continued to observe the Law, which is hateful to God. Hence the apostles say to their fellow apostle Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts 21:20).

Therefore it happened that the vessel of election was sent to teach the Gentiles, so that they themselves might have complete hope in their faith, hoping for nothing from the Law but in Christ alone.

Once the mystery had been revealed, such a gift of Christ was given that it would produce perfect salvation. For just as at a great banquet the finest gifts are given as keepsakes, so also, when the magnificent mystery was revealed, human beings were endowed with such an outstanding gift as the cause of joy and gladness that it was sufficient for their saving abundance.

[Note: [Col. 0382D] Some manuscripts read: “which was an open salvation.” But in the following verse, where our edition, together with the earlier edition and many manuscripts, reads “in great vows,” the Roman edition prefers “in great vows,” while some manuscripts read “in great life.”]

(Verses 10.) “So that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known through the Church to the Principalities and Powers in the heavenly places.”

God had such a good understanding of this matter that he not only gave this teacher to the Gentiles, but also intended that through him the truth of Christ should become known to the spirits in the heavenly places who are called Principalities and Powers.

They are called Powers because they are more powerful than the other spirits; they are called Principalities because they rule over the Powers. When they recognize through the Church—which has been drawn to life in manifold ways—that the mystery of the one God remains in Christ, they may cease from error.

The purpose is that ecclesiastical preaching may also benefit them, and that they may abandon their assent to the devil’s tyranny, by which he armed himself against faith in the one God through impious presumption.

This understanding is set forth in the twenty-third Psalm, where God is shown to be Lord of the universe, as the Spirit of God says through David: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Psalm 23:1).

And in what follows:

[Note: [Col. 0383D] Several manuscripts read: “Lift up the gates of your Principalities,” and so forth.]

“Lift up the gates of your Prince, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (ibid., 7 ff.).

It is therefore said to these Principalities who are in error in the heavenly places, or to his ministers on earth, that they should remove the gates of their prince—that is, of the devil—from their minds, through which the error of asserting many gods entered.

For these gates are temporary, since every deception is closed by time: “The way of the wicked will perish” (Psalm 1:6). But they are urged to lift up the eternal gates at the prompting of justice, because truth endures for everlasting ages.

Hence he says in the hundred-and-seventeenth Psalm: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous will enter through it” (Psalm 117:20). For it is clear that the righteous enter heaven through faith, into the kingdom of God, which never decays, as the prophet Daniel bears witness, saying among other things: “Another kingdom will arise, one that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44).

But the wicked, because of their unbelief, enter the Tartarean underworld.

This King of glory, then, is Christ, who, rising from the dead after conquering death, appears to be Lord and King of glory. He is manifested through the power of his authority, by which he subdued the underworld, because he is the Son of God who preached that the kingdom of the one God exists in heaven and on earth, for the condemnation of the devil’s tyranny.

(Verses 11–12.) “According to the purpose of the ages in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have freedom with confidence through faith in him.”

He says that Christ was revealed to the world at the time when God purposed to display his mystery for the salvation of humanity, so that knowledge of God’s mystery might bring salvation to mortals. It was as though, at the dedication of Christ’s kingdom, he bestowed this grace upon believers as a ceremonial gift.

Although it happened long ago, it nevertheless appears new to a creation that did not know it.

(Verses 13.)

[Note: [Col. 0383D] The Roman edition reads: “For this reason I urge you not to lose heart.”]

“For this reason I ask that you not lose heart because of my tribulations for you, which are your glory.”

Having revealed the hope contained in the mystery of Christ, he warns them not to be scandalized because of the tribulations inflicted upon the saints by the faithless.

For it contributes to their glory if the disciples are not scandalized by the tribulation of their teacher, having been strengthened by this hope: the sufferings of the faithful will be raised up into the glory of the future age. For this is the testing of the faithful, whether they turn their attention to the hope of their faith.

(Verses 14–16.) “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his majesty, to be strengthened in power through his Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0384D] The same edition reads: “through his Spirit in the inner man.” Hence it begins verse 17 as follows: “that Christ may dwell,” and so forth.]

He says that he prays on bended knees because God graciously summoned the Gentiles to know the mystery of his will. Since he is rich, he asks that God also grant this: that they may be strengthened by his will in the Spirit, so that the carnal destruction inflicted by the faithless may not disturb them, but that they may remain steadfast, awaiting the reward of this matter in the future.

(Verses 17.) “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner man.”

He asks that they be strengthened still more, so that they may not doubt but rather believe that Christ dwells in them, whom they do not see with these eyes. The Spirit given to them by God’s gift should instill this in them, so that they may be certain about Christ: that he lives, that he is the Son of God, and that he dwells through faith in our hearts. When we have his faith in our hearts, we seem to possess him himself.

This benefits us by making us secure concerning his assistance, because he does not abandon us but is always present on account of the faith he sees in us. Indeed, his Spirit, who is also the Spirit of God the Father, is given to us for this reason: that in his place he may keep us safe if we assent to him, and that he may reveal hidden things. Through him, certainly, we should not doubt that Christ himself dwells in us.

For this is another Paraclete; there is a distinction of persons among them, but not of nature, since he receives from Christ and proceeds from God (John 15:26). In those who share unity of nature, each belongs to the other. Hence the Lord says: “All things of the Father are mine, and all mine are the Father’s” (John 16:15).

(Verses 18.) “So that, rooted and grounded in love, you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth and length and height and depth.”

He says that Christ or the Spirit dwelling in us provides this: that we may be founded in the love of God, bound to him by his benefits, and able, together with the saints—who are the apostles and prophets—to know the immeasurable and inestimable God, who surpasses everything in the majesty of his power.

When he says “breadth and length and height and depth,” he surely means that, just as in a sphere length is equal to breadth, and height equal to depth, so in God all things are equal in the immensity of infinity.

A sphere is enclosed within a defined boundary; God, however, not only fills all things but also surpasses them. He is not enclosed, but contains all things within himself, so that he alone is ineffable and infinite. Nor can adequate thanks be given for this grace, since, although he is so great, he graciously chose through Christ to visit a human being subject to sins and death.

[Col. 0384D] (Verses 19.) “And to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge.”

After the infinite, incomprehensible knowledge and ineffable mercy of God the Father, he also wishes us to recognize the love of Christ, because it surpasses knowledge—understood, implicitly, as human knowledge—so that Christ’s love may be regarded as beyond human understanding.

For who can grasp the reasoning of this mystery of love: that God became human for the sake of humanity, and then died for human beings; that the Lord died for servants, the Creator for his creature, the pious one for the impious? Why did he love us so greatly? Or for what purpose did he desire something belonging to us, when he needs nothing? Is this love not beyond human knowledge? Or what human being could show anyone such love? Even though human love is unequal to it, it therefore surpasses human imaginings.

He wants us to know this: that our understanding cannot attain or discern the depth of Christ’s benefits toward us. Therefore we should always be suppliant and devoted to him, and, although we cannot in any way repay what we owe, we should persevere in his faith even to death.

For in the magnificence of his majesty he did for us things unworthy of himself,

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Some manuscripts read: “things worthy of himself,” but this is not sufficiently correct.]

so that we too might serve him as much as we are able.

“That you may be filled with all the fullness of God.”

Because faith is complete neither in the Father alone nor in the Son alone, he therefore added: “That you may be filled with all the fullness of God,” so that, through confession and thanksgiving, honor might be reserved for the Son just as for the Father; and so that all things which are from God the Father might be believed to have been made and restored through the Son, so that the full perfection of divinity might exist in the profession of believers.

For nothing will be lacking to the Christian when he recognizes that God the Father is in every respect immeasurable, and confesses that Christ’s love is ineffable and surpasses human understanding.

(Verses 20–21.) “To him who is able to do all things, and more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us: to him be glory in Christ Jesus and in the Church, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Several manuscripts read: “according to the truth that works.”]

He refers these words to the person of the Father. Since he knows better what is useful, what ought not to be requested, when things should be given, and what kind and how great they should be, he himself governs those who believe in him by his providence and power.

To him belongs glory in Christ Jesus because through him he provides everything for us, and because the Father’s honor is in the Son and in the Church—that is, in the people whom he graciously adopted.

For the glory of a father is in the splendor of his children, as the Lord says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

“Throughout the ages of ages. Amen”—that is, truth eternally.

## CHAPTER IV

(Verses 1.) “Therefore I urge you, brothers, I, a prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.”

He exhorts them, so that by walking rightly in the Lord’s commandments they may attain the promised glory. For just as a skilled physician urges the sick to conduct themselves properly so that they may recover health, so the teacher of the Gentiles exhorts them to perform works worthy of their faith, so that they may receive what was promised to the saints, knowing that this achievement contributes to his own glory.

(Verses 2–3.)

[Note: [Col. 0386D] The Roman edition reads: “with all gentleness … bearing with one another in patience … preserving the unity of the Spirit.”]

“With all humility of mind and modesty, with magnanimity, bearing with one another in love, diligently preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

He now forbids dissension and urges them to devote themselves to love, lest they lose the Spirit of unity and peace. Consequently, they are to bear with one another patiently.

Modesty produces progress, because when they tolerate one another and correct one another with gentleness of mind, they are brought to improvement, and peace will remain in them. Through this they will rightly be called sons of God, because the Lord said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

Disturbance or restlessness produces contention, which is accustomed to defend even what it knows to be evil, lest it appear to yield. From this discord arises, corrupting the bonds of peace.

(Verses 4.) “One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.”

He added this because of peace and harmony: since the Church is one body, the people should have one mind, because what is believed is one.

(Verses 5–6.) “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all.”

He continues to commend unity, so that, since unity is what we are called to, we may disagree in nothing. For if there is one Lord—that is, Christ, as he himself says in the Gospel, “Your teacher is one, Christ” (Matthew 23:10)—one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all and in all believers, then the people ought to have one mind and one heart.

For the things he enumerates belong to unity; they agree in every respect.

He says that God the Father is above all and through all because he owes what he is to no one. He says “through all” because all things are from him, and it is necessary that he be above all things that are from him. “And in us all” means in the faithful.

He is in us through confession, because we confess him, and because he has given us his Spirit, through whom he is undoubtedly in us. He is not in the pagans, because they deny that he is the Father of Christ.

(Verses 7.) “But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.”

Since people have different gifts, they might think that this harmed unity. He corrects this misunderstanding by showing that it is not contradictory, because there is diversity in the gifts of offices, not in nature.

He says that each person receives as much grace as the Lord has chosen to give—not, however, without a measure of equity, since he assigns to each according to his capacity, so that each may draw as much as he thirsts.

[Col. 0386D] (Verses 8.) “Therefore he says” (Psalm 67:19): “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.”

This is written in the sixty-seventh Psalm. He began to bestow these gifts after his triumphs. For, conquering death, he was exalted upon the cross, as he himself had said: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

He stripped the underworld when he removed the captives whom it held in bondage because of Adam’s transgression or because of their own sins, taking with him those who consented to him. From there he ascended into heaven and brought them in (Matthew 27:52).

Some of them, rising in their bodies, appeared to many as a testimony that death had been conquered. Thus, if anyone might not have been willing to believe in Christ’s resurrection, they would be held accountable through the resurrection of those whom they knew to have died, for they saw people whom they recognized as having lived previously.

Although captives are led away unwillingly and as strangers, the Savior led away both his own and willing captives. For by appearing to those who desired liberation, he is said to have captured them.

### (Verse 9)

“But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he had also first descended into the lower regions of the earth?” It is true that he descended for this reason: that he might ascend—not like human beings, who descended in order to remain there. For by sentence of condemnation they were held in the underworld, but that sentence could not hold the Savior, because he conquered sin. Having therefore triumphed over the devil, he descended into the heart of the earth, so that his manifestation might be a proclamation to the dead, and so that all who desired to belong to him might be set free. Nor could he fail to ascend, since he had descended for this purpose: that by the force of his power, having trampled down death, he might rise again with the captives for whose sake he permitted himself to suffer.

### (Verse 10)

“He who descended is himself also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.” This is what the Lord says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). This is also contained in the psalm, for it says: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his return is even to its summit” (Psalm 18:7). Thus, descending from the heavens to earth, he was born as a human being; afterward, having died, he descended to the underworld. From there, rising on the third day, he ascended above all the heavens before all mortal beings, so that he might show creation that death had been mocked.

### (Verses 11–12)

“And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and some as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry.”

The apostles are bishops (Acts 11:26); the prophets, however, are interpreters of the Scriptures. Although in the earliest beginnings there were prophets, such as Agabus and the four virgins who prophesied (Acts 21:9), as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles for the instruction of beginners in the faith (Acts 7:2 and following), nowadays interpreters are called prophets.

Evangelists are deacons, as Philip was. Although they are not priests, they can nevertheless evangelize without a presiding chair, as did the blessed Stephen and the Philip mentioned above (Acts 8:5).

Pastors can be readers, who nourish the listening people through reading, because “man lives not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

Teachers, however, are exorcists, because in the Church they restrain and chastise the disorderly; or else they are those who used to instruct children who were to be trained in letters and readings, as is the custom of the Jews—a tradition that has passed over to us but has grown obsolete through negligence.

[Note: The old edition and most manuscripts read, “and to instruct children through readings”; the Roman edition removed *covem imbuendi*. It seems preferable to us, with the Vatican manuscript, to read *imbuendos*.]

Among these, after the bishop, the one who is said to prophesy because of the disclosed hidden meaning of the Scriptures is understood to hold the higher place, especially since he brings forth words of future hope. This rank can now be that of the presbyterate.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “For in Christ are all the ranks.”]

For in the bishop all the ranks are present: he is first a priest—that is, the chief of the priests—and a prophet, an evangelist, and all the other offices of the Church that must be fulfilled in the ministry of the faithful.

Nevertheless, after Churches had been established in every place and their offices ordered, the arrangement became different from what it had been at the beginning. At first, everyone taught and everyone baptized, whenever an opportunity arose, regardless of the day or time. Philip did not look for a particular time or day on which to baptize the eunuch (Acts 8:38), nor did he insert a fast. Nor did Paul and Silas delay the time when they baptized the jailer of Philippi with all his household (Acts 16:33).

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “nor did Peter have clerics.”]

Nor did Peter have deacons or seek a particular day when he baptized Cornelius with his entire household (Acts 10:48). Indeed, he himself did not baptize them, but commanded the brothers who had come with him from Joppa to do so; for, besides the seven deacons, no one had yet been ordained.

Therefore, as the people increased and multiplied, at the beginning everyone was permitted both to evangelize and to baptize and to explain the Scriptures in the Church. But when the Church had spread throughout all regions, meeting places had been established, and rulers and the other offices had been arranged in the Churches, no one among the clergy who had not been ordained dared to presume to exercise an office that he knew had not been entrusted or granted to him.

The Church began to be governed by another order and provision. For if everyone could do the same things, the matter would be irrational and commonplace, and would appear utterly insignificant. Hence it is that now neither do deacons preach among the people, nor do clerics or laymen baptize, nor are believers immersed on just any day, except when they are ill.

For this reason, the writings of the Apostle do not correspond in every respect to the order that now exists in the Church, because they were written during the earliest beginnings. He even calls Timothy, whom he himself had made a presbyter, a bishop.

[Note: The Roman edition, together with one Vatican manuscript, reads, “because at first they were presbyters”; other editions and manuscripts more correctly read, “because at first the presbyters,” and so forth.]

For at first presbyters were called bishops, so that, when one departed, another might succeed him. Indeed, in Egypt the presbyters confirm if the bishop is not present.

But when subsequent presbyters began to be found unworthy of holding the primacy, the arrangement was changed by the foresight of the Council, so that merit, rather than rank, would create a bishop, appointed by the judgment of many priests, lest an unworthy man should rashly usurp the office and become a cause of scandal to many.

Under the Law, priests were born from the tribe of Aaron, the Levite (Exodus 28:43). Now, however, all belong to the priestly race, as the apostle Peter says: “For you are a royal and priestly race”; and therefore a priest can be made from the people (1 Peter 2:9).

“For the building up of the body of Christ.”

He says that the ordering of the Church has been composed for the joining together of the human body in the unity of its confession, so that, although differing in dignity, all may be one in Christ, having one head—Christ, that is, the author of life.

[Note: The old edition and not a few manuscripts read, “for the joining together of the human race”; the Roman edition and other manuscripts more correctly have the reading found in the text.]

### (Verse 13)

“Until we all attain to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God.”

He says that this ordering is to remain for as long as all those destined for life are united in one faith and in the knowledge of Christ.

“To a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

He urges us to labor in such a way that the perfection of faith may be grasped. Its principle is this: faith must hold Christ to be perfect and fully God; it must not measure him by human standards, but regard him as perfect God in the fullness of divinity.

For when he says “perfect,” he does not mean a man measured by temporal age and stature. Rather, by this expression he wants us to become perfect in the fullness of our understanding of the divinity of the Son of God.

### (Verse 14)

“So that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by the wickedness of human beings, by cunning, for the remedy of error.”

He wants us to be founded and stable in the discipline of the Catholic faith, which the apostle Peter professed when God revealed it (Matthew 16:16). We must not be driven about in error by the pestilential assertions of various heresies devised by human wickedness, so that through them the error of the deceiving enemy may be introduced under the name of truth.

For this is the remedy of falsehood: to introduce error under the pretext of truth. And he warns us not only against its appearing under the name of truth, but also lest, just as before receiving the faith we wandered in our weakness of understanding through various errors, we should, after becoming believers, run about unstable and uncertain concerning the hope that has been promised.

For once they have become Christians, they ought to be founded and established, because there is no ambiguity in our faith; it is commended by the power of miracles.

### (Verse 15)

“But speaking the truth in love, let us grow in all things into him who is the head, Christ.”

He says that this is the truth: that, looking to Christ’s love—by which he loved us and handed himself over for us—we should subject everything to him, knowing that he is the author of life for all, so that, like members under a head, they may be subject to him.

If others, through error or ill will, do not confess that Christ is the head of all things because all things were made by him according to the Father’s will, nevertheless we who adhere to the Catholic faith ought to carry out this confession with all devotion and care, so that we bring gain, not loss, to this faith, persevering in this assertion, so that the conversations of perverse minds armed against the truth may be restrained.

### (Verse 16)

“From whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual part, produces the body’s growth for the building up of itself in love.”

He explains why he said that Christ is the head of all things. “For from him,” he says, “the whole body”—that is, the entire company of Archangels, Powers, Principalities, and Authorities—exists.

Although each of these has its own proper number and constitutes legions, as the Lord himself said (Matthew 26:53), nevertheless, because all are from one and through one, he calls them all together one body.

For just as the members, although they belong to one body, nevertheless differ in function and dignity, so creation was established by God through Christ in such a way that from the powers of the Cherubim and Seraphim, which are beneath God’s throne, and from the angels whom the Lord himself calls holy (Mark 8:38), there is a kind of chain, descending in ordered succession even to the firmament. Thus everything is joined together, yet distinguished according to merits—by merits, I mean not only those of offices but also of natures.

For the fact that he says all things are joined together does not mean that they will be of one nature.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “But how do the members in the body perform distinct offices?”]

Rather, just as the members in a body differ in their offices, not in their nature, so among all these beings it is the natures themselves, not members, that produce distinctions.

This, then, is what is being worked toward: that creation may be brought into one understanding and may be one body in understanding, since all have one confession, so that it may agree in love of the Creator for its own advancement. For it rebuilds itself as a temple of the Lord, since it had been destroyed by the madness and fury of the devil.

### (Verses 17–18)

“This, therefore, I say and testify in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind, darkened in understanding, alienated from the faith of God because of the ignorance that is in them.”

After the Creator has been made known and the reasoning has been shown that creation ought to follow—namely, faith in its God—he solemnly charges them before God not to walk or think otherwise than they have been taught. He warns them not to be found like the Gentiles, who neither receive the faith nor observe the way of life commanded by the Law, having an obscured understanding so that they do not contemplate the truth of the divine name.

For, pursuing vanities—that is, idolatry—they are restrained by the devil, lest they walk in the path of the one God, so that he may make them companions in his own destruction.

### (Verse 19)

“And the blindness of their heart: having become desperate, they gave themselves over to shamelessness for the practice of every impurity and greed.”

He indicates that the Gentiles possess blindness of heart because they despair of the future resurrection. As though they would not exist beyond this life, they pollute their lives by the most disgraceful conduct, unwilling to submit themselves to the law of faith. For that law forbids pleasure on account of the hope of future life, which they therefore judge worthy of ridicule, so that they may seem justified in dishonoring themselves and desiring what belongs to others with greedy craving, as though no life existed after this passing.

### (Verses 20–21)

“But you did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus.”

It is clear that Christians have not learned despair after death, but hope with respect to both outcomes. Life is promised to the faithful, but death—which is eternal punishment—to the faithless, so that whether death or life is learned in Christ, the one who follows him will rise through him to life, while the one who separates himself from him will through him be handed over to Gehenna; for he will be condemned by Christ himself as judge.

And because there are some in the Church who, under the name of Christ, do not follow Christ’s truth, he therefore says, “as the truth is in Jesus.” If they have been taught as the truth is in Jesus, then they appear to have learned Christ, heard him, and been taught in him.

For Christ teaches concerning himself what he is, how great he is to be believed to be, what hope exists in him, and what those who believe ought to be like. Whoever has learned Christ knows that he rose from the dead, so that he might be a pattern for the faithful. Therefore there is great hope for those who love God amid this death.

### (Verse 22)

“That you put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error.”

The one who has heard Christ has learned this: to withdraw from his former way of life, which he now calls the “old man” because of the past time of ignorance.

The human being, therefore, is one and the same. If he follows his former vices, he is called old; but if he walks in the newness of life, estranged from secular error—whether in conduct or in understanding—he is called new.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “whether in disposition or in understanding.”]

He is nevertheless called a corrupted old man because of his adulterous understanding and disgraceful life.

### (Verses 23–24)

“But be renewed in the understanding of your mind”

[Note: The same edition reads, “in the spirit of your mind.”]

“and put on the new man, who was created according to God in truth and righteousness.”

It is just and true to follow the right path. The one who follows the right path is the one who, devoted to his Creator, walks in his will—a will unknown to the Gentiles.

The one renewed in the spirit of his mind is said to have put on the new man, who is Christ. For one puts on Christ who, reborn through faith in Christ, is an imitator of the life that Christ handed down, so that he may appear to have been created according to God.

For a person is created in the one in whom he has understanding; and therefore the truth and righteousness of God are unknown to the Gentiles. When believers acknowledge God as Creator and observe his commandments, they are created in righteousness and truth.

### (Verse 25)

“Therefore, having put away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor” (Zechariah 8:16), “because we are members of one another.”

Because we have been created in truth and righteousness and reborn in baptism, we are commanded to put away falsehood and assume truth, and not to deal deceitfully with a brother, so that, since we are members of one body, we may support one another truthfully in our own affairs.

### (Verse 26)

“Be angry and do not sin.”

Since one cannot be forbidden to become angry—for anger is a natural movement, arising from causes and often tending toward the correction of the offender—he therefore says that one should be angry (Psalm 4:5), but warns that one must not sin through anger.

For when we become angry, we commonly go beyond measure and are found to sin ourselves: while rebuking those who sin, we become excessively angry and burden the sinner more heavily than he deserves.

This, therefore, is what he teaches: that anger itself should be restrained, and that no one should show himself excessively righteous toward an offender. For some people sin in such a way that they seem to deserve blows so severe that they cannot endure them; and one who perhaps could have been corrected is removed from life—not without sin on the part of the angry person.

Hence Solomon says: “Do not be excessively righteous, for there is one who perishes through his righteousness” (Ecclesiastes 7:17).

But we ought to be imitators of God, who possesses a measured righteousness. For although it would be just for the wicked to be punished, in his patience he endures them so that some of them may be corrected. He endures us, his own servants, when we sin, and does not strike anyone quickly.

### (Verse 27)

“Let not the sun go down upon your anger;”

[Note: All editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read, “and do not give place to the devil”; but nearly all the manuscripts have the reading found in the text.]

“do not give place to the devil.”

He wants anger to pass away and not be retained in the heart, so that, having arisen with the day, it may also set with the day. For if it remains in the mind, it gives the devil an opportunity to boast.

An angry mind must think evil thoughts, which is what the devil desires. He finds a mind prepared for evil, and, inserting himself into it, deceives the human being who was made for life. For it is the human being’s part to think, but the devil’s to bring to completion.

### (Verse 28)

“Let the one who used to steal steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something from which to give to those suffering need.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “from which he may supply what the needy person requires.”]

He urges that the conduct of the new man remain steadfast and that we not return again to former vices and sins. For it will do no good to be called new when a person is shown by evil deeds to be old.

Therefore, the Christian is commanded not only not to take what belongs to others, but also to supply from his own labor what is needed by those suffering want, so that, devoted to good works, he may repay what he previously stole and henceforth store up treasure for himself in the future.

For the one who ceases from theft may obtain pardon, but not glory. What great thing is it, or what merit is there, to abstain from what belongs to others? It advances toward merit when someone gives from his own possessions to the needy.

### (Verse 29)

“Let no evil word proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear.”

In God’s servant everything ought to appear good, and his purity ought not to be stained in any respect. For what good is it to have a clean life and a foul mouth, when the Lord says that each person will be justified or condemned by his words (Matthew 12:37)?

Nor can the one who speaks evil be believed to live well, since evil speech leads to many vices. A person can speak evil by uttering obscenities, by slandering the good, by speaking deceitfully, or by lying.

[Note: The better manuscripts read this way; others, together with the editions, read: “These things produce error. Not sufficiently correctly.”]

Such things produce horror. Good and sober conversation, however, gives grace and an example to those who hear, so that they may honor God in his words, built up in the faith of Christ.

### (Verse 30)

“And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.”

When we act well, the Holy Spirit, given to us, rejoices in us, seeing his instructions advance our interests, as the Lord said: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10).

The Holy Spirit therefore rejoices in our salvation, not for his own sake, since he has no need of joy. Conversely, if we do not obey him, he is grieved because he does not achieve an increase in us; for he wants us to belong to life.

He is not, however, grieved in such a way as to suffer, since he is impassible. Rather, when he is said to be grieved, this is expressed for our sake, because he abandons us when we have injured him by despising his instructions.

His grief, therefore, is our unworthiness, which prevents us from being called children of God. For he is the Holy Spirit who sanctifies the children of God, remaining in us.

[Note: The old edition, together with some manuscripts, reads, “who signifies”; the Roman edition, together with several manuscripts, reads, “who seals”; other manuscripts more correctly read, “who sanctifies,” and so forth.]

### (Verse 31)

“Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice.”

He says that all these things, which can bring destruction upon souls, must be removed. For anger produces indignation; indignation produces clamor, like the voice of a madman, which is foreign to God’s servant; and through clamor blasphemy creeps in, which cannot be anything but evil.

These things make life bitter and lead to death. Therefore we must guard against all of them. The fear of God ought to moderate and set a limit to circumstances as they arise.

But since some people, while suppressing anger and clamor, can retain malice in their hearts until they find an opportunity for retaliation, he therefore added that these things must be removed together with all malice. For not only is it malice to blaspheme; it is also malice to feign peace on one’s face while meditating discord in one’s heart.

### (Verse 32)

“But be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.”

He exhorts us to become kind and compassionate toward one another after the example of God the Father, just as the Lord also says: “Be compassionate, so that you may be like your Father who is in heaven” (Luke 6:36).

If the Lord has had mercy on his servants through his Son, how much more ought the servants themselves to have mercy on one another and forgive if one sins against another?

These are the commands of the one who has shown mercy. If he is despised in these matters, he will undoubtedly revoke the sentence by which he had granted mercy. And it will happen just as the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the man who, having received mercy from the Lord, was found to be wicked toward his fellow servant (Matthew 18:33).

## CHAPTER 5

### (Verse 1)

“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.”

This is what he said above: by this exhortation we are commanded to be imitators of God the Father, so that, if we obey, we may be regarded as God’s beloved children.

For the father’s beloved child is the one who imitates his good qualities.

### (Verse 2)

“And walk in love, just as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma.”

Just as he wants us to be imitators of God the Father in kindness and mercy, so also of Christ, his Son, in love, so that, just as he loved us and handed himself over for us, we too ought to lay down our lives for one another.

The apostle John also said this, that, following the Lord’s example, we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers (1 John 3:16).

If Christ’s death is a fragrant aroma to God, God willingly accepted his death. If this is true, those who crucified him according to God’s will did not sin.

But this is not so. Christ is said to have offered himself to God by allowing himself to be killed, remaining in the will of God his Father. For the one who is justly killed, offering himself to the devil, does his will so that he deserves to be killed.

Thus Christ, while adhering to God’s will, displeased the devil; and for this reason the devil killed him, because he offered himself to God by carrying out righteousness.

For in the offering, righteousness and truth are signified. God regards these, and this is the sacrifice acceptable to him. Therefore the innocent person who is killed pleases God—not because he is killed, but because he preserved righteousness even to death.

Christ accepted this death for life; hence it is called a fragrant aroma to God. Yet in the Letter to the Romans he says that God handed him over for us all (Romans 8:32).

Now we must ask how God handed him over, or how he himself offered himself to God, since, as far as the words are concerned, this appears contradictory.

God is said to have handed him over when he permitted him to be killed, just as the Lord says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

Power was given to him, but to one who was willing; that is, he was permitted to do what he wished. And this is what it means to hand over: by not intervening, he hands over. For if he had not wished to permit it, Christ would not have been killed.

God therefore permitted him to be killed, but by those who wished to kill him—not under compulsion, but willingly. They are therefore not free from punishment, because they were permitted to do what they wanted; condemnation applies to them because they desired it.

God permitted this, however, because he knew that it would benefit many against the devil.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “that it would be beneficial to many against the devil.”]

For it was fitting that what the enemy, ignorant of the future, thought he was doing against himself but believed he was doing for himself should be permitted, so that, bearing the responsibility for his ignorance, he might be tormented by regret for his deed.

But whether Christ himself offered himself or God handed him over, it is one and the same thing, because their will is one.

### (Verse 3)

“But fornication and every impurity or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints.”

What he says is clear. Yet how serious a matter greed is—something we overlook when it is compared with fornication and impurity, and which consequently appears to us as though it were a fault of no importance—can be observed from this comparison, since it is a grave sin.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “From this it must be observed how serious greed is, since it is compared with fornication and impurity, from which we nevertheless dissemble and thus regard it as something of no importance,” and so forth.]

Those among whom any of the things he forbids is found cannot therefore be holy.

### (Verse 4)

“Nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor coarse joking, which do not pertain to the matter; but rather thanksgiving.”

Because some people are accustomed either to do something shameful or to provoke amusement through foolish talk, as though it were not a sin, he prohibits this, because God’s servants ought always to appear sober and modest. For sin is committed through foolish talk.

Hence Solomon says: “The fool does evil through laughter” (Proverbs 10:23).

And the Lord says in the Gospel that for every idle word people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment (Matthew 12:36).

Nor can things said precisely in order to insult someone be regarded as unpunished; therefore such things do not pertain to what is beneficial for salvation.

He urges us to do and say those things that advance our benefit and the praise of God, in whose law one must meditate day and night, as it is written in the psalm (Psalm 1:2).

From their conduct and behavior, God’s servants should be recognizable even when they are silent, so that just as truth differs from falsehood, God’s servants may differ from the servants of the devil.

### (Verse 5)

“For know this: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—for greed is idolatry—has an inheritance in the kingdom of God and of Christ.”

He shows why these things must be removed: whoever is such will have no share in the kingdom of heaven, which belongs to the Father and the Son.

To teach that greed is a dangerous matter, he calls it idolatry, than which no sin is greater. Let us therefore see why greed is called idolatry.

Idolatry seizes and claims for a creature the honor due to God, since, in the name of deity—which belongs only to the Creator—it asserts that the creature shares in that honor.

Greed is equated with this because the greedy person similarly claims for himself and hoards what belongs to God. Greed denies the use of things that God has granted commonly for everyone’s benefit, since it gathers them to itself precisely so that others may not use them.
