This causes things to be sold more dearly, so that the poor may not live. If such things were not hoarded, the abundance of all things would provide for everyone’s benefit. Indeed, among the ancients, because greed did not exist, neither did high prices.

It is rightly compared with idolatry, because it harms many. It is likewise hostile to the Creator: God wishes and commands that the poor be assisted from the things he created, while greed resists this. Consider whether it can exist without the devil.

### (Verses 6–7)

“Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Therefore do not become their partners.”

Empty speeches are vain. Vanity, however, is the worship of idols, which certainly does not originate from God but from error.

He therefore teaches that we must not assent to the words of such people. They are always clamoring, and through a certain seductive deception they set the custom of antiquity against the faith, judging that present realities, rather than hope for the future, should be asserted.

Therefore vengeance comes upon them from heaven, so that they may know that what they refused to believe is true. He teaches that God’s servants must remain far removed from this vanity, lest they become partners in their punishment.

### (Verse 8)

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

Darkness is ignorance, because no one sees in darkness. Ignorance, however, is paganism—or unbelief—from which they were drawn by God’s grace into faith and made light, that is, truth, because things are revealed in the light.

Indeed, while celebrating their mysteries in darkness, the pagans are deceived in a cave with veiled eyes. Having become Christians from among them and having come to know the truth, they are called children of light, because God is light, and they receive faith in him in truth.

### (Verse 9)

“Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.”

He says this so that they may conduct themselves in such a way that they may rightly be called children of light.

For the works of light are performed openly and without fear, whereas the works of darkness are performed secretly because they are unlawful. Every sin fears being done openly.

### (Verse 10)

“Prove what is pleasing to God.”

From the magnificence of holiness and goodness it can be discerned by what works God is pleased. For he himself said: “Be holy, just as I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2).

And the Lord said: “Be compassionate, just as your Father is” (Luke 6:36).

These things please God. For in holiness there is purification, and in mercy there is complete and perfect righteousness.

### (Verse 11)

“And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness.”

He warns us not to be polluted by consenting to the acts of wicked people, since such acts are unfruitful with respect to good but productive of gain for evil.

### (Verse 12)

“Rather, reprove them; for it is shameful even to speak of the things they do secretly.”

He wants them not only to be separate from evil actions but also to rebuke the evil deeds of those who act shamefully in secret.

Sins are then shown for what they are when they are rebuked, so that the children of light may be admired. When they are justly rebuked by them, sinners will not be able to contradict them but will rather revere them.

Everything, however, is revealed when it is rebuked by the light. It is true that sins become visible when they are rebuked, because the one who sins, so long as he is not corrected, scarcely seems to himself to be sinning.

“For everything that is revealed is light.” Where something is manifest, there is no ambiguity, nor can what is openly a crime be excused. Just as, when the sun appears, it can no longer be denied that it is day, so, when sin has been revealed, the rebuke cannot be considered false.

### (Verse 14)

“Therefore he says: ‘Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will touch you.’”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “and Christ will touch you.” Below, where Erasmus and subsequent editions read *qua alienatur a vero* (“by which [the mind] is estranged from truth”), the Amerbach edition and several manuscripts have *quae alienatur a vera* (“which is estranged from the true [reading]”); other manuscripts most correctly restore the word *via* (“way”). Finally, where Erasmus, together with subsequent editions and several manuscripts, reads *haec species mortis est* (“this is a form of death”), Amerbach and other manuscripts prefer *haec spes mortis est* (“this is a hope of death”).]

He signifies by this sleep a dullness of mind that is estranged from the true way. This estrangement is a form of death, from which he urges the person to rise, so that, coming to his senses, he may recognize the truth, which is Christ.

The unbelieving and vicious, sunk in filth under despair of life, are warned to rise or emerge and to have a share with Christ, so that they may pass from darkness to light and from death to life.

### (Verses 15–16)

“Therefore see carefully how you walk, not as unwise people but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

Since above he commanded that unbelief and the vices of life be rebuked by God’s servants, he now adds that these things must be rebuked prudently, because of the danger of scandal.

One must conduct oneself prudently among unbelievers, especially at a time when unbelievers are ruling and presuming upon an irreligious king. If a Christian sees that an opponent is unruly and angry, he should withdraw from him and should not provoke him to blasphemy or to stir up a disturbance; he should speak where an opportunity is given.

For just as, when questioned among powerful unbelievers about what the faith is, one must not remain silent or deny what it is, so, if there is danger in disputing with them, one should refrain. It is harmful to sow seed upon thorns.

This is the mark of a prudent person: to know how to answer each individual. There is someone who, although an unbeliever, is not entirely unapproachable, so that he will not even tolerate hearing words of faith.

There is another in whom the zeal of unbelief burns so fiercely that one should discuss the faith neither with him nor even in his presence. For when he clamors and blasphemes, he becomes a cause of scandal to many.

Hence Paul and Barnabas, when they heard people blaspheming against them, shook out their garments and withdrew from them (Acts 13:46).

### (Verse 17)

“Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.”

The Lord Jesus teaches that one must pursue peace. And the chosen vessel says: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all” (Romans 12:18).

And to Timothy he says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all” (2 Timothy 2:24).

This is the will of the Lord: that the things his servants must do be done with modesty. For disturbance and clamor, or contention accompanied by vehemence, produces enmity.

He added this because of what came before, where he wants God’s servants to rebuke the sins of sinful people, so that, since disagreement and quarrel commonly arise from this, they may rebuke sinners with restraint and gentleness, lest, provoked to anger, the sinners rush into litigation.

He therefore warns that this must be handled prudently, so that it may produce progress.

### (Verse 18)

“And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.”

Those who are sober can confidently rebuke others. For good conduct inspires fear in the offender, and the one being rebuked cannot take the correction harshly when he knows that the person admonishing him lives an excellent life.

For where there is drunkenness, there is also debauchery; and debauchery provokes shameful conduct. Therefore it is fitting that they remain sober, so that the standards of good conduct may be preserved.

[Col. 0398A] (Verse 19.) “But be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to God.” The Holy Spirit loves a reasonable life; for if we live well, we shall be filled with him, as he says, so as to confess and exalt God’s gift with varied vocal song, so that praise may be sung to God by every tongue. For wherever the Spirit is, he always meditates on spiritual things, so that this may not be only on the lips but may burst forth from the heart, because of the Lord’s ancient saying through the prophet. For he says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

(Verses 20, 21.) “Giving thanks always for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.” We are commanded to give thanks to God in all his gifts, who also deigned to adopt us through Christ his own Son, through whom we came to know him and learned that God—“for God is spirit”—must be worshiped, each submitting to the other because of the fear of Christ, who commanded humility to be practiced (John 4:24).

(Verses 22–24.) “Wives, be subject to your husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the Savior of his body. But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything.” Wives are commanded by natural law to be subject to their husbands, because the husband is the wife’s source; hence, he says, just as to the Lord, so they ought to be subject to their husbands. Thus Sarah called Abraham “lord” (Gen. 18:12); for just as Christ is the head of the Church, so also the husband is the head of the wife. For the Church took its beginning from Christ, and therefore is subject to him; likewise the woman took her beginning from the man, so that she may be subject to him. Yet there is this difference: the woman is of the same substance as the man, whereas the Church can participate in Christ in name, not in nature.

[Note: The older edition and several manuscripts read *quia mulier consubstantia* (“because the woman is consubstantial”); the Roman edition reads *consubstantiva* (“of the same substance”); other manuscripts read *consubstantialis* (“consubstantial”).]

(Verses 25–28.) “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but so that she might be holy and immaculate. So also husbands ought to love their wives.” Wives are commanded to be subject and to show reverence to their husbands; husbands, however, are admonished to love their wives in such a way that they even lay down their lives for them, having, because of love, a zealous concern for their affection and discipline, so that they may be religious and holy.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “He loves himself.” The same edition, together with the ancient edition and a few manuscripts, reads: “because, if she commits fornication…”]

He who loves his wife loves his own body. By natural reasoning, the woman is a portion of the man’s body; and thus, in the woman, the man loves himself. If she commits fornication, he sins against himself, because the two are one flesh. Therefore persons do not divide substance so that number arises in nature through persons; rather, they exist in the unity of nature.

(Verses 29.) “For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ also does the Church.” By the example of the Savior he urges husbands to love their wives: just as Christ nourishes and cherishes his own body, so also the husband nourishes and cherishes the woman, because she is his flesh.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “nourishes his own work,” and so forth.]

(Verses 30.) “Because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones.” This must be understood spiritually. For this reason he said that we are his members: because he is the head of the whole Church. Since we began to exist through him, he is called our head, as the one from whom the whole body subsists; thus every spiritual creature is his member—provided that it bends the knee in his name.

(Verses 31, 32.) “For this reason a man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24). To commend unity, he gives an example of unity, so that, just as man and woman are one by nature, Christ and the Church may likewise be understood to be one through faith. “This mystery is great, but I speak of Christ and the Church.” He signifies that the sacrament of the mystery is great in the unity of man and woman. He does not disclose it, however, but sets forth another reason that does not conflict with the mystery mentioned, a reason that he knows pertains to the advancement of the human race—that is, to the Church and the Savior. Just as, after leaving his parents, a man clings to his wife, so also, after abandoning every error, the Church clings and submits to her head, which is Christ.

Nevertheless, let each of you love his own wife as himself; and let the woman fear her husband. Since man and woman share one nature, the man is therefore admonished to love the woman as himself; but the woman, because she is lower in status on account of her condition, not her nature, is commanded to be subject to the man and to fear him.

# CHAPTER VI

(Verses 1, 2.) “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just: Honor your father and mother.” A law is given to children: since they exist through their parents as their source, they should obey them. For it is just that they show reverence to those through whom they exist.

(Verses 3.) “Which is the first commandment with a promise: so that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth.” This promise is contained in Exodus (Exod. 20:12), namely, that children should honor their parents, so that it might be well with them and they might reach a more advanced age. Yet how did he call this the first commandment, when it is clear that the first commandment is stated thus: “You shall have no other gods besides me”? Then: “You shall not make for yourself any likeness of those things that are in heaven above or on the earth below.” The third: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” The fourth: “You shall observe my Sabbaths.” The fifth, however: “Honor your father and mother,” and so forth (Exod. 20:3ff.).

But because the first four commandments concern God, they are understood to be contained on the first tablet; the remaining commandments concern human beings: that one should honor one’s parents, not kill, not commit fornication, not steal, not give false testimony, and not covet anything belonging to one’s neighbor. These six commandments appear to have been written on the second tablet, of which the first is: “Honor your father and mother.” For this reason, therefore, he said: “Which is the first commandment with a promise,” in order to distinguish between the commandments that concern God and those that concern human beings.

(Verses 14.) “And you, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but educate them in the discipline and correction of the Lord.” So that the Law may be observed, by which it is decreed that children honor their parents, another law is also given by the Apostle to parents: they must form their children in such a way that they do not despise the commandments of the Law. For if they are brought up in the fear of the Lord, they will be able to observe what has been commanded.

If parents provoke their children to anger, they themselves do not keep the measure of the Law; for they seem to compel their children to become transgressors. In anger no one recognizes what is useful. Therefore children ought to learn self-control from the example of their parents, so that they may pursue what is useful. Fathers must remember that they too were once children and surely did not wish to be embittered by their fathers. Children, too, must recognize that they will become fathers and would not wish to be dishonored by their children. Therefore both should show one another what they demand from one another.

(Verses 5.) “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would Christ.” Since our religion is higher than all others and alone possesses power, promising the kingdoms of heaven to believers, it was necessary to prevent pride from arising among human beings on this account. Therefore everyone is commanded to discharge the duties owed according to his present condition or service, so that they may encourage the minds of unbelievers all the more toward the worship of God, which they see to be both just and humble.

When masters see that slaves have improved and have advanced faithfully in rendering service, they fulfill what they owe with complete freedom. Slaves, too, when they observe the gentleness of their masters, eagerly desire the faith by whose peaceful restraints human duties are governed. For even one who is in a subordinate condition, if he has a servant, does not wish to be despised by him; therefore he himself must not despise his master. Just as he wants his master to act toward him, so he ought to act toward his servant, and in this way he will be able to please God.

(Verses 6–8.) “Not serving for the eye, as pleasing human beings, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with goodwill as to the Lord and not to human beings, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive that from the Lord, whether slave or free.” Because of the fear of God, he wants just and faithful service to be rendered to human beings. For the slave serves God, whose ordinances he observes in serving his earthly master; and he hears that God will repay him for his righteous actions on the day of judgment, as he testifies in every other matter.

This may also contribute to the salvation of masters. For when they see what is difficult to achieve—slaves made faithful servants by the grace of God—they may praise the glory of God together with them.

(Verses 9.) “And you, masters, do the same toward them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him.” Earthly masters must not be ignorant that God, the Lord of all, is their common Lord. Therefore they should demand such service from their slaves as they themselves would not endure being demanded from them. For “with whatever measure one measures, it will be measured back to him” (Matt. 7:1). The Lord is a just judge: he distinguishes causes, not persons.

(Verses 10.) “Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might.”

[Note: The older edition and some manuscripts read, “After all merits”; the Roman edition and other manuscripts read, “after all exhortations.” Below, on the basis of not a few manuscripts, we have restored *the enemy’s imprudence*, where all editions and several manuscripts have *the enemy’s impudence*.]

After all the admonitions and exhortations, after the order of discipline had been religiously handed down and the arrangement of the mystery made clear, he wants them to be strong in faith and confident in God’s power. Knowing that the hope of the promise is firm, they should be ready for the service of God, raising the helm against the waves stirred up by the enemy’s imprudence. For he raises a storm against God’s servants, but he himself suffers shipwreck.

(Verses 11, 12.) “Put on the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the nations.”

The armor of God is steadfast faith, by which alone Satan has always been defeated. “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against Principalities and Powers of this world, against the rulers of these darknesses, against the spiritual forces of wickedness that are in the heavenly places.”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “against the schemes of the devil.”]

The Apostle is certain that the destruction inflicted by faithless servants of God is carried out at the instigation of the devil, whose height is great and impossible for human beings to reach. He therefore urges that the armor of God be taken up against these things, for by its power alone all the devil’s devices are overcome and destroyed.

He is the one whose satellites they are—those whom he calls “rulers of these darknesses”—the most wicked spirits who dwell in the heavenly places, in the firmament of the world. These are leaders of error, rulers of darkness, that is, those placed over ignorance and faithlessness. The “rulers of darkness” must be understood as governing perversely, as though they were teachers of unbelief.

(Verses 13–17.) “Therefore take up the whole armor, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in everything, having girded your loins with charity, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in readiness for the Gospel of peace. Above all these things, take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

Since we wage war against exceedingly savage enemies, cunning in every form of evasion, we must therefore watch with every precaution and concern, so that whatever they attempt, they may find us fortified and prepared. For God must help those whom he sees watching in prayer and expecting victory from his weapons.

In such a war, a sober mind and a pure conscience are necessary, because the battle is not against fleshly wickedness but against spiritual forces. Against earthly enemies the body is strengthened with food and the mind is inflamed with drink, so that one may gain courage to resist. Against spiritual wickedness, however, one must fight spiritually, and the weapons of sobriety and abstinence must be taken up, so that, filled with the Holy Spirit, we may conquer unclean and wandering spirits.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “Thus, therefore, let us gird our loins in truth … thus let us be prepared,” and so forth.]

Thus we shall gird our loins in truth if we are prepared to resist error. For everyone who wishes to work girds himself, so that, once impediment has been removed, he may work more diligently.

(Verses 18–20.) “With every prayer and supplication, praying at every time in the Spirit, and watching for this with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints, and for me, that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, so that I may boldly make known the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am acting as an ambassador in chains, so that in it I may speak with boldness, as I ought to speak.”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “the opening of my mouth with freedom,” and so forth.]

If we live rightly, the Holy Spirit remains in us, and we can obtain what we ask. To pray in the Spirit at every time, therefore, means to direct prayer to God with a clean conscience and uncorrupted faith. For he prays “in the flesh” who prays with a polluted mind, intending to sin again—not through accident or sudden lapse, but deliberately.

Yet it is possible not to commit a sin leading to death if one prays perseveringly, so that the mind, with constant attention, may always be intent upon God’s Law, meditating day and night on what God loves. Then they can also pray for the saints. For it is not unworthy that the members should be concerned for one another; nor can it seem rash if capable disciples intercede for their teacher, assisting him so that, having set aside impediments, he may use freedom to preach, as was handed down by the author. Otherwise, oppressed by the force of tribulations, he might blunt the sharpness of his teaching through fear itself, losing its severity.

Therefore he urges that they pray for him in two ways: first, so that his understanding may be filled with the Spirit to express the mystery fully; and second, so that he may be given the boldness to assert it. God gladly hears such a prayer, for he sees his embassy despised in his Apostle; and therefore, angered in his own cause, he will not deny its effect.

For if it is customary and lawful not to inflict destruction upon human ambassadors, with what presumption and audacity are not only destruction but death inflicted upon God’s ambassadors? Hence he also says: “For which I am acting as an ambassador in chains.” He was not permitted to speak freely, but, while reporting God’s words under subjection and constraint, he was subjected to bonds, blows, and deaths. For he was stoned, and he fought with beasts at Ephesus (1 Cor. 15:32).

(Verses 21, 22.) “But so that you too may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn what concerns you and console your hearts.”

Through Tychicus the Ephesians learn what the Apostle is doing, and he likewise learns what the Ephesians are doing. There was no doubt about the Apostle, since what he was doing was divine; but it was necessary to know what he was doing among the faithless and amid their ambushes. Concerning the Ephesians, however, it was necessary to learn whether or not they were making progress. Therefore, so that they might obey and listen willingly to Tychicus’s words, he commends him, calling him both this most beloved brother and a capable minister of God.

“Peace to the brothers, and love with faith from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” He wishes that peace, which is the gateway of love, may be with the brothers, and love with faith, so that, having entered through peace, they may remain in love, which comes from faith. For this is from God the Father and his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0404A] “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruptibility. Amen.” The Apostle, foreseeing that many would in the future hold a hopelessly mistaken understanding of our Lord Jesus Christ, says that eternal grace will remain with those who love Christ, thinking rightly about him and in accordance with the will of God the Father. For grace will be taken away from those who call him degenerate.

[Col. 0403]

# ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE PHILIPPIANS

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0403B]

The Apostle delivered the word of faith to the Philippians. For he was warned in a dream, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 16:9), to go to them and open their ears to receive the word of the Lord. After remaining with them for many days, he instructed them in the Lord’s teaching.

And because, after his departure, they did not turn to something else, as the Galatians did, but remained in the faith and did not receive false apostles, he praises them highly in this epistle, rejoicing in the purpose of their hearts. In their praise the censure of others is contained. For the Corinthians, although they had listened to the Apostle for a long time, were overthrown after his departure by various false apostles; hence these Philippians are rightly praised.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0403C]

(Verses 1.) “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ.” He does not call himself an apostle because he is writing to people who held a right opinion about him; therefore he suppresses his dignity, which was already evident to them. He does, however, confess his condition, because the one who confesses Christ as Lord is freer in this respect and possesses salvation.

“To all the saints in Christ Jesus.” As is his custom, he writes to saints—but to those who are saints in Christ Jesus, that is, those who confess Christ as God and man. For Photinus denies that Christ is God, and Mani denies that he is man; therefore they are unclean. He is not writing, then, to those who suppress the truth with their own lies.

“Who are at Philippi.” He indicates to whom he is writing.

“With the bishops and deacons,” that is, with Paul and Timothy, who were certainly bishops; at the same time he also mentions the deacons who ministered to him. For he is writing to the common people. If he were writing to bishops and deacons, he would be writing to their persons, and he ought to have written to the bishop of that place, not to two or three, as he did to Titus and Timothy.

(Verses 2.) “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” It is clear that God is the Father, while Christ is our Lord Jesus. Does he not appear to be more a lord than a father? Among human beings in the world, perhaps; but with God there is harmony between the Father and Christ the Lord.

Here, that is, in the world, the Lord is for this reason greater than the father: either he is also lord of the father himself, or the father begets a son not of his own condition but of another. God, however, begot him in such a way that those whom he begot are under his power; although born free, they are nevertheless his servants. When he hands them over to his own Son, he also makes them servants of his Son, so that the Son may be their Lord, as he says: “Father, those whom you gave me were yours, and you gave them to me,” so that in the Father and the Son they may be servants of the one God (John 17:9).

(Verses 3–5.) “I indeed give thanks to my Lord upon every remembrance of you, always in all my prayer making supplication for you all with joy, because of your partnership in the Gospel.” First he gives thanks to the Lord, by whose will all prosperous things come to the faithful. In all his prayer he remembers them with exultation, because they have become participants in the Gospel, as the Apostle Peter says, among other things: “So that you may be participants in the divine nature” (2 Pet. 1:4).

“From the first day until now.” The Apostle foresaw their devotion and recognized the firmness of their faith from its very beginnings, and he rejoiced in them, knowing that they would always serve as an example to many.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and their right faith.” This is by no means an inferior reading.]

(Verses 6, 7.) “Confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus, as it is right for me to think this about you all, because I have you in my heart and in my bonds, and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel; for you are all participants with me in joy.”

Secure in the goodness and justice of God, and not doubting their faith, he trusts that, aided by God’s help, they will persevere in faith until the day of the Lord, on which those who have persisted in faith will be rewarded. Nor could he think anything else about people whom he had always found unbending in devotion to God, seeing their course so direct and tireless that he considered them worthy to share in his joy. For people of one faith ought to rejoice together in the hope of future immortality and glory.

(Verses 8.) “For God is my witness, how I long for you all in the inward parts of Jesus Christ.”

He calls God to witness in order to commend a righteous man's affection. For one who feels deeply about someone, in order to make this credible, calls God as witness; and through this he also arouses their longing for him, so that those who are longed for may themselves long.

[Note: Some manuscripts do not recognize the word *justi* (“of the righteous”); some instead have *cujusmodi* (“of what kind”). Below, the Roman edition restores *ut magis desiderent* (“so that they may long more”), whereas the other editions and manuscripts read *ut asiderati desiderent* (“so that those who are longed for may long”).]

He therefore longs for all of them, not with human desire but in the love of Christ; not with a fleshly affection but with that of the Spirit, so that he may possess them as participants both in the understanding of the mystery of divinity and in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

(Verses 9–11.) “And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and in every kind of discernment, so that you may approve what is useful, so that you may be sincere and without offense for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.”

With God’s help, he wants to instill in them the order of Christian discipline: since they have been strengthened in faith, they should not be ignorant of the sacrament of their belief. Knowing how to distinguish what is useful from what is contrary, they should adorn the Lord’s teaching with works of righteousness, producing the fruit of immortality in an abundance of every good thing, so that the teacher of the nations may appear glorious in them.

[Col. 0405B] (Verses 12–17.) “But I want you to know, brothers, that what concerns me has turned out for the advancement of the Gospel, so that my bonds have become manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium and in all other places; and that more of the brothers, trusting in the Lord because of my bonds, have begun to speak the word of God more boldly and without fear. Some indeed preach Christ because of envy and contention, but some because of goodwill. Some out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel; others announce Christ out of contention, not sincerely, supposing that they are stirring up affliction for my bonds.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “that what has happened to me has turned out more for the advancement,” and so forth.]

These things require no explanation; nevertheless, because of our concern that nothing should become doubtful, let us set them out more clearly in order.

Since above he declared them to be participants in his joy, he now indicates what his preaching has accomplished, as though he were writing to dear friends: his sufferings for Christ have become known to everyone. Through this humility he shows himself to be glorious, so that those who love him may have an opportunity for rejoicing; for when his bonds are made manifest in Christ, his dignity increases.

“In the whole praetorium and in all other places,” that is, throughout all Judaism and among all the Churches of the nations. Judaism has precedence because the promise was made to the Jews, as it is said: “For salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22).

Therefore he says that many of the brothers, following his example, dared to speak the word of God with confidence. His steadfastness encouraged many, so that, having learned from the Apostle’s example that God is present to protect those who love him, they did not fail to preach the Gospel.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “so that they would not be afraid to preach the Gospel.”]

But he also says that other false brothers, moved not by confidence or love of God but by contentious zeal, preached the word of God as though they were envious. Thus many of the brothers announced Christ with a sincere but differing intention. Some did so with goodwill, for the sole glory of God; others, moved by affection for the Apostle and certain of God’s protection.

Conversely, he again presents two other groups who did not preach with a sincere mind. Some, envious of the Apostle, did this out of contention; others announced Christ through the cunning of pretense, so that they might stir up seditions against the Apostle, as though he were the author of this sect who had gathered many into his conspiracy. For envy against the Apostle grew greater when many appeared to be teaching from his side.

(Verses 18–21.) “What then? Provided that in every way, whether by pretext or in truth, Christ is announced, I rejoice in this, and I shall also rejoice. For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my expectation and hope, because I shall be put to shame in nothing; but with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. For to me, living is Christ, and dying is gain.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “This will advance my salvation … according to my expectation and hope.”]

His first joy is in the brothers who announce Christ with goodwill. Then he also says that he rejoices because the deceit of human beings, which had been devised against him so that Christ might be preached to his envy and affliction, had been turned to account. What they had prepared for his death, he says, advances his life. For he says that his life consists in Christ being preached to everyone, and that he is also ready to die so that this may be fulfilled, knowing that a great and effective reward can be given him for this desire.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads, “and that an effective reward can be given.”]

Unskilled wickedness always plots against itself because it does not understand what it is doing. To trample upon the malice of those who, through a pretense of righteousness, were laying ambushes for his life, he declares that he is fortified by God’s protection, with those whom he calls partners in his joy assisting through prayer for the sake of their common eagerness and through the provision of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit would open paths for the preacher contrary to their will and plans, giving grace and confidence to his words so that he might restrain the seditions that had arisen.

Therefore he says that he is put to shame in nothing in the teaching of Christ, because there is both a great hope of promise and because nothing shameful, dishonorable, or deceitful is found in it, as among the pagans, but only open simplicity. For this reason he does not yield to adversity with complete steadfastness, so that Christ may be magnified in his body, whether he is killed or escapes after being beaten. The greatness of the hope in Christ is considered from this fact: he is ready not only to be beaten and afflicted for him but also to die.

He says that Christ is his life, whether in the present or in the future, as the evangelist John also testifies, saying: “What was made, in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings” (John 1:3–4). For the sake of this life he hands over his mortal body, so that he may receive it eternally; and therefore he counts it gain to die for Christ.

(Verses 22–26.) “But if living in the flesh is the fruit of labor for me, I do not know what I should choose. I am constrained between the two, having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is very necessary for your sake. And being certain of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and the joy of faith, so that your glory may abound through Christ Jesus in me, through my coming again to you.”

It is clear what he is saying: if, while he is in the flesh, his living is not fruitless, then he has the fruit of his labor. “What I should choose,” he says, “I do not know.” He is pressed for two reasons. He has the desire to depart and be with Christ, considering this much better, so that he may already be present with God and enjoy what he has desired and what was promised. Yet he says that it is necessary for him to remain in the flesh for the instruction of believers.

Although he considers departing and being with Christ much better, he nevertheless declares that he is certain that he will remain in the flesh for the progress of the faithful, so that their glory may abound in the Lord and advance the Apostle’s praise when they see him again. For they increase in knowledge and become more firmly grounded in faith.

What affection he had for believers! Although he says that what is much better for him is to depart, he does not choose it; instead he wills what is advantageous to many, certain that what advances the salvation of many is also pleasing to the Lord.

Who, desiring the third heaven, would not despise every present concern? Who, longing for the higher paradise, would not set all these things aside? Who, remembering the hidden words, would not avoid human speech? Who, after so many sufferings, would not choose rest? But because he placed love above everything, he followed what would benefit the brothers.

(Verses 27, 28.) “Only live in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ.” He wants them to display a life worthy of the Lord’s discipline, so that he will not regret having wished to remain in the flesh.

“So that whether I come and see you or, being absent, hear about you, you are standing firm in one spirit, striving together with one mind for the faith of the Gospel, and in nothing frightened by your adversaries. This is for them an exhibition of destruction, but for you of salvation.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “which is for them an occasion of destruction.”]

He wants them to be of one mind in faith and devotion against their adversaries, so that, when absent, he may hear the same things about them that he saw when present. In no way fearing the threats or terrors of their adversaries, they should preserve the faith, knowing that tribulation endured for Christ advances the salvation of those who suffer, but the destruction of those who inflict it.

(Verses 29, 30.) “For this has been granted to you by God for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him, having the same struggle as you saw in me and now hear about me.”

Although he exalts God’s grace in everything, he nevertheless advances their praise when he says that God has granted them to suffer for Christ. For he grants or gives this only to those who love Christ. Therefore he says: “It has been granted to you for Christ’s sake,” so that it may be understood as granted by God the Father to those who love Christ, so that, as proof of their merits, they may suffer for Christ. Following the example of their teacher, they should strive with complete confidence to triumph over the unbelieving.

# CHAPTER II

(Verses 1–4.) “If there is therefore any exhortation in Christ, any consolation of love, any participation in the Spirit, any inward affection and compassion, complete my joy by being of the same mind, having the same love, united in soul, thinking one thing, doing nothing out of irritation or vain glory, but in humility of mind considering one another superior to yourselves, not each looking to his own interests, but to those of others.”

He says this: if there is among you a true exhortation of hope in Christ, by which we console one another; if there is the consolation of common love; if there is participation in the Holy Spirit, through which we are joined in one new body; if there is any inward affection—that is, if I am in your heart just as you are in mine; if there is compassion, that is, if there is an affection of piety in love—then complete my joy.

He indicates that the things he lists are to be proven true when the commands that follow have been observed: they must be of one mind and humble in spirit, not provoking one another but rejoicing in love, so that the Apostle’s joy may be complete in them.

Thus he binds them together: if they do not preserve these things, they will not appear approved in the others either. Since they do not wish to appear disapproved in other matters, they should preserve these as well, so that they may be perfect.

Without doubt there were among them dissenters and restless people, and those who pursued vain glory, wishing to contend and conquer with savage spirit, where there is no reward; but this produces quarrels and breaks love.

For what kind of people can there be in a community in which there are only golden and silver vessels, and not also wooden and earthen ones? Yet through the practice of good, they can be changed into gold and silver, because the defect lies not in nature but in the will.

(Verses 5, 6.) “For have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.”

Christ was always in the form of God because he is the image of the invisible God. But the Apostle is discussing the Son of God when he became incarnate and was made human, saying: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus,” that is, in God and man.

“Although he was in the form of God,” he lived among human beings and appeared through his words and works to be God. The form of God differs in nothing from God. For this reason he is called the form and image of God: so that it might be understood that he is not God the Father himself, but is what God is.

Therefore he “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.” Knowing that he was in the form of God, he did not steal when he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Elsewhere in John’s Gospel the Jews, he says, persecuted Jesus because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18). Rightly, therefore, he made himself equal with God. For the one who makes himself equal to someone to whom he is inferior is considered to be committing robbery.

But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Knowing, therefore, that Christ was in the form of God, he showed himself equal to God; but, in order to teach the law of humility, when the Jews seized him he not only did not resist: “But he emptied himself”—that is, he withdrew his power from its operation, so that, humbled, he might appear to be weakened by inactive power. [Note: Some manuscripts: “to be formed by inactive power” (otiosa virtute informari).] Taking the form of a servant, while he is seized and bound and driven by blows, becoming obedient to the Father even unto the cross, he did not defend the equality which he knew himself to possess, but subjected himself. He teaches us to imitate this patience and humility, so that we may not only refrain from putting ourselves before those who are our equals, but even bend ourselves low, following the example of our author.

Yet he is not said to have received the form of God, but to have been in the form of God; whereas he received the form of a servant when he was humbled as though he were a sinner. Servants, however, are made from sin, as was Ham, the son of Noah, who was the first deservedly to receive the name of servant (Gen. IX, 25). For I do not think, as some do, that he received the form of a servant when he was born a human being. See what he says: “Have this mind in yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus,” that is, in God and in a human being. Before the incarnation, either “Christ” or “Jesus” can be said, because the two names together signify both the son of a human being and the Son of God. For what does he say, among other things, before the birth? “The rock was Christ, and let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him” (I Cor. X, 4).

Whenever Scripture wishes to signify either God or a human being, it sets down one of the two: either Jesus or Christ. For when the Son of God had been born a human being, he was in the form of God, because, while he appeared to be a human being, he performed the works of God, so that it might be evident from the deeds that the one who was thought to be merely a human being was God. For the works signified the form, so that, since his works were certainly not the works of a human being, the one who was in the work—or form—of God might be understood to be God.

For what is the form of God except the likeness by which God appears, when he raises the dead, restores hearing to the deaf, cleanses lepers, and performs other such deeds? How, moreover, is he said to have been made like a human being if he was merely a human being? And in what sense was he found in appearance as a human being if he were not also God? It is because, before he permitted himself to be humbled, he was always seen in the power of God; afterward, having been weakened, he was found in the appearance of a human being. For on the mountain he certainly appeared as God (Matt. XVII, 2); and, walking with his feet upon the sea, he was seen and understood to be not only a human being but also God. Finally, those who were in the boat said: “Truly this is the Son of God” (Matt. XIV, 33).

When, therefore, this power ceased, he appeared as though a human being; for this is why he says “as though,” to signify that he is also God. He says that he was made like human beings because of weakness. He explains this in what follows, saying: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.” This is why he was found in appearance as a human being: retaining his own power so that it might not appear in him, he was seen and killed as a human being, although he does not know death.

**(Verses 10–12.)** Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

He shows what and how much humility merits, so that we might desire it all the more, with pride trampled underfoot. Hence Solomon says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Prov. III, 34). And therefore the Lord says: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11).

This, then, is humility: if a person does not defend even what he knows to be owed to him. Thus that Pharisee (Luke XVIII, 11 and following), although speaking truthfully about himself, is said to have exalted himself; and for this reason he was humbled. Christ, however, did more: although he is God, he became flesh and humbled himself among human beings.

Now let us see how the name that is above every name was given to Christ—as though the Son of God had been in need, or had been imperfect; for whoever is in need is imperfect. If he was in the form of God, he was equal and coequal with God: how, then, was it given to him? He says that it was given to the one who humbled himself and appeared as a human being, emptying himself and becoming obedient unto death.

If, then, he was born perfect, how could he have been in need? Whoever denies that the perfect Son of God was born from God the Father is an Arian. For before the passion he showed himself equal to God the Father, as I mentioned above. It is therefore clear that he was born perfect; for in his birth he seems to have attained everything. He was born in the fullness of divinity for the performance of all that he accomplished, so that he received the gift before he performed the things for which he was born.

The Father’s gift, then, appears to be this: that he is the Son, and that his name is above every name—that is, that he is God. For the name of God, by nature and not merely by appellation, is above every name. Hence “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow,” of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, as he indicates in the Epistle to the Romans, saying among other things: “From them is the Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom. IX, 5).

He explains in this epistle what “all these” are, saying: heavenly, earthly, and infernal; for there are no others. Some, however, think that the name which is above every name was given to the human being—a view which is wholly and in every respect inappropriate. For if Christ the Son of God is himself both God and human being, God, having become human while remaining God, could not have needed what he already possessed. Or if, insofar as he was human, he needed the things that belong to God, then the Son of God, who is God, would have given himself what he lacked insofar as he was human.

But this is said from ignorance. And why is the Father said to have given it, when the one who had become human had nothing lacking? [Note: Some manuscripts of the Laudian codex: “or could not the divinity of the Son have supplied to its body ...”] Or could not the divinity of the Son have supplied to his body and soul what they lacked? But perhaps, because everything comes from God the Father, he is therefore said to have given it.

If everything comes from the Father, why should it not be said that he gave everything to his Son through generation? And although he begot a Son equal to himself, order nevertheless requires that everything be done in the name of the Father. After the cross the Father granted this to the Son: that everything should be saved in the name of the Son.

Thus the Lord says concerning his disciples to the Father: “Father, those whom you gave me I have guarded; for they were yours, and you gave them to me” (John XVII, 12). And he says to the disciples: “Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you will receive” (John XVI, 24).

The one who was born, then, received this so that after the cross it might be revealed what he had received from the Father when he was begotten. [Note: The old edition and several manuscripts: “For he did not then receive it.”] He received the name from the Father when he began to be known by creation; for it becomes clear what he had received, on account of the things he accomplished, before he accomplished them. Thus before the cross he said: “Everything has been handed over to me by my Father” (Matt. XI, 27).

How, then, can this be referred to the body, so that the name of God was given to the body, when it is established that Christ is both human being and God? For it is neither fitting that God should be changed into flesh, nor could flesh become what God is. But perhaps the claim is that he was God by adoption—and this too is a coloring of the argument. For then Christ would begin to be true God in part and adoptive in part, or there would be two gods.

But Scripture signifies something else: it signifies that the gift was given to the one who emptied himself, who received the form of a servant, who was made a human being in the likeness of a human being, and who obeyed the Father. If a human being obeyed God the Father, what great thing was it that the Apostle said? But this is great: that, although he was equal, he obeyed.

And what praise is there if, having been made in the likeness of a human being, he was made a human being, so that a human being is said to have been made like a human being? But this cannot be. No one becomes in the likeness of something unless he is something else before becoming like the thing whose likeness he assumes; he was made like it in cause, not in substance.

And who is it who emptied himself? [Note: The Laudian codex: “A human being. Therefore he was acting.”] A human being. Then he possessed it. And how did he receive it? But how could a human being, a frail thing, empty himself? And was a human being in the form of God? But perhaps [Note: Some manuscripts: “the human being was in the form of the Son of God.”] the human being was in the form of the Son of God.

Come, then: in whose form was the Son of God? And if the human being was already in the form of God—that is, was the Son of God—then he was already perfect before the passion. He therefore received nothing after the passion.

But let us see what is written concerning him: “Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

Let us now consider the words and thus attend to the force of the expression. Certainly the name that is above every name is the name of God. But if this name is not established by nature, it is not above every name; an appellative name exists only in the word, not in the nobility of nature. Nor does creation bow the knee to an adoptive god, but to the true God, not to one who is co-created with it.

And how can it be that a human being is in the glory of God the Father? Even if the human being were an adoptive god, he could not be in the glory of God the Father; for this belongs to the one who was born from God. To be in the glory of God the Father is to differ in nothing from God, so that the glory of the Father and the Son is one through their common substance and power. This is the unity of nature.

What, I ask, is contradictory if the Son is said to have received a gift from the Father, when everything belonging to the Son comes from the Father, from whom all things are also believed to exist? We call the substance of God “nature” for this reason: because Christ was born from it.

**(Verses 12–13.)** Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed—not only in my presence, but much more now in my absence—work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.

He testifies that God assists good endeavors; for he always refers every grace back to God, so that willing is ours, but bringing to completion is God’s. For who could overcome the principalities and powers, the rulers of this darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, whom we have as enemies because of their envy, except God alone? For they are indignant that we are called children of God.

This exhortation, then, is not something new, but urges them to be subject to the Gospel in the customary manner, taking care over their own conduct. For good conduct works salvation.

**(Verses 14–18.)** Do everything without murmuring and hesitation, so that you may be blameless and simple, as children of God, without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life for my glory on the day of Christ; because I did not run in vain or labor uselessly. But even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice and ministry of your faith, I rejoice and congratulate all of you. For the same reason you also rejoice and congratulate me.

So that they might possess the fruit of their faith and works, he exhorts them to do everything pertaining to Christian discipline without hesitation and murmuring. For if something is done carelessly and without devotion, it does not reach its proper result, because it falls under reproach. Rather, they should act with complete simplicity, as blameless children of God, so that, remembering their profession, they may live in accordance with it.

Thus, among those who do not believe, they should appear equally distinguished in life, conduct, and morals, just as the sun and moon are exalted in splendor among the stars. For just as the stars are darkened when the sun appears, so the unjust and faithless appear shameful and disfigured in the presence of the faithful and just. In this way the Apostle’s glory will be established at the coming of the Son of God, whose planting has produced such fruits. His labor and effectiveness will then be shown not to have been in vain.

Therefore, he says, even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice and ministry of your faith, I rejoice. If he should be overwhelmed by the faithless, he indicates that he ought to congratulate himself for having gathered them into his fellowship; for he knows that his death will have achieved its purpose. It is a great sorrow if someone suffers for those in whom he accomplishes nothing.

For this reason he testifies that he rejoices in them and that they ought to congratulate him, so that both people and their worthy teacher may share mutually in their common joy.

**(Verses 19–24.)** I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn about you. For I have no one equally minded who will sincerely care for you; for all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know his proven character: how, like a son with his father, he served with me in the Gospel. I hope, therefore, to send him immediately, as soon as I see how things stand with me. I trust in the Lord that I myself will also come to you soon.

These matters are clear and require no interpretation. After this letter he signifies that he will send Timothy, through whom he may learn what is happening among them. Timothy was of one mind with the Apostle; therefore he is marked as being especially concerned for them, unlike certain people who, while wishing to commend themselves, were negligent regarding the discipline and conduct of the brethren. They did not preach with a devout spirit, but for the sake of their own profits.

And because Timothy was an outstanding man, he says that he had found him proven: he was with him as a most beloved son, serving the Gospel of Christ. He calls him his son because he had been ordained by him. [Note: The Roman edition: “He hopes to send him ahead, and that he himself will also come to them shortly.”] He hopes to send him ahead, and that he himself will also go to them shortly.

**(Verses 25–27.)** But I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow soldier, and your apostle and minister of my service, since he longed for all of you and was distressed because you had heard that he had been ill. Indeed, he was ill almost to the point of death; but God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow.

All these matters are clear. He signifies that he will send Epaphroditus to them with this letter. They and Epaphroditus were sorrowful because of their mutual longing, on account of his illness, so that, when they saw him, they might be refreshed by his recovered health, and he might be free from the anxiety he felt about seeing them.

He had become their apostle through the Apostle, when he sent him to them to exhort them; and because he was a good man, the people longed for him.

What, then, is the meaning of Epaphroditus’ becoming ill almost to the point of death while the Apostle was present—the one who raised the dead? Did the Apostle not pray for him, or did he fail to obtain that he might be healed more quickly? But signs are performed for the sake of unbelievers. In this man the illness did not occur to his detriment, but to his increase.

The trials of believers are various. One is tested through illness, another through the loss of loved ones, another through the loss of money, another through tribulations: whether he is found steadfast in need, seeking no help from an opposite source, so that he may increase his merits.

The Apostle’s request, therefore, was not disregarded; rather, better provision was made for the one for whom he asked. But what does it mean that, whereas in another epistle he urges that one ought not to grieve over the departure of the brethren, here he indicates that he himself would have grieved if Epaphroditus had departed from the body?

He had said that, if Epaphroditus had died, he would have had sorrow upon the sorrow he already had because of his illness; for he was necessary to the churches. To the Thessalonians he says: “See that you do not grieve over those who sleep, as the others do who have no hope” (I Thess. IV, 12). But he said that he would be sad over the death of Epaphroditus because he required his comfort and assistance, not because he would mourn him as one lost.

**(Verse 28.)** Therefore I sent him with urgency, so that when you see him you may rejoice again, and I may be more encouraged.

He signifies that Epaphroditus and the people of Philippi had mutual affection: when they saw him, they would be stirred again to joy, and the Apostle’s spirit would rejoice, because a person is more encouraged when he sends someone to visit his dear ones.

**(Verses 29–30.)** Receive him, therefore, in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor, because for the work of Christ he came close to death, delivering his life over to destruction, in order to supply what was lacking in your service toward me.

Although the affection between Epaphroditus and the people was indivisible, the Apostle nevertheless commends him in order to make him still dearer to them—especially because there might have been some who did not feel such affection toward him. For there is diversity in every people.

This is why he recalls his struggle: he did not hesitate to die for the work of the Gospel. That is, he was not deterred by the threats and pressures of unbelievers, but persevered in exhorting the faithful, in order to fulfill what was lacking to the people in their service, according to the Apostle’s arrangement.

Therefore, whoever does not hold back his life from death but delivers it over to destruction gives it up with respect to the present life, just as the Lord also says: “Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it” (Matt. XVI, 2). This loss is destruction, because, according to the world, whoever gives up his life for Christ loses it; nevertheless, he will preserve it for the future.

### Chapter III

**(Verse 1.)** Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but it is necessary for you.

He shows his concern for their progress, because he is not reluctant to write to them what is necessary for their benefit.

**(Verse 2.)** Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers; beware of the mutilation.

He designates those who, out of envy toward the nations, were overthrowing the Galatians through the perverse character of their conversations, persuading them to be circumcised. He teaches that they must be avoided and despised in every way, like dogs that first bark and then viciously injure the flesh with their bite.

**(Verses 3–4.)** For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit, who glory in Christ Jesus and place no confidence in the flesh—although I myself have confidence even in the flesh.

It is clear that believers circumcise their own hearts, so that, when the cloud of error has been cut away, they may see and recognize the Lord of creation. This is to serve God in the Spirit and to glory in the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave the law of the Spirit so that the glory of the flesh might be emptied.

Nevertheless, the Apostle also had this confidence, so that, if he wished, he could glory in the circumcision of the flesh; but, knowing that this glory was empty, he rejected it.

**(Verses 5–7.)** [Note: The Roman edition: “If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh ... I more, circumcised on the eighth day.”]

If anyone seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the Law a Pharisee, according to zeal a persecutor of the Church of God, according to the righteousness that comes from the Law living blamelessly. But whatever gains I had, these I counted as losses because of Christ.

As far as observance of the Law, the preservation of its righteousness, zeal for the Pharisaic sect, and zeal for ancestral tradition in persecuting the Church are concerned, he had no equal. In other respects he had companions who were likewise Jews by nature.

But the things that seemed to be gains according to human judgment were found to be losses in comparison with Christ. [Note: The Laudian codex: “in comparison with Christ they are truly losses.”] Why losses, unless because the time had already come when the Law was no longer to be observed? All these things were empty and impediments preventing access to grace; and they were carnal, whereas ours are spiritual.

He says that he was of the tribe of Benjamin in order to exalt his lineage above those who derive their origin from the sons of Jacob’s concubines, or on account of those who were proselytes. [Note: The Roman edition: “to exalt it, either on account of those who …”] Hence he says: “I more, circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel,” to show that he was first among the Jews; but that he despised this because of the hope promised by Christ.

They were called Hebrews on account of Abraham. The letter was changed because of the sound, so that they would not be called “Abraei” but “Hebrews,” just as among the ancients, when “medidie” was said and sounded awkward, the letter was changed so that “meridie” would be said.

For if their origin is from Abraham, their name too should be derived from him, not from Heber, who is six generations after Abraham (Gen. XI, 14). If the human race began to be restored in Abraham, and he is the father of faith, then both the name and the Hebrew language should derive from him. For when the first language, which had no name, was restored to this people, it received its name from him.

There is no reason, then, for the name to derive from Heber. Abraham was a Chaldean, [Note: Some manuscripts: “Yet the Hebrews do not have the Chaldean language.”] but the Hebrews nevertheless do not have the Chaldean language.

**(Verses 8–11.)** Indeed, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have counted everything as loss and consider it refuse, in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which comes from the Law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness that comes from God through faith, in order to know him and the power of his resurrection and the sharing of his sufferings, being conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain the resurrection that is from the dead.

Above, when he was speaking of the race of Abraham, the Law, its righteous deeds, and the merits of those who observe it, he counted all these things as detriment in comparison with the promises of the Savior. Now he adds that not only these things, but also everything, is loss because of “the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.”

After the Law and its righteous deeds, what else could all these things be, unless the knowledge of Christ is set above the very life of body and soul? For, as he says to the Colossians, “In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Coloss. II, 3). Everything that exists must therefore be considered of no account if it enables one to attain the excellence of this wisdom and knowledge.

The righteousness that comes from faith, not from the Law, is therefore sufficient—indeed, more than sufficient—for salvation. It comes from the knowledge of Christ, through the grace of God granted to us. Knowledge of the mystery of his incarnation, passion, and resurrection is the perfection of life and the treasure of wisdom. For where there is wisdom, there is also life, because where there is folly there is no life.

Thus Solomon says: “The fool works wickedness through laughter” (Prov. X, 23). Whoever understands that Christ became human and suffered for his sake, and that, having conquered death, he rose again, follows him after despising and rejecting everything, seeking means of pleasing him, so that he may in some measure repay him and thereby deserve to obtain still greater promises in the resurrection.

**(Verse 12.)** [Note: The Roman edition: “Not that I have apprehended it, or am already perfect; but I pursue, if somehow I may comprehend.”]

Not that I have already received it, or am already justified, or am already perfect; but I pursue, if I may comprehend that for which I have also been comprehended by Christ Jesus.

Throughout the epistle he testifies that he rejoices in them and praises their obedience and faith. Lest they be puffed up, as human beings, by thinking that they were already worthy, he now openly declares through his own person that he still lacked the completion of justification, so that they might strive to add to their good works.

If one who possesses such dignity confesses that perfection is still lacking in him, how much more should they understand that they must labor to attain the merits of justification?

Therefore he adds: “But I pursue,” he says, “in order to comprehend that for which I have also been comprehended by Christ.” While he was wavering in error and mental agitation, distrustful of the way of the Lord, the mercy of God, as though pursuing him while he fled, seized him on the road as he went to disturb and afflict the Church, so that he might learn the gift of God [Note: Some manuscripts: “might learn, the grace of which he was rejecting.”] and the grace which he was rejecting, and might know that even to die for it was gain.

Thus he could not harm believers, but only himself, if he did not believe—he who, through ignorance, was pursuing the means of salvation.

For this purpose he was apprehended—that is, he was found after being sought by God’s foreknowledge—and he learned the mystery of Christ, so that throughout his life, increasing his merits, he might apprehend the appointed reward by pleasing the one whom he had learned had been killed for his sake. [Note: The gloss of Gill and the Roman edition in the text, with some manuscripts: “that is, by the presence of God.”]

**(Verses 13–14.)** Brothers, I do not consider that I have yet apprehended it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to the appointed goal the prize of the heavenly calling of God.

This is what he said above: he signifies that he labors for the purpose of advancing daily toward what is better, always stretching himself toward higher things, so that, forgetting what lies behind, he may pursue what is better—not because the former things are evil, but because they are small in comparison with the merit that must be attained.

He must advance toward what is better in order to reach the appointed heavenly reward; for he declares that, because of such an astonishing and invisible prize, one must certainly contend with seriousness.

**(Verse 15.)** Let all of us who are perfect think in this way.

Above he denies that he is perfect, with respect to the promise that merit is still to be added. But in comparison with others who attend less carefully to divine matters, those who proceed along the path of perfection with diligent care are to be called perfect. This, then, is what they ought to think, so that they may advance toward what is better.

And if you think differently in any respect, God will reveal that also to you. He says this so that, if they should devise anything further for the practice of an improved way of life, they might consider it a gift of God and not be puffed up by it.

**(Verse 16.)** Nevertheless, let us walk according to what we have attained, thinking the same thing and following the same path.

Lest presumption arise from this and something be thought to have been revealed that was not from God, he adds: “According to what we have attained, let us think the same thing.” That is, in the conduct of faith, they should not think outside the rule of discipline, but should think what is common and modest within evangelical truth.

**(Verses 17–19.)** Become imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have our example. Many walk—those of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears—as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they think about earthly things.

He wishes them to be vigilant, lest they be caught by the subtlety of wicked people, and to observe how each person conducts himself and teaches, so that they may join themselves to those in whom they recognize the mind of their teacher.

The people whom he indicates belong to the number of those who were overthrowing the Galatians. For walking deceitfully, they were subverting the Churches of God, preaching under the name of Christ that Judaism ought to be observed, as though Christ had been promised to them.

He mentions them with grief and tears because they were obstructing the salvation of believers, raising questions about foods to be eaten and not eaten, as though salvation lay in food, or as though the belly were God, whom they thought was pleased with foods clean according to the Law. They gloried in their circumcised shame—that is, they thought about earthly things.

But one who thinks about spiritual things glories in faith, hope, and love. [Note: The same in the Roman edition: “This does not pertain to this passage.”] This passage does not concern the statement “Their god is their belly” being said on account of profit or gluttony.

**(Verses 20–21.)** But our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to his power by which he is able also to subject all things to himself.

Those who care for spiritual things are said to conduct themselves in heaven, although they are still on earth; just as the evil principalities and powers, although they are still in the firmament, nevertheless have their conduct on earth.

The deeds of Christians, therefore, are in heaven, where their hope of salvation also is—which is Christ, whom every faithful person awaits for the transformation of the body of flesh. [Note: Some manuscripts: “so that what is from one thing ...”] He will make what is from the earth, clothed in spiritual attire, conform at his coming to the body of his glory, according to his power—that is, according to his strength—by which he is able to subject all things to himself.

This means that through the resurrection of the dead and the transformation into glory, the power of the Lord will appear manifested, restraining all principalities and powers, so that he himself may be shown to be God and Lord of all.

### Chapter IV

**(Verse 1.)** Therefore, my most beloved and most longed-for brothers, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved.

He exhorts them to persevere in the same faith. Their steadfastness is his joy in the present and his crown in the future. For when disciples are victorious in the contest, their teacher will be worthy of a crown.

**(Verses 2–3.)** I urge Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to think the same thing in the Lord. I also ask you, my true companion, to help them, women who labored with me in the Gospel, together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

He urges Euodia and Syntyche to increase in prudence, with the assistance of those whom he mentions, so that, just as they had advanced in the works of the Gospel, they might also advance in the knowledge and wisdom of God. He declares that all of them, by the merit of their faith, are held in the book of life. [Note: The editions after Erasmus: “To embrace prudence.”]

**(Verse 4.)** Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice.

The Apostle is joyful in their works and faith. To increase his own gladness, he desires them to advance in this pursuit and always rejoice in the Lord. This is why he repeats himself: to show that he truly rejoices in them.

**(Verses 5–7.)** Let your modesty be known to all people. The Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing.
