[Note: The Roman edition: “but by every prayer and petition … let your requests be made known,” etc.] But in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses every mind, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus. [Note: Some manuscripts: “which surpasses every understanding.”]

Now he wishes to win others by their example. When their modesty—that is, their reasonable conduct—has become known, their works will shine, and there will be people who imitate their goodness. Thus they will obtain an increase not only of their own deeds, [Note: The Laudian codex: “but also the merit of others.”] but also of the merit of others, so that, as it is said, they may eat the labors of their fruits (Ps. CXXVII, 2).

For when the fruit of their works gains others for good work, the labors of those who have been won will benefit the people whose example led them to begin imitating good works.

“The Lord,” he says, “is near. Be anxious about nothing.” That is, they must be prepared and vigilant in prayer and petition, giving thanks to God, setting aside worldly anxiety, hoping for and keeping before their eyes what the Lord has promised. Hence he also teaches that thanks should be given to him; for when the Lord is at hand, worldly anxiety ceases.

Why should they be anxious about something that will soon perish? And therefore, he says, let your requests be made known to God. This knowledge is produced by persistence and vigilance in prayer.

Then, with the fortifications of his peace—which surpasses every mind—may he guard your hearts in Christ Jesus. He said this because the one who has peace with God fears no hostile mind; every person who loves God in Christ Jesus is safe in the peace of God. For who would not fear the one whom he knows to be a friend of God?

**(Verses 8–9.)** Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is holy, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable—if there is any virtue, if there is anything worthy of praise in discipline—think about these things. What you have learned, received, heard, and seen in me, practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

In his conclusion he sets out what remains for imitation of perfection, so that, thinking about and practicing those things that not only do not fall under blame but are also worthy of praise, they may follow the Apostle’s example and have the God of peace with them.

Our God is truly the God of peace. He does not urge peace as one who, though powerful, has not been asked, or as one who, though weak, is fearful; rather, he urges it to such an extent that he even forgives sins committed against himself. He could, of course, by the terror of his manifested power and ineffable greatness, compel even the unwilling not to peace but to submission. [Note: The Vallian manuscripts: “to display the terror of his power ... and even [to compel] the unwilling.”]

But such peace belongs to the world, not to God, whose very nature is peace.

(Verse 10.) But I rejoiced greatly in the Lord [Note: The Roman edition reads, “greatly, because you have blossomed again . . . so that you may think of me as you did before.”] that at last you have flourished again, so as to feel concern for me as you did before; for you were occupied. He shows that their eagerness had become more ardent, because, having applied diligence to what they had grown negligent in, they renewed their former work, remembering their Apostle, so that they might send their fruits to him to be stored in the heavenly granary, where neither moth nor rust destroys (Matt. 6:19).

(Verses 11, 12, 13.) I do not say this because of want; for I have learned to be content with whatever I have. I know both how to abound and how to be brought low (everywhere and in all things I have been instructed), both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me. He testifies that he rejoices in their work not for his own sake, but above all in their own progress, being helped by God; so that he would be saddened neither by want nor elated by abundance, knowing that abundance often puffs a person up, while endured poverty acquires heavenly riches. Nevertheless, he declares their work toward him to be kind, for it benefited the needs of many.

(Verses 15, 16, 17.) And you yourselves know, Philippians, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone; for even when I was in Thessalonica, you sent something for my needs once and again. [Col. 0420A] I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that increases to your account. He recalls these things so that, when they hear that their works are remembered and praised, they may not doubt that they are credited to them before God, but may apply themselves still more earnestly to the zeal of faith.

(Vers. 18.) Yet I have received everything and abound; I have been filled by what I received from Epaphroditus, the things sent from you, a fragrance of good sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God. He does not remind them idly that this ought to be done, nor does he exhort them to something other than what he professes to have been done; rather, it appeared to have been done either less diligently or less generously than they had been accustomed to do it. Thus, by recalling their earlier works, they would know that they had done less than they had begun to do. Although he does not condemn what they had done, he indicates that they had previously been more devoted to this work; [Col. 0420B] nevertheless, God regards it as pleasing and accepts it as a welcome sacrifice. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “and that it is pleasing and acceptable to God.”] Finally, the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). How pleasing, then, is a work that cleanses every stain and defilement of a human being!

(Vers. 19.) But may my God fulfill all your desire according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. For this reason he distinguished the words by saying, “my God,” so that, according to the merits he had bestowed, assistance might be present for them and for their desires, in the abundance of his goodness, in the glory of Christ Jesus. The glory of Christ Jesus consists in this: that, by God’s will, the desires of Christians are fulfilled according to evangelical discipline.

(Vers. 20.) Now to our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen. Here he made no distinction, but said generally, “To our God and Father be glory.” He is called God because of fear, but Father as a matter of honor, and because every origin is from him. For he himself said through the prophet Malachi: “If I am God, where is my fear? And if I am Father, where is my honor?” (Mal. 1:6).

(Vers. 21.) Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “Let him be greeted in Christ Jesus.”] Greet this one in Christ Jesus who sanctifies himself, so that he may be regarded as worthy of Christ, who said: “Be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God” (Lev. 19:2).

(Vers. 22.) The brothers who are with me greet you. The greeting of brothers offers mutual consolation, for it presents, as it were, images of those who have been separated. All the saints greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household. By this he indicates that he has a more devoted affection toward those who are of Caesar’s household; he shows these brothers to be superior to those mentioned above, because he also calls them saints.

(Vers. 23.) The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. Since questions arise concerning the person of the Savior, here, in order to affirm the solidity of his divinity, he desires that the protection of his grace be with our spirit.

[Col. 0421]

## On the Epistle of the Blessed Paul to the Colossians

263 **PROLOGUE**

[Col. 0421A]

The pseudo-apostles were striving to overthrow the Colossians, so that, after the preaching of Epaphras or Archippus, they might entangle their simple minds in philosophical arguments and prevent them from rejecting the theories of the elements by which human life is supposedly governed. Therefore the Apostle exhorts and admonishes them throughout the epistle not to think that there is any hope except in Christ, lest they be deceived.

## CHAPTER ONE

(Verses 1, 2, 3.) Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy, a brother, to those who are at Colossae, holy and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. In his customary manner he writes the opening of the epistle to them, in which he proceeds to address his letter to holy and faithful brothers, wishing that the grace of God might remain with them through Christ.

(Verses 4, 5, 6.) We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love that you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven, which you heard before in the word of the truth of the Gospel, which has come to you, just as it has also come into the whole world. Since God considered it worthy to entrust these people with his Son, he gives him thanks in his prayers. Then, because of the love that they had for the saints, [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “believing that through this hope is made firm,” and so forth.] he was confident that because of this love their hope was firm with God, who is believed to reward those who believe in and love one another, with Christ as the author, whose name has reached all nations, so that they may increase in his faith.

(Verses 7, 8.) And it is fruitful and growing, just as it is among you also, from the day on which you heard and recognized the grace of God in truth, just as you learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf, who also made your love known to us in the Spirit. He speaks eagerly of our growing and bearing living fruit as an example to the other nations. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “to refresh them and bear fruit,” and so forth.] Thus, because they received the grace of God, they might advance both in number and in works, adding to their faith those who would become their brothers in Christ. For many were drawn by the example of their good works, as Epaphras testified, he who ministered to them the grace of Christ in the place of an Apostle. They immediately absorbed it as spiritual drink in the love of the Lord, which is not in the flesh but in the Spirit. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “of the good works of others.”]

[Col. 0421D] (Verses 9, 10.) For this reason we also, from the day on which we heard, have not ceased praying and asking for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of him in every good work, pleasing in all things. Having heard of their devoted and ready will concerning the faith of Christ, the Apostle prays for them, so that, having more fully recognized the will of God, they might complete by rational works the devotion that they had learned upon hearing the faith of Christ. Thus, their faithful dedication of mind [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “the building of the mind”; other manuscripts, more fittingly, “the dedication of the mind.”] and the strength of their faith would not lose the fruit of their labor by undertaking something rashly and without understanding. For what is done with a devoted and prudent spirit is gladly accepted.

(Verses 11, 12, 13.) Bearing fruit and increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory, for all endurance and long-suffering with joy, giving thanks to God and the Father, who called you to share in the lot of the saints in light, who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love. He wants the increase of their works to take place together with knowledge, so that they may not be ignorant of the hope of their faith. For they are then firm and stable if they attend to what has been promised for the sake of faith and to how great is the power of the glory of God’s majesty in endurance: that with long expectation he bears with the human race, which by its irreverence not only neglects the Creator but also persecutes those who love him. They too, therefore, must be patient, bearing the insults and curses of unbelievers; or, if oppression is inflicted, they must await the judgment of God, neither doubting concerning him nor failing to rejoice instead in the promised life, with thanksgiving to God, who deigned to call and bring the nations into the promise of the Jews, which is eternal light—that is, eternal life and everlasting truth.

For having been freed from the condition of darkness—that is, rescued from hell, where we were held by the devil both through our own fault and through Adam’s sin, he being the father of all sinners—we have been transferred through faith into the heavenly kingdom of the Son of God. Thus God might show us with what love he loves us, when, raising us from the depths of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his true Son. For now all believers who are devoted with steadfast mind, when they depart from this world, are led into heaven by the Angel at the Father’s right hand—something that was not granted before death had been conquered.

(Vers. 14.) In whom we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins. God transferred us into the kingdom of this Son of his, through whom he redeemed and emancipated us. For the forgiveness of sins makes people free, so that, once freed from their debts, they cannot be held liable. For without the faith of Christ no one has escaped from hell, because one bound by sins cannot leave the gates of Tartarus.

Who is the image of the invisible God. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “The image of the invisible God cannot be visible.”] The image of the invisible God cannot itself be visible, otherwise it would not be an image; for what is invisible cannot be depicted, nor can what is visible see what is invisible. Either what is seen is a body, or a figure, or some formed substance that the eye’s vision apprehends; yet all of these are bodily. But God, who is alien to all such things, how can he have a visible image?

He is therefore called this so that the Son may be understood to be such as the Father is. Since he is from the Father and differs in no respect from him in the nature of divinity, he is called his image and form, lest the impious believe in another God, although this is already contained in the very name. For this reason he is called the true Son of God, so that he may be believed to be from him.

But because of a mistaken understanding, this too was added, that he should be called his image: so that when he appears, whether in human form or even in fire, as to Moses (Exod. 3:2), it may not be understood that the Father himself is present, but the Son; and through his being called the Father’s image, he may be believed to differ in nothing from him. Hence he says to Philip: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also. How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:9).

This is the unity and substantial identity of the Father and the Son: that they are in one another, so that whoever sees the Son sees the Father also. Now let us see in what way the Son was seen, so that we may consequently understand how Philip, by seeing the Son, also sees the Father. They saw the Son through understanding of divine works, certainly not with bodily eyes. The works that the Son performed he declared to be the Father’s, in order to show the unity of their power.

In the same manner he was also seen by Jacob, from whom he received the name Israel, that is, “a man seeing God” (Gen. 32:28). For this reason, then, he is called the image of the invisible God, so that he might be understood to be the one who was seen as God through understanding. But the Father never appeared in any manner at all, as it is said in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

(Vers. 16.) The firstborn of all creation. He testifies that the Son was begotten before every creature, begotten and not created, in order to distinguish his birth from the making of creation. And to make this entirely clear, he adds:

Because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, or Dominions, or Principalities, or Powers; all things were created through him and in him. He signifies not only that Christ is magnificent and glorious because he was born before all things came to be, but also says that all things were created in him—that is, that all power belongs to him; and therefore all things proceed from him, since all things are made through him. This means that he is the head of the whole creation, because things began to exist in order that they might be through him.

The things made by him are therefore said to have been made through him because he was born for the purpose of making creation: that is, to make it in him and through him. For his birth does not benefit himself but us, because he did not need to be born, [Note: The Roman edition alone likewise reads, “who already existed.”] since he was already present in these things.

How does he become the one Son of God the Father? How does he himself know the things that are unbegotten and belong to God the Father? He was in God, having proceeded from God, in such a way that there was one God. Thus it comes about that there is neither diminution of the Father nor advancement of the Son in his birth.

And in order to convey more openly what and how great the Son’s power is, he shows what exists through him—namely Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers—so that it may be believed that absolutely nothing is less in him than in the Father.

(Vers. 17.) And he himself is before all things. He is before all things because he alone was born from God the Father, from the unbegotten substance of God. These things, however, subsisted through his power, which he possesses by generation from the Father; [Note: The Roman edition reads, “not because there is a shared substance between them.” Below, instead of “they subsist in him,” some manuscripts read, “they subsist for him.”] not because they share substance with him, but because they began from nothing at the will of God the Father, with the Son acting.

And all things subsist in him. They subsist in him because without him they are nothing. Unless they are subject to him, they will go astray in error and become liable, as it were, to destruction.

[Col. 0424B] (Vers. 18.) And he himself is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold the first place in all things. Christ is the head of the Church, provided that all, heavenly and earthly, think as one, so that they may be the Church—that is, of one faith. Otherwise, severed from the head of the entire body, that is, separated from their Creator, they rave in a kind of madness and vanity.

He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold the first place in all things. Since all things exist through him, they had to be restored through him after, through a certain negligence, they had become subject to decay; otherwise it would have been an insult to him if his work had been restored by another. Thus, just as he was born before all things, so he would again be first before all things through the resurrection of the dead, life having been restored to its former state.

For he was born before all things from God in order to create all that did not exist. But afterward he was born again, having assumed flesh from a virgin, in order to abolish the sin that had entered the world through the virgin Eve. Thus, having been born, he died and rose again, so that he might recreate afterward the things he had first made, since through error they had become, as it were, dead; therefore he is always first and chief in all life.

(Vers. 19.) Because in him the Father was pleased to have all fullness dwell. The fullness is in him and remains in him, because he is always able to do all things, so that nothing is excluded that cannot be accomplished through him: that he might create, restore, raise up what had fallen, and give life to what had died.

Hence he says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26); and: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid., 21–22).

What could be more just than that he should give judgment to the one through whom he made these things? [Note: So the old edition and manuscripts; the Roman edition reads, “and that all fullness itself . . . should dwell in him”; and, “that is what we have said: that he has in himself what it means to be,” and so forth.] Thus all the fullness of divinity would dwell in him, in accordance with what we have said: that he possesses all power in himself. This means that he is perfect God; for whoever does not possess all these things is not God.

[Col. 0425A] (Vers. 20.) And through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “whether the things that are in the heights.”] This is what he mentioned above: that, in order to restore through him all the things he had made, when they had already begun to differ from one another through a certain error, and also from their author—for error still exists in the carnal heavens—he humbled him by clothing him in flesh, so that, having become human, he might show and teach how the things in the firmament and those above the earth could be reconciled to the Creator.

To bring this to perfection, he allowed himself to be killed for the sake of human beings, so that those whom he had taught among the beings above might not, after departing from here, be held by the second death. Thus his teaching might bear the fruit of the original creation, and all things made through him might live in him as in their author, as Peter confesses in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 3:15).

(Verses 21, 22.) And you, once alienated and enemies of his purposes in wicked works, but now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, must be presented holy, immaculate, and blameless in his sight. He recalls what a great gift of God toward the nations this is, in order to show that they are debtors—and indeed very great debtors—in thanksgiving to God. Though they were enemies of his purposes, by which he had decided to visit the human race through his servant Moses, they did not receive his teaching and authority. Devoted to their idols, or rather to wicked works, they worshiped the works they themselves had made.

But the mercy and providence of God sought them out, so that they might freely obtain the grace of God, returning to him with a clean conscience. Thus, when nothing of their former error was found in them on the day of judgment, they might be joined to their Creator, who, in order to benefit the human race, became incarnate and was made human, so that in his flesh he might conquer death.

(Verses 23, 24.) If indeed you remain founded, established, and immovable in the hope of the Gospel that you heard, which has been preached in all creation under heaven. Of this I, Paul, became a minister; I now rejoice in sufferings for you and fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ for his body, which is the Church. He declares that he rejoices in the tribulations he suffers because he sees their progress in the faith of believers. For tribulation is not fruitless when it gains for life the one for whom he suffers.

He says that these sufferings are inflicted on Christ, whose teaching they persecute. Thus he both burdens the faithless with the guilt of their impiety and proclaims to the faithful the love of God, whose Son continues even now to suffer injuries for us.

Now, therefore, he wishes them to understand why he writes to them when he says: “If indeed you remain founded in the faith,” so that they may know that Christ’s passion benefits them if they remain in the faith they have received.

For this reason he declared from the beginning how great and infinite is the omnipotence of Christ’s majesty, in order to teach that hope must be placed in him alone: for all things belong to him, and nothing can live without him, neither in heaven nor on earth. He is before all things, and all things subsist in him, because he holds the first place in all things.

Thus, if anyone thinks that he ought to devote himself to one of the elements, or to angels, or to Powers, let him know that he is in error. For this one is the only Son of God, the head of every principality and beginning, whose Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world, beginning with Moses, who said to the Jews: “The Lord your God will raise up for you from among your brothers a prophet like me. You shall listen to him; for whoever does not listen to that prophet shall be exterminated from the people” (Deut. 18:15–16).

Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “Moses wrote about me” (John 5:46). Therefore this one alone must be heard and worshiped, and no one is to be compared with him, because the one who holds the head has the remaining part subject to him. For whoever humbles himself before those who are subject is wholly in error: because, not holding the head, he is a trunk from which the entire body is sustained unto life.

(Verses 25, 26.) Of this I became a minister according to the dispensation of God that was given to me for you, to fulfill the word of God in the mystery that was hidden from ages and generations. He confidently says that he was made a minister of the Gospel among the nations by God through Christ, so that the mystery begun by the Lord might be fulfilled through a suitable and effective servant—the mystery that had been unknown for ages.

(Verses 27, 28.) But now it has been revealed to his saints, to whom God desired to show what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the nations, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory, whom we proclaim. He asserts that the mystery hidden for ages has now been revealed, [Col. 0426C] that is, displayed in the time of the Apostles: namely, that the nations also were to be admitted to the faith of Christ without circumcision of the flesh, Christ having been promised to the Jews.

Previously, before the preaching of faith, the nations were commanded to be circumcised if they wished to approach the Law. Now, however, by the mercy of God, they were commanded to be received into the faith just as they were. The Jews considered it unworthy that Christ—in whom the hope of the Jews lay—should also make the nations participants in his glory.

(Vers. 29.) Admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ. For this I labor, contending according to his working, which works in me with power. He says that this is true wisdom: the wisdom found in the Lord’s discipline when Christ is recognized.

The Apostle testifies that he himself carries this out with great care, so that, instructing every person in this wisdom, he may present that person perfected to God in the understanding of Christ, so that he may grasp the mystery of the birth from God, the birth from Mary, and the whole of his work, heavenly and earthly.

He says that he has a struggle against the faithless in this matter, with signs of mighty works assisting him, so that through these unbelief may be overcome and restrained. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “the life of unbelief”; other, more numerous and better manuscripts read, “unbelief having been overcome.”] For whoever has dared to contradict him with a certain subtlety of diabolical cunning must yield, corrected by shame, before the power manifested.

267 ## CHAPTER TWO

(Verses 1, 2, 3.) For I want you to know how great a concern I have for you and for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh, so that their hearts may receive consolation, being instructed in love unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “of the mystery of God and the Father in Christ”; below, “of the sacrament of God and the Father.”]

He testifies that he is no less concerned for those whom he had not seen at all in the flesh than for those to whom he preached while present. Thus they might know that, because he had not seen them, they were loved by him with no less affection than the others with whom he was present. He wished to encourage their minds in love, so that through the epistle they might become ready and receive the knowledge of God’s mystery in Christ, recognizing that these are the riches of wisdom and knowledge: to recognize Christ as worthy of worship in the fullness of his divinity.

The whole mystery, therefore, of the sacrament of God is in Christ. For he is the one in whom every creature will perish unless it places its hope, so that all power may be in him. Whoever knows him may be considered to possess knowledge of all things that exist, and no other is to be sought for worship, because the power of all powers is in him; for they all receive from him. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “all possess from him what they possess.”]

Although he is one, he can do all things. Therefore he is also called the head of all, so that all things may appear to subsist through him. The treasures of wisdom and knowledge are therefore rightly said to be hidden in him.

For the whole principle of the knowledge of all creation, heavenly and earthly, must be in him who is the head of all those things—whether of angels, or of the sun, or of the moon, or of the stars, or of other things. All knowledge of them is in their author, so that whoever recognizes him seeks nothing further, neither wisdom nor power, because he has recognized the one in whom perfect power and perfect wisdom are found.

Whatever someone thinks he has found elsewhere, he will find fully and abundantly in him. For who was wiser than Solomon? Who was more prudent than Daniel? God gave them wisdom above others for this very reason: to make known to unbelievers that he is the author of all wisdom.

Finally, Nebuchadnezzar, admiring Daniel’s wisdom, says to him: “Truly your God is himself the living God, and the one who reveals mysteries” (Dan. 2:47). [Note: The same Roman edition reads, “He himself is the true God.”]

The fact that all wisdom and knowledge are in Christ is hidden from every unbeliever because they do not read astrology in the Gospels, geometry in the Apostle, or arithmetic and music in the prophets. These subjects are despised by our people for this reason: they do not pertain to salvation, but rather lead into error and turn people away from God. While they devote themselves to these argumentative investigations, they do not care for their souls.

For what wisdom is as true as knowing what benefits one and rejecting what harms one? It harms because it prevents the soul from caring for itself. Therefore, rightly, whoever recognizes Christ finds the treasure of wisdom and knowledge: for he has recognized what is useful to him.

[Col. 0428A] (Verses 4, 5.) I say this so that no one may deceive you with subtle speech. For although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order, [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and seeing the order of your conduct.”] and supplying what is lacking in the usefulness of your faith in Christ. He admonishes them lest their understanding be led astray in the conversations of wicked people and in the cunning of iniquity, because the wise men of the world strive by a certain art and by the minutiae of arguments to entangle simple minds, so that by reasoning about worldly things they may draw them away from the hope that is in Christ.

Therefore the Apostle says that he is present there in spirit, so that, keeping him in mind with reverence, they might avoid such people. For if the spirit of the prophet Elisha saw the fraud of Gehazi, who went to Naaman the Syrian to receive in Elisha’s name what had not been commanded him, and saw that Naaman, who was departing with a ready spirit, gave him more than had been requested (2 Kings 5:26), how much more could the Apostle see in spirit the things he had spoken! For grace was greater in the Apostles than in the prophets.

And in order to make them more ready concerning the evangelical tradition, he says that he rejoices in the ordered character of their conduct, so that, knowing what pleases God, they might become firmer in it and, having been made worthy to advance the usefulness of their faith, might learn its meaning.

(Verses 6, 7.) Therefore, just as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and confirmed in the faith, just as you were taught, [Note: The Roman edition reads, “abounding in it.”] walking in it with thanksgiving. He admonishes and exhorts them not to let their devotion diminish, to withdraw from the faith they had attained, or, having been overthrown by false stories, to receive Christ in a manner different from what they had learned.

For many corrupters of the faith were going about to seduce the simple, deceitfully and hypocritically announcing Christ. He urges them to avoid such people with the greatest care, so that, stable and firm upon the foundation of the Trinity, they might give abundant thanks for the mercy of God in hope of future things.

(Verses 8, 9.) See to it that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deceit, [Note: The same edition adds, “and empty seduction.”] according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ; because in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. He calls it earthly philosophy, by which those who desire to be considered wise in the world are commonly seduced.

It is composed of arguments and of certain subtle minutiae, as though it had investigated the principles of nature. It contains certain elements that are exhortations to a good life or lessons, sometimes arranged according to measurements, sometimes according to numbers, and sometimes according to the qualities and quantities of the elements.

Whoever falls into its arguments scarcely, and only rarely, escapes. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “Whoever falls into its arguments scarcely or never escapes.”] For he is detained by plausible causes and fabricated notions, judging nothing to be so true as what is observed and understood in the elements.

And because the things that exist in the present and are perceived by the eyes appear pleasant and delightful, they seduce some who, in despair of the future, think that spiritual reasoning should be despised and ridiculed. They assign all power to the stars, subject to carnal reasoning, so that they may not have to believe that heavy things can be lifted into heaven, or light things descend to earth, or that anything bodily can be generated without an admixture of material things. Thus they resist the power and providence of God.

For they know that many things are recorded in the ancient divine books of the Hebrews as having been done through Moses, which human reasoning cannot comprehend. In the same way, things are recorded in the new books as having been done by the Lord or through the Apostles, which carnal reasoning forbids people to believe.

He therefore calls this tradition or philosophy false and empty, because it was not ordered by the power of God but by the weakness of human reasoning, which confines God’s power within its own knowledge, so that he is not believed capable of doing anything other than what carnal reason allows.

For they assign a diversity of divinities to the individual elements for worship, so that they may bind the minds of the ignorant and prevent them from reaching out to the true God. For this reason he warns them to beware of this tradition, because it is a worshiper of the world, not of God, who is one. It does not lead to Christ but draws people away from Christ, in whom is the perfection of divinity.

For everything that the Father has, he gave to the Son, when he begot him bodily in the fullness of divinity. Since he himself is the head and creation is his body, whatever the heavenly creation is thought capable of doing is to be believed to exist wholly and fully in Christ, so that no one may think that anyone else is to be worshiped.

Whatever someone considers great in another, he will find greater in Christ, because all receive from him, as the members receive from the head. He himself, however, is always full.

(Vers. 10.) And you have been filled in him, who is the head of every Principality and Power. This signifies that more is given to believers than can be comprehended in the elements. For whoever is in Christ has been filled with the abundance of divinity, which the elements do not possess.

Finally, the Holy Spirit dwells in believers—something that could not be granted to the elements, because it was unworthy and incongruous that the invisible should dwell in visible substance, and the incorporeal in things that are perceptible to the senses. Let their worshipers hear this and come, and believe in Christ, so that they may become greater than those whom they now worship.

(Verses 11, 12.) In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism. In him you also rose together through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. Those are circumcised in Christ who, having cut away the worship of every human tradition, are joined to Christ—circumcised in heart, not in flesh; that is, serving in spirit, not in flesh. Thus they are converted from earthly things to heavenly things, from human things to divine things, and from error to truth, joined through love to their head and author.

They were buried with him in baptism; but they rose again through faith in the God of whom they believe that, following Christ’s example, he will raise them from the dead. For there the old human being is put off and the new is assumed; one dies to sins so as to live to righteousness; one renounces the elements so as to be joined to Christ, holding the pledge of the future resurrection in the example of the Savior, who rose from the dead.

He therefore admonishes them to persevere in renouncing the pomp and deceptions of Satan. For this reason Satan persuades people to worship the elements: he wishes to turn them away from God and make them participants in his apostasy. Since he cannot persuade them to worship under his own name—for that name itself is detested—he tries to fulfill his will under another’s name.

(Verses 13–15.) And when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, [Col. 0430B] forgiving us all trespasses, having erased the document that stood against us, the decree that was contrary to us; and he removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross; and, stripping the principalities and powers, he displayed them openly in authority, triumphing over them in him.

[Note: [Col. 0429D] Thus the old edition and manuscripts read, except that those copies prefer *of the decree . . . them in the same place*, whereas the more authoritative ones read, *the decree . . . them in it*. The Roman edition restored the passage as follows: *forgiving you all trespasses, having erased the document that was against us, in the decrees . . . and stripping principalities and powers, he displayed them openly, triumphing over them through himself.* [Col. 0430D]]

He says that the Gentiles were dead: first, because they refused to receive the Law, which was given as a testimony to the Creator and for the condemnation of vices; and then because, on account of the impiety of their sins, they were unworthy of life. Therefore he distinguished them from the Jews, as though they had been enemies of the one God. The Jews, however, living in confession of the one God, learn, when Christ comes, the mystery of God, which they were awaiting for their justification: so that in what had been withheld from them—for it is impossible to be without sin—they might receive forgiveness.

Therefore, after treating the case of the Gentiles, he introduces the Jews as well, saying, “forgiving us all trespasses,” so that after the particular case he might add the general one, because he forgave all trespasses to all. But since, as the Lord says, “To whom more has been forgiven, he ought to love more” (Luke 7:43), he therefore admonishes the Gentiles that, considering the causes of their evils and what sort of grace they received from God in Christ, they should be wholly devoted to the service of the one from whom they had been freed from a diverse punishment of death.

How, then, did he forgive us all trespasses? “By erasing,” he says, “the document that was hostile to us.” And what does “erasing” mean? He adds, saying, “And he removed it from the midst.” Thus he erased it when he removed it from the midst. And he removed it from the midst when, he says, he fastened it to the cross. To fasten it to the cross, he declared, means to strip the principalities and powers publicly [Col. 0430D] and to triumph over them in Christ.

These things, as they appear, are obscure, and therefore must be clarified with care. This is the protection of God, which the Apostle explains through the significance of various causes. For he recalls many things that were done so that the human race might attain forgiveness: not only that he might remit our personal trespasses, but also that he might remove that sin which arose from Adam’s transgression—which he called “the document in the decrees”—and which did not allow us to rise from the dead. For if he had not removed this also from the midst, those who had received forgiveness would, after departing from here, have been held there in the underworld.

Moreover, all trespasses were therefore forgiven so that they might rise from the dead. Since death comes from sin, when sin is removed there is a resurrection of the dead. This could in no way have happened unless he had fastened sin to the cross. For while the Savior, by not sinning, conquers sin, which held the human being liable, and, moreover, is killed by it though innocent, he thus crucified sin. For conquered sin is said to have been put to death: the cross is not the death of the Savior, but of sin. For when an innocent person is killed in this way, he makes guilty those by whom he is killed.

By “sin,” however, let us understand the principalities and powers, through whose activity the first Adam sinned. This name must be referred to its authors, whose death he signified by their being stripped. For their death is this: having been conquered by the Savior, they are put to death when they are stripped of the souls whom they held in captivity. They were made guilty because, while they held souls with this authority on the grounds that those souls had sinned, they themselves were found to be still greater sinners when they killed the one who had conquered them without sinning.

And so they were justly stripped, as he said, publicly—that is, on the cross—which means that they were openly triumphed over by God in Christ. For the one who is publicly conquered and whose spoils are displayed is triumphed over: he is shown prostrate before everyone, he who had insulted the others.

The “decree” of which he speaks is not what the pagans call fate. For they do not assert that fate is contrary to everyone: they say that some are made happy by it and others unhappy. This decree, he says, was contrary to everyone [Col. 0431C], for the sentence was adverse to all human beings.

(Verses 16–17.) Therefore let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or in regard to a festival, or new moons, or a sabbath: these things are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ’s.

Since every hope of life and confidence is in Christ, he commanded that we should be subject to no superstition or law. Therefore those who make a great noise, or whisper anything that does not pertain to faith in Christ, are to be despised; but we must follow only the one through whom death has been conquered and the resurrection of the dead restored.

For some of the Jews are accustomed to judge believers because they eat foods forbidden through Moses, although God made all things clean. The Jews, however, were judged unworthy to eat these things and were prohibited from them by those who were better. They also commonly reproach us because we disregard their festivals, or because we do not observe the beginnings of the months, which they call new moons; and especially because we do not keep the sabbath days, so that they may be spent in leisure and luxurious feasting—a practice that pertains more to offense than to grace.

All these things, however, are the body of Christ, because they are names of the elements according to their effects. Hence in the Gospel he says, “For the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath” (Matthew 12:8). Through him all things were given through Moses in such a way that they might be a shadow or figure of things to come, so that when the truth appeared, the figure would cease.

For just as, when the emperor is absent, his image has authority, but when he is present it does not, so these observances were to be kept in their proper time before the Lord’s coming, but in his presence they lack authority. Does someone acting in place of a lord rule while the lord himself is present? If the deputies of governors lose their authority when the governors are present, how much more must servants, when their lord is present, be seen to be subject to his service!

(Verses 18–19.) Let no one deceive you, wishing, in humility of mind and worship of angels, to exalt himself over what he sees vainly, puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast to that head from which the whole body, supplied and compacted through joints and connections, grows with the growth of God.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] The Roman edition reads: *in the things which he does not see . . . supplied and compacted through joints and connections.*]

What he earlier warned must be avoided under the name of philosophy, he now teaches more openly must be avoided by those who, devoting themselves to earthly wisdom, assert that the things which lie before the eyes or appear are to be worshiped. Thus souls held fast by the worship of these things are kept bound beneath the firmament, lest they stretch themselves beyond the firmament toward the higher heavens, to worship God, who is over all.

This is accomplished by the work of the enemy, so that he may always keep souls humbled upon the earth, where he knows that he himself will remain forever cast down from heaven by the just judgment of God, while pretending religion, although this is the greatest sacrilege.

For they are puffed up when they discern the motion of the stars, which he calls angels—not by divine authority, but by human superstition, which accomplishes nothing except harm—unwilling to hold the faith of Christ, who is the Creator and Lord of all. For all things have their origin from him; therefore they are also called his body, if indeed they acknowledge him.

Turning to him, they are rebuilt, joined together in his faith, with the Gospel supplying all as though they were members of the body in the love of Christ, so that they may bring increase to God. For when they return to the one whom they had abandoned through error, diminishing the riches of his possessions by denying that they belong to him, they bring increase to God, because they are acquired from those who had been lost.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] The Roman edition reads: *they return to God, having abandoned him through error, diminishing,* and so forth. [Col. 0432D]]

This concerns the pagans. Again, speaking of the Jews, he says that they too serve under the elements, not serve the elements.

(Verses 20.) If, then, you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though living in the world, do you still make decrees?

Everyone who is baptized in Christ dies to the world [Col. 0432D], for he renounces all the errors of superstition in order to worship only the faith of Christ. When the things that belong to natural justice are removed, the discipline given by God remains, through which one lives to God by the hope that is in Christ. But he dies to those things to which he had been subjected through error, while denying those whom he had presumed to be gods.

[Note: [Col. 0432D] All editions read, *whom he had presumed to be*; but we have restored the word *gods* from several manuscripts.]

Thus it happens that, through the hostility of renunciation, the human being and the worship of the elements are said to be mutually dead. For when he says “world,” he signifies the error of the flesh; everything that is seen is assigned to the flesh.

Hence the Apostle John also says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15)—that is, let us love neither the elements by which the world has been compacted, nor the errors invented by human tradition, but Christ alone, who died for us, so that he might associate us with his body, though we had been lost.

Those, therefore, who have been buried with Christ have died to the elements, so that they care for none of these things; for they have learned to hold fast to heavenly things, which can grant perpetual life. These things neither grant the present life nor permit the future things to be grasped.

But whoever, after baptism, doubts about certain matters, thinking that some things from the former practices are to be venerated, shows that he is living according to the elements, which he decides should be worshiped or hesitates to despise. Such a person will remain within the circles of the world, alienated from God, because, clothed in the old human being, he will not be able to pass beyond carnal things.

(Verses 21–22.) Do not touch, do not handle, [Note: [Col. 0433D] The Roman edition reads, *do not taste*, which things are all destined for corruption through use itself.] do not taste, do not handle—things that all lead to destruction and corruption through misuse—according to the precepts and teachings of human beings.

He prohibits them in every way from hoping in worldly things, because such hope is empty: they must not worship, assent to, or consider these things, since what they promise belongs to corruption. Their use and worship produce destruction, because the precepts and teachings are not of God but of human beings, in which there is vain hope. For human error devised these things against the Creator, so that, by prohibiting faith in the one God, it might introduce superstition concerning many gods.

(Verses 23.) These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in a pretense of religion and humility of mind, for the affliction of the body, but not with any honor for the satisfying and care of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] The same Roman edition reads: *in the observance of religion and humility of heart.*]

This is why they think that they possess the reasoning of wisdom: they apply the name of religion to human tradition, so that it may be called religion although it is sacrilege. For whatever is against the author is devised with a sacrilegious mind.

Thus he fabricates a name so that he may assert false things as true, and he humbles human minds upon the earth, lest they raise themselves toward heavenly things. Or, worshiping earthly things, they fall away from the heavenly realms above and harm the body, whose head is Christ, according to the structure of the original order.

For, weighed down by this, they could not be joined upward to their head, so as to be restored in him and honored when made whole. Instead, as though truncated at the first part of the body, they give themselves wholly to the world in order to satisfy the perception of the flesh.

For the nourishment of carnal perception is human tradition, which says that what the providence of the flesh has handed down is sufficient.

[Note: [Col. 0434D] The Roman edition reads *alone, prudence teaches*; but below it presents, together with the other editions and several manuscripts, *every bodily birth*, whereas some manuscripts read *human bodily birth*.]

It appears to possess the reasoning of wisdom according to the flesh, because every bodily birth is from the elements. Accordingly, they say that it is not unfitting to incline toward those things by whose governance the human race is ruled, so that it may subject itself to what it sees as the brightest things in the world. Nor, they say, should spiritual things be sought, because permission has been granted to use these alone as guides. By this reasoning they neglect the author.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0434A]

(Verses 1.) Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.

He asserts that those who think upon heavenly things have risen with Christ in baptism—where Christ’s seat is, where God the Father has granted his Son the right hand, so that he may reign and judge; for it is not fitting for a judge to sit on the left.

The resurrection, however, has two forms: first, that the soul rises from the earth to the heavens; then, after receiving the body, that it rises, caught up to meet Christ.

(Verses 2.) Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth.

He exhorts us to seek the heavenly realms above, which are the dwellings of the Eternal, and to disregard all those things that are in the firmament and beneath the firmament [Col. 0434B]. For whoever occupies himself with these superstitions will suffer hindrance; he will not be able to transcend the things to which he has bowed as though to lords.

(Verses 3.) For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

According to the world’s understanding, Christ appears dead, as do his disciples, although it is evident that he lives with all these. Therefore the life of Christ and of his followers is hidden from the carnal and worldly in God, outside the world, in his heavenly kingdom, in which they live.

(Verses 4.) When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

Christ is our life, because we read in the Acts of the Apostles that he is the author of life, who is not believed by the faithless to be the coming judge (Acts 3:15). But when he comes in heavenly power and is seen to be what was in no way believed, then those also who believed in him will appear with him. It will be revealed to all unbelief that he lives with his own in glory.

This consolation produces confidence in hope, so that, secure concerning the future life, we may put everything else aside and follow Christ.

(Verses 5.) Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols.

Since he signifies in the Epistle to the Romans that all sins together constitute a body (Romans 6:6), he now, in describing individual offenses, calls them members, so that after receiving and preserving the evangelical teaching from the fullness of the Savior, they might devote themselves to a good life, abstaining from every disgrace and evil desire, lest they lose the fruit of divine knowledge.

For it is greatly harmful to know the truth and not affirm it by pursuing it in one’s deeds. Hence the Lord also says among other things: “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not obey him will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

He compares greed with idolatry so as to demonstrate that nothing is more wicked than it. Under one name he designates two exceedingly evil and impious kinds of conduct, which he urges us by every means to avoid. For idolatry is the first and most serious crime [Col. 0435A]. What is more harmful and more disastrous than attributing the honor due to God the Creator to pieces of wood and stone or to other metals, when even they do not tolerate a servant being called by the name of his master, whom not nature but a certain condition subjects to slavery?

The other crime is greed—not different in wickedness, but different in name. Therefore he says to Timothy: “For greed is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). It is capable of every offense, seeking to fulfill the impossible desire of its appetite, always drinking and always thirsting.

He therefore not without reason displays both evils under one name. For they are nearly fulfilled by one and the same action. Just as idolatry attempts to take glory away from the one God, lest he alone possess the name of divinity, which belongs peculiarly to him and is worthy of him alone, so greed extends itself even against God, so that, if it could happen, one person alone might appropriate his creature, which God made common to all.

Therefore God says through the prophet: “The gold is mine, and the silver is mine” (Haggai 2:9). Both evils, then, are enemies of God; both deny God what belongs to him.

(Verses 6.) On account of these things the wrath of God is coming.

He says that the judgment of God will come on account of the evils mentioned, so that vengeance may be taken upon those who, having despised God and his Law, preferred to follow what had been forbidden.

(Verses 7.) In these things you also once walked, when you were living in them.

He does not conceal how great a benefit the grace of God through Jesus Christ bestowed upon them, so that they may rejoice that they escaped the wrath that is suddenly to come upon the unbelievers of the whole earth, and may present themselves in such a way that they can obey the commands of the one by whom they have been freed from the second death.

(Verses 8–11.) But now you too must put away all these things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy. Let no filthy speech proceed from your mouth. Do not lie to one another. Strip off the old human being with his deeds, and put on the new, who is renewed [Note: [Col. 0435D] After *in knowledge*, some manuscripts, together with the commonly received Bibles, add τὸ Θεοῦ, “of God”; but this word is shown to be superfluous both by the authority of many sacred copies and by this very passage.] in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him. Here there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; but Christ is all and in all.

He now prohibits those things that appear to be lesser sins, lest, because he earlier commanded the graver sins to be put to death, they should think that these may be admitted, or that, as though they were not dangerous, they need not be avoided.

At the same time he wishes them, having stripped off the old human being—that is, being seen to be undefiled both in word and in deed—and having become new in Christ through knowledge of the truth, which was formerly hidden but has now been revealed to believers through the new law, to become like the image of the one who created them.

This image is to be understood in a life of good conduct, as he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “As we have borne the image of the one who is from the earth, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49).

He, therefore, is the Creator of the human being, whose image he commands us to bear in holiness and good works, which proceed from knowledge of the Son of God. For no one can have a good and pure life unless he has someone before whom he may exhibit it, from whom he may expect, if not a reward, at least praise. But with God both praise and reward are hoped for, because God’s justice does not permit the one who has conquered the vices of the flesh to go without a crown.

In this knowledge, therefore, no one is excluded as unworthy, as though he did not deserve to approach the faith of Christ. For all who approach become one: they are erased with respect to what they were and inscribed with respect to what they have begun to be. Since they share one faith, they also share one merit in that very faith, so that those whom faith joins cannot be distinguished on account of their different nature, nation, or condition.

For Christ is all and in all these people. Since they are all his members, Christ is all, so that, while their confession of hope in him is one, Christ is in all. Thus they are all his body, so that their confession and nature correspond.

This image, which he says is created through knowledge of the Savior, is nevertheless one thing, and the image according to which the first human being was made is another. This image exists even in a woman when she acknowledges the one who created her and, obeying his will, abstains from a disgraceful life and perverse conduct. But that image exists only in the man, as he likewise says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7).

But if the woman also did not cover her head, she too would be the image of God. Yet it was unfitting that one made subject to the man should be called the image of God. For in Genesis he likewise says: “And God made the human being; in the image of God he made him” (Genesis 1:27), so that, just as God is one, one human being might be made by him; and just as all things are from the one God, so the whole human race might be from one human being upon the face of the whole earth.

One, therefore, made one, so that the one might bear the image of his unity. And in the man and woman alike there is a likeness of the mystery of the Father and the Son.

He nevertheless distinguished the barbarian from the Scythian, just as the slave from the free—not in Christ, in whom all are one, but in the savagery of their character and the ferocity of their nation. He wished these people to be understood as worse than barbarians before they believed, although the books of the Greeks praise their justice, which they followed under nature’s guidance.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] The Roman edition reads: *So great was theft regarded as a sin among them that the Greeks, who with great diligence . . .* [Col. 0436D] Since they were later degenerating, however, they began to be more blameworthy than they had previously been praiseworthy.]

Indeed, the Greeks praise them for having naturally grasped the paths of justice that the Greeks investigated with great diligence and instruction. But how all things degenerate! Later they began to be more blameworthy than they had previously been praiseworthy.

After their women began to live according to the law of men—women whom, they say, were originally called Amazons, because they subjected all Asia contrary to nature—the men too became, as it were, rabid like dogs: savage, wild, uncultivated, more than barbarian, changed to such an extent that they were trained to eat human flesh.

What wonder, when the Romans themselves were also once very different from what they are now? Among their women, too, the use of wine was unknown for the sake of chastity, just as the use of water is now. So strongly did the authority of discipline prevail that a subordinate vessel did not do what it wished.

(Verses 12–13.) Therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness of mind, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving each other, if anyone has a complaint against anyone; just as Christ forgave you, so also do you.

He urges them to do these things so that they may gain profit, for these things establish merit before God. Abstaining from sins is produced by fear: one is afraid that, by doing evil, one may be subjected to punishments. But the things he now urges them to do concern the advancement of merit; they arise from the will, not from necessity.

Therefore, whoever abstains from unlawful things has praise; but whoever restrains himself from lawful things has both praise and reward.

(Verses 14–15.) And above all these things have love, which is the bond of unity; and let the peace of God rejoice in your hearts, in which you were also called in one body; and be grateful.

Because love is greater than all things, he urges them to devote themselves especially to it. For then all the things he commanded above to be observed can be brought to the fulfillment of their rewards, if they walk the path of the Law under the guidance of love. One who does something out of love acts with the whole mind.

There is no hypocrisy or pretense in love. Therefore the Apostle John says: “There is no fear in love. For the one who fears is not perfect: perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Hence the Lord also prefers to be loved rather than feared.

This is the love that embraces unity; this is what makes all people one body; this is what possesses true peace, which it preserves with a pure heart. Peace can exist without love, but love always carries peace with it.

(Verses 16.) Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.

He urges them always to meditate on things that sound forth Christ; to keep in their hearts things that always give thanks to God the Father, so that a melodious voice may serve him, the psalm praise him, and the hymn exalt him. And let this be known only to him who sees what is hidden in the mind, from whom reward is hoped for.

He commanded that singing be done to him in the heart, lest it be done for human approval and the fruit be lost.

(Verses 17.) And whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

Since above he commanded that God be praised in the heart and thanks be given to him, he now urges that the name of the Lord Jesus be praised and exalted both in word and in deed, throughout our entire conduct. When our words are free from reproach and our deeds are good, the Lord Jesus is magnified, whose teaching makes his disciples blameless.

Then we truly give thanks to God through him, if we preserve the measure of his commands.

(Verses 18.) Women, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

Thus he commanded that women should be subject to their husbands, as God commanded, saying among other things to the woman: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16), so that by this same custom and discipline she may fear her husband as her lord, from whom she began to exist.

(Verses 19.) Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them.

He softens the strictness of the law governing men, lest anyone, because of the power by which he prevails, be excessive in ruling over his wife. He ought to consider affection, because the woman is his flesh, lest by humiliating her too much he provoke her and she conceive hostile thoughts.

(Verses 20.) Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to God.

Nothing else can please God except what is just and pious. Children can have God favorable toward them if they render their parents the honor that is due, being ready to serve them but reluctant to despise them, knowing that children ought never to plot against their parents.

[Note: [Col. 0437D] Erasmus and Gill, in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, read: *ought not to behave insolently*.]

(Verses 21.) Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, lest they become discouraged.

He commands fathers to be moderate toward their children, lest, constrained by them, they offend against them and thereby offend God, which they do not wish. For anger is an inconsiderate thing, to such an extent that the angry person sometimes spares not even himself.

Fathers should remember that they themselves were once children; children, however, should consider that they will become fathers. Thus, with the judgment of both sides equally balanced, children will be subject and fathers moderate.

(Verses 22.) Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, serving not merely for appearance, as those who please human beings, but in simplicity of heart, fearing the Lord.

For God cannot be served in any other way than with a pure heart, since he sees what is hidden in souls. Thus he also commands that human beings should be served.

Whoever serves merely for appearance does one thing in secret; but whoever serves from the heart is the same outwardly as inwardly. If he is faithful in this service, he will deserve the Lord’s favor, because he himself said: “The one who is faithful in what is least is also faithful in what is much” (Luke 16:10).

For if he is not faithful to the one who judges at present—

[Note: [Col. 0438D] Some manuscripts read: *who judges for the present*.]

—how will he be able to show faithfulness to the one whom he hears will judge after death? Therefore he wishes the slave to be just and obedient in the matter of his earthly master, so that he may also be faithful and obedient in the matters of God.

For if he is capable in the present life, where he knows that there are no rewards except corruptible ones, how much more eager will he be in devotion to God, whom he knows will give immortal rewards to the faithful!

(Verses 23–25.) Whatever you do, work from the heart, as for the Lord and not for human beings, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance of the Lord Christ, whom you serve. For whoever acts unjustly will receive what he has done unjustly, and there is no partiality with God.

To make them ready in obedience and faith, he promises that they will receive from God in the kingdom of Christ the reward of their good works. To make this approved and acceptable, he wishes them to obey as they would the Lord, from whom they expect their reward.

But if a slave acts unjustly, he will offend not only a human being but also God, whom he has despised by committing fraud against his earthly master. If he acts well, he will not be regarded by God as merely a human being’s slave, as though he were inferior; rather, he will be rewarded as free among human beings but as Christ’s slave—a name of dignity.

## CHAPTER IV

(Verses 1.) Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and equitable, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

So that earthly masters may not be lifted up by pride, presuming upon their mastery, he moderates and restrains their minds, so that, after considering the human race, they may recognize that God the Creator made all people free, not slaves and free persons.

But this has come about through the world’s injustice: when one person invades another’s territory, he then leads free people into captivity. Hence the ancients called them *manu capti*, “captured by the hand,” and from this, *mancipia*, slaves.

This accident and condition is still visible today: some are redeemed, while others remain slaves. But before God the slave is the one who has sinned (John 8:34). Thus, because of sin, Ham heard that he was a slave: “Cursed is the boy Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers” (Genesis 9:25).

The ancients agreed with this judgment [Col. 0439C], to the extent that they defined all wise people as free and all foolish people as slaves. For the wise person abstains from sins, so that the one who follows what is right is free; but the slave is the one who, through the imprudence of folly, subjects himself to sin.

Thus Ham was called a slave because of his folly: foolishly, he laughed at his father’s nakedness. He therefore shows masters that they are not truly masters but masters only as an image or likeness; they are masters of bodies, not of souls.

For the invisible God alone, the Lord and Creator of all things, rules over bodies as well as souls. Considering this, therefore, let them demand just services from their slaves—such services, certainly, as they themselves wish to be required to render by the common Lord.

For although they do not serve God as is fitting, while they do not deny that he has power over all things and that his daily gifts are supplied for human use through the ministry of creation, they demand such burdensome services from their equals—not to say their brothers—that they cannot be endured. They do not consider that they themselves, whether they wish it or not, are slaves; and let them see what their merit is.

(Verses 2–4.) Persevere in prayer, keeping watch in it with thanksgiving; praying also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also bound, so that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak.

He shows that those who are prudent concerning the mystery of the Lord Christ—

[Note: [Col. 0439D] The words *and cautious*, restored from the manuscripts of Remigius, Laudianus, and Vallensis, are found here.]

—and cautious in avoiding the vices of sins must persevere in prayer, so that they may grow in merit as the adversary’s temptations fail.

He considers them worthy to such an extent that he judges that they can also assist him by their prayers in boldly asserting the Gospel, for the manifestation of which he had received his commission.

(Verses 5–6.) Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be seasoned with the salt of grace, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.

Since it is necessary for us to walk among unbelievers and to engage in conversation for the sake of ordinary worldly life, this is what he admonishes: our conduct itself must be accompanied by wisdom because of the scandal of the Gentiles, lest they receive through us an occasion for blasphemy and be stirred up to persecution.

For what need is there to speak with someone whom you know to be unmanageable and stubborn-minded, ready to offer insult? Therefore he gives this instruction: at the appropriate place and time, under the guidance of modesty, words of religion should be brought forth; or, if such a person is present in the midst, one should remain silent.

One must act differently with the powerful of the world, differently with those of ordinary status, and differently with the humble. Again, one must act differently with the gentle and differently with the irritable, to whom one ought to yield. This is what it means to redeem the time.

For when you yield to one who lies in wait for the words of the Lord and rages against the boldness of the moment, you gain the injuries of the hostile moment. If the head—that is, the king—assents to the body, then there is freedom to speak the words of God with gentleness, so that they may be provoked to goodness.

But to those who make a disturbance and are eager for abuse, one must always yield; for you conquer while you yield.

[Col. 0440C] (Verses 7–9.) Tychicus, the beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow slave in the Lord, will make known to you everything concerning me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn what is happening among you and console your hearts, together with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is happening here.

He says that he sent these brothers so that each might learn from the other what was being done. Although above he says that he is spiritually present with them and sees what they are doing, messengers are nevertheless necessary.

For someone becomes more concerned when he sees a person coming to examine his conduct. He is more afraid if he suspects that what he is doing is being observed. For although God sees everything and we know that everything is known to him, because we do not see ourselves being seen by him, we do contrary things.

### (Verses 10, 11)

Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, receive him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are from the circumcision. These alone are my fellow workers for the kingdom of God; they have been a consolation to me.

Here Aristarchus appears to be a man of good conduct and merit, since by his devotion to the Lord he is designated a participant in and companion of the Apostle’s labors. In order to commend Mark, he does not conceal his relationship, so that, when he is learned to be related to the praiseworthy man Barnabas, he may be held in honor. He also adds Jesus, whom he says is called by the name Justus. He bears witness to these alone because they, being from the circumcision, were a help to him, agreeing with and sharing his judgment: namely, that they should preach that circumcision ought no longer to be practiced. Therefore he calls them his companions in the kingdom of God. But to preach that one must be circumcised, observe Sabbaths and keep new moons is not spiritual but earthly.

### (Verse 12)

Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, greets you. He makes the letter dearer to them when he bears witness to one who is from among them. He is always concerned for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and fully accomplished in every will of God. He testifies that he desires for them such things as are conducive to salvation, so that he may show that the man who is their fellow citizen and especially dear to them through the affection of their common bond shares in his devotion for their advancement.

[Note: Codex Laud., “a participant in his defense.”]

### (Verse 13)

For I bear him witness that he has much labor for you and for those who are in Laodicea and Hierapolis. In order to make them concerned for their salvation, he shows how great another’s vigilance is on their behalf; for a person becomes more concerned through shame when he sees another laboring in his cause.

### (Verse 14)

Luke the beloved physician greets you, and Demas. Luke was truly beloved by the Apostle, because, setting everything else aside, he always followed the Apostle. He is also said to have written the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

### (Verse 15)

Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nympha and her household church. Since he was similarly concerned for those who are in Laodicea, he reminds them in the letter to greet these people, considering Nympha especially dear, and he greets her household as well. For she appears to have been so devoted that her entire household was marked with the sign of the cross.

### (Verse 16)

And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you yourselves read the one that is from Laodicea.
