Since the Apostle’s instructions are general, and his letters were written for the benefit of all the churches, he therefore commands that this letter also be read to the Laodiceans, so that through it they might learn what they ought to do; and he instructs the Colossians to read the letter from Laodicea, in accordance with the meaning stated above.

### (Verse 17)

And say to Archippus: “See to the ministry that you received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.” Through the Colossians themselves he admonishes their leader to be concerned for their salvation. And because the letter is written solely for the sake of the congregation, it was not addressed to their ruler but to the church. After Epaphras, who instructed them, this man received responsibility for governing their church.

### (Verse 18)

This greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. Remember my chains. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. He says that he confirms the letter by subscribing it with his own hand, reminding them to keep in mind the sufferings he endured for the salvation of the Gentiles, so that they might conduct themselves in such a way that he would not regret suffering injuries on their behalf.

[Col. 0441]

## IN THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0441C]

In order, by the example of these people—that is, the Thessalonians—to encourage others toward growth in faith, he praises them because, remaining in the grace they had received, they increased toward the reward promised them by pursuing better things. He exhorts them, however, to strive toward perfection, so that the dignity they had acquired through their virtues might encourage the rest. For they had drunk in so great a spirit of faith that, in hope of things to come, they endured with devoted hearts the persecutions inflicted upon them by their fellow citizens, the Macedonians, for the name of Christ. Thus, in order to record in writing their merit and his own joy at their progress, he writes to them as follows:

## CHAPTER ONE

### (Verse 1)

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace.

[Col. 0441D] 277

[Note: Amerbach’s edition and quite a few manuscripts contain the names of the bishops in the letter.]

The letter contains the names of three bishops, but its meaning and wording belong to the Apostle alone. Since they rejoice together in the joy of the Thessalonians’ progress, the letter is written to the congregation with their agreement, wishing them peace and grace in the exaltation of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

### (Verses 2, 3)

We give thanks to God always for all of you, remembering you in our prayers without ceasing, mindful of your work of faith and labor of love, and of your expectation of our Lord Jesus Christ before our God and Father.

Since all good things come from God, they first give thanks to him for the Thessalonians’ progress. He deemed them worthy not only to give his gift to people subject to sin, but also to adopt them as sons, at the same time helping them endure every hardship so that they might become more worthy. Therefore they say that they remember them in their prayers, because they were increasing in the work of faith beyond the other churches, so that by God’s will they might complete the work they had begun, ready in their devotion to love and patience, and in hope of the Lord’s coming before God, who deigned to incarnate his Son for human salvation.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “and of the coming of faith,” and so forth.]

For it is pleasing to God if one makes progress in Christ.

### (Verses 4, 5)

Knowing, brothers beloved by God, your election, because our gospel came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in great fullness, just as you know what kind of people we were among you for your sake.

They indicate that they were humble among the Thessalonians, in order to give them an example of gentleness—not that there was any lack of great things that could urge them toward faith, since the strength of evangelical teaching was supplied by the power of signs and wonders, in the Holy Spirit—that is, not in an apparition but in the truth of fullness. Thus no need lacked assistance, but grace appeared abundantly both in teaching and conduct and in the healing of the sick. The perfect work of the Holy Spirit thus appeared in the churches of the Thessalonians, so that, seeing themselves inferior in nothing to the churches of the Jews, they might rejoice in the gift of God, who had deemed them worthy to become participants in the promise made to Abraham.

### (Verses 6, 7)

And you became imitators of us and of the Lord himself, receiving the word amid great affliction with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia.

Eager for belief, they endured with confidence in things to come the insults and injuries they suffered from their fellow citizens. Hence they are called imitators of the apostles and of the Lord himself: the Lord also suffered the same things from the Jews, and the apostles, following the faith of God, endured persecutions, rejoicing because they had been considered worthy to suffer insults for the Lord’s name (Acts 5:21), knowing that great rewards had been promised for these things. For a servant is shown to be worthy when, out of love for his master, he affronts his master’s enemies. Remembering this, they rejoiced in the hope of the promise amid affliction. Thus it is a great encouragement to progress when he says that they had become like Christ and the apostles, to provide an example to the other believers in those places where their reputation was spreading.

### (Verse 8)

For the word of the Lord has been proclaimed from you not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone forth everywhere.

This is like what he says to the Romans: “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Romans 1:8). But in this case there is something more, because not only their faith but also the work of their faith reached every place.

### (Verses 9, 10)

So that we have no need to say anything. For they themselves report concerning us what kind of entrance we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who rescued us from the coming wrath.

They say that the report of their entrance and of the Thessalonians’ conduct, together with the preaching of the Gospel, had traveled so widely that it was unnecessary to relate these things; for it is superfluous to speak of what is known. It had reached everyone in the surrounding regions, so that they also reported to others with what devotion the Thessalonians had received the apostles. And because they had been ready for everything they had heard from the apostles, they abandoned dead gods and awaited Christ from heaven. They had heard that he had died for the sake of human salvation, risen after conquering death, and been taken with his flesh into heaven by means of a ministering cloud, to the confusion of the wise men of the world. For, after considering worldly matters, these men think that the nature of flesh, being heavy, cannot be raised into heaven. The Holy Spirit brings this about in order that those wise men born of the earth may be put to shame.

278

## CHAPTER TWO

### (Verses 1, 2)

For you yourselves know, brothers, that our entrance among you was not empty; but after suffering much and being treated shamefully, as you know, at Philippi, we spoke to you the gospel of God with bold freedom in our God amid great struggle.

He suffered the affliction he now recalls (Acts 16:16 and following) at Philippi with Silas, because of the pythonic spirit he had driven out of the girl, as has already been said in its proper place. He did not yield to that affliction but proved stronger, daring to preach and not fearing to speak, certainly in hope of the promised reward. Thus they too might be secure amid persecutions, rejoicing because of the future recompense. He therefore says that this is the mark of a devoted and faithful preacher: that he does not fear to speak the word of God in affliction. He indicates that the one who, overcome by present terror, fears to preach is empty. For one who is secure in the promised hope does not yield, so that he may be crowned.

### (Verses 3, 4)

For our exhortation did not arise from deceit, impurity, or an idol, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak—not as pleasing human beings, but God, who tests our hearts.

He says this because of the false apostles, who preached deceitfully and fraudulently, without being sent, in order to lead the Gentiles around to serve the law of works. But this man proves in many ways that he was chosen and sent to preach: he was found stronger in afflictions and blameless in conduct, so that there was nothing in him that appeared less worthy of God, with signs following. Some preached Christ for the sake of profit, serving human favor; they were more lax in their rebukes, since they had no authority, and weak in tribulation, because their word did not arise from the heart but from deceit. For anyone who does something without hope gives way when tribulation arises.

### (Verse 5)

For we never lived among you with words of flattery, as you know, nor with an occasion for greed. God is witness.

Now he explains what he indicated above when he says, “not with an occasion for greed,” calling God as witness. He did this from the heart, not in hypocrisy, as though he were despising small offerings so that perhaps larger ones might be presented. Thus he also confronts them, since they knew and recognized that he had flattered no one. For the false apostles desired that an occasion for greed be given them, so that, taking advantage of the opportunity when they saw the true apostles accepting everything that was brought to them, they themselves might plunder simpler people without provoking envy.

### (Verses 6, 7)

Nor did we seek glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although we could have been a burden to you, as apostles of Christ.

[Note: The old edition reads “to be honored”; the Roman edition, “to be held in honor”; the manuscripts, and Gill in the margin, more appropriately read “to be a burden.”]

He weighs the case of the false apostles so heavily that he says he refused, although he was permitted to demand services, in order to restrain those who had neither means nor shame and nevertheless demanded honor for themselves. They wished to commend themselves rather than God’s teaching. But the Apostle, who sought glory not in the present but in the future, made himself humble so that God’s preaching might be exalted.

### (Verse 8)

But we were gentle among you, as a nurse cherishes her own children. So, being affectionately desirous of you, we were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own lives, because you had become very dear to us.

He shows that he had such affection for them—and because it was genuine, he wants it to appear proven by deeds more than by words, since deceit can lie hidden in words—that, stirred by these exhortations, the apostles might have their whole disposition in love.

### (Verse 9)

For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: working night and day so that we would not burden any of you.

This is what he says in the Acts of the Apostles: “All the necessities for me and those who are with me, these hands have supplied through labor.” Hence in another letter also he says: “Let the one who does not work not eat.” This too is directed against the false apostles, who pretended to be preachers while eating without working. Thus, in order to provide an example of how Christian life should be governed and to expose impostors, he devoted himself to human labor, eclipsing the false apostles. Moreover, those who devote themselves to work turn away from evil thoughts, occupying their minds and keeping themselves from dangers.

### (Verses 10, 11, 12)

You are witnesses, and God also, of how holy, righteous, and blameless our conduct was among you who believe. As you know, we treated each one of you as a father treats his children, exhorting, consoling, and charging you to walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory.

These things are clear. He reminds them how they came to believe when he preached, what kind of man they had experienced him to be, and what instructions he had given them, so that they might become worthy of God, who called them from earth to heaven in order to awaken their joy.

279

### (Verse 13)

And for this reason we also give thanks to God without ceasing: that when you received from us the word of the message of God, you accepted it not as the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God, which is at work in you who believe.

They give thanks to God, who opened their understanding to receive his Gospel. For the glory of preachers lies in this: when their hearers readily believe. They received the word with such devotion that they showed that they understood it to be God’s teaching.

### (Verses 14, 15, 16)

For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your fellow citizens as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, and do not please God and are hostile to all people. They prevent us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby continually filling up their sins. But wrath has overtaken them at last.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and you from your fellow citizens.”]

He complains of the impiety and unbelief of the distrustful Jews, who are enemies not only of their own salvation but also of that of others, preventing them from believing and being saved. They have been murderers from the beginning; for they ought at least to have spared the common Lord, since they did not spare his fellow servants and those appointed over them. Thus their sins are filled up, to such an extent that they may never deserve to obtain mercy. Therefore he says that the Thessalonians suffered the same things from their fellow citizens, imitating the patience of the saints and of our Lord Jesus Christ. He introduces the Jews as the perpetrators of this crime, so that both the great glory of those who suffer for the Lord’s name and the vengeance prepared for the hostile and faithless may be recognized.

### (Verses 17, 18)

But we, brothers, having been separated from you for a short time—in person, not in heart—have hastened all the more eagerly to see your face, with great desire. Therefore we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, both once and again—but Satan hindered us.

They say that they were separated from them not in spirit but in body. Love is neither divided nor separated; nevertheless, for the sake of greater instruction, they say that they desire to see their face. For in divine matters human powers of understanding fail to grasp what can be said; indeed, a single day is not enough for writing down what can be brought forth in one hour. Not to mention that some matters of our religion are mystical and, because of carnal perceptions, ought not easily to be made public lest offense be caused. For not everything should be said to everyone; what is said must be measured according to each person’s capacity—one way for the inexperienced, another for those firmly established. For this reason the bodily presence of the teacher is required, because in this way the truth of love is perfected. Although love is not divided, bodily absence produces longing; indeed, the will is fulfilled by a kiss and an embrace of the spirits.

He asserts that Satan was an obstacle to this, for Satan also stretched out hostile hands against the apostles so that the truth might not be disclosed to human beings. He stirred the minds of the faithless so that they would hold the apostles with blows and chains, preventing them from speaking the word of God. For the leaders of the Jews said to the apostles: “Did we not strictly command you not to speak in that man’s name, Jesus?” (Acts 5:40). But because what is not from God cannot stand, Satan’s obstacles are dissolved.

### (Verses 19, 20)

For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? For you are our glory and joy.

It is clear that the perfection of disciples is the joy and crown of their teacher. These are the people who will bring forth the fruits of their own labors. For the fruit of the teacher is an obedient disciple, whose good conduct advances the teacher, allowing him to reap the fruit of his labor. The disciple’s labor in a good work gives a crown to the teacher, with Christ as judge.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0447A]

### (Verses 1–4)

Therefore, when we could no longer bear it, we thought it best to be left alone at Athens, and we sent Timothy, our brother and fellow worker for God in the gospel of Christ, to strengthen you and to exhort you concerning your faith, so that no one might be shaken by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this; indeed, when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were going to suffer affliction, as happened, and as you know.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “that you were going to suffer affliction.”]

He has explained the causes of the longing mentioned above. They wanted to be present among the Thessalonians in order to strengthen their minds, so that no one would be scandalized by the apostles’ afflictions, supposing that those who performed such great signs could at some point become weak—so humbled as to be subjected to blows and chains.

[Col. 0447B] To excuse this circumstance, he testifies that Timothy was sent as a suitable teacher, one who could show that Christians’ merits increase when they give thanks for suffering on the Lord’s behalf, from whom they await the reward for this. At the same time, Timothy could pour out prayers to God that they might remain steadfast. They had foretold that they would suffer this persecution so that, by declaring beforehand their knowledge of what was to happen, they might show that they could escape and avoid these injuries. But because great hope lies in such things, he says that they willingly endure what has been inflicted.

### (Verse 5)

For this reason, when I could bear it no longer, I sent him in order to learn about your faith, lest somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor should prove fruitless.

He says this because of certain people who could have been seduced by Satan’s cunning. In every congregation there is a firm part and a weak part, and he was concerned for the latter, lest he lose the fruit of their belief. Since he could no longer endure being ignorant of what was more certainly happening among them, he sent Timothy, the bishop he had appointed, through whom he could learn the truth.

### (Verses 6, 7, 8)

But now that Timothy has come to us from you and has announced to us your faith and love, and that you always have a good remembrance of us, desiring to see us, just as we also desire to see you, for this reason, brothers, we have been comforted concerning you in all our necessity and affliction through your faith; for now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord.

He has explained why he writes to them with such an eager speech. When the messenger came and declared the steadfastness of their devotion in faith and love for the Apostle, he was made joyful by their common harmony and wrote to them, secure in the fruit of their faith and good conduct.

### (Verses 9, 10)

For what thanksgiving can we render to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God, praying most abundantly night and day that we may see your face and supply what is lacking in your faith?

He says that nothing is worthy enough to serve as adequate repayment for the salvation acquired by the Gentiles. And since they had advanced through perseverance in faith and through the practice of a better life, he desires all the more to see them, so that they may learn the things that pertain to their perfection—namely, the mysteries of spiritual realities, which ought not easily to be made public—so that they might know who and how immense is the one whom they hoped would be their judge.

For it is one thing to receive faith and another to receive an exposition of faith. One discussion concerns the nature of the Father and the Son, and another concerns their persons. The Father is unbegotten, while the Son is begotten. As far as the persons are concerned, they appear different, although there is an indivisible unity of nature; for unity is not in the person but in the substance. The Holy Spirit, however, must not be thought degenerate because he is placed third. Therefore, whoever does not doubt concerning the second person also admits the third.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”]

### (Verse 11)

May God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you.

He asks that their journey be arranged in the proper order: first by God the Father, because all things are from him; then by the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist. Thus the power and providence of the Father and the Son might commend his coming, make him acceptable to those hearing him, and remove the devil’s obstacles to directing his journey.

### (Verses 12, 13)

May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all, just as we do for you, so that he may strengthen your hearts, blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “in us and in all”; and shortly afterward, “your hearts blameless.” The old edition and the manuscripts read as in the text, except that some manuscripts have “our hearts.”]

In order to increase the joy he takes in them, he desires that they be multiplied in every good thing, so that when he comes to them he may find in them more that deserves praise than he had heard from Timothy. He desires that they be found blameless with the saints in the love of God the Father and at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, when the examination of each individual before his tribunal begins to approve them. He calls him God because of the terror of his majesty, but Father because of the kindness by which he deigns to adopt those who believe in him as sons—something that will be revealed at the coming of the Lord.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### (Verse 1)

Finally, brothers, we ask and exhort you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God—and just as you are walking—you should abound more and more.

This is what I said above: he wants them to increase in good works according to the apostolic commands, so as to complete his joy.

281

### (Verses 2–6)

For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God: your sanctification—that you abstain from fornication, that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor, not in the passion of desire like the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one transgress or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger in all these matters, as we told you beforehand and solemnly testified.

Although he praises them throughout the entire letter, he nevertheless warns them not to be led by any stealthy deception into unlawful things and to incur the vengeance they have learned is the punishment of evil. They should know that this pleases God: to keep their bodies undefiled and also to deal straightforwardly with their brothers, lest, found to be like the Gentiles, they be cast out from the title of adoption.

### (Verses 7, 8)

For God did not call us to impurity but to holiness. Therefore whoever disregards these things disregards not a human being but God, who has given his Holy Spirit to us.

In order to bind them more firmly to what he teaches, he introduces the person of God, saying: “Whoever transgresses the commands disregards not a human being but God.”

[Note: Codex Laud. inserts “the teaching of God.”]

He says that God gave us the Holy Spirit for this reason: so that we might live holy lives, because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subjected to sins (Wisdom 1:4).

### (Verses 9, 10)

Concerning brotherly affection, we have no need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another (John 15:17). Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout Macedonia.

Although he praises them for doing this also, he nevertheless warns them to practice it more earnestly. When he says that they have been taught by God himself, he indicates that they ought to be readier in brotherly love. For because of his great love God had mercy on us; having become imitators of him, we rightly show that we have been adopted by God as sons.

### (Verse 11)

But we exhort you, brothers, to abound more and more, to strive to live quietly, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk honorably toward those who are outside and may lack nothing.

Again he exhorts them to abound in good actions through deliberate effort. To show that this truly is what pleases God, he repeatedly emphasizes it. The path of righteousness must be followed, so that one may rightly arrive at mercy. Those who are poorer in possessions should work with their hands, so that by this very activity they may be removed from common restlessness and evil thoughts, so that even unbelievers may praise their discipline and be moved toward faith.

### (Verses 12, 13)

But we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “so that you may not be sad.”]

For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.

The reason is clear. If it is believed that there will be a resurrection of the dead, those who depart bearing the sign of the cross should not be mourned. But the unbelievers truly should be mourned, because they pass from here into Gehenna, so that they may learn that what they refused to believe was true. The faithful, however, will rise to glory, so that those who were considered foolish in this world because of their faith may be seen to be wise; for they provided glory for themselves. These are the ones who, through Jesus—that is, departing under the hope of this faith—will be brought with him at his coming, so that they may be seen by human beings.

Yet although he himself forbids mourning the departure of the dead, elsewhere he says: “lest I should have sorrow” (Philippians 2:27). But this has already been explained in its proper place.

### (Verses 14–17)

For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore encourage one another with these words.

He declares that he speaks with the Lord’s own authority when he says: “This we say to you by the word of the Lord.”

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “For in order to demonstrate faith, hope,” and so forth.]

In order to demonstrate the sure hope and established glory of the resurrection promised to the saints, he explains the very order in which it will take place, at the command of Christ the Judge, with the Holy Spirit revealing it. Thus those who have sent their loved ones ahead of them in death may not grieve because of this hope, learning that at the Lord’s coming those who die in Christ will rise first.

For Christ the Lord himself, by the will of the Father, like the first angel from the heavenly army, will descend from heaven to wage war in God’s name against the Antichrist, as is contained in the Apocalypse of the Apostle John (Revelation 12:7 and following). When he has destroyed him, the dead will rise at his command.

[Note: Some editions and manuscripts read: “the angel of God with the heavenly army.”]

This, then, is what it means to descend with the trumpet of God: to wage war in God’s name. For, as he himself said to Jesus the son of Nun (Joshua 5:14), he is the leader and prince of the army of the Lord; for this reason he is called an archangel. When he descends with the trumpet of God, he is God, because Scripture contains both claims. Thus in Exodus, where we read that the angel appeared to Moses in a flame, we immediately recognize from what follows that he himself is God—that is, the Son of God. For the same Scripture says: “And Moses approached and turned aside, because he could not look upon the face of God” (Exodus 3:6).

Therefore he is God, because the Son of God is true God. He is leader and prince because he is the head of all things, since all things are through him. After those who died in Christ have risen first, then we who are alive will be caught up together with them, carried by clouds to meet Christ in the air, so that all may come with the Lord to battle and he may see alive those whom he had killed, because just as the clouds served the Lord, so they also serve those whom he has deemed worthy to call his brothers.

And so we will always be with the Lord. In that very rapture death will occur, as if through sleep, so that the soul, having departed, may be restored in an instant. When they are taken up, they will die, so that, arriving at the Lord, they may receive their souls in the Lord’s presence; for with God they cannot remain dead. Therefore he commands them to encourage one another with these words. With this hope he commands them to console one another, since they still thought, in the manner of the Gentiles, that the departure of their loved ones ought to be mourned.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### (Verses 1, 2, 3)

Concerning the times and seasons, brothers, there is no need to write to you. For you yourselves know accurately that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, as labor pain upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “they will say, ‘Peace and stability.’”]

This is what the Lord spoke in the Gospel when he said: “Watch, because you do not know the hour when your Lord will come” (Mark 13:32). And again: “If anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There he is,’ do not believe it” (Matthew 24:23). For he will appear suddenly and unexpectedly, as lightning appears from east to west, bringing with him the host of God the Father’s army for the destruction of the Antichrist and his followers.

When the faithless feel secure in the devil’s kingdom, after the saints—namely, Enoch and Elijah—have been killed, and when they rejoice in victory, sending one another gifts, as the Apocalypse says (Revelation 11:7 and following), then sudden destruction will come upon them. At his coming Christ will destroy all of them, so that the saints, seeing that they have escaped, may glory.

### (Verses 4, 5)

But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day might seize you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; you are not of night or of darkness.

By darkness he signifies ignorance and falsehood, and by day knowledge and truth. Therefore he says that Christians are not in darkness, while the Gentiles and unbelieving Jews are sons of darkness, because they are worshipers of falsehood. Accordingly, he indicates that the faithful ought to be secure, because they do not remain ignorant of the Lord’s future coming but await it attentively, so that he may come. Those who are ignorant and distrustful of him, however, he will suddenly seize unprepared and destroy.

### (Verses 6–11.)

Therefore, let us not sleep, as the others do, but let us keep watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who become drunk are drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, clothed with the breastplate of faith and love, and with the helmet of the hope of salvation, because God has not destined us for wrath but for the attainment of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that whether we keep watch or sleep, we may live together with him. Therefore encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.

What he says is clear: he warns us not to act carelessly because we are secure in the name of the Savior. For this reason, he says that we must be armed with three defenses, namely faith, hope, and love. For while faith remains, it arouses hope; hope, for its part, is necessarily anxious concerning the promise and does not sleep; but love offers itself devotedly to God, for love admits nothing hostile. Therefore the Lord Jesus died and rose again for us, so that whether we keep watch—that is, live—or sleep, that is, die, we may enjoy eternal life together with him. This is what he said above: that at the Lord’s coming the faithful, both dead and living, will be taken up to meet the Lord, and will always live with him. He teaches that this should be kept in mind, so that they may build one another up in this understanding.

[Col. 0452A] ### (Verses 12–13.)

We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, who preside over you in the Lord, and who admonish you; and to hold them in the highest honor in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “those who labor among you.” And below: “Be at peace with them.”]

This is what he also says in another epistle (1 Tim. 5:17): that presbyters who labor in the word of teaching are to be honored with double honor. For a person suffering want may become weary of undertaking work that benefits his hearers. What benefit is there in possessing honor without fruit? Or what great thing is it to offer material things to one who supplies spiritual things? For just as riches produce negligence concerning salvation, so poverty, while seeking to be satisfied, turns away from righteousness. Hence Solomon asks neither to be made exceedingly rich nor destitute (Prov. 30:8).

Nevertheless, he says that this must be done in love, so that the honor shown to the priest may arise not more from fear than from love, and so that it may also benefit the one who renders it. What is not done willingly does not reach its proper effect; for although it may benefit the recipient for the present, it will provide no benefit in the future to the giver. And because dissension produces many evils, he urges them to be at peace.

### (Verses 14–17.)

We urge you, brothers: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient with everyone. See that no one repays evil to anyone for evil; rather, always pursue what is good, both toward one another and toward all. Rejoice always in the Lord, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.

Since it is necessary that among the people some should be disorderly, others fainthearted—that is, timid—and still others weak in faith, he therefore urges those who are restrained, magnanimous, and firmly grounded in faith, with an earnest appeal, to care for these people so that they may be able to progress, bearing with them; lest, if evil is repaid, they make themselves worse.

[Note: Some editions and manuscripts read: “who are modest.” Below, however, the Laud manuscript reads: “make themselves worse.”]

For this reason he urges them to pursue nothing other than what is good, not only in the case of the brothers but also in the case of everyone. Unbelievers can be drawn to faith by good works, through which one always rejoices in the Lord—that is, in what is good. One must also pray without ceasing, for persistent prayers move the mind of the judge to grant mercy. In all good actions, however, thanks must be given to God, who has granted this teaching in Christ Jesus our Lord.

### (Verses 18–22.)

Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies. Test everything; hold fast to what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil.

He says this so that no one who speaks through the Spirit may be silenced too readily—for the Spirit is extinguished when the speaker’s initial fervor is lulled by contradiction—lest, because they do not understand that spiritual things are being spoken by him, they injure the Holy Spirit and sin through ignorance. Nor should anyone who seems to reveal the Scriptures be refused a patient hearing. Rather, everything that is said must be examined and then judged, lest, while rejecting the grace given to a brother, they resist its author.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “is carried away by contradiction.”]

Therefore he urges that everything spoken be tested, and that whatever has been said soberly and well be retained. Whatever agrees with the sayings of the apostles and of the Lord himself is to be regarded as well spoken and retained; but one must abstain from whatever appears hostile to the faith. For the spirit of the world often deceitfully speaks good things, as though imitating the good, and inserts evil among them, so that through the good things the evil may be accepted. Since the sayings are thought to come from one spirit, they are not distinguished from one another; rather, what is illicit is commended by the authority of the name through what is permitted, not by the reason of virtue.

For people often teach unspeakable and contrary things under the name of the apostles and of the Lord himself. Therefore he urges that everything be tested, because the Lord’s utterances cannot be contradictory. Hence also the epistle of the apostle John says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1). For if a spirit says many good things but brings forth something opposed to the faith, it must be recognized as not being the Holy Spirit. No error can be found in the Holy Spirit.

Yet through the exercise of speech it presents some things as spiritual and others as carnal, because every error is assigned to the flesh; or, certainly, by some contrivance of cunning it fabricates good things in order to insert evil among them, as I mentioned above. Thus, in Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla, the prophets of the Cataphrygians, the spirit of the world, by a certain imitation of the good, pretended to be good, so that through many plausible things, and even true ones, it might falsely claim to be the Holy Spirit.

284

### (Verse 23.)

May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Christ is the God of peace, for he says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27). Since everything the Father has belongs to the Son, the Apostle wishes him to sanctify us, so that he may enlighten us with the piety of his mercy and direct all our conduct toward perfection, so that the spirit given to us may remain whole.

[Note: All editions read: “and every vow”; all manuscripts read: “and every action.”]

For the spirit is whole if we devote ourselves to a good life, possessing a pure soul and a blameless body, so that the whole person may be perfect. The body can be pure while the soul is defiled by an evil thought; therefore he says that the spirit in a person must be pure. But if an evil life or thought intervenes, the spirit will not remain whole, because it abandons a person subject to sins. For when soul and body disagree, although the body is without understanding, they become alien to the spirit; and, as though losing them, the spirit will not remain whole. The spirit is given to a person for this purpose: that it may remain in him and be, as it were, his head. It will therefore not be whole, because it loses its members when a person departs from it by doing what the Holy Spirit hates.

[Col. 0454B] ### (Verses 24–25.)

For God is faithful, who called you, and he will also act. Brothers, pray for us.

He calls God faithful in his promises, so that they may conduct themselves rightly, secure in the reward. And because those who live rightly according to the Gospel will easily be able to obtain what they ask, he urges them to pray for him; for many easily obtain what they desire.

### (Verse 26.)

Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.

Holy kisses belong to Christian greeting; all others are carnal, because whatever is done without Christ is carnal and therefore mortal. For whoever despises the author of life is in death.

### (Verse 27.)

I adjure you by the Lord that this epistle be read to all the brothers.

He binds them by obligation to take care that the epistle be read to all the brothers, so that they may know both his praises and his admonitions, through which they may become perfect.

[Col. 0454C]

### (Verse 28.)

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

He wishes them to progress in good works so that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ may remain in them forever.

[Col. 0453]

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE THESSALONIANS

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0453C]

Since in the first epistle delivered to the Thessalonians he wrote, among other things, about the coming of the Lord and the resurrection of the saints, he now writes another to them in which he indicates, although obscurely—for he could not write openly—the abolition of the Roman kingdom, the appearance and condemnation of the Antichrist, and the disorderliness of certain brothers.

## CHAPTER ONE

### (Verses 1–3.)

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and in the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

He writes to them in solemn language; for, according to his customary manner of expression, the opening of the epistle is contained in these words. The same three persons are named as its authors, just as in the first epistle (1 Thess. 1:1).

We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing exceedingly and the love of each one of you all toward one another is increasing.

They declare themselves indebted to God in thanksgiving for their progress. And to show that this was no ordinary debt, he says, “as is fitting,” testifying that great thanks ought to be returned to God for so immeasurable a gift. For after receiving the first epistle, they persisted in becoming better than they had been, so that they appeared rich and abundant in that which, after devotion to the Lord and God, we have been commanded to possess: that we love one another (John 13:34).

### (Verses 4–5.)

So that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God because of your patience and faith in all your persecutions and afflictions that you endure, as an example of God’s righteous judgment, so that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer.

He testifies that his glory consists in their conduct and in the persecutions they have endured, to such an extent that their example is set before the other churches, so that by imitating them the others may grow in devotion amid sufferings for Christ and may deserve to obtain what has been promised to the saints on the day of God’s righteous judgment. For love of God they did not hesitate to despise the world.

The afflictions themselves are examples of future merits: in those who suffer, they lead to glory; in those who persecute, to destruction.

### (Verses 6–9.)

For it is just before God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to you who suffer affliction, rest with us at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, bringing vengeance upon those who do not know God and upon those who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his power.

Since he said that an example of God’s righteous judgment would appear both in the good and in the wicked, he consequently adds: “For it is just before God,” so that he may repay each person according to his works. What could be more just than that those who in this world oppress the good and make them outcasts through persecutions should in the future suffer the same things they inflict, while the others should be at rest with the remaining saints—those who, coming from the great tribulation, will receive an eternal kingdom at the Lord’s coming from heaven?

He will come with his heavenly army and with fire as his minister, to bring vengeance upon the pagans who do not know that God is the Father of Jesus Christ, and upon the Jews who, while saying that they know God, do not believe the Gospel of Christ, which God the Father gave to him to deliver to his servants. The presence of the Lord and the glory of his majesty will burn all of them with fire, so that they may pay the deserved penalty of eternal destruction.

[Note: Thus read the majority of the better manuscripts; the edition, together with certain other manuscripts, reads: “always suffering.” The latter reading is less suitable.]

They will suffer continually, yet will not utterly cease to exist, so that the punishment itself may in some way perpetually generate them for consumption.

### (Verse 10.)

When he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at among all who have believed, because our testimony to you was believed on that day of the Lord’s coming.

This contains a twofold meaning: he will come to punish the wicked and to glorify the good. He will appear glorious and wondrous to those who believe through the example and faith of the apostles, when they have been crowned, while the Gospel bears witness on the day of the Lord. But he will appear severe to unbelievers when they begin to be confined by eternal punishments. For the glory of the disciples is the crown of their teacher, and his truth is the punishment of unbelievers, because what was preached was not believed.

### (Verses 11–12.)

For this reason we also always pray for you, that our God may consider you worthy of his calling and fulfill every good purpose and work of faith in power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.

He adds prayers to his joy, so that, because they are devoted, God may deem them worthy to help them complete the work they have begun, to the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Thus the perseverance of the disciples may be a testimony to their teacher, bringing him glory. For the authority of a teacher consists in the confidence of his disciples, when they make themselves more worthy in the grace they have received.

## CHAPTER TWO

### (Verses 1–4.)

Now we ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, not to be quickly shaken from your understanding or disturbed, either by a spirit or by a word or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were already present. Let no one deceive you in any way, for unless the apostasy comes first and that man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—the one who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “the man of iniquity, the son of destruction.”]

He begs them not to adopt lightly and readily the opinion that the Lord’s coming is imminent. He gives such instructions that even if someone should speak as a prophet through the Spirit, he must not necessarily be believed; nor should assent be given if something is presented through a treatise or a letter perhaps written in the name of the apostles. For deceivers often fabricate a letter under the name of some distinguished person in order to mislead, so that the authority of the name may commend what could not be accepted on its own.

He says this so that, while the unwary might be caught in the very disturbance, they would not be led astray into worshiping the devil. For this reason he will make these claims: appearing under the name of the Savior and deceiving the saints, he will wish to be worshiped, so that he may deceive those who believe in Christ.

But so that shameless Satan may not have the place or opportunity for deception that he thinks he possesses, he has specified the time and signs of the Lord’s coming. For the Lord will not come before the Roman kingdom has suffered its collapse and the Antichrist appears, who will kill the saints, restoring liberty to the Romans, though under his own name. Knowing that the Lord will come to suppress him, he will appropriate his name. And so that his kingdom may appear to be genuine, he will draw with him those who will perish together with him. Thus he will sit in the Lord’s house, in the seat of Christ, and will assert that he himself is God, not the Son of God.

Therefore in the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John 5:43). For this reason he is to be expected to come from the circumcision, or circumcised, so that the Jews may have confidence in believing him. Thus, when the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians, he teaches that everyone ought to be cautious in a matter of this kind.

### (Verses 5–6.)

Do you not remember that, while I was still with you, I used to tell you these things? And now you know what is restraining him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Were these things being said to you? And now it is hidden. What, etc.”]

He says that the only thing remaining is for the one who will come before the Lord to be revealed, so that the Lord’s coming may now be expected. Above he expressed this as though under a veil, saying: “Unless the apostasy comes first.” As I mentioned above, this is to be understood as the abolition of the Roman kingdom, so that when it has collapsed and the Antichrist has come, the Lord’s coming may then be believed to have arrived.

### (Verse 7.)

For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only the one who now restrains it must continue to do so, until he is removed from the midst.

The mystery of iniquity began with Nero, who, in his zeal for idols and at the instigation of his father the devil, killed the apostles, and continued through Diocletian, and finally Julian, who was unable by a certain art and subtlety to complete the persecution that had been begun, because it had not been granted from above. Satan uses these ministers so that, for the time being, under the multitude of gods, he may deceive human beings concerning the manifestation of the one true God, for as long as the Roman kingdom stands—that is what he means by: “Until he is removed from the midst.”

### (Verses 8–9.)

And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming; whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power and signs and lying wonders.

He says that the Antichrist will appear after the collapse of the Roman kingdom, as has been mentioned. For at the end of time, knowing that destruction is threatening him, and after the Roman kingdom has collapsed and he has been cast down from heaven to earth—thrown onto the earth, as was said in the Apocalypse of the apostle John—the devil will prepare for himself one in whom and through whom, by the permission of the just God, he will perform certain signs of power and commend himself, so that he may be worshiped as though he were God.

He will imitate God, so that just as the Son of God, born or made human, demonstrated his divinity through signs and powers, so Satan too will appear in a human being, showing himself to be God through lying powers, as was said above. The revelation of the mystery of iniquity is this: when the Antichrist appears, it will be recognized that he is, as it were, the god of those whom the common people formerly worshiped as gods at his command; he will be their first or highest god, and he will make this credible through the powers of his signs.

He called them “lying wonders” because he wants people to believe through the signs that he is what he is not, in order to deceive those whom he is about to ensnare. This was therefore foretold to the saints so that they might know what to avoid.

### (Verse 10.)

And with every deceit of iniquity for those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved.

He says that the deceit of his iniquitous wonders will benefit those who are destined to perish. Because they rejected the love of the truth through which they could have been saved when the apostles preached, they were handed over to the devil. For those who do not wish to be saved are abandoned by God.

### (Verse 11.)

And therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, in order that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity.

The operation of error is to entrust oneself to falsehood: those who refused to agree that the brightness of light is day suppose that darkness ought to be called day, so that, made guilty of a more deliberate offense, they may be condemned without contradiction as enemies of the truth and supporters of iniquity.

287

[Col. 0458A] ### (Verses 12–13.)

But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning for salvation, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, to which he called you through our Gospel, for the attainment of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Here God’s foreknowledge is being proclaimed, because he knows the minds of all before their birth; for those who will believe are not hidden from him. Therefore from the beginning he knows that these people will be faithful, since by believing they increase faith rather than diminish it. Sanctified through faith in the truth of the Gospel of the Son of God, they are acquired for the increase of the glory of Christ’s body, just as he says in another epistle: “so that all things may grow into the increase of God” (Col. 2:19). For all who, abandoning the devil, flee to the faith of Christ increase God in the body of Christ, whereas previously they had caused diminution.

### (Verse 14.)

Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to our traditions that you learned, whether through word or through our epistle.

So that God’s foreknowledge may remain directed toward their salvation, he urges them to stand firm and persevere in the tradition of the Gospel. They must be vigilant, lest, growing sluggish through idleness and leisure in the works of God, they fail to complete what they have begun. For he foreknows that they will believe and be able to remain faithful if they are repeatedly urged by admonition.

### (Verses 15–16.)

Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, console your hearts and establish you in every good work and word.

Since the Father and the Son are one power, one divinity, and one substance, he did not hesitate first to name our Lord Jesus Christ and then God our Father, by reason of his condescension, not by reason of his nature. He loved us to such an extent that he gave his Son for us (John 3:16): God for human beings, the Lord for servants, the true Son for adopted children. Thus his death is our life, his resurrection our justification, and his second coming the rest of our life and glory forever. This hope is therefore the consolation of present afflictions, by which those who are founded in it may grow in good works and teaching.

## CHAPTER THREE

### (Verses 1–2.)

Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, just as it is among you, and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil people; for not everyone has faith.

For the rest, he urges them to pray that God may deign to direct his teaching in an untiring course and pour it through the mouth of his Apostle into the ears of his hearers; and that he may restrain and quiet the disturbances of evil people who distrust the truth. He also asks that the Apostle may grow in confidence of speech, for the fruit and conversion of many.

### (Verse 3.)

But God is faithful, and he will strengthen them and protect them from evil.

Since God promised that his help would not fail faithful people and those of good conduct in their need, for their strengthening, and since these people were zealous for good things both in faith and in deed, he calls God faithful in his promises, because his providence would be directed toward them.

### (Verse 4.)

We have confidence in the Lord concerning you, that you are doing and will do what we have commanded.

Because he was confident that they deserved to be wholly protected by God, he does not doubt that they are doing and will do what he commands them in the Lord’s name.

### (Verse 5.)

May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “into the love of God and the expectation of Christ.”]

He desires this from God for them, which he does not doubt can be granted: that their hearts may progress in the love of God toward awaiting the Lord’s coming.

[Note: The edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “when the world has been despised.”]

He wishes them to condemn the world and desire the coming of the one who conquered the world.

### (Verse 6.)

We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that you received from us.

Since not everyone in the whole people obeys the word of teaching—not the law, but rather their own desire and judgment—he commands that they turn away from such people, so that they may recognize that they themselves are in error.

### (Verses 7–9.)

For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we did not live disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment; rather, in labor and hardship, working night and day so as not to burden any of you—not because we do not have the right, but so that we might offer ourselves as a model for you to imitate.

He says that they are not ignorant of his work and labor, which he diligently carried out so that he would not need another’s bread, in order to give them an example for imitation.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “which he diligently practiced.”]

For he would not have been blameworthy if he had received bread from those to whom he was supplying spiritual food for their souls, food that would also secure immortality with glory for the body. Freedom can truly be exercised when a person subjects himself to no one for the sake of his belly or money, but is content with his own bread. It is especially praiseworthy when, although he is permitted and has the opportunity to receive, he exercises restraint. Such a person can benefit his hearers; for they will respect this strictness, and what he commands will not be capable of being disregarded.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “nor did we receive bread from anyone without payment.”]

### (Verse 10.)

For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: if anyone does not wish to work, neither should he eat.

He taught not only by words but also urged them by his actions; for a teacher is competent when he fulfills in his works what he teaches in words. Those learning then know that what they hear is true if they do not see it neglected by their teacher. Although what is taught is plainly recognized as true, nevertheless, if the teacher begins to neglect it, the hearers will make little progress. Actions persuade more powerfully than words.

Therefore those who, despite negligent teachers, make progress through words alone, both in action and in understanding, are to be rewarded with great prizes. He was thus a model for those among the people who possessed moderate or limited means, so that they might learn not to lose their freedom.

Hence Solomon also says: “Seldom bring your foot to your friend, lest, having had enough of you, he hate you” (Prov. 25:17). For someone who frequently comes to another’s table must necessarily, being devoted to idleness, flatter the one who feeds him, whereas our religion calls human beings to freedom. Therefore, he says, if anyone refuses to work, let him cease from eating. But since no one can live without food, let him apply himself to labor, so that by living according to his own judgment he may have God as his gracious protector.

### (Verse 11.)

For we hear that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but acting as busybodies.

Those who desire to be idle do this so that an opportunity may arise by which they can make their entrance into the houses of the rich desirable. They go about carefully gathering reports and opinions, knowing what they wish to hear from each person, so that, when willingly sought out, they may be fed. This conduct is utterly contrary to the Lord’s discipline; for their belly is their god, and they provide for their necessities through shameful attentiveness.

### (Verse 12.)

Now to such people we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they should eat their own bread.

To persuade them more easily, he introduces the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and exhorts them to obey, because obedience is useful to them.

### (Verses 13–15.)

But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “do not grow weary in doing good.”]

If anyone does not obey our word in this epistle, take note of that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame; yet do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

Because above he had commanded each person to eat his own bread, lest some seize upon this as an occasion for stinginess and inhumanity, he immediately added: “But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.” For the humane and generous person is not blamed; the blame belongs to the one who, although able to endure labor, wishes to spend his life in idleness.

If the authority of the epistle does not correct such a person, he commands that he be marked out and that no one associate with him, so that, being put to shame when everyone avoids him, he may submit to the Apostle’s commands. He wishes this to be done, however, without anger or insult: they should patiently withdraw from him, yet if circumstances require them to speak with him, they should admonish him to allow himself to be corrected and no longer despise the Apostle’s commands. Nor should they maintain familiarity with him until he becomes obedient.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “until he becomes obedient.”]

For if he is provoked to anger by insults, he will become worse; he will be incited to contention and will begin to defend his error. Afterwards he will be ashamed to correct himself, lest he appear later to admit what he had previously excused.

### (Verse 16.)

May the God of peace himself give you peace always and in every place. The Lord be with all of you.

He always pursues them with good wishes for what belongs to him, as though they were dearly beloved children, continually wishing that peace—which is the guide to eternal life—may remain with them. For the Lord promised to be with those who are peaceful.

289

### (Verse 17.)

This greeting is in my own hand, that of Paul; this is the sign in every epistle. This is how I write.

Because of falsifiers and adulterators of the Scriptures, he testifies that in every epistle he always adds his greeting in his own hand, so that a letter that has not been subscribed by his hand cannot be accepted under his name.

290

[Col. 0462A]

### (Verse 18.)

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you.

This greeting was written by the Apostle’s hand, in which he wishes the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ to be with them. Amen.

[Col. 0461]

## ON THE FIRST EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO TIMOTHY

289

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0461B]

Timothy was the son of a faithful Jewish woman and a Greek father; for this reason he could not be circumcised as a small child. Through his mother’s diligence he learned the sacred writings, and by devoting himself to them he established a good life for himself (Acts 16:5). When the Apostle wished to take him as a companion, knowing that he would be a suitable steward of evangelical truth, he was compelled to circumcise him because of the Jews, who insisted that one born of a Jewish mother could not be received uncircumcised into the ministry of teaching, on account of the testimony of his ancestry. Having already been made a bishop, Timothy is therefore instructed by this epistle how he ought to order the Church.

## CHAPTER ONE

### (Verses 1–2.)

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, his genuine son in faith. Grace, mercy, and peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

He shows that he became an apostle by the command of the Father and the Son, so that he might preach salvation in God the Father and hope in Christ his Son. Since no one denies that salvation is in God, nor should anyone doubt that hope is in Christ Jesus, who, having been raised from the dead, is recognized as having given an example of this hope, he writes to Timothy in this way so that he may be secure concerning his ordination, because he was chosen to teach by the command of the Father and the Son.

He calls him a true son, but in faith, as he says to the Corinthians: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Cor. 4:15). This is a true and enduring generation, which knows neither decline nor sickness or pestilence, and which knows neither hunger nor thirst.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For those who are in the kingdom of God lack nothing.”]

He has learned to lack nothing in the kingdom of God, because glorious immortality will be granted by God in the kingdom of God and of Christ. He wishes grace, mercy, and peace from them to remain with Timothy.

### (Verses 3–4.)

Just as I urged you to remain in Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might command certain people not to teach differently, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which produce disputes rather than God’s edification, which is in faith—so do this.

A son should not have to be entreated by his father. Yet because of affection and to show him a model of humility, the bishop entreats his fellow bishop not to allow the Jews to teach the people something different from what had been handed down by the Apostle, nor to take pleasure in the myths that Jews customarily tell concerning the descent of their origins, concerning Abraham, Isaac, and the other patriarchs, and concerning circumcision and the things later handed down by Moses, lest they be ensnared into observing what had been given in a carnal manner.

For what need is there to mention genealogies, which are plainly endless through succession, and to discuss what was done, and when, under each of them, rather than seeking salvation more briefly through faith? From this arise disputes, when it is examined what was done, when, how, and why; such discussion impedes salvation.

### (Verses 5–7.)

The goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfailing faith. Certain people, having wandered from these, have turned aside to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the Law, although they understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions.

Since love is greater than everything else, he says that it is the goal—that is, the consummation of perfection—of all the commandments, provided that it arises from a pure heart and a good conscience. True love cannot coexist with an evil life or a feigned faith; in love the whole Law and the Prophets are fulfilled (Matt. 7:12).

But certain Jews, ignorant of the mystery of the Law and the Prophets, because they had been handed down to be observed until Christ, went astray, thinking that after Christ had been preached the Law of deeds was still to be observed in new moons, circumcision, and the distinction of foods. For this reason he says that they have turned aside to empty talk, because they wished to teach what they did not understand.

### (Verses 8–11)

We know that the Law is good, if someone uses it lawfully, understanding this: that the law was not established for the righteous but for the unrighteous and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked and profane, those who kill their fathers and mothers, fornicators, murderers, men who have intercourse with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, which accords with the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which has been entrusted to me.

He does not deny that the Law given through Moses is good, but only on the condition that its meaning be understood and the manner in which it was given be properly grasped. For he knows the Law, and the reason for which it was given, who, after Christ has been preached, abandons it in that aspect in which it is called the law of works; but, with regard to the love of God, he makes use of it, asserting and affirming what was said by the Savior in the Law and the Prophets. For he uses the Law lawfully who can distinguish what was given for a time from what is perpetual, and understands that what pertains to the sacrament of Christ ought not now to be observed for the future, as though he were still expected to come who has already come.

If, therefore, everything is understood in its proper place, it is good; otherwise, it becomes bad for one who asserts it perversely. For it is sin not to explain each thing in its proper place. Moreover, since the righteous have no need of the law—that is, those who, having received the remission of sins, have been justified—they should no longer live under the Law from which they have been freed by God’s gift through faith in Christ. Instead, having thereafter kept the law of nature, which acknowledges the Creator and urges one not to sin, they should await the day of judgment, on which the righteous are to be rewarded for preserving the natural law. Had the human race taken this law as its guide, the law written down and given through Moses would not have been necessary.

[Col. 0463B] But because it was treated with contempt, as though it possessed no authority, Scripture was confirmed, so that it might be known that it had to be observed, both for the present time and because the one who established it will call to account in the future those by whom it was neglected and those by whom it was observed. Thus he says that the Law was given not only because of evil actions and bodily vices, but also because of the faithlessness with which they despised the Creator, so that they might learn to live well and give thanks to the Creator.

### (Verses 12–14)

And I give thanks to him who strengthened me in Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful and appointed me to the ministry, although previously I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an abuser; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly, while I did not yet believe.

But the grace of our Lord [Col. 0463C] overflowed, together with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.

For this reason every unbeliever suffers weakness of mind, constrained by carnal reasoning so that he does not believe what is spiritual. Therefore he says that he gives thanks to Christ because the appearance of his majesty strengthened the weakness of his mind. He had thought it impossible that what was preached concerning the Lord’s power, his twofold birth, his resurrection, and hope could be true.

Once strengthened, he appeared to be one who was worthy and capable of being an administrator of the Lord’s sacrament, so that he might establish through the Law as true what he had previously judged incredible out of his zeal for the Law, and rejoice in the persecutions that he had formerly inflicted on believers as though justly—grieving because he had inflicted them, but rejoicing because he endured them. For he had learned such great hope in the one whom he had formerly denied that he rejoiced more in suffering [Col. 0463D] than he had previously exulted in persecuting.

He had not done this out of malice, but out of error; and when a person repents, error can readily be forgiven. But one who knows that the things he denies are true does not act from error but from ill will. His wound is incurable, for envy compels him to call false what he knows to be true.

### (Verses 15–16)

The saying is trustworthy and worthy of complete acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display all patience and long-suffering [Note: [Col. 0463D] The Roman edition has the same reading here and below, for the information of readers.] as an example for those who were going to believe in him [Col. 0464A] for eternal life.

What is more welcome and delightful than to proclaim forgiveness to sinners? For who is without sin, so as not to receive this gift with complete thanksgiving, acknowledging and praising God as its author in Christ? In order to wash humanity from sins, he descended from the heavenly realms to earthly things and assumed the flesh of sin [Note: [Col. 0463D] The same Roman edition reads: “he assumed the likeness of the flesh of sin.”]. He mingled himself with earthly things in order to make humanity heavenly. He allowed himself to die in order to restore to paradise, immortal, the one rescued from death.

Who would not extol without limit these benefits that God bestowed upon humanity, the Lord upon his servant, the Creator upon his creature—so that he might show even greater generosity in human benefits than when he made what did not exist, after he had made it? For, though he had been abandoned by them, despised, and assailed with insults, he added benefits without being asked, so that he might be more gracious and more to be preferred in restoring than in creating, showing that he alone could accomplish all these things.

Thus Christ brought aid to humanity without violating or losing his own purity and power. He willed to be born as a human being, fully certain that contact with flesh could not defile him. He mingled with human life, knowing that he could not be corrupted by sins. He allowed himself to be killed, not unaware that death could not rule over him, but knowing that he would crush it by his power.

He did these things, therefore, to teach that he could do all things. This humility does not diminish him but contributes to his glory—and not only to his glory, but also to the glory of those who believe in him. For it is an honor to be the servant of one who is powerful.

Although many Jews had certainly believed before the Apostle—among them some who had killed the Lord himself—the Apostle nevertheless humbles himself, still grieving over his unbelief, and calls himself the foremost of all sinners. Because he had been more deeply imbued than others with the Savior’s sacrament and had drawn nearer to understanding his greatness, he accuses himself all the more: he had recognized such goodness only late, and not of his own accord, but because he was anticipated by the Savior’s mercy. Thus he became a witness to the divinity of the one whom he had previously considered merely a dead human being.

This accusation of the Apostle is praise of the Savior, who called his persecutor to grace as an example for all other believers, so that through his patience and long-suffering he might show the others how benevolent he would be toward those who hastened to him, since he had been so benevolent toward an enemy.

### (Verse 17)

To the King of the ages, immortal and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

These words refer to the person of God the Father, whom he calls alone immortal and invisible because all immortality comes from him, and therefore it belongs to him alone in the fullest sense. For whoever is immortal does not possess this from himself, but from him.

Likewise, in the Gospel we read that the Lord said: “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18). Again, he himself says: “A good person brings forth good things from a good treasury” (Matthew 12:35). Yet no one except the one God is good, because he himself is the fountain of goodness, from which the others drink so as to become good.

He is also the only invisible God, [Col. 0465A] because no one has ever seen him. He does everything through the Son, whom we therefore call “seen,” although he appeared otherwise than he is [Note: [Col. 0465D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “although he appeared otherwise than he is”; nevertheless, by this expression we indicate him. This is not entirely correct.].

He therefore attributes honor and glory in truth to God the Father, by whose compassion and providence Christ delivered sinners from death.

### (Verses 18–20)

This command I entrust to you, my son Timothy, in accordance with the prophecies previously made concerning you, so that you may wage the good warfare in them, holding faith and a pure conscience. Some, having rejected these, have suffered shipwreck with regard to the faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I handed over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme.

After recalling what and how great were the benefits bestowed by God the Father and Christ his Son upon sinful human beings—who, although they deserved punishment, not only forgave them but also justified them and adopted them as sons—the Apostle shows in what order he would form the people through ecclesiastical discipline. He exhorts holy Timothy, mindful of his election, to fulfill that for which he was predestined.

For he was predestined when he was taken up by the Apostle for this purpose: to be ordained, having been judged worthy to become a bishop, so that he might fulfill the evangelical warfare in faith and a pure conscience. One who teaches faithfully cannot have a bad conscience. He then displays the faith of his preaching if he abstains from everything contrary, because by the example of good works he urges many to belief, as they place their confidence in the hope proclaimed.
