For one who despises faith is undoubtedly of bad conscience. Such a person is either proclaimed a hypocrite or an open blasphemer, as were Hymenaeus and Alexander, who, abandoning the faith, suffered shipwreck—that is, were stripped of the truth or deprived of life. For what is truth if not life?

He says that he handed them over to Satan so that they might be corrected because of their blasphemy. This handing over means that, provoked by their blasphemies, the Apostle pronounced a sentence against them. The devil, however, who is ready to receive into his power those who are hostile to God, seized them when he heard the sentence, so that they might understand that they were subjected to punishment for this reason: because they had blasphemed.

For this reason, among other things, it is said in the Gospel: “Do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14), showing that bodily illnesses are sometimes inflicted because of sin. And that these things happen through the ministry of the devil, the Lord made clear when he said, among other things: “And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years, to be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13:16).

## CHAPTER II

### (Verses 1–4)

Therefore, exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are placed in a position of greater authority, so that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life in all godliness and chastity [Note: [Col. 0465D] The Roman edition reads here, and below: “so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life.”]. For this is good and acceptable before our Savior God, who [Col. 0466A] desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

This is the ecclesiastical rule handed down by the teacher of the nations, which our priests observe: that they pray for everyone, making supplication for the kings of this age, so that they may keep the nations subject, and so that, established in peace and tranquility of mind, we may be able to serve our God. We also pray for those to whom lofty power has been entrusted, so that they may govern the commonwealth in justice and truth, with an abundance of resources supplied, so that, once the disturbance of sedition has been removed, joy may follow; for “bread strengthens the heart, and wine gladdens the mind” (Psalm 103:16).

We make requests, moreover, for those who are in various kinds of need, so that, rescued and delivered, they may praise God as the author of their safety. We also offer thanksgivings for the things that God’s providence provides for us daily for the sake of life, so that in all these things God the Father may be praised, from whom all things come (1 Corinthians 8:6), and his Son, through whom all things exist. Thus, when everything hostile and inimical to this rule has been put to rest, we may be able to serve God in devotion and chastity; for disturbance and captivity preserve neither devotion nor chastity. For how can one be devout who is stripped naked? [Note: [Col. 0466D] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “and whence chastity, where …”]. And how can one be chaste where one is not master of oneself?

In order, therefore, that these things may be preserved, rest is necessary, so that the services pleasing to God may be rendered to him who desires all people to be saved and to know the truth. “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

[Col. 0466C] If God, then, who is called almighty, desires all people to be saved, is his will not fulfilled? But in every expression a meaning and a condition lie concealed; therefore the apostle Peter says: “Every Scripture requires interpretation” (2 Peter 2:20). God desires all people to be saved, but only if they come to him; for he does not desire them to be saved against their will, but desires them to be saved if they themselves also desire it. For certainly he who gave the law to everyone excluded no one from salvation.

Does not a physician make his offer publicly for this very reason, to show that he wishes to save everyone, provided that he is sought out by the sick? For salvation is not genuine if it is bestowed upon one who does not want it; nor can one rejoice in a salvation received who has accepted medicine unwillingly—even if that is possible—not to mention that medicine cannot be effective unless the sick person applies his mind to it. For this medicine is not bodily but spiritual [Note: [Col. 0466D] The same reading is found in the old edition and in some manuscripts: “which benefits neither the doubting nor the unwilling.”], and it benefits neither those who doubt nor those who are unwilling. It is faith that grants salvation; unless the whole mind receives it willingly, it will not only provide no benefit but will also do harm. For the grace of faith has the power to pour divine healing into those devoted to it, but to bring upon the undevoted a disease through which the whole person perishes.

### (Verse 5)

For there is one God, and one mediator between God [Col. 0467A] and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.

He signifies that God and Christ have one will in saving human beings. Thus he confesses that God the Father is one, since all authority comes from him, and that Christ Jesus is one mediator between God and human beings. For, sent by the Father and made an arbiter, he reconciled God and human beings by restoring them to knowledge of him. Because the Father and the Son are one—not one person, but one in the undivided nature—the Son of God, in order to be the arbiter of God and human beings, assumed flesh and was born human. Thus, in order to be mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus was not without divinity: in God there was humanity, and in humanity there was God. And so that he might be mediator from both sides, and reconcile both, he first accomplished this in himself.

For, while preserving the unity of God, he could not be called the mediator of God and human beings as though there were another God who would restore to favor the human being estranged from God. Rather, the one who did not transgress the law that had been given became the arbiter between the one who sinned and the one who did not know sin: so that the latter might forgive, and the human being thereafter remain in the faith of God.

[Note: [Col. 0467D] The Roman edition reads: “because there is one”; the other editions and manuscripts read: “… there is one,” supplying “God.”]

### (Verses 6–7)

He gave himself as a ransom for all, testimony to which was given at its proper times. For this I was appointed a herald and apostle—I speak the truth, I do not lie—a teacher of the nations in faith and truth.

Because the human being, reconciled to God, was now liable to infernal death, the Savior, in order that he might bring his own decision to effect and enable the human being to ascend to the God with whom he had been reconciled, allowed himself to die contrary to the law. Descending to the underworld, he condemned death for the impiety it had exercised against him, taking away those whom it held, so that thereafter no one who bore his sign could be held by it.

He displayed testimony to this when he rose again; for the destruction of death is the resurrection of the dead. This is the hope that this Apostle, sent to the nations, was appointed to preach, so that they might learn from him what hope there is in Christ. For this reason he is called a teacher, so that he might teach faith and truth.

### (Verse 8)

I therefore desire men to pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger or dispute.

He teaches that the mind must be peaceful in prayer, so that prayer may attain its effect. The hands are holy when the heart is pure. Yet he commands prayer in every place in such a way that a suitable place is understood—not, certainly, an unsuitable or filthy place—since the Lord forbids praying in public display. Rather, he teaches this so that they would not think prayer should be offered only in the Church (Matthew 6:5–6).

### (Verses 9–10)

Likewise, women should adorn themselves in orderly dress, with modesty and chastity, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or expensive clothing, but—as is proper for women professing godliness—with good works.

He teaches that women should pray in humble dress, not ostentatiously. For one who wishes to be heard must humble herself, removing pomp from herself, so that she may call forth God’s mercy. Proud attire neither obtains what it seeks nor causes a person to be rightly regarded. For what prudent person would not shrink from a woman dressed ostentatiously? [Col. 0468A] How much more does God the Author shrink from seeing a body made free by him bound with metals!

For humble dress accords with a good profession, so that a woman may be judged to be no different from what she appears to be. But the woman who prefers to appear with pomp in the house of God obtains what she wants—not for God’s sake, but for the sake of human beings—so that she may appear glorious, receiving nothing from God except a stain. For the more splendid she appears to human beings, the more she is despised by God.

### (Verses 11–12)

Let a woman learn in silence, with complete submission. For I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to remain in silence.

He commands not only that a woman should have humble dress, but also that authority should be denied her and that she should be subjected to a man, so that both in dress and in obedience she may be under the authority of the man from whom she derives her origin.

### (Verses 13–15)

For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, became a transgressor (Genesis 1:27). Yet she will be saved through the bearing of children, if she remains in faith and love and holiness with chastity (Genesis 3:6).

He prefers the man to the woman because he was created first, so that the woman may be inferior, since she was created after and from the man. He adds another point: the devil did not deceive the man but the woman; the man, however, was deceived through the woman. Consequently, no boldness should be granted her, but she ought to remain in humility, because through her death entered the world.

“She will be saved,” he says, “through the bearing of children,” provided that she remains in faith, love, and a pure life. By “these children” he means those who are reborn through faith in Christ. For if these children persevere in their own regeneration, the woman will be saved with them when she rises from the dead—not as though she were saved by them, but through their regeneration. For when those who have been destined for eternal life believe, they reach the resurrection from the dead, and she will be saved because they believe and lead chaste lives.

For the resurrection remains suspended as long as all those predestined for salvation have not believed.

## CHAPTER III

### (Verse 1)

The saying is trustworthy: if anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work.

Because a bishop ought to be a person of good life, one who desires the office of bishop desires a good work. In desiring this, he appears to seek a good life—provided that he does not turn aside from the requirements set out below, lest he seem to have acted from ambition or a desire for money.

### (Verse 2)

For a bishop must be above reproach.

He describes what kind of person a bishop ought to be, so that no one may seek the office of bishop unless he is faithful and able to abstain from everything contrary, so that he may not be unworthy of his profession.

The husband of one wife.

Although having a second wife is not prohibited merely as a matter of number, nevertheless, in order that someone may be worthy of the office of bishop, he ought to reject even what is permitted because of the exalted character of the office itself. For the one who desires that position ought to be better than the others.

[Col. 0469A] ### (Verses 3–4)

Sober, chaste, well ordered, hospitable, teachable, not addicted to wine, not violent but moderate, not quarrelsome, not harsh, but governing his own household well, keeping his children submissive with all chastity [Note: [Col. 0469D] The same Roman edition reads: “composed, hospitable, apt to teach … not quarrelsome, not greedy.”].

He says that a person who observes these good qualities he enumerates ought to be made a bishop. For these are signs of episcopal dignity. But if someone, pursuing higher things, has dedicated both his body and his soul to God and does not join himself in marriage, he will become all the more worthy. For he placed the other condition lower so that no one might doubt the superior one.

### (Verse 5)

But if someone does not know how to govern his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?

It is clear that someone can then be proved likely to be a suitable ruler if he has first governed his own household correctly; for “the one who is faithful in very little is also faithful in much” (Luke 16:10).

### (Verse 6)

Not a recent convert, lest, puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil.

It is true that those inexperienced in the faith are accustomed to be lifted up by pride, especially if they receive an office. For novelty and authority inflate them, and they think themselves more worthy than others. Seeing the honor conferred on him in the first year of his new birth, he thinks that he has been called not so much for his own progress as for the progress of others, as though he were giving a benefit to religion rather than receiving one from it. Through this, being puffed up, he falls into the devil’s snare [Note: [Col. 0469D] The same Roman edition reads: “he incurs the devil’s judgment.”].

When Satan finds an opportunity in his pride, he casts him down. Therefore it is written in Solomon: “God resists the proud” (Proverbs 3:34). Hence the same Apostle says in another epistle: “The one who thinks he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Galatians 6:3). And the Lord says: “The one who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

### (Verse 7)

Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those who are outside.

Following the Lord’s teaching, he says that the future bishop ought to have a good testimony from outsiders, because, as the Lord says, the one who is faithful in little things is faithful also in great things. “And if you have not been faithful in another’s mammon, who will give you what is yours?” [Note: [Col. 0470D] The word *mammon* had been deleted in the Roman edition, but for what reason?]

Thus, if someone is not found faithful in worldly affairs and human conduct, there can be no doubt that he will not be suitable in divine matters either. But if he has shown faithfulness to human beings, much more will he show it to God.

Lest he fall into reproach and the devil’s snare.

If the bishop does not have the fear of God before his eyes, but accommodates himself chiefly to the present age, God abandons him as faithless and a false prophet, and he will appear deformed and stained to everyone, because he acts otherwise than he preaches, accusing himself by his own words, having been assigned to the flock of Satan. For he proves that he truly preaches only if he attempts to practice what he preaches.

Great care must therefore be taken in choosing the one who receives the task of governing the house of God. For if suitable administrators of earthly affairs must be sought, how much more of heavenly affairs!

[Col. 0470A] ### (Verses 8–10)

Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain, holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience. And these also must first be tested, and then let them serve without blame.

In giving such extensive instructions concerning the selection of deacons, whom we know to be ministers of the priests, he indicates what kind of people he wants bishops to be: as he himself says, above reproach, not engaging in public business or shameful and base profits. For he knows that they conduct business in order to obtain profits, and that they profess nothing other than what they practice.

He calls these profits shameful when gain is pursued under a pious profession; for a person is exposed as shameful when he presents himself as pure.

After the bishop, however, he placed the ordination of the diaconate [Note: [Col. 0470D] The Roman edition has: “He placed the ordination of deacons next.”]. Why, unless because the ordination of bishops and presbyters is one? Both are priests, but the bishop is first, so that every bishop is a presbyter, though not every presbyter is a bishop. For this one is a bishop who is first among the presbyters.

Finally, he indicates that Timothy was ordained a presbyter; but because he had no one senior to him, he was a bishop. Thus he also shows how a bishop should be ordained. For it was neither right nor permitted that an inferior should ordain a superior; no one gives what he has not received.

### (Verse 11)

Women likewise must be chaste, not devoted to discord, but sober and faithful in all things.

Because he commands that a bishop be made holy, and likewise a deacon, he certainly does not want the people to be different, since the Lord says: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). Therefore he also wants women, who appear to be inferior, to be without blame, so that the Church of God may be pure.

But the Cataphrygians, seizing an opportunity for their error because he addresses women after the deacons, defend with empty presumption that women themselves ought to be ordained deacons. Yet they know that the apostles chose seven deacons. Was no woman then found suitable, when we read that holy women were among the eleven apostles?

But in order to make their own opinion appear to rest on the Apostle’s words rather than on the meaning of the law, the heretics oppose the Apostle’s words to the Apostle’s meaning. When he commands that a woman should be silent in the Church, they, on the contrary, claim for women even the authority of ecclesiastical ministry.

### (Verses 12–13)

Let deacons be husbands of one wife, governing their children and their own households well. For those who have served well acquire a good standing for themselves and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

He now adds what he had said less fully about the ordination of the diaconate. He also shows that deacons themselves ought to be husbands of one wife, so that those may be chosen for God’s ministry who have not departed from God’s ordinance. For God decreed one wife for a man, with whom he is blessed; no one is blessed with a second wife.

If they have governed their children and their households well—that is, their servants or members of their household [Col. 0471A]—they will be able to become worthy of the priesthood and to have confidence before God, knowing that they can obtain what they ask, since thereafter they restrain themselves from intercourse with women.

For in former times Levites and priests were permitted to have wives for sexual use because they had much leisure away from their ministry or priesthood. There was a great number of priests and a large supply of Levites, and each served the divine ceremonies at a fixed time according to David’s institution (1 Chronicles 6:31–32). He established twenty-four classes of priests so that they might serve in rotation. Thus Abijah belonged to the eighth class, and Zechariah exercised the priesthood in its turn, as is contained in the Book of Chronicles (1 Chronicles 23:4 and following). Consequently, when it was not their turn to serve [Col. 0471B] at the altar, they attended to their households; but when the time of their ministry approached, after purifying themselves for several days, they came to the temple to offer sacrifice to God.

Now, however, there ought to be seven deacons and several presbyters, so that there may be two in each church, and one bishop in the city. Consequently, all ought to abstain from intercourse with women, because they must be present in the Church every day and cannot have time afterward to purify themselves legitimately as the ancients did.

An offering must be made every week, and, even if not every day for visitors, at least twice a week for residents; nor are there lacking sick people who are baptized almost every day. In former times this was permitted because they were not seen in the temple for a long period but lived privately.

For if he commands laypeople to abstain for a time for the sake of prayer, so that they may devote themselves to prayer, how much more does he command Levites and priests, who ought to pray day and night for the people entrusted to them! They ought therefore to be purer than the others, because they are God’s agents.

### (Verses 14–15)

I am writing these things to you, my son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon. But if I delay, so that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth [Note: [Col. 0471D] The Roman edition reads: “how you should order the Church, which is the house of the living God.”].

As far as his knowledge was concerned, this was contained in the expectation that he would see him soon. But because something else often pleases God, whose providence is known to him alone, he says: “Lest I perhaps delay, I am writing to you so that you may know how to order the Church, which is the house of God.” Although the whole world belongs to God, the Church is nevertheless called his house; its rector today is Damasus.

For the world is in transgression, disturbed by diverse error. Therefore it is necessary that the house of God and the truth be said to exist there where he is feared according to his will. To those servants who profess these things about him—that he himself deigned to teach them—he gave the assurance that his words should not be denied, signing them with powers that no one else can perform, so that the unbelief that was accused might perish without excuse. For the signs and wonders are the foundation of this truth.

### (Verse 16)

And, by common confession, great indeed is the mystery of this devotion.

No believer denies that the sacrament of the truth preached in the Church is worthy of admiration; he calls it devotion. To those who acknowledge his magnanimity and clemency, he grants eternal and divine gifts, apart from the remission of sins, which he bestows here in the present.

He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

He says that the sacrament of God’s mystery, which is Christ in the flesh, was manifested—what had been hidden in the Spirit. For the Son of God, born as a human being, who was secretly with God, made himself known to creation through his works and preaching. This is what it means for him to have been justified in the Spirit: that the one who was in the flesh was shown through works and power to be who he was.

Then he appeared to the angels, no longer in the form of humility but in power. For he appeared humble in the flesh only until, after conquering death, he rose from the dead and his majesty was seen. Although he was born as a human being, he was not merely human. Thus the angels, recognizing the mystery that had previously been hidden and manifested in the flesh, bow the knee to him as to God and give thanks because they have learned the truth.

This truth was preached to the nations so that they might be freed from error; through it the world makes progress and is not condemned. It was believed in the world. For this reason the sacrament of God was believed in the world, so that its faithlessness might not be able to obtain pardon for its error, as the Lord says concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they will have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22).

It was taken up in glory. For what they despised as weak and deformed [Col. 0472C] was taken up in glory. After the cross, the person and power of the Savior were manifested openly, and, with the clouds serving him, he ascended gloriously into heaven.

## CHAPTER IV

### (Verses 1–5)

The Spirit clearly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences have been seared, who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

The Holy Spirit does not conceal what he has revealed about the future for the instruction and protection of the churches, so that the churches, having been forewarned, may be watchful lest they be deceived by such people. What could he have stated more clearly and openly, in order to avoid—or rather condemn—men of this destructive teaching, than to call their false assertion and feigned doctrine a doctrine of demons? Thus, when the words of this assertion are heard, it would be understood that this doctrine was composed by the devil.

The Holy Spirit had foretold that the things they assert about the incarnation of the Savior are false. This is now denounced among the Marcionites, although they have almost disappeared, [Col. 0473A] among the Patricians, or especially among the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0473D] Valesius, in the Addenda to his annotations on Socrates and Sozomen, says that the reading here should be “Patripassians.” Concerning the Patricians, see Philaster and Augustine, *On Heresies* 61.].

For these people deny that Christ was born, forbid marriage, and teach that one must abstain from foods. He says that their conscience has been seared—that is, corrupted through pretense. Just as a branding iron corrupts the skin and inflicts a mark, so deceit marks the conscience that, through the fraud of malevolence, knows one thing and professes another, marking it for destruction.

He now denies that these people can be changed so as to be saved [Note: [Cols. 0473D–0474D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “he denies that they imitate these people”; the others read more smoothly, as in the text.]; for just as a branding cannot be changed, so their mind cannot be corrected. Nothing is worse than pretense. For they are like the Jews who, understanding that Christ worked by the power of God, nevertheless said that these things were done by him through Beelzebul.

In order to mistreat the Maker of humanity, they do not grieve that they themselves were born, yet they forbid marriage and deprive Christ of flesh. And in order to advance his dishonor, they teach abstinence from the things that he instituted for our use, so that, because these things are despised, they may appear to be evil and to have been invented by an evil author.

Hence the Apostle shows that all things were made good by God, provided that they are received with thanksgiving. For they will be impure to the person who does not praise the Creator in them. Nor can these things benefit those who receive them in such a way as to mistreat their author.

(Vers. 6.) By setting these things before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine which you have embraced. What could be so true, so clear, and so provident as this: that Christian instruction be transmitted without corruption, so that its fruit may be praised as fruitful and sound in the Lord’s threshing floor [Col. 0473C]—that is, so that on the day of judgment it may not be rejected and judged destined to be burned by fire? This is the mark of a good teacher and a competent minister of our Lord Jesus Christ, especially since he says that Timothy was nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine which he had embraced. For one who had been thoroughly instructed in all the books of the Hebrews, after receiving faith, became a perfect teacher.

(Vers. 7, 8.) But reject profane and old-womanish tales, training yourself for godliness. For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for everything, possessing the promise of the present life and of the life to come. “Profane words” are understood as words opposed to the truth; “old-womanish tales” are certain ravings. Some people customarily drag these matters into controversy by their clamorous arguments, [Col. 0473D] so that an empty subject is treated as though it were a serious discussion, although its only result is vanity. He therefore warns us to turn away from things that are contrary, and likewise from things composed in a kind of old-womanish vanity; for there are some who, carried away by the heat of their spirit, throw themselves into such disputations.

He urges that attention be given to godliness, because it brings great profit. Those who devote themselves to mercy, repaying their aged parents in return, will not lack God’s assistance in the present life, and in the future they will possess immortality with glory. But he says that bodily exercise is useful only for a little while; for fasting and abstaining from foods, [Note: [Col. 0474D] Some manuscripts: “while the authority of the Creator remains.”] while the authority of the Creator remains, are of little benefit unless godliness is added to them, whose works are aided by the prayers of many in winning the Lord’s favor.

Indeed, the Gospel passage testifies that those who are generous to their brethren and serve them in various ways advance to eternal life (Matt. XXV, 41), while those who dissent from this work go into eternal fire. Bodily exercise is nothing other than restraints upon the flesh. If, then, someone—because mercy is a great matter—nevertheless suffers a lapse of the flesh, what will happen to such a person? Without doubt, he will be punished, because the one thing ought to have been done and the other by no means omitted (Luke XI, 42). But if someone has practiced bodily discipline alone, he will suffer everlasting punishments, as the Lord promised in the Gospel [Col. 0474B] (Matt. XXV, 41); for the whole substance of our discipline consists in mercy and godliness.

Carnal people, however, undertake one kind of bodily exercise, and spiritual people another. Carnal people nourish their bodies with rich food and banquets, so that they may advance with swift motion toward destruction; spiritual people, on the other hand, temper their bodies with fasts and abstinence, so that, having become sluggish with regard to desires, they may be worthy of the future resurrection. The latter chastises his body because of the hope of the future; the former cherishes it because of despair concerning the future, caring for it for a time so that it may move more quickly toward sin.

(Vers. 9, 10.) This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance. For to this end we labor and suffer persecutions, because we hope in the living God, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers. It is entirely worthy [Col. 0474C] and deserving of acceptance to suffer persecutions for the sake of the hope that is in God, because hope in the present life is fleeting, whereas in God’s promise it is firm and stable. For he is the salvation of all, because all live from him and through him, insofar as the present life is concerned; but insofar as the promised salvation is concerned, the faithful do. For he promised those who understand that after this life—which ends in death—he would give them another life, one that would flourish in immortality. Therefore he says: “especially of believers.”

(Vers. 11, 12.) Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in purity. Insofar as age was concerned, Timothy was young; but insofar as his character and conduct were concerned, [Col. 0474D] he was mature and serious. He therefore admonishes him in this way, so that his progress might be an example of good works in every respect; so that in a young man a disciplined and serious way of life might appear marvelous; so that his actions might excuse his age, and he might be regarded not as a young man but as an elder; so that older men might blush unless they showed themselves serious in conduct and character according to his example, while young men might have their contemporary as their teacher. Wonderful was the most holy young man Timothy, whose example should restrain undisciplined youth and punish the irreverence of the elderly.

[Col. 0475A] (Vers. 13, 14.) Until I come, attend to the reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate. He wants Timothy to be attentive and devoted to the practice of reading, striving with all care and diligence to exhort and teach. Exhortation occurs when by gentle speech we invite some people to a good work; teaching, however, occurs when we disclose to the minds of listeners things that lie hidden.

For if the ruler of the people neglects these duties, he neglects the grace given to him. He is appointed leader of the people for this purpose: to be concerned for their salvation by admonishing and teaching, so that his ordination may bear fruit. God appointed him for this very reason, that he might advance the salvation of his people. Therefore whoever is negligent after being placed in this authority will be regarded as a despiser of God, called least in the kingdom of heaven; for one who does not consider teaching worthy will not be able to do what is required (Matt. V, 19).

He indicates, however, that the grace of the one who is ordained is given through prophecy and the laying on of hands. Prophecy is the means by which someone is chosen as a suitable future teacher; the laying on of hands consists of mystical words by which the one chosen for this work is confirmed, receiving authority—as his own conscience bears witness—so that he may dare to offer sacrifice to God in the Lord’s place.

(Vers. 15, 16.) Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Attend to yourself and to the doctrine; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you. He admonishes Timothy to be an example to all not only in good works but also in the practice of teaching. For he indicates that the progress of his discipline must appear [Col. 0475C] not only in teaching but also in conduct; for a good tree produces good fruits (Matt. XII, 17). Likewise, good doctrine cannot have evil works, so that when good works are seen, they may be understood as the fruit of divine teaching, and hearers may be able to advance.

[Note: [Col. 0475D] The Vallianus manuscript reads: “Then they understand that the things said are true and to be feared.”]

Then they understand that the things said are true and to be feared, when they see them observed with great reverence by the very person who teaches them. This benefits the ruler of the people in two ways: he will receive the reward both of his own good works and of those who hear him; whereas if he is negligent, he will have to give an account both for himself and for them.

# CHAPTER V

[Col. 0475D] (Vers. 1, 2.) Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity. Because of the honor due to age, he teaches that an older person should be invited gently to a good work [Note: [Col. 0475D] “He teaches” is absent from all printed editions and many manuscripts, but is restored from several others.] so that he may accept admonition more readily; for once admonished, he may fear being rebuked later, which is shameful for an elder.

Among all peoples, old age is certainly honored. Hence both the Synagogue and later the Church had elders, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church. I do not know through what negligence this practice has grown obsolete, unless perhaps through the laziness—or rather the pride—of teachers, who wish to seem to be the only ones of any importance.

He judges that younger men should be admonished as brothers, with an affection born of love, so that when they see that they are being admonished out of love, they may correct themselves more readily, especially when they see that the conduct of the one admonishing them does not differ from his preaching. Older women, however, should be treated as mothers, so that when they see themselves being taught with gentle speech, they may not take it harshly, since they are making progress honorably. It is harsh for elders when they are rebuked by younger people. He wishes this to be softened by a certain moderation, so that both the speaker and the hearer may advance.

He teaches that younger women should be admonished as sisters, so that they may readily accept the discipline of good conduct. For when they see that the things pertaining to a good life are not pressed upon them imperiously, they consent, presenting themselves humbly to the one who admonishes them [Col. 0476B]. Things that cannot be obtained by authority are usually obtained by kindness; for even animals, when they guard their limbs jealously, nevertheless yield to gentleness.

(Vers. 3.) Honor widows who are truly widows. He says that those widows should be honored who have deliberately chosen widowhood: although they could have married, in order to become better and worthy of God, they rejected a second marriage, emulating the most holy Anna, who served God with fasts and prayers night and day, having experienced intercourse with one husband (Luke II, 36).

(Vers. 4.) But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her own household piously and to repay her parents with mutual gratitude; for this is pleasing before God. He says that a widow must first be tested in this life and conduct, so that she may then be worthy to be called a widow of the Church—one who submits to ecclesiastical discipline not so much for the sake of gain as for the sake of protection. Merits must come first, [Note: [Col. 0476D] Roman edition: “so that the honor due to one who approaches may be bestowed.”] so that the honor due to one who approaches may appear to be bestowed. For a woman who has piously cared for her affections and governed her household well has kept God’s law and has become worthy of the Church’s reward.

(Vers. 5.) But she who is truly a widow and desolate hopes in God and persists in prayers night and day. A widow who has children or grandchildren should not readily be admitted to the Church’s support, because if she has governed her household piously and diligently, her own people must repay her, just as she repaid her relatives. But if, as often happens, impiety has brought it about that the old woman is despised by those whom she treated piously, it is right that she be received by the Church, because she has lived faithfully according to the Lord’s law.

A widow who is therefore desolate and despised by her own people hopes in God. Seeing that she has assistance from no quarter, she is devoted to God with her whole heart, expecting from him alone the help necessary for life and salvation.

(Vers. 6.) [Note: [Col. 0476D] The Vallianus manuscript reads: “Thus he indicates that such a woman is a widow of God.”]

But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives. He indicates that a woman who is called a widow ought to be such that she devotes herself to prayer in order to win the Lord’s favor, serving God night and day, and showing that for this reason she rejected a second marriage: to devote herself to the Lord’s discipline.

For if, under the name of widow, she devotes herself to pleasure or luxury, she must be regarded as dead while alive, because it is a kind of imposture to do one thing and profess another. [Note: [Col. 0477D] The same manuscript reads: “wanting not the service and devotion of God, but the honor attached to the name of widow.”] Such women want not the service and devotion of God, but the honor attached to the name of widow, although the profession of that name itself indicates its meaning: having rejected a husband, she chose God, whom she should serve with her whole mind, for the sake of the promised life.

(Vers. 7.) Command these things also, so that they may be irreproachable. He wants a widow to display such care in her actions and conduct that she cannot be blamed. Removed from the hope of worldly living and from the duty of caring for the body, she has turned to God for this purpose: to live a commendable life. When the opportunities that usually open access to sins have been removed, good conduct can remain unharmed [Col. 0477B].

(Vers. 8.) [Note: [Col. 0477D] The Roman edition reads, “But if anyone.” And below, “because, like the faithless.”] But if anyone does not care for his own people, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. He says that this widow, who was negligent toward her own affections and failed to raise her family in the discipline and correction of the Lord, must not be honored; for, like the faithless, she has not obeyed the law of the Lord and must therefore be considered worse. For one who lives under the law and in the fear of God but despises it must necessarily be worse than one who is not subject to the law: the latter is ignorant, whereas the former despises knowingly.

(Vers. 9, 10.) Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one man, who has testimony for good works: whether she has raised children, received strangers as guests, washed the feet of the saints, assisted those suffering oppression, and followed every good work. If a widow is commended by the distinction of her former works, he teaches that she should be chosen. Her name is entered into the Church’s records by the judgment of the Lord, and her former life declares her worthy. Instructed in divine service and wearing out her life in such service, she should be received into the bosom of the Church, to whose lawful ministries she once devoted herself.

(Vers. 11.) But refuse younger widows. For when they have lived in pleasure, they want to marry in Christ. He prohibits the admission of young widows to this profession, for trust should not readily be placed in an unstable age, especially since there are examples of some who, after professing this way of life, possess the name but not the works of widowhood, and, turning toward marriage, become entangled in its attractions.

For one who thinks that she may live in Christ amid pleasures does not remain innocent at all. Luxury draws her toward its members, so that she becomes subject to sin; for pleasures are the doors of sin. It is not unknown where one is headed when one loves a dissipated life.

(Vers. 12.) They incur condemnation because they have nullified their first faith. He shows what awaits such women, so that they may not rashly undertake what is difficult to fulfill. Or, if the mind is devoted to this dedication, let her keep it for the time being within herself; [Note: [Col. 0477D] All editions and some manuscripts: “because he says that it is rash.”] for she has learned that it is rash to profess [Col. 0478A] what should not yet be entrusted to a youthful age.

For one becomes liable to condemnation who turns away from what he had rightly undertaken. However praiseworthy it is if someone fulfills what is believed to be beyond her strength, so much more deserving of punishment will she be if, through rash presumption, she dares to impose upon herself what she cannot bear. Nor should forgiveness be granted to one who is found faithless from the beginning.

(Vers. 13.) At the same time they also learn to go around from house to house, and not only to be idle but also talkative and inquisitive, speaking about things that ought not to be spoken of. Certain virgins or widows, commended by their profession—for the name of this matter is glorious—are welcomed into the houses of the rich. They act in such a way that they may comply with their wishes, going about and seeking things to report to them in which they take pleasure, so that the idle may be rewarded with gifts. In an evil custom they seek more from stories than from what they do with their hands, so that they may go out haughty and adorned, acting contrary to their profession.

This practice often proves harmful to them even in the present life, for what they always think hidden is revealed. What does it mean that they speak about things that ought not to be spoken of? They are nearly married women, participants in many secrets, flatterers, and complainers about servants.

(Vers. 14, 15.) Therefore I want younger women to marry, bear children, [Note: [Col. 0478D] The Vallianus manuscript and several others read: “to be heads of households and govern the home.”] be heads of households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already turned aside after Satan. Since what he said above about such women is contrary and unlawful and will lead them to death, he therefore gives the counsel and command that they do what is lawful.

It is better to care for one’s own household [Note: [Col. 0478D] Most manuscripts read this way; others, as do the editions: “than to flatter in another’s house … to go about conspicuously.”] than to commit adultery in another’s household; and it is much better to marry than, under a good and pious profession, to walk conspicuously in evil. It is better to seek one’s livelihood with modesty by one’s own hands than, shamelessly and in idleness, to await another’s provisions.

For in this way Satan finds an opportunity to overthrow unsuspecting souls, when those who make a pious profession behave unjustly; nothing is more dangerous than for one’s conduct to contradict one’s profession. Satan does not envy open evil, because he rejoices in it. [Note: [Col. 0478D] All editions and some manuscripts read “but the righteous man”; other manuscripts have the better reading, “but this man.”] But the one whom he sees deceiving others he works to expose as his own son, not God’s; and this outcome does not displease God.

(Vers. 16.) If any believing man or woman has widows, let him or her provide them with sufficient support, so that the Church may not be burdened with their maintenance and may have enough for the true widows. What wonder if apostolic authority was able to foresee what would happen? For what he said is evident: the widows of believers now greatly burden the Church, as do those who appear wealthy in the world. Because of their old age, they remove these women from the work of spinning and weaving, and thus deprive them, in part if not entirely, of clothing and food, so that the women are driven by their very poverty to the Church in order to live.

Those wealthy people ought not only to give generously to their own needy, but also to feed and clothe other poor women. This causes great harm. For when assistance is given to these women, less—or nothing—is given to others who ought to receive more and who are worthy of being supported at the Church’s expense. The Church is thus burdened when it is forced to clothe many whom it ought to clothe only a few; and the people, who could willingly and frequently provide for a small number, are compelled to abandon larger numbers, so that they either complain or come to their aid more slowly.

For although he commands that a widow who was the wife of one man be chosen, now among them are found not only wives of two or three husbands, but also women who have lived more disgracefully. This sometimes happens through negligence, [Note: [Col. 0479D] Some manuscripts: “sometimes through the influence of someone making a recommendation.”] and sometimes through the influence of someone making a recommendation.

(Vers. 17.) Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching. Good and faithful stewards should be judged worthy not only of exalted honor but also of material support, so that they may not be distressed by lack of means but may rejoice all the more in their faith and teaching. For a person becomes more diligent when poverty does not humiliate him, and his authority increases [Note: [Col. 0479D] The Vallianus manuscript reads: “when he also rejoices,” and so forth.] when he sees that even in the present life he receives the fruit of his labor—not so that he may abound, but so that he may not fail.

(Vers. 18.) For Scripture says: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. XXV, 4); and: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X, 7). The one who proclaims the kingdom of God ought to have such a reward that he is neither saddened nor exalted.

301 (Vers. 19.) Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter [Col. 0479C]. Since the honor of this order is exalted—for such men are vicars of Christ—an accusation against this person should therefore not readily be admitted. It ought to seem incredible that this man, who is a bishop of God, has behaved criminally, just as it is credible that an actor is utterly disgraceful.

(Vers. 20.) Those who sin, rebuke before everyone, so that the rest may have fear. [Note: [Col. 0479D] The editions and some manuscripts read: “For indeed”; the Roman edition: “For truly”; other manuscripts have the better reading found in the text.] A presbyter’s crime should not readily be believed; nevertheless, if it is proved or manifest that he has behaved irreverently, he commands that the man be rebuked publicly, so that the others may also be terrified. This benefits not only those who have been ordained but also the people; for when they see a distinguished man rebuked because of his error, they must take care for themselves.

(Vers. 21, 22.) I testify before God, and Christ Jesus, [Col. 0479D] and the elect angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality or turning aside to another side. Do not lay hands quickly on anyone, [Note: [Col. 0480D] Roman edition: “nor share in the sins of others.”] nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.

He places this testimony before God the Father, Christ his Son, and his elect angels, whom the Lord calls holy in the Gospel (Mark VIII, 38). They are therefore elect because there are also others who are reprobate, who are not angels of God but of the devil, agreeing with his apostasy.

Under this testimony, therefore, he commands that the things concerning the ordering of the Church be observed, and that nothing be done without prior consideration, lest anyone readily receive ecclesiastical dignity unless his life and conduct have first been examined. Thus, once proved worthy, he may be appointed a minister or priest, so that afterward, if he should appear blameworthy, the ruler of the people may not perhaps regret having failed to determine fully what kind of person he was appointing [Note: [Col. 0480D] The same Roman edition reads: “not having provided with complete certainty.”]

Nor should one whose sins are suspected be ordained, lest the one ordaining him be stained by his vices and offenses. If, then, the offenses are entirely hidden, the ruler will be free from guilt, because his conscience is clear. Suspicion makes a person anxious; he sins if he does not investigate and nevertheless ordains.

The one who is to be ordained ought to be proved better than the others. It is not enough that he be without crime; his merits in good works must precede him, so that he may be considered worthy of ordination. If a bishop observes these things, he will present himself as pure in religion, and for this he will receive a reward in the future.

(Vers. 23.) No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses. He now gives a specific recommendation, so that Timothy may govern himself by sound teaching. For God wisely wishes to be served in such a way that people do not become weak through excessive austerity and afterward require the help of physicians. One must practice moderation, so that, if possible, the service once begun may be advanced gradually rather than diminished through lack of consideration.

Immoderation unsettles the soul itself, so that when it is anxious about illness, it is not wholly devoted to divine service. Lack of foresight causes harm. When the soul is established in tranquility, it raises its whole heart to God, entreating with sound judgment [Note: [Col. 0480D] The Carnian manuscript reads: “the things that ought to be brought to peace.”] for the things that should be requested.

(Vers. 24, 25.) The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but the sins of others follow afterward. In the same way, good works are manifest, and those that are otherwise constituted cannot remain hidden. He wants it understood that there will be no excuse for those who cling to people whose sins [Note: [Col. 0480D] The same manuscript reads: “when brought forward, are a greater burden.”] are plainly visible, so that, although such people ought to be avoided, they may instead be treated as honorable.

This therefore means that the man of God must be separated from such people, especially the steward of Christ, who also has authority to rebuke them. If they promise to amend themselves, they are to be retained. But he shows that the evil works of others follow them, because although they are judged good while alive, they are exposed after death. Thus those who previously displayed themselves as suitable are later revealed as impostors.

For the same reason, just as evil deeds, so good deeds are manifest. A good life and modest conduct cannot be hidden; together with godliness, they make people perfect. But just as certain evils are hidden for the present, so also are certain good deeds. No one can know everything about other people; rather, he proves and judges from what he sees and hears. He considers whether what is said agrees with the person of whom it is said, whether good or evil. Whatever has been hidden from human beings will be made public on the day of judgment.

This is why these things have been said: so that they may know that people of this kind have a more serious case than others. For one who, although evil, displays himself as good is worse than one who is openly evil.

302 # CHAPTER VI

(Vers. 1.) Let all who are under the yoke as slaves consider their own masters worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the doctrine may not be blasphemed. He wants slaves, through their obedience, to cause their masters to give thanks to God; for when they have rendered faithful service to them according to God’s discipline, perhaps the masters themselves will submit to this discipline.

(Vers. 2.) Those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers; rather, they must serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved, receiving benefits. If he commands that pagan masters be served with every form of diligence, how much more believing masters! A slave then proves himself subject to the fear of God if he obeys a believing and earthly master with his whole heart. He must not think that his master should be despised because he is called a brother on account of their common faith; for the one who thinks a believing master should be despised will deserve the greater rebuke.

(Vers. 3.) Teach and exhort these things. He wants the Lord’s doctrine to be made manifest, so that its detractors may see that there is nothing in it for which they can find fault. At the same time, let them consider the hidden disgrace in their own sacred practices, and let them be ashamed of what will leave them without excuse.

[Col. 0481C] (Vers. 4, 5.) If anyone teaches otherwise and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with the doctrine that accords with godliness, he is puffed up, knowing nothing, but is sick over questions and disputes about words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people who are corrupt in mind and deprived of the truth, supposing that godliness and the worship of God are a means of gain. Withdraw from such people.

He commands that those who disagree with Catholic discipline be rejected, especially those who, when convicted and corrected, refuse to yield because of the disturbance of a perverse mind, taking pleasure and nourishment in disputes. A haughty person does not allow himself to be defeated; indeed, in seeking popular approval, he bursts into conflict. This is something gentle and good men must avoid.

For contention is never without quarrel; and it would be little enough if quarrel alone arose, but blasphemies and enmities also result, things alien to the servants of God. Yet those whose minds are corrupt and who are deprived of the truth judge these things useful. They consider the worship of God and godliness a means of gain, expecting nothing from the future but looking for ways to get through the present life, like the worldly sects that are known to have been invented for the sake of present profits. They are not unaware that some people willingly hear the claim that one ought to flourish in this life; therefore they must withdraw from such persons.

(Vers. 6.) But godliness with contentment is a great gain. [Note: [Col. 0481D] Roman edition: “Godliness, when someone is content with his own lot.”] He calls it great wealth and acquisition if a believer is content with what is his. The person acquired by God’s mercy for future life is richer both in himself and in other respects if he considers what he has sufficient for the present, not hesitating to give generously from it. For every greedy person is impious, harming both himself and others.

(Vers. 7, 8.) For we brought nothing into the world, and it is clear that we can take nothing out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these things. He plainly declares that mortal people labor in vain to pursue abundance and wish to become wealthy, since they know that they possess nothing as their own in the world. What benefit does human desire produce, except that it becomes its own enemy? It brought nothing into the world and will be able to take nothing away. Why does it impose anxiety upon itself and seek to accumulate? A person will leave this world as he entered it.

Job also writes this and confesses it in his suffering, saying: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return to the earth . . . . Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I, 21). If the greedy did not retain possessions to their own destruction, few would store up what could benefit many, with advantage even to themselves.

(Vers. 9, 10.) But those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the root of all evils is greed, which some have desired and, having strayed from the faith, have pierced themselves with many pains.

Nothing is so harsh and destructive as for an ecclesiastical person, especially one who holds a high position, to pursue the wealth of this world [Col. 0482C], because he harms not only himself but also others. He provides people with a contrary example; many imitators of him will necessarily arise to their destruction. The more honorable his rank, the more he encourages others to imitate him, especially in a matter toward which life in this world is naturally inclined. For greed can admit every evil.

Therefore it is called the root of all evils: in order to satisfy its desires, which is impossible, it commits sorcery, murder, obscenity, and every kind of crime. Nor is it secure in the present, because it is always covetous; and in the future it is condemned.

(Vers. 11.) But you, man of God, flee these things. He urges and commands the man of God to cut himself off from them, so that he may be secure here and receive divine rewards in the future [Col. 0482D]. For one who despises greed, which persuades so many, is not crowned without reason.

(Vers. 12.) Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, and tranquility of spirit. Fight the good fight of faith; seize eternal life, to which you were called, and confessed the good confession before many witnesses. Since greed is an unjust thing, he commands the man of God to reject it by pursuing righteousness, godliness, and the other virtues he mentions. He will not be able to avoid greed unless he clings to the things opposed to it.

But how can a greedy person be faithful, when by his actions he denies what he appears to confess in words? How can he be a lover of the brotherhood, whose hands are closed? How can he be patient, when he is always reaching out toward what belongs to others? Or how can he possess tranquility of spirit, when day and night he burns with the greed of desire?

But since this iniquity was foreign to Timothy, the man of God, he is commanded to undertake the good fight of faith. Faith’s victory occurs when all vices and crimes are subdued, so that one may attain the rewards of eternal life. The confession of this faith is contained, from the very beginnings of faith, in the Church’s records, with the one asking and the other answering as witnesses.

(Vers. 13–16.) I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who testified to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, that you keep the commandment unstained and irreproachable until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0483B]. He will display him at the proper times—the blessed and only sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal power. Amen.

With great vigilance and foresight he gives these commands to the ruler of the Church, for in the person of the ruler the salvation of the whole people rests. He is not so careful merely out of concern for Timothy, but for Timothy’s successors, so that by Timothy’s example they may preserve the ordering of the Church, and, handing on a model to those who would come after them, may begin with themselves.

Finally, he says: “that you keep the commandment unstained until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He binds this command so firmly that he testifies that he gives it before God and Christ. To inspire fear, he recalls Christ’s passion; one who despises the reason for which Christ suffered must necessarily become liable for that passion.

He did not omit the day of judgment, which will come at the time predestined by God’s will. He declares him alone blessed and powerful, King of kings and Lord. For he alone possesses blessedness, power, dominion, and kingship in himself and from no one else; and he likewise possesses immortality.

The Father possesses all these things, and the Son likewise possesses them from the Father. But inaccessible light belongs to the Father alone, because he has never appeared to anyone. Finally, he adds: “whom no human being has seen or can see.” This is not because the Son’s light is something different—for the Psalm says: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXIII, 10), that is, that the Father’s light is in the Son [Col. 0483D]—but because no one has seen the Father, and therefore he dwells in inaccessible light.

No one has the capacity to see God the Father except Christ: whoever is from God has seen God. The Son, however, because he himself accomplishes all things, is said both to appear and to be seen. Therefore the feature peculiar to the Father is what was stated above: “To him be honor and eternal power. Amen.” This is the truth.

(Verses 17, 18, 19.) Command those who are rich in this present age not to be high-minded, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who grants us all things abundantly for enjoyment.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “abundantly for enjoyment . . . so that, having become rich in good works, they may be ready to share and willing to communicate, storing up for themselves,” etc.]

Let them be ready for good works, rich in good deeds, ready to distribute and willing to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life. That is the true life which we hope is to come, which is bounded neither by decline nor by time; for it is eternal, and therefore rightly called true. The present life is only an image of life, not its reality. And because an image is not altogether emptiness, that life is acquired in this one. In order that we may hasten toward it, we learn from the image—of which the reality is superior—that it is attained neither by pride nor by hope in riches, but by humility and hope in God, who promised it.

For our hope must be placed in him, because he supplies what is necessary for our use—not in riches themselves, but in their giver. What hope can there be in something perishable and uncertain? Some depart from these riches, and those who seem to remain with them gain no profit from them in the future, but rather loss, unless they share them with the needy. For riches are not eternal, so that they should be preferred to the life to come. They make people proud, as though they promised immortality.

We have the example of the resurrection in Christ; yet many do not love Christ as they love riches, for which no example is seen of their having delivered anyone from death. Christ redeemed us, not riches. He displayed in himself the likeness of the future life, so that, rejecting all these things, we might follow him and attain immortal and heavenly riches. Therefore we must strive to be rich in good deeds and, through these earthly resources, acquire spiritual riches. Let us sow on earth, so that we may reap in heaven, where an eternal treasure is stored.

(Verses 20, 21.) O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have fallen away from the faith. Grace be with you.

He gives the same admonition: that the matters stated above should be preserved, while those opposed to religion should be avoided—matters that usurp only the name of knowledge and are deceptive in their profession, so that they may deceive the simple. They pretend to have faith, from which they have fallen away, in order to introduce faithlessness. And he added his signature in his own hand, saying: “Grace be with you.”

[Col. 0483]

## ON THE SECOND EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO TIMOTHY

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0483D]

He now writes another epistle to Timothy, so that, already instructed in ecclesiastical discipline, he may urge him to martyrdom by his own example and show what the hope of the promise is. For some will turn away from sound doctrine because it seems harsh to them, and will turn to fables—that is, to human inventions.

## CHAPTER ONE

(Verses 1, 2.) Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God according to the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, his beloved son.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “The Apostle now writes to Timothy . . . to teach what the hope of the promise is through the faith of Christ, and by his own example . . .”]

By this he indicates that he was called an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, in order to teach what and how great the future promise is in the faith of Christ, so that through his preaching he might increase the number of those being saved through the Lord’s discipline. For servants are worthy who, by their diligence and faith, enlarge the affairs of their masters. He writes this to him as to a most beloved son, so that he may become an imitator of it, handing the same things on to others. Thus, through the succession of generations, he may remain an unfailing and capable teacher, through whom the asserted truth may gain many for the promised life.

Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

He wishes that the Father’s grace, given in mercy, may be present with him, and likewise the grace of Christ Jesus our Lord, because God bestows his grace through Christ, so that there may be one grace belonging to both.

(Verses 3, 4, 5.) I give thanks to my God, whom I serve with a pure conscience from my forefathers, because I have an unfailing remembrance of you in my prayers, desiring greatly to see you night and day, remembering your tears, so that I may be filled with joy when I recall the sincere faith that is in you, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice; and I am certain that it dwells in you also.

Since it is fitting to remember good things, he therefore gives thanks to God, because he remembered Timothy, a remarkable man; this itself too is a gift of God. For the person who thinks about good men is not without merit. And because the God of Christians is the same as the God of the Jews, he testifies that he gives thanks to that God whom he served through his forefathers. For when his ancestors hoped for what he had begun to preach, their faith was one and the same.

And because he entered into the service of his parents, and because he was still among them when they served God, he rightly says: “Whom I serve from my forefathers.” How? “With a pure conscience,” he says; for he once persecuted the Church in such a way that he did so out of love for God, not from malice.

For similarly it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews that Levi, who received tithes, gave tithes to Melchizedek, because, it says, Levi was in Abraham’s loins when Abraham offered tithes to Melchizedek (Heb. 7:9–10). So here too he says that he served God through his forefathers, because Levi too is said to have offered tithes in his forefather. For Levi is the father of Jacob, the grandfather of Isaac, and the great-grandfather of Abraham.

He therefore declares that he remembers Timothy very deeply and eagerly longs for him because of his tears, which, as may be understood, he shed out of love for the Apostle when the Apostle was departing from him. He therefore longs, not without reason, for one who loves him, so that he may be filled with joy through their shared gladness, because of the sincere faith which he indicates was also in Timothy’s grandmother and mother, and certainly in Timothy himself. Thus all this affection is on account of the faith that was inviolable in them.

(Verses 6, 7.) For this reason I remind you to rekindle the gift of God that is in you through the laying on of my hands; for God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sobriety.

He indicates that he remembered the sincerity of his parents’ faith in order to make Timothy stronger. For who, hearing the praise of those whose very qualities he shares, would not grow, adding courage to such strengths? Thus he rekindles in himself the gift of God’s grace received through ordination to the presbyterate, while he warms his spirit with the cheerfulness of his mind, rejoicing in himself, just as one rejoices in the freshness of ordination.

Finally he added: “For,” he says, “God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power.” The renewed man emerges from fear, receiving a spirit of joy because of justification. For every unrighteous person is in fear, not strong but weak; not in love but in hatred; not in sobriety of mind but wounded by error. But if he is free from these things, through faith he will be strong, beloved, and sober.

(Verses 8.) Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner.

He teaches that one must possess steadfastness and should not tremble in one’s confession. There is no reason to be ashamed of it, because although Christ appeared to be a man, by his deeds he showed himself to be God. Although he was crucified, he nevertheless rose from the dead and, while many saw him, was taken up into heaven as a cloud received him (Acts 1:9). This is therefore not a cause of weakness but of power, because where weakness is thought to be, there power appears. Thus the one proved to have conquered is foolishly said to have been weakened.

In the same way, there is nothing in the Apostle that should bring shame. For although he is said to have been humbled by afflictions and beatings, in that very respect he confounds his detractors, because in signs and wonders he is seen to be manifestly marvelous by God’s will. Thus it is understood that he was humbled not by weakness but willingly, for the advancement of a certain merit. For this reason God permits his servants to be humbled by the wicked, so that he may not appear to grant rewards to them unjustly.

(Verses 9.) But work with me for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “who delivered us.”]

Because death was conquered by the power of God, so that we might be saved, it is fitting that we repay our Redeemer in some measure. Since we cannot respond to all his benefits, let us at least carry out his embassy faithfully and diligently.

And he called us with his holy calling.

The calling is holy when people are chosen to govern God’s holy people. The elder, who is chosen as a leader of holiness, is called to holiness.

Not according to our merits.

This is true: if you examine the matter thoroughly, no human being can appear worthy to be Christ’s representative, for all those whom he chose had previously been sinners. Thus, in comparison with others, they were found worthy; but with respect to the matter itself, all are unworthy.

But according to his purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times.

God, in his gracious determination, long ago resolved to save sinners—for God knew beforehand what would happen in humanity, before he made the human being and before the human being sinned. He predestined how humanity would be restored, at what time, through whom, and by what means people could be saved, so that this gift might appear to be granted neither on account of the merit of those who are saved nor on account of those through whom they are called, but by God’s grace through the faith of Christ.

(Verses 10.) But now it has been revealed through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ.

He testifies that God’s gift, which had been hidden in mystery before eternal times, was revealed through Christ’s incarnation and coming, when people began to receive remission of sins.

(Verses 11.) He indeed destroyed death, but brought life to light by eternity through the Gospel, for which I was appointed a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “But he brought life and eternity to light.” The same wording occurs below.]

He shows in what way Christ saved his people, saying that he destroyed death, which was the enemy of humanity, so that humanity could not rise from the underworld. Then he brought life to light by eternity, so that, having risen from the dead, he could no longer die. For life that is defined by time is obscure, while it sleeps, while it is ignorant, and while it behaves badly. He shows how life is brought to light: through the Gospel, eternity is given to believers, with the teacher of the Gentiles preaching.

(Verses 12.) For this reason I also suffer these things.

While preaching God’s gift, he suffers the devil as an enemy, so that the devil may stir up afflictions against him, because he has snatched people from the devil’s jaws.

But I am not ashamed.

Secure in this, because a great promised reward is reserved for afflictions, he is not ashamed but glories in them.

For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit for that day.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “for that day . . . who, through hope and confidence . . .”]

This is what he means: he is secure in the hope and confidence of the Savior’s majesty, because what he entrusts to him is safe. And what does he entrust to him except his salvation? Thus, by suffering here for him, he may find salvation with him when he begins to judge, so that, while punishing the unbelievers, he may pronounce this man worthy of eternal life.

(Verses 13, 14.) Hold to the pattern of sound words that you heard from me in faith and love, which are in Christ Jesus; guard the good deposit entrusted to you through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Keep the pattern of sound words . . .” [Col. 0488D] “Guard the good deposit.”]

He calls his commandments, together with his deeds, a pattern of saving doctrine, and commands Timothy to follow it, so that he may preserve it with the help of the Holy Spirit.

(Verses 15, 16.) You know that all those in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.

Those whom he mentions were full of deceit. They pretended to be friends of the Apostle so that, by associating with him, they might learn something with which to slander him or set others against him. After they saw that they had been exposed, they withdrew from him.

May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains.

This refreshing is to be understood in two ways: he refreshed him by his support during the necessities of custody, and he supplied whatever was needed either by the Apostle or by those in need. Because of his hope in the things that had been promised, he was not ashamed to approach and seek out a man held in custody. Those whom he mentioned above, because they were ashamed of Christ’s cross, abandoned the Apostle in his need.

(Verses 17, 18.) But when I was in Rome, he sought me out with great diligence and found me.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “But when I had come to Rome.”]

May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day.

When the Apostle came to Rome and appealed to Caesar, he was guarded by soldiers. At that time Onesiphorus, out of love and respect for his teaching, sought him out with great diligence and found him. His visit was so acceptable to the Apostle that he commends him to the Lord in this way, so that he may find mercy from the Lord on the day of judgment. Just as he sought the Apostle and found him, so, when he seeks mercy, may he find it with the Judge.

For this is his prayer: that the Lord, the Father of heaven and earth, may grant him to find favor with the Lord of the human race, namely, the Son. This is like the passage in Genesis: “And the Lord,” it says, “rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven” (Gen. 19:24).

And how much he served me at Ephesus, you know better.

Since some people usually serve persons more than causes, wishing to please the powerful, the Apostle shows that Onesiphorus’s goodness was universal, so that he would not seem to have commended him merely because he had served the Apostle. It was evident that he had been generous to everyone.
