[Note: The Roman edition reads: “the household of Onesiphorus in general.”]

## CHAPTER TWO

(Verses 1, 2.) You therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and in the things that you heard from me through many witnesses. Entrust these things to faithful men who will be capable of teaching others also.

He commands Timothy to be steadfast and strong in teaching the grace of God that was given in Christ Jesus—not only in grace, but also in the mysteries concerning Christ. He wishes the secrets to be entrusted to faithful and worthy men who can teach others, not indiscriminately to ordinary and negligent people. For a teacher must be chosen with great care.

(Verses 3, 4.) Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.

What he says is clear: no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24). Worldly affairs must necessarily serve greed, and unless people have lied, they cannot have completed such transactions. It is therefore a sin, though a slight one. The ecclesiastical person proves himself to God for this reason: devoted to him, he fulfills the office he promised, concerned with God’s affairs and separated from worldly business. For it is not fitting for one person to have a double profession.

(Verses 5.) Even if someone competes, he is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For even if someone competes in the contest . . .”]

He wishes God’s soldier to be so trained in God’s works and in the office assigned to him that he may attain the reward of glory: vigilant with his whole mind in divine service, despising present things and loving heavenly things. For he proved himself for this purpose, so that, laboring here, he might be rewarded in heaven.

(Verses 6, 7.) It is necessary that the laboring farmer be the first to receive a share of the fruits. Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things.

Timothy was a saint of such great abstinence that he restrained himself even from lawful things. This is what is meant: he abstained from sharing in the treasury, although the Lord had ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (1 Cor. 9:14). Therefore the Apostle first commands him to take what is his due, since he is first, and then distribute it to the others.

(Verses 8, 9.) Remember that Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, is of the seed of David according to my Gospel, for which I suffer hardship even to chains, like a criminal; but the word of God is not bound.

Because there were to be many sons of the devil who would deny that the Son of God had become incarnate, he mentions this because they deceitfully tried to assert it under the name of the apostles. He added, “according to my Gospel,” in order to exclude the false conversations of evil minds. For the heretics should not be believed about the apostles more than the apostles themselves, who testify to their own preaching—a preaching which Paul complains that he carries out with hardship.

He was afflicted by trials and prisons because he offended both Jews and Gentiles, as it seemed to them, by preaching unbelievable things. He made the Jews angry because of the Law, which he taught was coming to an end; and he made the Gentiles his enemies because he preached one God in Christ. Thus they treated him like a criminal, binding and imprisoning him in the hope that he might be silenced, not knowing that the word of God could not be bound.

Indeed, when he was often imprisoned, he suffered no loss but gained advantage. For there was never a lack of someone to whom he could preach in prison, so that those whom he could not freely invite to the faith he might nourish with the word of God while he was in chains.

(Verses 10.) Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory.

So that he might save through his preaching those predestined to life, he was subjected to dangers, knowing that he would gain the progress of their sought-for salvation.

(Verses 11, 12.) The saying is trustworthy: if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him.

He indicates that one can attain Christ’s immortality and glory if one remains in the form of baptism, where all sins die, so that, renewed, we may flee all former vices and crimes and, following the footsteps of our author, be seen to have died to sins.

If something further is added to the matter—that we should not endure tribulations and afflictions for the Lord’s name with reluctance—then, by enduring these things, we shall reign together with him. For it is fitting that one who suffers reproaches and dangers for him should appear glorious in his kingdom.

If we deny him, he too will deny us.

This is true, because if we have not confessed him before human beings, then he too will say to us in that necessity of the coming judgment: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). This signifies punishment.

(Verses 13.) If we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.

No one can take away from the Lord what he possesses. For who is stronger than he, through whom all things came into existence? Nothing can be added to the perfect one, because the person who believes him contributes nothing to him, just as the person who does not believe in him takes nothing away from him. Whatever is done therefore concerns our progress, so that we may not remain in ignorance. He is not made firm by us, since he is firm in himself and with himself.

(Verses 14.) Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord.

Do not quarrel over words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear.

He warns that controversies should be avoided, while commands should be given under the fear and dread of God. For controversy can still generate scruples in those who are less firmly established. In disputes, people often bring forward such arguments, after sharpening the blade of malice, that they disturb the minds of beginning believers.

(Verses 15.) Take diligent care of yourself, so that you may present yourself to God as approved, a worker who is not ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.

[Note: The Laud manuscript reads: “that [he may make himself approved] by spiritual disputation.”]

Since some say that controversy benefits those who hear, the Apostle, knowing that it does more harm, commands each person to take care that, rejecting disputation, he may make himself approved. He calls those who rely on disputes “not ashamed,” because contention necessarily forces out something—or rather, many things—that are said against conscience. Thus a person loses inwardly in the mind, though he departs outwardly as the victor.

No one allows himself to be defeated, even when he knows that what he hears is true. But the person who speaks to those who are willing and peaceable handles the matter rightly and with a good conscience. There should therefore be discussion among God’s servants, not disputation.

(Verses 16, 17.) But avoid profane novelties of words, for they advance greatly toward emptiness, and their speech spreads like cancer.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “for they advance greatly toward impiety.”]

He continues the same point, that controversies should be avoided. It is not fitting for people of one faith to quarrel; rather, in discussion they should bear with one another and agree in good statements. If something appears unacceptable, it should be passed over peacefully.

Opponents and dissenters usually provoke one another; one of them is catholic and the other profane. The catholic person is therefore the one to whom the Apostle commands that he despise and avoid empty fables. He should be peaceful, always bringing words forth from his conscience, and should not allow impious words to be uttered in his presence.

For such things give some people an opportunity to advance toward worse things. There is no shortage of people who, hearing profane speech, conceive an evil thought. This is why controversy is harmful.

(Verses 18.) Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have wandered from the truth by saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they have subverted the faith of some.

Now he reveals the names of those on whose account he warns that controversies must be avoided. He identifies them as profane and impious, wandering from the truth. They denied what is the distinctive mark of Christians: that they should believe they will rise from the dead in the future.

[Note: All editions read: “what is manifest among Christians.” Some manuscripts, however, read: “what is outstanding,” and others: “what is excellent.” Both readings are suitable; one manuscript even reads: “what is distinctive among Christians.”]

As we learn from another Scripture, they said that resurrection takes place in children. There was no shortage of someone who would give perverse assent to this against the faith he had received at the beginning.

(Verses 19.) But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

The foundation of God is faith, which contains what God promised. This faith cannot be overthrown by the inventions of faithless people and heretics. Although they deny the future things that we believe, God will nevertheless grant what we believe he will grant, as his promise bears witness.

The seal of God’s promise is therefore our faith, which confirms God’s words. On the day of judgment God will recognize those who bear his sign, who dissent from the iniquity of the faithless and the heretics, which thinks it can weaken God’s promise. Nothing is so unjust as to oppose God’s faithfulness.

Thus Moses said concerning Dathan, Abiron, and Korah, when they dared to offer sacrifices against God’s command (Num. 16:35): “The Lord knows those who are his.” By these words he showed what destruction awaited those who perverted God’s words.

(Verses 20.) But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor.

By this statement he signified that there are different kinds of people in the Church: some good and eminent men, whom he wishes to be understood as gold; some merely good, whom he designates as silver; and others who are not good, whom he calls wooden and earthen vessels.

I think this is clear to everyone, for the Apostle’s frequent rebuking speech demonstrates it in the Church of the Corinthians. Now it is openly evident in our Church, and it is confirmed by clear readings in the temple at Jerusalem, which was a type of the Church.

For there were Sadducees there, from whose root came Hymenaeus and Philetus. After the Apostle had spoken of their perverse opinion, he immediately added this, showing that it is not surprising to see dissenting people in the Church. In the Church of the Corinthians, of which I spoke, there were also some who, dissenting, denied the resurrection.

Yet the mad Novatian, in order to flatter his error, teaches that this must be understood differently, so that the great house is believed to signify the whole world, which contains the diversity of human beings. But it is clear that the Apostle used the example of a rich and wealthy household which, although it is abundant, nevertheless has wooden and earthen vessels. In the same way, the Church, although it is called holy, nevertheless has vicious people and those who hold perverse opinions, as I mentioned above.

[Note: In the Roman edition, here and below “Novatian” is not written, but “Novatus.”]

He shows that these people are worthy of dishonor, though not destined to perish; rather, they are to be purified through fire, because they are necessary in some respect to the household.

But Novatian, lifted up by pride, in order to defend the general truth and holiness of his Church, decided that the passage must be understood as though the Church were with him and contained everyone purified, on account of those matters for which he accuses us as guilty.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “who accuses us as guilty.”]

But why was there any need at this point to say something about the world, or why should he assert that the world signifies the great house? For the Lord says to the apostles: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19). How then can those who are denied to be of the world be enclosed within the world?

And the same Apostle says: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5:12). In one house, all belong under one name; for everyone is reckoned under the name of his one Lord. But the world contains people of diverse professions, so that they profess to have different gods and lords.

He therefore does not call the world the great house, but the Church, in which all are under the name of one Lord.

(Verses 21.) Therefore, if anyone purifies himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.

Here another heresy is convicted of its fraud: it asserts that certain souls are evil by nature and cannot be compelled toward good. Yet this passage says that evil people can be changed into good and the filthy can be purified.

Hymenaeus and Philetus could have cleansed their understanding if they had wished, so that they might become a sanctified vessel prepared for honor.

(Verses 22.) Flee youthful desires.

Youthful desires are hostile; they are worldly pleasures enslaved to every enticement, and therefore they must be fled by God’s servant.

But pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, together with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.

He commands that these things be pursued, although they seem to youthful age to be wayward and harsh. For the person who chooses righteousness does nothing contrary to it; the person who loves faith keeps the commandments; the person who follows love is humble toward everyone; and the guardian of peace provokes no one to quarrel.

(Verses 23.) Avoid foolish and uneducated questions, knowing that they generate disputes.

Senseless questions belong partly to unbelievers and partly to heretics. Those of unbelievers compel modest people to dispute; for, changed by the excessive contradiction of their impiety, they become angry and say something contrary to their own purpose.

[Note: The Vall. codex reads: “for they are provoked by the excessive impiety of their contradiction . . . contrary to their own purpose.”]

Some heretics are accustomed to pretend patience—although they cannot hear anything harsh from a catholic—in order to commend their perverse conversations. For this reason one must pass them by without engaging them.

(Verses 24, 25, 26.) The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, apt to teach, patient, and modest, correcting those who hold different opinions, in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to the knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.

These things require no interpretation, for they are clear. Nevertheless, he has shown how beneficial modesty is. If this quality has pleased certain heretics because they appear humble, how much more praiseworthy and fruitful will it be in a catholic, if he is gentle—one in whom useful understanding and conduct worthy of imitation are seen!

## CHAPTER THREE

(Verses 1–5.) But know this: in the last days perilous times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, arrogant, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, impious, faithless, loveless, slanderers, without self-control, fierce, haters of what is good, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God, having the appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid such people.

This is the prophecy of the holy Apostle, in which he foresaw how many evils would arise among heretics and Jews. In them all these things, which are hostile to the faith, are marked out.

For the Apostle himself said: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5:12). Those who think wrongly about God and are not afraid to profess what constitutes an insult to him—how can they be benevolent in human society?

Therefore he said: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its power,” because they profess themselves to be Christians even though they are extremely wicked in their conduct and perverse in their understanding. For God’s praise and power lie not more in profession than in deeds.

(Verses 6, 7.) For among them are those who creep into households and capture little women burdened with sins, led by various desires, always learning but never able to arrive at the knowledge of the truth.

Although this applies to all heretics—that they enter households and capture women through deceptive and crafty words in order through them to deceive men, after the manner of their father the devil, who deceived Adam through Eve—it applies especially to the Manichaeans.

For none are so intrusive, deceptive, or cunning as they, who are known to worship one thing while professing another, to hold one thing inwardly and claim another outwardly. They defend chastity and, with their law favoring them, live disgracefully. They praise mercy, although they are found to be unjust among themselves. They assert that the world must be despised, yet always appear carefully groomed. They boastfully proclaim that they devote themselves to fasts, although all of them appear well-fed; they merely make themselves look pale by some contrivance so as to deceive.

Thus the Apostle prophesied especially about these people, who clearly did not exist in the time of the apostles, just as the Arians did not. For the emperor Diocletian identifies them in his decree, saying: “This filthy and impure heresy, which, he says, recently emerged from Persia” (see *Collection of Mosaic and Roman Laws*).

They find women who, out of vanity, desire to hear something new, and through what pleases them they persuade them to accept shameful and unlawful things. Such women are eager to learn but lack the judgment to test what they hear. This is what it means always to learn and never to possess the knowledge of the truth.

(Verses 8, 9.) Just as Jannes and Mambres opposed Moses, so these people oppose the truth—men corrupted in mind and rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not make further progress, for their ignorance will become evident to everyone, just as the ignorance of those men did.

This example comes from the apocrypha (Exod. 7:1 and following). Jannes and Mambres were brothers, Egyptian magicians or sorcerers, who thought that by the contrived rivalry of their magical art they could resist the works of God performed through Moses.

But when Moses’ power increased through his deeds, they were humbled and, in the pain of their wounds, confessed that God was working through Moses. Thus he likewise says that these people will make no further progress in asserting their impiety, because their incompetence and deception will become public. Although unwillingly, they will finally confess their own ignorance.

(Verses 10, 11.) But you have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, endurance, persecutions, and sufferings.

He wishes Timothy to imitate the things he enumerates. In the end these things will lead not to repentance but to joy.

(Verses 12, 13.) You have seen what happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and what persecutions I endured; and the Lord delivered me from them all. Indeed, all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. But wicked people and deceivers will advance toward worse things, themselves wandering and leading others into error.

He recalls how much and what kind of suffering he endured in order to show God’s assistance, by which God defends his servants and keeps them safe from Satan’s shamelessness. He does this to make them secure and raise them up, so that they may not fear what the faithless can inflict, but may be cheerful amid persecution, certain that all who conduct themselves rightly in Christ are hated even by the members of their own body.

But wicked people advance toward worse things when they see that many assent to them, so that they lead others into error. For when they are known to be wicked and deceivers, yet nevertheless flourish and prosper in the world, they attract some people to become their imitators. Such people will be punished not only for their own errors, but also for the errors of those whom they destroy by their example.

(Verses 14–15.) But you, continue in the things that you have learned and that have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them, and because from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation. He indicates that it is of great benefit to possess knowledge of the Old Testament; for he calls them “sacred writings” because they point to the person of Christ and declare his incarnation for the redemption and salvation of humankind. He urges him to advance in these things; for antiquity is the strength of novelty, since he knows that the authority of the one from whom he learned is firm. For he saw signs and wonders performed through him, before which every argument gives way.

[Col. 0495A] (Verses 16–17.) Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for correction, for restoration, for reproof, and for instruction in righteousness itself, so that the man of God may be prepared, [Note: [Col. 0495D] Some manuscripts: “instructed for every good work.”] equipped for every good work. It is clear that every Scripture whose author is shown to be God is useful; for it was given for this purpose: to advance the unlearned, to restore the deformed, and to draw the unrighteous toward righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfected in every good work. For, progressing step by step in the new humanity, it establishes him as a man of God.

# CHAPTER IV

(Verses 1–2.) I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is going to judge the living and the dead, by his appearing and his kingdom: proclaim the word; be urgent in season and out of season; [Col. 0495B] reprove, exhort, rebuke with all patience and instruction. He gives such careful command that God’s gift be preached without violation that he urges this duty and perseverance in it with an appeal to God the Father and Christ his Son. Through continual preaching and frequent rebuke, he is to summon people toward better progress, doing so at the appropriate time; and, so that they may more readily agree with the one who reproves them, he urges that it be done without bitterness.

(Verses 3–4.) For there will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but, according to their own desires, [Note: [Col. 0495D] Roman edition: “they will heap up teachers for themselves.”] they will accumulate teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to myths. This too is a prophecy of the holy Apostle, who, knowing what was to come, carefully commands that one persist in teaching, so that those formed in faith and good works, instructed in sound discipline, may remain steadfast and, when at the end of time some begin to turn from truth to error, remain immovable. For he says that there will be people who want to be taught according to their desires, so that they may turn away from steadfast and truthful teachers to those who will teach them what they gladly hear. For truth will seem harsh to them, and, abandoning their own teaching, they will devote themselves to myths. They do not want their evil deeds to be reproved; therefore they want teachers who will serve their morals. Their ears itch to hear tales of vanities fabricated under the name of teaching, by which they may be entertained. Nothing is more characteristic of the Manichaeans, who have I know not what diverse inventions, designated by inflated names, although they are frivolous things and certain ravings.

[Col. 0495D] (Verses 5–6.) [Note: [Col. 0495D] The same Roman edition: “But you, keep watch; act manfully in all things.”] But you, be sober in all things, endure patiently, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry; for I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is near. He admonishes and exhorts him to keep watch in ecclesiastical discipline, to act manfully, and to explain the Scriptures, so that the wise and instructed may avoid empty myths. For the Apostle, knowing that his passion was imminent, wished to leave in holy Timothy an example of devout conduct and sound teaching, so that suitable teachers might never be lacking in succession. Yet he calls his own passion a libation, for he is being offered in sacrifice to God, who suffers on behalf of his righteousness.

(Verses 6–7.) I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. What remains is that the crown of righteousness has been reserved for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing. He recalls that he preserved everything useful and beneficial both for himself and for others. For he offered himself as a model to his hearers not only in words but also in deeds, so that he might be a faithful steward to his author through the truth of his preaching; and, having struggled with every care and skill against the rulers and powers of the world, he left an example of how they might be overcome. Thus, unviolated teaching and the lawful contest of the struggle made them worthy to be crowned, [Col. 0496B] because God, the righteous judge, will give the most abundant rewards to those who love him and await his Son from heaven.

(Verses 9–12.) Make every effort to come to me as soon as possible. For Demas has deserted me, loving this present age, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia; Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in ministry. But I sent Tychicus to Ephesus. Since the whole instruction of the ecclesiastical man is contained in the letter, [Note: [Col. 0496D] Some manuscripts: “all instruction in ecclesiastical law.”] nevertheless, because of his great affection, he desires his presence. He bears witness to Mark for this reason: he remembers his former labors.

(Verses 13.) When you come, bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, [Col. 0496C] and the books, especially the parchments. The Apostle was Jewish by birth and possessed nothing alien to that identity. Where, then, did he get a cloak? But because he was from Tarsus, whose inhabitants are known to have been received into the Roman community and thereafter called Roman citizens, it is therefore necessary that they also have a senate-house in which, according to Roman custom, they might assemble wearing cloaks. For whoever at that time went out to meet the Romans with gifts was granted perpetual immunity and called a Roman citizen, as were their brothers, according to the testimony of the same Apostle. It may therefore be that, if it was not his own—for he had devoted himself entirely to the Law—he possessed his father’s cloak.

(Verses 14–15.) Alexander the coppersmith showed me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. [Col. 0496D] You too, avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words. This Alexander and the aforementioned Demas were associates. At first they were with the Apostle, pretending friendship toward him; but because deceitful people are revealed by time, both withdrew from him. This man, the coppersmith, who was bolder in evil, withdrew from him in such a way that he also became a contradictor of his words. Since he had dared to contradict the Apostle, he rightly warns that he must be avoided, leaving him to God’s judgment.

(Verses 16.) At my first defense no one stood by me; rather, everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them. [Col. 0497A] He calls the pressures and tribulations inflicted upon him his defense; for suffering is life for Christians, and persecution is defense. The pressure inflicted on him for the sake of righteousness defends him on the day of judgment, making the faithless guilty. At the very beginning, therefore, of the pressure inflicted upon him, he complains that he was abandoned. Yet because he knows this to be customary, he does not wish it to be counted against them, since when the Lord was seized by the Jews, the disciples also abandoned him—especially since it is written in the prophet: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7).

(Verses 17.) But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the proclamation might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear. For this reason he says that he was fortified by the help of our Lord and increased in strength, so that he might fulfill the proclamation among all the nations. Therefore he asks forgiveness for those who abandoned him in his necessity, so that, accepted by God, he might not seek vengeance. For he believes that he was helped all the more by God because he was abandoned by human beings.

(Verses 18.) And I was delivered from the lion’s mouth. The Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will save me for his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory forever. Amen. His fellow Apostle Peter says similarly: “Because our adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). But because he found no opportunity in the Apostle by which he might deceive him, he stirred up pressure and punishments against him through his sons, so that, even if he were not taken from this life as a sinner, he might nevertheless be taken from it as a righteous man, lest he encourage many to faith. When he had nearly accomplished this, the Apostle, delivered through God’s providence, insults him and testifies that he is weak, since he was snatched from his mouth: he was unable to accomplish what he desired. Thus he rejoices that he was rescued from death by God’s help, and he is so confident in God’s providence that he believes he will be delivered from future temptations—not merely delivered for the present, but also saved on the day of judgment and destined to reign with the Lord Christ throughout the eternal ages.

(Verses 19–21.) Greet Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth; but I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Make every effort to come before winter. Aquila and Prisca are those with whom he stayed and worked with his hands (Acts 18:3). Onesiphorus is the one to whom he bears witness in the second Epistle (2 Timothy 1:16). Yet how is it that, while the Apostle was present—the one who raised the dead—Trophimus became ill? [Col. 0498B] But signs were performed for unbelievers; and because merit is established before God for different reasons, a person who gives thanks to God either in tribulation or in illness, and seeks no assistance from the opposing side, advances in merit before God. Because of the rains and cold, therefore, he urged him to come to him in autumn.

Eubulus greets you, as do Pudens, Linus, and Claudia, and all the brothers. As usual, the letter is completed with the greeting of the brothers.

The Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0497C] Roman edition: “with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.”] be with your spirit. This is the Apostle’s subscription, which he says is the sign in every letter. And because the Son of God is also the son of man, and is called both Jesus and Christ—so that both man and God may be signified—he is designated by two names. Yet by both names his dignity is indicated, which is why the names were given.

[Col. 0497]

# ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO TITUS

317 **PROLOGUE**

[Col. 0497C]

The Apostle appointed Titus bishop; [Note: [Col. 0497D] Since these commentaries on the Epistle to Titus precede, in the manuscripts, the commentaries on both Epistles to Timothy, it seems necessary to note once that elsewhere too they are not arranged in the same order as in the Bibles. For after the Epistle to the Philippians follow the two to the Thessalonians, then that to the Colossians, and finally that to Titus. Primasius and Sedulius also followed this order.] and therefore he warns him to be diligent in ecclesiastical ordering—that is, concerning certain people who, through a kind of pretence, display themselves as worthy to hold a high office, and likewise concerning the heretics from the circumcision who must be rebuked.

# CHAPTER I

(Verses 1–4.) Paul, servant of God but an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the faith of God’s elect and the acknowledgment of his truth, which accords with godliness, in the hope of eternal life that the truthful God promised before the ages of the world; but in his appointed times he manifested his word in the proclamation entrusted to me according to the command of God our Savior—to Titus, a genuine son according to the common faith. Grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior.

He declares that the ordained gift which God had promised before the ages was manifested, in the time of the Savior, through the preaching of the apostles; for this is how he had promised it. He also says that it was entrusted to him, so that he might make known to the nations God’s predestined mercy. Thus Titus, his true son—that is, according to the Gospel, for what is eternal is true—might carefully contemplate and proclaim this will of God, and proclaim God’s grace and peace, so that, having received the gift of peace, they might be reconciled with God the Father; for all things are from him; and with Christ Jesus our Savior, because he too delivered us from death.

(Verses 5–11.) For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might set right what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in every city, as I also directed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not accused of debauchery or disobedience. For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward—not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not violent, not seeking shameful gain, but hospitable, kind, prudent, just, holy, self-controlled, holding firmly to the trustworthy word that accords with teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it. For there are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those from the circumcision, whom it is necessary to rebuke. They overturn whole households, teaching what they ought not to teach for the sake of shameful gain.

What has been read is clear. He wishes a bishop to be appointed who is holy in his works and prudent in his words, so that he may exhort the brothers and refute those who contradict him, especially those who came from the Jews and taught people to Judaize under the name of Christ (Galatians 2:4), whom elsewhere he calls false brothers. Although reborn in Christ, they were not pure Christians; for they wanted to venerate partly the Law and partly Christ. These are the people he says overturned households with this perverse teaching. They pursued shameful gain in two ways, because they acted thus especially in order to please the Jews, from whom they hoped to receive support, so that they might profit both money and the foreskin. These were their sources of gain, just as the Lord says to the Jews: “You travel sea and land to make one proselyte” (Matthew 23:15). He calls these two things shameful gains, because the person who teaches under the name of God, not for the sake of devotion but for profit, is a seeker of shameful gain; likewise, the person who wishes to acquire someone through circumcision. Hence he says elsewhere: “And their glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:19).

(Verses 12–13.) One of them, their own prophet, said: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.” This testimony is true. One of the Cretans, improved through the Lord’s discipline, expressed what ought to be thought about the uneducated Cretans: that they were evil and wanted to eat while remaining idle. For they wanted to be nourished by wickedness; although they are of no benefit, they eagerly desire to do harm. Thus the evil is twofold. Such were the Cretans; hence he calls this man a prophet, but in the matter of the Cretans. For he asserts that he spoke so truly about them that he was a prophet; it is impossible for a prophet to be mistaken.

(Verses 14.) For this reason rebuke them severely, so that they may be sound in faith [Note: [Col. 0499D] Roman edition: “not attending . . . commandments of people turning away, etc.”] and not attend to Jewish myths and commandments of people who turn themselves away from the truth. He commands that they be persistently corrected, so that they may be converted and pursue what is just and worthy of God’s law, turning away from Jewish myths. For no one is justified before God by the Law—how much less by human commandments! Whatever is set against the truth is a human invention. For, not knowing the power of the Scriptures and the inner meaning of the words of the Law, they follow the outward appearance rather than the substance. Therefore they are said to tell myths rather than the truth. They think that one must never depart from what Moses handed down—for example, concerning foods, marriages, new moons, the blood of a weasel, or an unclean house for seven days—although they know that their forefathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were justified without these things and were called friends of God. The prophet Ezekiel also testifies that because they profaned God’s law and his ordinances, they received precepts and commandments that were not good, in which they could not be justified.

Hence the Lord also says to the Jews: “Moses wrote these things for the hardness of your heart” (Mark 10:5). For this reason the Apostle Peter likewise says: “Why do you place a yoke upon the necks of the brothers that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10). For if these things had been useful, they would have been given at the time when the Law was also given on tablets. But because, after so many signs and wonders and after the Law had been promulgated, they were found irreverent, distrustful, and stiff-necked, they received such and so many commandments that they could not breathe freely under them. Thus it came about that the good also suffered together with the wicked, while they were to receive their reward. These commandments, therefore, were given as punishment, so that, when the promised gift of God arrived, God’s mercy might release everything that he had previously forbidden. Not understanding this, the Jews remain under the yoke and wish to bind the freedom of others with these chains. Therefore he warns that such people must be rebuked, so that they may turn away from them.

(Verses 15.) To the pure all things are pure; but to those who are defiled and without faith, nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled. He indicates that those are pure who know both why these things were forbidden and why they were afterward permitted. For if it is read in Genesis that everything God made is good (Genesis 1:31), there is no doubt that it is also pure. Those who do not understand this are impure, for they are accusers of Scripture. If the things made are read to be good, why are they forbidden as though accursed? Since they are not accursed, because they are good, it is understood that they were forbidden on account of hardness of heart, because the people were judged unworthy to use God’s entire creation. For the minds and consciences of those who seem to have been prohibited from better things are defiled, because they accuse God’s creation in order to excuse themselves.

(Verses 16.) They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him, since they are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for every good work. Although this statement applies to all heretics, he is understood here to be speaking about the Jews, who alone claim to know the God of Abraham but deny him by their works, as the Lord says: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). How, then, can they know the God of Abraham when they are ignorant of his mystery and faith, not following the works of the Gospel but disturbing others through legal observances concerning new moons, circumcision, and other matters? They are impious and irreverent. These are the works of those who do not know God.

# CHAPTER II

(Verses 1.) But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine. This is the doctrine that knows God and is called sound doctrine; for God’s doctrine is salutary.

315 (Verse 2.) Older men are to be sober, serious, prudent, sound in faith, love, and patience. He shows what people of sound doctrine are like, so that he might signify that those who are less sober, less serious, faithless, without love, and impatient are disciples of unsound doctrine. God is not known through these works, nor his righteousness.

(Verses 3–5.) Older women likewise are to be in a manner worthy of religious conduct, [Note: [Col. 0501D] Roman edition: “in an appearance worthy of religion.”] not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teachers of what is good, so that they may train the younger women to love their husbands, love their children, to be prudent, chaste, pure, managing their households, subject to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed. He commands older women to be such that they may serve as examples of good conduct to the younger, so that, if they have unbelieving husbands, they may rejoice with them rather than cause the name of God to be blasphemed, when their husbands see that, because of fear of God, they are more devoted in their service to them.

(Verses 6–8.) Likewise exhort younger men to be self-controlled, offering yourself in all things as an example of good works, in teaching, integrity, seriousness, and a sound, irreproachable word, so that the one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us. Since youth commonly exceeds proper limits and is indeed more ready to fall, it is commanded to be restrained by salutary reins, so that, once bridled, it may be governed by divine laws. To ensure that this may not be difficult or burdensome, he commands the teacher to be a model, showing how the things he teaches are to be practiced, so that those who are profane and hostile to the faith may be ashamed when they see that he proves by his deeds that the things he teaches in words are true.

(Verses 9–10.) Servants are to be subject to their masters in all things, [Note: [Col. 0501D] The same Roman edition: “obedient in all things.”] excellent, not argumentative, not defrauding them, but showing complete good faith, so that they may adorn the teaching of God our Savior in all things. He says that the Lord’s teaching is adorned by good works and faith. The doctrine is then pleasing, [Note: [Col. 0501D] All editions: “pleasing and beautiful”; but nearly all manuscripts agree with us. Below, instead of “to be unbecoming,” some manuscripts have “to be unlovable.”] if the person who professes it does not make it hateful by denying it in his deeds, but makes it lovable and true; for what is true cannot be unbecoming. When, therefore, the things said are fulfilled by subsequent deeds, they are shown to be true and consequently beautiful. Then masters can not only refrain from preventing their servants from having faith, but can also rejoice, because they see that their servants’ faith benefits even themselves. For no one who keeps faith with God can be faithless toward human beings.

(Verses 11–12.) For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, teaching us that, having renounced impiety and worldly desires, we should live temperately, justly, and devoutly in this age. He says that God’s gift has shone upon humanity through Christ—that is, the truth of the one God has been manifested in Christ—so that, by a devout profession, we may proclaim the Creator in the unity of the Trinity. What was previously hidden from the human race has now shone forth through God’s mercy, so that, avoiding the darkness of error—that is, fleeing the ignorance and impiety of worldly things—we may be found devout toward the God who is the Father of all, professing him in the truth handed down by the Gospel of his Son. And, so that we may receive a reward for this, let us perform good works. For just as there is no hope for one who proclaims only the Father if he does not profess the Son in the same truth, so the hope of the person who has only a profession of faith without good works is also futile.

(Verses 13–15.) Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing [Note: [Col. 0501D] Roman edition: “of the glory of the great God ... his own special people.”] of the glory of the blessed God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a plentiful people, zealous for good works. He says that this is the blessed hope of believers, because they await the appearing of the glory of the great God, which is to be revealed, with Christ as judge, in whom the power and glory of God the Father will be seen, so that they may receive the reward of their faith. For Christ redeemed us for this purpose: so that, pursuing a pure life and filled with good works, we might be able to become heirs of God’s kingdom.

Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

# CHAPTER III

(Verses 1–2.) Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey orders, to be ready for every good work. He reminds them what the salvation of believers is, so that, when they are rebuked, they may know for what good they are being prepared and may not take it harshly, certain that they are corrected for their salvation; and so that they may be slow toward evil but ready toward good, not ignorant of what ought to be rendered to each. [Note: [Col. 0502D] All editions with some manuscripts: “What the hope of believers is . . . for what good end they are to be prepared”; the other manuscripts read as in the text.] To speak evil of no one, not to be quarrelsome, [Col. 0502C] but to be gentle, showing all meekness toward everyone. He wishes Christians to appear humble toward all people; for in this way the faithless may be called to the future hope.

(Verses 3.) For we too were once foolish, disobedient, wandering, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. [Note: [Col. 0502D] Thus the old edition and nearly all manuscripts; but the Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “He recalls that Christians must avoid these evils, which unbelief possesses.”] He recalls that Christians have been given these good qualities, which unbelief does not possess, so that, shining in every righteousness, they may be shown to be worshipers of God. For although once they were foolish, now they appear to be sound in judgment in all things, and God is praised in them.

(Verses 4–7.) But when the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior appeared, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. This good that appears to flourish in Christians arises from the root of divine devotion. For God, in his mercy, saved us through Christ; reborn by his grace, we received the Holy Spirit abundantly, so that we might rely upon good works, with him assisting us in all things, and through these works attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore we ought to obey him with complete devotion and submit to his commands, because whatever is beautiful in us he himself paints with spiritual features.

(Verses 8.) The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to affirm these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are good and useful for human beings. Nothing is more evident: mercy and kindness are good in the present and useful in the future; here they receive praise, and on the day of judgment a crown. For everyone who believes in God ought to devote himself to mercy, through which he lives. He is therefore admonished so that the ruler of the people may be diligent in these things.

(Verses 9.) But avoid foolish questions, genealogical enumerations, contentions, and disputes about the Law, for they are useless and vain. He calls foolish those questions that produce no salvation and contribute no knowledge useful for living. In these words he marks the doctrines of many heretics. Although everything that is not true ought to be called foolish, one person introduces mythical matters, while another, through the craftiness of evasive argument, proposes something filled with poison, as do Arius and Photinus. The myth is not the Law but heresy, insofar as the matter concerns that period among the Jews when certain people claimed for themselves the prerogative of the origins of the patriarchs, who arose from marriages, although no merit before God derives from this.

Others insisted that the baptism of pitchers and other vessels and the blood of a weasel had to be carefully purified (Leviticus 11:29); and they claimed that Moses’ burial was hidden so that he might not be raised by magicians. If this were true, the burial places of the other saints would also have had to be hidden. They also claimed that Solomon built the temple with the assistance of demons, a work on which a vast multitude labored. What could be more mythical than this?

[Col. 0504A] (Verses 10–11.) Avoid a heretical person after the first rebuke, knowing that such a person is perverse and sins, being condemned by himself. Heretics are those who attack the Law through the words of the Law. They establish their own interpretation through the words of the Law, using the authority of the Law to commend the perversity of their minds. Since impiety knows that the authority of the Law has great force, it devises deceit under its name, so that, because an evil thing cannot be acceptable in itself, it may be commended by the goodness of the name. Therefore he says that such people should be rebuked once, so that they may be without excuse; for if rebuked more often, they will become more practiced in evil. It seems that the one who rebukes them repeatedly is compelling them to become more eager for the destruction of many. For this reason they are to be dismissed, so that, becoming more negligent, they may perhaps perish alone.

(Verses 12.) When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make haste to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. After sending the letter, he also wishes to see him personally out of affection and to strengthen him more fully in ecclesiastical discipline.

(Verses 13–14.) Diligently send on Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they lack nothing. Let our people also learn to devote themselves to good works for necessary needs, so that they may not be unfruitful. Each was a distinguished man in wisdom and works. Therefore he commands that the believers provide them with the support they need, so that they may be refreshed, since it was fitting that those who supplied spiritual things should not lack material necessities. Although he calls Zenas a lawyer, Apollos was nevertheless accomplished in the Scriptures; [Col. 0504C] but because Zenas had held this profession in the synagogue, he calls him by that name.

(Verses 15.) All who are with me greet you. For the sake of brevity, he indicates that they all greet him together. Greet those who love us in faith. He wishes those to be regarded as worthy of his greeting who love him faithfully with the affection of Christ our Lord. The grace of God be with all of you. Now he greets all the brothers and the household of Titus in general.

[Col. 0503]

# ON THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED PAUL TO PHILEMON

317 **PROLOGUE**

[Col. 0503D]

Philemon was not endowed with the dignity of an ecclesiastical office, but was a praiseworthy man, one of the common people. Concerning Onesimus, his servant and household member, he writes a letter to him so that he may not only forgive him but also give thanks to God, because he has received him in such a way that he does not regard him as a servant but as a most beloved brother.

# CHAPTER I

(Verses 1–3.) Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon, the beloved brother and our fellow worker, and to Apphia our most beloved sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in his household. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. In order to give dignity to the letter he was sending, he began with his own humiliation. For just as being bound on account of sin is disgraceful, so, conversely, to endure the bonds of imprisonment for Christ is the greatest glory. At the time when he sent this letter, he was in custody. Although Philemon was not a cleric, he nevertheless took part in ecclesiastical necessities because of his devotion; hence he calls him his fellow worker. For there are many who, although worthy, make excuses, judging themselves unworthy of so great a ministry; and for this reason they truly appear worthy.

(Verses 4–6.) I give thanks to my God, always mentioning you in my prayers, hearing of your faith and love that you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, so that your participation may become acceptable in the acknowledgment of every good thing that is in us in Christ. He says that he rejoices and gives thanks to God in his prayers because Philemon was firm in faith and devoted to good works. For whoever loves Christ must prove this in his servants, knowing that the Lord will charge him with whatever is shown to have been expended upon his servants. [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Vallian codex: “He ought to prove this toward his children.”] The Apostle nevertheless says that he adds this to his prayers: that his activity may take place with knowledge of goodness—that is, that he may act in this matter with such a mind that he may expect a reward for it in the future.

(Verses 7.) For I had great joy and consolation because of your love, because the hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother. It is clear that he indicates himself to be joyful for this reason: Philemon was supplying what was necessary for the needs of the saints. Therefore he rejoices all the more, certain that by this he was obeying the commands of the one who is acknowledged to be greater.

(Verses 8–9.) Therefore, although I have great confidence in Christ to command you what is fitting, nevertheless, because of love I rather appeal to you—such a man as Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus. Insofar as reason demanded, it would have been fitting for the teacher to command the disciple, relying on apostolic authority. But because Philemon was a good man, he moves him through affection to obey, presenting himself as though of the same age and as a prisoner of Christ Jesus—that is, bound by the Lord’s affairs, or subjected to bonds for his name, as the apostles themselves were. Such were Judas and Silas, who, although they were prominent among the brothers as members of the common people, bound themselves to the Lord’s works [Col. 0505C] (Acts 15:22 and following), so that they might struggle together with the apostles for the faith of God. [Note: [Col. 0505D] The Roman edition alone: “for the Son of God.”] Hence Silas is found to have shared the Apostle’s labors.

(Verses 10–14.) I appeal to you for my son, whom I fathered in my imprisonment, Onesimus, formerly useless to you but now very useful both to you and to me, whom I have sent back to you. You, therefore, receive him as my own heart. I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf in the bonds of the Gospel; but I wanted to do nothing without your consent, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.

It is not a great thing for a humble person to humble himself; but it is praiseworthy for a lofty man to humble himself. Therefore the Apostle asks the man whom he has the authority to command, so that in all things he may be an example for the advancement of merit. The Apostle baptized Onesimus, a fugitive returning to divine assistance, while he was in the custody of the city of Rome (Acts 28:16), seeing in him the hope of usefulness. He commends him in such a way as to signify that he had become suitable for his purpose, although previously useless, both for worldly and for divine service.

### (Verses 15–16)

Perhaps for this reason he withdrew for a time, so that you might receive him forever—not now as a slave, but, in place of a slave, as a beloved brother, especially to me; and how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord? Onesimus, having offended his own master, fled after a long journey [Col. 0506A] to the Apostle, in order to show that he had not withdrawn for the purpose of becoming liable for an offense, but so that, with his sins erased, he might return useful—to such an extent that he would become not only equal to his master in merits, but also a brother to the teacher himself. And lest Philemon, as commonly happens, should experience some disdainful arrogance toward him as a master toward a slave, he humbles him when he calls him a brother “both in the flesh and in the Lord,” so that, once the grounds of human condition have been removed—for we all descend from one Adam—we may recognize ourselves as brothers, especially when faith intervenes, which cuts away all pride.

### (Verse 17)

If, therefore, you regard me as a partner [Note: [Col. 0505D] The same Roman edition: “You have me as a partner.”], receive him as you would me. He shows that he has such affection for Onesimus that he says that Philemon, whom he praised above, [Col. 0506B] is his partner if he receives this man as he would receive the Apostle. For this is what Solomon said: “The freeborn shall serve the wise slave” (Eccles. X, 28). This saying is intended to terrify Philemon, so that he might receive him at least for this reason, if he could not be moved by charity.

### (Verses 18–19)

But if he has wronged you in anything, or owes you something, charge it to me. Now he removes the excuse for anger, lest Philemon perhaps complain that he had been so wronged by him that he seemed wholly undeserving of forgiveness. If that were the case, he says that it should be charged to him, through whom those who formerly sinned are to become heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

### (Verse 19)

I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me even your own self. If there is any offense on Onesimus’s part, he declares that his own guarantee [Col. 0506C] is sufficient to make satisfaction on his behalf. And, to speak truthfully, he raises his own claim and says that he demands less from him than he is shown to owe. For he is compelled to make satisfaction for the slave, because he burdens himself with the debt.

### (Verses 20–21)

Yes, brother, let me have this benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. For now he flatters him, so that his obedience may be voluntary and thus able to bear fruit. He urges him in this way to do more than is being requested of him; for it commonly happens that one who sees that a good opinion is held of him presents himself as a better man.

### (Verse 22)

At the same time, prepare a lodging for me; for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. To make him more attentive and more obedient, he indicates that he will come to him; for those who are absent are commonly despised. And why should the Apostle still disdain to be here, he who always suffered weariness and deaths, massacres, persecutions, and imprisonment, and whose rest was nowhere except in Christ alone? [Note: [Col. 0505D] In many excellent manuscripts the passages beginning “But for the progress” and continuing to the end of the commentary are lacking; nevertheless, they are found in several other manuscripts, as well as in all the editions.] But for the progress of believers, and also to confound the enemies of the cross of Christ and increase the glory of God, he offered his flesh to sufferings, so that he might acquire crowns of immortality for both his soul and his body.

### (Verses 23–24)

Epaphras, my fellow prisoner [Col. 0507A] in Christ Jesus, greets you; as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. He testifies that all these men share in his glory.

[Col. 0508A] ### (Verse 25)

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen. This subscription belongs to the Apostle, confirming the letter that was sent. [Note: [Col. 0507A] We have stated in the Preface placed before all these commentaries the reasons why the Commentaries on the Epistle to the Hebrews did not seem suitable for inclusion in this edition; consult that Preface.]

# ON THE TRINITY, OTHERWISE A TREATISE ON THE APOSTLES’ CREED

[Col. 0507]

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

The book that we present was first published by the editors of the Roman edition among the genuine works of Saint Ambrose under the title *Treatise on the Apostles’ Creed*. Yet although those most distinguished men did not tell us either from what library it had emerged or what was the quality of the exemplars from which it had been committed to the press, we did not on that account hesitate in our judgment. From our first reading of it, we were struck with wonder that learned men, distinguished for critical acumen, could have admitted as a legitimate product of the holy Doctor this little work, wholly lacking the genius and style of Ambrose.

Our wonder became much greater when, after comparing the aforementioned edition with two copies—one of which we possess transcribed from the Royal Library and the other from the Vatican—we understood how greatly the edition differs from them. At that point we did not know whether we should detest more the insolence of the impostor who presented this treatise, so shamefully interpolated and mutilated, to the illustrious head of the Roman edition as sound and complete, or lament the misfortune of learned men upon whom that same edition later imposed. Indeed, one could scarcely find clearer evidence elsewhere of how easily even the most learned men may be deceived. To pass over others, it is established that Petavius himself was led into error (*De Trinitate*, Book IV, chapter 3, no. 6, and chapter 15, no. 5), among other places where, discussing the word *suppositum*, he argues as follows:

“It follows,” he says (*ibid.*, chapter 5, no. 13), “that the name *suppositum*, which is less familiar in the usage of the Latin Fathers in the sense commonly heard in the schools, namely as ‘hypostasis’ or ‘person,’ occurs nevertheless in Ambrose, in the book *On the Apostles’ Creed*, chapter 12. ‘This nature,’ he says, ‘he assumed for the salvation of the whole human race in the unity of the suppositum.’”

Here one may observe that the most learned man fell into a double error: both in attributing this commentary to Ambrose and in quoting as words proceeding from its true author those words which are nothing other than the interpolator’s.

Therefore, so that no one in the future may stumble over the same stone, we shall present the complete text of the work, with the additions sewn into the margin, on the authority of the aforementioned manuscripts. Yet from the conjunction *therefore*, which immediately follows the opening word, it is understood that something preceded which has been lost. It is also certain that the title itself, which we place at the head from the manuscripts, is considerably better than the one the Roman editors wished to insert into this book on their own authority; nevertheless, it is not entirely free from defect, since it does not convey the form and conception of the entire subject treated.

For this little book is divided into three parts (chapter 15, at the end). The first concerns the Trinity; the second deals with the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation; the third discusses the resurrection of the dead and refutes what the heretics had objected against this truth. The Author of the Work also adds near the end that he collected this material from the writings of the Fathers. And indeed we have recognized here not a few passages either slightly altered according to the Author’s skill or often borrowed in the very same words—passages drawn from Hilary, Ambrose, or Augustine. To these are added substantial fragments from the books of Tertullian and from Jerome’s *Commentaries on Isaiah*. Since the latter work was composed only after Ambrose’s death, it alone could expose the forgery, without any need to resort to differences of style or to differences in the translations of the testimonies cited from Holy Scripture. In order to make the matter clearer and at the same time attend to brevity, we have taken care to mark in the margins, opposite the relevant passages, whatever we found inserted into this little book from other sources.

Moreover, if anyone asks whose work we consider this little book to be, we shall answer frankly that, given the great scarcity of copies, we can establish nothing certain about this matter. This much, however, may be stated with certainty: its author is an ancient writer—not only because the Royal codex containing this commentary is at least six hundred years old, but also because the work mentions no heretic except an ancient one. Nor shall we regret our conjecture too greatly if we believe that this little book was composed against the sect of the Priscillianists (of whom Augustine speaks in Book 70 of *On Heresies*) and that it is contemporary either with the First Council of Toledo or, at the least, with the Second Council of Braga, commonly dated to the year 563.

For the same doctrines are discussed here as are established against the same heretics in the Rule of Faith of the Council of Toledo, in Saint Leo’s fifteenth letter to Turibius, and in the Second Council of Braga. It is therefore highly probable that this same treatise was written not to expound the Apostles’ Creed, but to defend the Toledan Rule of Faith. As for the fact that certain errors are mentioned in that rule which are not mentioned in this work, we believe that this arose either because the Author selected only the principal errors for refutation, or because [Col. 0509] those very heretics, in keeping with their innate fickleness and instability, had already renounced those errors.

It is also very likely that the same book was marked with Ambrose’s name for no other reason than that it was known that the holy Bishop had written many works against the aforementioned heretics. Paternus, bishop of Braga, testifies that by reading these works he had been converted from that heresy to the faith; and our Author may perhaps have borrowed several passages from those works.

[Col. 0509]

# ON THE TRINITY, OTHERWISE A TREATISE ON THE APOSTLES’ CREED (C, S)

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0509A]

No one, therefore, who has sound understanding of the omnipotent God, who is Trinity and Spirit, should suppose that He is any visible or tangible body. Rather, let him understand Him as a simple, rational, and invisible nature, [Note: [Col. 0509C] The Roman edition adds: “Whom no structure at all consolidates, to whom nothing external accrues, and whom no creature, no substance, and no dominion precedes. But faith, ascending higher and penetrating more inward things, shows God to be the fountain of all virtues, the beginning of all visible and invisible things, and the Creator of all heavenly and earthly creatures. This is an undivided unity and an inseparable Trinity, eternal in itself, receiving nothing from elsewhere; not bounded by time or place, nor found to need anything; but, with supreme simplicity and unity, always fertile. So great is the essence of unity, inseparable and undivided in the Three, that although it perceives all heavenly and earthly things, even the smallest, it is nevertheless said to understand nothing outside itself, but to behold each thing within itself. In this Trinity there is true eternity, unchangeable unity, and eternal and perfect charity. Finally, God is thought more truly than He is spoken, because He is incomprehensible. He did not wish to be proclaimed according to sex . . . but most magnificently as omnipotent, eternal, and unbounded . . . power in the gift.”] which seems to have been consolidated by no structure at all, nor to have had anything external or from elsewhere added to it, and which no substance, creature, or dominion has ever preceded.

The holy and inseparable Trinity, therefore, is the fountain and source of all virtues, and the Creator of visible and invisible creatures—that is, of heavenly and earthly creatures. It receives nothing external into itself, lest it appear bounded or be found in need of anything, since it is always pure, uniform, mysterious, and, so to speak, fertile through union. For so great is the inseparable [Col. 0509B] and undivided essence of unity in the Three that the holy Trinity seems to act upon nothing outside itself. In this holy and inseparable Trinity there is true eternity, [Note: [Col. 0510C] The Vatican codex reads: “unchangeable unity.”] unchangeable truth, and eternal and perfect charity. And therefore God is thought more truly than He is spoken, because He is always incomprehensible.

The omnipotent God, then, who has neither sex nor age nor defined bodily members, willed to be proclaimed in the most excellent, most evident, [Note: [Col. 0510C] The Royal codex reads: “most magnificently to be entreated.”] and most magnificent manner. Eternity is therefore in the Father, form in the Image, and use in the Gift (Augustine, Book VI of *On the Trinity*, chapter 10, from Hilary, Book II of *On the Trinity*). These three, however, are one God—not existing in the singularity of one person, but established in the essence of one Trinity.

There is therefore one who loves [Note: [Col. 0510C] The Roman edition reads: “Him who is from Him”; “one is loved by Him from whom He is; one is the love of both, the Holy Spirit, nevertheless the same God. And as He is good, true . . . let Him be called charity and Spirit; nevertheless He is one God. He cannot be composite, since it is impious to suppose that anything preceded Him; and nothing was made except by Him, as the Evangelist says: ‘All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made.’ He alone is eternal, because He lacks beginning and end—that is, God the Father . . . begot the Word, with whom He brought forth the Holy Spirit. Hence we believe that the substance of the Son and of the Holy Spirit exists before every creature, outside all times: the Father is the begetter, the Son is begotten, and the Holy Spirit is the holiness and Spirit of the Begetter. For although the Father is Spirit . . . only the Third Person is properly called the Holy Spirit. Since, therefore, He is coeternal, etc.”] Him who is from Him; and one who loves Him from whom He is; and love itself is one and the same in both—that is, the Holy Spirit. And yet these three, as has been said, are one good, true, just, light, life, truth, Spirit, and charity: God.

Since God is eternal and the author of all things, He cannot be understood as composite, lest things prior to God exist from which He is thought to be composed. He alone, therefore, made every creature that is not what He is. No one can be called eternal except one who lacks beginning and end—that is, God the Father, who has with Himself the coeternal and co-omnipotent Word and Spirit. This understanding clearly proves that the substance of the Son and of the Holy Spirit existed before every creature and outside all times, and that their origin always remains in God the Father.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, was not begotten, but is the sweetness, holiness, and eternity of the Begetter and the Begotten. For although the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, the Spirit is nevertheless properly called the Holy Spirit. Since, therefore, He is coeternal and common to both, He is called by the name that both possess.

## CHAPTER TWO

[Note: [Col. 0510C] The same Roman edition reads: “With what great rashness—or, not to say, blindness—the Arians speak.” The Royal codex reads: “The Arians are blinded.”]

The reader understands with what rashness and misery the Arians are judged, when they say: “There was a time when the Son did not exist.” Could there ever have been a time when the Father existed without life, without wisdom, without power, without the Word, who is Christ? Far from it, since He Himself plainly declares it, the Father saying: “My heart has uttered a good Word” (Psalm XLIV, 2). Confirming this, blessed John says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John I, 1–3).

Whatever is incorporeal and invisible cannot be separated by differences of place. If our speech, power, or wisdom cannot be separated from us except when we depart from the body, how could these things be separated from the immortal and omnipotent [Col. 0511B] God, who made all things from nothing through His Word? For whose Father would He be, according to the impious heretics, if the nature of the Son were separated from Him? And again, whose Son would the Son be if His origin were not referred to the Father, so that one would be He who begot and the other He who was begotten from Him?

The Father, therefore, who is the origin of divinity and goodness, is rightly understood and perceived both in the Son and in the Holy Spirit: in the Son, as Word, power, and wisdom; in the Spirit, as proceeding from Him. It is therefore right and catholic that we confess one God according to the truth of substance [Note: [Col. 0511D] The Vatican codex reads: “the unity of substance.”], while recognizing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each in his own subsistence. The divinity of the holy Trinity must therefore be believed to exist without any end [Note: [Col. 0511D] The same Roman edition adds: “although it is difficult for the human mind to grasp it by comprehension. Hence it is not improperly said that . . .”], and it is difficult even for the mind to apprehend. This alone do we comprehend concerning it: that it cannot be comprehended.

There is therefore one divinity in the Three, and there are Three in whom there is divinity. There is therefore no confusion in unity [Note: [Col. 0511D] The same Roman edition adds: “nor division in the Trinity.”], nor division in divinity. And therefore both the confusion of the foolish Sabellius and the separation of the impious Arius must be rejected equally, for they produced teachings contrary to one another but equally impious. [Note: [Col. 0511D] The same Roman edition adds: “For Sabellius taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one substance and one three-named person; but, by considering all to be one person, he designated each as nothing.”]

Sabellius, by supposing that everything merely received different names, designates each thing as nothing, since what something is ceases to be what it is when what is said to belong to each one is poured into the other. Arius, meanwhile, impiously asserts that the Son is a creature of the Father and that the Holy Spirit is a creature of the Son.

## CHAPTER THREE

But having rejected and spurned these impieties, let us say, as blessed Paul the Apostle says: “There is one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things” (1 Corinthians VIII, 6).

By saying “from whom,” “through whom,” and “in whom” are all things, we do not divide the nature, but confess the unity both of nature, of will, and of operation. There is therefore one God in these Three, and these Three are one God. The Apostle confirms this, saying: “From Him and through Him and in Him are all things; to Him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans XI, 35).

The prophet David speaks correspondingly: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear Him” (Psalm LXVI, 8).

The Father is therefore Father without beginning; for there is nothing else from which He is Father. The Son is Son without beginning—strictly speaking—for He is from the Father and is the Creator of all times. Therefore He does not receive His beginning from time (John I, 1), because He is the Word, the power, and the wisdom that both made and precedes all time (1 Corinthians I, 24).

The Holy Spirit, meanwhile, is truly Spirit, proceeding from the Father [Note: [Col. 0512D] The same Roman edition adds: “and the Son.”]; but He is not Himself the Son, because He is not generated [Note: [Col. 0512D] The same Roman edition adds: “nor the Father, because He proceeds from both, neither begotten nor unbegotten, nor made. For everything that exists is either neither born nor made; or born but not made; or neither born nor made; or made but not born; or made, born, and reborn; or made and born but not reborn.”], but proceeds from the Father.

Everything that exists is either unbegotten, begotten, or made. There is therefore that which is neither born nor made; that which is born but not made; that which is neither born nor made; that which is made but not born; that which is made, born, and reborn; and that which is made and born but not reborn.

Now, remembering what has been proposed, let us designate the substances of each thing. That which is neither born nor made is the Father, for He is from no one. That which is born but not made is the Son, who was begotten by the Father. That which is neither born nor made is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father [Note: [Col. 0512D] The Roman edition reads: “and proceeds from the Son.”]. That which is made but not born is heaven, earth, and the other things that exist. That which is made, born, and reborn is the human being, who is first born carnally and reborn spiritually in baptism. That which is made, born, and not reborn consists of the animals.

## CHAPTER FOUR

To teach each point by examples: concerning the Father it is written, “There is one God the Father, from whom are all things” (1 Corinthians VIII, 6); concerning the Son, “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (ibid.); and again, “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy II, 5).
