Concerning the Holy Spirit: “No one knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him; so also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians II, 11); and again, “The Spirit searches even the deep things of God” (ibid., 10).

That the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are without beginning is demonstrated by the following: what the Father is did not begin to be; and if He did not begin, neither did the Son begin. The Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father [Note: [Col. 0513D] The same Roman edition reads: “who proceeds from both”], did not begin either, because His procession is continuous and He is from the One who did not begin. The Father did not begin to be; and because He did not begin, neither did the Spirit begin to be, since He is in the Father and belongs to Him.

The Evangelist again testifies that the Son did not begin, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1–2). Therefore, because He was, He did not begin; because He was with God, He did not begin; because He was God, He did not begin; and because He was in the beginning with God, He did not begin. For God was born from God in such a way that He does not know what it is to have begun.

The Father was not defrauded because He is unbegotten or because He begot the Son; nor was the Son defrauded because He was begotten or because He is begotten from the Unbegotten; nor was the Holy Spirit defrauded because He belongs to both—that is, to the Father and the Son. Yet He belongs to them in such a way that He is not poured back into either the Father or the Son, because He is God, having neither beginning nor end, since He is coeternal with the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0513D] The same Roman edition adds: “and consubstantial with the Father and the Son.”]. He breathes where He wills, upon whom He wills, upon as many as He wills, and as much as He wills, by His own will (John III, 8).

He therefore fills with His grace whom He wills, as many as He wills, and as much as He wills; He is not Himself filled. He grants perfection; He does not receive it. He sanctifies; He is not Himself sanctified.

## CHAPTER FIVE

He, therefore, just as the Father and the Son, is both life and life-giving, both light and illuminating, both good and goodness, both holy and holiness (Romans VIII, 15). [Col. 0513C] He is the Spirit of adoption; He is the One who distributes His gifts to each person as He wills (1 Corinthians XII, 11). He is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of knowledge and piety, of counsel and strength, and of the fear of God (Isaiah XI, 2).

He is the Holy Spirit, through whom the Father is known and the Son glorified; and He is known by those alone, and alone knows all their things through the unity of nature. He is the One of whom the Son said: “My Father will give good things to those who ask Him” (Matthew VII, 11)—that is, either the Spirit Himself or all His graces.

Therefore, just as the Lord Christ is called the Word, power, wisdom, righteousness, pearl, light, way, resurrection, and by the other names written concerning Him, so the Holy Spirit is called, as has already been said, wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. This does not mean that He is different according to the differences of these names, but that He is one and the same fountain and source of all virtues, who has always dwelt in the Lord Christ, as the sharer in His nature.

These are the seven eyes which the prophet Zechariah says are present in one stone (Zechariah III, 9), that is, in the Lord Christ. [Note: [Col. 0513D] The same Roman edition reads: “The property of each is that it is immovable; [Col. 0514D] but there is one worship,” etc.]

The individual distinction is therefore immovable; but the worship, veneration, and sanctification of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are always one. For it is not fitting either that the Son should have been lacking to the Father or that the Holy Spirit should have been lacking to the Son, as the impious heretics falsely claim.

Therefore, guarding against these errors, let us preserve the good purpose that we have received from the holy Fathers. Let us adore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, understanding the Father in the Son, and the Father and Son in the Holy Spirit: distinguishing before we unite, and uniting before we distinguish; venerating unity in the Trinity and confessing the Trinity in unity.

The whole holy Trinity must therefore be adored by us, because it is wholly royal, because it has one power and one glory above the world and above time, uncreated, invisible, incomprehensible, and inscrutable. It alone knows in what order it exists within itself; but it is adored equally by us.

In this invisible and ineffable holy Trinity we should understand nothing to be so proper and so fixed as peace and tranquility. For there is no dissension in the nature of God, nor should it be thought capable of being dissolved, since it is always peace and charity.

If four substances—namely, heat, blood, phlegm, and moisture—make a human being, and there is one human being, how can you fail to understand the Trinity in unity or unity in the Trinity? God the almighty Father, therefore, possessing the almighty Word and the Spirit, is beyond human understanding and incomprehensible and eternal beyond anything that can be conceived.

We can know Him insofar as the weakness of our condition permits only when we know the Lord Christ, who is His form [Note: [Col. 0514D] The same Roman edition reads: “His character and image.”] and only-begotten Son. For, as He Himself says: “Whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father who sent Him, and who is in Him and remains in Him” (John XIV, 9). And again: “This is eternal life: that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (John XVII, 3).

The almighty Father, therefore, acquired the name “Father” through the Son, because no one can be or be called a father without a son, nor a son without a father. It is honorable to confess that the only-begotten Son of God, the Word and Wisdom, and His Holy Spirit are substantially equal to the Father in all things.

For who has fitted either color, form, or size to the Word and Wisdom, insofar as He is Wisdom, or to the Holy Spirit, so as to require degrees and establish orders where all things invisible, united, and peaceful always remain?

## CHAPTER SIX

First of all, therefore, we must believe that there is one God, who made all things from nothing through His Word and gave them life through the Holy Spirit; who, although He contains the universe, is Himself contained by no one.

The prophet David comprehended this in a single verse, saying: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their power” (Psalm XXXII, 6).

He is the Holy Spirit who, at the beginning and creation of the world, hovered over the waters (Genesis I, 2). He is the One through whom Moses and Aaron performed signs before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and of whom the magicians said: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus VIII, 9). He is the One who spoke in Moses and in all the holy patriarchs, prophets, and apostles (2 Peter I, 21), of whom the Apostle says: “We were all given to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians XII, 13).

He is the One who fashioned the flesh of the Word of God in the sacred womb of the Virgin (Luke I, 35). He is the One whom the Father sent upon the Son after His baptism (Matthew III, 16). He is the One by whose power Jesus, full of the Spirit, returned from the Jordan and went back into Galilee (Luke IV, 14). He is the One whom the Father gives to those who ask Him (Luke XI, 13). He is the One who, called by the Son our Advocate with the Father, is named another Paraclete, whom the Son promised that He would send to us (John XIV, 16).

If He were not of one nature with the Father and the Son, He would never be called another Paraclete from the Son. He is therefore called another Paraclete so that we may recognize the equality of nature and power. One, then, ascending from us to the Father, and another coming to us from the Father, He reveals the Father’s constant and most loving affection toward us. He never permits us in the temptations and miseries of this world to be without either an advocate or a comforter.

He is the One who, together with the Father, sent the Son for the salvation of the human race, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, speaking in the person of the Son: “The Lord sent me, and His Spirit” (Isaiah XLVIII, 16; Matthew XII, 28). He is the One in whom Jesus cast out demons. He is the One whom the Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead on the third day, gave to His disciples, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 22–23).

He is the One who, descending upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, bestowed upon them diverse tongues and gifts (Acts II, 3), fulfilling the prophecy of the holy prophet Joel (Joel II, 28). He is the One who, speaking in the holy martyrs, conquered the devil and the adversaries of Christ. He is the One who filled Paul and set him apart for the apostolate [Note: [Col. 0515D] The same Roman edition reads: “for the ministry of the apostolate.”] (Acts XIII, 2).

He is the One who works His diverse gifts in each of the members of the Lord Christ until the end of the world (1 Corinthians XII, 6). He is the One who not only drives sadness, grief, and evil and shameful thoughts from us, but also grants us the remembrance of God, so that we may rightly say with the prophet David: “I remembered God and was glad” (Psalm LXXVI, 4); and again: “I shall remember Your wonders” (ibid., 12).

He is the One who, coming to us when we rightly believe and act well, drives away darkness, distress, and faintheartedness, illuminates us with His light, and mingles the mind of Christ with our understanding, so that we may contemplate our life, which is hidden in Christ, and consider what our condition will be in the eternal ages and in those that are to come, following Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens and, seated at the right hand of God and present everywhere, has left no place empty of His presence.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] The Roman edition reads: “Even if we think that, according to the dispensation of the body assumed for our salvation, He is contained within the space of one place . . . nevertheless the nature of His divinity and incorporeality is not bounded.”]

Provided that we do not suppose that He is confined within the space of a single place according to the dispensation of the body assumed for our salvation, or bounded according to the nature of His divinity and incorporeality. Divinity cannot be separated by differences of place. The Savior Himself confirms this, saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except He who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

The Spirit, the Word, the Power, the Wisdom, the Radiance, the Image, the Vapor, and the Radiance of God without stain—which all undoubtedly demonstrate the person of the Son—therefore needs no place in order to accomplish His works. There was never a time when the Father existed without the Son, or the Son without the Father, or the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER SEVEN
What is proper to God, therefore, is not to have begun, but always to be the same—what he always is. God confirms this by speaking of himself to Moses: “Go and say to the children of Israel, ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). [Note: The Roman edition reads again: “This, in turn, is the Holy Spirit, who was not made, just as neither the Father nor the Son was made. This one…”] This is the Holy Spirit, who was neither born nor made, but is uncreated, just as the Father and the Son are.

This is the Holy Spirit who raises those who have fallen and gives those lying prostrate the opportunity to rise again; and he dispenses each thing according to the diversity of merits and the will of the Father and the Son, all of whose things he knows, not by investigation but through the unity of nature. He is the one of whom the prophet says: [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “The intelligent, manifold, mobile, undefiled Spirit of the Lord, possessing all power and observing all things.”] “The Spirit of the Lord is manifold, pure, undefiled, and holy” (Wis. 7:22). Just as light does not admit darkness, so the Holy Spirit by nature possesses the quality of being incapable of every impurity.

He is the one who withdraws himself from thoughts that are without God. He is the one who pours himself into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets. Unless someone possesses the Holy Spirit, neither the Father nor the Son—whose Spirit he is and with whom he is one God—comes to that person to make a dwelling with him.

He is the Spirit of wisdom, who is therefore called manifold because he contains many things; [Note: In the same Roman edition, the words “and whatever he has, that he also is” are absent.] and whatever he has, that he also is; yet he is one in all things and is not himself changed into any of the things he performs—like the image from a ring, which passes into wax but does not leave the ring. The Lord confirms this by saying to Moses: [Col. 0516D] “Therefore I will take from the Spirit that is in you; [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “and place it upon them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you.”] and I will give it to the seventy” (Num. 11:17)—as though fire were transferred from one flame to another without diminishing the one from which it is taken.

Because of this immutability and diversity of operation, the Lord said concerning Saint John the Baptist that he came “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). This is the Spirit whom God sent into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6); and in whom we cry, “Abba, Father.” Both expressions are found: [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “that God sent into our hearts the Spirit crying, ‘Abba, Father,’ and in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’”] both that we received the Spirit crying, “Abba, Father,” and that we received the Spirit in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15). He therefore explained what he meant by “crying”: namely, that he makes us cry out.

This is the Spirit who pleads for us with inexpressible groanings when human weakness does not know what it ought to pray for (ibid. 26). The holy Apostle taught us this not only by word but also demonstrated it to us by his own example (2 Cor. 12:7–8): when, unaware, he was praying against his own benefit and perfection that the thorn of the flesh, which buffeted him, might depart from him. Later, instructed by that same Holy Spirit, [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “he said that it had been given to him for the increase of his virtues, when he heard: ‘Power is made perfect in weakness.’”] he said that it had been given to him lest he become elated by the greatness of his revelations and suffer some loss of the good.

But because the Lord loved him, and because he has always been accustomed to display the power of his divinity through weakness, he did not do what Paul ignorantly requested. He is the Holy Spirit 326 who has poured himself forth in the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, as the fountain of every grace.

This is the Spirit of the Lord Jesus [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “the Spirit of the mouth of the Lord, who…”] (ibid. 9), who at the end of the world will destroy the Antichrist by his power (2 Thess. 2:8). This is the Holy Spirit whom none of the heretics possesses. Although they all suppose that they possess the baptism of Christ, nevertheless, unless they come to the Church of Christ, they cannot possess the Spirit of Christ. Blessed Paul the Apostle confirms this, saying: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). And again: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

Confirming this, blessed John the Apostle and Evangelist (1 John 4:2–3) says: “By this the Spirit of God is recognized: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God. And this is the Antichrist, whom you have heard is coming, and who is now already in the world.” And again: “Who is the one who conquers the world, except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” (1 John 5:5 and following). “This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies that Jesus is the truth, because there are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one.”

## CHAPTER VIII

Justly, therefore, to those who confess him as Lord without the Holy Spirit [Col. 0517D], he will say at the judgment: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46); and, “Since you do not gather with me, you have scattered the peoples and my members, for whom I shed my blood.”

Therefore the offering of heretics, who do not possess the Holy Spirit, contributes not to the worship of God but [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “to the abominations of demons.”] to the worship of demons. Whatever the heretics say in their synagogues—that is, in the conventicles of Satan—is not the teaching of the Lord, [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “but the howlings and tricks of demons.”] but the howlings and tricks of demons.

These are the people to whom the Holy Spirit, through the prophet Isaiah, says that the Jewish people prepared a table, saying: [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “and preparing a table for the demon and filling a drink-offering for Fortune.”] “And you prepare a table for Fortune” (Isa. 65:11). Therefore the Apostle rebukes both them and sinners who, without judging themselves, boldly approach the most holy body and blood of Christ, saying: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons; you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10:21). [Note: These words concerning the offering of heretics are absent from the Roman edition. [Col. 0518D]] Let this suffice concerning the offering of heretics; now let us return to the order of our discussion.

## CHAPTER IX

Whatever, therefore, we have said about the Holy Spirit, we have likewise left untouched and unexamined as something also performed by the Father and the Son, although we know for certain that the holy and inseparable Trinity never operates anything outside itself. To make clear that what I have said is so, I shall briefly explain it.

The Trinity effected the incarnation of the Word, yet the incarnation pertains only to the Word (Augustine, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, ch. 15). The Trinity produced the voice from heaven over the Son after his baptism, yet it pertains only to the Father. [Note: The same Roman edition says: “For he says, ‘You are my beloved Son.’ The coming…”] The Trinity effected the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Son in the form of a dove (Luke 3:22), yet it pertains only to the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0518C] [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “and the Holy Spirit descended, he says, in bodily form like a dove upon him. Which…”]

Blessed Paul confirms this threefold operation remaining in unity, saying: “There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4 and following).

These three, therefore, bestow one grace upon believers, [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “because the persons of the holy and inseparable Trinity are not of one substance and another, nor is their operation different.”] because the substance of the holy and inseparable Trinity is not one thing and another. Although the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each said to operate individually, they nevertheless operate all things together. Wisdom founded, the Spirit gave life, and he ordered all things by righteous judgment.

He therefore distributed the world into various forms by his justice and, by his grace ordering all things, incomprehensibly dispenses, contains, and governs its members in such abundance. The governance of this providence is so just, [Col. 0518D] [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “so provident.”] so provident, so hidden and secret, that what is thought to be punishment is medicine for the one who suffers.

One God, therefore, existing in the holy Trinity, performs these things. Confirming this concerning himself, he says through the prophet Isaiah: “I am the Lord, and there is no more outside me” [Col. 0519A] (Isa. 45:6–7), that is, apart from my Word and my Spirit, my power and my wisdom, which are always in me. [Note: The Roman edition adds: “And again the same prophet says: ‘In you God is, and there is no other besides you.’ And elsewhere: ‘He will send them a man who will save them; judging, he will save them…’ ‘By myself I have sworn: unless righteousness goes forth from my mouth, and my words do not turn back.’ And elsewhere: ‘Whatever word goes forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty until everything I have willed is accomplished.’ The Son is therefore truly the Word of the Father, since he did not return empty; for, looking upon the pledges, he says: ‘For you are God, and we did not know it, God of Israel, Savior.’ We did not know, because he was veiled in flesh. And again: ‘He had no appearance or glory, and his face was despised and not esteemed,’ so that divine power might be concealed by a human body. And another prophet says: ‘He is a man, and who will know him?’ And again: ‘This our God will not be reckoned as another beside him’; and: ‘After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings.’ And again it is written: ‘A man existing in affliction and knowing how to endure,’ and so forth.”]

There is no other God and Savior, concerning whom the same prophet says: “And the Lord will send them a Savior, who will save them from their sins” (ibid. 5). And again the prophet cited above speaks in the person of the Father: “By myself I have sworn, because a word shall go forth from my mouth and shall not return to me empty” (Isa. 19:20; 45:23; 55:11).

The Word of the Father truly did not return to him empty, because he placed at the right hand of the Father the pledges of our salvation—that is, the true soul and true body which he had assumed. Seeing in the Spirit that this would happen, the prophet says: “Truly you are a hidden God” (Isa. 45:15), that is, hidden in the flesh, “God of Israel, Savior.” And again: “His face was hidden and despised” (Isa. 53:2), so that divine power might be concealed by a human body. And again: “He is a man, and who [uncertain OCR: “quies” for *quis*] knows him?” (Jer. 17:9). And again: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him, who appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36). And again: “A man in pain and knowing how to bear infirmities” (ibid. 38).

These words clearly indicate a true human body and a true soul: he knew how to bear infirmities and overcame them by his divinity, making peace through the blood of his cross, both with the things in heaven and with those on earth (Isa. 53:4; Col. 1:20). Through these words it became clear that in the Lord Jesus Christ there is not truth in part and falsehood in part, but complete truth—namely, both God and man.

## CHAPTER X

But human wisdom does not understand this. Blessed Paul condemns it, saying: “Let your faith not rest in the wisdom of human beings, whose thoughts the Lord knows to be vain, but in the power of God” (1 Cor. 2:5); and again: “Not taught by words of human wisdom, [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the manifestation of the Spirit and of power.”] but taught by the Holy Spirit” (ibid. 13). Let faith, therefore, not rest in human wisdom, and let there be no heresy.

The Son and the Holy Spirit, therefore, are always in the Father. The Son himself confirms this, saying: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30)—one with respect to the nature of divinity, “are” with respect to the distinct properties of the persons. And again: “Behold, the hour is coming … when you will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32). And again: “The works that I do, the Father who remains in me himself does them” (John 14:10).

The Son, therefore, is always in the Father—the one who says to Moses: “He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14). He is the one with whom the Father rejoiced when the world had been completed, because he had founded such a mass of earth upon the seas and set it upon the rivers, so that the heaviest element might hang over the delicate waters at his command.

When the Father was making firm the foundations of the earth, no one was with him except those who were in him—that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Let the impious heretics therefore be ashamed, those who say that the Son of God or the Holy Spirit is a creature, or that there was a time when they did not exist. For the author of time cannot at any time have a beginning.

Whatever the Son speaks is the word of the Father and the word of the Holy Spirit; whatever the Father speaks is the word of the Son and the word of the Holy Spirit; whatever the Holy Spirit speaks is the word of the Father and the word of the Son of God.

Thus, in these words, under the mystery of the holy Trinity, the knowledge of the one who fills all things and in whom all things are is proclaimed. For the Son says: “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26); nevertheless, because of the fellowship and unity of nature, he is sent by the Son. This Son was seen by the prophet Isaiah in the form of one reigning; but, because of the fellowship of majesty and the unity of substance, the Holy Spirit spoke in the prophet.

In the Cherubim and Seraphim, where the vision itself is described as having occurred, the Lord is partly revealed and partly concealed: “with two wings they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew” (Isa. 6:2). The things that existed before the world and those that will exist after the world are therefore veiled—things “which eye has not seen and ear has not heard” (1 Cor. 2:9). But the things made in the six days have come to our knowledge through sacred reading.

We therefore confess not only one operation in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but also equality; [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “For where there is the same operation, there is equality.”] for where there is equality, there are the same nature and the same substance.

Therefore, the Evangelist says (John 5:19), the Jews persecuted him because he not only violated the Sabbath but also, by saying that he was the Son of God, made himself equal with God. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “Therefore the Lord says (when the Jews … that he was making himself equal to God): ‘The Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.’ He shows this more clearly elsewhere, saying: ‘I and the Father,’ etc.”] The Lord himself confirms this, saying: “I and the Father are one”; “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; and again: “What the Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can snatch it from my hand.” Immediately he adds: “And no one can snatch anything from the hand of my Father” (John 10:30; 14:10; 10:29).

If, then, no one can snatch from the Son’s hand what the Father has given him, and these same things are in the Father’s hand and are not snatched away from him, it is clearly proved that everything belonging to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—who belongs to both the Father and the Son—is common to them: the things of the Father are held in the Son’s hand, and the things of the Son are held in the Father’s hand.

The Lord Christ, therefore, the Son of God and man, who was always with the Father and in the Father, spoke in two ways: sometimes according to the glory of his divinity, and sometimes according to the man assumed from our nature. The Father is therefore in the Son, and the Son in the Father; in both is the Holy Spirit. [Note: The same Roman edition adds: “Although our knowledge of the mystery of the holy and inseparable Trinity is confused, our confession nevertheless belongs to us. Thus the holy Apostle, although he testifies that the judgments of God are incomprehensible, does not nevertheless declare them entirely inscrutable and hidden. Therefore he did not say, ‘The judgments of God are impossible to find,’ or ‘They never present themselves as comprehensible,’ lest he seem completely to cut off the hope of those who seek. Rather, he said, ‘They are incomprehensible,’ and so forth.”]

For this reason, ignorance is the proper confession of the mystery of the holy and inseparable Trinity. Since the holy Apostle testifies that the judgments of God are inscrutable (Rom. 11:33), the wise reader now understands how inscrutable and hidden he must be whose judgments are inscrutable and hidden.

Yet the holy Apostle did not say, “The judgments of God are found with difficulty,” or “Never,” lest he seem completely to cut off the hope of those who seek. Rather, he said: “The judgments of God are inscrutable.” Therefore, however much someone may advance in knowledge and, devoted to wisdom, search out hidden things, created nature can never comprehend fully the substance of the uncreated. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “as it is, it can never comprehend it fully.”]

When someone has discovered one thing, another again presents itself for inquiry; when he has found that, he will discover countless others. [Note: Vatican manuscript: “other unchangeable things”; Roman edition: “other, even higher things, occur.”] So abundant is the material continually offered to the investigator that ignorance of what remains envelops his knowledge of what came before. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “the investigation of what remains envelops the preceding knowledge in forgetfulness.”]

Thus the wisest Solomon, understanding the natures and difficulties of things, and setting a limit to his wisdom, says: “I said, ‘I will become wise,’ but it withdrew farther from me than it was; and profound depth—who will find it?” And again: “There are many works of the Lord hidden away.” And again: “Just as you do not know the way of the spirit, or how the bones are joined together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things.” And again: “Do not seek things higher than you, and do not investigate things stronger than you.” And again: “Just as it is not good for one who eats much honey, so one who investigates majesty is overwhelmed by glory” (Wis. 7:17; Eccl. 7:24–25; 11:5; 3:12).

And truly, nothing is so true, nothing so evident. For it is written: “Who understands his offenses?” (Ps. 18:13). If human beings do not understand their own offenses, how much less will they be able to discover the nature of God and his counsels! Confirming this, the prophet says: “Who has declared his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

## CHAPTER XI

In this one God, the almighty Father, creator of visible and invisible things, we therefore believe. His judgments and counsels are hidden, but never unjust. Yet this Father is Father without having any father himself. Therefore the Son begotten from him—whose generation human speech cannot express—cannot be inferior to him, because, as has been said, he is his Word, power, and wisdom.

We confess the Lord God, God the Son of the most high Father, the only one from the only one; and we confess that with the Father and the Holy Spirit he is one God. Although human speech cannot explain his [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “majesty.”] equality, we have learned the holy and venerable mysteries of his incarnation from the holy Archangel Gabriel, who addressed the holy virgin Mary, married yet alone conscious by ear of having conceived through the Word. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “who addressed the Virgin, pregnant with the Word.”]

For he says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

This generation, therefore, by which he was born from a virgin for our salvation, does not make him later than the Father, either in time or in power. He is not a temporal parent, so that the Son might be disadvantaged by temporal succession; rather, the eternal Father begot an equally eternal Son. Nor was he born or made from outside, as the heretics falsely claim; true faith holds that he was generated from the Father’s own substance.

It is therefore honorable to confess a true Son from the true God, in whom the eternity and omnipotence of the perfect and holy Trinity reside. Thus, just as it is fitting for us to believe in the Father, so also in the Son, [Note: The Roman edition reads: “because, just as the one who was begotten is wholly what he is, so is the one who wholly begot him.”] because the one who was begotten is wholly what the one who begot him is.

We also believe in the Holy Spirit. Earlier, by his gift, we demonstrated his majesty, power, and equality, which he possesses with the Father and the Son. He proceeds from the Father and possesses, together with the Father and the Son, the common divinity, operation, and substance. While distinguishing the persons in their properties, we nevertheless confess the divinity of the holy Trinity to be inseparable: what we distinguish by names and persons, we unite in power, divinity, and unity.

The name of the holy Trinity is therefore a great mystery and secret. Consequently, when our discourse concerns spiritual things, nothing carnal at all should be placed before the eyes of the heart.

The holy and inseparable Trinity possesses invisible light, inseparable power, incomprehensible substance, and unending life; everlasting peace attends it, and no creature ever penetrates it or disturbs it.

If, therefore, someone calls either the Son or the Holy Spirit something outside the majesty of the Father, he seems to seek his hope from himself—that is, from a nature like his own, not from a superior nature. For everything created was made from what previously was not and is like itself, insofar as this is concerned.

God the Father is therefore Father to the Lord Christ by proper generation; to us, by voluntary adoption. He is Father to Christ by nature, but to us by grace. He is God to Christ [Note: The Roman edition reads: “by unity of substance, but to us by gift and power.”] by the unity of the mystery, but to us by power.

Whoever therefore holds anything other than this, and does not believe accordingly, [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Let him be anathematized by the holy catholic and apostolic Church.”] let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER XII

The Holy Spirit himself, as has already been said, is also the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. He is the one who, like the Father and the Son, fills the whole world. He is the one whom the Son declared to be holy and good. He is the one whom the prophet David, like the Lord Christ, declared to be good and upright (Luke 11:13). For he says: “The word of the Lord is upright”—this concerning the Son; and: “My heart has poured forth a good word.”

Concerning the Holy Spirit: “Renew an upright spirit within me”; and: “Your good Spirit will lead me on an upright path” (Ps. 32:4; 44:1; 50:12, 14; 142:10). [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “He is entreated as the principal and upright Spirit.”]

He is the one who foresees future things as though they were present. He is the one who announced to us many years beforehand the birth, miracles, persecution, passion, cross, death, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and coming of Christ the Lord for the judgment [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “of the living and the dead.”]

Just as the Father is without beginning, [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “he has a Son without beginning, coeternal, begotten from himself, not after himself; likewise the Holy Spirit is coequal with the Father and the Son.”] so he has the Holy Spirit and the Son without beginning and coeternal; the Son is begotten from himself, not after himself.

Therefore, just as the Father precedes every antiquity of time, surpasses it in eternity, and exceeds it in longevity, so he begot the Son as his companion in power and in that equality which we have mentioned. But this power, this wisdom, this Word who is the Son, to use the words of the Apostle (Phil. 2:6 and following), “although he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

For this reason the Son of God is called Christ; [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “Christ is called man.”] this nevertheless signifies his birth according to the flesh, his passion, and his death. But this miraculous and unique birth, by which [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “Christ was born a man.”] Christ was begotten, took place from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, as the faith of the holy creed testifies. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “of this holy creed.”]

This only Son of God in divinity is therefore also found to be the only one in his bodily birth, through which he assumed our humanity in order to save it. For he alone was born of a virgin who experienced neither conception by a man nor corruption through childbirth.

We therefore confess that he was born according to the flesh from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary. For the Archangel Gabriel had already promised the blessed virgin Mary that this would happen, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

This Son [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “God’s Son and the man Christ Jesus.”] of God was crucified and buried for our salvation under Pontius Pilate. The true flesh assumed from the Virgin was truly crucified, truly buried, and truly raised on the third day.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, the creator and sanctifier, came to the womb of the holy Virgin in order to assume flesh from her and form the human being there, so that through the union of the Word and the human being, Christ, the perfect mediator between God and human beings, might be born from the first formation—arising without deception of his humanity and without corruption of his divinity: destined to die because he was created, but destined to overcome the bonds of death as the Creator.

We must not therefore say that there is any separation between the Word and the human being assumed by him. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “We do not posit any separation of persons; but from two . . . united natures, we confess one Christ, God and man, the Son of God, in the unity of person.”] Because from two natures—namely, divine and human—mystically composed, we confess one Christ, the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XIII
Therefore it is permitted for us to believe these things, not to dissect them: to seek humbly, [Note: [Col. 0524D] The Roman edition likewise has, “not to inquire arrogantly.”] not to investigate arrogantly. The Word, therefore, and substance of God, which is incorporeal in every respect, could not be inserted into a human body except through some spiritual nature, that is, through a soul. Thus, when the soul received the Word of God through a secret rational process, without any involvement of a man, God was born from the Virgin. [Note: [Col. 0524D] The same Roman edition has: “With a rational soul as intermediary, the Word of God assumed flesh by the working of the Holy Spirit; and thus without any …, etc.”] [Note: [Col. 0524D] The Roman edition likewise has: “Finally, just as God, granting human beings participation in himself, … thereafter lost …”] Accordingly, just as the Son of God, by granting everyone participation in himself as an example—according to the fact that he is the Word and Wisdom of God—is not diminished by sharing in that participation, so the holy soul of Jesus, which was both sorrowful and troubled on account of our sins, contracted nothing thereby. This is the soul whom God loved above his companions (Ambrose, *On Luke*, book X, no. 127); this is our life, of which the Apostle says: “And your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3); this is the soul that loved righteousness and hated iniquity (Ps. 44:8); this was sorrowful, not for death, but even unto death (Matt. 26:38); this was troubled on the cross, not for itself, but for us. It was not the Power, nor the Wisdom, nor the Word of God [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition likewise has: “He assumed this for the salvation of the whole human race in the unity of the person assumed.”] who assumed it for the salvation of our souls and, adorning it with every virtue and holiness, brought it into partnership with divinity.

Concerning this soul, therefore, which in every respect is like our souls, the Savior says: “I have power to lay down my soul, and to take it up again”; and: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, and I take it up again” (John 10:18). This is the blessed soul that cried out on the cross to the divinity, saying: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). The man, therefore, who was about to die through the separation of divinity cried out. For since divinity is free from death, death could not exist unless life departed, because divinity is life; for what is always immortal and incorruptible never suffers either death or corruption.

God, therefore, who is the Word and the Spirit, who breathes where he wills (John 3:8), did not unwillingly abandon the flesh or soul he had assumed. Rather, because he willed it, he left it and laid it down where he willed, in the manner he willed, and when he willed, and took it up again. He was not deprived of the flesh by anyone’s right or power; he divested himself of it. For he who could have avoided death had he not willed it, unquestionably died because he willed it.

The Apostle confirms that this is so when he says: “Divesting himself of the flesh, he stripped principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2:15)—namely, through the death of the man he had assumed—so that, as the blessed Apostle himself says, “through the death of the man he had assumed he might destroy him who held the power of death” (Heb. 2:14), that is, the devil, and free those who throughout their entire life were subject to bondage.

The prophet Isaiah had foretold long beforehand that this would happen, saying: “As a sheep he is led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he was silent; thus he did not open his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition likewise has: “silent; thus he did not open his mouth.”]; and again: “He was offered because he himself willed it, to exhaust the sins of many”; and again: “He handed over his soul to death, and was reckoned among the wicked; and he himself bore the sins of many, and he himself pleaded for transgressors” (Isa. 53:7 ff.).

Therefore Christ the Lord endured the cross, not by necessity but by his will, saying to Peter, who through the weakness of fear was scandalized by the mystery of the cross and trembled through human dread: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings. For the cup that the Father has given me, do you not want me to drink it?” (Matt. 16:23; John 18:11; Matt. 26:23).

Otherwise, if he had not been offered by his own will and had not desired to endure the cross, he who could identify and foretell the betrayer, and who said to the apostles, “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night” (Matt. 26:31), could have avoided those who had been sent to arrest him. Instead, he met them fearlessly and said: “Whom do you seek?” (John 18:4). They immediately fell backward [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition has: “They went backward and fell to the ground.”], because they could not endure the voice of the God who was present.

It was therefore not necessity but will that caused him to suffer—not merely his own will, but also that of the Father, to whom he says: “I willed to do your will, my God” (Ps. 39:9). [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition likewise has: “And elsewhere: I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”]

Through the true flesh of the immortal mediator between God and human beings, we mortals have been redeemed, made alive, saved, and freed from the snares and captivity of the devil. Over him he gave us power, saying: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition likewise has: “Therefore the incarnation of such great humility and ineffable mystery was made for this reason …”]

The whole incarnation, with all its humility and mystery, was therefore accomplished so that we might receive power over the devil, who, recognizing through his pride that he was a creature, fell into such madness that he desired to make himself equal to the Most High Creator, saying: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). [Note: [Col. 0525D] The Roman edition has: “who, not recognizing that he was a creature, wished through pride to make himself equal to the Creator, saying: I will ascend above the clouds.”]

The Apostle confirms this, saying: “What was impossible for the Law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and, because of sin—that is, the sin of the first man—condemned sin in the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0526D] The Roman edition likewise has: “God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh; that is, Satan in the flesh of the Savior, as he also says in another epistle: triumphing over them.”] (Rom. 8:3; Col. 2:15); [Note: [Col. 0526D] The Roman edition likewise has: “them in himself, so that, as the Apostle says elsewhere: As all die in Adam, so also all might be made alive in Christ.”] so that, just as all die in Adam, so also all might be made alive in Christ, who through the passion of the cross dedicated for us, from his side, a laver and a drink for martyrdom (1 Cor. 15:22).

## CHAPTER XIV

For this reason, then, it is fitting for us to consider more carefully who offers, to whom he offers, [Note: [Col. 0526D] The Roman edition likewise has: “what he offers. He who offers became for us the way …”] what he offers, and for whom he offers—the one who has become for us the way, the truth, and the door. Concerning this door the Holy Spirit says through the Prophet: “This is the door of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it”; and again: “He shall not be put to shame when he speaks to his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 117:20; 126:5).

But no one will come to this door except those who have deserved, through the grace and help of God, to be lifted up from the gates of death, that is, from sins. I therefore recall with steadfast confession the punishments of the one in whom I believe, nor am I ashamed of those things which the Redeemer of the world assumed for my salvation and overcame by his power.

You may laugh, Jew and Gentile, that I place my hope in one whom I confess to have been crucified and dead. Yet I glory in these wounds, through which I understand—though you do not—that I am pleasing to my Redeemer. For, as the Apostle says, “the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:24–25).

Behold, I mention Pilate the judge, by whom he was judged who is destined to be the judge of the world. Why should the punishments of that blessed body diminish the dignity of my faith, when a swift resurrection followed and destroyed them? [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and there is no reason that the punishments of that blessed body should diminish the dignity of my faith.”] This is not the end of my faith and confession; hear what follows: “On the third day he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42)—that is, the righteous and sinners, Gentiles and Jews, souls and bodies.

Does our belief now seem to you stable [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and firm.”] and blessed, since it rests upon one whom not even death could confront or resist [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition likewise has: “could resist? And, he says, the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”]?

## CHAPTER XV

Finally, it never became more apparent how greatly our Redeemer abounded in mercy and patience than when he undertook the office of this mystery, assuming, that is, our substance and accepting both the rights of the gallows and of the tomb.

Our prosperity was therefore purchased through his adversity, and divine and human [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition likewise has: “nature entered into a kind of sacred exchange with one another in the person of our Redeemer.”] nature entered into a kind of sacred exchange in our Redeemer: divinity was to receive testimony from humanity, and humanity a reward from divinity. That is, our God was to display, through the wounds of his body, the greatness of his love toward us, and our mind and body were to recognize that the grace of obedience was repaid to humanity through fellowship with divinity [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Vatican manuscript has: “that the grace of obedience was recompensed to him.”].

We must therefore consider with what faith and devotion we ought to cling and serve this Lord, who has bestowed such abundant gifts upon us; [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition has: “who not only had no limit in his generosity, but so exceeded every measure …”] for he set no limit to his generosity, giving the faithful in reward as much as he himself possessed in his kingdom. He even chose to become a sharer in our nature, so that we might believe ourselves capable of becoming his co-heirs—not in order to thrust our substance down from the citadel of divinity, but to draw us, weak as we are and lying in the extremity and necessity of death [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition likewise has: “lying …”], upward to the glory of resurrection.

Because he displayed in himself whatever he promised us, he taught by rising again that the substance of this flesh would not perish; and by his ascension he showed where his dwelling would be after the resurrection. This, therefore, is the great—indeed, by the confession of all, great [Note: [Col. 0527D] The Roman edition likewise has: “great in the confession of all;” [Col. 0528D] “the sacrament of the mystery of piety. For it was manifested in the flesh, just as the outcome of events revealed what had lain hidden in the mystery.”]—sacrament of the mystery of piety, which, as the Teacher of the Gentiles announced, was manifested in the flesh (1 Tim. 3:16), just as the outcome of events revealed it.

It is clear that he was justified in the Spirit, because the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2:5), offered us in himself not only an example of happiness to be hoped for [Note: [Col. 0528D] The Roman edition likewise has: “not only of happiness to be hoped for, but also of happiness to be attained. For, just as through his works and power, by the testimony of truth, he shone forth in his bodily birth as what he was …”], but also an example of happiness to be attained [Note: [Col. 0528D] The Vatican manuscript has: “an example of unity.”]—an example of truth.

This sacrament of piety, through which our Creator and Redeemer embraces us, shone forth through the testimony of his power; and so, having been assumed into glory in his ascension, it was celebrated with the service of angels. Therefore human nature is not to be despised, since through the Lord Christ it deserved to enter into the substance and fellowship of the Holy Trinity.

I think that, with God granting it, enough has been said concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the incarnation of the Lord our Savior. But since, at the conclusion of our doctrine [Note: [Col. 0528D] The same manuscript has: “in the faith of our doctrine.”], the resurrection of our flesh is affirmed, these matters must be repeated by us more firmly and more frequently on account of the heretics.

## CHAPTER XVI

For the Word of God, who is the Lord Christ, who is the firstborn of every creature and the firstborn from the dead, came to his own image, which he himself had previously fashioned. Concerning this image it is written: “And God formed the human being according to his image and likeness” (Gen. 1:27).

And, assuming flesh for the sake of flesh from the holy Virgin Mary through a rational soul, and purifying like things—that is, soul and flesh—through like things, he became in every respect a human being without sin.

Through the soul, therefore, as mediator between God and flesh, he who, as the Apostle says, makes all rich, became poor, so that by his poverty we might be enriched with divine [Col. 0528C] and heavenly riches (2 Cor. 8:9). He did this through that sign of salvation which God gave to the human race, as the prophet Isaiah says (Isa. 7:14 ff.): “Behold, the Lord will give you a sign: behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.” Before he knew how to call his father or his mother, he ate butter and honey [Note: [Col. 0528D] The Roman edition has: “Emmanuel; before he knows how to call his father or mother, he will receive the strength of Damascus; and he will eat butter and honey.”]—that is, he was filled with the Holy Spirit, whose teaching is sweeter to us than honey and the honeycomb. Receiving the spoils of Samaria from the Magi, he was proved to be human, king, and God.

Concerning this wondrous sign also, the holy Simeon says to the Virgin Mary: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34). Concerning this sign the blessed Apostle Paul likewise says: “Jews demand signs, and Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. 1:22).

Therefore Christ came for the sake of his own image, which he had first fashioned in the human being and which he had seen disfigured in humanity by the devil’s art, in the likeness of sin [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Roman edition likewise has: “of sinful flesh”], so that through the passion of the cross and death he might restore the human being to the original image (Rom. 8:3) [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Roman edition likewise has: “condemned to death through the wood of transgression, through his passion …”]. This image can indeed be obscured through negligence, but by nature it cannot be erased.

Concerning this image the Prophet says: “Although the human being walks in the image of God, yet he will be troubled in vain” (Ps. 38:7). No one, therefore, exists who does not possess some image, either of holiness or of sin.

We walk in the image of God when the good thoughts implanted in us by God remain within us and lead us to good works. The memory of God therefore excludes from our heart all crimes and sins which the devil strives to sow and depict there.

Hence the Prophet says: “Lord, in your city you will reduce their images to nothing” (Ps. 72:20). It is of no benefit to have read or heard something unless you have stored in the treasury of memory the good things you have read or heard.

Just as there are three elements in a human being—body, soul, and spirit—so there are three higher faculties that lead us either to good or to evil: thought, speech, and action. The Holy Spirit briefly comprehended these three in the first Psalm, saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1).

These are the devil’s three attendants (*terni stratores*) [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Roman edition has: “*sternistratores*, corrected from the Vatican manuscript as *terni stratores*. A *strator* is one who saddles the prince’s horse and brings it to him when he is about to mount. The Royal manuscript’s *terni statores* is no less suitable; these same persons are called *stratores*, as are lictors and attendants, by whom a person is brought before judges.”], who lie in wait for the wretched soul, so that they may incite it to sin either in word, deed, or thought.

By spirit, soul, and body, therefore, we act either well or badly; we are either chaste or commit fornication. Thus, just as the greedy and plunderers are servants of Mammon, and just as gluttons and drunkards are servants of the belly and lust, so every sin rules over human beings.

The Prophet confirms this by saying: “There will be five cities in the land of Egypt, speaking the language of Canaan” (Isa. 19:18)—that is, the five bodily senses, which speak to the wretched soul oppressed by the darkness of Egypt. For Egypt is interpreted as “pursuing,” or “troubling,” or “confining.”

Unless, therefore, with Christ’s help, we overcome the extremely cold north wind through the warmth of faith—Christ, who both teaches what is good and delights in better things [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and delights in better things”]—it will immediately stir up in us the heat of desire and lust.

Let the flesh therefore be weakened by fasts, and let every desire be circumcised with a spiritual knife [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and let every desire be circumcised with a spiritual knife.”]; and let sin not reign in our mortal body (Rom. 6:12), so that we may be able to escape the companionship of the world and the reproaches of the devil.

Fasting, therefore, is the soul’s contrition and humiliation; affliction, however, belongs to the body.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0530A]

Let what has been said concerning the image of God, according to which the human being was made, suffice. Now let us return to the sequence of our discussion.

He was therefore born from a virgin mother among human beings, without a human father, because he had God as his Father in heaven, whom he had not come to deny by being born from another.

Because of the sentence imposed upon the virgin Eve (Gen. 3:16), which she received after sin—although she had been immortal, she became mortal after the transgression—he himself came through the Virgin. And just as death gained dominion through a virgin, so through the Virgin Mary came the one who would conquer death.

The occasion of death entered through the wood, but through the Lord’s death it was driven out through the wood. Woman was brought forth from the side of the sleeping man (Gen. 2:22); likewise, the Church was formed from Christ’s side on the cross through his passion [Col. 0530B] and the sleep of death.

Woman was formed from the man’s side; and therefore the Lord is struck in the side, so that the man might suffer on behalf of the woman, from whose side she had been formed and who had persuaded him [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Roman edition likewise has: “persuaded him to transgress.”] to transgress.

But let us see, since the subject requires it, what answer should now be given to the heretics who maintain that Adam’s soul was either a portion of God or was made before his body was fashioned from the earth. This is entirely alien to the Catholic faith and foreign to it.

For it is written that God formed the human being from the clay of the earth and, after forming him, breathed into him the breath of life; and the human being became a living soul (Gen. 2:7; Wis. 15:11) [Note: [Col. 0530D] The Roman edition likewise has: “taking dust from the earth.”].

The example of Eve the woman teaches that this is so: after she had been formed into a woman from Adam’s rib, she afterward received her soul from God. This pattern of creation is preserved in us until the end of the world [Note: [Col. 0530D] The same Roman edition has: “as the Wise Man rebukes the impious: ‘For he did not know him who formed him, who inspired into him an active soul, who breathed the spirit of life.’ And David, etc.”], as the prophet Isaiah testifies, saying: “He who forms the spirit of the human being within him”; and David: “He who fashioned their hearts individually” (Ps. 32:15).

Therefore, according to so evident an example [Note: [Col. 0530D] The Roman edition likewise has: “in accordance with testimonies of truth so clear”], the soul is neither prior to the body, nor created beforehand, nor from God’s substance, nor—as the heretics wish—in bodily and irrational creatures, having long ago existed somewhere; they have no proof for this claim.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Therefore every day the God of majesty creates souls in bodies already fashioned [Note: [Col. 0530D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and infuses them. Hence Moses the lawgiver condemns those who strike a pregnant woman, saying: If the child has been formed, he shall give soul for soul, eye for eye.”] and sends them into them, as Moses the lawgiver testifies concerning pregnant women who have a child formed or not yet formed (Exod. 21:23–24).

The Lord confirms this when he says: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17) [Note: [Col. 0530D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and I work. Therefore he did not breathe the breath of life into the face of the human being only once, but breathes it every day.”].

Just as it is impious to say that the human soul is from God’s substance, or that soul comes from soul, so it is impious to say that it was made before the body was fashioned, since Adam himself proclaims: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23).

God is one thing and the human soul another, because the soul was made by him, not from him. God is invisible, incorruptible, impenetrable, and undefiled [Note: [Col. 0531D] The Roman edition likewise has: “sinless and unfailing, impassible and undefiled.”]; he cannot be corrupted in any respect, nor can he be harmed in any respect.

The human soul, however, which is not God, is capable of sin and exists in misery; it is led into falsehood, tempted, blinded, troubled, fails, [Note: [Col. 0531D] The same Roman edition omits this word; it has “is corrupted”] is corrupted, and taken captive. Therefore it needs the power of a liberator.

This change in the soul, this variation, clearly shows me that the human soul is neither God nor from his substance. For if the human soul is God’s substance, as those who say this maintain, then God’s substance is saddened, God’s substance is deceived, God’s substance is blinded, [Note: [Col. 0531D] The Roman edition has: “God’s substance suffers.”] God’s substance is corrupted, God’s substance is taken captive, and it is now judged and, on the day of judgment, after assuming flesh, will be condemned with the devil to eternal fire. Anyone who has sound judgment understands how impious this is.

The Lord himself cries out, strengthening his apostles, and says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). According to these madmen, then, as has already been said, will God judge a portion or nature of himself? Certainly not.

Therefore, in the very bodies in which we were born, [Note: [Col. 0531D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and into which our souls enter at God’s command, they will rise, if they have done good …”] and from which our souls departed when we died, our souls will enter again after the resurrection at God’s command. They will rise, if they have done good, to the resurrection of life, to receive the glory of the heavenly kingdom; but if they have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment and everlasting disgrace and confusion.

The blessed Apostle confirms that this will happen, saying: “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

Then, according to the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah (Isa. 24:2), there will be no distinction between noble and base, [Note: [Col. 0531D] The Roman edition adds: “priest and people”] priest and layperson, servant and master, maidservant and her mistress, rich and poor, [Note: [Col. 0531D] The Roman edition adds: “the lender and the borrower”] lender and debtor, buyer and seller (as Jerome has it in this passage of Isaiah).

All will therefore stand equally before the tribunal of Christ, and there will be no partiality with God. Holy Job likewise announces this in almost the same words, saying: “The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master” (Job 3:19).

And the Savior in the Gospel, to whom all judgment was entrusted because of the glorious passion of the man he had assumed, testifies in a full statement, saying: “For when the Son of Man comes with the holy angels in the majesty of his Father, then he will repay each one according to his works” (Matt. 25:31).

All these things will therefore happen, because the Lord has spoken through the prophets of what is to come. He says: “I have multiplied visions, and I have been represented by the hand of the prophets” (Hos. 12:10).

## CHAPTER XIX

As the prophet mentioned above approaches this secret of the incarnation, he marvels and says: “O watcher, what of the night? What of the night, watcher? The secret is mine; the secret is mine. Woe is me.” [Note: [Col. 0532D] The same Roman edition has: “as if he were saying: when I, the prophet, heard these things, namely …, etc.”]

“When I had heard these things,” says the prophet (Isa. 21:11; 24:16)—namely, that the God of majesty would put on flesh, and when I foresaw that the prophecy had to be fulfilled in him—“I spoke to myself with the inward feeling of my heart,” because I cannot recount everything that I see. My tongue cleaves to my throat; my voice is closed by grief and fear, because such great mysteries are present before my eyes.

I see present things that are destined to come. I understand that the Samaritan watcher [Note: [Col. 0532D] The Roman edition likewise has: “that he is the one who cared for that man who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, …”] is the one who cared for the man who, descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers (Luke 10:33).

This is the watcher to whom blessed Job said: “O watcher of human beings, why have you set me against you, and have I become a burden to myself? Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?” (Job 7:20) [Note: [Col. 0532D] The Roman edition has: “Why have you set me against you? Yet I am a burden upon you. And why have you not caused my iniquity to be forgotten, and provided purification for my sin?”].

This is the watcher who says: “I am continually at my post, standing so many days and nights” (Isa. 21:8) [Note: [Col. 0532D] The Roman edition likewise has: “I stood throughout the whole day, and I stood over the camp all night.”]; and concerning whom the Prophet says: “Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep who guards Israel” (Ps. 120:4).

Because of these names used by the prophets, and because persons are frequently exchanged among them, they contain many parables and are obscure. But now let us return to the sequence of our discussion.

## CHAPTER XX

The heretics who deny the resurrection of the flesh commonly set against us that testimony of the blessed Apostle in which he says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50), while cunningly suppressing what follows. For after he had said, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God,” he continues: “Nor shall corruption possess incorruption” (ibid.).

These words were therefore spoken not so that the nature of our holy bodies would perish, but so that this corruptible nature would put on incorruption, as the same Apostle confirms, saying: “So also is the resurrection of the dead: it is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body” (ibid. 15:42 ff.).

These are the four orders of the resurrection, which were prefigured in that priestly staff which blossomed in the tabernacle of the Lord (Num. 17:8; Lev. 26:19).

The statement “flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” must therefore be understood in the same way as that with which God threatens the sinful people, saying: “I will make the heaven above you like bronze and the earth which you tread like iron”—not that the nature of the elements is changed, but that the magnitude of punishments is shown through bronze and iron.

The Lord Christ therefore manifested to us the true resurrection that would take place in himself, displaying to his doubting disciples, after his resurrection on the third day, the marks of the nails and the wound of the spear (Luke 24:40).

## CHAPTER XXI

Let us not therefore despise our flesh by living wickedly and luxuriously, in which the Lord Christ was both born and suffered and rose again. Let us not despise the clay of our flesh, which, baked into the purest vessel in the deity of the Lord Christ, which is fire, reigns in heaven.

We must indeed ask why the Apostle said: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29). Our God, who is living, divine, and eternal fire, consumes not these bodily materials but the consciences of sinners, and kindles our hearts with his love.

Therefore the angels, who are full of love, are themselves also called fire (Ps. 103:4). So too are all the saints who have been kindled by that fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” [Note: [Col. 0533D] The Roman edition likewise has: “and what do I desire except that it be kindled?”] (Luke 12:49); and again: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (ibid. 12:35).

Concerning this the Apostle also says: “Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Rom. 12:11). The divine word is therefore fiery and fervent.

The Lord himself confirms this when he says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, I have given my words in your mouth as fire” (Jer. 5:14). The prophet himself declares that this fire was burning within him, saying: “It became in my heart like a burning fire” [Note: [Col. 0533D] The Roman edition likewise has: “he says, it became like a burning fire, consuming in my bones.”] (ibid. 20:9).

When it is therefore said, “Our God is a consuming fire,” this does not mean that God, who is spirit, is fire, but that he illuminates the righteous, while to those enduring punishment he appears to be fire.

This is enough concerning the saying, “Our God is a consuming fire.” Now let us return to the sequence of our discussion.

## CHAPTER XXII

How, then, is the resurrection of the flesh denied, when long beforehand the Lord Christ, speaking through the prophet in his own person, said: “My flesh rests in hope” (Ps. 15:9); and in another passage: “His flesh shall not see corruption” (Acts 2:31); and again: “His burial has been taken away” [Note: [Col. 0533D] The Roman edition has: “His burial shall be in peace; it has been removed from the midst.”]; and again: “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God”; and again: “All flesh that is to worship shall come before the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0533D] The Roman edition likewise has: “that it may worship in my presence in Jerusalem, that is, in heaven, etc.”] (Isa. 69:23; 1 Tim. 2:8)?

This means either in the heavenly Jerusalem, or in every place where it has fallen or has been buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “I want men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands.” For if the sun, which is a creature and is commanded to rise, is seen throughout the whole world and extends its rays, how much more must the Creator and almighty God be believed to be present and fill every place [Note: [Col. 0533D] The Roman edition likewise has: “to penetrate and fill every place.”]!

The Prophet says to him: “Where shall I go from your presence? If I descend into hell, you are there” (Ps. 138:7–8), and so forth.

If, then, all flesh is to worship the Lord, and, conversely, the corpses of men who have transgressed against God are to be handed over to eternal fires, there will be a true resurrection of the flesh in both directions.

Therefore we must not deviate either to the right or to the left from this holy and catholic faith: that is, we must follow neither Jewish nor heretical error. Some of them, being carnal, love flesh alone; others, ungrateful for God’s benefits, shrink from admitting that the Lord Jesus Christ had flesh at his birth and, risen again, possesses it forever.

This is the true resurrection, which grants glory to the flesh without removing its truth. As has already been said, the Apostle declares: “This corruptible nature will put on incorruption, and this mortal nature will put on immortality”; and again: “We do not wish to be stripped”—understand, of the flesh—“but to be clothed over, desiring the glory that is from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0534D] The Roman edition likewise has: “which is from God.”]; and again: “so that we may be found clothed and not naked, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (1 Cor. 15:53; 2 Cor. 5:2–3).

No one is clothed over except one who was already clothed, just as our Lord, who was transfigured into glory on the mountain, was so transfigured when he displayed Moses and Elijah as witnesses (Matt. 17:3). Not only his garments but also his face shone like the sun. When his face is mentioned, I think that his other members too were seen.

## CHAPTER XXIII
To this glorification, then, all the righteous will be transformed in the resurrection, as the Evangelist John bears witness, saying: “Beloved, we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). And the righteous man says: “But I shall appear in righteousness in your presence; I shall be satisfied when your glory is manifested to me” (Psalm 16:15). Our bodies, therefore, will rise to remain forever either for glory or for punishment (Dan. 12:2). Witnesses to this are Elijah and Enoch, who through so many ages have remained thus until the second coming of the Lord Christ.

The blessed Job confirms that this is so, saying:

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “I know that he is eternal who is to redeem me, to raise my skin from the earth, which endures these things. For these things have been fashioned for me by the Lord; I am conscious of them; my eye has seen them, and no other; but all these things have been completed for me in my bosom.”]

“I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. This hope of mine has been laid up in my bosom” (Job 19:25 ff.). Let the heretics, then, be ashamed, who falsely claim that either the Lord’s body was airy or imaginary, or that ours will be so, or that there is transmigration of souls.

## CHAPTER XXIV

It is truly impious and unjust to say that Job—who saw his wounds with his own eyes and touched the putrefaction and worms of his body with his own hands (Job 7:5)—will rise in another flesh or another soul. What we have said, therefore, concerning blessed Job applies also to Peter, to Paul, and to all the saints who gave up their souls amid various torments for God.

The heretics mockingly ask us whether there will be a distinction of sex in the resurrection—that is, whether women will rise together with men.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “or whether females will rise distinguished from males.”]

Blind and ignorant, they do not understand the Lord’s saying:

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “The lost are ignorant; the blind do not see.”] “The queen of the South will rise at the judgment with the men of this generation, and she will condemn them” (Luke 11:31).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Therefore there will be a distinction of sex there. Nor is this surprising, because where there is true flesh, there is a distinction of limbs and persons. And where there is such a distinction, there is without doubt John.”]

Where, therefore, there is true flesh, there is a distinction of sex; and where there is a distinction of sex, John is John and Mary is Mary. There will accordingly be a true resurrection of the flesh, but without the works of the flesh; for, as the Truth says: “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).

An angelic likeness, therefore, is promised to us; the substance of the flesh is not denied. For when it is said, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage,” this is spoken of those who are able to marry, yet will not marry. If, in this present life—which is a temptation upon the earth—many,

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “in this miserable life, which is piracy.”] for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, castrate themselves and do not marry, and if not only men but also women do this with Christ’s help, how much more will such things not merely not be done in that blessed life, but not even be permitted to be contemplated!

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “How much less, then, will such things be done in that blessed life—or even, and so forth.”]

It is therefore Catholic and correct to confess that both sexes will rise in the resurrection of the flesh, without the works of sex. For, as has already been said, while we are still placed in this life, we strive, with God’s help, not to fulfill the works of the flesh that lusts against the spirit. The Apostle confirms this, saying: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” (Romans 8:9).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “And again: Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh; for by denying …”]

By denying that those who clearly were in the flesh are “in the flesh,” he condemned in them not the substance of the flesh but sins—that is, the works of the flesh. And again: “So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4); for although our outward person is corrupted—

[Note: The Roman edition: “yet the inward person is renewed from day to day.”]
