—our inward person is renewed. We know that this happens not only in the kingdom of heaven and in baptism, but also daily in penitents, in whom the destruction of the flesh contributes to spiritual progress.

What, then, will there be for one who has neither the works of the flesh nor the growth of limbs, and for whom neither hair nor fingernails grow? We shall all rise into the perfect man, who is Christ—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “and we shall rise into the measure of his fullness.”]

—as it says: “until we all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13). If, during forty years in the wilderness, the hair and fingernails of the Fathers did not grow, nor were their garments or sandals worn out (Deuteronomy 29:5), how impious it is to seek such things in the kingdom of heaven, where pain, groaning, and sorrow will flee, every wise reader understands.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Are such things, then, to be sought there? How impious this is, every faithful person understands.”]

## CHAPTER XXV

Against this doctrine—so true, so firm, and supported by such clear proofs and every virtue—the heretics customarily set before us that saying of the Apostle (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection*, chapter 52): “Not all flesh is the same flesh, but there is one flesh of human beings, another of cattle, another of birds” (1 Corinthians 15:39), and so forth.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “They do not understand, wretched and lost men, the things that follow there: that the blessed Apostle spoke of the dignity of the human body in the resurrection, not of a difference in flesh, and so forth.”]

These wretched men do not understand that the blessed Apostle spoke of the body’s honor, not of a difference of kind. There is, then, one flesh of human beings—that is, of the servant of God—and another of cattle—that is, of the pagan, the sinner, and the heretic, who, although he was in honor, redeemed and honored by the blood of Christ, did not understand; rather, he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them (Psalm 48:13).

There is another flesh of birds—that is, of the martyrs, who are borne aloft on the wings of the Holy Spirit and ascend to heavenly things. There is another of fish—that is, of those who, after the water of saving baptism, are taken up into heavenly life.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Those who, through the water of saving baptism, are taken up into heavenly life.”]

There is one glory of the sun—that is, of Christ; another glory of the moon—that is, of the Church; and another glory of the stars—that is, of the seed of Abraham and of those who show themselves to be his children through faith and good works.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “who are adopted as his sons.”]

“For star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41)—that is, the apostles and prophets: the latter desired to see and hear Christ, while the former saw and heard him.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “in brightness, as the apostles differ from the prophets. The latter desired, and so forth.”]

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Finally, he says, there are also heavenly bodies—that is, Christians—and earthly bodies—that is, Jews.”]

There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies—that is, of Christians and Jews. Finally, to demonstrate the resurrection of all, he concluded his statement by saying: “So also is the resurrection of the dead” (ibid., verse 42).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “So that this may more easily be understood, let us set forth examples of our transformation, which …”]

To make this understood, let us set forth examples from our condition as it occurs in this age. When an infant grows into a child, a child into a young man, a young man into a man, and a man into an old man, he does not perish through each successive age, but is always the same person he was.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “For in these transformations the age changes, but not the nature.”]

Thus, age gradually perishes here, but not nature. In that heavenly Jerusalem, however, where this sun and moon will shine sevenfold, there will be no differences of age. There will be neither infant nor old man, nor anyone small who does not complete his days; rather, as a child of the resurrection, each will attain the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age, so that no one will lack years, nor have years in excess.

In that time, therefore, when the age of all will be one, both saint and sinner will be perfected by a similar resurrection, and they will not differ from one another in age.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Therefore, in that day … they will not differ from one another in time or age.”]

But one will be drawn to eternal rewards and receive blessings a hundredfold, while another will be dragged away to eternal punishments. Although human beings are born in different ways within the human race, there will be one and the same resurrection for all in the resurrection of the flesh—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “the restoration of one nature.”]

—for Adam was born in one way, Eve in another, Cain and Abel in another, and all human beings have been born and are born in various ways; but the man Christ Jesus, who is the mediator between God and human beings, was born in another way (Genesis 2:22; 4:1; 1 Timothy 2:5).

Although a human being is born from different beginnings, there is nevertheless one human nature, which does not differ in the resurrection of the flesh and of all the limbs.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “For all flesh and all the limbs will be one and the same.”]

The Lord’s own statement makes clear that all these limbs are present, when he spoke of the man who did not have a wedding garment (Matthew 22:11)—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “the wedding garment, which was one …”]

—and who did not observe the command: “At all times let your garments be clean.” He ordered that man to be bound hand and foot and cast out, so that he would not recline at the banquet, sit upon the throne, or stand at God’s right hand, but would be sent into the fiery Gehenna, where there is weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth (compare Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 35).

## CHAPTER XXVI

Moreover, it is sufficiently impious to doubt concerning our hairs, which the Lord has declared to be numbered (Matthew 10:30). They have been numbered in vain, then, if they are at some time to perish. But they do not perish, because we shall rise, with all our limbs, in the likeness of the Lord Christ.

If, in this temporal fire, which consumes everything it receives, almighty God displayed his power in the three youths, preserving their hair unharmed in the furnace of burning fire (Daniel 3:50), will he not resurrect our hair in the resurrection? He certainly will, without any increase or diminution.

There will therefore be no variation or loss in the resurrection of the dead—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “or loss.”]

—as there is now the frailty of the flesh in us, which is weighed down by the mass of its burden, which is painted, disfigured, blinded, injured, wounded, healed, dies, decays, and is returned to earth and dust.

[Note: Manuscript of Regius: “which is driven away, calmed.”]

[Note: The Roman edition: “But on the day of judgment it will be restored in the simple nature of the first Adam and in the glory of the second.”]

Yet after all these things, on the day of judgment, it will be restored in the simple nature of the first Adam and in the glory of the second.

There will therefore be a true resurrection of the dead in the flesh, and a distinction of sex, but without the activity of flesh and blood. “The hour is coming,” says the Lord, “when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and will come forth” (John 5:28–29).

They will hear with their ears and come forth on their feet, as Lazarus did, and all those whom the Savior raised (John 11:44). Those, then, who had been placed in the tombs will themselves come forth from the tombs.

All flesh will therefore come forth not only from the earth but also from the sea and from the rivers, so that they may see the salvation of God (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 31). For he will command the fish of the sea and of the rivers, the beasts of the earth, and the birds of the sky; and they will spew forth the bones and flesh of all the dead, so that some may rise to eternal life and others to everlasting disgrace and confusion.

Then the righteous will see the punishments and torments of the wicked, “for their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be in the sight of all flesh” (Isaiah 66:24).

Since, therefore, we hold this hope with complete certainty, just as we presented our limbs to serve uncleanness and iniquity leading to iniquity (Romans 6:13), so let us present them to serve righteousness for sanctification of life, so that, rising from the dead, we may walk in newness of life, and the life of the name of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh because of his Spirit dwelling in us (2 Corinthians 3:18).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “that, walking in newness of life, the life … may be manifested in us, and that, rising from the dead, we may be transformed into his image from glory to glory.”]

It is therefore just—truly just—that those who have always carried the mortification of Christ in their body (2 Corinthians 4:12) should also have his life manifested in their body.

Stripping ourselves, therefore, as the Apostle says (Colossians 3:9), of the old man with his deeds, let us not seek again the garment of error and the cloak of sin—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “the cloak of sin.”]

—but let us put on the new man, who is Christ—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “let us put on the new man.”]

—as his bride says at night: “I have taken off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song of Songs 5:3).

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “This work, then …”]

This art of majesty and power—that is, the resurrection—is performed by that potter who, through the prophet Jeremiah, speaks to the sinful people, saying: “Can I not, like this potter, restore and renew you, O house of Israel?” (Jeremiah 18:6).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Can I not make you, O house of Israel, says the Lord.”]

He also displayed this wondrous work of his majesty in the hand of Moses (Exodus 4:6–7), which, after being changed to whiteness, he subsequently restored to its former color.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “his wondrous power … since he immediately changed it to the whiteness of leprosy and soon restored it to its former color.”]

The very word “resurrection” clearly indicates that it is not one thing that dies and another thing that is raised. What dies in the human being is also what is given life.

Thus, according to the resurrection of the dead—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “what existed rises again.”]

—what existed rises again, even when it goes astray; it does not cease to be known. Finally, that wounded man from Jericho (Luke 10:34) is carried entirely to the inn—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “That wounded man from Jericho is immediately carried to the inn … through the grace of that compassionate Samaritan … it hung in suspense.”]

—and the wounds of his sins are healed unto immortality through the grace of the one who has mercy.

The prophecy, then, which truly hung upon the flesh of the Lord Christ has been fulfilled. The Holy Spirit, desiring to teach us, spoke it, saying: “Who is this who comes up whitened, leaning upon his beloved and overflowing with delights?” And again: “My beloved is white and red” (Song of Songs 8:5; 5:10).

He is red, therefore, by reason of the incarnation, but white by reason of his divinity. The blessed Evangelist John confirms that this is so when he says that the horse on which the Lord sat was red (Revelation 6:4)—namely, the holy body that he assumed from the holy Virgin.

To him, as he ascended into heaven, it is said: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? And why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isaiah 63:1–2).

[Note: The Roman edition: “The brightness of the garments from Bozrah? And: Why are your garments red, and your clothing like that of one who has trodden the winepress?”]

The meaning is: Who is this who ascends from the earth, whose garments are sprinkled with blood?

In the prophet Zechariah it is said that horses of various colors followed him (Zechariah 1:8)—that is, those who are shown as red in martyrdom, or dun-colored in flight, that is, varied in virtues, or white in virginity.

But when this horse is again described by Saint John as red and white (Revelation 19:11)—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “the immortality of his divinity.”]

—his divinity, immortality, and incorruption are revealed. Therefore all who follow him not only wear white garments but also sit upon horses (ibid., verse 14)—namely, incorruptible and immortal bodies.

And so all the saints imitate him, with his help, because they do not defile their garments and, by the gift of his grace, remain virgins. Therefore, as has been said, they will be in white garments, following the Lamb—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “wherever he goes.”]

—the one who took away the sin of the world.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

The Son of God therefore assumed the whole human being from the Virgin, and he will raise the whole person, complete and entire—that is, soul and body—fulfilling his own statement: “Everything that the Father has given me, I will not lose anything of it, but I will raise it on the last day” (John 6:39).

We understand the Lord Christ to have said this both concerning himself and concerning his members, for he speaks through the mouth of himself and of his members in all the holy books.

The head in the body and the body in the head cry out to God—that is, the Church in Christ and Christ in the Church—because nowhere are the members separated from the head, nor the head from the members.

Then his adversaries will see him, those who pierced him and cried: “Take him away, take him away, crucify him!” (John 19:15).

Then the angels’ prophecy will be confirmed. While the apostles stood astonished, they said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

It must also be asked whether, after the resurrection, we shall eat and drink in the kingdom of heaven (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 60), just as the Lord, after his resurrection, ate and drank to demonstrate that he had a true body, as did Lazarus (John 11:44) and the others whom he raised.

The Lord therefore ate to demonstrate the truth of his body (Luke 24:43) and to strengthen the doubting apostles, who thought him a spirit and an apparition. He ate a honeycomb in order to fulfill the prophecy that speaks in his person, saying: “I ate my honeycomb with my honey; eat, friends, and drink deeply, neighbors” (Song of Songs 5:1).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “my bread.”]

For the sake of this prophecy, and to manifest his true body after the resurrection, the Lord ate and drank. Blessed Peter the Apostle confirms this, saying:

[Note: The Roman edition: “He raised him from the dead, and so forth.”]

“But God raised him from the dead, and he was made manifest to us who ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead” (Acts 10:40–41).

After the resurrection, our food will therefore be the Word, the vision of God, his praises, and alleluia, together with those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

After the resurrection, therefore, we shall neither eat nor drink, nor will incorruptible and immortal bodies need to be sustained by earthly nourishment; otherwise, where there is food, there will also be diseases and the other things we suffer in this age.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Just as the Lord assumed true flesh, truly suffered, truly rose again, and truly showed his hands and side to his disciples after the resurrection (John 20:14; Luke 24:40), so he truly ate, truly walked on his feet, and spoke with a true tongue to all the apostles and to Cleopas—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “with Cleopas and Ammaon.”]

—and truly reclined with them at supper in a real bodily posture. He took bread with real hands, blessed it, broke it, and offered it to them.

But the fact that he suddenly vanished from their eyes was an act of divine power, not of a shadow or apparition. Otherwise, even before the Passion, when they had seized him and led him out of Nazareth in order to throw him down from the brow of the mountain on which their city was situated (Luke 4:29), there would be doubt that he passed through their midst—that is, slipped from their hands.

Or did he not have flesh because he made a whip from cords and drove all his enemies and persecutors out of the Temple (John 2:15; John 20:26), where all the power of his divinity shone forth?

The fact that after the resurrection he entered to the disciples through closed doors was an act of the same power as his vanishing from their eyes.

People of this age say that Apollonius the magician, while standing before the emperor Domitian in the imperial chamber, suddenly disappeared (Philostratus of Lemnos, book 8, chapter 2; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 5, chapter 3). We have mentioned this not to compare a magician filled with a demon to the Lord Christ, but to refute the madness of the heretics.

If such a thing is permitted to a magician—provided that it is true—is it not permitted to the Lord? Lynceus, as the tales relate, could see through a wall (Pliny, *Natural History*, book 8, chapter 8). Could the Lord, through closed doors, not enter unless he was an apparition (Matthew 14:29)? He who, even before the resurrection, walked upon the sea with a poised step, and granted this very power to the Apostle Peter, who began to walk upon the waters in faith but soon began to sink through unbelief, unless the Lord’s right hand had quickly sustained him (Jerome, commentary on Isaiah, near the end; also on Matthew 24).

Eagles and vultures perceive corpses across the sea. Will the Savior not see his apostles unless he opens the doors? Finally, tell me, I ask, what is greater: to hang such a vast mass of earth upon three fingers, to balance the heavens in the span of his hand, and to measure the waters with his hand and the mountains with a scale (Isaiah 40:12), or for God to pass through a closed creature?

You attribute the greater thing to the Creator and criticize him for the lesser. The Apostle Peter, as has already been said, walked upon the waters (Matthew 14:36), and the soft waves would not have yielded to a heavy and solid body unless he had hesitated somewhat. Yet you criticize God because he entered through closed doors.

Peter’s faith therefore hesitated for a moment, and immediately the body recognized its nature, so that we might know that it was not the body that walked upon the waters by its weight, but faith.

## CHAPTER XXX

Do not, according to your own judgment, either equate the Lord’s power with the tricks of magicians or make it inferior to them, so that he would appear to have been what he was not, and be thought to have eaten without teeth, broken bread without hands, walked without feet, spoken without a tongue or head, or shown his side without a body.

“But how,” he says, “did they not recognize him on the road if he had the same body that he had before?”

You are mistaken—very greatly mistaken—if you do not hear the Evangelist saying: “Their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him”; and shortly afterward: “Their eyes were opened,” he says, “and they recognized him” (Luke 24:16, 31).

Will you be so foolish as to say that he was one person when he was recognized and another when he was not recognized? Certainly he was one and the same.

To recognize and not to recognize belonged to the eyes of those who saw, not to the one who was seen, so that the prophecy of the holy Jeremiah might be fulfilled, in which he says:

[Note: Absent from the Roman edition: “Why have you become like a stranger in the land, and like a native turning aside to an inn?”]

“Why will he be like a settler in the land, and like a man turning aside to stay?” (Jeremiah 14:8).

Finally, so that you may know that the error involved not the Lord’s body but the eyes, which had been closed: “Their eyes were opened” (John 20:16), and immediately they recognized him.

Mary Magdalene also, as long as she was seeking the living among the dead, did not recognize Jesus; but when she recognized him—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “among the living, she immediately …”]

—she immediately confessed him as Lord.

Jesus was also standing on the shore while all the disciples were together in one boat (John 21:7), though the others did not recognize him. John recognized him first and said: “It is the Lord.”

It was fitting, and entirely appropriate, that virginity should first recognize the virginal body. He was therefore the same, yet he was not seen as the same by everyone.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Immediately afterward the Evangelist adds, saying:

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “And none of those reclining dared to ask him, ‘Who are you?’”]

“And no one dared any longer to ask him, ‘Who are you?’” (John 21:12).

For, eating and drinking together with him, they saw a true human being and God—not, however, as though one were God and another human being, but as one and the same person, the Son of God and the Son of Man.

He was recognized as a human being and worshiped as God, fulfilling what the Lord himself had invoked from the Father for them, saying: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

It is therefore worthy—entirely worthy—that the flesh of the human being should be brought into the heavens, whose inhabitant God deigned to be. Nor can it be thought contrary to merit that a human being should be made a citizen of heaven, whose womb the Spirit, who is God, did not disdain.

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “whose region … God is; to dwell there.”]

It was therefore just that he should bring to immortality and place in the heavens the body in which God, by dwelling in it, deigned to visit the earth, and through which he became a participant in our condition.

Where, then, should God’s dwelling be, if not in the kingdom of God? And where is the kingdom of God, if not in the heavens, where we too shall all be, through his gift and help, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53)?

Then all flesh will see the salvation of God (Isaiah 40:5) and recognize that the Redeemer and Savior is the one who wrestled with Jacob (Genesis 32:24), who was Jacob’s strength and helper, and who, overcome in that voluntary Passion—

[Note: The Roman edition: “overcome in that wrestling, he prefigured that he would bless those who crucified him, and so forth.”]

—thereby prefigured that he would bless those who crucified him and pray for them, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

He also confirmed what he had previously foretold through David: “When those who ate my flesh drew near to me, I prayed” (Psalm 108:4).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Instead of loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed”—as if he were saying: “You who persecute me …”]

The flesh of the Word is eaten, not the Word; flesh, not God, who is spirit, is consumed. “You,” he says, “who persecute me, scourged me; you spat upon my face; you crucified me. Yet I summon you to repentance: for I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn back and live” (Ezekiel 18:32).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “For it is written that I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he be converted, and so forth.”]

The blessed Apostle confirms that this is so, saying: “Although you were once alienated and enemies in mind through your evil works, he reconciled you in the body of his flesh through death—

[Note: In the same Roman edition there is added: “in order to present you holy.”]

—that he might present you holy …” (Colossians 1:21–22).

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0543A]

As for the objection they make, claiming that the Apostle said, “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8), these words were spoken not to condemn the nature of the flesh—whose creator is God, and in which many saints pleased God and reign with Christ—but to reject the mind and works of the flesh (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 46).

When, therefore, the clay of our flesh, as has already been said, has flown to heaven on spiritual wings with the support of angels, it will there have forever the true and peaceful pledge of its salvation, toward whom we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “the Apostle says: ‘in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.’ And, as Isaiah says: ‘Their little ones will be carried upon shoulders and comforted upon knees.’”]

The prophet Isaiah bears witness, saying: “They will be lifted upon shoulders and carried to their places” (Isaiah 66:12). And again: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isaiah 60:8)—

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “with their young. And again: ‘They will bring all your brothers … among the nations, on horses and chariots, in wagons of mules, with coverings, into the holy city Jerusalem.’”]

—that is, to the dwelling places corresponding to their merits, concerning which the Lord says: “There are many dwelling places with my Father” (John 14:2). And again: “They will bring all your brothers from all the nations to Jerusalem, on horses, mules, quadrupeds, wagons, and litters, says the Lord God” (Isaiah 66:20).

So that no one might perhaps doubt that a human being placed in this body can fly through the air, the same Apostle confirms it, saying: “By faith Enoch was translated, so that he would not see death” (Hebrews 2:5).

For Elijah also, placed in this body—

[Note: Absent from the same Roman edition: “in which he remains to this day.”]

—in which he remains to this day, was taken up as though to heaven in a fiery chariot, that is, by the conveyance of angels, who are spirits and a flame of fire and do the will of God (2 Kings 2:2).

The prophet Habakkuk was led by an angel from Judea to Chaldea and brought back again in a moment of time (Daniel 14:35). The Apostle Paul himself was caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2) and into paradise—

[Note: Absent from the same edition: “And from there he was brought back into the world.”]

—and from there he was brought back into the world.

To make it still more evident that these vehicles of the saints are spirits—that is, the angels of God—the example of Saint Philip, one of the Seven, teaches us. The Spirit of the Lord snatched him away from Gaza and suddenly placed him—

[Note: The Roman edition: “in Azotus. Finally, these very things are confirmed by the words of our Lord and Savior, for he says …”]

—in Azotus (Acts 8:39–40).

These statements, examined more clearly and, so to speak, searched out and articulated limb by limb, are sufficient insofar as the Lord has deigned to assist my purpose. Nevertheless, lest we seem to have omitted anything, we must confirm the matter by the words of the Lord and our Savior himself.

For when he was speaking about the field, the wheat, and the weeds, he said: “At the consummation of the age—

[Note: The Roman edition: “the Son of Man will send his angels, he says, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals and separate the weeds …”]

—my Father will send angels to separate the weeds” (Matthew 13:41), that is, sinners, from the wheat, that is, from the righteous.

These are the angels who carried Lazarus, tested in the struggle of poverty and infirmity alike, into the bosom and rest of Abraham (Luke 16:22).

[Note: The same in the Roman edition: “which is the everlasting glory of the blessed. May the holy angels lead us there, where Christ reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.” With these words he closes the treatise.]

## CHAPTER XXXIII
Truly, as it is written: “I have tested you in the furnace of poverty” (Isa. 48:10). People are therefore tested in different ways: one through want and bodily weakness, another through wealth and bodily health. Yet none of these things is either the supreme good or the supreme evil; for the supreme evil is eternal death, and the supreme good is eternal life. All these things, therefore, which mortal life possesses, are intermediate: in each there is temptation. For many whom neither poverty nor weakness has broken have been broken by health, and riches destroy them. The wisest Solomon confirms this when he says to the Lord: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, but grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. 30:8)—namely, lest he become arrogant in the former, or, when subjected to the latter, perjure himself or blaspheme.

But that these things, which we have called intermediate, are foreign to us, the Lord confirms when he says: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book 7, near the end; likewise book 8, no. 85). Riches, then, are foreign to us because they lie outside our nature; for they are neither born with us nor pass away with us. Knowing this, therefore, let us not serve what is foreign, since we ought to have no God except Christ. We are guests, then, in our own possessions; for whatever belongs to the world remains in the world, and whatever we gather for our heirs, we lose. We carry nothing with us except either good or evil works.

Riches, then, are not evil in themselves, but they are evil for those who use them badly; for the good things that God made are very good. Thus the philosophers of this world call nothing the supreme good except peace, honor, and virtue; and they designate nothing as the supreme evil except wickedness, dishonor, greed, and shame. The promise and recompense of all good things is therefore eternal life, while the threat and recompense of all evils is the second death.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

Although these matters may seem to have been stated incidentally, they are nevertheless necessary and useful to us; and therefore we must now return to our order of exposition. When, then, the clay of our flesh, as has already been said, has been baked into a vessel, so that what was formerly weighed down upon the earth by a heavy burden may, after receiving the wings of spiritual grace and the assistance of angels, fly up to heaven, there it possesses forever the true and peaceful pledge of its salvation.

What could be found truer, more evident, or more luminous than this? Nevertheless, lest we seem to have omitted anything, accept the fullest and firmest illustration of our hope: that bird of the East called the phoenix, remarkable for its singularity and monstrous in its posterity. It willingly buries itself, tearing and cutting itself apart by a natural death; yet it is again a phoenix, again the very same bird and not another (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 13; *Apostolic Constitutions*, book 5, ch. 6; Cyril, *Catechetical Lectures*, 18; Lactantius, Ambrose, and others).

As evidence of this, and to strengthen our hope, the Holy Spirit, who is God, also placed the following in the sacred Scriptures: “And they shall flourish like the phoenix”—that is, they shall flourish out of death, out of their burial, just as the phoenix rises from its ashes. If the flesh of a bird rises from its ashes, will human flesh not rise from its ashes? And where is what the Lord Christ declared, that human beings are worth more than many sparrows? Where also is what he promised us through the Prophet, saying: “Your youth shall be renewed like that of the eagle” (see Rabbi Kimhi and other interpreters on this passage; likewise Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 52, ch. 23; Albert the Great, book 23 *On Animals*; Gesner, Aldrovandi, and others)?

They relate that the nature of this bird is as follows: when it has reached extreme old age, it is said to rise so high in the air that it reaches the clouds and fire. Touched by that fire, it immediately plunges into a most secret spring and immerses itself three times; then it is restored to the strength and appearance of its former youth.

The blessed Apostle promised that this would likewise happen to us, saying: “The fire will test what sort each person’s work is.” Birds of different kinds swallow grapes, olives, and other fruits; and after excessive heat, passing their seeds through their excrement, vines and trees grow again. If birds do this for your sake at God’s command, will God not do this for you on account of your faith and his recompense? Believe me: he will, because of his promise. For when once we were nothing, by the command of the Lord God of all creatures we came into being. He who made from nothing what did not exist will therefore be able again to make what he had previously made from nothing.

### CHAPTER XXXV

For if human flesh will not rise, as blind heretics falsely claim, how does Isaiah, filled with the Spirit of God—one who should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist—say: “All flesh shall come to worship before the Lord in Jerusalem, and they shall see the corpses of the men who transgressed against God”—that is, either the Jews, or the impious, or sinners—“their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Jerome, on the final chapter of Isaiah)?

Many wish that this worm or fire be understood as the consciousness of sins that torments those placed in punishments, because through their own vice and sin they have been deprived of so great a good, in accordance with what is written: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled for yourselves” (Isa. 50:11); and again: “As a moth consumes a garment and a worm consumes wood, so sorrow torments the heart of a man” (Prov. 25:2). For just as joy of mind sometimes alleviates bodily pains, so grief of mind weakens and torments the body, as the Prophet says: “A joyful mind makes life flourish, but a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. 17:22). If, then, mental distress is added to bodily illness, the weakness is doubled.

These statements, however, are made in such a way that they do not deny that the punishments of those who transgress and deny God are eternal, as Scripture says: “The almighty Lord will punish them on the day of judgment, giving fire and worms to their flesh; and they shall burn, so that they may feel it forever” (Judith 16:20–21).

Our Lord and Savior confirms that this will indeed happen when he says: “All who have done good shall rise from the dust of the earth for the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29); and again: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41); and again, concerning the man who did not possess a wedding garment: “Take him, bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid. 22:15).

Since, then, hands and feet, weeping and outer darkness—which pertains to the eyes—and the gnashing of teeth are most truly proclaimed by the Lord as belonging to the future resurrection in the flesh, I am astonished at certain heretics who attempt to introduce a body of air, one that after the resurrection is gradually to be dissolved into thin breezes.

Just as the saint is the garment of God and is clothed with a tunic of salvation and joy, so, conversely, the sinner, who bears the image of the old and earthly man, deserves to hear: “Behold, you shall all be devoured by the moth like an old garment” (Isa. 51:8). The diversity of character is therefore marked in the sacred Scriptures by various names. Just as the diversity of trees and musical instruments in the divine Scriptures signifies the diversity of spiritual grace, so also the diversity of wild beasts and serpents signifies the diversity of sins. God therefore wished these different kinds of musical instruments to be named and employed in the divine books in order to lead the Jewish people away from carnal sacrifices and invite them to spiritual and praiseworthy offerings.

But now let what has been said suffice, although, given the greatness of the subject, nothing can ever be said sufficiently about the causes and matters mentioned above. And therefore, holy, venerable, perfect, and inseparable Trinity, whom we worship and adore wholly in faith, this work is yours: with your help and illumination, I have excerpted it from the books of your fatherly servants for my edification. Your perfection is for the glory and praise of your name throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[ON THE ORTHODOX FAITH AGAINST THE ARIANS]

[Col. 0547]

### NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

[Col. 0547] This work, which the Roman editors entitled *On the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son* contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and ancient editions, was composed against those heretics who, while denying that the substance of the Son was the same as the Father’s, refused to call him ὁμοούσιον—that is, “of the same substance”—and instead attempted to introduce the word ὁμοιούσιον, that is, “of similar substance,” while insisting that the word *substance* should be removed from divine matters as though it were unknown to the sacred pages. Epiphanius writes that these men were called Semi-Arians (*Against Heresies* 74). Here our author clearly showed that, by proscribing the term ὁμοούσιος, the Arian heresy would be restored in its entirety; he demonstrated that the Son is God just as the Father is, and answered the arguments by which his opponents disputed that ὁμοούσιον should be expunged. He shows that this same word is contained in the sacred books; and although the unity of substance cannot be clearly conceived or explained, he proves that it should not therefore be rejected, since nothing among created things can be found that is comparable to it. Moreover, of all the many names attributed to the Son in Scripture itself, there is none that does not indicate some one of his mystical qualities rather than reveal the infinite majesty of the divine nature.

Finally, he teaches that the distinction of persons does not introduce a plurality of gods, and that nothing is thereby taken away from the Son’s invisibility or immutability, even when he occasionally presented himself to be seen.

This book exists among the works of Gregory of Nazianzus (*Oration* 49) and of our Ambrose, to both of whom the published works ascribe it. In the former, however, it is enriched by a preface in which he answers someone who accused the little book of obscurity and ambiguity, as well as by a brief epilogue; this is the form in which we present it.

Those who attribute this little work to Gregory of Nazianzus are known to have been led to that opinion chiefly by the authority of Augustine. For they interpret as referring to this work what Augustine reports: “Gregory also, the holy bishop of the East, says most plainly that God is invisible by nature; when he appeared to the fathers, as to Moses, with whom he spoke face to face, he could have been seen, while preserving his invisibility, through the assumed arrangement of some visible matter” (*Letter* 148, new edition, no. 10).

Nevertheless, learned men object that this book is demonstrably the offspring of a Latin writer, not only because the ancient translation called the Italian translation is cited in it, but also because the following words occur there (ch. 6): “A certain reason which among the Greeks is called λόγος”; and likewise: “And this is what the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον, that is, when one thing is the very same with another.” Add to this that Augustine’s passage may be referred to some unquestionably authentic work of Gregory of Nazianzus—for example, *Oration* 34, where precisely the same subject is discussed.

Perhaps someone might answer the first objection by saying that Rufinus, whom this little work reports as its translator in the case of Nazianzus, was accustomed to use great freedom in translating Greek and therefore that there would be nothing absurd in asserting that he rendered these same passages in the wording that he considered most suitable to the taste of Latin readers. The second argument, however, will scarcely move anyone who compares the passage of our author with Augustine’s words quoted above. After citing the example of Moses speaking face to face with God, our author adds: “And yet he is understood to have been seen in such a way that he appeared through the assumed arrangement of some visible [lacuna] matter, while his invisibility was of course preserved” (ch. 8). Who could easily fail to be persuaded that these very words were present to Augustine’s mind when he wrote the earlier passage?

As for Ambrose, it is certainly clear that this writing bears his name both in all editions of the works of the holy Doctor and in some manuscripts. Hence we would readily have suspected that this little book was none other than the work briefly written *On the Faith* by Niceta, bishop of Nicaea or Nicetus, and joined to the volumes of Saint Ambrose, which, as Cassiodorus testifies, he sent to the emperor Gratian (*On the Institution of Divine Literature*, book 1, ch. 16). But since Cassiodorus asserts that the work discusses not only the Father and the Son but also the Holy Spirit—and this agrees less well with the present book—we prefer to regard this as different from that work.

Why it has taken the place of another work and assumed the name of Ambrose is readily apparent: the subject matter is related. There are, moreover, certain slight features not wholly at variance with Ambrose’s manner of expression, such as the statement that heretics, if they had the opportunity, would twist the matter into another interpretation through distorted reasoning. There is also the phrase: “Let the philosophers look to it; let the heretics, their disciples, look to it.” Nor would the statement, “you who even now harass and disturb everything by violence, ambition, and the power of kings,” be too unlike Ambrose if this treatise were attacking rigid Arians such as Auxentius, against whom Justina and her son, the emperor Valentinian, were stirred up against the holy bishop.

In other respects, however, the work differs from Ambrose’s style and genius, so that its author seems not only unlikely to have been Ambrose but not even his translator, contrary to the opinion held by some. You may infer both points from the fact that Augustine, who was thoroughly versed in the writings of his teacher and exceedingly eager to praise him whenever the opportunity arose, nevertheless does not mention him here, but only Gregory, bishop of the East. Add to this that the biblical version differs greatly from the one Ambrose uses everywhere.

P. F. Chifflet, who assigns the same little book equally to both Fathers, brings forward several conjectures that he considers especially strong in support of this attribution when transcribing it for his Vigil. Nevertheless, we do not think that anyone will readily allow himself to be persuaded by these conjectures without manuscript authority or the testimony of any writer, since they are either extremely slight or altogether nonexistent. Certainly neither Hermann, in his life of Ambrose, nor Quenellius, in his appendix to the works of Saint Leo (*Explanations*), was persuaded by them. Both attribute this writing to Gregory, bishop of the Eliberitan see in the province of Baetica (Dissertation 14, pp. 719–720).

Quenellius attempts to establish his opinion by the following arguments:

1. It is clear that the same book proceeded from a Latin author.
2. Jerome testifies of Gregory of Baetica that he wrote an elegant little book *On the Faith* (*On Illustrious Men*).
3. From Augustine’s time onward, the same little book bore the name of some Gregory, thereby providing Augustine with an occasion for error.
4. Its subject agrees with the age of Gregory of Eliberis, against whom we know that the anger of the emperors was also aroused.
5. Finally, this author shows himself hostile to the defenders of three hypostases, a position that was customary among the Luciferians, to whom he had attached himself.

We will not deny that these conjectures possess some weight and force. Yet anyone unwilling to accept them will at least not call into question the antiquity and elegance of the little work we are examining if he considers that it was cited by Augustine and attributed to such great lights of the Greek and Latin Churches. Moreover, a fragment torn from it was inserted into a book circulated among the works of Hilary of Poitiers (*On the Unity of the Father and the Son*), and also into a sermon (*Sermon* 150 in the old edition, now 113 in the new appendix) that for a very long time was attributed to Augustine.

[Col. 0549]

### ON THE ORTHODOX FAITH AGAINST THE ARIANS, OTHERWISE A TREATISE ON THE DIVINITY AND CONSUBSTANTIALITY OF THE SON (C, G, S)

### CONFESSION OF FAITH

[Col. 0549A]

We believe in God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, born uniquely from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born, not made, of one substance with the Father, which the Greeks call ὁμοούσιον; through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth; who for us human beings and for our salvation descended, was incarnate, and became human; suffered, rose again on the third day, ascended into heaven, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit.

But those who say, “There was when he was not,” and, “Before he was born he was not,” and who say that the Son of God is mutable or changeable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes. Amen.

### PROLOGUE

Moved by love for the catholic faith, I had previously published a little book against the Arians. When I had given it to a friend to read, because he approved of it, he thought that it ought to be transcribed. I earnestly requested him first to conceal the author’s name and have it read by learned and prudent men, so that, if anything in it seemed to have been stated too much or too little, it might be corrected through the advice of many.

For no one is so arrogantly convinced that he possesses the fullness of heavenly doctrine that he thinks he clearly comprehends all the mysteries, since the Apostle Paul says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2); and again: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; then face to face” (ibid. 13:12). But if all judged that everything written there stood in accordance with the true faith, then I too would not refuse it to those who requested it. It is evident that he did so. And because the matter was judged worthy both of catholic confession and of a response to heresy, many wished either to read or to copy it.

But someone, whether out of devotion to learning or as a service of charity, subjected what we had written to more scrupulous examination and declared certain passages either superfluous or ambiguous, saying that some people might understand them differently from what I had intended. I therefore arranged those same matters again in plainer language in this little book, both to show the simplicity of my meaning and to remove the scruple from my readers.

For this is what they say can be criticized: that when we set forth the Word of God as a person of the Son, we seem to understand this Word in the manner taught by grammarians, namely, as air struck by the breath of the mouth and made intelligible to the hearing. But we know not the wisdom of this world, which is being destroyed, but that wisdom which is from God, which identifies the Word of God as God when it says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1ff.).

Therefore I confess that I am astonished that anyone could have thought this meant that we denied the proper person of the Word, who is the Son. No one names merely in words someone whom he repeatedly professes truly to exist in his own person. For how could we have confessed a true Son or a true Father if we did not truly preserve the proper personhood both of the Father and of the Son?

But because we said “one God,” we are thought to have denied the persons. Hence what we stated seemed, perhaps, to have this meaning. We name the Father and the Son in such a way as to designate one God in these persons and names. Moreover, although the Father and the Son are called by two names, they are one in reason and substance; and when I establish the Father and the Son, I designate the unity of kind.

These statements were judged capable of being understood as though these names had been placed between the Father and the Son like a name and a surname belonging to one person, although the preceding and following statements could have prevented such a suspicion. For since I had said that the Son of God was born not from elsewhere but properly from the Father—whole from whole, complete from complete, perfect from perfect, and consummate in power—how could I have made the Father himself the Son of himself and in this way called one person by two names? Especially since I had condemned this sect, namely Sabellianism, in the same little book, and had written about the distinction of persons according to their names. For no one can say of one person, “They are one,” or speak of a unity of kind, unless persons are being designated.

What catholic does not know that the Father is truly Father, the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit truly the Holy Spirit? As the Lord himself says to his apostles: “Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). This is the perfect Trinity existing in unity, which we confess to be of one substance. For we do not make a division in God according to the condition of bodies; rather, according to the power of the divine nature, which is not in matter, we believe that the persons signified by the names truly exist and testify that the divinity is one.

Nor do we say that the Son of God is an extension of some part of the Father, as some have thought; nor do we receive the Word as a word without a reality, like the sound of a voice. Rather, we believe that the three names and three persons are of one essence, one majesty, and one power. And therefore we confess one God, because the unity of majesty prevents several persons from being called gods.

Finally, we name the Father and the Son in the catholic manner, but we neither can nor ought to say “two gods”—not because the Son of God is not God, indeed, true God from true God, but because we know the Son of God to be from no other than that one Father himself, and therefore call them one God. The prophets taught this, the apostles taught this, and the Lord himself taught it when he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). “One” refers, as I said, to the unity of divinity, while “are” designates the persons.

The Apostle also says: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him. But not everyone possesses knowledge” (1 Cor. 8:6).

Having explained these words, which caused scruple—not in me, who know what I said, but in others—I think that the opportunity for a bad interpretation has been removed. The confession of faith is clear, the person is established together with the names, and one divinity has been designated.

Or, if anything in the words still seems ambiguous to readers, the words must be compared with their meaning, because it is not simplicity of words but obstinate perversity of understanding that gives off the odor of guilt. When our meaning agrees with the truth, the words too ought to agree with the most sincere reason. Therefore, let the academic disputant withdraw from Christian simplicity.

### CHAPTER I

We know that many serious heresies boil forth from many people and, like poison, pour the virus of their cancer into the innermost heart. Yet those whose first proposition reveals the whole purpose of their heart can either be easily defeated or easily avoided. But those whose teaching in many respects agrees with ours can easily strike minds that are innocent and devoted to God through a fraudulent association, while they defend their own evils by means of our good things.

Nothing can be more dangerous than these heretics, who, although they proceed correctly through everything else, nevertheless infect, by a single word like a drop of poison, that pure and simple faith of the Lord and, consequently, of apostolic tradition.

We must therefore guard ourselves vigorously lest something of this kind secretly insinuate itself into our minds or ears, because nothing drives a person so forcefully toward death as violating faith under the pretext of faith. Just as gypsum mixed with water falsely imitates milk in color, so here an inimical tradition is introduced under the appearance of a plausible confession. For this reason, it is not the similarity of the confession but the meaning of the mind by which the confession itself is confirmed that must be weighed.

Finally, if you attend more carefully and accurately, you will undoubtedly recognize why they wanted the term “substance” removed from the evangelical and apostolic faith and from the tradition of the Fathers: the Arian heresy has been introduced in a subtly abbreviated form by removal of this term.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] The Laet. and Tell. manuscripts read, “I maintain this neither on the basis of opinion,” etc.; all editions read better, as in the text.]

I do not assert this as a conclusion drawn from suspicion or opinion, nor do I act, as they suppose, like an Academic disputant, twisting simple meanings through verbal subtlety. Rather, I bring into the light of knowledge arguments that have been distorted and composed through a perverse artifice, so that an injustice once recognized and understood may more easily be avoided by human beings.

What cause, [Note: [Col. 0552D] The Tell. manuscript and the Amerbach edition read, “what true reason exists.”] or what explanation existed for their laboring, not without great effort, to remove what had been handed down for teaching and belief to all the Churches, and what our Fathers, apostolic men [Note: [Col. 0552D] The Vigilian edition reads, “flooded by the Holy Spirit.”] purified by the Holy Spirit, had established by catholic reasoning against all heresies, especially the Arian heresy, as a kind of barrier of truth blocking every entrance to pestilential doctrine? It can only have been so that they might pretend that the Son of God is mutable and changeable, as though he had not been constituted from the Father’s own substance, and so that they might now freely, securely, and without hesitation hand down and insinuate to the Churches what they had always taught—namely, that he had a temporal beginning, an origin from nothing, and a name derived from another [Note: [Col. 0553D] *Elogium* sometimes has the same meaning as a formula of condemnation.].

### CHAPTER II

You see, then, that in their treatise they have set everything forth not in evangelical faith but in deceitful malice, in order to seduce the simple. It should no longer be merely suspected but evident to all that they posited “God from God” in the manner Arius used to teach, so that the Son was made from God, not born from God.

If he was born, he is of one substance; if he was made, he is not the true Son; and if he is not the true Son, he is not the true God. Or if he is true God and is not from the Father, there are two beings, each possessing a will of its own and a different authority. If they are one only through agreement and association, then he is not, as I have already said, truly God in substance.

He will therefore be God as Moses was to Pharaoh (Exod. 7:1): by power, not by kind. The Son too will have to be believed in the manner in which it was said to the people through Isaiah: “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Isa. 1:2); and elsewhere: “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). He will also be regarded as firstborn in the same way that Israel was called by God his firstborn son (Exod. 4:22). Likewise, he will be considered “firstborn of all creation” as though he were firstborn in the order of created things, so that they may assign to him a certain sequence in the creation of the world’s affairs.

Finally, once the term ὁμοούσιον, “of one substance,” had been removed, they substituted ὁμοιούσιον, “like his maker” [Note: [Col. 0553D] Thus the Roman and Chifflet editions; the old editions and manuscripts read, “they set in place the term ‘similar to its bearer.’”], although likeness is one thing and truth another. Human beings too were made in the image and likeness of God (Gen. 1:26), yet they are not God; nor should one believe that what is God has become human. In the same way, they want the Son of God to be like him, but they say that he is like him from elsewhere, not from the Father’s one holy and blessed substance.

If he is not from the Father’s substance, then he is ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων—that is, “from things that do not exist,” as Arius himself taught. For once that which the Father is has been removed, wherever the Son may have come from, it is necessary that he have both a beginning from nothing and an origin in time; for nothing exists without a beginning except God alone.

Hence the Son says, as the Lord himself stated: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He said this in order to display the names of two persons in the majesty of one divinity [Note: [Col. 0553D] The Laet. manuscript reads, “to display the names of one deity.”], just as the Prophet says in the voice of God: “My heart has poured forth a good Word; I speak my works to the king” (Ps. 44:1). You see, therefore, that this good Word is the Son of God, whom we believe to have been born from nowhere other than the Father’s breast—or, so to speak, from the womb of God’s heart. Accordingly, he calls him king, because he is the King of kings: the Lord God to whom all divine works submit, who said: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

Of him the Evangelist also says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1ff.). Therefore, what was in the beginning must be believed always to have existed; yet it must also be believed to come from no other than him who has no beginning—that is, from the Father’s heart—for he says: “My heart has poured forth a good Word” (Ps. 44:2). He did not say, “In the beginning the Word was made,” but: “In the beginning,” he says, “the Word was.”

Whatever beginning you wish to assign to the Word, you will already have been contradicted, because he says: “In the beginning was the Word.”

Not that we speak of two beginnings on account of the diversity of things, but because the Word, the Son, is always with the Father and was born from the Father. Therefore, since his origin has no beginning, he must be believed eternal with the Father. For neither can the Father ever be named without the Son, nor can the Son be called without the Father; and thus the Son is always, because the Father is always.

“And the Word was God,” he says. Whatever is God always exists; for if he did not always exist, he could not be true God. The same applies to the name Wisdom, since according to the Apostle he is the Wisdom of the Father (1 Cor. 1:24). “I came forth,” he says, “from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24:5). Therefore he is from no other than the Father, because he is always with the Father.

For this reason he is called the Wisdom of God, so that it may never be believed that the Father existed without Wisdom—that is, without his Son. This is that ineffable Wisdom which, in Solomon, is described as established, begotten, or created at the beginning of God’s ways (Prov. 8:22) [Note: [Col. 0554D] The Tell. and Laet. manuscripts, as well as the old editions, read “which at the beginning”; below, “but with a beginning.” The Roman and Vigilian editions read, “but when a beginning.”]. Yet he speaks of it as established in such a way as to show that it had always been with God. What beginning could you assign to God, so that you could mark a beginning for his Wisdom? God did not establish his Wisdom as though he had once existed without Wisdom. Rather, when he calls it “the beginning of his ways,” he indicates the beginning of the movement of some work, so that the beginning of God’s Wisdom is that it proceeded from God to create all things, heavenly and earthly—not that it began to exist in God.

Wisdom was therefore created—or rather, begotten—not for itself, which always existed, but for those things that had to be made by it. Since its greatness and nature could not be known, its power and strength were to be recognized from the effect of its works, so that what we judge from created things might cause us to fear more when we marvel at what has been made. [Note: [Col. 0554D] The Vigilian edition reads, “so that, while we fear the Creator from created things . . . . .”]

But if you say that Wisdom was created in such a way that you understand the Son of God to be a creature, the Apostle confronts you, condemning those who worship the creature. He says: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonored their bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:24–25).

This, I say, is that Wisdom of God which says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24:5), the creator and maker of the universe—that is, the Son of God, through whom all things exist and in whom all things exist. For, as the Apostle said: “In him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Principalities, or Powers. All things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. 1:16–17).

Hence Solomon also says: “Although she is one, she can do all things; remaining in herself, she renews all things, and through the nations she passes into holy souls” (Wis. 7:27). Confirming this, the Apostle says that Christ dwells in the inner person (Eph. 3:16), so that through him by whom all things were made in the beginning, all things may also be saved at the end.

### CHAPTER III

But you say to me: They worship the name ὁμοούσιον, “of one substance,” rather than the Creator, while preserving precisely what the Apostle said: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess” (Phil. 2:10). Moses also says: “Let all the angels of God worship him” (Deut. 32:43). David says: “All kings shall worship him” (Ps. 71:11). This would not indeed be said in the Scriptures unless he were himself the Word, the Son, the maker of all things.

But you say that he ought not to be called ὁμοούσιον because the word does not occur in the divine Scriptures. I ask you in turn, my fellow human being, who forbid this: must it not be named because it is not written, or because it may not be believed in this way?

And if it must be believed in this way, why should it not be confessed in this way? For the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Or if it must not be named for the reason that it must not be believed either, then the assertion of the Arian stain has prevailed—an assertion that denied the Father and the Son to be of one substance for this reason: it introduces the Son of God as made, sometimes out of nothing, sometimes from the Father but from another substance, whenever and however and from wherever it wished—provided only that it contrive to make him come into existence from elsewhere, and not from that which the Father is. Although it says that he was born, this is merely in words; for it again understands everything that is born to have been made, since we too are called begotten by God, although it is established that we are a creation.

Or, if you are not an Arian and acknowledge that the true Son was born, not made, from the true Father, why do you not say that he is of one substance with the Father? You fear in vain, man, to profess what you believe; and you believe in vain if you do not believe in this way, and rightly you are marked out as a heretic. [Note: The Tell. manuscript and the edition of Vigil., “although you have not altered the statement.” The sense is not correct.] And although you have altered the statement in which you seem to have prohibited the Son of God from being called a creation, yet when you add, “Like one of these things that has been made,” you plainly show that you did not wish him not to be called a creation for the reason that he ought not to be understood as made; rather, you do not want him made in the same way as one of these things that has been made, but nevertheless made. For you call him made in another sense—as a perfect creation, through whom all things were made—provided that you also understand him to have been made, though not in the same way as the rest.

But, to return to the point that you say that the term ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*), that is, “of one substance,” is not found in the divine Scriptures, suppose for the moment that this is so, on the ground that wherever “substance” is read, a thing belonging to God, and not God himself, is to be understood. Yet you also profess something else that is not written, namely, “God from God, light from light.” What do you say to this? Either hold everything with me, or abandon everything. For if you fear to say “of one substance” because it is not written, you must likewise fear to profess “God from God” and “light from light.”

But I prove that “God from God,” “light from light,” and the term “of one substance” [Note: Teller: “in the Lord’s Scriptures.”] are contained in the divine Scriptures. For when the Son of God himself, who is God, says in his Gospel, “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:27), we rightly and deservedly profess “God from God,” because we recognize that the Son of God, true God, was born from God the true God, the Father. But this is not in the sense in which we are called gods (Psalm 81:6), or in which Moses was called the god of Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1); rather, because he is the true Son, [Note: The edition of Vigil.: “born from the true Father, not made.”] he was born from the true Father. He is truly and confidently to be called “God from God,” and likewise “light from light.”

You say with me that it is not written, but you do not understand it with me at all. For it is written concerning the Father, “God is light” (1 John 1:5), and concerning the Son, “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world”; and, “The light shines in the darkness,” that is, Christ in the world, “and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:9). Those whose heart was blinded by the darkness of ignorance did not recognize Christ as true God and the true Son of God. But the Lord himself says, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” [John 8:12]. Therefore, because the Father is light and the Son is light, rightly he is “light from light.”

Yet you assert “light from light” as though from the Father, who is the true light, another light had been made—one that was not from the very substance of the Father; as though it were like any other light which, although made by God, is nevertheless entirely different from the one who made it. For this reason you say “light from light,” not “light out of light.” After I have said this beforehand, even if you do not understand it with me, nevertheless, however you pronounce the words, you utter the very expressions although they are not written. Do you not likewise profess with me the term “of one substance,” which you do not think is contained in the Scriptures, unless you have there found a way to conceal by secret deceit your malicious meanings in both cases—so that you might express the same thing with me in the sound of your voice, while nevertheless separating the meaning of the statement far from mine?

So too those heretics who deny the resurrection of the flesh say, in order to deceive simple souls, “Woe to those who do not rise in the flesh.” But if you examine why they say this, knowing that they utterly deny the resurrection of the flesh, they will tell you: “Indeed, woe will be to the one who has not been baptized in the flesh, so that while his soul remains in the body it may rise through baptism from the death of its sins, as from the tomb of its crimes, in that same flesh.” For they defend only the resurrection of the soul in the flesh through the grace of the life-giving washing; they exclude the salvation of the flesh itself. By a plausible confession these people secretly mislead the minds of the innocent. And just as a deadly draught, tempered with the sweetness of honey, kills by its deceptive pleasantness, so this evil too, by flattering the ears and contaminating the understanding of its hearers with a certain corruption, infects them with the contagion of an adhering vice.

## CHAPTER IV

Finally, even now they could name *homoousion*, as they do the other terms, merely in words, if they had a way to twist it toward another meaning by a perverse interpretation. But when they saw that they were trapped by this word, they utterly refused to mention it, lest either by professing it they should appear to believe it, or by believing it they should be seen to have professed it. With subtle ingenuity they excused themselves by saying either that it was not written, or that God ought not to be called “substance,” lest he be thought corporeal.

“For God,” they say, “causes substance to exist, but God himself is not thereby reckoned as a substance; especially,” they say, “since every substance admits opposites. But God, who can admit nothing diverse, ought not to be called substance.”

I would forgive you if you said this simply, if you wished to know the reason for the matter, if you approached this question as an inexperienced person, if you were not yourself the one who had always asserted that the Son of God was either from another substance or from things that did not exist. But since you are the very person who has often been convicted on this point, often confessed it, often denied it, and even more often has been condemned for altering it in another way; and who even now, agitating everything by force, ambition, and power [Note: The Ambrosian edition with the Tell. manuscript reads, “now agitating by ambition”; the Vigil. edition with the Laet. manuscript reads, “by force, ambition,” while the Vigil. edition alone adds “and power.”]—how do you think I can forgive you for repeatedly retracting the same position? Yet, lest this perversity appear to be condemned by prejudice rather than examined, I shall answer you briefly concerning this objection.

You therefore prohibit “substance” from being named in God, as though everything called substance were regarded as belonging to one and the same kind. Do you not know that heavenly things have one mode of constitution and earthly things another, and that even among heavenly and worldly things there is great difference? Angels received the substances of their respective constitutions in one way, and the individual powers in another, as the Apostle says: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars” (1 Corinthians 15:41). So also in this world, just as there are different kinds of things, so there are different bodies of living creatures, and each has the substance proper to its kind, as the Apostle says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh” (ibid., 39).

If, then, the things made by God possess different qualities of substance, do you suppose that the substance in God is like that possessed by one of these created things, so that it can receive opposites? Far be it. For what is the substance of God? It is that very thing which God is: simple, unique, pure, unmixed with any composition, clear, good, perfect, blessed, whole, entirely holy. Do you suppose that what is God is something empty and void? For it is blasphemy to think empty the one through whom all things have been established, who brought forth all things by his word, ordered them by his reason, perfected them by his power, and by whose will and command the universe is governed and all things serve.

And rightly you read that it is written concerning God: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14); and, “He who is has sent me” (ibid.). The Lord himself, the Savior, says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). God therefore exists in substance, in his own essence; knowledge of him is eternal life [Note: All editions and the Laet. manuscript read this way; the Vigil. edition cut out “in his own essence,” while the Tell. manuscript substituted “in his own judgment.” The received reading should not be altered; it means the same as if one wrote, “in the order of substance through his essence.”]—and he is as great as he cannot be said to be. He is rightly esteemed only when he is called beyond estimation, whether you wish it or not.

Therefore, that which a thing is, is the substance of the thing whose existence is maintained. Yet what has already been said concerning how great and of what kind it is can neither be conceived by the mind, assessed by perception, nor defined by the spirit. It is enough that what is believed to exist is established to exist: so that from that very reality which God is there is the Son, in order that he may be the true Son, and that the true Father may be in the Son and the Son in the Father. This is *homoousios*, that is, “of one substance with the Father,” just as the Lord himself says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10); and, “I and the Father are one” (ibid., 10:30); and, “I came forth from the Father” (ibid., 16:28); and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (ibid., 14:9).

[Col. 0558D] And rightly so, because the Son of God was born from God the Father; and therefore, in the unity of substance and in the majesty of deity, they are one, just as Jeremiah prophesied: “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen the word of the Lord?” (Jeremiah 23:18). And again: “If they had stood in my substance, and if they had heard my words, I would have turned them away from their very evil pursuits” (ibid., 22). And in Solomon: “My substance is sweetness” (Wisdom 16:21).

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0559A]

Since, then, you recognize this unity of substance in the Father and the Son not only by prophetic but also by evangelical authority, how do you say that *homoousion* is not found in the divine Scriptures—as though *homoousion* were something other than what he says: “I came forth from God the Father” (John 16:28), and, “I and the Father are one” (ibid., 10:30), or something other than what the prophets openly proclaimed concerning the substance of God?

The meaning of the name is this: that you believe in the unity of substance in the Father and the Son, although you cannot define the reality itself, which is ineffable; so that whether you say “light from light,” or “word from word,” or “spirit from spirit,” or “lord from lord,” whatever you say of him, you nevertheless believe the Father and the Son to be of one essence, and understand the Son from that very reality which the Father is. For if you introduce some comparison with visible things, by the very dissimilarity of the things you will not display an argument but introduce disputatious controversy, as the one whose voice is recorded said: “To whom will you compare me?” (Isaiah 46:5). Therefore, since nothing can be likened to God, let it suffice that he be believed as he himself is apprehended; he willed himself to be believed, not pointed out.

Finally, if concerning this very thing that you profess with me you wished to make some comparison in God, I do not know whether you could define more clearly what you compared. For example, when you say “light from light,” if you were compelled to explain it through a painstaking account, I ask how you believe light to be from light: whether as a lamp from a lamp, or as a sun from a sun—so that by this example you introduce either two lamps or two suns, as though two gods? Or do you designate as “light from light” the radiance of the same lamp’s light or the brightness of the sun shining from that same sun, likening the Son to the archetype of the Father’s light and displaying him as the splendor of its brightness? Of this the Prophet said: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10); or Solomon, when he says: “She is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wisdom 7:26); or when the Apostle here proclaims our Savior to be the image of the invisible God, because the image of the sun is its own light, which proceeds from that same sun (Colossians 1:15). [Note: The word “sun” is absent from the edition; we restore it from the Tell. manuscript, as necessary to the completeness of the sense.]

But it would take too long to state how much could be said in answer to these matters, which generate disputes, something the Apostle forbids (2 Timothy 2:24). For it is established that the light which God is cannot be estimated, comprehended, or defined; nor can anything among the things of this world truly be compared with the divine majesty, since nothing among all these things that are seen or spoken of can be assessed by a fitting likeness according to what God is—especially since he surpasses the intellects and perceptions themselves.

Therefore he warned you to believe the divinity of the substance and to recognize the true Son from the true Father, but not to inquire into the quality of the reality, since you cannot know what its quality or magnitude is. This is what the prophets and the apostles proclaimed.

## CHAPTER VI

Finally, according to our capacity, our strength, and our faith, let us contemplate what God is and see whether anything can be compared with him.
