Certainly this is the one of whom, even when he is spoken of, nothing adequate can be said; when he is estimated, he cannot be estimated; when he is compared, he cannot be compared; when he is defined, he grows beyond the definition itself. He covers the heavens with his hand and encloses the whole circumference of the world in his fist. All things do not know him in his entirety, yet they know him with awe. This world serves his name and power, and even the momentary succession of the elements bears witness to him.

See, then, whether anything can exist to which the Father and the Son could be compared, because the Son is such as the Father is. He would not himself say that he is one with the Father unless he knew himself to be such as the Father is.

There is a certain reason, called *logos* (λόγος) among the Greeks, which distinguishes the persons or names between the Father and the Son, because the Son himself is also called “reason.” Yet this reason is called by many names: sometimes Word, sometimes Power, sometimes Wisdom, sometimes Right Hand, sometimes Arm, sometimes Pearl, sometimes Treasure, sometimes Nets, sometimes Plow, sometimes Fountain, sometimes Rock, sometimes Cornerstone, sometimes Lamb, sometimes Man, sometimes Calf, sometimes Eagle, sometimes Lion, sometimes Way, sometimes Truth, sometimes Life. Thus, although he is God, all in all, these names make known the mysteries of the divine arrangements, but do not properly define or display the majesty of the Son of God himself.

For what is the Son from that which the Father is? Another, yet the same. For this reason too he is called Word: because he proceeded from the Father’s own divine mouth, and the Father neither commanded nor did anything without him. He is called Power because he is truly from God and always with God, and all the Father’s power resides in him. He is called Wisdom because, coming from the Father’s heart, he disclosed the heavenly mysteries to believers. He is called Right Hand because through him all divine works have been perfected. He is called Arm because all things are held together by him. He is called Pearl so that nothing might be regarded as more precious than he. He is called Treasure so that it may be recognized that in him all the resources and riches of the heavenly kingdoms are stored. He is called Nets because through him and in him the diverse multitude of the nations is gathered from the sea of the world into the Church, like fish through the water of baptism, where the distinction between the good and the wicked is recognized. He is called Plow because hard hearts are subjected to the sign of his cross, so that they may be prepared for the necessary seed. [Note: The Ambrosian edition reads, “so that they may have what is more necessary in it”; the Tell. manuscript, “so that they may have what is necessary in it”; the Vigil. edition most aptly reads as in the text.] He is called the Fountain of Living Water because through him thirsty hearts are watered by the grace of heavenly water. He is called Rock because he grants strength to believers and hardness to unbelievers. He is called Cornerstone because, as the one Mediator, he joined together in himself the two walls of the New and Old Testaments. He is called Lamb so that Christ’s innocence and passion might be demonstrated. He is called Man because for our sake he deigned to be born according to the flesh for us human beings. He is called Calf because he endured suffering for our salvation. He is called Eagle because, after his venerable resurrection, he flies as king of the birds to the Father’s throne. [Note: This is the reading of the Tell. manuscript and the Vigil. edition; the Ambrosian edition instead reads, “so that, as king, he might ascend high to the Father,” etc.] He is called Lion because he is the King of kings, who crushed death and the devil by the power of his strength. He is the Way because through him there is ascent. He is the Truth because he knows no falsehood. He is the Life because he gives life to all things.

You see, then, that through these names the meanings of the divine arrangements and works are foreshadowed, but God himself is not thereby properly defined. The Father, then, is God—boundless, eternal, incomprehensible, beyond estimation. His Son too is God and our Lord, as great as the Father; yet he is from no other source than the Father, for he says, “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28), that is, “light from light.”

## CHAPTER VII

But lest the heretic derive some occasion from my establishing two names or two persons—that is, those of the Father and the Son—as though I were saying that there are two gods, in the way they fabricate two from their difference, we name the Father and the Son in such a way that we mark one God in these persons and names. Let the philosophers look to themselves, and the heretics, their disciples, who vary according to a diversity of powers. For us, however, there is one God, the Father, as the Apostle said, “from whom are all things, and we are from him”; and one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, through whom are all things, and we through him (1 Corinthians 8:6).

For what else is understood by “two” than a substance divided into parts between two, and, along with the names themselves, a nature separated, with both the will and commands of acting and ordering divided? The Father and the Son, although believed to be two persons, are nevertheless one in reason and substance. For the association of unequal things is an offense against the better, and another who is not truly God is compared as an insult to the one who is the true God. But when I establish the Father and the Son, I assign them unity of kind; and although I divide that unity among persons, the distinctions of the persons are again joined by the same names into their unity through the natural covenant of the law.

Therefore the Son is as great as the Father will be seen to be: wholly from the Whole, entire from the Entire, perfect from perfect and consummated power, as the Apostle says: “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). For Jeremiah too, the most universally accepted of the prophets, knowing this unity of deity in the Father and the Son, says: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him, who found every way of prudence and gave it to his servant Jacob and his beloved Israel. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36 and following). Isaiah proclaims the same thing, saying: “Thus says the Lord God: Egypt has labored, and the commerce of the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans, tall men, will pass over to you; they will be your servants, and they will walk behind you bound in fetters, and they will supplicate you, because God is in you, and there is no other God besides you; for you are God” (Isaiah 45:14).

Do not suppose that I have said this with the arrogance attributed to Sabellius, who professes that the Father himself is the Son himself. We do not force everything into one meaning in such a way that we are caught by the deceit of other heretics. Rather, because in the very name of the persons their undivided authority is recognized, and the Son is named from the Father not by kind but personally, we therefore ascribe entirely to the Father what is the Son, and entirely to the Son what is the Father. Nothing will be regarded as not belonging to the Father if it is judged to belong to the Son, nor as not belonging to the Son if it is maintained to belong to the Father, because the unity of majesty does not permit them to be called gods in the plural, since it is established that the Father and the Son are of one substance; hence each is called one God.

We fear above all that, unless the Father and the Son are one, the begetting of the author may be brought into disrepute. For this pleased the heretics: that the almighty, invisible, boundless God should degenerate in the Son, changed not only in power but in condition, as though the Father could not have from himself one who was such as he himself is. We therefore defend the true Son from the true Father, who always was and is of one substance with the Father. This is what the Greeks call *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, “with one, another same thing,” [Note: Earlier editions read, “so that the person hearing might be named expressly”; the Vigil. edition and manuscripts, “so that the person might be heard through the names”; some manuscripts read “expressly.” As for the author’s explanation of *homoousion* as “with one, another same thing,” Ambrose gives it somewhat more fully in *On the Faith*, book III, chapter 15, section 126; we have noted that passage as apparently derived from Basil.] so that the persons might be named distinctly, and not so that the terms should separate the substance.

## CHAPTER VIII

But, in order to expose the whole mystery of the Arian heresy—why they do not wish the Son to be believed to be from the Father’s substance—I shall state the matter briefly. They say: Since God the Father is almighty, invisible, unchangeable, immutable, perfect, always the same, and eternal, while the Son is visible, because he was often seen by the patriarchs, and changeable and mutable, because he displayed himself in various forms: if, they say, he were from the Father’s substance, it could never happen that before the assumption of flesh he should be seen either as visible or as mutable. Rather, he would have remained in the equality in which the Father is, since he was from the Father’s substance, because what is from the Father must be believed incapable of being seen, changed, or transformed.

They add to their argument that when he entered into Mary and filled the Virgin’s womb, something was certainly born from her other than what had come. Hence, they say, the substance, now corrupted, changed its state, lost its order, and, through an immediate transformation in the very process of formation, became from God a human being, from spirit flesh. And every transformation, they say, is the destruction of what previously existed. Consequently they argue: If the Son were from the Father’s substance, then the Father too would already appear diminished, either through the transmission or through the ending of his substance. Therefore they preferred to believe that the Son was from another substance, since he could be transformed, changed, and seen, because this cannot be believed of what is from the Father’s substance.

This is the cause of their error, this the origin of the Arian heresy: they do not understand God’s power, nor recognize the ordering of so great a mystery, so that they compare God with human conditions. To them one must first answer that the Son of God was not seen as he was as God, but as human beings were able to receive something from God. Second, he is not himself changeable and convertible in the various forms, but it is an expression of God’s power that, when he deigns to reveal himself to individuals as he wills, he changes his appearance, not his substance; nor does he lose the property of his quality, but he applies a moderation of majesty according to the merit of the one who sees. He himself nevertheless remains the same, as he always is, in the property of his substance, as it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 101:28).

For although there are many things among those seen in this world that are transformed from one thing into another, so that they cease to be what they were and become what they previously were not—for example, when mud is formed into a human being, it ceases to be mud; or when fish or birds emerge from water, they are no longer water, because they are something else; or when potter’s clay hardens into a vessel; or when a stone, burned, is dissolved into lime; or when sand is changed into glass, and other examples too numerous to recount—there is nevertheless a great difference, foolish heretic, between the things that have been made and the one who made everything as he willed. Created things serve the condition assigned to them; but the one who made them belongs to his own will and possesses his own right. He cannot be changed by any compulsion into something other than what he is; rather, he reveals himself as he wills and to whom he wills. For if angels have often been seen in the form of human beings and nevertheless are nothing other than what they know themselves to be, and do not change their substance when they take the form of a human body, how much more is this true of our Lord himself, who made all things and by his own institution granted to those very angels that they could do this?

It also follows that, as has already been said, we affirm that the Son of God was seen by the patriarchs in such a way that not everything in him which is God was seen. Rather, they perceived in him, by means of an image, the arrangements of future events that were to be fulfilled at their respective times. For who could see the Son of God before he assumed visible matter as it pleased him, or before he deigned to put on the human being himself?

Although he was seen by Abraham (Genesis 18:1), he was seen in the form of a human body, so that it might be shown that in the final times he would come as a human being.

Jacob too is seen in one place in the form of an angel (Genesis 28:13), and elsewhere likewise in human form. He therefore displayed himself as an angel to indicate that he was the messenger of the great counsel; but as a human being, with whom he is also described as having wrestled, so that he might especially indicate the image of the future wrestling that he would have with Israel when he came according to human nature. But so that Israel might believe him to be the Lord with whom he wrestled in such a great struggle under the appearance of a human being, he received the name Israel, that is, “a human being seeing God” (Genesis 32:24). “I have seen God face to face,” he says, “and my life has been preserved” (ibid., 30). Certainly he had seen the form of a human being that the Son of God had assumed.

He appeared to Moses in the bush in a flame of fire (Exodus 3:2), to demonstrate light to believers and judgment to unbelievers, because Christ is salvation to believers and punishment to unbelievers, as the Apostle says: “To some, an odor of life unto life; to others, an odor of death unto death” (2 Corinthians 2:16).

He went before the people of Israel as a guide on their journey, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exodus 13:21), to show through the cloud the grace of baptism and through the fire the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle Paul writes that the Fathers were baptized in the cloud (1 Corinthians 10:2), and the Acts of the Apostles declares that the Spirit is like fire (Acts 2:3).

You see, then, heretic, that throughout the divine Scriptures the figures were foreshadowed to the Fathers in honor of God, yet God himself was not revealed as he is in his proper nature. Finally, when Moses prayed that he might see God’s face clearly, what did God immediately say to him? “You cannot see my face,” he said; “for no human being shall see my face and live” (Exodus 33:20). By this very denial of sight, the glory is indicated—a glory that is as great as it must be believed to be and that is declared invisible. Thus, although Moses had arranged, indicated, and expressed the structure of heaven, the orders of the world, the cycles of the elements, and finally the adornments of the whole universe—of him the Lord himself bore witness, saying, “There shall be no prophet like my servant Moses, to whom I spoke face to face, mouth to mouth” (Numbers 12:7–8)—yet he could not see God clearly. He was deservedly worthy of every prophetic gift, but not to such a degree that, being merely human, he could behold God.

We defend all these words as the words of the Son, whom we know to have spoken with Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 31:18), and who had come from the Father to conduct and explain these matters, because it was fitting that from the beginning all things should be ordered, explained, and maintained through him, so that this might establish the chief rationale for having a Son. Yet he is understood to have been seen in such a way that he appeared to be visible through the arrangement of some visible matter, assumed, as I have said, while his invisibility remained intact—the majesty that, diffused beyond all sight, had withdrawn him from the view of everyone. For he was not revealed to human eyes in such a way that the whole deity in him appeared; rather, as in a mirror, when he wishes to enclose faces conceived within his own light as though in a complete image of a human being, [Note: Earlier editions and the Tell. manuscript read, “so that his majesty might be within that appearance”; the Vigil. edition with the Laet. manuscript reads more coherently, “so that the appearance of his majesty might be within that vision”—that is, vision is granted under these conditions.] the radiance of his majesty went before him, and what was seen displayed the image of the truth, not God himself in his proper nature.

So too, when he deigned to put on a human being, he did not inflict defilement on eternity by changing spirit into flesh; rather, by assuming a human being, he bestowed immortality and the eternity of heavenly life. For although the Apostle says that he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, we do not understand him to have been emptied in such a way that the same Spirit became something other than what he had been; [Note: The Gill. and Roman editions read, “that the same Christ became”; other editions and manuscripts read, “that the same spirit became.” The latter is by no means implausible, since above we read, “that he might change spirit into flesh.”] instead, setting aside for a time the honor of his majesty, he put on a human body, and by assuming it became the salvation of the nations. For just as when the sun is covered by a cloud its brightness is restrained, not blinded, and that light which, diffused throughout the whole world, bathes everything in clear radiance is enclosed by a very small obstruction of cloud but is not taken away, so the human being whom the Lord Jesus, our Savior—that is, God and the Son of God—put on did not obstruct God in him, but concealed him. [Note: The Vigil. edition reads, “he did not cut off the divinity in him,” etc.]

Finally, when on the mountain he raised himself slightly beyond the human being himself, the apostles, almost blinded by the brightness of his light, fell to the ground, being human beings (Matthew 17:6). They would have risked their lives had the Lord in his mercy not helped them by once again restraining the honor of his majesty, in accordance with the statement: “No one has seen God and lived” (Exodus 33:20). Thus, just as the sun’s radiance remains unharmed when it does not shine all the way into our sight—for what is not seen is due to the weakness of us, whose eyes are covered by the darkness of clouds—[Note: The Vigil. edition reads, “so too that divine majesty, which, as I have said, had put on a body, shows that it was hidden not through any loss of its own,” etc.] so he proves that he was hidden not through any loss of his own radiance, but through the benefit of the flesh, for whose sake, as I have said, the Son of God endured being the Son of Man.

Indeed, the Virgin conceived from the Spirit of God, and what she conceived, that she bore—namely, God joined to his human being, as I have already said. He himself said: “What is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit” (John 3:6), because God is spirit and he was born from God. So too the angel said to the Virgin Mary: “The Spirit of God will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

You see, then, that the Spirit himself, that is, the Son of God, came to the Virgin, and from her proceeded the Son of God and of a human being. Yet the Son of God was not changed by that garment of flesh; rather, he remained the same in the human being as he had been before the world with the Father—through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made—as the Evangelist says: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:10).

But it is the belief of a madman that one can be liberated by him who, in order to liberate, was lost; in order to be born, was crushed; and in order to recover immortality, passed over into death. But far be it, heretic, that the meaning of your wickedness should be admitted by Catholics. For we believe the Word and the Spirit—that is, the Son of God—to be immutable and unchangeable. When he assumed man, he did not alter his state, lose his rank, or change his substance; rather, he illumined the defilements of that same body [Col. 0566B] with the eternal light of his glory, so that through the pathway of his body the light of the Holy Spirit and the grace of eternal life might overflow to us.

Although we believe him to have suffered and to have been buried, it was that man who suffered—the man whom the Son of God took up, whom he assumed, whom he bore. But because everything that that man suffered was referred to its author, his death and suffering are therefore judged to be the Lord’s; for it is evident that what belongs to God is immortal, while what belongs to man is subject to decay.

On the third day he rose again—not God into man, but rather man into God.

He ascended into heaven, offered to his Father that man as a most pleasing gift, and sat at the Father’s right hand, according to what is written: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

He sent us the Holy Spirit from what is proper to him, from his own one substance, as protector, sanctifier, and guide into eternal life, as it is written in the voice of God: “I will pour out from my Spirit upon my servants and my maidservants” (Joel 2:29). And again: “The Spirit will go forth from me” (Isa. 57:16). And the Lord himself, our Savior, says: “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:15)—namely, from that which is the Son, since the Son also comes from that which the Father is.

After the appointed time, he will come to judge the living and the dead, so that he may grant rewards to believers and punishments to unbelievers.

His kingdom is eternal and immortal; it has neither beginning nor end. To him be honor and glory for ever and ever. [Col. 0566D]

## CONCLUSION

You who read this, I beseech you by God: do not twist the simplicity of its meaning into ambiguity, or draw from it anything other than what has been said. For we confess the Father to be truly Father, the Son of God to be truly the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit to be truly the Holy Spirit, confessing three persons of one substance and one divinity. We condemn the sect of Sabellius and Photinus, as well as that of Arius, and any others that oppose the rule of truth. We embrace the teaching of the Council of Nicaea, preserving it with every effort of our soul and in complete faith [Col. 0568A]; for we know that this teaching was set against all heresies with unconquerable truth.

## [ON THE DIGNITY OF THE PRIESTHOOD]

[Col. 0567]

## NOTICE ON THE BOOKLET ON THE DIGNITY OF THE PRIESTHOOD

Anyone who does not examine this little work altogether superficially will have no doubt that it was falsely attributed to Saint Ambrose. This is evident not only because it contains Jerome’s translation and asserts that senators are to be recognized not by the broad stripe but by the *chlamys*, as Blondellus observes (*De Forma Regni Christiani*, chap. 7), but much more because it contains nothing inconsistent either with Ambrose’s intellect or with his age.

Nevertheless, this same booklet has secured a place in all editions of the works of the holy Doctor; and in written manuscripts also, if one is excepted, it is honored by the prefixed name of Ambrose. Since there is such great agreement among them concerning the pseudepigraphical author, it is surprising how great is their diversity in identifying the work’s subject. For since copies occur so frequently in libraries—fourteen alone being found in the Vatican—there are almost as many titles for it as there are manuscripts.

In some places it is headed *Pastoral Book*, or *On Pastoral Care*; elsewhere, *On the Observance of Bishops*; at other times, *On the Life and Ordination of Bishops and the Simoniacal Heresy*; elsewhere, *A Sermon on Bishops and Priests*. Sometimes it is entitled *On the Apostle*, from the passage where he says, “Faithful is the saying,” and sometimes *A Sermon on Shepherds*; occasionally, *A Sermon on the Mysteries*; and in some places, *On the Ordination of a Bishop through Simony*.

But the codex of the Church of Saint Martial at Limoges differs from the others less in its subject than in its identification of the author, for it bears this title: “A Sermon of Gilbert the Philosopher, Pope of the city of Rome, who was surnamed Sylvester, on the Formation of Bishops.” Our Mabillon had this booklet copied from the same codex and published it in the eleventh part of his *Analecta* as a previously unpublished sermon, undoubtedly misled by that novel title. Nevertheless, he deserved well of scholars in bringing it to light for the first time under the name of this author.

Everything is, in fact, sufficiently appropriate both to the person and to the period (chap. 1, toward the end). For a bishop addresses there men of his own order, and it is well established that the same age suffered especially from the stain of simony. Yet since that manuscript continually differs from all the others—not indeed in meaning, but in wording—it may be questioned whether the same Sylvester should truly be regarded as its author, or whether it was some interpolator. We leave this to be determined by the judgment of readers.

Moreover, from those various manuscript titles it is abundantly clear that two matters are treated in this work: namely, that the dignity of the episcopate is explained and magnified (chapters 2, 3, and 4), and that the crime of simony is vigorously attacked (chapter 5 and following). Since the same treatise is found in the manuscripts designated partly as a sermon and partly as a booklet, it may perhaps be disputed which term more appropriately suits it. Certainly, in the first part there are many features sufficiently characteristic of a sermon; but since toward the end it is explicitly called a booklet, we have thought it preferable to present it among the booklets, or treatises.

[Col. 0567]

# ON THE DIGNITY OF THE PRIESTHOOD

[Col. 0567]

## 357 CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0567B]

If anyone, brothers, recalls the saying in which the Lord rebuked the prudent servant for retaining the money entrusted to him, which he had received for putting out at interest, saying: “You ought to have placed my money with the bankers, and on my arrival I would have collected it with interest” (Luke 19:23)—

[Note: [Col. 0567C] The old edition and Mabillon have: “If anyone, brothers, recalls the Lord’s oracle, by which he rebuked the prudent servant concerning the money kept for himself, which he had received for putting out at interest”; the Roman edition has: “by which he rebuked the wicked servant … for spending it.” Most manuscripts differ from the old edition only in omitting the word “Lord”; several of them read not *fratres* (“brothers”) but *frater* (“brother”). Others restore the passage as in the text.]

—he will no longer, as an idle hearer, reserve the grace of the divine gift entrusted to him solely for his own use. Rather, by making it available to everyone and putting it out more generously, he will possess it securely, so that through it he may provide the fruit of edification to many and, like a beautiful tree laden with fruit, may not be judged to occupy the earth fruitlessly while he lives. For he is adorned by his own fruits, and all who have received fruit from him are nourished. The blessed Apostle also invites us to this very thing: “Do not seek what is your own, but what belongs to others” (Phil. 2:4). And elsewhere: “I do not seek what is useful to myself, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33).

[Note: [Col. 0568C] Quite a few manuscripts read “is proved fruitless”; one reads “is rejected.”]

Therefore, we who have been entrusted with the administration of the divine words, and who have undertaken to feed and nourish Christ’s flock, believe that we shall not escape punishment without incurring great danger if we do not live in this manner, or even if we fail to preach. [Note: [Col. 0568C] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “not without the harm of immense danger”; the others have the reading in the text. The Roman edition too would have followed them, had it not removed the word *noxam* (“harm”).]

And although the wickedness of this life holds us back from preaching these things, the necessity of the command nevertheless summons us [Col. 0569A].

Woe is already upon me if I do not preach; if I leave the treasure entrusted to me buried in the earth—that is, hidden for a long time in my heart; if I keep the lamp of the divine word pressed down beneath a bushel, instead of setting it on a lampstand and displaying it to the eyes of all; and if I fail to unlock the barriers of human ignorance with those keys of the kingdom of heaven which all of us priests received in the blessed Apostle Peter. Then I might deserve to hear, in accordance with the measure of my speech: “Well done, good and faithful servant! Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:22).

[Note: [Col. 0569D] All editions, and some manuscripts, have this reading. Others have in part: “fearing those rebukes and punishments, struck under the fear of God’s penalty”; in part: “struck by fear of punishment because of the tongue’s penalty”; and some: “fearing these rebukes and punishments of God, struck by fear of penalty.”]

Therefore, fearing subjection to those rebukes and punishments, struck by fear of penalty and invited by fraternal love, I no longer address the ordinary people beneath me, whom I have been accustomed to admonish continually; rather, I turn my words now to the very preachers of the people. And, like an obedient servant addressing my fellow servants—that is, as a bishop addressing priests, and as a prelate addressing pontiffs—I shall not hesitate boldly to preach admonitions concerning salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0569D] All editions have “common duties of salvation”; Mabillon has “duties of salvation”; all manuscripts most fittingly have “admonitions concerning salvation.” Latinius rightly observes that in this passage our author differs greatly from the one whom he himself described as Ambrose in Book 1, chapter 1, *On Duties*.]

Nor shall I claim for myself a privilege of knowledge if, out of regard for charity, I put these matters before my fellow priests; nor do I profess myself to be perfect in life when I admonish others concerning perfect life. Rather, when I dare to speak these things to them, I shall hear together with them what I say.

## CHAPTER II

Now, supported by divine assistance, with whatever ability I possess and aided by the prayers of those to whom our discourse is directed, I shall undertake the desired journey and, as though placed in the midst of my fellow priests, address the priests themselves. Hear me, most blessed fathers [Col. 0569C], and, if you deem me worthy, most holy brothers.

Hear me, Levitical stock, priestly shoot, sanctified offspring, leaders and rulers of Christ’s flock. Hear me as I entreat and fear you alike, as I anxiously care for the common good and wish to demonstrate the honor of the episcopate, so that when we display its prerogative of honor, we may also require corresponding merits; and so that we may not go astray in our work when we know the truth in our hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0569D] Some manuscripts add: “and deem me worthy.”]

For it is fitting that the priestly dignity should first be known by us, and then preserved by us, so that the saying of the Psalmist may be refuted by us: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

The honor, therefore, brothers (Dist. 96, c. *Duo sunt*, § *Honor*), and the sublimity of the episcopate cannot be matched by any comparisons. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be far inferior—as though you were comparing lead’s metal with the splendor of gold [Col. 0570A]—since you see the necks of kings and princes bowed at the knees of priests, and, after kissing their right hands, trusting that they are fortified by their prayers.

What should I say now about the multitude of common people, whom the Lord not only deemed worthy to place beneath the priesthood, but whom he also commanded by evangelical precepts to be protected by it in accordance with paternal right?

Thus the Lord certainly says to the blessed Peter: “Peter, do you love me?” And he replied: “You know, Lord, that I love you” (John 21:15–16). When he had been questioned a third time and had answered three times, the Lord repeated three times: “Feed my sheep.” The blessed Apostle Peter did not receive those sheep and that flock only at that time; he received them together with us, and all of us received them with him [Col. 0570B].

Since they are entrusted to priests to be governed, they are rightly said to be subject to their rulers, because, while the evangelical command shines forth, we nevertheless see this also established: “The disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his lord; but it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and for the servant to be like his lord” (Luke 6:40).

## CHAPTER III

You ought to understand, brothers, that we have prefaced all these remarks for this reason: to show that nothing in this world is more excellent than priests and nothing more exalted than bishops. Thus, when we display the dignity of the episcopate to the eyes of bishops, we may recognize properly what we are and demonstrate what we are by profession through our conduct rather than by our title; so that the title may correspond to the conduct, and the conduct respond to the title.

Let the title not be empty while the crime is monstrous; let the honor not be exalted while the life is disfigured [Note: [Col. 0570D] Two manuscripts read: “and a life beset by dangers”; hence also, “and a dangerous life.” One reads “and a life prone [to sin],” and another, together with Mabillon, “and a penal life.”]; let the profession not be godlike while the conduct is illicit; let the dress not be religious while the advancement is irreligious; let the rank not be lofty while the transgression is shameful; let there not be a higher chair in the Church while the priest’s conscience is found to be lower; let us not imitate the speech of a dove while possessing a dog-like mind; let us not display a sheep-like profession while possessing a wolf-like savagery. Then the Lord may rightly answer us through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

Therefore, brothers, just as the *chlamys* adorns a senator, agriculture a farmer [Note: [Col. 0570D] “Just as weapons [adorn] a barbarian” was excised in the Roman edition.], weapons a barbarian, skill in navigation a sailor, and the quality of his work reveals each craftsman as its maker, so the bishop is designated only by episcopal conduct. He should be known by his good works to be a bishop more through his merits than by the fact that he is called one by name [Col. 0571A].

For just as we said that nothing is more excellent than a bishop, so nothing is more pitiable if a bishop imperils himself in regard to holy life, if a priest is held in crime, and if a pontiff is stained by the marks of vices.

[Note: [Col. 0571C] The phrase “and if a pontiff is stained …” was absent from all editions and many manuscripts; we have restored it from a manuscript of better quality.]

And just as it is easier to fall on level ground, so it is more grievous when one has fallen from lofty dignity [Note: [Col. 0571C] Mabillon’s edition reads: “thus one who has fallen from on high incurs a grave ruin.” Below it reads: “Episcopal honor indeed is great before men; but after a fall, God forbid, the grief in the Church is great.”], because a fall from on high is dashed down in a more serious collapse.

Episcopal honor is illustrious before human beings; but if it suffers a fall, the grief is great. For the higher the episcopal rank is above others, the heavier the fall if it declines through negligence.

Great sublimity must have great caution [Note: [Col. 0571C] The same editions add: “It requires great caution; greater honor needs greater vigilance. From the one to whom more is entrusted, more is demanded; and the powerful will suffer powerful torments, while the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do what was fitting will be beaten with many blows. For God requires something different from a bishop …”]. Great honor must be surrounded by even greater care. From the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required, as it is written: “The best things are always mingled with the worst”; and elsewhere: “The mighty will suffer mightier torments” (Wis. 6:7); and: “For one who knows the law and does not do it, it is a great sin” (Jas. 4:17); and: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten severely” (Luke 12:47).

For God requires one thing from a bishop, another from a presbyter, another from a deacon [Note: [Col. 0571D] Some manuscripts add: “another from a subdeacon, and another from a cleric.”], and another from a cleric, and another from a layman—or from each individual according to his condition.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] Mabillon’s edition adds: “Although God examines the deeds of all individually in his judgment, more is nevertheless required from the one to whom greater care has been entrusted; greater punishments will be paid by the one to whom the care of governing a greater number of peoples has been entrusted, if that administration is neglected.”]

Although God examines the works of all human beings in his judgment, more is nevertheless required from the one to whom more has been entrusted; for greater punishments are suffered by the one to whom the care of governing a greater number of peoples has been committed.

## CHAPTER IV

And so that we may portray for all priests, in particular, the manner and form of the episcopate [Col. 0571C], we must review the apostolic rule, which depicts its several episcopal actions one by one.

[Note: [Col. 0571D] The Codex Baluzius reads: “The apostolic rule must be reviewed by us in every respect; it distinguishes the individual features of the episcopate, lest any priest complain that he has been rebuked in this work by our inventions rather than reproved by apostolic sayings. Thus to all …” The manuscript is also followed by Mabillon’s edition, with a few minor differences.]

Thus the blessed Apostle says to all bishops: “Faithful is the saying” (1 Tim. 3:1), as though he were saying: “I speak truthfully about what I am about to say,” so that no one might think that I have lied.

He adds: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (ibid.)—that is, if you desire to be a bishop, you desire something great: [Col. 0572A]

[Note: [Col. 0571D] The Baluzius manuscript lacks the following passage: “But if you also embrace a good work … you desire to be.” Mabillon gives the whole passage as follows: “That is, do you desire to be a bishop? What you seek is great; but if you also embrace a good work, you seek something great indeed. For you cannot be a bishop if you wish to despise episcopal actions. And again he introduces and says: ‘A bishop must be …’—namely, if you are reproved, you are subjected to the disgrace of guilt. Guilt leads to liability; one subject to liability is subject to punishment; one subject to punishment is liable to servitude; and one liable to servitude loses freedom. Behold what episcopal freedom becomes through these stages, which we have called criminal. But so that you may not be reproved, preserve actions irreproachable in every respect. After this he adds: ‘The husband of one wife.’ If you attend only to the literal sense, he condemns bigamy, so that one who wishes to attain the rank of bishop may not know a second union. But if it is understood allegorically, he forbids a bishop to have two wives—that is, after the Catholic doctrine, not to adopt heretical understanding, but to associate himself only with the faith of Christian sincerity, so that a bishop may be called the husband of one wife alone, namely, the Church. He next says: ‘Sober.’ By ‘sober’ he means not merely sparing of wine but restrained in conduct, so that he may not indulge excessively in wine and may rejoice with a sober mind. If he does not do this, he will not be a bishop.”]

—but if you also embrace a good work. For if you wish to be one in any other way, you cannot be a bishop, because he continues: “A bishop must be irreproachable” (ibid., 2).

He says “irreproachable,” for if a bishop is reproved, he is disgracefully subjected to guilt. Indeed, guilt leads to liability, liability to punishment, and punishment all the way to death. Behold what becomes of episcopal dignity.

A little later he says: “The husband of one wife” (ibid.). If we look only at the surface of the letter, he forbids a bigamist to be ordained bishop; but if we ascend to a higher meaning, he forbids a bishop to usurp two Churches. And if you search even further inwardly, he warns that a bishop must not be found, after Catholic doctrine, to possess a heretical understanding [Col. 0572B]. Rather, he must associate himself only with the Christian, orthodox, and Catholic faith, so that a bishop may be called the husband of one wife alone—that is, of the Catholic Church.

Then he continues and says: “Sober” (ibid.), that is, sparing not only of wine but also of vices, so that he may not indulge in wine beyond what is appropriate and may always be found sober in mind.

He added what follows, saying: “Prudent.” For he means not worldly prudence, of which it is said that it is foolishness with God (II Cor. III, 19), but spiritual prudence—that is, prudence circumspect in action and skilled in speech—so that he may be “wise as a serpent and innocent as a dove” (Matt. 10:16).

[Note: [Col. 0572D] Mabillon’s edition again adds: “If he is not such, he is not a bishop.”]

And again he introduces and says: “Well adorned.” If we attend only to the literal sense [Col. 0572C], we shall seek for priests no other adornment than a more splendid garment—for example, beaver and silk clothing (1 Tim. 3:2)—and he will think himself superior among bishops who has put on the more splendid garment.

[Note: [Col. 0572D] Some manuscripts read: “no other adornment in a priest than …” Below, instead of “he considers himself superior,” several manuscripts read “more richly endowed”; Mabillon’s edition has “more holy.”]

But the holy Apostle does not wish to be understood in this way, for he teaches that a bishop is adorned not in flesh but in mind, so that the priest who has a soul ordered toward God may please God [Col. 0573A].

[Note: [Col. 0573C] Mabillon’s edition adds: “Whoever does not do these things will not be a bishop; and the unjust person incurs infamy by despising the holy Apostle.”]

After this he added: “Hospitable” (1 Tim. 3:2), so that, out of regard for humanity, he may receive into his hospitality those who have no lodging, bring the needy who lack a roof into his house, and not consume alone the gifts of Christ that Christ’s goodness has bestowed upon him. Since God loves a cheerful giver, let him contribute to Christ’s poor without complaint.

Then he continues and says: “Able to teach” (ibid.), that is, the bishop should possess such strength of wisdom that he may not only teach adequately the people entrusted to him, but also be able to repel from the Catholic Church the contradictions of every heresy, lest through his ignorance he fail to teach the ignorant and, overtaken by such a circumstance, what is written should happen to him: “When the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14) [Col. 0573B].

[Note: [Col. 0573C] Mabillon’s edition reads: “and let that happen to him in such a case which is written.” This is not bad; nevertheless, the manuscripts and the other editions agree with one another, except that some codices read *praevento* for *praeventus*.]

But whoever does not know himself to be such as we have described should not seek the priesthood, nor presume to usurp another’s place [Note: [Col. 0573C] The same edition has: “lest he deprive another of his place—one who could illuminate all by the splendor of his wisdom.”], especially that of one who is able to illumine the hearts of peoples with the splendor of his wisdom.

He adds and says: “Not given to wine” (1 Tim. 3:3), that is, not devoted to much wine, so that if he is believed or observed to be a bishop, it may be unknown whether he has drunk or not; lest, after a heavy drinking of wine, he become enamored of the allurements of women [Note: [Col. 0573D] The same edition adds: “and delight in lust, because through wine, as the Apostle says, all lust is nourished. If he cannot do these things, he cannot be a bishop.”], and lest through wine, as the Apostle says, all debauchery be nourished (Eph. 5:18).

Finally, he continues, saying: “Not violent, but gentle” (1 Tim. 3:3)—that is, he must not have hands inclined to slaughter, nor strike the consciences of others with wicked suspicions, lest, when he is found eager for violence, he be judged more an athlete than a bishop [Col. 0573C].

Rather, he should patiently endure injuries inflicted by others, so that he may display a calm gentleness to all people and show firm patience to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] The same edition adds: “so that through weak endurance he may display tranquil gentleness. Again he says … let him release it, so that the one who proclaims God’s praises and offers the divine sacrifices may not bring forth the poisons of lawsuits. For God cannot be blessed from the priest’s mouth while a human being is cursed, since that person is known to possess the image of God; nor can evil and good in any way be compatible in him. If he does not do these things, he will not be a bishop.” All other editions and manuscripts agree among themselves, except that the Baluzius manuscript and the Roman edition prefer “that sweet and bitter water should proceed”; the Roman edition has “that water should flow forth.”]

Again he added, saying: “Not quarrelsome” (ibid.), that is, the bishop must not loosen his tongue for abuse, lest through the same tongue by which he offers praise to God and tastes the divine sacrifices, he produce the poisons of lawsuits. For it is not fitting that blessing and cursing should proceed simultaneously from the bishop’s mouth; nor that by the same tongue through which God is praised, a human being should be cursed, since a single fountain cannot produce both sweet and bitter water [Col. 0574A].

Next he continued, saying: “Not greedy” (ibid.), that is, not desirous of dishonest gain:

[Note: [Col. 0573D] The same edition adds: “lest the bishop be overcome in anything by desire for profit and, made liable to wrongdoing for the sake of shameful gain, nourish greed, which is the root of all evils … but rather let him distribute those very things to Christ’s poor and purchase for himself the kingdom of heaven. And he connects the following, etc.” The Codex Souch differs from the other editions and manuscripts in reading: “who used only the stipends of his own Church.”]

He must not be held captive by the desire for profit or nourish greed, which is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10). Content only with the stipends of his own Church, he should not seek at all what he understands to be superfluous; rather, from the very poverty of his Church, he should willingly distribute to Christ’s poor, as it is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:5).

[Note: [Col. 0574C] This is found in several, and better, manuscripts. The others, including the edition of Erasmus and later editions, do not differ from them except in reading “remains forever”; they omit the remaining words of this passage. Amerbach, together with some manuscripts, had omitted the entire text.]

And elsewhere: “He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever; his horn shall be exalted in glory” (Ps. 111:9) [Col. 0574B].

And he joined what follows, saying: “One who knows how to rule his own household well, having his children submissive with all chastity” (1 Tim. 3:4).

He can rule his own household well who has preserved the chastity of his body.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] Mabillon’s edition adds: “to rule well, namely, to hold the household of his body under authoritative control, and not himself be subjected to the body or be driven headlong, unbridled, into the reins of lust, so that he may guide his children toward the rule of chastity by the example of purity. If he does not do these things, he cannot be called a bishop. Then he says: ‘If anyone does not know how to rule his own household …’ The old edition and manuscripts agree with one another, with a few exceptions, where they read ‘truly rule his own body’; but the Roman edition had revised it to: ‘rule his own body with such authority that he is not subjected to its will, lest desire …’”]

“His household,” he says—that is, let him rule his body with authoritative power, lest he himself become subject to his body and, devoted to the desire of lust, plunge into destruction. Rather, let him teach his children the rule of chastity by the example of purity.

“For if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?” (ibid., 5). This is what we said above: if he is unable to cultivate the house of his own heart, how will he care for the affairs of many? And if he cannot remove the beam of sin from his own eye, how will he be able to cut the splinter from another’s eye (Luke 6:41)?

[Note: [Col. 0574D] Mabillon’s edition adds: “from whose eye will he remove the splinter? Whoever does not do this will not be a bishop.”]

He continues and says: “Not a recent convert” (1 Tim. 3:6), that is, one who has recently come to the faith from paganism, or certainly one who has been transferred from secular military service to the clerical office.

Such men, therefore, should not seize the priestly rank indiscriminately, lest, lifted up into pride, they fall into judgment and the devil’s snare; for what they do not learn over a long period they cannot preserve in a short one.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] The Roman edition reads: “Those who have not learned it even in a short time cannot preserve it over a long period.” The only difference in the other editions and manuscripts is that Mabillon’s edition uses the singular and adds: “but, having fallen and being ignorant, he will undergo the judgment that the devil, in his pride, deserved to undergo.”]

And, concluding the rule and episcopal form, he finally added, saying: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. 3:7)—that is, from heretics and schismatics who establish profane assemblies for themselves outside the holy Catholic Church [Col. 0575A].

[Note: [Col. 0575C] The same edition adds: “who establish profane assemblies, among whom nevertheless the Apostle says that bishops ought to have a good testimony concerning their spotless life and holy conduct, lest they take occasion to slander and begin to defame the Catholic doctrine of the holy religion. If he cannot be such, how can he be a bishop? As I think, in this work, etc.” The Alnensis Codex differs from the others and from the editions in reading: “may they receive an opportunity in their wickedness to slander the bishop.”]

Nevertheless, the Apostle says that, with these as witnesses, the bishop must have a good testimony concerning his spotless life and holy conduct, lest his enemies perhaps gain an opportunity to slander him and begin to defame the Catholic doctrine.

## CHAPTER V
Having thus prefaced these matters, I believe that in this work we have been freed, as it were, from a great burden of debt, since we have set against the bishops not our own testimony but that of the holy Apostle, lest they should laugh at our work as though it were [Note: All editions and manuscripts, with a few exceptions, read: “lest they should laugh at our work as though it were vulgar fables”; in Mabillon’s edition there is a lacuna at this point, as follows: “lest, like clouds: But when …”]. But since the authority of the holy Apostle Paul has smiled upon us at every point, let them, if they dare, criticize the Apostle himself rather than us.

And although the length of this little book is already constraining us, and time presses us to bring this work to an end, concern for our brothers’ sake nevertheless delays us—especially for those priests who, dulled by the torpor of their minds, defame the priestly honor [Note: The Roman edition reads: “and who lament that a new rule has been prodigiously brought forth in this storm”; it also has “and Gehazi.” Among the other editions and manuscripts there is this difference: the older edition and certain manuscripts prefer “rule and storm,” whereas several manuscripts more correctly read “rule in this storm.” Mabillon’s edition continues as follows: “and, following the example of the leprous Gehazi and the magician Simon, they bought the grace of the Holy Spirit at a price and sold it, in no way …”]. They lament that, amid this storm, a new and portentous rule has been brought forth; following Gehazi and Simon’s doctrine, they bought the grace of holy episcopacy with money, not at all fearing that, having bought priestly honor with money, they would be condemned by the blessed Apostle Peter together with Simon, as he says: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be bought with money” [Acts 8:20]. [Note: Mabillon’s edition reads: “you thought that you possessed it for a price; and let them believe that they received leprosy with Gehazi from the holy Elisha, when they likewise judge the priestly rank to be sold for a price. And if, with more severe diseases, etc.” The older edition and manuscripts agree with our text. The Roman edition, however, after “Elisha” adds: “when he said: ‘Naaman, leprosy shall cling to you and to your seed forever.’” To whom, etc.]

And they believe that they have received the leprosy of Gehazi from the holy Elisha [2 Kings 5:27], since they judge that the priestly rank can be acquired with money.

When we have said this to them, it ought to have been enough for them to possess their own leprosy by purchasing it. For just as, when the head has been corrupted by more powerful diseases, the rest of the body must necessarily be fatally drenched by the overflow of the disease above, so those who seem to be the head of the Church corrupt the body of their brethren with a pestilential disease, so that nothing in the structure of the whole body can escape uninjured, since the deadly poison of negligent priests’ depravity [Note: Mabillon’s edition reads: “that the virus of their depravity would not infect it.” And you may see throughout the Church priests whom not merit but money has advanced: a foolish and unlearned priest has seized the rank.] infects it. Thus you see throughout the Church men whom not merit but money has advanced to the episcopal order, and a foolish and unlearned people who have chosen such a priest for themselves.

If you wish to question them faithfully about who appointed them priests, they immediately answer and say: “I was recently ordained bishop by the archbishop, and I gave him one hundred solidi [Note: The same edition adds: “so that he might confer the episcopal rank upon me.” Below, instead of *sacello* (“chapel”), that edition alone, felicitously, restores *locello* (“little box”) twice.] so that I might deserve to obtain the episcopal grace; if I had not given them, I would not be a bishop today. Therefore it is better for me to bring gold out of my little box than to lose so great a priesthood. I gave gold and purchased the episcopate.” [Note: The same edition reads: “Yet, if I live prosperously, I shall ordain a presbyter and receive gold; I shall make a deacon and receive a quantity of silver; and from the other orders as well, one by one, and from blessing abbots and churches, I trust that I shall extract a profit in money. Behold, the gold that I gave I have intact in my little box. I answer: ‘Indeed …’” The older edition and manuscripts agree among themselves, against the Roman edition, which cut out the words “and from the other … I trust that I shall extract,” although those words are supported by the older authorities.]

If I live, I do not doubt that I shall immediately recover those solidi. I ordain presbyters, consecrate deacons, and receive gold; and from the other orders as well I trust that I shall extract a profit in money. Behold, I have also recovered the gold that I gave in my little box: therefore I received the episcopate for nothing.

Indeed, this is what I grieve over: the archbishop made the bishop in a carnal manner. For on account of money he ordained one spiritually leprous [Note: Mabillon’s edition reads: “He ordained him. You gave money and thought that you had acquired God’s grace, and by this very act you received leprosy. Again, you accepted money and did not fear to sell God’s grace for a price; at the same time you handed over leprosy and completed a miserable transaction. You appointed an abbot over monks on account of money, and exalted a leprous man to the death of the monks. And ignorant men …” Among the editions and manuscripts there is this difference: for “miserable transaction,” some manuscripts read “wondrous transaction.”]. “May your money perish with you,” he says, “because you acquired the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price” [Acts 8:20–21], and you carried out a miserable transaction to the destruction of souls.

Ignorant and unlearned men shout at their ordinations and say: “You are worthy and just”; but their miserable conscience says: “You are unworthy and unjust.” [Note: The same edition adds: “Such a bishop declares to the people: ‘Peace be with you,’ while inwardly he does not have peace with himself.”]

For a bishop of this kind announces to the people: “Peace be with you.” To carnal eyes he appears to be a great bishop, but to divine eyes he is seen as greatly leprous. By money he acquired an undeserved rank [Note: The Roman and Mabillon editions add: “and lost God in his inner man.” In the remainder they agree with the manuscripts and the older edition, except that the latter consistently uses the second person by apostrophe.], and before God he lost the inner man. The flesh received dignity, and the soul lost honor. The servant-flesh became mistress of the soul, and the soul, which had been mistress, became the flesh’s servant. The flesh rules peoples, and the soul serves the demon. He purchased priesthood for the flesh and prepared loss for the soul.

And what does it profit such a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul [Matthew 16:25]? What he gave when he was ordained bishop was gold; what he lost was his soul. When he ordained another, what he received was money; what he gave was leprosy. These are the merchandise of the wicked, to their destruction.

Yet I question our brother and fellow bishop—for I too am a bishop, and I speak with a bishop. Tell me, then, brother bishop, for a little while: when you gave money, what did you receive?

“I received episcopal grace.”

Then I ask you: Why is this grace called by such a name?

He replies: “Why do you ask? I suppose it is called grace because it is given freely.”

Then, if grace is given freely and is not valued in gold, why did you purchase grace with money?

He replies: “It would not have been given to me if it had not been bought with money; nor would I have been ordained bishop if I had not given money.”

Therefore, as is evident from your answers, you did not receive grace when you were ordained, because you did not merit it freely. And so, brother, if you did not receive grace, how could you become a bishop? For the Lord also says to his disciples: “You received without payment; give without payment” [Matthew 10:8]. Why, then, did you think that you possessed grace for a price, although it is given freely? For, as I see it, by giving gold you lost it, and you did not acquire holy grace.

Still, adding one further question, I inquire of my brother bishop, lest we appear to have omitted any trustworthy proofs. Who gives episcopal grace, brother—God or a man?

You undoubtedly answer: “God.”

Yet God gives it through a man: a man lays on hands, and God bestows grace; a priest extends his suppliant right hand, and God blesses with his powerful right hand; a bishop initiates the order, and God grants the dignity. O justice, O fairness! If money is given to a man who does nothing more in the ordination than the service entrusted to him, why is everything denied to God, who bestows the very order upon you? Does it seem just to you that the servant should be honored while the master suffers injury, that the priest should unjustly receive money while God suffers injury at a man’s hands?

But since God expects nothing from you for the order he has granted, why does the priest shamelessly expect money from you? God wished to grant it freely to man, and the rapacious bishop demands money from man [Note: The same edition reads: “from man? God gave it freely to him, as the benevolent giver; the priest, as the malignant one, enslaved him.”]. God, certainly in his kindness, gave it freely to man, and the malicious priest robbed him without cause? For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it [1 Corinthians 4:7]?

## CHAPTER VI

Behold to what evils the divine order is driven; behold to what disgrace priests have fallen—priests who deserved to hear from the judge of the world: “You are the light of the world” [Matthew 5:14]. Behold to whom the nations are subjected—those to whom the Lord said: “You are the salt of the earth” [ibid., 13]. [Note: The same edition reads: “If you have been appointed by the Lord as the light of the Church … are you bound and shackled by the excesses mentioned above?” And: “And not only because, while doing these things, you yourself perish deservedly …”]

Therefore, if the bishop is the light of the Church and is ordained by the Lord so that, by the radiant eloquence of his preaching, he may illumine the hidden places of consciences with the light of knowledge, why is he himself held bound in palpable darkness? And not only does he himself perish deservedly while acting wickedly; he also undeservedly destroys others with himself.

For if you deserved to possess the flavor of salt so that you might season the fields of the foolish [Note: The Roman edition reads “season hearts”; one manuscript reads “season insipid things”; the others, together with the edition, read “season fields.” Mabillon continues: “why, stupefied by such a disgraceful vice, do you offer yourself to be trampled under the unclean feet of swine?”], why, made foolish by such a vice, did you offer yourself to be trampled under the unclean feet of pigs, so that you can season neither others nor yourself?

You willingly sought the function of the eyes in the body—that is, in the Church—so that through you the rest of the body might possess the guidance of light [Note: Mabillon’s edition reads: “you sought it voluptuously … and you yourself do not provide light.”]; and now, darkened by a certain bleary film and fog of vices, you neither make yourself fit for the light nor provide light to others.

Of these eyes the Gospel says: “If your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light” [Matthew 6:22]—that is, if the bishop, who has deserved to preside in the body as its light, is adorned with holy simplicity [Note: The same edition reads: “adorned with the innocence of simplicity”], the whole Church is irradiated by the splendor of light.

“But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark”; that is, if the bishop, who seemed to provide light to the body subject to him, is clouded by the blindness of wickedness, what will the other members do, from whose eyes the light has been taken away?

That is: what will the secular multitude do when the bishop has urged the people toward a similar abyss of crimes by illicit pleasures and forbidden actions, so that nothing will now seem illicit to anyone that is committed by the bishop as though it were lawful? Rather, people think that whatever the bishop finds pleasurable is praiseworthy. [Note: The same edition reads: “and no one will fear to do what the bishop does not hesitate to do. The name by which you are designated itself accuses you. For you are unhesitatingly called bishop by all; and what else does *episcopus* mean than ‘overseer’? Since you look upon all from your higher seat in the Church, and everyone’s eyes look toward you, so that you may give them food at the proper time, why do you display yourself like a foul mirror to the eyes of all, so that they cannot adorn you with their darkness?”]

Nor should anyone say that he hesitates to do what the bishop does not hesitate to do. For you are unhesitatingly called bishop by all, especially since you are designated by that very name—provided that conduct agrees with the name and the name corresponds to conduct. For what else does *bishop* signify than “overseer,” especially since he sits on a higher seat in the Church and looks upon everyone in such a way that everyone’s eyes also look toward him?

Therefore, since this is so, why do you display yourself like a foul mirror to the eyes of all, so that they cannot adorn themselves more beautifully by your darkness?

## CHAPTER VII

Let it suffice for now that we have somewhat extended our discourse to our fellow priests, in which we have shown both their excellence and their fall, lest, trusting in the loftiness of their honors, they should fail to seek perfection of conduct [Note: The same edition reads: “and should not believe themselves priests if they were called so only in name and not in deed. And although I know that many priests who neglect to embrace these things will maliciously disparage me for this little book, I nevertheless believe that many more who strive to attain them will faithfully pray for me.”], and should think that, in the mere name of priest, they have more cause for glory than in their works.

And although I know that, because of this little book, many priests who do not wish to do the things we say will maliciously disparage me, I nevertheless believe that many who do these things, or strive to do them, will faithfully pray for us. But just as we are not at all weighed down by the wounds inflicted by detractors, so we are indeed helped by the prayers of approved and holy men.

Come now, holy Spirit, who have aided us in this work by divine inspirations: help all priests [Note: The same edition reads: “help them to do what you yourself commanded in this little work, so that you may rightly grant them the kingdom of heaven which you promised to give to the saints, who live and reign with the Father and the only-begotten Son in the Trinity, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.” The older edition and certain manuscripts read: “help and grant … whom you inspired to speak … so that … the kingdoms of the ages, which you promised to give to the saints in the kingdom of the ages … Amen.” Most manuscripts more appropriately agree with the text; excepted is the Michaelinian manuscript, which ends: “which you promised to give to your saints, who live and are glorified with the Father and his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”], and grant that they may do what you yourself inspired us to express in this little work, so that together with me you may grant them the kingdoms of heaven, which you promised to give to the saints at the end of the ages, forever. Amen.

## [TO A DEVOTED VIRGIN]

[Col. 0579]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LITTLE BOOK

In this treatise, the Devoted Virgin—that is, one who has publicly professed virginity—is warned away from the use and companionship of secular men. The pretexts commonly used to justify such association are rejected, and its dangers and harms are set before her eyes; some discussion is also added concerning the virtues that she should especially embrace.

This is why the Roman editors prefixed to the customary inscription the title: “On the Form of Life for a Virgin.” Although this writing bears the name of the blessed Doctor at its head in all editions of Ambrose’s works, it has not been possible to find any manuscript of it; from this you may understand that there was not much evidence for attributing it to Ambrose. Concerning the author, then, we seem able to conclude only this: that he was devoted to the ascetic life, since he speaks in this way: “Far be it that you should be called my sister, since you associate with such people.”

But concerning the work itself we can state with complete certainty that it is far removed from Ambrose’s eloquence and learning. Compare it with his genuine books *On Virgins*, and you will undoubtedly agree with us in your judgment.

[Col. 0579]

## TO A DEVOTED VIRGIN (C, G, S)*

### 365 CHAPTER I

[Psalm 44:11–12.] “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house; for the King has desired your beauty” [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “and he himself is the Lord your God, and the daughters of Tyre shall worship him.”], “for he himself is the Lord your God, and they shall worship him.”

You have vowed yourself to be his bride; you are called devoted to God. What have you to do with secular men, or what dealings do you have with them? What do you wish to know with them? The destruction that they pursue? If you seek chastity, they do not possess it; if you seek faith, who among them is faithful, whom you might follow? But if you seek Christ, he does not remain in them. I do not know what you seek, what friendships or what conversations you have with them.

You have vowed your soul to destroy everything that belongs to this age; how, then, do you seek the world, to which you have renounced? Do you wish to return to your vomit like a dog, or, like a washed sow, again to wallow in the mire, as it is written [1 Peter 2:22]? The Apostle says: “If I rebuild what I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor” [Galatians 2:18]. [Note: The same Roman edition repeats this below. It also adds: “And elsewhere it is said: If anyone wishes …”]

He repeats the same thing, saying: “Whatever is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes” [1 John 2:17], which is not from God but from this world. Again, elsewhere he says: “If anyone wishes to be a friend of this world, he will be constituted an enemy of God” [James 4:4].

What do you say, devoted to God? Why do you wish to please men? What do you desire or seek? If you seek God, he is with you; but if you seek man, you did not vow yourself to this. What are men? Men of this age. “And the world is passing away, and its desire; but whoever does what is written remains forever” [1 John 2:18].

What do you desire? I do not know. If gold, silver, life, splendid clothing—these did not please you with God; God does not admire these things, but rather “a contrite and humbled heart” [Psalm 50:19].

Why do you seek the men of this age, whom the holy Apostle Paul judges, saying: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things; but our citizenship is in heaven” [Philippians 3:19–20]? If, therefore, our citizenship is in heaven, we ought to seek the things that are above, where Christ is, not the things on earth [Colossians 3:1].

I ask you, sister: who are these men of this age? You do not follow your spiritual brothers, but you follow carnal men—who, if they are not satisfied, will murmur. You have cast your pearls before swine, who will trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart. Have you not heard: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” [Philippians 3:2]?

Who are these men? The men of this age, who do not follow Christ’s footsteps. I ask you: what do they display to you? Tell me. Chastity, which they do not possess? What, then? Faith, which they do not find? Doctrine, which they do not follow except the devilish wisdom of this age? Fasting, which they hate? Abstinence, which they condemn? Humility, which they oppress? Sobriety, which they neglect? A sincere mind, which they do not possess except as a double mind? Modesty, which they cast away from themselves? I do not know what you wish to pursue with them.

### 366 CHAPTER II

“But what do you say? I am converting them to myself.”

But if they are converted to you, it is not good for you. What does a wolf seek with a lamb? Or what does a dog seek except bread? Why does a lion roar [Isaiah 31:4], except for prey?

Guard yourself chaste, if you can. Why do you wish to teach what you yourself do not do? As the Apostle says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God” [1 John 4:1].

But if you receive instruction from them, they will teach you what they do or pursue: desire, fornication, lust, greed, fraud, uncleanness, shamelessness, debauchery, drunkenness, wickedness, filthy speech, folly, sorceries, murders, anger, quarrels, and every evil.

What do you say, wretched woman, or what excuse do you offer? You vowed your soul so that you would withdraw from those men; what, then, do you seek now?

I ask you: are you not ashamed when they make themselves stories about you, saying: “Look, the woman devoted to God who follows us. She has abandoned her own way and wandered beyond the boundaries of her field; she has not found the road to her dwelling. Come, let us seize her beforehand and lead her into our way”?

You have fallen, wretched woman, onto the broad and spacious road that leads to death. What is evil appears good to you; you follow them madly and do not know that you are falling straight into a pit. Do you not remember that the way leading to life is narrow and constricted [Matthew 7:13–14]?

The way that is good seems laborious to you. You have forgotten that it was said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” [Acts 14:21]. But now you wish to pursue your own will.

Have you not read Solomon saying: “Good things were created for the good from the beginning, and likewise evil things for the wicked and sinners” [Ecclesiasticus 39:30]? [Note: The same Roman edition adds: “and evils for sinners? … The beginning of every necessity for human life is water and fire, iron and salt, and so forth. All these things are good for the godly; thus for sinners they will be turned into evils. Human life too will be judged spiritually; because the spiritual person, etc.”]

Again, he himself says: “The beginning of human life shall be spiritually judged” [ibid., 31]. “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” [1 Corinthians 2:15].

Where are you, devoted to God? You are spiritual in judging others, but you yourself are judged. What do you seek with them? “What partnership has the faithful person with the unfaithful” [2 Corinthians 6:15]? Or what partnership has a holy person with the flesh?

You can be a virgin in body, but not with a corrupted mind. Your eyes, however, have been blinded by the excessive heat of lust, and a beam lies within them. Your ears are full of every kind of masculine filth. Your feet are swift and not sluggish toward the outer door.

Where is holiness? Where is modesty? Where is sobriety? Where is dignity? Where is chastity? Where is restraint? Where is faith? Where is self-control? Where is a pure mind? Where are all those things for which you pledged your faith, which you have lost?

For it would have been better for you not to have vowed than to have vowed and not performed it [Ecclesiasticus 5:4]. You cannot serve two masters, either God or Mammon, as it is written [Matthew 6:24]. “With the perverse you will be perverted” [Psalm 17:27]. An old cloth cannot be joined to a new one; for it takes away its strength, and a worse tear results [Matthew 9:16].

Birds of a feather flock together, and truth will return to those who practice it. Far be it that you should be called my sister, since you associate with such people.

“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad. For each tree is known by its fruit” [Matthew 12:33]. “Whoever a person is, he joins himself to one like himself” [Ecclesiasticus 13:20].

The dove, released from a man’s hand, immediately returned to him in the ark; but the raven, when released, followed flesh [Genesis 8:7]. You too wish to follow the raven, so that you may not return to Christ’s door.

You associate with the beasts of the field and the birds of heaven. Like the raven, you do not remember the Lord who delivered you from the flood; you do not seek your shady and good dwelling, where you once had temporal rest.

The storm is not before your eyes, and you have forgotten Christ’s love; you cling to the love of the men of this age, who have no love in themselves except a devilish one. They pursue another flesh and do not cease until they die.

Withdraw, wretched woman, from those men, lest they devour your chosen flesh, overturn your ankles, and leave you naked and stripped, like [a shelter] in a cucumber field. [Col. 0583A]

What will you do now, since you are naked and stripped? You will go to your neighbors, whom you previously hated, asking them for a covering for your shame. But they do not wish to give one, saying: “Where is your splendid garment, which you used to wear before?”

What will you say, and what will you answer her whom the cold has bound? They rejoice in the evils that have come upon you. Then you will lament, saying: “Woe to me, wretched woman, to whom such things have come! What benefit did that captivity bring me, which took captive me, wretched and unhappy? Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings before the dawn and dwell at the farthest end of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” [Psalm 138:7–10].

Then you will say: “I will go and return to my first husband, because it was better for me then than now” [Hosea 2:7 and following], “who gave me my garments and my oil in their time. But what shall I do now?”
