Then you will return to your home with weeping, from which you had gone forth rejoicing. You will sit in the corner of your house, mourning and grieving, weeping day and night, seeking someone to grieve with you—and there will be no one. You will find no comforters.

And those whom you once hated will give you alms and shake their heads over you, saying: “Look at the woman who was devoted to God; now she has become like dung in the road and like a city under siege. Where is her chastity? Where are all those things that followed her?” For they abandoned her because chastity was their leader: she lost chastity, and all those things fled.

But what will you do now, wretched woman? Where are those whom you pursued? Let them redeem you, if they can. What exchange can you give for your soul, which you defrauded through your disobedience, so that you would not listen to your brothers or sisters who warned you not to join yourself to secular men?

But what shall we do for you now, or what shall we say—we whom you refused to hear—except that we should mourn over you ourselves, saying: “Spare, Lord, spare”? Perhaps he will deign to hear our weeping and groaning, so that he may give you the disposition to turn back to him once more, to remember your sins, saying: “How abundantly my father’s hired servants have bread, while I am perishing from hunger! I will rise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your daughter. Receive me as one of your maidservants, so that I may live” [Luke 15:17–19].

What if, perhaps, he has killed that fattened calf for you? For I am jealous for you, because I betrothed you to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ. For I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the love that is in Christ Jesus [1 Corinthians 11:2–3].

### CHAPTER III

See, then, and beware of these men, so that you may be called my sister and lady. Enter your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father [Matthew 6:6], so that he may give you a good mind and understanding, enabling you to know whom you ought to follow and whom to avoid.

For there are many who pretend to be what they are not, but lie. And you do not know that your soul is at stake, lest they lead you captive like an ox being led to slaughter, or like a dog to be tied up. Do not hasten like a bird into a snare.

Listen to me: remove your foot from them; sit diligently in your house; work with your hands at what is good, so that you may have something with which to share with those who endure need. Pray without ceasing, and do not appear too readily in the streets.

Fight the good fight; run more swiftly, so that you may grasp that for which you were grasped by Christ [Philippians 3:12]. Let people hear you and rejoice in your good disposition and in the mind by which you live.

Give alms, and behold, all things will be clean for you [Luke 11:41]. Do not be reluctant to visit the sick; through them you will be strengthened in love.

You shall not swear at all [Note: The Roman edition adds: “neither by heaven nor by earth; but let your word be …”], neither by truth nor by falsehood; but let your speech be: “Yes, yes; No, no”; whatever is more than this is from evil [Matthew 5:34–37].

“Be angry and do not sin”; do not turn aside to make excuses for sins with men who practice iniquity [Psalm 140:4]. Humble yourself, daughter, before the Lord, for God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble [1 Peter 5:5].

Draw near to the Lord, so that he may illumine you, and you will not be ashamed in his presence [Psalm 33:6]. Withdraw from the pleasure of the world, and clothe yourself with steadfastness in virtue. Put aside the garments of this age, and clothe yourself with the garment of perpetuity.

Abandon the foods of this age, and take for yourself the food of the saints [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “take for yourself the food of the holy of holies.” This is not an unsuccessful reading.]. Remember that Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego, and Daniel refused the meat and wine of the Gentiles and took vegetables and legumes for themselves [Daniel 1:8 and following].

Remember that the Maccabean mother suffered because of pork, and that her sons were roasted or fried in oil [2 Maccabees 7:1 and following]. Walk, daughter, in holy attire, with modesty, sobriety, and dignity.

Put away falsehood and speak the truth with your neighbor. Pray, daughter, without ceasing; fast frequently and give alms, for almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit one to go into darkness [Tobit 4:11].

Almsgiving is a good gift, which cleanses every stain and filth. You will be blessed if, after reading all these things, you do them. Be zealous for what is good, so that you may forget what is evil.

May the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit bless you with the blessing with which he deigned to bless our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Pray for me, daughter, for I too am concerned for you, as it is written: “Pray for one another” [James 5:16]. Again: “A brother helping a brother will be exalted” [Proverbs 18:19].

May the Lord exalt you in holiness and love, as it is written: “Whoever loves his brother has fulfilled the Law” [Romans 13:8]. May the Lord fulfill all your petitions [Psalm 19:7].

May God the Father grant this to you through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord and God, king, judge, savior, and redeemer, who is blessed with the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## [SERMONS HITHERTO ASCRIBED TO SAINT AMBROSE]

[Col. 0585]

## NOTICE ON THE SERMONS PUBLISHED HITHERTO UNDER THE NAME OF AMBROSE

Almost no one who has examined the sermons found in the older editions of our Ambrose has failed to recognize that a considerable part of them was wrongly attributed to that holy man and circulated among the works of other Fathers, especially those of Saint Maximus. The Roman edition not only failed to remedy this inconvenience but additionally wished to include others even more alien than the first to Ambrose’s intellect and style.

Nor is this the only fault of that edition in this matter. Besides, it tore a good many sermons away from the class of authors to whom they belonged and sent them to foreign homes; it also altered many things, both in the titles and in the text itself, by its own authority, so that they might appear more Ambrosian. As a result, people who were otherwise extremely perceptive were led into error.

Therefore, so that in future we might free readers from such fraud, we decided to call all the sermons that bear the name of Ambrose in any editions back for examination. In this judgment, after applying as much diligence and severity as we were able, we found no sermon whatsoever—apart from four homilies, namely those on the funeral of Valentinian, on the funeral of Theodosius, on not handing over the basilicas, and on the relics of the saints Gervasius and Protasius, which we have published in their proper places—that we thought could be attributed to Ambrose with any degree of probability or resemblance to the truth.

Indeed, everything in them seemed to us so greatly to differ from the holy Doctor’s diction and method of treatment that we do not doubt that all who examine them with the attention they deserve will yield to our opinion.

What Cassiodorus (Book 5 of *On the Institution of Divine Literature*) asserts—that in his own time there existed homilies or sermons bearing the name of Ambrose on their title page—must lead us to say, unless we suppose that his memory was deceived or that he was misled by someone’s false report, that those copies had already disappeared long before. As for the books containing the sermons now attributed to that same Bishop, we consider them to possess no authority. For the most part, they either exhibit a more recent hand or were books intended for choral use—namely, lectionaries and homiliaries—whose evidentiary value no one will deny to be extremely slight.

But even in this matter it is not sufficiently safe to place confidence in the older manuscripts. Experience teaches that, in order to make them more saleable, antiquarians very often inscribed great names on the homilies or sermons they contained. This is plainly evident in these sermons. For although we possess no copies of them older than the Lyon manuscript, whose variant readings we owe to the friendship of the most distinguished Baluze, and the Gallese manuscript, which our Mabillon testifies to have been examined and collated by him and to have been written a thousand years ago, nevertheless each of these contains sermons falsely parading an author: the Gallese manuscript, Augustine; the Lyon manuscript, Ambrose. Most of them must be restored to Saint Maximus, as Mabillon himself declares concerning the Gallese manuscript. From this judgment concerning the Lyon manuscript one may form an opinion, since the same sermons are exhibited in almost identical form in both manuscripts.

Nor will anyone be surprised that so many sermons have been ascribed to blessed Maximus, since it is well known how eminent this Saint was in preaching. That a considerable portion of his sermons was transcribed under the name of Ambrose may have happened, besides the scribal frauds already mentioned, for this reason also: because, after diligently reading through the works of our holy Doctor, Maximus inserted large extracts from them—especially from the *Commentary on Luke*—copied word for word, and thus gave careless scribes an opportunity for error. From this one might likewise perhaps infer that no other author need be sought for the books or sermons *On the Sacraments* than Maximus himself; this conjecture is supported by both place and date.

What we have said thus far makes it clear that only those sermons from which the first volume is almost entirely composed, and a considerable part of the second as well—sermons that Ambrose himself arranged in book form—can certainly be called Ambrosian. We therefore shall not appear to have acted rashly in publishing none of the sermons examined here among the genuine and authenticated works of the holy Doctor. Since some of these sermons are circulated only under Ambrose’s name, while others have also been published elsewhere, we shall present only the former, lest the volume be enlarged by material of lesser utility. Nevertheless, to make it clearer that we have by no means exercised a freer criticism, we shall briefly preface each sermon with the reasons that led us not to regard it as Ambrosian. Nor shall we object if any reader, employing stronger arguments, should succeed in vindicating these sermons for our Ambrose.

As for those discourses circulated among the works of other Fathers, since they suffer above all from the additional prejudice that they have been assigned no more to Ambrose than to Maximus or anyone else, we have cut them away with less hesitation. So that this alteration may cause no inconvenience, two indexes will be provided. In the first, the omitted sermons will be arranged in such a way that one may see at a glance not only the place each formerly occupied in the Ambrosian editions, but also under which Father it is found elsewhere. In the second index, a threefold series of the sermons we retain will be compiled, so that all the Ambrosian editions—the ancient edition, the Roman edition, and our new edition—may be compared with one another, set out opposite one another. But first, certain matters specifically concerning the omitted sermons must be noted.

## Sermons on the Temporal Cycle

The first two—the first and third sermons of the Roman edition—are attributed to Augustine in the Gallese manuscript, but in the Corbie, German, and several other manuscripts they are assigned to Maximus, whose character they wholly breathe. The same may be said of the following sermon, whose title the Lyon manuscript gives in this genuine form: “To Be Delivered before the Nativity of the Lord.”

The fourth of the omitted sermons, which is the sixth of the Roman edition, is assigned to Caesarius in the Augustinian Appendix. We do not oppose this opinion, content merely to point out that it contains comparisons which, when they are read in the sermons mentioned above, appear to indicate interpolation. The sermon omitted after this one—that is, the twelfth of the said edition—is likewise attributed to Caesarius by the same Appendix; certainly no one who reads it will assign it to Ambrose. Nor shall we argue otherwise concerning the following sermon, which is also found in the Appendix of Augustine’s sermons. Since some manuscripts assign it to Ambrose and others to Augustine, we, together with the Corbie manuscript, assert it to belong to no one.

The sermon that follows these begins in the frequently cited Appendix only with the words: “The Lord says in the Gospel,” and so forth. The Gallese manuscript likewise divides it in such a way that these same words form the beginning of a new sermon. How foolish this division is can be recognized at first sight. Both this sermon and the following one, which appears to be its continuation, are rightly assigned to Maximus; and the one numbered twenty-four in the Roman edition was likewise long ago vindicated for that same Bishop.

Of the two sermons that follow, the first was formerly placed among the Augustinian sermons as number fifty-six; it has now been restored to Caesarius, whose diction it closely resembles. The second was restored to the same Father with no less justification. Yet a considerable part of it is inserted into a sermon attributed to a certain Rabanus, whose heading is: “On the Lord’s Fast and the Discipline of the Lenten Fast.”

Sermon thirty-nine of the Roman edition bears the title: “Why Christ Fasted in the Desert,” and so forth. In the Augustinian Appendix it is number 147. It, together with two others—namely, numbers thirty-seven and thirty, one of which discusses Christ’s first temptation and the other his second—is by one and the same author, but most certainly not by Ambrose. They differ from his style as greatly as they approach that of Maximus.

The sermon placed as number forty-one in the Roman edition, large fragments of which are found in Rabanus Maurus’s homily on the Third Sunday of Lent, is assigned to Saint Caesarius in the Augustinian Appendix. Nevertheless, what Gennadius records—that Maximus wrote discourses “On the Special Fast of Lent,” in which one must not jest—fits this sermon quite well. Yet it appears no less to be Caesarius’s than sermon twenty-six of the Roman edition, which no one would doubt was written by him.

The forty-second sermon of the aforesaid edition contains nothing at all that does not have the character of Saint Maximus. The same must likewise be concluded concerning the forty-seventh, whose beginning the same Roman edition had incorrectly altered, and which Gennadius indicates belongs to Maximus under the title: “On Judas the Traitor.”

To these let the forty-eighth be added, together with the forty-ninth and fiftieth, which depend upon it. Everything cries out that these are Maximus’s. Here, however, we cannot refrain from protesting against the Roman editors, who, both here and elsewhere—and especially in the last of these sermons—did not hesitate to alter many passages contrary to the other editions and manuscripts.

Sermon fifty-one, as well as the two immediately following it, is also found among the sermons of Maximus. We have no doubt that these are the very sermons mentioned by Gennadius under the titles: “On the Cross of the Lord,” “On His Tomb,” and “On His Resurrection.” Numbers fifty-five and fifty-six likewise belong to Maximus; the latter is a continuation of the fifty-third, just as is number fifty-seven [reading uncertain].

Number fifty-eight is restored to Caesarius in the Augustinian Appendix; it contains nothing at all to explain why it was ever attributed to Ambrose. Nor did number sixty deserve to be reckoned under his name with any stronger claim. Besides being vindicated for Maximus in his editions and in numerous manuscripts, what it says concerning the baptism of the Apostles openly conflicts with what may be read in *Apology for David*, chapter 9, section 50.

Among other considerations, number sixty-one is claimed for Maximus by the fact that it appears to refer us to sermon fifty-seven, which we have said above belongs to that Bishop. But what it says here concerning the Saturday fast before Pentecost does not agree with what was stated on the same subject in number sixty. Consequently, some doubt may arise whether it ought perhaps to be assigned to an author more recent than Maximus himself.

Sermon sixty-four is nothing other than Basil’s homily on that passage from the Gospel according to Luke: “I will pull down my barns,” and so forth, though with some additions and excisions. We have seen Ambrose use this same Basilian homily in his book *On Naboth*; yet it cannot be inferred from this that Ambrose was also the author of this sermon. Indeed, if the passages that Saint Ambrose imitated from that homily in the same book are compared with this sermon, it will immediately be recognized that our Doctor interpreted Basil’s thoughts in a much nobler manner than the translator of this sermon. The latter, rendering [Col. 0589] word by word in servile fashion, is as far as possible from Ambrose in his entire expression, and especially in those patches which he repeatedly wove in from his own material.

Mabillon thinks that number sixty-six, which is found under the same number in the Appendix of the Augustinian sermons, may be referred to number eleven, which he himself published as Maximus’s. Yet its style, in our judgment, differs so greatly from this Father’s manner of writing that we would more readily assign the sermon to some later author.

In the Roman edition, several discourses had been appended to the sermons on the Temporal Cycle. The first three of these—namely, the sermons on the Basilicas and on the funerals of the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius—we have presented in their proper places. The fourth we wished to leave solely to Maximus, whose style it bears and whose name it already bears in the *Library of the Fathers*.

## Sermons on the Saints

The second of the sermons called “On the Saints” was published under both Augustine’s and Maximus’s names; but diction, as well as its affinity with number fifty-eight, assigns it to Maximus alone.

We have placed the fifth sermon, which was delivered by Ambrose on Gervasius and Protasius, the martyred brothers, among the letters. That this is its genuine place was demonstrated in the Admonition prefixed to it.

Sermon six was long ago restored to Maximus, and it is not obscure that it was spoken by no one but the Bishop of Turin.

Number ten is attributed to Ambrose in the Appendix to Augustine’s works, perhaps with greater likelihood than to Augustine. Yet in our view it must be denied to both, and with equal justification. For if one examines its diction, one will readily admit that it is no more Ambrose’s than Augustine’s; at the same time, one will observe that its author appears to be later than Chrysostom.

Number twelve is also found in the Augustinian Appendix, but it is additionally extant among the works of Maximus, to whom it is assigned by the consensus of scholars. The same conclusion must be reached concerning number thirteen, since it is a continuation of sermon twenty-four on the Temporal Cycle, which we have seen above to belong to Maximus.

Before number seventeen, the Roman edition places a certain fragment omitted from the ancient editions; the same Augustinian Appendix, however, presents this sermon in full. To make clear that it contains nothing Ambrosian, one need only compare it with what Ambrose wrote concerning Saint Laurence in the books *On Duties*.

Number eighteen is read among the sermons of Maximus, and in it his talent and diction are evident.

Number twenty is also found among Maximus’s works. If it is to be assigned to him, as it appears it should, it must have been given the heading “On Saint Michael” by some ignorant person, for the reason that on this feast the Gospel forming the subject of the sermon was customarily read. Among the same Bishop of Turin’s works, number twenty-one is extant with its true title, namely, “On Hospitality.” It is therefore credible that this is the very sermon which Gennadius testifies was written by the same Bishop “On Avarice and Hospitality.” The Roman edition therefore had no reason to entitle it “On the Feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist.”

## Sermons from the Earlier Volumes

The sermon “On the Forbidden Tree” leads the sequence in the Augustinian Appendix. It is there observed that this sermon has variants in Ambrose’s text, but these were introduced by the editors either for elegance or in order to give it a closer kinship with Ambrosian style. It is therefore not surprising that someone of even more learned judgment, deceived by these alterations, considered that there was nothing preventing the sermon from being attributed to the holy Doctor. Its author is entirely unknown.

The Manichaeans are attacked in it, but not the strict Manichaeans, since these do not deny that wine is good. It is therefore necessary either that they were Marcionites or that they belonged to those heretics whom Ambrose refutes in the book *On Paradise*, where the same subject is treated, though in a very different manner.

Our Mabillon had two sermons on Saint Elisha published in the first part of the *Museum Italicum* as though they had not yet entered the public domain. The reason for this error must be attributed to the confusion of the Roman edition, where they had been placed in the wrong location. For the rest, we shall by no means object to their being declared Maximus’s.

The genuine title of the sermon on chapter 7 of Job is: “On Not Fearing Carnal Enemies and on Giving Thanks after Food.” Gennadius indicates it under this title, and also signifies that it belongs to Maximus, among whose works it is likewise found.

The expositions or sermons on Psalms 21, 109, and 117 are rightly counted among those of Maximus. The Ambrosian editions present certain periods from these sermons in their first volume which are not found in Maximus; but these are of little importance. The third sermon, however, has been restored to Maximus in the Roman breviary.

The exposition of chapter 31 of Proverbs may be read in its pure form under Augustine’s name, without those additions which the Roman edition inserted into it in order to make it appear more Ambrosian.

The two sermons on chapter 3 of Ecclesiasticus, “On Almsgiving,” are attributed to Saint Maximus in the editions of that Father as well; their diction beautifully reflects his style.

The same must also be thought concerning the sermon on chapter 1 of Isaiah, and likewise concerning the two sermons on chapter 13 of Daniel. All of these are read among Maximus’s works, and Gennadius asserts them to be his, giving the title of each.

The first of the sermons on chapters 3 and 4 of Jonah belongs to no one other than Maximus, to whom the editions of that Father, as well as [Col. 0591] Gennadius, assign it. The second was published by Mabillon in the *Museum Italicum* under Maximus’s name. The fact that he considered it unpublished must be attributed to the disorder of the Roman edition.

Finally, since the sermon on chapter 1 of Malachi is a continuation of the sermon on chapter 7 of Job, which we previously proved to be Maximus’s, it is clearly to be assigned to the same author.

[Col. 0591]

# SERMONS HITHERTO ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT AMBROSE (C, G, S)

## [SERMONS]

### 391. SERMON I. First Sunday of Advent

[Col. 0603A]

First published in the Roman edition; but the remarks concerning the fast of Advent—which was not known by that name in the Church until long after Ambrose—clearly show that it was wrongly attributed to him. Moreover, at that time the Author imposes confession of sins and abstinence from marital intercourse as virtually necessary, something especially foreign to Ambrose. Finally, the correctors of the *Decree* observed that the words quoted there concerning the marital bed are found not in this sermon but in a certain sermon on Lent.

1. This season, dearly beloved brothers, is rightly called the Advent of the Lord, and it was not without reason that the holy Fathers began to celebrate the Lord’s Advent and delivered sermons to the people concerning these days. They instituted this practice so that each believer might prepare and amend himself, and thus be able worthily to celebrate the birth of his God and Lord.

For if one of you were about to receive an elder into his house, he would cleanse the house itself from every impurity and unclean thing and, according to his ability, prepare whatever was honorable and necessary. If a mortal does this when he is about to receive a mortal, how much more ought a creature to cleanse himself so as not to displease his Creator appearing in the flesh?

The Just One comes to us sinners in order to make the just from sinners; the merciful One comes to the impious in order to make us merciful; the humble One comes to the proud in order to make the humble from the proud. What more need be said? He who is good by nature comes to human beings who were full of every evil.

2. Therefore we exhort you, during these days, to give alms more abundantly, to assemble more frequently in church, and to make a most pure confession of your sins. Not only should you diligently abstain from every impurity, but also from your own wives; and you should drive far from you hatred, anger and indignation, shouting and blasphemy, pride and boasting, together with every carnal pleasure, so that when the day of the Lord’s Nativity arrives you may celebrate it for your salvation.

Just as many are concerned with bodily wealth and costly garments, so that they may appear more honorable than others on that day, so you should be more concerned with spiritual wealth and garments. For just as the soul is better than the body, so spiritual delights are better than bodily ones. It is far better to adorn the soul with virtues than to clothe the body in costly garments.

3. This admonition, brothers, has been given to you so that those who are good may become better through it, and those who remember that they are evil may certainly be converted, so that all alike may deserve to rejoice spiritually on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. May he grant this who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

### 392. SERMON II. On the Coming Nativity of the Lord

In the old edition it is incorrectly entitled, “Also on the Nativity of the Lord”; more correctly, in the Lyon manuscript: “The Following Sermon on the Coming Nativity of the Lord.” From this one may understand that it was customary in the Church of Lyon for priests, over several Sundays, to prepare the people to celebrate the Lord’s Nativity. Although it is attributed to Augustine in the Vindobonensis manuscript and to Ambrose in some others, it may more properly be placed among the sermons of Maximus, since it is a continuation of the sermon that appears as number four in the Roman edition and has been proved to be Maximus’s. Erasmus also seems to have noted this in the margin.

1. I believe that last Sunday I said more than enough about how we ought to receive the Lord’s Nativity adorned and clean, and how we ought to observe its approaching feast free from all ambition. [Note: Royal manuscript: “in the preceding discourse [lacuna] and to refrain, on the coming of its feast, from all wicked ambition, so that,” etc.] I say “retain” so that, even when the day of its solemnity has passed, the blessedness of its sanctification may nevertheless remain among us. For this is the grace of the Nativity of the Lord and Savior: it passes forward to those predestined and remains behind with the devout.

We ought, therefore, to be pure in holiness, clean in chastity, and bright in integrity, so that the closer we see the festive day approaching, the more carefully we may conduct ourselves. If women commonly wash away the stains from their clothing with water when they are about to celebrate a festival, why should we not, when we are about to receive the Lord’s Nativity, wash away the stains of our souls with tears?

2. [Note: Lyon manuscript: “And indeed those little things [reculae] if they have been so stained and darkened with dirt”; Vindobonensis manuscript: “But if those things, the little rooms [res cellulae], have been so stained”: two others, “[lacuna] if the things have been so stained with dirt.”] If their garments are so deeply stained and darkened with dirt that water alone does not remove the stains, they add the softness of oil and also the sharpness of soap. So, if our sin is so grave that tears alone cannot wash it away, let us add to it, by the oil of mercy, the sharpness of fasting.

For no offense is so grave that it cannot be cleansed by abstinence and extinguished by almsgiving. The holy prophet says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33). Great, therefore, is almsgiving, which cools the burning masses of crimes with the spring of its benevolence and, as though by a channel of generosity, overwhelms the fires of wrongdoing. Thus, although God is offended and provoked by crimes, he is compelled by almsgiving to free the one whom he had resolved to punish for his sins.

For in a certain sense he is compelled by us, when he is forced, because of our deeds, to change his sentence and, in one and the same person, to be moved now by the severity of a judge, now to show the gentleness of a father. God is our Father when we do good; he is our Judge when we sin.

The Lord is therefore compelled by our works to grant us his mercy. Hence he himself says in the holy Gospel: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven is forced” (Matthew 11:12). Let us examine what meaning this statement possesses.

3. The kingdom of heaven is none other than the Lord Christ, who reigns in heaven. The verb “to be forced” is customarily used when something relatively rare is thickened by continual activity.

From the time when John the Baptist announced the Savior’s coming, the kingdom of heaven—which previously lay among the Jews loose and diffuse—began to be thickened by the continual activity of believing peoples, and all that rarity of the kingdom began to be solidified by the frequent preaching. It was so rare among the Jews that it passed to the Gentiles; so fluid that it flowed out to the peoples.

Now, however, it is compressed by such a density of believers that it remains fixed and solid without end, as Scripture says: “And of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:33).

We therefore force the kingdom of heaven and, in a certain sense, do violence to it, as the Gospel reading says: “And those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12). I say that we do violence to the Lord—not by compelling him, but by weeping; not by provoking him with insults, but by entreating him with tears; not by blaspheming through pride, but by grieving in humility. [Note: Vindobonensis manuscript: “not by contending.”]

O blessed violence, which is not struck down by indignation but pardoned by mercy! Blessed, I say, is the violence that elicits goodness from the one who suffers the violence and grants benefit to the one who inflicts it. An evil deed is admitted, yet no one complains of injury; violence is admitted, and religion is propagated. [Note: The same manuscript: “and no one is accused concerning the injury.”] For whoever is more violent toward Christ will be regarded by Christ as more religious.

We therefore attack the Lord on the road, since he himself is the Way (John 14:6), and, like robbers, we strive to strip him of his goods. We desire to take away from him the kingdom, treasures, and life. But he is so rich and generous that he neither refuses nor resists; and when he has given everything, he nevertheless possesses everything himself.

We attack him, I say, not with sword, club, or stone, but with gentleness, good works, and chastity.

4. These are the weapons of our faith, with which we fight in the contest. But, if we are to use these weapons in doing violence, let us first in a certain sense do violence to our own bodies: let us conquer the vices of our members so that we may obtain the rewards of virtue. [Note: Some manuscripts: “let us purge the vices of our members.”] We must first reign over ourselves, so that we may be able to seize the Savior’s kingdom.

The Gospel says: “And those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12). We are therefore robbers; but robbers seize nothing except what belongs to another. I recognize the statement as true: Christ was seized by the Church from the Synagogue, and the kingdom of a foreign people was possessed by force.

For the Savior, sent under the Law, born under the Law, and raised according to the Law, was neglected by the Jews and seized by the Gentiles. When he was rejected by the priests, he was found by sinners, as he himself says: “Publicans and prostitutes go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 21:31). [Note: Royal manuscript: “was rejected by priests.” The same manuscript also omits the following passage, from “We are therefore robbers” through “Therefore, brothers, as we are about to receive the Lord’s Nativity.”]

We are therefore robbers.

5. This is not surprising, since we descend from such an ancestor. For it is written concerning our patriarch Benjamin: “A ravenous wolf” (Genesis 49:27); for he seizes what is not his. Thus we too, like the sons of a ravenous wolf, seize for ourselves the shepherd of foreign sheep, as he himself says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

Christ is seized when he is abandoned by the Jews and preached by foreigners. Christ is seized when he is killed by the Jews and buried by us. Christ is seized by the disciples who keep watch and lost by the Pharisees who sleep; for they themselves confessed this by lying when they placed guards at the tomb after the Lord’s resurrection, saying: “His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping” (Matthew 28:13).

From this we understand spiritually that all who sleep lose Christ, while those who keep watch find him. Therefore the Apostle says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

You see, then, that the person who sleeps in such a way as not to guard the Savior is dead. Therefore those Pharisees, as though dead, could not preserve the living one.

For this reason, brothers, let us not sleep but keep watch around the Lord our Savior, so that, with guards continually posted, no one may take him away from the tomb of our hearts, and we may never say: “They came, and while we were sleeping they stole him.”

For we have enemies who, if we fall asleep, strive to take Christ from our hearts. Therefore let us guard him with vigilant care in the tomb of our souls; there let him rest, there let him sleep, and there, whenever he wills, let him rise again.

6. [Note: “Therefore, brothers, as we are about to receive the Lord’s Nativity,” and all that follows to the end have been restored from the Royal and Vindobonensis manuscripts, since they are absent from the others and from the editions.] Therefore, brothers, as we are about to receive the Lord’s Nativity, let us cleanse our consciences from every filth and take care to adorn ourselves not with silken garments but with costly works.

Bright garments can cover the limbs, but they cannot adorn the conscience—except that it is a matter of still greater shame to walk with bright limbs while moving about with polluted thoughts. Let us therefore first adorn the disposition of the inner person, so that the clothing of the outer person may also be adorned. Let us wash away spiritual stains, so that bodily garments may shine in us.

It is of no benefit to shine in clothing and be filthy in sins. For where the conscience is dark, the whole body is obscure. But we have the means by which to wash away the stains of conscience, as it is written: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Blessed is the command of almsgiving, through which we work with our hands and are cleansed in heart—through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

### 394. SERMON III. On the First Day of the Lord’s Nativity

It was absent from the ancient editions. It plainly exhibits nothing of Ambrose; and those words, “because of the length of the divine office … because of the discord among the kings,” and so forth, are wholly unsuitable to him. They may perhaps be less alien to Caesarius, whose style this entire sermon sufficiently resembles.

1. As we celebrate, brothers, the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us consider the meaning of the Gospel reading that has just been read. The holy Evangelist says that, by decree of Augustus Caesar, the whole world was enrolled for a census, and that for this reason Joseph went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, in order to be enrolled there with Mary, his pregnant wife, and to pay the census tax for both of them, since they belonged to the same family (Luke 2:1 and following).

For such was the peace when the Son of God appeared in the flesh, lasting for twelve years, that all, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles” (Isaiah 2:4). The Son of God, the author of peace, was therefore born in a time of peace so that he might teach all his followers to love peace.

For just as Caesar Augustus sent Quirinius to collect the census, so the true Augustus, God, sent preachers into the world to collect the census of faith. Let us therefore render, brothers, the census of faith and good action.

Let no one remain behind; let us all go up from Galilee—that is, from the instability of the world—into Judea, that is, the region of right confession, so that we may deserve to be Bethlehem, that is, the house of bread, namely, of him who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41).

2. The Gospel further relates that, after the blessed ever-virgin Mary had given birth to Christ, she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger. These things too are not without mystery. Christ wished to be wrapped in swaddling clothes so that he might free us from the snares of death.

The Gospel rightly says, “They went,” to show that he was born on the road; and this because he had come to show himself to us as the Way. He wished to be placed in a narrow manger who had come to prepare for us the breadth of the heavenly kingdom.

He did not wish to be wrapped in silken or gilded cloths but in humble ones, because he had come to restore to us the robe of immortality. He permitted himself to be bound by those who were hastening to release our feet and hands for the performance of good works.

What should we say about these things, brothers? We must exclaim with the Psalmist: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Psalm 115:12).

He indeed found a cup which he could offer in return; let us, however, give what we can: alms, vigils, tears, and peace. Let us forgive those who sin against us, so that our sins may be forgiven us by God.

3. The shepherds who, when the Son of God was born, kept watch over their flock and saw angels signify the holy preachers. The greater their care for souls, the more frequently they deserve to have revelations through angelic speech.

When an angel appears, the shepherds are troubled, because it is natural for human beings to tremble at the sight of angels, while it is characteristic of good angels to offer consolation to those who fear. Hence the angel immediately addresses the shepherds, saying: “Do not fear,” and adds why: “Behold,” he says, “I proclaim to you great joy, which will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10).

He rightly says, “For all the people,” because people from every nation came to the faith.

4. While one angel was speaking with the shepherds, suddenly a multitude of angels appeared and uttered this cry: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

By this event we are morally admonished that, when one brother is reading, teaching, or performing any good work, the multitude of the faithful should burst forth in praise of God and rise to imitate the good it sees.

When the Son of God appears in the flesh, glory is sung to God in the highest, and peace on earth is announced to people of good will. Let us therefore also be people of good will, so that we may deserve to live in peace.

5. Yet, because of the shortness of the day and the length of the divine office, we touch upon the meaning of the Gospel reading only briefly, so that we may admonish you concerning those matters that especially pertain to your salvation.

We must be admonished to strive to reckon the affliction that has come upon us because of the discord among the kings as resulting from our own sins. Therefore, so that you may deserve to be freed both from this persecution and from eternal condemnation, let each person correct whatever he recognizes as blameworthy in himself on this day on which the Son of God is born.

Let the adulterer vow chastity to God; the avaricious person, generosity; the drunkard, sobriety; the proud person, humility; the slanderer, charity; and let him fulfill these vows, according to that verse of the Psalm: “Vow and repay to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75:12). Let us make our vows faithfully; he will grant the ability to fulfill them.

6. It is indeed very honorable, brothers, that there should be no one who does not offer something to the Lord today. We give gifts when we receive kings or friends, and shall we give nothing to the Creator of all things who comes to us?

For he requires nothing from us more than ourselves. Let us therefore offer ourselves to him, so that, freed by his ineffable mercy from present evils and eternal torments, and received into the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, we may be able to rejoice forever.

This may he grant, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, to whom belong all honor and glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Second Nativity of the Lord the Savior

It appears to have been compiled from the works of various Fathers, especially Augustine. For not only in his book *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 58, but also in his sermons 188 and 194 of the new edition, one finds numerous passages that would persuade you that they were transferred into this sermon. If you compare it with Jerome’s *Commentary on Galatians*, chapter 4, and also with sermons 98 and 197 of the Augustinian Appendix, you will likewise agree with us that it is a compilation.

1. It is true what Saint John the Baptist says of the Lord the Savior: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Indeed, this is first confirmed by the very seasons themselves. For behold, at Christ’s nativity the day grows longer, while at John’s nativity it grows shorter: when the former rises, the light increases; when the latter is born, it diminishes. For time itself, in a certain sense, serving its appointed parts, suffers loss when the servant is born; but when the Lord is born, it gains increase. The day plainly advances when the Savior of the world arises; it suffers decline when the final prophet is born. For it is written: “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16). Therefore it was necessary that observance of the Law should be obscured where the calling forth and grace of the Gospel shone forth, and that prophecy of the Old Testament should cease when the grace of the New Testament succeeded it. Thus, at the Lord’s nativity, the day advances.

[Note: All editions, together with the Lugdunensis manuscript, read: “when they cause loss, the servant is born … it attains increase”; the other manuscripts read more harmoniously, as we have printed in the text.]

[Note: Where the text has “the calling forth,” three manuscripts omit the phrase; and instead of “grace shone forth,” the Lugdunensis has “glory shone forth.”]

**2.** It is no wonder that the day advances on which the new Sun of justice gleams; it is no wonder that the day is illuminated by the most splendid light of truth. For the Evangelist says of Christ the Lord: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being” (John 1:9). Therefore, if he was the true light that enlightens humanity, why would he not enlighten the world? And so the day that gave birth to this light first shone forth itself in the brilliance of that same light, and, having already completed its appointed span, dispelled the darkness of night with the radiance of the Lord’s light. For the length of night would have occupied the entire day, had Christ’s coming not shone forth amid the day’s brevity. Just as by his rising he dispersed the darkness of the human race’s sins, so on the day of his nativity he cut away the darkness of gloom and, by one and the same rising, brought light alike to human beings and to the days. Hence it is no wonder that the day grows longer, clothed in the double splendor of its radiance.

[Note: We have restored the reading from all the manuscripts: “on which the new … shines forth; it is no wonder that the day advances.”]

**3.** But let us see further how the Lord the Savior increases and John the Baptist decreases.

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “We have said elsewhere.”]

We said above that John indeed represented the figure of the Law and the prophets. Therefore, when the Gospel flashed forth, the Law had to decline, and when the Christian people arose, the Jewish people had to diminish. For who doubts that, at the Lord’s nativity, the meeting places of the Synagogue were emptied, while the crowds of the Church multiplied, and that each day Christ wonderfully increases through his Christians, while John diminishes through the Jews?—that these shine with the splendor of the Lord’s day, while those labor under the darkness of night? For night, in a certain sense, settled more heavily upon the Jews from the moment when they said concerning the Savior’s death: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25). They were plainly darkened by greater shadows of night from the moment when they attempted to kill the day of truth.

**4.** But so that we may demonstrate more convincingly what we are saying, let us briefly explain the nativity of each. Behold, when Christ is born, the angels rejoice, the shepherds keep watch through the night, the Magi arrive, and a star goes before them; and all the most beautiful things that are in heaven and on earth are offered to the Lord himself. Glory is offered him through the angels, radiance through the star, worship through the Magi, and simplicity through the shepherds. And because all these things were destined to belong to him alone, they all serve the one who is being born.

But when John is conceived, Zechariah becomes mute, the solemn priest falls silent, and Elizabeth the mother hides herself, signifying the silence of the Law after his birth, the loss of the priesthood, and the concealment of the Synagogue. There is no doubt that, when John was born, he took away from the Pharisees the righteousness of the Law, just as, when he was conceived, he took from his father the service of speech. Thus the Lord always increases, while John the Baptist decreases.

**5.** He does not decrease because anything is taken away from his merits, but because the Savior’s glory is daily accumulated, he appears to become lesser. John is finally called a lamp, as the Lord says: “He was a burning lamp” (John 5:35). The lamp’s light is therefore obscured when the sun’s ray shines forth, and it undergoes a certain decline when it is surpassed by the splendor of a brighter light. For what wise person would seek a lamp in the sun? It is not extinguished, but it is no longer necessary. That is: who would come to John’s baptism of repentance when he can be saved by the Savior’s baptism? The former is not condemned, but the latter is judged more useful and necessary, because in it the forgiveness of sins is granted.

[Note: The Lugdunensis manuscript omits this sentence, beginning with “because in it …”.]

# SERMON V. On the Nativity of the Lord III

[Col. 0612B]

In this sermon there is a passage at number 4 that we have no doubt was taken verbatim from Ambrose’s *Commentary on Luke*, book II, section 50. As for the material extending from the words at number 6, “For what is done so silently,” to the end, it is beyond dispute that it has been copied word for word from the *Commentary on Psalm 71*, which is commonly attributed incorrectly to Rufinus.

**1.** By what grace, or with what praises, I should proclaim this day of the Lord’s nativity, I truly do not know; for amid so great a festival, human speech is not sufficient to magnify God.

[Note: Some Paris editions read “how I should approach the Lord’s nativity”; all the others read “how I should proclaim it”; the manuscripts read “how I should proclaim it.”]

For if, when Christ was being born, he was praised by the voice of angels, should he not now be praised even more by a human voice, when he reigns? For our solemnity surpasses the festivity of that time. Then they marveled only at the Lord who was being born; we contemplate him as being born, and likewise as risen and reigning.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “then they received him”; below, where all editions and more manuscripts read “we receive the one being born,” the Lugdunensis manuscript has the better reading, “we contemplate the one being born.”]

Therefore praise ought to be all the more fruitful at this time in proportion as the miracles are greater.

**2.** But since human frailty cannot offer praise worthy of him, let us turn to the proclamations of the angels; and because we cannot rightly equal them, let us accompany them in devotion. That is, on this festival let us rejoice in the same joy as they, expressing the same declaration and saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Plainly a worthy and just declaration, which at Christ’s nativity presents honor to God in heaven and peace to human beings on earth. For before the Savior’s rising, neither heavenly beings offered reverence nor earthly beings possessed rest.

But observe what the declaration itself says: “Peace to people of good will” (ibid.). Not to all people indiscriminately, but to people of good will, so that you may understand that Christ’s peace is not a matter of entitlement but of merit.

[Note: An old edition reads: “For the angels did not merit it on that night when the shepherds, keeping watch over their flock as they observed the watches of the night, first learned of the Lord’s birth before all others … they learned it through the angels’ announcement. It is astonishing that they could know the world’s redemption before the rulers … There is therefore no longer any reason for astonishment.” The Roman edition reads: “For it is not social condition but the will that merits it. The shepherds heard this first of all on that night when, while the Lord was being born, they kept watch over their flock. They were the first of all human beings to know of the Savior’s birth, when the angels announced it; for the angels announced the world’s redemption first not to kings or judges, but to rustic people. Nor is it surprising, then, that …” We have restored the passage from three manuscripts.]

For it is not social condition but the will that merits it.

**3.** With this declaration the angels rejoiced on that night when the shepherds, keeping watch over their flock as they observed the watches of the night, were the first of all to learn of the Lord’s birth; they were the first of all human beings to recognize the Savior’s coming, when the angels announced it.

Therefore it is not surprising that the shepherds of the world were able to know the world’s redemption before its rulers; for the angels did not announce it to kings or judges, but to rustic people. It should no longer be surprising, then, if innocence was deemed worthy to know Christ’s grace before power, and simple rusticity to recognize the truth before proud domination. For what the shepherds learned, the rulers were unable to learn.

Hence the blessed Apostle also says: “None of the rulers of this age knew it” (1 Corinthians 2:8), and so forth.

Thus at the Lord’s nativity the angels rejoiced together with the shepherds, proclaiming glory to God on high; for, as it were, with neighboring and joined choirs they proclaimed God’s glory.

**4.** Hence I believe that these same angels, on this same festival of the same Lord, rejoice with us in a similar nearness of joy. For those who customarily addressed the shepherds because of Christ’s birth cannot, because of the joy of this same Christ, fail to seek out the priests.

Indeed, what they said then to the shepherds who were keeping watch over their flock in the middle of the night signified the mystery of this present time. For by that event it was certainly shown that the flock represented the people, the night the world, and the shepherds the priests, who, keeping watch over the people with unceasing concern, are by no means abandoned by the angels on Christ’s account.

**5.** Therefore on this day the Lord was born according to the flesh, so secretly and so silently that the world entirely failed to perceive his birth. The world did not know it, because he was born outside his father’s awareness and conceived outside the ordinary course of nature.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads “conceived without the father’s knowledge and born outside nature.” Subsequently, where all editions and some manuscripts read “for Joseph received the conceived child,” the Lugdunensis and Silvanectensis manuscripts do not recognize the word “conceived.” Finally, where all editions read “she gave birth,” all the manuscripts prefer “she placed the child.”]

For Joseph received a son whom he did not beget; Mary brought forth a child whom the ordinary process of her sex had not created. Thus the Lord was born in such a way that no one suspected his coming, no one believed it, and no one perceived it. How could they believe that this would happen when, after it happened, they scarcely believe that it did happen?

**6.** For the fact that the Savior would descend into the Virgin so secretly and quietly had already been attested beforehand by the prophet David, who said: “He will descend like rain upon fleece” (Psalm 71:6).

For what happens as silently and without disturbance as rain being poured into a tuft of wool? It strikes no one’s ears with sound, nor does it sprinkle anyone’s body with moisture through violent impact.

[Note: All editions read “but without disturbance of the people”; the Roman edition reads “of the sheep entirely,” and so forth. All manuscripts agree with the text, except that the Lugdunensis has “outside” instead of “of dew.” This is incorrect.]

Rather, without disturbing anyone, it draws into itself the whole rain poured through its many parts throughout its body, knowing no single opening’s cleft, but, with solid softness, taking hold of many openings; and what appears closed because of its density is open because of its fineness.

**7.** Rightly, then, we compare Mary to fleece, for she conceived the Lord in such a way that she absorbed him with her whole body and suffered no cleft in that same body, but was soft in obedience and firm in holiness.

Rightly, I say, Mary is compared to fleece, from whose fruit saving garments are woven for the peoples. Mary is plainly fleece, since from her soft womb came forth the Lamb who himself, bearing his mother’s wool—that is, the flesh—covers the wounds of all peoples with soft fleece. Every wound of sin is drenched with Christ’s wool and warmed by Christ’s blood; and, so that it may recover health, it is clothed in Christ’s garment.

# SERMON VI. On the Nativity of the Lord IV

This sermon is concerned almost entirely with the fact that the Lord’s nativity was called by the common people the new sun, that is, the new year, since formerly the year began on that day. It appears to be by the same author as the fourth of the preceding sermons, since near its conclusion there are passages very similar to those in which the sun’s lamp, which precedes it, is discussed here. What we have below at number 7 concerning the carpenter can also be found in Sermon 135 of the Appendix to Augustine; but that too seems to have been drawn from Ambrose’s *Commentary on Luke*, book III, near the beginning. Hence perhaps it may be conjectured that blessed Maximus was the author of this sermon.

**1.** In a certain sense the common people rightly call this holy day of the Lord’s nativity the new sun, and they confirm this with such authority of their own that Jews and gentiles alike agree in this expression.

We should gladly embrace this, because when the Savior rises, not only is the salvation of the human race renewed, but even the sun’s own brilliance is renewed, as the Apostle says: “To restore all things through him, whether those in heaven or those on earth” (Ephesians 1:10).

For if the sun is darkened when Christ suffers, it must shine more splendidly than usual when he is born. And if it spreads darkness over the Jews as they bring about death (Luke 23:45), why should it not display radiance to Mary as she gives birth to life? Or why should we not believe that, when Christ was born, the sun came more brightly in service, when a brighter star went before the Magi as a sign?

And if the star performed during the day the service belonging to another time, why should we not believe that the sun too, during the nocturnal hours, shortened the night somewhat by arriving earlier than usual? Finally, I think this is why the night grew shorter: the sun, hastening to serve the Lord’s nativity, brought forth light to the world before the night had completed the course of its appointed time.

**2.** Indeed, I would not even say that it was night, or that it possessed any darkness, on the night when the shepherds kept watch through the night, the angels rejoiced, and the stars rendered service. Nor should we marvel that everything was made new at Christ’s nativity, since this itself was new: that a virgin gave birth.

But if the nativity occurred beyond the ordinary, then service too was offered beyond the ordinary. Therefore, when the Lord arose, the shepherds kept watch, the angels rejoiced, the sun served, and the star ministered.

The angels and shepherds expressed their joy with voice and words; but these elements, because they could not do so with a voice, testified to their joy through their service.

[Note: The Lugdunensis manuscript reads “with whatever voice they could.”]

Thus, contrary to custom, the sun shone forth like morning at this festival. Nor is this surprising. For if at the prayer of Joshua the son of Nun it stood fixed in the daytime (Joshua 10:13), why would it not hasten forward in the night at the nativity of Jesus Christ?

**3.** The common people therefore call this day the new sun; and when they say “new,” they certainly show that there is also an old one. By the old sun I mean the sun of this world, which undergoes eclipse, which is shut out by walls, and which is obscured by clouds. By the old sun I mean the sun subject to vanity, afraid of corruption, and fearful of judgment. For it is written: “The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood” (Joel 2:31).

By the old sun, I say, I mean the one that is present at human crimes, that does not shrink from witnessing adulteries, and that does not avoid homicide. And although no human being wishes to be a witness when some crime is committed, this sun alone stands present at all wicked deeds.

**4.** Since it is therefore evident that this is the old sun, whom shall we find to be the new one except Christ the Lord? Concerning him it is written: “For you the sun of justice will rise” (Malachi 4:2). Of him the prophet also says, speaking in the person of sinners: “The sun has not risen for us, and the light of justice has not shone for us” (Wisdom 5:6).

For when the entire world was oppressed by the darkness of the devil and the age, filled with crimes, was possessed by gloom, this sun deigned, at the end of time—that is, when night was already descending—to pour forth the rising of his nativity.

First, before the light—that is, before the sun of justice illuminated the world—he sent, like a kind of dawn, the prophetic oracle, as it is written: “I was sending my prophets before the light” (Jeremiah 7:25).

Afterward he himself shone forth with his rays, that is, with the splendor of his apostles, and dispelled the world’s great gloom with the light of truth, so that no one would stumble in the darkness of the devil.

[Note: The manuscripts read thus; all the editions, on the contrary, read “so that the darkness of the devil might offend no one.”]

**5.** This, then, is the new sun that penetrates barriers, opens the underworld, and searches the heart. This is the new sun that gives life through the Holy Spirit to the dead, restores what is corrupted, and raises up those already dead; or the one who, through his heat, cleanses what is filthy, dries up what is fluid, and boils away what is diseased.

He himself, I say, is the one who sees all our works in all our actions, and who does not so much condemn crimes as correct them.

This is plainly the just and wise sun, which, unlike the sun of this world, does not circulate indiscriminately around the good and the evil alike. Rather, by a judgment of truth, it shines upon the holy and sets for the sinner.

This is the difference between the two suns: the former fears judgment, while the latter threatens judgment; the former is an agent of corruption, while the latter is Lord of eternity; the former is a creature, while the latter is the Creator.

**6.** Nevertheless, before this world’s sun rises, a lamp customarily precedes it, still before daylight, for the necessary uses of human beings. Christ the Sun also has his lamp, which preceded him, as the Prophet says: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm 131:17).

[Note: All editions read “which preceded his rising”; all manuscripts read “which preceded him.” Again, all editions together with the Lugdunensis read “a shining lamp”; the Vallis Clara manuscript has “a burning lamp”; the Silvanectensis, more suitably, has “a burning and shining lamp.”]

What this lamp is, the Lord shows when he says of John the Baptist: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35).

John himself, like the faint light of a lamp that goes before, says: “Behold, after me comes one whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen; he himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3:16).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “One stronger than I will come, whose …”]

At the same time, understanding that his own light would be darkened by the sun’s rays, he foretells: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). For just as the lamp’s brightness is destroyed by the sun’s arrival, so John’s baptism of repentance was emptied of its force when Christ’s grace came upon it.

**7.** Let us see, then, from what source this new sun of ours is born.

It is true that he arises with God as his author; therefore he is the Son of the Godhead—of the Godhead, I say, incorruptible, whole, and undefiled.

I clearly understand the mystery. For this reason the second birth occurred through the immaculate Mary: because the first had been established undefiled through the Godhead, so that the one whose first birth had been glorious would not have a second birth that was shameful. That is, just as the Godhead had brought him forth as a virgin, so the virgin Mary would give birth to him.

He is also said to have a father among human beings, as we read in the Gospel when the Pharisees say: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter, and is not his mother called Mary?” (Matthew 13:55).

Here too, observe the mystery. Christ’s father is called a carpenter. And plainly the carpenter is God the Father, who fashioned the works of the whole world. Plainly he is a carpenter, the one who determined that Noah should build the ark in the flood. He is the carpenter who ordered Moses to make the tabernacle, established the ark of the covenant, and raised up Solomon’s temple.

I would call him a carpenter who smooths rigid minds, cuts away proud thoughts, and exalts humble deeds.

[Note: All editions and two manuscripts read “who polishes rigid minds”; the Vallisclara manuscript, however, has the better reading, “who softens them.”]

This carpenter uses a curved tool around trees, as we read in the Gospel, where John says: “Now the axe has been laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 3:10).

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds “not producing good fruit.”]

For his entire work is to arrange useful trees within the structure of the heavenly building,

[Note: The editions together with the Lugdunensis manuscript read “may arrange them in the future”; the Vallisclara and Silvanectensis manuscripts have the excellent reading “may arrange them within the structure.”]

but to consume fruitless trees, uprooted from their roots, in the fire of the flames.

# SERMON VII. On the Kalends of January

Since many Christians retained for several centuries the games and profane ceremonies instituted by the gentiles for celebrating this day, the holy Fathers took the greatest care to deter them from such practices both in synods and in sermons. This is clearly known from the Council of Trullo, canon 62; the Second Council of Tours, canon 17; and the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 11. Various sermons by Chrysostom, Augustine, Maximus, and others on this subject confirm it.

Ivo of Chartres also cites a sermon of Ambrose on this topic. Its opening words do not agree with this sermon, although other portions correspond sufficiently. But whether Ivo saw this discourse or another, we think that neither was Ambrosian. For we would not believe that these superstitions had prevailed at Milan, since in the genuine sermons from which the treatises of the first volume are composed, the holy Bishop nowhere attacked them. See also what we noted on this subject in volume I, book II, *On David’s Interpellation*, chapter 1, section 5. Add that several manuscripts also attribute it to Augustine.

**1.** I have a considerable complaint against most of you, brothers. I am speaking of those who, while celebrating the Lord’s nativity with us, devoted themselves to the holidays of the gentiles and, after that heavenly banquet, prepared for themselves a meal of superstition; so that those who had earlier been made joyful by holiness might afterward become drunk with vanity, not knowing that whoever wishes to reign with Christ cannot rejoice with the world, and that whoever wishes to find righteousness must avoid luxury.

For the one is the way of eternal life, while the other is the despair of temporal wantonness: one ascends to the former through virtue; one descends to the latter through destruction.

**2.** Therefore whoever wishes to share in divine things must not be a companion of idols. For it belongs to the portion of an idol to intoxicate the mind with wine, distend the belly with food, and torture the limbs with dancing, and to become so occupied with depraved actions that one is forced not to know what God is.

Hence the holy Apostle, foreseeing these things, says: “What partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what portion has the faithful with the unbeliever? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Therefore, if we are the temple of God, why is a festival of idols celebrated in God’s temple? Why, where Christ dwells—Christ who is abstinence, moderation, and chastity—is feasting, drunkenness, and wantonness introduced?

For the Savior says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), that is, God and Mammon. How, then, can you devoutly celebrate the Lord’s Epiphany, when you have already celebrated the Kalends with the utmost devotion, as far as it lay within you?

**3.** Janus was a human being, the founder of a single city called Janiculum. In his honor the gentiles named the January Kalends. Therefore whoever observes the January Kalends sins, because he offers the service of divinity to a dead human being.

That is why the Apostle says: “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear that I may have labored over you in vain” (Galatians 4:10).

He observed the day and the month who on these days either did not fast or did not go forth to the Church. He observed the day who yesterday did not go forth to the Church but went out to the field.

Therefore, brothers, let us avoid with every effort the festivals and holidays of the gentiles, so that when they feast and rejoice, we may be sober and fasting; thus they may understand that their joy is condemned by our abstinence.

**4.** We must avoid not only the company of the gentiles but also that of the Jews, whose very conversation is a great pollution. For they insinuate themselves into people by cunning, penetrate houses, enter governors’ residences, and disturb the ears of judges and public officials. For this reason they prevail all the more because they are all the more shameless.

This, however, is not a recent evil among them, but an ancient and inherent one. For long ago they also persecuted the Lord the Savior within the governor’s residence and condemned him by the governor’s judgment (Matthew 27:2 and following).

Therefore, within the governor’s residence, innocence is oppressed by the Jews, secrecy is betrayed, and religion is condemned. For when Christ is killed, all truth and righteousness are condemned in him, because he is innocence, the worship of holiness, and the mystery itself.

# SERMON VIII. On the Holy Epiphany I

[Col. 0618C]

In the Appendix to Augustine there is a sermon numbered 135, with which this sermon of ours agrees in its discussion of the frequent celebration of festivals. We observe an even closer relationship between this sermon and the first of Maximus’s sermons, since in both it is shown that the changing of water into wine is a symbol of the resurrection of bodies. Hence we conjecture that the author of both is the same. Indeed, in the margin of Erasmus’s edition this sermon is attributed to that same Maximus. Among his sermons there is also one on the feast of Easter that begins with precisely the same words as this one.

**1.** We ought to rejoice, dearest brothers, because vows follow upon vows and joys are heaped upon joys. For behold, our hearts are still rejoicing in the solemnity of the Lord’s nativity, and already we glory in the festival of the holy Epiphany.

Therefore we ought to give thanks to the Lord, who frequently visits us in order often to make us joyful,

[Note: The old edition reads “so that he may demand more abundantly”; three manuscripts read “conscious, he demands”; the Roman edition reads “so that he may repeat more frequently”; the Lugdunensis has the reading printed in the text.]

and who more frequently demands from us so that he may bless us more abundantly.

Although the gentiles, vainly indeed, rejoice in numerous solemnities because of the diversity of their gods, the visitation of the one God provides us with more festivals than their superstitious presumption concerning many demons provides them. For just as we surpass them in the truth of religion, so we surpass them in the number of our vows.

**2.** Today, therefore, we celebrate the joys of the Epiphany. Someone may perhaps ask what this word means, namely because *epiphainein* (ἐπιφαίνειν) in Greek is rendered in Latin as *apparere*, “to appear.” Therefore, because the Savior first appeared in the world at that time, the day itself was called Epiphany by that same name.

[Note: All manuscripts read: “namely because *epiphania* in Greek is rendered in Latin as ‘to appear’”; Erasmus and Gill read “… is rendered ‘appearance’”; the Roman edition reads: “namely, because *epiphainein* in Greek, etc.” We prefer Amerbach’s reading.]

**3.** Let us inquire, then, how he appeared—not because he had not previously been in the world, since the world was made through him (John 1:10), but because it was then that Christ God first shone through signs and miracles into the hearts of believers, and the radiance of faith came into the darkened consciences of human beings.

Since God is everywhere and possesses all things, he is said to have appeared as though he had not previously been seen. But he appeared not so much to the eyes of human beings as for their salvation. For although he had previously been born of a virgin and was visible to bodily eyes, he did not appear, because the eye of faith did not yet know his power.

Hence it is said to the Jews through the prophet: “You will indeed see, but you will not see” (Isaiah 6:9); that is, although they would behold the Savior with bodily eyes, they would not see him by spiritual light.

Afterward, when he declared his divinity through wonders, appearing to human minds as something new and unexpected, he infused certain eyes of the heart, so that understanding might recognize the one whom sight had not recognized.

Thus it comes about that we contemplate Christ the Lord through faith, although we have never seen him; whereas the Jews, who looked upon him with their eyes and touched him with their hands, still to this day do not see him.

**4.** Let us therefore inquire what sign he performed in order to declare his divinity to the peoples. It is said that he first performed this miracle: that he changed water into wine (John 2:11). A great sign indeed, and sufficient to establish belief in God’s majesty. For who would not marvel that the elements were transformed into something other than what they had been? No one can change nature except the one who is Lord of nature.

**5.** We must now believe that mortal human beings can be changed into immortality, since a lowly substance was changed into a precious substance.

I do not want you, hearer, to look merely at the names “wine” and “water.” If you wish to confirm the power involved, look at the reality of the things; for through this deed something deeper is demonstrated.

When the Lord changed water into wine, he did not do this merely so that drunkenness would not be lacking for those reclining at table, but so that eternity might come to the believers.

[Note: The old edition reads “so that eternity might exist”; the Roman edition, “so that eternity might abound.” Below, all editions read “not so that he might supply the storerooms of the banqueters,” whereas the manuscripts in both places have the reading printed in the text.]

For this reason Christ came into the world: not to stock the storerooms of banquets, but to provide for human salvation; not to fill jars with a substance of pleasant odor, but to water souls with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when he wished the guests to taste the flavor of excellent wine from lowly water, he wished believers even more to taste from this lowly flesh the wisdom of heavenly resurrection.

**6.** For this entire sign certainly contains the mystery of the resurrection. Water, lowly, pale, and cold, changed into wine—that is, precious, red, or fiery—signifies that the substance of human beings, mortal by its condition, lowly through weakness, pale through death, is to be changed in the resurrection into glory: precious through eternity, colored with glory, and set aflame with the spirit of immortality.

[Note: The old edition reads: “the substance, lowly by its created condition, pale through weakness, cold in death, into resurrection”; the Roman edition: “cold through death, into resurrection”; the manuscripts agree with our text.]

This, then, is what it is worthy to believe the Lord intended to accomplish: that through this earthly sign the heavenly mystery, which was to come, might already be perceived by the wise.

For if it is marvelous to replenish the wines that had failed the guests, how much more marvelous is it to restore to human beings the life that had been exhausted? And if it is glorious to change water into wine, how much more glorious is it to change sins into righteousness, and to regulate morals rather than cups!

**7.** I dare to say that those jars supplied that precious substance not only to that banquet but to the whole world, except that they supply it to us in a better way.

For it is clear that from those vessels they drew drunkenness, whereas we draw righteousness; they received a cup of wine, whereas we receive the cup of salvation; and, if it is permissible to say so, among them what they had drunk passed away, whereas among us what we have received remains.

# SERMON IX. On the Holy Epiphany II

What is said here about the apostles believing in Christ after seeing the miracle, since it is not found in the preceding sermon, clearly belongs to another sermon. The same passage is found in Maximus’s sermon on this very feast, as are several other passages in which his sermon agrees considerably with this one and with the preceding sermon. Hence it may be conjectured that the three have the same author.

The words “And if at times I have strength,” which fit poorly with what precedes, begin a new sermon in the Lugdunensis and Vallis Clara manuscripts. As for the author’s complaint about weakness of voice, we had already noted in book I *On the Sacraments*, chapter 6, that this complaint is common to many preachers. You may consult that passage yourself.

**1.** Your holiness remembers, brothers, our preceding preaching, in which we described how the blessed apostles immediately believed in him after witnessing a single miracle—namely, the Savior’s changing of water into wine. For the Evangelist says of the Lord: “He manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John 2:12).

[Note: The Regius manuscript, after prefacing several verses from the Gospel, arranges this homily as follows: “We have described the blessed apostles …”]

This event was not written down merely so that the glory of the faith of those under whom it occurred might be displayed, but also for our sake, since by the same example of devotion we are summoned to the glory of faith.

For what Christ accomplished, he accomplished not only for those who were present with him at that time, but also for us who would follow afterward, so that although our predecessors preceded us in time, they would not precede us in the grace of signs.

The power displayed to them in the miracles of present things has been preserved for us in the treasure of the written word, so that the page might provide us with what the historical event was accomplishing in them.
