[Note: The manuscripts read thus, except that some prefer “what was being done in us” instead of “what was being done for us”; the editions read: “indeed, in us is done whatever is presented to us, whatever is insinuated into us.”]

Rather, whatever the mirror of the Scriptures dictates while it insinuates itself into us is accomplished for us, so that we may see with spiritual light the power of the Lord that they beheld with bodily eyes.

## 2

“And he manifested,” he says, “his glory to his disciples, and his disciples believed in him.” How rightly the devotion of the servants follows the Lord’s power, and how the disciples inscribe in their hearts what the Master teaches by his deed! [Note: All editions, together with the Reg. manuscript, read: “Behold to whom the power of the worker is manifested, and the faith of the manifest believers is proclaimed”; the other manuscripts have the reading found in the text.] Behold, the power of the worker is now manifested to you who believe, and the faith of the believing apostles is openly proclaimed. The faith of the apostles is plainly worthy of proclamation: at the sight of a single sign, they believed in the Savior’s omnipotence. And while the apostles marveled that water had been changed into wine, they themselves likewise were changed from the entire dregs of sins and, in keeping with the character of the miracle, were transferred from the worthless superstition of the pagans into the precious devotion of believers. And just as water changed into wine is endowed with flavor, redness, and warmth, so what was tasteless in them received flavor through knowledge; what was pale assumed the color of grace; and what was cold grew hot with the ardor of immortality.

## 3

The faith of the apostles, therefore, is to be magnified. It was recorded in the Gospel narrative both for their praise and to benefit us as an example. But what is worse is that their praise remains, while their example does not move us; for the later we are in time, the lower we are in merit. They, at the sight of a single sign, immediately believed in the Lord; whereas we, though we have received so many further marvels of his benefits, doubt. We doubt, I say, because we love present things too much while we do not believe in future ones; we love riches in this world while we hesitate to receive them from Christ; we are lifted up by anger without restraint while we do not fear the judgment of recompense.

But whoever knows that it is written, “By the judgment with which you have judged, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:2), is without doubt gentle, moderate, and mild. He compels more by goodness than he forces by severity; a friend of indulgence and familiar with pardon, so that, while he frequently grants it, he may always receive it from the Lord. [Col. 0621D] For it is indeed the mark of a prudent ruler to conduct earthly honors in such a way as to acquire the honor of heavenly dignity.

## 4

And although bodily weakness sometimes dulls the vigor of our speech, nevertheless your devotion makes us stronger. For the more attentively you listen, the more willingly we preach; and the power of speaking is added to us when you lend your ears to understanding. Who would not try to sow the seeds of the heavenly word there where fertile soil of a pure heart receives it? Who, I ask, would not wish to place the Savior’s word there where worldly anxiety does not choke it, but the power of spiritual disciplines nourishes it?

Therefore, brothers, since on holy Epiphany we rejoiced when we saw the Savior’s miracles, we must do what the disciples of that time then did.

## 5

As for what I said—that we have now seen what was done long ago—we have plainly seen it, and we see it every day. [Note: All editions read: “Christ’s miracles, so that they may not pass away through iniquity”; all manuscripts have the reading found in the text.] For Christ’s miracles are such that they do not pass away through antiquity, but grow strong through grace; they are not buried in forgetfulness, but are renewed through virtues. For in the omnipotence of God nothing has been abolished, nothing has passed away; because of his greatness, everything is present to him, and all time is today for him. Hence the holy Prophet also says: “A thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Ps. 89:4).

If, then, all the time of the ages is one day for the Lord, on the same day on which the Savior worked miracles for our ancestors, he worked them also for us. We too, therefore, have seen the Lord’s miracles, just as our ancestors did, when we contemplated them with equal amazement. We too have tasted from those same jars; for they drank a cup of wine from them, while we have received the cup of salvation.

## 6

After seeing the Lord’s sign, therefore, we must do what our predecessors did. For if the same grace of divinity has shone forth in us, then the same devotion of faith ought also to be found among us. The Evangelist says of the Lord, after this miracle had been accomplished: “And he manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (John 2:11). We must therefore believe, just as the apostles then believed.

But someone else says: “We too are Christians, and we believe in the Lord our Savior.” Yet one must believe through one’s works, not through speech; not with the tongue, but with the heart, lest it also be said to us: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

# SERMON X. On Holy Epiphany III

This sermon reports that on this day some maintain that Christ was baptized in the Jordan, while others deny it. On this matter one may consult Jerome, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, Leo the Great, Letter 16 of the new edition, and others. Our task here is to point out that it has much in common with Sermon 1 of Saint Maximus, as well as with another sermon in the Appendix to Augustine, no. 134, which the manuscripts and editions commonly attribute to the same Maximus. [Col. 0622D] Anyone who compares only what is discussed there by Ambrose near the end of Book II of his *Commentary on Luke* with what is discussed in this sermon concerning the figure of the dove will readily recognize that it has no real affinity with Ambrose.

## 1

Most people commemorate that on this holy day of Epiphany the Lord performed miracles of this kind: when requested to attend a wedding, he changed the substance of water into the appearance of wine (John 2:9), transferring the liquid of springs into a better use through his blessing. The servants drew water from wells and found wine in the jars; they lost, at a more useful cost, what they had filled them with and found what had been lacking. Then, for the first time, by this wonderful sign he declared the power of his divinity.

Others, however, testify that on this holy day he was baptized by John in the Jordan, and that, through the grace of his washing, God the Father was present by speaking and the Holy Spirit also descended. Nor is it surprising that the mystery of the Trinity was not absent from the Lord’s washing, since the sacrament of the Trinity completes our washing. For the Lord could not fail first to display in himself what he would afterward command the human race, since he accomplished everything not for his own sake but for the sake of our salvation.

## 2

But did he wish to be baptized for his own sake, although he had no sin, as Peter says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22)? [Note: The Roman edition, together with the Reg. manuscript, reads: “as the prophet says.”]

Certainly, he did so for our sake. We, who are liable to the sins of many crimes, needed to be cleansed in Christ’s baptism. Therefore the Lord came to the washing, not to be purified himself by the waters, [Note: The latest Paris edition reads: “but to purify us by the streams of water.” This is incorrect.] but to purify the streams of water for us. From the moment he plunged himself into the waters, he wiped away the sins of all believers. It was necessary that he should wipe away the sins of all, since he took upon himself the sins of all, as the Evangelist says: “This is the Lamb of God; this is he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Thus, in a wondrous manner, one is immersed and the salvation of all is restored.

## 3

God the Father, then, is present when the Lord is baptized; the Holy Spirit is present. See the Savior’s benevolence: although in his Passion he alone submitted himself to insults, in the washing he did not seek grace for himself alone, but wishes others to share in his glory. The Father is present, as I said, and the Holy Spirit is present also. And because God cannot be seen, the Spirit descends in the form of a dove, while the Father descends in a voice; and, since this alone was necessary to establish faith among human beings, he displays the Savior.

Our faith is established only through hearing and sight. Therefore the Spirit submits himself to the eyes in the form of a dove, while the Father offers himself to the ears in a voice. For unless these things had to occur for the sake of our belief, the Father and the Spirit, as the invisible God, could have descended to the Word, the Son, by an invisible movement.

Thus, for the sake of our faith, when heaven was opened, the Spirit descended to Christ, the Father to the Son, and the voice to the Word. For Christ is the Word, of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). Well, I say, is the Father called the Voice and the Son the Word, because the Word proceeds only from a voice. Voice and Word therefore correspond to one another, and in their shared mystery they provide for the salvation of human beings.

## 4

Let us consider in what manner the Holy Spirit descended to Christ in the form of a dove: whether there is some likeness between the dove and the Lord, as there is between the voice and the Word. There plainly is no small likeness. For I would even say that the Lord himself is a dove, because he is lively, gentle, and simple. He is a dove because he commanded his holy ones to be doves, saying: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

That Christ is a dove, the Prophet says in his person, describing his return to heaven after the Passion: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I will fly and rest?” (Ps. 54:7). When Christ the Lord, therefore, was inaugurating the sacraments of the Church, a dove came down from heaven.

I understand the mystery, and I also recognize the sacrament. For the dove itself is the one that now comes to Christ’s Church in baptism, which once hurried to Noah’s ark in the Flood (Gen. 8:9): then announcing security to him with an olive branch, now conferring eternity on the Church through the sign of divinity. Then it carried the sign of peace in its mouth; now, by its very substance, it pours peace—Christ—upon him.

## 5

The Lord, therefore, was baptized in the Jordan. Scripture frequently records that many miracles were performed in this river, among them saying: “And the Jordan was turned backward” (Ps. 113:3). I think that what happened when the Lord Jesus was present there is even more marvelous. Formerly, the waters had been turned backward; now sins have been turned backward. And just as then the force of the river lost the channel of its course, so now the force of sins has lost dominion over its error.

I think this had already happened at that time through the prophet Elijah. For just as Elijah divided the waters in the Jordan (2 Kings 2:14), so Christ the Lord effected a separation of sins in that same Jordan. Elijah commanded the waters to stand; Christ commanded crimes to stand still. And just as under Elijah the waves sought the beginnings of the springs from which they had issued, [Note: All editions read: “they returned … to the infancy of their origin, from which they had come,” etc.; all the manuscripts agree with us, except that one reads *originis* for *originem*, and another reads *originis suae initium*.] so under Christ the Lord human beings returned to their origin, from which they had arisen in infancy.

# SERMON XI. On Holy Epiphany IV

In the ancient editions this was entitled: “After Epiphany.” It was in fact delivered after the preceding sermon, which is known to have been preached on Epiphany itself, as can be recognized by comparing the two. In the Roman edition it bears the title: “To the Catechumens.” Nor is this unreasonable, for it can be understood from many testimonies, both of others and of Ambrose, that in various churches they were accustomed to take their name from that festival.

There is no reason, however, for anyone to think that this author was a contemporary of Felix and Elipandus, or a precursor in their errors, because he says that Christ was reborn in baptism. That statement means nothing other than that the Lord, emerging from the waters, displayed the form of the resurrection. Since the same things are read not only in the following sermon but also in nos. 135 and 136 of the Appendix to Augustine, this is certainly substantial evidence either that all these sermons proceeded from the same author or that the author of one drew extensively from another.

## 1

I believe that my preaching on the holy day of Epiphany has reached all of you, brothers, and especially you catechumens. On that occasion we explained that some asserted that water had been changed into wine, while most testified that on that same day the Lord had also been baptized in the Jordan.

Although different people believe that only one or the other of these events occurred, I nevertheless affirm that both occurred, and that one sign contains another. Both events did occur. For when the Lord was baptized, he both instituted the mystery of the washing and changed the human race, like worthless water, into the eternal substance of divinity through the savor of divinity.

Similarly, when he changed jars full of spring water into wine, he accomplished both things: he provided a form more necessary for a wedding and showed that human bodies, through the washing of the Holy Spirit, were to be filled with spiritual substance. Elsewhere the Lord himself made this clearer (Matt. 9:17), saying that new wine must be stored in new wineskins. For in the newness of the wineskins the purity of the washing is signified, and in the wine the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## 2

[Note: One Reg. manuscript inserted everything from these words to the later phrase “Therefore on this holy day” into the sermon that is ninth for us, beginning as follows: “Therefore you ought to listen carefully to these things, so that the worthless and thin liquid of souls, namely vices, etc.”]

You catechumens, therefore, ought to have listened to this especially attentively. You need it more than others, so that your understanding—which now grows cold like water through ignorance of the Trinity—may grow warm like wine through recognition of the mystery, and so that the worthless and thin liquid of your souls may be poured into precious and powerful grace. Thus, in place of wine, may we taste what is good, smell what is fragrant, and be able to say with the Apostle: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15).

[Note: The same Reg. manuscript reads: “For the unbeliever, like water, lies, grows cold, and is pale … The unbeliever, I say.”]

Before baptism, the catechumen lies like water, is cold, and is pale; but the believer is strong and red like wine. The catechumen, I say, is like water without flavor, without fragrance, and without value: neither sufficient for use, nor pleasant for refreshment, nor tolerable for preservation. For just as water, when kept too long, turns bad, rots within itself, and stinks, so the catechumen, when he remains a catechumen for too long, turns for the worse, grows worthless within himself, and perishes.

For the Lord says: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he does not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3). Whoever does not enter the kingdom necessarily remains in hell.

## 3

The believer is rightly compared with wine. For just as, from the substance of all created things, everything deteriorates with age while wine alone improves with age, so, while all other kinds of human beings perish through antiquity, the Christian alone improves with age. And just as wine, day by day, boils away its harshness and acquires sweetness of taste and pleasantness of fragrance, so the Christian, as time advances, boiling away the harshness of his sins, acquires for himself the wisdom of divinity and assumes the benevolence of the Trinity.

[Note: All editions and one manuscript read: “the benevolence of the Trinity”; two manuscripts read: “the goodwill of the Trinity”; the Lugd. manuscript best of all reads: “he acquires benevolence,” etc., referring this to the preceding phrase, “he acquires pleasantness of fragrance.” The Reg. manuscript reads: “he assumes for himself wisdom and the benevolence of the supreme divinity.”]

## 4

Therefore the Lord was baptized on this holy day. See how well he arranged it: he was born at his nativity and reborn at Epiphany, so that the hopes of human salvation would not be far separated from one another and so that we might continually give eternal thanks to the Savior.

## 5

Our hopes also were celebrated when the Church was joined to Christ, as John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). For this wedding, therefore, it is fitting that we should dance. King David, both king and prophet, although he sang many songs, is said to have danced before the Ark of the Covenant; lifted up by joy, he broke into dancing (2 Sam. 6:14).

In the Spirit he foresaw that through Mary the Church would be joined to Christ, born from his line, in the bridal chamber. Of this he says: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18:6). And for this reason [Note: All editions and manuscripts have this reading, although *prophetiarum* may perhaps be read where *prophetarum* appears. The Roman edition, however, incorrectly substituted: “he sang more than all the prophets.”] he sang more than the other prophetic authors: happier than all of them, he joined his descendants in marriage through these joys. Inviting all the nations to their proper hopes with customary sweetness, he also taught us what we ought to do at the wedding, since before the wedding he himself rejoiced with complete exultation.

# SERMON XII. On Holy Epiphany V

To what we have said above concerning the preceding sermon we will add only this: our sermons appear to have been composed as a continuous whole, whereas those cited above from the Appendix to Augustine display something of the appearance of patchwork compositions; consequently, these may perhaps have been interpolated from those same sermons. We do not deny, however, that this author also imitated certain things from the holy Fathers. For the reasons given here why Christ wished to be baptized are found also among others, including Ambrose himself, both elsewhere and especially in his *Commentary on Luke*, Book II, no. 83, and Book IV, no. 5.

## 1

The Gospel Scripture reports, as we recently heard read, that the Lord came to the Jordan for the sake of baptism and wished to consecrate himself in that same river through heavenly mysteries. We should not be surprised that the Lord and master of baptism himself did this, since he says: “Whoever does and teaches thus will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

He therefore wished first to do what he commanded everyone to do, so that, as a good teacher, he might convey his teaching not so much through words as exercise it through deeds, and confirm us at the end alike through taste and understanding.

## 2

It is clear that all this happened today. We can gather that it is true by reason itself. Reason requires that after the day of the Lord’s nativity, although years intervened, this festival should nevertheless follow at the same season; and I think that this festival too should be called a nativity.

For then he was born among human beings; today he was reborn through the sacraments. Then he was brought forth through the Virgin; today he was generated through the mystery. Thus the Lord arranged that human hopes should not be far separated from one another: at one time, those who rejoiced that he had been born on earth might rejoice that he had been sanctified in heaven; those who possessed the Son of God, with the angels announcing the Virgin’s childbirth, might retain him with the heavens bearing witness.

Thus human beings could be certain that the one whom the Virgin had borne was himself the Son of God, whom divinity acknowledged. New births deserve new acts of homage. There, when he was born according to humanity, his mother Mary embraced him in her lap. Here, when he is generated according to the mystery, God the Father embraces him with his voice, saying: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3:17).

The mother, therefore, caresses the child with her tender lap; the Father serves the Son with a loving testimony. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “supports him with a pious testimony.”] The mother, I say, presents him to the Magi to be adored; the Father reveals him to the nations to be worshiped. He is held in his mother’s lap when he is born, but the Father continually supplies him with the warmth of his own bosom.

For we read that he rests without interruption in the Father’s bosom, as the Evangelist says: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18).

## 3

The Lord therefore gladly rests in the bosom of the saints. Hence he gladly chose the bosom of John the Evangelist in order to recline there. The bosom in which Christ rests is not prepared by the embrace of the body, nor arranged by the ostentation of garments, but gathered through the working of heavenly virtues.

For Christ’s bosom in John the Evangelist was faith; in God the Father, divinity; in Mary his mother, virginity. Christ’s bosom is wherever there is a dwelling-place of virtues. There he reclines his head (John 13:25), wherever he finds a home for the heavenly commandments.

For this reason he says to sinners and unbelievers: “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to recline his head” (Matt. 8:20). The Lord Jesus, therefore, came today to baptism and wished his holy body to be washed with water.

## 4

Someone might perhaps say: “Why did the one who is holy wish to be baptized?” Listen, then. Christ is baptized not to be sanctified by the waters, but to sanctify the waters himself and, by his purification, purify the streams that he touches. [Note: The same Roman edition reads: “For Christ’s baptism is the consecration of the element.”]

For when the Savior is washed, all water is already cleansed for our baptism, and the spring is purified so that the grace of the washing may afterward be provided to the peoples who will follow. Christ therefore goes before through baptism, so that the Christian peoples may confidently follow after him.

## 5

I understand the mystery. For the pillar of fire also went before through the Red Sea, so that the sons of Israel might follow on an unhindered path (Exod. 13:21). It itself first crossed through the waters, in order to prepare a path for those coming after it.

As the Apostle says (1 Cor. 10:2), this event was a mystery of baptism. It was plainly baptism in a certain sense, where the cloud covered the people and the wave carried them. But all these things were accomplished by Christ the Lord, the same one who acts now. Just as then he went before the children of Israel through the sea in a pillar of fire, so now through baptism he goes before the Christian peoples in the pillar of his body.

The pillar is he himself: then he provided light to the eyes of those who followed; now he supplies light to the hearts of believers. Then, amid the waves, he made the path firm; now, in the washing, he strengthens the footsteps of faith. Through this faith, whoever walks without fear, like the children of Israel, will not fear the Egyptian persecutor.

# SERMON XIII. On These Words of the Gospel: “The Kingdom of Heaven Is Like Leaven”

[Col. 0628B]

The very first words of the opening argue against attributing this sermon to Ambrose. For he was not accustomed to speak in this way about the beginning of his episcopate, when, having been taken from the tribunals, he needed some time to learn the things he would teach others. This author could nevertheless have drawn certain things from Ambrose’s *Commentary on Luke*, Book VII, no. 187. But since the holy Doctor there testifies that he is reporting the opinions of others, there is nothing to prevent this author from having imitated others as well.

## 1

You yourselves know, brothers, that from the day on which I began to be with you, I have not ceased to admonish you all with the Lord’s commandments, presenting [Note: The word “divinity” is restored from the Lugd. manuscript.] divine precepts to you partly by exhortation and partly by rebuke. Thus I have often been a devoted father, but to some I have appeared a harsh teacher.

Whoever gladly embraced my sermon rejoiced to have me as a father; but the one who grieved that his conscience had been struck by my preaching experienced me as a harsh teacher. Yet it makes no difference to me, provided that Christ is proclaimed among you, whether through devotion or through correction. Indeed, correction itself is devotion, and it is applied to negligent children so that they may learn to fear what they neglected to love.

This does not mean that a father does not love all his children equally, but that a father’s indulgence displays affection according to differences of character: by encouragement he urges on the gentle child, while by severity he confronts the stubborn one, secure nevertheless in the correction of both. He chastises one with love and the other with severity, as the blessed Apostle says: “All discipline at the present time seems not to be joy but sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Heb. 12:11).

Therefore, since I believe that you have made progress through so many of my discourses, I am pleased to discuss certain matters from the divine Scriptures, so that I may understand that you grasp what I say with the liveliness of faith.

## 2

The Lord says in the holy Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened” (Luke 13:21). In another passage he says: “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in flour, until the whole was leavened” (Matt. 13:33).

There is no doubt that the force and power of leaven are known to everyone. Though small in size, simple in appearance, and common by nature, it possesses such strength within itself that, when it has been hidden in flour, its juice makes the whole mass become what it itself is. [Note: Thus the Valliscl. manuscript. But all editions print: “this juice will make the whole mass be what it itself is, thus always the whole”; the Lugd. manuscript differs in that it does not recognize *succus hoc*.] It spreads throughout the entire heap through the power of its diffusion, making the whole quantity of meal into leaven; and thus the thing itself, through its strength, acquires a mass proportionate to its own power.

Women do this so that they may carefully provide their husbands with healthier bread and useful food. But since the Law is spiritual (Rom. 7:14), and the Gospel subsists spiritually through the narration of parables, let us see what the leaven is, who the woman is, and what the flour is.

## 3

In the holy Gospel we read that the Lord Christ said concerning himself: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). If, then, the Lord is wheat, and the Lord is leaven—for leaven is ordinarily made only from wheat—then the Lord is rightly compared with leaven. [Note: The Valliscl. manuscript reads: “therefore rightly [compared] with grain.”]

Although human in appearance, small in humility, and cast down in weakness, he possessed such great power of wisdom within him that the world itself could scarcely contain his teaching. When he began to pour himself throughout the whole world through the power of his divinity, he immediately drew the entire human race into his own substance by his power, so that he might pour out the yoke of his Holy Spirit upon all and make all Christians become what Christ is. [Note: All editions and the Valliscl. manuscript read: “upon all, that is, Christians”; the Lugd. manuscript: “upon all, and that Christians.” But “and this” means the same as “and by this infusion.”]

For when the man Jesus the Lord was the one and only man in the world, like leaven hidden in the mass, he brought it about that all human beings should become what he is. Whoever therefore clings to that leaven of Christ becomes leaven himself, useful both to himself and suitable for all others: certain of his own salvation and confident of acquiring others.

## 4

Just as leaven, when it is to be sprinkled through a heap of flour, is broken, crushed, scattered, and entirely dissolved, so that by its strength it may bind that dispersed quantity of flour into one and reduce it to a solid body—which, when diminished into the form of dust, had grown weak—and by its joining make a useful mass out of what seemed useless through its own dissolution, [Note: Thus the Lugd. manuscript; the Valliscl. manuscript and all editions read: “bind into one strength.” Immediately afterward the Valliscl. manuscript alone reads: “and reduce it into one work.”] so the Lord Jesus Christ, when he was the leaven of the whole world, was broken, torn, and dissolved through various sufferings. His juice, which is his precious blood, was poured out for our salvation, so that by being mixed into it he might solidify the whole human race, which had previously lain dissolved in various places. [Note: All editions and the Lugd. manuscript read: “which had previously lain dissolved through various caves”; the Valliscl. manuscript more suitably reads: “which had previously lain dissolved in various places.”]

Thus we, who appeared to be flour from the nations, clung to him like leaven. We, I say, who lay scattered and utterly divided throughout the whole world, [Note: The Reg. and Valliscl. manuscripts read: “scattered and utterly divided,” etc.] were brought by the power of Christ’s Passion into his own body, as the blessed Apostle says: “For we are the body of Christ and members” (Eph. 5:30).

We, therefore, who came from the nations and were scattered like dust over the face of the earth, grew into the solid mass of his body through the sprinkling of the Lord’s blood.

## 5

But who is the woman said to have hidden the leaven in the flour, if not the holy Church, which daily tries to hide Christ’s teaching in our hearts? She, I say, is the woman who is also said in another passage to be grinding, as the Lord says: “There will be two women grinding; one will be taken and one will be left” (Matt. 24:41).

The holy Church grinds through the Law, through the apostles, and through the prophets when she makes catechumens and disperses and crushes the harshness of paganism, so that, softened and made suitable in the manner of flour, they may cling to the leaven of the Lord’s blood.

I would call the entire Passion of the Lord leaven; for the very symbol that is handed down is the leaven of our salvation. [Note: All editions read: “the symbol without which leaven”; the manuscripts restore the passage as in the text.] Without this leaven, or symbol, no one can attain the substance of eternal life.

## 6

And because the Gospel describes two women grinding, and we have said that one Church grinds beneficially, whom must we understand the other to be except the Synagogue? It too grinds through Moses and the prophets, but it grinds uselessly, as the Apostle says concerning the Jews: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2).

The Synagogue grinds uselessly, I say, because it does not temper its mass with Christ’s teaching. Therefore the Lord commanded that the leaven of the Synagogue be avoided, saying: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matt. 16:6).

For it was tempered with the blood and cruelty of the Jews who said concerning the Lord: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). Hence the Gospel says: “There will be two women grinding; one will be taken and one will be left” (Matt. 24:41).

The holy Church will be taken into eternal rest, for she has ground food of holiness for the Lord; the bloodstained Synagogue will be left at the mill, forever suffering the rotation of its faithlessness.

# SERMON XIV. Sunday of Septuagesima

It is acknowledged that the name “Septuagesima” is much more recent than the age not only of Ambrose but also of Maximus. The first and fourth Councils of Orléans, which prohibit the observance of Quinquagesima and Sexagesima, say nothing about Septuagesima; nor does the Rule of Saint Benedict mention it, but commands that the alleluia be sung until Quadragesima.

We have no doubt that the same word was falsely inserted in editions of Gregory the Great’s *Homilies*, homily 19, and in certain Masses of the *Sacramentary*, since it is not found in the manuscripts. The same must likewise be stated concerning the letter to Augustine the monk cited by Gratian, Distinction 4, chapter “Finally, the priests.”

## 1

“Redeem yourselves while you possess the price.” When, dearly beloved brothers, you begin a new period, you ought to renew your life. Throughout the whole year no day is called Septuagesima except this one; nor Sexagesima except the following Sunday; nor Quinquagesima except the third Sunday from now; nor Quadragesima except the fourth Sunday from now.

Because this period bears new names, therefore every Christian ought to renew his life. The Apostle urges this when he says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23); and again: “Although our outward person is being corrupted, yet our inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

## 2

For just as the one who passes from evil to good is renewed, so the one who passes from good to better is renewed. Whoever passes from luxury or any impurity to chastity has renewed his life. Whoever was accustomed to seize what belonged to others unjustly, if he begins to distribute what is his with mercy, renews his life.

Whoever passes from pride to humility, and whoever loved to slander his brothers, if he begins to love his brothers, undoubtedly renews his life. For one who was a member of the devil through evil living begins to belong to the body of the new man—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ—through right faith and good works.

You have often heard, dearly beloved brothers, that there are two men: Adam and Christ. One is called old; the other is called new. Therefore whoever is evil is old, imitating the one who was proud and disobedient in paradise. But whoever is good is new, following the one who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29), and of whom the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:8).

But because this period bears a new name, we therefore admonish those who are old through evil living to become new through good conduct.

### 3

We admonish those who are already new through good works to strive to be renewed in this new age through better works. For example, one who is new through chastity by abstaining from evil conduct should be renewed by ceasing to take pleasure in that very conduct. Likewise, one who is humble, obedient, merciful, and patient must be renewed daily, so that by advancing he may grow in these virtues, according to what is written: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. 83:8).

Let none of us, beloved, be secure merely because he has been baptized; for just as not all who run in the stadium receive the prize (1 Cor. 9:28)—that is, the appointed reward—but only the one who reaches the goal first by running, so not all who have faith are saved, but only those who persevere in the good work they have begun. And just as one who contends against another abstains from everything, so you too must abstain from every vice, so that you may overcome the devil, your persecutor.

Wretched men serve an earthly king amid dangers to their lives and immense labors, for a benefit that will quickly pass away and perish; why do you not serve the King who enjoys the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom and bestows it upon those who labor?

[Note: [Col. 0631D] One Reg. manuscript reads: “the heavenly King for the blessedness of the kingdom. Now, since through faith, etc.”]

Now, since through faith you have been called by the Lord to the vineyard—that is, to the unity of the holy Church—live and conduct yourselves in such a way that, with God’s gift, you may be able to receive the denarius, that is, the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom (Matt. 20:1 ff.).

### 4

Let no one despair because of the magnitude of his sins, saying: “My sins are many; I have persevered in them until old age and extreme decrepitude. I shall no longer be able to merit pardon, especially since the sins abandoned me, not I them.” Far be it from anyone of this kind to despair of God’s mercy. Some are called to God’s vineyard at the first hour, others at the third, others at the sixth, others at the ninth, and others at the eleventh—that is, some are drawn into God’s service in childhood, others in adolescence, others in youth, others in old age, and others in extreme old age.

And just as no one should despair, whatever his age, if he wishes to turn to the Lord, so no one should feel secure on account of faith alone, but rather fear what is said: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:12). We know that we have been called through faith; but whether we have been chosen for eternal life, we do not know. Therefore each person ought to be more humble in proportion as he is ignorant whether he has been chosen.

### 5

May almighty God grant that you not belong to the number of those who crossed the Red Sea on dry ground, ate manna in the desert, and drank spiritual drink, yet perished in the wilderness because of their murmuring. Rather, may you belong to those who entered the promised land and, laboring faithfully in the vineyard of the Church, deserved to receive the denarius of everlasting blessedness, so that, with Christ our Head, you who are his members may reign for ages upon ages without end.

## SERMON XV. Sunday of Sexagesima

[Col. 0632D]

That this sermon is not by Ambrose is demonstrated, in addition to the points stated above, by the fact that it indicates here that the observance of Sexagesima was established by Telesphorus, whereas Alcuin, in his book *On the Offices of the Church*, attributes the occasion for its institution to the adulterine decree of Pope Melchiades. Since it is clear that the collection of Mercator’s false Decretals did not gain currency in the Church until the beginning of the ninth century, it is altogether manifest that this sermon cannot be by an author earlier than that same century. Add to this the fact that what is stated here concerning the observance of Lent does not agree with the rite customarily observed at Milan during Lent, as may be inferred from our Admonition in the book *On Elijah and Fasting*.

### 1

The season called Sexagesima has arrived, beloved brothers. Therefore it is necessary that your life be changed, your morals corrected, the world despised, and the heavenly homeland loved more ardently. For the number six, from which sixty, Sexagesima, six hundred, and six thousand are derived, signifies perfection. Hence the one who made man on the sixth day wished to redeem him in the sixth age, on the sixth day of the week, and at the sixth hour. Therefore, since you have already celebrated Septuagesima, are celebrating Sexagesima today, and thereafter, with God’s favor, will celebrate Quinquagesima and Quadragesima, we ought to disclose to you the mysteries of these names.

[Col. 0633B]

### 2

Lent, plainly, has six weeks. Pope Telesphorus added a seventh week to it, and this season was called Quinquagesima. Then others added an eighth week, and that season itself was called Sexagesima. Afterwards a ninth week was added, and it was called Septuagesima. For just as Quadragesima is named from four and Sexagesima from six, so Septuagesima is named from seven. Therefore, if someone were now to add a tenth week, we would not call it “Decagesima,” but “Octogesima,” preserving the order of the number, because after seven, from which Septuagesima derives its name, comes eight.

### 3

Quadragesima is observed because Moses, Elijah, and the Savior are read to have fasted for forty days and nights. Quinquagesima is observed by some because it contains fifty days. If seven Sundays are subtracted from these, only forty-two days remain for abstinence; and on those two days some fast and others do not, namely, on the Lord’s Supper and Holy Saturday.

Sexagesima is celebrated because it contains eight weeks—that is, fifty-six days.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] The Ambrosian Library manuscript and one manuscript of Reg. read: “and sixty days.”]

If eight Sundays and eight Thursdays are subtracted, only forty days of fasting remain.

Septuagesima, extending from its beginning until Easter, comprises nine weeks—that is, sixty-three days.

[Note: [Col. 0633C] The same Ambrosian and Reg. manuscripts read: “that is, sixty-four days.”]

It is therefore celebrated by some because, if nine Sundays are subtracted on account of the Lord’s resurrection, nine Thursdays on account of the Lord’s Supper, and an equal number of Saturdays, lest we seem to keep the Sabbath with the Jews, no more than thirty-six days remain for fasting. May Christ our Lord grant you to observe these with complete devotion—he who lives and reigns with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. Where the Lord Healed the Withered Hand on the Sabbath

The Roman editors, failing to notice that Lent at Milan did not begin until the Monday after the First Sunday, arranged this sermon for the Friday after Ash Wednesday. For that reason they prefixed to it a long addition patched together partly from Sermon 63 of the Appendix to Augustine and partly from Book II, chapter 6, section 32, of Ambrose’s *On Abraham*. But if they thought that Ambrose could be vindicated in this way, nothing could be more absurd. We have restored the sermon in accordance with the old editions and the Gallican and Lyon manuscripts; but we do not foist it upon Ambrose, since a Gallican manuscript more reasonably attributes it to Maximus.

### 1

[Note: [Col. 0633D] The Roman edition reads: “But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand does. You see, brothers, what a judge concerned with morals you have. He advises you how he may receive your work; he first questions your mind: ‘Do not let your left hand,’ he says, ‘know what your right hand does.’ Attend carefully, brothers, and seek humbly and wisely the understanding of divine Scripture. For since the right hand and the left hand are bodily organs, devoid of reason, it does not belong to them to know or not to know anything; therefore he is not now speaking of the body. But by the right hand is understood the love of God; by the left, vanity or desire for the world. It is as though he said: ‘Let not the left hand know what the right hand does’; that is, let worldly vanity not destroy what the love of God does. When Abraham could not keep his nephew, who was turning away from him, and wished to dismiss him, he said: ‘Depart: if you go to the left, I will go to the right.’ On the left are the things belonging to the body and the world; on the right are the love of God and the virtues of the soul. Abraham therefore rightly said: ‘If you go to the left, I will go to the right,’ because the imprudent person places in the better part the things belonging to the world and the body—namely, riches and honors—whereas the prudent person prefers the virtue of the soul and the grace of attaining immortality: ‘For length of life is in her right hand.’ Finally, because this right hand had by now withered in man, the Lord Jesus entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and healed by spiritual medicine the man there who had a withered right hand, as another Evangelist relates. For the passage reads thus: ‘And it came to pass also on another Sabbath, that he entered into the synagogue and taught; and there was a man whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and Pharisees watched whether he would heal on the Sabbath, that they might find whereof to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts; and he said to the man who had the withered hand: Rise, and stand forth in the midst. And he rose and stood forth.’ And shortly after: ‘And looking round about upon them all, he said to the man: Stretch forth your hand. And he stretched it forth, and his hand was restored whole as the other.’ Carefully, brothers, I believe you have heard how the Lord Christ [not by applying …, etc.].]

Brothers, I believe you have carefully heard the Gospel reading that was recently read, in which the Lord Jesus Christ entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and healed by spiritual medicine a man whose hand was withered—not by applying the juices of herbs, nor by binding on medicinal compounds, but by commanding with a word and, in anger, restoring health to the body (Luke 6:6 ff.).

Anger, as the Evangelist says, restored strength to the right hand. From this we understand what kind of health belongs to the Lord’s kindness, since such is the medicine of his indignation—or how he benefits when placated, who shows such mercy even when angry.

By a word, therefore, he commands the fluids of the veins to flow into the withered right hand. It is not surprising that the one who restored the withered right hand also created so many bodies from dry dust and, by the command of his word, restored what at the beginning he had established through the work of creation. Recognizing its maker, the small part obeyed him to whom the whole body owed itself in its mass.

[Note: [Col. 0634D] All editions read “who created the whole body”; the Lyon manuscript reads “who created so many bodies.”]

### 2

But let us see what the withered hand in the synagogue is: a hand that benefits the body in no way because it has dried up in works. Let us investigate when it first began to wither. For the Savior’s action does not concern only one man, nor is the weakness of one man alone being remedied; rather, the infirmity of the entire human race is being healed.

No one doubts that the right hand, or the more distinguished part of the whole body, performs this service: it supplies daily nourishment to its body and, with a kind of providence, feeds and sustains the other members so that they may enjoy life.

### 3

This right hand, then, I would say, was the scribes in the Jewish people—or the teachers, who, like a more distinguished part of the Pharisees’ body, had been established by the Lord, yet neglected to offer to their other members the oracles of the prophets as food for eternal life. Therefore their teaching withered like a weak hand, because it did not seek the fountain of everlasting wisdom.

Finally, it happened that, as though contracted, the right hand could no longer hold the key of knowledge, as the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who hide the key of knowledge,” and what follows (Luke 11:52).

This key is the Lord Christ, by whom the hidden things of hearts are unlocked for belief in the faith.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] The Lyon manuscript reads “the hidden things of sinners,” but not very correctly.]

This is the key of which the Lord says to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

Therefore the right hand of the synagogue withered when it abandoned Christ. It had previously been in the leaders of the Jews, but it deteriorated; for whoever abandons Christ, the fountain, is immediately weakened and withers.

### 4

But I find that this hand was once better than the other members. Holy Moses, the leader of the Jewish people, was like the brighter right hand of his body when he deserved to receive from the divine power the Law that was to be handed on.

I say that holy Moses was the right hand: he nourished the children of Israel with heavenly manna, like a provident hand. This is plainly the hand that overcame Jannes and Jambres, the magicians, by the brightness of its snowy splendor (2 Tim. 3:8).

For thus it is written: “Therefore the darkness of the magicians was destroyed, because the shining right hand glittered through Moses’ merits.”

### 5

But let us see when this hand first began to be withered or dead. I affirm that it first withered in Adam, when he plucked the fruit of the forbidden tree against the Lord’s prohibition; then he lost the sap of immortality.

It was, in a sense, dried up when by his sin he caused the man made in the image of God to be dissolved into dust. And would that the hand alone had been held guilty of sin! What is more serious is that the whole body was condemned to death when the first right hand sinned.

Nor should you be surprised that the member of the right hand did not remain whole in Adam: the vigor of eternity had dried up. For just as Moses’ right hand, guarding the Lord’s commandments, shone with snowy radiance, so Adam’s right hand, transgressing the commandments, was contracted by a deadly pallor.

### 6

The Savior heals this hand of Adam in the synagogue; that is, he hastens to heal the weakness of the entire human race. He says also to the one who contracted it by offering it to idols: “Stretch out your hand.” He says this to the one whose right hand dried up through taking interest. “Stretch out your hand,” he says, to the one who uses it to seize the property of orphans and widows.

But you too, who think that you have a pure and healthy hand, beware lest avarice contract it. Rather, frequently stretch it out to the poor in mercy, more often to the stranger in hospitality; always stretch it out to the Lord on behalf of your sins. Be merciful; be generous.

Observe what the prophet says: “Do not let your hand be extended to receive and contracted when it is to distribute” (Ecclus. 4:36). For your hand will be able to remain healthy if it is contracted toward evil things but extended toward good works.

[Note: [Col. 0635D] The Roman edition reads “extended.” While it is extended toward works of virtue, let the left hand—that is, the desire of the flesh or of the world—not destroy what it does. Through the favor of Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.]

## SERMON XVII. On Holy Lent I

This sermon first received a place among the Ambrosian sermons in the Roman edition. Indeed, an extremely ancient manuscript of the Vallicellian Library, from which we corrected it, also ascribes it to our Doctor. But we do not consider such authority sufficient for it alone to be believed.

### 1

[Note: [Col. 0635D] The Roman edition reads: “Behold, the holy days are here … concerning which it has now been read.”]

Behold, the holy days and the acceptable season are approaching, beloved brothers, of which it is written: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). Therefore you ought to be more diligent in vigils, fasts, almsgiving, and prayers.

Let the one who has given alms until now give more during these days, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin (Ecclus. 3:33).

[Note: [Col. 0636D] The Roman edition reads: “Just as water extinguishes a blazing fire, so almsgiving will obtain forgiveness of sin.”]

Let the one who has fasted and prayed until now fast and pray more, because there are certain sins that are not forgiven except through prayer and fasting.

[Note: [Col. 0636D] The Roman edition adds: “As the Savior says: This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.”]

If anyone harbors anger against another, let him forgive him from the heart. If anyone has unjustly taken something from someone, let him return it to the person from whom he took it, if he wishes to have God favorable to him.

[Note: [Col. 0636D] The same edition adds: “Let him at least return what he took, if not fourfold, if he wishes,” and so forth.]

For although a Christian ought at all times to abstain from curses, insults, oaths, excessive laughter, and idle words, he ought to do so especially during these holy days, which have been established for this purpose: that the sins of the whole year may be wiped away through repentance during these forty days.

[Col. 0637A]

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0637D] The same edition reads: “Believe me most firmly, brothers, and do not doubt in any way, that if …” It repeats below: “but just as they did so only in sackcloth …”]

Believe—and believe most firmly—that if during these days you make a pure confession and repent in the manner we have described, you will obtain from the most merciful Lord, together with the Ninevites, forgiveness of all your sins. They deserved to be freed by repenting in sackcloth and ashes.

So too, if you cry out to God with your whole heart, following their example, you will call forth divine mercy upon yourselves, so that you may celebrate the day of the Lord’s resurrection more joyfully and securely, and after this life pass happily to the heavenly homeland—through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. On Holy Lent II

[Col. 0637B]

In the ancient editions this sermon bears the title *On Fasts*, while in some manuscripts it is entitled *On Fasting at the Beginning of Lent*. Not inappropriately so, since it was composed on the epistle assigned in the Gallican liturgy to the First Sunday of Lent and still read on that same day.

Moreover, one finds in it certain passages that the author seems to have imitated from Augustine’s Sermon 24, section 7, and Sermon 77, section 3. The author may be Maximus not only because the style suggests it, but also because the sermon is contained with other works of Maximus in the Gallican manuscript.

### 1

The holy Apostle bears witness concerning the prophets, saying: “In an acceptable time, he says, I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (2 Cor. 6:2). He himself continues: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation.”

Therefore I too testify to you that these are days of redemption, that this is, in a certain sense, the season of heavenly medicine. During this time we can heal the stain of all our vices and all the wounds of our sins, if we faithfully entreat the physician of our souls, so that we do not carelessly neglect his commands, like patients entrusted to him.

For then the sick person finds medicine for his illness if he observes the physician’s instructions with complete diligence.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “if he preserves the medicine that has been given.”]

For if he does one thing while another has been commanded, then, as the disease increases, the physician is not at fault; the transgressor is.

### 2

The physician is our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “I kill and I make alive; I strike and I heal” (Deut. 32:39). The Lord kills, in a certain sense, before he gives life. Through baptism he first kills in us murders, adulteries, crimes, and thefts; then he gives us life as new people through the immortality of eternity.

We therefore die to sins through the washing, but we are regenerated to life through the Spirit, as the holy Apostle says: “For you have died to your sins, and your life is hidden with Christ. For you have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Col. 3:3). We are killed, in a sense, when we cease to be what we were.

Through a new kind of mercy, death and life operate in one and the same person. The desire for sins dies; love of the virtues is brought to life.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] The same manuscript reads: “the fragrance of the virtues is given life.”]

In one and the same person the impious and the adulterer are put to death so that the merciful and chaste may be reborn; idolatry is destroyed so that religion may be propagated; the fornicator and the drunkard are extinguished so that the temperate and sober may be brought forth.

### 3

Thus the Lord mortifies in order to make alive; he kills in order to benefit; he strikes in order to correct. This, then, is his entire severity toward his people: that sins may be punished in them while the soul is preserved, and that detestable vices may be removed while excellent virtues are nourished.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] The edition reads: “that detestable vices may be removed … on this devout occasion of the Lord.” It adds below: “you would see them and believe them to be people reborn.”]

To such an extent do we see many converted through this devout killing by the Lord and advancing toward what is better, being changed from merely devout into outstandingly good people, that when you see them you would believe them to be different men, although you do not see their persons changed.

For what we previously were is so completely killed, removed, and extinguished in us that we believe what we afterwards become to have been born anew. Hence this second birth signifies that the end of the former life has already taken place.

### 4

When he says, “I will strike and I will heal” (Deut. 32:39), the Lord plainly strikes sinners with his commandments in order to heal them; he scourges them with his orders in order to correct them. He commands fasts, imposes continence, threatens judgment, and, instilling the grave fear of Gehenna, applies medicine, so that, while we fear future things, we may correct present ones.

### 5

In this way he restored the Apostle Paul to health by striking him (Acts 9:3 ff.). When Paul was a persecutor, impious and blasphemous, and was hastening to Damascus to devastate the churches, the Lord suddenly struck him with terror through a flash of heavenly brilliance, so that he might flood him with the light of the Gospel’s splendor.

He deprived him of the use of his bodily eyes in order to illuminate his spiritual sight.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] Thus the Vallicellian manuscript and the old edition; the Roman edition reads “changed his blindness,” while all the others read “illuminated his sight.”]

He terrified him through bodily weakness in order to save him through devotion to the faith. Thus Paul rose from the ground: with his outward eyes he did not see people or even the air, but with the eyes of his mind he saw Christ from heaven.

Finally, this blow from the Lord benefited him so greatly that from Jew he became Christian, from blasphemer an apostle, and from Saul Paul. It changed the former man, together with his morals, so completely that it even changed his name.

### 6

Since we have such a physician, who heals by striking and gives life by mortifying, let us submit to him with complete patience for treatment, so that whatever he perceives in us to be shameful, soiled by sins, or putrid with wounds, he may cut into, amputate, and excise. When all the wounds of the devil have been cut away, may he cause only what belongs to God to remain in us.

His first command is that during these forty days we devote ourselves to fasting, prayers, and vigils. Through fasting the wantonness of the body is chastised; through prayers the devout soul is nourished; through vigils the devil’s ambushes are driven away.

Then, when this season has been completed through observance of these commandments, the soul, purified and wearied by so many observances, comes to baptism and is refreshed by the inundation of the Holy Spirit. Whatever heat of various illnesses had dried it up is drenched with the dew of heavenly grace, so that, laying aside the corruption of the old person, it acquires the character of new youth.

In a wondrous way, in one and the same person holiness succeeds sin, righteousness succeeds iniquity, and infancy succeeds old age. Through this new kind of birth, the person who is reborn is another person from the one who sinned.

### 7

Thus Elijah, through forty days and nights of continuous fasting, deserved to extinguish the long and excessive drought of the whole world with the dew of rain and to drench the burning thirst of the earth with the abundance of heavenly rain (1 Kings 19:8).

We recognize that this was done as a figure of our own experience, so that we too, fasting through the course of these forty days, may deserve spiritual baptismal rain for our tribes, and so that heavenly rain from above may pour upon our long-dry earth and the life-giving flood of the washing may moisten the prolonged drought of the nations.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] The Roman edition, after the word “rain,” had removed “for our tribes.”]

Whoever is not watered by the grace of baptism suffers drought and burning in his soul.

### 8

Through the fast of these days and nights, holy Moses deserved to speak with God, to stand and remain in his presence, and to receive from his hand the commandments of the Law (Exod. 24:18).

Although his human condition kept him from God’s sight, the grace of fasting nevertheless brought him close to participation in divinity. For this is a portion of God’s virtues in us: that we fast frequently, since God himself always fasts.

Therefore, in whomever he perceives a greater abundance of his works, he is more familiar, intimate, and friendly with that person, as Scripture says: “And Moses spoke with God face to face, as one speaks with his friend” (Exod. 33:11).

### 9

For this reason the Lord Jesus Christ, intending to receive the glory of the resurrection, dedicated his virtues to a fast of forty days and nights (Matt. 4:2), to show that human life is not bread but the word of God.

Through these forty-day fasts, then, God is reconciled, the heavens are opened, and the underworld is unlocked. Therefore let us too, beloved brothers, fast continually and devoutly during this period, so that the Lord may be favorable to us, the heavens may be opened to us, and the underworld may not be able to hold us.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] The old edition reads: “so that the underworld may not prevail against us”; the Lyon manuscript: “so that the underworld may not prevail”; the Roman edition: “may not overpower us”; the Vallicellian manuscript has the reading adopted in the text.]

## SERMON XIX. On Holy Lent III

From the beginning this sermon displays such affinity with Sermons 39 and 41, which we rejected, that we may readily be persuaded that they belong to the same author. There is no reason to suppose that Lent, where this sermon was delivered, ordinarily comprised forty-two fasts, or seven weeks. What is said here about the forty-two stopping places should be understood only as a comparison between those same stopping places and Lent, a comparison begun by Gregory the Great in Homily 16 on the Gospels. There he expressly states, however, that in his own time only thirty-six days of fasting were observed.

### 1

We have often set forth the meaning of holy Lent, whose beginning we celebrate today, and we have frequently explained why we fast for so many days.

For we have said that the Lord Jesus Christ consecrated this same number by fasting, and that, taking no food through continuous days and nights, he formed one single body of fasting. That is, although the succession of day was interrupted by the arrival of night, the continuity of the fast was not interrupted.

Thus, before God there were indeed several periods of time, but one day of abstinence. He showed us that we ought to fast through this whole number without interruption: since we cannot complete the whole of Lent in one solid and uninterrupted fast, we should at least celebrate it through daily fasts without interruption. If anyone omits even one day of fasting, he violates the whole of Lent and, for the food of a short time, loses the fruit of a great labor.

### 2

But someone may say: “We have heard the meaning of Lent explained several times, and we have often heard that it was consecrated by the Lord. But we desire to hear why this same Lent contains forty-two days.”

We read in the Old Testament that when holy Moses delivered the children of Israel from the yoke of Egyptian captivity in order to lead them into the promised land, he reached that land by forty-two stopping places.

[Note: [Col. 0640D] The Roman edition alone reads: “by forty-two places.”]

He possessed the promises after as many periods of time as we rejoice to enjoy the promises made to us by the Savior.

I say that Moses reached rest by the same number of stopping places by which we hasten through fasts to heaven. For our fasts are certain stopping places through which we travel spiritually, walking by the virtues of the soul and, through daily progress, drawing nearer to the promised land. Thus the more devoutly one fasts, the sooner one arrives.

Faith and fasting are swift feet of the soul: they quickly climb from lowly things to higher ones and quickly proceed from earthly things to heavenly things. Concerning these feet the Apostle said: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10:15). The Lord commanded that these feet be washed, as the Apostle says of the widow: “If she has washed the feet of the saints” (1 Tim. 5:10). Worthy of honor are the feet of those who proclaim peace: spiritual and pure through their teaching, they walk over the hearts of human beings.

### 3

The people of Israel also reached the waters of the Jordan after forty-two years; through the same course of days the Christian people reach the waters of baptism.

And as the prophet says, “The Jordan was turned back” (Ps. 113:3), so there, when Israel entered the river’s waters, the current withdrew; here, when the Christian descends into the font, the sins of crimes flee away.

In a wondrous manner, there the river turned backward and returned to its source; here, the human being, called back thereafter, is restored to the infancy of his origin.

There the water seeks its own spring from which it had emerged; here it recognizes the human being from whom innocence had departed.

There the riverbed is emptied of its waves; here hearts are emptied of their crimes, so that there muddy water does not wet God’s servants, while here a foul conscience does not defile God’s ministers.

The Jordan is, in a sense, the fountain of the washing. Whoever passes through it, leaving behind his filth, enters the promised paradise.

### 4

In this forty-two-fold number, then, the people of Israel, leaving Egypt, crossed the waters of the Red Sea. We too, leaving the Egypt of the world in this same number, cross the pools of burning Gehenna.

The waves supported them; the flame of fire does not burn us. The water was made solid for them; the conflagration is cooled for us. Contrary to nature’s order, the sea is dried up by heat, while through the fountain of baptism Gehenna is softened.

In this mystical number, when the children of Israel reached Myrrha, they could not drink the water because of its bitterness. For the fountain had water but no sweetness: it was pleasing to look at but not pure in taste. When Moses threw wood into it, they drank its sweetness with pleasure. The sacramental power of the wood removed the harshness carried by the harmful water.

### 5

I think this was done as a figure. I believe that the bitter water at Myrrha represents the Law of the Old Testament. Before it was tempered by the Lord’s cross, the Law was harsh: it commanded that an eye be given for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and, like something austere, offered no refreshment of mercy.

But when it was tempered by the wood of the Gospel passion, immediately exchanging its bitterness for sweetness, it showed itself sweet for all to drink, as the prophet says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

Sweet are the words that command: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. If anyone takes your tunic, leave him your cloak as well” (Matt. 5:39).

This, then, is that bitterness which was changed into sweetness: the austerity of the Law was tempered by the grace of the Gospel.

The letter of the Law is bitter without the mystery of the cross; concerning it the Apostle says: “The letter kills” (2 Cor. 3:6). But when the mysteries of that passion are joined to it, all its bitterness is spiritually seasoned, and the Apostle says of it: “But the Spirit gives life.”

## SERMON XX. On Holy Lent IV

[Col. 0642A]

This sermon continues the preceding one, and therefore both should be attributed to a single author. After repeating here certain matters treated there, the author turns his discourse to the twelve springs and seventy-two palms. His statement that these represented the apostles and disciples seems to have been drawn from nowhere other than Origen’s Homily 27 on Numbers 33 and Jerome’s Letter 127 to Fabiola.

### 1

Your memories still retain, brothers, what we preached on the previous Sunday: that the forty-two stopping places were a figure of our Lent. Through these stopping places the people of Israel, departing from Egypt, entered the promised land by daily progress and, as though by certain steps of salvation, ascended from the yoke of slavery to the kingdom (Num. 33:3 ff.).

### 2

I say that those stopping places were a figure of our fasts not only in the quantity of their number but also in the observance of virtues. For the children of Israel did not travel through the desert merely with bodily steps as much as they advanced along the Lord’s way through religious actions.

They plainly walked on the Lord’s way—a way that both carried them upon the waves and fed them from heaven. For manna was not lacking for those who were hungry in the wilderness, nor did the land flee from those in danger at sea. There the sea was laid out as a path; here heaven is opened as food.

For the sake of God’s servants, the Jordan holds back its waters, and Myrrha changes its water. There, the wave that followed, turning backward, goes before them; here, the stream that once let fall bitterness, tempered for the better, becomes sweet.

And in a wondrous way the river lost its course, while the fountain lost its taste.

[The supplied source ends here.]

3. But since we said that the children of Israel, when they came to Marah, suffered from the bitterness of the water and could drink it only after wood had been thrown into it—and that in this too there had been a figure of the Old Testament—let us see where that people proceeded from there and arrived. They came to a place called Elim, where there were twelve exceedingly pure springs and a multitude of seventy flourishing palm trees. Behold the mystery of God: see how, after the bitterness of the Law, the streams of evangelical devotion overflow. There one single spring is harsh to drink; here there are several, and all are sweet to drink. There, after weariness, there is no refreshment; here, after toil, there are refreshment and victory. For springs are provided for the thirsty, and palms are offered to the victorious (Exod. XV, 27).

4. Palms, I say, are offered to the victorious, because to have reached the grace of the Gospel after the rigors of the Law is to have conquered. For it is a victor’s reward to moisten one’s mouth at a living spring and to strengthen one’s right hand with a triumphal palm. Through the spring, the tongue of the confessor is purified; through the palm, the martyr’s right hand is honored: the former because it exalted the glory of Christ, the latter because it refused the altar of sacrilege. For the palm of martyrdom is a certain reward, granting sweet fruit to the confessing tongue and glorious adornment to the victorious right hand. The palm is plainly sweet food for martyrs, shady rest, and honorable triumph; always green, always clothed with leaves, always ready for victory. And therefore the palm does not wither, because the victory of the martyrs does not wither.

5. Finally, the palms themselves are offered by the crowds to the Lord as he sits upon the ass and comes to the temple. When the disciples spread their garments and fortified Christ’s path with their clothing, he had no greater reward than the palms which the devotion of the crowd offered him. [Note: [Col. 0643D] All editions and the Lyons Royal codex read “the way [is] undefiled”; more suitably, Remigius and the Vallisclavian codex read “polluted,” etc.] By the garments spread along the road, this signified that the way in the world was polluted; by the palms offered, that he himself was the victor of the world (Luke XIX, 36). He himself, I say, is the victor of whom Scripture says: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V, 5). He is plainly the victor who destroyed diabolical death and illumined eternal life. Palms, therefore, are raised for Christ as he comes. It is written: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree” (Ps. XCI, 13). Therefore, rightly, banners of righteousness are raised for the righteous one who comes, and the titles of their triumphs attend their author.

6. Before the palms are raised, however, the Lord’s path to the temple is covered with the disciples’ garments, and, so that the Savior’s path may be undefiled, it is fortified with the apostles’ cloaks. I think this was done as a mystery. For Christ’s way, which leads to the temple, is his faith and teaching. Therefore the disciples, so that we might walk along this way without stumbling, stripped off the garments of their own bodies and spread them upon it through their martyrdom, so that amid the crowds of different peoples they might lay the garments of their limbs beneath the path of righteousness, cover the muddy myrrh-mire (myrrhago) of the world, [Note: [Col. 0643D] The Roman edition alone reads “and the muddy abyss . . .”; after *maran* it has: but the manuscripts and old editions everywhere write *myrrham*, *myrrha*, etc.] and show the Savior’s way to be undefiled.

7. After Marah, therefore, the people of Israel came to the twelve springs. We read in the Prophet: “Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel” (Ps. LXVII, 27). The Lord is Christ, who is learned only through the mouths of the apostles and the teaching of the disciples. The apostles are to be called springs,

[Note: The old editions: “because they are all exceedingly pure”; the Roman edition: “because they are like exceedingly pure rivers”; the manuscripts as in our text. Again, where the old editions read “the sacraments of abundant wisdom of the cup,” the Vallisclavian codex has “the abundant sacraments of the wisdom of the cup”; we prefer the reading of the Lyons codex.]

because, like exceedingly pure springs, they overflow with the grace of preaching, and after the bitterness of the Law, the abundant cups of sacramental wisdom drip sweetness from their channels. Nor is it surprising that the drink of the springs is sweet, when the food in the bosom of the palms is sweeter. The apostles, therefore, are the springs that watered the face of the whole earth with the river of their teaching and offered the drink of the divine mystery to peoples wearied by their labors.

[Note: The Vallisclavian codex: “offered the drink of the divine ministry.”]

8. The seventy palms generated beside the apostolic springs, I would say, are those seventy disciples whom the Lord sends out after the apostles, in a second rank, for the salvation of humankind. The evangelist Luke, describing them, says that they were sent two by two (Luke X, 1 ff.). Returning with joy after their labors on behalf of humankind, they truly rejoice before the Lord that even the demons are subject to them. Rightly, therefore, they are compared to palms, since, with the reward of palms, they became victors over the devil.

## SERMON XXI. On Holy Lent V

The opening words of this sermon indicate to us that it belongs to the same author as the preceding two. It is not surprising, however, that although he recognizes Lent as lasting forty days, he nevertheless compares it with the forty-two stations of the Israelites, since, as we have already said, the same comparison had already been used when Lent consisted of only thirty-six days. As for the statement that it was customary for these days to be called “stations,” this seems to have been taken from Tertullian, *On Prayer*, near the end of *On Fasting*, and *On the Soldier’s Crown*; similarly, Jonathan is mentioned here on the basis of Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 10, and Cassian, *Conferences* 21, chapter 29.

1. I believe, brothers, that you have understood why I compared our fasts with those stations in which the people of Israel, as though stationed in a military formation, overcame King Pharaoh by daily labor and defended themselves against their enemies by remaining at the stations as if in certain camps. Thus, whoever among their companions did not complete the distance of the day’s station was either overtaken by Pharaoh or engulfed by the wilderness. So we too must complete with every effort the journey of forty days appointed for us and fortify ourselves with the devotion of fasting as though in certain camps. For our fasts are camps for us, defending us against the devil’s assault.

[Note: The Roman edition alone: “brothers, on the preceding Sunday.”]

Finally, they are called stations because, by standing and remaining in them, we repel the ambushes of our enemies. Fasts are camps for Christians. If anyone strays from them, he is attacked by the spiritual Pharaoh or devoured by the wilderness of sins. The wilderness of sins is suffered by the one who is deserted by the fellowship of the saints.

2. Fasting, then, is a kind of wall for the Christian, impregnable to the devil and impassable to the enemy.

[Note: The German codex: “and an impregnable tower for the devil.”]

For who among Christians has ever fasted and been captured? Who has remained sober and been defeated? The devil attacks the drunkard; the enemy assaults the lustful. But when he sees fasting, he flees, fears, and trembles. He is terrified by its pallor, weakened by hunger, and struck down by infirmity—struck down, I say, by infirmity, because Christian weakness is strength. Hence the Apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am stronger” (II Cor. XII, 10).

But someone may ask how weakness can be strong. Weakness is strong when the flesh wastes away through fasting and the soul grows rich through purity. To the extent that nourishment is withdrawn from the flesh, to that extent the power of righteousness is increased in the soul. Thus a person is indeed weak for worldly works, but strong for divine ones. Then he thinks more of God,

[Note: The Vallisclavian codex: “then he does not fear judgment.”]

then he fears judgment, then he conquers the enemy. For the Savior says of the devil: “This kind is not driven out except by fasting and prayers” (Matt. XVII, 20).
