He is saying that one possessed by the devil can be cleansed only by fasts. See, therefore, what the power of fasting is, how much grace it bestows upon the one who fasts, and how great a medicine it provides for another; how it sanctifies its practitioner and so purifies someone else. For it is a wonderful thing: one person fasts, and the benefit of the one fasting profits another.

3. Therefore, brothers, let us not lay down the weapons of abstinence, and let us diligently undertake the fast of forty days without interruption. For this is the perfect number for conquering. After the Lord had fasted for forty days, he conquered the devil—not because he could not have conquered him even before fasting, but to show us that we can then be victors over the devil when, by fasting for forty days, we have become victors over bodily desires. He also showed that whoever violates this consecrated number through gluttony can easily be overcome by the enemy as weak and wretched.

For how can one overcome the devil’s wickedness in another who does not overcome gluttony in himself? First, then, human being, be victor over yourself, so that you may be able to be victor over another. For there are within you enemies of your own, who attack you every day. Greed surrounds you with the ambition for wealth; lust captivates you with the sweetness of banquets; heresy perverts through the falsehood of knowledge.

[Note: All editions: “perverts through perversity”; all manuscripts: “perverts through falsehood.”]

Conquer your own enemies, therefore, so that you may be able to conquer those of others.

4. For it is no small sin, brothers, to violate the Lent imposed upon the faithful by the Lord and to dissolve consecrated fasts through the voracity of the belly. For it is written: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (I John II, 6). If you wish to be a Christian, you ought to walk as Christ also walked.

[Note: The old edition and one manuscript: “you ought to do what Christ does”; the Roman edition: “you ought to do what Christ did”; but since neither of these words is found in the other manuscripts, the reading of the German codex seemed preferable.]

He who had no sin fasted for forty days; you, who sin, do not wish to fast for forty days. He, I say, had no sin, but he fasted for our sins. What sort of Christian are you, then, in your own conscience, when Christ hungers for you while you dine? When the Savior fasts for you, while you refresh yourself?

5. Therefore, as I said, it is no small sin to violate the fast that has been imposed. To prove this briefly by examples, we read in the Books of Kings that, when Saul, king of Israel, was waging war against the Philistines, he imposed a fast upon his entire army; and, while all were abstaining, they began to fight against their adversaries (I Sam. XIV, 24 ff.). He was plainly a good king, who conquered his enemies not so much by arms as by devotion, and fought more through religious observance than through weapons.

When Saul had imposed abstinence for the day upon all his men, and his son Jonathan, unaware of the command, was advancing victoriously through the enemy lines, he tasted a honeycomb after dipping the tip of his staff into it. So great was the indignation that was suddenly aroused that victory was delayed and the divine power offended. In the end, neither was the battle brought to completion nor was a prophetic response given to the king. From this we understand that Saul overcame his enemies not so much by the valor of his soldiers as by their abstinence. Finally, the fault of one was reckoned as cowardice to all, and weakness was produced in everyone by the offense of one. For strength fails in an army when fasting fails in its observance.

When Saul recognized this sin from the divine offense itself, he immediately said that Jonathan should not be spared, but that the sin committed should be expiated by the shedding of his blood.

See how great the religious observance of King Saul was, since he wished even to mitigate the Lord’s offense by an act of parricide,

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions instead read: “the observance by which he offended God,” etc.]

and how great is the guilt of breaking a fast, when it is punished only by the shedding of blood. If Jonathan, unaware that his father had imposed a fast, is handed over to death because he broke it, what does he deserve who knowingly breaks a fast imposed by Christ?

6. Therefore, brothers, let us guard the fast appointed for us with every observance, so that we may conquer our spiritual and bodily enemies. For, as you know, we also have bodily enemies. Let us fast, then, so that both our army and Saul may overcome and defeat them.

Nor, while engaged in abstinence, let us turn aside toward the honeycomb. For the honeycomb is a kind of pleasure of the world, or its vices, which, as it is written, temporarily fatten the throat, but “their end is bitterer than gall” (Prov. V, 4).

[Note: “Let us pray, then,” and what follows are restored here for the first time from the Vatican and German codices.]

Let us pray, then, that while we fast, the Lord may grant us that spiritual honeycomb which may become sweet to us upon the palate of the soul in eternal blessedness. With his help, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. On Holy Lent VI

This sermon is placed immediately after the preceding three in the ancient edition and in most manuscripts; hence one may conjecture that it came from the author of those sermons. Its style, however, is somewhat humbler; yet it removes it much farther from the diction of Ambrose than from that of Maximus.

1. We ought not to be so greatly saddened, dearest brothers, that during these days of Lent the trial of tribulation has come upon us, since we see that our Savior too was tempted because of Lent. We servants, therefore, ought to grieve less, because we have the example of the Lord. For wherever there is devotion like Christ’s, there is also temptation like Christ’s; the condition of fasting imposes upon us the condition of endurance.

We believe, moreover, that just as our Savior prevailed over the devil when he was tempted, so we too can overcome our enemies when we are afflicted. For Christ’s fasts can be tested, but they cannot be defeated. They contain hardships in their observance, but they bestow prosperity and salvation. Let us therefore see, among the other temptations, by what art the devil assails the Lord.

2. When the Savior was standing upon the pinnacle of the temple, the devil said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down,” and so forth (Matt. IV, 6). Truly, the cunning of diabolical deceit relies upon its customary argument. For it always tries to cast the devout down from higher things to lower ones, and hastens to lead them from holy and venerable actions to earthly and muddy ones, so that the one who stands in purity of mind upon the height of the temple may throw himself into the depths through the pollution of sin.

When he tries to cast the Lord down from the pinnacle of the temple, he is certainly attempting to remove him from the perfection of religious worship; for the pinnacle of the holy place is the heavenly perfection of the mystery.

3. The Lord is rightly said to stand upon the pinnacle of the temple, because it is written of him: “He walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. CIII, 3). The Lord in a certain sense walks upon the wings of the winds when he proceeds in the swift flight of our conduct and morals. For good morals are wings to us: lifted above the lowliness of earth, they raise us to the heights of heaven; by a kind of flight of the mind they lead us out of dark Tartarus and bring us to the delights of paradise.

Desiring to have the wings of such morals, the Prophet says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly and find rest?” (Ps. LIV, 7). The Savior, therefore, is said to stand upon this pinnacle of the temple—that is, to stand as though in a temple of our faith. Hence the Apostle says: “You are the temple of the living God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (II Cor. III, 16).

4. Standing in this temple and not departing from it, the Lord rebukes the devil, saying: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. IV, 7). That is: You shall not tempt him whom you think should be thrust down into lower things as a human being; rather, you shall recognize and worship him as God and Lord himself.

[Note: The old edition, with the Vallisclavian manuscript: “as God and man himself.” Not sufficiently correct.]

During these days of fasting, therefore, we are tempted in imitation of the Savior. Our enemies likewise try to hurl us down from the pinnacle of the temple—that is, from the observance of Lent. When they bring terrors upon us and prepare ambushes, they desire to lead us away from the fortress of religion. But the Lord says to them: “You shall not tempt holy men and servants of God. Those whom you think should be trampled down as lowly, you will find worthy of honor as valiant.”

5. For, as I said, there are many brothers whom our enemies lead away from the perfection of religion. When they fear present evil, they suppose that God has forgotten our salvation, not knowing that God forgets no one. We ourselves make him forgetful of us when we sin. When we do evil, he turns his face away; when we speak wickedly, he closes his ear. Thus God does not so much withdraw his goodness from us as our sins repel him.

The same Lord says through the Prophet to those who were placed in tribulations: “Is my hand not strong enough to rescue you?” (Isa. L, 2), and so forth. You see, then, that sins separate God and the human being. Take sins away from the midst, and you have made God near to you.

6. How can God forget us, brothers, when in the Gospel he says that even the hairs of our head are numbered before him? If he remembers our hairs, how much more does he remember our souls (Luke XII, 7). Through the act of numbering, we recognize his care and solicitude for us; for no one numbers anything except what he wishes to guard more carefully. No one numbers anything except one who fears suffering loss without knowing the number.

A shepherd frequently counts his flock so as to keep it safe. Finally, when one little sheep had strayed from a hundred sheep, the Lord, who is the good shepherd, returned to the number and carried it back to the flock upon his own shoulders (Luke XV, 4). So completely is the one who is counted held under protection that, when it strays, it is carried back upon the shepherd’s shoulders, lest anything be lacking from the number.

Do not suppose, therefore, brothers, that God forgets even the least person. God remembers everyone; he calls everyone to mind. Only let us not, through our intervening sins, impose forgetfulness upon him.

## SERMON XXIII. On Holy Lent VII

From what is said here about the fifty-day observance, it can be learned that its observance had not yet generally been received at that time. On this difference one may consult Cassian, *Conferences* XXI, chapter 24, and Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 19. The fact that no mention is made here of the sixtieth or seventieth day is certainly evidence that the authors of this sermon and of the preceding Sermons 14 and 15 were different. A complaint is also directed against those who kept the fast during Lent only on alternate weeks; Peter Chrysologus likewise attacks them in Sermon 146. There are, moreover, points in which this sermon agrees sufficiently with Sermons 145 and 147 of the Augustinian Appendix that it might perhaps be attributed to their author. Yet to attribute it to our Ambrose is contradicted by everything.

1. Some Christians, brothers, thinking that they observe the divine commands more religiously, omit the devotion of Lent, whose beginning we celebrate today, and falsely claim that they are observing a fifty-day fast, although this is commanded neither by the divine Scriptures nor handed down by the authority of our predecessors. They do this solely through presumption of mind; and while they think they are acting more devoutly, they behave more superstitiously.

The one who says he observes a fifty-day fast may perhaps scarcely be able to complete Lent. It is indeed good to fast at all times, but it is better to fast for forty days with Christ. For the Lord consecrated this Lent for us by his fast. I said “by his fast,” not “by his fasts,” for the Lord’s fast was one: over forty consecutive days and nights, he took no food at all (Matt. IV, 2).

2. Therefore, any Christian who does not complete the consecrated Lent by fasting will be held guilty of transgression and obstinacy, because by eating he himself annuls the law divinely given for his salvation. You annul the law when you do not keep the example of the Lord’s fast.

[Note: Absent from the Lyons and Vallisclavian codices: “But what sort of Christian are you ... while you dine?”]

What sort of Christian are you, then, when the Lord fasts while you dine? What sort of Christian are you, when Christ hungers while you refresh yourself? He endures hunger for your salvation, while you fear to fast for your sins?

Tell me, I ask you who dine during Lent: are you not guilty in your consciences when, while the whole people abstains, you alone devour food contrary to the Lord’s command? Are you not ashamed when you go out in public, lest you encounter someone who is fasting? Or do you not think, when you proceed to church, how you will offer the kiss of peace to the bishop, lest the very spirit of your kiss condemn you?

If you perhaps do not think about these things, you are surely greatly mistaken. For you ought to know that, during the days of Lent, when someone who has eaten encounters someone fasting, the one who fasts does not judge him favorably.

3. I say this because I hear that many of the faithful—what is more serious—abstain during Lent only in alternate weeks and violate that consecrated number of days through gluttony: they dine for the span of seven days and fast for the space of seven days.

To these I say: why do they defraud themselves by fasting during those seven days too, when such fasting does not profit them? For although someone abstains on certain days, although he does not eat the sweeter foods,

[Note: The Vallisclavian codex: “yet it is not credited to him,” etc.]

the fast of Lent is not credited to him if he does not fast for forty days.

It is shameful to say: old men and old women keep Lent,

[Note: Thus the edition; the Lyons and Vallisclavian codices instead read: “the rich and the young do not keep it.”]

but young men and young women do not. Let us therefore celebrate this most sacred season with every concern. Let no day pass us without fasting; let no week pass us without vigils. For the one who ascends to Easter by fasting and keeping vigil celebrates Lent.

Just as fasting during the rest of the year is a reward, so not fasting during Lent is a sin. The former fasts are voluntary; the latter are necessary. The former arise from free choice; the latter from law. We are invited to the former, but compelled to the latter.

4. But let us see where this most sacred number of forty days first began. We read in the Old Testament that in the time of Noah, when criminal wickedness had seized the whole human race, the cataracts of heaven were opened and rains poured down for that number of days (Gen. VII, 12). Through a certain mystery of Lent, a flood came upon the whole world—not so much a deluge as a baptism.

It was plainly a baptism, through which iniquity was removed from sinners while Noah’s righteousness was preserved. So now also the Lord has given us Lent in imitation of that time, so that, with the appointed number of days, the heavens may be opened, the rain of heavenly mercy may fall upon us, and, through the flood that occurs in baptism, the shower of the saving washing may illumine us.

As then it happened through the waves of water, so now may the iniquity of sins be extinguished in us and the righteousness of virtues preserved. The same pattern that operated under Noah operates now as well: baptism is a flood for the sinner and a consecration for the faithful. Through the Lord’s washing righteousness is saved and unrighteousness is slain.

We see this accomplished in one and the same apostle, Paul. Before he was washed by spiritual commands, he was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and Saul. But when the rain of the heavenly washing flowed down upon him, the blasphemer was slain, the persecutor was slain, Saul was slain; the apostle was brought to life, the righteous man was brought to life, and Paul too was brought to life.

So completely did he lose the old man with his deeds that, when his conduct changed, his name changed as well. Whoever, therefore, observes the Lord’s commands in this devotion of Lent will have the devil’s impiety slain within him, while apostolic grace will be preserved. In a certain sense he succeeds himself: he dies in that part by which he is a sinner, and he is brought to life in that part by which he is righteous.

5. Let us also see whether we can find this mystical number of Lent elsewhere in Scripture. We read that holy Moses nourished the children of Israel in the wilderness with heavenly manna for a period of forty years (Exod. XVI, 35). It is a good number, then, which always opens heaven; a good number, I say, through which Noah’s righteousness is saved and the children of Israel are nourished.

Let us therefore observe this number too, so that the heavens may be opened for us, the rain of spiritual grace may fall upon us, and the manna of spiritual mysteries may refresh us. In imitation of our fathers, through this observance of Lent we are both justified and fed: justified by the washing, fed by the sacraments.

6. But someone may say that, when the children of Israel were filled with manna in the wilderness, they were certainly not fasting. I say, however, that they were engaged in nothing but abstinence at that time, and therefore deserved the grace of heavenly nourishment.

First, because the whole wilderness is a fast; the anxiety of solitude drives away the desire for food. Then, in the wilderness, where could elaborate banquets come from? Where could expensive wines come from? Where could any sort of provision have come from over a period of forty years?

[Note: The old edition with the Vallisclavian manuscript: “because it is the anxiety of concern”; the Roman edition with the Lyons codex is better: “because it is the anxiety of solitude.”]

We understand, therefore, that the children of Israel fasted, because we know that they lacked an abundance of food and took food only when the Lord who bestowed it was pleased. The one who refreshes himself according to Christ’s will fasts for a sufficiently long time.

Indeed, the abstinence of the children of Israel in the wilderness pleased the Savior so much that the intemperance of some among them was also marked. Whoever, being more greedy, had gathered a double portion of manna for himself was struck by this punishment: he was found to have stored up not so much food as worms. Since he had desired more than a moderate refreshment, he was pressed by something like the goads of conscience, in the manner of worms.

7. Therefore, brothers, let us too observe daily and moderate fasts during Lent. As though placed in the wilderness, let us think of none of the world’s delicacies; let no sweetness of bodily desires disturb us. Let us be sober; let us be chaste. Though our life is among cities, let us possess the wilderness in our minds. If we live in abstinence in this way, we shall be refreshed by heavenly manna and pierced by no goads of worms.

## SERMON XXIV. On Holy Lent VIII

Whatever is inserted between the first words of this sermon and number 2 is found in the Augustinian Appendix, where it constitutes Sermon 251. Some passages are also found in Sermon 256 of the same Appendix. Hence we learn that Caesarius—if he may rightly be called the author of these sermons—sometimes repeated the same thoughts, and that this sermon of ours is full and complete, since the sermon called 251 is only a fragment of it. In Rabanus it is entitled “Homily Against Pagan Errors.” In it, as also in the following sermon, certain passages may be read that seem to have been borrowed from this sermon—unless one prefers to suppose that the same sermon was compiled partly from Caesarius, partly from Rabanus, and partly from others.

1. How greatly to be feared is that day of judgment, dearest brothers, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, the redeemer of all, has purposed to come with a flame of fire that will consume his adversaries and those who practice iniquity! On that day all the tribes of the earth will mourn. They will see the Son of Man coming upon the clouds of heaven with great power and exalted majesty. All the ends of the earth will tremble before him, and sinners will perish in it. Heaven will be folded up, the sea will dry up, and the mountains will burn like wax down to the underworld. The sun will be turned into darkness, the moon will not give its light, the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken.

Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. It will be the cross of Christ our Lord, in whose light the lights of the whole world will grow dark. Then the saints will be snatched up to meet Christ in the air, and so they will always be with the Lord. But sinners will be confounded and perish.

Then our Lord Jesus Christ will send his angels to the four corners of the earth, and they will gather his elect from the highest heavens to their boundaries. Then the Lord will separate his saints from the midst of sinners and send them to heavenly dwellings. But sinners will be sent into the furnace of fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. XXIV, 29 ff.). There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. VIII, 12).

Woe to those people who will have their dwelling with the devil, because the smoke of their torments will rise forever and ever. Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished. Among them there will be no voice except groaning, no rest except fire, no refreshment except flame, and no light ever except darkness. Such people will never come into God’s remembrance. Their food is torment, and their dwelling will be with the devil, where there is no sweetness but only stench.

2. O human being, who desire to possess the kingdom of God: while you can, amend the evil you have done. While you have time, cry out to almighty God. While you have time to mourn, while your soul still dwells in your body, while you are still alive, acquire a remedy that will benefit you—before the snare of punishments absorbs you into the depths of death, before hell receives you; where there is no indulgence, no recourse to confession, and no return to forgiveness.

3. We too, dearest brothers, should practice true repentance, so that the Lord may deign to rescue us from the punishment we described above. It is not enough for us to bear the name Christian if we do not perform Christian works. The Lord commands that our tithes be distributed every year from all our crops, livestock, and other possessions.

It is also written: “Give tithes from all your labor and from all your livestock, and I will open for you the cataracts of heaven; your harvests will multiply, and your vineyards will abound for you, and there will also be health in your houses” (Deut. XII, 6 ff.). But if you do not give tithes, says the Lord, I will send hail, frost, and storms upon you, and I will take away all your labor.

Nine parts have been allotted to you, but because you were unwilling to give tithes, you will return to the one-tenth alone. Moreover, pestilences will come upon your houses. Offer the first portion of your grain, wine, and oil to the church; the remainder you ought to distribute among the blind, the lame, the weak, lepers, orphans, widows, travelers, and strangers. Do the same with all your livestock and all your produce.

Whenever you make new bread from your harvest, bring the first portion to the church for a blessing. You may keep the remainder for yourself and your household. Do the same with grapes and with all your labor.

4. When standing in church, do not make a disturbance, but listen attentively to the divine readings. Whoever makes a commotion in church with idle words, loud laughter, or inappropriate wandering will give an account both for himself and for others on the day of judgment, because he neither hears the Word of God himself nor permits others to hear it.

When you come to church, do not quarrel. Do not utter, hear, or judge frivolous cases; do not engage in strife or joking, or relate other people’s stories. For those who do such things cause their prayers to vanish without fruit. Indeed, they come to church with a small number of sins and leave the church with many sins. To them the Prophet’s saying and warning applies very well: “Humanity has become like vanity; its days pass like a shadow” (Ps. CXLIII, 4).

5. Judges who hear cases should judge justly and should not accept gifts against the innocent, lest, while acquiring money, they lose their souls. No one has unjust profit without just loss: where there is profit, there is also loss—profit in the chest, but loss in the soul.

Tell me: where are the kings, where are the rulers, where are the rich? Where is their gold and their ornamentation? Everything has passed away like a shadow. Their gold, silver, and ornaments remained in the world, while they are tormented without end in hell, where their worms will not die and their fire will not be extinguished, because it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI, 7).

There they will have a dark life and an obscure dwelling forever: the wretched with the wretched, the proud with the proud, murderers with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, the wicked with the wicked, the false with the false, sacrilegious people with sacrilegious people. All will be tortured together in hell without end.

6. Believe me firmly, brothers: no one has a worse sin than the person who blasphemes and abandons God and worships idols. Nor can there be a worse corruption among the people than offering sacrifice to demons and abandoning the Catholic Church; nor than despairing of the Lord’s mercy and not believing in the resurrection.

Those who consult augurs, fortune-tellers, haruspices, diviners, or enchanters; those who trust in phylacteries and magical characters, sneezes, singing birds, divinations, astrologers, or any other evil arts—all will be condemned.

7. All these unhappy and wretched people who lead dances before the very basilicas of the saints and on the festivals of those same saints, and utter lascivious or shameful songs with their tongues. Thus, from the very place where they ought to have praised God and earned merit, they acquire condemnation for themselves; and, although they come to the church as Christians, they nevertheless return from the church as pagans.

8. Let no woman procure an abortion by means of a potion, or kill a fetus that has been conceived. The woman who commits this wickedness will be answerable for as many murders as children she could have borne, and will have to give an account on the day of judgment. Whoever is found guilty of such evils has lost the merit of baptism before God and his angels.

9. We testify to you before Christ our Lord that whoever has done evil, unless he has performed true penance, given proper alms, and unless death finds him engaged in good works, will never possess eternal life, but will descend with the devil into hell; for narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life (Matthew 7:14). Therefore one ought to abstain from every vice and evil not only because of fear of judgment, but because of love of God and the joys of eternal life, and at every hour to place one’s hope in God.

10. When a serpent comes to drink water, before drinking it first spits out its venom outside the spring, and afterward drinks. So too, when we approach the Lord’s altar to receive Communion, let us lay aside the most evil venom: anger, hatred, envy, falsehood, wickedness, greed, covetousness, pride, sacrilege, theft, sexual immorality, false testimony, discord, and perjury. These are the poisons of souls. Let us first drive them away from us, and so let us be satisfied at the Lord’s altar with his body and blood. Let us cleanse our hearts and bodies from every evil vice, so that with a chaste body, a pure heart, and a secure conscience we may be able to approach the Lord’s altar. Also throughout all the festivals, with the Lord’s help, preserve chastity, so that our solemnities may find us chaste and just.

11. We ask the Lord to send you a heavenly medicine, that is, chastity, charity, joy, patience, steadfastness, faith, gentleness, self-control, and mercy. And let us, dearest brothers, not cease to do good, to fast, to perform penance, to give alms, to clothe the naked, to visit the sick, to welcome strangers, to feed the poor, to serve God’s churches, to preserve the holy Scriptures, to love God’s servants, to place our hope in God at every hour, not to carry anger through to action, not to prolong the time of wrath, not to offer a false peace, not to abandon charity, and not to swear at all, lest we perhaps commit perjury. Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them likewise. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved (Matthew 10:22).

12. But you, dearest brothers, we admonish with fatherly love so that you may consider your danger. If you listen to us willingly, you will obtain eternal life for yourselves and lasting joy for us in the kingdom of heaven, to which may we deserve happily to attain, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. On Holy Lent IX

This sermon was long ago numbered among the Ambrosian sermons, since it was cited under Ambrose’s name by Gratian and Peter Lombard. On the authority of these men, as well as of the Vatican and Milanese manuscripts, it seems readily apparent that the revisers of the Decree attributed it to the holy Doctor. Yet we cannot help being astonished that the most learned Cardinal Bona, in *De rebus liturgicis*, book I, chapter 14, no. 5, regarded it as Ambrosian. For even the single fact that it teaches that one must necessarily fast each day throughout Lent except Sunday provided Possevin, in the *Apparatus*, with good reason for doubting this. If you add to this the fact that it permits one to take lunch at the ninth hour, and compare these matters with Sermon 8 on Psalm 118, no. 48, you will immediately discover how entirely non-Ambrosian it is. Moreover, we have corrected the alterations made in it by the Roman editors who first sent it to press, using a manuscript from the Vallicelliana Library.

### 1.

“Behold, now is the acceptable time,” in which you ought to confess your sins to God and to the priest, and to wipe them away through fasts, prayers, tears, and almsgiving (*On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter “Ecce”). [Note: In the Vallicelliana Library manuscript and in Gratian, these are the first words of this sermon; but the Roman edition prefixed, without witness or authority, the opening: “Behold, now is the acceptable time.”] Why, then, is the sinner ashamed to reveal his sins, which are known and manifest both to God and to all the angels and to all the elect souls? Confession frees the soul from death; confession opens paradise; confession grants hope of salvation. Therefore Scripture says: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26). These words show that the person who does not wish to confess his sins during his life does not deserve to be justified. Yet that confession does not free a person which is not made with penance. True penance is sorrow of heart and bitterness of soul for the evils each person has committed (*On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter “Poenitentia”). Penance is also to mourn past evils and not to commit again what must be mourned.

### 2.

Although all the days during which people live are suitable for penance, these days are nevertheless more suitable and appropriate for confessing, fasting, and giving alms, because during these days you can wipe away the sins of the entire year. Therefore I warn everyone and exhort each individual to correct whatever you recognize in yourselves to be blameworthy. Whoever recognizes in himself what is unbecoming to a faithful person should correct it: whatever he has done inadequately, if he has not faithfully paid his tithes. [Note: Roman edition: “who has not faithfully paid his tithes should now correct what he has done inadequately. What does it mean,” etc.]

What does it mean to give tithes faithfully except that one should never offer God either less or worse of one’s grain, wine, or the fruits of trees; of one’s livestock, garden, business, or even one’s hunting? For from every possession that God gives to a human being, he has reserved a tenth part for himself; and therefore a person may not retain what God has reserved for himself. He gave you nine parts but reserved the tenth for himself; and if you do not give God the tenth part, God will take the nine parts from you.

Likewise, if someone recognizes in himself that he has unjustly taken something from another, let him correct it by returning what he unjustly took. For the person who does not wish to return to God the tithes he has withheld, and does not take care to return to another what he unjustly took from him, does not yet fear God and does not know what true penance and true confession are (*16, q. 2, chapter “Nam qui Deo”*).

### 3.

Such a person cannot give good alms. Therefore, brothers, it is good that you return to God what belongs to him and to your neighbor what belonged to him, so that by giving alms from your just labors you may redeem your sins, according to what is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Daniel 4:24). [Note: The same edition reads: “It is written: Redeem your sins by almsgiving. And you ought further to know.”]

You ought to do this because each person must give to the needy according to what he possesses: that is, the one who has much must give much, and the one who has little must give little, as the holy Tobias taught his son to do (Tobit 4:7). [Note: Roman edition: “let him not fear to give alms according to his little means, according to,” etc.] Christians ought also to give alms with great zeal and immense eagerness, so that on the day of judgment they may deserve to hear from the Lord:

“I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me. Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25:35).

But if you do not perform these works of mercy that I have just mentioned, you will hear on the day of judgment: “Go into the eternal fire” (ibid., 41). [Note: Roman edition: “If through this declaration [you perform the works of mercy] … eternal [fire], which is prepared for the devil and his angels: Now because … I do not dare to be silent, so that I may reveal your danger … which threatens you unless you amend your life, what kind,” etc.]

### 4.

Since these are such days, I cannot refrain from speaking of the danger and great evil that exists among this people. If you do these things, he will say to you: “Come, blessed of my Father.” What kind of Christian is someone who does not fast at such a time, at least until the ninth hour? Behold, the Ninevites made even their little children at the breast, as well as their cattle and beasts of burden, fast so that they might escape the danger of death.

What kind of Christians, then, can those be who are healthy and yet are unwilling to fast with Moses, Elijah, and our Savior? They are accustomed to say: “We cannot work and fast.” But they cannot because they do not wish to. Let them at least work less, so that they may be able to fast. Therefore I warn and charge you before the Lord: let none of you, unless perhaps he is sick or an infant, eat or drink before the ninth hour until Easter, except on Sundays.

### 5.

I also advise that whoever lives near the church and can attend should hear Mass every day; [Note: The same edition adds: “and can do so without grave hindrance.”] and whoever can should come every night to the office of Matins. Those who live far from the church should strive to come to Matins every Sunday: that is, men and women, young and old, except the sick. Nevertheless, one or two should remain behind to guard the house.

### 6.

Let no one at all have relations with his wife before the octave of Easter. Whoever harbors anger or hatred against another should forgive him from his whole heart, if he desires to be saved. And except for those to whom the priest gives the counsel not to communicate, all Christians ought every Sunday to offer and receive Communion.

During Lent, however, I advise that you offer and communicate every day, or at least, as I said, every Sunday. Therefore lead a pure and clean life, so that you may be worthy to approach holy Communion. And you should know this: whatever you take away from the body by fasting, you ought to give entirely to the poor and not reserve it for yourselves.

### 7.

May almighty God grant that you retain these things that have been said and fulfill them in action, so that after the end of this life and after the completion of your labor you may reach eternal rest—through him who created you and wished to redeem you at the price of his blood, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. On Holy Lent X

This sermon belongs to the number of those first published by the Roman edition. It prefixed to it the title: “On the Proper Way to Perform Penance.” But no one, even from a first reading, can fail to see how undeservedly it assigned Ambrose’s name to it. We also find this attribution suspicious because, at the very outset, the Ninevites are mentioned, although in the whole remainder of the sermon nothing is said either about them or about their penance. The assertion that whoever omitted even a single day of fasting violated the whole of Lent is also found in Sermon 22; and what is discussed here on the occasion of winter changing into better weather seems likewise to have some affinity with that sermon. Hence one might perhaps conjecture that these sermons had one and the same author.

### 1.

It has now been read in the Gospel: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah” (Matthew 12:41). The Pharisees pretended to repent; therefore Christ the Lord calls them “an evil and adulterous generation” (ibid., 39), and elsewhere “a brood of vipers” (Matthew 3:7). They did not truly repent, and therefore they are rightly condemned.

### 2.

So too you, Christian, whom I know to be proud, claim that you repent, yet seek the works of the devil and neglect the Lord’s commandments. I desire to know what you repent of; I do not know what your repentance is. You claim to repent, though, clothed in the injustice with which you are girded, you have put pride on over it? You claim to repent, though you pursue another person’s flesh? You weary yourself in this way: you have returned like a dog to its vomit, or like a pig overcome by heat, wallowing in the mud of the earth.

I do not find what your repentance is. I have gone around and traversed the place of repentance, and I have not found your repentance. You who had destroyed the world are found in it again; you who had laid aside the pride of the flesh once more lower your shoulder, so that you may carry a heavier burden; you who had turned your back on greed meet it again face-to-face; you who had repudiated vanity return again to seek its favor; you who had fled the pageantry of the world have fallen again into its hands.

You walk puffed up, without a neck. Do you not know what is written: “What did our pride profit us, and what did riches with boastfulness bring us?” (Wisdom 5:8). And it continues: “All those things passed away like a shadow” (ibid., 9).

You had found yourself faithful and clean, having been renewed through the water of baptism, as it is written: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove your wickednesses from your souls” (Isaiah 1:16). The prophet urges them to wash; but although you were clean, you became filthy and cannot be washed again.

### 3.

But if you wish to be cleansed again, give alms, “and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Almsgiving is good for those who must be cleansed; it purges all filth. Humble yourself in everything, and you will find grace before God: “Submit yourself to God and entreat the Lord” (Ecclesiasticus 3:20); and: “Do not envy in order to act wickedly, for those who act wickedly will be destroyed” (Psalm 36:7).

Pray to the Lord every day with tears, if perhaps your sins may be loosed; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5).

Remember the son who was living far away, who by living dissolutely squandered his substance with prostitutes. Later, having been humbled and having come to his senses, he said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread, while I am perishing here from hunger? I will rise and go to my father and say: Make me like one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:17).

When he approached his father and threw himself down before him, he was joyfully received by him; indeed, the father killed the fattened calf for him.

### 4.

Remember, then, that Christ was also killed for you; he who was formerly the fattened calf. But because his other son was saddened that Christ had been killed—Christ who had formerly been the fattened calf—the father replied, saying: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But you ought to rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (ibid., 31–32).

O how blessed the people for whom Christ is killed! What joy the Father bears when what was dead comes to life and what was lost is found! To such a person it is then said, as it is written: “Behold, you have become well; now do not sin, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

### 5.

Therefore consider from where you have fallen, and weep; perform penance. Otherwise the Lord will come to you quickly and move your lampstand from its place.

Remember, son, that Christ left the ninety-nine righteous and sought the sinful human being; when he found him in a trackless place, he carried him back on his shoulders (Luke 15:4). Or remember that woman (Luke 15:8), that is, the Church, who had lost the drachma—that is, the sinful human being. She lit a lamp—that is, Christ, who is the light of righteousness—and, having found the coin in the dust, called the friends and neighbors of the Church to rejoice with her over the sinful person who had been found; and having raised him from the dung, she placed him among the leaders of his people, that is, among the apostles and prophets.

Behold what penance does for a sinful person: while he lies in dung, he is raised up among princes (Psalm 112:7).

### 6.

I call a person penitent who mourns what he had sinned and asks the Lord not to do again what he had committed. I call a person penitent who groans day and night and says with the Prophet: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will water my couch” (Psalm 6:7).

I call a person penitent who rejects what he had done badly and asks the Lord to obtain pardon. I call a person penitent who does not follow after his desire and deprives himself of his pleasures. I call a person penitent who loves what he previously neglected and abandons the evil he had done.

Therefore let the things that are good cling to you, and let the things that are evil be erased.

### 7.

If you do not perform penance, you will fall into the hands of the Lord according to the severity of his judgment, which we must avoid; for the Apostle says: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

Turn away, then, from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it, as it is written (Psalm 33:15). Say, therefore: “I have committed evil, and I have restored good.” Also produce worthy fruits of penance, and do not say: “I have sinned; what sad thing has happened to me?” [lacuna] “and do not add sin upon sin” (Ecclesiasticus 5:4). And do not say: “The mercy of God is great” (ibid., 8), for you should know that mercy and wrath belong to him.

Return, therefore, to the Lord and weep. Say: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm 50:6); and: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances, Lord” (Psalm 24:7); and: “Do not turn your face from me, nor in anger withdraw from your servant” (Psalm 26:9).

Behold the repentance of a person who humbles himself. How could the one who groans over such things not receive pardon? Who could hear him and not be moved? For “whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11). For it is written: “Why do you boast in evil, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Psalm 51:3).

### 8.

You promised to repent, and yet you still perform the works of the flesh? Do you not know that it is written: “It is much better not to make a vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiasticus 5:4)?

Sin does not cease to rule you, and you say that you repent and pray. Do you not know what is written? “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous deeds and take my covenant upon your lips?” (Psalm 49:16).

Behold what a threat of the Lord this is against every sinner. What do you say, you who claim to be penitent? Where is your repentance? It has been driven out by the heat of pride: while you strive to follow the desires of the flesh, you neglect the Lord.

Listen, then, son; withdraw your foot from the world, to which you renounced yourself long ago, so that henceforth you may be found faithful. What do you seek from the world, to which you have already renounced yourself? Repent, then, of the entire pageantry of iniquity. Take hold of the faith that you previously stained, because you had consented to the devil of darkness and had left the Lord, who is light, behind your back.

### 9.

Remember, son, that it is written: “What does this mean: I desire mercy and not sacrifice?” (Hosea 6:6). The Lord will have mercy on you if, after reading all these things, you do them, so that through your obedience and humility you may obtain grace; if you perform penance with your whole heart; if you keep the Lord before your eyes; if, having poured out the abyss of the cup of poison, you receive the cup of salvation; if day and night you meditate on the law of the Lord; if you cast all your care upon him.

Then you will rejoice and exult in the Lord, because you have conquered the evil one. Then your reward will be in heaven, because you have labored in this way. Then the Lord will be your helper on the day of judgment. Then you will stand with great confidence; then you will stand at the right hand of God with his saints, and it will be said to you:

“Come, blessed of my Father; receive the eternal kingdom” (Matthew 25:34), which my heavenly Father has prepared for you.

But to the unjust and sinners it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire” (ibid., 41), which your Father prepared for the devil.

Then the wicked will go into eternal fire, but the just into eternal life (ibid., 46). May our Lord Jesus Christ lead us to that life, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. On the Lord’s Fast in the Desert; On Lent XI

From the reading of this sermon we learn both that it was delivered during Lent and that its author frequently ascended the sacred pulpit. Since the subject of the sermon that he delivered on the preceding Sunday is found treated in Sermon 30 above among the rejected sermons, it is credible that the same sermon is indicated here, and therefore that both are by Maximus. Add that the same saint often uses beginnings similar to this one, and that in Homily 2 on this very Gospel he treats several matters that harmonize well with our sermon. It is also highly probable that, after delivering this sermon on Christ’s first temptation, the author added others on the second and third; the sermon on the third no longer survives, while that on the second is the very one presented above as Sermon 22. But here we retain the order of the ancient editions and manuscripts.

### 1.

Your Charity ought to remember that I preached this on the preceding Sunday and explained why the Lord fasted for forty days, or why he spent the very fast in the desert. For we said that he observed all these things not for his own justification—since he was a virgin in every respect—but for the sake of our salvation, so that those whose race had sinned through intemperance might be healed through abstinence.

### 2.

Let us see, then, what happened at that time and in that solitude. For the evangelist says that the devil was present there and that the Savior was tempted by his cunning. The sacred reading says that the Lord was hungry and that the devil said to him: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (Luke 4:3).

Observe the Lord’s strategy, by which he circumvents his adversary through deception. After many fasts he pretends to be hungry, so that he may provoke the devil by hunger once again, although he had already conquered him by fasting. He thus gives him, in a certain sense, hope of engaging in combat on the basis of weakness, so that when the devil attacks one who seems feeble, he may be gloriously defeated.

For this is the true victory: that the one who had overthrown Adam, immortal, glorious, and feasting, should now be defeated by a mortal, humble, and hungry man. When the devil sees the Lord hungry, he thinks him a human being and doubts that he is the Savior; therefore he says: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”

O miserable and final encounter of Satan! In the desert the devil does not find his customary weapons of temptation [Note: All editions read “the solid weapons of temptation”; the manuscripts more correctly read “the customary weapons of temptation”]. The pleasant trees of paradise are absent; Eve, his counselor, is absent; the attractive deception of the fruit is absent. And because he finds no food to offer the hungry man, he asks that stones be changed into food.

### 3.

Shut out on every side and deprived of every resource, he turns to the pavement. He plainly shows that the desert’s wasteland has resisted him, since he thinks that, because of the lack of things, even the elements can be transformed. Therefore he asks that stones be changed into bread.

Cunning and clever, he knows what he is asking; he knows that the deed he names has been done. For he remembers that in the Old Testament water flowed from a stone for those who were thirsty (Exodus 17:6). Here too he wants food to be provided from a stone for the hungry man. He recalls there the hardness of the rock dissolved into the liquid of springs; here too he desires the roughness of stone to be transformed into the sweetness of bread.

For he suspected that this was the Christ who was accustomed to perform such works from the nature of stones, as the Apostle Paul says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

I say that he suspected him to be the Christ when he asked him to make loaves from a stone; but when he saw him hungry, he thought him merely a human being.

### 4.

The Savior condemns his cunning with a marvelous answer. He does not do what the devil says, lest he appear to display the glory of his power at the adversary’s discretion. Yet he does not answer that it cannot be done, because he could not deny what he had often already done.

Thus he neither complies with the petitioner nor denies the tester; and by this means he both reserves the power of his might to his own will and refutes the adversary’s cunning with divine speech.

He therefore answered him: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4:4). That is: not by earthly bread, not by material food, with which you deceived Adam, the first human being, but by the word of God, in which are the nourishment of heavenly life.

The Word of God, however, is the Lord Christ, as the evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). Therefore whoever is nourished by Christ’s word does not seek earthly nourishment; for one who is refreshed by the Savior’s bread cannot desire the bread of the world.

The Lord has his own bread; indeed, the Savior himself is the bread, as he taught when he said: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). Of this bread the Prophet says: “And bread strengthens the human heart” (Psalm 103:15).

### 5.

Why, then, should I want the bread offered by the devil when I have the bread that Christ distributes? Why should I want the food because of which I remember that the first-formed man was cast down, that Esau was deprived of his birthright, and that Judas Iscariot was marked by the crime of betrayal?

Adam lost paradise through food; Esau lost the honor of primogeniture through lentils; Judas surrendered the exalted dignity of apostleship through a morsel. For from the moment he took the morsel, he no longer began to be an apostle but a traitor.

For thus you have it written, the Lord saying: “The one to whom I shall give the dipped bread, he will betray me.” And immediately after the morsel Satan entered into him (John 13:26).

It is not good food after which the Lord is denied, after which the enemy enters; it is not good food after which Christ is rejected and the Antichrist is devoured. It is not good food that lacks blessing and is filled with a curse.

Therefore we need that food which bestows life and nourishes the soul, after which Christ follows and the enemy is shut out. We ought to receive that food which the Savior, not the devil, follows; which makes its recipient a confessor, not a traitor.

### 6.

How appropriately, during the time of fasting, the Word of God said that it is what refreshes, to show that our fasts ought not to be occupied with the activities of the world but exercised in the sacred writings! For the person who attends to the nourishment of reading neglects the hunger of the body; nor can the one who acquires the nourishment of the heavenly word be concerned with the belly.

This is the refreshment that fattens the soul and enriches the inward parts, when we receive from the divine Scriptures the food of everlasting speech. This is the food that grants eternal life and excludes from us the snares of diabolical temptation.

That the reading of the sacred writings is life, the Lord testifies when he says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:64).

## SERMON XXVIII. On Holy Lent XII

From the opening words of this sermon it can be inferred that its author was accustomed to preach during Lent not only on Sundays but also on other days. What is discussed here concerning the kind of weather in which that fast occurred, and concerning the violation of a single day, seems to have some kinship with several preceding sermons; but this is too little to establish that those sermons were written by the same author. Perhaps there is stronger reason for assigning this final sermon to Saint Maximus, since it was inscribed under his name in the Remigius manuscript and in two German manuscripts.

### 1.

A few days ago, while preaching devotion to holy Lent, we brought forward examples from the sacred writings to prove that this number of forty was not established by human beings but consecrated by God; that it was not devised by earthly thought but commanded by heavenly majesty. [Note: Three manuscripts read “initiated by thought”; one reads “entered upon by thought.”]

Therefore the person who passes beyond the appointed number by eating on a single day is not accused as a violator of one day, but reproved as a transgressor of the whole of Lent. Hence it is good for a person to fast for the day without difficulty and at the same time attain the holiness of the whole of Lent. [Note: The old edition reads “that he fast the said number without difficulty”; the Roman edition, “that he fast the said number for a day without difficulty”; all the manuscripts omit “the said number.”]

These are not so much the commands of priests as of God. Therefore whoever despises them does not despise a priest but Christ, who speaks through his priest.

### 2.

Let us see, then, at what time the Lord imposed this observance upon us, and whether he did not wish all the elements to derive benefit, as it were, through this devotion.

Behold: during the appointed Lent [Note: All editions here and below write the word as one, *indicta*; the manuscripts partly join and partly separate the same word], as the earth bound by winter’s frost is loosened and the streams of water recover their channels when the ice has melted, so at this same time the sins of our bodies, contracted through wickedness, are released, and the purer course of our life, once the devil’s rigor has melted, recognizes its former channel.

The earth, I say, during the appointed Lent lays aside the harshness of winter; I, during the appointed Lent, cast away the harshness of sins. That earth is split by plows so that it may be suitable for earthly crops; my earth is plowed by fasts so that it may be suitable for heavenly seeds.

For just as the person who more frequently exercises a field by troubling it receives a more abundant return, so the person who more often cultivates the field of his body by fasting receives greater grace.

### 3.

Behold: during the time of abstinence, the grass of the crops comes back to life for the harvest, the shoot of the tree strives toward becoming a branch, the vine-shoot grows toward the bud, and everything rises from lower things to higher ones.

So at this same time the hope of human beings, which had nearly died, revives for the future; [Note: Several manuscripts read “hope meanwhile dead”; some also read “hope inwardly dead.”] lost faith is restored to glory; temporal life advances toward eternal life; and the whole human race, rising toward heavenly things, ascends from the lowest to the higher. [Note: All editions, with two manuscripts, read “from the lower regions”; several manuscripts, “from lower things”; a larger number, “from the lowest.”]

Now the farmer, carrying iron, prunes the vine-shoots; so now the bishop, expounding the Gospel, cuts away the filth of the peoples. Throughout this forty-day course all creatures perform this work, so that, having laid aside what is superfluous, they may proceed to Easter adorned and arrayed.

### 4.

Now everything is in labor so that then it may be found in fruit. For then, contrary to nature’s usual order, the thorn produces a rose, the reed gives forth the fragrance of a lily, and dry shrubs emit sweetness. Thus everything is adorned with flowers, so that creation itself may be believed to celebrate the festival of the great day with its splendor.

Therefore, during this same time of fasting, let us also bring forth roses from our thorns: righteousness from sins, mercy from severity, generosity from greed.

For these are the thorns of our body, which choke the soul, about which Scripture says: “It will bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Genesis 3:18). My earth brings forth thorns if it pricks me with the stimulation of bodily lust; it produces thistles for me when it torments me with desire for worldly riches.

For a Christian, greed is the root of his thorns; for a good man, ambition for honor is a thorn. They seem outwardly pleasing among their own people, but they wound.

### 5.

Unless we keep watch and fast, we cannot be rid of these things; rather, through abstinence the very thorns will be turned into roses. For by fasting, lust produces chastity, pride produces humility, and drunkenness produces frugality [Note: Thus read the majority of the better manuscripts; some manuscripts and all editions instead read “sobriety produces frugality,” which gives an absurd sense].

These are the flowers of our life, which emit a sweet fragrance for Christ and breathe a good odor toward God. Hence the Apostle says: “For we are the good odor of Christ for God” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

The Lord has therefore granted us this Lent so that during this period, after the manner of all creation, we may now conceive the shoots of the virtues [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “now desire”; the Roman edition and others, “now conceive”], in order that on Easter Day we may bring forth the fruit of righteousness.

### 6.

The Lord Christ himself exercised himself in this number of forty, not so that he might make progress himself, but so that he might show us the progress of salvation. For there was no thorn of sin in him that could be turned into a flower. He himself was the flower born not from a thorn but from a branch, as the Prophet says: “A branch shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1).

For Mary was the branch—pure, delicate, and a virgin—and from the integrity of her body she caused Christ to sprout like a flower.

7. Thus, after forty days [Note: [Col. 0664D] All printed editions omit “and nights,” but it is absent from none of the handwritten manuscripts.] and nights had passed, the Lord did not undertake these fasts because he was hungry; yet the evangelist says that afterward he was hungry. How, then, can it be that one who had not felt hunger or thirst throughout so many days afterward became hungry? He was indeed hungry, and we cannot deny that he was hungry; but he hungered not for human food, but for salvation. He did not desire the banquets of worldly fare, but longed for the holiness of heavenly souls. For Christ’s food is the redemption of peoples; Christ’s food is the accomplishment of the Father’s will, as he himself says: “My food is to do the will of my Father, who sent me” (John 4:34). Therefore let us too hunger for food—not food prepared for earthly banquets, but food gathered through reading the divine Scriptures. The former nourishes the body for a time; the latter restores the soul forever.

# SERMON XXIX. On Holy Lent XIII

This sermon was delivered approximately in the middle of Lent, on the Gospel of the man born blind, which is now read on the Tuesday of the fourth week. This sermon was absent from the ancient editions; but there is absolutely no reason why it should have been attributed to Ambrose in the Roman edition.

1. Give thanks, brothers, to the divine mercy, which has brought you safely to the middle of Lent [Col. 0664C]. Those, however, can praise God more sweetly and devoutly for this gift who, just as they learned at the beginning of Lent, have newly endeavored to live up to this point—that is, those who have daily taken care to seek forgiveness for their sins by fasting, giving alms, and hastening to the church with tears and sighs to pray.

2. But those who have neglected these things—that is, who have not fasted daily, or have not given alms, or have not been diligent and contrite in prayer—have no reason to rejoice; rather, wretched as they are, they have reason to mourn. Yet let them not mourn in such a way as to despair, because he who was able to give sight to a man blind from birth (John 9:1) can also now make these lukewarm and negligent people diligent and fervent in his service, if they wish to turn to him with all their heart. Therefore, those who live in such a way—that is, those who live impurely, or retain hatred in their heart against someone, or unjustly seize what belongs to others, or retain their own possessions immoderately—should recognize their blindness and hasten to the physician to be enlightened.

3. Would that, when you sin, you sought spiritual medicine as earnestly as, when you fall ill in body, you seek bodily medicine [Col. 0665A]. Who among this great assembly, if he were threatened not with death but merely with the loss of his eyes, would not give everything he possessed in order to escape the danger? And if you fear the death of the flesh so greatly, why do you not fear the death of the soul—especially since the pain of bodily death lasts not even one hour, whereas the death of the soul, that is, its mourning and punishment, never comes to an end? And if you love the eyes of the body so greatly, though you quickly lose them by dying, why do you not love the spiritual eyes by which you may behold God and your Lord without end?

4. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, work—work while it is day, because, as Christ our Lord says: “The night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4). The day is the present life; the night is death [Col. 0665B] and the time after death. If after this life there is no opportunity for working, as the Truth says, why does each person not labor while he has the time—that is, while he lives in this world? Fear that death, brothers, of which the Savior says: “The night is coming, when no one can work.” All who do evil do not fear this death, and therefore, when they depart from this life, they find everlasting death. Labor while you live, but especially during these days: fast from rich foods, and at all times abstain from vices. Indeed, those who fast from food but do not abstain from evil are like the devil, who does not eat and yet does not cease from evil. Finally, know that what you withhold from yourselves by fasting you ought to send on to heaven through the poor.

[Col. 0665C] 5. Put the admonition of today’s sermon into practice, brothers, lest the curse of the Jews come upon you. For they said to the blind man: “You be his disciple” (ibid., 28). What does it mean to be Christ’s disciple except to be a disciple of piety, truth, and humility? They said this with a wish to curse; but great is the blessing which he himself grants you to attain—he who lives and reigns through ages of ages.

# SERMON XXX. On Holy Lent XIV

The Gospel from which the theme of this sermon is taken is now read on Passion Sunday. In the Ambrosian Missal, and perhaps also in the Gallican one, it was read on the Second Sunday of Lent, which was therefore customarily called Abraham Sunday [Col. 0665D]. This sermon was not found in the ancient editions; and although the editors of the Decree testify that it is found in the Vatican codices, even the lowliness of its diction alone abundantly proves that it was never written by Ambrose. Nor does it depart so far from the style of Caesarius, among whose sermons we also have one that agrees with this one in its opening words.

1. Know, brothers, that each person is called the son of the one whose works he does. Thus, when the Jews had said that Abraham was their father, they heard from the Lord—as is read immediately before the Gospel passage you have heard today: “If you are Abraham’s sons, do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39). When they again said that they had God as their Father, they heard: “If God were your Father, you would certainly love me” (ibid., 42).

2. These words demonstrate most clearly that the wicked and greedy are sons neither of Abraham nor of God. The following words reveal whose sons they are, for he says: “You are from your father the devil” (ibid., 44). It is as though he were saying: “Why do you change fathers, now Abraham, now God? I will show you who your father is: your father is the devil—not by creating you, but by deceiving you.” Flee such a father, brothers; flee him, as the prophet admonishes. For he says: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11). By “people” he means vices and sins; by “the Father’s house” he means the world in which the devil reigns. He forgets his people who abandons his vices; and he forgets his father’s house who despises the false riches of this world, through which the devil holds him captive. It is clear that the devil does not love his children but hates them, because he loves only in order to destroy—just as a glutton loves a pig in order to eat it.

3. Beware, brothers, of lying (XXII, q. 55, c. *Cavete*), because all who love lies are sons of the devil, who is not only a liar but also the father and inventor of lying itself. Every pretense and every duplicity is lying; therefore lying is demonstrated not only in false words but also in feigned actions. It is a lie to call oneself a Christian and not do Christ’s works; it is a lie to profess oneself a priest or cleric and act contrary to that order. These things must be feared, because they are God’s words. The prophet says: [Col. 0666C] “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7). Therefore, brothers, pass from lying to truth, if you do not wish to have the devil as your father. For what is read elsewhere—“Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11)—must be understood as referring to the human insofar as he is human, insofar as he is carnal, not insofar as he is spiritual.

4. Finally, the Gospel reading admonishes you to be patient. Behold, although the Lord had heard many insults from the Jews, he patiently endured them; he bore them patiently and put up with them patiently. And if the Lord showed patience amid words of blasphemy—he who could have plunged his enemies into the abyss with a single word—why do wretched human beings, full of sins, not show patience when they hear harsh words or are corrected for their iniquities?

[Col. 0666D] 5. See to it, brothers, that by evil works or thoughts you do not stone Jesus; that you do not stone the Savior together with the unbelieving Jews, of whom it is said today: “Then the Jews took up stones to throw at him” (John 8:59). Perhaps you say: “The Jews did wrong when they wished to stone him and when they crucified him.” Know and firmly believe that Christians who live wickedly do this today, because they persecute Christ through their vices. For what is Jesus except truth, peace, and justice? Therefore, whoever abandons truth for falsehood, breaks charity for greed, hates peace, or conceals justice for some reward seems to be doing nothing other than stoning, crucifying, and killing Christ, because he extinguishes his gifts within himself.

[Col. 0667A] 6. Oh, how few there are in so great a multitude of Christians who do not persecute, stone, and kill Jesus! But woe to them, because Jesus conceals knowledge of himself from such people, departs from the temple of their hearts, reveals himself to those who love him, and dwells in them, as he promises below to the one who loves him, saying: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

7. Because we do not wish, brothers, to burden you by saying much, we ask that you not belong to the number of those who wished to stone Jesus; but rather share the portion of those who, loving him above all things, have received his grace in their hearts. May he himself grant this to you—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXI. On Holy Lent XV

[Col. 0667B]

In this sermon, which was first published in the Roman edition, the supplication customarily performed on Palm Sunday is described. Although investigators of ecclesiastical rites observe that it is mentioned by Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* 10), they nowhere find that it was so ancient in the Latin Church. Whatever may be the case concerning this ceremony, it is clear that this little sermon contains nothing that could reasonably establish it as Ambrose’s.

1. When our Lord Jesus Christ came to the city of Jerusalem six days before his Passion, the large crowd that had gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover according to Moses’ command took palm branches and went out to meet him, so that in the psalms they might display Christ’s victory among the people of Israel as though he were an earthly king; for it is customary to offer a palm to victors. Others in the same crowd were cutting branches from the trees (Matthew 21:8 and following), especially olive trees, because the events were taking place on the Mount of Olives. They carried them so that, wherever it was appropriate, they might spread a smooth path before the Lord as he came. From this arose the custom of today’s festival: as we sing psalms, we carry palm or olive branches in our hands, and we call the festival the festival of palms or olives.

2. Yet the branches of these trees are carried with no small sacramental significance. The olive, because it produces oil as a comfort for pains and labors—since wounds are treated with oil and heat is relieved—signifies works of mercy. Indeed, mercy itself is called in Greek *ἔλεος* (*eleos*). The root of the palm, however, is rough, but it has the greatest splendor at its end, showing that through the harshness of this life we must be raised to the beauty of our heavenly homeland. Hence the prophet and psalmist David sings of the righteous man: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree” (Psalm 91:13). Let us therefore carry olive branches in our hands, displaying the virtue of mercy in our actions. Let us also take palm branches, so that, in exchange for the good of mercy, we may await not earthly delights but the beauty of our heavenly homeland, to which Christ our Lord has gone before us. He is, according to the Apostle, “the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4).

[Col. 0668A] 3. We must not pass over the verse of the psalm that the crowd going out to meet the Lord sang: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest” (Psalm 117:26). The Lord’s coming and his incarnation were not only salvation for human beings on earth but also for the angels in heaven, because while human beings are saved on earth, the number of angels that had been diminished when the devil fell is restored in heaven. “Hosanna in the highest,” therefore, means the same as if one said: “Save us, you who are also salvation in the heavens.” And those who had asked for this salvation with great devotion doubled their cry, saying again: “Hosanna in the highest.”

4. May blessed Christ our Lord grant you to attain this salvation. He came in the name of God the Father, with whom God lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON XXXII. On Holy Lent XVI

This sermon, too, owes its publication to the Roman edition. Yet scarcely any other could have been attributed to our Ambrose with less justification, since it has nothing Ambrosian about it. Indeed, it does not even appear to be by the same author as the preceding sermon, since there the six days from Palm Sunday to the Passion are counted, whereas here only five are counted.

1. I see, brothers, that you have come together today to the church more attentively than usual and have brought branches of trees with joy. [434] But what benefit is there in doing this for those who do not know why they are doing it or what these things signify? [Col. 0668C] You ought to know that, as was read today—the fifth day before the Passion—our Savior sat on the Mount of Olives upon a donkey in order to enter Jerusalem (Matthew 21:7). When the crowd heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, they went out to meet him with palm branches. And when he was already approaching the descent of the Mount of Olives, the crowds coming down began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice.

2. Throughout these five days—from this day until the evening of Thursday, when he was betrayed after the supper—he taught every day in the temple and remained every night on the Mount of Olives. Since the lamb that was to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the month was shut up on the tenth day, this true Lamb, Christ the Lord, who was to be crucified on Friday, rightly entered Jerusalem on the day when that symbolic lamb was shut up.

3. Today the crowds spread their garments on the road (ibid., 8); and others, cutting branches from the trees, likewise spread them along the road of the Savior seated upon the donkey. Holy Mother Church celebrates this bodily so that something much greater may take place spiritually. Every holy soul is God’s donkey. Therefore the Lord sits upon a donkey and makes his way toward Jerusalem when, dwelling in our souls, he makes us despise this world and love our heavenly homeland. You throw garments onto the road before God if, by preparing a way for him to come to you, you discipline your bodies through abstinence. You cut branches from the trees if, by loving the virtues of the holy fathers, you prepare a way for the Lord to come to you. What was Abraham? What was Joseph? What was David? What were the other righteous men, if not fruitful trees of God’s Church? Learn obedience from Abraham, chastity from Joseph, and humility from David, if you desire to attain everlasting salvation.

4. And because the palm signifies victory, we rightly carry palms in our hands if we sing praises of victory to him in such a way that we also strive to conquer the devil by living well. Therefore, brothers, you must know that the person carries an olive branch without purpose whom the devil overcomes by deceiving him. Return, then, most beloved, to your consciences and see whether you are doing spiritually what you are doing bodily.

[Col. 0669B] 5. Finally, believing most firmly, understand that our danger lies in failing to announce the mysteries of our Savior to you, while your danger lies in treating them lightly. We therefore admonish you: the closer the Paschal solemnity approaches, the more carefully prepare yourselves by cleansing yourselves from all envy, hatred, insult, cursing, and detraction, so that you may be able to celebrate that day worthily.

6. Forgive those who have sinned against you, so that the Lord may forgive you your sins. Whoever has maintained hatred or anger against even one person will celebrate Easter to his own harm, because he will not eat life with Peter but will receive death with Judas in holy communion. May he avert this from you—he who created you by his power and redeemed you by his mercy, Jesus Christ [Col. 0669C] our Lord, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages. Amen.

# SERMON XXXIII. On the Fasts of Lent XVII

This sermon was delivered on the day when the Creed was customarily handed over to the catechumens, a practice which, as we have noted elsewhere, was customary in many churches on Palm Sunday. Since the sixth of the sermons omitted here begins with the words “With the divine favor,” and is attributed to Caesarius in the *Appendix to Augustine*, someone might perhaps infer from this that the same person was also the author of this sermon. Yet it is no less probable that it belongs to Saint Maximus, whose style it displays and whose name is also supplied by the Remigius manuscript.

1. With the divine favor, behold, we have now almost completed the prescribed fasts of Lent [Col. 0669D] and fulfilled the commands of Christ the Lord through devotion to abstinence.
