It remains now that, just as his servants Moses (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8) earned grace by observing this most sacred number, so we too may merit it by keeping this same period; and that those whose labor in observing the fast is alike may receive a similar reward in the attainment of recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] The Roman edition alone reads: “his servant Elijah … earned grace.”]

[435] 2. When the heavens were closed because of human iniquities, and no abundance of rain fell from above upon worldly affairs, while everything languished under the squalor of prolonged drought, and there was a great famine for the entire human race—for since heaven gave no rain, the earth produced no nourishment—then holy Elijah unlocked heaven by his fasts and made the earth fruitful by his prayers. He changed its drought into rain and dissolved its barrenness into fertility. So great was the abundance of rain that his prayers poured over the earth that dry things grew green again, dead things rose, and the weak were healed. Thus a kind of passageway of springs was infused into all things, so that, once purification had been accomplished through the rain, the faults of all creation were washed away [Note: [Col. 0669D] All editions read: “all the faults of creatures”; the Lyon and Valliscluse manuscripts read “the faults of all,” and so forth.] and, through the benefit of that flood, the appearance of the whole world rose renewed.

[Col. 0670B] 3. Therefore, let us too, observing the same fasts as Elijah, and adding prayers, unlock the closed heaven for our catechumens, so that the rain of saving purification may enlighten them [Note: [Col. 0670D] The Valliscluse manuscript reads: “may cleanse them with rain.”]. Heaven is closed to them as long as the Holy Spirit has not yet come from heaven to give life to their hearts. They suffer, in a manner of speaking, drought because they have not yet been watered by the grace of baptism. They also suffer great hunger, since, like hungry people, they long for the heavenly mysteries. Let us therefore unlock heaven for them, so that, when the spiritual rain comes from above, their earth may be filled with the water of the font, and, once the barrenness of sins has been removed, they may begin to produce the fruits of virtue. For the heavenly rain washes away the vices of sins, produces an increase of righteousness, shakes off the dry dust of desire, gladdens the useful purity of chastity, overwhelms the filthy dregs of greed, and nourishes the everlasting generosity of mercy. Just as, when Elijah’s rain came, the earth produced every kind of nourishment, so, when Christ’s washing comes, the soul produces every kind of righteousness. And just as there the springs of rain watered the earth so that the already dead seeds of plants might be made alive, so the spring of baptism waters the human race so that it may give life to hearts of souls that have been rendered dead. The merit, then, of those who observe these fasts is that through their prayers the world may either be renewed or their brothers may be born again.

4. Heaven must therefore be opened for our catechumens, since it is still closed to them. Heaven is closed to them because they do not yet see through the mystery of the Trinity. With heaven closed to them, they do not know what is taking place above heaven; nor can they know what the substance of the Son and the Father is unless they first transcend the elements of the world. A person will then be able to behold the divine mysteries of the Trinity when, by his own power, he has had the heavens opened, just as blessed Stephen the martyr opened the heavens for himself through his martyrdom and saw the Savior standing at the right hand of the Father, according to his own words: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55). Therefore, for the one whose heavens are closed, action must be taken so that they may be opened, enabling him to behold Christ above the heavens; for as long as they are closed to a human being, he cannot see Christ reigning.

5. We must inquire, then, how the closed heavens are to be opened. I think they cannot be opened in any other way unless we take up the keys of the apostle Peter, which he received by the Lord’s gift, as the Lord himself said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18). Indeed, let us ask Peter himself, so that, like a good doorkeeper, he may open the gate of the heavenly palace for us. Let us investigate more carefully what this key is. I would say that Peter’s key is Peter’s faith, through which he opened the heavens, entered the depths fearlessly, and trod upon the seas without dread. So great is the power of apostolic faith that all the elements are open to it—that is, the angelic gates are not closed to it, the gates of Tartarus do not prevail against it, and the streams of the waters do not subside before it.

[Col. 0671B] 6. Let us see, then, how this very key, which we call faith, is constituted and how it has been made firm. I think it was forged through the work of twelve craftsmen, for holy faith was conceived through the Creed of the twelve apostles. They came together like skilled craftsmen and forged the key by their counsel. I would call the Creed itself a kind of key, through which the darkness of the devil is unlocked so that the light of Christ may enter; the sins closed within consciences are opened so that manifest works of righteousness may shine forth. Therefore this key must be shown to our brothers, so that they too, as Peter’s disciples, may become accustomed to unlocking the depths for themselves and opening the heavens.

# SERMON XXXIV. On the Sunday of the Resurrection

[Col. 0671C] Since this sermon was absent from the ancient editions, the Roman edition was the first to publish it under this title. And indeed, it explains certain matters pertaining to the Gospel of this Sunday. But by presenting it under Ambrose’s name, it plainly acted contrary to the style and character of the holy Father.

1. You heard, brothers, that the holy women who came to the tomb with spices saw an angel. For it says: “And entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting at the right” (Mark 16:5). But lest there be any ambiguity concerning who this young man was, another Evangelist wrote: “For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and coming, rolled back the stone and sat upon it” (Matthew 28:2). Mary Magdalene, who loved Jesus more intensely, because she remained beside the tomb, was the first of all to see the Lord and announced him to the apostles. For the Evangelist John says: “Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord,’ and these things he said to me,” and so forth (John 20:18). Through this we are admonished to seek the Lord filled with spices—that is, with the fragrance of good works and virtues.

2. Yet there are some, beloved, who seem to seek the Lord; but because they are idle and strangers to virtue, they do not deserve to find him or to see him once found. After all, what were those holy women seeking in the tomb except the body of the Lord Jesus? And what are you seeking in the church except Jesus, that is, the Savior? But if you wish to find him, come at sunrise, as those women did—that is, let there be no darkness of vices in your hearts. Carnal desires and evil works are darkness. Those whose hearts contain such darkness do not see the light and do not understand Christ, because Christ is light. Therefore, brothers, drive darkness away from yourselves—that is, every pleasure and every evil work—and take care to possess spices, that is, pure prayer, saying with the psalmist: “Let my prayer be directed, O Lord, like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140:2).

3. Moreover, attend to what you heard: Mary Magdalene, because she persevered at the tomb, found the one whom she was seeking, since “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). Therefore, just as it is necessary for you to drive evil away, so it is altogether beneficial that you persevere most firmly in the good you have already begun, if you desire to see the Lord and reach your heavenly homeland.

4. Finally, because you are celebrating holy Easter, you ought to know, brothers, what Easter is. Easter is called a “passage”; this festival was given that name because on it the children of Israel passed out of Egypt, and the Son of God himself passed from this world to the Father. But what benefit is it to you to celebrate Easter if you do not imitate what you worship? That is, what benefit is it if you do not pass from Egypt—from the darkness of vices—to the light of virtues, and from love of this world to desire for the heavenly homeland? For there are many who rejoice in this festival and celebrate this solemnity, yet do so wickedly and to their own harm, because they have not passed from this world to the Father—that is, they do not pass from worldly desire and carnal pleasure to love of the heavenly homeland. Wretched Christians, who are in Egypt—that is, under the power of the devil—and rejoice in evil! Therefore I admonish you, brothers, to celebrate Easter properly, that is, to make the passage. All of you who are wicked and celebrate this festival, pass from vices to virtues; all of you who are good, pass from virtues to virtues; and let no one remain among you who does not make the passage.

5. And just as the Jews, when they celebrated Easter, ate unleavened bread for seven days, so every Christian who eats the flesh of the true Lamb, that is, of Christ, ought throughout the whole time of his life—which is measured by the cycle of seven days—to conduct himself simply and innocently. [Col. 0672D] See, brothers, see that the old leaven is not among you, as the Apostle admonishes, saying: “Purge out the old leaven” (1 Corinthians 5:7), that is, the conduct of the old person. Then you will be true Christians, if you have turned away from all evil, which is signified by the old leaven, and have faithfully kept what you promised in baptism. May he himself grant this to you, who lives and reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON XXXV. On the Mystery of Easter II

This sermon was published under the title of a little treatise in all the editions of Ambrose, although it is clear that it is a brief composition in which the author shows that the feast of Easter ought to be celebrated because human innocence and salvation have been restored [Col. 0673A]. That this author was someone other than Ambrose is made certain by the very diction.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. The mystery of Easter, for all believers reborn in Christ through faith, provides the renewed joy and glory of the annual blessedness of faith [Note: [Col. 0673D] So read the ancient editions and manuscripts, except that instead of *recidivatum* the Roman codex reads *residuatum*. But the Roman edition omitted *de fide* and printed *recidivum*.]. This sacred name derives from the Passion of the Lord himself, for Easter is the Passion of the Savior, as the blessed Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). For this purpose Christ took a human body and consecrated himself to the Passion through the mystery of Easter, so that whoever by faith had obtained participation in this gift might rightly be judged worthy of sharing in the Lord’s blessedness.

## CHAPTER TWO

2. Easter is truly the beginning of the year, the beginning of the first month, the renewal of young shoots, and, once the night of dark winter has been dispelled, the restoration of the delight of early spring. At this time, I say, God, the creator of visible and invisible things, suspending the structure of heaven on a hook fixed in the earth [Note: [Col. 0673D] The ancient edition reads *defixa humo*, “fixed in the earth”; two manuscripts read *defixo humo*, “with the hook fixed in the earth”; the Roman edition’s reading, as in the text, is better.], radiated with the sun’s heat, assigned the moon’s splendor as a consolation for the night, and adorned the hanging vault of heaven with the ornament of shining stars. Restricting the sea within the fixed boundaries of its shores, he commanded the surge of the hollow, roaring wave not to exceed the limits of its appointed boundary. And so that the level surface of the world might be withdrawn from the distant gaze of the eyes, wooded hills and lofty mountains were established as ornaments of the world’s structure, so that once again the beauty of the plains might bring greater delight to mortals.

## CHAPTER THREE

3. Humanity itself, formed through the condescension of the divine workmanship [Col. 0673C], was made lord of earthly creation for this purpose: that, obeying the divine ordinances, it might serve only the will of him who had appointed it lord over such great things from nothing. Yet at the very beginning (Genesis 3:6 and following), though not ignorant, it was corrupted by envy. While desiring, beyond God’s work bestowed upon it, to become what nature had not given, it lost the grace that the Creator’s mercy had attributed to it. Immediately, as a transgressor, it incurred the sentence of death through the desire arising from the devil’s deception and also transmitted it to the origin of the offspring that would come from it, so that the divine sentence might rightly be fulfilled here: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24). Thus, through the occasion of sin, the devil acquired dominion of death over all sinners and possessed all who had turned away from God, bound by the chain of sin and confined in the prison of grim Tartarus.

## CHAPTER FOUR

4. As divine judgment grieved over their destruction, God did not come through a prophetic servant or an invisible angel; rather, God came and dwelt among human beings through the substance of human flesh [Note: [Col. 0674D] The Roman edition alone reads: “but through the substance of human flesh assumed”]. He did this to give mortals an honorable pattern of life and to reveal eternal life in himself to temporal beings who believed, through the example of his death and resurrection. For just as unbelief and the worship of idols had closed the way to heaven, so the faithlessness of the transgressor had prepared the abyss of hell.

5. In their punishments the devil reigned through death until the coming of the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, when the substance of human flesh, joined to God, subjected an immaculate body to the condition of death. Christ, free from sin, descended to the depths of Tartarus; breaking the bars and gates of hell, destroying the dominion of death, he recalled to life the souls bound by sin from the jaws of the devil. Thus the divine triumph was inscribed in eternal characters, when he says: “Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

6. Recalling this happiness of restored salvation, Paul cries out: “Just as death entered this world through Adam, so salvation was restored to the world through Christ” (ibid., 22); and again: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly” (ibid., 47, 49). Adding, he says: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly”—that is, of the old person in sin—“so let us bear the image of the heavenly”—that is, let us preserve the salvation of the human being received, redeemed, restored, and purified in Christ. For the same Apostle says (ibid., 23): “Christ the beginning,” that is, the author of resurrection and life; “then those who belong to Christ,” that is, those who live in the form of his purity [438] and, secure in the hope of his resurrection, will possess with him the glory of the heavenly promise, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever follows me,” he says, “will not perish, but will pass from death to life” (John 5:24).

[Col. 0674C] 7. Thus the Passion of the Savior is the salvation of human life. For this reason he wished to die for us: so that we who believe in him might live forever. He wished to become for a time what we are, so that, having obtained the promise of his eternity, we might live forever with him.

## CHAPTER FIVE

8. This, I say, is the grace of the heavenly mysteries; this is the gift of Easter; this is the desirable festival of the year; these are the beginnings of things that bring forth life. From this comes the birth of infants from the sacred womb of the Church’s life-giving font [Note: [Col. 0674D] The Roman codex reads: “innocent ones, reborn in the simplicity of little children, bleating innocently,” and so forth.], reborn in the simplicity of little children, and their innocent consciences resound with bleating. From this chaste fathers and also modest mothers follow, through faith, an innumerable new offspring. From this, beneath the tree of faith, the adornment of candles shines forth from the womb of the innocent font. From this, they are sanctified by the gift of heavenly merit and nourished by the celebrated mystery of the spiritual sacrament. From this, the brotherhood nurtured in the bosom of the blessed Church, worshiping the substance of the one divinity and the name of the threefold power [Note: [Col. 0674D] The same codex reads: “and worshiping the threefold name of the power.”], celebrates with the prophet the psalm of the annual festival: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24).

9. What day, I ask? Surely that day which bestows the beginning of life, the dawn of light, the author of illumination—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who says of himself: “I am,” he says (John 11:9), “the day. Whoever walks by day does not stumble”; that is, whoever follows Christ in all things has passed, by his footsteps, to the throne of eternal light. Thus he himself, while still present for our sake in the body, prays to the Father, saying: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be who have believed in me, so that, just as you are in me and I am in you, they too may remain in us” (John 17:24).

10. This, I say, is the day of exultation and joy, on which, having attained the promise of perfect glory, we, the holy people, rightly destined to become like the angels, sing with the Prophet to the Lord, while we are still established in this world, the mystery of the praise that is to come: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it”—that is, the author of creation, redemption, and eternal life, the Lord Jesus Christ, who (Revelation 17:14) is “King of kings and Lord of lords,” reigning without beginning and without end in the Father with the Holy Spirit, now and forever and unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. On the holy day of Pentecost

This sermon should be joined to those added in the Roman edition. We are entirely at a loss to understand by what reasoning it acquired the name of Ambrose; so little Ambrosian material do we see in it. As for its attribution of the division of languages to pride, we think it was taken from Augustine’s Sermon 271.

1. Great, dearest brothers, is today’s festival, on which, as you have heard, the apostles received the Holy Spirit, who with the Father and the Son is one and perfect God, of the same substance, majesty, and power; who proceeds inseparably from the Father and the Son, not in time but from eternity; who is also called the gift of God, because even before there was an angel or a human being to whom he might be given, he was already by nature a gift capable of being given, since he is love and charity. Hence he was given secretly in the soul not only to patriarchs and prophets but also to the remaining righteous; and although he is sometimes recorded as having been given manifestly, never, nevertheless, so openly as today—that is, on the tenth day after Christ’s ascension—when he appeared in the form of fire above the one hundred and twenty believers. For it is written, as you remember: “And divided tongues appeared to them, as of fire, and it sat upon each of them” (Acts 2:3).

2. See, brothers, see what pride did and what humility deserved. Pride divided languages when human beings wished to build a tower reaching up to heaven (Genesis 11:3). Previously there had been one language, by which people understood one another and shared with one another the secrets of their minds; but, lest the proud complete what they had begun, the languages were confused and the nations were divided. Today, however, because they had received the Holy Spirit through humility, the 439 believers began to speak in all languages. Therefore cast pride away from you, brothers, since all the proud are sons of the devil; and be humble, so that you may deserve to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit and be called sons of God. Let your hearts and bodies be clean from the filth of every sin, because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sins (Wisdom 1:4).

3. If you first clean the vessels in which you wish to preserve something precious, and prepare and adorn your houses when you expect a powerful person, how much more must hearts be cleansed from hatred, anger, envy, and every evil, 440 and especially from impurity and greed, so that the Holy Spirit may not disdain to come to you and make his dwelling among you. And just as a noble person does not willingly dwell in a foul place full of dung, so the grace of the Holy Spirit does not visit a soul that persists in the stench of sins. Therefore, brothers, when the Holy Spirit comes, you must adorn the houses of your souls with the flowers of good works and fill them with the precious fragrance of chastity and the balm of benevolence, so that the Holy Spirit may delight to dwell in you, with the Father and the Son, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMONS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

[Col. 0675]

### 439 SERMON XXXVII. On Miracles

[Col. 0675D]

It is evident that the author of this sermon borrowed no small amount from Ambrose’s Commentary on Luke, Book IV, sections 58 and following. Indeed, what Gratian cites as taken from this sermon comes less close to its text than to that Commentary; this may perhaps be evidence that something was altered in the indication of the passage. The same sermon is attributed to our Ambrose in many manuscripts, but in some it is found without an author’s name; hence we infer that in other manuscripts it was inscribed according to the discretion of the scribes. Moreover, since this sermon is found in the Gallican manuscript, in which it is probable that all the sermons are Maximus’s, that too indicates that it belongs to this Father; this seems further supported by the imitation of Ambrose, which appears to have been familiar to him. In the same manuscript it is entitled “On the Two Little Boats”; in the Silvanus manuscript, “On the Chair of Saint Peter”; in the Remigius manuscript, “On Saint Peter”; in the others, as also in the ancient edition, it bears the title that we have placed at the beginning.

1. From this Gospel reading we can understand how many miracles the Lord Jesus Christ performs: it describes such great benefits bestowed by him upon the people that the crowds, stirred up to hear him, rushed upon him rather than asked him; and they did not expect the medicine of salvation through the grace of humility but through the offense of importunity. Thus, as the Gospel says (Luke 5:1 and following), when they rushed upon him, neither the wilderness separated the crowds from the Lord Jesus, nor the synagogue repelled them, nor reverence for his divinity held them back. For this is the custom of the sick: while they hope for medicine for their ailments, they are not restrained from importunate petition—neither by place, nor by time, nor by shame. Rather, the more the one who heals provides a remedy, the more importunate is the one who suffers.

2. Therefore, when the Lord Jesus could not remain on land because of the crowds pressing upon him, he saw two little boats on the sea and boarded Peter’s boat with all haste, so that the nature of the waters might repel the offense of their importunity, since the reverence due to the teacher did not restrain it at all. From Peter’s boat he then began to pour out the words of his teaching upon the people. See the Savior’s mercy: in body he is separated from the people, yet through the benefit of his teaching he is joined to them. Everywhere he shows mercy; everywhere he is beneficial. On land, through touch, he heals the sickness of bodies; at sea, through teaching, he cures the wounds of souls.

3. But let us see what this boat of Simon Peter is. [Note: All editions read, “which he judged more suitable, of the two, to be brought alongside”; all manuscripts, more elegantly, “which he judged more suitable, of the two, for teaching,” and so forth.] The Lord judged it more suitable than the other for teaching, since it both protects the Savior from insult and offers words of faith to human beings. For we find that the Lord had already sailed in another boat and had been assailed by grave insults. He sailed with Moses on the Red Sea when he carried the people of Israel across the streams of the waves; but he suffered grave insults, as he himself says in the Gospel to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me” (John 5:46). The insult to the Savior is the unbelief of the synagogue. Therefore he chose Peter’s boat and abandoned Moses’—that is, he rejected the faithless synagogue and took up the faithful Church.

4. For two boats, as it were, have been appointed by God to fish for salvation for human beings in this world, as in a sea, just as the Lord says to the apostles: “Come, I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matthew 4:19). Of these two little boats, one is left empty and vacant on the shore, while the other is taken out into the deep, loaded or full. The synagogue is left empty on the shore because it lost Christ together with the utterances of the prophets; but the Church, loaded, is taken out into the deep because it received the Lord together with the teaching of the apostles. The synagogue, I say, remains on land, as though clinging to earthly works; but the Church is called into the heights, as though examining the deep mysteries of heaven, into that height of which the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Therefore Peter is told: “Put out into the deep” (Luke 5:4)—that is, into the depth of discussions concerning divine generation.

[Note: The Vallisclausus and Silvanus manuscripts read: “into the depth of divine generation.”]

For what is as deep as what Peter said to the Lord: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16)? What is as earthly as what the Jews said about the Lord: “Is this not the son of Joseph the carpenter?” (Luke 4:22)? The former, by a higher understanding, affirmed Christ’s divine birth; the latter, with a viperous mind, judged the heavenly generation in a carnal manner. Hence the Savior says to Peter: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). But to the Pharisees he says: “How can you speak good things, when you are evil?” (Matthew 12:34).

5. The Lord therefore boarded this one boat of the Church, in which Peter was appointed teacher, since the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). This boat sails in the deep of this world in such a way that, while the world perishes, it preserves unharmed all whom it receives. We already see its figure in the Old Testament: just as Noah’s ark, while the world was shipwrecked, preserved unharmed all whom it had taken in, so Peter’s Church, while the world burns, will present unharmed all whom it embraces. And just as, when the flood had passed, the dove brought a sign of peace to Noah’s ark, so, when judgment has passed, Christ will bring the joy of peace to Peter’s Church, because he himself is the dove, or peace, as he promised when he said: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice” (John 16:22).

6. But since we read in Matthew (Matthew 8:24) that this same boat of Peter, from which the Lord now draws forth the mysteries of his heavenly teaching, was disturbed by rising winds while the Lord slept in it, so that all the apostles feared the danger of death, let us see what the reason is that one and the same boat here gives teaching to the people in tranquility, while there announces fear of death to the disciples in a storm—especially since Simon Peter was also there with the other apostles.

The reason for the danger is this: Simon Peter was there, but the traitor Judas was there as well. Although Peter’s faith secured the boat, Judas’s faithlessness nevertheless disturbed it. There is tranquility where Peter alone sails; there is a storm where Judas is added. Although Peter was firm in his own merits, he is nevertheless disturbed by the crimes of the traitor (1.4, canon “Turbatur”; and 24.1, canon “Non turbatur”).

Therefore, while the disciples were afraid and Peter was anxious, the Lord slept. It may perhaps seem harsh that, while Peter was anxious, he slept: he slept for Peter, lest he keep watch for Judas. Thus, through the offense of one, the merits of all are shaken. Christ falls asleep, and the blasts of the winds are stirred up; for whoever commits a sin immediately makes the Lord sleep for himself and raises up for himself a storm of unclean spirits. The devil’s storm must arise when the Lord’s calm falls silent.

[Note: Thus read the same two manuscripts; others and the old edition instead have: “He slept: he slept for Peter, he sailed for Judas”; the Roman edition reads: “The Lord slept.” In truth, he slept for Peter, but Judas disturbed the sea.]

7. Therefore, if all the apostles are endangered by the sin of one Judas, let us beware of the faithless man, let us beware of the traitor, lest through one we many be tossed about. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “By this example let us beware of the faithless traitor.”] Indeed, let us cast such a person out of our boat, so that the Lord may not sleep but keep watch within us; and while he keeps watch, may no storm of spiritual wickedness shake us. For where faith is whole, there the Savior teaches, keeps watch, and rejoices; there are rest, tranquility, and the healing of all. But where faithlessness is mingled with faith, there Christ is sluggish, sleeps, and is inactive; there are fear, storm, and universal danger. For according to our actions, the Lord either sleeps or keeps watch for us.

## SERMON XXXVIII. On the Grace of Baptism

This sermon bears this title not only in the old edition but also in several of the better manuscripts; in the Remigius manuscript, however, it is prefaced with the title “On the Feast of Epiphany.” It certainly seems clear that it was delivered to catechumens not long after that feast, so that they might be stirred to seek the grace of receiving baptism. It bears nothing characteristic of Ambrose; but it may be attributed to Maximus with greater justice. Since it agrees well with Sermons X and XI printed above, one may suppose that these are the three sermons designated by Gennadius when he reported that this same bishop had published a book on the grace of Baptism in very ancient books.

1. Since it is established, as we explained a few days ago, that Jesus Christ was baptized not for his own sake but for ours, we, dearest brothers—I am speaking to you catechumens—must receive the grace of his baptism with all haste and draw the blessing of consecration from the spring of the Jordan, which he blessed, so that our sins may be plunged into that stream into which his holiness was immersed (Matthew 3:13 and following). Thus the same water that surrounded the Lord may cleanse his little servants all around; so that the holy water may benefit us from Christ’s venerable washing and, through the same footsteps and mysteries by which it borrowed its blessing from the Savior, purify us with a more blessed nurture and pour upon Christians the grace it received from Christ.

[Note: All editions have “that we may be of more blessed fruit”; all manuscripts have “that we may be of more blessed nurture”; one has “more blessed.”]

2. Therefore, brothers, we must be immersed in the same spring in which Christ was immersed, so that we may be what Christ is. For, speaking with faith unharmed, although both baptisms belong to the Lord, I nevertheless think that this baptism, by which we are washed, is more gracious than that by which the Savior was baptized. The former is celebrated through Christ; the latter was celebrated through John. In the former the master excuses himself; in the latter the Savior invites us. In the former justice is incomplete; in the latter the Trinity is perfect. To the former the holy man comes and the holy man goes forth; to the latter the sinner comes and the holy man departs. In the former blessing is conferred upon the mysteries; in the latter sins are forgiven through the mystery.

Therefore, brothers, we must be baptized in the same stream as the Savior. But, if we are to be immersed in the same spring, we need not seek the eastern region or the river of the Jewish land; for Christ is now everywhere, and the Jordan is everywhere. The same consecration that blessed the rivers of the East sanctifies the streams of the West. Hence, even if the river has another name in the world, the mystery of the Jordan is nevertheless present in it.

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts; the edition, also not incorrectly, has “for where Christ now is, there too is the Jordan.”]

3. Finally, the work is carried out through the same mysteries through which it was then accomplished, except with fuller grace. Then we saw the Trinity with bodily eyes; now we contemplate the same Trinity with the eyes of faith. Then scarcely a human face looked upon Christ; now the human mind embraces him. Then the Holy Spirit surrounded a human being in the appearance of a dove; now he pours himself into the human interior by the very power of his divinity. Then the Father came to us on account of the Son through the long hearing of a voice; now he himself descends to us together with the Son.

[Note: All editions have “Then the Father came from the Lord”; the Remigius manuscript and the Vallisclausus manuscript have a lacuna, “to the Lord”; the Lugdunensis manuscript has the excellent reading, “then the Father came to us,” and so forth.]

Therefore grace is fuller where God does not descend to human beings in an assumed form but deigns to descend to his children in his own substance. There, as though addressing unbelievers, he wished to persuade them of faith through bodily signs; here, as though addressing believers, he confers grace through spiritual power. It is therefore a grace of greater fullness to see God as God is than to see him in such a way that one must search for him. Here the Trinity is perfect; there divinity still must be sought out. Grace is therefore fuller when one knows God in his own truth than when one suspects him in an assumed form.

[Note: The old edition has “to know God by his own power”; the Roman edition and the manuscripts more suitably read as in the text.]

4. Let us therefore do for ourselves what we see God doing for us; let us do toward ourselves what John wished to be done toward him. If he who was a prophet and a holy man desired the Savior’s baptism, how much more ought we sinners and unworthy people to seek this grace! See the Savior’s mercy: what is freely offered to us is not deserved by the prophet even when he asks for it.

5. We must consider, however, why John asked for Christ’s baptism but did not receive it. For the Lord says to him when he asks: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). We know that John the Baptist bore the figure of the Law. It was therefore right that he himself should baptize the Lord: namely, so that, just as the Savior was born according to the flesh from the Jews, so the Gospel might be born according to the Spirit from the Law; and that from the source from which he derived the succession of his origin, he might also receive the tradition of consecration. This, then, is what he says: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” For it was right that he himself should fulfill the commandments of the Law that he himself had established, just as he says elsewhere: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

## SERMON XXXIX. On the Camel

[Col. 0680D]

The Roman edition, in order to adapt this sermon to the Gospel for the fourteenth Sunday after Pentecost, prefixed an opening of its own devising. How absurdly it did so is shown by the fact that this sermon is known to have been delivered not long after Epiphany. Moreover, we find in it such a close relationship with Sermon 20, which we rejected, that we judge the two to have had the same author. Nor are there lacking features that seem to establish it as Maximus’s; but there is nothing to support its attribution to Ambrose.

1. [Note: The Roman edition has: “Among the Hebrews, mammon is called the riches of this world. It is called unrighteous mammon because only the unrighteous place their hope in it; the righteous, although they possess such things, do not regard them as their riches, but only heavenly and spiritual things. Therefore he serves mammon who trusts in the earthly things of this world. Elsewhere the prophet calls such people ‘men of riches.’ Do not call those things riches, brothers; do not love them, because if you serve them, you will perish with them. Therefore concerning such a rich man Jesus Christ says elsewhere,” and so forth.]

The Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24). I fear that this saying may perhaps apply to you, who either possess or seek the riches of this world. For just as the camel, an animal that is crooked and misshapen, is prevented by the very perversity of its body from passing through the exceedingly narrow opening of a needle, so the deformity of their life does not allow the rich, burdened with greed and disfigured by desire, to enter by the narrow way of the kingdom. For the same Lord says: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7:14).

2. Thus, in the camel, the structure of its limbs makes passage difficult; in the rich man, the enormity of his sins causes the impediment. For it is a kind of hump of the soul to think or act in a shameful manner; and it is a kind of crooked deformity of the mind to be continually intent upon worldly matters and to be called away from the threshold of the holy Church by worldly cares.

[Note: All editions read “the difficulty of gain,” and below, “continually upon unclean things”; the manuscripts more aptly read as in the text.]

Therefore it seems to me that, when the prophet spoke spiritually of this bodily deformity, he indicated rather the foulness of conduct when he said: “Let not the hunchback boast as the upright” (1 Kings 20:11). It is as though he said: Let not the sinner, distorted by the crookedness of his vices, boast as the righteous person, made straight by the simplicity of a good conscience. For although, sinner, you may rejoice in the height of your body, although you may delight in the evenness of your shoulders, your soul is nevertheless deformed by the crookedness of your conduct.

3. The rich man is therefore rightly compared to a camel. The latter is held back from passing through the needle by the thickness of its body; the former is detained from entering the Church by concern for his patrimony. Just as the small opening does not admit the camel burdened by the mass of its limbs, so the holy entrance does not receive the rich man weighed down by a heap of sins. Each has its own burden: the one is loaded with flesh, the other with sins. Just as the former is unfit for the exceedingly narrow opening of a needle, so the latter is unsuited to the most blessed kingdom of God. Nature makes the camel physically misshapen; the will makes the rich man morally crooked.

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts; the edition instead has “whom nature makes physically composed.” This is somewhat less elegant.]

4. I say these things, brothers, about those who have been detained by the fetters of their patrimonies from attending the most festive day of the holy Epiphany in the Church, and have been bound by a kind of earthly chain, so that they were unable to come to the house of the Lord. Not that anything holds them back by force, but that they are so entangled in their own affairs that they have already lost control over their way of life; and while they attend to the care of their patrimony, they do not seek the medicine of their souls at all.

5. Why, rich man, do you put the difficulty of the season before me? Why do you introduce some sudden necessity? If you have a heart, understand that the necessity of salvation is greater than every necessity; and that it is more beneficial first to care for life and then repair the losses of one’s property, lest, while we seek an increase in our patrimony, we experience the loss of our soul.

Perhaps you fear the judge whom you left in his office. Believe me: you ought to fear God the Judge more, for he will judge your judge himself. You fear the man who will soon receive a successor; do you not fear the Lord, whom no one ever succeeds? Consider, then, the approaching day of judgment, the unquenchable flames of Gehenna, the dreadful gnashing of teeth, the final torment of darkness; and, if you can, continue to entangle yourself in worldly cares while you abandon the Church. For I fear that, while you seek the riches of the world, you may instead find the riches of sins; and that, having discovered the treasures of this world, you may lose the heavenly treasures.

## SERMON XL. On Fasting and Almsgiving

[Col. 0682B]

In order to turn this sermon into one for the epistle of the twenty-third Sunday after Pentecost, the Roman edition altered its true title and inserted several words into the text; we have restored both. Its manner of expression is so opposed to that of Ambrose that it may be attributed to almost anyone rather than to him.

1. I do not doubt, brothers, that you are saddened whenever necessity makes me absent from you. For when you do not see the one you love, like good sons you are troubled by the goads of filial devotion. But although I sometimes leave you bodily, I do not leave you in spirit. Wherever I go, your love follows me; wherever I am, your brotherhood dwells with me. For whoever remains in Christ’s commandments must cling to Christ’s priest. Although he may appear to be far away, he becomes near when the grace of one faith represents him.

Let him consider himself separated from the priests who is separated from Christ by evil deeds. Therefore, brothers, since you do what the Savior commands, although you have been absent from me in body, you have not been lacking to me in love. Thus the distance of lands separated us, but the grace of Christ joined us together.

2. There are, however, some among you, brothers, whose faces we see in the Church but whose hearts we know to be in the fields; we observe their presence among the congregation, but we find their way of life in the countryside.

[Note: The old edition and the manuscripts have: “For the Apostle says of the earth”; the Regius manuscript has: “For they always think about the earth,” and so forth.]

The Apostle says of them: “Their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Philippians 3:19). For they are always thinking about the earth, dealing with the earth, and taking pleasure in earthly things. To them applies that divine saying: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). They sometimes come to the Church not because they are Christians in faith, but so that people will not think them non-Christians.

3. When fasting is imposed upon them, they always excuse themselves by citing the harshness of the season. In the summer months they say: “The day is long, the sun is scorching; we cannot endure thirst; we must refresh ourselves with drinks.” In winter they say: “The cold is severe, the chill is extreme; we cannot tolerate the cold; we must warm ourselves with food.” Thus people whose minds are always at the meal seek reasons for themselves to eat; and while they excuse themselves from fasting, they accuse the seasons established by the Creator.

[Note: The Roman edition added the word “accuse.” Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Their god is their belly.”]

4. Tell me, delicate Christian, who cannot endure the heat of the sun while fasting: is the heat that you will have to endure hotter than Gehenna? Is winter more terrible than the darkness into which you will be cast? Sinners will be thrown into the outer darkness; “there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12). As the Lord says, the gnashing of teeth, like that of winter, will always be in those darknesses.

Therefore, just as, when winter’s chill penetrates, people tremble throughout their bodies, so, when the cold conscience of sins intervenes, sinners will be shaken by the severe gnashing of their teeth. Thus the wretched sinner, while fearing winter’s harshness here, encounters the cold of darkness there; while avoiding the sun’s heat here, he will endure the heat of Gehenna there.

5. When these same people are told to give something to the poor, they immediately object: “The needs are endless; the taxes are heavy; we cannot discharge our fiscal obligations.” They heap so many arguments upon you that they seem to treat you as guilty for having wished to remind them of this at all. They do not understand that those who do not understand that the necessity of salvation must be preferred to every other necessity are enemies of the cross of Christ.

Paying tribute benefits the one who receives it; giving alms benefits the one who gives it. The payment of tribute brings advantage to the one who receives it, whereas the work of almsgiving confers merit upon the one who performs it. The payment of tribute, I say, brings loss to the payer; the distribution of alms gives profit to the distributor. For the merciful person becomes richer after he begins to have less by giving to the poor.

[Note: The Roman edition has “of Christ,” as was read today.]

6. Blessed, therefore, is almsgiving, which both refreshes the recipient and gladdens the giver: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Therefore it is better for him to give more.

[Note: All editions and the Lugdunensis manuscript have “it is better for him first to give”; the Vallisclausus manuscript more suitably has a lacuna, followed by “to give more.”]

He who supplies the poor is joyful and cheerful. He is rightly joyful, because with a few coins he acquires eternal heavenly treasures for himself. On the other hand, the person who pays taxes is always sad and sorrowful. Nor is he sad without reason: he is brought to make the payment not by love but compelled by fear. The debtor of Christ is joyful; Caesar’s debtor is sad, because love drives the former to pay, while punishment compels the latter. The one is summoned by rewards; the other is constrained by penalties.

7. The holy Apostle says: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded and not to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches” (1 Timothy 6:17). You see, rich man, that your riches are uncertain. Why, then, do you gather gold, in which there is no sure confidence? Let the greed for your gold cease: it is earth. Let the desire for your silver be taken away: it is filth. Gold and silver are cheap and rejected materials. Nature did not make gold and silver precious; human desire made them so.

[Note: The Lugdunensis and Vallisclausus manuscripts have: “May your gold be avarice”; the edition’s reading, as in the text, is better.]

## SERMON XLI. On What the Lord Says in the Gospel: “Foxes Have Dens,” and So Forth

This is the title that the ancient edition and the manuscripts gave this sermon. The Roman edition, however, prefixed the heading “On the Feast of Saint Basil,” failing to notice that, according to the same edition’s own editors, it is scarcely credible that in Ambrose’s time—whom they claim to be the author of this sermon—the feast of Basil was already customarily celebrated at Milan. Apart from several passages transferred here from the Commentary on Luke, Book VII, sections 30 and 31, it can therefore be asserted only that there is nothing Ambrosian in this sermon.

1. If your affection has carefully noticed the Gospel passage read today, it may have disturbed your thoughts for the very reason that, as Scripture relates, when one man asked to follow the Lord wherever he went as an act of religious service, the Lord instead said to another: “Follow me” (Matthew 8:22), and, rejecting and disregarding the former, chose another who was silent and unsuspecting.

Although voluntary service is ordinarily more acceptable than compelled service, and service pleases more when it is offered spontaneously than when it is demanded by command, why, then, is this man rejected? Why is he refused as though unworthy? For the Lord says to him: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58).

[Note: The Roman edition has a fuller version: “Your affection, brothers, has noticed the Gospel passage read today—how the Lord, who in the Law, as Scripture reports, commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and whom the Lord your God commanded you to obey so that it might be well with you, now says, ‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and so forth, he cannot be my disciple.’ This agrees with what happened elsewhere: when someone addressed him, ‘Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father,’ he replied, ‘Let the dead bury their dead; but you go and announce the kingdom of God.’ To the man who said, ‘I will follow you wherever you go,’ he replied, ‘Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.’ Why, then, when one man asked to follow him wherever he went as an act of religious service, did he instead say to another who hesitated to follow him, ‘Follow me’; and, rejecting the former, and so forth.”]

2. First, then, we must consider that the Lord is not a respecter of persons—for he is an impartial and just judge—but returns the affection of love according to the quality of one’s conduct.

[Note: The old edition has “according to the quality of these things”; the Roman edition, “according to the quality of merits”; the Lugdunensis manuscript, “according to the quality of conduct.”]

He chooses not the one who is ready in words but sluggish in devotion, but the one who is silent with his tongue and devoted in mind, of whom the Prophet says: “If you make yourself silent, you will be considered wise” (Proverbs 17:28). Of the one who speaks rashly, Scripture says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father” (Matthew 7:21). From this we learn that one must cry out to the Lord not so much with the mouth as with the heart.

3. Our Savior, therefore, who sees through the thoughts and understanding of human beings, hears the obedience of the voice but recognizes the trickery of the mind. He compares this man to an animal that indicates one thing by its voice but does another in its behavior. For the fox sounds with the bark of a dog but practices robbery through deceit.

[Note: Thus reads the Lugdunensis manuscript; the old edition has “and foresees his thoughts”; the Roman edition, “foresees them.”]

He therefore takes up the silent and unsuspecting man. His tongue was silent, but he spoke in spirit. We understand how devoted he was: as he himself asserted, he left his father dead in order to find the Lord of life. He says: “Permit me first to go and bury my father” (Luke 9:59). He had therefore left him dead, asking permission to return and bury him. Pain had not held him back, nor death delayed him, because he was hastening toward life. He had not yet closed the eyes of the dying man, nor yet buried his stiffening limbs; as soon as he learned that the Lord had arrived, he forgot filial devotion and judged that, in his greater devotion, he should love Christ more than his parent.

Perhaps he had read the prophetic passage that says: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11). Therefore he forgot his father while remembering the Savior. He had also heard the Lord’s Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

4. Thus, while Tobias is justified because he abandoned his meal for the sake of a burial (Tobit 2:3), this man is approved because, for Christ’s sake, he abandoned his father’s burial. The former did not fear that, because of the intervening task, he would forgo the feast of an earthly meal; the latter feared that, because of the intervening delay, he would lose the nourishment of heavenly bread. Therefore, although, in consideration of Christ, we owe burial to everyone, this man abandoned his father’s burial out of love for Christ.

5. Let us therefore first examine that man’s appeal and the response of the Lord and Savior. For he says: “I will follow you wherever you go” (Luke 9:58). A ready, indeed, [Note: [Col. 0685D] All editions: “but an arrogant response”; the Lyon manuscript [Col. 0686D]: “a declaration.”] but arrogant declaration. For the Lord was going to his Passion, descending to the underworld, and ascending into heaven. Could human frailty possibly accompany him in all these things? This presumption is foolish rather than a devout confession.

For the Lord also says to the apostle Peter, when he thought that he would follow the Savior in everything: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now” (John 13:33). And when Peter persisted stubbornly and declared that he would not be separated from him even by death, he hears—as though condemned for boasting—that he would deny the Lord three times. Thus the man who promised that not even death would separate him from confessing Christ is separated from Christ’s company by the questioning of a servant girl; and unless the Lord had established, as it were, a limit by saying that Peter would deny him three times, perhaps, questioned more often, he would have denied him more frequently.

6. What, then, is said to that presumptuous man? “Foxes have dens and the birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58). Observe what he is subtly compared with: this is a deceitful kind of animal, always intent on ambushes and practicing fraud through plunder. It permits nothing to be safe, nothing undisturbed, nothing secure, since it seeks prey even among human dwellings.

7. I think that this comparison was written not only on his account, but also on account of many Christians who confess God with their mouths, yet differ in their conduct through the deceitfulness of foxes. For every Christian who wishes to conceal his sins is spiritually a fox. Just as the fox, because of its deceptions, dwells in hiding places, so the sinner, remaining silent because of his conscience, lurks in the dens of his sins. And just as the fox does not dare display the deceitfulness of its ways amid crowds of people, so this man is ashamed to confess the wickedness of his conduct in the midst of the Church. I would plainly call every Christian a fox who lies in wait for his neighbor, who daily strives to gnaw away others’ boundaries, seize their fruits, and devour their animals; and—something characteristic of our own times—who no longer carries off young animals in the manner of foxes, but swine in the manner of wolves; who, although he could live by his own labor, hunts the property of others with the ferocity of wild beasts. [Note: [Col. 0686D] The Lyon manuscript: “although he could support himself by his own labor.”]

[Col. 0686C] 8. I also think that all heretics should be compared to foxes. Since they cannot dwell in the house of the Lord, they prepare for themselves certain assemblies like dark dens, in which they lurk obstinately and lie in wait for the Church, so that, if some innocent soul should happen to come forth, they may swallow it like a chick of a mother hen. “Foxes,” I say, “lie in wait for the Church”—that is, heretics lie in wait for that evangelical hen of whom the Lord says: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings!” But she, like Samson, tied burning torches to the foxes.

## SERMON XLII. Rebuke to the People Concerning What Is Written in the Gospel: “To Whoever Has, It Will Be Given”; and “We Have Sung to You,” etc.

[Col. 0686D] Nothing occurs to indicate why we should assign this sermon by name to one particular Father rather than another; but, if we are to think it Ambrosian, everything argues against it.

### 1

I had often resolved within myself, brothers, to withhold from you the words of the Lord’s preaching and not to distribute so frequently the mysteries of heavenly discourses. For it is useless to offer food to one who refuses it, and to present drink to one who is not thirsty. Why should the person to whom you offer it drink it less willingly than he rejects it disdainfully as turbid, so that both the purity of the cup is spoiled and the fastidious drinker finds grounds for his offense? Thus, too, it may perhaps be superfluous to pour out to your Charity the preaching of the Lord’s cup, since your soul, with its inward faculties closed, does not drink it so thirstily [Note: [Col. 0687D] Thus the Lyon and Vallisclara manuscripts; the editions instead read: “as it pours it out deceitfully.” Incorrectly.] as it pours it out deceitfully.

For whoever hears the Lord’s command with his ear but does not retain it in his heart pours it out. Carrying it only on the surface of his body and not sending what he has heard into his inward parts, he forgets it, pours out the sequence of the preaching, and thus [Note: [Col. 0687D] The Lyon manuscript: “returns home empty.” And below: “which of you, when,” etc.] returns home empty, although he had left the Church burdened with it.

### 2

Tell me, then: which of you, when he has returned to his lodging, will say: “Today we heard the bishop discussing almsgiving; he preached something useful: we ought to show mercy to the poor”? He also spoke at length about the accursed worship of idols: “Let us make sure that, without our knowing it, there is no idol on our property.” He also warned that the catechumen ought to hasten toward the grace of faith: “Let us offer faith to our household, so that whoever is faithful may receive it; otherwise an account of their salvation may be demanded from us, since their life depends upon our decision.”

No one thinks about the things of God; no one speaks about the day of judgment, as though we were destined either to live forever or to die forever. Believe me: we live in this world as those who will die in body; we die as those who live for the rendering of an account. Meanwhile the human being dies, but the cause of his deeds does not die. Since the cause remains alive, the person responsible for that cause must necessarily remain as well, as the prophet says: “Behold the man, and his works.”

### 3

I had therefore wanted to withhold from you the words of the Lord’s preaching—not because I was doing this in anger, [Col. 0687C] but in order to preserve the Gospel saying. For the Lord says: “To whoever has, it will be given, and he will abound; but from whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Luke 19:26). He therefore commanded that more be given to the one who has; and to the one who does not have, not only that nothing be given, but even what he has be taken away.

This saying may perhaps seem excessive to you; but I say that the Lord commanded rightly and wisely. The one who has is therefore commanded to receive more. He plainly deserves to receive who has labored with such personal concern as to acquire spiritual riches for his soul. For example, if someone has begun, with a firm resolve toward self-restraint, to preserve the virtue of chastity, he deserves to hear what reward awaits chastity, so that, hearing the glory of its reward and thus being encouraged to preserve virtue, he may more easily wear down the struggle he has begun. [Note: [Col. 0688D] The Vallisclara manuscript adds: “for the observance of virtue.”]

Another person who is ready to show mercy ought to hear that God will show mercy to him; and since God will repay this earthly substance with heavenly riches, he must, when he hears of the recompense of heavenly rewards, pursue the Lord’s work more eagerly and willingly, and add an increase of generosity to the good of mercy that he already possesses. Therefore the Lord says: “To whoever has, it will be given”—that is, whoever is rich in good works will be enriched still further by evangelical preaching.

### 4

But if you preach to a fornicator and tell him that he ought to remain a virgin, or to a miser that he ought to dispose of all his possessions and give them away, it is foolishness to him. He considers such preaching ridiculous, as the Apostle says: “The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

To preach what is perfect to such people is like trying to clothe a beggar covered in rags with silk, or delighting a hungry rustic with a pastry. The offering must be rejected by both. The beggar dislikes silk, because he desires clothing more necessary against the cold; the rustic finds the pastry bitter, because he seeks food that will satisfy his hunger.

From such persons, therefore, what is theirs must rather be taken away, as the Gospel says: “Even what he has will be taken away from him.” That is, the fornicator must be compelled to cast off the rags of his corruption, and the miser must be forced to set forth the bread of his greed.

### 5

I fear, brothers, that the Gospel reading applies to many of you, which says: “We have sung to you, and you did not dance; we have lamented, and you did not weep” (Luke 7:32). We announce to you, therefore, the joy of the heavenly kingdom, yet your hearts do not leap with any movement of gladness. We preach the dread judgment, yet your minds do not burst into tears for repentance. For it is a kind of unbelief neither to rejoice at prosperity nor to weep at adversity in matters divine.

The Lord therefore asks us for dancing—not, of course, the twisting movement of the body, [Note: [Col. 0688D] The Vallisclara manuscript: “but the holiness of an exalted faith.”] but the holiness of faith that lifts itself up. For just as one who dances bodily is now suspended in the air, now thrown upward to higher places, and now illuminates different places with alternating leaps, so one who dances spiritually, through the intervention of faith, is at one moment raised to the heights of the air, at another lifted higher than the stars, and at another surveys paradise and heaven through the various leaps of his thoughts.

And just as one who dances bodily, exercising himself through the movement of his limbs, creates a circle for his dance, so one who dances spiritually, always moving himself through the alacrity of faith, takes for himself the circuit of the whole world.

### 6

People customarily dance or sing especially at their vows—that is, at weddings. We too, therefore, have a wedding of vows at which we ought to dance or sing. Our vows are celebrated when the Church is joined to Christ, as John says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). For this wedding it is fitting that we dance.

Indeed, King David, both king and prophet, is said to have danced before the Ark of the Covenant, although he sang many things (2 Samuel 6:14). Lifted up by joy, he burst into dancing, for in the spirit he foresaw Mary, from his own offspring, to be joined to Christ’s bridal chamber. Hence he himself says: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Psalm 18:6).

Therefore he sang more than the other authors of the prophecies, because, more joyful than all others through these joys, he joined his descendants in marriage. Inviting them to his own vows with more than usual sweetness, he taught us what we ought to do at that wedding, since he himself danced before the wedding with such exultation.

The prophet David therefore danced before the Ark. What, then, should we call the Ark except holy Mary? The Ark carried within itself the tablets of the Covenant, while Mary carried the heir of that Covenant; the former held the Law within itself, the latter the Gospel; the former had the voice of God, the latter the Word.

Yet the Ark shone within and without with the splendor of gold, and holy Mary likewise gleamed within and without with the splendor of virginity. The former was adorned with earthly gold, the latter with heavenly gold.

## SERMON XLIII. Rebuke to the People for Not Frequenting the Church

Many distinguished men, thinking this sermon to be Ambrose’s, supposed that the council mentioned in it could only have been the Council of Aquileia [Col. 0689B]. But nothing indicates that the subject should be understood in this way rather than another. As for their having regarded the same sermon as Ambrosian, they followed the authority of the editions in this matter. Not to mention that it is found in an ancient Gallican manuscript in which all the sermons are attributed to Augustine, there is nothing in it, either in style or in subject, that suits our Ambrose.

### 1

Brothers, after these many days I ought to preach something more abundant and, returning from so great an examination of priests, refresh you with a pleasant discourse. I was right to say “an examination of priests,” because, just as bees make sweet honey from the little flowers of divine Scripture and skillfully compose whatever pertains to the healing of souls with their mouths, so priests are rightly compared with bees.

For, just as bees prefer bodily chastity, provide the food of heavenly life, and wield the sting of the law, so priests are pure for sanctification, sweet for refreshment, and severe for punishment. Those who are contained, as it were, in a hive of the grace of Mother Church are plainly to be compared with bees. In that hive they arrange the cells of various merits through the sweetest preaching, and from the one swarm of the Savior produce many swarms of Christians.

### 2

Although I have never ceased, brothers, to correct you with paternal affection, I am amazed that you have made no progress through so many admonitions of mine. I grieve that my frequent preaching does not correct you through some advance in salvation, but instead constrains you with a kind of sentence of accusation.

For the preaching of a priest is correction for the people who are to be saved, and a warning for those who are to be judged. We warn them before the judgment of what awaits them in the judgment itself, so that then, once every excuse has been removed, they may be found guilty both of their sins and of their contempt.

Therefore, although I sometimes wish to spare you by keeping silent, I prefer that you give an account of your stubbornness rather than that I bear the judgment of negligence.

### 3

I have discovered, brothers, that in my absence only a few of you come to the Church and that scarcely any of you proceed there—as though, when I departed, you had come away with me, and as though, when necessity dragged me away, that same necessity had dragged you along with me.

We are therefore alike absent from the house of God, but there is this difference: necessity makes me absent, [Col. 0690A] whereas your absence is caused by your will.

Do you not know that, although I am absent from the Church, Christ, who is everywhere, is not absent from his Church? You come, brother, to the Church and do not find the bishop there. But if you come faithfully, you will find there the Savior, the bishop of bishops.

For the Christian who comes to the Church only when the bishop is present appears to have come not so much for God’s sake as for a human being’s sake; nor does he seem to have fulfilled the duty of a Christian who fears God, but rather the service of a friend who pays his respects.

### 4

Why, though, do I rebuke you, when you can convict me with a single discourse? (Question I, chapter “What, then?”) I am convicted because in this respect I see the clergy more negligent than you. How can I correct sons if I cannot correct brothers? Or with what confidence can I be angry with the laity if, out of respect for my fellow ministers, I fall silent in shame?

I am not speaking about everyone, brothers. Certainly some are devoted, and others negligent. I name no one; let each person’s own conscience address him.

## SERMON XLIV. Encouragement to the People after the Rebuke

This sermon appears under this title in the Gallican and Lyon manuscripts; in the old editions, however, *consolatio* is used instead of *allectio*. The Roman edition devised a title differing not so much in sense as in wording. We do not doubt that this discourse was delivered after the preceding one; and we see that its author borrowed some material from Jerome, chapter 62 on Matthew, and more from Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book VI, sections 96 and 97. All these features lead us to think that its author was someone other than Ambrose.

[Col. 0690C] 1. My rebuke in the preceding sermons may perhaps have been rather bitter, because I addressed many of you more sharply with the severity of instruction and pursued matters that brought not flatteries but sadness to many. [Note: [Col. 0689] The Lyon manuscript: “my preaching … because I addressed many of you.”]

But it makes no difference to me. I rejoice, knowing that the sadness of the disciple is the joy of the teacher. The hearer makes progress when the preacher announces harsher things; salvation is born for him when the sadness of correction is imposed. For the blessed Apostle says: “The sorrow that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

### 2

I therefore rightly rejoice, because I bring about salvation. When I rebuke, let the son grieve at the harshness of my discourse; I nevertheless take delight when I understand that he is making progress through his grief.

The holy Apostle says: “What son is there whom the father does not chastise?” (Hebrews 12:6). A father does not always kiss his son; sometimes he also disciplines him. Therefore, when the one who is loved is disciplined, affection is exercised toward him.

Love, too, has its wounds, which are sweeter when they are inflicted more bitterly. Religious correction is sweeter than indulgent leniency. Hence the prophet says: “The wounds of a friend are sweeter than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:6).

### 3

Therefore, brothers, since I believe that, after so many useful words of my rebuke, you have advanced through the kindness of your understanding, let us discuss some matters from the sacred Scriptures.

Just as a spring that does not drip with its usual flow is stirred with branches and is then found to be more abundant, with turbid water first issuing from it so that a purer stream may follow, so your holiness had indeed been irritated by the harshness of the discourse, but has become more devoted through the sweetness of affection.

Your minds perhaps retained something turbulent, but now everything that is pure flows forth from your conduct.

### 4

Let us therefore see what the Lord says to his disciples: “But you—who do you say that I am?” (Matthew 16:15). The Lord does not ask this as though he were ignorant of what the crowds and the disciples thought about him; rather, as one who knew the minds of all, he wished each person’s faith to be made manifest.

While some believed in their hearts that the Lord was Jeremiah and others that he was John the Baptist, Peter alone confessed him to be Christ, the Son of God. [Col. 0691B] There are certain degrees of faith, and the one who believes more devotedly confesses more religiously.

### 5

For this devotion Peter is told: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:17ff.).

When he was called Simon, therefore, he was called Peter because of this devotion. We read that the Apostle said of the Lord himself: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Therefore, rightly, because Christ is the rock, Simon was named Peter, so that the one who shared the fellowship of faith with the Lord might also share with the Lord the unity of the Lord’s name; and just as a Christian is named from Christ, so the apostle Peter was named from the rock, Christ.

### 6

Nor can we reject the opinion of the crowds, who thought that the Lord was one of the prophets (Matthew 16:14). Some perhaps therefore thought that the Savior was Elijah, because Elijah ascended into the heavens just as the Savior did (2 Kings 2:11).

But Christ is not like Elijah. Elijah is carried off into heaven, whereas Christ returns; Elijah, as a weak human being, is carried upward in a fiery chariot, whereas Christ, as God, is borne by his own power. Elijah is led away like a human being, whereas Christ ascends like the Savior. Elijah follows the angels who lead him, whereas Christ goes before the angels who accompany him.

Finally, those same angels, returning to earth from the Lord and Savior, said to the Apostles: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

## SERMON XLV. On the First Adam and the Second

We present this sermon—or rather, fragment of a sermon—taken from a Vatican manuscript written at the command of Cardinal Bolognese in the year 1470. We do not offer it because we find anything Ambrosian in it, but because its writing is not inelegant and it is prefaced in the manuscript with the name of the holy Doctor. Since, as far as we know, it has nowhere else been published, it does not seem at all unworthy to give it a place at least in the appendix.

### 1

Listen, dearest brothers, to what the mystery of the Law is like. The first human being was from earth and heaven; the second from heaven and earth: the latter from God and Mary, who was from earth; the former from earth and the Spirit, who is from heaven.

Both, however, are from a virgin and without the mingling of intercourse: the latter from one who was incorrupt, the former from one who was untouched—because the earth had not yet been wounded by any seed, plowshare, or rain.

Through the first, life was lost; through the second, it was restored. The first lost the grace he had received; the second bestowed grace together with life. The first fell at the persuasion of a virgin; the second, through the birth of a virgin, raised up what was lying fallen. The first, by sinning, brought forth the punishment of death; the second, by suffering, bestowed forgiveness. The first was expelled from paradise on account of guilt; the second was fastened to the cross for the glory of the world.

### 2

Thus evil came through a woman—rather, good through a woman; for through Eve we fell, through Mary we stand. Through Eve we were cast down, through Mary raised up. Through Eve we were handed over to slavery, through Mary made free.

Eve took away our perpetuity; Mary restored it to us. Eve caused us to be condemned through the fruit of a tree; Mary absolved us through the gift of a tree, because Christ also hung upon the wood as its fruit.

### 3

Therefore, just as we died through a tree, so we were given life through a tree. A tree showed us our nakedness; a tree clothed us with the leaves of forgiveness. A tree inflicted on us the burning of sins; the tree of knowledge prepared refreshment through garments for transgressions. A tree produced thorns and thistles; the tree of knowledge brought forth hope and salvation. A tree brought sweat and labor; a tree bestowed peace and salvation. A tree disclosed the light of the body; a tree opened the eyes of the heart. The tree of the world insinuated cunning; the divine tree displayed wisdom.

The tree showed evil; the tree showed good. And, to return to the origin of the beloved one and say, with God’s consent, what we are permitted to understand: if Adam had not fallen bodily, Christ would not have needed to raise us spiritually in this life.

### 4

O mystery of Mary’s sacraments, as we have said! O discipline closed to the faithless and revealed to the faithful! The immortal fashions the mortal; the mortal gives birth to the immortal; the incorporeal is enclosed in earth, the corporeal in heaven. God becomes human, yet God is manifested. All this is brought about through Adam and washed away through Mary.

Therefore blessed is Eve, through whom the opportunity was given; rather, blessed is Mary, through whom the remedy was bestowed. Blessed is Eve, through whom the people were born; more blessed is Mary, through whom Christ was born.

Thus the one is better than the other—indeed, both are glorious—because Christ would not have brought joy to Mary unless he had first fashioned the former Eve, from whom Mary herself was born; nor would he have come to the people unless she had first sinned in the world.

The former is called the mother of the human race, the latter of salvation. Eve instructed us; Mary strengthened us.

### 5

Through Eve we increase; through Mary we reign. Through Eve we were led astray toward earth; through Mary raised up toward heaven. And, to disclose briefly the whole mystery of the Law and show that the two were one, just as all are one: Mary was then present in Eve; afterward Eve was revealed through Mary.

### 6

Thanks be to the Lord, dearest brothers, that we do not need to be taught what festival is being celebrated, since you come already instructed by devotion. For the prophetic and Gospel readings presented today have taught the same thing that your faith has taught us.

May our God therefore grant that, just as today, so at all times, your deeds may agree with the divine reading, and that you may possess this agreement in your conduct.

## SERMON XLVI. On Solomon

In all Ambrosian editions this little work bears the title of a booklet at its beginning, although it is truly a sermon in which three things that Solomon says are impossible to know are mystically explained.

Erasmus recognized its elegance and, at the same time, its difference from Ambrose’s style. Hermann, however, thinks that the latter feature is obscure; yet even the word “Psalmist,” which could also have been joined with “Arch-Pirate,” does not seem sufficiently Ambrosian to him. We, however, believe Erasmus’s judgment to be correct in both respects.
