As for Hermann’s opinion that the statement here—that Martha, the sister of Lazarus, was the woman healed from the flow of blood—is insufficiently well founded, one may consult Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 18, in Valesius’s edition; Sozomen, book V, chapter 21; and Philostorgius, book VII, section 3. Ambrose, too, carefully explains this healing in his *Commentary on Luke*, book VI, sections 57 and 58, although he does not mention Martha there.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

It is sufficiently remarkable, dearest brothers, that in this passage Solomon the prophet, wisest of all human beings, proposed that three things were impossible to know, and that there was still a fourth which he was unable to recognize: “The traces of a flying eagle, the ways of a serpent upon a rock, the paths of a ship sailing, and the ways of a man in his youth” (Proverbs 30:19).

That prophet Solomon declares that he does not know these things. Yet as soon as he had passed beyond the beginnings of childhood and entered the years of youth, when an age still weak and uncertain hesitates over which course of life to choose, he asked nothing else from God but wisdom. Already wise amid, as I have said, the first trials of life, he chose the love of those things that surpassed all others.

For in his Book of Wisdom he himself recalls that he had entreated the almighty Lord: “Give me,” he says, “the wisdom that sits beside your thrones” (Wisdom 9:4), “so that I may know the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements, the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things, the divisions and changes of the seasons, the courses of the year, and the arrangements of the stars, the natures of animals, and the tempers of beasts, the force of winds, and the thoughts of human beings, the differences of trees, and the powers of roots. For wisdom,” he says, “the artisan of all things, taught me” (Wisdom 7:21).

And elsewhere in the same book he says: “I called upon him, and the spirit of wisdom came into me” (Wisdom 7:7).

### 2

What, then, dearest brothers, is the reason that Solomon, so wealthy a possessor of wisdom, when he had understood everything that was hidden in the secret recesses of concealed arrangements, presents these things as impossible for him? He had obtained wisdom from God; he knew the entrance into the arrangement of the world: how this entire heaven that we see was suspended in lofty elevation; how the surrounding and diffused air was balanced in the middle by an even moderation; by what means the earth, slipping downward through its sluggish weight, remained in place; and by what principle the restless waves of the liquid element surged within the fixed limits of the shores.

He knew what the beginning of things was, what their end was, and what lay between. Nor were the divisions and changes of the seasons hidden from him. He understood how the mutual succession of the years followed as the sphere returned; for what reason the stars pursued their various courses, sometimes overtaking one another or suddenly following behind; from where their rising and setting came; and many other things that he had learned through the instruction of wisdom.

It is remarkable that he either could not know or could not see the things he says are impossible for him.

[Col. 0694B] 3. But because everything that has been gathered in the divine books through the announcements of the prophets has been reserved for its proper times, Solomon, before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, could rightly not know what the flying eagle was, what the serpent upon the rock was, what the sailing ship was, or what the way of a young man in his youth was.

The time had not yet come when the body would emerge from the shadow, or the truth from the figure. But for us, to whom our Lord Jesus Christ has shown that everything concerning him was written in the Law, for whom nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, and after no one other than Christ could open the sealed book with its seven seals, it has been permitted and granted that we may both see and know everything, as the Lord himself says: “Father, I confess to you that you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25).

And again: “To you,” he says, “it has been granted to know this mystery” (Luke 8:10).

I have recalled these things in order not so much to criticize Solomon for being unable to know as to say that the time had not yet come for him to know.

## CHAPTER II

### 4

But now, lest the proposed reading be delayed any longer, I have considered, with the favor of our gracious God, explaining briefly for you the matters that arise in this question:

“There are three things impossible for me to know, and a fourth that I do not recognize: the traces of a flying eagle, the ways of a serpent upon a rock, the paths of a sailing ship, and the ways of a man in his youth.”

For who, dearest brothers, has ever been able to know these things? Is it really easy for an eagle, suspended high above and swiftly raised by the movement of its wings, to leave visible traces of its beating and gliding, or to mark a path in the empty air, draw a line through its flight, and fix it in the fluid sky?

Who can detect the course of a ship in the waves? Who can understand its mark, by which embankments and boundaries it is carried? There is always frequent and restless change: as the following waves move, what has gone before is either overwhelmed or what follows is buried.

Who has recognized any sign of a serpent upon a rock, when stone is hard by nature and serpents slippery? Or how can the ways of a man in his youth be known, when it cannot be discerned from where he comes or where he goes?

These are the things that the prophet Solomon, wisest of men, said he could not know. Now, then, listen to what we should say about each of these matters.

### 5

In this passage we ought to understand the eagle as Christ our Lord, who, after his venerable resurrection—which taught the human race that it could return to life after death—flew back like an eagle to the Father, carrying off his prey with him: that is, the human being whom he had snatched from the jaws of the enemy.

This is the eagle whom the prophet Ezekiel reported that he saw among the living creatures joined to the wheels and bearing the mystical chariot in that fourfold throne and among the Cherubim: one living creature like a calf, another like a lion, a third like a human being, and a fourth like an eagle (Ezekiel 1:10ff.), just as John wrote in the Apocalypse that he had seen:

“The first living creature was like a calf, the second like a lion, the third like a human being, and the fourth like an eagle” (Revelation 4:7). [Note: [Col. 0695D] Thus the manuscripts and editions, except the Roman edition, which reads: “But another passage is necessary for treating the nature of these living creatures,” etc.]

But another passage is necessary for treating the nature of these living creatures. For now, let us explain what we have begun.

### 5*

This is the eagle of which it is written: “As an eagle protects its nest” (Deuteronomy 32:11)—that is, Christ protects the Church. And again: “In the shadow of your wings I will hope” (Psalm 56:2). And again: “Your youth will be renewed like that of an eagle” (Psalm 102:5).

For the nesting eagle, as it were, is always the mother of a single nest and never seeks another dwelling to produce offspring. When, after the eggs have been warmed and the young have emerged at the proper time, she raises the chicks while they are still featherless, holds them up before the face of the burning sun, and the one whose weak and feeble eyesight has yielded under the flashing impact of the rays is condemned by the mother’s judgment, separated from the company of its brothers, and cast down to the earth.

And just as this bird is hostile to serpents, which, while she carries them aloft through the air by the rowing of her wings, she tears and rips apart with her hooked beak and feet armed, as it were, with weapons; and when she devours them, extinguishes their harmful venom with her inner heat, so Christ our Lord loves one Church, like an eagle her nest. He protects it from the heat of persecutions beneath the shelter of his wings.

In the same way, he casts outside the Church those whose light of faith is weak, who, contaminated by worldly vices, cannot endure the fiery light of the Gospels.

### 6

And just as the eagle devours serpents and cooks their venom with her inner heat, so Christ our Lord, having struck down the dragon—that is, having torn apart the devil—extinguished, as though it were a deadly poison, the sin that held the human being liable to condemnation, when he assumed a human body. As the Apostle says: “And, through sin, he condemned sin in his flesh” (Romans 8:3); and elsewhere: “Although he was not a sinner, he committed sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

For this reason Moses also suspended the bronze serpent on wood in the wilderness. It was a precise type of Christ’s body, so that whoever looked upon it would not perish; for the human body had become, through transgression, a vessel of the serpent.

Likewise, elsewhere Moses threw his staff upon the ground, [Note: [Col. 0695D] The Roman edition reads: “Since it too was an image of Christ’s body and bore within itself a type of such great power, it swallowed up the power of all the Egyptians.” The manuscripts and other editions do not differ greatly from it in wording, but rather in the order of the words, which we follow.] and it was embodied in the likeness of a serpent. It too was an image of the Lord’s body; therefore it bore within itself a type of such great power that it swallowed up the power of all the Egyptians.

### 7

This, then, is what is meant by “the traces of a flying eagle.” For although, after his Passion and resurrection, our Lord ascended into heaven in the presence of the Apostles, what human being has such lofty and profound understanding that he could explain how such great majesty deigned either to come from heaven or to return there, when we are permitted to know only that he came or that he returned?

Who can understand how the Word came into the Virgin, so that she suddenly conceived; how the birth of a virgin brought forth such a blessed child; how God put on humanity, whom the whole world cannot either endure or contain?

This is what is meant by “the traces of a flying eagle”: the traces of Christ our Lord coming to earth and returning to the heavens cannot be grasped or recounted.

## CHAPTER III

**8.** “And the ways,” he says, “of a serpent upon a rock.” I have already said to your Charity that a gleaming, sinuous serpent, gliding with winding limbs, leaves no trace of its movement upon a rock, because the rock is hard. For the mark of this creature can be impressed only upon soft writing in the dust. Let us now see who this serpent is, or what the rock is upon which the serpent’s trace does not appear.

We must not doubt that this rock is our Lord. Thus the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); and the Psalmist: “You have set me on a rock,” he says (Ps. 60:3); and Moses in the song of Deuteronomy: “He fed them honey from the rock, and oil from the solid rock” (Deut. 32:13)—that is, he was to give them the sweetness of the Gospel, or the Holy Spirit through the anointing of chrism.

And elsewhere he says: “Blessed is he who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rock” (Ps. 136:9). This would certainly have been parricide, if that rock did not bear the figure of Christ’s body. For no one is blessed at a funeral who dashes his infants against a rock; rather, he is blessed because he joins them to the rock.

**[Note: [Col. 0696D]** So the old edition and the manuscripts; but the Roman edition had rearranged the passage as follows: “That he is the most cunning of all . . . it appears that he is the devil, who,” etc.]

**9.** I have therefore said that the rock means our Lord and Savior, as he is found throughout the Scriptures. That the serpent, by the very name, is the devil is apparent: he is “more cunning than all the beasts that are upon the earth,” that is, the devil. He is called a serpent because he creeps secretly and, insinuating himself subtly, tests the human mind. If he overcomes them, he entwines and plunges himself into the marrow and bones of human beings.

In the body of man, which almighty Christ God had assumed, he could imprint none of his wickedness, although he had dared to test it often, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me” (John 14:30); and elsewhere: “The enemy shall not prevail against him, and the son of iniquity shall do him no harm” (Ps. 88:23).

This, then, is the rock: the flesh of Christ, sprinkled with no wickedness of the enemy, in which no trace of the serpent—that is, of any sin—appears, as it is written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22).

## CHAPTER IV

**10.** Hear what he adds: “And the paths,” he says, “of a ship sailing.” We must likewise understand the ship as the Church, established upon the sea of this world. It is wearied by the frequent waves of the winds—that is, by the blows and lashes of temptations. The stormy waves, that is, the power of this age, strive to drive it upon the rocks.

Although it is often battered by the waves or storms, it can never suffer shipwreck, because Christ is raised upon its mast—that is, upon the cross; the Father sits in the stern; and the Spirit, the Paraclete, as helmsman guards the prow. Twelve rowers conduct it through the narrow straits of this world into harbor: that is, the twelve apostles and an equal number of prophets.

**11.** From there the caves of Montanus resound with the barking of a false song; he is girded about by two female prophetesses, Priscilla and Maximilla, like some Scylla surrounded by raging dogs. In this ship of the Church we pass safely beyond them.

From there we do not fall into the Charybdis of Photinus. From there we in no way plunge into that abyss, as did Dathan and Abiram—that is, into the depth of death represented by Ursacius and Valens. From there we do not fear Arius, the arch-pirate, who pursues us across the sea of this age in the manner of Pharaoh. We keep in heaven that star which led the Magi to Christ, through whom the kingdom of God, which will be the harbor of all blessings, awaits us.

From there that whale, Marcion, never swallowed us after casting us headlong from this ship of the Church. From there the pirate Sabellius did not capture us. From there the north wind will not be able to harm us, although violent blasts of Antichrist are destined to come from it, as it is written: “Evil shall blaze forth from the north” (Jer. 1:14).

From there we avoid the sandbanks of the Gentiles, dangerous heresies, and reefs concealed beneath the thin surface of the overlying water. For heretics, under the pretext of the Christian name, cover hidden rocks of unbelief with the deceptive confession of their mouths; and people, while they are believed to be Christians, run aground upon them.

**12.** This ship, then, is the Church. Although each day it encounters this world as a hostile sea, it is never dashed against a rock nor sunk into the depths.

We prove by divine testimonies that the ship signifies the Church, as it says: “There the ships of Tarshish passed” (Ps. 47:8); and elsewhere: “Against every ship of the sea” (Isa. 1:16). For there are churches of this world that place all their hope in what occurs in the present age, promising it to themselves not so much from God as from the powers of this world.

**13.** But when he says, “The ways of a ship sailing,” he signifies precisely that, in the time of persecution, she cannot in any way be overtaken, but is made vigorous through destruction and enriched through losses, as the Psalmist says in her person: “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:2).

For this reason she is compared in many places either to the sun or to the moon. Though struck, she is not moved; and if she is moved, she rises again.

**14.** “And the ways,” he says, “of a man in his youth.” This man is Christ our Lord, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man chosen by God among you, approved by mighty works, signs, and wonders” (Acts 2:22); and the Apostle: “That we may all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of Christ” (Eph. 4:16); and elsewhere: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

This is the man whose ways cannot be known in his youth. For who could estimate in his mind or comprehend how great were the works he performed while he dwelt on earth according to his humanity? What journeys of virtue did he undertake? Into what paths of beneficence toward the human race did he enter, when he restored strength to the feet of the lame; when he gave sight to the blind, or created it anew; when he granted speech to the mute and opened hearing to the deaf; when he dried up the abundant flow of blood in Martha; when he drove demons out of Mary; when he restored warmth to the body of Lazarus with his returned spirit, and what death had claimed for punishment, light received again into life?

What was that firm tread upon the waves? What was it that, after the multitude had been satisfied, more remained from the few loaves than had existed before? What was the poor provision of the Galilean wedding in wine, yet made precious by the Lord’s works? And what of the many other things mentioned in the Gospel, which, if they had all been written down, the world could not contain (John 21:25)?

Or, finally, what of his descent into hell, or his ascent into heaven? What of the fact that, during his Passion, the sun could not retain its ordinary fullness of light—not to mention the torn veil and the stone rolled away?

These, then, are the ways of his youth, which the prophet testified that he could not so much discover as declare himself unable to recount.

**15.** Here he also speaks of “the ways of a prostitute,” who, after she has been washed, says that she has done nothing wrong (Prov. 30:20).

This prostitute is a type of the Church, once established among the Gentiles and corrupted by the worship of idols. The violations of empty superstition had defiled her, and the multitude of false gods had made her an adulteress. She roamed through the unkempt groves and wooded sanctuaries, given over to luxury and enslaved to the pomp of the Gentiles, with wanton and shameful leaps and disorderly movements.

After our Lord Jesus Christ had bathed her in the pure fountain of baptism, she received through the grace of faith both cleansing from guilt and a new name. From a prostitute she becomes a virgin, because she has devoted herself to one Bridegroom.

For that prostitute Rahab of Jericho, who received the scouts of Jesus son of Nave as guests (Josh. 6:25), also bore a figure of the Church: she was marked by the sign of scarlet, whose color indicated the figure of Christ’s blood, and she escaped the destruction of the city, just as the Church, through Christ’s blood, fears no destruction of this world.

Thus the prophet says: “Take for yourself,” he says, “a prostitute as wife, and make children of prostitution” (Hos. 1:2). For everywhere, beloved brothers, the worship of idols is called prostitution, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “You permit your servants to commit fornication and to eat what has been sacrificed to idols” (Rev. 2:20).

Finally, whenever that once-noble city of the Hebrews, Jerusalem, had turned away from the truth and served idols, she was immediately called by the name of a prostitute, as Isaiah cries: “How has the faithful city, Zion, become a prostitute?” (Isa. 1:21).

This, then, is why Solomon says: “Such is the way of a prostitute, who, after she has been washed, says that she has done nothing wrong” (Prov. 30:20).

# SERMON XLVII

## On Proverbs 30, concerning the difference between Solomon and the other prophets

**[Col. 0699B]**

As soon as this fragment of a sermon appeared in the Roman edition, everyone noticed that it was not by Ambrose. It is not so easy, however, to bring its author out of obscurity—unless someone should infer that all these sermons belong to the same author because the passage about the adulterous woman is adapted to the Church in this sermon and in the preceding one, and is found explained in the same manner in Sermon 2, *On Almsgiving*, which we established in our censure of the omitted sermons to be Maximus’s.

To this we shall add that the Roman editors partly added and partly altered many things in this sermon, which we have restored from the Vatican manuscript.

**[Col. 0699C] 1.** Before the coming of Christ our Savior, many prophets, having conceived the Holy Spirit, announced future events. Among them Solomon is counted in his proper place and order, according to the times; but there is some difference between him and the others.

Therefore the others spoke only of the Spirit, whereas Solomon spoke both of the Spirit and of the wisdom joined to it. Finally, this is attested by the statement that we have heard recited from his words:

**[Note: [Col. 0699D]** The Roman edition: “the reading bears witness . . . .” While he professes ignorance of certain mysteries, he seems to indicate a distinction between the wisdom granted to him and the Spirit. He therefore says: “There are three things impossible for me to know, and a fourth that I do not understand: the paths of a ship sailing, the ways of a serpent upon a rock, and the traces of an eagle flying; and the fourth that I do not understand: the ways of a man in his youth. Such is the way of an adulterous woman, who, after she has done it, when she has been washed, says that she has done nothing wrong.”]

He says, then: “There are three things that I do not understand: the way of a ship at sea, the path of a serpent upon a rock, and the trace of an eagle flying in the air; the fourth that I cannot investigate is this: an adulterous woman who, after she has once been washed, believes that she has not sinned at all” (Prov. 30:19–20).

These words, considered in their ordinary sense, appear to have been gathered from common speech, but they contain holy mysteries throughout: three concerning Christ, and one concerning the Church.

**2.** For when he says that he cannot discover the way of a ship at sea, this statement is not without mystery. For who could gather among the waves the path that a ship had been able to traverse?

**[Note: [Col. 0699D]** The Roman edition: “Who could point out or prescribe amid the waves the path by which the ship had passed? For by its passage the ship cleaves the waves, and immediately the wave closes again, so that it can be seen that the ship passes, but it cannot be known where it has passed . . . . In order that it might be carried more securely among the waves, it is made of wood,” etc.]

For by its passage the ship cleaves and congeals the waves, so that it is known that it passes, but it is not seen where it has passed. It can be seen, but it cannot leave a trace.

Christ is the ship in which the souls of all believers embark. In order that it might possess complete stability amid the waves, it is constructed of wood and fastened with iron: that is, Christ upon the cross.

But he says that the ship leaves no trace because the powerful Word of God entered through the ear into the womb; having assumed humanity, he was born among human beings, and the Virgin Mary gave birth.

**[Note: [Col. 0699D]** The same edition: “The living and effective Word of God penetrates through the ear to the inward parts without injury, and, having assumed man, the Word is born among human beings without diminution of himself, and the Virgin Mary gives birth without corruption. The ship passes . . . traces remain, because he came,” etc.]

The ship passes through the sea without leaving any trace upon the waves. Christ came from heaven, was conceived through the ear, and was carried in the womb for the appointed time. Mary the Virgin remained such after she gave birth as she had been before the Word conceived through the ear.

**[Note: [Col. 0700D]** The Roman edition: “conceived through the ear and carried in the womb. Rightly . . . . he establishes a distinction between the Spirit and the wisdom infused into him, while by the Holy Spirit he indicates the mystery that he did not know through the wisdom granted to him. Finally, he would have noted . . . . upon the rock. It is common and belongs to all,” etc.]

Rightly, therefore, Solomon says that he does not understand the distinction between the Holy Spirit and wisdom, and he indicates the mystery that he does not understand.

**3.** Next he professes that he does not see the path of a serpent upon a rock. This is clear to all in the ordinary sense: in summer, when the earth is loosened into dust, a serpent emerging from its hiding place can mark out a path in the earth softened by the impression of its body. But when it reaches a rock, it does not make upon the stone what it made in the dust.

So, too, the serpent, the devil, found at the very beginning of the world a corruptible earth in Adam and Eve, who willingly listened to what he said (Gen. 3:1ff.). He made a path in their ears; he made one also in their feet, which had been forbidden the way to the tree; he made one in their hands, with which the fruits were touched; he made one in their sides, where marriage, not yet permitted, was celebrated.

**[Note: [Col. 0700D]** The same edition: “in their sides, since they celebrated what had not yet been granted to them as it could have been,” etc.]

Then the serpent was able to leave a trace in the primeval human being as in dust. He reached the rock, which is Christ—for Adam had been made such as Christ is from the womb of the Virgin—and saw the likeness covered by a body, but could not recognize the majesty.

**[Note: [Col. 0700D]** The Roman edition: “Adam was formed from clay, just as Christ is from the Virgin’s womb. He saw the likeness of a human being, but, with the body covering it, could not recognize the majesty.”]

He was also able to approach Christ when he was being tested; but Christ neither obeyed nor became angry, because anger is the devil’s work. When the devil’s words were despised, the serpent left no trace upon the rock.

**[Col. 0701A] 4.** As a third matter, he testifies that he did not understand—

**[Note: [Col. 0701A]** The Roman edition: “he testifies that he did not understand, namely, the traces of an eagle flying.”]

An eagle is understood to be Christ, who descended to the earth in his flight. This species of animal is not nourished unless the mother’s chastity has first been established, so that, with its eyes open and without blinking, it may look upon the entire sun.

Rightly, then, this animal is compared with the Savior. When it wishes to seize something, it does not walk upon the ground by its tracks, but chooses a lofty place. So Christ, suspended upon the high cross, made a thundering and terrible assault upon hell in his flight, seized the saints, and returned to the heights.

**[Note: [Col. 0701A]** The same Roman edition: “He made an assault from the underworld . . . . As for what he says about the ways of a man in his youth and the adulterous woman, this woman . . . . went about as a prostitute.”]

**5.** As for the fourth matter, which he speaks of concerning the adulterous woman, this woman is understood as the Church. Once she followed idols and prostituted herself after foreign gods, but when she came to know the truth, she abandoned the seats—

**[Note: [Col. 0701A]** The Roman edition: “which she had formerly chosen. Once she has been washed from sin by baptism, free from offenses, she says that she has never sinned.” The manuscript, however, reads as in the text, although in place of *sedes* we would prefer *sordes* (“filth”).]

—which she had formerly gathered. Once she has been washed in baptism, freed from them, she believes that she has never sinned. She becomes clean and new, laying aside the way of life of the world. She dies to the devil and is reborn to God.

**[Note: [Col. 0701B]** After the words “is reborn to God,” the Vatican manuscript ends. The Roman edition continues: “as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: ‘Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new’” [2 Cor. 5:17]. “Rightly, therefore, she says that she has done nothing wrong, because through the sacrament of regeneration her sins have been so abolished as though they had never been committed; nor are they in God’s memory, as the prophet Ezekiel testifies, saying: ‘He shall live and shall not die; for none of all his sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him.’ For this purpose Christ gave himself over to death, as the Apostle writes to the Ephesians, so that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle.”]

# SERMONS ON THE SAINTS

**[Col. 0701]**

# SERMON XLVIII

## On the feast of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr

We have committed this hitherto unpublished sermon to the press from three manuscripts, namely the Vallisclara, Remigius, and Regius manuscripts, all of which attribute it to our Ambrose. Although we are convinced that it is not the work of the holy Doctor, we nevertheless thought this little composition too elegant to leave unreclaimed from the moths.

**[Col. 0701C] 1.** While throughout the whole world the virginal flower of Mary binds unfading crowns and preserves, with stainless devotion, the palace of chastity bearing the scepter, integrity persevered toward the palm to such a degree that, among young women, it seized the trophy of holiness and, following in the footsteps of the Virgin Mother, reached the heavenly bridal chamber.

This is why Agnes declares that she has been betrothed with the ring of faith and cries out that she is bound by love.

**[Note: [Col. 0701D]** The Vallisclara manuscript: “O how wondrous it is,” etc.]

O virgin, what an example of your love you have handed down for virgins to imitate! What a holy answer you have given to virginal hearts by despising the riches of the world, abhorring the desires of the flesh, and loving only the beauty of Christ!

**2.** Come to the girl, girls, and learn what flames she kindled in her heart during the years of childhood for the love of Christ. She says that she keeps faith with her lover and longs only for the body of him who, out of love for all, did not refuse the destruction of death.

Learn, virgins of Christ, the love burning in a young girl and rejecting all the riches of the world as dung. For this reason the examples of the saints are handed down in writing: so that each person, according to sex and age, may hold to the measure of his or her purpose; and just as virgins strive through a virgin, so wives through a wife may strive to overcome the world for the love of Christ, rejecting the world’s delights through firmness of spirit and not shrinking from its hardships, so that they may attain everlasting pleasures and eternal joys.

**[Note: [Col. 0701D]** The same manuscript: “refusing sweet things, through austerities to delights,” etc.]

**3.** In saying this we do not condemn the chaste relations of married people; rather, we adorn the perseverance of virgins. For virginity is not to be set above evil things, but is to be preferred to the best things. What is purer than the pure and holier than the holy does not need to be praised by condemning evil things.

Therefore let holy marriages follow: wives devoted to religion and instructed by the divine writings should imitate Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, Anna, Susanna, and Sephora. But the virgins of Christ should follow only the Virgin Mother of the Virgin Light.

**[Note: [Col. 0702D]** The Remigius manuscript: “It is not to be placed beneath evil things,” etc.]

**4.** Agnes, most blessed, her attendant, raised up a great example of chastity when she preferred virginity to life, expelled every earthly love from herself through heavenly love, seized the trophy of Christ’s cross, and fought and conquered, armed by faith rather than by iron, both against lusts and against every form of torture.

At last, she looks upon the man who flatters her and refuses him; upon the man who threatens her, and she despises him; she looks upon the fire and laughs. She does not know how to love anything that passes away. And while she loves virginity exceedingly, she fears neither mockery, flames, punishments, nor executioners; finally, she did not even tremble before the sword of the raging persecutor.

The virgin is compelled to receive bodily adornments, but she refuses, because she had already received the adornments of the mind. And because she did not strive to please through the elegance of the human body, fearing to displease the Lord through the ugliness of her soul, she displayed inwardly, through faith, the brightness of her mind and the beauty of her soul, which she cultivated.

The more she knew that she made her soul beautiful, the more she was ashamed to be beautiful in her flesh. She strove to displease carnal people in the appearance of her flesh as much as she endeavored to please Christ and his angels.

**5.** The young man is disturbed at being despised by the girl. Thinking that he could win her favor with gifts, he brings gold, jewels in abundance, garments, and costly estates. But because the love of Christ has no price in money, the most sacred virgin remained steadfast in her condition even to the shedding of blood, since Christ had betrothed her with his own blood.

The wealth therefore returns to the one who desired her, while the unshaken virginity once offered to Christ endures.

Learn, virgins of Christ, the examples of maidenly discipline. Reject with complete determination the little gifts offered by men under the appearance of piety, and refuse them with every joy as though they were the bites of a rabid dog.

From one from whom you have received nothing that makes you fear God, do not accept what makes you love the world. Accept, accept, virgin—but accept what advances eternal love. Whenever you receive wealth from a man, receive it in such a way that you recognize yourself as Christ’s bride. He sees within your mind what you do and observes with what desire you accompany his virgins.

**6.** See, then, how Agnes follows Mary. After the insults, she could fear no punishment utterly, for even a brothel of disgrace was made a place of prayer for her. And where the devil had prepared for her the shame of corruption, there the Lord caused her to receive the crown and palm of her virginity.

This is to conquer enemies in their own dwelling: a virgin is led captive into the inner chambers of the king of lust; the king himself is conquered by the virgin whom he had captured; and he leaves defeated together with the virgin’s triumph. For the one who had held another is held; the one who had dragged another is dragged; the one who thought he would kill himself is killed.

**7.** Finally, to prove that the devil was then defeated by the virgin, let us recall the deed of that young man whom the enemy had armed against Agnes’s childhood in such a way that he ordered her to be dragged naked to a brothel through the crowd, under the voice of a heralding leader inviting the people to lust.

No one can doubt that this leader was the devil’s agent; and once the leader was defeated, it is known that the people were overcome as well. When the people and their leader had been defeated, it is evident to all that the tyrant was held captive.

It is clear that the devil was defeated whenever he took up arms against the virgin. For the stripped virgin is covered by her hair; naked before wicked men, she was clothed by good angels; condemned to a brothel of shame, she appeared in the bosom of chastity.

A place that had belonged to lost souls became an oratory of angels. Where chastity had always suffered shipwreck, virginity was crowned.

Finally, the people whom the herald had invited to lust were captured by the virgin; and those whom the devil brought to her polluted, she sent away from herself cleansed. For each one entered separately, and each awaited another’s entrance.

**[Note: [Col. 0703D]** “He remained fixed in place and waited.”]

When he did not believe that the one who left would be clean, he showed himself unclean. But having entered for lust, he was held by the virgin’s merits to adore the Lord; and he departed from there a servant of God, though he had entered as the devil’s servant.

**[Note: [Col. 0704D]** The Remigius manuscript lacks: “and as many became worshipers of Christ . . . as the devil had thought he had found corrupters of the virgin.”]

Thus as many worshipers of Christ were made as the devil had thought he had found corrupters of the virgin.

**8.** The young man therefore remained, he who had been the author of this rejection. He who thought he would overcome the defender of the virgin, when he challenged her radiance toward luxury, lost the life he seemed to possess and found the death he had sought.

Tears follow laughter, and lamentations put an end to insults. The virgin sees the judge grieving, and the man whom she had previously despised when he threatened her, she now hears as he begs.

As soon as she began to pray for the dead man, she raised from the dead and restored to safety the one who had been condemned to death; she summoned to joy the one who had been hurled into mourning. For the man who had died in incest rises chaste, and he becomes a preacher of chastity who had been its persecutor.

**9.** At this the sacrilegious men are disturbed in the temples. Since they do not fear Christ performing these miracles, they stir up a revolt of the base populace, so that reason, which urged an end to the sedition, driven out by shouting, could find no place in the minds of the people.

The father of the son who had been raised departed in grief and, as we read, left a substitute behind amid the raging crowds.

They therefore prepared crackling flames for the virgin body. But the body that had overcome the fires of lust found refreshment amid the flames; and she who had entered the pyre to burn began, through holy virginity, to grow cold, so that virginity might learn that flames and fires could have no power over it at all.

**10.** Do not suppose that those whom the fire consumed for the name of Christ perished. When you read that Elijah was carried away by fire and that the three boys were in no way consumed amid the flames; when you recall that Lawrence was consumed upon the gridiron and recognize that Agnes, like Thecla, escaped the flaming masses, do not imagine that there was any difference of faith among them.

For one faith exercised God’s saints in their passion and made them victorious in both cases through different kinds of glory. The martyr who was consumed rejoices, and the victor who escaped rejoices. God made Isaiah a martyr by cutting him in pieces, while he proved Daniel a most excellent confessor, who despised the fury and bites of lions.

By this he showed that both were victors over the devil: one dies and triumphs; the other escapes and reigns.

**11.** Come now, virgin, to the bridal chamber you sought, and for the love of the Bridegroom admit the sword of the executioner, so that unstained virginity may prove you Christ’s bride, and an approved confession may mark you as a martyr.

Blessed is the company of virgins who strive to follow the footsteps of your confession. For those who overcome the enemy with you in the world will have a crown with you in heaven.

Just as participation in eternal reward appeared to you when you followed in Mary’s footsteps, so we believe that eternal joys will not be denied to those who imitate you.

# SERMON XLIX

## On the feast of Saints Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla

The feast of the martyrs in whose honor this sermon was delivered is announced in the Roman Martyrology on the fifth day before the Nones of April. Concerning this entry, Cardinal Baronius observes in his Notes that this very sermon was wrongly attributed to Ambrose, since it belongs to Maximus. We gladly add our judgment to his.

**1.** Today is the feast of the most blessed Cantius, Cantianus, and Cantianilla.

**[Note: [Col. 0705D]** The Gallican manuscript: “of the most blessed Cabellus with the three little Cantii,” etc. [The reading is uncertain.]]

How fitting and pleasing it is that three martyrs are called by almost one name! Nor is it surprising that those who are alike in suffering should be alike in name; that those who have one calling before God should have one designation among human beings.

**[Note: [Col. 0705D]** The Gallican manuscript: “one confession.”]

For they were called together by the Lord. They did not suffer at different times, one after another, but all endured martyrdom together in the same blow.

This was granted to them by Christ’s parental affection, so that those who agreed in name might correspond in merits; those who were brothers by blood might also become brothers in holiness; and those whose limbs were animated by the substance of one body might have their souls crowned by the confession of the same faith.

**2.** The history of these blessed persons reports that, at the time of their passion, when the persecutor was seeking them, they mounted a vehicle and, with mules yoked together, wished to withdraw.

**[Note: [Col. 0705D]** The Gallican manuscript: “They wished to go ahead, and when they wished to travel toward the walls of the city.”]

As they were traveling not far from the city walls, one of the animals that had been harnessed beneath the vehicle suddenly collapsed.

**[Col. 0705C]**

Thus they were seized by the persecutors—

**[Note: [Col. 0705D]** The same manuscript: “seized for punishment.”]

—and held for punishment.

**3.** We must recognize how glorious this event was and how it was arranged by divine providence. For God always brings those whom he has chosen, as victors, into the palace of the heavenly kingdom by an exalted conveyance.

Just as Elijah, with a chariot attached, ascended as it were into heaven (2 Kings 2:11), so these men, with a vehicle brought up, reached martyrdom. As the chariot raised Elijah to rest, so it carried these men to glory.

And although that chariot was fiery, this one should not be considered inferior, because the former carried one prophet, while this one supported three martyrs.

**4.** But someone may say: “The fiery chariot carried him more gloriously than an earthly one.” This too was plainly not lacking to the holy men. For just as a fiery chariot carried Elijah, so fiery faith already carried the martyrs.

I say that Christ carried them—Christ who is light, who is fire, of whom it is written: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:29).

**5.** Therefore, when the persecutor pressed the blessed men of whom we speak, they mounted a vehicle. Why? To flee? Far from it. Not to flee, but to reach martyrdom more quickly; not to hide, but to show all who passed by more plainly that they were Christians.

Moreover, they could have hidden more secretly among the crowds in the city, and each of them could have entrusted himself more safely to flight in different directions. But when a man, after gathering a company, setting out the vehicles, and arranging the equipment, goes forth along the public road, this cannot be called flight; it is a departure.

The holy men, placed as it were in a triumphal chariot, testified by this deed, saying:

**[Note: [Col. 0706D]** The Gallican manuscript: “saying: ‘Behold, we go before you; why are you sitting still?’”]

“Behold the persecutor; behold, we are setting out; behold, we are going ahead. Why do you sit still? Why do you delay? Follow our footsteps. For we do not wish to seem to have been unwillingly led to punishment, since we declare that we are going ahead to glory.”

# SERMON L

## On the feast of Saint John the Baptist

**[Col. 0706B]**

The comparisons made in this sermon between the birth of Christ and that of his forerunner are found in certain sermons of Augustine, from which the author may have transferred them here. Although this author is not as far removed from Ambrose’s style as many others are, we nevertheless think that sufficient difference can be observed in it for us to reject it as the work of the holy Bishop.

**1.** In praising the holy and most blessed John the Baptist, whose feast we celebrate today, I do not know what I should proclaim above all: whether that he was born wondrously, or that he was killed even more wondrously.

He was born in prophecy; he was slain in truth. By his birth he announced the Savior’s coming; by his death he condemned Herod’s incest.

For this holy and righteous man, who had been generated by promise beyond the ordinary birth of human beings—

**[Note: [Col. 0706D]** The German manuscript: “beyond the birth of all human beings, from promise.”]

—earned this from God: that he should not depart from the world by the common death he shared with others, but should lay down the body he had received through the Lord’s gift by confessing the Lord.

**2.** John therefore fulfilled God’s will in every respect, because he was both born and died for the Lord’s work.

To recall briefly the course of his birth: when his father Zacharias and his mother Elizabeth were exhausted by old age and enjoyed no offspring; when the most fruitful time for bearing children had passed them by, so that even their hopes of receiving a child had already failed, they were granted a sudden promise through an angel. The holy Gabriel announced that John would be born, saying:

“Do not be afraid, Zacharias; behold, your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1:13).

**3.** “Your prayer has been heard,” he says. From this we understand that Zacharias begot John more by his righteousness in prayer than Elizabeth received him through procreation.

**[Note: [Col. 0706D]** All editions, together with two manuscripts, read *procurando susceperit* (“received him by obtaining”); the Lyon manuscript reads more suitably *procreando susceperit* (“received him by procreating”).]

This, I say, shows us that John was created by supplication, not by pleasure.

For when the inward parts of the maternal womb had grown cold through old age, and the exhausted limbs of the body had lost the grace of fertility, against the impossibility of the body and against the sterility of the womb, Elizabeth’s uterus swelled at Zacharias’s prayers, and she conceived John not by nature but by grace.

**[Note: [Col. 0707D]** “Hence it was necessary that the holy son should be born . . . .” is lacking in the German manuscript.]

It was therefore necessary that the holy son should be born who was generated not so much by embraces as by prayers.

### 4

We ought to marvel less that John merited such great grace at his birth; for the precursor and forerunner of Christ ought to have something resembling the birth of the Lord and Savior. For the Lord is begotten of a Virgin, while John is born of a barren woman: [Note: The old edition has, “he from a young woman, this one from one already wearied”; the Roman edition, the Lyon manuscript, and Theodore have the reading in the text, except that the Roman edition gives “she is immaculately brought forth, this one,” etc.; the German manuscript differs from Theodore only in preferring “virgin” to “young woman.”] the one is brought forth from an immaculate young woman, the other is born from an old woman already exhausted. His birth, therefore, also possesses something of glory and wonder. Although a woman’s birth may seem less noble than that of a virgin, just as we marvel at Mary because a virgin gave birth, so we marvel at Elizabeth because an old woman bore a child.

### 5

I think this event contains some mystery: John, who bore the figure of the Old Testament, was to be born from an old woman whose blood had already grown cold; but the Lord, who would preach the Gospel of the heavenly kingdom, was to emerge from the flower of a fervent young woman. Mary, conscious of her virginity, marvels at the fetus enclosed in her womb; Elizabeth, conscious of her old age, is ashamed that her womb has been burdened by pregnancy [Note: The editions have, “the womb burdened by the child”; the manuscripts more correctly read, “the womb burdened by childbearing.”] For the evangelist says: “She kept herself hidden for five months” (Luke 1:24).

### 6

But what is more wondrous than this: the same archangel Gabriel performs the service of announcing both births? He comforts the unbelieving Zechariah and encourages the believing Mary. The former, because he doubted, lost his voice; the latter, because she immediately believed, conceived the saving Word.

### 7

Nor should this be passed over in silence among John’s praises: before he was born, he already prophesied; while he was still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he confessed the coming of Christ—not by his voice, which he could not yet use, but by his joy. For Elizabeth says to holy Mary: “As soon as the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the child in my womb leaped for joy” (ibid., 44). John rejoices before he is born, and before he recognizes the appearance of the world with his eyes, he already recognizes the Lord of the world in spirit. In this I think the prophetic utterance is fulfilled which says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5). Therefore we should not wonder that, though shut up in prison by Herod [Note: So the manuscripts; all the editions, however, read, “sent into prison, shut up,” etc.], he continually proclaimed Christ to his disciples, since, while still shut up in the womb, he had already preached the same Lord by his movements.

## SERMON LI  
### On the preeminence of the same holy John the Baptist

[Col. 0708A]

That this sermon is by the same author as the preceding one may be inferred both from its style and from the fact that it immediately follows it in the old edition and in the manuscripts. Moreover, what is said from number 5 to the end concerning John’s greatness may have been imitated from Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, book II, number 110, and worked out by the author’s own ingenuity; but it seems that the author borrowed this very passage from the person who pieced together Sermon 197 of the Augustinian Appendix, where this fragment appears complete. For the two works do not seem to have come from the same hand, and our sermon is less of a patchwork than the one mentioned above.

### 1

As I am about to celebrate today the birthday of Saint John the Baptist, beloved brothers, I would prefer to remain silent and restrain by silence both my labor and my lack of skill. But the very power of his name does not allow me to keep silent: for the utterance of his name presses upon the hidden places of our heart, unlocks the secrets of our silence, and compels admiration to disclose what is concealed by dissimulation. If his father Zechariah received his voice when he named him (Luke 1:64), how much more should we obtain eloquence when we praise him? And if his father’s mouth opened when John was born into the world, how much more does John make our mouths fruitful when he suffers for Christ?

### 2

For when his father Zechariah had been punished with the silence of dumbness by the angel Gabriel because of his unbelief concerning John’s birth, and for a long time, mute and deprived of speech, had concealed the secrets of his mind, suddenly, when his son John was born, a dispute arose among the relatives about what name he should be called. Tablets were therefore brought to the father, so that he himself might write the name according to his own choice, and might say in writing what he could not say aloud. Then, wonderfully, as soon as he took up the writing tablets in order to set the stylus to them, he loosened his tongue, anticipated the letters with speech, and did not merely attest to John’s name but uttered it (ibid., 20).

### 3

Consider, then, the merit of the holy Baptist: he restored a voice to his father and eloquence to the priest. Consider, I say, his merit: John released the mouth that the angel had bound; the child unsealed what Gabriel had closed. Yet he himself is also an angel, as it is written of him: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Malachi 4:1). Look, then, at John: such is the power of his name that its utterance restored a voice to the mute, piety to the father, and a priest to the people. Before, there was a silent tongue, a father deprived of a son, and a man deprived of his office; but when John is born, he suddenly becomes father, prophet, and even pontiff. His use of speech is restored, affection receives offspring, and his office recognizes its priest.

### 4

Since, then, such is the power of his name, although we may wish to be silent when we are about to speak of him, we cannot remain silent. For John himself is called “the voice of one crying.” Who, then, can praise the voice and remain silent? Who can marvel at the cry and be mute? For he says of himself: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23). Notice what he said: he did not merely say, “I am a voice,” but “the voice of one crying”—so that the voice might penetrate the ears in order to bring about faith, while the cry might shake the hearts; so that the voice might proclaim the kingdom, and the cry threaten judgment.

### 5

Great, therefore, is John, whose greatness the Savior himself also attests, saying: “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Luke 7:28). He surpasses all, rises above everyone, precedes the prophets, and transcends the patriarchs; and everyone who is born of a woman is inferior to John.

### 6

But we must carefully inquire why the Lord said this—namely, “among those born of women”—rather than saying, “Among the sons of men there has not arisen anyone greater than John,” since women plainly cannot have children without men. He said this because the offspring of women are more numerous than those of men: for there is a son of a woman who is not a son of a man. Thus holy Mary bore a son who did not have a human father; for the Lord is the son of a woman and is not the son of a man, as the Apostle says: “Made of a woman, made under the Law” (Galatians 4:4) [Note: The Theodore manuscript reads, “Born of a woman.”]—so that he who had a mother on earth might have a Father in heaven. Therefore, in praise of John, the generation of the more fertile sex is mentioned, so that no one’s birth might be excluded from his comparison.

### 7

Someone may perhaps say: If John is greater among those born of women, is he then also greater than the Savior? God forbid. John was born of a woman, whereas Christ was born of a virgin; the former was poured forth from the recesses of a corruptible womb, while the latter was born from the flower of an undefiled womb. The Lord’s birth is therefore compared with John’s birth so that the Lord might not appear to stand outside the truth of human condition [Note: The same manuscript reads, “so that the Lord might not be outside nature.”]

## SERMON LII  
### On the life of the same holy John the Baptist

Although this sermon was cited by Gratian and Ivo under Ambrose’s name, it displays nothing of Ambrose. Nor does it have any affinity with the preceding sermons, as is clear from its beginning and from the fact that it is separated from them by a great distance in the Gallican manuscript. Indeed, anyone who examines it more attentively will find that it consists of fragments taken from various places: what is read here concerning Abel’s crying blood is found below in Sermon 59, while the discussion here of concubines, monks, and clerics appears to have been taken from Sermons 292 and 293 of the Augustinian Appendix and several others.

### 1

Last Sunday, when we asked pardon for our silence, we said that, for the sake of the common salvation, even when priests are silent, evangelical teaching does not remain silent, and that divine utterance supplies what their silence lacks. For divine Scripture always speaks and cries out, as it is written concerning John: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23). John did not cry out only at that time when, announcing the Lord and Savior to the Pharisees, he said: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Matthew 3:3). He cries out in us even today, and by the thunder of his voice shakes the wilderness of our sins. Although he has fallen asleep in the holy death of martyrdom, his voice nevertheless lives; for even today he says to us: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” Divine Scripture always cries out and speaks.

### 2

Thus God also says to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Genesis 4:10). There is, of course, no voice belonging to blood; yet the blood that was innocently shed is said to cry out—not so much by its voice as by the cause for which it was shed—and to appeal to the Lord, not by the presentation of words but by indignation at the deed committed. It accuses its guilt not so much through verbal statements as by fastening condemnation upon the conscience itself. For although an evil deed, once expressed in words, may perhaps receive an excuse, if conscience recalls it, it cannot be excused. [Note: All the editions read, “For conscience [its] own guilt”; the Lyon manuscript has a lacuna followed by “its guilty party.”] Conscience always silently convicts and judges its guilty party, without contradiction.

### 3

Today, then, John cries out and says: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” We are therefore commanded to prepare the Lord’s way—not a raised roadway, but purity of faith. The Lord travels an earthly path, but he proceeds through the hidden places of the mind. If anything on this way is rough in conduct, harsh through cruelty, or polluted in manner of life, we are commanded to cleanse it, level it, and set it in order, so that when the Lord comes he may not stumble over anything in us, but rather find a road purified by chastity, made easy by faith, and raised up by almsgiving. The Prophet describes the Lord as accustomed to travel by such a route, saying: “Prepare a way for him who ascends over the setting sun; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 67:5).

### 4

But let us see how John himself, who commands us to prepare the way for the Lord, prepared that way for the Savior. In every respect, when Christ came, he arranged and directed the path of his own way. For he was indeed fasting, humble, frugal, and a virgin. The Evangelist, describing all these virtues, says: “John himself had his clothing of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey” (Matthew 3:4–5). What greater humility can there be in a prophet than, rejecting soft garments, to be clothed in the roughness of hair? What more devoted faith than to be girded with a belt and always ready for every service of obedience? What more illustrious abstinence than, spurning the delicacies of this life, to feed on shrill locusts and wild honey? [Note: The old edition has, “What greater cause of humility”; the Roman edition and the Lyon manuscript have, “What greater humility.”]

### 5

Since all these things were useful to the prophet, I think that prophecy was contained in these very things. For when Christ’s herald wore clothing woven from the roughness of camel’s hair, what else does this signify except that Christ himself, when he came, would use the garment of a human body, which had been thickened by the roughness of sins? And what else does it signify except that, surrounded as though by the skins of the most unclean beast—that is, by the coverings of the Gentile people—he himself would bear its deformity? What else does the leather belt demonstrate except that this fragile flesh of ours, which before Christ’s coming ruled over vices, was after his coming restrained for virtue? That which before had been enlarged into fatness by indulgence would now be reduced to skin by abstinence.

### 6

How blessed, too, is the account we read of his end: namely, that the king’s daughter, a female musician, sought his head after that hostile pleasure [Note: The Lyon manuscript has, “after that hostile pleasure.”] What wonder if a dancing girl killed a prophet (Mark 6:27)? We know that luxury is always hostile to righteousness, and that iniquity continually persecutes the truth. A great mystery is contained in this event: for that dancing girl must be compared with the synagogue, which, while indulging in luxury, killed Christ. That this dancing girl is the synagogue the Lord declares to the Jews: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matthew 11:17).

### 7

Why John’s head was removed from his body is evident. John, as Scripture establishes, bore the figure of the Law; concerning the Lord we read: “The head of a man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:3). Therefore, when his head is removed from John’s body, Christ is in a certain sense separated from the Jews who practice the Law. The Law remained for them without a Savior, lifeless and mutilated; for from the moment they began to be without a head, the Jews no longer understand divine things.

### 8

Therefore, he makes a way for the Lord who, among the other virtues of self-restraint, does not exceed the bounds of marriage and does not stain the prescribed limit of wedlock by adulterous intercourse. For there are some who, although they have taken wives according to the law, contrary to the law of God associate concubines with themselves. They do not understand that, by contracting marriages, they have bound themselves with their own bonds: for the man who has taken a wife according to the law professes that he will do nothing contrary to the law. He therefore establishes himself as guilty who, taking an adulteress to himself, exceeds the right promised by his marriage.

### 9

But someone says: “I do not have a wife, and therefore I have taken a little maidservant as my companion.” Hear what Scripture says to Abraham: “Cast out the maidservant and her son; for the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (32, question 4, “Let someone say”). If, then, the son of a maidservant is not an heir, he is not a son either. Why, then, seek such a union, from which a son born cannot be heir either of succession (Genesis 21:10) or of blood? For he cannot share in an inheritance who does not possess the privilege of legitimate origin. Why, I ask, seek such a liaison, from which sons born are witnesses not of marriage but of adultery? Why receive illegitimate children of this sort, who bring shame rather than honor to their father? Scripture says: “The children of adulterers shall not be initiated, and the offspring of an unlawful bed shall perish” (Wisdom 3:16). If your woman is endowed with such character that she deserves to share your life, let her also deserve the name of wife. Grant your concubine freedom and the name of wife, lest you be an adulterer rather than a husband.

### 10

The Christian also makes a way for the Lord who offers him the faithful service of his profession and preserves the chastity he has promised, both in mind and in body. For there are many who, professing the solitary life, cannot remain solitary but seek companions for themselves—and would that they were brothers. [Note: The Lyon manuscript reads, “I have also found a Christian,” etc.] You have found a Christian monk who cannot get along with a brother but gets along more willingly with a sister; who does not follow an elder offering useful admonitions but follows a young woman who laughs in an unseemly manner. Even if his body is pure, his soul cannot be pure.

### 11

The cleric also makes a way for the Lord who lives according to the Gospel and obeys the priest in all things. For some, being insufficiently submissive, are displeased when they are rebuked by their elders. They say: “The bishop is excessively angry; he ought to be more patient.” Hear, then, excellent cleric: You demand patience from the priest, but do not demand discipline from yourself? Do you not know that I have sometimes been permitted to rebuke for the sake of salvation, while you have never been permitted to sin? The Apostle says: “Reprove in season and out of season; rebuke” (1 Timothy 4:2). Be submissive, therefore, to the priest in all things, if you wish him to be gentle with you. [Note: The Lyon manuscript reads, “You demand patience from the priest, but do not demand it from yourself,” etc.]

## SERMON LIII  
### On the birthday of the holy apostles Peter and Paul

This sermon contains absolutely nothing of Ambrose’s style. Although it is inscribed with the name of the holy Bishop in some manuscripts, in the older ones it is attributed to no one. It might perhaps be thought to belong to an ancient author because it speaks of numerous conversions of pagans, unless these are more appropriately referred to the preaching of the apostles.

### 1

Celebrating today the birthday of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, beloved brothers, we ought to refresh ourselves with various dishes and celebrate so great a feast with great joy. [Note: The sentence “For who would not celebrate the solemnity of such men with great joy?” is absent from all our manuscripts.] For who would not celebrate the solemnity of such men with great joy? Who would not display great preparations for the solemnity of such men, so that the more he spends, the more he might confirm that he loves the apostles?

### 2

Nevertheless, we do not need our own expense for our refreshment, for on his birthday Saint Peter himself refreshes us. His vessel is filled with every kind of provision—the vessel that was brought down to him from heaven when he was hungry. Therefore, whoever is hungry, like Peter, is himself refreshed together with Peter. Why, then, should we prepare our own meal when we are filled by an apostolic dish? Why should we seek earthly foods when we possess heavenly provisions? For Saint Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles that, after prayer, when Peter was hungry around the sixth hour, a certain splendid vessel like a linen cloth was brought down to him from heaven, and in it were all kinds of four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the air. And the Lord said to him: “Peter, rise; kill and eat” (Acts 10:11ff.).

### 3

Behold Peter, who says elsewhere: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). Now the vessel of his banquet is more splendid than silver, so that he who had rejected the appearance of silver for Christ’s sake [Note: The Vind. and Mich. manuscripts read, “who had rejected a gift of silver.”] might be enriched through Christ with the radiance of silver. When Peter is about to dine, there are no cooks’ preparations and no attentions from servants; but, what is better, divine services are not lacking. By a more useful exchange, what is lacking on earth abounds in heaven for the holy man. In order for Peter to be refreshed, the storeroom is not carefully unlocked; heaven itself is immediately opened. [Note: The same manuscripts omit: “We read in Scripture ... supplies.” They also omit, below, “Peter is rightly said to have ascended.”] We read in Scripture that holy Elijah was fed in the wilderness by ravens serving him (1 Kings 17:6). How much better is Peter served, to whom not a small morsel is offered by a foul bird, but an entire banquet is supplied by a multitude of angels!

### 4

After prayer, then, Peter is hungry (Acts 10:10). It is astonishing that hunger follows prayer for a holy man, since hunger is usually driven away by prayer, and the hungry soul is nourished only by supplications. But I think that after prayer Peter was not hungry for human food but for salvation; he was not tormented by bodily want but afflicted by the poverty of believers. For when the faithless and ungrateful Jewish people did not believe in Christ while Peter preached, Peter in a certain sense endured hunger in the exercise of his office. For the one who does not attain the fruit of his labor suffers hunger.

### 5

He therefore hastily ascends to the upper room for prayer (ibid., 9). Peter is rightly said to have ascended to the upper room for prayer, because whenever a holy person prays, leaving behind lowly and earthly things, he is lifted up to the heights of the mind, carried aloft, and made near to heaven by holy thought. There, while he was hungry—that is, while he was thinking in the higher place of his heart about the salvation of the Jewish people—a vessel full of animals of various kinds was offered to him, as though divinity were saying: “You hunger only for the Jews; behold, I satisfy the hunger of your faith by the diversity of all nations.” For the various animals gathered into one vessel signify the gathering of various nations into one Church. That Church shines with the brightness of linen in his splendid vessel, since it has neither spot nor wrinkle. In it the first animal from the Gentiles, the centurion Cornelius, is offered to God.

### 6

From this vessel, then, Peter refreshes us today. When we see crowds of Gentiles hastening to the faith of Christianity, we rejoice together with the apostles. Those whose birthday we celebrate today are not dead, for, having been reborn, they plainly live; they have become participants in Christ, who is the life of all. Although their bodies were struck down by suffering, the order of life has not been interrupted [Note: The editions together with the Lyon manuscript read, “the order of the living”; the other manuscripts more elegantly read, “the manner of living.” Below, the Roman edition alone reads, “who is the bread, the life of all.”] For continually they give thanks to God and offer praises to the Savior. Only this has changed: once the burden of their limbs has been dissolved, they cling more closely to Christ, as the Apostle Paul says: “To depart and be with Christ is much better” (Philippians 1:23). Therefore, death should not be called death when, through its intervention, we are rid of persecutors and joined to Christ. It should plainly not be called death when, by joining the dead to Christ, it makes the dying person’s death a gain, as the blessed Apostle says: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid., 21). But that is the true death which binds a living person also by the death of sins. For although he may appear to live, by his crimes he already seems bound over to death, as the Apostle says of the pleasure-loving widow: “She who lives in pleasure is dead” (1 Timothy 5:6).

## SERMON LIV  
### On neglecting the solemnity of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 0714B]

The old edition and the Lyon manuscript prefix to this sermon the title *On the Pearl*. Not correctly; but the Roman edition does much worse by entitling it *On the Feast of Saint Lucy*, etc., although the saint is not mentioned anywhere in the sermon. We have therefore restored the genuine title from the Remigius manuscript. As for the author of this sermon, he may indeed be the same as the author of Sermons 42, 43, and 44; but anyone who attributes it to Ambrose reveals that he is little acquainted with Ambrosian reading.

### 1

I think, beloved brothers, that what should suffice for your correction is the fact that, when I was going to leave you on the previous Sunday, I gave you none of the spiritual gifts of sacred Scripture, but only rebuked and reproved you for your sin and dismissed you without any consolation of preaching. For I wanted you to understand how gravely you had sinned, since you were not worthy to hear the divine utterances. This is the severe and abundant vengeance of priests: not to entrust the mysteries of the heavenly Scriptures to the unworthy, nor, as the Lord says, to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine to be trampled under their feet (Matthew 7:6).

### 2

Whoever attempts to enclose the heavenly pearl within the foulest sinner loses the grace of the heavenly pearl [Note: So the old edition; but the Lyon and Remigius manuscripts read, “within the foulest herd,” which is doubtless better.] For, as you yourselves know, a gem belongs only with gold, and a pearl is fitted only to precious necklaces. Be the finest gold, then; be a precious necklace, so that the spiritual pearl may be enclosed in you. For Christ the Lord is the pearl which that rich merchant in the Gospel hastened to purchase after selling all his possessions. He preferred to lose all the gems of the world that he possessed, provided only that he might buy the one pearl of Christ (Matthew 13:46).

### 3

Therefore, brothers, because of the magnitude of the offense you had committed, I did not wish to open to you the words of evangelical refreshment. Rather, I wished to inflict the injury of spirited indignation, first to correct you with spiritual blows and then to enrich you with the gifts of the pearl. I preferred, I say, to rebuke your sin sharply by accusing it rather than nourish it by gently ignoring it; for whoever does not rebuke a brother who is sinning somehow encourages him to sin. But do not think that I do not act out of love when I strike you so often. A son who is worthy of correction is loved more, as holy Scripture says: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

### 4

Tell me, was it not grievous that on that occasion you were so forgetful of your salvation that you failed to show due honor to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, although you know them to be teachers of the nations, authors of martyrs, and princes of priests? You were unwilling to celebrate their birthday with us in the fullest festivity or to attend that heavenly banquet in which, amid such joy for his martyrs, the Lord himself supplied us with the substance of life [Note: All the editions and the Lyon manuscript read, “the Lord demonstrated”; the Remigius manuscript most aptly reads, “the Lord supplied.”] Do you wish to know how many blessings you were deprived of? Ask the brothers who were present with me at that time how refreshed they departed from the Lord’s table and what spiritual riches they carried home with them.

### 5

I know one thing: if some honored or wealthy person had invited you to a meal on that day, on the occasion of his son’s birthday, even as far as ten miles away, you would undoubtedly have gone for the sake of the carefully prepared food and the extravagant portions. Therefore, brothers, whenever we celebrate the memory of martyrs, we ought to set aside all worldly activities and come without any delay [Note: The old edition has, “without any doubt”; the Roman edition and the manuscripts have the reading adopted in the text. Below, where all the editions and the Remigius manuscript read, “so sacred a victim,” the Lyon manuscript more suitably has, “as a sacred victim.”] to pay honor to those who won salvation for us by the outpouring of their blood, who were offered to the Lord like a consecrated sacrifice for our reconciliation—especially since Almighty God says to his saints: “Whoever honors you honors me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Therefore, whoever honors the martyrs honors Christ also; and whoever despises the saints despises the Lord also.

## SERMON LV  
### On the birthday of the martyrs Saints Nazarius and Celsus

This sermon is found neither in the editions of Amerbach or Erasmus nor in any manuscripts that we have been able to see. Anyone can understand that it is not Ambrose’s by comparing it only with Paulinus’s account, in which he describes the discovery of these martyrs’ relics. For Paulinus asserts that the discovery occurred only in the final years of the holy Bishop, whereas this sermon had already been delivered at their feast, which was celebrated throughout the Church. Their birthday is observed on the fifth day before the Kalends of August; their discovery, however, on the sixth day before the Ides of May. On these saints one may also consult Saint Paulinus, *Poem* 9, on the birthday of Saint Felix.

### 1

Even if we were rendering the pious tribute of our vows to martyrs from a foreign region, we would still be shown to be consulting our own interests and advantages. Faith would make them ours, and, although they were separated by whatever boundaries, they would procure for us the patronage we hoped for. Such intercessions belong to devotion, not to places; therefore, among God’s household, you will merit as much intercession as you have offered veneration. It is therefore fitting that religious devotion should reconcile strangers to us rather than, perhaps, the negligence of irreligious torpor estrange our own from us.

### 2

Let us recognize, beloved brothers, the more abundant generosity of divine gifts bestowed around our Church. The peoples of individual cities rejoice if they are fortified by the relics of even one martyr; behold, we possess whole peoples of martyrs. Let our land rejoice, the mother of heavenly soldiers and the fertile parent of such great virtues. Rightly, therefore, and as is due, the honors of these blessed martyrs are celebrated by the children of the mother Church, who, illuminating innumerable peoples by the power of their faith, alone felt the death inflicted upon them, but did not alone possess the benefits of their death. For the immense mercy of our God, manifold in goodness and skillful for salvation, sets before us the arduous palm of virtue—made precious by its rare seeker—and, in the triumphs of a few, provides for the advantage of many. He wishes their merits to become our intercessions; and while he commends true faith to us through the harsh struggle of martyrdom, he makes the suffering of those who preceded us an instruction for those who come after.

### 3

How great is the concern of our God for us! He examines them in order to instruct us; he crushes them in order to gain us; and he wishes their torments to become our progress. Rightly, then, we honor those who fight through their own dangers and serve our interests, who teach us, through contempt for light and life, how much affection we owe our God. Let us therefore know that we doubt the truth of religion at great peril, since we see it confirmed by the blood of so many. It is a matter of great danger if, after the oracles of the prophets, the testimonies of the apostles, and the wounds of the martyrs, you presume to examine the ancient faith as though it were new; if, after such evident guides, you remain in error; and if, after the sufferings of those who died, you contend in idle disputation.

### 4

We therefore congratulate you, dearest brothers, on your great faith, through which, while you receive exiles with overflowing love, you have also merited to possess inhabitants of paradise and citizens of heaven. Although holy Milanese Church retains the blessed martyr Nazarius wholly in body, it has nevertheless transmitted him wholly to the world in blessing.
