This is the glory of the holy martyrs: although a portion of them may be scattered throughout the world in ashes, the fullness of their virtues nevertheless remains undivided. Therefore, in so great a soldier of Christ, we venerate our faith. For the mother of martyrdom is the Catholic faith, in which this illustrious athlete, pouring out his blood, trampled death for that very faith. Faith, I say, is the mother of martyrdom; therefore, in the glory of the holy martyrs, let us venerate our faith.

How do we venerate our faith? Because, when these men unhesitatingly accepted death, the hope of immortality was clearly affirmed. They would never have sacrificed this life with such steadfastness unless they had judged with complete conviction that another life was incomparably more blessed. In the holy heralds of truth, therefore, there is the authority of the resurrection. They willingly perish in order to be restored to something better; through the narrow passages of tribulation, the way out into the vastness of joys is opened to them.

### 5

Hence blessed Nazarius, whose glorious victory over the enemy of the world the universal Church celebrates today with festive rejoicing, although he was born of parents not without distinction in the time of paganism, suddenly began, while still a boy, to detest both the military service and the teaching of his still-sacrilegious father. From his innocent mother, who was already marked by the insignia of Christian faith and devoted herself assiduously to Christ, he earnestly requested that the waters of sacred rebirth be shown to him. In spirit he was already faithful, and in faith already instructed, anticipating the waters of baptism.

For he had not yet received baptism, but was already perfected among the beginnings of religion; and although the laws had not yet been revealed to him, he was full of God. Suddenly he became God’s possession and dwelling place. Thus he merited to raise the summit of a tower reaching even to the heavens [Note: The Roman edition reads, “first to raise the height,” omitting “he merited,” evidently.] before he had laid its foundation; he was not yet aware of the sacraments, yet he had already been chosen for sacrifice.

### 6

What will we wretched people be able to answer to this? After the brightness of baptism, after the whiteness bestowed upon us through sacred rebirth, after we acquired the angelic dignity of the wedding garment, we have fallen back into the filth of sins and rolled again in the ancient mire of crimes. We soil the snowy garment with the foul contagions of iniquities and lusts; we stain with the spots of deadly corruption the silk garment on which the seal of the divine image had been impressed; and, after the singular indulgence of our God, we defile what was renewed, tear apart what was whole, violate what was cleansed, and repeat deeds that must now be purified not by water but by flames.

### 7

What was that gift of divine grace, and how remarkable, that, after receiving the saving bath, after countless signs of virtue, after traveling through innumerable regions everywhere in order to preach Christ, while almost the whole world raged against him through various punishments because of his confession of the Most High God—now being confined to be tortured by the most atrocious penalties, now being carried away into distant regions for exile—he overcame every torment with the breast of Christ’s strongest athlete, so that he carried away a splendid trophy from his prostrate enemy?

And when, amid the bloody commands of Caesar, he had been thrown into the vast waters of the sea, divine providence granted him permission to walk upon the waters. While nature itself stood amazed, he set his suspended steps upon the new paths of an unfamiliar route and trod the swelling backs of the sea. You would have seen the waters of the deep placed beneath the merits of the saint, and him, strengthened above by angelic words of encouragement, rejoicing in the praises of Christ Jesus. Behold, the profane enemy could never have benefited the blessed martyr by his service as much as he benefited him by his hatred.

8. But at last, when the contest had been brought to completion, he was released from condemnation by the cruel decree and consecrated by the sword, together with the boy Celsus, whom he himself had taken from the polluted world as a holocaust for God. Blessed was he in such an end: by it every fault departed from him in such a way that it could not return; by it he paid his debts so fully that he no longer feared the creditor; through it he enclosed the enemies’ sins within himself by faith and condemned them by faith; through it he sought innocence by devotion, found it through perseverance, and preserved it by death.

9. Since this is so, beloved, although this great witness of Christ is precious for his confession, more precious for his blood, more precious still for his cruel wound, and whiter than a garment dipped in blood; although he is considered, by the privilege of his tomb, the special possession of the people of Milan, he belongs to all through the common benefit of his intercession. For the overflowing affection and miserly faith of this city must not so diminish this martyr, by arrogating him to itself, that it should believe the benefits of his protection will extend only toward its walls. What is spread abroad through merits is not confined to places. You invoked the martyr everywhere, and everywhere he heard you—the one who is honored in the martyr. Therefore, under the governance of him who weighs your prayers and distributes his gifts, the effective advocate’s nearby presence will be granted in proportion to the devotion with which he is received. For prayer aided by works of chastity, justice, and almsgiving surpasses the world, penetrates paradise, and flies up even to the presence of the supreme Majesty, the angel conveying it, just as an angelic voice attests in a certain passage: “And when you were praying,” he says, “I presented your prayer in the presence of the glory of God” (Acts 10:4).

10. Blessed is the soul, beloved, whose vow, whose incense of compunction, whose holocaust of supplication is clouded by no unbelief, polluted by no stench of carnal allure, bloodied by no savagery, and stained by no hostility of hatred; but is fiery with faith, bright with conscience, fragrant with sincerity of heart, and perfected in concord and charity, and is carried through the service of heavenly messengers even to the face of God. Since this is so, let us honor the blessed martyrs, leaders of the faith, intercessors for the world, heralds of the kingdom, and fellow heirs of God.

11. But if you say to me, “What do you honor in flesh already dissolved and consumed, for which God now has no concern?”—where then, beloved, is that which Truth itself speaks through the Prophet: “Precious,” he says, “in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15)? And again: “But your friends, O God, are exceedingly honorable to me” (Ps. 138:15). We ought to honor God’s servants; how much more, then, God’s friends! Of them it is said elsewhere: “The Lord,” he says, “guards all their bones, and not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. 33:21).

Therefore I honor in the martyr’s flesh the scars received for Christ’s name; I honor the memory of the living through the perpetuity of his virtue; I honor the ashes consecrated by the confession of the Lord; I honor in the ashes the seeds of eternity; I honor the body that showed me how to love my Lord, and taught me, for the Lord’s sake, not to fear death. Why should the faithful not honor that body which even the demons revere—those who afflicted it in its punishment, but glorify it in its tomb? Therefore I honor the body which Christ honored by the sword, and which will reign with Christ in heaven.

468 **SERMON LVI. On the Feast of Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli**

In this sermon Eusebius is treated as a martyr, although among the ancients he is always placed in the order of confessors; in other respects, the history of this bishop agrees sufficiently with the sermon. We possess in Maximus another sermon on the same saint, in many respects very similar to this one; but whether the two proceeded from the same author or from different authors, it is clear that this sermon is not Maximus’s, since it was delivered in the Church of Vercelli itself. That its author was ancient is evident from the fact that he indicates that he is speaking in the presence of Exsuperantius, a disciple of Eusebius. Whoever he was, he was different from Ambrose; others had already recognized this, and the entire sequence of the sermon abundantly proves it.

1. To wish to add anything to the praise of the holy martyr Eusebius is to detract from it. For he was a teacher of doctrines so ineffable that his merits can more easily be recognized in his works than explained in words. Conscience retains as much about him as speech and narrative cannot recount.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] The Theod. manuscript has “as much as speech cannot recount.”]

Therefore his deeds should not be adorned with words, but briefly indicated in statements—especially since we know that we ought not to embellish with speeches what we see already adorned with virtues, since the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4:20).

2. Therefore, to wish to add anything to his merits is to detract from them—especially for me, who am both ignorant of his deeds, unskilled in sacred letters, and inexperienced in priestly functions.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] So the manuscripts and the old edition; the Roman edition, however, abridged the passage as follows: “since I am almost ignorant of the things I have done.” [Col. 0720D] “But they could have…”]

My holy predecessors could have praised these things more easily through practice, more authoritatively through experience, and more splendidly through learning. I speak especially of the lord and father, the blessed Exsuperantius, who was Eusebius’s assistant in the priesthood, his companion in martyrdom, and his partner in labor. In whose face we believe that we see the holy Eusebius as well, and as though in a mirror we contemplate the image of his goodness. For we easily recognize what kind of teacher he was when we see what kind of disciple he had. But because a glory like his teacher’s confession accompanies him, he prefers to keep his father’s praises silent, lest he seem likewise to boast of his own.

3. What, then, should I proclaim about the glory of the martyr Eusebius, whose glory this entire people is? And since Scripture says, “A wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 10:1), how great is the glory of one who rejoices in the wisdom and devotion of so many sons! For in Christ Jesus he himself begot us through the Gospel.

Whatever virtue and grace can be found in this holy people is found in the teaching of Saint Eusebius. From this, as from a kind of most lucid fountain of virtues, the purity of these streams flowed forth. Because he was strong in the vigor of chastity, he established the profession of virginity; because he gloried in the austerities of abstinence, he introduced the discipline of monks; because he was endowed with the attractions of gentleness, he stirred the affection of all the citizens toward God; because he shone through the administration of his episcopate, he chose many of his disciples as heirs of his priesthood.

Although, therefore, some leave their children treasures of gold and silver, no one left Saint Eusebius richer heirs—for all of them proved to be either priests or martyrs.

[Col. 0720B] 4. To say nothing of the rest, how remarkable is this: in this holy Church he established the same men as both monks and clerics, and ensured that priestly duties were contained within the same sanctuaries in which singular chastity was preserved; so that in these men there might be contempt for worldly things,

[Note: [Col. 0720D] The Theod. manuscript has “and careful attention to letters.”]

and the careful discipline of Levites. If you saw the beds of the monastery, you would judge them to resemble the Eastern discipline; if you observed the cleric’s devotion, you would rejoice in the observance of the angelic order.

5. I certainly do not think that this should be left unmentioned: when the detestable faithlessness of the Arians had disturbed all Italy together with the whole world, and the priests of that same plague had taken captive the simplicity of the holy martyr Dionysius, so that they retained the bond of his signature—by what wisdom did he free him from their hands?

For just as Saint Paul says, “I became as a Jew to the Jews, that I might win the Jews” (1 Cor. 9:20), so Eusebius pretended to be a heretic to the heretics, in order to free his son from heresy. He said that he agreed with their faithlessness and approved what they approved; but he said that he was seriously disturbed because they had put his son Dionysius before him in signing.

“For you,” he said, “who say that the Son of God cannot be equal to God the Father, why have you put my son before me?”

Moved by this reasoning, they immediately erased the signature of Saint Dionysius, granting blessed Eusebius the first place for signing. Rebuking and mocking them, he said: “Neither do I pollute myself with your crimes, nor do I permit you to make my son share in them.”

Thus, although the Gospel says that “the sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light in their generation” (Luke 16:8), behold, here a son of light was found more prudent than the darkness itself.

6. Then they, gravely indignant that their wickedness had been exposed, harassed him with new sufferings through the emperor Constantius.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] The Theod. manuscript has “they afflicted him with sufferings.”]

After many insults, they banished him into exile in the region of the East, where he suffered so much that he carried away the unconquered glory of martyrdom. Among the other kinds of suffering, he is said to have endured this painful punishment: when the Arians questioned him and he refused to profess communion with their faithlessness, they dragged him down the entire flight of stairs, feet first, along the sloping descent. Then, having been called back to the top and questioned again, when he gave the same answer, he suffered the same treatment; and this punishment followed each repeated questioning.

In this suffering of the holy martyr Eusebius, although his head was shaken, his body battered, and his limbs broken, his spirit nevertheless remained unconquered in faith. For the more the Arian faithlessness tore him bodily, the more the integrity of the Catholic faith inwardly refreshed him.

7. We may say that this ascent and descent of the stairs was what Jacob prophetically saw in his dream (Gen. 28:12). Just as Jacob saw those stairs reaching from below even to the heavens, so Eusebius ascended to heaven by these stairs, while the Arians descended to hell.

Therefore, brothers, I think that Saint Eusebius should be numbered among the choir of the Maccabean martyrs. For while they endured martyrdom in their individual limbs, he confessed the Lord through the suffering of his entire body; and their grace was not unequal, since the same day also joined them together in martyrdom.

**SERMON LVII. On the Burial of the Same Saint Eusebius**

Those who attribute the preceding sermon to Maximus also think that this one should be assigned to him. But in order to establish that it belongs to the aforementioned bishop, we judge both its style and its kinship with the second sermon on Eusebius, the Maximian sermon, to be much stronger evidence.

1. Today we celebrate the burial of Saint Eusebius. What is burial? Not that burial, certainly, which is attended to by the hands of clerics in burying the bodily remains in the earth, but that by which a human being, released from bodily bonds and about to go freely to heaven, lays aside his earthly body.

That is truly burial in which we cast away desire, cease to sin, stop committing offenses, and lay aside everything burdensome to salvation like a discarded load. For this day is observed with the greatest solemnity because it is truly the supreme festival: to be dead to vices and alive only to righteousness. Hence the day of burial itself is called a birthday, because, freed from the prison of sins,

[Note: [Col. 0721D] So the old edition and the manuscripts, except that Theod. reads “free” instead of “for freedom”; the Roman edition accepts neither, but instead has: “we are born to the Savior.”]

we are born into the freedom of the Savior.

2. But let us consider with what glory Saint Eusebius came to this day of burial. For some time before his death, he is said to have seen in a clear revelation that on the Kalends of August he was flying from mountain to mountain, and he interpreted this prophetically to mean that on that day he would depart from the body.

In this event I do not know what should first be admired: whether that he deserved to know the end of his life, or that he was able to know what grace would remain for him after his departure.

Saint David says: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end and the number of my days, and the rest” (Ps. 38:5). Behold, what the Prophet had desired, the Martyr received: the knowledge for which the former prayed, the latter attained;

[Note: [Col. 0721D] The Theod. manuscript omits from “the latter attains” to “he may deserve something greater.” Below, where all the editions read “he declared what remains,” the same manuscript has “he learns what remains.” [Col. 0722D] The Lugd. manuscript has “he assigned,” incorrectly.]

except that, if I may say so without compromising the faith, the latter received something greater. The former asks to know his end; the latter also recognizes what he will be after the end. The former does not know what is lacking until his departure; the latter learns what remains after his departure.

470 3. Therefore the martyr Eusebius saw himself flying on this day. As we know, only what is pure, light, and subtle can fly; neither is its purity hindered by excess, nor its liveliness or speed weighed down by bulk.

I say that flight is weighed down not so much by the mass of the limbs as by the weight of sins. Hence I think that among birds, too, the dove flies almost more swiftly than all the others because liveliness is accompanied by innocence.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] All the editions and the Lugd. manuscript read, “because liveliness and innocence accompany it”; the Theod. manuscript’s reading, followed in the text, is better.]

Finally, when Saint David desired to fly with purity of mind, he wished for wings belonging to no other creature than a dove, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? And I shall fly and find rest” (Ps. 54:7). For he understood that higher things are reached more easily through simplicity of mind than through the lightness of wings.

4. Therefore Saint Eusebius flew on this day. Let us now judge his innocence from his flight, and his purity from the very act of rising.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] The Theod. manuscript reads, “and his piety,” etc.]

Living like a dove in the house of God, he assumed spiritual wings and found rest on the mountain.

Although he himself said that he would fly from mountain to mountain, I nevertheless indicate that in this very translation there was a greater rest. For what else is it to fly from mountain to mountain than to hasten from the grace of the Savior to the glory of the Father? For they are the mountains, as the Prophet says: “A mountain cut from a mountain without hands”—that is, the Son from the Father, without the intervention of any act of creation.

**SERMON LVIII. On Saint Cyprian**

Another sermon on the same martyr preceded this one. In all written manuscripts and ancient editions it was numbered 72; in the Roman edition it was numbered 18 among the sermons on the saints; we have placed it among the published Maximian sermons. Since it is clear that both were delivered by the same preacher, there is no doubt that both should be attributed to the same Maximus.

1. A few days ago, when we celebrated the feast of the most blessed martyr Cyprian, we rejoiced most sweetly in his festival. Because he suffered at the time of the vintage, we too gathered sweet and varied fruits from his passion, as from a vintage. For he fattened and refreshed us with the new wine of his martyrdom.

There is indeed a new wine that refreshes and intoxicates the Christian, but that intoxication makes him more sober. For whoever is intoxicated with heavenly grace is sobered from the burden of sins.

[Note: [Col. 0723] The Theod. manuscript has “is relieved of the burden of sins.”]

2. Filled with this new wine, the holy Apostles, as Scripture says (Acts 2:13), spoke of God’s mighty works in foreign languages. In this event they appeared to be drunk and sober at the same time. They were thought drunk because speech of an extraordinary kind resounded loudly in them; they were sober because, according to the custom of the mind, they praised God with devotion.

[Note: [Col. 0723] The same Theod. manuscript has “their speech was alike, but their nature different.” And below: “or it happened through lack of understanding.”]

This did not happen through any arrogance or shamelessness, as though the holy men were speaking in an alien language; rather, it happened through divine providence, so that, since one language is insufficient for magnifying God, the devotion of the mind might be expressed through many languages.

2. We rejoiced because we received the fruit of refreshment from the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth. The vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, as the Prophet says, is the house of Israel—and that house is us (Isa. 5:7). For in faith we are Israelites; hence the Apostle says: “Those who are of faith are sons of Abraham” (Gal. 3:7).

Since, therefore, we are Israel, we are the vineyard of the Lord. Let us carefully ensure that from the branch of our works there grows not a sweet grape but a grape of gall, lest what was said to the Jews through the Prophet be said to us: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns, and not justice, but a cry” (Isa. 5:7).

How harsh the condition, that the possession which ought to have brought its master the fruit of sweetness should have pierced him with the sharpness of thorns! That is, although the Jews ought to have received the Savior with the whole devotion of faith, they crowned him with thorns in his Passion. That crown, insofar as it concerned the Jews, was an insult of abuse; insofar as it concerned the Lord, it was a crown of virtues. The Jews therefore pierce the Lord when they crown him; they pierce him when they crucify him. Hence Holy Scripture says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37).

471 3. Therefore, brothers, take care lest it also be said to you: “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isa. 5:2). That is, let us not place upon the Lord with wicked thoughts the thorns which the Jews placed upon him with bloodstained hands, and pierce him not with the sharpness of thorns but with the perversity of our works.

For there are thorns of the heart that habitually wound even the Word of God. The Savior mentions them in the Gospel, saying that the seed sown fell among thorns, which grew up and choked what had been sown (Matt. 13:7). He himself explains what these thorns are, saying that they are worldly cares. When they grow in a person’s heart, they choke the Savior’s commandments within him.

Whoever has ever been concerned about the world could be rightly concerned about Christ? Whoever is occupied with providing for the profits of his household could provide for the needs of the Church? Hence the Apostle says: “The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. 7:32).

4. Therefore, brothers, take care that your vineyard produce not thorns instead of grapes, and that your vintage bring forth not wine but vinegar. Whoever gathers a vintage and does not distribute it to the poor gathers vinegar, not wine. Whoever stores up his harvest and does not supply those in need has stored up not the fruit of nourishment but the thistles of avarice. For this reason Scripture says concerning our earth: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3:18).

**SERMON LIX. On the Feast of One Martyr, or of the Lord Domitian**

This sermon, together with the following one, is found in the Floriacensis manuscript, written a thousand years ago, where it is also attributed to Saint Ambrose. Nevertheless, since these sermons have until now been unpublished and we are bringing them to light, we wished to do so in recognition of the manuscript’s antiquity, although they contain nothing Ambrosian, as anyone can recognize from their first reading.

1. Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the day of a righteous man who is dead and is not here. But if you wish to know where he is, ask the reading you heard first: “If the righteous man is overtaken by death, he will be in refreshment” (Wis. 4:7).

For in this age, for whom and from where is there refreshment, when everything is full of tribulations? And when tribulations abound, everything is full of temptations. Whether it is feared or flatters us, this world must be feared; but God must be feared, while the world should rather be despised and more carefully avoided. If, therefore, we wish to be in refreshment when death overtakes us, let us be righteous.

2. Someone may perhaps say: “That is too much for me.” Let us consider what is written: “If the righteous man is overtaken by death, he will be in refreshment.” But when we ask what “righteous” means, the psalm terrifies us: “Every man is a liar” (Ps. 115:11).

Let us hear the Book of Wisdom: “If the righteous man is overtaken by death, he will be in refreshment.” Let us hear the psalm: “I said in my alarm, Every man is a liar.” Was Saint Domitian not a man? If he was a man, and every man is a liar, how was he righteous if he was a liar? Or how is he in refreshment if he was not righteous?

3. Let us consider, then, beloved. We have these thoughts filled with witnesses, and there is no small refreshment in what we hear the Apostle saying: “For Christ died for this reason, that he might be Lord of both the living and the dead; and whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. 14:9).

He is the righteous one; he will not lose his own. We are certain that Christ was not a liar. Christ was man and not a liar. How, then, is every man a liar? Because Christ was man in such a way that he was not only man. Unless he were both God and man, he would be a liar.

Such and so great a one died for us, and we fear death? He went before us and rose again; we are his members, and we follow our head.

4. The psalm itself also consoles us: “What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” (Ps. 115:13). What did he say? “I said in my alarm, Every man is a liar” (ibid., 11).

The lying man gives thanks to the Lord and cannot find what to repay him for the many benefits he has received from him. For what do we receive from him when we ask what we shall repay and find nothing? We did not exist, and he created us; the animals did not exist, and he created the animals. More than that, he made us in his own image. We had perished, and he sought us. He gave us the pledge of his Son’s death and promised us the life of his Son. In the saving baptism he cleansed us from all our sins.

And because by living here we afterwards contracted what he might forgive—for we might say, “Forgive us our debts”—he taught us to say this. He cleansed everything in the baptized person; he cleansed everything in the living person who had been reborn. He did not allow that person to die—he does not permit him to die, I mean in sin, which is an evil and eternal death. He warns the one who has been called, instructs him, helps him, forgives him, and frees him.

“What shall I repay the Lord for all that he has repaid me?” What do you say, man? What do you wish to repay? Whatever you find, you received from him.

5. Therefore we come—we come, if we live by faith. Then we shall be righteous, because “the righteous man lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). We shall therefore come to that reward which will be equal for all.

Children believe and come at the first hour; adolescents believe and come at the third hour; young men believe and come at the sixth hour; the more mature believe and come at the ninth hour; the aged believe and come at the final hour. They came at different hours, and received one reward. Thus the last became first, and the first last, because what the first received, the last also received (Matt. 20:10).

What is that denarius? Eternal life. Why is it equal for all? Because there no one lives more and no one less. Let us strive toward this; let us trust in the Lord; let us escape the life of temptation and possess the life of blessedness.

**Another Sermon on One Martyr**

1. This solemn day, this illustrious day of our homeland, shining with angelic beauty, has dawned resplendent today, clothed in the flourishing crown of this martyr. As the day unfolds through its hours, as the cycles of days and nights and the waxing and waning of the moon complete the months, as the charioteer Year drives the quadriga of the seasons to its goal on revolving axles, the joyful day of this holy Martyr has shone forth. On it, exulting as a warrior amid enemy lines, he conquered all his foes and hastened to the kingdoms owed to him.

2. In an uncertain contest victory is always suspect when either the judge rages against the venerable martyrs or the executioner roars. Now the sword, now the beast, now the flame, now tortures are feared. But once a manly breast has taken up the breastplate of faith, the brave spirit does not feel whatever the cruel mind inflicts. He stands unharmed amid fires and steadfast amid beasts and tortures; he is more released by axes than cut down by them.

But until the contest of the happy hour came to its prosperous end, the Christians remained in suspense, and with fearful hearts and fleeing glances they watched the funeral spectacle between Christ’s athlete and the enemy’s servants: lest the timid martyr expose his side to a wound; lest he escape some violent attack; lest, amid the tortures, he recoil in tender feeling even from the executioners’ barking.

Meanwhile a crown hung from heaven, woven with lilies of angels and roses blooming from the cross and blood of Christ; and a celestial garland, painted with varied beauty, shone from above like the many-colored face of a flowering meadow.

3. The soldier of God was therefore fighting, and contending by faith, not by the body. On one side the world enticed him with life; on the other it terrified him with death. The blind dust of the arena was stirred up in that conflict, but the confessor’s eye could not be closed. He saw on both sides what God was preparing and what the enemy desired.

Christ was his shield of protection; the hands of angels had made him a helmet of salvation; one God, one faith, and one baptism forged for him a triple breastplate. The Holy Spirit was his sword. The demons fought with their weapons, and he with his: they with black weapons, he with shining arms. He guarded his soul with the shield of faith and sowed his body in the earth; he watered it with his blood, so that it might offer abundant fruits to his God in the resurrection.

4. “Those who sow in tears,” he says, “shall reap in joy. Going forth, they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:5).

At that time, while the saints were fighting, the tears of the faithful flowed, stirred by devotion, until it became clear toward which side the dangerous contest of uncertain outcome was inclining. The pain of unjust persecution drew forth lamentable weeping, and each Christian feared in himself what he saw in another. Although they knew that glory in heaven had been prepared for the blessed martyrs, still, amid uncertain and varied outcomes and impending sorrows, tender charity wrung bitter tears from their hearts.

5. The martyrs went forth weeping, casting their seeds. O how narrow and confined is the way that leads to life! They went through beasts and swords, through straits and pressures, weeping in prayer and rejoicing in hope. They laid their bodies in the earth as their seeds, from which an eternal harvest of glory sprouted.

473 Then they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves, when they receive their flowers in the resurrection. “For the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, and shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon.” That green beauty never knows decay among the saints, especially when God supplies it, like an everlasting river, with continual streams and abundant refreshment.

Behold, from one grain of Christ’s body, which was buried, how great a harvest of martyrs sprang forth! Behold, from the first palm, how many victorious palms of confessors have arisen! O paradise, where the holy souls mingle in a gracious fellowship!

6. Among these, this most blessed martyr renews the festival today with greater strength. For by dying he conquered the adversary who was fighting, and he obtained from heaven the crown that had been hanging there. Let the children now rejoice in the triumphs of the martyrs, and let them hand on annual vows to posterity—those whose fathers both witnessed the hard contests of the saints and rejoiced in the crown of the victors.

**SERMON LX. On the Feast of the Holy Martyrs**

[Col. 0727A]

In the Theod. manuscript this sermon is entitled “On the Day of Saints Alexander, Eventius, and Theodolus,” although these same martyrs are nowhere named in the sermon itself. No better is the title prefixed to it in the Roman edition: “For the Common Feast of One Martyr,” since everything there is referred equally to all the martyrs. The title found in the other manuscripts and editions is therefore preferable. But the fact that in all of them, except the Gall. manuscript, it is attributed to Saint Ambrose is an evident error, as may be understood from its style and from what we prefixed to Sermon 52.

1. If my bodily weakness were able to pursue as much as I must say and you ought to hear, we would all certainly be excused: I by explaining the command, and you by carrying it out. But since we are struck by weakness and cannot say as much as we ought, let devotion of mind excuse us, though the speech of preaching does not; that is, although our tongue ceases from praising the Lord, let us nevertheless commend his wonders through works of faith. If we do not proclaim his glory in words, let us fulfill his grace in deeds,

[Note: [Col. 0727D] All the editions have “his glory”; all the manuscripts have “his grace.”]

since deeds precede words. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does and teaches in this way shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

You see, then, that action comes first and teaching follows, since doing good is the first teaching. When words cease, the excellent deed itself teaches a person while it is seen. Even if it does not stir the ears with its voice, it pierces the heart by its virtue. For who, seeing a good deed, would not rejoice, marvel, imitate it, and, using it as a silent teacher, be instructed by its example?

[Note: [Col. 0727D] The Lugd. manuscript has “and as though using such a swift teacher”; the Theod. manuscript has “and as though using a silent teacher,” etc.]

Deeds therefore precede words; indeed, without deeds words are of no benefit. For this reason the Lord also wished to act and then to teach, lest without good works the boasting of words should be useless and superstitious.

2. We are therefore taught better by deed than by voice. Thus the holy martyrs, although silent in voice, instruct us by the power of their works; although silent in tongue, they persuade us through the suffering of martyrdom.

Thus, although an eloquent orator may teach me by his eloquence, I learn what is useful to me better from the example of the saints than from an assertion in words. The eyes more quickly persuade me of what they see than the ear can convey what passes away. Oblivion quickly creeps into hearing, but the history of the eyes is always viewed.

Who would not at every hour and moment behold how, at that time, the blessed martyrs endured various punishments for Christ’s name and in a certain sense triumphed over the very penalties? For the more they suffered, the more victorious they believed themselves to be. The persecutor’s judgment upon the martyr is the martyr’s victory, as it is written: “And you may prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:6).

When the martyr is judged and condemned, then he conquers and casts down his judge. For by such a judgment he is not consigned to death but released into rest; and thus it is most clearly victory, not destruction.

3. It is therefore established that the holy martyrs teach more through suffering than through speech, although their very suffering is not without a voice. For we read that their souls cry out, or say, from beneath the altar of God: “How long, O holy and true one, will you not avenge our blood?” (Rev. 6:10).

God also says concerning Abel’s blood to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Gen. 4:10). Blood that has been innocently shed is therefore said to cry out—not so much by its voice as by its cause. So too the souls of the holy martyrs cry out when, through their very suffering, they commend their faith and innocence to our understanding.

**SERMON LXI. On the Feast of the Martyrs**

From the reading of this sermon we learn that it was delivered after the Lord’s resurrection. It is also recited at that time in the Roman Breviary, but under the name of Ambrose, although it differs very greatly from his diction. It is more plausibly Maximus’s, since Gennadius testifies that he composed a general homily on all the martyrs. It may also be added that the same sermon is found in the Gall. manuscript, whose sermons our Mabillon believes all belong to that bishop.

1. It is worthy and fitting, brothers,

[Note: [Col. 0727D] All the editions have “so that after the joy of Easter”; all the manuscripts have “after the joy of blessed Easter.” The same applies below, where the editions have “the Lord’s Easter,” while all the manuscripts have “the Lordly Easter.”]

that after the joy of blessed Easter, which we celebrated in the Church, we should join our joys with the holy martyrs and announce the glory of the Lord’s resurrection to those who share in the Lord’s Passion.

Those who are companions in humiliation ought also to be participants in joy. Thus the blessed Apostle says: “As you are companions in sufferings, so also shall you be in the resurrection” (2 Cor. 1:7); and, “If we endure,” he says, “we shall also reign together” (2 Tim. 2:12). Those, therefore, who endured evil for Christ ought also to possess glory with Christ.

## 2.

“Let us announce,” I say, “to the holy martyrs the grace of the Lord’s Passover, so that, while we proclaim that the bars of his tomb have been opened, the tombs of these men too may be opened; while we say that his dead body, with its veins still warm, suddenly came to life, the limbs of these men also, now cold, may be warmed by the heat of immortality.” For the same power raises the martyrs that raised the Lord. For just as they experienced the way of suffering, so also will they experience the way of life; for it is written in the psalm: “You have made known to me the paths of life” (Psalm 15:11).

This is certainly said in the resurrection in the person of the Savior.

[Note: Thus the Vallisclae and Theodoret manuscripts; the editions, however, with the Lugdunensis manuscript read: “who, while [the Roman edition: ‘so that while’] after death . . . begins to have the way of life known.”]

He, when he returns after death from the regions below to those above, begins to make known the way of life, which had not previously been known. For before Christ’s coming the way of life was unknown, because no one who had yet risen had worn it smooth by his footsteps.

[Note: All printed editions and the Lugdunensis manuscript read: “had been trampled by no footprint . . . had become known, its surface worn smooth,” etc.; the Vallisclae and Theodoret manuscripts read as in the text.]

But when the Lord rose again, the path became known and was worn smooth beneath the feet of many, of whom the holy Evangelist says: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with him and entered the holy city” (Matthew 27:52).

## 3.

Since, therefore, at his resurrection the Lord said: “You have made known to me the paths of life” (Psalm 11:15), we too can now say to the Lord: “You have made known to us the paths of life.” For he made the paths of life known to us who revealed to us the path leading to life.

“He made known to me the paths of life” when he taught me faith, mercy, justice, and holiness.

[Note: The Vallisclae manuscript adds: “chastity.”]

For by these paths one reaches salvation. And although, when the body is dissolved, the shadow of death surrounds us, life nevertheless does not abandon its own footsteps; but even amid the very laws of hell we walk without hesitation in the virtues of Christ. Hence the holy Prophet says: “Even though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me” (Psalm 22:4).

The Lord expresses the same thing more clearly concerning the believer when he says: “Whoever believes in me will never die” (John 11:27). And even if he dies, he will live.

## 4.

Therefore, brothers, let us compare with the holy martyrs the glory of the Lord’s Passover. Let us compare it, I say; and although they know everything better than we do, let us nevertheless proclaim to them how the Lord rose from the embrace of the tomb to the heights above.

Let them reveal to us how he returned from the depths of hell to the tomb. Let them make known to us, I say, how heat entered a body already lifeless and cold, how breath was restored, how blood was poured in, and how the beating of its former vigor stirred the veins frozen by cold moisture.

Let them make known to us, I say, how the loosened structure restored the shattered instrument of the body to its former condition by refitting the nerves, and how the life-giving Spirit revived the harmony of the inward parts, already silent, into its ancient concord.

Let the priests therefore proclaim what wonders the Savior performed after his resurrection on high; let the martyrs reveal how great a refreshment he brought to the dead in death itself.

# SERMON LXII  
## On the Tumult of War, or for the Common of Martyrs

Mabillon, in volume I, part II of his *Museum Italicum*, page 5, asserts that this sermon, together with two others—one of which the Roman editors had placed in volume I of the works of Ambrose, while the other had already been published among the sermons of Saint Maximus—belongs equally to this Father. This is handsomely confirmed both by the diction of the sermons and by the authority of Gennadius cited at the indicated place.

In any case, although the Roman edition wished to entitle this very sermon *for the Common of Martyrs*, there was no reason why it should do so. It will therefore more suitably be placed among the sermons *On Various Matters*, under the title found in the older edition and in the manuscripts.

## 1.

Perhaps you are troubled, brothers, because we continually hear of the tumult of wars and the incursions of battles; and perhaps your love is even more troubled by the fact that these things occur in our own times.

[Note: The Lugdunensis manuscript reads: “But this is the reason: the nearer we are to the destruction of the world, the nearer we are to the kingdom,” etc.]

But the reason is that, the nearer we are to the destruction of the world, the nearer we are to the kingdom of the Savior. For the Lord himself says that in the last days: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Mark 13:8); and elsewhere: “When you see wars, earthquakes, and famines, know that the kingdom of God is near” (Matthew 24:33).

Therefore this proximity of wars demonstrates that Christ is nearer to us. For this reason I should not fear the adversary who is coming, because through these signs I understand that the Savior is coming instead. For although the former inflicts temporal fear, the latter bestows eternal salvation.

[Note: So the manuscript; all printed editions instead read: “yet that one abandons eternal salvation.”]

The same Lord is powerful both to drive hostile terror away from us and to grant us his presence.

## 2.

Through these tumults of war, therefore, a certain destruction of the world is signified; for this disturbance precedes the judgment that is to come. It is an indication of God’s admonition to see what you fear, so that you may understand that more remains for you to fear.

[Note: The Lugdunensis manuscript reads: “a certain sign of disturbance.”]

For while we are cautious about the things we see, we become more cautious about those things that we hope for. A wise man is instructed by these earthly events how he ought to avoid the judgment of the age to come.

For when he sees the leading men preparing defenses upon the walls amid this common upheaval—

[Note: All printed editions read “the former men”; the manuscript, more appropriately, reads “the leading men.”]

—he is himself admonished how to prepare a defense for Christian souls in the future overthrow of the world.

We see the gates of the city being armed; we too ought first to arm within ourselves the gates of justice. These are the gates of justice of which the holy Prophet said: “Open to me the gates of justice,” and what follows (Psalm 117:19).

The city gate can then be fortified if the gates of justice are first fortified within us. Otherwise it is of no benefit to fortify walls with defenses while provoking God by sins.

The former is built with iron, stones, and stakes; the latter is armed with mercy, innocence, and chastity. The former is guarded by a multitude of weapons; the latter is defended by frequent prayers. And for the complete protection of cities, standards ordinarily precede the gates of rulers; but let the sign of the Savior precede the gates of our souls.

## 3.

Therefore, brothers, in view of the future judgment of the world, let us fortify ourselves with heavenly weapons. Let us gird ourselves with the breastplate of faith; let us be protected by the helmet of salvation; let us defend ourselves with the word of God as with a spiritual sword. For whoever is equipped with these weapons neither fears the present disturbance nor dreads the future judgment (1 Kings 17:50).

Indeed, protected by this devotion, the holy David, though unarmed, killed that exceedingly strong and armed Goliath, and by the sole power of faith struck down a warrior surrounded on every side by fortifications.

For although the holy David was not covered by a helmet, was not girded with a sword, and did not use a spear, he killed him not with an iron weapon but with a spiritual sword. Although he appeared unarmed to human eyes, he was sufficiently armed with divine grace.

Yet that spiritual sword was not a sword; for Goliath was not struck down by a sword but by a stone. We read in the Scriptures that Christ is figuratively designated by the word “stone,” as the Prophet says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 117:22).

Therefore, when Goliath is struck with a stone, he is overthrown by the power of Christ. And in what part of the body is he struck? In the forehead, of course. For the pagan and sacrilegious man is struck by Christ precisely where Christ was lacking; and the destruction of death is inflicted upon him where the sign of salvation is not found.

Although Goliath was protected on every side by armor, his forehead nevertheless lay exposed to death, because he did not bear the mark of the Savior. Therefore he is killed there where he is found naked of God’s grace.

## 4.

No one is unaware that these events took place figuratively. David had first girded himself with the equipment of armor (1 Kings 17:39); but when he found himself weighed down and hindered by it, so that he could scarcely walk, he threw it off without hesitation. By this he signified that the arms of this world are empty and luxurious works, and that whoever wishes to entangle himself in them will be weighed down and will not have a free course for walking toward heaven.

At the same time he taught us that victory must not be hoped for in weapons alone, but must be sought in prayer in the name of the Savior.

# SERMON LXIII  
## On the Centurion’s Servant in the Gospel, at the Dedication of a Basilica

This sermon is recognized as having been delivered at the dedication of a church. Yet, apart from its style, which is alien to that of Ambrose, and Paulinus’s silence concerning this dedication—since nothing is said either about the relics discovered there or about the saints who were patrons of that basilica—it is abundantly clear that this consecration was not celebrated by Ambrose.

[Col. 0731D] Nevertheless, the course of the sermon does not reveal by which bishop, in what place, or at what time it was performed.

## 1.

We read in the holy Gospel that when the servant of a certain centurion, who was more precious to him, was suffering from a severe illness of paralysis, and the centurion asked the Savior through the elders of the Jews to relieve his suffering—for, as Scripture says, he was at the point of death (Luke 7:2 and following)—the elders of the Jews said to the Lord, among other things, in order to commend him more favorably:

“It is fitting that you grant this to him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us” (ibid., 4).

If, therefore, the one who built a synagogue is commended to the Lord, how much more commendable is the one who built a church! And if he merits favor who provided a dwelling place for impiety, how much greater a favor does he merit who prepared a dwelling for religion!

And if he is visited by heavenly mercy who built a place where Christ is always denied, how much more should he be visited who had a tabernacle constructed where Christ is proclaimed every day!

[Note: The Lugdunensis manuscript reads: “who fashioned a tabernacle.”]

## 2.

In the centurion, the Lord approved not what work he had done, but with what intention he had acted. For the man who, at a time when they were not yet Christians, carefully built a synagogue would, had they been Christians, plainly have built a church with much greater care.

Yet although he builds a synagogue, he proclaims Christ. For by that very work he reminds the Pharisees that they ought to receive the Savior; and he demonstrates that he added a larger tabernacle for this reason: so that they might speak there of the Lord’s glory in many ways.

For if the founder of the synagogue believes in Christ, much more ought the inhabitant of that synagogue to believe.

## 3.

If, therefore, the centurion was justified because of a fragile or earthly work, then surely our most illustrious and provident Count should be justified because of a work so enduring and heavenly. Just as this Count is superior to the centurion in rank, so he ought also to be more devoted in faith.

He is a wise and religious count, who serves the emperor in war as much as he serves the Savior in peace; and just as eagerly as he hastens to rescue captives from the hands of enemies, so much more eagerly does he hasten to free himself from the devil’s sacrilege.

There he kills the enemies of an earthly king; here he pursues the adversaries of the heavenly Lord. There he conquers barbarians; here, demons.

Wise indeed is the man who, just as he is the emperor’s count, so also desires to be Christ’s companion. For by acting well and religiously he wishes his dignity to be perpetual, according to what is written in the Prophet:

“And you, good kings, make your ways and your purposes good, and hear the voice of the Lord your God; then the Lord will repent of the evil that he has spoken against you” (Jeremiah 26:13).

## 4.

When, therefore, the centurion asked the Lord to rescue the sick man from death, and the Lord wished to go to the centurion’s house, where the little servant lay, the centurion said:

“Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

The centurion therefore makes an excuse and declares himself unworthy that the Lord should enter beneath his roof. Behold, our Count is worthy, under whose roof the Savior enters today.

## 5.

Let us see what grace the centurion’s very excuse contains. For he says:

“Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but speak only a word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8).

O Christian faith, which has learned to obtain everything through humility! Behold, the religious centurion becomes more worthy to receive salvation when he professes himself unworthy. And when he considers his house unworthy, he makes it all the more honorable and pleasing.

For he was a man of great and perfect faith, who understood that Christ was the Lord of heaven, while he feared that the narrowness of his lodging would not receive him.

[Note: The remainder of this sermon, to its end, is absent from the Lugdunensis manuscript.]

Therefore, when the centurion objected, the Lord did not go to the house. The Lord did not go, but the Lord’s healing went; the Savior did not visit the sick man, but the Savior’s health visited him.

## 6.

But what shall I say about our holy brothers Vitalinus and Maianus? I know that they seek glory not from men but from God alone. Yet even if I were silent about their praise, the works themselves speak; for whatever we praised in others a little earlier pertains to their praise.

For although many people built this tabernacle, these men nevertheless contributed the expense with one accord. And what kind of expense was it, since they are of modest and limited means in this world?

It was that of which the Apostle says: “An abundance of faith and the riches of simplicity” (2 Corinthians 8:2).

For among holy men poverty itself is always rich. Hence I believe that these blessed men built this church no less with prayers than with expenditures. For it was fitting that the work of Christ should grow more through prayers than through mortar.

They spent their entire substance on the construction of this work, and yet they themselves certainly lack nothing. This is plainly, as we said, rich and wealthy poverty, which spends everything and possesses everything.

But this poverty has been blessed by God, like that widow of whom the Lord says in the Gospel:

“This poor widow has put in more than all the others; for all these gave offerings to God from their abundance, but she gave all the livelihood she had.”

# [LETTERS REMOVED FROM THE NUMBER OF THE AMBROSIAN LETTERS]

[Col. 0733]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE LETTERS REMOVED FROM THE NUMBER OF THE AMBROSIAN LETTERS

[Col. 0733B] We have judged that five letters should be removed from the catalogue of the Ambrosian letters. The first two—namely, *To the Sacred Virgin Demetrias* and *To the Sacred Virgins*—had been published in all editions of the works of Saint Ambrose. The three later ones—namely, *On the Discovery of the Saints Gervasius and Protasius*, *On the Discovery of the Saints Vitalis and Agricola*, and the letter to Florianus—were first brought to light by the Roman editors.

We briefly set out our judgment concerning each, so that the reader may understand by what considerations we were led to reject them.

The letter to Demetrias is rejected as Ambrose’s by every scholarly generation. Whatever a reader encounters there plainly proves that their judgment ought to be held valid, especially the discussions concerning the Pelagians, who were later than our Doctor.

Some years ago Quesnellius had attempted to attribute it to Leo the Great in his edition of the works of that pontiff. Recently Anselm rose up against him with great zeal and believed that it should be vindicated for his fellow-countryman Prosper, along with several other works.

Anyone may choose whichever side he wishes in that dispute; since it is certain to us that the letter is not Ambrose’s, we will not object. Moreover, since the same letter has often been published elsewhere among letters attributed to Ambrose, we would seem to burden this volume with unnecessary weight if we were to print it again.

For this reason, the order of the four letters that we shall present here will be led by the one addressed to the sacred virgins. This letter is rejected not only by the judgment of others but also by Baronius himself, who says that it was improperly inscribed with the name of Ambrose (under the year 324, no. 107).

We therefore cannot help wondering what occurred to the learned men who undertook upon their shoulders the great mass of the work begun by Bollandus, when they printed this letter under the name of our Ambrose. They ought surely to have noticed that its author was entirely ignorant of the customs that prevailed at Rome in the time of the holy Bishop.

Otherwise he would never have written what we read near the end of the letter:

“Constantia persevered in virginity, through which many virgins, both of modest birth and noble and illustrious, received the sacred veils.”

How empty and futile this statement is may be learned from Jerome’s testimony, where he says as follows in his *Letter on the Praises of Marcella*:

“At that time no noble woman in Rome had vowed the monastic way of life, nor did anyone dare, because of the novelty of the matter, to assume among the people a name that was then considered disgraceful and low.”

Therefore, if this letter is to be attributed to Ambrose at all, we shall accept the judgment written by John Bandinus in the margin of the same letter in a Vatican manuscript, from which we obtained a copy in a friendly hand, in these words:

“It is not by Ambrose of Milan, but by another Ambrose, a certain monk, who wrote this sermon in Greek. It exists in the Vatican Library and was later translated into Latin by another person.”

As for the remaining three letters, which, as we said above, first appeared in the Roman edition, anyone who undertakes to compare them with certain genuinely Ambrosian works will immediately recognize how greatly they differ from one another.

To make this more evident and clear, let what is reported in the first of them concerning the discovery of the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius be compared with what Augustine, Paulinus, and Ambrose himself record concerning that same discovery.

Nevertheless, it must not be denied that a passage from this same letter is found cited in a fragment of John of Damascus’s *Oration on Images*. But this proves nothing more than that, from the time of that saint onward—if indeed the fragment truly belongs to him—the letter had been accustomed to circulate under the name of Ambrose.

[Col. 0735] Nor does the following letter seem any less clearly to belong to some compiler, who interpolated Ambrose’s account of the discovery of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, which Ambrose left described in his *Exhortation to Virginity*, partly by adding, partly by changing, and partly by rearranging it.

Add to this the authority of Gregory of Tours, who explicitly states that in his own time the Acts of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius existed, but not those of Vitalis and Agricola (*Book I of the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapters 44 and 47).

Finally, the letter which in the Roman edition is addressed to Flavianus, but which in the manuscript of the Royal Library bears the title *On Morals and an Honorable Life*—although in both places it bears the name of Ambrose at its head—has a style and character that plainly contradict that attribution.

# LETTERS REMOVED FROM THE NUMBER OF THE AMBROSIAN LETTERS (C, G, S)

## 479. LETTER I

[Col. 0735A]

Before the martyrdom of the virgin Agnes is described, the love of the prefect’s son for her and her rejection of him are recounted. Then the virgin’s condemnation to a brothel is added, together with the miracles divinely performed on behalf of the same girl: the death of the young man who was desperately enamored of her and his restoration to life.

Next follows the virgin’s condemnation to the pyre because of the pagan uprising, and her bloody killing while she remained unharmed amid the flames. Soon afterward, the fury of the pagans against the Christians who were persisting in prayer at the Martyr’s tomb is described; then comes the killing of Emerentiana, the restoration of the health of the Empress Constantia, the temple built by that same ruler for her deliverer, and the account of her resolve, together with that of several others, to embrace virginity.

**Ambrose, bishop and servant of Christ, to the sacred virgins.**

## 1.

Let us celebrate the feast day of the most sacred virgin. From one side let the psalms resound; from the other let the readings ring out. From one side let the crowds of the people rejoice; from the other let the poor of Christ be lifted up.

Let us all therefore rejoice in the Lord, and for the instruction of virgins let us recall how the most blessed Agnes suffered.

[Note: “At that time there was . . . and the powers of darkness” are restored from the Noallian manuscript.]

At that time there was a certain virgin in Rome, born of noble parents, named Agnes. Striving against rulers and the powers of darkness, she lost death and found life in the thirteenth year of her age, because she loved the Author of life alone.

In years she was counted as a child, but in her character she possessed the old age of the mind.

[Note: All printed editions read: “but the old age of her mind was immense”; the Noallian manuscript is better, as in the text.]

In body she was a young girl, but in spirit she was gray with age. Beautiful in face, but more beautiful in faith and more distinguished in chastity.

## 2.

As she was returning from school, she was loved by the son of the prefect of the City.

[Note: So the Noallian manuscript; all printed editions instead read: “When he had sought out and found her parents, he began to offer many things and promise still more.”]

When his parents had sought her out and found her, they began to offer beautiful things and promise more beautiful ones. Finally, they had brought with them the most precious ornaments, which blessed Agnes rejected as though they were refuse.

As a result, the young man was driven on by a still greater stimulus of love. Thinking that she wanted to receive better ornaments, he brought with him every precious stone and its splendor.

[Note: All printed editions read: “He brought with him the splendor of precious stones of every kind.”]

Through himself, his friends, his acquaintances, and his relatives, he began to address the virgin’s ears. He promised riches, houses, estates, servants, and all the delights of this world if she would not refuse her consent to his marriage.

## 3.

Blessed Agnes is said to have given the young man this reply:

“Depart from me, kindling of sin, nourishment of crime, food of death; depart from me. For I have already been claimed by another lover, who has offered me ornaments far better than yours and betrothed me with the ring of his faith—one far nobler than you both in birth and in dignity.

“He has adorned my right hand with an incomparable bracelet and encircled my neck with precious stones. He has given my ears priceless pearls and surrounded me with blooming and sparkling gems. He has placed his sign upon my face, so that I may admit no lover besides him.

“He has clothed me in a gold-woven robe and adorned me with immense necklaces. He has shown me incomparable treasures, which he promised to give me if I persevere in his love.

“Therefore I cannot, to the insult of my former lover, even look upon another and abandon him to whom I am bound by love. His nobility is higher, his power stronger, his appearance more beautiful, his love sweeter, and he is more elegant in every grace.

“He has already prepared a bridal chamber for me. Its instruments resound for me in harmonious voices, and its virgins sing for me in most upright voices. I have already received honey and milk from his mouth. I am already bound in his chaste embraces. His body has already been joined to my body, and his blood has adorned my cheeks.

“His mother is a virgin; his father knows no woman. Angels serve him. The sun and the moon marvel at his beauty. The dead revive at his fragrance. The sick are strengthened by his touch. His resources never fail, and his riches never diminish.

“To him alone I keep my faith; to him I entrust myself with complete devotion. When I love him, I am chaste; when I touch him, I am pure; when I receive him, I am a virgin. Nor will sons be lacking after the marriage, where childbirth follows without pain and fertility increases daily.”

## 3.

When the utterly mad young man heard this, he was consumed by blind love and was tortured amid anguish of mind and body, gasping for breath.

Meanwhile he was thrown upon his bed, and through deep sighs his love was disclosed to the physicians. What the physicians had discovered became known to his father, and at the father’s request the words already spoken by his son were repeated to the virgin.

The most blessed Agnes refused, asserting that she could in no way violate the covenant of her former betrothed.

When her father said that he held the office of praetor in the insignia of the prefecture, and therefore ought not to have any man, even a distinguished one, preferred to him—

[Note: So the Noallian manuscript; the printed editions read: “that he was acting in the insignia of the prefecture.”]

—he nevertheless began to inquire most insistently who the bridegroom was whose power the holy Agnes gloried in.

Then one of his parasites came forward and said that she was a Christian from infancy and so possessed by magical arts that she claimed Christ as her bridegroom.

## 4.

When the prefect Symphronius heard this, he became glad. He sent a summons with great commotion and ordered her to be brought before his tribunal.

At first he secretly tried to persuade her with gentle words; then he assaulted her with threats. But the virgin of Christ was neither led astray by persuasion nor shaken by terror. Remaining with the same expression and the same courage, she mocked in her heart both the one who threatened and the one who flattered.

When the prefect Symphronius saw such steadfastness in the girl, he addressed her parents. Since they were noble and he could not use force against them, he brought against them the charge of Christianity.

The following day he ordered Agnes to be brought before him, and again and again he repeated the matter of the young man’s love.

## 5.

When all his speeches failed through fruitless effort, he ordered her to be brought before his tribunal and said to her:

“If the Christian superstition, whose magical arts you boast of, is not removed from you, you will not be able to cast the madness from your heart or give consent to the most reasonable counsels.

“Therefore you must hasten to the venerable goddess Vesta, and if perseverance in virginity pleases you, you must devote yourself day and night to her revered sacrifices.”

Blessed Agnes answered:

“If I refused your son, though he was afflicted by an unlawful love, yet still a living human being—a human being capable of reason, who can hear, see, touch, and walk,

[Note: All printed editions add: “and enjoy the good things in the brightness of this light”; the Noallian manuscript reads: “and enjoy the good things in the radiance,” etc.]

—and if for the sake of Christ’s love I can in no way look upon him, how can I worship mute and deaf idols, without sense and without soul, and in insult to the supreme God bow my neck before empty stones?”

## 6.

When the prefect Symphronius heard this, he said:

“I wish to give counsel to your childhood, and I still delay punishing you for blaspheming the gods because I regard your years as beneath understanding. Do not despise yourself so much that you incur the anger of the gods.”

Blessed Agnes answered:

“Do not despise my bodily childhood so much that you think I wish to win your favor. Faith is carried not in years but in understanding, and almighty God approves minds more than ages.

“As for your gods, whose anger you do not wish me to incur, allow them to be angry with themselves; order them to speak. Let them command me to do this; let them command themselves to be worshiped; let them command themselves to be adored.

“But since I see that you are aiming at something you will not be able to obtain, do whatever seems good to you.”

## 7.

The prefect Symphronius said:

“Choose one of two things: either sacrifice with the virgins of the goddess Vesta, or you will be prostituted with the harlots in the brothel. And the Christians who so steeped you in magical arts that you trust you can endure this calamity with an undaunted spirit will be far from you.

“Therefore, as I said, either sacrifice to the goddess Vesta for the honor of your family, or, to the disgrace of your ancestry, you will become a prostitute subjected to public degradation.”

Then blessed Agnes said with great steadfastness:

“If you knew who my God is, you would not utter such words from your mouth. Since I know the power of my Lord Jesus Christ, I securely despise your threats, believing that I will neither sacrifice to your idols nor be defiled by the uncleanness of others.

“For I have with me an angel of the Lord as guardian of my body. The only-begotten Son of God, whom you do not know, is an unassailable wall for me, an ever-watchful guardian, and a defender who never fails.

“But your gods are either made of bronze, from which cauldrons are better made for human use, or of stone—

[Note: All printed editions read: “from which streets are paved”; other words have been added from the manuscript mentioned above.]

—from which streets are better paved to escape the mud.

“Divinity does not dwell in empty stones; it dwells in heaven. It does not consist in bronze or in any metal; it abides in the heavenly kingdom.

“But unless you and those like you withdraw from the worship of these things, a similar punishment will overtake you. For just as they were melted by fire in order to be cast, so those who worship them will be melted in everlasting fire—not so that they may be cast, but so that they may be confounded forever and perish.”

## 8.

At this the mad judge ordered her to be stripped and led naked to the brothel, while a herald proclaimed that Agnes was a sacrilegious virgin who blasphemed the gods and had been handed over to the brothels.

As soon as she had been stripped and her hair had been loosened, divine grace granted such thickness to her hair that she appeared better covered by its strands than by clothing.

When she entered the place of shame, she found the angel of the Lord prepared there in such a way that he surrounded her with immense light, so that no one could look at her, touch her, or see her because of the brilliance.

For the entire chamber shone as though the sun were radiating in its strength; and the more eagerly anyone wished to look, the more he blunted the sharpness of his sight.

When she had prostrated herself in prayer before the Lord, a robe of dazzling whiteness appeared before her eyes. She took hold of it, put it on, and said:

“I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who, counting me among your handmaids, have commanded that this garment be given to me.”

The garment was so perfectly fitted to her little body and so conspicuous in its excessive whiteness that no one could doubt that it had been prepared by angelic hands.

Meanwhile the brothel became a place of prayer. All who entered worshiped and revered there, giving honor to God for the immense splendor, and they went out purer than they had been when they entered.

[Note: So the Noallian manuscript; the printed editions instead read: “everyone who entered would worship . . . giving honor to the immense light, and would go out purer,” etc.]

## 9.

While these things were happening, the prefect’s son, who had been the author of this crime, came to the place with his young companions, as though he intended to insult the girl. He believed that with them he could engage in the sport of his lust.

But when he entered and sent before him young men who were burning with desire and raging shamefully, and when they emerged with excessive reverence and immense amazement, he began to rebuke them for their weakness and judge them foolish, effeminate, and wretched.

Mocking them, he boldly entered the place where the virgin was worshiping. When he saw such a great light around her, he did not give honor to God. Instead, he rushed into the light itself and, before he could even touch her with his hand, fell on his face and expired, strangled by the devil.

His companions, seeing that he was delaying inside, thought that he was occupied with obscene acts. One of the young men, who was more intimate with him, entered as though to congratulate him on his insult. Finding him dead, he cried out in a loud voice:

“Most pious Romans, come to our aid! This harlot has killed the prefect’s son by magical arts.”

Suddenly the crowds rushed to the theater, and the raging people shouted variously. Some called her a witch; others proclaimed her innocent; others cried out that she was sacrilegious.

## 10.

When the prefect heard that his son had died, he came to the theater amid immense tumult and mourning. He entered the place where his son’s lifeless body lay and cried out loudly to the most blessed virgin:

“Most cruel of all women, you wished to demonstrate the proof of your magical art upon my son.”

As he continued to heap up words of this sort and others like them, and vehemently demanded from her the cause of his death, blessed Agnes said to him:

“The one whose will he sought to carry out received power over him.

“But why did all who entered to me come out unharmed? Because they all gave honor to God, who sent his angel, clothed me in this garment of his mercy, and guarded my body, which from the very cradle had been consecrated and offered to Christ.

“When they saw the angelic splendor, they all worshiped and went away unharmed. But this shameless man, as soon as he entered, began to rage and snarl; and when he prepared his hand to touch me, the angel of the Lord handed him over to the reprobate death that you see.”

11. The prefect says to her: “It will become evident that you have not done these things by magical arts if you pray to that angel himself to restore my son to me alive and well.” Blessed Agnes replied to him: “Although your faith does not deserve to obtain this from the Lord, nevertheless, since it is time for the power of my Lord Jesus Christ to be manifested, all of you go outside, so that I may offer him his customary prayer.” When everyone had gone outside, she prostrated herself face-down upon the pavement [Col. 0739D]—the same editions read, “prostrating herself with her face flat upon the ground”; Codex Noall has, “upon the face of the pavement”—and began to ask the Lord to raise the young man. While she was praying, the angel of the Lord appeared to her, lifted her up as she wept, strengthened her spirit, and raised the young man. When he went outside, he began publicly to cry out and say: “There is one God in heaven and on earth and in the sea, who is the God of the Christians; for all the temples are vain, and all the gods who are worshiped are vain and utterly unable to provide any help either for themselves or for others.” [Col. 0740A–B]

12. At these words all the haruspices and priests of the temples were thrown into confusion, and through them the people’s uprising became more violent than before. Everyone shouted with one voice: “Take away the sorceress! Take away the witch, who changes minds and alienates hearts.” But when the prefect saw such great wonders, he was astonished. Yet, fearing proscription if he acted against the priests of the temples and defended Agnes against their judgments, he left his deputy as judge over the people’s uprising, while he himself departed sadly because he had been unable to free her after the resurrection of his son.

Then the deputy, named Aspasius—unable to endure the people’s uprising [Note: [Col. 0740D] “Unable to endure the people’s uprising” is added from Codex Noall]—ordered a large fire to be lit in full view of everyone and commanded that she be thrown into the midst of the flames. When this had been done, the flames immediately divided into two parts and burned the rebellious crowds on either side; but the fire did not touch her in the slightest. The people, however, attributing this less to divine powers than to sorcery, uttered even louder cries among themselves and raised countless shouts to heaven. [Col. 0740C]

13. Then blessed Agnes stretched out her hands in the midst of the fire and poured forth this prayer to the Lord:

“Almighty, adorable, worshiped, and terrible Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, I bless you because through your Son I have escaped the threats of impious men and passed undefiled through the filth of the devil. Behold, now, drenched with the heavenly dew of the Holy Spirit, the fire beside me has been dissolved; the flame is divided, and the heat of this blaze is poured out upon those by whom it is supplied. I bless you, Father worthy of praise, who even amid the flames permit me to come to you without fear. Behold, now I see what I believed; I now possess what I hoped for; I embrace what I desired. I confess you with lips and heart, and I long for you with all my inward being. Behold, I come to you, the living and true God, who with the Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, and with the Holy Spirit, live and reign now and forever, for endless ages of ages. Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 0740D] All editions read: “Behold, even now, drenched with heavenly dew through the Holy Spirit, the pyre beside me dies”; Codex Noall has the wording given above.]

14. When she had finished the prayer, all the fire was extinguished so completely that not even the warmth of the blaze remained. Then Aspasius, deputy of the city of Rome, unable to endure the people’s uprising, ordered a sword to be thrust into her throat. By this death Christ consecrated his bride and martyr, bathed in the rosy redness of her blood.

Her parents, however, felt no grief at all. With complete joy they took away her body and placed it on their estate not far from the city, on the road called the Nomentan Way. When the entire crowd of Christians gathered there, they suffered an ambush from the pagans. On seeing the armed crowd of unbelievers approaching, everyone fled; some, however, escaped after being wounded by stones. [Col. 0741A]

15. [Note: [Col. 0741D] Thus Codex Noall; all editions, however: “But Emerentiana, who had been her foster-sister, a most holy virgin, although a catechumen, stood steadfast, fearless, and immovable.”]
