While her foster-sister, the most holy virgin Emerentiana, was praying amid such great crowds, she stood firm and immovable and reproached them in these words:

“Useless, wretched, fleeting, and most savage people! You kill those who worship almighty God, and in defense of stones you slaughter innocent human beings.”

While she was saying these and similar things to the enraged crowds, they stoned her. As she prayed beside the tomb of the most blessed virgin Agnes, she gave up her spirit. There is no doubt that she was baptized in her own blood, for while confessing the Lord in defense of justice, she steadfastly accepted death.

At that very hour a most violent earthquake occurred. Although the sky was exceedingly clear, such flashes of lightning, bolts, and thunder arose that the greater part of the mad crowd perished. As a result, no one thereafter caused any disturbance to those coming to the saints’ tombs. The parents of blessed Agnes came by night with the priests, took away the body of Emerentiana [Note: [Col. 0741D] The editions read, “of the holy virgin Emerentiana”], and buried it at the boundary of the little estate belonging to the most blessed virgin Agnes. [Col. 0741B–C]

16. Thus, while the parents of Saint Agnes kept vigil through repeated nightly watches at her tomb, in the silence of midnight they saw an army of virgins. All were clothed in gold-woven garments and passed by amid a great light. Among them they also saw the most blessed Agnes shining in the same way, with the Lamb standing at her right hand. When her parents and those who were with them saw this, they were held as if by a stupor of the mind.

But blessed Agnes asked the holy virgins to pause for a little while. Standing there, she said to her parents: “See to it that you do not mourn me as dead, but rejoice with me and congratulate me, because I have received radiant dwellings with these virgins and have been joined in heaven to the one whom, while placed on earth, I loved with complete devotion.” [Note: [Col. 0741D] The same editions read, “whom I loved with the full intention of my soul.”] After saying this, she passed on.

17. This vision was publicly spread by all who had seen it. Consequently, several years later the event was reported to Constantia, the daughter of the Augustus, by those who had witnessed it. Constantia herself was an exceedingly prudent virgin, but she was so covered with sores that no part of her body remained free from them, from head to foot.

Having received hope of recovering her health, she came by night to the martyr’s tomb. Although she was a pagan, she nevertheless poured out prayers faithfully with a believing disposition of mind. As she did so, she was suddenly overcome by the sweetness of sleep and saw in a vision the most blessed Agnes bringing her this message:

“Act courageously, Constantia, and believe that the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is your Savior; through him you will now obtain healing from all the wounds that you suffer in your body.”

At these words Constantia awoke healed [Col. 0742A]—so completely healed that not even a mark of any wound remained on her limbs. She therefore returned to the palace in perfect health and brought joy both to her father, the Augustus, and to her brothers, the emperors. The whole city was crowned; joy arose among the soldiers and its leading men [Note: [Col. 0741D] Codex Noall reads as above; the edition has instead, “among the soldiers and common people.” On this passage see Casaubon’s notes on Lampridius, p. 174]. As everyone heard these things, the unbelief of the nations was confounded and the faith of the Lord rejoiced. [Col. 0742B]

18. Meanwhile she asked her father and brothers, the Augusti, to build a basilica for blessed Agnes [Note: [Col. 0742D] The editions add, “and ordered a mausoleum for herself to be placed there.” Consult the Acts of Liberius in Labbe’s Councils, p. 37], and ordered a dwelling for herself to be established there. This report spread to everyone, and all who came as believers to her tomb were saved, whatever illness afflicted them. No one doubts that Christ continues to do this even to the present day.

Constantia, the daughter of the Augustus, persevered in virginity. Through her, many virgins—of modest, noble, and illustrious status—received the sacred veil. And because faith suffers no loss from death, even to the present day many virgins in Rome see the most blessed Agnes as though she were still bodily present; following her example, they persevere courageously and uprightly, believing without doubt that those who persevere will obtain the palm of everlasting victory. [Col. 0742C]

19. I, Ambrose, servant of Christ, having found these things written in hidden volumes, did not allow them to be covered by unfruitful silence. Therefore, in honor of so great a martyr, I wrote them down as I learned her deeds, and I judged that the text of her passion should be sent for your edification, O virgins of Christ [Col. 0742D]. I beseech the power of the Holy Spirit that our labor may bear fruit in the sight of God by leading you to imitate her [Note: [Col. 0742D] The same editions read: “beseeching the charity of the Holy Spirit that our labor may be able to find fruit in the sight of the Lord through your imitation. Amen.” Codex Noall has the wording given above]. To him be honor and glory forever. Amen.

## Letter II (formerly LIII)

Since God’s benefits ought not to be concealed, Ambrose recounts the vision in which Gervasius and Protasius appeared to him once and again during Lent, and on the third occasion Paul also appeared, commanding that a church be built for them after their remains had been exhumed. He adds that, after summoning his fellow bishops, the bodies of the saints were found; from a document discovered there he reports their conversion, death, and burial. He also inserts the martyrdom of Vitalis and Valeria.

AMBROSE, servant of Christ, eternal salvation in the Lord to the brethren throughout Italy.

1. In the divine books the person who has not taken care to give freely what he himself freely received is declared guilty. For he is accused of having withheld whatever would have benefited the Church of the Lord, since he was unwilling to hand on to everyone what he had received—not to be concealed. Hence the Psalmist and prophet sings:

“I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation. I have not concealed your mercy from the great assembly” (Ps. 39:11).

And, asking God for a kind of return for this work, he added:

“But you, O Lord, do not remove your mercy far from me” (ibid., 12).

It is as though he were saying to God: “Just as I have caused others to find mercy, so do not allow your mercies to be far from me.” Let us therefore explain why we have prefaced these words and invite your minds—since you think and believe piously concerning the Lord—to rejoice over the discovery of the saints’ bodies. [Col. 0743A–B]

2. During the days of the Lent that had recently passed, when the Lord had granted that I should share in the fasting [Note: [Col. 0743D] The Roman edition omits “and praying”] and prayers of those who fasted, I was engaged in prayer when sleep so overcame me that, neither fully awake nor wholly asleep, I saw with open eyes two young men, ephebes, standing with me. They were clothed in brilliant white garments—that is, a tunic and cloak—and wore boots, with their hands extended in prayer.

Although I felt no heaviness, I could not speak with them. But, as I have said, a part of me was under the influence of sleep, which prevented me from uttering a word in response to their questioning. When I fully awoke, their vision slipped away from my eyes. [Col. 0743C]

3. I therefore asked the mercy of the Lord that, if it had been a deception of demons, it might depart; but if it were true, that it might appear more fully. To obtain what I was asking from the Lord, I increased my fasting. In the same way, at cockcrow, the same young men appeared, praying with me. [Col. 0743D]

4. On the third night, when my body had been weakened by fasting, they appeared not to one who was sleeping but to one who was in a state of astonishment, together with a third person who resembled the blessed apostle Paul. A painting had taught me what his face looked like. He himself spoke with me while the other two were silent, saying:

“These are the men who, following my teachings, rejected estates and riches and followed the footsteps of our Lord Jesus Christ, desiring nothing earthly and nothing carnal. Remaining in the service of God for ten years in this city of Milan, they deserved to attain the point of becoming Christ’s martyrs. You will find their bodies in the very place where you are standing and praying. You will find an ark covered with earth to a depth of twelve feet. You will raise the ark above ground and build a church in their name.”

When I asked him their names, he said to me: “At their head you will find a written booklet in which both their origin and their end have been recorded.” [Col. 0744A]

5. I therefore summoned all the surrounding brethren and the bishops of the neighboring cities. Reporting everything that I had seen and heard, I was the first to approach as an excavator of the earth. The other bishops followed, and as we dug we reached the ark that Saint Paul had promised. When we opened it, we found the saints as though they had been placed there at that very hour, exuding a wondrous fragrance. At their head we found a booklet in which all the following things had been written in order: [Col. 0744B]

6. “I, Philip, servant of Christ, buried within my house the bodies of the saints, which I carried away with my son. Their mother was called Valeria and their father Vitalis. They begot them as twins in a single birth and named one Protasius and the other Gervasius.”

[Note: [Col. 0743D] The Roman edition reads: “They named them; and when Gervasius and Protasius had succeeded by intestate inheritance to their property—that is, after their holy father Vitalis the martyr and their mother Valeria of holy memory had died—…” [Col. 0744D] We have followed two Longpont codices, which insert the martyrdoms of Saints Vitalis and Valeria into this letter.]

7. Their father Vitalis, a consular soldier, had entered Ravenna with his judge Paulinus. When Paulinus began to seek Christians for sacrifice, a certain Christian named Ursicinus was brought before him, a physician by profession and a Ligurian by birth.

Then Paulinus ordered him to be tortured in his presence, saying: “Sacrifice, Ursicinus, to the immortal gods.” But he replied to him: “I will not sacrifice to deaf and dumb beings; I will sacrifice to my Lord Jesus Christ.”

When Paulinus saw that he could not change him from his steadfastness, after extensive tortures he ordered him to undergo the death sentence. The place where Christians were beheaded had the name by which it was called: “At the Palm.” For an ancient palm tree stood there. [Col. 0744C]

8. Thus, as we said, when the holy Ursicinus came to the Palm to be beheaded after extensive tortures, he was frightened. As he wished to escape his fate, Saint Vitalis cried out, saying:

“Do not, do not, physician Ursicinus, who were accustomed to heal others, wound yourself with the dart of eternal death. You have come to the palm through grievous sufferings; do not lose the crown prepared for you by the Lord.”

When Saint Ursicinus heard this, he knelt and urged the executioner to strike, repenting that he had been afraid. The executioner struck him and made him a martyr of Christ.

Immediately Saint Vitalis seized the martyr’s body and buried it with all the honor due to a martyr within the city of Ravenna. After that, Saint Vitalis refused to come again before the judge. For this reason the consular Paulinus ordered him to be seized—not merely because he had refused to return to him [Col. 0744D–0745A], but especially because he had been exposed as a Christian.

9. Then Paulinus’s servants seized him and brought him before him. When Paulinus saw him, he said to him: “How have you been deceived by sorcery, Vitalis, so that you do not sacrifice to the gods?”

He replied: “I do not sacrifice to deaf and dumb beings, but I sacrifice to my God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them, and to Jesus Christ his Son, who lives and reigns with him and the Holy Spirit.”

Then Paulinus ordered him to be hoisted upon the rack, so that through tortures he might compel him to consent to sacrifice. But Saint Vitalis was eager to return to God the precious jewel that the devil was striving to snatch away. He answered him:

“Endless folly rules you. Or do you think that I can deceive myself, when I have striven to free others from the danger of death or deception?” [Col. 0745B]

10. Then Paulinus the consular said to the officer: “Take him to the Palm, and do not behead him if he refuses to sacrifice. Instead, dig a pit in the ground until you reach water; there lay him on his back, cover him with earth and stones, and leave him there.”

When this had been done, God consecrated Saint Vitalis as a martyr for himself in such a way that the priest of Apollo who had given this advice to the judge Paulinus, filled with the devil, cried out there for seven days as one possessed:

“You burn me, martyr; you torture me, holy one.”

After seven days the devil cast him into a river, and he died. But Saint Vitalis, glorious martyr of Christ, grants benefits by his prayers and intercessions to all who believe in Jesus Christ, beside the city of Ravenna, even to the present day. [Col. 0745C]

11. His wife Valeria, wishing to take away the body of Saint Vitalis, was prevented by Christians and was often warned in visions not to violate the holy body, which had been properly laid to rest by an evil person. But when she persisted in her intention, Saint Vitalis appeared to her more clearly and said:

“Do not trouble me, woman, for you will never be able to prepare for me a tomb as glorious as the one the Lord Jesus Christ has ordered to be made for me.” [Col. 0745D]

12. As she was returning to the city of Milan, she encountered on the road men who were sacrificing to the idol Silvanus. When they saw her, they took her down from her vehicle and urged her to feast with them. But she resisted and said:

“I am a Christian; I am not permitted to eat from the sacrifices of your Silvanus.”

As soon as they heard this, they beat her with such a slaughterous attack that her own people could scarcely carry her, half dead, into the city of Milan. Within three days she departed to Christ. [Col. 0745D–0746A]

13. After their blessed father Vitalis had been crowned with martyrdom and their most blessed mother Valeria had departed to Christ, Gervasius and Protasius succeeded to their parents’ possessions by intestate right. They sold their own house, in which they had been born, all their parents’ belongings, and their small houses. They gave the entire price to the poor and set their own household free. They themselves shut themselves up in a single upper room and devoted ten years to reading and prayer. In this manner, in the eleventh year after their conversion, they reached the palm of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0745D] The Roman edition reads: “Rejecting the idols, under Count Astasius in the city of Milan, on the first day of June, they happily reached the palm. For at that time, when he arrived…”]. [Col. 0746A]

14. When Count Astasius came along on his way to the war that had been stirred up by the Marcomanni [Note: [Col. 0746D] The same edition reads: “the worshipers of the idols met him”], the worshipers of the temples came to him with their priests and said:

“If you wish to return joyful and victorious to our Augusti, compel Gervasius and Protasius to sacrifice to our gods. For our gods are exceedingly angered by their contempt and refuse to give us an answer.”

[Col. 0746B] 15. When Count Astasius heard this, he ordered them to be seized and brought before him. He said to them:

“I urge you to restrain the insults against our gods and devote yourselves earnestly to sacrificing to them, so that my expedition may be successfully carried out.”

Blessed Gervasius said:

“You must ask victory from heaven of almighty God, not from filthy and empty images, which are proven to have eyes without light, ears without hearing, nostrils without smell, a mouth without speech, hands without touch, feet without movement, and a belly without inward organs, and are known to be without breath.”

Angered, Count Astasius ordered him to be beaten with leaded clubs until he breathed out his spirit.

16. When he had been taken away, Astasius ordered Protasius to stand before him and said to him:

“Wretched man, at least you should strive to live, and do not become βιωθάνατος—that is, die a violent death—like your brother.”

Protasius replied:

“Who is wretched: I, who am not afraid, or you, who are shown to be afraid of me?”

The count said: “How am I afraid of you?”

Protasius replied:

“In that you fear being harmed if I do not sacrifice. For if you did not fear being harmed by me, you would not compel me to sacrifice. But I, fearing neither you nor your threats, despise them and count all your idols as dung. I worship the one God who reigns in heaven.” [Col. 0746C]

17. When Astasius heard this, he ordered him to be beaten with staves. Then, when he had been raised up, he said:

“Wretched man, why are you so proud and rebellious? Do you wish to perish as you have proved your brother to have perished?”

Protasius said:

“I am not angry with you—neither am I, nor is justice itself—because I regard the blind eyes of your heart. The unbelief that rules your understanding does not allow you to see what belongs to God.

For my Lord Jesus Christ did not curse those who crucified him; rather, he prayed that they might be forgiven, adding that they did not know what they were doing. Therefore I also pity you, because you do not know what you are doing. Go on, then, with what you have begun, so that the kindness of our Savior may come to me today together with my brother Gervasius.” [Col. 0746D]

18. Then Count Astasius ordered him to be beheaded. When this had been done, I, Philip, secretly took away the bodies of these saints by night with my son and buried them in my house, with God alone as witness, in this stone ark [Col. 0747A]. I believed that through their prayers I would obtain the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## Letter III (formerly LV)

Ambrose recounts the discovery, with the applause of the Christians, the astonishment of the Jews, and not a few miracles, of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, who had been buried at Bologna among the tombs of the Jews. He praises them both by their names and for their steadfastness in their sufferings, and adds several other matters pertaining to the same subject.

AMBROSE, servant of Jesus Christ and called bishop, eternal salvation in the Lord to his most beloved brethren [Note: [Col. 0747D] Codex Regius adds: “and to all the people, eternal salvation in the Lord.” The great and exalted testimonies of the martyrs are diminished rather than explained by our discourse. Therefore, invited by the people of Bologna, I could not in any way refuse my presence, since the time had come for the Lord to display his customary wonders. I brought with me gifts full of holiness and grace; gifts are customarily associated with the triumphs of princes. These gifts, too, are triumphal offerings, for the palms of the martyrs are the triumphs of Christ our prince. Therefore, since there is less in me than was expected, more is found in the martyrs. The name of the holy martyr is Agricola. The rest is found in the same sequence and with the same words, apart from one or two sentences, in *Exhortation to a Virgin*, from chapter 1, no. 2, through chapter 2, no. 10. But after the words “today we dedicate,” the invocation found in the cited work, chapter 14, no. 94, is added; afterward comes the conclusion, “They suffered,” etc., as below.] and to all the peoples throughout Italy, eternal salvation in the Lord.

1. The great and exalted testimonies of the martyrs about which I am going to write to you are diminished rather than explained by our discourse. Yet what discourse diminishes, power increases. Therefore, what is lacking in me shines forth splendidly in the martyrs. [Col. 0747B]

2. When I was invited by the people of Bologna, I could not, at the Lord’s prompting, refuse my presence, since the time had come for Christ to display to his faithful the wonders he is accustomed to perform.

For during the reigns of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, two men—Vitalis and Agricola—suffered martyrdom for Christ in the city of Bologna. Their bodies had been hidden among the tombs of the Jews so that the faithful would not find them. Thus, confessing Christ and dying for his glory, they had been dishonorably buried among those who denied him.

Our Lord Christ was pleased to reveal to me the place that had been hidden from everyone. There, after keeping many vigils in fasting and prayer, we finally found the martyrs’ remains as the Lord had revealed them to me, like people gathering a rose among thorns; and they were made manifest openly to all. [Col. 0747C]

3. The Christian people were present with applause and joy. The Jews, joking, said:

“Flowers have appeared in our land” (Song 2:12).

The Christians replied:

“The time of pruning has come” (ibid.).

Others said:

“Others have labored, and we have entered into their labor and received the fruit of the martyrs, so that what is written may be fulfilled: ‘The one who sows and the one who reaps receive a reward’” (John 4:38).

When the Jews heard the voices of the applauding Church, they laughed and said:

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2:12).

The Christians said:

“Flowering vines have given forth their fragrance” (ibid., 13).

Hence the prophet rightly says:

“Day pours forth the word to day, and night reveals knowledge to night” (Ps. 18:3).

It is as though he were saying: “Day to day”—that is, Christian to Christian—and “night to night”—that is, Jew to Jew. [Col. 0747D–0748A]

4. Certainly the demons themselves also confessed, and immediately departed from human bodies. Many who were afflicted with various illnesses were healed at once when they touched the saints’ cloths. The Lord worked many other wonders through his saints in the presence of the people while the sacred remains were being carried. [Col. 0748A]

5. Let others gather gold and silver, extract them from hidden veins, and collect precious garlands of jewels. This is a temporal treasure, and it is not rarely harmful to those who possess it.

We gathered the nails of the martyrs—many of them, since they had more wounds than limbs. We gathered the triumphant blood and the wood of the cross. For just as those who are invited to a great banquet customarily bring away gifts with them, so we took care to preserve for ourselves gifts full of grace and holiness from the banquet at Bologna. [Col. 0748B]

6. One of the holy martyrs was named Vitalis, and the other was named Agricola. Both names were fitting, so that those already marked out for martyrdom might also be recognized by their very names.

For the one was called Vitalis, as though by despising this life he were acquiring for himself another life, which is eternal. The other was Agricola, as though he would sow good fruits of spiritual grace and water the plantings of his merits and virtues with the outpouring of his blood. [Col. 0748B]

7. When Saint Vitalis was ordered by his persecutors to deny Christ, he confessed him with even greater steadfastness. They tortured him with every kind of torment, so that no place on his body was without a wound [Note: [Col. 0748D] Codex Regius reads, “to confess the Lord Jesus Christ”; they inflicted every kind of torture upon him, so that there was no place, etc.].

Therefore he poured out this prayer to the Lord:

“Lord Jesus Christ, my Savior and my God, command that my spirit be received, because I now long to receive the crown that your holy angel has shown me.”

When he had completed the prayer, he gave up his spirit. [Col. 0748C]

8. Saint Agricola, on the other hand, was so gentle in character that he was intensely loved by everyone; for this reason they delayed his passion. Yet this indulgence of the persecutors seemed to the martyr more bitter than any savagery, for their flattering words were not expressions of diligence but of deceit: they were delaying the crown.

For this reason they inflicted many more tortures and punishments upon Saint Vitalis in order to frighten Saint Agricola. But the Lord turned these things into a means of increasing his steadfastness. Finally, when they saw that they were accomplishing nothing, they fastened him to a cross, and thus he gave his spirit back to God. [Col. 0748D]

9. Saint Vitalis had been Saint Agricola’s servant; soon he became his companion in suffering, and now he has become his partner in glory.

Saint Vitalis rightly suffered first and went ahead as a servant because he was preparing a place for his master. The master followed in order to prove the faith of his prudent servant. The suffering of the servant is the discipline of the master: this one instructed, that one fulfilled; nothing is taken away from him by his servitude.

How can what Christ splendidly bestowed be diminished? The servant learned, by serving a human being, how to please Christ; the master acquired a double honor, one from his instruction and one from his martyrdom.

After they had deserved to become equals, they competed with one another in benefits: this one sent him ahead to martyrdom, and that one summoned him afterward. Thus neither social condition detracted from a person’s merit, nor did rank increase it; faith perfected both.

For it is written: “Whether free or slave, we are all one in Christ”; and: “Each person will receive from the Lord whatever good he has done” (Eph. 6:8).

With the Lord, slavery and freedom are weighed in an equal balance, since there is no greater dignity than to serve Christ, who valued us so highly that he gave his life for us. [Col. 0749A–B]

10. Beloved brethren, we have taken care to inform you briefly and in summary about the discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs, so that you may commemorate them in the churches.

The holy martyrs suffered under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian in the city of Bologna, in the province of Italy, on the day before the Nones of November, while Jesus Christ our Lord reigned. To him belong all honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. [Col. 0749C]

## Letter IV (formerly XXIX)

Ambrose urges Florianus toward mature and continuous repentance and prescribes what he should follow or avoid in both words and deeds.

AMBROSE, bishop, to FLORIANUS.

1. Beloved son, love tears; do not delay them. Be as ready for lamentation as you were ready and inclined toward sin. Let nothing make you secure concerning sin (Eccl. 5:5). [Col. 0749C]

2. If you cannot avoid anger, at least moderate it. It is a great glory, when you have been able to harm someone, to spare him; do not repay the person who sins against you according to his fault, knowing that judgment will come upon you.

For you will not have forgiveness unless you grant it to another. Hatred separates a person from the kingdom, removes him from heaven, and casts him out of paradise (James 2:13). [Col. 0749D]

3. In all your actions imitate the good, emulate the saints, and keep the examples of the saints before your eyes. Join good companions to yourself; for if you are a companion in conduct, you will also be one in virtue (Ps. 17:26).

It is dangerous to associate with those who live badly. It is therefore better to hate the wicked than to share their company. [Col. 0750A]

4. Empty speech quickly pollutes the mind, and what is willingly heard is easily done. Let that come forth from the lips which does not pollute the ears of the hearer [Note: [Col. 0749D] The Roman edition reads, “the human mind,” etc.].

A person’s character is revealed by his tongue; and whatever kind of speech is displayed, such a mind is proved to be present. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks,” as it is written (Matt. 12:34).

Restrain speech that does not edify those who hear, because the person who does not restrain idle speech quickly proceeds to harmful speech [Note: [Col. 0749D] The same edition reads, “leads toward what is harmful.”]. [Col. 0750A]

5. Do not defile your mouth with another person’s evil. Never disparage the sinner; rather, suffer with him. What you disparage in others, fear rather in yourself. You will certainly never disparage anyone if you have examined yourself properly.

Take as much care to correct your own life as you observe that of another. Do not defend anyone’s life by any deception. [Col. 0750B]

6. Neither wound nor death will terrify you if you have lived well and devoutly. Curiosity is a dangerous presumption. Love listening more than speaking, and attending more than talking.

The person who obeys in evil is like the person who does evil. An equal penalty binds both the doer and the accomplice [Note: [Col. 0749D] Codex Regius reads, “binds with perpetual punishment.”].

Whatever good you do with discernment is virtue; but undiscerning virtue is reckoned as vice. [Col. 0750B]

7. Let your testimony harm no one. Let your speech be irreproachable, accepted and praiseworthy by all. Let affection for no person turn you aside from right judgment, whether the person is rich or poor; consider the case, not the person.

Distribute justice for the sake of eternal recompense alone. For the person who seeks present gifts neither seeks nor hopes for future glory.

In judgment never abandon mercy [Col. 0750C]. It is an impious justice not to forgive human frailty [Note: [Col. 0749D] Codex Regius reads, “An impious mind is…”]. Condemn no one before judgment; judge no one according to the decision of suspicion.

8. Beware honors that you cannot hold without sin [Note: [Col. 0749D] The same codex reads, “To be elevated to honor is recognition of crimes”; [Col. 0750D] “in a higher rank,” etc.].

High office is scarcely maintained without the burden of sin. Therefore the Apostle says: “Nor seeking glory from human beings” (1 Thess. 2:6). For in a higher rank the fault is undoubtedly greater; the person who is lower is nearer to forgiveness.

9. No one administers earthly affairs without danger of sin [Note: [Col. 0750D] The Regius codex reads: “without sin, earthly matters, etc.”]. It is exceedingly rare for one who possesses riches to make his way toward rest. Hence it is written: “Amen, I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty” (Matthew 19:23). Whoever entangles himself in earthly cares [Note: [Col. 0750D] The Roman edition reads: “separate yourself from him.” Less suitably.] separates himself from the Lord. No one can embrace God’s grace and the world at the same time. It is difficult to devote oneself simultaneously to heavenly and earthly cares. It is difficult to love God and the world at the same time. Hate and renounce with your whole soul what the world loves. Separate yourself, as one dead, from the stain and attachment of this world; as one buried, have no concern for this age; as one deceased, deprive yourself of every earthly occupation. While you live, disdain what you will not be able to possess after death.

10. Give to everyone [Note: [Col. 0750D] The same edition reads: “Give yourself to all … lest perhaps you prefer him,” etc.]; do not choose whom you will pity, lest you pass over someone who deserves to receive—for it is uncertain on whose behalf you may please God more. Do not take from one person what you may give to another, lest you display yourself as merciful through another’s plunder; such pity condemns rather than benefits.

11. Do the good you do for the sake of mercy, not vainglory; for if praise is sought here, the reward in heaven is lost. [Note: [Col. 0751A] In the Regius codex these words, together with the following passage from Matthew, are absent. In that codex, moreover, after the word “is promised,” the letter ends in this manner: [Col. 0752A] “Whoever you are who read this, see to it that you do not despise in living what you regard with admiration in reading. Praise be to God. Amen.”] Of such people it is said: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:5). Reward is promised to the just in heaven, not on earth.

12. Read what I have written, and see to it that you do not despise in living what you admire in reading. Farewell, and love us, because we love you as a son.

[THE TWO PRAYERS HITHERTO ATTRIBUTED TO AMBROSE.]

[Col. 0751]

NOTICE.

[Col. 0751A] The following two prayers were indeed found in all Ambrosian editions, but written copies of them are exceedingly rare and difficult to discover. For our part, although we carefully examined the cases of the more distinguished libraries, we were able to find no manuscript of the first prayer and only one of the second. This is no slight indication that those by whom they were first published among the works of Ambrose could not have relied upon the authority of numerous copies. It is therefore not surprising that both have been regarded by more discerning judges as spurious compositions. For although the first has seemed worthy of our Doctor to not a few, nevertheless, on closer examination, its style is found to differ somewhat from Ambrose’s, and several passages quoted in it from the Old Covenant do not agree with the Septuagint version. As for the second, there is less difficulty in rejecting it, since, although not inelegant, it scarcely displays anything of Ambrosian gravity. We present it according to the Floriacensis codex, about seven hundred years old, in a form much more corrected than it formerly was. For the rest, we are by no means pleased that Theophilus Reinaudus thinks both prayers were attributed to the bishop of Milan because someone interpreted the characters “S. A.,” written before the same prayers in some manuscript, as referring to Saint Ambrose, whereas they indicated Saint Anselm. Indeed, even if the other considerations fit, the reasoning on one side differs too greatly from that on the other for us to believe that both had the same author.

[Col. 0751]

THE TWO PRAYERS HITHERTO ATTRIBUTED TO AMBROSE. (G,S)*

489 **FIRST PRAYER. In preparation for Mass.**

[Col. 0751B]

1. Most High Priest and true Pontiff, Jesus Christ, who offered yourself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross as a pure and undefiled offering for us wretched sinners, and who gave us your flesh to eat and your blood to drink, and established the mystery through the power of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:25): I entreat you by your precious blood, the great price of our salvation; I entreat you by that wonderful and ineffable charity by which you deigned to love us wretched and unworthy creatures so greatly that you washed us from our sins in your blood. Teach me, your unworthy servant, whom among your other gifts you deigned to call to the priestly office—not because of any merits of mine, but solely through the favor of your mercy—teach me, I pray, through your Spirit, to handle so great a mystery with that reverence and honor, that devotion and fear, which are proper and fitting.

490 2. Make me, Lord Jesus Christ, by your grace, always to believe, understand, perceive, firmly retain, say, and think concerning so great a mystery what pleases you and benefits my soul. May your good Spirit enter my heart, sounding there without sound and speaking without the noise of words the whole truth of these great mysteries. They are exceedingly profound and covered by a sacred veil.

3. Because of your great mercy, grant me today and always to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass with a pure heart and a pure mind. Free my heart from unclean, abominable, vain, and harmful thoughts. Fortify me with the devoted and faithful protection and the strongest guardianship of the blessed angels, so that the enemies of every good thing may depart in confusion through the power of so great a mystery and through the hand of your holy angel. Drive away from me, Lord Jesus Christ, and from all your servants, the harsh spirit of pride, vainglory, envy, anger, fornication, and impurity, of doubt and blasphemy. Let those who persecute us be confounded; let those who hasten to destroy everything perish. King of virtues, God who loves chastity and integrity, extinguish with the heavenly dew of your blessing all the burning fuel of lust in my body, so that the full integrity of chastity in soul and body may remain in me. Put to death in me the goads of the flesh and every stirring of lust, and grant me true and perpetual chastity, together with your other gifts that may truly please you, so that with a chaste body and a pure heart I may be able to offer you a sacrifice of praise.

4. With what contrition of heart and fountain of tears, with what reverence and trembling, with what chastity of body and purity of spirit must this divine and heavenly sacrifice be celebrated, where your flesh is truly received, where your blood is truly drunk, where the highest things are joined to the lowest, where the presence of the holy angels is present, where you are wondrously and ineffably constituted both priest and sacrifice! Who will be able to celebrate this worthily unless you, almighty God, make the one who offers it worthy? I know, and truly know, and confess this very thing to your mercy: I am not worthy to approach so great a mystery because of my excessive sins and my countless negligences. But I know truly, and with all my heart and mouth I confess and believe, that you can make me worthy—you who alone can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed and make sinners just and holy. By this your omnipotence I beg you to grant me, a sinner, to celebrate this heavenly sacrifice with fear and trembling, with purity of heart and a fountain of tears, with spiritual gladness and heavenly joy. May my mind perceive the sweetness of your most blessed presence and the watchful guardianship of your holy angels around me.

[Col. 0753C] 5. For I, Lord, mindful of your venerable passion, approach your altar, although a sinner, to offer you the sacrifice which you instituted and commanded to be offered in remembrance of you for our salvation. Receive it, therefore, I pray, most high God, most tender Jesus Christ, for your holy Church and for all your people, whom you acquired with your precious blood. And since you wished me, a sinner, to stand between you and this same people, although you recognize in me no testimony of good works, do not reject the ministry of the stewardship entrusted to me; and do not let the price of the salvation of those for whom you became a victim and deigned to be a saving redemption perish through me, your unworthy servant.

Therefore, Lord, if you deign graciously to regard the tribulations of peoples, the dangers of nations, the groaning of captives, the misery of orphans, the needs of strangers, the poverty of the weak, the despair of the sick, the failing strength of the aged, the sighs of the young, the vows of virgins, and the lamentations of widows, I bring these before you. For you have mercy on all, Lord, and hate nothing that you have made. Remember what our substance is, because you are our Father; do not be excessively angry, nor restrain from us the abundance of your compassion. For we do not cast our prayers before your face on the basis of our justifications, but on the basis of your many mercies.

Take away our iniquities from us, Lord, and mercifully kindle in us the fire of the Holy Spirit. Take away the heart of stone from our flesh and give us a heart of flesh that fears you, loves you, honors you, delights in you, follows you, and enjoys you. We pray, Lord, that in a serene countenance you may deign to look upon your household awaiting the duties of your sacred name. And so that no one’s vow may be fruitless and no one’s petition empty, suggest to us the prayers which you yourself may graciously delight to hear and answer.

6. We also ask you, holy Father, for the spirits of the faithful departed, that through this great sacrament of piety they may have eternal salvation, perpetual health, everlasting joy, and refreshment. Lord my God, may they today have great and complete joy in you, the living and true bread who descended from heaven and give life to the world; in the holy and blessed flesh of the spotless Lamb, namely, you who take away the sin of the world; and may they drink from the fountain of your mercy, which flowed from the side of our crucified Lord through the soldier’s lance, so that, comforted, they may exult in your holy praise and glory.

7. I ask your mercy, Lord, that the fullness of your divinity may descend upon this bread and this chalice. May that invisible form and incomprehensible majesty of your Holy Spirit also descend, just as once it descended upon the offerings of the Fathers; and may it make our offerings your body and blood, and teach me, your unworthy priest, to handle so great a mystery in such a way that you may peacefully and graciously receive the sacrifice from my hands for the salvation of all, both living and dead.

492 I entreat you, Lord, by the very holy mystery of your body and blood, by which we are daily fed and given drink in your Church, washed and sanctified, and made participants in your one supreme divinity, that you may give me your holy virtues. Filled with them, may I approach your altar with a good conscience, so that these heavenly sacraments may become salvation and life for me.

For you said with your holy and blessed mouth: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” And: “He who eats me will live because of me; he remains in me, and I in him. I am the living bread that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever” (John 6:51–52).

8. Most sweet bread, heal the palate of my heart, so that I may perceive the sweetness of your love; heal me from every sickness, so that I may love no beauty apart from you. Most radiant bread, in whom is every delight and the sweetness of every flavor, who always refresh us: may my heart eat you, and may the innermost parts of my soul be filled with the sweetness of your taste. The angel eats you with a full mouth; may the human pilgrim eat you according to his capacity, so that, refreshed by such provisions for the journey, he may not be able to fail on the way.

Holy bread, living bread, beautiful bread, pure bread, who descended from heaven and give life to the world, come into my heart and cleanse me from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Enter my soul and sanctify me within and without. Be the protection and perpetual salvation of my body and soul. Repel those who lie in ambush for me. Let my enemies withdraw far from your presence, so that, fortified by you within and without, I may reach your kingdom by the straight path, where we shall see you face to face—not through mysteries, as is done at this time—when you have handed over the kingdom to God the Father, and God is all in all.

Then satisfy me with yourself with perpetual satiety, so that I may neither hunger nor thirst forever; you who, with the same God the Father and the Holy Spirit, live and reign forever and ever. Amen.

**SECOND PRAYER. Also in preparation for Mass.**

1. Supreme and incomprehensible nature, power and blessed life, inaccessible light, true, singular, and one wisdom, unchangeable truth, holy, incomparable, and eternal love, timeless creator of temporal things, invisible and eternal maker of visible and invisible things, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one true Lord God in the Trinity:

The Father, having no one from whom you are, yet possessing wisdom—that is, the Son—to whom you are neither greater nor prior;

the Son, having the Father, from whom you are, yet having no one to whom you are lesser or posterior;

the Holy Spirit, having the Father and the Son, from whom you are, yet having none to whom you are unequal or inferior;

because everything in this divinity of yours, upon which time never comes, is eternal and coeternal, equal and coequal. In it one is the Father, another the Son, another the Holy Spirit; yet the Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. For just as your nature, our God, admits persons, so it in no way admits parts.

To you “above” and “below,” “before” and “behind,” do not apply, because you do not admit the features of bodies. Hence you are wholly present in all places without being contained by a place, and yet you are not wholly comprehended. For you are wholly present everywhere, since no part is found in you; yet you are not wholly comprehended, because although you become wholly present to each creature, you are also found wholly beyond creatures.

Therefore, when you fill heaven and earth, you are wholly there; when you fill one human being, you are wholly there. You are not changed among individual things, since you are wholly present in each; nor do you pass from place to place when, abandoning one, you seek another, for you move yourself without place or time.

Hence you are rightly worshiped; hence you are adored; hence you are recognized as unchangeable and uncircumscribed. Hence Christ Jesus, mediator of God and human beings, according to the essence of divinity was wholly with human beings on earth and wholly with the Father in heaven when he said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

He, although he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0755D] All editions read: “in the likeness of human beings, becoming obedient”; the rest has been restored from the Regius codex.], being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6).

2. Through him, blessed Trinity, through this assumption of humanity, through the humility of this submission, through his most sacred obedience, through his most blessed death, I first beseech and entreat you that I may love you as my Lord and God, thirst for you, and seek you with all my heart; and then that, according to my strength and measure, I may always regard my neighbor as dear and beloved in this same love of yours.

But you will grant this love, Lord, to no one unless you first grant him to hate vices. Therefore I implore you, compassionate and true mercy, my solid and only hope, to take away the reign of pride from my soul. It is a dreadful and fearful evil of the greatest magnitude: it cast the angels from heaven, expelled human beings from paradise [Note: [Col. 0755D] The Regius codex reads: “threatened [them] from paradise.”], and is the beginning of every sin. Whatever vice and iniquity exists belongs to it, and from this poisonous root its first offspring—namely the seven principal vices—arise: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony of the belly, and lust. A numerous multitude of descendants is also generated from each of them.

3. When vainglory has fully seized the mind, it immediately gives birth in it to a sevenfold wickedness: disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, contentiousness, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous novelty. But if true humility is set against it, all its wickedness is emptied out.

Therefore I beseech you, teacher of humility, to implant it in my heart and preserve it once implanted. While it regards itself as inferior to all, it immediately produces submission, extinguishes boasting, excludes hypocrisy, avoids contentiousness, softens obstinacy, guards against discord, and abhors presumptuous novelty.

You foresaw that the sickness of arrogance would be healed by this medicine of blessed humility when, through the human nature you assumed, you said to those coming to you: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). And again: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

4. From envy, moreover, hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in a neighbor’s adversities, and distress at his prosperity are propagated. O evil offspring, which, if admitted into the soul and allowed to rule, extinguishes every offspring of holiness!

Whoever envies or hates first kills no one other than himself; whoever whispers and detracts first tears up his own roots rather than those of others; whoever rejoices in a neighbor’s adversities and is distressed by his prosperity first attacks himself with another’s sword [Note: [Col. 0756D] Thus the Regius codex; the edition, however, reads: “with another’s sword he attacks his neighbor.”].

This second shoot of pride first sprang forth when Cain was persuaded by him of whom it is written, “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24), to shed his brother’s blood out of hatred born of jealousy. But that same envious Cain killed his own soul before killing another’s flesh, for it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15).

Here, Lord, it becomes clear whose first murderer he is who hates another—he in whom there is no life. In opposition to this, Moses, the meekest of all, admonishes us, saying: “You shall not hate your neighbor in your heart” (Leviticus 19:17). And because the one who envies and hates consequently whispers and detracts, Holy Scripture declares that this evil must be avoided: “You shall not be a whisperer among the peoples” (ibid., 16); and: “Do not speak evil of one another, brothers” (James 4:11).

Whoever speaks evil of his brother speaks evil of the law. Whoever whispers and detracts will consequently rejoice in his neighbor’s adversities and become sad at his prosperity. But the blessed Apostle counters this and says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).

And behold: one person envies and hates someone, whispers against someone, detracts from someone, rejoices in someone’s adversities, and saddens his spirit at someone’s prosperity because of earthly possessions and earthly honors; another does the same because of the success of virtues.

5. But so that this many-sided evil may be overcome in every respect, may that manifold good, I pray, confront it, Lord—good which, resisting with powerful strength, leaves no room for envy: namely, charity, which is the foundation of all virtues and good things. It does not envy, but rejoices with others; it does not hate, but loves; it does not whisper, but rebukes; it does not detract, but reproves; it does not rejoice in a neighbor’s adversities, but grieves; it does not become distressed at his prosperity, but receives consolation.

It rightly received such a name, because nothing can be found dearer than it. Whoever has it certainly has you. “God is love,” Scripture says, “and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:8).

To overcome the aforesaid evil of envy, therefore, vigilance of both heart and mouth must be joined: of the heart, so that it does not envy, rejoice in a neighbor’s adversities, or become sad at his prosperity; of the mouth, so that it does not whisper or detract. For it is written: “Guard your mouth with all vigilance; guard your heart, because from it life proceeds” (Proverbs 4:23). And again it is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21).

The evil hidden within is extinguished more quickly if the tongue is restrained outwardly from wicked speech. “Set a guard over my mouth, Lord, and a door of protection around my lips, so that my heart may not incline to an evil word” (Psalm 140:3). “Deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Psalm 119:2).

6. Anger follows envy; among all the vices, nothing is found harsher or more bitter than it. When it boils beyond measure, it cruelly inflames the mind, dulls the understanding, changes the tongue, darkens the eyes, and disturbs the whole body. From it quarrels, insults, shouting, indignation, swelling of mind, and blasphemies immediately arise.

Holy Scripture bears witness concerning it, saying: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:10), and: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

7. But, Lord, oppose to this most bitter evil of anger the sweetest good of patience, in which the salvation of our souls is especially established, since the Gospel says to us: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

When patience has received the stronghold and sovereignty in the mind, it immediately restrains every disturbance: it turns quarrels and insults into exhortation, suppresses confused shouting beneath ordered silence, conquers indignation and swelling of mind with gentleness, and repels blasphemies with thanksgiving.

But if anger, kindled to an immeasurable degree, should for a time overcome patience, is there no remedy, Lord? There certainly is. For when the Gospel announces the condemnation of this evil, saying: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:22), it immediately adds the means of restoration, saying: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (ibid., 23). And again: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against another in your hearts” (Mark 11:23).

Grant me this second victory, Lord God, if, blinded by fury, I should lose the first—when I offend someone’s spirit not out of zeal for you, but through my own fault.

8. Sadness also follows anger. When it penetrates the secret places of the heart, it immediately generates there malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness concerning the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things. The blessed Paul indicates how detestable it is among the other vices: “The sadness of the world,” he says, “brings about death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

But I beseech you, my God and Lord, oppose to worldly sadness the joy of future blessedness. Let it overcome by benevolence the malice contracted from sorrow, drive away with sincerity the rancor produced by weariness, strengthen faintheartedness with courage, raise despair through confidence in hope, repel sluggishness concerning the commandments through spiritual exercise, and restrain the wandering of the mind toward unlawful things through unwavering stability.

But if, with spiritual joy momentarily withdrawn, the evil of sadness should prevail, let me do, I pray, what the blessed James counsels: “Is anyone among you sad? Let him pray with an even spirit, and let him sing psalms” (James 5:13).

9. Avarice follows sadness, and it is marked by equal execration in both Testaments. In the Old Testament it is said: “There is nothing more wicked than the avaricious” (Ecclesiasticus 10:9); in the New: “and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Ephesians 5:5).

From it, certainly, seven wickednesses are born: betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardening against mercy. And behold, Lord God: every lover of the world rather than of you, for the sake of precious metals, burning and glittering stones, male and female slaves, estates and farms, delivers his neighbor to death, incurs fraud, practices deceit, and commits perjury. One is restless and violent because of a farm, another because of a hen. One is hardened against mercy so as not to return gold; another so as not to offer a drink.

But I ask you, my God, chaste and true lover, that I, to whom no possession on earth is due apart from you, may desire on earth nothing that is not you; that I may always remember the sentence: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job 1:21). And this one: “We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it” (1 Timothy 6:7). When these things are devoutly considered, they seem to bring contempt for the world, which is opposed to avarice.

495 10. After these things, gluttony of the belly remains. It begins indeed from necessity, but, exceeding the measure of necessity, passes over into pleasure. When it proceeds from what is permitted to what is forbidden, it immediately gives birth to foolish merriment, buffoonery, impurity, excessive talk, and dullness of the senses regarding understanding. Its deadly poison is somehow emptied out when not the quality but the lust of the appetite in foods is guarded against.

The first woman brought death into the world not through elaborate dishes, but through the pleasure of a single fruit (Genesis 3:6); the ancient enemy tempted our king not with meat but with bread (Matthew 4:3); and Sodom perished by fire and sulfur because, among its other evils, it ate bread to excess (Genesis 19:24).

11. Therefore I implore your mercy, God, that I may approach food as a sick person approaches medicine: not seeking pleasure in it, but relieving necessity. Remove from me, through your great mercy, every harmful desire for food, and graciously grant your servant a suitable abstinence from food, so that I may regulate my own appetite within the measure of necessity;

With all gluttony and drunkenness entirely removed from me, may I know how to abound through your power, know also how to suffer want, and learn in what things I may be sufficient for myself. Thus, Lord, yes, good Father, when the harmful juices of gluttony have been dried up, foolish merriment or buffoonery will not sprout—vices that lead especially to madness those in whom gluttony and drunkenness take control: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32:6).

Against them comes that sentence which says: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation! And woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25). In contrast, those who “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5:24) hear: “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:20). And again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

Impurity also, which according to the Apostle bars certain people from entrance into the kingdom of heaven, will never defile the vigilant person and will defile the sleeper only more slowly with its filth. Excessive talk, pressed down by fasting, will fall silent. Dullness of the senses concerning understanding will yield to the skill of spiritual insight, which holy moderation will propagate in the mind; for a belly contracted by abstinence raises human understanding to higher things.

12. Lust follows gluttony. When it exceeds the boundaries of license, it immediately generates blindness of mind, lack of consideration, instability, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, affection for the present age, and horror or despair of the future.

But I ask you, Lord, since you willed from the very time of puberty that I should be separated from the embrace of carnal intercourse, that I may not be touched by consent to its pleasure [Note: [Col. 0759D] All editions read: “by the sense of its delight.”]. For what does it profit, Lord God, to be a virgin in body if one should happen to be corrupt in mind? “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).

For one who has not yet professed chastity, it is better, according to the Apostle, to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians 7:9). But I beseech you, Lord, that one who may not marry may not be allowed to burn.

[Col. 0760B] 13. Behold, while I ask such things in concern for myself, I must remember charity, so that I may also pray for others.

Therefore I beseech you, God, lover of your Church, for its priests: that by both their words and the merits of their lives they may invite the people entrusted to them to their heavenly homeland.

For kings, governors, and those placed in high office: that they may show themselves fathers of orphans and judges of widows, sympathize with the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, seek nothing in judgment except what is just, and so administer present affairs that they may not lose future goods.

For virgins, the continent, and those who have renounced the world: that they may despise present things and seek future things, and not entangle themselves in worldly business; that, serving you as soldiers, they may please you, to whom they have proved themselves faithful.

For married people: that they may discharge the debt of the flesh to one another in such a way that they do not deviate from their longing for the heavenly homeland.

14. But what am I doing, Lord? As though I had forgotten my own sins, I presume to pray for others. O how greatly I have offended, and continue to offend, in many things! Yet despair does not steal upon me when I consider the tax collector justified in the temple; when I behold the thief confessing on the cross and passing from the cross into paradise; when I consider Mary washed in the fountain of mercy after many stains of crime; and when I see Peter recover the grace of the apostolate after his denial.

But I ask you, ineffable mercy, that since you have permitted me to draw confidence from such great examples, you may grant me the sighs of the tax collector, the confession of the thief, the tears of the prostitute, and the weeping of the apostle who denied you.

For if you foresee that my sins must be punished by a temporal scourge, I implore you with tears: while you rage against these sins in anger, may you always remember mercy in your anger. “For the one whom you love, you correct; and you scourge every son whom you receive” (Hebrews 12:6). Although these words threaten with the rod of the one who strikes [Note: [Col. 0760D] The same editions read: “although with the rod of punishment”], they nevertheless reveal a fatherly affection of mercy. Therefore, Lord, grant me endurance amid the scourges, so that I may not incur the mark of murmuring like an evil servant; but rather, like a good son, may I repay you with thanksgiving.

15. I also earnestly ask that I may always remember the day of death, the day of the final judgment, the condemnation of eternal punishment, and the blessedness of the future kingdom—for no one can do this continually except one who has been predestined to eternal life.

The day must be recalled continually, Lord, on which light battles with darkness, mercy struggles with cruelty, and our adversary, a most violent accuser, will disclose the evils we have done, said, or thought, and demand your justice for their punishment. Where am I then, Lord, unless you, who judge justly, also defend mercifully? Remember, I pray, that you yourself are my advocate, you who judge.

And if in that other age you still reserve something in me for punishment, I ask that you not hand me over to the power of demons while you cleanse away my crime through purgatorial punishment.

16. That day must never, Lord, be given over to oblivion, of which the prophet said: “That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah 1:15 and following) [Note: [Col. 0761D] “A day of cloud and whirlwind” has been restored from a manuscript.].

On that day, while heaven and earth burn, the angels will go forth and separate the wicked from among the just, and cast them into the furnace of fire (Matthew 13:49). On that day the reapers will gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to be burned. On that day the impious placed on the left will hear: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

On that day, when the doors of life have already been shut, the foolish virgins, their lamps extinguished, excluded from the bridal chamber, will weep and lament their condemnation, crying: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (ibid., 11); and then you will say to them: “I do not know you.”

On that day even those who shone through miracles will likewise lament when rejected, and will say: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?” (Matthew 7:22). And then you will confess even to these that you never knew them, adding: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Psalm 6:9). [Note: [Col. 0761D] The edition reads: “Who here … who, I say, here would not be afraid?”]

Who, Lord God, terrible in counsels and wonderful in majesty, doing marvelous deeds—who, I say, would not fear these things and tremble from the depths of the heart, when he hears even those condemned whom it happened to see shining with miracles in this life?

To this applies that sentence which says: “A human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything is reserved uncertainly for the future” (Ecclesiastes 9:1). In that judgment, if even the just will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the impious appear?

17. Moreover, Lord God, the punishment of eternal damnation must be meditated upon without ceasing: whatever punishments can now be imagined—and even whatever cannot be imagined—are perpetually present there. Its worm is immortal, its fire unquenchable, and its stench intolerable. Its earth is dark and covered with the shadow of death; it is a land of misery and darkness. Its streams are turned into pitch, and its soil into sulfur; it will burn forever. Its lake is mingled with blood and fire, and whoever it receives, it both submerges and consumes. O how dreadful! O how terrifying these things are!

18. But greater still, Lord, will be the torment of losing the sight of your brightness. For it is enough for complete misery not to enjoy your blessedness, in which the just, having received their bodies and been made equal to the exalted state of the holy angels [Note: [Col. 0762D] The Regius manuscript reads: “made equal, the inward light,” etc.], will look upon eternal light and shine like the sun. Nor will they need the sun or the moon, since they will have you as their everlasting light. They will neither hunger nor thirst; they will neither labor nor grow faint; they will neither mourn nor grieve, because your visitation will provide whatever satisfaction, whatever rest, and whatever joy there is; it will be everything in all things. Time will no longer approach them, because eternity will possess the whole of it; nor will those who have deserved to be clothed with blessed immortality fear death any longer. 497

But what more can I, a wretched human being, say about this blessedness? Whatever I might say about it is restrained by that sentence which I understand to have been spoken through the Prophet and the Apostle: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

[Note: The manuscript reads thus; the printed edition, however, has “God,” i.e., “what God has prepared for those who love him.”]

Certainly, in that blessed life there will be the good things I have mentioned above, but in a manner ineffable and still beyond our comprehension. Out of longing for this, Lord God, my creator and recreator, and out of love for it, I will carry out whatever you command me to do in this life. “Let there no longer be fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (2 John 4:18).

19. And that this supplication of mine may be effective, I seek the intercession of the blessed Virgin Mary, whom you made so worthy that she was the first among women to offer a new gift, and that no woman besides her should receive one so new: she was the first to offer a new gift, namely, that she should remain a virgin after giving birth [Note: [Col. 0762D] The manuscript reads: “that she might remain a virgin as a girl.”]; and no woman besides her should receive so new a gift, namely, that she should give birth to God as a virgin and remain a virgin after childbirth. 498

I implore the intercession of the Apostles, who, following in the footsteps of the Mediator’s most blessed poverty and of his sufferings, attained so lofty a summit that whatever they bound on earth was bound also in heaven, and whatever they loosed on earth was loosed also in heaven (Matt. 16:19); and at the end they would sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19:28).

I ask the prayers of the martyrs, who did not hesitate to shed their blood for the truth, nor love their lives even unto death, so that they might overcome the author of death. I beseech the prayers of the confessors, who, while living devoutly in Catholic peace, endured the battles of the tempting enemy, and also the conflicts of heretics through prolonged struggle; and, to speak truly, received the palms of a longer and hidden martyrdom.

My God, never despise the prayers of such people, if you yourself inspire them to intercede for me—you who live and reign over all things through everlasting ages and in every age. Amen.

# EXPOSITION ON THE SEVEN VISIONS OF THE BOOK OF THE APOCALYPSE

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE EXPOSITION OF THE APOCALYPSE

Having obtained from the library of a certain monastery a copy of this Commentary bearing the name of Saint Ambrose, Cuthbert Tonstall, bishop of Durham, determined to make it publicly available and at the same time attempted, in a preface of his own, to vindicate it for our Doctor. He does not, however, conceal the fact that one passage in it gives precedence, both in wording and in meaning, to Gregory, bishop of Rome; but he replies that there is no reason why Saint Gregory could not have imitated Ambrose in this matter. From Tonstall’s edition, which appeared at Paris in 1548, Gillotius admitted these Commentaries into the appendix to his edition of the works of Ambrose; the Romans did the same.

There can be no doubt, moreover, that this work was published from a very mutilated manuscript, since the names of Hilary, Augustine, Prudentius, Jerome, and Ambrose himself, and finally Gregory—who is cited there at least six times, occasionally even in his own words—were omitted from the editions. We have restored these names, along with very many other gaps, with the help of the best manuscripts. (See chapters 9, 11, 12, 13, 17, 21, and 22.)

Nevertheless, although those earlier editions were extremely imperfect, they still supplied adequate evidence for all critics to recognize that this spurious offspring had been falsely attributed to Ambrose. They were led to this conclusion by the work’s style, far inferior to Ambrose’s majesty of expression; by its ignorance of Greek literature; and finally by its mention (chap. 17) of the power of the Lombards as though it had already been destroyed. Indeed, this last point alone was sufficient to show that the holy Bishop could in no way be called the author of a commentary which must certainly have been composed after the year 774, when that people, after the extinction of its king Desiderius, was brought under the rule of Charlemagne.

But what if we add that this author speaks of Pope Gregory the Great as one already received among the saints and Doctors of the Church, together with Jerome and others; that he frequently uses testimonies from the creed of Athanasius (chapters 1, 6, and 20), as though it were already customarily sung throughout the Christian world as a rule of faith; and, finally, that he vigorously and indignantly attacks the greed of archdeacons (chap. 18), which had been restrained by the canons of the councils held at Paris, Chalon, and Aachen in the ninth century?

We have therefore discovered the period in which this author must have flourished. We must now inquire into his name. Nor was Ussher of Armagh (On the Succession and State of the Christian Church, chap. 1), although mistaken in thinking him a recent author, any less mistaken in asserting that he was called Berengaudus. For this very name is either written at the beginning in all the manuscripts except the Gemeticensis, or at least indicated at the conclusion—which was omitted from the editions—in these words:

“Whoever you are who desire to know the author’s name, pay attention to the first letters of the Expositions in the chapters of the Seven Visions. The number represented by the four missing vowels, if you use Greek letters, is LXXXI.”

But because these words themselves might perhaps appear obscure and enigmatic, we append here their explanation, written more than six hundred years ago in the Regius and Sagiensis manuscripts, by the same hand as the Commentary itself.

The author of this book is called Berengaudus, if one carefully attends to how he himself teaches that his name is to be discovered. For the first letters of the Expositions in the seven chapters of the Visions to which he tells us to pay attention are these: B, R, N, G, V, D, S. The four Greek vowels that must be added to these, expressing the number LXXXI, are these: short E, 5; again short E, 5; A, 1; and O, 70. Add together the number contained in each of these vowels, and you will undoubtedly have LXXXI—unless, as indicated above, you take E twice; otherwise this number will not appear to you in any entirely different set of vowels.

Join these four vowels, then, to the seven consonants above, and form syllables from them in this way: Berengaudos. Thus you have Berengaudos. But this is a Greek ending; the Latin ending is Berengaudus. For what ends in *-os* among the Greeks ends in *-us* among the Latins, as *Petros*, *Petrus*, and *Paulos*, *Paulus*. If, however, you prefer to retain the order of the vowels given above in discovering this name, placing A first and arranging the others among the consonants so that you say *Barenguedos*, the prescribed order of the vowels does not indeed oppose you; but from it a highly barbarous and wholly unfamiliar name is formed. It is therefore better, and much more correct, that he be called Berengaudus, as prescribed, rather than Barenguedus, because the former is customary and more elegant, whereas the latter appears to be an unfamiliar and entirely inelegant name.

Now, if anyone wishes to know what the author’s institution and way of life were, although we have no certain information about this, we nevertheless infer that he followed the monastic discipline of the Benedictine family from the fact that he repeatedly discusses, as an eyewitness, the vices that had gained access to monasteries at that time (chapters 9 and 21), and frequently inserts passages reproduced word for word from the Rule of blessed Benedict. Even if this argument is not accepted, it can at least not be denied that this work is by a man excellently learned in ecclesiastical literature, as the Regius manuscript states at the very beginning of the chapter. Dionysius the Carthusian had long ago reached no different judgment concerning it; and in more recent memory the most learned man, and one who had deserved exceedingly well of the Catholic religion, Lord Benignus Bossuet, bishop of Meaux, held the same view. We consider it wrong not to agree with his judgment.

# EXPOSITION ON THE SEVEN VISIONS OF THE BOOK OF THE APOCALYPSE (S)

499

## ON THE FIRST VISION

[Note: The Roman edition had cut off the words “Blessed John, up to the following passage,” although this fragment is found both in Gillotius’s edition and in all the manuscripts. In the Gemeticensis manuscript it is preceded by the first two verses of the same book of the Apocalypse, and in the Regius by the first verse.]

It is established that the Apostle and Evangelist blessed John published this book of the Apocalypse, although some have existed who said that it was composed not by him but by another. Yet the following passages show that it was his.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Verse 1

“The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him.”

*Apocalypsis* is interpreted as “revelation” or “manifestation.” The Father gave this gift of revelation to the Son insofar as he was human, and the Son himself gave it to himself—that is, the divinity gave it to the man whom he assumed.

“To make known to his servants what must soon take place.”

Since this book relates not only future events but also present and past ones, why is our Lord Jesus Christ here said to have revealed only future things to his servants? Because present things are easily known by sight and past things by hearing; future things, however, can be known only either through the teaching of the divine Scriptures or through revelation.

“And he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John.”

The meaning seems to me to be this: the Lord Jesus sent his angel, and through that same angel manifested to his servant John what must soon take place.

### Verse 2

“Who bore witness to the word of God.”

This passage clearly demonstrates that this book was composed not by another John but by the one who wrote the Gospel. He reclined at supper upon the Lord’s breast (John 13:25), in whom were hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3), and from whom he deserved to draw an immeasurable fountain of wisdom.

He therefore bore witness to the Word of God when he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

But a question also arises concerning what follows: “and the testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever he saw.” How, then, did he bear witness to Jesus Christ concerning whatever he saw, when he himself says in the same Gospel: “Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of his disciples which are not written in this book” (John 20:30)?

He bore witness to Jesus Christ concerning whatever he had seen by preaching to the nations everything he had learned from Christ, recounting the miracles he had witnessed, and writing only those things that he foresaw would be especially beneficial to posterity.

### Verse 3

“Blessed are those who read, and those who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep what is written in it.”

He establishes three forms of blessedness. But two are nothing if the third is absent: it does no good to those who read or hear God’s commandments if they do not keep what they read or hear.

For there are many who either hear or read God’s commandments, but this does them no good because, although they are present in body, they are absent in mind. Their minds are either devoted to acquiring possessions, agitated by lust, judging their neighbor, proud against their superior, imagining themselves destined for power, or distracted by other utterly vain concerns.
