To such people the prophet’s words may apply: “You will hear with your ears and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not perceive” (Isa. 6:9).

There are others who read and hear the divine Scriptures—that is, who apply their minds to understanding them—but they learn the divine Scriptures so that they may be regarded as wise and distinguished among human beings and may prosper in worldly affairs, not so that they may correct their reprehensible way of life. But they are not blessed, because they learned divine Scripture not out of love for God but out of love for the world.

The prophet speaks of such people: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22). And in the Gospel, in the parable of the sower, the Lord says: “What fell among the thorns are those who have heard, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and pleasures of life, and they produce no fruit” (Luke 8:15).

Those alone, therefore, are blessed who strive to learn God’s commandments so that they may hear them—that is, store them in their minds; they store them in their minds so that they may fulfill them in action; and they fulfill them in action so that they may attain eternal blessedness.

“For the time is near.”

This means the time of judgment. For if you place before your eyes the period from the Lord’s coming to the end of the world, you will find it long; but in comparison with earlier ages, it is short.

### Verse 4

“John to the seven churches that are in Asia: Grace to you and peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come.”

Through the seven churches, the one Catholic Church is signified, namely, on account of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit by which, enlightened, it shines forth in the world.

*Asia* is interpreted as “exalted,” because among the exalted people of this age Christ found a multitude of believers from whom he built his Church.

Observe also that the entire book is structured around the number seven: there are seven churches to which these writings are sent; seven lampstands, seven stars, seven lamps, seven horns of the Lamb, seven eyes, seven seals, seven angels sounding trumpets, seven thunders, and likewise seven angels holding bowls.

For the dragon, which signifies the devil, and the beast, which signifies the Antichrist, are each seen to have seven heads. Likewise, the beast upon which the harlot woman was seen to sit had seven heads. And if you pay careful attention, you will find that the entire book is divided into seven visions.

The first is the vision containing the seven letters sent to the seven churches and the other things included there. The second is that in which he saw a throne placed in heaven in the figure of the Church, and Christ seated above the throne. In the third, the Lamb opened the book and its seals. In the fourth, seven angels were seen sounding trumpets. In the fifth, seven other angels were seen holding bowls. In the sixth, the resurrection is described. In the seventh, the glory of the saints is displayed in the figure of the city of Jerusalem descending from heaven.

### Verse 5

[Note: The Roman edition had removed the passage beginning “Grace to you … who is to come.” We have restored it from the manuscripts and from Gillotius’s edition. Since the author has not infrequently allowed himself similar liberties in the scriptural texts, we shall likewise restore them, in accordance with the manuscripts and Gillotius’s edition.]

“Grace to you and peace from him who was, and who is, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne; and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness.”

Here the whole Trinity is shown. Through “him who was, and who is, and who is to come,” the Father is signified. He was before the foundation of the world, without any beginning; he is now, after the foundation of the world, governing and directing all that he created; and he will come after the end of the world with the Son and the Holy Spirit, to reign with his saints forever and ever.

Through the seven spirits, the Holy Spirit is understood, because he is sevenfold.

“And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness.”

He can truly be called a faithful witness who does not know how to lie; who will undoubtedly fulfill what he mercifully promised to his elect; who does not leave even the one who gives a thirsty person a cup of cold water without a reward (Matt. 10:42); whose words remain so firm that it would be easier for heaven and earth to be reduced to nothing than for any of all that he foretold he would do to be changed.

“The firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.”

How is Christ called the firstborn of the dead, when he was born at the end of time and an innumerable multitude of people preceded his coming?

[Note: The manuscripts read thus; the printed edition, conversely, has: “But ‘firstborn’ is properly used of the dead.”]

“Firstborn” is used in the sense of “first,” just as we call those who surpass the others not in age but in honor and dignity “first” among a people.

The dead are those of whom the Apostle speaks: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). Christ is therefore the firstborn of the dead because he is the first and head of all his elect.

“The ruler of the kings of the earth.”

A king is so called from ruling. Through the kings, therefore, the Apostles and the other saints are signified, for they know how to rule both themselves and others; through the earth, the Church is signified.

“Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

Thus, because he loved us, he washed us; and what this washing has brought us is made clear by what follows.

### Verse 6

“And made us a kingdom and priests for God and his Father.”

The Church of God is called the kingdom of God. Christ God therefore made the kingdom of God from human beings when he established them as those in whom he, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, would deign to dwell and reign.

For those who are signified by the kingdom are also signified by the priests. They are called priests of God because they are members of the supreme Priest, of whom the Psalmist says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

God’s elect may also be called priests of God in another sense: because every day, through compunction of heart, prayers, and other good works, they offer themselves to God, as the Psalmist says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. 50:19).

There is also a sacrifice of praise, which the holy Church is accustomed to offer to God every day. The same prophet speaks of it: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49:14). And again: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (ibid., 23).

### Verse 7

“Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him.”

He will come to judgment with the clouds, as he himself says in the Gospel: “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24:30).

But how will every eye see him, when Scripture says: “Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10)?

The wicked, placed on the left at the judgment, will see him in the form in which, while he was in the world, he could be seen by human beings, but not in the form in which he is God. The just, however, will see him in the brightness in which those now placed in heaven see him, and in which they will see him forever after the end of the world.

Even those who pierced him, willingly or unwillingly, will be compelled to see him: namely, the wicked Jews who crucified him, so that they may know whom they mocked, as it is written in the Gospel: “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37).

“And all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.”

By “all the tribes of the earth,” only the reprobate are understood. They will mourn because they despised God’s commandments and, for the sake of brief joy, acquired everlasting sorrow.

Alternatively: “Behold, he comes with the clouds.” The clouds may signify the Apostles and the other preachers. He comes with the clouds when his name becomes known to all the nations through holy preachers.

“And every eye will see him,” because all who had eyes saw him—namely, those eyes of which he himself says to the Apostles: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23). The wicked Jews had eyes, but they did not possess the eyes by which God is seen.

“And those who pierced him”—that is, those who persecuted him and his members, and who, for the most part, were converted to his faith, among whom was the Apostle Paul.

“And all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him.” By “all the tribes of the earth,” the entire multitude of the nations may be understood, which has been converted to Christ. Placed daily in the Church of God, it mourns its sins so that it may deserve to obtain forgiveness from God.

“Indeed, amen”: this is a confirmation of the statement.

### Verse 8

“I am Α and Ω.”

What Alpha and Omega mean is made clear by what follows: that is, the beginning and the end. As he himself said to the Jews: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

Our Savior may also be called the beginning because he is the beginning—that is, the creator of the human race and the author of salvation. He is the end because he is the end of the Law, the end of death, and the end of every transgression.

“Who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.”

He is now in the world, governing his Church; he was eternally abiding with the Father before the foundation of the world; and he will come to judgment in order to judge the world with equity.

### Verse 9

“I, John, your brother and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom, and in the patience of Jesus.”

He calls the disciples brothers because they had been redeemed by the one blood of Christ and born from the one mother, the Church.

He also calls himself their companion in persecution, because the persecution of Domitian had disturbed all the churches. He calls himself their companion in the kingdom because he confessed himself to be a member of the Church, just as they were, whom God had acquired.

He testified that he was also their companion in patience because they endured adversity with equanimity, as did he himself, who was held in exile on the island of Patmos for the love of Christ.

### Verse 10

“I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.”

He says that he was in the Spirit because such great mysteries as follow could be seen not with bodily but with spiritual eyes. “The natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14).

The Lord’s day signifies the time of the Gospel. Concerning this time the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). In this time the prophets foretold that the divine mysteries would be opened to the nations.

“And I heard behind me a voice like that of a trumpet saying…”

What we do not know is, as it were, behind us.

[Note: The Regius and Gemeticensis manuscripts lack the following alternative: “Alternatively: The voice of the Lord is behind us … to call us back.”]

Alternatively: The voice of the Lord is behind us because we are like fugitive servants; but the Lord cries out behind our backs in order to call us back.

John therefore heard the voice behind him because he had not yet perfectly understood the mysteries that were then revealed to him. The voice is said to have been like a trumpet. Concerning this trumpet the prophet says: “Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58:1).

A trumpet usually summons soldiers to battle; likewise, the word of God never ceases to urge us to fight against the devil and to conquer him.

### Verse 11

“What you see, write in a book, and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.”

Through these seven churches, the one Catholic Church is signified, as the interpretation of their names shows.

*Ephesus* is interpreted as “will” or “counsel”; *Smyrna*, “their song”; *Pergamum*, “division of horns”; *Thyatira*, “the enlightened”; *Sardis*, “the beginning of beauty”; *Philadelphia*, “saving the inheritance of God”; and *Laodicea*, “a tribe beloved by the Lord.”

Ephesus, therefore, which is placed first, signifies the beginning of each person’s conversion. It is interpreted as “will” or “counsel.” For what better counsel is there than a good will, which urges a person to renounce the devil and follow Christ, to abandon vices and embrace virtues?

And because those who wish to convert to God must implore the Lord’s mercy so that they may accomplish what they desire, Smyrna is placed next. It is interpreted as “their song.” For the person sings well who, with a contrite heart and humbled spirit, begs the mercy of his Creator. Concerning this song the Apostle says: “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. 5:19).

And because one who wishes to be heard by God must abandon vices and turn himself toward the performance of good works insofar as his strength permits, Pergamum follows in order. It is interpreted as “division of horns.”

The two horns here signify evil and good. We divide the horns when, discerning between good and evil, we drive evil away from ourselves and embrace good.

And because as long as we lie in sins we are in darkness, but when we reject evils from ourselves and begin to do good, we advance as if from darkness to light, Thyatira, which is interpreted as “the enlightened,” appropriately follows Pergamum.

And because the beauty of the soul increases through the performance of God’s commandments, and the more a person grows in carrying out God’s commandments, the greater the beauty he bestows upon his soul, Sardis follows Thyatira fittingly. Sardis is interpreted as “the beginning of beauty.”

It is called the beginning of beauty because the beauty of the saints begins in this life and is perfected in eternal blessedness.

Philadelphia follows, and is called “saving the inheritance of God.” What, then, is the inheritance of God except the entire multitude of the elect, as the Lord says to the prophet: “And Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. 19:25)? And in what does the salvation of the elect consist except in the performance of God’s commandments (Luke 19:10)? For the one who came to seek and save what was lost grants salvation of soul to those who each keep his commandments according to their own strength.

Laodicea is placed seventh because it is interpreted as “a tribe beloved by the Lord.” The tribe beloved by the Lord is the entire multitude of the elect, which is the Church. Through the renunciation of vices and the practice of virtues, it reaches the point of being called a tribe beloved by the Lord.

### Verse 12

“And I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me.”

Why did he remain turned away for so long? Why did he not turn at the first blow of the words striking his ears toward the one who was speaking behind him?

But he gave us an example. He did not turn toward the Lord who was speaking with him until he had heard the names of the churches to which he was commanded to write.

Above we briefly said that, through the interpretations of the names of the seven churches, the way that leads to life is shown. Whoever therefore desires to travel this way to God must investigate, either by reading or by hearing from others, how he ought to walk along it. For a traveler is foolish if he wishes to reach his desired destination but does not know the road, unless he first strives to learn its length, its roughness, its winding paths, and its dangers, so that when he begins to climb the route, he may pass more easily through dangers known in advance.

We have seen many people abandon the world in order to acquire eternal life by the way of contemplation; but because they did not know the roughness of the road, they suddenly fell.

Someone might object against this with a testimony from divine Scripture, which says: “Do not delay to turn to God” (Ecclus. 5:8). To this I reply that I am already turning to God when I do not cease investigating the way that leads to him.

And what does “I turned to see the voice” mean, when a voice is perceived not by the eyes but by the ears? But John, being in the Spirit, deserved to see with spiritual eyes the things that follow. Nor was there any need for words to resound there, where God, who was teaching, was within.

Alternatively: he properly hears the words of God who does not cease to contemplate with the eyes of his mind what he has heard, so that he may fulfill it in action.

### Verse 13

“And when I had turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like the Son of Man.”

The seven golden lampstands signify the seven churches, as he himself explained; and the seven churches represent the one Catholic Church.

They are called golden lampstands either on account of the persecutions that the saints endure throughout the ages or on account of the wisdom by which they are enlightened.

Christ was seen standing in their midst, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

### Verses 14–15

It follows:

“Clothed in a long robe and girded around the breasts with a golden belt; his head and his hair were white like white wool and like snow; his eyes were like a flame of fire; his feet were like aurichalcum, as though burning in a furnace; and his voice was like the voice of many waters. He held seven stars in his right hand; from his mouth proceeded a sword sharp on both sides; and his face was like the sun shining in its strength.”

If you wish to take the seven lampstands and the seven stars as two ornaments, you will find ten ornaments with which the Lord’s body appeared to have been adorned. But he himself explained what the two ornaments—that is, the seven lampstands and the seven stars—signified; what the remaining eight signify must be investigated by us.

For if you carefully examine the holy city of God, which consists of all the elect and extends from the beginning to the end, you will find it divided into seven parts.

The first part consists of the elect who lived from the beginning until the Flood. The second consists of the patriarchs and the other righteous people up to the giving of the Law. The third consists of those who lived under the Law. The fourth consists of the prophets. The fifth consists of the Apostles and those who believed from among the Jews. The sixth part consists of the multitude of the nations that came to the faith. The seventh consists of the elect who will be born at the end of the world and will fight against the Antichrist.

Having spoken, as the Lord grants, of these seven parts, let us return to our exposition. We shall speak of the eighth in what follows.

The *poderis*, which is a robe reaching to the feet, signifies the righteous who lived before the Flood. Its color is not stated, because they had no other law except the natural law. The natural law is to love one’s Creator and not to do to another what one does not wish to have done to oneself. No one endowed with reason is permitted to be ignorant of this law.

By the belt, the patriarchs and the other righteous who lived before the Law are signified. It is called golden because they are known to have been tested by many tribulations, like gold in a furnace: Abraham, who was rescued from the fire of the Chaldeans; Lot, whom the Sodomites afflicted; Isaac, who endured blindness; Jacob, who suffered persecution from his brother and his father-in-law; Joseph, who endured captivity and imprisonment; and Job, who endured the loss of his possessions and terrible suffering.

[Note: Gillotius’s and the Roman editions read “whom Scripture mentions”; the manuscripts, however, read “whom Scripture does not mention.”]

We must understand the same concerning the others whom Scripture does not mention. The belt is said to have been fastened around the breasts; by the breasts, the two commandments of love are signified, through which it is certain that the holy fathers pleased God.

“But his head and his hair were white like white wool and like snow.”

By the head, the Law is signified; by the hair that grows from the head, the multitudes of those who were saved through the Law are signified.

The hair is said to be white like wool and like snow because that people was cleansed from the darkness of vices through the Law.

“But his eyes were like a flame of fire.”

The eyes perceive everything around them, far and wide. Through the eyes, therefore, the prophets are signified, who were granted to foresee long beforehand the things that were to come. They are said to be like a flame of fire because, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, they contemplated the heavenly mysteries.

And his feet were like burnished bronze, as in a burning furnace. By the feet the apostles are signified, and the others who believed from among the Jews. Concerning these feet the prophet says:

> How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one who evangelizes peace, announces good things, and proclaims salvation, saying: “Zion, your God shall reign” (Isa. 52:7).

They are said to be like burnished bronze. For bronze, when mixed with certain medicinal substances, is melted in a furnace until it takes on the color of gold, and is called *aurichalcum*. By bronze, therefore, which is sonorous and quickly turns black, the Jews are signified, who seemed indeed to make the Law resound according to the letter [Col. 0772D]; but, their minds being covered by the veil of blackness, they were unable to understand the spiritual meaning hidden within it. Bronze was thus changed into burnished bronze when apostles were chosen from among the Jews. By the furnace, either the world, in which Christ dwelt for a time, or the tribulations that he endured, may be signified.

[Note: In this furnace also . . . in my temptations, were absent from the printed edition; we have restored them from all the manuscripts.]

In this furnace, too, the apostles were joined to him, as he himself says: “For you are those who remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22:28). In this furnace, therefore, through the teaching of the Gospel, they deserved to receive the splendor of gold.

And his voice was like the voice of many waters. [Col. 0773A] By the voice of many waters the multitude of the nations that hastened to the faith of Christ is signified.

And he held seven stars in his right hand. What this signifies he himself explains below. And from his mouth proceeded a sword, sharp on both sides. By the sword those elect who are to arise at the end of the world and fight against Antichrist are signified. Since a very great multitude of the nations, abandoning the worship of Christ, will worship Antichrist, that most wicked man, as God, those who will advance to cut down their errors are appropriately signified by the sword. It appeared to have two edges, because those teachers, instructed in the doctrines of the two Testaments, will easily overcome their enemies. That the sword itself appeared to proceed from the Lord’s mouth signifies what he said in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

In these seven ornaments the entire Church of the elect is included, which we divide into seven parts. Without these seven parts, therefore, it does not seem possible for anyone to understand this book in an orderly manner. Something must also be said about the eighth, which remains.

And his face was like the sun shining in its strength. By the face the Church is signified as it will be after the resurrection; and it is signified by the face because then, as the Apostle says, the righteous will see God face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). It was seen to shine like the sun because, as the Lord says, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

Certain things are found in the Scriptures that correspond to these seven parts, as is the passage in Joshua (Josh. 6:6 ff.), where the Lord commanded that the ark of God should go around the city of Jericho for seven days, once each day, with the priests carrying it, the trumpets sounding, and the people following. Jericho signifies the whole body of the reprobate, which is the city of the devil. By the children of Israel the elect are signified; by the priests, preachers; by the trumpets, the doctrine of preaching; and by the people who followed them, all the righteous are signified, who followed their doctrine and imitated their conduct. By the ark that they carried, Christ is understood, who, dwelling in the hearts of the saints, is carried by them.

There is no doubt that the preachers who came after Christ’s advent carried Christ not only by preaching him with their tongues, but also by loving him in their hearts. But how did those who preceded his advent carry him? They too certainly carried him: some foretold him in words, and others prefigured him by their deeds.

We must ask, however, what this circuit made over seven days signifies. We avoid entering the place we are going around. For when we travel along a road, if we encounter a pit, deep mud, or some other danger, we go around it if we can and avoid entering it, so that we may escape the danger. We go around Jericho, therefore, if we complete the journey of the present life according to God’s will. For although we live among the reprobate, we go around Jericho if we abstain from their depraved ways.

The Psalmist seems to have spoken of this going around when he says: “I have gone around and sacrificed in his tabernacle a sacrifice of jubilation” (Ps. 26:6). He went around and then sacrificed, because he first rejected the deeds of the reprobate, so that his sacrifice of jubilation might be acceptable to God. For many constantly praise God; but because they are unwilling to drive vices away from themselves, the sacrifice of their praise is not acceptable to God.

The first circuit, therefore, pertains to those righteous who lived before the Flood, who were called sons of God. They went around the city of Jericho for as long as they separated themselves from the society of the reprobate. After the ark of God and the people had gone around the city of Jericho, they returned to the camp; for each righteous person, when the time of his circuit has been completed, is led after death to the fellowship of the elect, which is the camp of the saints.

The circuit of the second day pertains to those who lived after the Flood and up to Moses. They too went around the city of Jericho because they separated themselves from the iniquities of the reprobate. Abraham, although he lived among the Amorites, abhorred not only their vices but also association with their bodies to such an extent that he did not wish to take a wife for his son from among their daughters. Blessed Peter also speaks of Lot, who lived among the Sodomites (2 Pet. 2:7); he was righteous in hearing and seeing, dwelling among those who day after day tormented his righteous soul with wicked deeds. The others did likewise.

The third circuit pertains to those who lived under the Law. The Law itself shows with what diligence they ought to have separated themselves from the society of the wicked. [Col. 0774C] The prophets, to whom the fourth circuit pertains, so despised and reproved the sins of rulers and wicked men that some of them were stoned for this, some were cut apart, and others died by the killing of the sword.

The apostles and those who believed from among the Jews, to whom the fifth circuit pertains, separated themselves with such zeal from the counsel and deeds of the unbelieving Jews that Luke relates it in the Acts of the Apostles. Let the nations, to whom the sixth circuit pertains, declare through the martyrs with what ardor they separated themselves from the society of the wicked. The seventh circuit pertains to those who will exist in the times of Antichrist; but this book also reveals how they will avoid the faithlessness of Antichrist and his ministers.

On the seventh day, therefore, when the priests went around Jericho with the ark and shouted, the walls of Jericho fell, and the entire people with its king was killed. For when preachers of truth preach at the end of the world and announce the end of the world, the end of the world will suddenly arrive; the entire city of the devil will be destroyed, and together with its own head, the devil, it will be condemned to everlasting death.

We also read in the Book of Judges that Samson, the strongest of men, had seven locks of hair (Judg. 16:13). Samson signifies Christ; by the hair all the elect are signified. And just as the hair clings to the head, so all the righteous cling to Christ, who is the head of all his elect. And just as Samson’s hair was divided into seven parts, so the whole number of the elect can be divided into seven parts according to the character of the times, as we demonstrated above.

This too, which is written in Solomon, may suit our interpretation: “Wisdom built her house; she carved out seven pillars” (Prov. 9:1). Wisdom built her house when our Lord Jesus Christ, from the beginning of the world to its end, built and will build for himself the Church from the multitude of the elect. She carved out seven pillars when, throughout these seven periods, he established in his Church preachers suited to each period, who would support it both by salutary admonitions and by examples of good works.

We may also adapt to our interpretation what the same Solomon says elsewhere: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. 11:2). First, therefore, we must ask what it is from which we are commanded to make portions. There is a certain good—and it is the highest good—namely, love, which will not be perfect unless it is divided. For it is divided into love of God and love of neighbor. Although it is one, it nevertheless has two arms, which, extending in every direction, join God to human beings and human beings to God.

There are also two lives: one called active, the other contemplative. Love of neighbor belongs to the active life, while love of God properly belongs to the contemplative life. We may therefore understand by seven the whole multitude of the elect, and by eight our Lord Jesus Christ, because he rose on the eighth day.

The saints of God give a portion of their love to seven when they are occupied in the exercises of the active life, namely, when they provide care for their neighbor, not only bodily but also spiritual. They give a portion to eight when the love of God again calls them back to contemplation of him.

Alternatively, we give a portion to seven when we show the saints of God the veneration due to them; we give a portion to eight when we render the worship due to God our Creator.

[Col. 0776D]

**(Verse 17.)** It follows: “And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead.” Behold John, who seemed able to stand on his own; when he saw the Lord, he fell as though dead. For the more deeply each holy man raises himself to contemplate the divinity of God, the lower he falls inwardly before himself, because he easily perceives how small his greatness is in comparison with God. Thus he fell as though dead because he recognized that he was nothing in comparison with God. He fell at his feet because he realized that he could in no way comprehend the mystery of his incarnation, which is represented by the feet.

And he placed his hand upon me, saying: “Do not fear.” Just as the hand in the body has many functions, so the hand of God has many meanings in the divine Scriptures. Job calls the scourge of God the hand of God when he says: “Remove your hand far from me, and let not your dread terrify me” (Job 13:21). And again he says to his friends: “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, because the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 19:21).

The Lord also touched Jeremiah with the hand of wisdom, as he himself says: “And the Lord stretched out his hand and touched my mouth, and said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth,” and so forth (Jer. 1:9). Likewise Daniel was touched by the hand of God’s strengthening when, lying prostrate on the ground because of the angelic vision, he saw a hand sent to him, which strengthened him; and he said to it: “Speak, Lord, for you have strengthened me” (Dan. 10:10).

John, therefore, was touched by this hand of strengthening, which raised him up by strengthening him, so that he would not cast himself down beyond measure.

**(Verse 18.)** “I am the first and the last.” If he is first, why did Arius say that the Son of God had a beginning? For if he had a beginning, he himself was not first; rather, the one from whom he received his beginning was first. He himself is therefore first and last, because just as he will have no end, so he had no beginning.

“And I was dead, and behold, I am living forever and ever.” This is clear.

“And I have the keys of death and of Hades.” Whoever holds the key of a house lets in whom he wishes and keeps out of the house whom he wishes. By the key, therefore, the power of the Son of God is understood. He possesses the keys of death and Hades because, in his mercy, he frees from condemnation to everlasting death those whom he wishes, while by his just judgment he allows those whom he wishes to remain in the same danger of condemnation.

**(Verse 19.)** “Therefore write what you have seen, and what is, and what must take place after this.” Here he shows that he has woven a prophecy not only concerning the present and the future, but also concerning the past. “Write what you have seen,” that is, what has been shown to you concerning the past; “what is, and what must take place after this,” that is, the present and the future.

**(Verse 20.)** “The mystery of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands.” What they signify is understood. What they signify, however, he makes clear by adding: “The seven stars,” he says, “are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven golden lampstands are the seven churches.”

We must therefore understand the seven angels as the rulers of the seven churches, since *angel* is interpreted as “messenger.” Those who announce the word of God to the peoples are appropriately called angels, that is, messengers. And just as the one catholic Church is designated by the seven churches, so all the rulers of the catholic Church are designated by the seven rulers of the seven churches.

## CHAPTER II

**(Verse 1.)** “And to the angel of the church of Ephesus write: Thus says the one who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands.”

By the right hand of God the power of God may be signified here; by the stars, the holy preachers. The holy preachers are therefore held in the hand of God because they are governed and directed by him, and are joined to him, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me” (John 15:4).

Christ walks in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, as the prophet himself says: “I will dwell among them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Lev. 26:12).

[Col. 0777A] **(Verse 2.)** “I know your works”—namely, those that you formerly practiced, before love grew cold in you—“and your labor and your patience,” that is, the persecutions that you patiently endure for my name.

“And you cannot endure the wicked” (Matt. 13). Since divine Scripture commands us to tolerate the wicked, why is he praised here for not being able to endure the wicked? It seems to me that this is said concerning heretics. For at times we ought to correct the evils of our neighbors by reproving them, namely at an appropriate time; at times we ought patiently to tolerate them, so that those whom correction does not amend may be prompted to amendment by patience.

There are some who do not know how to reprove their neighbors except when inflamed by anger. If one of them is provoked against his neighbor not only by a great matter but by even some small matter, he carries anger in his heart until he sees something in his neighbor’s actions that he can reprove. Then he becomes glad when he has inflicted upon his neighbor the vengeance of reproof. If he sees that this has displeased someone, he says that he did it out of zeal for God.

To you, therefore, I speak, whoever you are who act in this way. Why do you seek to deceive the one who observes the secrets of hearts? If the zeal of God is in you, why do your eyes wander in different directions in the manner of the devil, desiring rather to see evil than good—desiring to see in your neighbor an evil that you may reprove, rather than a good by which you may be edified?

There are also many who attack impatiently, even for the smallest offenses, those from whom they have suffered some injury; but those whom they love they not only do not reprove, even when they have seriously sinned, but also defend with all their strength.

O wretched friendship, which by silence and defense hands over to the devil the one whom it loves, while by reproving the one with whom it is angry it draws him away from the devil! That correction, therefore, is just which proceeds from zeal for God and brotherly love—correction offered not to avenge anger, but to save the soul of one’s neighbor.

But since we have said these things briefly, let us return to what we began. Therefore, when the Lord says to the bishop of the church of Ephesus, “You cannot endure the wicked,” we must understand this as referring to heretics. For everyone who is a pastor of the Church ought, as far as he can, to avoid the company of heretics, lest through the opportunity of familiarity they corrupt the hearts of the simple with the poison of their wickedness. For just as a quiet wolf cannot move among sheep without tearing those same sheep apart, so neither can a heretic move among the simple without harming them.

It follows: “And you tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you found them to be liars.” Some who taught perversely in the times of the apostles called themselves apostles, so that, through the reverence attached to the name, they might more easily plant perverse doctrine in the hearts of their hearers (2 Cor. 10:12). The Apostle Paul also condemns them, and the Lord indicates in the Gospel that they must be avoided when he says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7:15). This man therefore proved that these men were false and that their doctrine was false.

[Col. 0778A] **(Verses 3–4.)** “And you have patience, and you have endured for my name, and you have not grown weary”—that is, your patience appeared in this: that in the labors which you endured for my name, you did not grow weary.

“But I have this against you: that you have abandoned your first love.” There are many who at the beginning of their conversion are fervent in the service of God, but in the course of time grow lukewarm. It is clear that this happened to the bishop of the church of Ephesus.

**(Verse 5.)** “Therefore remember from where you have fallen.” From where have you fallen? From love. If you have fallen from love, you have fallen from God, because God is love. “And do penance” (John 4:16)—namely, because through your sluggishness and negligence you have been separated from love.

“And do your first works; otherwise I will come to you quickly and remove your lampstand from its place, unless you do penance.” If the church of Ephesus is signified by the lampstand, why will the Church lose its place on account of the pastor’s sin, when Scripture says: “Fathers shall not die for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; but each one shall die in his own sin” (Jer. 31:30)?

It seems to me, however, that by “place” the reward owed to him for his pastoral care is signified, so that the meaning is: Unless you do penance because you have abandoned your first love, and return to your first works, so that you fulfill in your conduct what you preach with your mouth, I will withdraw the reward owed to you for your pastoral care.

**(Verse 6.)** “But you have this”—namely, so that the lampstand may not be removed—“that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.”

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; but the printed edition reads, “I hate.” “Because you hated their deeds, which I too hated.”]

The meaning is: Because you have hated the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate, the reward owed to you for your pastoral care still remains yours.

The Nicolaitans were heretics, whom he said above that he could not endure.

**(Verse 7.)** “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” Since he says to all who have ears, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” he clearly requires the ears of the heart.

“To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” There were two trees in the middle of paradise: one was called the tree of life, and the other the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Their power was such that if anyone ate from the tree of life, he would not die forever; but if anyone ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:27), although he was immortal, he would immediately become mortal.

Paradise therefore signifies the Church; the tree of life in the middle of paradise is Christ in the midst of his Church. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which is also said to have been in the middle of paradise, signifies the devil, who does not cease to move among the faithful in order to deceive as many as he can.

The tree of life therefore pertains to the elect, while the tree of the knowledge of good and evil pertains to the reprobate. The elect eat the fruit of the tree of life so that they may live forever, because they keep the commandments of the Gospel so that they may live forever with the Lord. [Note: The printed edition has only, “they will live with the Lord”; the rest has been added from the manuscripts.] The reprobate eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and die, because they feed upon the suggestions of the devil and upon every vice and pleasure; thus they acquire eternal condemnation for themselves.

And just as the fruits of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil were more pleasing to the woman than the fruits of the tree of life, so the glory of this world, which the reprobate see with the eyes of the body, is more pleasing to them than the glory of the heavenly homeland, which is seen only with spiritual eyes.

But a question arises: Why is it called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, when it supplied the first human being with knowledge of evil, not knowledge of good? This seems to me to be answered as follows. When the first angel was created, he had knowledge of good, not knowledge of evil. He discovered knowledge of evil by himself, and for this reason he was cast down from that heavenly glory.

The first human being therefore ate from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil when he followed the suggestions of the one who possessed knowledge of good and evil. For the tree could not teach knowledge of evil; rather, it was the devil who persuaded the human being to transgress God’s command.

He therefore says: “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” The one conquers who perseveres in good works until the end of his life. To the one who conquers, therefore, Christ will give to eat from the tree of life, because to those who keep his commandments until the end of life he will give, with himself, the glory of his immortality in heavenly blessedness, so that they may live eternally with him whose commandments they strove to keep while placed in this world.

When he calls God his Father, this pertains to his humanity.

**(Verses 8–9.)** “And to the angel of the church of Smyrna write: [Col. 0779C] Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty.”

It may be that the church of the Smyrnaeans endured from its fellow citizens the same persecution in the seizure of its goods as did the church that was in Jerusalem. Therefore its tribulation and poverty, which it endured for his sake, are praised by the Lord. By this may also be understood voluntary poverty, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

“But you are rich”—poor in possessions, that is, rich in virtues.

“And you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan.” Jews are interpreted as “confessors.” Those Jews who blaspheme and deny Christ are not Jews—that is, confessors—but are appropriately called a synagogue of Satan.

**(Verses 10–11.)** “Fear none of these things that you are going to suffer.” Adversities are foretold to him so that he may more easily endure them when they come.

[Note: In the printed edition this passage had been omitted after the words “you may endure,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.]

“Behold, the devil is going to cast some of you into prison, so that you may be tested.” That is, the devil—that is, the devil’s ministers—will cast some of you into prison, so that you may be tested as to whether, because of fear of punishments, you will withdraw from the faith, or whether you will decide to die for the love of Christ.

“And you will have tribulation for ten days.” He indicated the period during which this persecution would rage with greater cruelty.

“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” The crown of life signifies everlasting glory.

“Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. Whoever conquers will not be harmed by the second death.” What the second death is, we shall explain below.

**(Verse 12.)** “And to the angel of the church of Pergamum write: Thus says the one who has the two-edged sword.”

By the sword the Lord’s judicial power may be understood. It is said to be sharp on both sides because of the two judgments: one that took place through water, and the other that will take place through fire. But this interpretation is excluded because that judgment has already been completed and, through God’s mercy, abolished. The sharpness of that judgment was erased when God said to Noah: “By myself I have sworn that I will never again bring the waters of the flood upon the earth” (Gen. 6:17).

It therefore seems to me that by the sword the divine Scripture should be understood. It is called sharp because it cuts away vices, and it is shown to be sharp on both sides because of the two Testaments. Both the Old and the New Testament continually admonish us to abandon vices and exercise ourselves in good works, so that we may be able to find the salvation of our souls.

**(Verse 13.)** “I know where you dwell, where the throne of Satan is”—that is, you dwell among those who have the devil as their enthroned ruler.

“And you hold fast to my name, and you have not denied my faith”—that is, although you continually endure persecutions for my name from those among whom you dwell, nevertheless you hold fast to my name and have not denied my faith.

“And in those days Antipas was my faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells.” “In those days,” that is, in the days when persecution was raging more fiercely among you, Antipas, my faithful witness, existed—this is understood—who was killed among you, where Satan dwells. He was killed among you, but not by you; rather, by those among whom you dwell, in whom the devil dwells.

**(Verses 14–15.)** “But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel; so you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans.”

We read in the Book of Numbers that Balak, king of the Moabites, at the suggestion of Balaam, placed beautiful women before the children of Israel, sacrificing to their gods. Their beauty not only inflamed them to commit lust, but also led them to eat of the sacrifices (Num. 25:1).

The Nicolaitans were heretics who detested marriage and taught the faithful to unite themselves promiscuously with whomever they wished, like beasts. Therefore, just as through the teaching of Balaam the children of Israel fell into the evil of fornication, for which many of them perished, so the Nicolaitans cast some of the faithful who were in Pergamum into the evil of fornication through their perverse teaching. They taught them not to be bound in any way by the bond of marriage, but to unite themselves promiscuously with whomever they wished.

When he says, “I have a few things against you,” he signifies that only a few of the faithful had been deceived by the heretics.

[Col. 0781A] **(Verse 16.)** “In the same way, do penance.” When he says “in the same way,” it seems to me that he is referring to the angel of the church of Ephesus, to whom he says, “Do penance,” because he had abandoned his first love. It is as though he were saying: Just as I commanded the angel of Ephesus to do penance because he had abandoned his first love, so you too should do penance because you have strayed from love, so that through your silence you might lose some of your own.

“Otherwise, I will come to you quickly.” The Lord’s coming is often understood as death. For the Lord comes to each person when, through death, he separates the soul from the body. “Quickly,” that is, unexpectedly, as the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the negligent servant: “The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour that he does not know; and he will divide him and appoint his portion with the hypocrites” (Matt. 24:51).

A human being consists of soul and body. The Lord divides the human being when he separates the soul from the body; he appoints his portion with the hypocrites when he hands over the soul, which is the second part of the human being, to be tormented with the wicked on account of its iniquities.

In what he says, “I will come to you quickly,” the meaning seems to me to be this: If you do not do penance, I will come to you quickly, so that I may dissolve you through the death whose coming you neglect to foresee.

It follows: “And I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth”—that is, I will appoint another in your place, and I will put the sword of my words in his mouth, by which he will cast down the adversaries of the truth.

**(Verse 17.)** “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” Wherever this sentence occurs, whether in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse, we must understand that what is said is mystical and difficult to understand.

“To the one who conquers I will give the hidden manna” (Exod. 16:14). We read in the Old Testament that the Lord fed the Jewish people with manna as they journeyed through the wilderness, until they came to the promised land. By manna, therefore, wisdom may be understood, which is Christ. For he is the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6:41).

All the elect who are placed in the wilderness and on the journey of this world are nourished by this bread until they come to the promised land, that is, to the heavenly blessedness which God promised to those who love him. It is called hidden because the wisdom of God is hidden from the proud and revealed to the humble, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

“And I will give him a white stone.” By the stone, which is a small stone and is called *calculus* from *calculare* (“to calculate”), we may understand the Gospel. Just as the ancients gathered a great multitude of such stones for dividing and reckoning numbers, so the teachers of the Church gather many words of the Gospel in their hearts. When they open up to their hearers its obscurities, spiritual meanings, and benefits, they seem to divide and distribute their numbers.

“And on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” What is this name of Christ that is said to be written on the stone of the Gospel?

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); and again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). The same evangelist says elsewhere that he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God (John 5:18).

If Christ made himself equal to God, why does Arius say that the Son is less than the Father? No one knows this name written on the stone except the one who receives it, because no one can know the omnipotence, divinity, and equality of the Son with the Father unless the teaching of the Gospel has been given to him.

But something else troubles us. A little earlier he said: “I will give the one who conquers the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and on the stone your name, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” If, therefore, only those who conquer the devil are given knowledge of the manna, the stone, and the name of Christ, then the impious, who do not conquer the devil but are conquered by him, although they seem to have received baptism and the faith of Christ, nevertheless remain excluded from this gift.

But someone may say: How does a learned person, instructed in the divine Scriptures, fail to know the mystery of the name of Christ, even though he loves the world and lives voluptuously?

To him I will oppose the likeness of two men who possessed a great quantity of honey. One of them was accustomed to eat from it, while the other, compelled by some necessity, abstained from eating it in every way. Which of these two seems to you to have known the taste of honey more fully? You will certainly answer me: the one who was accustomed to enjoy its sweetness.

And yet, if you had asked both of them about honey and what sort of taste it had, both would have admitted that it was exceedingly sweet. But one would describe what he had heard, the other what he had experienced. The tongue of the first would speak of what his palate did not know; the tongue of the second, of what delight had taught him.

The one who possessed honey not for use but to increase his profits signifies those who, from knowledge of the divine Scriptures, seek temporal glory rather than eternal glory.

[Note: The Gem. manuscript reads: “are more capable of temporal glory than of eternal glory.”]

The one who possessed honey in order continually to enjoy its sweetness signifies those who strive to learn God’s commandments not for temporal glory but out of love for God, so that through their practice they may deserve to attain eternal glory.

For the former, God’s commandments are not sweet, even though they preach them, because they love not the sweetness of the heavenly homeland but the earthly sweetness that produces bitterness. For the latter, the hope of the heavenly homeland makes God’s commandments sweet, as the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your sayings to my palate, Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103).

Only those who keep God’s commandments therefore know the name of God. Those who love the world, who cast themselves down into certain vices, and who fulfill the desires of their flesh do not know the name of God, because they cast his fear and love away from their minds.

Alternatively, the heavenly blessedness may be signified by the stone and by the name written upon it: by the stone, the heavenly homeland; by the name written upon it, the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. No one therefore knows this name except the one who receives the stone, because no one can know how great that heavenly blessedness is except the one who has deserved to reach it, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who await you” (Isa. 64:4).

### (Verses 18–19)

“And to the angel of the church of Thyatira write: These things says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like burnished bronze.” What these things signify has been explained above.

“I know your works, and your love, and faith, and ministry, and your perseverance, and that your last works are more numerous than the first.” Here he is praised in every respect; but, as what follows makes clear, he is reproved only for the fault of silence. [Col. 0783B]

### (Verse 20)

“But I have this against you: that you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols.”

This woman, who is compared with the most impious Jezebel, falsely claimed to be a prophetess so that, more easily and under the name of religion, she might introduce false teaching among God’s people. Just as Jezebel compelled God’s people to abandon the worship of God and venerate idols, so this woman also attempted, through perverse teaching, to separate God’s people from the worship of God, that is, from the true faith. For every soul that departs from God its Creator commits fornication. He calls “an idol-sacrifice” that which had been consecrated to idols. This woman taught that it did the faithful no harm if they ate flesh that had been sacrificed to idols. [Col. 0783C]

### (Verse 21)

“And I gave her time to repent, but she does not wish to repent of her fornications.”

Thus also blessed Job says concerning the wicked: “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abused it for pride” (Job 24:23).

### (Verses 22–23)

“Behold, I am casting her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation, unless they repent; and I will kill her children with death.”

Behold, no opportunity for repentance is promised to the woman and her children, because they despised the time for repentance granted to them by God; but to those who committed adultery with her, an opportunity for repentance is still promised. It seems to me, therefore, that those who committed adultery with her signify those who, while favoring her perverse assertions, had not yet been completely plunged into the pit of her wickedness. Her children, however, signify those who had already been entirely deceived by her and were unwilling in any way to receive the remedy of correction. [Col. 0783D]

By the bed onto which the woman was to be cast, hell is signified, in which the rich man also was buried, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “But the rich man also died, and was buried in hell” (Luke 16:22). By the great tribulation into which those who committed adultery with her were to be cast, unless they repented, and by the death with which her children were to be killed, the same punishment of hell is signified.

“And all the churches shall know that I am he who searches the kidneys and hearts.” By the kidneys, which are contained within the body and from which lust is said to proceed, hidden sins are signified; by the hearts, hidden thoughts. The meaning is this: They shall know—namely, on the day of judgment, when both that woman and all who were deceived by her will be condemned—all the churches, that is, all who are reckoned under the Christian name, not only the elect but also the reprobate, [Col. 0784A] because I am he who searches the kidneys and hearts—that is, I see not only sins that are manifest but also those that are hidden; I also behold the thoughts themselves, and on that day I will repay each one of you according to your works.

### (Verse 24)

“But I say to the rest of you who are in Thyatira, whoever do not have this teaching, who have not known the depths of Satan, as they say, I will not impose upon you any other burden.”

[Note: [Col. 0783] The printed edition has *dico, caeterisque qui Thyatirae*; the manuscripts have *dico caeteris; qui*, and so forth.]

What he says seems to me to pertain not only to the woman’s teaching but also to the false apostles who taught those who had believed from the Gentiles that they should turn to the Law and circumcision. Since the Jews took pride in observance of the Law, and after the Gospel had been given, keeping the Law according to the letter was nothing other than slavery to the devil, we may understand by “the depths of Satan” the Law itself, if it is fulfilled in a carnal manner.

What he says, therefore, is as follows: “I say to the rest of you who are in Thyatira”—namely, those who have remained steadfast in the faith—“whoever do not have this teaching,” that is, those who have not accepted the teaching of that most wicked woman; “who have not known the depths of Satan, as they say,” that is, who have not accepted the Law as the false apostles say, in order to fulfill it carnally. They did accept it in order to fulfill it spiritually; they did not accept it in order to observe it carnally (Acts 15:1).

For example, they said: “Unless you circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, you cannot be saved.” But these men, understanding circumcision not carnally but spiritually, circumcised from their hearts and flesh every vice. They said that they should keep the Sabbath by doing no work on it; but these men, accepting the whole time of their life as a Sabbath, took care, insofar as they could, to abstain from every servile work, that is, from sins.

“I will not impose upon you any other burden”—that is, upon you who have remained steadfast in the faith and have not accepted the false apostles. “I will not impose upon you any other burden” except what was commanded you by the apostles: to abstain from foods sacrificed to idols, from what has been strangled, from blood, and from fornication (ibid. 29). [Col. 0784D]

### (Verse 25)

“Nevertheless, hold fast to what you have until I come.”

It is as though he were saying: Since you are little ones and need milk, not solid food, hold fast to the faith you have learned until I come, so that through the grace of my inspiration I may urge you on to undertake higher works of virtue.

### (Verses 26–28)

“And to the one who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give authority over the nations, and he will rule them with an iron rod, and they will be broken like a potter’s vessel, just as I also received from my Father.”

By “the end” in this passage death is understood. Therefore, whoever has conquered the world and its desires and has persevered to the end will be given authority over the nations and will rule them with an iron rod.

But if “the end” means death, how are the elect said to rule the nations after death, when in that blessed life there is no one who is ruled with an iron rod, since nothing distorted or perverse is found there? Unless perhaps we understand it in the sense of the saying, “He who made the things that are to come.” For all things that are to be done according to God’s ordering already exist, as it were, as accomplished in his predestination, since it cannot happen that anything should be changed among all the things that God has determined to come to pass.

Likewise, for the saints whom God foreknew would become righteous and would persevere in good works, before their birth he granted this: that they should have authority over the nations and rule them with an iron rod, just as he says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; and I appointed you as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1:5).

In the second Psalm it is written that the Father said to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth. You shall rule them with an iron rod; like a potter’s vessel you shall break them” (Ps. 2:8).

The Father gave the Son authority to rule the nations with an iron rod; and the Son gave the apostles and the other preachers authority, so that they too might rule the nations with an iron rod and crush them like a potter’s vessel.

By the iron rod, therefore, the Gospel is signified, just as by the wooden rod the Law is signified. For the wooden rod used by Moses prefigured the Law given through him. That rod, as we read in Exodus (Exod. 17:6), struck the rock twice, and exceedingly abundant waters came forth, so that the people and the animals drank.

The rod, therefore, is the Old Testament; the two blows signify the Law and the Prophets; and the rock prefigured Christ. The rod struck the rock twice when the Old Testament, through the Law and the Prophets, foretold that Christ would come for the redemption of the human race. And because it was impossible for the things foretold through the Law and the Prophets not to be fulfilled, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota or one stroke to pass from the Law without being fulfilled” [Col. 0785D] (Luke 16:17).

The rod struck the rock twice when the prophecies of the Prophets and the Law somehow compelled God to deign to become human. The rock was therefore struck, and exceedingly abundant waters came forth, because Christ, coming according to what had been foretold, brought forth from himself streams of heavenly teaching, that is, the Gospel. The people and the animals drank: that is, Jews and Gentiles.

The same rod also blossomed in the tabernacle and produced nuts (Num. 17:8), because afterward, in the tabernacle of the Church, the Old Testament brought forth flowers of spiritual meanings, and those flowers produced the fruits of good works. We have said all this [Col. 0786A] in order to show that the Law was signified by the wooden rod.

And because the commandments of the New Testament are more severe than those of the Old, it is not unfitting that the Gospel should be signified by the iron rod and the Law by the wooden rod. In the former it is said: “You shall eat and be satisfied; you shall drink and become drunk; you shall sleep, and there will be no one to terrify you” (Lev. 26:5–6); and again: “You shall eat the oldest of the old, and when the new arrives you shall cast away the old” (ibid. 10), along with many other passages that pertain to bodily pleasures.

But here it is said: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this world”; and again: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Luke 13:24); and the apostle Paul says: “In everything let us present ourselves as ministers of God, in great patience, in vigils, in fasts” (2 Cor. 6:4); along with countless other passages found in the New Testament concerning the mortification of the flesh.

The Lord also makes clear in the Gospel how much more severe his commandments are than the commandments of the Law when he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:21–22).

And again: “It was said to the ancients: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you that whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (ibid. 27–28).

And again: “It was said to the ancients: Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce. But I say to you: Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, commits adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” (ibid. 31–32).

And again:

[Note: [Col. 0785] The printed edition lacked the passage beginning “And again” and ending “give him your cloak”; we have supplied this passage from the manuscripts.]

“It was said to the ancients: An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you not to resist evil; rather, if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and to the one who wishes to take your tunic, give him your cloak as well” (ibid. 38–40).

And again: “It was said to the ancients: You shall love your friend and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (ibid. 43–45).

These words of the Lord that we have quoted plainly demonstrate that the Gospel is signified by the iron rod, while the fragile and soft Law is signified by the wooden rod. By the potter’s vessels are signified the hearts of the Gentiles, filled with every error of demons; these were shattered by the touch of the iron rod, because, when the grace of the Gospel came, every error of the Gentiles was destroyed. Those who had previously been earthen vessels became iron vessels, exceedingly strong against all the assaults of demons and against the persecutions of wicked people. [Col. 0786D]

“And I will give him the morning star”—that is, I will give him myself. For he is the morning star, concerning whom Scripture says: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and he shall strike the leaders of Moab” (Num. 24:17).

[Note: [Col. 0787] So the manuscripts; the printed edition omits the words that intervene between “from the father” and “Therefore, the leaders of Moab.”]

“Moab” is said to mean “from the father”; and the Lord said to the Jews: “You are from your father the devil.” Therefore, the Lord struck the leaders of Moab when he emptied all the makers of error.

## CHAPTER III

### (Verse 1)

“And to the angel of the church of Sardis write: These things says he who has the seven spirits of God and the seven stars.”

The seven spirits of God are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet Isaiah shows descended upon the Lord when he says: “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:2).

Concerning these seven spirits, what the Lord has given will be discussed below; what the seven stars are has been explained above.

It follows: “I know your works, that you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead.” He had the name that he was alive—that is, the Christian name—but he was dead, because he did not have the works of faith, which is love. [Col. 0787B]

### (Verse 2)

“Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die.”

The one who always practices good works is watchful. This person is therefore commanded to watch—that is, to exercise himself in works of love—so that the little good he still seemed to possess would not perish. For just as the body is dead without a soul, so, even if we seem to possess various good things, they are dead if love is absent.

“For I have not found your works complete before my God.” They were not complete but empty, because they were not filled with love. Thus also the five foolish virgins were excluded from the company of the heavenly bridegroom, because they did not wish to have the oil of love in their vessels (Matt. 25:3). [Col. 0787C]

### (Verse 3)

“Therefore, keep in mind how you received and heard, and preserve it, and repent.”

That is: remember how you received the faith of Christ in baptism, where you promised that you would renounce the devil and all his works. Remember also what you heard from the teachers of the Christian faith who taught you Christ’s faith—namely, how you ought to live.

“Preserve what you heard, and repent,” because until now you have been sluggish in good works.

“If therefore you will not watch”—that is, if you do not rouse yourself to perform good works—“I will come like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come upon you.”

The Lord comes upon such a person like a thief in order to remove him by death from this worldly dwelling: one who rests in his wickedness, is unwilling to abstain from his vices, and does not even set death before his eyes. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “If the master of the household had known at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into” (Matt. 24:43).

By the master of the household we may understand the mind, because just as the master of a household rules over everyone in the house, so the mind is placed over all the acts and thoughts of the body. The master of the household therefore sleeps, and the thief comes and breaks into his house, when the mind rests in carnal pleasures, death arrives unanticipated, breaks into the house of the body, and takes away the soul. But if he is watchful—that is, if he perseveres in good works—he will endure death not as a thief but as a liberator. [Col. 0788A]

### (Verse 4)

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments.”

Behold, the disciples are placed above the negligent shepherd, so that he might at least make progress by imitating them. But it is surprising that he is said to have “a few names,” rather than “a few people.” This pertains to the great excellence of a saint, when God is said to know him by name. Thus it is said to Moses, a perfect man: “I know you by name”; and the Lord says in the Gospel: “He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out” (John 10:3).

These few, who deserve to be praised by the voice of God, have not defiled their garments—that is, they have not polluted with the filth of vices the purity they received in baptism.

“And they walked with me in white, because they are worthy”—that is, in good works. [Col. 0788B]

### (Verses 5–6)

“The one who conquers will thus be clothed in white garments.”

That is, the one who through repentance and tears has conquered the devil and driven every vice from himself will also obtain the same purity possessed by one who has been baptized.

He says these things in order to urge both the shepherd of the church of Sardis and all sinners to repentance.

“And I will not erase his name from the book of life.”

If he calls predestination the book of life, how can anyone be erased from the book of life, when the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30)?

Unless perhaps we understand it in this way: There are many who are thought righteous by human beings but are found unrighteous in the sight of God. Therefore, the people who judge them righteous already think that they have been written in God’s book. But on the day of judgment, when the deeds of the reprobate and the righteous are made known to all, this inscription and false presumption will be erased from their minds, when they see their condemnation for their wickedness.

“And I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.” This confession of the names of the righteous will then take place, when each person receives his reward according to the quality of his merits. [Col. 0788C]

### (Verse 7)

“And to the angel of the church of Philadelphia write: These things says the holy and true one, who has the key of David.”

We read in the Book of Kings that the Lord said to David: “And when you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall come forth from you, and I will establish his kingdom forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (2 Kings 7:12–14).

No one except a faithless Jew would doubt that this was spoken concerning Christ. And no one can enter a closed house except by a key. Therefore, the Son of God has the key of David, because he assumed a human being from the lineage of David—one whom he calls the key of David—through whom all things were unlocked: both what God spoke to David and what David spoke concerning him.

“He opens, and no one shuts; he shuts, and no one opens.”

The Lord Jesus Christ opened the Old Testament for the understanding of the divine mysteries hidden within it, and no one will be able to shut it. But he shut the superfluous observance of the letter of the Law, and no one will be able to open it.

He also opened the hearts of the Gentiles to receive the teaching of the faith, and no persecutor was able to shut them. But he shut and destroyed the worship of idols, and no persecutor was able to open it.

He also opened the way into the heavenly kingdom for his elect, and no power of demons can shut it. But he shut that same way for the reprobate, and no one will be able to open it for them. [Col. 0789A]

### (Verse 8)

“I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door that no one can shut, because you have little strength, and you have kept my word and have not denied my name.”

It seems to me that this angel of the church of Philadelphia was not sufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures, and therefore he is said to have had little strength for refuting the enemies of the true faith.

The meaning is this: Because you remained steadfast during persecution and kept my word—that is, you did not cease preaching my word—and did not deny my name, therefore, because you have little strength, I have set before you an open door in the divine Scriptures, so that you may understand the mysteries of the divine Scriptures. No one will be able to shut this door—that is, no enemy will be able to resist the wisdom that will be given to you. [Col. 0789B]

### (Verse 9)

“Behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan, who say that they are Jews and are not, but they lie.”

[Note: [Col. 0789D] The printed edition reads: “the synagogue of Satan, who opposed you”; the manuscripts have the wording found in the text.]

Behold, I will give some from the synagogue of Satan—“some” is understood—that is, from the Jews who are the synagogue of Satan, who opposed you and whose harassment you continually endured, so that they may believe in me through your words. [Col. 0789C]

### (Verse 10)

“Behold, I will cause them to come and worship before your feet, and they shall know that I have loved you, because you have kept the word of my patience.”

That is, when they believe in me through your words, they will worship before your feet, entreating that through you they may attain eternal life.

“And I will preserve you from the hour of temptation that is to come upon the whole world, to test all who dwell upon the earth.”

The hour of temptation signifies the day of judgment. He uses “temptation” to mean manifestation, [Note: [Col. 0789D] So all the manuscripts; the printed edition reads: “because the deeds of each person will be made manifest to all. From which hour of temptation,” and so forth. [Col. 0790D]] because at that time the cases of individuals will be made manifest.

In Exodus also we read: “God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3)—that is, so that it may be made clear and appear to all whether you love him.
