In accordance with this meaning, then, the hour of temptation signifies the hour of manifestation, when the deeds of each person will be made manifest to all. From this hour of temptation the Lord will save us and all his elect.

### (Verse 11)

“Behold, I am coming soon. Hold fast to what you have, so that no one may take your crown.”

“Hold fast to what you have”—that is, hold fast to the good that you have until the end of your life. “So that no one may take your crown”—that is, so that no one may possess without you the glory owed to you.

### (Verses 12–13)

“The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more” (Gal. 2:2).

The Church may be signified by the temple; by the pillars that support the temple, the preachers. For the apostle Paul calls Peter and James pillars of the Church, because the Church was built upon them, just as the Lord said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18).

But because of what follows—“and he shall go out no more”—this statement seems to pertain not to the present Church but to the heavenly one. For there have been many who were called pillars of the Church but who, because of their perverse teaching, went out from it, as happened with Origen and many others.

Therefore, by the temple the heavenly dwelling is signified; by the pillar, each of the elect. Thus whoever conquers all the assaults of the devil and all carnal pleasures becomes a pillar in the temple of God—that is, in heavenly blessedness. And just as a pillar remains with the firmest stability in the place where it has been set, so each of the elect receives from his Creator such firm stability in heavenly blessedness that he is never torn away from it, as the devil was torn away when he fell from heavenly blessedness through pride.

[Note: [Col. 0790D] The words “with the firmest stability” through “such firm stability” have been restored from the manuscripts.]

“And I will write upon him the name of my God.” This name of God is eternal. Therefore, the name of God, which is eternal, is written upon each righteous person when eternity with the Lord is granted to him.

“And the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God.”

That new Jerusalem is the heavenly one, which is built each day not from stones, as the old Jerusalem was, [Col. 0790C] but from holy people. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” that is, “vision of God.” Therefore, the name Jerusalem is written upon each of the elect when each is granted the privilege of deserving to see God without end.

Alternatively: The name Jerusalem is written upon each of the elect because he himself is Jerusalem, in whom God deigns to reign, namely, in the fellowship of the angels and of all the elect who are called the heavenly Jerusalem.

But it is surprising that Jerusalem is said to have descended from heaven, since we know that all the elect daily ascend from earth to heaven, rather than falling back from heavenly things to earthly ones. But when the Lord descended from heaven for the redemption of the human race, the saints also descended with him, because by the grace of predestination they were already joined to those whom he was coming to redeem by his mercy. [Col. 0790D]

“And my new name”—namely, so that he may be called the Son of God, just as I am the Son of God.

### (Verse 14)

“And to the angel of the church of Laodicea write: These things says the Amen, the faithful and true witness.”

“Amen” is interpreted as “truly” or “faithfully.” What is “Amen” is therefore “the faithful and true witness.”

“Who is the beginning of God’s creation.”

He does not call himself the beginning of God’s creation because he himself was created, but because all things were created by him. For example, an architect made a house. If you ask who was the beginning of the house, you will be told: the craftsman, who first conceived it in his mind and afterward built it, since the house itself could not give itself a beginning. [Col. 0791A]

### (Verse 15)

“I know your works: that you are neither cold nor hot.”

He was not cold, because although he did not have the works of faith, he considered himself righteous by faith alone. He was not hot, because he lacked love.

“I wish that you were either cold or hot.”

That is, I wish either that you burned with love or that you considered yourself a sinner, as you are, so that through fear of eternal fire and through repentance you might be driven to perform good works.

### (Verse 16)

“But because you are lukewarm, I am beginning to vomit you out of my mouth.”

If lukewarm water is swallowed, it produces disgust and is therefore easily rejected. We enter the Lord’s mouth when, through baptism, we are cleansed from every vice and become his members.

Therefore, if, growing lukewarm with respect to love, we neglect to practice the faith that works through love and that we promised in baptism, we are rejected from the Lord’s mouth like something harmful, disgusting, and foul-smelling. As he himself said concerning himself to his disciples: “I am the vine, and you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will cut off; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2).

[Note: [Col. 0791D] The printed edition has: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will cleanse it”; but all the manuscripts supply the omitted clause.]

### (Verse 17)

“Because you say, ‘I am rich and have grown wealthy, and I need nothing.’”

A person is rightly called rich and wealthy when, full of every virtue, he has grown even to the summit of perfection.

But this bishop of the church of Laodicea considered himself rich and wealthy in every virtue on account of faith alone, and thought that he needed nothing else in order to acquire eternal salvation, not considering what the Apostle says: “Faith without works is idle” (James 2:26). [Col. 0791C]

“And you do not know that you are wretched and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.”

We call a person wretched when, together with poverty and nakedness, he is also oppressed by some infirmity. Likewise, this man is called wretched and miserable because he was poor in virtues, blind in mind, and naked in good works.

[Note: [Col. 0792D] The printed edition lacked the words “blind in mind.”]

### (Verse 18)

“I advise you to buy from me gold tested by fire.”

By gold, wisdom is understood, as it is written: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 21:20). It is called “tested” because it makes all whom it possesses tested and perfect.

It is called “fired” because it kindles the minds in which it dwells with love of God and neighbor. And because true wisdom grows from the divine Scriptures, the Psalmist makes this clear when he says: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11:7).

The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings because they make pure minds free from vices. But since nothing can be purified except what is filthy, we must ask how the sayings of the Lord are said to be purified, when nothing filthy can be in them.

The sayings of the Lord, therefore, are said to be like silver tested by fire [Col. 0792A] because they test the minds of the faithful by the fire of repentance at one time and by the fire of love at another, cleansing them from every filth of vice.

The phrase “proved upon the earth” has in Hebrew: “separated from the earth.”

It is also said to have been purified sevenfold on account of the seven purifications contained in divine Scripture, namely, the seven virtues by which all vices are cleansed. Thus the vice of gluttony is cleansed through abstinence, pride through humility, lust through chastity, and hatred, avarice, envy, and many other vices through love. Likewise, the remaining vices have their own adversaries, by which they are either conquered or conquer.

And because above the Lord says that gold—that is, wisdom—is to be bought from him, we must ask at what price wisdom is bought, since Job says: “Gold of Ophir shall not be given in exchange for it” (Job 28:15), nor anything else that is considered more precious among human beings.

But blessed Job himself reveals at what price it is bought when he says: “The fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (ibid. 28). This does not mean that the one who fears is perfect in wisdom, since the Apostle says: “The one who fears is not perfected in love” (1 John 4:18); rather, it means that the one who begins to pay its price begins already to possess wisdom.

Its price is the fear of the Lord, renunciation of vices, repentance, tears, and works of mercy. Therefore it follows appropriately: “So that you may become rich.” For without this price no one can attain the enrichment of virtues, which is wisdom.

“And that you may clothe yourself in white garments.” The white garments are good works.

“And that the shame of your nakedness may not appear.” That shame of nakedness is the one of which the Psalmist says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth” (Ps. 50:7).

We must cover this shame of nakedness with good works. For although this bishop had faith, he is nevertheless said to have been naked because he was lacking in the works of faith.

“And anoint your eyes with salve, so that you may see.” By the salve, which removes darkness from the eyes and draws out tears, repentance and compunction of heart may be understood. For repentance removes the darkness of blindness from the eyes of the mind and sharpens them to see the reward of the righteous and the punishment of sinners. [Col. 0792C]

### (Verse 19)

“I reprove and discipline those whom I love.”

As Scripture says: “For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). [Col. 0792D]

### (Verse 20)

“Be zealous, therefore, and repent.”

That is, imitate the good and repent, because until now you have been sluggish in good works.

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me.”

The Lord knocks at our door when, through divine Scripture, he admonishes us each day to abandon our vices and turn to the performance of good works.

We hear his voice and open the door when we receive his commandments with the full attention of our mind. [Col. 0793A]

[Note: [Col. 0793D] So the manuscripts; the printed edition reads: “He enters into us when he rejoices in our progress.”]

He himself enters into us when he plants his love in our hearts. He dines with us when he rejoices in our progress. We dine with him when we exult in the hope of heavenly glory.

### (Verse 21)

“To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne.”

Christ conquered the devil, and his saints also conquer; but Christ conquered by himself, whereas his saints conquer not by themselves but through him.

The Father gave the Son authority, insofar as he is human, to sit on his throne; and the Son gave his saints authority to sit upon his throne as well.

But Christ sits at the right hand of the Father, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1), because he is equal to the Father. The saints, however, are not said to sit at the right hand of the Son but in their own seats, as the Lord said in the Gospel: “You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

They are not sons by nature, as Christ is, but by adoption; therefore they receive different seats according to the diversity of their merits.

May he of whom we speak grant this to us, so that in the distribution of those seats we wretched people may deserve to have a share: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## THE SECOND VISION

[Col. 0793C]

[Note: [Col. 0793D] The printed edition reads: “Reason demands that … it be described more clearly”; the Roman edition had removed the words from the middle.]

Reason demands that, after the seven epistles which John directed to the seven churches—which signify the one catholic Church—and in which the faithful are instructed how they ought to ascend to the heights of virtue, the condition and exalted state of that same Church should be described more clearly.

## CHAPTER IV [Col. 0793C]

**[Verse 1.]** After this I saw a door opened in heaven. By the door Christ is understood, who says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). It is said to be an open door because, for all who desire to come to him—even if they are weighed down by many crimes—he does not disdain to open the door of his mercy, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28).

[Col. 0793D] By heaven, however, the Church is signified. But if everyone who enters through the door into the sheepfold, that is, into the holy Church, will be saved, by what entrance did the wicked enter, those countless people who are contained within the holy Church? Let us ask the Lord about this; for he says: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Therefore, all who do not wish to observe what they promised in baptism have climbed into the sheepfold not through the door, but by another way.

“And the first voice that I heard, like the voice of a trumpet speaking with me,” [Col. 0794A] saying. We may understand the first voice as the Old Testament; but it seems better to me that by the first voice we should understand John the Baptist, of whom it is written: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people for the forgiveness of their sins” (Luke 1:76). John himself also calls himself a voice, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said” (John 1:23, from Isaiah 40:3). And because his preaching spread everywhere, the voice of his preaching is said to be like a trumpet.

But let us hear what this voice says: “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen afterward”; that is, leave earthly things and raise your mind to heavenly things. [Note: The same in the Roman edition: “Come up here,” that is, leave earthly things.]

Alternatively: In this passage the evangelist John represents those who believed in Christ through John the Baptist. At that time many arose who thought that John was the Christ. John, however, urged his hearers to raise their minds upward when he said that he was not the Christ, but that another would come after him, saying: “I am not the Christ; but one stronger than I will come after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loose. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (John 1:27); and again: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). He also admonished his disciples to climb upward when he clearly taught that he himself had to be abandoned and Christ followed.

Then follows: “And I will show you what must happen afterward,” as if he were saying: If you raise your heart upward—that is, if you follow Christ in faith—you will easily be able to recognize, even with Christ himself as your teacher, the things that I teach and the things that are to come.

**[Verse 2.]** “And immediately I was in the Spirit”; that is, when I began to believe in Christ, I became spiritual instead of carnal. “And behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one seated upon the throne.” By heaven, as we said above, the Church is signified; the throne set in heaven signifies the hearts of the saints who dwell in the Church. The one who was seen seated above the throne is God, who dwells and sits in the hearts of his saints, as the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

**[Verse 3.]** “And he who was seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius.” Jasper is green in color, while sardius is red. Through the greenness of jasper, therefore, the divinity of our Savior is signified; through the redness of sardius, his humanity. Our Savior thus contains within himself the greenness of jasper, because according to his divinity he is in all things equal to the Father, and the redness of sardius, because according to his humanity he exists as a perfect man, as it is written: “Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh” (the Creed attributed to Athanasius).

“And there was a rainbow around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” In Genesis we read that God said to Noah: “I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my everlasting covenant, which is established between God and every living soul” (Genesis 9:13). Through the bow, therefore, which appears as a sign of God’s clemency to human beings dwelling on earth, God’s mercy is appropriately understood.

The rainbow, that is, the bow, surrounded the throne of God, that is, the Church, because his mercy protects and governs us by surrounding us, [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the edition instead has: “and protects us from visible and invisible enemies.”] and defends us from invisible enemies. For in him, as the Apostle says, “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

This bow is said to have had the likeness of an emerald, which is of an exceedingly intense and pleasing greenness. The jasper of which we spoke above is also green, like the emerald. But its greenness is dull, whereas the greenness of the emerald is transparent; its beauty draws the eyes of those who look upon it toward admiration.

Through the greenness of jasper, therefore, as we said, the divinity of our Savior is understood. It is obscure and covered by certain clouds, because no mind can comprehend the divinity of our Redeemer as it is. The higher the mind raises itself to investigate it, the greater the darkness that confronts it.

Through the greenness of the emerald, however, which is transparent, the Lord’s mercy is rightly signified. The Lord’s mercy is so evident that no person possessing a sound mind can be unaware of it. For who can be unaware of the immense mercy of God, which he has shown toward the human race and shows daily, although it cannot be perfectly expressed in words?

The fact also that the greenness of this stone, when it is looked upon, sharpens dulled eyes for seeing can be applied to God’s mercy. When we lie in sins and our crimes weigh us down, we have the dulled eyes of the mind. But when we consider God’s mercy—how he has brought prostitutes and robbers, people overwhelmed by every kind of crime, and even his persecutors, back to salvation through repentance—we are restored to hope of forgiveness.

And because we were already being held in the pit of destruction, when we look upon the Lord’s mercy and place our hope in it, we flee to the one whom we had offended, so that by his mercy we may be freed from everlasting death. The Psalmist contemplated this mercy of God but could not express it in words, and therefore called God himself “my mercy,” saying: “My God, my mercy” (Psalm 143:1–2).

**[Verse 4.]** “And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the twenty-four thrones twenty-four elders seated, clothed in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns.”

In this book the twenty-four elders sometimes signify the fathers of the Old Testament, sometimes those of the New Testament, and sometimes both together. In this passage they signify the fathers of the Old Testament, who are said to have sat upon twenty-four seats. For when we sit, we rest from labor.

Through the twenty-four seats, therefore, the books of the Old Testament are signified. The twenty-four elders were seen seated upon twenty-four thrones because the fathers of the Old Testament rested, in a certain sense, from the labors and cares of this world in the reading and meditation of the divine books.

But we must ask: Since the throne signifies the Church, why are these seats said to have been arranged around the throne? Clearly, because whenever a householder desires his house to be safe from thieves and enemies, he surrounds it with a wall, hedge, or partition. Similarly, the Church is fortified by the books of the Old Testament against heretics and pagans who wish to overthrow the faith of Christ within it. For when the Church proves that the things it venerates were foretold long before Christ’s coming, it drives far away from itself the darts of the enemies who desire to destroy the faith of Christ.

These elders are said to have been clothed in white garments, and to have had golden crowns on their heads. Through the white garments, purity of life is signified; through the golden crowns, good works.

**[Verse 5.]** “And from the throne”—that is, from the Church—“proceed flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder.”

Through the flashes of lightning, the miracles that God works through his saints are signified; through the voices, preaching; through the thunder, the terror of the fire of Gehenna. For holy preachers present the eternal torments prepared for the impious to those whom they cannot recall from vices by love of the heavenly homeland, so that those whom they cannot restrain by encouragement they may at least restrain from vices by terror.

[Note: Fragment of the manuscript of Saint Ouen: “The blessed apostle and evangelist John saw seven lamps in the Apocalypse,” etc.]

“And seven burning lamps before the throne.” He explains what the seven lamps are when he says: “Which are the seven spirits of God.” By the seven spirits of God we must understand the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet Isaiah declares rested upon the Lord, saying: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:2).

These seven lamps, therefore—that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—are said to burn before the seat, that is, before the sight of his Church, because without the light of these virtues, placed as we are in the night of this world, we cannot walk along the paths of life toward the heavenly homeland.

When he says that Christ received these seven gifts from the Holy Spirit, this pertains to the mystery of his humanity. For according to his divinity he could not be increased in anything, since without him nothing could exist.

It may nevertheless be asked why, when the prophet said that these seven gifts would descend upon Christ, he began with the greater and proceeded downward to the lesser. But the reason will not seem unfitting if it is examined carefully.

Our Lord Jesus Christ descended from that heavenly blessedness in which he was in all things equal to the Father, deigned to come down to earth and become human, and wished to be made lower than the angels whom he himself had created. It is therefore not inappropriate that he received these seven gifts while descending, because by descending and humbling himself even unto death he fulfilled the Father’s will, as the Apostle says: “He humbled himself even unto death, and the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8).

We, however, who are lifted from the very pit of destruction to heavenly things, begin with the lesser, so that by growing we may arrive at the greater.

Let us briefly say, insofar as the Lord grants, how these seven gifts descended upon Christ.

The spirit of wisdom rested upon the man Christ when the Son of God, who according to his divinity is called the Wisdom of the Father, descended into him.

The spirit of understanding rested upon him when he was enriched with every virtue, as it is written in the Gospel: “Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and human beings” (Luke 2:52).

After understanding comes counsel. “Counsel” is so called from *consulere*, “to consult,” for if some danger threatens us, we seek counsel from a wise person about how we may escape the danger. Similarly, when we desire to rise to some dignity in this world, we seek counsel about how we may attain what we desire.

Christ, therefore, is our counselor. He gives counsel about how we may escape eternal dangers, and he himself accomplishes the counsel he gives when he frees us from eternal dangers. Likewise, he gives counsel about how we may attain the inheritance of paradise, and he himself brings us to those joys.

The spirit of counsel, therefore, descended upon the man Christ when he received from the Holy Spirit the teaching of the Gospel, in which the counsel of all people who desire to be saved consists.

The spirit of fortitude also rested upon Christ when he appeared strong among human beings to defeat the ancient enemy. He himself spoke of this strength in the Gospel: “When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace; but when someone stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his armor in which he trusted and distribute his spoils” (Luke 11:21).

After fortitude comes knowledge. Among human beings there are many kinds of knowledge; for there are different forms of knowledge belonging to different arts. There is knowledge in literature, in secular laws, in increasing temporal possessions, and also knowledge in avoiding dangers. There are even many who, through subtlety of perception, foresee certain future events.

The good sometimes possess these forms of knowledge, and sometimes the wicked. But the knowledge that descended upon Christ can be possessed by no one except the good. It was so great that no mind could comprehend it: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

It therefore seems to me that by the spirit of knowledge we should not understand some particular deed of his. For our Savior foresaw that, if he avoided the company of sinful people, many criminals would fall into the pit of despair. He therefore wished to conform himself to sinners through bodily association, eating and drinking with them and not refusing to be touched by prostitutes. He even promised paradise to the robber at the beginning of his confession (Luke 23:43), so that he might give hope of forgiveness to all sinners who desired to be saved.

But the Pharisees, who did not possess the spirit of knowledge, reproached him because he ate with tax collectors and sinners. He, however, possessing the spirit of knowledge, said to them: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:12 and following).

We need say nothing about the spirit of piety. For what is so pious as the one who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22), and who, although he could free himself from death by his own power, allowed himself to be seized and bound for the salvation of the human race, to be spat upon, struck with blows, scourged, and crucified?

The spirit of the fear of the Lord, which is placed last, pertains to the Passion—not because he was compelled by fear to die for the salvation of the human race, but because we must understand fear as obedience, concerning which he himself says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:36).

We also say that a son who is wholly obedient to his earthly father fears his father, although that obedience is not one of fear but of love. Concerning this fear the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10). It is not fear, however, but the love of God that will endure forever and ever.

Now we must briefly explain how these seven gifts of the Holy Spirit apply to each of the faithful. Since we, who lay in the snare of destruction through the guilt of the first transgression, are led back to heavenly things by God’s mercy from below, we begin with the fear of God, so that by progressing we may grow toward higher things, that is, toward wisdom.

By the same steps through which Christ descended to us by humbling himself and completed our salvation by dying, we too must ascend to him: namely, by carrying out his commandments, which are contained in the seven gifts of the Spirit.

The spirit of the fear of the Lord rests upon each sinner when, considering his sins, fearing God’s just judgment and the punishments of eternal fire prepared for the impious, he turns to repentance and tears, and begins to weep most bitterly over what he had done with delight.

The spirit of piety rests upon any sinner when, hearing Scripture say, “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33), and hearing the Lord say, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41), he begins to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and perform the other works of piety, so that by showing mercy to others he may make God favorable toward himself, whom he had offended by sinning.

For this reason the prophet Daniel also sought to urge a most wicked king to redeem his sins through almsgiving and acts of mercy toward the poor.

From piety one ascends to the spirit of knowledge. For although someone may appear to possess knowledge, he is foolish if he lives badly. What is more foolish than to cast the fear of God from one’s mind, [Note: The edition has: “to serve vices? Knowledge, however, is the greatest thing,” etc.; the manuscripts read as in the text.] serve vices, and rush headlong toward destruction?

If, then, it is foolishness to serve vices, and the best knowledge is to abandon vices and turn wholly to God, whoever begins to mourn his sins through the spirit of fear, and through the spirit of piety strives to be merciful toward the needy so that by showing mercy to others he may make God merciful toward himself, must possess the spirit of knowledge through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

For whoever desires to turn back to God must abandon vices; and whoever wishes to abandon vices must learn, through the teaching of the divine Scriptures or through the preaching of holy men, what kinds of vices there are, how they entangle human beings, and by what means they can be extinguished; what the deceptions of demons are, and how one must fight against them. This is to possess the spirit of knowledge.

And because Solomon says that “he who adds knowledge adds labor” (Ecclesiastes 1:18), from knowledge one ascends to the spirit of fortitude.

For just as a soldier does not fight against someone whom he holds bound, but rather against someone who wishes to resist him, so the devil does not fight against someone whom he holds bound by the chains of sins, but rather against someone who ceases to sin and turns back to God with his whole mind.

Therefore, whoever through repentance and works of piety deserves to be released from the devil’s chains, and desires to wage war against him through the spirit of knowledge, must receive the gift of fortitude from the Holy Spirit. Armed with it, he can utterly extinguish his inner enemies, that is, vices, overcome his external enemies, namely human beings, through patience, and repel all the darts of demons from himself with the shield of faith.

From fortitude one ascends to counsel. The counsel of our salvation consists in the evangelical commandments. Whoever has been able to extinguish vices within himself through the spirit of fortitude must pass on to examining and storing in his heart the commandments of the Gospel, where he will find counsel about how he may ascend to the summit of perfection.

[Note: Fragment of the Audian manuscript: “so that he may advance toward the commandments of the Law or the Gospel.”]

And because the commandments of the Gospel cannot be kept without virtues, from the spirit of counsel one ascends to understanding, in which the perfection of all virtues consists.

The faithful receive the gift of understanding from the Holy Spirit when they deserve to be enriched with every virtue. For the person who possesses true understanding is the one illuminated by faith, purified by chastity, adorned with patience, fortified by humility, radiant with charity, and perfected by the remaining virtues.

And because one ascends to the summit of perfection through the practice of virtues, wisdom is placed above understanding, in which the whole of perfection consists.

[Note: Gill has “through the exercise of virtues”; the Roman edition has “through the power of prayers”; the manuscripts agree with the reading given here.]

Concerning this perfection the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

There are many who try to ascend suddenly to the summit of perfection. But because they do not ascend by the steps of the virtues, they easily fall. For what benefit is there in abandoning one’s possessions if one does not cast from one’s mind anger, hatred, drunkenness, envy, pride, vainglory, and the other vices that kill the soul?

It does no good to climb a tree in order to escape a lion if one carries a serpent in one’s bosom and perishes from its poison. Nor does the Lord call the person perfect who has merely abandoned his possessions, but the one who has both abandoned his possessions and followed him.

We follow him when we imitate him. Therefore, that person ascends to the summit of perfection by the proper order who, after first renouncing vices, ascends through the active life—which is perfected by virtues—to the contemplative life, in which he is joined to Christ alone, who is the Wisdom of the Father and the Son of God, and becomes a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem.

[Note: Fragment of the Audian manuscript: “which advances through virtues … the heavenly Jerusalem is perfected.”]

Now let us briefly demonstrate how the ascent of the faithful through the seven steps of the gifts of the Holy Spirit corresponds to Christ’s descent.

The final step of Christ’s descent is the fear of God, through which we said that his Passion and death were signified; it is also the first step of those who ascend by turning to God. The Lord’s death corresponds to those who mourn their sins through the spirit of the fear of the Lord, because forgiveness of all sins consists in the Lord’s death. Perfect forgiveness of sins could not exist if he had not died for us.

The sixth step of Christ’s descent is piety, and the second step of the ascent of penitents. The piety of the faithful corresponds to the Lord’s piety because he bestowed his mercy upon those who were miserable according to the soul, freeing them from eternal death by his own death, [Note: The edition has: “and these show mercy to those who are miserable according to the body”; the manuscripts read as in the text.] while these show mercy to those who are miserable according to the body by giving them the necessities of bodily life. To such people he himself will say at the judgment: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 1:25).

The fifth step of Christ’s descent is knowledge, and the third step of the ascent of the faithful. The spirit of knowledge given to the faithful corresponds to the spirit of knowledge offered to the man Christ, because he did not disdain to conform himself to sinners in order to save them, while these flee to him through the spirit of knowledge so that they may escape sins, for he has the power to forgive sins.

The fourth step of Christ’s descent is fortitude, and likewise the fourth step of the ascent of the faithful. The fortitude of the faithful corresponds to Christ’s fortitude, because they conquer the devil by the same fortitude by which Christ conquered him—namely, Christ’s fortitude, not their own—as he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

The third step of Christ’s descent is the spirit of counsel, and the fifth step of the ascent of the faithful. The counsel of the faithful is joined to Christ’s counsel when they turn to observing the commandments of the Gospel, in which the perfect counsel of all the saints consists.

The second step of Christ’s descent is understanding, and the sixth step of the ascent of the faithful. The understanding of the faithful corresponds to Christ’s understanding when his saints deserve to receive from him the same virtues that he himself received from his Spirit.

The first step of Christ’s descent is wisdom, and the seventh step of the ascent of the faithful, because Christ is the Wisdom of the Father, and all wisdom arises from him.

The saints, therefore, who are joined to the Lord through the practice of virtues receive from him wisdom, in which the sum of all goodness consists (Proverbs 3:13). Through Solomon he says to them: “If anyone loves wisdom, let him turn to me, and he will find her; and when he has found her, he is blessed if he holds fast to her.”

**[Verse 6.]** It follows: “And before the throne there was something like a glassy sea, like crystal.”

We read that in Solomon’s temple there was a bronze sea in which the priests washed before approaching the altar to offer sacrifices (2 Chronicles 4:6). The brightness of bronze, however, is quickly clouded by a certain darkness.

Through the bronze sea, therefore, the Law of Moses is signified, which obscures the radiance of spiritual understanding by the darkness of the letter. And just as the brightness of bronze is revealed when it is rubbed with a file, so the spiritual understanding that is obscured in the Law by the surface of the letter is revealed by God’s grace when it is carefully examined by faithful people.

The priests washed in this sea because certain sins of the ancient people were cleansed through sacrifices and certain legal observances.

Through the glassy sea, therefore, and the crystal, the New Testament is appropriately understood. In this sea we find three things: sea, glass, and crystal. Through the sea, history is signified; through the glass, moral understanding; through the crystal, spiritual understanding.

Through glass, from which mirrors are made, moral understanding is appropriately understood. Just as a person can detect in a mirror whatever disfigurement he bears on his face, so moral understanding reveals whatever may be defective in human souls.

Through crystal, which is clearer than all gems and which often emits from itself flashes of brilliance and even fire, spiritual understanding is expressed. It illuminates whatever is obscure in the divine Scriptures, lights the minds of spiritual people with the flames of spiritual meanings, and kindles some people to love God and the heavenly homeland.

“And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind.” Taken historically, this cannot stand; for such a small number could not occupy both the circumference and the center of the throne. It must therefore be understood spiritually.

The four living creatures signify not only the four evangelists, but also all the teachers of the Church who follow their teaching.

The four living creatures stand around the throne because the teachers of the Church defend the people entrusted to them from visible and invisible enemies with all the strength they possess. They stand in the midst of the throne because they never cease admonishing each person to advance in every virtue and in all good works.

These four living creatures were therefore seen to have eyes before and behind because holy preachers look upon both the future and the past.

They have eyes before them because, as they contemplate the day of judgment, the condemnation of the wicked, and the glory of the righteous, they show their hearers what they ought to avoid and what they ought to desire.

They have eyes behind them because, as they look upon the life of the fathers who preceded them, they themselves advance by imitating them and place their life and teaching before their hearers, so that the hearers too may advance in their imitation. [Note: Codex Gemblacensis has: “that they too may advance in their imitation and teaching.”]

**[Verse 7.]** “And the first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature had a face like a human being, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle.”

Not all authors have interpreted the figures of the four living creatures in the same way. But it has been handed down to us by the ancients that through the lion we should understand Mark, through the calf Luke, through the human being Matthew, and through the flying eagle John. The reason is that Mark begins with the wilderness, Luke with the priesthood of the Jews, Matthew with a human being—that is, with Christ’s genealogy—and John with Christ’s divinity.

Some, however, following another order, think that Matthew is signified by the lion, Mark by the calf, Luke by the human being, and John by the eagle.

They say that Matthew is signified by the lion, which is the king of beasts, because he narrated that Christ, according to his human nature, descended from a royal lineage (Matthew 2:2). He also says that at the time of Christ’s birth a star appeared, which showed him to be King of heaven and earth, of angels and human beings. It brought the Magi from the East to worship him as King of the world.

He also says that the king of the earth, Herod, was troubled at the time of Christ’s birth, together with all his attendants. For just as any king of small power trembles and is disturbed if he learns that another king of great power is coming against him to invade his kingdom (ibid. 3), so when Christ came in the flesh, as the future King of the world, Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.

The gifts that he says the Magi offered to Christ also demonstrate that he is King, God, and Lord of all creatures.

They say that Mark was represented by the calf because of the simplicity of his language. Luke was represented by the human being because he treated Christ’s human generation more fully than the others. From him we learned how Christ was announced by the angel, how he was born, how he was placed in a manger, how he was circumcised, how he was presented in the temple, and how, by growing, he reached mature age. [Note: The edition lacked the words “how he was announced by the angel … how he was born”; these are not omitted in the manuscripts.]

There is no one who denies that John was signified by the eagle.

**[Verse 8.]** “And the four living creatures, each one of them, had six wings, and around and within they were full of eyes.”

Through the number six, which is a perfect number, the perfection of the saints is signified. No one can rise to it except through the teaching of the Gospel, for “the Law brought no one to perfection” (Hebrews 7:19).

If you join together the six wings of the four living creatures, you will find twenty-four. They therefore seem to me to have the same significance as the twenty-four seats, which we said signified the twenty-four books of the Old Testament.

Seats, however, since they always cling to the earth, bend those who rest upon them somewhat toward the earth; wings, on the other hand, lift those to whom they are attached toward exalted things.

The books of the Old Testament were therefore seats for the ancient fathers, because, understanding them according to the letter, they were not able fully to raise themselves to their spiritual meaning. But these seats were changed into wings for the fathers of the New Testament, because, understanding the books of the Old Testament spiritually, they are daily lifted through their teaching toward heavenly things.

Since this number—that is, twenty-four—is often found in this book, it seemed appropriate to say a little about the mysteries of this number.

The parts of this number are one, two, three, four, six, eight, and twelve. The one placed at the beginning signifies the one God. The two that follow indicate the two Testaments. Three pertains to the Trinity. Four follows three appropriately because through the teaching of the four Gospels the faith of the holy Trinity has been revealed to us.

After four comes six, which is a perfect number, because no one can ascend to the summit of perfection without the teaching of the Gospel; for the Law, as the Apostle says, brought no one to perfection (ibid.).

After six comes eight, because there are eight virtues that fight against vices, and without the exercise of these no one can ascend to the height of perfection.

After eight comes twelve, because through the teaching of the apostles we arrive at the faith that is the mother of all virtues.

The four living creatures are therefore said to be full of eyes around and within. By “around” we must understand the whole body. For when Ezekiel spoke of these creatures, he said that their whole body was full of eyes (Ezekiel 1).

The saints have eyes behind them when, hearing the Lord’s warning, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62), they labor with all their strength not to fall back into the evil things they remember having once done, although they do not cease to place those things before the eyes of their minds as a safeguard of their humility.

They have eyes before them when, hearing the Lord’s voice say, “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds watching” (Matthew 24:46), they do not cease to perform whatever good they can, so that at the time of their death, when the Lord comes, they may be found ready.

They have eyes on the left when they repel all the temptations of demons from their minds with the shield of faith. They have eyes on the right when they carefully guard against being exalted because of their good works.

Or they have eyes on the right and on the left when neither prosperity can raise them up nor adversity bend them down.

They have eyes below when, by extinguishing them, they trample down carnal desires. They have eyes above when, with the whole desire of their minds, they yearn for the heavenly homeland. They have eyes within when they guard their hearts from filthy thoughts.

And they had no rest day or night, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.” For the rest of the wicked is the present life; tribulation follows them, and it has no end. The righteous, however, are afflicted in this world so that they may possess eternal rest, as the Apostle Paul says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

Alternatively: the saints have no rest because they do not cease from praises of God and prayers, as the Lord says: “One ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1); and the Apostle Paul says: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (1 Thess. 5:17). [Col. 0804C] But we must ask how we can pray without ceasing. For there are many who, although they are constant in prayers, psalmody, and the celebration of Masses, and give abundant alms, are nevertheless puffed up with pride, burn with the fever of avarice, and gather money by whatever means they can—so much so that they even harass the very poor, whom they ought to pity, by various devices, in order to increase their own wealth from the poor people’s meager possessions. They say that they are doing this lawfully, although this is not God’s law but the devil’s trick.

Many are also found in monasteries who devote themselves to vigils, psalms, prayers, and the celebration of Masses, yet are very often and easily inflamed by anger. Some serve drunkenness and gluttony; others carry hatred in their hearts for a long time; some seek the favor and praise of men for the good deeds they appear to perform; some are weighed down by envy, others by detraction or by various other vices. And why say more? They disfigure and deform by disgraceful conduct all the holiness they claim in their words.

To demonstrate, therefore, the blindness of such people, I shall propose a certain comparison. A man was held fast in mud up to his neck. When he saw someone passing by, he stretched out his hand and cried: “Have pity on me and pull me out of this mud.” When the passerby had extended his hand in order to pull him out, the man plunged the hand that had been extended beneath the mud. When the one who had come to pull him out wished to withdraw, the man again asked to be rescued. When the other extended his hand a second time to rescue him, the man, as before, plunged his hand beneath the mud. When he did this repeatedly, the other, becoming angry, said: “Why do you ask to be rescued, when you wish to remain in your danger? Since you love your destruction, possess what you have chosen.”

In the same way, such people constantly beseech God to be rescued from their vices, yet they embrace those very vices so tightly that they cannot in any way be torn away from them. Let us therefore place before our eyes two men: one learned, constantly praying, singing psalms, and celebrating Masses, yet subject to certain vices; the other unlearned and ignorant, but faithful, fearing and loving God, [Col. 0805B] loving his neighbor, patient, and humble. Which of these, in your view, has kept the Apostle’s injunction: “Pray without ceasing” (ibid.)? Is it the man who prays constantly yet is subject to certain vices, or the one who does not know how to pray yet is free from vices and devoted to good works? It is clear to all that God hears the latter’s innocence and good works more readily than the words of the former, whose life is stained by certain vices.

He, then, prays without ceasing who at appropriate times beseeches God with mind and tongue and is constant in good works. When he sleeps or is occupied with some necessities of human life, his works shine in the sight of God, and those works themselves intercede for him before God, just as the angel says to Cornelius: [Col. 0805C] “Your prayers and your alms have been remembered in the sight of God” (Acts 10:4).

Let us hear, then, what the four living creatures say without ceasing: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.” [Note: [Col. 0805D] Edition: “calling the Spirit of the Lord three times”; manuscripts: “calling holy God three times.”] By calling God three times holy, they signify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But when they say, “Lord God almighty,” passing from plurality to singularity, they show that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one lordship, one divinity, and one omnipotence.

But we must ask: if the four living creatures signify not only the four evangelists but also all the teachers of the Church, why are they said to invoke the Holy Trinity without ceasing, when the saints of God are sometimes occupied in prayers, sometimes in reading, sometimes in preaching, and sometimes with various necessities? The holy preachers, therefore, while they retain the faith of the Holy Trinity in their minds and confess it with their mouths; while they fulfill the works of faith; while they preach that same faith and its works by every means available to them; while in prayers and thanksgivings they entreat and praise the one who is the triune and one God; and while, according to the Apostle, whether they eat or drink, they do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ—they invoke the Holy Trinity without ceasing [Col. 0806A] (1 Cor. 10:31). What follows—“who was, and who is, and who is to come”—has already been explained above.

### (Verses 9–10)

And when those living creatures gave glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, who lives for ever and ever, the twenty-four elders fell down before the one seated upon the throne and worshiped him who lives for ever and ever.

In this passage the four living creatures signify the four books of the Gospel; by the twenty-four elders the Fathers of the New Testament may be understood. The four living creatures, therefore, give glory, honor, and blessing to the one seated upon the throne, who lives for ever and ever, because the teaching of the Gospel is read and preached throughout the whole world, through which glory, honor, and blessing are given to the Father, Son, [Col. 0806B] and Holy Spirit.

At the voice of the four living creatures, therefore, the twenty-four elders fell before the one seated upon the throne and worshiped him who lives for ever and ever, because the saints of God, established throughout the whole world, hear the teaching of the Gospel and humble themselves in God’s presence so that they may live with him for ever and ever. And they cast their crowns before the throne, saying:

We said above that crowns signify good works. The saints therefore cast their crowns before the throne when they attribute whatever good they do to God rather than to themselves, according to the Apostle’s command: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

### (Verse 11)

But let us hear what they say: “You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and [Col. 0806C] power.”

Above, the four living creatures were said to have given glory, honor, and blessing to God. Here, however, the twenty-four elders say that God has received glory, honor, and power, substituting “power” for “blessing.” [Note: [Col. 0805D] Thus the manuscripts; the edition, however, has “and to have received blessing from God,” and here has changed “power” in place of “blessing.”]

But what can anyone give to God, or what can God receive from anyone, since he created all things, without whom nothing can exist, and who says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)? If the saints can do nothing without God, what can they give him?

Since human nature is such that people can possess no good of themselves unless they receive it from him who is supremely good, God gives his saints that with which they may repay him. [Note: [Col. 0806D] The edition reads, “from which he himself may reward them”; the manuscripts read, “from which they themselves may repay him.”] God has promised his saints the kingdom of heaven, provided nevertheless that they give the price of good works for it. Yet the elect do not possess this price unless they receive it from him; he himself gives the price with which they may purchase eternal life from him.

The saints therefore give glory to God when they do whatever good they do with the intention [Note: [Col. 0806D] Thus all the manuscripts; the edition, however: “that they may glorify God the Father, as the Son of God says . . . ‘Let them see,’ etc.”] that God may be glorified through them, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Let them see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). John also says that Peter glorified God by his death (John 21:19).

They give honor when, in everything they do, they seek God’s honor rather than their own. Above, blessing is placed third; here, however, power is placed in its stead. Since the saints, when they do great things, are blessed by men, “power” corresponds appropriately with “blessing.” But how much the saints detest human praise for the great works they perform is shown to us by the book of the Acts of the Apostles.

When Peter and John had healed the lame man and everyone’s eyes were fixed upon them, as though they had done this by their own power, Peter, avoiding the blessing of their eyes, said to them: “Men, brothers, why do you gaze at us as though by our own [Note: [Col. 0807D] The edition reads, “power or authority we had done this”; and below, “Jesus, in whose name this man stands before you”; the manuscripts supply the wording in the text.] power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob has glorified his Son Jesus” (Acts 3:12).

And later: “In whose name this man stands before you healed.” Similarly, when Paul and Barnabas had healed a sick man at Lystra and the people wished to sacrifice to them, they tore their garments, saying: “Men, what are you doing? We also are human beings, like you” (Acts 14:14).

We can also understand this of Christ, who clearly received glory, honor, and power according to his humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0807D] The same editions have, “and they were created? Therefore all …”; all the manuscripts, however, agree in supplying the entire lacuna, except for the reading found at [Col. 0808D]: “If they existed, how were they created? Therefore all …”.]

It follows: “For you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created.” If this is to be understood in the same sense as the passage, “who made the things that were to come,” then all creatures existed in God’s power and will before they were created; they were created at the time God ordained. May he himself, therefore, who created all things from nothing, deign to create in us a clean heart—he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## THE THIRD VISION

[Col. 0807C]

[Note: [Col. 0808D] The Roman edition, on its own authority, had cut out this entire prologue, up to “And I saw,” etc.]

After the form of the Church has been described, it is not inappropriate that the opening of the book should be placed next, by which the opening of the divine Scriptures is signified. For after the Church had been founded among the nations by the holy apostles and the other preachers, the books of the Old and New Testaments were expounded by the holy teachers according to the apostolic faith.

## CHAPTER V

### (Verse 1)

And I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and on the outside, sealed with seven seals.

What is meant by the right hand and the seals—that the Lord gave them—we shall explain below. The book written within and on the outside signifies not only the Old Testament but also the New. It is written within according to allegory and outside according to history. This book therefore contains within itself the Old and New Testaments, because spiritual understanding in the Old Testament is nothing other than the New Testament.

### (Verse 2)

And I saw a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice: “Who is worthy to open the book and to loose its seals?”

The strong angel signifies the Fathers of the Old Testament, who proclaimed with a loud voice because they foretold that Christ would come for the redemption of the human race. The angel’s question signifies the desire of the saints. For the saints desired to see Christ in the flesh and to hear his words, since they knew that all the mysteries of the Old Testament would be revealed by him, as he himself said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10:24).

### (Verse 3)

And no one was found worthy, neither in heaven nor on earth nor beneath the earth, to open the book and to loose its seals.

For no angel inhabiting heaven, no righteous person dwelling on earth, and no one among those who had already paid the debt of death ever appeared in the world who could redeem the human race from the power of the devil. This redemption is the opening of the Old Testament.

### (Verse 4)

And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it.

Here John represents those whom we have just mentioned, namely, the Fathers of the Old Testament. The saints wept greatly because there was no one who could reveal to them the mysteries of Scripture hidden from them, and no one who could rescue the fallen human race from the power of the devil.

But we must ask why he says that this book could be seen by no one, when above he says that he saw it in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne. The ancient Fathers, whose type John represents here, saw the book of the Old Testament, but did not see it; [Note: [Col. 0808D] Thus the manuscripts; the edition, however, reads, “the book of the Old Testament, and they did not see it according to spiritual understanding.”] they saw it according to the letter but did not see it according to spiritual [Col. 0808C] understanding.

### (Verse 5)

And one of the elders said to me: “Do not weep. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and loose its seven seals.”

It seems to me that the elder has the same significance as John and as the strong angel, for he signifies the Fathers of the Old Testament. The strong angel asks who is worthy to open the book; John weeps because no one is worthy to open the book; but the elder says that the book is to be opened by the Lion, that is, by Christ.

Through the strong angel, therefore, those are signified who, desiring Christ’s coming, asked at what time he would come. John signifies those who wept because his coming was delayed for so long. The elder signifies the prophets, who declared how and at what time he would come.

The Lion of the tribe of Judah signifies Christ, who arose from the tribe of Judah and from the offspring of David. He is called a lion because of his strength, since he conquered the devil and rescued his elect from the devil’s power. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, therefore conquered the devil in order to open the book and its seven seals, because the book could not be opened unless the devil were first conquered; that victory was the opening of the Old Testament. [Col. 0809A] How he opened the seven seals we shall explain below.

### (Verse 6)

And I saw, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.

The throne, the four living creatures, and the elders signify one Church with all its orders. The Lamb was seen not as slain but as though slain, because he tasted death only in passing and, rising shortly afterward, no longer dies; death shall have no more dominion over him (Rom. 6:9). He was seen to have seven horns and seven eyes.

What the seven eyes are he explains when he adds: “Which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.” Horns often signify kingdoms. It seems to me, therefore, that the horns have one meaning and the eyes another. Through the seven horns all the elect are signified, who are called the kingdom of God; their entire multitude we divided above into seven parts.

To the first horn belong the elect who lived before the flood; to the second, those who lived after the flood and before the Law; to the third, those who lived under the Law; to the fourth, the prophets; to the fifth, those of the Jews who believed in Christ; to the sixth, the gentile people; and to the seventh, those who will be born at the end of the world and will fight against the Antichrist.

### (Verse 7)

And he came and took the book from the right hand of the one seated upon the throne.

Above we said that Christ was signified by the one seated upon the throne. But because he himself said, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me, and whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9 and following), here the one seated upon the throne signifies the Father; the Father’s right hand is the Son; and the Lamb signifies the human being whom Christ assumed.

The Lamb therefore took the book from the right hand of the one seated upon the throne, because Christ as man received from his divinity the power to disclose the mysteries of the divine Scriptures.

### (Verse 8)

And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.

We must ask how the book could have been opened before the seals were loosed. This must be understood spiritually. The prophets sometimes foretold Christ’s coming, passion, and resurrection through certain figures, and sometimes in clear words. The patriarchs also prefigured all these things in their actions.

When Christ was born from the Virgin, when he suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, he opened the book of the Old Testament, because he fulfilled in deed the things signified there. Afterwards he opened to the teachers of the Church, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, those things that had been obscure in the Old Testament and in the New. This opening is the loosing of the seals.

The statement that the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb pertains to those same teachers of the Church. Whenever they recall the Lord’s birth, passion, and resurrection, and remember in whatever ways these things were prefigured by the holy Fathers and foretold by the prophets; whenever they do not cease investigating the things placed obscurely in the Gospel—the sealed book is opened to them.

They fall before the Lamb when, by meditating on the divine Scriptures and considering God’s immense clemency, they humble themselves in the presence of their Creator. The more they abase themselves through humility, the more they burn with love for him, because humility practiced in God’s presence nourishes the love of God.

The harps that the living creatures and elders are said to have held signify the mortification of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, avarice, and so forth” (Col. 3:5).

The golden bowls signify the hearts of the saints, filled with spiritual wisdom; they are said to have been full of incense. He himself explains what the incense is when he adds: “Which are the prayers of the saints.” And so that this incense may rise to God, the Psalmist prays, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.”

### (Verse 9)

And they sang a new song, saying:

A new people sings a new song; the new song is the song of the Gospel.

“You are worthy, Lord God, to receive the book and to open its seals” (Ps. 140:2).

This refers to his humanity, for according to his divinity he could receive nothing, since he has always possessed all things. Why he was worthy to receive the book and to loose its seals, he makes clear by adding:

“For you were slain, and you redeemed us for God by your blood, from every tribe and people and nation.”

Here he shows that the Church was gathered from all nations, for there were certain heretics who denied this.

### (Verse 10)

“And you made us a kingdom and priests for our God, and they shall reign upon the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0809D] The edition reads, “and we shall reign upon the earth. There are certain people who consider themselves and others …”; the manuscripts, however, all agree in supplying the entire [Col. 0810D] lacuna.]

If the saints of God are the kingdom of God, how are they said to reign upon the earth, that is, over the holy Church? The saints of God are therefore the kingdom of God because God reigns in them. They are also kings because they know how to govern themselves and others very well. They are likewise called priests because, kindled daily by the fire of charity, they are accustomed to offer themselves to God through compunction of heart and tears, as the Psalmist says: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19).

Or they are called priests of God because they are members of the High Priest, of whom the Psalmist says: “You are a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

### (Verses 11–12)

And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne and the elders and the four living creatures; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice:

“Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing.”

The throne, the four living creatures, and the elders signify the whole Church together with its teachers. The angels who appeared to surround the throne—that is, the Church—are the angels whom God has appointed for the protection of the Church, as the Apostle Paul says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

The immense number signifies an innumerable multitude. They are said to bless the Lamb with a loud voice because, whatever duties angels are appointed to fulfill, they never cease from praising God. Just as this book consists entirely in the number seven, and the prophet says that the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit rested upon Christ, so seven blessings are placed here, with which the angels are said continually to praise God.

### (Verse 13)

And I heard every creature that is in heaven and on earth and beneath the earth, and those that are in the sea and those that are in it, all saying to the one seated upon the throne and to the Lamb:

The creature that was in heaven signifies the angels; the creature that was on earth signifies human beings; and the creature beneath the earth signifies those who had already paid the debt of death.

When he says, “And those that are in the sea,” we should understand the waters of the sea; by the sea, the place in which the waters are contained. When he adds, “And those that are in it,” we may understand the fish that dwell in the waters.

But if by every creature that is on earth we may understand all human beings, how do all human beings praise God, when pagans and Jews should rather be called blasphemers of God than his praisers? We also find certain immoral people who are called Christians. Although they may appear to praise God, they do not praise him, because, as Scripture says: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9).

And if by every creature that is on earth we ought to understand all the souls whose bodies rest in the earth, how are those who are tormented in hell to be believed to praise God?

But by every creature that is on earth and beneath the earth we ought to understand only the elect. On earth they do not cease praising God in works and words; and when they are placed with the Lord in heaven, they never cease from his praises.

By the sea we may understand the Church; by the waters of the sea, the multitude of the faithful; and by the fish that dwell in the waters, the teachers of the Church.

The blessing follows, by which the faithful are said continually to bless God: “Blessing, honor, glory, and power to our God for ever and ever.” The elect continually bless God when they join works to words.

### (Verse 14)

And the four living creatures said: “Amen.”

“Amen” is a confirmation of the statement. The four living creatures therefore say “Amen” when the holy preachers continually desire that their hearers may advance more and more in good works.

And the twenty-four elders fell down and worshiped.

Here the twenty-four elders have the same significance as the four living creatures. The elders therefore fall and worship when the holy preachers, the more they see their hearers advance in good works, humble themselves all the more in God’s presence, as Scripture says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3:20).

The opening of the seals follows. This must be understood as pertaining only to the opening of the divine Scriptures. For the things said to have occurred under the opening of the seals also pertain to the opening of the Old and New Testaments. Just as the entire body of the elect consists of seven parts, so there are seven seals corresponding to each part, to reveal the things placed obscurely in the divine Scriptures or to show what the deeds of the holy Fathers signify. [Note: [Col. 0811D] The same editions read, “for the perfection of the divine Scriptures,” and below, “for the perfection of the Old and New Testaments”; the manuscripts in both places read, “for the opening.”]

The opening of the first seal therefore pertains to the things that took place before the flood; the second seal to the patriarchs; the third to those who lived under the Law; the fourth to the prophets. The remaining three openings pertain to the New Testament: the fifth opening to the martyrs; the sixth to the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the gentiles; and the seventh to the coming of Christ. Why the Lord’s coming is placed in the seventh position we shall explain below.

But we must ask why the opening of the Old Testament is represented through the vision of four horsemen. The rider is recognized as irrational in respect of the horse, but rational in respect of the one seated upon it. Similarly, certain legal precepts are shown to be irrational in respect of the letter, but highly rational in respect of allegory.

## CHAPTER VI

### (Verse 1)

And I saw when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals.

The opening of the first seal, as stated above, pertains to the things that took place before the flood. The Lamb opened the first seal when, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he disclosed to the teachers of the Church how the things done before the flood were to be understood spiritually.

To make clearer what the opening of the seals is, let us say a little about the opening of each seal. In Genesis it is written that God had planted a paradise of delight and placed there the man whom he had formed; it is described as planted with various trees (Gen. 2:8).

The paradise therefore signifies the Church; the trees of paradise signify the teachers of the Church. Just as the trees of paradise supplied the first human beings with food from their fruits, so the teachers of the Church do not cease to supply the souls of the faithful established in the Church with the nourishment of divine words.

We spoke above about the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The spring that flowed from the middle of paradise signified the Gospel, which springs up in the midst of the holy Church. From there it divided into four heads, because the teaching of the Gospel is divided into four books and encompasses all the boundaries of the earth.

[Col. 0813A] Adam also prefigured Christ, while Eve prefigured the Church. Just as Eve was made from the side of the sleeping man, so the Church was fashioned from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross, because she was redeemed and cleansed from her stains by his blood.

Two sons were born to Adam, Cain and Abel. Cain signified the Jewish people; Abel signified Christ. Cain offered the Lord gifts from the fruits of the earth, because the Jewish people, who were earthly, offered earthly gifts—that is, firstfruits, tithes, sacrifices, and the other things commanded in the Law. Abel, however, offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat.

The firstborn of the flock are the apostles, whom the Church brought forth first and from whom the Church was born; the fat signifies the faith of the apostles. Abel therefore offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat because Christ offered to God the Father the apostles whom he had chosen from the world, together with their faith.

Moved by envy because the Lord had looked upon Abel and his offerings, Cain killed him. Similarly, when the Jews saw the signs that Christ performed by his own power and that of the Father, they killed him, although according to the flesh he was their brother.

God cursed Cain because he had killed his brother Abel, and he told him that he would be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth. Similarly, the Jews were cursed not only by God but also by themselves when they said of Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). They are wanderers and fugitives upon the earth because, having no permanent dwelling of their own, they wander among all the nations.

It is enough to have said this much about the opening of the first seal.

I heard one of the four living creatures saying: “Come and see.”

The first living creature has the same significance as the second, third, and fourth, for they signify the teachers of the Church. The words “Come and see” summon us to spiritual understanding, as though he were saying: “Come—not with bodily steps, but with the steps of the mind—and understand spiritually what you have read as having happened historically in the first age.”

### (Verse 2)

And behold, a white horse, and the one seated upon it had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering so that he might conquer.

The white horse signifies the righteous who lived before the flood, who are called white because of their innocence. The rider of the horse is the Lord, who eternally presides over his saints.

The bow, which shoots arrows from a distance and wounds, can signify the Lord’s vengeance. By it he condemned the first human beings on account of their guilt of disobedience and punished Cain sevenfold for the crime of fratricide.

Likewise, the crown, as does the white horse, signifies the righteous who lived before the flood. He went out conquering so that he might conquer when he decreed that the entire multitude of the wicked should be destroyed by the waters of the flood.

### (Verses 3–4)

And when he had opened the second seal—

The opening of the second seal pertains to the construction of the ark and to the righteous who lived before the Law. To demonstrate the opening of the second seal, let us say a little about these matters.

[Col. 0814A] In Genesis it is written that God said to Noah: “Make yourself an ark of planed wood; you shall make compartments in the ark and coat it with pitch inside and out, and this is how you shall make it. The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits” (Gen. 6:14–15).

The ark signified the Church; Noah, the builder of the ark, signified Christ, the builder of the Church. The ark is described as having been made from planed wood. The planed wood—which kept out the waters and preserved the life of all the animals within it—signifies the teachers of the Church. By their teaching and writings they prevent the waters of various errors from entering the Church, and by their teaching and example they preserve the life of those who are within the Church. They are said to have been planed, that is, cleansed from every roughness of vice.

The compartments that were commanded to be made in the ark signify the various orders in the Church. One person lives in the married order, another in continence, another in the monastic order, another in the priestly order; while they strive to serve God, they dwell, as it were, in different rooms.

The pitch with which the ark is said to have been coated signifies divine Scripture. The boards from which the ark was made—which we said signified the teachers of the Church—were coated with pitch inside and out, because the teachers of the Church are coated within by the wisdom and teaching of the divine Scriptures, and outwardly by works of virtue.

The length of the ark is described as three hundred cubits, its width as fifty cubits, and its height as thirty cubits. The length of the ark therefore signifies faith, its width charity, and its height hope.
