The length of the ark extends to three hundred cubits because our faith consists in the confession of the Holy Trinity; the number one hundred is a perfect number. Our faith is therefore prefigured in three hundred cubits because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess equal perfection, as it is written: “As is the Father, such is the Son, such is the Holy Spirit” (Athanasian Creed).

Its width, likewise, is extended to fifty cubits, because faith works through love. But it is not inappropriate to understand charity as signified by the fifty cubits of width: seven times seven makes forty-nine, and if you add one to this number, you find fifty. Love of neighbor, therefore, is not inappropriately comprehended in the number seven, because it cannot be perfected without the seven virtues. [Note: The manuscripts read as above; the edition reads *septenis . . . extendit* (“extends … by sevens”); the Roman edition reads *ostendit* (“shows”).] In seven times seven, each believer extends love of neighbor, since whatever kinds of needs or adversities may befall his neighbors, he is prepared to come to their aid in those same ways: for example, when he supplies what is necessary to the hungry, the naked, the stranger, the needy, and the person confined in prison; when he consoles the grieving; when by his words he restrains the angry; when he reconciles the person harboring hatred in his heart and restores those who are at odds to peace; when he summons the person lying in sins to repentance; when he strives to draw with him as many as he can toward eternal life; and, to put it briefly, in whatever ways he wishes another to come to his aid for his salvation, he himself is ready to help others in every way he can. But if to seven times seven you add one, the result is fifty; similarly, if you add love of the one God to love of neighbor, complete and perfect charity is formed in you.

The height of the ark, moreover, was raised to thirty cubits, [Note: The edition reads, “because he possesses a pardonable hope”; the manuscripts read, “a useful hope.”] because the person possesses a useful hope who neither in conduct nor in belief deviates from the faith of the holy Trinity as it was handed down to us by the apostles, nor from the other teachings. For whoever presumes to possess hope of attaining eternal life without right faith undoubtedly deceives himself, because without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6). Thus the height of the ark arose from its great length and width and was completed upward in one cubit, because charity, which arises from faith, extends itself widely in concern for one’s neighbors. It is completed upward in one cubit, however, because all the hope and desire of the faithful tend toward the vision of the one God.

That Noah, at the Lord’s command, brought into the ark males and females from all the living creatures, clean and unclean (Gen. 7:8), signifies that the wicked and the good would be brought into the Church. But seven pairs of the clean animals, and two pairs of the unclean—male and female—entered the ark; for the elect are signified by the clean animals, while the reprobate are signified by the unclean. The clean animals, therefore, are placed in the number seven, because only those are elect who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, are not alienated from the working of the gifts of that same Holy Spirit; but the reprobate are placed in the number two, because they belong to the Church only in body and soul, while in mind they are outside the Church.

In what follows it is also written: “For Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent out a raven, which went out and did not return until the waters over the earth had dried up” (Gen. 8:6). By the raven, an exceedingly black bird, the Jews darkened by unbelief are signified. Noah therefore sent the raven out from the ark, because our Lord Jesus Christ separated the Jewish people from fellowship with the holy Church. After the raven he sent out a dove, which, when it found no place where its foot might rest, returned to him in the ark. A second time he sent the dove out of the ark, and it came to him in the evening, carrying in its mouth a branch of a green olive tree. A third time he sent out the dove, and it did not return to him again. The Holy Spirit is often signified by the dove, because he descended upon the Lord in the form of a dove (Luke 3:22).

But we must ask what the dove’s threefold sending forth and twofold return signify. The three sendings forth signify three periods: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. In this passage Noah signifies God, while the ark signifies the heavenly dwelling place of God. Noah first sent the dove out of the ark, because almighty God gave the grace of the Holy Spirit to the holy men who lived before the Law; and although they did not possess the Law, they fulfilled through the gift of the Holy Spirit the divine commandments that were later given. But the dove found no place where its foot might rest, because not only the other nations but even the Jews themselves, while they were in Egypt, had abandoned the worship of God to such an extent that at the time when Moses was born scarcely anyone could be found in whom the Holy Spirit would deign to dwell; and, in a certain sense, the grace of the Holy Spirit returned to the one from whom it had been sent when it abandoned sinful human beings.

A second time Noah sent the dove out of the ark, because God gave the grace of the Holy Spirit to people who kept the Law with a pure heart. The evening at which the dove returned to Noah signifies the time when Christ was born. Concerning this time the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16), because after the Gospel began to be preached, circumcision and many legal observances were of no benefit. For as long as observance of the Law pleased God, so long did the grace of the Holy Spirit accompany those who kept the Law; and just as the dove returned to Noah in the evening, so the grace of the Holy Spirit, abandoning the unbelieving Jews, returned, in a certain sense, to the one from whom it had been sent. By the branch of the olive tree we may understand or accept the Law; by the green leaves, those who were saved through the Law. Thus the dove carried the olive branch with its green leaves in its mouth when the grace of the Holy Spirit, in a certain sense, offered to God those whom it had saved through the Law.

A third time Noah sent the dove out of the ark, when he gave the grace of the Holy Spirit to those who kept the faith of the Gospel. It did not return to him again, because the faith of the Gospel will remain with the elect until, when the Lord comes for judgment, the elect who are found in this world will be caught up before the Lord into the air, and so will always be with the Lord (1 Thess. 4:16).

To demonstrate more clearly the opening of the second seal, let us say a little about the three patriarchs. It is written in Genesis that God tested Abraham and said to him: “Take your son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall tell you” (Gen. 22:2). Abraham rose during the night, saddled his donkey, and took with him two young men and his son Isaac. Abraham signifies Christ according to his divinity; Isaac, the human being whom Christ assumed; and the donkey signifies the apostles. Abraham therefore rose during the night, because the Son of God deigned to be born from the Virgin Mary while the world lay in the darkness of ignorance. He saddled his donkey when he entrusted his apostles with the commands of the Gospel. [Note: The edition reads *tradidit. Duos vero juvenes secum duxit* (“he delivered [them]. But he took two young men with him”); the manuscripts agree with our text.] The two young men signify the two commandments of charity. He took two young men with him because he delivered the two commandments of charity to his disciples with particular insistence and frequency. He also took his son, because he handed over the human being whom he had assumed to die for the human race, as he himself said in the Gospel to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that has been written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again” (Luke 18:32 ff.).

On the third day, raising his eyes, he saw the place from afar. The three days signify three decades of years and twice three months, the span of time during which Christ is said to have lived in the world. The place signified Jerusalem, in which Christ suffered. But why did he say that he saw the place from afar, when he preached daily in the Temple? Because although the Jews were near in body, through unbelief they had nevertheless withdrawn far from him.

And Abraham said to his servants: “Wait here with the donkey; I and the boy will hurry there, and after we have worshiped, we shall return to you” (Gen. 22:5). Similarly, Christ commanded his disciples to wait until he returned to them after rising again, when he said: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night; but after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” (Matt. 26:32). And when he was being seized, he said to the Jews: “If therefore you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8).

Abraham therefore took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it upon his son Isaac; but he himself carried fire and a sword in his hands. We said above that our sins were signified by wood. Isaac therefore carried the wood, because Christ bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness. By the hands of Abraham the power of our Lord Jesus Christ is understood; for it was in his power to die and, if he wished, not to die, as he himself said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). By the fire his passion is understood, and by the sword his death.

When he came to the place, he built an altar and arranged the wood upon it. And when he had bound his son Isaac, he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood. By the altar the cross is understood. The Son of God therefore built the cross upon which the human being whom he had assumed was to be sacrificed, because this happened with his permission. He arranged the wood upon the altar and placed his bound son Isaac upon the wood; for whatever we wish to suffocate, we place beneath ourselves so that it may be suffocated and perish under our weight. Similarly, our Redeemer, hanging upon the cross, placed the wood—that is, our sins—beneath himself, so that they might be suffocated and destroyed by his weight and power. The bonds of Isaac signified the Lord’s affliction upon the cross. [Col. 0818A] The matters that the angel spoke to Abraham do not pertain to this exposition.

Abraham raised his eyes and saw a ram caught by its horns among the thorns. He took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. The ram signified Christ; by its two horns the two commandments of charity are signified; by the thorns, the Jews. Christ therefore was caught by his horns among the thorns, because, loving the Jews as brothers and knowing that the calling of the Gentiles would be the Jews’ destruction, he did not wish to give the faith of the Gospel to the Gentiles at first. Instead, sending his disciples to preach, he commanded them, saying: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:5). And to the Canaanite woman he said: “I was not sent except to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24); and again: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (ibid., 26).

Abraham, however, pulled the ram away from the thorns and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son, because the Father and the Son himself separated the Son from love of the impious Jews and offered the human being whom he had assumed as a burnt offering for the salvation of the human race.

Concerning this same Isaac it is written that he had two sons, Esau and Jacob. Esau was a hunter and a farmer; Jacob, however, was a simple man who dwelt in tents. Esau signifies the Hebrew people, while Jacob signifies the people of the Gentiles. Isaac, the father of both, held the figure of the Lord, who made both peoples his sons—one through the Law and the other through faith. Esau was a farmer because the Jewish people served God for earthly benefits. For it was not said to them: “If you are poor in spirit, if you are meek, peaceful, and merciful, if you endure persecutions for my name, you will be blessed, and your reward will be abundant in heaven.” Rather, it was said to them: “If you keep my commandments and observe my judgments, I will give you rains in their seasons, and the earth will produce its growth, and the trees will be filled with fruit,” along with the other things that pertain to the pleasures of this age (Lev. 26:3). Esau was also a hunter, because he was accustomed to appease God by the shedding of the blood of rams, goats, and calves. Jacob, however, was a simple man who dwelt in tents, because the elect from among the Gentiles strove to please God by faith alone and by good will. [Note: The manuscripts read as above; the edition reads *ex gentibus soli fide*, etc. (“the elect from the Gentiles by faith alone,” and so forth).] By the tents we may understand either the various Churches into which the one Catholic Church is divided throughout the whole world, or the various orders.

Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting; but Rebekah loved Jacob. Isaac, as we have said, holds in this passage the figure of the Lord; by Rebekah we may understand the foreknowledge of God. Isaac therefore loved Esau because he ate of his hunting, because God loved the Jewish people insofar as he was appeased by their continual offerings. But the mother loved Jacob because God, knowing that the people of the Gentiles would be much better than the Jewish people, loved them much more through the grace of his foreknowledge. While Esau was occupied in hunting, in order to offer his father food from wild animals so that he might be blessed by him, the mother brought Jacob forward to receive the blessing. For while the Jewish people were devoted to legal observances and were slow to come to receive the faith of Christ, the mother—grace—offered the people of the Gentiles to God for the reception of the blessing that was owed to the Jews, because they had eagerly embraced the faith of Christ. How this people of the Gentiles merited this gift of blessing is attested by the works of Jacob, understood symbolically, which he is described as having performed in order to receive the blessing.

Rebekah therefore said to her son Jacob: “Bring me two of the finest young goats, and I will make from them food for your father, such as he likes to eat; and he will bless you before the Lord, before he dies” (Gen. 27:9). He went and brought them and gave them to his mother. She prepared food as she knew his father liked it, clothed him in Esau’s garments, which she had at home, wrapped the skins of the young goats around his hands, and covered his bare neck. She gave him the stew and handed him the bread that she had baked. By the two young goats we may understand the confession of the sins of the Gentile people and repentance. Jacob therefore offered two excellent young goats to his mother, because through confession of sins and repentance, which is the way for those proceeding toward faith, the Gentile people hastened to receive that same faith. They are said to have been excellent because the repentance of a sinner accompanied by renunciation of vices is highly acceptable to God, as our Lord himself says in the Gospel: “There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7). By the one sinner he wished the people of the Gentiles to be understood, and by the ninety-nine righteous persons, the Jews. They are called righteous because, on account of their observance of the Law, they falsely considered themselves righteous; for to these same righteous persons the Lord says: “Woe to you who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts” (Luke 16:15). They are placed in an imperfect number because the Law brought no one to perfection (Heb. 7:19).

By the pleasant foods prepared for Isaac from the two young goats, we must understand the works of repentance. John the Baptist speaks of these foods when he says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3:8). By the very good garments that Esau—that is, the Jews—had left at home, we may understand the excellent commandments of the Law, such as: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6:5), and many others without which no one can be righteous. These are the excellent garments that the Jews had left at home—that is, in the Old Testament—because they were unwilling to observe them. Clothed and adorned with these, the Gentile people went to God the Father with the food of good works. Along with the food he also brought bread. Bread often signifies the word of God, because the person proceeds appropriately to God the Father with the food of good works who does not cease to exhort all others whom he can to perform good works.

But we must also ask why the mother covered Jacob’s hands and bare neck with the skins of young goats. For when the skin is stripped from a young goat, the flesh appears; from it, therefore, pleasant foods can be prepared. Similarly, when vices are stripped away from any sinner, the goodness of nature appears with understanding; [Note: The edition reads *quae si fide Deo coquantur* (“which, if cooked for God by faith”); the manuscripts read *decoquatur* (“is cooked”).] and if this is cooked by faith, pleasant foods are prepared for God from the goodness of nature. By the neck, because pride often appears in the neck, we may understand the elation of the mind; by the hands, works are signified. Each believer therefore wraps his neck in the skins of young goats when, in order to lay aside the elation of his mind and preserve his humility, he does not cease to recall past sins before the eyes of his mind. He wraps his hands when, so that he may not become exalted over his good works, he often brings past sins back before the eyes of his mind.

After Isaac had eaten the food, Jacob also offered him wine. If the works of the active life are signified by food, we may understand by wine, which makes human minds estranged from themselves, the contemplative life, which renders the minds of certain elect persons insensible to love of the world. After Isaac had taken the food and drink, he blessed Jacob, because those receive from God the blessing of the heavenly homeland who strive to please him by good works until the end of their lives.

This same Jacob, when he was fleeing from his brother Esau, came to a certain place. After placing a stone beneath his head, he slept there; and in his sleep he saw a ladder set up on the earth with its top reaching to heaven, and the Lord resting upon the ladder, while the angels of God ascended and descended by it (Gen. 28:12). By the stone Christ is understood; Christ is our foundation, concerning whom the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:12). We place our head upon the stone if we build our wall from good works upon Christ. [Col. 0820D] [Note: The manuscripts read as above; the edition reads *Christus intelligitur: Fundamentum enim aliud*, etc. (“Christ is understood: ‘For no other foundation,’” and so forth).]

The vision of the ladder agrees with this interpretation. The two larger pieces of wood forming the ladder, which stand on either side and are raised from the lower parts to the higher, signify the two commandments of charity. The rungs, however, which are inserted crosswise between those two pieces of wood on either side, signify the other virtues. And just as the two pieces of wood cannot be held together without the rungs, nor the rungs without the two pieces of wood, so charity cannot exist without the other virtues, nor the other virtues without charity. And just as the various rungs, unless they are inserted into the two larger pieces of wood on either side, cannot provide people with a means of ascent, [Note: This entire sentence—“so the other virtues … cannot provide an ascent”—has been restored from the manuscripts.] so the other virtues, unless they arise from love of God and love of neighbor, cannot provide an ascent to those who wish to go to heaven, as the apostle John says: “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). And just as the ladder appeared to touch the earth on one side and heaven on the other, so charity is joined below to one’s neighbors and above to God. Hence the angels of God were shown ascending and descending by it, because the love of God sometimes raises God’s saints, who are signified by the angels, to lofty heights through the grace of contemplation, and sometimes the love and care of their neighbors brings them back down to lower things. He saw the Lord resting upon the ladder because whoever strives to ascend to the Lord by the path of the virtues, after completing the course of his journey, finds the Lord, the author of all good things and the giver of rewards, with whom he will rejoice without end.

When this same Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia of Syria and had come to the Jordan, after transporting everything that belonged to him, he remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and immediately it withered. And he said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has risen.” But he replied: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” And he said to him: “What is your name?” He answered: “Jacob.” Then he said: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 32:26 ff.). By Jacob in this passage every sinner and penitent is signified. That the angel wrestled with Jacob in the figure of the Lord, and he with the angel, signifies what the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). And who are the violent except sinners and penitents? When they see that on account of their crimes they are liable to everlasting death, they knock at the gate of paradise with prayers for so long that the entrance to the heavenly kingdom is opened to them. Jacob therefore wrestles with the Lord when any sinner, fearing the punishments of eternal fire, persists in prayer until divine mercy comes to his aid, as what follows makes clear.

When he saw that he could not overcome him, he touched the sinew of his thigh, and immediately it withered. And because lust arises from the thigh, carnal pleasures can be understood by the sinew of the thigh. The Lord touched the sinner’s thigh-sinew when he extinguished all carnal desires from which sins arise, because it is impossible for us to abstain from sins so long as we lie dissolved in carnal pleasures. The angel therefore—that is, the one who wrestled with him in the person of the Lord—said to him: “Let me go, for dawn has risen” (Gen. 32:26), as if he had said: “Cease now to weep out of fear of eternal fire, because tranquility has now returned, with the vices that had plunged you into the pit of perdition extinguished.”

And because it is not enough to abandon evil unless we strive to do good, what follows is: “Jacob said: I will not let you go unless you bless me”—that is, “I will not cease from prayers unless you enrich me with virtues, so that I, who until now have lived according to the flesh, may henceforth live according to the spirit.” [Note: The same edition reads, “And he said to him: You shall not be called”; the manuscripts agree with us.] And he said to him: “What is your name?” He answered, “Jacob”; and he said to him: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name”—that is: “You shall no longer be called the supplanter of vices, but you shall be called a man who sees God. And you who formerly wept lest you be plunged into hell will now weep because for some period you are kept away from the vision of almighty God,” saying with the Psalmist: “Woe is me, that my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5).

This same Jacob is also said to have limped on one foot after the wrestling that he had with the angel. Whoever limps, however, supports his whole body on the sound foot, while touching the ground lightly with the other. The two feet therefore signify two kinds of nourishment. There is nourishment for the body, and there is nourishment for the soul. The nourishment of the body consists of food, drink, and clothing; the nourishment of the soul consists of the word of God and good works. Thus each believer touches the earth lightly with one foot and rests entirely upon the other, because he uses the things of the world only insofar as they are needed to support the body, as the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8). But he applies himself wholly to the things that pertain to the salvation of the soul, lest he ever stray from the way of God, which is the soul’s salvation. To demonstrate the opening of the second seal, we have said a little of many things; now let us continue the sequence.

It follows: “I heard the second living creature saying: Come and see”—that is, understand spiritually the things you have learned were done by the patriarchs. [Note: The Gill edition reads, “And behold, a red horse. This color approaches the golden,” and so forth. The Roman edition, after the word *rufus* [“red”], added the following: “and the one who sat upon it: it was given to him to take peace from the earth.” We have restored the remainder from the manuscripts.] “And behold, a red horse; and the one who sat upon it was given power to take peace from the earth, so that they might kill one another. And a great sword was given to him.” By the red horse those righteous persons who lived after the Flood and until the Law are signified. And because the color red comes somewhat close to the color gold, as though one were to mix blood-red with gold, the holy men who lived before the Law are not incongruously compared with this color, because they shone with wisdom, which is signified by gold, and were steadfast in persecutions and adversities, which are signified by blood. The rider of this horse is the Lord, who dwells in his saints.

To this rider it was given to take peace from the earth. If peace is good when it comes from God, how was it taken from the earth? But there is a good peace, and there is a bad peace. The sons of God had a bad peace with the sons of men before the Flood, when they took their daughters and gave their own daughters to them (Gen. 6:1); and therefore they were destroyed with them in the waters of the Flood. The Lord also commanded the children of Israel not to make a covenant with the Canaanites, nor to take their daughters, nor to give their own daughters to them (Exod. 23:32). The Psalmist speaks of good and bad peace when he says: “With the elect you will be elect, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (Ps. 18:26). God therefore took this peace from the earth when he separated righteous people from the wicked in mind, though not in body.

“And so that they might kill one another.” Once peace has been taken from them, it follows that one should be killed by another; for often the righteous kill the unjust, and the unjust the righteous. Thus Aram, Abraham’s brother, according to Jewish tradition, died in the fire of the Chaldeans because he refused to worship the fire; Abraham killed four kings with their armies on account of their wickedness; and the sons of Jacob killed all the Shechemites because of the violation of their sister. By the great sword we may understand the waters of the Flood, by which the whole world was destroyed. We may also understand by the great sword the destruction of the five cities, whose inhabitants perished by fire and sulfur, together with their land, which was plunged with them into the abyss.

And when he had opened the third seal. The opening of the third seal pertains to the Law and to those who lived under the Law. To demonstrate, therefore, the opening of the third seal, it seemed appropriate to say a little about Moses and about those things in the Law that appear irrational. It is written in Exodus that, when Moses was born, he was hidden by his parents for three months. Afterward his mother made him a basket of reeds, coated it with bitumen and pitch, placed the child inside it, and set it among the reeds on the bank of the river (Exod. 2:1 ff.). Moses prefigured Christ. The three months during which Moses was hidden signify three periods: one before the Flood, the second after the Flood until Moses, and the third from Moses until the coming of the Lord. [Note: The manuscripts read thus; the edition, on the contrary, reads: “In these three periods, how human beings awaited the coming of Christ . . . it was foretold.”] During these three periods the coming of Christ according to the flesh was hidden from human beings; nevertheless, it was foretold by the perfect.

By the basket of reeds the blessed Virgin Mary is signified. The mother therefore prepared the basket of reeds in which Moses was to be placed, because the wisdom of God, who is the Son of God, chose blessed and glorious Mary, ever-virgin, in whose undefiled womb he would form the human being who was to be united to him by the unity of person. By the bitumen, which cannot be dissolved by water, we may understand the virginity of blessed Mary, which could not be violated by any heat of the flesh. By pitch, which [Note: The edition reads, “is the guardian of bitumen”; the manuscripts read, “is the guardian of wine.”] guards the wine, we may understand humility, the guardian of the other virtues. Concerning this she herself speaks, saying: “Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid; behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48).

By the river the world is signified; by the reeds in which Moses was placed, the Jews are signified, for later he is read to have been found in the papyrus by Pharaoh’s daughter. The reeds have the same signification here as the papyrus. Reeds tend to wound the hands of those who touch them, while books were formerly made from papyrus. By the reeds, therefore, the Jews are signified, because they killed the prophets—that is, the spiritual physicians who wished to heal their wounds. They are also signified by the papyrus, because they boasted of the Scriptures handed down to them by God, which they read but did not keep. [Note: In the edition, “Pharaoh’s daughter . . . prefigured” had been displaced and placed after the words “she took him.”]

Pharaoh’s daughter, that is, the daughter of the devil, prefigured the people from among the Gentiles. Pharaoh’s daughter therefore took Moses up from the papyrus (Exod. 2:5), because the Church from among the Gentiles, receiving the faith of Christ, took that same Christ away from the Jews who refused to believe.

Afterward, while Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro, his kinsman, the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from a bush. He saw that the bush was burning but was not consumed (Exod. 3:2). By the bush that produced flames from itself but was not consumed, we may understand the blessed Virgin Mary, who brought forth the Son of God from her womb without losing her virginity. But because of what follows, I think the bush should be understood as Christ, insofar as he is human. The flame of the bush signified his divinity. The bush therefore burned but was not consumed, because when the Son of God assumed a human being, just as his divinity was not changed into humanity so that he would lose what he was, so neither was his humanity, burning through the divinity, so consumed by the divinity that it lost its humanity. Rather, from the two substances, humanity and divinity, one Christ remained and remains, as it is written: “Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh” (*Athanasian Creed*).

And the Lord spoke to Moses from the midst of the flame of the bush: “Do not come near; remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground. I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. But come, I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may lead the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 3:5 ff.). And shortly afterward: “Moses said to the Lord: Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and lead the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (ibid., 11). And later he speaks to the Lord concerning the children of Israel, saying: “They will not listen to my voice, but will say: The Lord did not appear to you” (Exod. 4:1); and again: “I beg you, Lord, send whomever you are going to send” (ibid., 13).

These words show that Moses obeyed the Lord’s commands unwillingly, in order to lead the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt. But we must ask why so great a man of the Lord carried out the Lord’s command unwillingly. In truth, we must understand his resistance spiritually; for the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them in figure, and they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

By Moses, therefore, the apostles are signified in this passage. At the beginning of their preaching of the Gospel, the apostles, knowing that the election of the Gentiles meant the rejection of the Jews, did not wish to hand over the teaching of the Gospel to the Gentiles so that they might be rescued from the power of the devil. Hence, in the vision of the four-footed animals and reptiles, the Lord rebuked Peter for despising the Gentiles, saying: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10:15). To this interpretation, therefore, pertains what the Lord said to Moses: “Do not come near; remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3:5), as if the Lord had said to one of the great apostles: “Although you raise the dead, although you heal the sick by the shadow of your body, nevertheless do not dare to compare yourself with me in anything, because the great things you do are not from you, but I work through you.”

Sandals protect the feet so that they do not touch the ground. By the ground the Gentiles are signified. “Remove,” he says, “the sandal from your feet”—that is, take hatred and contempt for the Gentiles away from your heart. “For the place on which you stand is holy ground”—that is, the world in which you dwell has been redeemed by my blood.

And in what follows the Lord said to Moses: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” He replied, “A staff.” He said to him, “Throw it on the ground.” When he had thrown it down, it became a serpent, so that Moses fled; and the Lord said to him, “Take it by its tail.” When he had seized it, it became a staff again (Exod. 4:2). By the staff the Jews are signified. Moses held the staff in his hand because the apostles held the Jewish people in their hearts through love, and labored with all their strength [Col. 0825C] to lead them to salvation through the teaching of their preaching. Moses threw the staff from his hand because the apostles, seeing that the Jews in no way wished to believe in Christ, cast their love for them from their hearts. By the serpent, however, the devil is signified. The staff therefore became a serpent because the Jews, having been made worse by the apostles’ preaching—those who had previously been called the people of God—became sons and members of the devil. Moses fled because the apostles, leaving the Jews, passed over to the Gentiles. By the tail, which is the end of the body, the Jews who are to be born at the end of the world are signified. Moses therefore seized the serpent’s tail, and it became a staff, because the holy preachers will in a certain way seize the Jews at the end of the world, when through their teaching they will be converted to the faith of Christ and, from sons of the devil, will be made sons of God.

For that event also has the same meaning: at the Lord’s command Moses put his hand into his bosom, drew it out leprous, put it in again, and drew it out healed. By Moses’ hand the Jews are signified. Moses put his hand into his bosom because the apostles, desiring the salvation of the Jews, did not cease to preach to them the teaching of the faith. Moses drew out his hand and found it leprous because the Jews, made much worse by the apostles’ preaching, fell into the most grievous leprosy of unbelief and blasphemies [Col. 0826A]. Moses put his hand into his bosom again and drew it out healed because, at the end of the world, the holy preachers will receive the Jews into their bosom when they preach to them the faith of Christ and lead them back to the health they had lost.

It is also written in what follows that, when Moses was returning to Egypt, the Lord met him and wanted to kill him. Immediately Zipporah took a very sharp stone, circumcised the flesh of her son’s foreskin, touched his feet, and said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” (Exod. 4:25). And he released him after she had said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” on account of the circumcision. If the Lord wished to kill Moses, why did he not do what he wished, since the Psalmist says: “All that the Lord willed, he did” (Ps. 134:6)? But “will” is often used for “threat”: the Lord therefore threatened Moses with death because he was carrying an uncircumcised son, just as he says to Abraham: “Every soul among you that has not been circumcised shall perish from its people” (Gen. 17:14).

But leaving these matters aside, let us return to the spiritual meaning. Moses here signifies those from the Gentiles who believed. At the beginning of the faith, the apostles and the other preachers, considering the weakness of the Gentiles who were receiving the faith of Christ, did not wish to give them the more severe commands of Christ at first, lest, frightened, they should not dare to approach the acceptance of Christ’s faith. The apostle Paul demonstrates that this was so when he speaks in his letter to those who had believed from the Gentiles, saying: “As to infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able, and indeed you still are not able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:2). The apostles likewise commanded those at Antioch who had believed in Christ, saying: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you except that you abstain from foods sacrificed to idols, from fornication, from what is strangled, and from blood.”

The Lord therefore threatened Moses with death because he hesitated to circumcise the flesh of his son’s foreskin, because the Lord threatened believers from the Gentiles with death on account of their lukewarmness in love when he set before them the commands of his Gospel, where it is written: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few are those who go by it. Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many are those who go by it” [Col. 0826D] (Matt. 7:14); and again: “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:27); along with many other passages concerning the cutting away of vices found in the Gospel and in the sayings of the apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] So the manuscripts; the edition has instead: “and few are those who go by it, or who enter through it. And again,” etc.]

By the stone, however, Christ is understood; the sharpness of the stone signifies the hard commands of the Gospel. Zipporah therefore took a very sharp stone and circumcised the flesh of her son’s foreskin because the Church, seeing that her children could in no way attain perfect salvation unless she uprooted all carnal desires from their bodies, took the more severe commands of the Gospel and cut away from the bodies of her children all nourishment of vices [Col. 0827A]. In the feet the end of the body is signified. Zipporah therefore touched her son’s feet after the circumcision because the one receives saving circumcision who perseveres in the good he has begun all the way to the end of life. After Zipporah had touched her son’s feet, she no longer calls him “son,” but “bridegroom”; and the bridegroom of the Church is Christ. She herself is also called his bride, as John the Baptist says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). She calls him a bridegroom of blood because she has been redeemed by Christ’s blood. Therefore, after the circumcision of vices and the completion of life in good works [Note: [Col. 0827D] All editions have “the completion in works”; all manuscripts have “the completion in works of life.”], the children of the Church are no longer called sons but bridegrooms, because they are joined in heaven through the union of members to him who is called—and is—the bridegroom of the Church on earth.

[Col. 0827B] And since we cannot mention everything that was done through Moses in Egypt, let us set down a few things that were done by the Israelites after their departure from Egypt. The children of Israel, in order to escape Pharaoh and the Egyptians, passed through the middle of the dry sea, and the waters were like a wall for them on their right and on their left (Exod. 14:22). In the same way, the people of the Gentiles, in order to escape the devil and all his satellites, passed through the water of baptism. Those who had previously been sons of the devil were reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, who was signified by the pillar of fire, and became sons of God. Thus the water of the sea saved the children of Israel but killed Pharaoh with all his satellites, because the water of baptism saves the image of God and extinguishes the sins to which it had been enslaved [Note: [Col. 0827D] Gill’s edition has: “saves the image of God the Savior and extinguishes the sins to which it had been enslaved”; Rom. emended it as follows: “bearing the image of God the Savior, it extinguishes the sins to which the people of the Gentiles had been enslaved”; we have followed the agreement of the manuscripts.] [Col. 0827C]; and the devil is extinguished for each person who faithfully renounces him together with all his pomp. The waters that were a wall for them on their right and left signified our faith, which we received in baptism and which is our wall, defending us on both sides from invisible and visible enemies.

After crossing the Red Sea they came to Marah, where they found bitter waters that they could not drink. The Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, and when he put it into the waters, they were turned into sweetness (Exod. 15:23). By the bitter waters the Law of Moses is signified; by the wood we must understand the passion of Christ, since it was completed on the wood of the cross. The people who came out of Egypt therefore found bitter waters [Col. 0827D] because they received the Law, which they could not fulfill. But for the Gentiles coming to the faith of Christ, the bitterness of the Law was turned into sweetness through Christ’s passion and resurrection, because they understood it spiritually, not carnally. The fact also that they found twelve springs at Elim and camped beside the waters (ibid., 27) has the same meaning. By the waters of the twelve springs the teaching of the New Testament is signified, which flowed throughout the world from twelve springs—that is, from the twelve apostles. By the seventy palms the Old Testament is signified, because through the interpretation of the Seventy Interpreters it reached the knowledge of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0828D] All editions have “because the interpretation”; all manuscripts have “because through the interpretation.”].

Leaving these matters aside as well, let us speak briefly about certain things in the Law that appear irrational. The Lord commanded the children of Israel: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. 23:19); and again: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together, and you shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen” (Deut. 22:10–11). What sin does anyone commit if he boils a kid in its mother’s milk? Or what wrongdoing does a farmer commit if he breaks up the earth with the plow using oxen and asses? Or what offense does anyone commit if he wears a garment woven from wool and linen? But all these things are to be understood spiritually [Col. 0828B]. By the kid, each sinner is signified; our mother, however, was our first parents, from whom we were all begotten; the mother’s milk is the vices that proceeded from original sin—for if original sin had not existed, there would be no vice. The Psalmist speaks of this mother’s milk, saying: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. 50:7). A kid is therefore boiled in its mother’s milk when any sinner is burned by the fire of vices until the day of his death. The Lord therefore commanded that a kid not be boiled in its mother’s milk—that is, that a sinner not be permitted to remain in sins until the day of his death, but be recalled to the practice of good works before the day of his death [Col. 0828C], lest he perish.

“You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22:10). By the ox we can understand the apostles and the other preachers; by the ass, the Jewish people. We plow when, according to the tradition of the saints, we exercise ourselves in good works. Therefore, whoever strives to observe simultaneously the teaching of the apostles and the traditions of the Jews plows with an ox and an ass together. The apostle Paul sought to recall the Galatians from this teaching when he said: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you so that you do not obey the truth? For I tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. 3:1). We may also understand by the ox any wise preacher and by the ass a foolish one. It is therefore commanded that one not plow with an ox and an ass together [Col. 0828D]—that is, that a fool not be joined with a wise person in the ministry of preaching.

This command, “You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen” (Deut. 22:11), may be understood according to the preceding interpretation [528]. By wool, which is the clothing of sheep, we may understand the teaching of the apostles; by linen, which grows from the earth, the teaching of the Jews. We put on a garment when we surround ourselves with good works. He uses a garment woven from wool and linen who, together with the traditions of the apostles, wishes also to observe the traditions of the Jews [Col. 0829A].

The Lord also commanded Moses that, if anyone had been cleansed of leprosy, he should come to the priest and offer the priest two sparrows. The priest was to sacrifice one of them, cause its blood to run into living waters, and, dipping the living sparrow into the water in which he had caused the blood of the sacrificed sparrow to run, sprinkle the leper seven times with cedar wood, scarlet wool, and hyssop; then he would be duly cleansed (Lev. 14:3 ff.). By the priest Christ is understood. The two sparrows signify the teachers of the two Testaments. By the living waters the commands of the Gospel are signified, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38). He calls them living waters because they grant eternal life to those who perform them.

By the sacrificed sparrow, as we have said, the teachers of the Jews—namely, priests, scribes, and Pharisees—are signified. The blood that gave life to the sparrow is spiritual understanding, which lay hidden in the observances of the Jews. Just as a sparrow becomes dead without blood, so many Jewish observances, if spiritual understanding were absent, would appear vain. After the sparrow’s blood had appeared and flowed into the living waters, the sparrow died, because after the spiritual understanding that lay hidden in Jewish observances had been manifested through the grace [Col. 0829C] of our Lord Jesus Christ, certain legal observances were of no benefit; and those themselves who, on account of their observance of the Law, rejected the faith of Christ were dead in soul. The sparrow’s blood was therefore mixed with the living waters because all Scripture that pertains to the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0829D] So the manuscripts; the edition has instead: “is filled with spiritual interpretations.”] is filled with examples of the Old Testament understood spiritually.

By the cedar wood the Father is signified; by the hyssop, the Son; by the scarlet wool, which has the brilliance of fire, the Holy Spirit. The one who wished to be duly cleansed was sprinkled with these three, because no one can be cleansed from the leprosy of sins through the water of baptism unless it is done under the invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But if the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are signified by these three, why is a fourth, living sparrow added? We have said that by the living sparrow the preachers of the New Testament are signified. The priest therefore joined the living sparrow to the cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop because our Lord Jesus Christ, in the invocation of his own name and of the Father and the Holy Spirit, joins the ministry of priests, and through their invocation and through the water of baptism washes us, who are signified by the leper, from our sins. The sparrow is commanded to be dipped into the living waters because the one who teaches others ought to be learned in the divine Scriptures [Col. 0830A]; for if a blind man attempts to lead a blind man, both fall into a pit (Matt. 15:14). The leper is commanded to be sprinkled seven times because no one’s purity can be perfect without the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit. For who can be saved without fear of God, without piety, and without the other virtues? But when each person is taught by the preachers of the faith how he ought to live according to the commandments of God, he is sprinkled seven times with living water. After the leper’s cleansing, the living sparrow was allowed to fly away into the open country because, after completing the duty of their preaching, the holy preachers deserve to fly away into the territory of the heavenly homeland.

In another passage it is also written that the Lord commanded Moses that the children of Israel should offer a scapegoat to the priest. The priest was to place his hands upon its head [Col. 0830B], confess over it the sins of the children of Israel, and send it into the wilderness by the hand of a prepared man, so that it might carry the sins of the children of Israel into the wilderness. The man who led the scapegoat into the wilderness was not permitted to enter the camp unless he had first washed his garments (Lev. 16:10 ff.). The priest therefore has the same meaning as the scapegoat; both signify our Lord Jesus Christ. The priest confessed the sins of the children of Israel over the scapegoat because the Son of God placed the sins of the human race upon the man whom he assumed, so that he himself might die for them. By the wilderness, whose habitation all pleasure-seekers dread, the cross is signified, which is exceedingly dreadful to all the guilty. The prepared man therefore led the scapegoat into the wilderness because the Jews who had been foreknown for the perpetration of this crime [Note: [Col. 0829D] All editions have “had been appointed”; all manuscripts have “had been foreknown” [Col. 0830D].] crucified our Lord Jesus Christ. The man who had led the scapegoat into the wilderness was commanded first to wash his garments and then enter the camp, because the Jews who killed Christ could not enter the camp of the Church unless they were first washed by the water of baptism.

And in Deuteronomy Moses commanded the children of Israel, saying: “If you pass through a field and find a bird nesting upon its young, do not seize the bird together with its young, but let the bird fly away into the open country, and keep the young captive, so that you may live for a long time in the land that the Lord your God will give you” (Deut. 22:6). Could the release of a little bird increase anyone’s days? [Note: [Col. 0830D] So the manuscripts; but the edition has: “Could the little bird, once released, increase another’s days?”] [Col. 0830D] No; rather, it is to be understood spiritually.

By the bird every holy soul is signified; by its young, good works are understood. For just as a bird gathers its young beneath its wings in order to cherish and nourish them, so every holy soul conceals its works within the secret places of the heart and continually increases and nourishes them, so that from them it may receive a full reward. We find the bird with its young when we embrace some righteous person with love on account of his good works. We permit the bird to fly away into the open country when we rejoice that the one whom we loved has ascended through death to the heavenly kingdoms [Col. 0831A]; but we keep his young captive if we retain his good works in our mind and advance through imitating them. In this way we acquire for ourselves the length of life that is given only to those established in heavenly blessedness.

We have said a little of many things concerning the opening of the third seal; now let us continue in order.

**(Verse 5.)** “I heard the third living creature saying: Come and see”—that is, understand spiritually [529] the Scripture of the Law [Note: [Col. 0831D] Only the Roman edition has “who read Scripture.”]. “And behold, a black horse, and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand.” By the black horse we may understand the teachers of the Law. The blackness of the horse signifies either the obscurity of the Law that they taught or its harshness. Moses too had a veil over his face because the splendor of his countenance—that is, the spiritual understanding in the Law—could not be seen by dim eyes [Col. 0831B]. The rider of the horse is the Lord; the balance demonstrates the equity of legal judgment, as in this passage: “Life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, foot for foot” (Exod. 21:23), and whatever blemish anyone has inflicted, he must likewise be made to endure.

**(Verse 6.)** “And I heard a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying.” The voice that came forth in the midst of the four living creatures may be understood as the voice of the Church imploring the Lord’s mercy. “Two pounds of wheat for a denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius, and do not harm the wine and the oil.” Great and exceedingly obscure are the things he has brought forth.

By wheat, from which the finest bread is made, we may understand divine Scripture, which is the bread of souls [Col. 0831C]. The two pounds of wheat signify the two Testaments into which divine Scripture is divided. From these two pounds of wheat the holy fathers, who expounded them in many ways, prepared for us a great abundance of food. The denarius signifies the Lord. The two pounds of wheat are therefore joined to the denarius because whatever holy Scripture says pertains to the omnipotence, greatness, goodness, and severity of the one God; for whatever good we do toward our neighbors comes from him, not from us.

By the roughness of barley, the works of the saints are signified. They appear harsh in their performance, but hope makes them sweet, as the Lord says: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30). There are three two-pound measures of barley. Therefore, not inappropriately [Col. 0831D] they signify, through the number six, which is perfect, the works of the saints, because the perfection of the saints increases through good works. The three two-pound measures of barley are therefore joined to the denarius because whatever good the elect perform in this world, and whatever adversity they suffer, they do and suffer for the love of the one almighty God.

Alternatively: by the horse those who were saved through the Law are signified; by its rider, the giver of the Law himself; by the balance, the equity of his judgment. It follows [Col. 0832A] that by the two pounds of wheat and the three two-pound measures of barley we should understand the Old Testament. By the two pounds of wheat, therefore, the two commandments of love are signified, which are especially commended in the Law and the Prophets, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. 22:40). By the three two-pound measures of barley we may also understand the Old Testament, because the Hebrews divide it into three parts: the Prophets, the Law, and the Hagiographa. Nor is it inappropriate that the Old Testament is signified by barley, which has a rough husk, on account, namely, of the harshness of the legal commandments. For just as barley contains within the roughness of its husk a kernel from which bread is made, so beneath the letter of the Old Testament spiritual understanding is contained [Col. 0832B], from which the teachers of the Church prepare the bread of spiritual doctrine for the nourishment of the faithful. The apostle Paul writes that the Law brought no one to perfection—that is, none of those who understand and practice it carnally; but those who understand and practice it spiritually it undoubtedly raises to the summit of perfection (Heb. 7:19).

The three pounds of barley are therefore doubled so that they reach the number six, which is perfect, when the Old Testament is understood first historically and afterward spiritually by the teachers of the Church, and its spiritual understanding is fulfilled through works. By the denarius eternal life is signified, as the Lord teaches in the Gospel (Matt. 20:2). The Church therefore prays to the Lord and says: “Two pounds of wheat for a denarius, and three two-pound measures of barley for a denarius”—that is, deign to grant the denarius of eternal life to those who follow the two commandments of love according to the teaching of the Law and the Prophets, namely, the fathers of the Old Testament; and likewise to those who understand and practice the Old Testament spiritually, namely, the faithful of the Church.

By the harshness of wine we may understand the active life; by the richness of oil, the contemplative life. Therefore, when he says, “Do not harm the wine and the oil,” it is as if he said: Do not harm those who have sought to serve you through the works of the active life or of the contemplative life when you come to judgment.

**(Verse 7.)** It follows: “And when he had opened the fourth seal.” The opening of the fourth seal pertains to the prophets, who foretold Christ’s coming, passion, and resurrection, as well as the calling of the Gentiles, both in plain speech and through various figures. Our Savior therefore opened the fourth seal when he granted the teachers of the Church understanding of the prophets. But it is not necessary for us to say anything about the sayings of the prophets, since those same teachers have expounded them. And because not only what was written by the prophets but also what was done by them has a spiritual meaning, let us say a little about what was done through David, Elijah, and Elisha.

[Col. 0833A] It is written in the Book of Kings that, when David wished to go into battle against the Philistine, he said to Saul: “Your servant was tending his father’s flock, and a lion or a bear came and carried off a ram from the middle of the flock. I pursued them, struck them, and rescued it from their mouth. They rose against me, and I seized them by the jaw, strangled them, and killed them. For your servant also killed both the lion and the bear” (1 Sam. 17:34 ff.).

David signifies Christ. By the lion and the bear the persecutors of the Church are signified: by the lion, emperors and the other rulers of the earth; by the bear, the Jews who persecuted the Church of God; by the ram, the martyrs. The lion and the bear came and carried off the ram from the middle of the flock [Col. 0833B] because persecutors took some of the faithful from the Church and killed them for Christ’s name. And just as David pursued and struck the lion and the bear and rescued the ram from their mouth, so our Redeemer pursued some of the persecutors when he inflicted upon them in the present age the punishment they deserved—on the first Herod, and again on the second and third, and on many others. He struck them when he condemned them to eternal death; he rescued the ram from their mouth because he freed the faithful people from their tearing jaws.

Again, they rose up against David because, in the times of persecution, while some were being punished, others rose up against Christ in order to extinguish his name and worship completely. But David seized them by the jaw and strangled and killed them (1 Sam. 17:35). By the jaw, which is close to the mouth, the blasphemies of the Jews and pagans are signified. Christ seized the jaw of the persecutors, strangled, and killed them when, after emperors believed in Christ, all pagan worship and error were so strangled that none of the persecutors dared open his mouth to blaspheme Christ; [Note: [Col. 0833D] “And all were extinguished when the Gentiles believed in Christ” is restored from the manuscripts.] and all were extinguished when the Gentiles believed in Christ.

That same David, when he went to war against the Philistine, took with him his staff, which he always held in his hands. He chose five very smooth stones from the brook and put them into the bag he carried with him; he took a sling in his hand and went out [Col. 0833D] against the Philistine. By the staff, with which a person is supported, the apostles are signified. They, as it were, supported Christ when they completed the work for which he had come into the world, as the apostle Paul says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. 3:9). By the bag his humanity is signified. By the five stones, the five books of Moses, which he put into the bag, are signified, because he gave the man whom he had assumed knowledge of the five books. By the sling we may understand his tongue.

David’s going out against the Philistine can be understood allegorically in two ways [Col. 0834A]. Our Savior went out against the Philistine when he was led by the Holy Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil and to conquer the devil. David put five stones into his bag but struck down Goliath with one, because our Savior possessed equally the knowledge of the five books, but from one of them—Deuteronomy—he drew three testimonies by which he conquered the devil’s three temptations. And just as David cast the stone with the sling and killed Goliath, so our Lord Jesus Christ brought forth testimonies through the tongue of holy Scripture and overcame the devil.

Alternatively: David went forth to battle against the Philistine; likewise Christ hastened to his passion in order to conquer the devil. David brought down Goliath with a stone; likewise Christ destroyed the devil by his death. [Col. 0834B] Since David did not have a sword in his hand, he took the Philistine’s sword [Note: [Col. 0833D] All editions have: “and cut off his head. [Col. 0834D] This is the sword,” etc.] and killed him with his own sword; he cut off his head. The devil’s sword is death: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24). This is the sword with which he first killed the human being, and then the human race, until it was redeemed by Christ. We encounter this sword when we sin; but Christ did not have this sword because he had committed no sin, and no deceit had been found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22). He was not subject to original sin either [Note: [Col. 0834D] So all the manuscripts; all editions instead have: “he was liable to it, because he had not been born in sin. Christ, therefore,” etc.], because he was not born from the intercourse of man, which cannot be without sin. Christ therefore, who did not owe death as a debt, borrowed death from the devil, who was its author, and through death killed that very prince of death.

By the head of the Philistine the human race is signified here [Col. 0834C]. David cut off the Philistine’s head because Christ separated the multitude of the elect from the devil’s body. He carried it to Jerusalem because he placed the multitude of the elect in the heavenly blessedness that is called Jerusalem.

Concerning Elijah and Elisha, although their deeds are full of spiritual meanings, let us bring forward only those that are mentioned by the Lord in the Gospel. When the Lord came to Nazareth, his fellow citizens said to him: “How many things we have heard were done in Capernaum; do them here in your homeland as well.” He said to them: “Amen, I say to you: There were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut up, and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Sarepta of Sidon. And there were many lepers in Israel in the days of Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:23 ff.).

It is written in the Book of Kings that, when Ahab, king of Israel, began to persecute Elijah, he departed at the Lord’s command into the wilderness and sat beside the Cherith brook. Ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook (1 Kings 17:3 ff.).

Elijah prefigured Christ. By the Cherith brook we must understand the Law. Cherith is interpreted as “falsehood,” not because the Law is false. Wise people customarily set parables before their hearers so that what they wish to say may be understood more clearly, and they introduce speaking beasts and birds. If you attend only to the words of the parables, you will see that they are falsehood; but if you attend to their meaning, you will recognize the truth. Likewise, certain legal commandments, if you attend only to the letter, will appear useless to you; but if you attend to the spiritual understanding, great truth shines forth for you in the letter.

Thus certain legal commandments are falsehood to the Jews because they understand them carnally, but truth to us because we take care to understand them spiritually. By the ravens the priests of the Jews are signified, darkened by the veil over their hearts. By the meat, the perpetual sacrifice that was offered morning and evening is signified. The loaves signify the loaves of the Presence, which were continually placed before the Lord. He drank from the brook because Christ delighted in the observances of the Law.

After many days the brook dried up because, when Christ came in the flesh and preached the Gospel, observance of the Law ceased and from that time was of no benefit, as the Lord says: “The Law and the prophets lasted until John,” and so forth (Matt. 11:13). Again he says to Israel through the prophet: “Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain. Incense is an abomination to me; I will not endure your new moons and sabbaths; your assemblies are wicked” (Isa. 1:13).

And the Lord said to Elijah: “Go to Sarepta of the Sidonians and remain there; for I have commanded a widow there to feed you” (1 Kings 17:9). He arose and went to Sarepta. Elijah went to Sarepta because Christ, abandoning the faithless Jews, passed through his apostles to the Gentiles [Col. 0835C]. Sarepta is interpreted as “burned” or “a scarcity of bread.” The Gentiles, who were the city of the devil and who are signified by Sarepta, had been burned by the fire of vices. Concerning this fire Scripture says: “All of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled for yourselves” (Isa. 50:11). Those are girded with flames who are burned on every side by the fire of vices. They are also called “a scarcity of bread,” because no preacher had ever approached them to provide them with the nourishment of God’s word.

When he came to the gate of the city, a widow appeared, gathering pieces of wood. The woman has the same meaning as the city: she signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles [Col. 0835D]. She was a widow because, as her sins demanded, she had lost God as her husband. He called her and said to her: “Bring me a little water in a vessel, so that I may drink.” He asked for something small in order to reach something greater. By “a little water,” which refreshes the soul of one who thirsts, we may understand the willingness of the hearers; for just as water refreshes the tongue of one who thirsts, so the ready disposition of the hearers refreshes the minds of preachers. As she was going to bring it, he called after her, saying: “Bring me also a morsel of bread in your hand.” What we do not know is, as it were, behind our back. Elijah therefore called after the woman because the holy preachers preached to the Gentiles the God whom they did not know [Col. 0836A]. Hence, by the morsel of bread we may understand the beginnings of faith.

And because those who first strive to confess their sins properly come to faith, it is rightly added:

“Then the woman said to him: ‘As the Lord your God lives, I have no bread, except for as much flour as a handful can contain in the jar, and a little oil in the cruet.’” A cruet was a vessel in which oil was kept. We may understand flour as reason, and oil as works of mercy. Thus the Gentile people, recognizing that they had seriously gone astray, confessed that there was nothing good in them, except only that they seemed to possess a little reason and a little of the works of mercy. For the Gentiles had little reason, since they were rational in part but, for the greatest part, irrational. What is more irrational than saying to wood or stone, “You are my God”? They also had little mercy, because nature itself often impelled them to assist the wretched. By the vessels containing the flour and oil, their hearts are signified.

“Behold, I am gathering two pieces of wood, so that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat and die.” The wood gathered in the city has no usefulness except to be burned in the fire. The pieces of wood, therefore, signify the errors discovered by the Gentiles through the devil’s deception. The woman gathered two pieces of wood because the Gentile people gathered various errors from the teaching of philosophers and poets, for which they would be handed over to everlasting fire. But what does she mean by saying, “That we may eat and die”? We eat in order to preserve life in the body; yet she says that she will eat precisely in order to die, because the teaching of the Gentiles brings death rather than life.

To her Elijah said: “Go, and do as you have said; nevertheless, make me from that little flour a small hearth-cake and bring it to me; afterward you shall make one for yourself and your son.” Bread often signifies faith, while ashes signify repentance, as blessed Job says to the Lord: “Therefore I rebuke myself and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). Bread, then, is covered with ashes when an unbeliever comes to faith and first strives to mourn the evils he has committed, so that he may approach more suitably to receive the faith of Christ, which is given in baptism. Thus Elijah commanded the woman to make bread from the flour and bring it to him, because the holy preachers exhorted the nations to prepare for God, and bring to him, food of faith from the good of reason that they had received from God. For each person coming to baptism brings faith to the preacher when, in response to the priest’s question about how he believes, he makes his confession. Elijah ate the bread that he had commanded the woman to make because the progress of his children is the reward of preachers. Therefore Elijah commanded the woman to prepare bread for him first, and afterward for herself and her son, because the conversion of the sinner is first credited to the preacher. Afterward, the convert prepares bread for himself when, exercising himself in good works, he obtains the inheritance of the heavenly homeland.

But when Elijah said, “The jar of flour shall not fail, and the cruet of oil shall not diminish until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the earth” (1 Kings 17:14), this signifies that faith and good works will not fail from the hearts of the elect until the Lord comes to judgment with all his saints.

Likewise Elisha prefigured Christ, while Naaman signified the people of the Gentiles. There were many lepers in Israel, yet none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian, because when Christ came in the flesh, both Jews and Gentiles were surrounded by the leprosy of their sins. But while the Jews remained in their iniquity, the Gentiles were cleansed from the leprosy of their sins.

Therefore Elisha commanded Naaman, saying: “Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh shall recover, and you shall be cleansed” (2 Kings 5:10). He went and washed seven times in the Jordan, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was cleansed from his leprosy. The water of the Jordan prefigured baptism, because Christ was baptized in it. Naaman was washed in the waters of the Jordan and cleansed from leprosy, because the people of the Gentiles were purged from the leprosy of their sins by the water of holy baptism. His sevenfold washing prefigured the sevenfold Spirit, through whose operation the forgiveness of sins is given in baptism. For just as the body is visibly cleansed by the waters of baptism, so the soul is invisibly cleansed from all sins through the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Gehazi, however, who received the price of healing from Naaman and inherited his leprosy, signifies those who sell their teaching to people. The Lord calls such men in the Gospel not shepherds but hirelings (John 10:12). Elisha, therefore, bestowed healing, while Gehazi accepted the price, because perverse teachers demand the price of healing from those whom divine mercy saves. They consequently become heirs of their leprosy because, remaining in the evils that those people despised by the grace of God, they acquire everlasting condemnation for themselves.

Of the openings of the four seals, which certainly pertain to the Old Testament, we have said a little of much, in order to show that the opening of the seals is nothing other than the manifestation of the spiritual meanings in the Old Testament, which has been made for us through Christ.

### (Verse 8.)

Next: “And behold, a pale horse, and the one seated upon it—his name was Death, and Hades followed him.” These things said of the fourth rider seem to pertain to Antichrist. But since we have interpreted the preceding three riders in a favorable sense, so that they would correspond to the openings of the three seals, the correctness of the order compels us to understand this rider also in a favorable sense, so that he may agree with the opening of the fourth seal, which we have shown to pertain to the prophets.

The pale horse, therefore, signifies the prophets. Pallor occurs in human beings in various ways: sometimes through fear, sometimes through sickness, sometimes when death overtakes the whole body, and people grow pale in many other ways. The prophets, then, who foretold to the sinful people that they would be given over to plunder, the sword, and destruction, are not inappropriately said to have borne a pale color. The rider of this horse is the Lord, who dwelt in his prophets.

But it seems very difficult that he is said to have had the name Death, for he himself is the life of all his elect, as he says: “I am the life” (John 14:6). Yet if we examine the divine Scriptures carefully, we shall find that our Lord Jesus Christ is also called Death. For just as he is the life of all the elect, to whom he daily grants eternal life, so he can also be called the death of the reprobate, whom for their crimes he daily delivers over to everlasting death. For he has authority to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matthew 10:28). He is therefore said to have had the name Death because he brought death upon the sinful people of Israel, as he plainly demonstrates in the song of Deuteronomy when he says:

“Fire has been kindled in my anger,
and it shall burn to the depths of hell;
it shall devour the earth with its produce,
and burn the foundations of the mountains.
I will gather evils upon them,
and exhaust my arrows against them.
They shall be consumed by famine,
and birds shall devour them with the bitterest bite.
I will send upon them the teeth of beasts,
with the fury of those that drag themselves upon the earth,
and of serpents.
Outside, the sword shall lay them waste,
and inside, terror,
and so forth” (Deuteronomy 32:22 and following).

[Note: After the word “last,” the Gem. manuscript adds “and so forth” and does not continue the testimony of this song. The editions extend it to the word “burn”; we have followed the authority of the other manuscripts.]

Hades followed this rider because Hades swallowed up all who despised the threats that the prophets had uttered to the people from the mouth of the Lord. Hence it follows:

“And authority was given to him over the four parts of the earth, to kill with sword, famine, death, and the beasts of the earth.”

By the four parts of the earth, the whole land of Israel is signified.

[Note: All editions read “the whole earth is signified”; but all the manuscripts add τὸ Israel (“Israel”), which the following context shows to be necessary.]

How they were destroyed by sword, famine, death, and the beasts of the earth, the books of the Prophets and Kings clearly demonstrate.

But we must ask why the opening of the four seals pertains to the Old Testament, while that of the three pertains to the New. There are four elements by which we subsist according to the body. Thus the Old Testament is appropriately represented by the number four, because the law of Moses promises the Hebrew people nothing other than what pertains to the four elements. The New Testament, however, is represented by the number three because the faith of the holy Trinity, without which we cannot be saved, is especially commended in it.

### (Verse 9.)

“And when he had opened the fifth seal.” The opening of the fifth, sixth, and seventh seals, as we have already said, pertains to the opening of the New Testament. Although the New Testament is the opening of the Old Testament, many things are nevertheless set forth obscurely in it, and these must be explained.

The Savior opened the fifth, sixth, and seventh seals when he disclosed to the teachers of the Church those things that he himself had spoken in parables and performed figuratively.
