But we do not need to say anything about the interpretation of the New Testament, since it has been expounded wonderfully and in many ways by the holy fathers.

The opening of the fifth seal, therefore, pertains to the martyrs. Christ opened the fifth seal when he made known to the teachers of the Church what he had said through parables and certain figures about the persecution and glorification of the martyrs. He also opened the fifth seal when he bestowed upon them the heavenly glory that he had promised and glorified them before human beings in the world.

“I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus, which they possessed.” Christ is the altar of God. The souls of the saints therefore rest beneath the altar, because just as the limbs are placed beneath the head and cleave to it, so the souls of the saints, established in heavenly glory, are subject to Christ the Savior and are joined to him through the union of the members.

### (Verses 10, 11.)

“And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, holy and true Lord, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?’”

Since Scripture commands us not to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17), and the Lord says in the Gospel, “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5:44), what does it mean that the saints, established in heaven, seek vengeance upon their enemies?

We know that the saints desire the last day, on which they will receive from the Lord both their bodies and the full reward of their labors. The Lord showed his disciples that this day should be desired when, foretelling the signs of the day of judgment, he said: “When you see these things happening, look up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21:28). And in the Lord’s Prayer we continually ask, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10).

But because the resurrection and glorification of the saints will take place on the day of judgment, and the day of judgment will be the condemnation of the wicked, the saints ask vengeance upon their enemies when they ask that the Lord’s day come, because on that day they will be condemned with everlasting condemnation.

Yet a question arises: Why do the saints desire the Lord’s day, when the prophet says, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18)? We know that the day of the Lord is the condemnation of the wicked, as we have already said. Why, then, did the prophet need to say, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord,” when no wicked person is found who desires either his own death or the Lord’s day, since he fears being condemned on it?

And because what the prophet said is true, we must investigate what it signifies. The sins of the wicked are their condemnation. Whoever, therefore, desires to lie with a prostitute desires his own condemnation. Whoever desires to become drunk desires his own condemnation. Whoever desires to steal a horse, an ox, or anything similar desires his own condemnation. Whoever desires to inflict some injury upon his neighbor desires his own condemnation.

Therefore, since the condemnation of the wicked will be the day of judgment, whoever desires to commit those crimes for which he will be condemned on the day of judgment desires the Lord’s day—that is, desires his own condemnation.

[Note: The passage from “Whoever desires to become drunk” through “who desires to steal a horse” has been restored from the manuscripts.]

“And individual white robes were given to them.” The white robes are the glory of the holy souls. The saints of God now possess individual white robes because, while their bodies rest in the earth, they enjoy eternal blessedness in soul alone.

[Note: So the manuscripts; the edition reads instead: “The souls enjoy the blessedness of eternal life in robes.”]

They will then receive double robes when, after the resurrection, their souls together with their bodies possess the glory of the heavenly homeland without end.

“And it was said to them that they should rest for a little while longer, until their fellow servants and their brothers, who were to be killed as they had been, should be completed.” The little while is the time up to the day of judgment. It is called little because, in comparison with the time to come, it is very short.

The saints, therefore, who desire the day of judgment to come, on which they will receive both their bodies and the full reward of their labors, are commanded to await a little while, until the number of their brothers is complete, because the day of judgment will not come until the entire number of the elect has been fulfilled.

But we must ask why only the souls of those killed for Christ’s name are said to have rested beneath God’s altar and to have received individual robes, when the souls of all the elect rest beneath this altar and possess those same robes.

By the souls of the slain, therefore, we must understand not only the martyrs but also all the souls of the just, since they too died to the world in order to live to God, as the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). He also says of himself: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14); and: “All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12); and: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

John himself, the author of this book, is also described as having drunk the Lord’s cup, since he rested without being killed by the sword.

### (Verse 12.)

“And when he had opened the sixth seal.” The opening of the sixth seal pertains, as we have said, to the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. Because Christ spoke many things in parables about the destruction of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles, and also performed certain deeds that signified this, he opened the sixth seal when, through the grace of his inspiration, he disclosed to the teachers of the Church the things he had said and done figuratively. He also opened the sixth seal when he fulfilled in deed what he had foretold.

“There was a great earthquake.” In this passage, the Jews are signified by the earth. There was a great earthquake when this people was devastated by the Romans.

“And the sun became black like sackcloth.” The same Jewish people is signified by the sun. The sun therefore became black like sackcloth because the Jewish people, which on account of its knowledge of the one God and its observance of the Law shone like the sun in the world among the other nations, became hateful to all people because of its iniquities. Penitents wear sackcloth to indicate that they are sinners. The sun therefore took on the blackness of sackcloth because the crimes of the Jews became evident to all the nations.

“And the moon became like blood.” The moon has the same significance as the sun; it signifies the Synagogue. The moon therefore appeared to have the appearance of blood because it became clear to all that the Jews had been destroyed on account of the shedding of the blood of Christ and his saints.

### (Verse 13.)

“And the stars of heaven fell upon the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind.” By the stars, the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees are signified. By the fig tree, however, we can understand the land of the Jews. Its unripe fruits are called useless fruits, which quickly fall when that tree is shaken by the wind.

The fig tree was shaken by the wind and cast off its useless fruits because the land of the Jews was invaded by the Romans and expelled from itself a useless people, hateful to God, so that it might become a dwelling place for the faithful. The stars therefore fell upon the earth like unripe figs because those who shone in the people like stars through their teaching of the Law were overtaken by the same punishment as the rest of the multitude.

### (Verse 14.)

“And the sky receded like a scroll being rolled up.” By the sky, the Old Testament is signified. When a scroll is rolled up, its writing is hidden from the eyes of those looking at it. The scroll was therefore rolled up for the Jews because they did not wish to understand the spiritual meaning in the Old Testament that pointed to Christ.

The sky therefore receded like a rolled-up scroll because the Old Testament abandoned the Jews and passed to the Gentiles.

“And every mountain and island was moved from its place.” Since the land of the Jews is mountainous, by the mountains we may understand those who lived in the cities, and by the islands those who lived in the plains. They were moved from their places because all were either exterminated or led into captivity.

### (Verses 15–17.)

“And the kings of the earth, the princes, the tribunes, the rich, the strong, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains, and they said to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of the One seated upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, because the great day of their wrath has come, and who will be able to stand?’”

By the kings of the earth, the princes, and the tribunes, we can understand those who appeared to rule this people; by the rich and the strong, the slaves and the free, the rest of the multitude.

How they hid themselves in caves and among the rocks of the mountains, Josephus plainly relates when he describes the destruction of Jerusalem (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 6, chapter 11 and following). Their affliction was so great that, when they were consumed by prolonged famine and were afflicted externally by their enemies and much more grievously within by brigands, they hid themselves in wells, sewers, and certain hidden places in the earth, desiring to die so that they might bring their prolonged misery to an end by the shortcut of death.

They knew that they were suffering these things because of their crimes and that after death they would undergo the punishments of hell. They therefore desired that the mountains beneath which they were hiding might crush and conceal them, away from the face of God and from the face of his Christ, whom they knew they had gravely offended.

When the Lord was being led to his passion, he also foretold to the women who were lamenting that they would suffer these things, saying: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children, because behold, days are coming when they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren women who did not bear, and the breasts that did not nurse!’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains: ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills: ‘Cover us.’ For if they do this with the green wood, what will happen with the dry?” (Luke 23:28).

He calls himself green wood, and them dry wood, as though he had said: If they do these things to me, who am wood according to my humanity but green according to my divinity—that is, who am God and man—what will happen to those who are dry wood, that is, who do not possess the greenness of faith? The unstated conclusion is: “They will perish most miserably.”

The fig tree also, which the Lord made dry by cursing it before his passion because he found no fruit upon it (Matthew 21:19), signified those same Jews, whom he condemned by an everlasting curse because he found no fruit of faith in them.

# CHAPTER VII

### (Verse 1.)

“After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth.” Having first spoken of the rejection of the Jews, he now begins to relate how the Church gathered from the Gentiles came into being.

By the four angels, four kingdoms are signified: the Assyrians, the Persians, the Macedonians, and the Romans. But because the power of the four kingdoms had passed to the Romans alone, by the four angels the Romans alone are understood, since they had claimed for themselves the power of the four kingdoms. By the four corners, however, all the nations contained within the four regions of the world are signified, and the Romans had subjected them to themselves.

“Holding the four winds of the earth, so that they would not blow upon the earth, or upon the sea, or upon any tree.” By the winds that raise the clouds, watering the earth and making its surface joyful and fruitful, the peace desired by all mortals is signified. This peace gladdens human minds and grants them the opportunity to attend to their own interests. By the earth and sea, all the nations are represented; by the trees, those who held authority among them.

The four angels therefore held the four winds so that they would not blow upon the earth, because the Romans, who are signified by the four angels, filled the whole earth with slaughter, plunder, and the deaths of human beings, and did not allow the human race to be peaceful and tranquil.

### (Verse 2.)

“And I saw another angel descending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God.” The other angel is Christ, of whom it is written: “And his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isaiah 9:6). He is the sun, of whom it is written: “But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Malachi 4:2).

Christ descended from the rising of the sun, that is, from himself, because he did not assume flesh through the intercourse of a man, but from himself, since he himself created for himself immaculate flesh from the flesh of the Virgin.

The seal of the living God is his divinity. For while he was present in the flesh, he possessed the seal of the living God because he performed works that demonstrated that he was the one Son of God, as he himself says: “The works that I do themselves bear witness about me” (John 10:25).

### (Verse 3.)

“And he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels, to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: ‘Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads.’”

God’s crying out is his acting. For by his coming he caused the Romans to cease their assault upon the human race, and peace came to be throughout the whole world, as the Psalmist says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace” (Psalm 71:7), until the seeds of faith were scattered among all the nations and those who had been foreordained to eternal life were sealed with the seal of faith.

### (Verse 4.)

“And I heard the number of those who were sealed: one hundred forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the sons of Israel.” By the one hundred forty-four thousand, the elect of the present Church are signified. Twelve times twelve makes one hundred forty-four. All who preserve the faith of the twelve apostles and imitate their actions are included in this number.

But we must ask why they are said to have been gathered from every tribe of the sons of Israel, when many more from the Gentiles than from the Jews have believed. Yet if we attend to the interpretations of the names, we shall find all the elect in the names of the twelve tribes.

[Note: The edition reads, “the twelve tribes pertain entirely to the elect”; but the manuscripts have restored the passage for us.]

The names of the twelve tribes pertain to all the elect.

### (Verses 5–8.)

“From the tribe of Judah, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Reuben, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Gad, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Asher, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Naphtali, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Manasseh, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Simeon, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Zebulun, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Joseph, twelve thousand sealed; from the tribe of Benjamin, twelve thousand sealed.”

Judah is placed first, while Benjamin is last. If we wish to examine the interpretations of the names, we find Judah below and Benjamin above.

[Note: So the manuscripts; the edition instead reads: “We find Judah below in repentance, but Benjamin above in the homeland.”]

For whoever desires to ascend to God begins with lesser things, so that by gradually increasing he may arrive at greater ones, as the Psalmist says: “The saints will go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83:8). And because the saints ascend to God by the path of the virtues, he adds: “The God of gods will be seen in Zion” (ibid.).

Judah is interpreted as “confession.” Judah is therefore placed first because whoever desires to return to God after sins must first confess his sins, as the apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16), namely, so that through confession of sins and repentance he may make God, whom he had offended, favorable to him.

And because the person who repents healthfully and mourns the evils he has committed brings joy in heaven and turns God’s eyes of mercy toward himself, as the Lord says, “Turn to me, and I will return to you” (Zechariah 1:3), Reuben is placed second. His name is interpreted as “son of vision,” because through repentance he has become a son of vision who had previously been a son of perdition.

After Reuben comes Gad, which is interpreted as “girded,” because it is necessary that the person who repents of having done evil and asks not to fall back into the same things arm himself against all vices and cut off carnal pleasures from himself. For it cannot happen that one abstains from sins while resting in carnal pleasures.

[Col. 0844B] And because the one who fights manfully against vices already begins to be blessed, Asher is placed in order; his name is interpreted as “blessed.”

[Note: The edition reads, “which is interpreted as blessedness.” It then continues, “Next comes Naphtali, which is interpreted as expansion,” and so forth; the manuscripts, as we have it in the text.]

After Asher comes Naphtali, which is interpreted as “my expansion.” Everyone who knows that he has offended God and wishes divine mercy to come to his aid must himself also show mercy to whomever he can and in whatever way he can, as the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). The mind of the person who, through the love he ought to show his neighbors, is merciful to all whom he can, is expanded in every direction.

After Naphtali comes Manasseh, which is interpreted as “forgotten,” because it is fitting that the person who mourns his sins and gives alms to the poor so that his sins may be forgiven should abandon those sins in such a way that he appears to have completely forgotten them.

And for this reason Simeon follows, which is interpreted as “hearing.” The person who pleads that the evils he has committed may be forgiven is heard by God when he completely abandons all vices.

Next comes Levi, which is interpreted as “added” or “taken up.” The person who has already practiced repentance for the sins he committed, who has fought against vices and conquered them, who has shown mercy toward the needy and by these works has merited that his sins be forgiven, casts the fear of eternal fire from his mind, now secure in pardon, and is wholly taken up into the love of God and the heavenly homeland. He is added to those who are called and truly are the children of God.

Next comes Issachar, which is interpreted as “reward.” But we shall see the interpretation of this name more clearly if we set forth what his mother Leah said when he was born. She said: “God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband” (Genesis 30:18). And therefore she called his name Issachar, that is, “reward.”

Our flesh ought to be our maidservant; our husband is our God. We give our maidservant to our husband when we subject our flesh to the service of God, compelling it to keep watch, fast, and abstain, and subduing its pleasures. Issachar was therefore given by God to Leah as a reward because God grants those who discipline the flesh and extinguish vices the reward of being enriched with virtues.

And for this reason Zebulun is placed after Issachar, which is interpreted as “dwelling of strength.” Who is strong except God? Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord is strong and powerful, the Lord powerful in battle” (Psalm 23:8). And what is the dwelling of strength except the dwelling of God? God dwells in the one in whom faith, patience, chastity, humility, charity, and the other virtues abide.

And because rewards for merits increase through the practice of the virtues, Joseph follows, whose name is interpreted as “increase.”

Benjamin is placed last, indeed also above, and is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” The Son is called the right hand of the Father, and the Gospel says that the saints of God will be placed at God’s right hand. The elect become sons of the right hand when, taken from this life, they are placed in heavenly dwellings, where there is nothing left-handed but everything is right-handed (Matthew 25:33).

Therefore, since we have carried the interpretations of the names of the twelve tribes to the point at which they are placed in heavenly dwellings, it is fitting that we transfer what follows to the glorification of the holy souls.

### (Verses 9, 10.)

“After this I saw a great crowd, which no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne…”

[Note: So the manuscripts and the edition of Gill; but the Roman edition, conversely, adds after the word “Lamb”: “clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands.” After the word “saying,” however, it cuts off “Salvation to our God … and to the Lamb.”]

“And in the presence of the Lamb … And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.’”

By the earlier crowd, which is comprehended by number, the elect who labor in the Church of God in each age are signified, as we have already said. And because “many are called, but few are elect” (Matthew 20:16), and the crowd of the elect is small in comparison with the reprobate, the elect who labor in the Church of God in each age are appropriately signified by the number one hundred forty-four thousand.

But in heavenly blessedness, where in each age they are gathered from every nation, tribe, and language, their multitude becomes so great that it cannot be comprehended by any number.

By the white robes, purity of souls is signified; palms are given as a sign of victory. The holy martyrs do not possess palms alone, although victory is especially attributed to them; all the elect who, while placed in this world, fought bravely against visible and invisible enemies possess them in heavenly blessedness.

The palms are the rewards of the saints’ victory. They are also said to cry out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” The saints of God never cease praising God, yet there is no weariness in praising God, because just as the vision of God is sweet to the saints, so also is the praise of God.

### (Verses 11, 12.)

“And all the angels stood around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell on their faces before the throne and worshiped God, saying: ‘Amen. Blessing and glory and wisdom and thanksgiving, honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever. Amen.’”

Earlier, myriads of myriads of angels are said to praise God around the throne; here, however, they are not comprehended by any number, but all are said to stand around the throne.

By the angels mentioned earlier, who are comprehended by number, we can understand those who are sent into the world for various duties; by those who are mentioned without number, we can understand those who dwell with the Lord in heaven.

Here too seven blessings are enumerated, as above, to show that those who guard the world by their governance bless God in the same way as those who dwell with the Lord in heaven.

### (Verses 13–14)

And one of the elders answered and said to me: “Those who are clothed in white robes—who are they, and from where have they come?” And I said to him: “My lord, you know.”

He asks in order to teach. By the elder, therefore, the teachers [Col. 0846B] of the Church are understood; by John, however, the hearers. For the holy preachers, in whatever ways they can, make known to their hearers the glory of holy souls, so that they may kindle their minds to love of the heavenly homeland.

And he said to me: “These are those who have come out of the great tribulation; and they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

Here he shows that this refers not to the elect who labor in this life, but to those who rest with the Lord in the heavenly life. For the saints do not come into the world from the great tribulation, but in order to endure great tribulations [Note: [Col. 0846D] The Roman edition reads, “as Job says”; but we prefer to retain the author’s lapse with the manuscripts and Gill.], as Solomon says: “Man is born to labor, and the bird to fly” (Job 5:7). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10). And Paul says: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:21). Here, indeed, is the time of tribulation; there, the time of peace.

The saints, therefore, come from the great tribulation because, having been taken away from this life, where the time of tribulation is, they are placed in eternal rest. They have washed their robes because, while placed in this life, they cleansed their souls from every stain of sin: first, indeed, through baptism; afterward through repentance and tears, works of mercy, and the other good works. They are also said to have been made white in the blood of the Lamb because the souls of the elect, previously enveloped in the blackness of sins, received the brightness of purity through the redemption of Christ’s blood.

[Col. 0846D] ### (Verse 15)

Therefore they are before the throne of God, and they serve him day and night in his temple.

For the saints of God stand in the presence of God and continually enjoy the vision of him. He calls the heavenly homeland the temple of God, and the service of God the love of God. For what service is so acceptable to God as to be loved with the whole heart and with all one’s strength? And who loves God so ardently as those who constantly contemplate his face?

And he who sits upon the throne dwells over them. The saints of God are the throne of God, as we said above. Those, therefore, who are designated by the throne of God are the ones over whom God dwells. God dwells over his saints when he illumines, surrounds, and protects them with his light. [Col. 0847A]

### (Verse 16)

They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore.

Since the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6), why are the saints of God here said never to hunger?

But, as we said above, he is speaking not of the elect [Note: [Col. 0847D] The edition reads: “who are placed in this life, who, seeing …”; the lacuna has been supplied from the manuscripts.] who dwell in this life, but of those who rejoice with God in heavenly blessedness. For the righteous who are placed in this life, seeing the injustices of human beings, hunger and thirst for righteousness, desiring all people to be righteous as they themselves are. They also hunger and thirst so that their own righteousness may increase daily; they hunger and thirst for eternal life.

But the souls of the saints shall hunger and thirst no more [Col. 0847B] [Note: [Col. 0847D] The same editions read: “because they have hungered and now have deserved to receive eternal life”; but the manuscripts read as in the text.] because they have now deserved to receive what they hungered for.

And the sun shall not fall upon them, nor any heat. By the sun we may understand the tribulations that the saints endure from human beings; by the heat, the temptations of demons or carnal pleasures. And because the saints, placed in this life, conquered the persecutions of wicked people by enduring them, overcame the temptations of demons, and extinguished carnal desires within themselves, once placed in heavenly blessedness they feel no labor forever.

### (Verse 17)

For the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne, will rule them.

God rules his saints when he orders their wills in such a way that they can desire nothing except what God wills.

And he will lead them to fountains of waters of life. [Col. 0847C] Christ is the fountain of life, who says: “I am life” (John 14:6). For what is without him is dead; but what is in him is life. Christ leads his saints to the fountain of life because he leads them to himself, so that they may be one with him.

By the waters we may likewise understand the saints themselves, for he is also the fountain of waters, since all the holiness of the elect proceeds from him, as he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. For the time of weeping was here; the time of rejoicing will be in that blessedness, as the Lord says: “Blessed are those who now mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

## CHAPTER VIII

### (Verse 1)

And when he had opened the seventh seal.

The opening of the seventh seal pertains to the birth of Christ; but we must ask why it is placed seventh rather than fifth. It is written in Genesis that God made everything that took its origin from heaven and earth in six days, but rested on the seventh; and therefore he called the seventh day the Sabbath, that is, rest (Gen. 2:2).

But what is our rest except Christ? It is therefore not inappropriate that the birth of Christ is placed at the opening of the seventh seal, because he is the rest of all his saints, which is signified by the seventh day. [Col. 0848A]

And because the things that took place at Christ’s birth possess a spiritual meaning, Christ opened the seventh seal when he revealed to the teachers of the Church, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, the things that had taken place symbolically.

There was silence in heaven for about half an hour. By the silence, the peace that came about throughout the whole world under Octavian Augustus when Christ was born is signified. The silence lasted half an hour because the peace that the Church had among the pagans at the beginning of the faith lasted only a short time; for it was interrupted by the emperor Nero, who, after Peter and Paul had been killed, ordered all Christians to be persecuted.

### (Verse 2)

And I saw seven angels standing in the presence of God, and seven trumpets were given to them.

The order of these seven angels follows below. For just as a herald is sent before a king or prince to announce his arrival, so John, because the things signified through the angels were great, wished to mention them before he came to narrate them.

### (Verse 3)

And another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand [Note: [Col. 0848D] The Roman edition had omitted [this], and reads: “and there were given to him … before the Lord”; or, as Gill reads, “before the throne.”], and much incense was given to him, so that he might offer it from the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar that is before the Lord.

This angel signifies Christ. He came because he appeared in the world through the mystery of the Incarnation. The golden altar signifies the Church. He is said to have stood before the altar: Christ lay among unbelievers who considered him merely a human being; but he stood with the faithful who believed that he was true God. He therefore stood before the altar because he manifested to the apostles and to the other believers, from whom the Church then consisted, that he was God. By the censer that he held in his hand, the hearts of the apostles and of the other faithful are signified. It is said to have been golden because the hearts of the disciples, purified by faith and gilded by the wisdom they had learned from Christ, were radiant. He is said to have held the censer in his hand because the hearts of the apostles were in the hand of God, as Solomon says: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever he wishes, he inclines it” (Prov. 21:1).

Was the heart of this Solomon in the hand of God when he worshiped idols? Was the heart of Antiochus or Herod in the hand of God? Were the hearts of kings who persecuted the saints of God in the hand of God? [Col. 0848D] They were in the hand of the devil, who inclined them toward whatever crimes he wished. But the hearts of spiritual kings—that is, of the saints—are in the hand of God; and therefore wherever he wishes, he will incline them.

535* It follows: “And much incense was given to him.” The much incense is the commandments of the Gospel. Incense is placed in a censer so that, after receiving the heat of fire, it may spread the fragrance of its scent all around. Similarly, Christ placed the teaching of the Gospel in the hearts of his disciples, who, kindled by the fire of charity, spread the fragrance of their faith among all nations. Hence it follows: “So that he might offer it from the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar that is in the presence of God.”

There are many kinds of prayer. The faithful pray with words, entreating God that all their sins may be forgiven. They also pray by giving alms, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:42). And it is written elsewhere: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Eccl. 3:33). They also pray by forgiving their neighbors for the wrongs committed against them, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:15). They likewise pray by keeping the commandments of charity, as it is written: “Charity covers all offenses” (Jas. 5:20).

Therefore, the one who keeps the commandments of God prays to God profitably. For it benefits us nothing to implore God’s mercy with words and to provoke it by our deeds. God therefore gave upon the golden altar, from the prayers of the saints, when he placed the faith, teaching, and actions of the apostles and of the other preachers upon the hearts of believers, so that they might have from them instruction and an example to imitate.

### (Verse 4)

Hence it follows: “And the smoke of the incense ascended from the prayers of the saints, from the hand of the angel, in the presence of God.”

By the smoke of the incense are signified not only the prayers of the faithful, but also the fragrance of good works, which continually rises from the Church in the presence of God. This smoke is said to ascend from the hand of the angel because whatever good the faithful do, they do through God’s activity, as he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

### (Verse 5)

And the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and cast it into the earth. [Note: [Col. 0849D] “And there were … and earthquakes” is found in the Roman edition; where the present text has “they were moved,” it reads “earthquakes.”]

And there were flashes of lightning, voices, thunder, and an earthquake.

The fire signifies the Holy Spirit. The angel, therefore—that is, Christ—filled the censer, that is, the hearts of the disciples, from the fire of the altar, that is, from the Holy Spirit, when, after his ascension into heaven, he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven on the tenth day, filled the hearts of the disciples, and gave them knowledge of all languages.

And if the Church is signified by the altar, why is the Holy Spirit said to have been the fire of the altar before he was given, as the same John says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”? [Col. 0849D] The Holy Spirit was the fire of the altar before he was given because the Church already possessed him through the grace of forgiveness.

For before his Passion the Lord promised that he would give the Holy Spirit to his disciples. And when the same John had reported the words of Caiaphas—“It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish”—he added: “Now he did not say this of himself, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation; and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11:50–52).

Were those who were going to believe in Christ, who were scattered throughout all nations and served idols, already children of God? They were already children of God through predestination, because they had already been predestined to eternal life. They were gathered together afterward when, through the faith they received in baptism, they were joined to the body of the Church.

The angel therefore sent into the earth the fire that he had placed in the censer because, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, he poured out through the mouths of the apostles the teaching of faith that he had placed in their hearts into the hearts of the Jews, who through unbelief were earth.

There were flashes of lightning, voices, thunder, and an earthquake. By the flashes of lightning are signified the miracles that were performed through the apostles; by the voices, preaching; and by the thunder, the threat of eternal fire. By the earthquake we may understand the conversion of the Jews. For through the preaching of blessed Peter they were converted to repentance, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles relates: “When they heard these things, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, ‘Men and brothers, what shall we do? Show us’” (Acts 2:37).

And it is written below that at this first preaching of Peter three thousand of them believed, and afterward an innumerable multitude. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to pour this fire—that is, the Holy Spirit—upon us who are earth, so that we may be made spiritual from carnal [Note: [Col. 0849D] The Codex Gemblacensis reads: “may we become, he himself assisting us, who lives [Col. 0850D] and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit through immortal ages of ages, amen.”], through him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CONCERNING THE FOURTH VISION

[Col. 0850C]

By the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have said a little about the opening of the seven seals. Now let us bring forth something about the sound of the trumpets of the seven angels that follows.

The seven angels signify the teachers who were sent by God, and who will be sent until the end, to instruct the people of God. And because, with God inspiring them, the mysteries of the divine Scriptures were made clearer to the teachers of the Church than to others, the order of the argument required that after the opening of the seals—which signifies the opening of the divine Scriptures—the seven angels should be placed, through whom all the teachers of the people of God are signified, those who received the knowledge of the divine Scriptures more abundantly.

And just as we divided the whole body of the elect into seven parts, so the seven angels also appeared to sound with trumpets. Through them all the teachers of the people of God are signified, although they differ somewhat from that order.

For above, through the *poderis* [Note: [Col. 0850D] This is a robe reaching to the ankles; it is absent from the manuscripts.], which is a tunic reaching to the ankles and is placed first among the Lord’s ornaments, and likewise below through the first horn of the Lamb, we said that the righteous who lived before the Flood were signified. Through the golden belt on the body of Christ, and through the second horn, the patriarchs and the others who lived before the Law were signified. Here, however, through the first angel, the teachers who lived from the beginning of the world until the Law are signified; through the second, the teachers of the Law.

### (Verse 6)

And the seven angels prepared themselves to sound the trumpets.

The sound of the trumpet signifies preaching. For the holy preachers are always ready for this: through the teaching of their preaching, to win for God as many people as they can.

### (Verse 7)

And the first angel sounded his trumpet.

As we have already said, the first angel signifies the preachers who lived before the Law. The first angel therefore sounded his trumpet because the holy men who lived before the Law, although they had no law except the natural law, should be believed to have urged everyone they could [Note: [Col. 0851D] The edition reads “they attempted to persuade”; the manuscripts read “they should be believed to have urged them.”] to fear and love God their creator, and not to do to another what one would not wish to suffer oneself.

And there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was cast upon the earth.

The things that are said to have occurred when the seven angels sounded their trumpets should, as it seems to me, be understood in a favorable sense, just as, conversely, the outpouring of the seven angels’ bowls that follows should be understood in an unfavorable sense.

By the hail, therefore, which strikes, the words of holy men are signified—words that struck the hearts of wicked people by reproving them. It is described as having fire and blood mixed with it. By the fire the Holy Spirit is signified, who, dwelling in his saints, became the minister of their words. By the blood Christ is understood, who was often foretold by the Fathers and prefigured by their actions. The earth demonstrates the people of the world subjected to sin.

[Col. 0851C] And a third of the earth was burned … and all the green grass was burned up.

By the third part of the earth we must understand those who were saved through the teaching and examples of good people, who burned up and destroyed whatever was wicked within themselves by the fire of the fear and love of God.

The trees signify those who held authority among them. Many of these were saved through the teaching and examples of good people (Gen. 20:17), such as Abimelech through Abraham, and Job’s three friends through Job (Job 42:8).

By the green grass, which is said to have been entirely burned, those are signified who were earlier signified by the third part of the earth and of the trees that was burned—that is, the elect who existed at that time. For green grass is difficult to ignite, whereas dry grass is easily consumed. By green grass, therefore, the elect are signified; by dry grass, the reprobate.

Concerning this dry grass the prophet says: [Note: [Col. 0852D] The manuscripts read this way; the edition, however, reads: “the people is grass.” By the green grass, therefore, faithful men are signified.] “Truly the people is grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:7).

By the green grass, therefore, those who were green in faith are signified, who burned up by the fire of charity everything in themselves that was reprobate.

### (Verse 8)

And the second angel sounded his trumpet.

The second angel signifies Moses and the other teachers of the Law.

And behold, a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea.

By the great mountain the Law of Moses is signified, which is likened to a mountain because of the weight of its burden [Col. 0852A], and is said to burn with fire because of the spiritual understanding that shone forth in the Law. The Hebrew people themselves are signified by the sea because of the magnitude of their crimes.

### (Verse 9)

And a third of the sea became blood, and a third of the creatures that had souls in the sea died, and a third of the ships perished.

Every remission under the Law took place through the shedding and sprinkling of blood. Hence Moses also sprinkled the people with blood, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you” (Heb. 9:20). Moses likewise sprinkled Aaron and his sons with blood so that they might be made clean to offer sacrifices to God; nor could there be remission without the shedding of blood (Exod. 24:8).

By the third part of the sea, therefore, the elect who existed at that time are signified. By the blood in this passage we may understand the remission of sins. The third part of the sea was therefore changed into blood because the elect who existed at that time deserved to be cleansed from their sins through observance of the Law.

The third part of the creatures that had souls in the sea, which is said to have died, has the same meaning as the third part of the sea that was changed into blood. By the sea, as we have already said, the multitude of sins is signified. Fish, when they are removed from the waters, lose their souls.

The elect, therefore, as long as they are in the waters of their vices, have marine souls—that is, souls enveloped in the darkness of sins. But when they are drawn out of the waters of vices, whether through baptism or repentance, they seem to lose their former souls when they are made good from evil, and they die to the devil in order to live to God.

The third part of the fish therefore gave up their souls because the elect who existed at that time died to sin through observance of the Law and began to live to God.

By the ships, which have the waters beneath them and rise above them, the rulers of that people are signified. The third part that perished signifies those among them who were righteous, according to the meaning we have stated: they perished and died to sin, and lived to God.

### (Verse 10)

And the third angel sounded his trumpet, and a burning star fell from heaven like a torch.

The star has the same significance as the angel, for it signifies the prophets. But we must ask how it is said to have fallen from heaven to earth.

The saints ascend in a certain way into heaven when divine love raises them to contemplate heavenly things. They fall to earth when love of their neighbors draws them back below, so that through their preaching they may lead sinners back to the way of truth. The torch is kindled so that it may dispel the darkness of night.

The words of the prophets were therefore a torch because they drove the darkness of sins away from human minds. We may also understand the Holy Spirit through the fire of the torch. Inflamed by him, the prophets both corrected many people from their iniquities and foretold what was to come.

And it fell upon a third of the rivers and upon the fountains of waters.

By the rivers and fountains, the twelve tribes with their families are signified; by the third part, those among them who had been appointed to eternal life are represented. The star therefore fell upon a third of the rivers because those who had been predestined to eternal life received the teaching of the prophets and planted it in their hearts.

### (Verse 11)

And the name of the star is called Wormwood.

Wormwood is extremely bitter. By Wormwood, therefore, the threats of the prophets are signified, which they laid before the sinful people, foretelling them that unless they repented, they would be given over as spoil and captives to their enemies; and that if they did not repent even then, they would be condemned to everlasting death.

And a third of the waters became wormwood.

Those whom we said above were signified by the third part of the waters—that is, the elect—took on the bitterness of repentance through the threats of the prophets.

And many people died from the waters because they had become bitter.

For the bitterness of repentance brought death to those who deserved to be saved. They died according to what they had been when evil, and they lived according to what they had begun to be when good.

### (Verse 12)

And the fourth angel sounded his trumpet.

The fourth angel signifies Christ and his apostles.

And a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon and a third of the stars, so that a third of them was darkened; a third of the day did not shine, and likewise a third of the night.

The sun, moon, and stars pertain to one matter. For by the sun the Jewish people are signified; by the moon, the Synagogue; and by the stars, the chief priests and the Pharisees.

But if we wish to apply the darkening of the sun, moon, and stars to those who refused to believe in Christ, the preceding order will be disturbed. Above we demonstrated that the burning of a third of the earth, which is said to have occurred under the sound of the first angel’s trumpet; the changing of a third of the sea into blood, which appeared to have occurred under the sound of the second angel’s trumpet; and likewise the changing of a third of the waters into wormwood, which is read as having occurred under the sound of the third angel’s trumpet, should be understood in a favorable sense and therefore as pertaining to the elect.

It follows, then, that we should interpret the striking of the sun, moon, and stars in a favorable sense. Through the third part of the sun, therefore, which was struck—that is, darkened—those from the Jewish people who believed in Christ are signified. For they were darkened in the eyes of the impious Jews, but they shone in the presence of God.

Similarly, through the darkened third part of the moon and stars, those who believed in Christ from among the rulers of the synagogues, the priests, and the Pharisees are signified. For they too, on account of the true light—that is, Christ—which they had received, were darkened to those whose mind’s eyes the devil had blinded so that they would not believe in Christ. For the brightness of the sun blinds sore eyes more than it illuminates them.

We may also understand by the third part of the day the apostles, and by the third part of the night those who believed from the Gentiles. The apostles were darkened to those who not only rejected their teaching but also persecuted them everywhere.

Concerning this darkening of theirs the Lord says: “You will be handed over by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death. [Note: [Col. 0853D] “And you will be hated by all people for my name’s sake” is restored from all the manuscripts.] And you will be hated by all people for my name’s sake” (Luke 21:16–17).

### (Verse 13)

And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the voices of the three angels who were about to sound their trumpets.”

By heaven in this passage the Church is signified; by the eagle, Christ and his apostles are demonstrated. The eagle therefore flew through the midst of heaven and cried out because Christ preached the Gospel first through Judea, while his apostles preached it throughout all nations. They also foretold in many ways the persecutions that the Church would suffer from its adversaries.

Therefore he gives three woes. The first pertains to the heretics, who attempted in many ways to attack the Church of God. The second pertains to the pagans, who persecuted that same Church of God and killed a very great multitude of the faithful. The third pertains to the Antichrist, who will wage war against the people of God at the end of the world.

We must not suppose that the three woes pertain to the elect, who endured various calamities from the impious; rather, they pertain to those same impious people who inflicted those calamities. Hence he says: “Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth.” For the impious, who seek nothing except earth, are rightly called inhabitants of the earth. But the righteous, who always desire heavenly things, are rightly called inhabitants of heaven, as the apostle Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

## CHAPTER IX

### (Verse 1)

And the fifth angel sounded his trumpet.

The fifth angel signifies the defenders of the orthodox faith of the Church. They sounded the trumpet when they labored in every way for the defense of the faith.

And I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth.

By the star the founders of heresies are signified, because just as stars shine in heaven, so they too shone in the Church through doctrine and wisdom before they fell. It fell from heaven to earth because, cut off from the Church, they were joined to the body of the reprobate, who are signified by the earth.

But we must ask why he first placed the heretics, who are signified by the star and the locusts, and afterward the persecutors, who are signified by the armored horsemen, about whom he will speak below under the sound of the sixth angel’s trumpet.

This is because, before the Roman emperors began to persecute the Church of God, heretics had already arisen, such as Nicolaus, who existed in the time of the apostles, and many others.

And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him (Acts 6:5).

By the key, the free will of the heretics, which they possessed for evil, is signified; by the abyss, their hearts; and by the pit, their mouths. The key of the pit of the abyss was therefore given to the heretics because God permitted heresies to exist, as the apostle Paul says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

### (Verse 2)

And he opened the pit of the abyss.

The star that fell from heaven opened the pit of the abyss because the heretics opened their mouths to bring forth the evils that lay hidden in their hearts.

And smoke rose from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace.

By the smoke the teaching of the heretics is signified. For just as smoke, driven by the wind, quickly vanishes, so the teaching of the heretics vanished like smoke through the teaching of the holy Fathers. By the furnace, the hearts of the impious are often signified, as the prophet says: “Their hearts are like a burning oven” (Hos. 7:4).

And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.

By the sun Christ is often understood; but in this passage his members, that is, the holy preachers, are signified. By the air, the faithful people subject to them are signified.

But how were the elect darkened, whom heretical depravity was unable to deceive? They were darkened to those whom the heretics were able to deceive, who are signified below by the locusts. Yet their brightness could not be hidden from the other faithful, just as a lamp cannot be hidden under a bushel.

### (Verse 3)

And locusts came out of the smoke upon the earth.

From the smoke—that is, from the teaching of those who were called founders of heresies—a great multitude of heretics was generated. They came out upon the earth because, separated from the fellowship of the elect, they were joined to those who are called earth—that is, to unbelievers. [Col. 0855C]

And power was given to them, like the power that the scorpions of the earth have.

God is often said to have given what he permits. For God permits the impious to act wickedly so that from their evils he may produce good.

By the scorpions we may understand demons. For just as scorpions, when they are not noticed, infect and destroy human bodies with their poison, so demons inject the poisons of evil persuasions into unwary people. By drawing them into the commission of crimes, they kill their souls after infecting them with the poison of their own wickedness.

The power of the locusts—that is, of the heretics—is therefore like the power of the scorpions—that is, of the demons. For just as demons are always intent on deceiving everyone they can, so the heretics labored with all their strength to plunge everyone they could into the pit of their destruction. [Col. 0855D]

### (Verse 4)

And they were commanded not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree.

What the grass of the earth signifies, the green thing also signifies. For just as above (see ch. 8), under the sound of the first angel’s trumpet, all the green grass that is said to have been burned signified the elect who existed in the earliest times, so here too, by the grass of the earth and every green thing, the faithful people are signified. By the trees, however, the teachers of the Church are signified.

The heretics were therefore forbidden to harm the grass of the earth, or any green thing, or any tree, because God did not permit them to deceive those who possessed the greenness of faith—that is, those who fulfilled in their works the faith that they professed—nor the holy preachers who were not thorns or thistles, from which neither grapes nor figs are gathered, but rather trees bearing the fruits of good works, from which the faithful people were refreshed.

Hence it follows: “Except those people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.”

What is the seal of God except charity, about which the same John speaks, saying: “God is charity” (1 John 4:8)? We may also understand by the foreheads, which very often display the qualities of minds, the hearts of the reprobate.

Those, therefore, were easily deceived by the heretics who did not have the seal of the living God—that is, charity—in their hearts.

[Col. 0856B] ### (Verse 5)

And they were commanded not to kill them.

When he says that they were commanded not to kill them, it seems to me that this pertains to the demons. For the wickedness of demons is so great that, if God had permitted it, as soon as a person committed a mortal crime they would kill him. But God waits for impious people so that at some time they may return to him through repentance and be saved, or so that the righteous may be tested through them.

For the Psalmist also, when speaking about the impious, prayed, saying: “Do not kill them, lest my people forget” (Ps. 58:11). And it is written in the Book of Judges that God left the Canaanites and Philistines, so that he might test Israel through them and so that they might learn how to fight against their enemies (Judg. 3:1–2).

God therefore commanded—that is, he did not permit—the destruction either of all heretics or of all the impious, so that the righteous might have people by whom they could be tested, like gold that is tested by fire.

Hence it follows:

“But that they should be tormented for five months.” By the five months we may understand the whole period of the present life, which consists of five ages. The first age is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, and the fifth old age—although blessed Gregory, in order to correspond the ages of human beings with the six ages of the world, divided old age into two parts.[^c0080-1] Thus, during the five months—that is, throughout the whole period of the present life—not only heretics but all the impious are tormented. For whether they wish it or not, whenever they recall death and the punishment that follows death, they are tormented inwardly, although they may appear to rejoice in the prosperity of the world, because they know that they will be eternally tormented for their crimes. Conversely, although the righteous are afflicted outwardly in various ways, inwardly they rejoice in the hope of heavenly glory, which they believe they will attain.

We may also understand by the five months the whole period of this world. The first month is from the creation of the world to the Flood; the second, from the Flood to Moses; the third, from Moses to David; the fourth, from David to Christ; and the fifth, from Christ to the consummation of the age. During these five months, therefore, all the fabricators of errors are tormented, either in the manner we explained above, or because they see their false inventions overcome by the truth.

“And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a human being.” We said above that demons are signified by scorpions. For just as a scorpion wounds the body with its sting in order to introduce poison through the wound and thereby kill the person, so the devil wounds the mind with anger, or pride, or lust, or some carnal delight, in order through this to pour in the poison of his malice and kill the soul.[^c0080-2] The torment of the locusts is therefore said to be like the torment of a scorpion, because heretics, imitating their father the devil, wounded the minds of the ignorant through smooth and carefully contrived words, and, pouring in the poison of their error, killed their souls. We may indeed understand the killing of souls by “torment.”

### (Verse 6)

“And in those days people will seek death and will not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them.” This statement concerns the elect. “In those days”—that is, in the days when the grace of the Gospel shines throughout the whole world—people will seek death. Paul sought death by persecuting the Church of God, but he did not find it, because Christ, who is an impenetrable wall, placed himself before him and violently brought him back from the death he sought to the life that is Christ himself.

There were also many others who sought death, either by persecuting the Church of God or by committing other evils; but death fled from them, because through the preaching of the saints they were recalled to life. We too have seen some who sought death and did not find it; they desired to die, and death fled from them. For we know that there were some who, loving the world more than was proper, had labored for a long time and in many ways to become rich, desiring to live luxuriously and fulfill the desires of their flesh,[^c0080-4] but when they could not attain what they desired, they rejected the false promises of the world and turned toward acquiring heavenly riches. By persisting in good works for their attainment, they deserved, as we believe, to reach them.

We have likewise seen some leave monasteries, pass over into the world, and place themselves in the service of powerful men, so that through their support they might obtain the earthly riches and possessions that they could not have by themselves. But when they could not attain what they desired, they abandoned the world, returned to their monasteries, and ended their lives in good works. These, then, sought death and did not find it; they desired to die, and death fled from them.

Concerning such people the Lord speaks to the prophet under the figure of Jerusalem, saying: “Behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns, and I will enclose it with a wall, and she will not find her paths. She will pursue her lovers and will not overtake them; she will seek them and will not find them” (Hos. 2:6). Our lovers are carnal desires. We pursue our lovers when we labor to become possessors of riches, so that we may have the means to satisfy our carnal desires. We pursue our lovers but do not overtake them when, because God’s mercy intervenes, we cannot attain what we uselessly desire.

### (Verse 7)

“And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle.” Horses often signify holy preachers, as the prophet Habakkuk says in his song: “You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters” (Hab. 3:15). God made a way in the sea for his horses, in the mud of many waters, when at the beginning of the faith he granted peace to the world, so that his apostles could travel through all the nations—signified by the sea and the mud—and scatter the seeds of faith.

God’s horses were prepared for battle when the holy preachers were armed with both word and virtues for the purpose of rescuing the human race from the power of the devil. The locusts, however, are said to have been like horses prepared for battle because, just as the holy preachers labored with all their strength to rescue as many people as possible from the devil’s snares, so the heretics were always armed for the purpose of ensnaring as many as they could and drawing them into the abyss of their damnation.

“And upon their heads were what appeared to be crowns like gold.” Gold often signifies wisdom, as we have already said above; through the crowns of the locusts, worldly wisdom is shown. The crowns of the locusts were therefore not gold itself, but had the appearance of gold, because the worldly wisdom in which the heretics placed their greatest confidence was not gold—that is, wisdom—but rather folly, as the apostle Paul says: “The wisdom of this world is folly with God” (1 Cor. 3:19).

“And their faces were like human faces.” A human being is a rational animal. By human faces we may understand knowledge of the divine Scriptures, which the heretics strove to possess so that through it they might more easily deceive the simple. The locusts therefore appeared to have human faces, but this was likeness, not reality; for the heretics appeared indeed to possess knowledge of the divine Scriptures, but they were far from the truth because they did not understand them correctly.

### (Verse 8)

“And they had hair like women’s hair.” By hair, which is cut without sensation, we may understand a great multitude of fools who were easily deceived by the heretics. For just as hair is cut without injury, so these were cut off from the Church without any loss. By women, however, we may understand the various churches.

The locusts therefore had hair like women’s hair, because just as the holy Churches of God had their assemblies, which gathered at appointed times to celebrate the divine offices, so the heretics had insane peoples who gathered in various places—not for divine mysteries but to celebrate diabolical rites.[^c0080-5]

“And their teeth were like lions’ teeth.” The function of teeth is to grind up whatever they have seized and consume it, then plunge it down into the pit of the belly. We may therefore understand persecutors of the Church by lions and teeth: by lions, the rulers; by teeth, those who, under their command, tore the saints of God.

The teeth of the heretics were therefore like lions’ teeth, because just as pagans persecuted the Church of God and entangled whomever they could, through terrors and torments, in the abyss of destruction, so the heretics, associating powerful men with themselves, persecuted the Church of God and, afflicting many in the manner of teeth with threats and oppression, plunged them into the belly of their malice.

### (Verse 9)

“And the sound of their wings was like the sound of many horses running into battle.” By wings we may understand the words of the heretics, because just as wings lift birds from the earth, so the heretics exalted themselves through their eloquence. By horses, however, preachers are signified, as we have already said above.

The sound of the locusts’ wings was therefore like the sound of many horses running into battle, because just as the holy preachers uttered the voices of their preaching when they went forth to battle against the devil, in order to free the human race from his power, so the heretics ran about everywhere, spreading false doctrine, so that they might deceive as many as they could and subject them to the devil.

### (Verse 10)

“And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails.” The prophet Isaiah says that a prophet who teaches lies is a tail (Isa. 9:15). The heretics, therefore, who, on account of their knowledge of the divine Scriptures, considered themselves prophets, are not inappropriately likened to scorpions’ tails, because their doctrine was false and poisonous; hence they are also said to have had stings in their tails.

By the stings are signified the blasphemies that they inserted into the divine Scriptures. Just as a scorpion would be harmless if it lacked its sting, so the doctrine of the heretics would be good if they did not defile it with blasphemies.

“Their power was to harm people for five months.” What the five months signify has been explained above.

### (Verse 11)

“And over them they had as king the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon, and in Latin his name is Exterminator.” It is certain to everyone that the devil is the prince of the heretics, as the Lord says to Job: “For he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25). Hence he is also called the Exterminator, because he is the exterminator of all goodness.

### (Verses 12–13)

“One woe has passed; behold, two woes are still coming.” And the sixth angel sounded his trumpet. The martyrs are signified by the sixth angel. The sixth angel sounded his trumpet because the martyrs of Christ offered the doctrine of faith to unbelievers.

“And I heard a voice from one of the horns of the golden altar that is before the Lord, saying to the sixth angel.” As we have already said above, the Church is signified by the golden altar. The altar’s four horns therefore signify the four evangelists. He says that he heard a voice from one of the four horns of the golden altar because there is one faith and one doctrine taught by the four books of the Gospels.

### (Verse 14)

What this voice says to the sixth angel is revealed by what follows: “Go, and release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” First, let us explain what the four angels, the bonds, and the Euphrates signify; afterward we shall investigate more carefully why the Gospel commands the sixth angel to release the four angels.

For just as above, at the opening of the sixth seal, four angels were seen standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth so that they would not blow upon the earth or upon any tree, so here, at the sound of the sixth angel’s trumpet, four angels are reported to have been bound at the great river Euphrates. These four angels therefore have the same meaning as those others: they signify the four kingdoms, namely, the Assyrians, the Persians, the Macedonians, and the Romans.

And because, as we said above, the power of the four kingdoms had passed to the Romans, the Romans are signified in this passage by the four angels. By the Euphrates, however, the world is understood.

What the bonds of the four angels signify is made clear above. For it is written there that John saw an angel descending from heaven, holding the seal of the living God, and he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the earth and the sea, saying: “Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees until we have marked the servants of our God upon their foreheads” (Rev. 7:2–3).

We said that Christ was signified by the angel who held the seal of the living God. The bonds of the four angels, therefore, are the words of the Lord—not in the sense that the Lord commanded the persecutors to cease from persecution until the seeds of faith had been scattered throughout all the nations, but because what he did by his power is said to have been commanded by his words.

Before Christ’s coming, the Romans could in no way be satiated with slaughter, plunder, and the shedding of the blood of the human race.[^c0080-6] But when Christ came in the flesh, he bestowed peace upon the world, and the Romans, who could not restrain their hands from shedding the blood of the human race, were bound by peace and restrained from shedding blood.

The voice that proceeded from the four horns of the golden altar therefore commanded the sixth angel who held the trumpet to release the four angels, because the doctrine of the Gospel commanded the preachers of the word of God not to be terrified by any threats or terrors of impious people, so that they would not cease from the work of preaching. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

For when the Roman emperors and the other rulers of the earth saw the Christian religion increasing daily and the worship of idols being emptied of power, they threatened death to all who worshiped or preached Christ. Thus the sixth angel—that is, the martyrs—released the four angels, that is, their persecutors,[^c0080-7] when, because of their unconquerable steadfastness in evangelizing, the persecutors armed themselves to attack them.

### (Verse 15)

Hence it follows:

“And the four angels were released, who had been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year, to kill a third of humanity.” The four angels were released because impious people, casting aside peace and with the hands that peace had bound now unbound, persecuted the people of God.

When it says, “They had been prepared,” it reveals the will of the impious, because before the time of persecution arrived they were prepared in their intention to kill the people of God. Now, as was said above, the third part of humanity signifies the elect.

Moreover, since the four angels are said to have been prepared for the hour, the day, the month, and the year in order to kill a third of humanity, we may refer this to all the impious who existed from the beginning of the world and will exist until its end. The hour signifies the period from the beginning of the world to the Flood; the day, the period from the Flood to the Law; the month, the period under the Law; and the year, the period under grace. Thus, throughout these four periods, the reprobate always persecute the elect.

### (Verse 16)

“And the number of the mounted army was twenty thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.” Those who are signified by the four angels are also signified by the mounted army, namely, the persecutors of the Church.

The army of persecutors is said to be mounted because, just as God has his horses—that is, the holy preachers who carried him throughout the whole world—so the devil has his horses, that is, all the impious, upon whom he sits and whom he drives to commit various crimes.

They are said to number twenty thousand times ten thousand; for by a finite number the innumerable multitude of persecutors is expressed.[^c0080-8]

### (Verse 17)

“And thus I saw the horses in the vision, and those who sat upon them had breastplates of fire, hyacinth, and sulfur.” In this passage, the insane peoples are signified by the horses, and the rulers of the earth by those who sat upon the horses. By the breastplates, which repel the blows of swords, the hardness of the hearts of the reprobate is signified—a hardness that does not allow the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, to approach their hearts.

These breastplates are said to be fiery, hyacinth-colored, and sulfurous. By fire, plainly, the cruelty of the persecutors’ minds is signified; by hyacinth, which has the appearance of the sky, the honor of divinity that they offered to their gods; and by sulfur, which stinks, the blasphemies that they uttered against Christ are signified.

The persecutors are therefore said to have had fiery, hyacinth-colored, and sulfurous breastplates because partly through the unbelief of their minds they had hardened their hearts, so that they not only did not believe in Christ but also persecuted his servants; partly for the defense of false gods; and partly because of the blasphemies that they uttered against Christ, saying that he was a magician and a deceiver.

“And the heads of the horses were like the heads of lions.” By the heads of the horses the Roman emperors are signified, because they appeared to be the heads of all the persecutors, and because of their insatiable rage they are also likened to lions.

“And from their mouths proceeded fire and smoke and sulfur.” By fire the impious commands of the emperors are signified, by which the people of God were ordered to be killed; by smoke, the honor of divinity that they commanded to be offered to their gods. And rightly the falsehood of idolatry is signified by smoke, because just as smoke vanishes before the face of the wind, so the worship of idols perished in the presence of evangelical preaching. By sulfur, as was said above, the blasphemies that they directed against Christ are signified.

### (Verse 18)

“By these three plagues a third of humanity was killed”—that is, the multitude of martyrs—through the fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths.

Fire proceeded from their mouths, that is, the most impious command by which they ordered the holy martyrs of God to be killed. Smoke also proceeded from them, because they commanded that the honor of divinity be offered by all people to their gods. Sulfur also proceeded from them, that is, blasphemies against Christ, as they commanded that the Christian religion be utterly extinguished from the world.

### (Verse 19)

“For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails.” Above, the heads of the horses are said to be like those of lions. In the mouths of lions, however, are their teeth, with which they crush and tear apart everything they seize.

We may therefore understand executioners by the teeth. They were placed in the mouths of the lions—that is, in the power of the persecutors—and by their command they tortured the bodies of the saints with various torments. The persecutors therefore had the bodies of the saints in their mouths, that is, in their power, but they did not have their souls, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

The power of the persecutors was therefore only in their mouths, because they had the bodies of the saints in their power but did not have their souls: they could kill those whom they could not conquer.

By their tails the doctrine of philosophers and poets is signified. “For their tails were like serpents, having heads, and by these they do harm.” The doctrine of the philosophers is rightly likened to serpents, because it was full of the poisons of lies. These serpents are said to have heads because all the errors of the Gentiles had their own authors.

The power of the horses was therefore in their tails, because the persecutors of the Church sought through the doctrine of the philosophers to overthrow the Christian religion.

### (Verses 20–21)

“And the rest of the people, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands,[^c0080-9] so as not to worship demons and idols of gold and silver, bronze and stone and wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders, their magic arts, their fornication, or their thefts”—“they perished” is understood.

The third part that was killed was therefore saved—that is, the elect, many of whom were killed for the name of Christ; the rest would have fallen willingly if necessity had demanded it. The others, however—that is, the pagans who refused to believe in Christ and repent of their iniquities—perished.

# CHAPTER X

### (Verse 1)

“And I saw another mighty angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow upon his head.” Since above he had narrated the adversities suffered by the Church from heretics and pagans, it remains for him to narrate its prosperity and how it grew amid persecutions.

For it is evident that the Church grew through persecutions: the more greatly it was oppressed, the more it was strengthened and increased. Thus we read that the children of Israel, as a figure of this same Church, multiplied all the more as they were increasingly oppressed by the Egyptians.
