> [Note: [Col. 0887D] Thus the manuscripts read; the printed edition, on the contrary, has: “created vice and other riches, so that human beings might use them abundantly and effectively.”]

When they have affirmed this shameful teaching as virtue, they will easily deceive earthly people, who are more inclined toward evil than toward good.

Hands often signify works. They will therefore have Antichrist’s mark on their right hand because they will perform evil works corresponding to Antichrist’s teaching. They will also have it on their forehead, by which the mind is often signified, because from their wicked works it will be recognized what utterly evil minds they bear.

### (Verse 17)

And so that no one may be able to buy or sell except one who has the mark of the name of the beast or the number of its name. We know that human life cannot continue unless people sometimes sell or buy. Antichrist’s persecution will therefore rage more cruelly against the faithful insofar as this is forbidden to them, without which they cannot live.

Antichrist’s ministers will do this so that, in a time of necessity, they may discover those who secretly wish to preserve the faith of Christianity.

### (Verse 18)

Here is wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a human being, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six. Many people have said many things about this number and have discovered numerous names in whose letters this number is found. Yet they could not foresee whether Antichrist possesses any of those names. But I do not dare to define anything concerning so uncertain a matter. For who knows whether the name that will be given to him by his parents will contain this number?

## Chapter XIV

### (Verse 1)

And I saw, and behold, the Lamb was standing upon Mount Zion. If we carefully examine the text of the following passage, we shall see that what is said about the hundred and forty-four thousand pertains rather to the elect whose souls rejoice with the Lord in heavenly blessedness than to those who labor in this life.

The Lamb therefore signifies Christ. Zion, however, is interpreted as “contemplation.” By Mount Zion we must understand the heavenly homeland. The Lamb was therefore seen on Mount Zion because Christ stands in heavenly blessedness with his saints.

> [Note: [Col. 0887D] Gill’s edition reads, “Christ stands.” And with him the hundred and forty-four thousand, chosen from the twelve tribes. The Roman edition reads, “Christ stands.” In the preceding passage also: “the hundred and forty-four thousand, from the twelve,” and so forth. The manuscripts, however, read as in the text.]

And with him were a hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads. In the third vision preceding this one, a hundred and forty-four thousand chosen from the twelve tribes are said to have been sealed with the sign of faith.

Those hundred and forty-four thousand, as the exposition of the names of the twelve tribes demonstrates, pertain to the elect who labor in this life. But these hundred and forty-four thousand signify the elect who rejoice with the Lord in heavenly glory, as the text of the present passage clearly indicates.

But why does it say that they have the name of the Father and of the Son written on their foreheads, while it remains silent about the Holy Spirit? Obviously, wherever we read of the Father and the Son, we must understand the Holy Spirit as well.

We can understand the foreheads as the hearts of the saints. They therefore have the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit written on their foreheads, because the love of God can never be torn from their minds, as it was torn from the hearts of certain angels who fell from heaven because of pride.

### (Verse 2)

“And I heard a voice from heaven, like the voice of many waters and like the voice of a great thunder.” John often represents the faithful of the present life; by waters, however, peoples are signified. And because the elect are gathered daily from all nations and placed in heavenly blessedness, the saints of God established on earth, who are signified by John, continually hear the voice of many waters, because they perceive with the ears of their hearts the teaching of the saints who dwell in heaven and, insofar as they are able, imitate their deeds. Hence the same voice is also said to be like thunder, which ordinarily terrifies the hearts of those who hear it; for they are terrified when they consider that they cannot ascend to their perfection.

“And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps.” The voice of harpists is exceedingly sweet to those who hear it; and what is sweeter to the faithful than the remembrance of the saints dwelling in heaven, when they contemplate in their minds how great their glory is and earnestly pray that they may one day attain it?

### (Verse 3)

“And they were singing, as it were, a new song before the throne, and before the four living creatures and the elders; and no one could sing the song except those hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth.”

Here there is great obscurity. For he says that the hundred and forty-four thousand were not defiled with women and were virgins, and therefore sang a new song which no one could sing except they alone. Yet we know that some of the apostles and martyrs had wives. Shall those who strove to preserve bodily virginity sing praises to God, while these others remain mute in God’s praises? This is especially impossible since we know that people of little merit from both sexes preserved bodily virginity until death, such as infants and children, whom their age does not permit to lose virginity. We have also seen certain people burdened with particular sins preserve bodily virginity until death; we believe that they must be cleansed by purgatorial fire, so that they may eventually deserve to be counted among the just. Shall we dare to prefer such persons to the apostles and martyrs whose having had wives Scripture does not conceal, so that they may offer that most sweet song to God while Peter and his equals are excluded from it?

For just as the vision of God is sweet to the saints, so also is the praise of God; and just as they cannot be satiated with the vision of God, so neither can they be satisfied with the praises of God. And the closer they are to the Lord God according to the quality of their merits, the more fervent they are in praising God. Who, then, can adequately consider how great a portion of the saints’ glory is taken away if they are regarded as excluded from the praises of God?

We do not say this in order to disparage virginity, which is a great virtue and the companion of the angels—provided that they do not defile it with vice. For who can appreciate how great a good it is to possess integrity of body and soul? Since, therefore, we cannot understand what was said above about virgins as referring only to those who preserved bodily virginity, we must investigate who the virgins are and who those are who will not be able to sing the song of virgins. For if we carefully attend to the surface of the passage, we shall find that this is said not only of virgins but of all holy souls.

We said above that the hundred and forty-four thousand signify the souls of the saints, who never cease continually to praise God in heavenly blessedness. By the throne, however, and the four living creatures and the elders before whom they are said to sing the new song, the faithful placed in this life, from whom the Church is constituted, are signified, as we said in the second Vision.

The hundred and forty-four thousand, therefore, are said to have sung the new song before the throne, the four living creatures, and the elders. The New Testament is called a new song, as the prophet says: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is from the ends of the earth” (Isa. 42:10). It is called the New Testament because another Testament precedes it, which is called the Old; or because it makes new peoples, when it makes children of God from children of the devil.

The faithful placed in this life also have their songs, but in those songs there is often confession of sins, often supplication for sins, and often remembrance of eternal torments. Therefore they frequently move those who sing them to tears; they often teach them to pray amid the praises of God; and they often lift the minds of the faithful toward hope of the heavenly homeland. In that song of the heavenly spirits, however, nothing sad and nothing that disturbs the mind resounds; and the more fully it is uttered,

[Note: [Col. 0889D] All editions: “the greater or the more abundant the joy and gladness”; some manuscripts: “the greater the joyful gladness”; the rest, as we have it in the text.]

the more abundant joy and gladness it pours into the minds of those who sing. Therefore, just as the New Testament is called new because the Old preceded it, so that song of the heavenly spirits is called a new song because another song, which is old, preceded it for those who daily pass into heavenly blessedness, while the song to which they attain is new.

And they are said to have sung this song before the throne of God—that is, in the presence of the throne—for whatever is in our presence we behold without interruption. In the presence, therefore, of the faithful, who are signified by the throne, the four living creatures, and the elders, the souls of the faithful are said to have sung the new song, because the holy men placed on this earth continually behold with the eyes of the mind the glory of the saints dwelling in heaven and labor with all their strength to reach their company one day.

“And no one could sing the song except those hundred and forty-four thousand.”

[Note: [Col. 0890D] The Roman edition has: “had strangled, except those … from the earth.”]

That is, no one among those who are signified by the throne, the four living creatures, and the elders. For now the faithful placed on earth see the glory of the saints dwelling in heaven “through a mirror and in a riddle,” and, because they ardently desire that song, they seem almost to hear it, but they cannot sing it, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

They are said to have been purchased from the earth; for those placed on earth have been purchased by the precious blood of Christ. But it is better to understand “purchased” as “taken up.” For they have been taken up from the earth and placed in heavenly blessedness.

### (Verse 4)

“These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins.”

Here again a question arises. For if there are different orders in that blessedness—apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins—how can all the souls of the saints be called virgins, and virgins to such an extent that they are said not to have been defiled with women? And if what the Lord says is true—indeed, it is true, since it is impossible for God to lie (Matt. 5:28): “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart”—how could all the souls of the saints have remained pure from the defilement of women throughout the entire course of the present life?

We must therefore inquire how this is to be understood. For many were adulterers and fornicators before baptism; but when they believed in Christ, repented of their sins, and sought the baptismal font, whatever was filthy in them was erased by the grace of the Holy Spirit through the waters of baptism. Persevering until the end of life in the good which they promised in that same baptism, when the Lord came to remove them by death from this earthly dwelling, their souls were found to be virgins—that is, intact and clean from every corruption of vices. Their souls are therefore rightly called virgins, because all their corruption was erased by the waters of baptism and by good works.

There were also many who committed great crimes after baptism, but when they strove through repentance and tears, through mercy and through other good works, to erase the evil they had done, and persevered in a good purpose, their souls were found to be virgins when the Lord came, because whatever was blameworthy in them had been cleansed by the remedies of charity.

There were also married people who loved God with all their strength and strove to lead their lives in virtue. Their souls, therefore, are rightly called virgins, because if they contracted any stains from sexual union (Gen. 2:24), these were erased by good works.

[Note: [Col. 0891D] All editions: “concerning the other stains”; all manuscripts: “concerning the other orders.”]

The same is to be understood concerning the other orders.

We may also understand by women the bodies of the saints and by men their souls. For just as man and woman are called one flesh, so body and soul are one human being. And just as woman is inferior to man and therefore must be ruled by him and endure his dominion, so the body is far inferior to the soul and therefore must be governed and subdued by the spirit, and its desires must be broken. Because the saints strove to do this, they were not defiled with women, since from the union of their bodies they drew no stains by which they would grievously offend God.

“These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

Where does he go who fills all things and is wholly everywhere? But how he goes, the Apostle teaches when he says: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:18). God therefore goes by showing mercy to some and withdrawing his mercy from others. The saints follow him because to those to whom he grants his mercy, they too grant it, and from those from whom he cuts it off, they too cut it off.

We cannot understand this of the elect placed on earth. For they often show mercy to those to whom God does not show mercy, as Samuel, who mourned for Saul (1 Sam. 15:35), whom God had cast away from his presence. The saints also sometimes wish to condemn those to whom God shows mercy, as Jonah, who desired that the Ninevites should be destroyed, although God had determined to save them.

“These were purchased from among all as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb” (John 4:3).

In the Law it was commanded that the firstfruits of crops be offered to God (Exod. 22:29). By the firstfruits of crops the elect are signified. For just as small firstfruits were offered to God from the multitude of fruits, so from the multitude of peoples a small number of elect is chosen and offered by the angels to God in the temple of heavenly glory, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14). The saints, therefore, have been taken from humanity in the manner of firstfruits and placed in heavenly blessedness.

### (Verse 5)

“And no lie was found in their mouth.”

What is said here seems exceedingly difficult. There are certain lies that are very serious, and there are others that must be counted among the lighter sins. In our times, I do not know whether anyone could abstain from the latter throughout the whole course of life, unless he were an infant who did not know how to speak.

It therefore seems to me that this is not said of every lie. There is, however, a very grave lie: when we lie about what we promised in baptism. This lie was not found in the mouth of the saints, because they strove to preserve until the end of life what they had promised in baptism.

And if there were some who committed many sins after baptism, nevertheless no lie was found in their mouth, because before death they strove through repentance and works of charity to erase the evil they had done.

“For they are without blemish.”

This also demonstrates clearly enough that the things contained in this passage refer not to the faithful who labor in this life, but to those who rest in the heavenly dwellings. For who can be without blemish while placed in this life, when the same John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

The souls of the saints, however, are without blemish, because if they contracted any stains from their worldly dwelling, these were erased either through repentance and tears and works of charity, or through scourges, or certainly after death by purgatorial fire.

I have said what I have understood. If someone should wish to apply the text of this passage to the present Church, and should judge that the hundred and forty-four thousand signify either preachers or other righteous people still living in this life, and that the new song which no one but they could sing signifies the Gospel, let him consider that the holy Gospel is often preached not only by the elect but also by the reprobate. We believe that the Lord spoke of such people in the Gospel:

“Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out many demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will confess to them, ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’” (Matt. 7:22).

The Apostle Paul also speaks of such people, saying: “There are some who proclaim Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, thinking that they will stir up affliction for my bonds” (Phil. 1:17).

But if someone should decree that the sequence of this passage applies to the virgins of the present time—that is, to those whom the love of God daily impels to preserve integrity, together with the other good works—I think that in this he possesses a sound understanding. Yet he must observe that this understanding cannot accommodate interpreting the Gospel as the new song in this place. Rather, the new song is the spiritual joy that increases in them from preserving virginity.

No one, therefore, can sing the new song except they alone, because no one can possess the joy of virginity except those alone who habitually offer it daily to God, adorned with the other good works.

Similarly, if someone wishes to apply this interpretation to those who, having won the palm of virginity, have already deserved to ascend to the heavenly kingdom, he does not depart from a correct understanding. But he should know that this understanding does not permit the new song to be interpreted as some song composed with voice, tongue, or lips. Rather, it is the reward of virginity, which they deserve to receive eternally from the Lord. No one can sing this song except they alone, because no one receives the reward of virginity except those who, while placed in this world, have striven to preserve it with an undefiled mind for the love of Christ.

The prophet Isaiah speaks of such people, saying:

“Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I will, and hold fast to my covenant—I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will not perish” (Isa. 56:4 and following).

### (Verse 6)

“And I saw another angel flying through the midst of heaven, having an eternal Gospel, to evangelize those seated upon the earth, and every nation and tribe and tongue and people, saying with a loud voice.”

Again he briefly encompasses everything. For just as earlier, when he wished to narrate the evils of Antichrist, he began with the coming of Christ, and, first recounting the persecutions which the Church suffered from the devil, arrived at Antichrist, so here, wishing to describe the day of judgment, he begins with the coming of Christ and, under the appearance of three angels,

[Note: [Col. 0893D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions instead read: “comprehending all things.”]

briefly repeats everything and arrives at the day of judgment.

This angel signifies Christ and his apostles, as well as the other preachers of Christ. He is said to have possessed the eternal Gospel because the teaching of the Gospel was given by Christ, the apostles, and the other preachers for them to proclaim to the nations. That Gospel is called eternal because it grants eternity to all who practice it.

It is also said to have been preached to those seated upon the earth, because the nations to whom the Gospel was preached were seeking nothing other than earth and had placed all their rest in earthly things. Let us hear, then, what this angel preaches.

### (Verse 7)

“Fear the Lord and give him honor, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of waters.”

He appropriately placed fear of the Lord first and honor afterward. For fear of the Lord impels a person to repentance, while repentance urges him to perform good works. We therefore render honor to God when we perform good works, as the Lord himself says: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

The hour of judgment began from the time when the Gospel began to be preached. Those, therefore, will be judged severely on the day of judgment who, hearing the word of the Gospel and despising it, refused to receive the faith of Christ. Likewise, those who did receive the faith of Christ but refused to fulfill it in their works will be judged severely; for from the one to whom more is entrusted, more will be demanded.

Concerning those who did not hear the word of God, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18).

### (Verse 8)

“And worship him who made heaven and earth, and the sea and the springs of waters”—that is, abandon the deaf, mute, and blind idols, and worship him who made all things from nothing.

“And another angel followed, saying…”

The other angel signifies the teachers of the Church who, after the persecutions had ended, governed the Church of God.

“Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen.”

By Babylon, as we said above, the city of the devil is signified, which consists of all the impious. It had fallen because all the worship of demons had been destroyed through faith in Christ. It is said to have fallen twice because it had fallen both on the side of the persecutors and on the side of the worship of the devil.

“She made all the nations drink of the wine of her wrath.”

The wine of wrath is the errors of the pagans, by which they provoked God to anger. But since Babylon is nothing other than all the nations—that is, all the reprobate—how did she make all the nations drink of the wine of her wrath? In truth, when one person taught another, and that person a third, and the third a fourth, and the devil’s error thus passed into all human beings, Babylon indeed made all the nations drink the wine of God’s wrath.

### (Verses 9–10)

“And a third angel followed them, saying with a loud voice: If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark upon his forehead or upon his hand, he also will drink of the wine of God’s wrath, which has been mixed with unmixed wine in his cup.”

The third angel signifies the preachers who will exist in the times of Antichrist. For they will preach that no one should worship Antichrist, or incline the ears of his heart to his most wicked teaching, or imitate his works. If anyone does so, they will testify that he must be condemned to everlasting punishment.

By the wine of God’s wrath the final condemnation inflicted upon the impious on the day of judgment is signified. “Unmixed wine” means pure wine. By unmixed wine, therefore, the justice of God is signified; by the cup, we may understand the judgment of God.

The wine is therefore mixed with unmixed wine in God’s cup, because the final condemnation by which the impious will be condemned will be mixed with justice in God’s cup—that is, in God’s judgment—for it will be carried out by the most just judgment of God.

The impious will therefore drink the wine of God’s wrath when it is said to them: “Depart, you accursed, into the eternal fire,

[Note: [Col. 0893D] The editions had omitted: “which has been prepared for the devil” [Col. 0894D] “and his angels.”]

which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

### (Verse 11)

“And they will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torments will rise forever and ever.”

Fire consumes, while sulfur emits from itself a most foul stench. They will be tormented bodily with fire who refused to extinguish the fire of vices within themselves. They will be tortured by the stench of sulfur—those for whom the stench of lust was sweet.

They will be tormented in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb, so that they may be tormented before those in whose presence they were not afraid to perpetrate many evils.

“And they will have no rest day or night, those who worshiped the beast and its image, and whoever received the mark of its name.”

Why does he say that the reprobate will have no rest either by day or by night, when the elect will possess eternal day, while the reprobate will possess perpetual night? He has spoken according to human usage.

### (Verses 12–13)

“Here is the patience of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.”

That is, such is the patience of the saints, and such is the fruit it produces, as is demonstrated in what follows.

“And I heard a voice from heaven saying to me: Write, ‘Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.’”

Such, then, is the patience of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus: that they may be blessed forever.

But what does he mean when he says: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord”? For who can a dead person die? Certainly no dead person can die unless he first receives his soul again, so that he can die once more.

Those are blessed, therefore, and those die in the Lord, who first die to the world and afterward in the flesh; who first extinguish in themselves the old man—that is, every spiritual and carnal wickedness—so that they may say with the Apostle: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). For those die in the Lord of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

“From now on,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labors.”

“From now on”—that is, from the time of their death—the saints will rest from their labors.

“For their works follow them.”

How do they follow them? Had not Cornelius’s works preceded him, to whom the angel said: “Your prayers and your almsgiving have been remembered in the presence of God” (Acts 10:4)?

But he uses “follow” for “accompany.” For an army that accompanies a king is said to follow him, although some go before, others follow, and others proceed on his right or left.

The works of the saints therefore follow them because the reward of their works accompanies them forever.

We can also understand this spiritually of those who will be killed in the times of Antichrist for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed will they be, and they will die in the Lord, who die for the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Now that he has narrated the punishment of those who will believe in Antichrist, and has briefly encompassed the blessedness of those who persevere in the faith of Christ to the end, it follows that he should describe the day of judgment, on which all these things will be completed.

### (Verses 14–19)

“And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and seated upon the cloud one like the Son of Man, having upon his head a golden crown and in his hand a sharp sickle. And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to the one seated upon the cloud: Send forth your sickle and reap, because the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is ripe. And the one seated upon the cloud sent his sickle upon the earth, and the earth was reaped. And another angel came out of the temple which is in heaven, himself also having a sharp sickle. And another angel came out from the altar, who had authority over the fire, and he cried with a loud voice to the one who had the sharp sickle: Send forth your sharp sickle and harvest the clusters of the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe. And the angel sent his sharp sickle upon the earth, and harvested the vine of the earth and cast it into the great lake of God’s wrath.”

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The edition of Gilbert has: “his sharp sickle upon the earth, and reaped the earth”; for both angels are said to do this. The Roman edition, however, has: “his sharp sickle upon the earth, and harvested the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great lake of God’s wrath.” We have restored the passage as it is found in the manuscripts.]

I have set out almost the entire passage so that its winding structure may be seen more clearly from every side.

Both of these angels signify Christ. Likewise, the two sickles have one meaning: they signify the fire by which the whole world is to be destroyed. For just as the world was first destroyed by water, so at the end of time it will be destroyed by fire.

But we must ask why one Christ is represented by two angels and one destruction by two sickles. The first angel appeared to sit upon a white cloud and to possess a golden crown; the second is not said to have possessed a golden crown or to have sat upon a white cloud. The first is said to have cut off the harvest of the earth, while the second cut off the clusters of the vine of the earth. The place into which the first cast the harvest of the earth is not stated; the second, however, is said to have cast the clusters of the vine of the earth into the great lake of God’s wrath.

It seems to me, therefore, that by the harvest of the earth the elect are signified, and by the clusters—from which wine arises, which makes human minds lose their reason—the reprobate are signified.

This is the harvest of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “At the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, ‘Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to be burned; but gather the wheat into my barns’” (Matt. 13:30). Those who are signified there by the wheat are signified here by the harvest. And those who are signified there by the weeds are represented here by the clusters of the vine of the earth.

And because Christ will appear in one way to the just and in another way to the unjust, he is fittingly represented by two angels. The just will see him in that same glory in which he is beheld by the angels and holy spirits in heavenly blessedness. The impious, however, will see him in the form in which he appeared to human beings while placed on earth. “The impious will be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isa. 26:10).

He will therefore appear gentle to the just and terrifying to the unjust. Hence the first is described as seated upon a white cloud and as having a golden crown upon his head. By the white cloud his immaculate body is signified; by the golden crown the multitude of angels and saints who will accompany him when he comes to judgment is expressed.

Likewise, one destruction is represented by two sickles because the just will be destroyed in one way and the unjust in another. The destruction of the just should rather be called redemption, as the Lord says: “Look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near” (Luke 21:28). It is rightly called redemption because it frees them from temporal evils and leads them to eternal joys.

The destruction of the impious, however, will be grievous both here and more grievous after death, for condemnation and perpetual mourning will remain in them. The just, because of their hope of eternal reward, will receive death joyfully; but the impious, fearful because of perpetual condemnation, will be punished by a most sorrowful death.

The other angel who came out of the temple and cried with a loud voice to the one seated upon the cloud, saying, “Send forth your sickle and reap,” signifies the elect who labor on this earth. By the temple from which he appeared to come out, the Church is signified.

He therefore cried out to the one seated upon the cloud to send his sickle upon the earth and reap, because holy men, seeing that the world lies in wickedness and shuddering at its miseries, pray daily that the kingdom of God may come, in which, freed from every distress, they will receive their own bodies and rejoice with the Lord forever.

The dryness of the harvest indicates its ripeness. For just as the harvest grows until maturity, when it becomes dry, so the number of the elect will increase until the end of the world, and their maturity will be perfected when their number has been completed.

Similarly, the fourth angel who came out from the altar and had authority over the fire has the same meaning as the second, who appeared to come out of the temple. For he signifies the elect laboring in this life.

The altar signifies the Church, just as does the temple. By the fire we may understand charity, which the Holy Spirit nourishes in the hearts of the saints through spiritual sustenance. They are said to have authority over this fire because they both possess charity and are possessed by it.

This angel therefore cried out to the third angel bearing the second sickle, whom we said signified Christ, to harvest the clusters of the vine of the earth, by which the impious are signified. For holy men, seeing the human race daily deceived by demons, seeing also the impious flourishing and the world continually declining toward worse things, pray that the day of judgment may come—a day on which the wickedness of the demons will perish together with its authors, every transgression will come to an end together with the transgressors, and everlasting righteousness, which will have no end, will be brought forth.

The vine signifies the world, which has produced and nourished the entire multitude of the impious. The lake, which we call hell, is called the lake of God’s wrath because the vengeance of God’s wrath will be completed there.

### (Verse 20)

“And the lake was trodden outside the city.”

By the treading of the lake we may understand the plunging of the impious into hell. By the city, the heavenly Jerusalem is signified, which consists of all the elect. The lake will therefore be trodden outside this city, because the impious will be separated from the fellowship of the just and thrust into hell, as the Lord says in the Gospel:

[Note: [Col. 0897D] The edition omitted: “and they will cast them … and there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”]

“The angels will go out and separate the evil from among the just, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 7:14).

### [Col. 0898A] 557

“And blood flowed from the lake as far as the horses’ bridles, for one thousand six hundred stadia.”

By blood the punishment of the impious is signified. By the distance of one thousand six hundred stadia, which the blood flowing from the lake occupied, false Christians are signified. Although this number is derived from the number four, it is spread in every direction while preserving that same number, and it does not cross beyond its limits.

[Note: [Col. 0898D] All editions: “spreading the same number, it is spread”; all manuscripts: “[while] preserving … it is spread.”]

Similarly, false Christians receive in baptism the faith of Christ, which consists in the four books of the Gospel. But abandoning the narrow and constricted way, which is enclosed within the limits of the number four and leads to life, they walk along the broad and spacious way of this world, which leads to death (Matt. 13:3).

Nevertheless, they do not depart from the number four, because although they do not possess the works of Christianity, they do not lose the name of Christianity.

The blood therefore flowed out from the lake and occupied one thousand six hundred stadia, because the punishment that will engulf the demons and all unbelievers will also entangle the false Christians who appeared to possess the faith but did not possess the works of faith.

By the horses, false pastors of the Church are signified, who undertake the office of governance not for the love of God but for the love of the world. By the bridles by which the horses are governed, their false doctrine is signified.

False pastors do indeed have doctrine in their mouths, lest they appear wholly alien to their office; but, following the example of the Pharisees, they say and do not do. And because they cannot teach anything other than what the Gospel speaks, and in their preaching they announce to sinners the punishments they will suffer unless they reform, the blood reaches the horses’ bridles, because they themselves will experience the punishments with which they threatened sinners unless they reformed, since they refused to abandon their own vices.

## CHAPTER XV

### (Verse 1)

“And I saw another great and wondrous sign in heaven: seven angels having the seven last plagues, because in them the wrath of God is completed.”

Just as earlier, before proceeding to the account of the seven angels sounding the trumpets, he took care to mention them, so here, before coming to the account of the seven angels holding bowls, he mentions them, to indicate that great mysteries are contained in their vision. But concerning these we shall say what the Lord grants in what follows.

### (Verses 2–3)

“And I saw something like a glassy sea mixed with fire, and those who conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name standing upon the glassy sea, holding the harps of God and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and saying the song of the Lamb.”

We explained above what the glassy sea signifies, in the second Vision (on chapter 4). There, however, it is said to be like crystal, whereas here it is mixed with fire. And because crystal possesses exceptional brightness and, when it receives the sun’s heat, ordinarily emits fire from itself, crystal there and fire here have the same meaning. For they signify the spiritual understanding found in the divine Scriptures.

The glassy sea is therefore mixed with fire because divine Scripture is mixed with spiritual meanings. Those who conquered the beast were therefore seen standing upon the glassy sea because the saints of God who will fight against Antichrist will plant their feet upon the commandments of the divine Scriptures and will not be able to be moved from their faith by any assault of the winds.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] The edition reads: “and by no impulse of vices”; the manuscripts: “[and by no impulse] of winds.”]

By the harps which they held, the mortification of the flesh is signified. The song of Moses signifies the Old Testament; the song of the Lamb signifies the New. They therefore sang the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb because the saints will preach both the Old and the New Testaments.

Let us hear what sort of song it is.

(Vers. 4.) “Great and wondrous are your works, Lord God almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages. Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify [Col. 0899B] your name? For you alone are merciful; because all nations will come and worship in your presence, for your judgments are manifest.”

This song agrees with the Old and New Testaments, for seven blessings are found in it, which can be fitted to the seven periods of which we spoke above (On chaps. 5 and 7).

The first blessing is: “Great and wondrous are your works, Lord God almighty.” This can apply to the first period, in which heaven and earth were made, together with all the creatures, which are exceedingly wondrous.

The second is: “Just and true are your ways, King of the ages.” This corresponds to the second period, in which all the creatures that possessed the breath of life were destroyed by the waters of the Flood through God’s most just judgment.

The third is: “Who will not fear you, Lord?” This corresponds to the third period, namely, that of those to whom the Law was given, who practiced the commandments of the Law more through fear than through love.

The fourth is: “And will glorify your name.” It is clear that this applies to the prophets, who glorified God’s name both in their preaching and in their writings.

The fifth is: “For you alone are merciful.” We placed Christ’s coming in the fifth period, in which our Lord, who alone is merciful, deigned both to become human for the salvation of the human race and to suffer and die.

The sixth is: “Because all nations will come and worship in your presence.” It is clear that after the Lord’s ascension all nations came to faith in Christ; these we placed in the sixth position.

The seventh is: “For your judgments are manifest.” It is clear that this pertains to the day of judgment, when God’s judgments will be shown to be just and true [Col. 0899D]. May the mercy and compassion of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ deliver us from condemnation in that judgment. [Note: Codex Gem. reads: “May he deign, to whom are honor and glory through all things, etc.”] He lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## ON THE FIFTH VISION

The fifth vision, to whose meaning we have now come, with the Lord’s help, agrees for the most part with the preceding vision. Up to this point we have spoken, insofar as the Lord’s grace has deigned to grant it, about its meaning [Col. 0900A] (On chap. 8). For just as seven angels were seen there, to whom seven trumpets were given, so here it is mentioned that seven bowls were given to seven angels. And just as, at the trumpet-blast of the first angel, great hail struck the earth, so also, at the pouring out of the first angel’s bowl, human beings—who are often signified by the earth—are said to have been struck by the most grievous wounds. Again, just as at the trumpet-blast of the second angel a third of the sea was turned into blood, so likewise, at the pouring out of the second angel’s bowl, the whole sea is described as having been turned into blood.

[Note: The manuscripts read as above; the edition instead has “is described.” But how these things … we shall explain, following the same meaning.]

The others follow the same meaning. How they agree with the preceding things we shall explain below. These therefore have the same signification as those: they signify [Col. 0900B] the preachers who existed from the beginning and will exist until the end.

They are set forth twice, however, because, as we demonstrated above, the things that were seen to take place at the trumpet-blasts of the first, second, third, and fourth angels pertain to the elect. But the things reported to have occurred at the trumpet-blasts of the fifth, sixth, and seventh angels, to which the three woes are joined—woes in which the persecutions suffered by the Church from heretics and pagans, and to be suffered from the Antichrist at the end of the world, are described—pertain in one respect to the reprobate and in another to the elect. The wicked acquire everlasting punishment from the evil they inflict upon the righteous; the just acquire everlasting glory from the evil they endure.

Everything, therefore, that is described under the pouring out of the seven angels’ bowls pertains to the reprobate [Col. 0900C]. Hence the first angels are said to have blown their trumpets, by which God’s army was summoned to battle; but the angels who follow are reported to have poured out bowls full of God’s wrath upon the wicked.

(Vers. 5.) “After this I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened.”

In Exodus it is written that Moses made the tabernacle in the desert. Later, when the people were already dwelling in the promised land, Solomon built the temple. The desert, therefore, signifies this world; the tabernacle, which is transferred from place to place, signifies the present Church, which daily passes from the desert of this world to heavenly blessedness and proceeds from virtue to virtue, so that it may see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. LXXXIII, 8).

Thus the curtains of the tabernacle, which were decorated in various colors, were covered with skins and haircloth, to indicate that mortification of the flesh and humility are the guardians of the virtues [Col. 0900D].

What else is signified by the promised land except the heavenly homeland, which God promised to those who love him? And what is represented by the temple, which was built from excellent stones, except the heavenly Jerusalem, which is built daily from living stones (James I, 12)?

[Note: All editions read: “What, then, does he say, ‘The temple of the Church was opened’? The temple …” But the manuscripts repair the lacuna, as in the text.]

What he says, “The temple of the tabernacle was opened,” is therefore equivalent to saying: “The temple of the Church was opened.” But what is the temple of the Church other than the heavenly homeland? The Psalmist desired to dwell in this temple when he said: “One thing I asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4). This temple, therefore, was opened through Christ, because through him the entrance to the kingdom of heaven has been opened to all the faithful.

(Vers. 6.) “And seven angels came out of the temple, having seven plagues, clothed in pure and shining stone, and girded around their breasts with golden belts.”

If the temple signifies the heavenly homeland, and the seven angels signify the preachers, how are they said to have come out of the temple? Do the saints descend from that heavenly homeland to preach?

The holy preachers are said to come out, as it were, from the heavenly homeland when they are sent by him who is the glory of the saints and from whom all their teaching proceeds [Col. 0901B].

They are said to have had seven plagues. Earlier, too, they were said to have had seven plagues, because in them the wrath of God was brought to completion. If they had seven plagues of God’s wrath, how did they become holy?

The saints of God had the seven plagues under their authority, not as their punishment. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28).

The seven principal vices, from which all evils arise, are signified by the seven plagues. The seven angels were therefore seen to have seven plagues, because on the day of judgment the holy preachers will have the seven principal vices—that is, all workers of evil—under their authority, so that they will be punished with everlasting punishment by their judgment [Col. 0901C].

The wrath of God was brought to completion in the holy preachers—that is, through them—because by their judgment God’s wrath will be fulfilled.

We can understand the seven plagues in another way. Above, we divided the entire body of the wicked into seven parts (On chap. 1). The seven plagues, therefore, are the sins that correspond most suitably to each part. Those who lived before the Flood and deceived God’s people through unions with women will be judged in one way (Gen. VI, 2); those who, after the Flood, devised idolatry and various errors by which the human race was deceived will be judged in another; those who lived under the Law and did not keep God’s commandments in another; the false prophets who deceived God’s people in another [Col. 0901D]; the wicked Jews who killed the Lord and persecuted his apostles in another; the persecutors of the Church who tried to extinguish the faith of Christ in another; and the ministers of the Antichrist, who will abandon Christ and follow the Antichrist, in another.

The saints of God will have these plagues under their authority, because each of them will condemn to everlasting punishment, by his judgment, those who lived in his own time and despised their admonitions.

The pure and shining stone with which the seven angels were seen to be clothed signifies Christ. Of him the Apostle says: “All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” [Col. 0902A] (Gal. III, 27).

The golden belts with which they are said to have been girded around their breasts signify the wisdom of the preachers. This wisdom so encloses the hearts of the saints within itself that it does not allow them to wander outside it through various errors.

“And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God who lives for ever and ever.”

Although the four living creatures signify the four evangelists, they also signify Christ both collectively and individually. But because brevity does not allow us to explain how each one signifies Christ, let us understand Christ through this one living creature.

The bowls are the hearts of the saints, which are rightly called golden because of wisdom. One of the four living creatures therefore gave the seven angels seven golden bowls, because Christ filled the hearts of his saints with wisdom [Col. 0902B].

But if they were filled with wisdom, how are they said to be full of God’s wrath?

In the Gospel the Lord says concerning the wicked Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV, 22). Did the Jews, then, have no sin before Christ’s coming? They were sinners beforehand, but they did not yet have the sin of unbelief, the sin of blasphemy by which they called him Beelzebul, the sin of murder by which they crucified him, and many other crimes that they incurred through his coming.

In Christ’s bowl [Note: Codex Gem. reads: “in which wisdom was contained”], in which the life of the world was contained, the Jews, by the demands of their own guilt, found death. The seven angels’ bowls were therefore full of God’s wrath, because, as far as the reprobate are concerned [Col. 0902C], the preaching of the saints contained God’s wrath within itself: because, by despising their preaching, they incurred God’s wrath.

(Vers. 8.) “And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from his power.”

Above we said that the temple signifies the heavenly homeland. But if smoke is inside a house, it obscures the eyes of those looking in from outside, so that they cannot see perfectly what is happening within the house.

The temple of the heavenly homeland is therefore now full of smoke, because the elect, placed in this life, while they raise the eyes of their minds to contemplate heavenly things, are obscured by a certain darkness that they cannot cross. He calls this obscurity smoke.

Paul suffered this darkness when he said: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.” And again: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

It should be noted that the elect suffer this dullness as long as they remain in this life. But when they have passed into that heavenly blessedness, it will be taken away from the eyes of their minds.

Hence it follows: “And no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” Surely the righteous do not enter that heavenly blessedness every day? We should understand this as referring to the entrance of their bodies. For in that heavenly blessedness the righteous do not enter with their bodies until the seven plagues of the seven angels are completed [Col. 0903A].

We spoke above about the seven plagues. The final plague will be when the Antichrist infects the human race with his errors. When the seven plagues have ended—for the examination of which the day of judgment will take place—the saints will receive their bodies and dwell without end with the Lord in the temple of the heavenly homeland.

The Psalmist speaks of this dwelling: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

# CHAPTER XVI

(Vers. 1.) “And I heard a loud voice from the temple saying to the seven angels: Go and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth.”

The voice from the temple is the voice of the Lord commanding the preachers to announce God’s word not only to the elect but also to the reprobate, so that the former may have the means of correction [Col. 0903B] and the latter the means of receiving a harsher condemnation.

The earth signifies sinners. The preachers therefore pour out their bowls upon the earth when they announce God’s word to sinners.

(Vers. 2.) “And the first went and poured out his bowl upon the earth, and a grievous and most terrible wound came upon the people who had the mark of the beast and upon those who worshiped its image.”

The first angel signifies the preachers who lived before the Law, just as the one who was seen to blow the first trumpet in the preceding vision does (On chap. 8). But there the elect are signified by the third part of the earth that was burned; here the reprobate are signified by those who suffered the grievous and most terrible wound.

The angel therefore poured out his bowl upon the earth because the holy men who lived before the Law offered words of admonition to the wicked in order to correct them [Col. 0903C]. But a grievous and most terrible wound was inflicted upon them, because through the preaching of the saints they became worse and despised God’s commandments. The grievous and most terrible wound is the contempt of God’s commandments.

But if the grievous and most terrible wound pertains only to the reprobate, and only those who had the mark of the beast suffered it, we must ask what the mark of the beast is.

If we wish to understand the mark of the beast as pride—because on account of it the devil fell from heaven—we must recognize that many of the elect had the wound of pride but were healed by the medicine of humility.

There is, however, another most evil vice that always excludes from itself the medicine of repentance. For we know that the devil is irrevocable, so that he cannot in any way be corrected from his iniquities. Whoever is irrevocable therefore does not seek the medicine of repentance, just as the devil is estranged from this medicine.

Those, then, who could not be recalled from their crimes by the teaching of the holy Fathers had the mark of the devil, who remains incorrigible and impenitent.

But because many in our own time suffer from this vice, it is necessary to say something about its magnitude. There are some so irrevocable that, although they know their assertion to be wicked, they can in no way be called back from it, fearing to be defeated by human beings. To avoid being refuted, they try to defend their falsehood with lies, perjuries, and blazing contentions. While they fear being defeated by human beings, they are defeated by the devil [Col. 0904A].

Other vices are healed by the medicine of repentance. This alone excludes that saving medicine from itself, lest they appear to have been defeated through confession and repentance.

And because they praise their evil so that they may appear to have overcome, what the prophet said is fulfilled in them: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. V, 20)!

It is said that there is a certain bird that defeats and eats a serpent but is shortly afterward killed by its venom. In the same way, these people rejoice that they have defeated their neighbors, but such a victory is the destroyer of their souls.

Whoever, then, is of this sort bears the mark of the devil.

By the image of the beast we can understand vices [Note: The edition reads: “because it itself, that is, the devil, is the author”; the manuscripts read: “because he himself is the author”], because he himself is the author of all evils.

Whoever serves vices therefore worships the image of the beast. Paul likewise says that the belly was the god of false preachers: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. III, 19). Similarly, he called greed the service of idols (Col. III, 5).

(Vers. 3.) “And the second poured out his bowl upon the sea, and it became like the blood of a dead man, and every living soul in the sea died.”

This angel signifies the teachers of the Law, just as does the one who was seen to blow the second trumpet in the preceding vision (above, on chap. 8). There it is said that a third of the sea was turned into blood [Col. 0904C], by which we said the elect were signified. Here, however, the whole sea is read to have been turned into blood (Gen. IX, 5).

Under the Law, the vengeance for criminal crimes was the shedding of blood. The transgressors of the Law are therefore signified by the sea. It was turned into blood because they received everlasting vengeance for their contempt of God’s commandments.

“And every living soul in the sea died,” because many of those who were in the sea—that is, among the number of the reprobate, who are signified by the sea—and who before receiving the Law appeared to be alive, that is, righteous, were shown by their transgression of the Law, once they had received it, to have been unrighteous.

Even now there are many in the Church who, before they rise to ecclesiastical or secular honors, appear holy and righteous. But once they have received honors, when they turn God’s gift to evil, it becomes clear to everyone that they were dead and not alive.

(Vers. 4.) “And the third poured out his bowl upon the rivers and upon the fountains of waters, and they became blood.”

This angel signifies the prophets. By the rivers and fountains of waters the twelve tribes, together with their families, are signified. For in the preceding vision we said that the prophets were signified by the third angel who blew the trumpet.

[Note: All editions read: “But there a part of the rivers”; the manuscripts read: “a third part of the rivers.”]

There it is read that a third part of the rivers and fountains was turned into wormwood. By this we said those who, through the teaching of the prophets, took on the bitterness of repentance and through it merited salvation were signified.

Here, however, at the pouring out of the third angel’s bowl, the rivers and fountains are read to have been turned into blood.

The angel therefore poured out his bowl upon the rivers and fountains of waters when the holy prophets announced God’s word to the wicked people. But they became much worse through the preaching of the saints: they not only despised God’s commandments but also killed the ministers of God’s word. They were turned into blood because they inflicted everlasting death upon themselves.

(Vers. 5, 6.) “And I heard [Note: The Roman edition reads: ‘the angel of the waters saying: Just are you, Lord … We can understand by the angel of the waters …’] the fourth angel saying: You are just, who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have judged these things; because they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and you gave them blood to drink, for they are worthy of it.”

We can understand by the fourth angel the angel of that people who, seeing that the wicked people had been condemned by God’s just judgment, praises the most just sentence of almighty God.

And because they poured out the blood of the saints and prophets, they drank blood, because in place of the temporal death they inflicted upon the righteous, they received everlasting death.

(Vers. 7.) [Note: All editions read: “And I heard a voice from the altar saying: Yes, Lord”; all manuscripts read as in the text.]

“And I heard the altar also saying: Lord God almighty, your judgments are true and just.”

By the altar we can understand the holy men who lived at that time. They praised God’s just judgment because he had inflicted a most just condemnation upon the wicked people, just as we read that Daniel and the three youths did.

(Vers. 8, 9.) “And the fourth poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given power to afflict people with heat [Note: The manuscripts read as above; the edition instead printed *affligere* in the margin for *afficere*, and the Roman edition admitted it into the text; moreover, it excised the entire scriptural verse that follows]. and with fire. And the people were scorched by great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God who has power over these plagues; and they did not repent so as to give him glory.”

The fourth angel signifies Christ and his apostles, together with the other preachers, just as we said that the fourth angel in the preceding vision signified them.

There the Jewish people were signified by the sun; by the third part of the sun, moon, and stars were signified the faithful from that people who believed in Christ.

The fourth angel therefore poured out his bowl upon the sun because Christ and his apostles openly foretold that the wicked Jews would be destroyed by the Romans.

For just as a servant receives a sword from his master not so that he himself may be slain but so that he may slay the guilty, so the Romans received the pouring out of the bowl, in which God’s wrath was contained, not so that they themselves might perish in it, but so that they might pour it out upon the Jews in vengeance for Christ’s blood.

Hence it follows: “For it was given power to afflict people with heat and fire.”

By the heat we can understand the siege, and by the fire famine and the sword, by which almost all the Jews were consumed. Power was therefore given to the sun to afflict people with heat and fire, because God gave the Romans power to afflict the wicked Jews with various calamities, killing some and uprooting others [Col. 0906A] from their land.

“And the people were scorched by great heat.” Whoever wishes to know how great was the heat with which the Romans afflicted the Jews should read Josephus, and will find that no nation in all the kingdoms of the earth perished more atrociously (*The Jewish War*).

“And they blasphemed the name of God who has power over these plagues.” The Jewish people were so impious that, although they knew they were suffering unheard-of evils because of their crimes, they not only did not cease from blaspheming Christ but also spewed forth much worse blasphemies against God in their afflictions.

Hence it follows: “And they did not repent so as to give him glory.” They would have given glory to God if, repenting of their iniquities, they had believed in Christ and kept his commandments.

(Vers. 10, 11.) “And the fifth poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast, and its kingdom became dark; and they chewed their tongues because of the pain, and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their wounds; and they did not repent of their works.”

The fifth angel signifies the orthodox Fathers who fought against the heretics, just as we said that the fifth angel in the preceding vision, who blew the fifth trumpet, signified them (above, chap. 9).

And just as the heretics were signified there by the locusts, so here the heretics are signified by the throne of the beast. The beast signifies the devil.

The heretics are therefore rightly called the throne of the beast, because the devil dwells in their hearts.

The fifth angel therefore poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast because the holy men, exposing the errors of the heretics, strove to reveal what punishment was impending for them [Col. 0906C].

“But its kingdom became dark,” because, through the teaching of the holy Fathers, it was shown to those for whom the teaching of the heretics had seemed brilliant that it was wretched and dark.

“They chewed their tongues because of the pain,” because each one reproved the errors of the others. For neither did Arius follow Eunomius, Sabellius, or any of those men, nor did they follow him; but each one, wishing to establish his own heresy, reproved the errors of the others.

[Note: “For neither did Arius …” The statement that each one reproved the others’ errors has been restored from all the manuscripts.]

They are also said to have blasphemed God because of their pains and wounds. The heretics grieved because they were continually refuted by Catholic men; their wounds were the errors of each one.

The heretics blasphemed God because of their pains [Col. 0906D], because the more they were overcome by Catholic men, the greater the blasphemies they devised in order to defeat them. Their own errors, which they professed, likewise impelled them to blaspheme God.

They are also said not to have repented. For scarcely will you find any of the founders of heresies who repented of his errors.

(Vers. 12.) “And the sixth poured out his bowl upon the great river Euphrates, and its water dried up, so that a way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun.”

This sixth angel has the same signification as the one who was seen to blow the sixth trumpet. For he signifies the holy martyrs. Those who are signified there by the horsemen, by whom a third of humanity is described as having been killed, are likewise signified here by the great river Euphrates—namely, the persecutors of the Church of God.

The angel therefore poured out his bowl upon the river Euphrates because they fearlessly foretold to the persecutors themselves what condemnation awaited the persecutors of the Church.

The water signifies the persecution itself. He dried up its water because the holy martyrs persevered in preaching God’s word until all persecution came to an end, with some of the persecutors cast into hell and others submitting themselves to the Christian faith [Col. 0907B].

By the kings we can understand the multitude of nations that flowed together to the faith of Christ.

The way for the kings was therefore prepared when the water was dried up, because, once the persecutions had ended, free opportunity was given to all nations to come to the faith of Christ.

But how are they said to have come from the rising of the sun—that is, from Christ, who is signified by the sun—when they came not from Christ but to Christ, abandoning the devil?

Perhaps we should understand the devil by the sun, so that they came from him to Christ. But it is better to understand Christ by the sun, because of the prophetic saying: “But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in his wings” [Note: The phrase “and healing will be in his wings,” absent from the edition, is found in all the manuscripts] (Mal. IV, 2).

They come, therefore, from the rising of the sun—that is, from Christ—because, by his inspiration and urging, they come to him. It is his gift both to will and to accomplish what is good, as he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

Whoever comes to Christ comes from Christ, because he grants that they come and he receives those who come.

(Vers. 13, 14.) “And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet; for they are spirits of demons performing signs.”

[Note: All the manuscripts likewise contain everything that is read from these words, “the calling of the nations,” up to “he will come.”]

Having described the calling of the nations and how they came to the faith of Christ, he mentions the Antichrist, who is to come near the end of the world.

The three unclean spirits signify the disciples of the Antichrist, who will preach him throughout the whole world. Although they will be human beings, they are called unclean spirits and spirits of demons because demons will dwell in them and speak through their mouths.

They were seen to come out of the mouth of the Antichrist and the mouth of his false prophet because through their teaching they will be made sons of the devil. They were also seen to come out of the mouth of the dragon because the devil will speak through the mouth of the Antichrist.

They are likewise rightly compared to frogs, which are unclean reptiles and live in mud. Just as frogs remain in filthy waters, so the disciples of the Antichrist will easily deceive those who have not feared being defiled by various vices and crimes.

The frogs’ hoarse and repulsive voice also signifies their utterly impious preaching, full of blasphemies [Col. 0908A].

“And they go out to the kings of the whole earth to gather them for battle on the great day of almighty God.”

By the kings of the earth not only kings but also peoples are signified. The disciples of the Antichrist will gather them for battle on the great day of almighty God—not because they dare to fight against God on the day of judgment, by whom they will be judged with such terror [Note: The edition reads: “that they dare to fight against God”; the manuscripts read: “that they dare to fight against God.”], but they will gather them for battle in order to persecute the Church, so that on the great day of almighty God they may be condemned to everlasting punishment.

And because, when the persecution of the Antichrist has ended, the Lord will soon come to judgment, he adds:

(Vers. 15.) “And behold, I am coming like a thief.”

The day of the Lord, as the Apostle says, will come like a thief in the night. For when they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them.

“Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (I Thess. V, 2–3).

The wicked, who rest in the pleasures of their flesh as though in the softness of a little bed and who do not wish to foresee the evils that follow, are appropriately said to sleep.

The Apostle admonishes them, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V, 4).

The righteous, however, who strive to foresee the evils that follow, who extinguish carnal pleasures within themselves, and who arm themselves with the weapons of the virtues so that they may be able to fight continually against visible and invisible enemies, are appropriately said to keep watch; and therefore they are blessed.

The garments of our souls are good works [Col. 0908C]; the guarding of the garments is the guarding of God’s commandments.

We therefore guard our garments if, by doing what God has commanded, we fulfill them. The one who is alien to good works is naked.

The wicked will walk naked when they are led to the day of judgment empty of good works. Their shame will therefore be seen, because their crimes will be made manifest both to angels and to human beings.

(Vers. 16.) “And he gathered them into the place called in Hebrew Armageddon.”

Armageddon is interpreted as “a rounded mountain” or “a rising up toward what is first.” Both interpretations can be applied to the day of judgment.

It is rightly called a rounded mountain, because at that time the whole world will be destroyed by globes of flame. Likewise, “a rising up toward what is first” is rightly said, because all human beings will be restored to their former state by rising again.

(Vers. 17.) “And the seventh poured out his bowl into the air.”

This seventh angel signifies the holy preachers who will exist in the time of the Antichrist, just as we said that the one who is read above to have blown the seventh trumpet signifies them (On chap. 9).

The air signifies vain people. The angel therefore poured out his bowl into the air because the holy preachers will announce to vain and impious people that they are to be condemned to everlasting punishment.

“And a loud voice came from the temple, from the throne, saying” [Col. 0909A]:

The loud voice is the voice of the holy preachers. The Church is understood by the temple. The voice therefore came out of the temple because the voice of holy preaching proceeds from the Church. It is also said to have come from the throne because the Church of God is God’s throne, and he sits and rests in it.

What this voice says he makes clear by adding: “It is done”—that is, the end of the world is at hand, in which everything foretold by the Lord and by the saints will be fulfilled.

(Vers. 18.) “And there were flashes of lightning, voices, and peals of thunder, and there was a great earthquake, such as had never occurred since human beings were upon the earth—so great an earthquake.”

[Note: Such an earthquake, “so great,” was omitted in the only edition.]

The flashes of lightning signify the miracles that God will perform through his saints. For we read above that Elijah and Enoch will perform many signs [Col. 0909B]. The voices signify the preaching of the saints; the peals of thunder express the terror of eternal fire.

The earthquake often signifies the movement of hearts. Some will be moved from evil to good, such as the Jews who will believe in Christ. Others will be moved from good to evil: those who will abandon the faith of Christ and follow the errors of the Antichrist.

(Vers. 19.) “And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell.”

The great city is the city of the devil—that is, the entire multitude of the reprobate. By the three parts into which it was divided are signified the Jews who refused to believe in Christ, the pagans, and false Christians.

When he says, “And the cities of the nations fell,” it seems to me that this pertains to the day of judgment. The cities of the nations will then fall when, by the fire that will precede the Lord’s coming to judgment, all the nations will be destroyed, as the Psalmist says: “Fire will go before him and burn up his enemies round about” (Ps. XCVI, 3).

“And Babylon the great came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath.”

How is Babylon said to have come into remembrance before God, when nothing can be added to or removed from his memory, before whom past and future stand just as present things do?

He used “remembrance” for “time.” Babylon will therefore come into remembrance before God when the time comes in which he has determined to judge the world and repay each person according to his work.

The wine of the indignation of God’s wrath is everlasting punishment, because, when judgment has been completed, all the wicked will be condemned together with the author of iniquity, the devil [Col. 0909D].

(Vers. 20.) “And every island fled, and the mountains were not found.”

The mountains and islands have the same signification as the cities of the nations, which are said shortly above to have fallen. The nations are signified by the islands, and their rulers by the mountains. They are said to flee when they are destroyed by the fire on the day of judgment.

(Vers. 21.) And great hail, each stone about the weight of a talent, fell from heaven upon the people. In the Gospel it is written that a certain householder, setting out for a foreign country, gave five talents to one of his servants, two to another, and one to a third. But the first and second, by trading, doubled the talents they had received from their master; the third dug in the ground and hid his master’s money (Matt. XXV, 15). Therefore, whatever temporal goods or whatever skills we have received from the Lord will be reckoned to us as the reception of talents. The righteous, accordingly, who are represented by the first and second servants, double their talents when they spend the temporal goods they receive from the Lord on good works and urge as many as they can to do good. But the wicked, who are represented by the third servant, hide their talents in the ground, because from the temporal goods they have received from the Lord they nourish vices rather than virtues.

By the hail, which crushes and destroys the things that grow from the earth, the vengeance of almighty God is signified, by which he will crush the wicked and cast them into hell. It is said to be like a talent because he will punish each person according to the quality of his talent; and the more someone has sinned, the greater the torments he will be compelled to endure.

But what follows is very obscure: “And people blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, for its plague was exceedingly great.” For who in that [Note: [Col. 0909D] All editions read *districto justorum judicio* (“the strict judgment of the righteous”); all manuscripts read *districto justoque judicio* (“the strict and just judgment”).] strict and just judgment would dare to blaspheme God? Yet they are said to blaspheme because the blasphemies of the reprobate, which they now conceal in their hearts, will then be made manifest to all.

## CHAPTER XVII

(Vers. 1.) And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying. Just as above, while briefly comprehending the day of judgment under the sound of the seventh angel’s trumpet, he returned to matters he had omitted and, describing the holy Church under the figure of a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet, added the sufferings she endured from the devil and will endure from Antichrist at the end of the world; so here too, while briefly touching upon the day of judgment under the outpouring of the seventh angel’s bowl, he returns to matters he had omitted and, under the figure of a prostitute, describes the devil’s city and subsequently reveals what punishments it will suffer for its crimes.

The angel holding the bowl signifies the holy preachers; John, however, represents all the faithful. Hence it is also added:

(Vers. 2.) “Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great prostitute who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication; and all who inhabit the earth have become drunk with the wine of her prostitution.”

In some passages this prostitute specifically indicates Rome, which at that time was persecuting the Church of God; in others, more generally, it indicates the devil’s city, that is, the entire body of the reprobate. The angel therefore shows John the condemnation of the great prostitute because the holy preachers, both by word and in writing, show the faithful what punishments the wicked suffer for their crimes, so that, terrified by their punishments, they may abstain from sins.

She is said to sit upon many waters because the devil’s city is built from the multitude of nations, which are signified by the waters. The kings of the earth are said to have committed fornication with her because they increased Babylon’s crimes rather than destroyed them.

563. “And all who inhabit the earth have become drunk with the wine of her prostitution.” The wine of her prostitution is the various errors and various crimes of the wicked city. For just as a prostitute is offered to all who wish to fornicate with her, so that she may be polluted by their impurities, so all the wicked submit themselves to demons, obeying their evil suggestions and plunging themselves into every crime, as the prophet says to Jerusalem: “You laid your body like the ground, and like a road for passers-by” (Isa. LI, 23).

By “the inhabitants of the earth” he calls all the reprobate. Their drunkenness, however, is Babylon’s wickedness, because just as a drunkard fills himself with wine until he becomes alienated from his own mind, so the reprobate fill themselves with every kind of wickedness until, having become alienated from their own minds, they cast away from themselves the fear of God and every form of goodness, as blessed Job says: “They drink iniquity like water” (Job XV, 16).
