(Vers. 3.) And he carried me away in the spirit into the wilderness; and I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast, full of blasphemous names, having seven heads and ten horns.

The whole multitude of the wicked is signified by the wilderness, because they themselves abandoned God and therefore have been abandoned by God. The prostitute was therefore found in the wilderness because the devil’s city consists of the multitude of the wicked.

The beast, as he himself explains below, signifies the devil. Scarlet has the color of blood, and by blood death is often signified. The devil, therefore, is blood-red because he is the author of death and every destruction.

The beast is said to be full of blasphemous names because the devil himself is the author of every blasphemy. What the seven heads and ten horns signify the angel explains below.

(Vers. 4.) And the woman was surrounded with purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls; she had a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations and the uncleanness of her prostitution.

Purple is dyed with blood, while scarlet has the color of blood; and these are royal garments, by which secular power is signified. [Note: [Col. 0911D] The phrase “By blood, however, death is often signified,” taken from the manuscripts, has been restored to its proper place.]

By blood, moreover, death is often signified. Purple and scarlet therefore have the appearance of blood because secular power is deadly and brings eternal danger to those who embrace it more than heavenly glory. We may also understand by the blood-colored garments the works of the wicked, for which they will be condemned to everlasting death.

What follows—“and adorned with gold”—often signifies wisdom through gold. The woman was therefore adorned with gold because she possessed the wisdom of this age, which is foolishness before God.

Through gems and pearls secular eloquence is signified. Through the golden cup, which she is said to have held in her hand, the teaching of philosophers and poets is signified. It is said to be full of abominations and the uncleanness of her prostitution because the teaching of philosophers and poets was full of lies and every kind of error devised to deceive the human race.

(Vers. 5.) And upon her forehead a name was written: “Mystery, Babylon the Great, Mother of Prostitutions and of the Abominations of the Earth.”

Through the forehead and face a person is recognized; similarly, the wicked are understood from their works, as Solomon says: “A boy is known by his pursuits” (Prov. XX, 11).

Through the forehead and face, therefore, the works of the wicked are signified, because from their works it is understood that they are children of the devil and citizens of the wicked city.

[Col. 0912B] (Vers. 6.) And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.

Had Babylon actually drunk the blood of the saints? Rather, she was drunk—that is, alienated from every spiritual understanding. She was drunk because the vengeance for the blood of the saints had made her so culpable and so alienated from God’s mercy that she was not worthy in any way to be able to seek her own salvation.

And I was greatly astonished when I saw her. The faithful are astonished when they see the reprobate so alienated from the fear of God that, without any trembling, they inflict many evils upon the innocent and plunge themselves into every kind of wickedness, even though they know that God leaves no crime unpunished unless it has first been erased by repentance and by the other remedies through which sins are healed.

[Col. 0912C] (Vers. 7.) And the angel said to me: “Why are you astonished? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and the ten horns.”

The beast has here the same significance as the dragon was said above to have: it signifies the devil. What the seven heads and ten horns signify he himself, as we have said, explains below.

“The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise from the abyss, and it will go into destruction.” The beast—that is, the devil—existed before Christ’s coming, possessing the human race; it is not now, that is, he does not possess the human race as before, because through Christ he has been expelled from the hearts of the elect. But he is about to rise from the abyss because in the time of Antichrist Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out and deceive all the nations, as the following passages make clearer. And he will go into destruction because, together with all the reprobate whom he has deceived and all his followers, he will be condemned to eternal punishment.

(Vers. 8.) And those who inhabit the earth will marvel, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, when they see the beast that was and is not.

By those who inhabit the earth we must understand those who will be lovers of the earth more than of God, whom Antichrist will easily deceive. The reprobate, therefore, whose names are not written in the book of life—that is, who are not predestined to eternal life—will marvel when they see the beast, that is, the devil performing signs through Antichrist, and worship the devil in Antichrist.

(Vers. 9.) And this is the meaning for one who has wisdom. That is, what follows contains great obscurity, and the understanding must be sharpened greatly in order to comprehend it. Let us also ask the Lord to open this obscurity for us.

(Vers. 10.) The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have fallen, one is, and another has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain for a short time.

Above we said that the seven heads of the dragon signify those reprobates through whom the devil deceived the human race; we also divided them into seven groups, as we did the rest of the multitude of the reprobate.

And because this beast of which we are speaking has the same significance as the dragon was said to have, for they signify the devil, the seven heads of the beast also have the same significance as the seven heads of the dragon were said to have.

They are also called mountains because those who were greater in crimes and deceived the others were higher than those who were deceived by them, as he says below concerning Babylon: “For her sins have reached up to heaven” (below, chap. 18).

They are likewise called seven kings because they offered leadership to the others who were going to destruction. The prostitute is therefore said to sit upon these mountains because from them the devil’s city was formed in all its errors and crimes. For just as the apostles are called the foundations of the Church, so, conversely, the inventors of errors are the foundations of the devil’s city.

Of these heads, or mountains, or kings, five have fallen, one existed, and another had not yet come. The devil’s first head had fallen because those who existed before the flood, through whom those who were called the sons of God were deceived, had descended into the sewer of hell (Gen. VI, 2). Likewise, the second group, those who existed after the flood and up to the Law, were submerged in the same pit of destruction.

The third had also fallen: these were those who persuaded the people of God, to whom the Law was given, to worship idols. Likewise, the false prophets, who are placed in the fourth position, had already fallen into the destruction of their own perdition because they had been deceivers of God’s people.

But the wicked Jews, who killed the Lord and persecuted his apostles, who are placed in the fifth position, had already been devastated by the Romans at the time when this vision was shown to John. Five heads of the beast had therefore already fallen—those called mountains and kings—because all the preceding groups, including the wicked Jews placed in the fifth position, were already suffering the punishments of their destruction.

“One existed,” because the pagans, namely those who persecuted the Church of God and are placed in the sixth position, were then persecuting the Church of God. For this reason John himself was being held in exile on the island of Patmos.

“Another had not yet come,” because Antichrist, who is placed in the seventh position, had not yet come. “And when he comes, he must remain for a short time,” because the Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming, as he himself says in the Gospel: “And unless the Lord had shortened those days”—that is, the days of Antichrist’s persecution—“no flesh would be saved” (Mark XIII, 20), by “all flesh” signifying the elect alone.

(Vers. 11.) And the beast that was and is not is itself the eighth, and is of the seven, and it goes into destruction.

The beast—that is, the devil—who before Christ’s coming ruled the human race and now does not hold it subject in the way he then did, is itself the eighth. For the seven are the divisions of all the reprobate, while the eighth part of them is the devil together with the other demons.

It is of the seven because the demons arise from the fellowship of the reprobate; and just as they were the authors of their destruction, so they will also be their companions in torment. Hence it follows: “And it goes into destruction.”

What follows, up to the place where the angel is seen to descend from heaven, pertains specifically to the destruction of the Roman Empire.

(Vers. 12.) And the ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but will receive authority as kings for one hour after the beast.

Four beasts were shown to Daniel in a vision (Dan. VII, 3), by which four kingdoms were represented. The fourth beast, which was strong and terrifying and by which the Romans were signified, is described as having ten horns. These signify the kingdoms that destroyed the Roman Empire, as Saint Jerome explains, following the assertion of certain others (*Commentary on Daniel*, chap. VII).

The ten horns in this passage therefore have the same significance as those are said to have had: they signify the kingdoms by which the Roman Empire was destroyed. They first seized part of Asia for themselves; afterward the Saracens conquered the whole of it. The Vandals claimed Africa for themselves, the Goths Spain, the Lombards Italy, the Burgundians Gaul, the Franks Germany, and the Huns Pannonia. The Alans and Suevi, moreover, devastated many regions that lay under their dominion.

At the time when this vision was shown to John, these kingdoms had not yet received authority. But they received authority as kings for one hour because the power of each of these peoples lasted only a short time. They received the kingdom after the beast because, once the devil’s kingdom had been destroyed through Christ, these peoples received an impious power. [Note: [Col. 0913D] The edition reads: “These peoples received their own power. They will have one purpose, that is, one will in evil. And they gave their strength and power to the beast.” [Col. 0914D] The manuscripts agree with our text: “For their strength,” etc.]

(Vers. 13, 14.) These have one purpose, and they gave their strength and power to the beast.

They had one purpose, that is, one will in evil. They gave their strength and power to the beast because their strength and power were demonic.

These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them. They fought with the Lamb who persecuted the Church of God and killed God’s people. But the Lamb will conquer them because we know that, with few exceptions, these peoples have now accepted the yoke of Christ’s faith.

For he is King of kings and Lord of lords, and those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful. The kings and rulers are the chosen and faithful. Christ, therefore, is King of kings and Lord of lords because he is the King and Lord of all the saints. And those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful, that is, holy; they are called to this purpose, that they may remain with him forever, and are rightly called chosen and faithful.

The reprobate, too, are called, as the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16). [Col. 0915B] But the reprobate are called so that they may be without excuse; the chosen, so that they may remain with him forever. [Note: [Col. 0915D] The Roman edition had placed here: “And he said to me: The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits,” followed by material found in the manuscripts and in Gill’s edition immediately before verse 18.]

(Vers. 16.) And the ten horns that you saw upon the beast—these will hate the prostitute.

He calls Rome the prostitute because, in defense of false gods, she persecuted God her creator. The ten horns therefore hated the prostitute when the peoples signified by the ten horns took up arms to destroy the Roman Empire. [Note: [Col. 0916D] The manuscripts read as here; the edition reads: “took up arms.” “And they will make her desolate and naked.” “They made her desolate and naked when all the peoples removed themselves from her authority.”]

“And they will make her desolate and naked.” They made her desolate and naked when all the peoples removed themselves from her authority.

“And they will eat her flesh.” Since luxuries nourish the flesh, we can understand by “flesh” the wealth of all the peoples. They ate her flesh when they received the riches of all the peoples that were brought to Rome and converted them to their own uses.

“And they will burn her with fire.” We know that very many cities, villages, and forts that were subject to the Roman Empire were burned by these peoples.

(Vers. 17.) For God put it into their hearts to do what pleases him, to give their kingdom to the beast until the words of God should be fulfilled.

“God put it into their hearts,” that is, he permitted them to do what pleased him and what had been foretold by his prophets and apostles, who predicted that the power of the Roman Empire would be destroyed by these peoples.

They gave their kingdom to the beast until the words of God should be fulfilled because, in accordance with the permission of the most just God, they followed the devil’s suggestions in committing crimes for as long as it took for the words of God to be fulfilled—that is, for the things foretold by God and his saints to come to pass.

(Vers. 15.) The waters that you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples, tribes, and languages.

By the waters all the peoples whom the Romans had subjected to themselves are signified.

(Vers. 18.) And the woman whom you saw is the great city that has power over all the kings of the earth.

This is clear, for we know that at that time the Romans ruled over all the kings of the earth. But someone may say: How are the Romans signified by the prostitute, when in the times in which these peoples inflicted various disasters upon the human race the Romans were Christians?

To this we reply that by the prostitute are not understood the elect who belonged to that same people and who, for love of heavenly glory, despised the glory of the world; rather, the reprobate are meant, whether they were pagans or Christians. Their power, therefore, was destroyed by those peoples who were oppressing the human race through an impious domination.

## CHAPTER XVIII

(Vers. 1.) After these things I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was illumined by his glory.

What follows pertains generally to the wicked city, that is, to all the reprobate. And in order to demonstrate Babylon’s overthrow more fully, he returns to its first ruin, by which it was overthrown through Christ.

This angel signifies Christ, who deigned to descend from heaven to earth in order to raise human beings to heavenly things. He is said to possess great authority because he possesses the same authority as the Father, being equal to the Father in all things.

The earth was illumined by his glory because through the teaching of his faith the human race was rescued from the darkness of ignorance and unbelief.

(Vers. 2.) And he cried out with a loud voice, saying.

Christ’s voice is the teaching of the Gospel. What this voice cried out he makes clear by adding: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.”

For God’s saying is his doing. He said that Babylon had fallen because he himself caused it to fall. It is said to have fallen twice: it fell first when, through the teaching of the Gospel, it lost a very great multitude of the elect, who were cut off from it through faith in Christ and became citizens of the holy city, that is, the Church. It will fall a second time when, on the last day, it is punished by everlasting death, which in this book is called the second death.

“And it has become a dwelling place of demons.” Did demons not dwell in Babylon before Christ’s coming? They did indeed dwell there, but their dwelling was not recognized. When the multitude of the elect was converted to the faith, Babylon became a dwelling place of demons because those who accepted Christ’s faith came to know truly that it had always been a dwelling place of demons.

“And a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird.” The demons are the unclean spirits and the unclean birds. They are called birds because they fly continually through this air like the winds. They are called guardians of Babylon because just as angels guard God’s elect so that they may not sin so wickedly as to perish, so demons watch over the wicked lest they ever turn back from their iniquities and be saved.

(Vers. 3.) For all the nations have drunk of the wine of her wrath, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have grown rich from the power of her luxuries.

What the wine of wrath is, and what the fornication of the kings with Babylon is, we have briefly explained above. By the merchants of the earth we may understand lovers of the world, who hand over their souls to destruction in order to acquire money.

Jesus son of Sirach speaks of such merchants, saying: “He has put his soul up for sale, because in his lifetime he cast away his inner self” (Eccl. XX, 10). He has put his soul up for sale who did not fear to hand it over to demons in order to acquire money.

He calls luxuries Babylon’s power because, just as the elect labor with all their strength to acquire heavenly riches, so the reprobate strive with all their efforts to accumulate perishable riches for themselves. Concerning such people the prophet says: “They labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IX, 5).

(Vers. 4.) And I heard another voice from heaven saying:

Heaven signifies the Church in this passage; the voice from heaven is the voice of the preachers proceeding from the Church. But what does this voice say?

“Come out of her, my people.” Through his preachers the Lord urges the elect to come out of Babylon, not bodily but in mind. How they ought to come out of Babylon he teaches in what follows, saying:

“And do not share in her sins.” Those properly come out of Babylon who make themselves strangers to her evil works, as the Psalmist says of himself: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and with those who act unjustly I did not enter” (Ps. XXV, 4).

“And do not receive her plagues.” What are Babylon’s plagues except the vices that kill souls? We may also understand Babylon’s plagues as the punishments prepared for the wicked, so that the meaning is: If you abstain from Babylon’s crimes, you will be strangers to the punishments that she will suffer eternally.

(Vers. 5.) For her sins have reached up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.

Almighty God always observes Babylon’s iniquities. But when he does not exact vengeance, he appears not to see what he does see. By saying this, therefore, he indicates the time when all the wicked will be punished with everlasting punishment. [Note: [Col. 0917D] The edition and the manuscript of Regius read “does not exact”; the editions alone add: “By saying ‘another voice,’ he indicates this.” The manuscripts agree with our text.]

(Vers. 16.) Repay her as she herself repaid you.

The elect are commanded to repay Babylon as she repaid them, either because God’s saints will judge the wicked, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX, 28); or because they are members of him to whom the authority of judgment was handed over by the Father.

The righteous will therefore repay the wicked for the evils they suffered from them when Christ, who is their head and whose members they are, condemns them to everlasting punishment.

“And repay her double according to her works.” Babylon persecuted God’s elect in two ways when she inflicted many evils upon their bodies and souls. She will herself receive punishment in two ways because bodies will be tormented together with souls. And those twofold punishments will be doubled because, in place of the temporal and brief punishments with which she afflicted the righteous, she will receive eternal punishments.

“In the cup that she mixed for you, mix a double measure for her.” By the cup we may understand the tribulations that the saints suffered from the wicked.

(Vers. 7.) As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give her torment and mourning.

As much as she glorified herself—that is, exalted herself in pride and entangled herself in every vice—so much greater torment will she receive.

“For she says in her heart: I sit as queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning.” Babylon in a certain sense calls herself queen when she exalts herself amid the prosperity of this world. She says that she is not a widow because she trusts that she cannot be separated from the temporal goods to which she is joined and from which she nourishes her luxury.

She says that she will not see mourning because the wicked, although they know that they will be punished for their crimes, pretend not to see what they do see and drive the memory of death from their minds, lest sad reflection disturb the joy of their hearts.

(Vers. 8.) Therefore her plagues will come in one day: death, mourning, and famine.

On the day of judgment everlasting death will come upon her, which in this book is called the second death. Mourning will come upon her, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII, 12).

Famine will come upon her, that is, hunger for rest. They will desire to rest from the punishments they suffer, but they will in no way attain that rest.

(Vers. 9, 10.) And she will be burned with fire, that is, with eternal fire, because the Lord who will judge her is mighty.

And the kings of the earth who committed fornication with her and lived in luxury with her will weep and mourn over her when they see the smoke of her burning, standing far away because of fear of her torments, saying: “Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city, because in one hour your judgment has come!”

What the fornication of the kings with Babylon is we explained above. But it is very astonishing that they are said to stand far away, when they themselves are to be plunged into the same punishments as the other reprobates signified by Babylon.

They will therefore stand far away in mind and will, not in body, recoiling from their crimes for which they will be tormented eternally. They will stand far away through desire, desiring one thing—rest—and suffering another—eternal torments.

(Vers. 11.) And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her because no one will buy their merchandise anymore. [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Roman edition reads “because no one will buy their merchandise”; but the manuscripts and Gill’s edition consistently read here and elsewhere *mercedes, mercedem*, and similar forms.]

Since above we said that the merchants of the earth signify lovers of the world, in this passage we may understand by merchants those who sell the good they appear to do.

There are many to whom knowledge of secular laws has been given, who bring the cases of the poor before the courts. But because they do this not out of love for God but in exchange for rewards, they receive no reward from God.

This misery has grown so strong that one can scarcely find anyone among those who hold positions with rulers who will say a word to support the needs of a poor neighbor without accepting a reward.

We may also understand by the merchants of the earth those who seek praise from human beings for the good they do. We may likewise understand them as those who sell ecclesiastical offices, something which divine Scripture strongly condemns.

And although many bishops appear free from this crime, their ministers are often polluted by it. Yet whatever is done wrongly by disciples is charged to their teachers.

There is another very wicked crime committed by those who are called archdeacons. For they accept payment from adulterous priests and, by remaining silent, consent to the evil that they could correct through the authority they received from the bishops.

There are also some among such priests who, fearing condemnation for their crimes, are more assiduous than the others in serving the archdeacons. If anyone wishes to speak a word against them, they defend them and pretend not to know what they do know. They are condemned by that prophetic sentence which says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. V, 20)!

To you, therefore, who are such a person, I speak: behold, you have sold a priest’s soul to the devil. For who persuaded the priest to commit fornication except the devil? Therefore the one who persuaded him to fornicate also persuaded him to give you payment, so that he could commit this crime without fear.

Through the priest’s hand, therefore, the devil gave you the price of his soul’s destruction. Behold, you accepted the payment and handed over your brother’s soul, redeemed by Christ’s blood, to that same devil from whom it had been redeemed.

It is written in the Law that if anyone sold a person who was his brother, he should be put to death (Exod. XXI, 16). If, then, the one who sells a person to another person is guilty, how much more guilty are you, who sold a person redeemed by Christ’s blood not to another person but, more disastrously, to the devil!

Such merchants will therefore weep and mourn in hell because no one will buy their merchandise anymore. For they will lose what they appeared to possess and fall into the evil that they neglected to foresee.

[Col. 0919D] (Vers. 12, 13, 14.) Merchandise of gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, every kind of thyine wood, every kind of vessel made of ivory, every kind of vessel made of precious stone, bronze, iron, and marble, cinnamon, spices, ointment, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle, sheep, horses, chariots, slaves, and human souls; and the fruits desired by your soul have departed from you, and all the fat and splendid things have perished from you, and the merchants of these things will no longer find them.

In all the things that have been enumerated, Babylon’s avarice and luxury are condemned.

For at the judgment the Lord will not say to the reprobate: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire because you were murderers, proud, fornicators, and adulterers.” Rather, he will say: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink,” and the other works of mercy, from which avarice restrains the reprobate so that they are not merciful toward the poor.

Avarice is the nurse of luxury; the nourishment of luxury is described in this passage, and luxury is nourished by avarice.

If we examine carefully, we will find that everything enumerated in this passage to demonstrate Babylon’s avarice or luxury pertains to the five bodily senses.

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. God gave them to human beings and animals: to animals merely for preserving their lives, but to human beings both for preserving life and so that reason might use them to guide the soul entrusted to it along the path of righteousness.

The righteous, therefore, who strove to walk according to the rectitude of reason through these five bodily senses acquired the friendship of almighty God. But the wicked, perverting the good of reason into evil and forcing these bodily senses to serve luxury and the other vices, likewise incurred the anger of the just Judge.

Therefore, if you wish to join with these things what is written below—namely, the voice of harpists and musicians, of flute players and trumpeters—you will find that all Babylon’s riches described here pertain to the five bodily senses, as we said above.

Gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls pertain to sight; fine linen, purple, scarlet, and the other fabrics pertain to touch; cinnamon, spices, ointments, and frankincense pertain to smell; wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, and the other foods pertain to taste; and the voice of harpists and musicians and of flute players pertains to hearing.

Babylon’s condemnation, therefore, as this Scripture shows, consists chiefly in riches, because riches are the nourishment of vices, and from them avarice—which may now be called the queen of the world—feeds her daughter luxury.

### (Verses 15–17)

Those who had grown rich will stand far away from her, because of fear of her torments, weeping and mourning and saying: “Woe, woe, that great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls; for in one hour such great riches have been laid waste!” The statement that Babylon’s rich stand far away is to be understood according to the higher meaning that we discussed concerning the kings.

### (Verses 18–19)

And every shipmaster and all those who sail to the harbor [Note: All printed editions read “who sail from afar”; the Gembloux manuscript reads “who sail to the place”; Saguntine and Regius manuscripts read “who sail into the harbor,” etc.], and sailors who work upon the sea, stood far away and cried out, seeing the place of her burning, saying: “What city is like this great city?” And they threw dust upon their heads, weeping and mourning and saying: “Woe, woe, that great city, in which all who possessed ships at sea grew rich from her wealth; for in one hour she has been laid desolate!”

By this sea we can understand the present world; by the shipmasters, wicked rulers; and by those who sail from place to place, together with the sailors who work upon the sea, those who daily practice various occupations in the world for the plundering of the poor and the increase of their own sins. These, then, will weep and mourn when they see the place of Babylon’s burning; for they themselves will constitute Babylon, and they themselves will mourn and weep. They will see Babylon’s fires because, by enduring their own fires, they will see what they neglected to perceive while living in the world, so that they might correct themselves.

They are also said to have cast ashes upon their heads; for the head often signifies the mind, and ashes signify sins. They will therefore place ashes upon their heads, because the memory of their sins will never depart from their minds.

### (Verse 20)

“Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you holy apostles and prophets, because God has pronounced your judgment upon her.”

By heaven we can understand the angels; by the apostles, the fathers of the New Testament; and by the prophets, the fathers of the Old Testament. They will rejoice when the entire host of the wicked, together with the demons who are the authors of their iniquities, has been destroyed. They will also rejoice because then all wickedness will come to an end [Note: So the manuscripts; the editions, conversely, read: “and the righteous will be led to everlasting joys.”], and everlasting righteousness will be brought forth.

### (Verse 21)

And one mighty angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: “With such force Babylon, that great city, will be thrown down, and it will never be found again.”

This angel signifies Christ, who is called mighty because the human mind cannot comprehend how great Christ’s strength is. By the great millstone, the entire multitude of the wicked is signified; and the sea signifies hell, into which all the wicked will be plunged. The angel therefore threw the millstone into the sea, because our Lord Jesus Christ, on the day of judgment, will plunge the entire multitude of the wicked into hell by his just judgment.

### (Verses 22–23)

“And the sound of harpists and musicians, and of flute players and trumpeters, will no longer be heard in you.”

This was mentioned above.

“And every craftsman and every craft will no longer be found in you, and the sound of the mill will no longer be heard in you, and the light of the lamp will no longer shine in you, and the voice of the bridegroom and the bride will no longer be heard in you.”

We must ask why he counts crafts, the sound of the mill, the light of the lamp, and the voice of the bridegroom and bride among Babylon’s crimes, since all these things can be practiced without guilt, and human life cannot continue without them. All these things must therefore be understood spiritually.

By crafts, then, we can understand the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19). Wicked craftsmen and sons of Babylon learn these arts so that they may advance Babylon’s wickedness; for “they are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22).

A mill crushes and pulverizes whatever it receives beneath it. We can therefore understand wicked judges by the mill. The mill gives forth its sound when wicked judges pronounce unjust judgments in order to crush the innocent.

By the light of the lamp, the glory of this world is signified. Concerning this lamp Scripture says: “The lamp of the wicked will be extinguished” (Prov. 24:20). The lamp of the wicked is extinguished when, removed from this life, they lose temporal joy and incur eternal sorrow.

Likewise, by the bridegroom we can understand lovers of the world, and by the bride, the earth. For just as love binds a bridegroom and bride so that they become one flesh, so love of the world joins its lovers to the earth so closely that they become one with it and, if it were possible, would never wish to be separated from it.

Such craftsmen, then, will no longer be heard in Babylon, because they will be condemned forever together with her.

“For your merchants were the rulers of the earth.”

The Church has her merchants, and Babylon has hers. The merchants of the Church store their treasures in heaven, “where thieves do not break in and steal” (Matt. 6:19); but Babylon’s merchants store their treasures on earth, “where thieves break in and steal.”

“And by your sorceries all the nations were deceived.”

Babylon’s sorceries are the various errors by which the human race has been deceived.

### (Verse 24)

“And in her was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who have been slain upon the earth.”

The blood of the saints was found in her—that is, the crime of killing the saints—just as the Lord says to the wicked Jews, with all the reprobate understood: “All the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth will come upon you” (Matt. 23:35).

## Chapter XIX

### (Verses 1–8)

And I heard what seemed to be a loud voice of many trumpets in heaven, saying:

“Alleluia! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth by her prostitution, and he has avenged the blood of his saints at her hand.”

And again they said: “Alleluia!” And her smoke rises for ever and ever.

And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell upon their faces and worshiped God, who sits upon the throne, saying: “Amen, alleluia!”

And a loud voice came forth from the throne, saying: “Give praise to our God, all his saints, and you who fear him, small and great.”

And I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great trumpet, and what seemed to be the voice of many waters, and what seemed to be the voice of great thunder, saying:

“Alleluia, because the Lord our God, the Almighty, has begun to reign! Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give him glory, because the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself. And it was granted to her to clothe herself in shining, bright fine linen; for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.”

I have set out the entire passage so that its subtle meaning may more easily be examined from every direction. For it is written that “alleluia” was sung five times by seven voices: first and second by the voice of many trumpets; third by the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures; fourth by the voice that came forth from the throne—not now was “alleluia” sung, but its interpretation, namely, “Give praise to our God, all his saints.” For *alleluia* means “praise the Lord”; and fifth, it was sung once by three voices: by the voice of the great trumpet, the voice of many waters, and the voice of great thunder.

The Scripture of this book often shows that the entire multitude of the elect is to be divided into seven parts, if its meaning is examined with greater subtlety [Note: The editions and the Regius manuscript read “to be divided”; the editions add, “if its subtle meaning or interpretation is carefully investigated”; other manuscripts read more suitably, as we have in the text.].

The righteous who lived before the Flood belong to the first part. Those who lived after the Flood until the Law was given belong to the second, as we have often already shown. They had no other law except the natural law, that is, love of God and neighbor. Everyone knows that he ought to fear and love above all the one by whom he was created and by whom life and the means of sustaining life are supplied to him; and that he ought not to do to another what he does not wish another to do to him. No one who is of sound mind is permitted to be ignorant of this law.

The many trumpets therefore signify the elect who lived before the Flood and those who lived after the Flood until the time when the Law was given. They uttered a voice because, through the teaching of their preaching, they recalled from their errors as many people as they could. They sang “alleluia” because, according to their knowledge of the natural law, they strove to please God through good works. They said “alleluia” a second time because those who lived after the Flood, living according to the same law, justly adhered to their Creator.

But we must ask why, at the second pronouncement of “alleluia,” Babylon’s smoke is said to have risen for ever and ever. Fame may be signified by smoke. We know that Noah and his sons are placed first in the second part; in their time the human race was destroyed by the waters of the Flood. Afterward, Sodom and Gomorrah, and the other cities associated with them, were consumed by heavenly fire. Babylon’s smoke therefore rises for ever and ever because this fame will never depart from the mouth of the faithful.

The twenty-four elders, however, signify the fathers who lived under the Law. They are joined by the four living creatures, through whom the New Testament is represented, because, if it is understood spiritually, the New Testament is contained in the Old Testament. They sang “alleluia” because, observing the legal commandments, they strove to please God through good works.

The throne signifies the prophets, because they were God’s seat, and through them he established his judgments. A voice came forth from the throne because holy preaching proceeded from the prophets. They sang praise to God because they strove to serve him with all their strength.

The great trumpet signifies Christ. The voice of the trumpet is the preaching of the Gospel. The voice of many waters signifies the multitude of nations confessing Christ. The voice of great thunder signifies the elect who will be born at the end of the world; and rightly by thunder, because they will announce the terror of the day of judgment.

The three voices therefore sang “alleluia” once, because they have preserved and will preserve until the end the faith of the holy Trinity and the teaching of the Gospel, which proceeded from the great trumpet, that is, from Christ.

Thus the two parts—the first and the second—belong to the law that we have called natural. The two that follow—the third and the fourth—belong to the law given through Moses. The remaining three—the fifth, sixth, and seventh—belong to the law of the Gospel, to indicate that they must remain in the faith of the holy Trinity until the end of the world.

Let us hear what these three parts proclaim:

“Alleluia, because the Lord our God, the Almighty, has begun to reign”—that is, let us praise the Lord, because, after the kingdom of the devil, our destroyer, has been overthrown, he himself has deigned to reign in us, he who is our Lord and Savior.

“Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give him glory, because the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself.”

Let us therefore rejoice; let us therefore exult, because the mercy of our Creator has deigned to unite his Church, which is ourselves, to himself in such a way as a bride is united to her bridegroom, so that we may be one flesh with him, as Scripture says: “The two shall become one flesh” (Gen. 2:24; Eph. 5:32). The apostle taught that this is to be understood of Christ and the Church.

“His wife has prepared herself”—that is, the Church, who is called the Lamb’s wife, has adorned herself with various virtues.

“And it was granted to her to clothe herself in shining, bright fine linen.”

He himself explains what the fine linen signifies: “For the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints.”

### (Verse 9)

And he said to me: “Write: Blessed are those who have been invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.”

The meal of the elect is now, when they are nourished in the Church by evangelical food. The supper, however, will be then, when after the resurrection they enjoy eternal glory in heavenly blessedness. And because the meal now taking place receives both good and evil people, not all who appear to recline at it are blessed; only those will be blessed who are received into that supper which will take place after the end of the world.

### (Verse 10)

And he said to me: “These words of God are true.” And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said to me: “See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who possess the testimony of Jesus. Worship God.”

The redemption by Christ’s blood has granted the faithful this: that they should become children of God and companions of the angels. Therefore the angel fears being worshiped by a human being who worshiped, above the angel himself, the man who is God; for this reason he calls himself John’s fellow servant and the fellow servant of the other faithful.

The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. It is entirely certain that the fathers of the Old Testament, who foretold Christ’s coming, passion, and resurrection, possessed the spirit of prophecy; hence they are also called prophets. Whoever, therefore, bears testimony to Christ possesses the spirit of prophecy.

### (Verse 11)

And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and the one seated upon it was called Faithful and True.

We must in no way think that this passage refers to Christ’s coming in which he will come for judgment, but rather to the elect who will be born at the end of the world. For, when the end of the world is at hand, the Lord will come in his saints, in order to fight through them against Antichrist and his ministers. And just as he will be proclaimed by those saints, so too his form is described here.

Heaven signifies the Church; the white horse signifies the human being whom the Son of God assumed, and upon whom he was seen to sit. He is also said to be called Faithful and True. These two names—Faithful and True—have one meaning in this passage [Note: The words “the Son of God” are absent from the edition.].

The Son of God is rightly called Faithful, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144:13). He calls himself True in the Gospel, saying: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

It follows: “And with righteousness he judges and fights.”

God will not fight against the wicked on the day of judgment with weapons; rather, they will be conquered and crushed by his righteousness. For the Lord will bring all the sins and crimes of the wicked before their eyes, so that they may know that they have been condemned by the most just judgment of God.

### (Verse 12)

His eyes were like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems.

By the Lord’s eyes the Spirit of God is signified, as the author of this book explains in the third vision: “The Lamb had seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.”

And because a flame both burns and illuminates, the Holy Spirit is suitably called fiery, since he both illuminates the hearts of the faithful and sets them aflame with love of God.

“And upon his head were many diadems.”

By the many diadems the multitude of the saints is expressed.

“He had a name written that no one knows except himself.”

Since above he says that he was called Faithful and True, and shortly afterward that his name was called the Word of God, what does he mean by saying that no one knows his name except himself?

The saints of God do know Christ’s name, which is “Son of God,” and they do not know it. They know it in part, and in part they do not know it. For in all creatures that beget and are begotten, no son can be coeternal with his father; the begetter must necessarily precede, and the one begotten must follow. But the nature of the Son of God is not like this. For just as the Father is without beginning, so also is the Son.

Although we cannot consider how this can be, we nevertheless truly believe and confess that the Son is in every respect equal and coeternal with the Father. Concerning this generation of his the prophet says: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

### (Verse 13)

And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name was called the Word of God.

By the garment we can understand Christ’s body, and by the blood our sins, for which he himself died, or the death itself that he endured for us. But because, by dying, he destroyed the sins of his elect, and by rising again trampled down death itself, as the apostle Paul says: “Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9), it seems better to me that by Christ’s garment we should understand the multitude of the saints, who are his members.

By the drops of blood with which the garment is said to have been sprinkled, the martyrs are signified, who did not hesitate to pour out their blood for love of Christ. Thus, in that heavenly blessedness, they adorn with their splendor Christ’s garment, which consists of angels and holy human beings.

### (Verse 14)

And the armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in white, clean fine linen.

We said above that the form of Christ described here corresponds to the way he will be proclaimed by the saints at the end of the world. Heaven therefore signifies the Church in this passage. By the armies that appeared to come forth from heaven while following Christ, the saints who will be born at the end of the world and will fight against Antichrist are understood. By the horses, bodies are signified; by the riders of the horses, souls.

They therefore appeared to have white horses because they will present themselves before God pure and shining, insofar as human frailty permits.

What the fine linen signifies he explains above: “The fine linen,” he says, “is the righteous deeds of the saints” [Note: So the manuscripts; the edition reads: “as was explained above. The fine linen, therefore, is the righteous deeds,” etc.].

### (Verse 16)

And upon his garment and upon his thigh he had written: “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

By the garment, as we said above, the saints are signified; by the thigh, from which human origin is said to proceed, the human being whom Christ assumed is signified.

On his garment, therefore, he had written that he himself is King of kings, because in the works of the saints it is recognized that the one who possesses such servants is the true God. He also has written upon his thigh that he is King of kings and Lord of lords, because in the works that he performed while present in the flesh it was made known that he is the true Son of God.

We can also understand by the thigh the fathers of the Old Testament, from whose lineage Christ derived his human origin. They prefigured him and openly foretold that he would be King of kings and Lord of lords.

### (Verse 15)

And from his mouth came forth a sharp sword.

By the Lord’s mouth we can understand the same preachers whom we mentioned, who will be born at the end of the world and through whose mouth God will speak, as he himself said in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). And through the prophet he says: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you will be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19).

By the sword we must understand divine Scripture, as we said above, as the apostle Paul says: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:17). It is called sharp because divine Scripture is exceedingly sharp for cutting away vices.

“So that with it he may strike the nations.”

Christ will strike the nations with his sword when, through the teaching of his saints, he destroys the errors of foolish people [Note: All editions read “of unbelieving people”; all manuscripts read “of foolish people.”].

“And he will rule them with an iron rod, and they will be broken like a potter’s vessel.”

We have said that the Gospel is signified by the iron rod. Christ will therefore rule the nations with an iron rod when, through the teaching of the saints, he both converts the Jews to his faith and protects the elect from the errors of Antichrist.

“And they will be broken like a clay vessel.”

As long as someone lies in sins, he is rightly called a clay vessel. But when, through repentance and tears, he has turned toward the practice of good works, the clay vessel is broken; and from a clay vessel he becomes a solid and firm vessel, exceedingly strong against the blows of demonic temptations.

“And he will tread the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.”

When Isaiah was speaking about the Lord’s passion, he introduced the Lord saying: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isa. 63:3). There the winepress signifies the Lord’s cross; here, however, it signifies not the cross but the place of punishment into which the wicked are to be thrust.

The winepress has the same meaning here as the pit was said above to have: into it the clusters of the vineyard of the earth, by which the wicked are signified, are said to have been plunged. The treading of the winepress also has the same meaning as the treading of the pit that we described there; for it signifies the final plunging of the wicked into hell.

What the wine of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty signifies, we explained above (on chapter 14).

### (Verse 17)

And I saw another angel standing in the sun, and he cried out with a loud voice to all the birds that were flying through the midst of heaven.

This angel signifies the preachers who will exist at the end of the world; they were also signified somewhat earlier by the horsemen. By the sun we must understand Christ.

The angel therefore stood in the sun because the holy preachers will be so firmly established in Christ that no force of persecution will be able to tear them away from his faith.

By the birds all the faithful who will exist at that time are signified. They will fly through heaven because, while placed on earth, they will dwell in heavenly things in their minds. We can also understand the Church by heaven. The saints fly through heaven because, possessing two wings—that is, the two commandments of love—they fly everywhere, showing mercy to some and recalling others from iniquities.

### (Verse 18)

“Come, gather together for the great supper of God the Almighty, so that you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of tribunes, and the flesh of the mighty, and the flesh of horses and of those who sit upon them, and the flesh of free persons and slaves, and of small and great.”

Those represented by kings and rulers, by free persons and slaves, and by the others are themselves represented by the horses and their riders—namely, the rulers of the earth and the peoples subject to them.

What else is God’s supper except the destruction of the wicked? The righteous will eat the flesh of the wicked when they receive vengeance for the evils that the wicked inflicted upon them. And because the righteous, seeing the punishment of the wicked, advance in good works, as the Psalmist says: “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. 57:11).

### (Verse 19)

And I saw the beast, and the kings of the earth and their armies gathered to wage war against the one seated upon the horse and against his army.

This shows that the passage does not refer to the Lord’s coming according to what was said above, but rather to that time when he will fight against Antichrist through his saints, as we have already said.

The beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies will gather to fight against Christ and his saints when Antichrist and the innumerable multitude of nations deceived by him rise up to persecute the Church of God, in order to extinguish Christ’s name utterly from the world.

### (Verses 20–21)

And the beast and the false prophet who performed signs before it were seized—signs by which he deceived those who had received the mark of the beast and those who had worshiped its image. These two were thrown alive into the lake of burning fire and sulfur; and the rest were killed by the sword of the one seated upon the horse, the sword that proceeded from his mouth. And all the birds were filled with their flesh.

The beast and his false prophet will be seized when what the apostle Paul says is fulfilled: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:8).

If Antichrist is to be killed by the spirit of the Lord’s mouth, how are he and his false prophet to be thrown alive into the lake of fire?

There is a life of the righteous, and there is also a life of the wicked. Concerning the life of the righteous, the prophet says: “The righteous will live by his faith” (Hab. 2:4). Concerning the wicked widow, Paul says: “The wicked widow, though living, is dead” (1 Tim. 5:6) [Note: So all the manuscripts; the edition, conversely, reads: “The prophet says that the righteous lives by faith”; but concerning the wicked life Paul says that “a widow living wickedly is dead.”].

The righteous appropriately call the life of the wicked death. Likewise, the wicked consider the life of the righteous death, as they will say at the judgment: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor” (Wis. 5:4).

Antichrist and his false prophet, then, are thrown alive into the lake of fire—that is, alive in their wickedness, persevering in it until the end of their lives.

But when he says that the rest were killed by the sword of the one seated upon the horse, he uses “killing” in the sense of confusion. For the saints, whose teaching is signified by the sword of the Lord’s mouth, will insult the unbelievers after Antichrist has been killed, because they considered that most wicked man, worse than all other human beings, to be immortal and a god, although it will be evident that he was put to death by the worst of deaths. They will then be confounded and waste away in their iniquities.

All the birds, therefore, were filled with their flesh because, after Antichrist has been overthrown, all the elect will rejoice and exult indescribably, since divine mercy will have delivered them from so wicked an enemy, and all who persecuted them will have vanished like smoke.

## Chapter XX

### (Verse 1)

And I saw an angel descending from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand.

Wishing to narrate the devil’s condemnation, he returns to Christ’s coming. For there are three condemnations of the devil.

He was condemned first when, because of his iniquity, he was cast down from heavenly blessedness. His second condemnation is the one of which the author of this book now begins to speak: when, through Christ’s death, the human race was snatched from his power, and he himself, as the present Scripture shows, was bound in the abyss [Note: In place of *religatus* (“bound”), some codices read *relegatus* (“banished”); but these two words are easily exchanged in manuscripts.]. His third condemnation will be when he is plunged into hell to be tormented eternally with all the wicked.

This angel, therefore, signifies Christ. His descent from heaven is his incarnation. He himself possesses the key of the abyss—that is, of hell—because he withdraws from entering it those whom he wishes, and justly permits those whom he wishes to fall into its condemnation.

By the great chain his power is signified.

### (Verse 2)

And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.

Christ seized the ancient serpent, that is, the devil, when through his death he destroyed the devil’s dominion. By the thousand years we must understand the entire period from Christ’s coming until the end of the world.

Christ therefore bound the devil not with bodily chains but with the bonds of his immense power, expelling him from the hearts of his elect and holding him excluded from deceiving them by his divine strength.

### (Verse 3)

And he threw him into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he might deceive the nations no more until the thousand years were completed. After this he must be released for a short time.

We can understand the devil’s binding in three ways.

We can understand it simply: that by the power of God Almighty he is kept bound in the abyss until the appointed time.

We can also understand the abyss as the hearts of the wicked, so that, excluded from the hearts of the elect, he is held confined and bound within the narrowness of the hearts of the reprobate.

We can understand it in a third way as well. The devil desires nothing other than the deception of human beings. While, by the guardianship of God Almighty—who does not cease to guard and defend his elect—he is kept from deceiving them, his most wicked will is held bound as though by certain chains.

By the nations whom he is not permitted to deceive, we must understand the elect alone. The short time in which he is said to be released after the thousand years is the time of Antichrist. Then, because of the sins of human beings, the devil will be given power to fight against the human race with all his strength.

### (Verse 4)

And I saw thrones, and those seated upon them, and judgment was given to them.

Since above he narrated how divine mercy daily delivers its elect from the devil, that most savage enemy, it follows that he should describe the glory to which their souls are daily led.

By the thrones, therefore, the heavenly homeland is signified; by those seated upon them, the souls of the saints. That judgment has been given to the saints, whose souls rest in heavenly blessedness, we can recognize from this: at their tombs we often see demons expelled from possessed bodies, perjuries exposed, and many miracles performed.

And the souls of those who had been killed for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus, and of those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark upon their foreheads or their hands. They lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.

By the souls of those who were killed for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus, we can understand the martyrs who were killed at various times. By those who did not worship the beast and its image, I think we are to understand those who will be killed by Antichrist.

These, then, lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years because, although they were killed in body, they nevertheless live with Christ in heavenly blessedness according to the soul.

But we must ask how the elect who will be born when the end of the world is at hand are said to reign with Christ for a thousand years, when the period of a thousand years does not pertain to the future time, which is without end, but rather to the present time, which will be completed at the end of the world and in which the faith of the Gospel, flourishing throughout the whole world, daily directs the elect toward receiving eternal life.

I think this should be resolved as follows. The time from Christ’s ascension until the end of the world, designated by the thousand years, has been assigned to all the elect, so that during it they may enjoy heavenly glory with the Lord without their bodies.

And we know that all the elect are members of Christ, and that from many members one body is formed; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it. The joy of the saints who came before will therefore also belong to those who will be born at the end of the world, because they will become one body with them and will possess in others what they themselves lack.

### (Verse 5)

But the rest did not live until the thousand years were completed.

The rest—that is, the reprobate—did not live, because after death they are not led to the life that is given to the souls of the saints in heaven; rather, they are plunged into hell, which in this book is called the first death [Note: The Roman edition and the Regius manuscript read: “which is called the second death … Blessed and holy is the one who has,” etc.].

### (Verse 6)

This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; over such the second death has no power.

We must ask what the first resurrection is. For he would not call it the first resurrection unless there were also a second, nor the second death unless there were also a first.

We therefore rise first through baptism from the death of the soul. But since he says that those who have a share in the first resurrection are blessed, this does not seem to me to have been said of baptism, because not all who appear to rise through baptism from the death of the soul are blessed. Some, after baptism, bring death upon themselves by sinning: by lying about what they promised in baptism and by persevering in their evils.

There are also some who, after committing crimes by which they brought death upon themselves, return to life through repentance and tears and other good works. The Apostle speaks of them, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

But we cannot call this the first resurrection either, because first, through baptism, and second, through repentance and tears, our souls are recalled to life.

We must therefore investigate which resurrection he calls the first.

Four are the lives of the faithful: the first evil, the second both good and evil, while no evil can cling to the third and fourth. The first is before baptism, and is wholly evil; the second is after baptism, and may be called both good and evil. For no believer can pass through the period of the present life without some sins, as this John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

The third is wholly good, and this is the life to which the sequence of the present reading pertains. It extends from Christ’s Passion to the end of the world; in it the saints, without their bodies, enjoy eternal life with the Lord. He also calls this the first resurrection when he says: “This is the first resurrection.” The period, therefore, from Christ’s Passion to the end of the world is called the first resurrection.

The fourth life of the saints will be after the reception of their bodies, and it will be ended by no limit. Therefore, since the present life may rightly be called death in comparison with heavenly life, the saints rise in the first resurrection when, having been removed from this wretched life, they are placed with the Lord in heavenly blessedness.

And just as this is the first resurrection of the saints, so there is also a first death of the wicked, when they abandon the present life and are plunged into punishments. The second death, however, will be the final condemnation, as he explains in what follows. Blessed, therefore, will be those who have a share in the first resurrection, and over them the second death has no power; for only those are and will be blessed who before the end of the world have deserved to be enrolled in the company of the saints.

For, as the end of the world approaches, the purifying fire will burn many as it purifies them; but, having been acquitted before the judgment, they will be received into the fellowship of the saints. Over them the second death—that is, the final condemnation—will have no power, because they will now be placed not with the goats on the left, but with the sheep on the right.

“They sat as priests of God and of Christ, and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (Matthew 25:33). By the name “priests” he includes all the elect; for all the elect are called priests, either because they are members of the High Priest, or because they do not cease to offer themselves to God through good works.

### (Verse 7)

“And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and he will go out and deceive the nations that are over the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog.”

What is here called a prison was above called the abyss. But meanwhile a question arises. Earlier, following the opinion of certain persons, I said that by the abyss the hearts of the wicked could be signified, in which the devil, expelled from the hearts of the faithful, is held bound. If, then, the hearts of the reprobate are signified by the abyss, how is he said to come out of the abyss—that is, from the hearts of the reprobate—whom he will never abandon? Is he perhaps going to abandon the reprobate and attack the elect? By no means.

I therefore think that the binding of the devil is to be understood literally: he is held bound by divine power in some place of the abyss, or certainly in hell, until the day of his release. He will deceive the nations that are over the four corners of the earth, because his most wicked doctrine through Antichrist will traverse all the nations contained beneath the four regions of the world. He will deceive no other nations except those who are spiritually called Gog and Magog. For Gog means “roof,” and Magog “from the roof.”

By Gog, therefore, which means “roof,” are signified those who conceal their wickedness in their hearts and will appear righteous to human beings, although in mind they will be reprobate. Magog, however, which means “from the roof,” signifies those who burst forth from the roof of their heart into open miseries, displaying to everyone that they are impious.

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Thus the manuscripts and Gill’s text; Gill’s margin and the Roman edition’s text instead read, “into open wickedness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0931D] In the printed edition, “Magog from the roof” had been omitted.]

The devil will therefore easily deceive such people through Antichrist.

### (Verse 8)

“And he will gather them for battle, whose number is like the sand of the sea.”

He will gather them for battle because he will arm them to persecute the Church of God.

“And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.”

We said above that the disciples of Antichrist would be praisers of vices and would teach everything pertaining to carnal pleasures. Therefore they went up over the breadth of the earth because they will enter upon the broad ways of this age, which lead to death.

The camp of the saints and the beloved city have one meaning: they signify the Church. They will therefore surround the camp of the saints because they will persecute the Church of God with all their strength, so that they may utterly extinguish the name of Christ from the world.

### (Verse 9)

“And fire went forth from heaven from God and devoured them.”

Fire will come down from heaven because, when the Lord comes for judgment, fire will go before him. It will consume not only the entire host of the wicked but also the world itself, as David says in the ninety-sixth Psalm: “Fire will go before him and burn his enemies round about” (Psalm 96:3).

Although the reprobate live among the elect, they are “round about,” because, just as enemies attack a city in order to capture it, so the Church is attacked by the reprobate.

David also says in the forty-ninth Psalm: “Fire will blaze before him, and a mighty tempest around him” (Psalm 49:3). Some explain this verse to mean that after the burning of the elements rain will descend to wash away the ashes of the conflagration. But such an explanation seems utterly absurd to me. For we know that rain rises from the sea and from the earth, either through mist or through the drying action of the sun.

And just as water raises whatever is light from the bottom to the upper regions, so the air raises water—either transformed into mist or reduced by the sun’s heat to the thinnest and almost invisible vapor—up to the places where its completion occurs. There it gathers together and is first changed into a dense mist, which we call a cloud. Then, as the wind drives it, the tiniest drops are mingled together and made heavy by their mingling; they fall to the earth and produce rain.

Behold the earth, the air, the sea, and the other elements: they will be consumed by fire. From where, then, will rain arise, especially since, according to the Apostle, creation will then be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:21)? Will God, who created all things from nothing, not be able to cleanse his creation without the help of rain—especially since the world itself will be restored after the fire to a better and much more beautiful condition?

Or what else are ashes but clean earth? Whatever filth the fire consumes, it turns into clean ashes. Will God not be able to restore clean ashes to a better condition together with another earth, so that the rain of cleansing is not necessary for it?

Let us give another explanation. Every cleansing of filth is either absorbed by the earth or flows into rivers, and with the rivers into the sea. But how will the earth, after it has been tested by fire, absorb its filth and become filthy again? Or how will it flow into rivers and with the rivers into the sea, when the sea will no longer exist, as the following passages of this book seem to acknowledge? And if the sea will be restored to a better state, just as heaven and earth will be, how will it be polluted by the filth of the earth?

If someone should say that the sea will suffer this pollution before its renewal, and that the impurities will be reduced to nothing when it is transformed, will God not be able, just as with water, to reduce those same impurities in the earth to nothing, so that it is not necessary for them to flow into the sea?

By the mighty tempest, therefore, we can understand the final destruction of the wicked, which Wisdom testifies through Solomon that it will bring upon the impious at the final judgment, saying: “I also will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you; when sudden calamity falls upon you, and destruction rushes upon you like a tempest” (Proverbs 1:26).

“And the devil who was deceiving them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet are.”

This will be fulfilled when the Lord says: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41).

[Note: [Col. 0933D] The printed edition had omitted “which was prepared for the devil and his angels.”]

### (Verse 10)

“And they will be tormented day and night for ages of ages.”

May the mercy of our Redeemer deign to free us from that torment—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## ON THE SIXTH VISION

By the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have reached the sixth vision, which is shorter than the others because in it the general resurrection, the condemnation of the wicked, and the glorification of the righteous are described only briefly. And rightly the final resurrection is placed in the sixth position, because the number six is perfect, and whatever has been promised to the saints will be completed in the resurrection.

### (Verse 11)

“And I saw a great and white throne, and the one sitting upon it.”

This throne of God will not be adorned with gold and gems but with righteous human beings. For this is the throne of which the Psalmist says: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom” (Psalm 44:7).

The throne of God, therefore, is the entire multitude of angels and saints.

“From whose presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them.”

How heaven and earth flee from the presence of the one sitting upon the throne, the Psalmist shows, as we already said above, when he says: “Fire will blaze before him” (Psalm 49:3); and again: “Fire will go before him” (Psalm 96:3).

Earth and heaven will flee—that is, the appearance of earth and heaven—because through fire they will be changed from their present appearance, so that they can be reformed into another, much better and more beautiful one. When he says, “No place was found for them,” he does not mean that they will lose their former place, but their appearance.

### (Verse 13)

“And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne.”

By the great and small dead, only the reprobate are signified. On the day of the resurrection they will stand dead before God, in the death that we have said is the first, shortly afterward to be cast into the second death.

By the great dead, I think those are signified who were either greater in their crimes or higher in the dignities of this world. By the small are signified those who were subject to them, or certainly those who sinned less.

“And the books were opened; and another book was opened, which is the book of life.”

The many books pertain to the reprobate; the one book, which is the book of life, pertains to the elect. The reprobate have many books because they have fallen into many errors. Pagans worshiped many gods and cast themselves down into many errors. Likewise, heretics devised many perverse doctrines hateful to God. False Christians, too, are daily entangled in many crimes.

The reprobate therefore possess many books because they offend God in many ways. The elect, however, have one book because they worship one God, confess one catholic faith, and are joined by one bond of charity.

But we must ask what these books are. Will books perhaps be made from some visible or invisible material in which the deeds of individuals will be written?

The many books, then, are the deeds of the reprobate. The many books will be opened when the crimes of the reprobate are made manifest to everyone. By the book of life, however, we can understand the predestination of almighty God. The Lord reveals in the Gospel that the names of the disciples are written in this book when he says: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

The Apostle Paul speaks of this book, saying: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also glorified” (Romans 8:30).

### (Verse 13)

“And the dead were judged according to what was written in the books, according to their works.”

[Note: [Col. 0935D] In the printed edition, “They were judged according to what was written in the books” was not repeated; in the manuscripts, however, it is repeated in this way.]

The dead were judged according to what was written in the books because each will be judged according to his own errors and in accordance with the character of his crimes. Heretics will be judged in one way, pagans in another, and false Christians in another. Each of them, the worse he has been in his own error, will be judged more severely.

“And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and death and hell gave up the dead who were in them; and each was judged according to their works.”

He now returns to matters that he had passed over. First the general resurrection will take place, and afterward judgment will be carried out. The Lord makes this clear in the Gospel when he says to the disciples: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28).

First he mentioned the regeneration—that is, the resurrection—and afterward he said that they would sit to judge the peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0935D] The printed editions omitted “that is, the resurrection.”]

And in the Gospel of this John the Lord says: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29).

At the Lord’s command, therefore, the dead will come forth from their tombs because the bodies of all the dead, made alive by the reception of their souls, will come out of their graves. Those who have done evil will come forth to the resurrection of judgment because they will rise for this purpose: to be judged in the bodies in which their souls sinned, so that those whom they had as partners in iniquities they may have as companions in torments.

The present reading also shows that the resurrection will occur before the judgment, since after it says that the dead were given up by the sea, death, and hell, it relates that the wicked are to be judged.

The catholic faith that we frequently chant also demonstrates this when it says of the Lord: “At whose coming all human beings must rise with their bodies and give an account of their own deeds” (Athanasian Creed).

Yet we must ask what death, the sea, and hell signify.
