We know that the waters have been consecrated for the washing away of our sins, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

The sea, therefore, pertains to the resurrection of the elect; death and hell, however, pertain to the reprobate.

[Note: [Col. 0936D] The same printed edition reads, “to the rejection of the reprobate”; the manuscripts, except the Regius manuscript, do not have “rejection.” The word “dead” may, however, be taken to refer to the resurrection.]

The sea in this passage therefore signifies baptism. As though the sea were to give up its dead, the elect who have received that purity in baptism will rise in that same purity, having no stain of sin. The sea will give up its dead because the washing of holy baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit will present all the elect, at the time of the resurrection, clean and immaculate in the presence of their Creator.

By death we can understand the bodies of the wicked, which are held dead in the recesses of the earth; by hell, their souls, because they are held confined in the chambers of hell. Hell will therefore give up its dead because it will send back the souls devoured by the first death, which it holds, to receive their own bodies.

Death, too, will give up its dead because it will present the bodies that it had reduced to dust, so that they may be made alive by divine power through the reception of their souls.

### (Verses 14–15)

“And death and hell were thrown into the lake of fire … and whoever was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the furnace of fire.”

Death and hell were thrown into the lake of fire—that is, souls together with bodies. By death we may also understand the demons, since they were the authors of death. Death and hell will be thrown into the lake because the demons will be plunged into hell together with the other wicked.

## CHAPTER XXI

### (Verse 1)

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more.”

Heaven and earth, and the other elements that we now see, will be consumed by fire—not so that they may be utterly destroyed, but so that they may be restored through fire to a better condition, as we already said above. The Psalmist indicates this when he says: “They will perish, but you will remain; and they will all grow old like a garment, and you will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101:27).

When he says, “The first heaven and the first earth passed away,” he demonstrates that the appearance of that heaven and earth will pass away. Their appearance, not their essence, will pass away when they are changed into a better condition.

When he adds, “And the sea is no more,” we can understand it literally, so that the sea will be entirely destroyed. Alternatively, the sea will no longer exist because it will lose its proper form, just as heaven and earth will, in order to be restored in a more beautiful form.

But I think this should be understood spiritually. Whatever has been said about the renewal of heaven and earth must be understood both historically, as we said above, and spiritually.

We can therefore understand heaven as the souls of the saints and earth as their bodies. A new heaven will be made when the souls of the saints, through the reception of their bodies, are restored to the nature and form of human beings. A new earth will be made when the bodies of the saints, which were previously mortal and corruptible, are made immortal and incorruptible.

Often, however, the wicked are signified by the sea, as the prophet Isaiah says: “The wicked are like a boiling sea that cannot rest, and its waves cast up mud and mire” (Isaiah 57:20).

The sea, therefore, will no longer exist because the entire multitude of the wicked, having been thrust into hell with their deceiving demons, will leave the present face of the world clean from their polluted habitation.

### (Verse 2)

“And I saw the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.”

The city Jerusalem is the Church, constructed from all the righteous. It will descend from heaven because, when the Lord comes for judgment, the entire multitude of the saints will come with him, as the prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes” (Isaiah 3:14).

And the most wise Solomon says in Proverbs: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Proverbs 31:23).

She is said to be prepared and adorned like a bride because, just as a bride adorns herself with various jewels and ornaments in order to please her bridegroom, so the Church is adorned with various virtues so that she may be able to please her Creator, who is her bridegroom.

### (Verse 3)

“And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: ‘Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them; and they will be his people, and the Lord himself will be with them as their God.’”

We know that the city Jerusalem and the Lord’s tabernacle often signify the Church. In this passage, therefore, the city and the tabernacle are called the Church because God dwells in her, as he himself says through the prophet: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Leviticus 26:12).

### (Verse 4)

“And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.”

The souls of all human beings were created immortal, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28).

Although souls may die through sin, or by the death that we have called the first and the second, they do not die in such a way that they cease entirely to exist; rather, their evil condition is called death.

God has also appointed two periods for them: the present life, which quickly comes to an end, and the future life, which cannot come to an end. He has assigned one to weeping and sorrow, and the other to joy and gladness.

For example, if someone were willing in this present and very brief period to weep and mourn for his sins, and by afflicting himself to extinguish carnal desires, then in the other period that follows this one, which is without end, he would rejoice and exult forever.

But if someone chooses to rejoice in the present period and fulfill the desires of his flesh, then in the future he will mourn and be sad forever.

It seems to me that Solomon spoke of these two periods when he said: “A time for weeping and a time for laughing” (Ecclesiastes 3:2). The time of weeping is now for the elect; the time of laughing will be then, when what the Lord says in the Gospel is fulfilled: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:5).

But to sinners he says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25).

God will therefore wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints because after the resurrection nothing sorrowful will be able to happen to the saints from which tears could arise.

“And death will be no more.”

The first human being was made immortal; but by sinning he both lost immortality and brought death into the world. After the resurrection, however, death will be no more because the prince of death himself, the devil, together with all his attendants, will be kept confined forever in hell; the immortality that the first human being lost by sinning will be restored to the righteous; and the possibility of sinning, which brought death into the world, will be taken away from them.

“Neither will there be mourning.”

Since above he says that God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, why was it necessary to mention mourning in this passage? But there is some difference between the shedding of tears and mourning. For sadness often draws forth tears, but so do joy, desire, and gladness.

[Note: [Col. 0937] Thus the manuscripts; the printed edition reads, “often joy, often gladness.” Not well.]

Mourning, however, always arises from great sorrow; mourning is the weeping of many days.

Paul mourned for those who had sinned and had not done penance. Solomon also says: “The mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but the mourning of a fool lasts all the days of his life” (Sirach 22:13).

The Church is now in mourning because through the deceptions of demons she daily loses a great part of her own. But in that life there will be no mourning because through the deceptions of demons she will not be able to lose any of her own.

“Neither will there be an outcry.”

In Genesis it is written that God said to Abraham: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come to me” (Genesis 18:20). The prophet Isaiah explains what the outcry of Sodom is when he speaks about Israel: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and they did not hide it” (Isaiah 3:9).

The proclamation of sin is therefore called an outcry.

We can also understand outcry in another way. The Psalmist says: “When I was in distress, I cried to the Lord, and he heard me” (Psalm 119:1). Moses, too, when placed in distress, cried to the Lord.

Where, therefore, there will be neither sin to proclaim nor any tribulation, no outcry will be necessary.

“Neither will there be pain.”

There is bodily pain, and there is also pain of the mind. These pains are so connected that one cannot exist without the other: bodily pain afflicts the mind, and likewise pain of the mind torments the body.

In that life, therefore, there will be no pain, where no adversity can befall either body or soul.

“For the former things have passed away.”

These former things have passed away because they passed away with the age. The elect, who—as we already said above—assigned the present life to pains and afflictions, have found everlasting joy after the end of the present life.

### (Verses 5–6)

“And the one who was sitting upon the throne said: ‘Behold, I make all things new.’”

We have already said something above about the renewal of created things.

“And he said to me: ‘Write, because these words are most trustworthy and true.’”

This too was said above.

“And he said to me: ‘I am Alpha and Omega.’”

He explains what “Alpha and Omega” means by adding: “The beginning and the end.”

“I will give freely to the one who thirsts from the fountain of the water of life.”

Holy Scripture is often signified by the fountain of living water, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38).

But, to preserve the order of interpretation, by the fountain of living water we should understand the glory of the heavenly homeland. This fountain, proceeding from the Lord himself, does not cease to satisfy the minds of all the righteous with its indescribable sweetness.

But how is this glory given freely to the righteous, when they endure many adversities to receive it, shed many tears, offer countless prayers, distribute many alms, and exercise themselves in other good works?

They receive eternal life freely because they receive from him the price of eternal life, which consists in good works, who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). He himself gives the price, and he himself grants eternal life in exchange for the price.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] Gill’s printed text has “he gives the price, and without a price”; in the margin, and in the Roman edition in the text, “he gives the price, and by his own price.” The manuscripts support us.]

### (Verses 7–8)

“The one who conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son.”

Whoever conquers the devil, overcomes every vice, and perseveres in good works will possess these things—that is, the things mentioned above: namely, that he himself may drink from the fountain of eternal life, which is everlasting glory.

“But for the timid, the unbelieving, the abominable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake of burning fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

Since fear is extremely necessary for human beings, why did he place fear first among eight very evil vices? But there are good fears, and there are evil ones.

There is a very excellent fear, of which the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm 18:10). There is also the very necessary fear of death and the fear of eternal fire. There is even the fear of good people when they are loved by those who fear them.

There are other fears that sometimes help and sometimes harm, such as fear of evil people, fear of judges, and fear of masters. There are also very evil fears, and I think these are meant here.

There are some who are often moved to tears by fear of punishments; but because they fear the roughness of the road that leads to life, they hesitate to abandon their vices and are afraid to undertake the rigor of a good life.

There are also many to whom God has given knowledge of the temporal laws. When placed in judgment, they see some people unjustly oppressed by the powerful. Fearing human anger more than the anger of God, they allow those whom they could have helped and rescued from danger through the instruction they received to come to great harm by their silence.

There are others who not only do not help them but, because of fear of human beings, pronounce a sentence of condemnation against them.

There is also the fear produced by greed, along with other very useless fears, about which it would take too long to speak.

“Unbelieving” does not refer only to those who do not believe, such as Jews and pagans, but also to those who do not believe in the resurrection.

There are also many others who are called Christians but do not believe in God’s justice. Because they love vices and want to fulfill the desires of their flesh, they do not believe the threats of the divine Scriptures, so that they think they will not be condemned for such things.

For the lustful say that no one will in any way perish because of sexual intercourse. Drunkards likewise say that they will in no way be punished for excessive drinking of wine. Similarly, the greedy, the extravagant, and the proud defend their vices.

I think that “the abominable” are those who abominate the commandments of the divine Scriptures and the corrections of good people. We may also understand by “the abominable” those who are so shameless that they are not ashamed to commit certain detestable acts in the sight of everyone. They are often abominated not only by the righteous but also by some of the unrighteous.

“Murderers” does not refer only to those who kill particular human beings, but also to those who carry hatred in their hearts, as this John says: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Fornication follows. There are many kinds of fornication. In whatever ways the desire of lust is fulfilled apart from a lawful wife, it is called fornication.

The Apostle Paul speaks of the evil of fornication when he says: “The one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18). He sins against his own body because he violates and corrupts its integrity, violently drawing out and expelling its harmless fluids.

There is also fornication of thought, of which the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28).

The prophet also called Jerusalem a fornicator because, abandoning God, she worshiped idols (Ezekiel 16:15 ff.). Likewise, when we obey the suggestions of demons and subject ourselves to them, we are not inappropriately called fornicators.

Sorcerers are those who infect human bodies with poison in order to destroy them. But there are other sorcerers much worse than these: namely, those who sow discord among brothers. The former kill bodies; the latter, souls. The death of the soul is much worse than that of the body.

Idolaters are not only those who worship idols but also all the greedy, as the Apostle Paul demonstrates when he calls greed the service of idols (Colossians 3:5).

But what follows is extremely frightening: “And all liars.” He then adds: “Their portion will be in the lake of burning fire and sulfur, which is the second death.” The Psalmist says to the Lord: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7); and elsewhere: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11).

If every human being is a liar, and if God will destroy all who speak lies, and if all liars will have a share in destruction with the other wicked about whom we have spoken up to this point, who will be able to be saved?

For we know that no human being can pass through this life without ever lying—unless it is an infant who cannot speak.

But we must understand that this is not said about every kind of lie, just as the statement sung in the thirty-sixth Psalm is not about all sinners: “Because sinners will perish” (Psalm 36:20), nor is the statement in the hundred and forty-fourth Psalm: “The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners” (Psalm 144:20).

If sinners will perish, and he will destroy all sinners, and we are all sinners according to the statement of this John—“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)—then we shall all perish.

But we must understand that this is not said about all sinners, but only about those who plunge themselves into grave sins and do not wish to do penance for their iniquities.

Likewise here, we must understand that this is not said about all liars. There are lies that are counted among light sins, and I think that no human being can entirely abstain from them. There are also serious lies that plunge a person into the condemnation of death.

But because in these times there are many who lie almost constantly without any reverence for almighty God, it has pleased us to say something about this vice. First, however, let us speak about light lies, and afterward about the more serious ones.

We often lie through judgment, imagining that we see what we do not see, or hear what we do not hear, or know what we do not know. For often, when we look at certain people from a distance, our sight deceives us, and we say that people are present who are not.

Often, too, in dim conditions, when we see stones or shrubs at a distance, we are deceived by the darkness and say that they are human beings or animals.

Often we are deceived through forgetfulness. When we forget what we have done, seen, or said, we claim to have done what we did not do, or not to have done what we did; to have heard what we did not hear, or not to have heard what we did hear; to have seen what we did not see, or not to have seen what we did see; to have said what we did not say, or not to have said what we did say.

Often, too, when we hear what we desire, we say that what we hear is true, although it frequently turns out to be false. And when we hear what we do not want, we say that it is false, even though it is true.

Often we also lie in jest, in order to provoke laughter in those who hear us.

But often we lie out of excessive credulity. When we have heard certain people whom we consider truthful telling plausible stories, we believe what we hear. When we repeat it to others, we say that it is true, although it is false; and we frequently affirm it with an oath.

There are also many who, having partly forgotten the deeds of the Fathers that they have either read or heard in the divine Scriptures, when they begin to recount them to others, either insert certain lies or try to make one account out of many. Just as someone who mixes tin with gold or silver makes a useless material, so these people, when they strive to make one account out of many, render it useless by lying. For it is better to remain silent than to relate the deeds of the saints falsely. [Col. 0942A]

There are also many learned in the divine writings who, believing the Jews more than they ought, accept some of their exceedingly empty fables and insert them into their own traditions. For we know that the Jews strive to twist into perverse meanings everything found in the Old Testament concerning Christ, so that they may extinguish the glory of Christ’s name among as many people as they can. And not only do they overturn the prophecies concerning Christ, but in other passages as well they introduce many exceedingly empty [Note: [Col. 0941D] The printed edition has “and exceedingly obscure fables”; the manuscripts have “and exceedingly absurd fables.”] and absurd fables. I therefore marvel why credence is given to the enemies of Christ and of our entire religion, or why anything is accepted from them, except only what is known to have been approved by the ancient Fathers. For they have as their father the devil, who did not stand in the truth, because he is himself a liar and its father; and whoever the devil possesses, he makes liars (John 8:44). [Col. 0942B]

We also often lie out of fear. For when we fear that some trouble may be inflicted upon us by those more powerful than ourselves, we sometimes devise lies by which we may be freed. Travelers, too, commonly invent certain lies in order to escape from robbers. Likewise, slaves and children often insert certain lies so that they will not be beaten. There are also many who, placed in foreign regions, lie because of poverty or some necessity, so that they may acquire food or some necessities for the body.

Often, too, we lie out of love and anger: we praise those whom we love beyond measure, and condemn those with whom we are angry more than is proper. But these seem to me more serious than the preceding kinds. [Col. 0942C] There are other lies similar to those already mentioned, which it would take too long to pursue; for not only the unjust but often the just as well slip into such lies. And for this reason it seems to me that the Psalmist said: “Every man is a liar” (Psalm 115:11).

There is also another kind of lie that would seem to be without guilt, unless Scripture said that every lie is from evil; examples of it are found in the divine Scriptures (1 John 2:21). [Note: [Col. 0942D] The printed edition has “In Exodus”; Gill places it in the margin, while the Roman edition has it in the text. Gill, however, places “In Genesis” in the text together with the manuscripts.] For in Genesis it is written that Pharaoh commanded the Hebrew midwives to kill the males and preserve the females (Exodus 1:16). But they, fearing God, preserved the male children. When Pharaoh rebuked them for this, they said that all the Hebrew women possessed knowledge of midwifery and that they gave birth before the midwives came to them. Was it not better to preserve the children by lying than, by telling the truth, to commit so many murders?

It is also written in Joshua that he sent two spies to explore Jericho (Joshua 2:2 and following). They entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab, who hid them in the inner parts of her house. When their pursuers came, she said that, when the gate was being closed, they had fled in the darkness. By this lie she freed them from their pursuers, and she herself, together with her entire family, was freed from danger of death. For this deed she is praised by blessed Paul the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews; for he says: “By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace” (Hebrews 11:31). [Col. 0943A]

It is also written in the Book of Kings that David, fleeing from his son Absalom, sent two spies from Jerusalem to investigate the actions of that same son (2 Samuel 15:32 and following). When Absalom heard of this, he sent men to seize them. But they, fleeing, entered the house of a certain man, whose wife hid them in a well that he had in the vestibule, placing a covering over it. When their pursuers came and asked for them, she replied: “They passed on, having tasted a little water” (2 Samuel 17:20). By telling the truth, she could have destroyed those whom she saved by lying. The stains of such lies, therefore, are wiped away by the charity from which they proceed, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). [Col. 0943B]

Now let us speak of more serious lies. There are lies of unbelief, lies of blasphemy, and others that proceed from hatred; others are generated by envy, others by greed, and others by vainglory. The remaining vices likewise have lies suited to themselves.

The unbelieving Jews and pagans have very many lies. Apart from denying that Christ came in the flesh, they possess many errors by which they are deceived and perish. There are also lies of blasphemy, by which those same Jews and pagans, and likewise heretics, blaspheme God and his Church, together with all the divine mysteries, in many ways.

There are also lies that proceed from hatred. For some, because they harbor hatred in their hearts against their neighbors, fasten false accusations upon them. Those whom they cannot kill with the sword they often cast into great ruin, and even into death, by false accusations. [Col. 0943C]

There are also other lies that envy produces. For the envious, when they see certain people excelling in worldly dignities, wisdom, or some skills, never cease to despise and mock them, and to place themselves above them, so that they may appear more distinguished in the eyes of those who believe their lies than those whom they despise.

There are also lies of mockery, which properly belong to the envious. For the envious always mock the deeds of better people, and seek by their lies to obscure the actions of those whom they cannot equal.

There are many who, pretending to be friends of those whom they hate or envy, draw them by their cunning persuasions into committing certain crimes. When they have hurled them into some wicked deed as into a pit, they turn against them and persecute them more fiercely than the others; and those who seemed to be friends are shown to have been the worst enemies. [Col. 0943D]

Greed, too, has its lies. How many there are who, in order to seize the possessions of others, devise many deceptions and various schemes, so that they may take away from others what will somewhat satisfy the abyss of their greed, which is insatiable! There are also many who, in exchange for receiving rewards, become false witnesses against their neighbors, and by lying either plunge them into slavery, or deprive them of their inheritance or property, [Note: [Col. 0943] “They often even cause death” has been restored from the manuscripts.] and often even cause their death. [Col. 0944A]

There are other lies that vainglory engenders. For there are many lovers of vainglory who, in order to be regarded by people as great and outstanding, say that they have done great things that they have not done, or that they can do what they cannot, or that they possess what they do not possess, or that they know what they do not know. Thus their lies may lift them to a height which they cannot climb.

And because this vice is considered by some to be nothing, we know that even in monasteries certain people are stained by it. There are many who, after appearing to have left the world, so establish themselves as great and famous among the simple-minded and among those brought up in monasteries that they say they once possessed great riches, boast that they were fighters and hunters, and lie about many other things concerning themselves, so that they may be regarded as great by those whom they can deceive with their lies. [Col. 0944B]

To you, then, who are such a person, I speak: Behold, when you were in the world, you could scarcely labor throughout the entire year to obtain simple food sufficient for you and all your household; but once placed in a monastery, you become the possessor of treasures, estates, and great riches. You could scarcely catch one little fox, but after becoming a monk you have become a most powerful hunter. You feared certain of your lowliest neighbors, but once placed in a monastery you have made yourself a most valiant fighter. Behold, this was not leaving the world but acquiring it.

You say that you killed a man, [Col. 0944C] and have laid upon yourself the guilt of murder. The lying tongue did what the hand could not accomplish. And do you want me to prove that by lying you made yourself guilty of murder?

Saul, as we read in the Book of Kings (2 Samuel 31:4), killed himself with his own hand out of fear of the Philistines. A certain man came to holy David and said that he himself had killed Saul, who was persecuting him. But David, understanding by the prophetic spirit that he had lied, ordered him to be punished as a murderer. Laying the guilt of murder upon him, he said: “Your blood be upon your head; for your mouth has spoken against you, saying: I myself killed the Lord’s anointed” (2 Samuel 1:16).

We know that the rich of this world, when they come to conversion, sin gravely if they begin to boast of their riches and power. [Col. 0944D] And if he is guilty who tells the truth, how much more are you, who lie in almost everything?

There are also others who lie almost without interruption and can scarcely say anything without an admixture of falsehood. To everything they hear they always fabricate some lies, saying that they have seen what they have not seen, heard what they have not heard, and done what they have not done. When they are caught by truthful people, they say that no one can speak the truth well who cannot lie well.

O fool, how empty is your assertion! Behold, Christ spoke many things well and truthfully, and he could never lie; you ought rather to have followed his footsteps, insofar as virtue afforded you the strength. Likewise, the apostles and the other preachers taught and wrote many things without any admixture of falsehood.

And Scripture says that every lie is from evil (1 John 2:22). If lying is evil, how can evil be spoken well? O unhappy man, [Note: [Col. 0945D] The printed edition and certain manuscripts have “how empty it is”; Gem. has the better reading, “how near it is.”] how near is the anger of almighty God to you, whom you do not fear constantly to offend without cause!

For although the other vices are contrary to the Lord, they nevertheless seem to contribute something to the body. Greed, although it is altogether hateful to God, nevertheless seems to contribute something to the body, because it gathers riches with which it may satisfy its desires. Likewise, lust seems to contribute something to the body, because in its fulfillment the pleasure of the flesh is extinguished. [Col. 0945B] Drunkenness, too, although it offends God, fulfills the desires of the appetite. In the same way, the other vices are taken up for the fulfillment of the desires of the flesh.

There are also certain lies that seem to add something to the body, such as the lies of greed mentioned above. But you acquire nothing for the body, and yet you do not fear offending God without interruption. Behold, your lie would be slight if it occurred only rarely; but through continual repetition it becomes exceedingly serious and intolerable.

For just as mud is lighter than lead, but through accumulation becomes heavier and more dangerous, so that animals often sink in it, in the same way certain light sins, through accumulation, become more serious than some sins considered grave. And know that, as he himself said, “God is truth” (1 John 5:6); nothing can be more contrary to truth than a lie. [Col. 0945C]

Their portion, therefore, will be in the pool of burning fire and sulfur, which is the second death. What the second death is, he clearly demonstrates in this passage. May the mercy of our Redeemer deign to free us from the vices mentioned above, lest we fall into the second death—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## THE SEVENTH VISION

The seventh vision, to which by the Lord’s gift we have come, pertains entirely to that time which will occur after the resurrection (above, ch. 15). The order required that, after describing the general resurrection, he should describe the glory of the saints, which they will possess without end after the resurrection; this is described under the figure of the city of Jerusalem in the present vision.

### (Verse 9)

“And one of the seven angels who had the bowls came and spoke with me, saying: Come, and I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”

Earlier, in the fifth vision, John says that seven angels holding seven bowls were shown to him, and that in what follows one of them showed him the city of the devil and its condemnation under the appearance of a prostitute. Likewise here he says that one of those same seven angels showed him the city of God under the figure of Jerusalem. These individual angels therefore have the same significance as those seven: they signify the preachers who have existed and will exist until the end. John, however, represents the other faithful.

The angel therefore promises John that he will show him the city of God, because the holy preachers strive, insofar as they can, to show the other faithful how great is the blessedness of the righteous, so that they may kindle them to receive eternal life.

He also calls it the bride, the wife of the Lamb. That the Church is rightly called the Lamb’s bride is shown by John the Baptist, who says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). That she is also called a wife is shown by Scripture, which says: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

It is as though the Son of God left his Father when, descending from that heavenly blessedness to earth, he assumed humanity, which he would give for his bride, the Church. He left his mother because, setting aside a mother’s affection, he surrendered the body that he had assumed from her for his Church; and he united her to himself in such a way that he is the head and she is the body.

### (Verse 10)

“And he lifted me up onto a great and high mountain.”

This mountain is Christ. Concerning this mountain the Prophet says: “And it shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the top of the mountains” (Isaiah 2:2). The mountains upon whose summit the mountain of the house of the Lord is said to be prepared signify the Fathers of the Old Testament. [Note: [Col. 0945D] “Therefore upon their … he has surpassed it” is restored from a manuscript; it is absent from the other manuscripts and all printed editions.] The mountain of the house of the Lord is therefore said to be prepared upon their summit, because it was foretold by them and, coming in the flesh, surpassed them in wondrous height.

Upon this mountain of the house of the Lord—that is, the Church—the house itself has been built, because it is founded upon Christ, as the Apostle Paul says: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11). [Col. 0946C]

### (Verse 11)

“And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven, from God, having the glory of God.”

It should be noted that Ezekiel’s final vision agrees with John’s vision in certain respects. For this reason it seemed appropriate to insert a few things from that vision into this work. He says (Ezekiel 40:2 and following) that a mountain was shown to him, upon which there was a city, [Col. 0946D] and in it a temple. Yet, while mentioning the city only briefly, he spoke at length about the structure of the temple.

The temple there therefore has the same significance as the city here: both signify the Church. But by that temple the Church of the present time is designated, whereas by the city Jerusalem the Church is indeed designated, but the Church as it will be after the end of the world.

But someone may say: How does this description of Jerusalem—that is, of the Church—pertain to the future, when the form of the Church in the present age seems to be described in this vision?

To this we reply [Col. 0947A] that the Church, so long as she remains in this life, cannot be perfectly recognized, but is held hidden as if beneath a veil. For it is unknown who is rejected, who is chosen, or to what end each person will bring his deeds. In that life, however, her form will be manifest to all. Then it will clearly appear to everyone who the wall was, who the gates were, who the foundations were, who the stones of the structure were, and who the precious stones were.

But we must ask how she is said to descend from heaven, when she is believed to ascend daily toward the heavenly dwelling in which she will remain without end. As long as we consider the deeds and merits of the saints with our minds, they continually increase in our hearts; and the more we contemplate them, the more their magnificence is elevated for us. But when we raise the eyes of our mind to contemplate the greatness of almighty God, the greatness of the saints, compared with God’s greatness, is greatly humbled for us. [Col. 0947B]

The saints therefore ascend for us when we consider their deeds and merits; but they descend when we raise the eyes of our mind to contemplate God’s omnipotence.

It is also said that she had the glory of God. Certainly, she had God’s glory, not her own. Often, for example, the sun shining in water imparts its brightness to the water, so that the water dazzles the eyes of those looking at it just as the sun does. Thus, just as water has the sun’s brightness, but not from itself, rather from the sun, so the saints have God’s glory, but not from themselves; rather from God, by whom they are illumined.

“Her light was like a precious stone, [Note: [Col. 0947D] Thus the manuscripts; the printed edition reads: “and like a jasper stone, and crystal … whose light he compared to that of the Church.”] like a stone of jasper, like crystal.” [Col. 0947C]

Behold, he has set down three stones, comparing the light of the Church to the light of these stones: one without naming it, and two by naming them. We may therefore understand the precious stone as the Father, the jasper as the Son, and the crystal as the Holy Spirit.

The first is unnamed because the Father is from himself. The second and third are named because the Son is from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.

We may also understand the precious stone as hope, the jasper as faith, and the crystal as charity. But someone may say that in that life faith and hope will not be necessary. For “who hopes for what he sees?” (Romans 8:24).

To this we reply that, just as a garment dyed from some material, once the dyeing is complete and the material has been discarded, retains within itself the most beautiful color, so in that life, although faith, hope, humility, abstinence, and the other virtues will reach their end without charity, the splendor that the saints acquired through the exercise of those virtues will remain in them forever.

### (Verse 12)

“And it had a great and high wall.”

This is the wall of which the Prophet says: “The city of our strength is Zion; the Savior will be placed in it as a wall and a rampart” (Isaiah 26:1). By this wall, therefore, Christ together with all his members is signified, so that by the one part the foundation is signified, while by the remaining structure his members are represented.

“Having twelve gates.” [Col. 0948A]

It is written in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 46:1 and following) that the temple shown to him had three gates: the eastern, the southern, and the northern. God commanded that the eastern gate should always remain closed, with only the Prince entering and departing through it.

By the eastern gate is figured the blessed and glorious virgin Mary, who remained closed before the entrance of the Prince, that is, Christ, and after his departure remained closed forever.

The southern gate signifies the Old Testament, while the northern gate signifies the New. Those who are said to come from the southern side signify the Jews; those who come from the northern side signify the nations.

The Jews, therefore, who possessed knowledge of God and to whom the Law had been given, are not inappropriately said to come to the Church from the side of the sun—that is, from the southern side, where the sun burns more intensely. They entered through the southern gate because, recognizing that Christ had been prophesied in many ways in the Old Testament and prefigured in various forms, their Scriptures drew them toward receiving the faith of Christ.

The Gentiles, however, abandoning and renouncing idolatry and the one who said, “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13), are not incongruously said to come from the northern side. They entered through the northern gate because, hearing the teaching of the Gospel and admiring the miracles performed through Christ and his ministers, they ran to receive the faith of Christ.

It was also commanded that no one should return by the way through which he had entered, but should depart opposite it: whoever entered through the southern gate should leave through the northern gate, and whoever entered through the northern gate should leave through the southern gate.

The Jews, whom understanding of the Old Testament led to receive the faith of Christ, ought not to return by the way they had come—that is, to fulfill the legal observances in a carnal manner—but rather to leave through the northern gate and turn to the study and investigation of the teaching of the Gospel, so that they might learn to fulfill spiritually what they had previously striven to do carnally.

The Gentiles, however, who entered through the northern gate—that is, who through the teaching of the Gospel became sons of the Church—ought not to return by the way they had come, namely, to return to investigate the errors of the philosophers. Rather, after receiving the faith and teaching of the Gospel, they should turn to the southern gate, that is, to the investigation of the teaching of the Old Testament. When they found that Christ had been foretold in it in many ways, their faith in Christ would be strengthened.

By the twelve gates that Jerusalem is said to have, the twelve apostles and their teaching are signified.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The manuscripts read “I saw twelve corners,” “twelve corners,” and so forth; but the printed edition’s “I saw twelve angels,” and so forth, is preferable.]

“And in the gates I saw twelve angels.”

The twelve angels signify the other preachers, namely, the successors [Col. 0949A] of the apostles. They are said to have been in the gates because, holding firmly to the unshaken faith of the apostles and following their teaching, they strove to draw to the faith of Christ as many as they could.

“And names written, the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.”

By the names of the twelve tribes we can understand the Fathers of the Old Testament, who did not deviate from faith in the Holy Trinity. We can also understand the Old Testament itself by those same names. The names of the twelve tribes were written on the gates because the teaching of the apostles and of the other preachers is full of examples from the Old Testament.

### (Verse 13)

“On the east three gates, and on the north three gates, and on the south three gates, and on the west three gates.”

He set down the four regions of the world to indicate that almost all the nations contained within the four regions of the world have gathered into the Church. He said that he saw three gates facing each region, that is, twelve in all, to indicate that no one can enter the Church except through confession of the Holy Trinity.

And because the teaching of the apostles is nothing other than the Gospel, and the Gospel itself is divided into four books, while the teaching of each book consists in faith in the Holy Trinity, this city is rightly said to have four sides, with three gates on each side. Joined together, these make twelve. [Col. 0949B]

### (Verse 14)

“And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them were the twelve names of the apostles of the Lamb.”

He himself explained what the twelve foundations signify when he added that the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb were written on them. I was reproved by someone for saying that Peter is the foundation of the Church, in the passage where the Lord says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

If Peter is the foundation of the Church, as are the other apostles, as the present reading plainly demonstrates, then the Church was built upon him, just as upon the others. But if the Church was not built upon Peter, then neither was it built upon the others; therefore this present assertion of John is false, because he says that the twelve apostles are the twelve foundations of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0949D] The printed edition reads: “Therefore this present assertion of John is true, because he said that there are twelve foundations of the Church”; the manuscripts rightly have the wording given in the text.]

Nor does what the Apostle says drive us away from our understanding: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11). For Peter is not one foundation and Christ Jesus another, because Peter is a member of Christ Jesus, just as he himself said to his disciples: “You are in me, and I in you” (John 14:20).

Christ is therefore the foundation of all his apostles, and likewise they are foundations of those who came to faith through them. There is therefore one foundation, namely Christ, by whom all the foundations are held, and upon whom the entire structure of the Church has been built.

Paul speaks of this foundation, saying: “But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw: the fire will test what sort each person’s work is” (1 Corinthians 3:12). [Col. 0950A]

Here he set down six kinds, three valuable and three worthless. Gold often signifies wisdom. He builds gold upon the foundation of Christ who stores in his heart wisdom by which he may crush vices and nourish virtues, imitating the Psalmist, who said: “In my heart I have hidden your words, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 118:11).

By silver the word of preaching is expressed, concerning which the same Psalmist says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11:7). He builds silver upon the foundation of Christ who teaches others the good that he has learned, so that he may draw them to perform good works.

By precious stones, good works are signified. He builds precious stones upon the foundation of Christ who fulfills in his works the good that he teaches.

There are some who do not possess words of exhortation by which they may perfectly instruct others; but when they exercise themselves in good works, they build precious stones upon the foundation of Christ.

Likewise, those who know little and teach it to others build silver upon Christ, provided that they fulfill by their works what they teach. For many build upon Christ the understanding they have received by teaching others, but by evil works they destroy within themselves what they have built.

By wood, hay, and straw, minor sins are signified. But there is another interpretation that excludes us from this meaning. For sins are not built upon Christ, but the works of the virtues. When we sin, we withdraw from the building that is made upon Christ; and the more seriously we sin, the farther we are separated. But when through repentance we return to doing good works, we return to the building that is made upon Christ.

We may therefore understand wood as earthly works, when someone devotes himself to earthly labor in order to have a means of living, lest perhaps, compelled by necessity, he be forced to steal. For the Apostle commands that, working quietly, each person should eat his own bread; [Note: [Col. 0950D] “And again: ‘Whoever is unwilling to work, let him not eat,’” has been restored from the manuscripts, just as the same wording appears below: “and let each woman have her own husband.”] and again he says: “Whoever is unwilling to work, let him not eat” (1 Thessalonians 3:12).

By hay we can understand earthly affection, when someone loves a wife, children, and brothers out of fleshly attachment. The Apostle himself also commands that husbands love their wives, wives their husbands, children their parents, and parents their children (Ephesians 5:25, 28).

By straw, however, we can understand those who, because lust torments them and they cannot remain continent, take wives. The Apostle also commands this, saying: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (Titus 2:4).

And because such ways of life cannot exist without frequent offenses, he says that such people will be saved through fire—that is, through purgatorial fire. This will happen if they abstain from serious sins and, through the generosity of almsgiving, merit being able to be saved after death through purgatorial fire. [Col. 0951A]

For just as gold that has been made dirty by admixture with other substances is purified through fire, so these people are cleansed through fire from the stains they contracted through worldly actions, so that they may become worthy to be joined to the number of the elect.

### (Verse 15)

“And the one who spoke with me had a golden reed, in order to measure the city, its gates, and its wall.”

The angel who spoke with John signifies Christ in this passage. In the present age he rules all the nations with an iron rod, as has already been said above; but in the future he will measure the city of God, which will consist of all the nations, with a golden reed.

We said above that by the iron rod the discipline of the Gospel is signified. Iron, however, is heavy and extremely hard. Concerning the hardness of the iron rod the Lord says [Col. 0951B] in the Gospel: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7:14).

But the love of God and hope of the heavenly homeland make this hardness sweet and light, as he says again: “For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

The iron rod will therefore be changed into a light, sweet, and golden reed, because the saints will receive perpetual sweetness and glory in exchange for the hardships they endured for Christ.

He will measure the city, its gates, and its wall when he restores to each person a reward according to the quality of his works.

But we must ask why, when he is said to have measured the city, he added the gates and the wall, since all these things are included under the name of the city. Yet, as past and future things teach, the apostles are signified by the gates, apostolic men by the city, and the remaining multitude of the faithful by the walls. The following passages make this clearer.

### (Verse 16)

“It follows: And the city is set out as a square, and its length is as great as its width.”

By the city’s squareness [Note: [Col. 0951D] All printed editions have “perfection is signified … or whatever else can be squared … For it has six sides … but the sides signify perfection,” and so forth; the manuscripts agree with the wording given here.] the perfection of the saints is signified. For a square stone, however one turns it, will stand upright.

If you carefully examine a square stone, or anything else that can be squared, you can discover that the perfection of the Church is depicted in it. For it has six faces, eight horns, and twelve edges.

The six faces demonstrate the perfection of good works, because the number six is perfect. It has eight horns, four of which face heaven and four earth.

The four horns therefore signify the Gospels, which are doubled because they especially commend love of God and neighbor. Four face heaven to indicate that God must be loved above all things; four face earth to indicate that neighbors must be loved as ourselves.

The twelve edges demonstrate the faith of the twelve apostles. From each horn three edges project, to indicate that from the teaching of Christ, which is the Gospel and which is also divided into four books, faith in the Holy Trinity passed into the apostles, [Col. 0952A] so that through them it might pass to all the nations.

We have said all this concerning the square stone in order to show that by the city’s squareness the perfection of the Church is signified.

And because this city has an equal square, its length is said to be as great as its width. For eternal glory is signified by length, while charity is signified by width. The length of this city is therefore as great as its width, because the greater each faithful person has been in charity while placed in this life, the greater the glory he will possess in heavenly blessedness; and the lesser his charity, the lesser will also be his glory.

And he measured the city at twelve thousand stadia: its length, breadth, and height are equal. The twelve thousand stadia have the same significance as the twelve gates, for they signify the apostles. Above, this city is said to have equal length and breadth; here, however, its length, breadth, and height are said to be equal. We may therefore understand these three dimensions as faith, hope, and charity: length signifying faith, breadth charity, and height hope. But how can they be equal, when the Apostle says: “And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13)? Although charity is greater than all the virtues because it endures forever, equality can nevertheless be ascribed to these three virtues in a certain respect. For the Apostle says that faith works through charity, and that faith without works is dead (Jas. 2:2). If it is dead, the one to whom it is dead possesses nothing; and if faith works through charity, then faith is dead in the one who does not possess the works of charity. Faith, therefore, is as great as the works of charity. Similarly, hope is as great as faith and charity, because hope of glory is as great as the works of faith, which is charity. For in proportion as each believer has been able to enlarge himself through works of charity, in that same proportion he may confidently expect his glory in the heavenly homeland to increase.

**(Verse 17.)** And he measured its wall all around, one hundred and forty-four cubits, the measure of a man, which is that of an angel. If we consider what precedes, this cannot stand according to the literal sense. Above, it says that he measured the city at twelve thousand stadia; here, however, it says that the city’s walls were measured at one hundred and forty-four cubits. The space of twelve thousand stadia is much greater than the space of one hundred and forty-four cubits; therefore, by the greater space we may understand those who are of greater merit. [Col. 0952D] The same editions read, “the space by which those who are of greater merit are understood is greater”; but the manuscripts read as in the text.

Above we said that the twelve apostles are signified by the twelve stadia. Martyrs, therefore, confessors, and the other perfect men who followed the apostles’ teaching in every respect and imitated their deeds will be measured within their circumference, because they will possess the same glory as the apostles. By the walls, however, which are made of smaller stones, the remaining multitude of the faithful is signified. They will occupy a smaller circumference than those of whom we spoke above, because those who are of lesser merit will receive lesser rewards. Their measure consists in the number twelve, because they preserved the apostolic faith undefiled; for twelve times twelve makes one hundred and forty-four.

When it says that the city and the walls were measured by the measure of a man, which is that of an angel, it shows that the angel appeared to him in the likeness of a man. [Col. 0953D] Gill reads, “and the walls are the measure of a man,” or, “he says that the angels were measured by the measure of a man.” The Romans corrected this to, “and the walls are the measure of a man,” or, “by the measure of a man,” and so forth; but the manuscripts restore the passage more suitably.

We may understand this in another way. It says that the measure of a man is the measure of an angel, and by that measure it says that the city and the walls were measured, because holy men will possess equality with the angels and will be measured by their measure, since they will possess the same glory as the angels, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30).

**(Verse 18.)** And the structure of its wall was of jasper; but the city itself was like pure gold, like pure glass. Here too he establishes a certain distinction between the walls and the city. He says that the walls were constructed of jasper, but that the city itself was like pure gold and pure glass. By the greenness of jasper, faith is signified. Through jasper, therefore, simple and imperfect men are not inappropriately represented: they are saved by faith, as the prophet says: “But the righteous shall live by his faith” (Hab. 2:4). Holy and perfect men, however, who are represented by the city, are appropriately likened to pure gold, because they were filled with wisdom, which is often figured by gold, and because they were tested by various tribulations, like gold purified by fire. By pure glass, which is clearer than all metals, the angels are signified, for no stain of sin has ever been able to defile them.

**(Verse 19.)** The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every precious stone. Above we said that the twelve apostles are signified by the twelve foundations; by the precious stones, however, all the righteous are signified. The twelve foundations, therefore, will be adorned with twelve stones, because in that blessedness the apostles and the other preachers will have as their adornment those who believed through them, since they will receive their reward on behalf of all these.

The first foundation was jasper. [Col. 0954D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “Jasper is green and of a dense color.”

Jasper is green and of a compact color. It signifies the faithful who live in the world and who, while abstaining from vices, nevertheless allow their greenness—that is, their faith—to be somewhat darkened by worldly actions. Yet they do not cease to redeem their sins by almsgiving and other works of mercy. Nor is it without reason that such people are placed first. The apostles, as has often already been repeated, were afraid to impose the Lord’s stricter commandments upon those from the nations who had first come to faith, lest, frightened by the severity of the commandments, they should not dare to approach the acceptance of Christ’s faith. Therefore they wrote to them: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no burden upon you except that you abstain only from sexual immorality, from foods sacrificed to idols, from what has been strangled, and from blood” (Acts 15:28). And in another passage, Peter, recounting the conversion of the nations, says to the Jews: “And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and cleansing their hearts by faith” (ibid. 8ff.). [Col. 0954D] All the editions read, “they imitate God”; all the manuscripts read, “they imitate these men.” Whoever, therefore, imitates these men is included under the figure of jasper.

The second was sapphire. Sapphire is blue in color, like hyacinth, but it has interspersed spots of the same color, though darker. It seems to me that by this stone certain men living in the world are signified: they desire heavenly things, but are still occupied with worldly actions, and from that occupation appear to contract certain stains. Because they place heavenly things above all their concerns, they are said to possess the color of heaven. They are placed second because they strive to love God above all things and their neighbors as themselves.

The third was chalcedony. Chalcedony has a red color, but it is dark unless it is thinned by excavation; the hollow itself gives it a most beautiful and pleasing color. This stone also signifies certain men living in the world whose great holiness before the time of persecution was hidden from people. But when they had been refined by various tribulations inflicted by their persecutors, the extent of the splendor of holiness hidden within them became evident to all. They are appropriately placed third, because, remaining steadfast in confessing the Holy Trinity, they deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom.

The fourth was emerald. It is of extraordinary beauty and greenness, so much so that it tinges with its greenness the things around it. It signifies the holy preachers who, green with faith and distinguished by virtues, spread the splendor of their faith everywhere by preaching. They are placed fourth because they disseminated the teaching of the Gospel, which is divided into four books, throughout many places.

[Col. 0954D] **(Verse 20.)** The fifth was sardonyx. Sardonyx is white, inclining slightly toward red. It signifies simple and innocent men, who are represented by the white stone because of the purity of their lives. Since, by keeping vigil, fasting, abstaining, and afflicting their bodies in various ways, they impose martyrdoms upon themselves, they seem to possess a kind of red color. They are appropriately placed fifth, since the number five often signifies the five bodily senses. [Col. 0955D] The same editions read, “are signified.” Because the five bodily senses are signified by five; but all the manuscripts agree with our restoration.

Blessed Gregory also says that through the five bodily senses knowledge of external things is signified. Since these men devoted themselves to imparting to others the knowledge of external things that they had acquired, they rightly occupy the fifth place in the structure of the holy city.

The sixth was sardius. Sardius is tawny in color; because it seems to incline somewhat toward red, it is slightly darkened. By the tawny color, which approaches the color of gold, the tribulations that the saints suffered from their enemies are signified; the red color signifies martyrdom. Through sardius, therefore, holy and perfect men are represented who, after experience of every virtue, after various persecutions, and after the monstrous torments they endured from their enemies, deserved to attain the palm of martyrdom. They are appropriately placed in the sixth number, which is perfect, because they were perfect in virtues and adorned that perfection with martyrdom.

The seventh was chrysolite. Chrysolite is entirely golden, and gold often signifies wisdom. Through chrysolite, therefore, wise men in the Church are represented; because of the radiance of their wisdom, they may rightly be called golden among human beings. They are suitably placed seventh because, filled with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, they turned many away from wickedness by their words and examples.

The eighth was beryl. Beryl is of extraordinary brightness, with blue mixed into it. It signifies people of pure life, wholly separated from worldly actions. To avoid staining the brightness of their lives in any way, they even wished to withdraw from the society of other people. Their brightness was turned toward the color blue because, always intent upon heaven, they are shown to have led an angelic life among human beings. They are appropriately placed eighth, for twice four makes eight. [Col. 0955D] “Twice four makes eight” is restored from the manuscripts.

These men fulfilled the number four because they followed the commandment of the Gospel, which says: “Go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). They doubled the number four because they persuaded many others to ascend with them to the same summit of perfection.

[Col. 0955D] The ninth was topaz. Topaz is said to be of an airy and golden color, scattering its radiance in every direction. Gold often signifies tested men, who are tested by the fire of tribulation. The tribulations themselves are various. Sometimes holy men are tested by various temptations inflicted by demons; sometimes by tribulations imposed upon them by wicked people; sometimes by afflictions that they impose upon themselves; sometimes they are tested by God’s scourges; and sometimes by the exercises of the active life.

It seems to me, therefore, that the stone topaz signifies those who are first tested through the works of the active life and afterward pass over to the contemplative life. [Col. 0955D] This restoration is supported by all the manuscripts; in the editions [Col. 0956D] it read: “those who ascend to the contemplative life through the works of the active life, who first through the active ….” For the person who has first been tested through the exercises of the active life ascends to the contemplative life by a suitable progression. Whoever passes suddenly to the height of the contemplative life without the exercises of the active life easily falls. The fact that this stone is said to scatter its rays in every direction signifies those men represented by it who, by preaching, drew many to the works of the active life and also led many with themselves to the height of the contemplative life. They are appropriately placed ninth, since three times three makes nine.

Holy men who, for love of the Holy Trinity, first afflicted themselves through the good works of the active life, then drew to their imitation by their exhortations all whom they could, and afterward ascended to contemplate the divinity of that same Holy Trinity, leading many with them, are appropriately placed ninth. They multiplied the talent they received from the Lord not merely twofold but threefold.

The tenth was chrysoprase. Chrysoprase is said to be green and golden in color. Because it is placed tenth, we may understand by it certain teachers of the Church who, while present in the body, taught many by their words and instructed many more through their writings—and still instruct them daily—such as Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and many others. [Col. 0956D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “and instruct. They also [are] lights of the Church … because in the greenness of faith, steadfastness, and wisdom they were radiant like gold.” They may also rightly be called lights of the Church. They are signified by the green and golden color because they were firm in the greenness of faith and radiant with wisdom like gold. By the number ten we may understand the Old Testament, on account of the ten commandments of the Law. Since no one can understand the Old Testament without the teaching of the New Testament—for spiritual understanding in the Old Testament is nothing other than the New Testament—they are appropriately placed tenth, because they possessed the fullest knowledge of both the Old and the New Testaments.

We may also understand the number ten in another way. The number ten divides, orders, and completes all numbers. In the same way these men, in a certain sense, divided the Scriptures when, by interpreting them, they distributed them among sentences and books. They ordered them when they disclosed their obscurities and revealed what proper order the things that seemed disordered actually possessed. They completed them when they supplied what appeared to be lacking.

The eleventh was hyacinth. Hyacinth, the species that gave its name to the hyacinth color, is most precious and has the color of a clear sky, like sapphire. But sapphire has spots, whereas the beauty of hyacinth is marred by no spots. It signifies holy men who are free from every pollution of sin, inhabiting the earth in body but heaven in mind. One of this kind was the Apostle, who said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

They are appropriately placed eleventh. [Col. 0957D] All the editions read, “the number eleven”; all the manuscripts, “the number ten.” The latter is better, since unity is discussed below. By ten, as we said above, the knowledge of the divine Scriptures is already signified; the one that follows ten, making eleven, pertains to the contemplation of the one God. These holy men completed the number ten because, filled with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, they led many to eternal life through their preaching. They completed the number one because they were constant in the contemplation of almighty God. Neither the urgency of preaching drew them away from contemplation, nor constant contemplation from preaching. They bore the likeness of angels, who always fulfill their angelic office and are never separated from the contemplation of almighty God.

The prophet seems to have spoken of such men when he said: “The lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7). John the Baptist was such a man, of whom the Lord said: “This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you” (Luke 7:27).

The twelfth was amethyst. The number twelve often signifies the apostles. Amethyst, however, is purple, and we know that purple is a royal ornament. Through amethyst, therefore, the apostles and those like them are signified, for they were God’s ornament because they preached him throughout the whole world. Peter was God’s ornament, of whom it is written that he glorified God by his death (John 21:19). Similarly, the other apostles were God’s ornament because they glorified him by preaching, performing miracles, and dying for his name.

**(Verse 21.)** And the twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate being made from a single pearl. This cannot stand according to the literal sense. If each gate was made from a single pearl, how can twelve pearls be said to have been in each gate? Spiritually, however, it must be understood that there are twelve pearls from which the individual gates are said to be made—that is, one hundred and forty-four—through which the successors of the apostles, the teachers of the Church, are signified. They followed the faith and teaching of the apostles and imitated their deeds. Because of the purity of their lives and their outstanding holiness, they are signified by the whiteness of pearls.

And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass. Above we said that perfect men and holy angels were signified by pure gold and pure glass. Here, however, the street of the city signifies the minds of the faithful; and by pure gold and transparent glass, the purity of the minds of human beings and angels is signified. For just as no vain thought could ever enter the minds of angels and stain them, so after the resurrection no useless thought will ever enter the minds of the saints and defile them.

**(Verse 22.)** And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. By the temple, in which offerings and sacrifices were made, the present Church is signified, in which not bodily but spiritual sacrifices are offered to God daily. For just as the ritual of sacrifices was carried out there according to the nature of sins, so in the Church there ought to be sacrifices of repentance, sacrifices of prayers, tears, and contrition of heart, according to the measure of faults.

The prophet speaks of such sacrifices, saying: “The sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit” (Ps. 50:19); and again: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness” (ibid. 21). If there is a sacrifice of righteousness, [Col. 0958D] the same editions read, “there is also [a sacrifice] of wisdom,” whereas the manuscripts read, on the contrary, “there is also [a sacrifice] of patience”; there is also a sacrifice of abstinence, of humility, and of the other virtues. These are the sacrifices that offer the Lord a most pleasing fragrance, not the flesh of animals that was burned upon the altar.

John therefore said that he did not see a temple in the holy city because none of the things we have mentioned will be necessary in that blessedness: “For God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (above, 5:4). The Lord and the Lamb will be its temple because the saints will be in him and will dwell in him, as he himself said to his disciples: “As I am in the Father, and you in me, and I in you” (John 11:20).

**(Verse 23.)** And the city has no need of the sun or the moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God will illumine it, and its lamp is the Lamb. By the sun the New Testament is signified, and by the moon the Old Testament. Without these two lights, the Church cannot walk along the way of righteousness through the darkness of this age without frequent stumbling. But in that blessedness, where there will be no darkness, no offense, and nothing imperfect that could be corrected, the light of the New and Old Testaments will not be necessary. The saints will enjoy without end the light of him who is the author of light and who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1:9).

**(Verse 24.)** And the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. By the nations all the elect are signified. But how will they walk? They will walk in mind, not in body—not by changing place, but by contemplating omnipotence, divinity, and majesty.

They will walk by the light of the Church because, so that they may complete this journey, they will be illumined by that light which almighty God will give to the whole Church. By the kings of the earth, however, the apostles and the other preachers are signified. Their glory and honor are those whom he calls the glory of the preachers, namely, those who believed through them, as the Apostle Paul says to his disciples: “For you are our glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 1:14). They will therefore bring their glory and honor into it when they present to the Lord those who believed through them.

**(Verse 25.)** And its gates shall not be shut by day, for there shall be no night there. Above we said that the twelve gates, which are said to have been made from twelve pearls, signify the apostles. Here, however, where they are mentioned without a number, they have another meaning: they signify the hearts of the faithful.

The faithful who are placed in this life suffer night—that is, demons and wicked people. They shut the gates at night when, against every temptation of demons, they close the entrances to their minds and repel such things from themselves. They also shut the gates at night when they fortify their hearts against the wickedness of evil people, so that they do not listen to a slandering tongue, return evil for evil, or cursing for cursing, so that, according to the prophet, they may “shake their hands free from every gift,” stop their ears lest they hear bloodshed, and close their eyes lest they see evil (Eccl. 33:16).

But in that blessedness, where there can be no demon or reprobate to give evil counsel—those represented by night—the guarding of the gates, that is, of the minds, will not be necessary. According to the literal sense also, there will be perpetual day there, with no night following.

[Col. 0959C] **(Verse 26.)** And they will bring the glory of the nations and their honor into it. Above he says that the kings of the earth, that is, the holy preachers, brought their glory into the holy city. We said that by this glory the nations who believed through them were signified. If the glory of the preachers is the nations, what is the glory of the nations? Perhaps we should understand this according to Solomon, who says: “The glory of the elders is their children’s children, and the glory of children is their fathers” (Prov. 17:6). The glory of the elders—that is, of the apostles—is their children’s children, that is, the nations who believed through the apostles and through their children, namely, their disciples. The glory of the children, however, will be their fathers, because the nations will rejoice that they have fathers of such merit and excellence, since they will have deserved to share in their glory.

When it says “they will bring,” we may refer this to the angels, who on the day of judgment will lead the saints of God to receive the promised rewards, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather his elect from the four winds of heaven, and from the summit of the heavens” (Matt. 24:31).

**(Verse 27.)** And nothing unclean shall enter it, nor anyone who does what is abominable and false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life. He calls those people unclean who have defiled themselves with various crimes. Those do what is abominable who perform evil, for God abhors nothing except wickedness, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “You have mercy on all, O Lord, and you hate nothing that you have made” (Wis. 11:25).

It may be asked why it is said that falsehood is done. What we do is no longer falsehood, because what has been done cannot fail to have been done and therefore cannot be falsehood. But he has put “done” for “spoken.” We commit the sin of falsehood by speaking, not by acting. We may also understand by falsehood every sin. For we know that God is truth, whereas sin is the deception of souls. Whatever, therefore, is contrary to truth and pertains to the deception of souls, even if it appears true, may rightly be called falsehood.

Nothing unclean, therefore, will enter that holy city, nor anyone who does what is abominable and false, because on the day of judgment the angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous and cast them into the furnace of blazing fire (Matt. 13:49). For the door of the heavenly kingdom will also be closed to those who have not had the oil of charity in their vessels, and the Lord will say to them: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12).

## CHAPTER XXII

**(Verse 1.)** And he showed me the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, in the midst of its street. In his final vision Ezekiel was shown a torrent that went out from the temple and flowed into the sea. He speaks of it as follows: “And the angel,” he says, “led me a thousand cubits and brought me through the water up to the ankles. And he led me a thousand cubits and brought me through the water up to the knees. And he led me a thousand cubits and brought me through the water up to the loins. And he led me a thousand cubits, and I could not cross the torrent, because the waters of the torrent had risen and could not be crossed” (Ezek. 47:3ff.).

By the torrent we must understand divine Scripture, which goes out from the temple—that is, from the Church—from the mouth of the preachers. The angel signifies the Lord.
