The prophet represents those who wish to learn the divine Scriptures so that they themselves may progress through them and instruct others through their knowledge. The number one thousand often signifies the perfection of some thing. The first crossing therefore pertains to understanding the historical sense, the second to the moral sense, and the third to the spiritual sense.

[Col. 0960D] [Col. 0959D] In the editions these words—“Therefore the angel leads [the prophet] … [to] understand the Scriptures”—were placed above, after the words “signifies the Lord”; but in the manuscripts they are more suitably located here. [Col. 0960D]

The angel therefore leads the prophet a thousand cubits when the Lord grants one of his faithful the desire to understand the Scriptures. He leads him through the water up to the ankles when he grants him understanding of the historical sense. For whoever desires to investigate the moral and spiritual understanding of the divine Scriptures must first possess an understanding of the historical sense.

Second, the angel leads the prophet a thousand cubits when the Lord kindles his faithful one to receive moral understanding. He leads him through the water up to the knees when he reveals to him the meaning of moral knowledge.

[Col. 0961A] [Col. 0961D] Everything intervening from the words “Third, the angel raises the prophet as far as the mysteries” is restored from all the manuscripts. [Col. 0962D]

Third, the angel leads the prophet a thousand cubits when, after moral understanding, the Lord elevates his faithful one through desire to unfold the meanings of spiritual understanding. He leads him through the water up to the loins when he opens to him the meaning of spiritual knowledge.

Fourth, the angel leads the prophet a thousand cubits when, after understanding the Scriptures, the Lord raises his faithful one to contemplate divine and heavenly mysteries. He could not cross the torrent because no one can investigate the depth of divine and heavenly mysteries as they truly are: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part,” as the Apostle says, “but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away” (1 Cor. 13:9–10); and again: “Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face” (ibid. 12).

Considering that he could not cross this torrent, Paul himself said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor, or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Rom. 11:33ff.). And the prophet Isaiah says: “The eye has not seen, O God, besides you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you” (Isa. 64:4).

Behold, the angel led the prophet as far as the appointed place but did not lead him across, because almighty God brings his saints as far as the contemplation of the secret and hidden mysteries of his divinity, but does not lead them across, because human frailty cannot perfectly comprehend those inscrutable and divine mysteries.

Just as one who has smelled royal foods and tasted their sweetness beforehand desires them more than one who has neither seen nor smelled them nor learned by tasting what their sweetness is like, so the saints who often taste, through the grace of contemplation, the sweetness of the heavenly homeland burn daily with far greater love for it than those who, because of the sweetness of the world, do not perceive the sweetness of eternal life.

The same prophet says in what follows that he saw trees on both banks of the torrent, whose fruit was for food and whose leaves were for healing. The two banks signify the two Testaments. Between these two banks flows the great torrent of the Scriptures, produced by the holy Fathers. By the trees, the teachers of the Church are signified; they are said to have been planted on both banks—that is, in the teaching of the Old and New Testaments. Drawing the waters of true knowledge, they produce both fruit and leaves. By the fruit, good works are signified; by the leaves, words of preaching.

The fruit serves as food and the leaves as medicine, because each teacher administers the healing medicine of saving words to a sick soul when he has first nourished it with examples of good works.

[Col. 0962A] Behold, Ezekiel said that he saw the torrent going out from the temple; John, however, says that he was shown not a torrent but a river proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb (Ezek. 47:5). A torrent is accustomed to dry up from excessive heat of the sun, whereas a river is not dried up by any heat. Therefore divine Scripture is not inappropriately expressed by the torrent, which will dry up when the sun comes—that is, when the Lord comes for judgment—because after the resurrection divine Scripture will no longer be necessary.

By the river, however, which is not dried up by any heat of the sun, the perpetual glory of the saints is understood. It is said to proceed from the throne of God and of the Lamb because the river of the saints’ glory will proceed from him from whom, while they were placed in the flesh, the stream of all good things proceeded.

This river is said to be bright as crystal. Since this stone is often mentioned in this book, it is appropriate to say a little about its nature and significance. This stone is clearer than all other stones. It is formed in extremely cold places, from which the cold never departs. Because it adheres on its lower side to a somewhat softer rock, it sets down a small root in it and rises upward as it grows. It has six angles and becomes pointed at the top, while preserving the same order of six angles all the way to its summit.

It signifies every perfect man. The stone to which it adheres signifies Christ. The brightness of crystal signifies the purity of the minds of the saints. Its six angles demonstrate the perfection of good works. It carries the order of its six angles all the way to the summit because the saints strive to bring the perfection of good works to the end of their lives. At the top it becomes pointed because all the intention of the saints is directed toward him who is one, and in whom they themselves also become one.

This river, therefore, which signifies the glory of the saints, is said to possess the brightness of crystal because it shines for each of the faithful according to the quality of his works, as the Apostle says: “For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41). It is said to proceed from the throne of God and of the Lamb because all the glory of the saints will proceed from him who is the author of every good. It is also said to flow in the midst of the street of the city because it will gladden the hearts of the saints with the perpetual sweetness of joy.

[Col. 0962D] “And on both sides of the river, the tree of life” (Ezek. 47:7). Ezekiel was shown very many trees on both banks of the stream, about which we spoke above; here, however, he says that the tree of life occupied both sides of the river. There, many trees signify many preachers; here, by the one tree of life, one Christ is signified, who is the life of all the faithful. By the two sides, moreover, we can understand angels and human beings. Therefore the tree of life will possess both sides of the river, because Christ will possess holy angels and human beings equally.

“Bearing twelve fruits.” The twelve fruits are the apostles and all who followed their teaching. The tree of life will bear twelve fruits because in that blessedness Christ will establish the entire multitude of the faithful. “Yielding its fruit each month.” The individual months are the periods from the beginning of the world to its end, about which we have often spoken. Thus it will yield its fruit in each month because it will present to the Father, in that blessedness, all the elect who existed in each period and who will exist until the end.

“And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” The leaves of the tree are the words of the Gospel, which have brought healing to many nations. The meaning is this: he will establish in heavenly blessedness all the nations that have been saved from the illnesses of their souls through the teaching of the Gospel.

[Col. 0963B] (Verse 3.) “And every curse shall be no more.” By saying “every curse,” he shows that there are many curses. The first man incurred the curse of death when he sinned, and from him it passed to all human beings (Gen. 3:17). Paul also says of Christ that he became a curse for us (Rom. 5:11), because for our salvation he accepted death, which is the curse of the first man (Gal. 3:13). Cain, too, was cursed by God for the crime of murder (Gen. 4:11). And Moses says to those who despise the Law: “Cursed is he who has not remained in the words of this book” (Deut. 27:26).

[Note: All printed editions read “in all these”; all manuscripts read “in the words of this book.”]

Similarly, when we sin gravely, we ourselves condemn ourselves with the worst curse. Therefore “every curse shall be no more,” because there will be no sin, nor anything that provides an occasion for sinning. The curse of the first man, too, will be erased in the resurrection, when immortality has been bestowed upon all the elect.

“And the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it” (1 Cor. 15:53). If the saints of God, placed in this life, are now the throne of God, how much more will they be so then, when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality”?

“And his servants will serve him.” What is this service by which the servants of God will serve God? Clearly, loving him and praising him without end.

(Vers. 4.) “And they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.” The greatness of the glory and sweetness that will be bestowed upon the saints cannot be grasped by the human mind, as the apostle Paul says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). But all sweetness and delight will be surpassed by this: they will see God face to face. The name of God is the Son of God; therefore his name will be on the foreheads of the saints, because that very radiance and appearance will show that they are sons of God.

(Vers. 5.) “And night shall be no more.” John says elsewhere: “God is light, and there are no darknesses in him” (1 John 1:5). What darkness, then, could those suffer among whom God will continually be seen? If we wish to understand this saying as referring to demons and the impious, there will be no night because the demons, together with all the impious, will be shut up forever in the sewer of hell.

“And they will not need the light of a lamp, nor the light of the sun.” We said above that by the light of the moon and the light of the sun the Old and New Testaments are signified. The lamp, therefore, has here the same meaning that we said above belonged to the moon. Concerning the light of the sun and moon—that is, of the Old and New Testaments—we have said something above. The saints, therefore, will not need this light, “because the Lord God will illumine them, and they will reign for ever and ever.”

Up to this point is the seventh vision. What follows concerns the admonition of John himself and of the other faithful.

(Vers. 6.) “And he said to me: These words are most faithful and true.” He repeats this twice so that no one, considering the obscurities of the wording and those things that seem irrational according to the letter, may become unbelieving. For there were certain people who, not understanding the divine mysteries contained in this book, wished to cut it out of the catalogue of the divine Scriptures.

“And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants what must shortly take place”; that is, the Lord God who gave the spirit of prophecy to all the holy prophets himself sent his angel—that is, the one who was speaking these things—to show his servants what must shortly take place. He is the one who also showed John all the mysteries contained in this book.

Since this Scripture pertains not only to the future but also to the past, why does he say that he was sent by God merely to show those things that were to take place shortly? Surely because the past is easily recognized, whereas future things, unknown to human beings, can be understood only through the revelation of the Holy Spirit or through the ministry of angels. Otherwise, whatever we do not know is future for us, because it is future that what we do not know should come into our understanding—namely, what God predestined us to know. For knowledge of evil was not predestined for us; rather, it descended from original sin.

587 (Vers. 7.) “And behold, I am coming quickly.” He speaks this in the person of Christ, signifying that he is soon to come for judgment.

“Blessed is he who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book.” He keeps the words of the prophecy—that is, the commandments of God—who fulfills them by doing them and is constant in meditating upon them, fulfilling the saying of the Psalmist: “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2).

(Vers. 8, 9.) “And I, John, who heard and saw these things, and after I had heard and seen them, fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who was showing me these things. And he said to me: See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers the prophets and of those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.”

[Note: So the manuscripts; the editions, however, read: “Why the angel of the Lord did not wish to be worshiped by John, we have sufficiently explained above in the exposition of the fifth Vision. Pure fabrication.”]

Why the angel did not wish to be worshiped by John, blessed Gregory has sufficiently explained. We, however, must ask why John repeated what had previously been forbidden him. But if we examine the text of this book carefully, we will see that this was not done without purpose. When the angel had shown him Christ seated on his throne, together with the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, he is by no means said to have wished to worship the angel. Likewise, when he had shown him how the seven seals were opened by the Lamb, and what was done under the sound of the seven angels’ trumpets, as well as what is said to have been done under the pouring out of the bowls of the seven angels, he is nowhere said to have wished to worship the angel.

But when the account reached the place where the angel showed him how the bride of Christ—that is, the Church—was joined to Christ, namely where it is written: “Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give him glory, because the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his wife has prepared herself; and it was granted to her to clothe herself in shining, bright linen”—for, he says, “the linen is the justifications of the saints”—then immediately he wished to worship the angel.

[Note: The editions read “and let us give him glory, and so forth”; immediately, “the angel.” The manuscripts, however, read as we have placed it in the text.]

Similarly, in what follows, when the fall of Antichrist, the binding of the devil in the abyss, and the glory of the resurrection had been shown to him, he in no way wished to worship the angel. But when, at the end of this vision, it had been shown to him how, after the glory of the resurrection, the Church would be joined to Christ and reign with him forever, immediately he wished to worship the angel.

For the Church is joined to Christ daily through faith and through the other good works signified by the linen. After the resurrection, however, it will be joined to him in a far higher and nobler manner—not now in parts, as at present, but all together, remaining with him forever and reigning without end. Thus John wished to worship the angel twice because the angel showed him the Church’s two unions with Christ.

(Vers. 10.) “And he said to me: Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near.” Scripture is sealed for those by whom it is not understood. John is therefore commanded not to seal the words of the prophecy of this book—that is, not to conceal its obscurities by remaining silent about them, but rather to make it known by explaining it to all who wish to understand it—for the day of judgment, which is described in various ways in this book, is near, and we must behold in our hearts the danger that threatens, lest it seize and destroy us unawares like a thief.

But why did John, in accordance with the angelic command, not wish to reveal and explain the obscurities of this book, especially since, because of those same obscurities, certain people fell into error and heresy, saying that after the resurrection Christ would reign carnally in the world with all the saints for a thousand years? What he did not do by writing, we believe he did by preaching.

(Vers. 11.) “He who does harm, let him do harm still; and he who is in filth, let him become filthy still; and let the holy person be sanctified still.”

[Note: The same editions read “let him become filthy still,” not as a command; the remainder has been restored from the manuscripts.]

The one who says, “He who does harm, let him do harm still; and he who is in filth, let him become filthy still,” spoke not by commanding but by threatening. Human beings often use this form of speech to frighten certain persons subject to them, as teachers who are accustomed to say to idle boys: “Do not read, do not read.” Understanding that this is a threat, not a prohibition, they immediately begin to read. In the same way masters frighten servants who are languishing in idleness, so that they may complete more quickly the work assigned to them.

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “And he who is righteous, let him be justified still; and let the holy person be sanctified still. Behold, I am coming, and so forth.”]

(Vers. 12.) “Behold, I am coming quickly, and my reward is with me, to repay each person according to his works.” The people of this world keep the rewards they owe those who serve them either in purses, in granaries, or in certain places on earth. Christ, however, always carries the rewards of his servants with him. From him proceeds now all the goodness of the saints, and from him will proceed in the future all their glory.

(Vers. 13, 14.) “I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end. Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates.”

By “robes” in this passage we can understand our souls. Since we sin continually, it is necessary for us continually to wash our robes—that is, our souls—by praying, keeping watch, fasting, and giving alms.

By the tree of life we can understand wisdom, as Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is he who holds her fast” (Prov. 3:18). The saints have authority over the tree of life—that is, over wisdom—because whoever possesses wisdom is powerful enough to uproot every vice, overcome the temptations of demons, and perform every good work, as Solomon says: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. 16:32).

Such people, then, enter the city through the gates—through that gate which says in the Gospel: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and will find pasture” (John 10:9).

We can also refer this to the future. For the tree of life, as we have often said, signifies Christ. Just as many branches proceed from a single tree trunk, so from one Christ comes the multitude of the saints. Therefore, whoever does not cease to wash his soul with spiritual washings—that is, with good works—will have authority over the tree of life, because, having become its members, they will be able to accomplish great things through him. For just as all the strength of the branches proceeds from a single tree trunk, so all the power of the saints proceeds from one Christ.

[Note: The Gill edition reads “to wash themselves with good works”; the Roman edition, “to wash themselves”; the manuscripts, “to wash their souls.” Below, both editions read “the gate will be opened, because [it is opened] to the righteous”; the manuscripts, on the contrary, read “it will be opened, and it will be closed to the unrighteous,” and so forth.]

By the gate of the city we can understand the mercy and clemency of God. This is the gate that will be opened to the righteous and closed to the unrighteous, because divine mercy will receive the righteous within the court of paradise, while the impious will be strangers to that mercy.

[Note: The Gill edition reads “will receive.” It continues: “I, Jesus”; the Roman edition reads “will receive.” It continues: “Outside are dogs … and he who makes a lie. I, Jesus.” The authority of all the manuscripts, however, restores so great a lacuna.]

From this gate the foolish virgins will be driven away, those who will not have the oil of charity in their vessels (Matt. 25:12).

(Vers. 15.) Hence it also follows: “Outside are dogs, sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, those who serve idols, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.”

By “dogs” we can understand false preachers, concerning whom the apostle Paul says: “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Phil. 3:2); and the prophet: “Mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56:10); and again: “The dogs are shameless; they have not known satisfaction. They are shepherds who have no understanding” (ibid., 11).

We have spoken above concerning the other vices contained here. Therefore all who have been defiled by these vices will be driven away from that blessedness and condemned to eternal punishment.

[Col. 0967B] (Vers. 16.) “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches. I am the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star.”

David is the root of his entire stock, because, just as many branches arise from one root, so a great offspring arose from one David. Since David was the root of Christ, inasmuch as Christ arose from his stock, how does Christ say that he is David’s root? Christ, therefore, is both the root and the son of David.

He is the root of David because David was created by him, just as all other human beings were. He is David’s son because he proceeded from David’s offspring according to the flesh.

He also calls himself the morning star. The morning star, which we call Lucifer, is rightly called Christ, because just as that star, rising in the morning, spreads its radiance throughout the whole world, so Christ, coming into the world, illumined the entire face of the world. He is not improperly called Lucifer, because when he came into the world he brought light with him, by which he extinguished the darkness of this world.

Job speaks of this Lucifer, saying: “Who brings forth the morning star in its time” (Job 38:32). God the Father brought forth Lucifer in his time when, at the appointed time, he sent his Son to redeem the human race.

(Vers. 17.) “And the bridegroom and the bride say: Come.”

[Note: Gill has in the text: “And the bridegroom and the bride, that is, Christ, [say]”; in the margin: “or, the Spirit.” The Roman edition reads: “And the Spirit and the bride say: Come; that is, Christ,” and so forth. But all the manuscripts agree with us.]

The bridegroom and the bride—that is, Christ and the Church—invite all human beings daily through the Scriptures and through preachers to receive eternal rewards.

“And let him who hears say: Come.” Those who hear are not only those who understand the divine Scriptures, but also those who know the good things by which they can be saved. There are many who hear—that is, who have learned the divine commandments—but do not come because they neglect to fulfill them in action.

Therefore whoever hears must come. And whoever has already begun to come to God by the way of good works must also draw others along with him by admonishing them.

“And let him who thirsts come”—that is, let him who thirsts for eternal life recognize that he must come to it by the way of good works.

“Let him who wishes take the water of life freely.” This was explained above (at chap. 12).

(Vers. 18, 19.) “I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God will take away his part from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book.”

Since above the angel commands John, saying, “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book,” what does it mean that here the same John condemns with a terrible curse those who add anything to the writing of this book—especially since many things are found in this book that seem, according to the letter, useless and vain unless spiritual understanding is applied to them, by which they may be understood?

We must understand that this was said not about interpreters but about heretics. An interpreter adds or subtracts nothing; rather, he either reveals the obscurities of the history by explaining them or demonstrates a moral or spiritual understanding.

He therefore curses the heretics who, in the divine Scriptures, added certain falsehoods to confirm their heresy and removed certain things that seemed contrary to their heresy.

(Vers. 20.) “He who testifies to these things says: Surely I am coming quickly. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”

[Note: The editions read “Lord Jesus Christ.” He says “I am coming quickly”; the manuscripts more correctly read as in the text.]

Christ says, “I am coming quickly”; John asks, “Come, Lord Jesus.” We too ought to ask for Christ’s coming in many ways.

We ask for his coming in the Lord’s Prayer, saying daily: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10)—that is, the time that will come after the resurrection, when all the saints will reign with Christ without end.

We lie in sins; we must implore his coming by repenting, weeping, praying, practicing abstinence, and giving alms, so that he may return to us by showing us his mercy, from whom he had departed, provoked by our evils.

We are placed in the darkness of ignorance; the Lord must be entreated to come and illumine our hearts with the light of his wisdom.

We are attacked by invisible enemies; the Lord must be asked to come and defend us from them by his invisible power.

We suffer visible enemies; the Lord must be implored to come and grant us patience and endurance in adversity, so that we may not be overcome by evil but may overcome evil with good.

There are other enemies within, and far worse ones, by whom we are ceaselessly assailed: greed, gluttony, lust, envy, anger, hatred, pride, vainglory, swelling of mind, contempt for our neighbors, blasphemies, and many others that it would take too long to list.

These, then, are the worst enemies, who come forth from us, remain with us, and constantly do battle against us. They also possess innumerable arrows of evil thoughts, with which they continually wound us.

If, therefore, the inner enemies were absent, the outer enemies could in no way harm us. For these inner enemies are the traitors of our city, and the outer enemies can capture the city of our heart in no way except through them.

Let us therefore ask the Lord to come and utterly destroy these monstrous enemies within us, because unless they are destroyed, we cannot be saved.

(Vers. 21.) “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ also be with us, and may he give us the weapons of the virtues. Armed with these, under his leadership and standard, may we be defended both from inner and outer enemies, so that we may deserve to share in eternal life—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

# THE AUTHOR’S ADMONITION

[Col. 0969B]

[Note: This author’s admonition was omitted in the earlier editions; we reproduce it from all the manuscripts except the Gemeticensis, whose single leaf had been torn out. See what we prefaced concerning it in our Admonition to this book.]

Whoever wishes to know the author’s name, pay attention to the first letters of the expositions in the chapters of the seven Visions. The number of the four missing vowels, if you supply the Greek ones, is eighty-one.

Behold, with as much brevity as I could, I have written this book. But I beseech you, to whom God has given knowledge of letters and into whose hands this book has come for reading, not to cast away the discourses of this book because of their foul and exceedingly rustic diction. Rather, imitate the man who, having found a gem in a dung heap, washed it for a long time with clear water until it returned to its former brilliance. In the same way, wash away with the water of your wisdom the stains of my ignorance, and adorn the discourses of this book—which are necessary—with your beautiful and well-ordered words, so that the usefulness of the book may no longer be rejected by proud readers because of its rusticity.

For I know that many, puffed up with knowledge of letters, will spit upon and mock this unpolished composition of mine. They will also be indignant with me, asking why I, an uneducated and ignorant man, presumed to forge a volume of exposition on a book of such great obscurity.

To them I reply that, just as the sprinkling of manure benefits barren soil more than any precious metal, so divine Scripture expressed in ordinary language benefits uneducated people more than if it were delivered in philosophical or poetic speech. Let them know that our Lord Jesus Christ first entrusted the mysteries of his teaching not to philosophers but to fishermen, so that through fishermen he might come to philosophers.

For he who gave the she-ass sensible speech to correct the prophet’s foolishness (Num. 22:30) has himself deigned to grant some understanding of this book to me, unworthy and most insignificant of all human beings.

As I reflected upon Solomon’s saying, “Wisdom hidden and treasure unseen—what benefit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20:32), and at the same time considered that grave danger threatened me if I concealed in silence the very small treasure that almighty God had deigned to bestow upon me; and as I also considered that I was not suitable for teaching what I understood, since no one could be found who, in the manner of a disciple, would deign to hear the words of my ignorance, I resolved within myself to pursue this small knowledge that divine mercy had granted me in whatever style I could, lest, hiding my Lord’s talent, I should be condemned together with that servant who went away, dug in the earth, and hid his master’s money (Matt. 25:18).

And because I am not capable of doubling my Lord’s money, I hand it over to the money-changers, so that when he comes he may receive what is his with interest.

You, to whom I have begun to speak, I call a money-changer. For just as a money-changer adorns unworked money with his own inscriptions so that it may be suitable for producing profit, so you are able, by your wisdom and your well-ordered words, to adorn this money of the Lord that I entrust to you, so that it may become suitable for accomplishing profits for our Lord Jesus Christ.

Know that you will receive an excellent reward from him if this book—which, as I think, is necessary for the Church of God—through your diligence and learning loses the stains of its diction and, adorned with your fitting words, becomes more useful for the edification of those who read or hear it.

I do not, however, permit you to change the meaning of this book into other meanings, unless, God forbid, something is found in it that is contrary to the truth. In that case I decree that it must be wholly removed or certainly changed for the better.

# ON PENANCE

[Col. 0969]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOK ON PENANCE

[Col. 0969C] Gillotius was the first to publish this book On Penance from a codex of the Sorbonne library, in which the name of Ambrose had been falsely inscribed as its author. He nevertheless placed it only after the complete works of the holy Doctor and demonstrated by very strong arguments that it was spurious.

His supports for this judgment are these: its diction is affected and entirely unlike that of Ambrose; it is also harsher and scattered here and there with certain words suggestive of an African writer; Ambrose mentions only two books On Penance published by him; this author makes no mention of the Novatians; and finally, the same author openly reveals at the end of the book that his name was Victor.

The last point alone was certainly sufficient to establish that this treatise was not by Ambrose, but it is not by itself sufficient to determine who that Victor was. Since the aforementioned Gillotius had learned from Gennadius and Trithemius that a book On Penance had been composed by Victor, bishop of Cartenna in Africa, he thought that this work should be attributed to no other Victor. Many later embraced this opinion, since it was not entirely without the appearance of truth.

Yet this opinion finally vanished after that most perceptive investigator of ancient manuscripts, Sirmondus, read this little work attributed also to Victor of Tunnuna, a bishop in Africa, in a manuscript of Saint Mary of Reims and in another of the abbey of Hérivaux, as Labbe testifies.

We say nothing about the Hérivaux manuscript, which we were not permitted to see. But concerning the Reims manuscript, against which we corrected this book, we willingly follow Sirmond’s testimony. For the following inscription appears there:

“Here begins the book of Saint Victor On the Lapsed, bishop of Ton(n)una, the historiographer.”

The fact that Tonensis is written there instead of Tunonensis must without doubt be attributed to the scribe. The addition “historiographer,” however, is explained by the fact that a chronicle composed by the same man was transmitted to posterity.

[Col. 0971]

# ONE BOOK ON PENANCE (C, G, S)*

589 ## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0971A]

As I am about to describe the duties and merits of penance, dearest brother, I think that words are not needed but deeds. A salutary and necessary matter should not so much be spoken of as taught; although its entire activity is imbued with bitterness, it produces the fruit of sweetness in its effect and clings to the throat while imparting a saving remedy to the heart.

Penance, I say, is condemnation of the former way of life and a promised correction in the future. It is as though one is led into another life when the devout mind does not look back at the things behind it.

I teach this not so much by words as by actions; and although the role of a righteous person does not suit me, at the beginning of my discourse I nevertheless accuse myself. For a cautious confession of error has a share in righteousness. Although, as you teach, it belongs to God to punish sins, penance practiced in humility nevertheless anticipates the sentence of the judge. For it is written: “He granted the penitent a share in justice, corrected those who were failing to endure, and appointed them to the lot of truth” (Ecclus. 17:20).

Come, then, penitent: confess your own crimes; disclose to God the secrets of your iniquity; lay bare the hidden things of your heart; and remove the covering of inward transgression.

Everything that you have done in secret is known to God. If the tongue does not speak it, conscience cannot conceal it. In vain do you deceive yourself with hidden consolation and think that what you committed without a witness can remain concealed.

Everything closed is open to God, and whatever the night of hidden thought darkens shines in the open. Establish yourself as guilty through the duty of confession; arrange your case in your own sight, with yourself as accuser. Pronounce judgment against yourself with severity before you feel the anger of the judge, and, in order to draw out mercy, exercise discipline upon yourself first.

Believe me: everything of which you are suspected immediately becomes pardonable when such penance of righteousness has been found in you, as Scripture says: “To the penitent he granted a share in justice, corrected those who were failing to endure, and appointed them to the lot of truth.”

[Col. 0972A] Behold, the Lord awaits the gift of confession, provided guilt does not overwhelm the one who confesses. Although the human conscience is known to the divine understanding, he prefers the tongue to reveal what the hidden things of the heart cannot conceal.

Penance, therefore, is what joins together different duties in a single act. On one side it makes the penitent public; on the other, it restores the confessed person as innocent. On one side it puts guilt up for sale; on the other, it excuses the crime. On one side it sets sins more closely before the sinner; on the other, it obtains pardon for the penitent. The Lord does not permit the confessed person to be punished when he recognizes that the penitent has been restored from condemnation.

O magnificent treasure of divine goodness! O singular ordinance of the most merciful judge! For this reason he wishes to draw from the guilty the voice of confession, so that he may find nothing that ought to be avenged. Whereas among the judges of this world the one who confesses is immediately led to punishment, before the Lord the one who confesses proceeds at once to pardon. Nor does he extract this confession from the penitent through any tortures, since the sufferer appears to perform the duty of terror upon himself.

The groans of the one who confesses are gains for the pious judge, and the joy of the judge is confession without interrogation. The Lord gains what is not punished in his servant.

[Note: The edition reads: “what is not punished in hell”; the Roman manuscript: “… in the servant.”]

Much is conferred upon the author when one appointed for punishment is granted pardon. For he wishes it to be a loss to vengeance that mercy does not wish the person to perish; nor does he desire to avenge one whom he is ready to pity. He himself says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he should turn back and live” (Ezek. 18:32).

In harmony with this, Solomon’s Wisdom says: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:16).

Therefore the clemency of our judge does not desire the guilty to perish from life, but to perish from the sentence; nor does it desire the death of the dying person, but hastens rather to save the one who confesses: “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but that he should turn back and live.”

Behold the true author of life, who does not wish the death of the dying, but the laments of the converted; and who wishes always to be generous in mercy, lest justice retain the one who has been judged.

## CHAPTER TWO
Therefore he experiences loss in the one who dies, [Col. 0973A] [Note: [Col. 0973D] The Remensis manuscript reads: “who [experiences loss] in the living person who has perished.”] he who does not rejoice in the one who has perished; for in the giver of life it is necessary that the cause of sadness arise from death—not as though what grieves him in the lost and dying person proceeded from the law of bodily sensations, since in an incorporeal creator not everything that comes from the body can occur—but because he derives no joy whatsoever from the death of the one who perishes, the action of sadness is immediately apparent: it is the feeling of one who pities, not the anguish of one who suffers; [Note: [Col. 0973D] Thus the edition and the Sorbonne manuscripts; the Remensis manuscript, however, reads: “and sadness, purified as it proceeds.”] and sadness flowing from compassion, not any external suffering endured. It follows, then, that he grieves over the lost one who rejoices over the one found, and that he does not rejoice over the dead who rejoices over the living.

The Lord makes this clear in the Gospel through the parable, saying: “But you ought to rejoice and be glad, because your brother was dead and has come to life again; he had perished and has been found” (Luke 15:32); and again: “So there will be joy,” he says, “in heaven before your Father and his angels over one sinner doing penance” (ibid., 7).

Hence, through the prophet Isaiah, the Lord summons the penitent, saying: “I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, do not forget, and let us be judged. You speak first of your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:25). What, I ask, could be more pleasing than this promise? What could be found sweeter than this invitation? To summon the judge, to declare oneself guilty against oneself for one’s own sake—not so that he may punish, but so that he may absolve; not so that he may take vengeance on the one who confesses, but so that he may justify the one convicted by his own confession.

“But I will not remember,” he says, “but you, do not forget.” This means: “The memory of your deed will not remain with me if you do not forget your own error; and the disgrace of your crime will be erased if, compelled by remembering it, you do not cease to confess it to my ears.”

You see, then, that God is intent upon the sinner’s crimes if there is no act of repentance, and that the anger of the just judge hangs over the guilty person, since he is not pleased by the groaning of one who confesses. But he leads into oblivion those things that you have been unable to make known, and the stain of the crime is erased if you do not wound your conscience by silence.

“I am he,” he says, “who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember; but you, do not forget.” He did not wish there to be any point of time, any instant at all, in which forgetfulness of sins might enter your breast—not so that you might be captivated by the enjoyment of what you had previously committed, but so that a sigh might arise in you not from longing for past things, but from remembering your grief.

Always place your fall before your eyes and mourn; lament your burial at every moment; continually feel that you are dead, and recognize without doubt that you are destined to die. The Lord will not count this against you as punishment, but will turn it toward glory. He will remember you in such a way that he will forget what you previously did in sin, offering you, in place of temporal mourning, eternal and infinite consolations, once your sins have escaped punishment, as he himself says: “Blessed are those who now mourn, for they shall be comforted. But you, do not forget, and let us be judged” (Matthew 5:5).

“Meanwhile, let us be judged,” he says. [Col. 0974A] Surely the Lord is not to be judged, since he says that he is to be judged together with the sinner? Far from it. “Let us be judged,” he says: you confessing, I forgiving; you offering what is owed, I granting forgiveness for sins; you declaring your iniquities, I justifying you in complete compassion.

Finally, consider what follows: “You speak first of your iniquities,” he says, “that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26)—not that you may be condemned; so that the reward of the one converted may remain in you, not the punishment of the one who merely confesses; so that judgment may accompany you as one made just, not the mark of the condemned. And then you will be free from all your iniquities when you have become a witness and accuser against yourself.

“You speak first,” he says, “of your iniquities, that you may be justified.” But surely he does not summon you, brother, to confess your iniquities as though he were ignorant of them, since he knows them before they occur? And does he desire to hear from you as though he were unaware, when by his foreknowledge he ordinarily judges what has not yet been born?

Or do you not know that the judgment concerning the unequal merits of the twin offspring conceived at the same time in the womb of holy Rebecca and born from it at the same time was declared through foreknowledge?

## CHAPTER III

He therefore wants you to know more fully what is happening within you, so that, when you disclose your illness to the physician, he may administer the antidote necessary for you. For you will be able to obtain the full benefit of medicine only if you do not conceal the wounds of your conscience from the physician.

Otherwise, how will you be healed if you do not reveal what is hidden within you? For I think that, unless the physician is called in, the sick person is not cured. He therefore waits a long time for the causes of your pain to be shown to him, so that, once you have been healed, you may understand the remedy of medicine; for you will weigh what is owed to the physician by a proper estimation if you have first recognized your disease within yourself. [Note: [Col. 0973D] The Remensis manuscript and the Sorbonne manuscripts read: “you will weigh it according to a proper assessment.”]

And, not to keep you longer, your penitent confession is medicine: it heals you, it gives you life. It does not allow your wound to retain its putrefaction, but as soon as you have groaned, it applies a [Note: [Col. 0974D] The edition and the Sorbonne manuscript read: “from there, a notable scar”; the Remensis manuscript has the better reading: “from there, a knot-like scar.”] knot-like scar.

Today, if some bodily illness afflicts you, and you feel your limbs weighed down by an inward weakness, or understand that your wound is becoming cancerous with corruption and the filth of putrefaction, you immediately run to the physician, seek a remedy from his skill, keep watch before the door of the one who is sleeping, and stand at his doors as a morning visitor. You desire to pray with entreaties, promise gifts, offer presents, and spend your entire fortune for the sake of your health. And although most often his incompetence either aggravates the illness or at least delays it for a long time, nevertheless you persist in constant attendance.

You hope for slow remedies from one human being, and you do not despair of receiving useful assistance, even though you do not yet feel the effect of restored strength. Yet you do not run to your God, the physician who gives freely, the willing dispenser of remedies, who in healing the illnesses of your soul knows no weariness, does not await a reward from your health, but rather desires to reward you by rewarding the one who has been healed.

And certainly the temporal physician treats only what pertains to the body; God, however, heals the soul, which sins wound repeatedly. The former brings forth remedies useful for the present; the latter applies an everlasting medicine.

And yet a human physician cannot even help himself unless God comes to his aid. For the skill of medicine often labors in vain if God does not wish to prolong the sick person’s time of life. Indeed, we sometimes see physicians unable to help even themselves when, overtaken by bodily diseases, they are deprived of the benefit of health. Therefore medicine will provide no benefit when medicine itself does not assist the physician.

Believe me: no one restores you better than the one who made you; and no one justifies except the one who scourges and heals. He alone knows how to mend the breaches in his work and to restore the shattered form of our clay to its original condition, as he himself says through the prophet: “As clay is in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand” (Jeremiah 18:6).

Nor does he accomplish this after any interval of time. As soon as you have declared your illness, he immediately grants assistance. Almost no time intervenes between the aid being implored and the remedy being bestowed. He waits only for you to confess; there will be no delay before you are healed.

“You speak first,” he says, “of your iniquities, that you may be justified.”

The same Spirit promises this through the prophet Ezekiel to the unrighteous: “On whatever day the wicked person turns away from his wickedness and does justice, on that day all his injustices will perish; in the injustice he committed, he will not die” (Ezekiel 18:27). And elsewhere: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:15).

## CHAPTER IV

But perhaps you say: “I have no one who knows, and what I have committed is wholly unknown to anyone.”

What then? If you have no human accomplice, do you at least not know God, the foreknower and unavoidable witness of your conscience? And if no human being knows your deeds, surely God knows your deeds and even those still to come.

For what does he not see who sees everywhere and sees everything? He says to Job: “Who would think that anything could be hidden from me? Give me a place in which God is not, who is wholly hidden, [Note: [Col. 0975D] Gill and the Sorbonne manuscript read: “who is wholly hidden, and he will be hidden in your deeds, as you suppose”; in the margin, opposite the first occurrence of “hidden,” the manuscript has what may be “eye,” a conjecture admitted into the text by the Roman edition. We have preferred the reading of the Remensis manuscript.] and then you too will be hidden in your deeds, as you suppose.”

But God is everywhere, and he is wholly present in everything, as he himself says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66:1); and: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24).

Hence the most blessed prophet David also says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you will be there. If I take up my outstretched wings, to dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand, O Lord, will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:7 and following).

It is therefore useless for you to say that you have no witness, when you hear that God is wholly everywhere and diffused through all things by the expanse of his majesty, and that whatever is thought to be hidden is known to him.

“But I have no accomplice,” you say. You would have said this correctly if you did not have the example of Cain, the first of parricides.

Parricidal wickedness had persuaded him to go with his righteous brother into the field. The inexperienced and newly formed brotherhood, thinking that he had no reason to guard himself against his brother, obeyed his commands in the goodness of his simplicity. The two brothers walked together in a single company, and the accursed parricide chose a place without a witness in which to carry out his wicked plan.

But surely, even if he had no human witness, could anything have been hidden from the eyes of God? Or could he conceal it by seeking solitude, when nothing is hidden from the gaze of the Creator?

When the original perpetrator of the unspeakable deed judged the place suitable for committing his crime, he rushed into madness and, with the devil’s prompting, killed his very patient and wholly unresisting brother. The deed itself was plainly evident in its execution; but, as Cain had thought, it remained hidden as though without a witness. [Note: [Col. 0975D] The edition reads “as he had thought it”; the Remensis manuscript, “as Cain had thought.” Below, where Gill, with the Remensis and Sorbonne manuscripts, reads “the crime could find no admission,” the Roman edition, following Gill’s margin, reads “the crime could find no opening.”]

The most cruel of men believed that the crime could find no admission without a witness, though by the very deed he acknowledged the crime that he wished to conceal. But behold the Lord of all things, for whom whatever is thought hidden is manifest, and from whom what takes place in the secrecy of thoughts cannot be concealed. Scripture says: “The thought of a human being will confess to you” (Psalm 75:11); and again: “Your eyes saw my unfinished substance, and in your book they will all be written” (Psalm 138:16); and again: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:10).

Hence the same prophet David says: “You saw my thoughts from afar” (Psalm 138:2), and addresses the parricide in a voice of indignation. Knowing the savage spirit of the atrocious deed he had committed, and knowing that he would deny it, God pretends, as it were, not to know what had happened, so as to increase the guilt of the wicked parricide.

“And the Lord said to Cain: ‘Where is Abel your brother?’ And Cain said: ‘I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?’” (Genesis 4:9).

O detestable madness! O extraordinary audacity! He confidently denies what he had committed without a witness, and believed that, without a witness, the crime could not be made public, although the very act itself exposed the guilt of his conscience. [Note: [Col. 0976D] The Roman edition, following Gill’s margin, reads: “with the denial itself.”]

What are you doing, unhappy Cain? You have no human being as a witness. Behold, you have blood poured out as an informer: it itself exposes and accuses you. Its voice appeals against you to the Creator, and the spilled blood provokes judgment, lest vengeance pass over the parricide who lies hidden.

“What have you done?” he says. “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (ibid., 10).

But when the parricide realized that what he had thought hidden had been betrayed, and, convicted by blood as a witness, recognized that he had pretended in vain to deny his defiant crime, he confessed the deed. He desired a harsher judgment to be pronounced against him, since his conscience could not excuse the parricide he had committed.

Meanwhile, the more severe punishment was delayed, so that a slow sentence might torment the author of so great a crime for a longer time, and so that the speed of the punishment inflicted might not seem to lessen the condemned person’s suffering. [Note: [Col. 0976D] Thus the Remensis manuscript and Gill in the text, except that Gill writes “more long-lived.” In the margin Gill has: “a punishment made longer by its duration, since he considered the crime of parricide diminished by the slowness of dying”; the Roman edition adopted this reading, though it retained “would lessen.”]

Thus his punishment was prolonged by its penal duration, lest the slowness of dying should make light of the crime of parricide.

Why, then, do you flatter yourself about not having an accomplice, when you see that Cain was at once convicted and punished by the testimony of innocent blood?

## CHAPTER V

“But I have no witness,” you say, “who might disclose my deeds.”

Tell me, I ask, if you have no witness, do you therefore have no testimony from your conscience? Or can you escape yourself and evade your conscience?

I speak of the conscience in which nothing we do dies; it accuses and judges us in our deeds. Though it does not possess the use of speech, it nevertheless does not know how to keep silence. A witness may be taken away by death; the absence of a witness may help you for a time. [Note: [Col. 0977D] The Sorbonne manuscripts and Gill read: “the testimony of conscience may help”; nothing correct remains afterward. In the margin, however: “may help. The testimony of conscience is also always with you.” The Roman edition reads: “the testimony may help. But conscience is always with you.” The Remensis manuscript restores the passage best.]

But conscience is always with you and is never without you. It clings to your breast and never abandons you. Like a kind of attendant, it never leaves your side for any interval of time; it holds you guilty and always keeps you captive under its power.

If at any time the activity of more prosperous circumstances draws your mind away, and pleasure begins to delight your senses through enjoyment of what you have done, conscience suddenly pricks you; it strikes and pierces you to the marrow, interrupts your pleasure, and disturbs the whole region of your breast with sorrowful sighs. And since it seems to be held wounded by reproach, no remedy is found for a human being by which it might be healed. For it is always offended when someone else is chastised, and it is itself struck first by another’s wound.

Do you wish to know how great is the severity of conscience? An accomplice may be bribed with gold; he may be bought with money. Conscience admits no corruption; its testimony remains whole, surrounded by the complete firmness of faith.

Indeed, a defense is procured against a witness, arguments of cunning are sought through the ingenuity of advocacy, and the truth of testimony is distorted by the craftiness of shameless speech. Even the judge is bought, so that the character of the deed may be excused.

All these things are useless where conscience is concerned. And although a human being dies, conscience certainly does not die; after the death of the body, it is judged in the soul. Do you think it benefits you not to have a witness when you experience the daily and perpetual judgment of conscience?

But certainly divine vengeance will not accompany the one whom his own conscience has judged. For there the power of the judge must necessarily be inactive, where the guilty person is himself his own witness and accuser against himself.

Without doubt, the cause of sin will be doubled if a rebellious conscience refuses to confess its deeds. For then the sinner becomes impious: he remains hardened in refusing to confess his sins, so that a fitting sentence may condemn his crimes and his stubborn conscience may suffer the punishments of defiance.

The judge’s anger is broken when the strictness produced by repentance and severity is softened by the opposition of confession. The judgment drawn from indignation is shaken by satisfaction, and the intention of the one threatening is tempered by the modesty of the most humble prayer.

Learn this from the Ninevites, whose confession erased the sentence already pronounced and turned aside the impending anger, lest the repentance of those who confessed should prove fruitless.

A sentence had already been brandished from heaven over the wretched city, and the axe of divine punishment pressed upon the necks of the unhappy inhabitants. The heavenly sword had already been drawn from its sheath, and fierce anger boiled for vengeance upon the crimes committed. The herald’s voice threatened the peoples with destruction, and the prophet’s cry announced imminent ruin to all who were about to perish: “After three days,” he said, “the city of Nineveh will be overthrown.”

Alas, what are you demanding from our God by your crimes? What punishment are you purchasing through your sins? You have forestalled the most merciful compassion of our God himself, from whom you have demanded vengeance so near at hand and before its time.

I seem to see how great an anguish constrained the wretched people, and what kind of necessity had seized them with trembling. Fear had deprived them of counsel, and despair had no remedy. For time had been driven forward with such precipitous speed that not even the interval allotted to them could loosen the dreadful suspicion of their crime.

“After three days,” he says, “the city of Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4).

And what sort of overthrow was that which was announced to those who were about to perish? It certainly did not signify an enemy’s attack, nor the clamor of weapons or the terrifying blare of trumpets, against which perhaps defensive preparations might have enabled those resisting to meet the advancing forces. Nor could the opposing sides engage in battle, or those destined for captivity cast their lot upon the protections of flight. [Note: [Col. 0978D] The edition, Gill, and the Roman edition read: “defensive forces might meet them”; Gill in the margin and the Remensis and Sorbonne manuscripts in the text read: “defensive protections might meet them.”]

Rather, the destruction of divine indignation and heavenly vengeance was being proclaimed—a destruction from which the one to be punished could be withdrawn neither by flight nor by the means of warfare.

For who could avoid the calamity that had been inflicted, when an ethereal crash was beginning to pour it forth?

## CHAPTER VI

But behold: counsel does not abandon the wretched in their fear, and despair finds a remedy in danger. Returning to themselves, they question their consciences in the role of judges, run to the stronghold of repentance, and, holding up the shield of confession, turn aside the arrow.

Everyone goes to the healing of confessed crimes, and the crowd exposed to death unites in the duty of making satisfaction. They impose upon themselves the necessary fast of those who are about to perish; in their very bodies they chastise their souls with the whip of humility. They put on sackcloth instead of clothing, sprinkle themselves with ashes instead of perfume, and, prostrate on the ground, lick the dust.

They bury their death with tears and accompany their life with lamentation. They make their guilt public through groans and disclose the hidden crimes of their deeds.

Every age and sex, without distinction, adapts itself to mournful duties. All adornment is laid aside, all finery cast down. But those bodily squalors were truly the ornaments of repentance, and the virtue of their appearance was the highest beauty of confession.

Food was even denied to nursing infants, and an age not yet infected by its own sins bore the burdens of others. Dumb cattle hungered for their food, and the brute animals received none of their natural fodder.

A single wailing of creatures of different kinds was heard throughout the walls of the city; sorrowful laments of mourners resounded through every house. And, to put it briefly, the earth endured the roaring of those who confessed, while the stars themselves rang with the voice of repentance.

What is written was fulfilled: “The prayer of one who humbles himself pierces the clouds” (Ecclesiasticus 25:31).

Finally, in this way he appeased the offended God; in this way he made the stern one gentle; in this way he softened the angry one and hid the sword-point of vengeance in its [Note: “in its sheath” or “in its case”; the transmitted Latin, *in techa*, is textually uncertain.] sheath: because conscience passed judgment upon itself.

Confession rescued the guilty from punishment, and repentance claimed for itself those already delivered over to vengeance. The sentence of condemnation was immediately erased by the tears of those who confessed, and the confession that acknowledged the crime absolved those liable to punishment.

The merciful God saw that the penitents had taken judgment upon themselves and condemned their errors by that acknowledgment; immediately he granted forgiveness to those whom he had destined for punishment and at once spared the afflicted, so that, removed from punishment, they might become gains for compassion.

The testimony of prophecy that we set forth a little earlier was proved: “I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember; but you, do not forget, and let us be judged” (Isaiah 42:25).

“You speak first,” he says, “of your iniquities, that you may be justified”; and again: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:15); and again: “Turn to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and compassionate, patient and of great mercy, and one who turns aside the judgments inflicted against wickedness” (Joel 2:12).

Hence the most blessed David also says: “I myself have acknowledged my sin, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 31:6); and again: “For I myself know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5).

You see, then, that the one who sins daily needs judgment upon himself, so that when conscience is stripped bare, it may be covered; and when it is made public, it may be covered. [Note: [Col. 0979D] Thus the Remensis manuscript; the edition and Gill read: “so that, when conscience is covered, it may be…” In the margin: “perhaps ‘is uncovered’”; this conjecture was admitted into the text of the Roman edition. Even there, however, the word *nudatur* (“is stripped bare”) is absent.]

Although everything we do is known to God and is not hidden from his senses before it happens, he nevertheless prefers that you strip bare the secret of your heart and expose the crimes of your conscience, so that, by the gift of his indulgence, he may cover the nakedness of your shame.

How does he wish to send away the one who confesses, stripped of forgiveness? Concerning such people the most blessed prophet sang, saying: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” [Col. 0979D] (Psalm 31:1).

Although this applies more clearly to those reborn, whose iniquities and crimes are covered and concealed in baptism, sincere confession occupies a trustworthy place of forgiveness, and the penitent conscience is secure if it does not doubt the remission of indulgence.

## CHAPTER VII

On the contrary, the mass of sin is increased if what is committed is denied. We recalled this above in the case of Cain, who, while thinking that he could deny his deed to his Creator, was not released from punishment for himself; thus conscience, in the atrocity of its deed, deprived him in vain, through denial, of the fruit of repentance.

He was convicted as one who denied, not confessed willingly, and his defiance was punished in the crime because confession through repentance did not follow the interrogation.

It is therefore worthwhile to disclose here, step by step, the sevenfold reason for that vengeance and to demonstrate, by proof of the evident matter, what cause compelled so harsh a sentence to be heaped upon him—lest the enormity of the vengeance open a path of slander toward the suspicion of injustice. Yet the punishment ought to accompany the discovery of such an extraordinary crime with force, since it was to serve as an example for later generations.

For he is mistaken who thinks that the parricide was held by a single crime, since all his offenses are crowded together in the testimony of such a deed. I hear the Lord saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37 and following). Hence the whole Law and the prophets depend upon these two commandments.

Since everything belonging to the Law depends upon these two precepts, and since I see that Cain neither loved God—whose first creation he violated—nor intensely hated his brother, whom he killed under the impulse of wickedness, it is clear that he had thereby paid the due of vengeance, because all crimes are found united in his deed.

And rightly a sevenfold punishment was inflicted upon him, in whom every crime held dominion. Yet I find seven particular crimes in him, each of which received its own punishment.

His first crime was that he did not divide correctly; that is, he first ate from the firstfruits of the earth before he offered them.

The second was that, when his offering appeared to have received the rejection it deserved, he conceived a rebellious spirit. Since no fault of rejected offering belonged to his righteous brother, the accursed man thought that he ought to avenge himself upon the Creator, if he appeared to kill the brother who had been approved by God on account of this.

The third crime was that, filled with the gall of envy and poisoned by the bitterness of jealousy, he envied his most innocent brother with savage hostility.

The fourth was that he deceived his obedient brother by trickery, so that they might go together into the field: there the righteous man was to begin martyrdom under the simplicity of a lamb, while the unjust man would stain the earth with parricide.

The fifth was that the wicked author of cruelty killed his brother.

The sixth was that, after committing the crime, he not only denied it but also thought God ignorant of some deed, although he had perceived that God had punished the secret of his conscience when he had rightly declared the rejection of his offering.

The seventh crime was that, after the death, he did not believe that he would be punished for the parricide once exposed, although, because of the disgrace of the publicized crime, he asked to be killed immediately.

Therefore vengeance was justly exacted sevenfold upon Cain, in whom as many punishments were imposed as there were crimes. As many wounds were inflicted upon him as causes could be counted, so that justice would neither exceed the measure of vengeance nor pass over the number of crimes with an appropriate punishment.

I have repeated this for the reason that the opportunity for the explanation already introduced might not pass by.

## CHAPTER VIII

For a long time now I have felt that I have strayed from the purpose of the work I began and diverted the swift course of my discourse into another direction. But it is easy to return to what was omitted, and the path of the subject from which one has deviated is quickly recovered when the argument does not wander beyond the boundaries of the proof inserted between them.

“Therefore,” he says, “I have acknowledged my sin, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 31:6); and again: “For I myself know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5).

He taught this not only in words but also fulfilled it in deeds. For it is not enough, for the completion of spiritual wisdom, to put virtue forward in words unless teaching is adorned by actions. Only then is appropriate authority granted to instruction if it rests upon one’s own example.

Finally, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does and teaches in this way will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19), so that teaching may be confirmed by deeds and the credibility of deeds may receive testimony from teaching.

Otherwise teaching will not be founded upon strenuous effort if it misuses the glory of virtue through the ornament of words. The tongue will be rich in eloquence, but the conscience will not be full of the wealth of works; and the one who enjoys another’s privilege will be deprived of his own merit.

Let us therefore see what he did who sang these words.

At one time, two sins had crept upon the king, and the license of royal power had enticed the ruler into committing a crime. For, when he wished to cover adultery, he fell into homicide.

Yet he committed both deeds not through the violence of royal rank nor through an ambition for power. Although the adultery arose from the license of unlawful desire, the homicide had not been committed out of hatred.

Therefore a prophet is sent by the Lord to plead before him the causes of the adultery and the killing of the murdered man, and, under the guise of a fabricated story, to draw a judgment from one who did not know what was being judged.

But when the prophet had explained what he had proposed, the king, moved by the matter, pronounced against himself an unmarked sentence under the appearance of truth; and the unknowing arbitrator brought vengeance upon himself.

When the judge who had been forestalled saw that he himself had been struck by his own judgment, and the most just examiner proved him guilty to himself, he realized that he could not escape the punishment of a judgment in which he himself was held under the condition of the condemned. He seized the most health-giving counsel in such a crisis and, since he could not appeal against the justice of the judgment, fled to the inner chamber of repentance.

He knew that his sin had been exposed and covered his iniquity with no cloud of denial. He immediately gave testimony against himself and, once the voice of confession had been uttered, promptly obtained forgiveness of his sins: “I have sinned,” he said, “against the Lord.”

But the prophet did not delay absolution or postpone the effect of forgiveness. As soon as the guilty man, once exposed, had offered confession, the prophet, by God’s will, brought forth forgiveness for the crimes, saying: “The Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).

What he sang in the psalm was fulfilled: “I have acknowledged my sin, and I have not covered my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 31:6).

## CHAPTER IX

Let us also disclose another example of repentance in holy David. For this distinguished king had so devoted himself to divine worship through faithful service, as an institution of life worthy of imitation, [Note: [Col. 0981D] The edition and the Sorbonne manuscript read: “an instructor in a life worthy of imitation”; the Remensis manuscript has the better reading, as in the text.] that he left us not examples of his conduct but memorials.

Against the prohibition, he had ordered the people to be counted and had wished to know the number of the whole army. His royal will was obeyed, the total number of the army was reported to him, and he began, to his own glory, to know what harmed him. He magnified his prosperity by increasing the number of his subjects and counted the gains of the multiplied army among his principal joys.

Immediately another prophet is sent to him. The cause of his sin is not subtly suggested to him, as had first been done; rather, a penal choice is now proposed because of the deed. [Note: [Col. 0981D] The Remensis and Sorbonne manuscripts read: “a punitive choice is punished”; the edition has the better reading: “a punitive choice is proposed,” and so forth.]

“And the word of the Lord came to Gad the prophet, saying: ‘Go to David and speak: Thus says the Lord: I set three things before you; choose one of them, and I will do it to you.’ And Gad came to David and reported to him, saying: ‘Choose what you wish to happen to you from these three: either a famine for three years over the land, or that you flee for three months from the face of your enemies, while they pursue you, or that for three days there be death in the land. And now know and see what I should answer the one who sent me the word’” (2 Samuel 24:11 and following).

What struggle of counsel was then at work in his mind? What turmoil of thought arose in his choice? On one side the fear of enemies, on another the devastation of famine, and elsewhere the blow of divine punishment terrified him. He wished to encounter none of these things, but the offense could not remain unavenged.

Amid the very constraints of this choice, when he was enclosed between the extremities of both dangers, taught by the example of the forgiveness that had preceded, he more sharply chose punishment in the very deliberation [Note: [Col. 0982D] Thus the Remensis manuscript; the edition reads: “punishment in the very will.” The latter is less coherent.] and exposed himself to the greater punishment, so that he might summon compassion.

For the rigor of justice is softened when one presumes upon mercy, and the first matter brought before the most compassionate judge is a plea for compassion. The one who forgives those who confess their errors does not condemn the stubborn according to their will.

Therefore this devoted king, while wavering amid the storm of deliberation, did not let go of the anchor of repentance. Trusting in the compassion of the one who terrified him, he did not consider the magnitude of the vengeance:

“And David said to Gad: ‘I am in great distress in these three things; but it is better for me to fall into the hands of the Lord, because his mercy is very great, than to fall into the hands of human beings’” (ibid., 14).

Immediately agreement with vengeance follows, and a merciful punishment accompanies the choice that pleases mercy. An immeasurable slaughter of the slain takes place, and a multitude of the people is struck down by an angelic blow.

Seventy thousand of the army are struck down, and a pitiful ruin of the camp presses more bitterly upon his tender heart. He presents himself as the author of the deed to the weapon of punishment, and puts on the breastplate of confession against the sword raging with justice. Urging that he himself be punished more than those being punished, he cries out and wishes the sentence to be diverted onto himself, so that he may recall the blow from the people.

“Behold, I am here,” he says. “I, the shepherd, have sinned; I have acted wickedly. But what has this flock done? Turn your hand against me and against my father’s house” (2 Samuel 24:17).

Behold, punishment is struck by the duty of satisfaction, and indignation is resisted by the weapons of confession, so that vengeance might proceed no further against him and the heavenly devastation poured out against the people might cease.

By one act of repentance he both purchased compassion for himself and immediately suspended vengeance from the people. Therefore, rightly granted forgiveness, he sang, saying: “I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Psalm 31:5), because, when he stood under the despair of one convicted, he was judged worthy to be cleansed.

But the enormity of your sins weighs you down, and, held captive under their power, you do not dare to raise your eyes toward heaven. I approve the fear of your conscience, but I do not approve your counsel. I would rather have you suspicious about obtaining forgiveness than utterly despairing of the restoration of salvation.

## CHAPTER X
The shame of asking constitutes a certain part of confession: one who is conscious of his sins does not doubt the Author’s forgiveness, but is ashamed of the greatness of his guilt. To have acknowledged one’s offense is the beginning of confession, and remorse brings one close to forgiveness.

“But the abundance of my sins,” you will say, “drives me backward.” On the contrary, the more heavily you are burdened with sins, the more insistently you must devote yourself to confession, so that what you are not worthy to demand through friendship you may be able to obtain through shameless persistence. For you hear the Lord say in the Gospel that “he to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke 7:47). Furthermore, you make God impious if you suppose that he rejects the converted person [Note: [Col. 0983D] The Roman edition alone has “and denies affection to the returning person.”] and denies affection to one who returns, when you know that those who are lost are sought out through compassion.

The Apostle proves this when he says: “And if we should prove faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (1 Timothy 2:12).
