Or do you not know that the Lord, when tempted nine times in the wilderness, deferred punishment, and even on that tenth occasion [Note: [Col. 0983D] The editions and the Sorbonne manuscript read “could have condemned,” if this refers to the preceding sins; the Remiremont manuscript has the reading adopted in the text.] could not have condemned the people’s stubbornness if, after the preceding nine offenses, they had practiced repentance, since he himself said: “Behold, now they have provoked me ten times in this wilderness” (Numbers 14:27)?

Read the Book of Judges, and you will find that innumerable times the children of Israel did evil before the Lord and were handed over to the attacks of the nations. Yet, when the people again turned back, they were delivered from their various captivities through chosen leaders, and their offenses could not be avenged whenever appropriate repentance followed what had been done. For although punitive correction was not absent, there was nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0984D] Thus the Remiremont manuscript; the edition instead reads “the cutting off of treachery.” This is not entirely correct.] no severing of destruction, but an appeal for conversion.

For when a chastised son is received back into affection, it is clear that he has been admonished to make satisfaction, not punished. The correction does not appear to arise from hatred but from love, since, after the scourging, the returning son is repeatedly not denied the rights of affection.

Finally, hear the Lord, through the prophet, rebuking a fornicating woman of this kind—one devoted to disgrace and polluted by defilements—and declaring that he wished to take her to himself by right of conversion: “And I said,” he says, “after you had committed all these acts of fornication, ‘Return to me’; but you did not return, shameless Judah” (Jeremiah 3:7).

The same Lord makes this clear in the Gospel when he rebukes the hardened, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

Believe me: the Lord awaits the final act of our life, and in whatever condition our final end finds us, in that condition he will judge us. If, that is, you are surrounded by multiplied errors, if the shadows of your crimes circle above your head, if the darkness of your sins overspreads your eyes, if the yoke of sin bends your neck, and if, within the inner chamber of your conscience, the disgrace of your offenses repeatedly festers as a wound—if you have not cast your soul into the wretchedness of despair, then, when you pour forth in confession a single utterance from the innermost secret of your heart, he will not deny you the remedy of forgiveness. He came to save souls, not to destroy them; he plainly urges the one who has turned back toward life, as the Lord himself says: “The Son of Man did not come to destroy human lives but to save them” (Luke 9:56); and again: “For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had been lost” (Luke 19:10).

Otherwise, you make the devil too powerful if you suppose that the Lord cannot snatch a captive from his jaws—or that, just as the devil is always watchful to destroy, the Lord does not strive in the same way to gain.

## CHAPTER XI

Let the final confession of the thief, therefore, introduced to you as a kind of confidence in the present situation, provide immense hope to the desperate: the confession of one who did not despair at the very end upon the cross.

Throughout his life that man had stained every act with robberies, and had always played in the world the role of an armed agent of diabolical savagery. He had never remembered God, had heard no commands of the Law—or, if he had heard them, being more inclined toward crimes, had paid no attention. He placed all his hope in despair and practiced cruelty in the manner of criminal accomplices. For this reason he was condemned to the cross and hung upon the wood, fastened there together with his crimes.

At last the lost man came to his senses, and, standing in the midst of his punishment, purchased for himself a great profit from death. He recognized the God with whom he was hanging; he trembled before the Judge to whom he was clinging; he made public the crimes of his conscience; he immediately acquired the baptism of blood through the shedding of his own blood; and, clothed in purple as a confessor, he entered paradise with the Lord.

This is the true deliberation of repentance; this is the chief practical purpose of confessing: that you believe the Son of God, whom you acknowledge as Creator, also to be Judge, since he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). And, in order to grasp the hope of eternal salvation, you must not plan merely for the present life but think about the future judgment.

First, the condemned man exposed himself before the Judge’s sight and, confessing his crimes, fulfilled the duty of the penitent. Then, when he saw the punishment of the cross, he understood that the judgment was common to the one fastened there, not the cause of his condemnation. Yet he believed him to be God at the very moment when Judea stubbornly denied him. Not forgetful of the future judgment while on the cross, he entrusted the memory of himself to the judgment of the one who would reign.

The Gospel makes this clear: “But the other thief,” it says, “answering, rebuked him, saying: ‘Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? We indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserved; but this man has done nothing wrong.’ And he said to Jesus: ‘Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom’” (Luke 23:39 and following).

But observe what he suddenly earned, what he heard from the mouth of Truth, and what he received through the grace of the Judge: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., 42).

## CHAPTER XII

“But,” you say to me, “I have added sins to sins; though I had already been raised after falling, I fell again, and the wound of my conscience, almost healed, has broken open again through the festering of sin.”

Why are you afraid? Why do you tremble? The one who healed you before is still the same; you will not have to change physicians. He will not labor to investigate the cause of your illness, nor will he newly test the power of a remedy against you. He will heal you with a medicine he knows. The one who knows the origin of your sickness does not wait for an experiment with his help. From the source at which you were healed before, you will be healed again. You will not distrust the remedy of healing, and the physician will be confident of your restoration.

Certainly he will chastise your lack of self-control and strike your impatience with severe rebuke; but he will not deny help, since he does not despise the sick person.

Hear the Prophet say: “Will not one who sleeps add this also—to rise again?” (Psalm 40:9). Or does one who has suffered shipwreck not sail again? Or, when someone has lost a harvest, does he, once he has despaired, not plow or sow again?

Our course is tossed upon a certain sea of the world. We must sail, and our sails must be set against the snares of evils. The storm rages, the wind rises, the tempest grows wild. If you hold the rudder in such a way that you do not lose the tackle of your ship, you will make for harbor with your cargo unharmed.

But if, struck by adverse waves, entangled among enclosing rocks, and hindered by gusts of wind, you suffer shipwreck amid the conflicting straits of a swollen whirlpool, you must return for ballast, repair the vessel first, purchase replacement cargo, face the dangers again, and trace the causes of the former disaster. If you are to be allowed to restore what was lost, you will not hesitate to entrust yourself once more to the former danger, even with uncertain hope.

For undoubtedly you will become a beggar if, after shipwreck, you refuse to return to the practice of trade. Nor will you later be able to complain about your poverty and hardships if, captured by the lot of shipwreck and overcome by the stupor of idleness, you become a beggar through misfortune.

And if a worldly merchant takes such care that, usually, after the loss of a shipwreck he does not despair of repairing his former losses through the profits of his industry; if, stripped by assaults, he does not allow his nakedness to be exposed but strives to grow from little [Note: [Col. 0985D] The Remiremont and Sorbonne manuscripts read “and with doubtful commodities.”] and seeks, through uncertain hopes, to acquire better profits—if sin itself is acting as a procurer—how much more must you consider the losses of your soul and immediately repair the destruction in which the losses of future hope are counted [Note: [Col. 0986D] The edition reads “the losses may be rewarded”; the manuscripts are better: “the losses may be counted”], and in which the profit of eternal life is disastrously forfeited!

## CHAPTER XIII

You must go to the treasury of a suitable benefactor. With the interest offered by repentance and satisfaction, draw up a bond; send written acknowledgments; purchase from him the gold refined by the gift of God. Fill your ship with whatever merchandise you can obtain, even if it is not precious. Spend your entire wealth in acquiring that precious pearl, by which you may adorn the shamefulness of your soul, so that when you arrive at the great city with your merchandise delivered, you may be richer in more worthy profits and most blessed goods.

For if the stupor of sluggishness overtakes you and bodily idleness begins to dominate your senses, and you seek no means of restoring your soul, you will be subjected to the tortures of your creditor and held liable to interest.

That generous sentence will be pronounced, from which, conscious of your own condition, you will not be able to escape or postpone by lodging an appeal: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him” (Matthew 25:29); and: “Drive the useless servant outside into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 30).

You do not tolerate wearing a tunic made from the woolen fabric of the cheapest workmanship. Your clothing horrifies you when it is disfigured by a stain. Yet does your soul not horrify you when it is polluted by the filth of sin and the contamination of crime?

Unless it is because, at that same moment, you hurry to wash your tunic so that you may put it on clean and without any blemish of ugliness, while you do not desire to recover the whiteness of your soul, stained by the squalor of crimes; nor do you wish to wash your conscience, which you know to be muddied by the filth of offenses and the contamination of sins.

Who, I ask, falls and does not seek to rise? Who becomes ill and does not desire to recover? Who is in danger and does not wish to escape? Who has become poor and does not wish to restore his patrimony?

If the nature of things allows a person, when such circumstances arise, to be unable to return to his former condition, then let him compete with his former state in order to receive worse things; let him lower his hands, wrap his half-awake eyes in stupidity, fall asleep never to awaken, lie down never to rise, and dull his sluggish mind through the stupor of sleep.

Later you will regret your delay, when you have thought of nothing that benefits your soul. You will always lie there sick, naked, exhausted by poverty, and, so to speak, drunk with the intoxication of sleep, destined to hear that sentence from which you will never be free: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Psalm 75:6).

Rise, brother, rise; cast off the torpor of an unsound resolve. Keep watch—keep watch always—and be concerned for your salvation, rather than sleeping in despair.

Beware the nighttime thief, lest he break through the wall of your house, and avoid the noonday archer and his flying arrow. Security that is off guard lies open to assaults, and it is easy for one who sleeps to be crept upon and struck mortally.

Confidence belongs to the one who keeps watch; nothing is safe for the one who sleeps. It is fitting for a sober mind to have sleep as its servant, not its master. The enemy flees when he does not find you sleeping. “Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds watching” (Ephesians 5:14), because he says: “Rise, sleeper; rise from the dead” (Matthew 24:46); [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Gill edition reads “and put on Christ”; the Roman edition reads “and you will touch Christ”; the Remiremont and Sorbonne manuscripts read “and touch Christ.”] and touch Christ.

## CHAPTER XIV

“But I do not dare to pray,” you say, “because my conscience holds me back; for I have gone astray not once but repeatedly and often.”

But I will say this: if shame prevents you from praying, let obstinacy in sin cease, and what you fear will become the benefit of fear, not the cause of despair.

To reverence the authority of the Judge is not shamefulness but modesty. Although permission to sin may be frequent, the conscience nevertheless becomes excusable when the recollection of sin has produced timidity.

Let the example of Ahab, that most impious king, teach you. He had coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite because it was adjacent to his own property. He offered a price—or, at least, an equivalent vineyard. Naboth refused, asserting that he could not in any way transfer an ancestral possession to another.

Stung by this refusal, he returned home sadly because the desire of his appetite had come to nothing. Then his sacrilegious wife Jezebel asked the reasons for his sadness and, when she learned them, as though applying nourishment to his wounded heart, cast into it the fuel of consolation. Through this scheme, after many false accusations had been contrived by the counsel of the impure woman, innocent Naboth was stoned and killed.

When the woman had accomplished the crime of her deadly wish, she entered her husband’s presence like a victor, intending to report the death of the slain man as a cause for rejoicing. So that she alone would not remain implicated in the crime, she acted with the cunning of the first woman, binding her husband to the consciousness of the offense and fastening both spouses with a single chain of guilt.

“Rise,” she said, “take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, who refused to give it to you for a price; for behold, he is dead” (1 Kings 21:15).

But he, grieving that he had provided the occasion for the murdered man’s death, shuddered at the announcement of the crime and turned the cause of his death into sorrowful lamentation. Tearing apart his royal garments, he clothed himself in mourning attire, bearing witness not so much to the guilt of his conscience as to the first thought of repentance.

“And it happened,” it says, “when Ahab heard that Naboth the Jezreelite was dead, he tore his garments and clothed himself in sackcloth” (ibid., 16).

Could Ahab therefore have been free from guilt for the bloodshed [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Remiremont and Sorbonne manuscripts read “because it was established/known.”] because he had repented of the design rather than of the parricide, while the impiety of the murder remained with the profane woman, who thought she ought to purchase the vineyard with the price of shed blood?

But behold: just as a dog returning to its vomit becomes hateful, so Ahab, forgetting his repentance, immediately set aside his mourning and went to possess the vineyard of the slain man. He lost the merit of innocence because, led on by desire for the vineyard, he became entangled in consent to the murder of the slain man.

Soon the venerable prophet Elijah was sent to him, and a sentence was pronounced against him with indignation, so that the repentance he had previously undertaken might be nullified and the repeated presumption of the crime provide an occasion for vengeance.

And Elijah said to Ahab: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring evil upon you, and I will cut you off after you, and I will exterminate from Ahab the one who urinates against the wall, the despised and abandoned one in Israel. And I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because of all by which you have provoked God and caused Israel to turn aside” (ibid., 21 and following).

But when he could not escape the blow of the sentence, he suddenly turned his mind back to his former repentance. He confessed his guilt with tears, cast down his royal power through sackcloth, put on the sackcloth of repentance, and, reverencing the face of the one who threatened him, made his offense public with silent groaning; he did not excuse his conscience.

“And it happened,” it says, “when Ahab heard these words, he reverenced the face of the Lord, and went away weeping, and tore his garments, and clothed himself in sackcloth.”

Then the Lord said to Elijah: “Have you seen how Ahab has reverenced my face? I will not bring the evil in his days, but in the days of his son I will bring the evil” (ibid., 27 and following).

Behold what timid reverence accomplished, and how great a movement of severity fear restrained! It was not the display of prayer, nor elegance of speech, nor abundance of eloquence that pleased God, but an abundance of tears. His mouth was silent, but his heart groaned; his eyes wept, but his conscience lamented; and the piety of the Author praised the modesty of his repentance.

It was not enough for the guilty man to escape the punishment he deserved unless reverence received the testimony of approval. He was approved in fear, though he was condemned in crime. Nor was the first mourning for the death of the slain man useless; by repeated lamentation he cleansed the guilt he had repeatedly renewed.

## CHAPTER XV

Nor should Manasseh, the king and son of Hezekiah, be left unmentioned. He surpassed the boldness of all profane men, stretched out impious hands against God, and, degenerating from his father’s ways, raised the insane head of idolatry entirely above the worship of God.

Possessed by sacrilegious madness, he established altars of execrable superstition in the house of God; he polluted it with images of demons; he filled the sacred altars of the temple with stone figures [Note: [Col. 0988D] The edition and the Sorbonne manuscript read “filled, sought omens”; the words inserted here have been borrowed from the Remiremont manuscript.]; he cultivated sacred groves; he dedicated his sons to profane fire; he sought omens; he defiled his life with magic arts; he led the people into the observance of idols; he polluted them with ceremonies; he enslaved them to the devil; and he practiced everything prohibited by the divine laws, beyond all the insolence of a mind given over to despair.

For these many and great crimes he was led away as prey, bound in chains, weighed down with fetters, and subjected to the punishment of captivity. Transported to Babylon, he paid the penalties of his impiety, so that, hardened and previously forgetful of God, he might feel the divine vengeance to which he had been handed over.

Finally, seized by an appropriate scourge, he was converted, and, placed amid punishment, acknowledged the God whom he had not sought when he was in royal power. Affliction benefited the desperate man, and, through recognition, the wickedness provoked by the goad of correction was corrected. That vengeance became medicine for his ruined mind, and the chastisement contributed greatly to his salvation. It struck the impious man for this reason: to make him acceptable to God, from whom the devil had alienated him through his powerlessness. What had been inflicted upon his folly benefited the health of his soul.

The faith of the Lord’s Scripture admits this: “And the Lord spoke against Manasseh and against the people, and they did not listen. And the Lord brought against them the commanders of the forces of the Assyrians, and they seized Manasseh and bound him with chains and fetters, and brought him to Babylon. And immediately, when he was afflicted, he sought the Lord his God, and humbled himself greatly before the face of the God of his fathers, and prayed to God; and the Lord heard him and restored him to Jerusalem, to his kingdom. And Manasseh knew that the Lord himself is God.”

Behold how much he wept over and washed away his sin through sudden lamentation from a converted heart, and wiped away with tears what he had stained through his wickedness. Yet, conscious of his guilt, he prayed, and deserved to purchase forgiveness through satisfaction—so much so that he restored to their former reverence the sacred things he had previously polluted through the contamination of profane actions, and returned everything to the worship of the fear of God.

When the convert had been fully restored, that prophetic oracle of the divine mouth was fulfilled: “When you have turned back and groaned, then you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:25).

## CHAPTER XVI

But why should I mention those kings whose praiseworthy origin from an elect race did not allow them to depart from the city of sacred religion through the worst persuasion, when that savage and foreign ruler Nebuchadnezzar was punished by divine judgment [Note: [Col. 0989D] The Roman edition, following the marginal reading of Gill, has “and a foreign prince.” Below, however, both readings appear in the body: “whom sacrilege had been”; the Remiremont manuscript has “whom sacrilegious men,” and so forth.]? Through the correction brought by punishment, he was compelled to acknowledge the one whom he had dared to deny through sacrileges, and to believe in his powers, whom previously, through the ferocity of his spirit, he had not known.

Indeed, the one whose proud and obstinate spirit had previously not feared to have himself proclaimed God later did not dare to speak falsely concerning his incomparable majesty. Corrected by profound amazement at what had happened to him, he not only ceased from everything else but confessed with all his heart the one true God, with decrees proclaiming his praise.

But if, conscious of evil, you are afraid to pray, you have the teaching of the publican. Even if you are apprehensive that, when you pray for your sins, you may not deserve to be heard, consider his example.

He had entered the temple with his neck bent beneath the weight of sins and with the eyelids of his eyes pressed down by the grave disease of iniquity. He did not dare to look toward heaven. Timidly he drew back his step and presented himself at the extreme rear—not so much in a physical place as before the judgment of his conscience. He did not advance his foot toward supplication with irreverent boldness but restrained his steps. [Note: [Col. 0989D] Thus the Remiremont manuscript; the edition instead reads: “he publicly declares himself guilty through modesty, repeatedly recalling his sin by striking his breast.”] Publicly displaying his shame, he repeatedly recalled his guilt by striking his breast and battered his conscious heart with the admonition of his fist.

The words of his mouth were not heard, but his groans; and his entire confession was expressed in only five words.

The Lord makes this clear in the Gospel, saying that two men went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee and the other a publican. When the Pharisee had taken his stand, he prayed to himself in this way: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or even like this publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.”

But the publican stood far off and did not wish even to raise his eyes toward heaven; rather, he struck his breast, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:11 and following).

But observe what the reverent supplication demanded from the examiner of hearts. Through the munificent reward of his shame, the publican perceived the God whom he desired to have as merciful.

And immediately that shame deserved justification, since it was proved in confessed humility, the Lord saying: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (ibid., 14).

## CHAPTER XVII

Where, then, do you place the example of that sinful woman who appears to have exposed her crimes not with words but with tears? Although her tongue was silent while she prayed, her conscience confessed through the duty of repentance.

The Lord was reclining in the house of a certain Pharisee, who had prepared a banquet for him as for an invited guest [Note: [Col. 0990D] The edition reads “the inviter”; the Remiremont and Sorbonne manuscripts read “the invited guest.”].

When a prostitute discovered this, she boldly entered the Pharisee’s house and stood beside the reclining Lord’s feet. She washed his holy feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed his feet without ceasing, and moistened them with precious ointment. With nearly all the limbs with which she had previously sinned, she was expiating the stains of her crimes.

Then the Lord, before whom our bones are distinguished, as the prophet says, “All my bones will say, ‘Lord, who is like you?’” (Psalm 34:10), struck down the murmuring of the slanderous Pharisee, praised the woman’s hidden thought and manifest faith with admirable approval, and preferred the service of the confessing woman to the preparations of the host. He was more delighted by what the woman had done than by the meal; he rejoiced more in her conversion than in being fed. Since he was not at all led by desire for food, he was nourished by the banquet of confession.

“Do you see this woman?” he said. “I entered your house: you gave me neither a kiss nor water for my feet, but she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.”

And he turned to the woman and said: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:45 and following).

Is this a small thing? Later observe what she hears: “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

A sinner before, she was immediately absolved and became a daughter; she was sent away at once in the Lord’s peace, she who had been ravaged by the warfare of her crimes.

This is that prophetic oracle: “When you have turned back and groaned, then you will be saved”; and: “You speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26).

Since, therefore, you recognize from so many and such great examples that the sacrifice of repentance is pleasing, and since you need not fear that the reward of a contrite heart and humbled spirit will perish before the merciful Judge—for Scripture says, “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19)—why do you not hurry to rise from the depths of luxury and from the whirlpool of worldly pleasure, and breathe again from your drunken actions in order to undertake the duties of repentance? [Note: [Col. 0991D] The Gill edition reads “nor from the depths”; the Roman edition reads “if from the depths”; the Remiremont manuscript reads “why not from the depths.”]

Nor should you suppose that, because you have distanced yourself far from him, his ear is therefore closed to you. As soon as you knock, he will open the doors and, in compassion, include you within the enclosures of his fold—provided only that the complaint of your grief moves him.

The farther you had withdrawn, the more swiftly he will draw near, as the prophet says: “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm 33:19).

Of such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).

## CHAPTER XVIII

“But perhaps repentance seems harsh to you after the pleasures of the world.”

It is true: I perceive the disorder of your condition; I see the sickness of your spirit. But if you desire to be healed, do not consider the violence of the treatment or fear the remedy. When the surgeon’s instrument is applied to your wound, the incision makes the healing swifter. For the diligence of healing is most disastrously softened when the festering corruption is not immediately cut away.

The taste of the antidote is bitter, but what is unpleasant to the throat is life-giving and salutary.

The Lord heals us not as strangers: all sinners whom he heals he keeps as his own, not as outsiders. Every hour, every day, he is intent upon healing; neither time nor any obstacle of delay holds him back. [Note: [Col. 0991D] Thus the Remiremont manuscript; the edition and the Sorbonne manuscript instead read “and is hindered when he has been found,” followed by the text at [Col. 0992D].]

Indeed, his power is hindered only when there is no one to be healed. The Lord’s benefit must be idle when there is no one toward whom he ought to show mercy.

The chastisement of repentance is harsh, but it becomes gentler when the measure of the guilt is considered. For a long time the ambition of worldly display delighted you, and the dominion of the age claimed you as its servant—now relaxed in luxury, now plunged into drunkenness.

Some saw you absorbed in the practice of gambling; others saw you at banquets; others thrown to a prostitute; still others enslaved to brothels, smeared with perfumes, drenched in spices, and with your eyes polluted by alien sights.

You shone in clothing, glittered with gold, and were adorned with gems and the most precious pearls.

Therefore repay deed for deed and, even if late, at least return a compensation of time for time. Divide your life between both ways of living with equal moderation. You belonged then to the devil; now belong to God. Indeed, belong now to yourself, though earlier you had belonged to another.

And perhaps, if you consider the matter, you have squandered a great deal of time, so that the brief period remaining has become even more constricted. Devote yourself now to yourself, not to time. I said, devote yourself—not so that you may grow sluggish, but so that you may apply yourself to the business of confession.

Return to the road from whose paths you had wandered. Condemn the things you did; seek what you once were. First find yourself, so that you may find what you seek; and if you find yourself, seek nothing apart from yourself.

Put on sackcloth; sprinkle yourself with ashes; pray always while fasting, and fast while praying. These things are more precious because they afflict the body, so that the beauty of the soul may be restored.

Humble clothing is despised, but what is not displeasing to God is highly fitting. The adornment of the body is cheap, but it is itself the chief ornament of holiness.

And perhaps you still complain about the unworthiness of your clothing, though you have lost the wedding garment. When you appear disfigured by the nakedness of your ugliness, do you not consider how you may be clothed again?

Do not fear, I beg you, lest, like the man who was invited and entered the royal banquet, you be driven away from the feast of those reclining at table with a similar reproach of condemnation and hear this said to you: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” (Matthew 22:12).

And when you have found no argument with which to excuse yourself, let him say: “Bind him hand and foot, take him away, and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid., 13).

That man, certainly, because he had neither sought nor received the garment, is said to have been cast out. He entered when invited, but reclined without being clothed.

If, then, the one who had never possessed the garment went out in this way because he did not seek it, how will the one who received the garment, lost it, and could not be clothed again be punished?

## CHAPTER XIX

But, I suppose, you doubt that a lost garment can be recovered, or that the one who gave it only recently could refuse it when you ask for it.

In the Gospel, consider the younger son, who, after losing his patrimony, was reduced to begging, to such a degree that, driven by poverty, he wanted to become a swineherd (Luke 15:15 and following).

Exhausted by utter want and poverty, and not even permitted to eat the food of the pigs, he returned to the former soundness of his own mind. He began to burn with longing for his earlier life and, thinking about the abundance of his father’s house, condemned his guilt through the judgment of conversion.

At last, after deliberating as a penitent and speaking with himself in the secret chamber of his heart concerning satisfaction, he returned like an exile restored to his ancestral home, naked and destitute.

Then the father, who had seen the plan in his son’s heart before the lost son poured out his words in confession, anticipated the affection of the grieving man and mercifully received the one who was returning.

He rushed upon his neck, reconciled him with kisses, and, while he was still trembling and saying nothing, the father wonderfully reassured him. [Note: [Col. 0992D] The Remiremont manuscript reads “the father rightly confirms him.”]

But that very prudent penitent and excellent confessor, secure in his father’s intention yet still uncertain about his own satisfaction, disclosed the carefully considered course of his confession: he expressed in words what he had turned over in his heart.

“Father,” he said, “I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:21).

The father, therefore, placated by the confessor’s prayers, ordered the first robe to be brought and immediately commanded that the naked son be clothed in the garment he had recently lost.

He ordered a ring to be given him and restored the seal of the pledge. He enclosed his feet in the protection of commandments. For his restoration he ordered the fattened calf to be slaughtered—that is, he commanded a most pleasing sacrifice to be offered for the reconciled man, one acceptable both to heaven and to the hosts of angels.

A harsher stubbornness had been aroused in the elder brother’s hatred of his brother, and the elder son, reproaching the crimes of the one who had been received, objected.

The command was not revoked; the father’s compassion did not change. His brother was affirmed, and he was called a son. The one who had formed a perfect plan in repenting had called forth the father’s full affection for himself.

“I was glad and rejoiced,” he said, “because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (ibid., 24).

You see, then, that the former robe was restored to the converted son as the reward of repentance, and that the father celebrated the return of the confessing son with every expression of joy.

The lost patrimony signifies the sacrament of baptism, in which all the structures of the heavenly kingdoms have been established. That son—that is, the faithful Christian—had received the freedom of the Father but lost it through the pollution of lust and luxury. Living far from his God, he had polluted himself with every kind of disgraceful action, and, enslaved to the devil to whom he had surrendered himself through his utterly depraved conduct, he began to tend pigs—that is, unclean spirits.

Since he was not permitted to feed upon their food, because, under the pretext of the flesh, he could not gorge himself on demonic husks, he labored, abandoned on every side and deprived of everything, exhausted by the lack of good fruit.

But when he returned, he immediately received everything of which he had been deprived, and, with the substance of his former possession accounted restored, he remained in reconciliation with his father.

Return, then, brother—return. Rise again from death, and be restored from perdition.

## CHAPTER XX
The good shepherd seeks his wandering sheep, and rejoices more over the one found than over those not lost. He carries it back on his shoulders, restores it to the fellowship of his flock, and encloses it in the lodging-place of its former security; nor does he consider the number of those left behind, since by restoring one lost sheep he sought to complete the full hundred [Col. 0993D]. The woman searches intensely for the lost drachma, lights a lamp, cleans the house with brooms, and invites her friends and neighbors alike to rejoice over the drachma that has been found. Can anyone think that God does not rejoice at the restoration of the converted person, when he sees the parable expressly applied to the person who repents? For he himself says: “I tell you, thus there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (ibid., 10).

Consider finally that remarkable saying of the Lord in which he declared: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; for I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX, 12). The Lord therefore calls [Col. 0994A] sinners to repentance, and our physician desires to benefit the sick more than the healthy. Yet he does not pass over the righteous because he receives sinners; for the life of the righteous is a divine calling, just as he left the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains while he sought the one that had strayed—rendering to the former the due reward of justice, and intending to bestow upon the latter the benefit of mercy. The Apostle proves this when he says: “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace” (Rom. IV, 5).

Finally, listen to the arrows with which the Lord strikes the hearts of sinners in the Gospel, and you will understand how highly he valued the sacrament of repentance. “There were present,” he says, “some who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. Then [Col. 0994B] Jesus said to them: ‘Do you think that these Galileans were sinners above all other Galileans because they suffered such things? I tell you, unless you repent, you will all likewise perish’” (Luke XIII, 3 ff.). “Or those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think that they were sinners above all the people who lived in Jerusalem? I tell you, unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.”

And he added an illustrative example to confirm the matter, mentioning a fig tree which, being barren and fruitless, was ordered to be cut down; but, through the intervention of the vinedresser, its destruction was permitted to be delayed until, after the ground around it had been dug with suitable cultivation and a basket of manure had been applied, it might be given time to produce the fruits of repentance. But if a tree that had produced no fruit of its kind was ordered to be cut down before its time, with what instrument must that tree now be cut off, or with what axe felled, which, overgrown with brambles and crowded with foreign thorns, had received no cultivation for its restoration? [Col. 0994C] For the likeness of the tree is an example of the faithful person who, barren of the fruit of faith, has conceived nothing that might contribute to the gain of future hope. It had been planted in a vineyard, and that vineyard specifically signifies the Church, in which that tree had been planted. But the cultivator of this vineyard seems to represent the priest, who applies the digging of the unfruitful plantation to the cultivation of the Lord’s commandments; and the basket of manure signifies the work of repentance.

And if no fruit could be found on it at all after the delay of time, it would later be torn up by the roots and wither completely—that is, cut down at the future judgment and cast away as useless wood [Col. 0994D]; becoming discarded material, it would burn as fuel for eternal fire. Although [Note: [Col. 0993D] The edition and the Sorbonne manuscript: this may be understood of Christ among the people. And below, “that these things have been shown by the proofs which we have brought forth with care from remedies for the sick [Col. 0994D] … and have been made abundantly clear”; the Remigius manuscript in both places: as in the text.]

this may also be understood of Christ and of the Jewish people.

### CHAPTER XXI

I believe that these proofs, which we have brought forward with care from remedies for the sick in order to raise and restore your courage, have made it sufficiently and abundantly clear to your understanding that God, the fountain of mercy, does not desire the destruction of sinners, but rather prefers that the wicked person be corrected, so that as many offenses as are counted, so great may be the practice of repentance. Let no one despair of the swift restoration of his return who hears the Lord himself urging the sinner to repentance.

The Apocalypse of the most blessed John explains this more explicitly. In it he rebukes the angels of the churches, so that, deprived of their former errors, they may bend themselves to the lamentations of repentance; for it is thereby proved that the Lord desires the ruin of no one, since he imposes repentance upon the fallen. To the angel of the church of Ephesus he says: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do the first works; but if not, I am coming to you, and I will move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent” (Apoc. II, 5).

And yet the one to whom the care and conversion of repentance are entrusted is called an angel, and he is urged to complete his former works, so that he may be shown to have lost nothing of all his merits. The warning, however, threatens more severely the one who does not repent if he persists in the stubbornness of his hardened state. For the severity of punishment will be inexcusable if the first correction does not bend an untamed neck; and the person forewarned by the authority of the threat will perish to his own harm if, through obstinacy, he does not subject his neck to the yoke of satisfaction.

He plainly declares that the person who is corrected with the worthy humility of confession in order to return to his former state will indeed return to it. This is explained more fully a little later, when the angel of the church of Thyatira is chastised with the blows of rebuke. “I have many things against you,” he says, “because you tolerate the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and teaches and seduces my servants to fornicate and to eat things sacrificed to idols. And I gave her time to repent, and she did not wish to repent of her fornications. And I will cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her will be in great tribulation unless they repent of all their works. And I will kill her children with the sword; [Col. 0995C] and all the churches will know that I am the searcher of heart and kidneys, who repays each person according to his deeds” (Apoc. II, 20).

What could be said that is more humane, what more merciful? “And I gave her time,” he says, “to repent, and she did not wish to repent.” You have nothing, sinner, nothing with which to excuse yourself. There is no reason for you to doubt without cause; there is no reason for you to despair without cause. Arm yourself for confession with these examples; equip yourself for repentance with these instructions.

### CHAPTER XXII

The Lord delays punishment so that he may find repentance, and, making use of intervals of delay, prolongs his patience, lest mercy lose what ought to have been accomplished by judgment. He does not look at past evils or reckon up errors, but praises what has been corrected. You have the promise of the one who urges you to repent: if you do not repent, he will hold it against you. “And I gave her time,” he says, “to repent, and she did not wish to repent.” Similar is that prophetic saying: “And I said, after she had committed all these fornications: ‘Return to me’; and she did not return to me” (Jer. III, 1).

But if, driven by the enormity of your crimes, you cast yourself into the whirlpool of despair; or if, checking your step, you hesitate to uproot the accumulated burden of your journey; or if, through the downhill slide of a warped mind, you bring your footsteps onto a downward slope by slippery practice, then at once the hope of restoration is taken away from you. The abyss of crimes will seize you and swallow you into the chasm; your eyes will be closed by the night of sin, so that they may not see the ray of the true light shining through [Col. 0996A]. The blindness of death will oppose itself, and deceptive angels will lead you here and there in a kind of game.

All crimes will become pleasing to you, and the license to sin will become wholly attractive. The devil will hold you bound under the hope of freedom [Note: [Col. 0995D] Thus the Remigius manuscript; the edition reads: “the devil [will hold you] given over to his own freedom.”], so that it will be free for you to sin, but not to live. He will not allow you to look back upon what you once were, when, by the allurements of sin and the sweetness of crimes, the most deceitful tempter has drawn you away. And, to put it in a word, he will deceive you with the pleasure of perishing so completely that it will seem more delightful to you to perish than to return.

For no sin is committed without its own pleasure; nor can it otherwise ensnare the mind unless it entices the one it has deceived by the sweetness of desire [Note: [Col. 0996D] The edition reads “otherwise bait [inescare]”; the Remigius manuscript, “otherwise ensnare [inviscare].”]. The deadly preparation of the fatal cup must be a sweet and pleasant mixture for the throat, lest the first taste of bitterness recall the drinker [Col. 0996B]. Thus the poison of that tree seemed good to the first woman to look upon and sweet to eat; but, after its false sweetness had deceived the lips of the eater, the violent subtlety of the draught infected the one who was dying and extinguished what had remained vigorous and alive. Through intemperance, her desires fell into their opposite, and she was driven from the paradise of blessedness and the estate of security into the exile of the world and the spectacle of the age.

### CHAPTER XXIII

I beg you, brother, fear, flee, and dread these things. Do not allow the enemy to rejoice over your destruction and to raise the victor’s brow in the sight of God. Beware the return of the seven unclean spirits, to which an eighth has joined himself as the leader of all evils. And if no one can endure a single devil, who could sustain the dominion of eight?

The Lord says: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and not finding it, says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it returns, it finds it empty, swept with brooms, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 43).

If an enemy’s hand had seized you, surrounded by military siege, and under a barbarian attack had kept you captive in the robber’s power, what weeping would you utter, what cries would you give, what laments would you pour forth? Day and night you would sigh continually; you would seek no food and desire no drink. Exhausted by thirst and weakened by hunger, only the dryness of harsh skin and wrinkled emaciation would appear upon you. Your hair, clotted with filth, would stand stiff, and the shaggy locks of your unkempt head, together with your long beard, would make your limbs look dreadful. You would surrender your patrimony beneath the redeemer’s sword; constrained, you would walk naked, poor, and stripped of every possession. You would seek to escape, or, if an avenue of flight were offered, you would cautiously consider how to overcome the danger amid the greatest uncertainty.

The author of crime holds you captive—not with iron bonds, but with chains of offenses he has bound you. He has put the fetters of lust upon you and enclosed you on every side in stricter confinement. He has given you a law by which you think everything permissible that is not permitted. He has plunged you alive into the pit of eternal death. And do you not groan over the loss of your salvation, the wasting of eternal hope, and the ruin of everlasting life?

You walk about adorned in splendid clothing; you celebrate meals with sumptuous foods; you are soaked in wine; you fatten your soul with daily banquets; and you do not cease to cultivate the gluttony of your muscular body—to say nothing meanwhile of your other crimes. Do you think—yes, do you think—that this too is not a manifestation of divine judgment: that you do not know how you ought to repent of your crimes? The Apostle proves this when he says: “Because they did not retain God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a depraved mind, to do what is unfitting” (Rom. I, 28). And again: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, God sent them an operation of error, so that those who did not believe the truth might be judged” (II Thess. II, 10).

Finally, he fears concerning such people that, when he comes to Corinth, he may mourn over many of those who have not repented of the impurities, fornications, and lusts they have committed (II Cor. XII, 21).

### CHAPTER XXIV

Consider the sumptuous dinners of that rich man and the abundant profusion of his plentiful dishes, enclosed in purple, costly crimson, and the gleaming fabrics of woven silk—wholly occupied with the hope of the present age, yet considering nothing of the future. Listen to what was reserved for him after all these things. After purple came flame; after banquets, want. He who had once drunk a drop of precious nectar sought a drop of water, and asked from the one to whom he had denied, in this world, the crumbs of his banquets even the comfort of a moistened fingertip.

Confess, I beg you, everything of which you remember yourself guilty. Confess, and anticipate the face of God by the duty of satisfaction. Humble your heart before him, and bow your neck in his sight. Bend your knees, and prostrate yourself upon the ground with your face cast down. That heavenly advocate will immediately receive your groaning and will not fail to intercede for you with his Father, who is accustomed to offer faithful protection to the penitent.

He will plead his case not with arguments according to the prescribed style of eloquence, but will immediately obtain the benefit of pardon—he who does not expect any honorarium from the one who has been overcome [Note: [Col. 0997D] The Remigius and Sorbonne manuscripts read: “not with arguments, and he will plead the prescribed rule of genuine patience . . . he who expects no fee from a suspect.”]

The Apostle proves this when he says: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God is the one who justifies; who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died, indeed rather was raised, who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us” (Rom. VIII, 33).

The most blessed apostle John, composing his epistle, also writes and says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus; and he himself pleads for our sins” (I John II, 8 ff.).

Everything that the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life, has spoken is law. By his own example he taught that what he commanded us in writing should be done. For he would not wish anything to be done by us that he himself had not done, or that he would not approve when done by us. Nor could what he himself had commanded displease him, because the one who commanded it had himself first done it.

The teaching of the command would indeed be empty if the authority of the teacher did not precede it in action. But whatever the Lord commanded and did cannot be empty when he commanded it to be done in imitation of himself.

The same Lord therefore set these things before his disciples for their observance: “Pay attention to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, forgive him; and if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to you, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him, and he will be forgiven you” (Luke XVII, 4).

And when the holy apostle Peter had consulted him on this matter and said, “Lord, if my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?” Jesus said to him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII, 21).

Therefore, does the one who commands us to forgive seven times the debts of a brother who sins against us fail to preserve toward us the form of his own command? Or can the one who said, “I desire mercy more than sacrifice” (Hos. VI, 6), deny us the treasure of mercy? This is what I said earlier, after obtaining pardon: we would have to believe that the Lord Jesus had lied in everything he taught if he did not wish to preserve toward us the form of his own commandments.

### CHAPTER XXV

And rightly he immediately adapts to this statement the parable concerning two servants. One of them, because of a very large debt, was ordered to be sold, together with his wife and children, for the payment of the debt. He fell at his master’s feet and begged for patience, promising that, if time were granted him, he would repay the whole debt. Through the master’s mercy he deserved to have everything forgiven him.

Yet he, who had been kept bound under such a condition for punishment, was unwilling to show mercy to his fellow servant who owed him a debt, because he had forgotten the benefit that had very recently been bestowed upon him. He was immediately handed over to the torturers, and from his torments the same debt that had earlier been forgiven was demanded.

For this reason the Lord established this form of prayer, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12), so that you may know that as much can be forgiven you as you yourself have forgiven your debtor—or rather, so that you may appear to spare yourself when, entreated by another, you have pardoned him.

For without doubt you will be judged by your own judgment if, desiring that you yourself be forgiven, you are unwilling to forgive another. The Lord says: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you” (Matt. VII, 2).

I want you to read more attentively the beginning of the prophet Zechariah, and there you will find something to strengthen your courage more powerfully. “The Lord,” he says, “was angry with our fathers with great anger” (Zech. I, 2). Who, hearing this, would not tremble? Who, terrified by the thunder of this voice, would not wither? Whom would this declared indignation not disturb? For what state of health could be maintained where such vehement anger of the Author was announced?

And it would have been little to say merely “anger,” unless “great” had also been declared—as though, if it were not great, his anger could be endured, even if it were slower. But let us see what outcome such agitation announces. I suppose he says: “I will trouble you with the tumults of war; I will punish you with the cruel domination of captivity; I will afflict you with hunger; I will shake you with disease; I will consume you with death; unexpected devastation by wild animals and beasts will carry you away; exile will drive you, fugitives, scattered everywhere.”

For this is left to the understanding: that a more violent punishment follows great anger. “The Lord,” he says, “was angry with our fathers with great anger, saying to them” (Zech. I, 2). Let us hear what he said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you.”

O indignation flowing from piety! O great anger that brings mercy! I ask: if he who is angry in this way shows mercy, how does he show mercy? Or if he shows mercy in this way, how does he grow angry in indignation? Another prophet proclaims this: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have been weakened by your iniquities. Say to him: ‘You are powerful to forgive our sins’—not so that you may receive iniquity, but so that you may receive good things—and offer him the fruits of your lips, and your heart will feast on good things” (Hos. XIV, 2).

And elsewhere: “Return,” he says, “you apostate children, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVI, 8). And again: “Return, returning children, and I will heal your affliction” (Jer. XIV, 22). In harmony with these words, blessed David sang the consolations of sinners, saying: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. CV, 1).

### CHAPTER XXVI

I do not say this so that I may seem to have given excessively broad rein to license, or, under the pretext of divinely granted pardon, to have provided repentance as an incentive for further sinning [Note: [Col. 1000D] The same manuscript: “may seem to have given the reins of license.”]. By this speech I raise up the one who is falling; I do not push down the one who is standing. Nor do I prejudice innocence when I exhort the sinner to repentance.

For, as we have already said above, innocence demands from God the due reward of its life; repentance, however, awaits the benefit of mercy. Not to sin is fear, but to repent is more than fear. Secure prosperity often lies exposed to offenses; but the one whom fear corrects becomes more cautious in avoiding what is past, because the person who takes care not to fall again where he has already fallen will always be more watchful.

Thus experienced dangers make a helmsman watchful, and the person who has once suffered shipwreck through confidence sometimes fears to enter even safe harbors. Finally, divine Scripture says: “The one who has not been tested—what does he know?” (Ezek. 33), showing that the one tested through temptation is always made more cautious, and that through fear the person who was previously heedless is corrected by the knowledge gained from temptation.

To such an extent does the Lord desire to forgive sinners—he who does not desire the death of the dying, but rather that he return and live—that those whom he repeatedly assigns to punishment for their crimes, when appealed to by repentance, he hastens immediately to absolve. He puts the sword back into its sheath and changes the sentence of punishment through satisfaction.

### CHAPTER XXVII

Although this has already been proved above by the example of the Ninevites, nevertheless receive also the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah concerning the same matter, so that the example may be proved to you more fully by the testimonies.

“The word,” he says, “which came from the Lord to Jeremiah, saying: ‘Rise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear my words.’ And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the stones, and the vessel that he was making fell from his hands. And again he made that vessel into another, as it pleased him to make it.

“And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Shall I not be able to do with you as this potter does, house of Israel? Behold, as the potter’s clay, so are you in my hands. At one moment I speak concerning a nation or a kingdom, to uproot and destroy them. And if that nation turns from its evil thoughts, I will repent of the evil that I was thinking of doing to them, and I will not do it. And at another moment I speak concerning a kingdom or a nation, to build and plant it. And it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice; I will repent of the good that I said I would do to them, and I will not do it.

“And now say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: Behold, I am fashioning evils against you, and I am devising a plan against you. Let each person turn from his evil way; make your thoughts better” (Jer. XXIII, 1 ff.).

Our potter therefore urges us to turn away from the worst ways and from wicked thoughts, so that conversion through repentance may fashion our fractures and defects into another vessel. He desires the substance of his work not to perish through repentance, lest the sentence hold the guilty person whom confession excuses.

The Wisdom of Solomon agrees with this: “But you have mercy on all, Lord, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance; for when you wish, power is present with you, and although you are Lord of all, you make yourself merciful to all” (Wis. XI, 24).

Let us therefore turn and confess to the Lord while we live in the passage of this age, and let us prepare the provisions of repentance for our judge. Let the courses of our time not be idle, and let us live—not born for sinning, but for doing good. Or if we have become liable to sin, since it cannot be absent from the theater of this world that we sin, let us remember ourselves, so that we may desire to escape the precipice of Gehenna.

Let us therefore repent in faith, pray from the heart, and weep from the depths. And as the Prophet says: “Let us adore and fall down and weep before the Lord who made us; for those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Ps. XCIV, 6).

Happy—alas, exceedingly happy—is the work of tears, by which rewards are gathered in the future! Blessed is the growth of the seed poured out in weeping, so that it may be harvested in gladness! For it is written: “Blessed is the person who recognizes his own wailing.”

Let us lift our eyes toward the mountains, from which our help will come; for as the eyes of servants are toward the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant toward the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us (Ps. CXXII, 3).

### CHAPTER XXVIII

Nor should we prolong the resolve of our conversion through the pleasures of time in such a way that, knowingly sinning and delighting in perishing, we sink ourselves into the abyss of crimes until extreme old age. For it is uncertain what limit will close the span of life granted to us by divine favor.

Perhaps what is thought to be the beginning, or the middle, is already bounded by the limit of the approaching sunset, and the summons of the angry Lord may be the due end of conversion delayed. Hence the oracle appears to urge us not to delay our conversion: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not defer it from day to day; for his anger will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclus. V, 8).

And again: “Son, you have sinned; do not add again, but pray also concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you. Do not add sin upon sin, and say: ‘The mercy of God is great’; for mercy and anger are from him” (Ecclus. XXI, 1).

Nor should we allow ourselves to become slaves until death, or give our bodies over to the domination of crimes. Rather, let us obey the Apostle who says: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey it” (Rom. VI, 12). Since sins cannot be entirely absent, at least let them not reign—that is, let there not be a precipitous license to sin without regard for escape.

Or if anyone thinks that time still remains for him to sin, and that, after lust has been satisfied and the powers of the body have already commanded the mind, he may then return to the judgment of repentance, let him tell me the final time of his life, so that, by calculating it, he may learn, and by declaring it, may know, and so may flatter himself—so to speak—with regard to the length of time allotted to him.

But since our final departure is unexpected, and the course of our life is uncertain because of our ignorance of death, how can anyone suppose that time remains for confession when he does not know the time appointed for him, especially when Scripture says: “While living and in health you will confess, and you will praise God, and you will take your place among the holy age with those who are alive and offer confession” (Ecclus. XVII, 27)?

A delay of time should produce confession, not despair, because condemnation is increased in the one who, with stubborn obstinacy, presumes upon divine patience. This was shown to have occurred in the days of holy Noah, when patience was extended for a hundred years, and then the unappeasable flood poured across the world, as judgment overflowed.

Hence the blessed Apostle says: “Or do you despise the wealth of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s goodness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his deeds” (Rom. II, 4).

### CHAPTER XXIX

I want you to tell me: what glory belongs to present things? What are the fruits of this age? What is the usefulness of things that pass away?

The power of a kingdom, as I have said, ends in death. The ambition of authority is cut short by succession. The abundance of riches is often taken away from us while we are still alive. The fulfillment of pleasure is spoiled when sadness intervenes. The joy of delights is violated by the dread of fear. And everything that is grasped by desire—whether body or soul desires the body—is cut down by the sickle of the end [Col. 1002A] [Note: [Col. 1001D] The Roman edition: “either body or soul is cut short by the heel of the end”; but the Roman and Gill manuscripts establish our reading.].

Nor can that obtain the perfect privilege of blessedness which is not enclosed by the infinity of eternity. For what is measured by unavoidable necessity must be fleeting; it will doubtless remain subject to change, unstable, and weak, since its life is sometimes cut short by an accidental event.

When all these things have therefore been ended by death, what will be our own possession in death itself? If we have nothing that conscience may patch together through the increase of good works, and if we have been unable to possess anything good from ourselves, what will we carry with us when we return to our homeland? How naked and deformed our soul will remain if we do not at least clothe it with the veils of repentance and the garments of confession! Unless we hasten to conceal its shame and strive to cover the soul’s nakedness, its naturally invisible beauty will become visibly deformed by the filth of sins.

### CHAPTER XXX

Those are the transactions we must pursue; those are the riches we must embrace; that is the power we must seek—the power that time does not take away, place does not remove, and persons do not withdraw; which remains in an everlasting state; which is preserved by eternal privilege; which is not taken away by any end; and which is neither pressed down nor constrained by the yoke of death.

For there the goods of conscience are secure: there it will no longer be possible to sin after the evils of the present age; there the devil has no access; there is no place for darkness. Nor will the deceiver, nor the one who could be deceived, be found there at all.

There all things are good; there all things are blessed; there everything is prosperous. The day of light will not change by increase; the sun will not appear slower in rising, brighter in shining, or darker in setting. Night will be entirely absent; there will be no moon; nor will the flashing of the stars glow with greater brilliance. No one will feel hunger; tears will be wiped away; there will be no fear, no dread arising from nothing. Gladness will possess all things; peace, the whole; joy, whatever had been subject to sadness.

The prophet Isaiah sets all this forth clearly (Isa. LX, 2 ff.). What will then be the glory of the blessed there, and what the punishments of the wretched? What groans, what sighs of sinners, and what blessedness of the saints? The former will share companionship with God; the latter will be given over to the torment of Gehenna’s flames. These will enjoy incomparable refreshment; those will be slaughtered by unrestrained fire. These will be delighted by the streams of paradise and the heights of the groves, refreshed by tireless rivulets [Col. 1002D]; those, surrounded by a lake of fire, a flood of flame, and the darkness of black night, will be driven onward by inextricable punishments. Finally, these will enjoy heavenly goods, while those will be consumed by the devouring power of all Gehenna and eternal death.

### CHAPTER XXXI

If someone, weakened by the stain of poverty in this present age, has no means at hand by which he can sustain his hungry appetite with even the most ordinary food, and sees others burdening their tables with sumptuous dishes, drinking wine from jewel-studded vessels while stuffed with banquets, and prolonging their feasts through the ambition of elaborate preparations seasoned with exotic flavors, what sighs do you suppose rise from the deepest part of his entrails? What complaints does he utter in the pain of his gut? At times he even sheds tears, when his desire for what he sees begins to grow somewhat stronger, and he feels his ineffective longing burning more and more from desire.

What then will be the groans of the unhappy, and what torment in that comparison, amid inconsolable grief, when they see the procession of blessed souls enjoying heavenly abundance and everlasting riches, while they themselves are deprived of a drop from a finger wet with dew and, in addition, endure an unquenchable flame, with no hope of being reserved for pardon?

We cannot bear the heat of the sun; we scarcely tolerate the warmth of the baths; we feel the fires of furnaces and withdraw far away. Who could bear the surging Gehenna, or endure the din of the infernal furnaces boiling with the smoke of the abyss? Who could withstand the masses of infernal darkness, where only the howling of the burning is heard and the wailing of those cruelly punished resounds?

These things, I beg you, how much they must be fled, how much guarded against, and with all our strength, with our whole soul and mind, avoided!

### CHAPTER XXXII
Since the gates of pardon stand open, since a harbor of repentance is offered to those tossed about and battered by the storm of their crimes, since care is promised to sick minds and a willing physician offers vital medicine to the wounded; since mercy is ready at hand before justice draws its sword from the hilt, let us take up the weapons of repentance and soften the severity of the Judge by the duty of satisfaction. For the gift of pardon is assured to the one who is permitted to repent; for without doubt the one to whom no compassion is shown is not permitted to confess. [Col. 1003C]

This is demonstrated by the condemnation of the ancient serpent at the very origin of the world, whom the unanticipated thunderbolt of the sentence struck down: absolute severity deprived him of possession of his desired state. The regions consumed by heavenly fire—Sodom and Gomorrah—bear witness to this: because of the excess of their crimes, no opportunity for repentance was reserved for them, lest perhaps, warned in advance, they might have been able to evade the justice of vengeance. The destruction of Pharaoh in Exodus proclaims this; the unexpected ruin of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram testifies to it; the punishments of Antiochus and Herod declare it; the shipwreck of Ananias and Sapphira through sudden retribution indicates it. Vengeance did not postpone its assault upon them until a later time, and, with pardon denied, severity accompanied and cut them down.

Let the day of our departure not find us unprepared, [Col. 1003D] nor let it enclose us within the devil’s camp at that time of winter or Sabbath. Let us be watchful against the fraudulent ambushes and open threats of the ancient enemy. For he is aroused more fiercely against those who have turned back, and, as though mocked, he pursues his deserters with greater severity. Then, when he was deceiving us, he had enticed us with flatteries; now he harasses us with temptations and cruelties. Then he had been like a friend; now, like an enemy, he rages. Through a fall he has made the cautious more careful, but the one who has been thrown down often knows how to overthrow the one who throws him down.

Let us flee the pompous allurements of the world and reject its ambitions utterly. The Apostle John persuades us of this when he says:

“Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the desire of the world. And the world will pass away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God remains forever” (1 John 2:15).

Let us be washed in the baptism of repentance, so that we may be able to see the Lord with a pure heart. Let us remove wickedness from our souls in the sight of God’s eyes; let us learn to do justice; let us seek judgment, rescue the one suffering injury, judge for the orphan, justify the widow, and then we shall plead our case with the Lord. And if our sins are like crimson, he will make them white as snow; but if they are like scarlet, he will make them like white wool. And because he will sprinkle us with hyssop, [Col. 1004B] we shall be cleansed; he will wash us, and we shall become whiter than snow (Psalm 50:9).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[605] There are three things which the Lord, by his own will, has established and preserves in relation to us: goodness, I say, mercy, and justice. Goodness is that by which we have already begun to exist; mercy is that by which we are summoned to repentance; justice is that by which we shall be judged in the future. For the present, these preserve within themselves the order of time—past, present, and future: the past, in which, by the Lord’s authorship, we are created and born; the present, in which, once converted, we earn mercy; the future, in which, according to our works, we shall be rewarded when justice distributes its gifts.

Therefore, while we have the kingdom of mercy in our hands and the gifts of compassion have been placed within our power, let us here [Col. 1004C] cleanse our consciences from every defilement, and henceforth prepare ourselves, through a good manner of life, with spiritual instruments. Let us avoid the desires that wage war against our souls, and let us in no way tolerate a profane conscience. We shall obtain everything that we believe by faith if we order ourselves through righteous actions into a blameless life. We shall merit the remission of all sins; we shall rise to eternal life in the resurrection of believers; [606] and, to dare to say even more, we shall enter the kingdoms of heaven with the righteous, with whom we have merited to have a share through repentance, as Scripture says:

“But to those who repent he gave a share in righteousness, and he assisted the failing to endure, and appointed them to the lot of truth” (Ecclesiasticus 17).

[Col. 1004D] These things, dearest brother, which I would use to exhort you together with myself to practice repentance, I have written down insofar as the modest capacity of my intellect was able to gather from the Lord’s readings. If, as I suppose, you already pursue these things earnestly according to your own purpose, and, seated in the chariots of confession, are hastening toward pardon, accept me as your companion in this endeavor, so that, joined in common fellowship, we may hurry toward the goal of indulgence. Or, if hindered by the inertia of laziness, I cannot follow your speed, remember me; and when you have merited a reward from God’s generosity, I ask that no forgetfulness of Victor take hold of you in your prayers.

## ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 1005]

### NOTICE

[Col. 1005] This little work, or rather fragment, came forth from the library of Saint-Denis in France. Gillotius recovered it from an ancient codex in which, appended to the three Ambrosian books *On the Holy Spirit*, it was entitled *The Fourth Book of Saint Ambrose on the Holy Spirit*. Yet this heading did not deceive the learned man, since he observed that the passages of Scripture repeatedly cited in this treatise are not in the version used by Ambrose, and that the style of the whole little work differs from Ambrose’s. He further noted that the author declares at the end that he has discussed the Holy Spirit only briefly, whereas Ambrose, on the contrary, treated the subject at very great length.

For this reason he judged that the fragment should be published for no other reason than that he considered it the work of an ancient author and very worthy of being read. Since the Romans likewise retained it in their appendix for this reason, we too have thought that it should not be rejected.

[Col. 1005]

## ONE BOOKLET ON THE HOLY SPIRIT (C, G, S)

[Col. 1005A] [605] “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:9 and following).

With divine method and divine eloquence the Apostle has brought the mystery of the Lord’s Trinity and of our faith into the minds of believers. For after he had said, “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you,” he added, “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” What else, then, did the Apostle teach than the unity of the Trinity? For the Spirit of God is the Spirit of Christ; and the Spirit of Christ and of God is neither divided nor separated from Christ, since neither can God be shown to be separable from his Spirit, nor Christ from his Spirit. If God is inseparable from his Spirit, then Christ likewise is inseparable from his Spirit. Therefore the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are inseparable from God and Christ; and thus God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit are manifested as undivided, because the Spirit is eternally in God and Christ.

For what else does he insist is signified by this chain and connection than an understanding of unity, since through the Spirit God and Christ—who are inseparable from one another—are united, and, to speak more fully, are understood to be one?

[Col. 1005C] This is the divine mystery; creation does not naturally or inseparably possess this: that the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, or the three may be one, and the one indivisibly, may be recognized as existing.
