Therefore the Apostle, secure because he learned this foundation of faith from Holy Scripture and came to know it through divine revelation, is no longer afraid to proclaim in one place the one God, in another the Holy Spirit with the Lord, and elsewhere the Spirit with God and the Lord. [Col. 1006A]

For whether he has said “one God,” he knows that he has fulfilled the name of the Trinity. Or if he mentions only God and the Lord, he knows how to say, “But God himself, and the Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you” (1 Thessalonians 3:11), and he takes care not to say, “May they direct it.” If he mentions God and the Holy Spirit, he knows that he has not dishonored Christ. If, when circumstances require, he assigns the persons of God, the Lord, and the Holy Spirit, he knows how to say, “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). For it is impious to speak of three gods, and it is extremely irreligious not to confess the One in the name of the Trinity.

Finally, let us consider the following words, by which he confirms and strengthens this meaning. After saying, “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him,” he added, “But if Christ is in you” (Romans 8:9). It is therefore clear that Christ dwells through the indwelling Spirit of Christ. But if Christ dwells through the indwelling Spirit of Christ, then God also dwells through the indwelling Spirit of God. Finally, he added: “And if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you” (ibid. 11)—that is, the Spirit of God. Thus it is proved that the Holy Spirit is none other than God and Christ, through whom God and Christ dwell. Whoever does not have him dwelling within cannot have God or Christ.

But someone may say: If God dwells in us through his Spirit, and if the Spirit is one and the same with God and Christ, how is it said again: [Col. 1006C] “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies”? How are God and Christ one, when Christ is raised from the dead by the Spirit of God?

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). Truly, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?” Truly this is what “the eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (2 Corinthians 11:2). God prepared this for those who love him: that Christ the Lord, while existing in the form of God, should take the form of a servant, so that he alone might be found to be both.

Since Christ is therefore both—namely, God and man—this raising is not attributed to his divinity because his divinity could suffer or die; rather, it is because the Word, God, became flesh and dwelt among us. Otherwise, if his divinity could have suffered, there would have been no need for him to take the form of a servant. He took the form of a servant for no other reason than that through it he might both suffer and die for the salvation of those who love him. Therefore it is rightly said that the Lord of majesty was crucified, and that the Lord Jesus Christ was raised from the dead, because by his voluntary goodness and divine purpose he himself undertook and endured everything through the suffering of his temple. Thus the fact that Christ [Col. 1007B] was raised from the dead contributes to the glory of God and demonstrates Christ’s omnipotence.

We must also examine the following passage no less carefully, because the Apostle, speaking with lofty and profound doctrine, says:

“If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead, who raised Christ from the dead, will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:11).

First, then, it is clear that God and Christ accomplish everything in us through their indwelling Spirit. Thus it is established that the Holy Spirit accomplishes everything, because it is he who raised Jesus from the dead who will also give life to our mortal bodies through the indwelling Spirit of Christ [Col. 1007C] in us. He did not say that the one who raised Jesus from the dead raises him by himself, or that he raises Christ by himself, but through the Spirit of Christ dwelling in us: “His Spirit, who raised Jesus from the dead, will also give life to our mortal bodies.”

And indeed we read in the Gospel that the Lord says: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes” (John 5:21). It is not said there that God and Christ raise the dead through their Spirit. What, then? Is this contrary to that statement? Far from it. The meaning of those words is given back to us, and through the Gospel of the blessed Paul we are taught by what means God raises the dead—namely, through the indwelling Spirit of Christ in us. Thus it is most plainly handed down that the Holy Spirit accomplishes all divine works.

Therefore, in another place the same Apostle teaches, saying: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4). How is the Spirit “the same” if the Spirit is something other than God and the Lord? Or what does “the same Lord” mean if the Lord is something other than God and the Spirit? Or how will you understand “the same God” if God is something other than the Lord and the Spirit? If in essence—that is, in *ousia* (οὐσίᾳ)—in divinity and authority they were different from one another and not one, they could in no way be called the same, since they would be found to be altogether different. The Apostle would then be found to be a false witness and defiant toward God, attributing sameness where there is no sameness. But far be this from us. The Apostle was not mistaken in his understanding; rather, he knows God, the Lord, and the Holy Spirit as one Spirit working all things in all.

And lest the minds of his hearers retain any scruple—since, after showing the persons of the Trinity, he had said that God works all things in all, while knowing that he must truly prove both the Trinity and the unity, although no error could seem possible where he had already said the same thing so often—the Apostle nevertheless, according to his customary manner and the caution of his prudence, or, to speak more truly, under the governance of the Holy Spirit, whom he often professes to have as his revealer and teacher, as he says, “Taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Corinthians 2:13), and elsewhere, “God has revealed them to us through the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2:10), restored everything to unity, saying:

“To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in one Spirit,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 12:8).

And concluding in the final part, he says: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit” (ibid. 11)—the Spirit whom above he had called God. Since, therefore, God and the same Spirit work all things, we must receive and believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in whose name we are recreated through the baptism of regeneration, are one God, which is one name. For by one and the same manner, by the same powers, and also by the same prophecies through which we learn of God the Father, we are likewise instructed concerning the Holy Spirit and the Son.

[Col. 1008C] But perhaps someone may say: He said “all things” that pertain to the ordering of the Church, not all the things that God, the Lord, and the Spirit accomplish. Therefore, something should be said about all things, or at least about a few of them, by which it may be proved that the Holy Spirit is present in absolutely all divine works and himself fulfills them all.

Moses is filled with the Holy Spirit; through the Spirit of prophecy he is taught foreknowledge and foretells future events. What of all the prophets afterward? Did they not prophesy filled with the Holy Spirit, announce the plagues threatening the people, and preach the coming and passion of the Lord, as the Lord himself confirms when he says through the mouth of the prophet Zechariah: “Accept, nevertheless, my words and my ordinances, which I command by my Spirit to my servants the prophets” (Zechariah 1:6)? Thus it is clear [Col. 1008D] that all the prophets prophesied in the Holy Spirit.

We have also received and learned that the Law itself was given and written through the Holy Spirit. For Moses says: “And the Lord gave two tablets of stone written with the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18). The Gospels make clear that the finger of God is called the Holy Spirit. For when the Lord had cast out a demon and was accused by the Jews of expelling demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, according to Luke he is said to have replied: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20); while according to Matthew: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). From this it is clear that the Spirit is called the finger of God.

Since, then, it is established that the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God, it is clear [Col. 1009A] that the Holy Spirit wrote the tablets of stone which Moses received as written by the finger of God. The Holy Spirit gave them, because the finger of God is nothing other than God, since he works in all things.

As for the very miracles which divine power performed in Egypt for the instruction and testing of sinners, is it not clear that they were accomplished by the finger of God, as the Lord confirms when he professes that he casts out demons by the finger of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit? For that same one—the Holy Spirit—accomplished and carried out those things in Egypt.

The Lord brings this home to our understanding when he professes that he casts out demons by the finger of God, teaching that his works are the works of the Holy Spirit, since the works of the Holy Spirit are the works of Christ. The works of Christ [Col. 1009B] are the works of the Father, as we read in the Gospel according to John, where the Lord himself says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever he does, the Son likewise does in the same way” (John 5:19); and: “Just as the Father raises the dead, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes” (ibid. 21).

Therefore, by this progression and reasoning we recognize that the works of the Holy Spirit are the works of the Father, because whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does; and whatever the Son does, the Holy Spirit does. Thus the Trinity is always one God and one Spirit, working by itself, yet from itself working the same things and all things in all.

Because the Egyptians refused to recognize this Holy Spirit in his powers and divine might, they were compelled by plagues [Col. 1009C] to confess him. Lest those who now hear these things should fall into the same plagues, they are warned by the Lord that they may not begin too late to say, “It is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19). Thus it is clear that one and the same Spirit works all things in all (1 Corinthians 12:8).

Is not the birth of the Lord Jesus himself according to the flesh also proclaimed as having taken place through the Holy Spirit, when the angel Gabriel evangelized to Mary and said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 2:35)? And again the angel appears to Joseph in a dream, saying: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife, for that which has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20). From this it is evident that he himself works and accomplishes everything and in all things.

[Col. 1009D] But some say: He does indeed perform all divine works, and God is understood from his works; nevertheless, he is not proved to work by his own authority, since God and the Lord perform everything through him.

His authority is already sufficiently established when he is proved to be God, recognized as God, found inseparable from God, and shown to possess unity with God and the Lord. But since inquiry is made concerning his authority—which Scripture has not concealed—we must be instructed. First, this is shown when it is said: “But all these things the one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:8). He divides; it is clear that he does not work under another’s command. And it must be observed that what he divides as he wills is not written to be alien things.

Again, we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “As they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2). What could be clearer or more evident for manifesting the divinity and authority of the Holy Spirit than the words, “Set apart for me”? He did not say, “Set apart for God,” but “for me”; nor did he say, “for the work to which we have called them,” but “for the work to which I have called them.”

He has therefore given us sufficient proof of his authority and divinity, since he attributed the separation of the apostles to no one but himself and said that he had called them to a work not belonging to another but to himself. One who was alien from God, the Lord, and divine authority could never have done this.

And so that the one authority and divinity of the Holy Trinity, to be reverently honored, may shine forth more clearly, we must contemplate the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah, which the Holy Spirit himself interpreted for us through the Apostles. We read it as follows:

“And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?’ And I said: ‘I, I am; send me.’ And he said: ‘Go, and say to this people: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not perceive,’” and so forth (Isaiah 6:8).

And earlier, in the same vision, he had said that he saw the Lord of hosts sitting upon the throne of his glory, and that he heard the Seraphim saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his majesty” (ibid. 3).

Certainly the Lord of hosts, to whom this praise and glory are rendered, is shown in the prophets as one and the same, and he himself is the one who spoke to Isaiah, saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?” Although one and the same is signified in the prophets, the Apostles and the Church understand the Trinity.

Hence the custom arose throughout almost all the Eastern Churches and in some Western ones that, in the offerings of sacrifices made to God the Father, the people join their voice with the priest, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his majesty.” Therefore, according to the prophet, it is established that this must be referred to the person of God the Father.

The Evangelist John, however, informs us and teaches that it must be understood of the Son. For after he had inserted the testimony quoted above into the Gospel and interpreted it, he added: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him”—that is, of the Lord Christ.

The Apostle Paul, when the Jews at Rome opposed his teaching and blasphemed the way of the Lord Christ, raised his voice and said: “Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet, saying: ‘Go and say to this people: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not perceive,’” and so forth (Acts 28:26).

Since, then, the Apostles teach one divinity in the prophecy, while the Church nevertheless understands the Trinity, we are most certainly taught that the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one and the same God. And since they are understood and acknowledged as one God, they must necessarily also be understood as possessing one authority.

Again, the Lord teaches the Trinity of this unity in the Gospel, saying: “Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” and so forth (Matthew 28:19). Although he had expressed the significance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he nevertheless taught us to observe one name for the Trinity itself, namely: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his majesty” (Isaiah 6:3).

Thus the usage of Scripture is clear: when it names one God, it does not remove the understanding of the Trinity; and when it mentions the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it does not abolish the name of the one majesty.

And what more can be said? The page and the time would fail me if I wished to review or enumerate everything written to prove the divinity of the Holy [Col. 1011B] Spirit. These things have been said briefly to blunt the shamelessness of those who attempt to deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit—or, to speak more truly, the Trinity itself. They deny it when they do not confess God as he is; when they do not believe as divine Scripture has taught us and as we ought to believe, but according to the desire of their own understanding.

Let them understand how far they are from the faith of God, and how alien from the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, since they strive to grieve and deny the Holy Spirit, by whom believers are sealed for the day of our redemption. Let those who think such things know that they are contriving actions which can have no connection either with pardon or with the remission of their sins, because it is written: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12:31). Rather, let them not fail to recognize that they are subject to the sentence which the divine judgment pronounced through the mouth of Isaiah: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isaiah 66:24).

## ON THE HARMONY OF MATTHEW AND LUKE IN THE GENEALOGY OF CHRIST

[Col. 1011]

### NOTICE

[Col. 1011B] We also owe this little writing to Gillotius, who brought it to light from two handwritten codices, one Dionysian and the other Victorine, in which it is attributed to Saint Ambrose. But although he declares that it does not differ from our Doctor either in subject matter or in style, we certainly cannot endorse his opinion. Instead, we confidently refer the matter to a simple reading of the little document itself, and especially of these words: “But a solution to this question of such a kind is given by the Fathers.”

[Col. 1011]

## ON THE HARMONY OF MATTHEW AND LUKE IN THE GENEALOGY OF CHRIST (C, G, S)

[Col. 1011C] [609] In the generation of Christ, Matthew and Luke appear to disagree, because one of them—Matthew—constructs the sequence of the same generation by descending, while the other—Luke—constructs it by ascending. Matthew, beginning his account from Abraham and descending as far as David, then carries the line through Solomon down to Joseph. Luke, beginning with Joseph, proceeds through Nathan to David, and from David up to Abraham, finally ascending from Abraham to Adam while unfolding the order of the generations.

Thus it happens that, beginning with David and proceeding downward, since one traces the path of descent through Nathan and the other through Solomon, almost the whole order of the reckoning differs. But because Holy Scripture sometimes admits things that are different, while it never admits things that are contradictory, and because we are not permitted to believe in contradiction, we are compelled to seek the hidden truth.

Matthew, then, reckons the generation of Christ by descending, showing that the Son of God, through the assumption of flesh, became the Son of Man. Luke weaves the same genealogy by ascending, demonstrating that the sons of men become sons of God through the grace of adoption.

For this reason Matthew, wishing to carry the sequence of the genealogy down to the birth of Christ, began not from the first parent Adam but from Abraham, to show that the assumption of flesh by the Son of God was not an institution belonging to the first creation but the fulfillment of a promise made later.

Luke, however, beginning from Christ’s baptism, did not end with David or Abraham, nor even with Adam. Passing through David, Abraham, and Adam, he ascended to God, so that he might plainly indicate that those who through the generation of the flesh are sons of men pass through the regeneration of baptism into adoption as divinity’s children.

Therefore Matthew wished to count in the genealogy only natural sons, while Luke includes adopted sons among the natural ones, so that it might be shown both that the assumption of flesh was genuine in Christ’s birth and that adoption comes to us who are reborn not by nature but by grace.

This, then, was the reason why Matthew and Luke placed different fathers in the sequence of the generations: the former, as we have said, counted only natural fathers, while the latter counted adopted fathers together with the natural. To make this clearer, let us compare the accounts of both.

The order of Christ’s genealogy according to Matthew [Col. 1013A] is as follows:

“Abraham begot Isaac; Isaac begot Jacob; Jacob begot Judah; Judah begot Phares; Phares begot Esron; Esron begot Aram; Aram begot Aminadab; Aminadab begot Naasson; Naasson begot Salmon; Salmon begot Booz; Booz begot Obed; Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot David; David begot Solomon; Solomon begot Roboam; Roboam begot Abia; Abia begot Asa; Asa begot Josaphat; Josaphat begot Joram; Joram begot Oziah” (Matthew 1:2 and following).

Here the Evangelist omitted three persons: Ochoziah, Joas, and Amasiah. For Joram first begot Ochoziah; Ochoziah begot Joas; Joas begot Amasiah; and Amasiah finally begot Oziah, of whom it is now said, “Joram begot Oziah.” This must be understood as meaning that he begot him through the persons mentioned above, because he came forth from his seed through them.

The Evangelist may have omitted them either so that the number might correspond to the number of the decade, or because Joram had joined himself to the family of Jezebel. It had been said through the prophet concerning the house of Ahab that no one would reign except in the fourth generation; therefore his memory is removed from the holy genealogy up to that point.

Oziah, who is also called Azariah, begot Joatham; Joatham begot Achaz; Achaz begot Ezechias; Ezechias begot Manasses; Manasses begot Amon; Amon begot Josias; Josias begot Jechonias; Jechonias begot Salathiel.

The historical truth is that Josias begot Eleachim, who was also called Joachim or Jechonias. Eleachim begot Joachim, who likewise, like his father, was called Jechonias. This latter Jechonias finally begot Salathiel.

We shall therefore say either that one person was omitted for the reason stated above, or for some other reason; or that the Jechonias of whom it is said, “Josias begot Jechonias,” is not the same as the one of whom it is said, “After the Babylonian captivity, Jechonias begot Salathiel.” The former was the father, the latter the son. Because of the separation and interruption caused by the captivity, the connection of the generation was not repeated between them so as to say: “Jechonias begot Jechonias; Jechonias begot Salathiel.”

Jechonias therefore begot Salathiel; Salathiel begot Zorobabel; Zorobabel begot Abiud. Up to this point the order of the genealogy is woven from the ancient books; what follows is confirmed by the authority of the Evangelist:

“Abiud begot Eliachim; Eliachim begot Azor; Azor begot Sadoc; Sadoc begot Achim; Achim begot Eliud; Eliud begot Eleazar; Eleazar begot Mathan; Mathan begot Jacob; Jacob begot Joseph.”

In this way we believe that the genealogy descended naturally. Now let us retrace the sequence of the genealogy according to Luke.

[Col. 1014A] Luke says:

“Jesus himself was beginning about thirty years old, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was of Heli, who was of Matthat” (Luke 3:23).

At first sight a contradiction seems to arise. Matthew says that Joseph was the son of Jacob, and Jacob the son of Mathan. Luke says that Joseph was the son of Heli, and Heli the son not of Mathan but of Matthat.

The Fathers offer the following solution to this question: Mathan, who descended through Solomon, had a wife named Estha, by whom he begot a son, Jacob. After Jacob’s death, Matthat, who descended through Nathan, married the same woman and begot by her a son, Heli. Thus Heli and Jacob were uterine brothers, born of one mother but not of one father.

First Heli took a wife and died without children. Afterwards Jacob took his brother’s wife in order to raise up offspring for his brother, and by her he begot Joseph. Joseph, therefore, was the son of Jacob according to generation, but the son of Heli according to the Law.

Then the sequence of the genealogy is unfolded:

“Joseph, who was of Heli, who was of Matthat, who was of Levi, who was of Melchi, who was of Janne, who was of Joseph, who was of Matthathias, who was of Amos, who was of Nahum, who was of Hesli, who was of Nangae, who was of Matth, who was of Matthathias, who was of Semei, who was of Joseph, who was of Judah, who was of Johanna, who was of Resa, who was of Zorobabel, who was of Salathiel” (ibid. 23 and following).

I do not think that this is the same Zorobabel or Salathiel who were counted above in Matthew’s genealogical sequence, since that Salathiel was not the son of Neri but the son of Jechonias, and Zorobabel begot not Resa but Abiud and the others, among whom Resa is not counted.

Or, if they are the same, it must be said that here the line of both reckonings first converges into one, and then immediately, according to the method that we indicated at the beginning of this genealogy, diverges again:

“He who was of Neri, who was of Melchi, who was of Addi, who was of Cosam, who was of Elmodan, who was of Her, who was of Jesu, who was of Eliezer, who was of Jorim, who was of Matthat, who was of Levi, who was of Simeon, who was of Judah, who was of Joseph, who was of Jona, who was of Eliachin, who was of Melcha, who was of Menan, who was of Matthata, who was of Nathan, who was of David” (ibid. 27 and following).

What follows from this point up to Abraham is the same in both accounts. It should certainly not seem contradictory that, in the genealogical line, more persons are counted according to Luke from Joseph to David than according to Matthew from David to Joseph, since the successions of generations themselves multiplied more abundantly in that part where, as the fathers died sooner, the sons succeeded in greater number.

## ON THE DIGNITY OF THE HUMAN CONDITION

[Col. 1013]

### NOTICE
[Col. 1013D] The little book placed below by us follows immediately after the books of the *Hexaemeron* in all editions of the works of Ambrose. The older editions, however, had prudently and necessarily added this caution in these words: “which by some is attributed to Saint Ambrose as its author”; but the Roman edition, removing those words entirely, assigned the treatise without qualification to the holy Doctor. Nevertheless, no one who persuades himself that this work is Ambrose’s ought to see anything Ambrosian in it. For, apart from the fact that nowhere does it breathe the spirit of Ambrose, it is certainly a patchwork, whose first and last parts are found in Alcuin under the heading “Sayings of the blessed Albinus the Levite on the passage of Genesis, ‘Let us make man,’ etc.”; likewise in the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, printed at the end of the sixth volume of the Augustinian edition; and also several sayings in the treatise of Paulinus of Aquileia *On Saving Teachings*, which is likewise contained in that Augustinian Appendix. As for the middle section—namely, from the words “and therefore, dearest son” up to “those other words, dearest son, take this to heart”—we suspected that it was by Alcuin himself, both because it is more obscure and because it is later; since it is almost longer than the other two sections, and since we were unable to find it elsewhere, this was the reason we retained the little work in its entirety.

[Col. 1015]

## A LITTLE BOOK ON THE DIGNITY OF THE HUMAN CONDITION (G,S)*

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1015A]

“Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). The dignity of the human condition is therefore understood to be so great that man was created not merely by the word of command of the one commanding, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the Holy Trinity and by the work of divine majesty. Thus, from the honor of his first creation, he might understand how much he owed his Creator, since the Creator immediately bestowed upon him such a privilege of dignity in his creation; and thus he might love the Creator more ardently, the more wondrously he understood himself to have been created by him. And this is so not only because he was created in such an eminent manner by the counsel of the Holy Trinity, but also because the Creator of all things created him in his own image and likeness—something he granted to no other creature.

### CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 1015B]

This image must be considered more carefully in the nobility of the inner man. First, just as the one God is always wholly present everywhere, giving life to all things, moving and governing them—as the Apostle confirms: “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28)—so the soul is wholly active everywhere in its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. Nor is it greater in the larger members of its body and smaller in the smaller members; rather, it is wholly present in the smallest and wholly present in the largest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God that the soul possesses within itself.

It also bears a certain image of the Holy Trinity. First, because just as God is, lives, and knows, so the soul, in its own manner, is, lives, and knows. There is also another trinity in it, by which it is made in the image of its Creator, the perfect and supreme Trinity, which consists of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Although it is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses within itself three dignities, namely, understanding, will, and memory. The same thing, though expressed in other words, is indicated in the Gospel when it says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. 22:37)—that is, with all your understanding, all your will, and all your memory. For just as the Son is generated from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so from understanding is generated [Col. 1016A] will, and from both of these together memory proceeds, as anyone wise can easily understand. For the soul cannot be perfect without these three, nor can any one of these three, insofar as its blessedness is concerned, be complete without the other two. And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God possessing three persons, so understanding is soul, will is soul, and memory is soul—not three souls in one body, but one soul possessing three dignities.

In these three, therefore, our inner man wondrously bears his image in his own nature. From these, as from the soul’s more excellent dignities, we are commanded to love the Creator: so that he may be loved in proportion as he is understood, and in proportion as he is loved, he may always be held in [Col. 1016B] memory. Understanding of him alone is not sufficient unless the will is directed toward his love; indeed, these two are not sufficient unless memory is added, by which God remains always in the mind of the one who understands and loves him. For just as there cannot be a moment in which man does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy, so there ought to be no moment in which memory does not possess him as present.

And therefore, [Note: [Col. 1015C] The Roman edition here and twice again below cut out this apostrophe, “dearest son.”] dearest son, it seems rightly said to me that the inner man is the image of God. For the soul is called the whole inner man, by which that clayey mass, moistened with juices lest it dry out and dissolve, is given life, governed, and held together. God is called that ineffably great and immeasurably wise power, as it is written: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146:5); and incomparably sweet, as he says elsewhere: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:5). From him, through him, and in him are all things that exist; by him all things that exist are governed; in him all things that exist are contained. By “all things,” I mean the whole universe, which is the totality of everything other than him who made it and was not made. But he is [Note: [Col. 1016C] The Roman edition reads: “from whom, through whom, and in whom.”] the one from whom, and the one who is from him, and the one through whom. God is called “the one from whom”—the Father—by us poor in understanding and poorer still in words; the one who is from him is called the Son; the one through whom, the Holy Spirit.

God is therefore called Father because he is the one from whom all things are, and he is wisdom, by which all things are ordered; and love, by which all things will to remain as they have been ordered. The one from whom, therefore, and the one who is from him, and the one by whom they love one another: those two are three, and those three are one because the two are from one in such a way that they are nevertheless not separated from him. They are from him because they are not from themselves; and in him because they are not separated. And the one itself is what they are, as he himself is what it is; and the one himself is what they are, as they themselves are what he is; and they are not the one itself who is he himself, [Note: [Col. 1017C] The same edition reads: “and not they themselves who are themselves.” These two expressions mean: God is the two.] nor are they themselves he himself who they themselves are. This power is God; and God himself is three; and each one of these three is God; and all three together are not gods but God.

The Creator therefore made the human soul, which is called the whole soul, in his own image, as has been said. When I say “mind,” I do not signify something other than the human soul, but I use “soul” for one reason and “mind” for another. Everything that lives is the human soul; but when the soul acts within itself, from itself, and through itself, it is customarily called mind alone. When it fulfills the functions assigned to it, however, it is more commonly called soul.

The mind therefore gives birth to knowledge, and loves to know what it knows. By “knowledge” I do not mean that by which something is suddenly known that was previously thought unknown, but that by which anything and everything that is known or unknown can be known. The mind therefore gives birth to this knowledge, and when it has been born it may be called knowledge. There are now two: the mind and what the mind itself knows. A third remains, common to both. Every mind loves to know whatever it knows. Love is no less between two—namely, the lover and what is loved. There is therefore one love of both, which is also the third. Yet it cannot be denied that this whole is one soul, and that one soul is these three; for just as these three are truly one soul, so this one, this second, and this third are no less truly one soul.

Let this creature, then, so eminent, compare itself with its Creator, who is eminent above it, except for this one point, which must be set far above it: all goodness, every good, and all the sweetness of goodness and good in the Creator comes from himself; whereas the creature receives from another not only what it is but also the fact that it is such, and not from itself. And he himself is always what he is. The soul too, in its own way, is unchangeable; for once it has begun to exist, it is always a soul, and it knows and wishes to know.

Let the soul therefore compare itself, as I have said, with its Creator insofar as it can, so that the mind may be called Father because it gives birth to knowledge; knowledge may be called Son because it is from another and is not other than that very thing which he himself is, from whom it is; and love may be called the Holy Spirit because it belongs to both of those who love one another. Hence, in our Scriptures, love—that is, charity—which exists in God toward us and in us toward God, is often itself called the Spirit. And this, dearest son, is what you should understand concerning the image.

### CHAPTER THREE

Now understand something about likeness, which must be discerned in lesser things. Just as God the Creator, who created man in his likeness, is charity, good, and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful, and possesses the other marks of holy virtues that are read of him, so man was created to possess charity, to be good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful. The more each person possesses these virtues within himself, the nearer he is to God and the greater likeness he bears to his Creator. But if—God forbid—someone degenerates from this most noble likeness of his Creator and wanders through the byways of vices and the divisions of crimes, then what is written will happen to him: “And man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

What greater honor could man have than to be created in the likeness of his Maker and adorned with the same garments of virtue with which the Creator is adorned, of whom it is written: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Ps. 29:1)—that is, he is adorned with the splendor of every virtue and the beauty of complete goodness? Or what greater disgrace, or more unhappy misery, could there be for man than, having lost the glorious likeness of his Creator, to fall into the shapeless and irrational likeness of brute beasts?

Therefore, dearest one, let everyone consider more carefully the excellence of his first creation, recognize within himself the venerable image of the Holy Trinity, and strive to possess the honor of the divine likeness for which he was created through nobility of conduct, the practice of virtues, and the dignity of merits. Thus, when he appears as he is, man may then appear like the one who wondrously created him in his likeness in the first Adam and more wondrously restored him in the second (1 John 3:2).

# EXORCISM

[Col. 1017]

## NOTICE

[Col. 1017C] The following exorcism was copied from a Vatican codex six hundred years old, in which it is presented as the work of Ambrose. Although it is also found in the Roman Ritual, since there it has been divided into various parts and in several places differs through additions or alterations, we have not hesitated to present it here according to the manuscript, especially on account of the brevity of the text.

[Col. 1019]

## EXORCISM (S)

[Col. 1019A] 613 Almighty Lord, Word of God the Father, Jesus Christ, God and Lord of all creation, who gave your holy apostles power to tread upon serpents and scorpions; who, among the other commands of your wonders, deigned to say, “Cast out demons” (Matt. 10:8); by whose power Satan, overcome, fell from heaven like lightning: I humbly beseech you, with fear and trembling, by your name, that, having forgiven all my sins, you may deign to grant me, most unworthy as I am, confidence and the ability to attack this cruel dragon faithfully and without fear, strengthened by the power of your arm.

I adjure you, therefore, every most unclean spirit, every phantom, every assault of Satan, by the power of the name of Christ, who, after his baptism in the Jordan, was led into the desert [Col. 1019B] and conquered you in your own dwelling, to cease attacking the one whom he formed from the clay of the earth for the honor of his glory, and to tremble in this wretched human being not before human weakness but before the image of almighty God.

Yield, therefore, to God, who reduced you to servitude in his humbled servant Job. Yield to God, who through Moses his servant drowned you and your army in Pharaoh and his army in the abyss. Yield to God, who through his boy Daniel destroyed you in Bel and struck you down in the dragon. Yield to God, who through his most faithful David drove you away from King Saul by spiritual songs. Yield to God, who condemned you in Judas the betrayer.

For he now drives you with divine scourges, before whom, trembling with your legions, you cried: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of David? Have you come here before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8:29). He presses you with everlasting flames, who at the end of time will say to the wicked: “Go, accursed ones, into the everlasting fire which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). For you, impious one, and your angels, the worm that never dies is prepared; for you and your angels an unquenchable fire is prepared. For you, accursed one, are the prince of murder, the author of incest, the head of sacrilege, the teacher of the worst arts, the instructor of heretics, and the inventor of every obscenity.

Come out, therefore, impious one; come out, criminal; come out with all your deceit, because God has willed man to be his temple. Why do you delay any longer? Give honor to God the almighty Father, before whom every knee bows. Give place to Jesus Christ, who shed his blood for man. Give place to the Holy Spirit, who revealed you through his blessed apostle Peter in Simon, condemned your deceit in Ananias and Sapphira, struck you in King Herod when he did not give honor to God, and through his apostle Paul covered you, the wicked magician, with the darkness of blindness, and through that same apostle, by a word of command, ordered you to come out of the pythoness.

Depart now, depart, deceiver. The desert is your dwelling; the serpent is your habitation. Humble yourself; prostrate yourself. There is no longer time for delay. For behold, the ruling Lord is drawing near; soon fire will burn before him and consume his enemies round about. If you deceive man, you cannot mock the Lord. He casts you out whose eyes see nothing hidden. He expels you to whose power all things are subject. He excludes you who has prepared eternal Gehenna for you and your angels. From his mouth will come a two-edged sword; he will come in the Holy Spirit to judge the world by fire. Amen.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT AMBROSE

Part Two, containing minor works not admitted into the Benedictine edition.

# ACTS OF SAINT SEBASTIAN THE MARTYR

## NOTICE ON THE ACTS OF SAINT SEBASTIAN

[Col. 1019C] 1. Baronius, in the year 286, no. 2, considers the Acts of him and his companions authentic and worthy of being appended to the *Annals*. Joannes Hessels of Louvain, Molanus’s teacher, writes the following in his judgment concerning certain histories of the saints—a judgment otherwise sufficiently severe, as we have indicated elsewhere: “The entire passion of Saint Sebastian pleases in every respect; in it is contained the passion of many others.”

2. “Those Acts,” says Galesinius, “are thought to have been written by the notaries of the holy Roman Church.” We have no doubt of that; but perhaps not in the form in which they are now in our hands. For their author was held to be Saint Ambrose eight hundred years ago. Thus writes an anonymous and not unlearned monk who described the translation of Saint Sebastian’s relics into Gaul, mentioned below, in chapter 6, no. 22: “The Alarces go together to a place that was no longer unknown; for from the account of his passion, splendidly published by Saint Ambrose, they had learned that, at the third milestone from the city, at the place called the Catacombs because of the stationing of ships, that same most blessed martyr had appeared in a vision to a certain matron named Lucina and commanded her to bury him at the feet of the apostles Peter and Paul.”

And in the Epilogue, no. 100: “If anyone, fastidious and desiring to be satisfied with more refined food, should set aside our bran and seek the work of the most holy Father Ambrose, which he published concerning the triumph of this heavenly citizen, he will find there a dish [Col. 1021B] most richly filled. Having tasted its exceedingly delicious wheat with the palate of the mind, he will be able to grow fat with delight.”

2. Nor is it surprising that he himself, like the accounts of other saints, either first committed Sebastian’s splendid struggles to writing—Sebastian was born at Milan, and the purpose was to inflame the Milanese with an equal ardor of virtue—from what he had heard from his elders or found in commentaries, or interpolated material handed down by others. Nor does the style depart greatly from Ambrose’s elegance and gravity.

3. Rosweyde, our associate, transcribed these Acts from manuscripts of Rebdorf near Eichstätt, the Eichstätt Fathers Preachers, M. Welser, and Saint Martin of Trier. We collated them with manuscripts of Saint Gislenus, Saint Omer, Saint Maximinus, Ripatorium, [Col. 1022A] and others, as well as with the edition of Bonino Mombrizio. Livinus Brecht of Antwerp, a Minorite, published at Louvain the version he took from a manuscript at Mechelen—though with the style somewhat altered, as Molanus testifies and becomes clear to the reader—and dedicated it to Viglius Zuichemus, president of the imperial council, under this title: *A Memorable History Containing the Conversion and Struggles of Several Illustrious Martyrs, Together with a Golden Exhortation to Contempt for the Present Life and Desire for the Eternal Life, a Little Work by an Author Indeed Uncertain, but Newly Reviewed and Purged by Brother Livinus Brecht*. In the dedicatory letter he writes: “We have judged it right to communicate to the Christian reader the illustrious struggles of the martyrs, most carefully written down, if I am not mistaken, twelve hundred years ago.”

5. Gentianus Hervetus translated the same Acts from the Greek of Symeon Metaphrastes into Latin; Aloysius Lippomanus published them, and Surius reproduced them from him. They were also written by James of Voragine, Francis Haraeus, Zacharias Lippelous, Ferrarius in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*, Baronius in volume II of the *Annals*, M. Antonius Georgius, Joannes Basilius Sanctorius, our associates Ribadeneira and Rosweyde, Petrus de Natalibus, book II, chapter 106, Gabriel Flamma, and countless others. Saint Augustine’s hundredth sermon *On Various Subjects* was delivered on the feast of him and Saint Fabian; Saint Gregory’s homily 37 was delivered in the basilica of Saint Sebastian. Many others’ sermons concerning him are extant. We have also read the same martyrdom in a manuscript of Nicholas Belfortius, a canon regular of Soissons, written in verse by Oliver Conrad, a Minorite.

[Col. 1021]

# ACTS OF SAINT SEBASTIAN THE MARTYR (C,G,S)

## CHAPTER ONE. SAINT SEBASTIAN ENCOURAGES THE MARTYRS

[Col. 1021C]

1. Sebastian, a most Christian man, an educated citizen of the Milanese region but a citizen of Narbonne, [Note: [Col. 1021D] Most manuscripts read “of the Milanese region”; some read “a citizen of the district.” Saint Ambrose, in *On Psalm 118*, octave 20: “Let us use the example of the martyr Sebastian, whose feast is today. He was born in Milan. Perhaps the persecutor had already departed, or had not yet come into that region, or was milder. He noticed that there was either no contest or that it was growing cold. He went to Rome, where, because of zeal for the faith, bitter persecutions were raging. There he suffered—that is, there he was crowned. Thus, where he had arrived as a guest, he established a dwelling of perpetual immortality.” Baronius, however, in volume II, year 284, no. 12, writes: “Saint Ambrose and others report that he was born at Milan of a father from Narbonne and a Milanese mother.” Metaphrastes reports that he was born at Milan but says nothing of his parents. Sauffaius says that he was born at Narbonne in Viennese Gaul, of a Gallic father and a Milanese mother. Neither Tristanus Calchus nor Joseph Ripamontius contradicts this; the latter adds that, left a widow by the early death of her husband, his mother returned to Milan with her only son. Rabanus and various manuscripts read: “On this same day, Saint Sebastian of Milan, who to such an extent …” Metaphrastes says that he was of illustrious lineage. The *Menaea* reads: Εἷς τῆς συγκλήτου βουλῆς ὑπῆρχεν, “He belonged to the senatorial order.” Guilielmus Catellius, in book II of his *History of Occitania*, testifies that even now at Narbonne a house of Saint Sebastian is pointed out, after which a church was built and called that of Saint Sebastian’s birthplace.] was so dear to the emperors Diocletian and Maximian that they entrusted him with command of the first cohort and ordered him always to stand in their presence. For he was a man of complete prudence: truthful in speech, just in judgment, provident in counsel, faithful in entrusted matters, vigorous in intervention, distinguished in goodness, and eminent in every moral excellence. The soldiers revered him as a father; all who presided over the palace revered him with the deepest affection. For he was a true worshiper of God, and it was necessary that everyone love the one whom God’s grace had suffused.

[Col. 1022C] 2. Every day, therefore, he diligently rendered service to Christ, but he acted in such a way that this remained hidden from the sacrilegious emperors—not terrified by fear of suffering, nor constrained by love of his property, but solely for this purpose: under the cloak of earthly imperial service he carried on Christ’s hidden soldiership [Note: [Col. 1022D] Some manuscripts read “hidden military service.”], so that he might strengthen the spirits of Christians whom he saw failing amid torments and restore to God the souls whom the devil was attempting to snatch away.

3. Finally, after he had rescued many minds of martyrs from fear of suffering and urged them toward the crown of perpetual glory, it became clear who he was, because light could not remain hidden in darkness. When the most illustrious men Marcellian and Mark, two twin brothers, had been imprisoned for Christ’s name, he provided them daily [Col. 1023A] with consolation and offered both them and their servants, who had been imprisoned with them, saving counsels of faith, so that they might reject the fleeting flatteries of the world and not fear the momentary kinds of torment.

## CHAPTER TWO. THE CONSTANCY OF MARCELLIAN AND MARK SEVERELY ASSAILED

4. When they had accepted these most blessed consolations and endured the executioners’ blows with persevering courage, they were ordered to undergo the sentence of death. The arrangement was that, at the very moment when they were to be beheaded, if they consented to sacrifice, they would be restored to their parents, wives, children, and possessions. For they were not only, as we have said, men of most illustrious birth, but also wealthy [Note: [Col. 1023D] Other manuscripts read “enriched”; others, “adorned.”]. Their father was named Tranquillinus, and their mother was called Marcia. Their parents followed them with their wives and children, for they were excessively attached to their grandchildren. Thus it happened that, from Agrestius Chromatius, prefect of the city of Rome, they obtained a delay of thirty days [Note: [Col. 1023D] Others read “from Agrestinus.” In the catalogue of city prefects, it is recorded that under the consulship of Carus and Carinus the prefect was Titutius Roburrus; under Carinus and Numerian, Ceionius Varus, who also held the prefecture in the following year, when Diocletian and Aristobulus were consuls. The name of Chromatius appears to have been erased from the records out of hatred of religion. Whether Vopiscus means him, Roburrus, or Ceionius is uncertain, when he writes in his account of Carinus: “He made one of his secretaries prefect of the city.” The *cancellarii* were those who kept watch at the barriers, whether of the imperial palace or of the tribunals.] during which they were to be dealt with in order to induce them to consent to burn incense to idols.

5. Their friends therefore approached them and began to say: “How can you have so hard a mind and such an iron breast that you can endure to cast aside your father’s gray hairs [Note: [Col. 1024D] Others read *patitur* (“suffers”).] and bring new pains of childbirth upon your mother, already decrepit? For she overcame the pains of her childbirth through consolation when, in one labor, she bore two sons and poured forth upon their father a double affection for his children. But now this is an incurable sorrow, an inconsolable punishment, an irremediable anguish, an incomparable [Note: [Col. 1024D] Alternatively, “mourning.”] childbirth, by which hope and joy are taken away, life is despised, glory rejected, and, with every affection of piety disregarded, the cruelty of death is desired [Note: [Col. 1024D] The next three words are absent from the Saint-Omer manuscript.] rather than feared. We beseech you, dearest friends: at last put an end to these disasters, and, once reminded, remember that you are fathers of beloved sons.”

6. While the friends were saying these and similar things, their mother arrived crying aloud that she was wretched. With her head uncovered, displaying the gray hairs of her old age, she tore open before them the garment that covered her breast. While everyone wept, she showed them her loosened breasts, which they had sucked, and in lamentation and tears recalled the caresses she had bestowed upon them in infancy. She said to both of them:

“You have always been the more affectionate toward me, my son; and you have always been the more bashful. In this one I gave birth to my own image; in you I poured forth your father’s features. You are more useful to your father; this one is more like him. Alas, wretched me! Incomparable griefs surround me on every side, unheard-of misery, and a double bereavement beyond all comparison with any tribulations.

“I pass over the fact that my sons are rushing voluntarily to death. If enemies were taking them from me, I would follow the raiders through the midst of the battle lines; if violent judgments shut them away, I would break into the prison and die there with them. This is a new kind of dying, in which the executioner is asked to strike, life is desired so that it may perish, and death is invited to come. This is a new sorrow, a new misery, in which the youth of children is willingly surrendered and the pitiable old age of parents is forced to remain alive.”

7. While the mother continued with these and similar words, their feeble father, already weighed down by old age, was led in by the hands of servants. Sprinkling the dust of the earth upon his swan-white head, he addressed heaven with these cries:

“I have come to bid farewell to sons who are voluntarily going to their death, so that all that I had prepared for my sons to provide at my burial, unhappy man that I am, I may spend in burying my sons. O sons, staff of my old age and double light of my inmost being, happily born and prosperously raised, of most excellent memory and singular intelligence, imbued with knowledge of all the liberal arts: what sudden madness, born of your own will, has made you lovers of death?

“This has never pleased the living; it has never induced those about to die to love it. Wherever it has been able to reach anyone, it has been violently imposed, and no living person has accepted it willingly. If a naked debtor suffers it under a greedy moneylender, he can in no way love it; indeed, he is known not merely not to love it but to fear it. By what reasoning does one desire it who overflows with every good and is utterly indebted to no one?

“Come here, old men, and mourn with me over sons whom you feel to be the inmost organs of your fatherly being. Come here, young men, and weep over young men dying of their own accord. Come here, fathers, and prevent such things, lest you suffer such things yourselves. Fail through weeping, my eyes, and cover yourselves with darkness as you pour forth rivers of tears, lest I see by the sword those whom I trembled to touch when a light rod merely brushed them, and whom I feared to see even when they were mildly saddened.”

8. While the old man continued these and other words, behold, the wives of both men arrived with their own children. Holding their little ones before their husbands’ eyes, they poured forth these cries in lamentation:

“To whom are you leaving us to serve? To whom are you handing over the love of our marriage? Who, do you think, will be masters of these children, and the most eager invaders of your houses? Who will seize your household? Or who will divide among themselves the servants whom you raised?

“Alas, with what iron-hearted, with what impiously cruel conduct you despise your parents, reject your friends, cast away your wives, disown your children, and voluntarily present yourselves to the executioner!”

## CHAPTER THREE. SAINT SEBASTIAN STRENGTHENS THOSE WHO WERE WAVERING

9. While these things were being said and those things reported, amid the tears of their wives and the sighs of their children, Christ’s soldiers began to soften and bend their spirits toward grief. As we said above, Saint Sebastian was present at this spectacle, a man Christian in every respect, whom his military dress concealed and the shadow of his cloak kept from view.

But when he saw God’s athletes wearied beneath the immense weight of the contest, he threw himself among them and said:

“O most valiant soldiers of Christ, O most fully equipped warriors of the divine battle: through extraordinary courage you have bravely reached the palm of victory, and now, through miserable flatteries, are you laying down your everlasting crown? Let the courage of Christ’s soldiers now learn from you to be armed with faith rather than iron. Do not cast away the trophies of your victories through women’s flatteries, and do not release the necks of your conquered enemy, which lie beneath your feet, to return again to victorious and renewed battles—an enemy whose persistence, however savage and unjust it has been against you, becomes more savage still when its anger is renewed.

“Raise, therefore, from earthly affections [Note: [Col. 1025D] Others read “from full affections”; others, “from earthly sights.”] the glorious trophy of your contest [Note: [Col. 1025D] Alternatively, “of glory.”], and do not lose it through the tears of little children.”

10. Those whom you see weeping would rejoice today if they could know what you know. For they think that this life is the only one, and that, if it should end, no portion of the living soul can remain once the body has failed. If they knew that there is another life, ignorant of death and unacquainted with sorrow, in which immortality reigns and perpetual joys dwell, they would surely hasten with you to reach it. Counting this life as nothing, they would desire that life which remains in exultation and knows no end.

For this life is fleeting and so unfaithful that it has been unable to keep faith even with its lovers. From the beginning of the world it has deceived all who believed in it, disappointed all who awaited it, mocked all who relied upon it, and made absolutely no one secure, so that everyone has been proved to have been lied to by it.

And if only it were guilty of lying alone and did not force its lovers to run through every crime! It gives gluttony to gluttons [Note: [Col. 1025D] Papias: “gluto,” from *gula* (“throat”); “ganeo,” a spendthrift.], it pours drunkenness into the intoxicated, it gives adulterers the shipwreck of chastity, and hands incestuous persons over to abominable perversion. It urges the thief to steal, the angry man to rage, and the liar to deceive. It sows divorces among husbands and wives, discord among friends, quarrels among peacemakers, injustice among the just, and scandals among brothers. It takes justice from judges, chastity from the chaste, skill from craftsmen [Note: [Col. 1025D] Some manuscripts read “from the arts.”], and discipline from character.

And, to mention the more serious crimes it inflicts upon its lovers: if a brother has ever killed his own brother, if a son has killed his father, if a friend has been slain by a friend—at whose instigation were these crimes committed? At whose prompting, through whose hope, through whose assurance were these abominations perpetrated? Are they not seduced by love of the present life into committing these things, and, while loving it more than is just, pursuing human beings with unjust hatred?

Why does the pirate slaughter the sailor? Why does the bandit kill the traveler, the rich man oppress the poor, the proud man the humble, and every guilty person burden whatever innocent person he can? They do these evil things because they desire to serve this life and suppose that they will endure for a longer time in its love. Therefore crimes are committed for no other reason than that this most wretched carnal life may be served by carnal people.

11. Finally, it is this life that commands them to commit crimes, orders wicked deeds, and persuades them to injustice. After it has been fattened on every cruelty and every filthiness, it hands those who serve it over to its daughter, namely, everlasting death. For from it and from its womb eternal death was born at the time when the first human beings served their appetite, their lust, and the delights of their eyes. Therefore those who had been made for eternal life were cast into this region of death; from here they were again rolled down into hell, carrying nothing with them except their sins.

This, then, is the life that deceives you, dearest friends, so that you may recall your friends, who are going to everlasting life, by an unjust counsel.

## CHAPTER FOUR. THE PUNISHMENTS OF HELL AND THE JOYS OF HEAVEN IMPRESSED UPON THE MINDS OF THE MARTYRS
12. This is what incites you, most holy parents, to call back your sons, as they set out for the heavenly [Note: [Col. 1025D] *Comitatus*: often the emperor’s companions; elsewhere, the office of a *comes*; commonly today, the place or district subject to his jurisdiction. Here it signifies the court. Thus Possidius in the *Life of St. Augustine*: “where at that time the *comitatus* of the younger Valentinian had been established”; and St. Ambrose, *On the Death of Valentinian*: “He ordered her to come to the court.”] court, to incorruptible honor, to the friendship of the eternal Emperor, by your most foolish lamentations. This is what has made you, most chaste wives of the Blessed, under the appearance of piety, hand impiety over to the minds of the Martyrs, and bring death instead of liberation. For if they had yielded to your attempt to call them back, they could indeed have remained with you for a short time; afterward, however, they would have had to be separated, and separated from you in such a way that you would see them nowhere except amid everlasting torments: where devouring flame consumes the souls of unbelievers, where dragons eat the lips of blasphemers, and where serpents feed upon the breasts of unbelievers with their bites. There howling and groaning resound, and a confused outcry, which the force of torments drives forth and the heat of the fire wrings out. This very tribulation, moreover, which will receive the faithless there, is defined by no limit and enclosed by no end; nor, after the burning of the terrible flames, is it consumed, but whoever has been burned is restored for fires that come alive again.

13. Permit them, then, to escape this punishment, and consider rescuing yourselves. Permit them meanwhile to reach the crown appointed for them. Do not be afraid; for they will not be separated from you, but will go to prepare for you in heaven starry dwellings, in which you may remain with them and with your children in perpetual joy. And if houses made of stones delight you, how much more ought the beauty of those dwellings to invite you, where there are dining rooms shining with pure gold, which have *zetas* furnished with gems and pearls [Note: [Col. 1027D] Papias: *zetae*, houses that have water beneath their floors. Hence the force of the word. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XXIV, chapter 4, interprets *zeta* as *diaeta*, and Casaubon does likewise in his notes on Lampridius, who for this reason calls it a *zeta*; but Salmasius writes *dieta* and *zeta*. Thus they observe *zabulon* for *diabolum*, *zabolenum* for *diabolenum*, and *zarritum* for *diarritum*, together with Martinius. Passeratius, however, derives it from ζεῖν, “to boil,” because it receives the sun more fully, or from ζῇν, “to live.” Here and elsewhere it signifies a kind of dining room. [Col. 1028D] Below: *zetarius*, the curator of the *zetae*, or dining rooms.], where the purple flower of roses never withers; where flowering groves flourish in perpetual greenness; where fresh meadows always flow with honeyed streams [Note: [Col. 1028D] The Audomarus manuscript: “verdant.”]; where the grass breathes the fragrance of saffron flowers, and the fields, exhaling [Note: [Col. 1028D] Another reading: “whitening.”] pleasant and most delightful odors, are rich with them. There the breezes, possessing eternal life, breathe nectarous fragrance into the nostrils. There light shines without the sun’s ray, serenity exists without cloud, and the eyes enjoy day without the darkness of night. There no delight is obstructed by any occupation [Note: [Col. 1028D] Another reading: “occasion.”], nor is security disturbed there by any anxiety whatever. Bellowing, howling, groaning, lamentation, and mourning are never heard or named there. The eyes of the inhabitants have never seen there anything foul or deformed, gloomy, black, dreadful, or filthy. Rather, their open eyes uninterruptedly enjoy the beauty of the pleasant groves, the brilliance of the joyful air, and loveliness together with every elegance; and nothing at all that could disturb the mind is presented to their ears. For there the organs of hymns resound continually, sung by angels and archangels to the praise of the King. Bitterness and the harshness of gall have no place there; thunder is never heard there, nor have flashes or lightning ever appeared. There cinnamon shrubs produce their growth, and balsam bushes spring forth. The fragrance of the air diffuses delight through every limb, and no food there produces excrement. For just as the ears are satisfied by good news, the nostrils by a good odor, and the eyes by a pleasing sight—and this refreshment cannot break out into digestion—so there the refreshment received by the mouth tastes sweet as honey to each person, according to what delights him. Indeed, immediately whatever the soul desires, everything serves its longing, and fulfillment, ready for all its pleasures, serves it.

14. For whoever in this mortal life has fought against his desires and his pleasures, whoever has not exhausted them here, receives them there in their entirety from his Creator. For He created human beings in such a way [Col. 1027D] that they might live, and placed death beside the entrance of pleasure, so that those who wish to escape the fear of death may seek eternal life. And when they have learned that there is another life beyond this one, they may inquire whether it too can be cut short by old age or ended by death; and when they have recognized it as immortal, they may inquire whether eternity itself can again either bestow honor upon the just or inflict punishment upon the unjust.

## CHAPTER V. The Use of Wealth and Pleasures

15. And when they have specifically proved that this is so, it remains for them to ask why riches were made by the Creator, if they are to be despised according to His law; or why the variety of four-footed animals, birds, and creeping things was made by the Creator, if each person must renounce them [Note: [Col. 1028D] Other manuscripts: “gluttony.”]; and why natural pleasure, deeply implanted in bodies by the Creator Himself as an incitement [Note: [Col. 1028D] Another reading: “for defilement.”] to lust, was established, if its use makes not only the user guilty before its author but also delivers him over to everlasting fires. [Note: [Col. 1028D] Another reading begins: “Someone therefore asks: Why …?”]

The question is therefore asked: Why were riches given by the Creator, if they are to be despised? We answer: These riches, made by the Creator, address their lovers in a certain way, saying: “Love us in such a way that we may never be separated from you. We cannot follow you when you die; but while you live we can go before you—if you yourselves command it.” The greedy moneylender gives gold to a man so that he may receive it doubled; the avaricious farmer commits various seeds to the earth so that, if it can happen, he may seek to receive a hundredfold what he gives as onefold [Note: [Col. 1028D] Another reading: “may be able.”]. The debtor returns gold doubled to his creditor, and the earth returns seed a hundredfold to the farmer. Shame upon the wickedness! A debtor can repay interest to a moneylender; the earth can restore seed multiplied a hundredfold to its farmer; and can God not return His riches to you increased, if He has received them from you?

16. You ask now: Why did He give me riches, if they must be returned to Him by me? He entrusted them to you so that you might know how great is the rest they provide, how great their pleasure, how great their luxury, and how great their delights can be; so that, through these things, having acquired affection for your riches, you may entrust them for safekeeping to our Lord Jesus Christ. If you do not wish to entrust them to Him, either gluttony will seize them, or luxury, the mother of lust, will take them from you; or—and you know this very well—death, attacking unexpectedly, will wrest them from you in such a way that you will no longer foresee either possessing or seeing them at all.

Suppose you were crossing through the midst of barbarian battle lines and found a strong man who had always loved you, who had even given you a purse full of money, saying to you: “Give me the money I gave you to keep, because these barbarians are lying in wait to take it from you; and when they have taken it from you, they will tear you apart with their swords.” Would you not fall at his feet and beg him to receive it himself, knowing that he would return to you more than he had received and would also free you from your enemies? It remains, then, for you to have Christ as guardian of your riches.

[Col. 1029A] 17. Let us come to pleasures. Whoever has ears to hear will hear them saying: “If you are truly our lovers, entrust us to Him who will restore us to you whole and undefiled in that region where we may remain with you continually. For if in this life we should wish to claim you for our service, having as it were been experienced here, in that life we will altogether deny you the office of our service.” Allow us meanwhile to serve those who are dying, because mortal days have been shortened for this very reason: that we may serve immortals continually. For thus it is written (Matthew 24:22): ‘For the sake of the elect the days will be shortened,’ so that our service may not be long.

“We serve the unjust in rapid [Note: [Col. 1029D] Another reading: “with a swift onset.”] course; we serve the impious, the wicked, and the disgraceful, not willingly, but because He who subjected us has so ordained. Yet we will be freed from the slavery of corruption and recalled to the freedom of the glory of the children of God.”

Therefore every pleasure, preserved for the future life, is not lost. Treasures stored away are not thought by the one who hid them in the earth to be of no concern; rather, he trusts that he possesses them all the more securely the more secretly and safely he has placed them.

18. Let the abundance of all pleasures, then, be stored up, so that they may not be touched in this life, which passes away. For if they are used here, they will be lost in that life which never passes away. Suppose that this life were extended across a span of a hundred years: once the final day had passed, would it not immediately appear as though it had never existed, leaving only traces like those of a guest who stayed with us for one day? But that life remains continually and endures without interruption; even as the years pass, it grows young and flourishes, and it takes the beginning of renewal from the very point at which its end is received. Truly degenerate and deprived of every good is the one who is not captivated by love of this life so beautiful; who fears to surrender this life, destined to perish, and receive that life which knows no utter destruction, in which delights, pleasures, riches, and joys begin in such a way that they know no end, and take their beginning in such a way that they cannot end completely.

19. For whoever refuses to be a lover of this most splendid life not only loses this one and fails to reach that one, but, as I have already said, is also seized and held by perpetual death. In it there is unceasing flame, enduring tribulation, and everlasting punishment; there dwell dreadful angels whose arms are the heads of dragons, whose eyes shoot fiery arrows from themselves, whose teeth protrude like those of elephants, and whose tails, like those of scorpions, goad toward torment. Their voices sound like the roar of lions; their appearance inspires fear, pain, and death alike. If only death could come to those placed in such distress! But what is more bitter is that they are kept alive for this purpose: to be ruled by tortures; they are restored for this purpose: that their limbs, eaten away by the bites of serpents, may then be touched again and again by repeated and renewed bites.

## CHAPTER VI. The Happiness and Glory of the Martyrs

[Col. 1030A]

20. This is the whole reason for the struggle, which teaches that the punishments of martyrdom ought to be endured patiently. Therefore, friends, do not—parents, do not—venerable wives of the saints, do not call back from life to death those whom you love; do not lead them from joy to mourning, drag them from light to darkness, or summon them from eternal rest to everlasting punishments. This is to cast a hook with the devil, as though for fish, and to invite someone to a brief sweetness in which the torture of the inward parts lies hidden, and death is wrung out through the torments of the inner being.

Is it not to prefer fleeting joys to the compensation of eternal delights, and, so that they may laugh for a very little while, to hand them over to everlasting tears? In gladiators, who offer themselves voluntarily, we all condemn this conduct: they consider the pleasures of a single year and do not consider what fruit will arise from those very pleasures. They are tortured by sword blows, or by successive slaughter, and display their inner organs before the eyes of the people after the covering of the belly has been split open, so that the fat which thoughtless feeding had supplied may be offered to the devil for him to devour.

By the very counsel of the enemy through which these things are done, the Martyrs of God, who are going to eternal life, are recalled—those whom people entreat to incur everlasting torments so that they may live for a few days [Note: [Col. 1029D] Another reading: “are taught”], and not fear the perpetual death that ought especially to be feared.

21. Perhaps you bring forward against this argument the following objection: Why does a Christian not fear torments, and why is he not terrified by the present punishment [Note: [Col. 1030D] Ripuarian manuscript: “by the torments of punishment”] of the executioner? He is not broken by fear for this reason; he is not led away by pain for this reason: he knows that, at the price of one pain, he is purchasing the joy of perpetual health, and that through momentary tribulation he is reaching perpetual happiness and everlasting joy.

But if this pain is to be feared, if the executioner is to be feared, and if the executioner’s new and elaborate cruelty is also to be feared, then which is more worthy of fear, more horrifying, more to be fled and guarded against: this pain, which blazes up today and vanishes tomorrow; this pain, which burns today and cools tomorrow; this pain, which is inflicted within an hour and removed within an hour? Or that pain which is enclosed by no end, extinguished by no passage of time, and consumed by absolutely no old age?

For this pain is either light and can be endured tolerably, or it is severe and, in a glorious struggle, quickly offers an end. But that pain of punishment and torture of fire, which is given to lovers of this life, although more vehement than every kind of torment, begins without ever coming to an end; it rages afterward more fiercely than when it began; no limit to its raging, no end whatever, appears. It carries with it every kind of punishment and is continually renewed so that it may rage, increased so that it may torture, and inflamed so that it may burn more fiercely.

22. Let us therefore exhort those whom we love to escape from this destruction, and bravely prepare ourselves to escape it. Let us not fear enduring pain in the body for a single hour, since we desire to rejoice with Christ forever. Let us permit our soul to leave this body with the palm of martyrdom, so that we may escape eternal punishments and reach the starry dwellings full of delights.

Let us turn our tears into joy, for we ought not to mourn as though they were going to die those whom we believe will reign with Christ. Let us congratulate the victors over their enemies, with the enemies’ necks trampled underfoot; let us rejoice with those clothed in the purple robe of martyrdom, and glory in their having become consuls of heaven.

Behold the day on which the tyrant thought he would conquer: while he captures, he is captured; while he holds, he is bound; while he tortures, he is tortured; while he insults, he is mocked; while he slaughters, he is killed. Now, therefore, let us also awaken our affections to love of martyrdom, so that we may bravely seize the one who wished to gain victory through our captivity. As though awakened from a deep sleep, let us open the eyes of our minds, so that, seeing the pits which the enemy had prepared for our destruction, we may, with God’s help, escape them; and when the devil himself, together with his attendants, falls into the very pit he had prepared, let us say with the prophet: “They dug a pit before my face, and they themselves fell into it” (Psalm 56:7).

## CHAPTER VII. Zoe and Nicostratus Converted by Sebastian’s Prayer and Miracles

23. When the most blessed Sebastian, clothed in a military cloak and girded with a belt, was uttering these words from his own mouth, suddenly, for nearly an hour, he was illuminated by an immense brightness coming from heaven.
