Beneath that very radiance, he was clothed by seven most illustrious Angels in an exceedingly white mantle [Col. 1031C], and a young man appeared beside him, giving him peace and saying: “You will always be with me.”

24. These things were taking place [Note: [Col. 1031D] Some manuscripts: “beside”; this is not approved.] inside the house [Note: [Col. 1031D] Under the authority of the illustrious prefect of the City, among his other administrative offices, there is the *primiscrinius*, or *numerarius*, concerning whose office others have written much. [Col. 1032D]] of Nicostratus, the *primiscrinius*, where Marcellianus and Marcus were being held. Nicostratus had a wife named Zoe. Six years earlier, she had become mute through the severity of an illness, yet she had not only failed to lose the faculty of hearing and understanding; she possessed the use of her ears even better than before.

When she had understood everything that Blessed Sebastian had said and had seen such a great light around him, while all were trembling and held in astonishment at the miracle, she gestured with her hand to everyone, as though reproaching those who did not believe such an evident declaration. Then she fell at his knees and began to entreat him by signs made with her hands. But when St. Sebastian saw that she could not express the secrets of her heart through the speech of her tongue, he inquired into the cause of her silence and learned that the power of speech had been taken from her by the excessive force of her illness.

Then Blessed Sebastian said: “If I am a true servant of Christ, and if all the things this woman heard from my mouth and believed are true, may my Lord Jesus Christ command that the function of her tongue return to her and open the mouth of her who opened the mouth of His prophet Zechariah.” And he made the sign of the cross over her mouth.

At these words of St. Sebastian the woman cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Blessed are you, and blessed is the word of your mouth; and blessed are those who through you believe Christ, the Son of the living God. For I saw with my own eyes an angel coming to you from heaven and holding a book before your eyes; from its reading the whole discourse of your speech flowed forth. Blessed are those who believe everything you have said, and accursed are those who have doubted even one word of all that they heard. For just as the rising dawn excludes all the darkness of night and restores to every eye the light that blind night had denied, so the light of your words has wiped away every gloom and all the blindness of ignorance, and has restored to the eyes of those who rightly believe a serene day after the darkness of night. From me, moreover, it has not only driven out the darkness of unbelief; it has also opened the door of my speech, which had been closed for six years.”

25. When Nicostratus, her husband, saw that such power of Christ had been manifested in his wife, he began to fall at Sebastian’s feet and ask pardon because he had held the saints of God in chains at the command of the emperor and the prefect. Removing the iron bonds from their hands and embracing their knees, he began to beg them to consent to depart, saying: “How blessed I would be if I could deserve to be bound for the sake of your salvation! Perhaps I could be cleansed by the shedding of my blood, so that I might escape that death of eternal punishments and reach that life which God has deigned to reveal to us through the mouth of my lord Sebastian.”

## CHAPTER VII [Note: [Col. 1032] Migne printed CHAPTER VII instead of CHAPTER VIII]. The Steadfastness of Marcellianus and Marcus; an Address to the Neophytes

[Col. 1032C]

26. When he asked Marcellianus and Marcus to depart, they said to him: “If you have received the glory of faith, which you never possessed before, how can we, abandoning the faith which we have always possessed from infancy, give you the cup of our passion—something we can offer you to drink, but cannot give away? For Christ is rich in all things, and in the generous abundance of His fullness He offers better things to all who come than they ask.

“For if, when you were unbelievers, you were granted the light of recognizing the truth, how much more, now that you believe, will everything you already seek be granted to you? Divine mercy is always prepared freely to provide everything for you; and it multiplies each person by the gift of its grace in proportion as his mind receives the standard of a higher faith.

“Your faith, therefore, took its beginning from instruction, and within the space of one hour you received everything that lengthy teaching scarcely bestows. No memory of your parents prevents you from believing. No tender affection, nurtured from childhood toward your sons, calls you back. Suddenly you despise what you have always loved and seek what you have never known. Entering by roads of which you were ignorant, you have suddenly arrived at Christ; and in your spirit you have already entered heaven, because on earth you sought no consolation.

“O incomparable proclamation of your deed! O example of virtue worthy of imitation! The sacred water of baptism has not yet led you to Christ; you have not yet even taken up the military standards through the beginnings of your training; and already you seize weapons for the true King. Releasing His soldiers from the bonds of iron, you yourselves, fearless, desire to be killed instead of those who are to be killed.”

27. When all who were present heard these words, they jointly displayed through their tears repentance for their former persuasion. Marcus said: “Learn, dearest parents—and let your wedded affection learn, O wives—to set the shield of virtues against the battle of the devil and against all the arrows of the passions of carnal desire; amid the battle lines of the tyrannical army, do not yield to the enemy, fight more fiercely, hold your position [Note: [Col. 1033D] Others read: “press on toward joy”; others: “press on toward the sword”; others: “press on toward the step.”], and reach the King bravely.

“Let the attendants of demons rise up as much as they wish and rage; let them tear our bodies apart with whatever punishments they choose. They can kill the body, but they cannot conquer the soul fighting for the truth of the faith. Wounds received for the Emperor make soldiers more glorious. For the devil now rages with the fury of his tyranny precisely in that place where he foresees that he can be tormented by the trophy of your perseverance. Therefore he inflicts torments so that his hope may not perish; he threatens death in order to terrify; he promises life in order to take it away; he promises security in order to remove it.

“This is the whole cunning of the war, this the plan of the deception: to rescue the body from punishments and subject the soul to vices. Let us, on the contrary, strive not to yield to the enemy, to despise the body, and to aid the soul. Why should the strongest [Note: [Col. 1033D] Another reading: “the soldiers of the Leader.”] commanders turn their backs on the most wretched soldiers and fail in a war in which they can be victorious? Or why should those who know that this is the nature of humanity, not its punishment, fear to die?

“Why, I ask, should those fear to die who believe that this life is false, and that the true life cannot be found unless one has cast this false and fleeting life away from his soul—a life which commands its lovers to do nothing but sin, urges them to crimes, and thrusts criminal acts upon them, demanding nothing else from its lovers except that they should never think at all about enduring life and should despair that the kingdom of God will come?”

28. Now let us see what circumstances this slave is subject to and what dangers she serves, so that, once we have proved that she cannot even govern herself, we may remove our service from her domination and seek another whom it is right to serve. How many of her lovers have been suddenly crushed by a heavy fall, struck by the crash of heaven, consumed by lightning and fire [Note: [Col. 1033D] Another reading: “devoured by flames and conflagrations.”], destroyed by shipwrecks, covered by chaos, swallowed by Charybdis, or slaughtered by the sword! And when these wretched people lose this life amid suffering, they cannot find that other life at all.

For torture does not lead to that life; the cause does. Thus, by one and the same kind of punishment, eternal salvation is bestowed upon the innocent and punishment is inflicted upon offenders.

## CHAPTER IX. The Others Converted by Sebastian Together with the Prisoners

29. While Marcus continued with these and similar words, all who were present began to give thanks to God, and all wept in repentance because they had preferred the love of the flesh to the love of God and had dared to recall the minds of the saints from the contest of martyrdom.

When all who had come to deceive the saints unanimously believed in Christ, Nicostratus, together with his wife, pressed the matter, saying: “I will take neither food nor drink unless the mystery of the Christian religion is entrusted to me.” St. Sebastian said to him: “Change your rank, and begin to be Christ’s *primiscrinius* rather than the prefect’s. Hear my advice, then, and gather together all whom prison has enclosed, whom chains hold, and whom the workhouses confine. When you have done this, I will bring in a bishop of the sacred and inviolable law, so that with all who wish to believe you may receive the sacrament of the mystery.

“For if the devil has tried, and continues to try, to take Christ’s saints away from Him, how much more ought we, by an act of piety, to care for these whom the devil has unjustly gained and restore them to their Creator?”

Nicostratus replied: “How can holy things be entrusted to the wicked and criminal?” St. Sebastian said: “Our Savior deigned to present His presence to us for sinners and revealed the mystery through which all sins and crimes may be taken away from a person and all the virtues of the Lord bestowed. At the beginning of your conversion, therefore, if you offer this first gift to Christ, the reward of His recompense will stand ready for you: the crown of martyrdom, bearing with it the unfading flowers of every virtue, destined to serve the joys of eternal life [Note: [Col. 1034D] Ripuarian manuscript: “giving off fragrance.”].”

When Nicostratus the *primiscrinius* heard this, he went to Claudius the *commentariensis* [Col. 1034C] and ordered all the persons to be brought to his house, saying: “Since at the next hearing they are all to be examined, I want them to be present with those Christians who are in my keeping, so that no person may be absent from the prefect’s inquiry” [Note: [Col. 1034D] Other readings: “the prefect”; “the praetor”; “the prefect of the praetorium”; “the inquiry of the praetorium.”].

30. When all had been led to the house of the *primiscrinius* and stood there bound by the links of their chains, the man of God, Sebastian, addressed them in this way: “If diabolical crimes yield to divine virtues, your guilt is shut out from death and recalled from fleeting joys [Note: [Col. 1034D] Another reading: “from the desired joys.”]. The unjust enemy had acted through his attendants so as to overthrow the minds of Christ’s soldiers, raised upright to the summit of the virtues, and, when they stood at the very height of perfection, to attempt to plunge them into the mire of hell.

“For this reason, the spirit of the enemy, provoked to combat, has grown hot, so that, removing you—whom the enemy had already won—from his captivity, we may return you to your Creator. For the devil is recognized as neither your lord, nor your creator, nor your father; but God is proved to be Father, Lord, and Maker.

“And if, abandoning him, you went over to the one who was so much your enemy that he led you to the punishments of perpetual death and brought you to this lethal end, how much more must you return to Him who handed over His only Son to suffering and death in order to free us from eternal sufferings and perpetual death?”

As St. Sebastian continued with these and similar words, they all fell prostrate with tears. With knees bent, they began to utter the groaning of their hearts and to cry out in penitential words that they had sinned and acted impiously. They poured out bitter tears and declared with unanimous voices that they wished to believe in Christ. Then Blessed Sebastian ordered all of them to be released from the bonds of their chains.

## CHAPTER X. All Prepared by Polycarp for Baptism

31. After this, St. Sebastian went to the presbyter Polycarp, who was hidden because of the persecution [Note: [Col. 1035D] The feast of St. Polycarp the presbyter is celebrated on February 23], and related to him everything that had happened. When he heard it, St. Polycarp gave thanks to God and came with him to the house of Nicostratus the *primiscrinius*. Seeing the crowds of believers, he greeted them with great joy and said:

“Blessed are all of you who have heard the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ saying: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light’ (Matthew 11:28–30).

“You, therefore, our brothers, whom the water of baptism has not yet washed and made beloved sons consecrated to Almighty God—because you attempted to recall the most blessed soldiers of Christ from their holy purpose—needed repentance, so that through it you might come to pardon. But now, because you have advanced to such great glory that you desire to run joyfully and willingly embrace even the passion from which you sorrowfully wished to recall others, know that you have attained both pardon and the palm.

“This is an ancient device of Christ. He Himself deemed and willed to give us as a teacher to the nations the one who not only recalled the minds of the faithful from their purpose of piety, but also stoned those unwilling to depart from Christ. The Lord Himself bestowed this man upon us as an apostle: from Saul He gave us Paul; from an apostate He made an apostle; and from a persecutor He gave His Church a teacher.

“He who had been the author of persecution became a lover of passion; and he who had previously rejoiced in the afflictions of others afterward rejoiced in his own persecutions. He, therefore, who at that time exercised this power in His apostle has now rescued the captivity of your souls from the prison of hell itself and from the very jaws of dragons, and has opened for you, now returning from darkness to light, the gates of eternal life.

“Therefore, because all the demons, who are the children of darkness, are sorrowful, while all the holy angels, who are the children of light, rejoice, let each one of you come forward and give his name, so that, while the fast continues from today until evening, the joyful sacrament of baptism may find a fitting time.

“For it is right that light, departing from the mortal world, should approach our immortal minds, so that we who in this age have wallowed in the mire of darkness may, washed and cleansed by the water of sanctification and clothed in purity, proceed joyfully to Christ.”

As St. Polycarp continued with these and similar words, all rejoiced, and each person hastened to offer his name before he was asked.

## CHAPTER XI. The Catechumens Are Baptized, and Claudius with His Sons

32. While these things were taking place, Claudius the *commentariensis* came to the house of Nicostratus the *primiscrinius*, where they were occurring, and said to Nicostratus: “The prefecture has been greatly disturbed because you ordered the persons of the accused to be entrusted to the custody of your house. For this reason the prefect has ordered you to be brought before him. See that you appear prepared to give an answer when questioned.”

Nicostratus therefore entered the prefect’s presence. When he was asked why he had wished the persons whom the prison’s barriers held to be placed under the custody of his own house, he replied: “At the command of Your Highness I accepted Christian persons into my house for safekeeping. To inspire them with fear of suffering, I made them associate with persons under accusation, so that, if they would not consent to your command and to my persuasion by their own agreement, they might at least consent through the experience of others and fear that a similar punishment would enclose them.”

The prefect, hearing this with great satisfaction, dismissed him, saying: “I will arrange for you to be rewarded with a large sum by their parents when their sons have been restored to them safe through your agency.”

[Col. 1036C] 33. Returning to his house with Claudius the *commentariensis*, Nicostratus the *primiscrinius* began to recount everything: how St. Sebastian, although he was a friend of emperors, was most Christian and perfect in divine learning; how by his exhortation he had recalled the souls of Christians; and how he had taught with sufficiently convincing reasoning that this present life is fleeting and imaginary, and that, even while it is thought to be held, it is taken away. He also related how a light had suddenly come from heaven and shone around him, and how he had made his wife, who had been mute for six years, speak.

34. When Nicostratus had told this to Claudius, Claudius fell at Nicostratus’s feet, saying: “From a wife whom I have lost I have two sons. One is afflicted by the disease of dropsy [Col. 1036D], and the other is oppressed by various wounds. I ask you to order that they be examined. For I do not doubt that He who was able to make your wife speak after six years can, if He wishes, restore health to my sons.”

Saying this, he hurried to his own house, had his two sons brought in, and, introducing them into the house where the saints of God were, threw them at their feet, saying: “No sign of doubt has remained at all in my heart. Believing with my whole heart that Christ whom you worship is Himself the true God, I have brought you my two offspring, trusting that through you they may be delivered from the danger of death” [Col. 1037A].

All the saints of God said to him together: “All those who are afflicted here today by any illness will be healed as soon as they have become Christians.”

35. When Claudius cried out that he believed and desired to become a Christian, Saint Polycarp ordered each person to give his name. First of all, Tranquillinus, father of Marcellianus and Marcus, gave his name. After him, their six friends: Aristo, Crescentianus, Eutychianus, Urbanus, Vitalis, and Justus; after them, Nicostratus, chief secretary, his brother Castorius, and Claudius, the records officer. After them, Claudius’s sons, Felicissimus and Felix. After them, Marcia, mother of Marcellianus and Marcus, with their wives and children; likewise Symphorosa, wife of Claudius, and Zoe, wife of Nicostratus. After them, the entire household that was in Nicostratus’s house—thirty-three persons of mixed sex and age—and thereafter all who had been bound and brought out from the filth of the prison—sixteen persons.

36. Accordingly, all these sixty-eight were baptized by the presbyter Saint Polycarp and received by Saint Sebastian; Beatrix [Note: Saint Beatrix is commemorated on July 29.] and Lucina [Note: The story of this Lucina is given on January 16 in the Life of Saint Marcellus. She is commemorated on June 30.] became godmothers for the women.

First, as soon as he had immersed Claudius’s sons—one dropsical and the other covered with wounds—in the name of the Holy Trinity, they were lifted from the font so completely healed that no sign of any former illness remained in them. After them came the little children, and then Tranquillinus, father of Saints Marcellianus and Marcus, who had been so tightly bound by the pain of gout in his feet and hands [Note: Another reading: “contracted”] that, as was said above, he could scarcely be carried in people’s hands.

When they were removing his garments and he said that he was being tortured by intolerable pain, the presbyter Polycarp asked him: “Tranquillinus, if you believe with all your heart that the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, is able to grant you health and forgive you the remission of all your sins, declare it with your own mouth.”

Tranquillinus replied: “I both desire and believe that remission alone be granted for my sins. Besides, even if I should remain in pain after the sanctification of this baptism, I will no longer be able to doubt the faith of Christ. For I have tested it, and, believing with all my heart, I have assented in my mind that the Son of God is the Lord Jesus Christ, who is able to grant salvation both to souls and to bodies and to recall them from eternal death to everlasting life.”

When he had said this in a loud voice, all the saints shed tears for joy and begged the Lord that the fruit of his faith might be displayed. Therefore, as soon as Saint Polycarp, confessor and presbyter, anointed him with the oil of chrism [Note: Another reading: “of oil”], he asked him again whether he believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. As soon as he answered, “I believe,” his hands, which had been knotted, were released, and his knees and the soles of his feet were restored whole. It was as though, with his feet renewed, a little child were descending into the font, while he cried out: “You are the one and true God, whom this wretched world does not know.”

37. After he had been baptized in this order, everyone else was baptized as was fitting. During the ten days that remained of the postponement they had obtained [Note: Some manuscripts add: “and six”], they continued in the praises of God, spending their days and nights in hymns and songs. Like faithful soldiers, they prepared their hearts to fight and to engage in martyrdom for Christ’s name, so that even among the women and little children the love of martyrdom burned, and they prepared one another for confession of the holy name against the forces of the devil.

## CHAPTER XII. Tranquillinus Refutes the Errors of the Pagans before Chromatius, Prefect of the City

[Col. 1038B]

38. [Note: Rosweyde’s autograph had written: “Book II.” Since this division is found in no manuscript, we have omitted it.] When the appointed days of the postponement had been completed, Agrestius Chromatius, prefect of the city of Rome, ordered Tranquillinus, father of Marcellianus and Marcus, to come before him. When he asked him about the disposition of his sons, Tranquillinus replied:

“No speech is sufficient to express my thanks for your benefits. For unless the reins of your moderation had restrained the judgments that were rushing forward, I would have lost my sons, and they would no longer have had me as their father. All who are possessed by paternal affection and goaded by the stimulus of love congratulate me; and I believe that your Excellency also shares my joy, since life has been granted to those who were about to die, joy restored to the anxious, and security restored to the troubled [Note: Another reading: ‘established’].”

39. Then the prefect, supposing that his sons wished to bow their necks to his idols, said: “[Note: Manuscript S. Gist.: ‘Come, therefore, today, and let the due incense be offered by your sons to the gods.’] On the appointed day, let your sons offer incense due to the deities. Through this, you too may remain safe with your sons, and your sons may be restored to you.”

Hearing this, Tranquillinus said: “Most illustrious of men, if you wish to weigh the scale of your judgment toward me and my sons with an even balance, you will be able to recognize that this Christian name possesses great power.”

The prefect said: “You are mad, Tranquillinus.”

Tranquillinus replied: “I suffered madness in both soul and body; but as soon as I believed in Christ, I recovered the health of both my soul and my body.”

40. The prefect said: “It appears that I granted an interval to your wicked sons for this purpose: not only would you fail to remove them from their error, but they would entangle you in their errors.”

Tranquillinus said: “By your glory, examine the very name ‘error’ and see what actions are called by the name of error.”

The prefect said: “You tell me what actions receive the name of error.”

Tranquillinus said: “The first error is to abandon the way of life and gladly walk along the way of death.”

The prefect said: “And what is the way of death?”

Tranquillinus said: “Does it not seem to you to be the way of death to bestow the name of deity upon dead men and worship their images through wood and stone?”

[Col. 1039A]

41. The prefect said: “Then the gods whom we worship are not gods?”

Tranquillinus said: “They are so far from being gods that it is read in your public books [Note: Another reading: ‘in your books’] how badly they were born; what wicked, cruel, and criminal parents they had; how unjustly, deceitfully, and fraudulently they lived; and how miserably they died.

“Before Saturn ruled the Cretans and ate the flesh of his own children, was there no God in heaven? Or did the island of Crete have a king while heaven had no God? He greatly errs who thinks that Jupiter, his son, rules the thunderbolts—a little man in whom wickedness and lust held sway. Whom did he not persecute, seeing that he did not spare his own father? Or what disgrace did he not practice, seeing that he took his own sister as his wife?

“In the forum, in the streets, in the houses, and everywhere, we read daily that filthy Juno boasts that she was both sister and wife; and the most shameful and incestuous honor of the abducted Ganymede is not denied by those very people who worship Jupiter.

“Therefore, most exalted sir, do you not err in worshiping those whom Roman laws order to be condemned according to the character of their deeds, while abandoning the almighty God who reigns in heaven and saying to a stone, ‘You are my god,’ and to wood, ‘Help me’?”

42. The prefect said: “Ever since you began to blaspheme the gods and withdraw from their worship, the Roman world has been oppressed by various disasters.” [Note: This was a customary accusation against Christians, refuted by various Church Fathers, especially Paulus Orosius and Saint Augustine.]

Tranquillinus replied: “That is not true. For if you review the decades arranged in Livy’s style [Note: Another reading: ‘of the books,’ incorrectly. Some manuscripts read ‘of Livy’], there you will find that, while they were offering incense to Jupiter, twenty-three thousand young men of the Roman army fell in a single day.

“You also do not forget that the Senonian Gauls occupied even the Capitol [Note: Thus all the manuscripts. It would perhaps be better to read ‘attacked’: [Col. 1040D] for after this they were bought off with a payment and soon driven out by Camillus.] and subjected the entire Roman force to their mockery. The Roman world suffered various famines, unspeakable plagues, various captivities, and various bloodshed before men worshiped the one God.

“Now, however, ever since the invisible and true God began to be worshiped by believers, the Roman Empire rejoices in increased peace [Note: Another reading: ‘in lofty peace’]. But what is worse is that the God who grants this is not acknowledged; rather, whatever is granted by the Creator is attributed to his creatures.”

43. The prefect said: “If the one who grants something beneficial to human beings is to be worshiped, then no one but the sun will be regarded as god. By its sight it makes the depths of the earth fertile, so that the seeds it receives may give birth and restore grains of its native offspring upon the stalk; and it grants to all the benefits of our well-being, providing equally light, renewal, and vigor.”

Tranquillinus replied: “Here too the error is boundless. If someone today grants his clients what they ask through a servant, it is utter folly, if the person who granted the favor is neglected and the servant through whom he granted it is honored.

“To offer an analogy for what I have said: when ships carry provisions to the Romans, are thanks given to the ships rather than to the rulers? [Col. 1040A] If, then, people attribute the provision of grain not to those who sail but to those who command, how much more must thanks be given to God alone, at whose will these elements serve all our needs, and the sun itself is daily closed equally over land and sea at the end of the day and opened again with the renewal of day?”

## CHAPTER XIII. The Incarnation of the Word Explained to a Pagan

44. The prefect said: “If, then, the one whom you worship is one and invisible, do you not worship Christ, whom the Jews crucified?”

Tranquillinus said: “You would rightly ask this if you were intending to believe. To unbelievers, everything they do not want appears vain. For once the will of mortals has turned headlong toward something, it desires everything it censures to be censured by others, and it wants everything it praises to be praised by everyone. But a wise person strives, according to the merit of each thing, either to impose blame upon it or to bestow praise [Note: Another reading: ‘to expend’].”

The prefect said: “I am asking you about your Christ. If what you worship is something that cannot be seen with these eyes, you do not worship Christ, who was seen, heard, and questioned, and in whose passion everything appropriate to human weakness is read as having been completed?”

Tranquillinus said: “Listen to an analogy and understand the truth. For example, if today you saw your ring, containing a precious gem, rolling about in a sewer or manure heap, and sent your servants to retrieve it; but they were unable to free it and, while trying to rescue it, also soiled themselves in some way; then, afterward, you yourself, laying aside these silken garments that you are wearing, put on a servant’s tunic, descended into the sewer, placed your hands in the filth, and brought out the golden ring and the gem together in your hands, and, rejoicing, invited all your friends to a banquet and celebrated over the ring and the gem because they had been freed from such great filth—”

The prefect said: “To what does this illustration refer?”

Tranquillinus replied: “To show you that we worship one invisible God.”

The prefect said: “And what is the gold? Or what is the gem that was rolling about in the manure heap?”

Tranquillinus replied: “The gold is the human body, while the gem is the soul enclosed within that body. Body and soul make one human being, just as gold and gem are shown to make one ring.

“However precious the ring may be to you, a human being is far more precious—one hundred times more precious—and dear to Christ. You sent your servants to rescue the ring from the filth, but they were utterly unable to retrieve it. God, speaking from heaven, also sent his prophets to them to rescue the human race from the filth of this world [Note: Another reading: ‘to snatch it away’]; but they were altogether unable to accomplish this, despite all their efforts.

“You laid aside your golden garments, put on a servant’s clothing, descended into the sewer [Col. 1041A], and placed your hands in the filth to free the ring from the filth. The majesty of the Godhead likewise stripped itself of the splendor of its divinity, though it did not leave the heavenly realm; it put on the servant’s clothing of our body and, descending here from heaven into the sewer of this world, placed its hands in the filth of our sufferings. Taking upon himself the suffering that was due to our merits, he restored us to the glory of his fingers.

“For we who, through unbelief, were rolling about in the filth of the world have been washed clean of our pollution through faith and restored by divine hands, like your ring.

“Could not your servants, who denied you as their master when they saw you in servant’s clothing, have been killed as rebels? So also those who deny Christ as their Lord because he emptied himself of majesty and assumed the form of a servant will in no way be able to escape the punishments of eternal fire.

“Therefore, for us who believe in him, the water of the eternal font comes to our aid, so that eternal fire may be conquered by the eternal font and unbelief overcome by faithfulness.”

45. The prefect said: “As I see it, you did not ask for an interval in order to remove your sons from this purpose; rather, you prove to have prepared these old wives’ tales and brought them to our tribunal [Note: Another reading: ‘deliberated upon’].”

Tranquillinus said: “The disciples of Christ do not deliberate beforehand about what they will say in the presence of judges. For he warned them in this way, saying: ‘When they hand you over to the authorities of this world on account of my name, do not think about how or what you should say; for it will be given to you divinely in that hour what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of God who speaks in you’ (Matthew 10:19).

“Therefore, I did not discover these things through deliberation but through believing in my Creator. Though I had been contracted and weakened by the pain of gout in my feet and hands [Note: Another reading: ‘shaken’], as soon as I believed in Christ I recovered the health of all my limbs, as though I were a little child.

“It is therefore established in my heart that the one who deigned to renew me is the one who created me; and just as he granted restoration to my body, so also he promised to grant it to my soul after this life—provided that I am not broken by doubt or fear of human beings, but persevere in confessing his name and preserve intact the faith that God enabled me to discover.”

[Col. 1041D]

46. The prefect said: “You do not know, Tranquillinus, how fiercely the anger of the invincible rulers rages against Christians; and therefore, as though secure, you pursue what seems right to you without fear.”

Tranquillinus said: “It is foolish fear by which human indignation is feared more than divine indignation. If we were to come among barking dogs, and in their senseless fury they began to attack us with their bites, could they take from our minds the fact that we are rational human beings, while they are dogs, irrational and mad? In the same way, those who grow angry with us because we believe rightly can indeed rage and inflict unjust punishments [Col. 1042A], but they will never be able to take from our hearts the conviction that we believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be our Creator and rejoice that he is our Redeemer and Restorer.”

Then the prefect ordered him to be taken back by the records officers, saying: “I will hear you at the next session.”

## CHAPTER XIV. The Prefect of the City, Chromatius, Is Catechized

47. After this, he sent for him and ordered that he be brought secretly to him during the night. Offering him an immense weight of gold, he said: “Show me the medicine by which you recovered your health.”

Tranquillinus replied: “Know that those who think God’s grace can either be sold or bought will suffer great anger and wrath from God. Therefore, if you wish to be freed from the pain of gout, believe in Christ, the Son of God [Col. 1042B], and you will be freed; and just as you see me today, so you will be healed.

“I could scarcely be carried in people’s hands, and for eleven years I was bound throughout all the joints of my body by knots of pain; scarcely could bread be brought to my mouth except by the hands of others. Immediately after I believed that Christ was the true God, I received the joys of my healing and became whole, because I acknowledged the true God as my Savior.”

48. Then the prefect dismissed him, saying: “Bring to me the one who made you a Christian, so that, if he promises me health, I too may become a Christian.”

Immediately Tranquillinus went to the presbyter Saint Polycarp and told him everything that had been done and said. He secretly led him into the house and presented him to the prefect.

The prefect said to him: “Although the severe hostility of the rulers is directed against Christians, nevertheless, in the hope of recovering my health, I will offer you whatever it may be, up to half of the property of my inheritance, if the members of my body are released from this knotted condition of condylomas [Note: Greek κόνδυλωμα, properly a swelling or inflammation in the condyles or joints of the fingers [Col. 1042D]. The manuscripts read condologmatum; some have doloris, ‘of pain’].”

Then Saint Polycarp, smiling, said: “The Lord Jesus Christ is powerful enough to open the doors of your ignorance [Note: Another reading: ‘doors’] and show you that he himself is the restorer of your body. For those who bring money, as well as those who accept money when it is offered, not only provide no medicine to the suffering, but also take upon themselves an incurable disease.”

The prefect said to him: “Tell me, then, what must I do so that I may obtain what I hope for?”

Polycarp said to him: “If you believe with all your heart, as Tranquillinus believed [Col. 1042D], you will be saved.”

The prefect said to him: “Explain to me in what manner I ought to believe.”

Then Saint Polycarp catechized him and ordered him to fast for three days. He summoned Saint Sebastian to him, and for three days and three nights he fasted with him. Together they prayed with tears that the Lord might reveal the faith of his name for the salvation of the man who desired to believe.

## CHAPTER XV. The Idols of Chromatius Are Broken

49. When the third day that had been appointed arrived, they came hastening together to the house of the awaiting prefect [Col. 1043A]. Entering, they said: “Peace to your faith.”

He returned their greeting most courteously, invited them to sit beside him, and said: “What proceeded from Tranquillinus’s mouth is confirmed by the evidence of my eyes. I see him completely healthy, though I had seen him contracted by the pain of gout in his feet and hands.

“When I asked him what kind of medicine had saved him, I received this reply from him: ‘While I placed my faith in idols, I was weak and contracted by excessive illness. But when, through the demonstration of Christians, I learned of the one God in heaven, I denied all the things I had worshiped without reason and handed over the faith of my soul to Christ [Note: Another reading: ‘I handed over my soul through faith to Christ’].

“‘As soon as I confessed that the one and true God reigns in heaven, all the health that I had lost over eleven years immediately returned to me, and all illness was at once removed from me.’

“I heard this with my ears, tested it with my eyes, and believed it in my heart. It remains for you to do for me what you did for Tranquillinus, so that I too may recover the health of my body.”

50. The presbyter Polycarp said: “If a human soul does not endure passing pains, what will it do with those pains for which there is never any end and no succession at all? These pains bear the image of those pains; and as far as living fire differs from its picture, so far do the pains that the body suffers now differ from those that the soul will suffer, if, ignorant of its Creator [Note: Another reading: ‘if it despises the gift of its Creator’], it fulfills the duty of this present life.

“Come, then, first consider those pains with us, and be concerned about that punishment which has a fire that always burns and a worm that always devours.”

51. Then Chromatius, prefect of the city of Rome, together with his only son Tiburtius, gave his name, saying: “You should be assured of my faith in this matter, since I also desire that my son become a Christian with me.”

Saint Sebastian said: “Take care that you do not hope to become a Christian merely because you have been led by the recovery of your body; rather, through hope of eternal life, make your mind pure so that it may behold the reason of truth. For unless you acknowledge who your Creator is, you will not be able to find the salvation you seek.”

Chromatius said: “Then do we not see rustic and very simple people becoming Christians, so that among a thousand men you scarcely find one who can attain even a knowledge of eloquence? Were all these people able to reach this inquiry when they became Christians?” [Col. 1043D]

Saint Sebastian said: “This response of yours confirms the assertion of our side [Note: Another reading: ‘affirms’]. For from the beginning of the world God dealt with farmers and shepherds of sheep; and when he came near the end of the world, he did not choose grammarians and orators, but fishermen and simple people, and entrusted to them the knowledge of himself.”

52. Chromatius said: “Why, then, do you say that I must first acknowledge who my Creator is, since, unless I acknowledge him, I cannot find salvation?”

Saint Sebastian said: “Because you have worshiped many gods and many goddesses. Unless, therefore, you drive them from your heart, break their images, and come to know the one and true God, you will not be able to find life and salvation.”

Chromatius said: “Tell me, then, who is the one and true God.”

Saint Sebastian replied: “If you send your servant to draw water, when he comes to the spring he first looks to see whether any dirt is hidden inside the pitcher, and he does not dare put water into the vessel unless he sees that it has been cleansed of dirt. How, then, could we hand over to you the fountain of truth unless you first make yourself free from all the dirt and filth of idols?”

Chromatius said: “And in what manner can I become free from these things?”

Saint Sebastian said: “Give us permission to break all the idols that we find in your house if they are made of stone, burn them if they are made of wood [Col. 1044B], melt down those made of gold, silver, or bronze, and distribute their value among the needy.”

Chromatius said: “And when you have done this, what benefit will come to me?”

Saint Sebastian said: “You will immediately obtain health for all the nerves of your limbs, by the knots of which you are constricted [Note: Another reading: ‘of all your limbs’]. You will begin to run on your feet as though you had never suffered pain, and you will recognize that you loved as gods the enemies of your salvation [Note: Another reading: ‘whom you considered worthy of worship’]. But you will recognize that this one is your parent: the one who, as soon as you have found knowledge and worship of him, restores and saves you.”

53. Chromatius said: “Do not lower yourselves to this insult. I will order my servants, and they will break everything.”

Saint Sebastian said: “If the doubtful, timid, and unbelieving break them, the devil will find an opportunity, through whatever negligence they display, to harm them. As soon as they have been harmed, the unbelievers will say that they were harmed because they broke the idols.

“For no one without a breastplate is protected from the blows of arrows. In battle, a trained hand uses a helmet, shield, and spear, so that from the protection of the weapons and the force of striking it may gain courage and not turn its back. In the same way, the soldiers of God, who are fortified by the shield of faith and protected by the breastplate of Christ’s covering, possessing the helmet of faith and salvation, can safely enter the conflict. They fight most fiercely and conquer bravely, because day and night they wage tireless battle against the invisible enemy; they are covered in all their limbs, armed with faith rather than iron.”

Chromatius said: “Let the will of God and of you be done.” Then the presbyter Saint Polycarp and the blessed Sebastian girded themselves and prayed. After the prayer, they broke more than two hundred images of idols and began to give thanks to their God.

## CHAPTER XVI. Chromatius Is Healed after the Instruments of Judicial Astrology Are Broken

54. After this they approached Chromatius and said to him: “When we broke the idols, you ought to have received health, unless perhaps some sign of unbelief remains in your mind. For we are certain of this: either something remains that has not yet been broken, or, if everything has been broken, make clearer to us what you harbor in your mind.”

Then he said: “I have a room made entirely of glass, in which the whole discipline of the stars and mathematical mechanics has been constructed by a mechanical art [Note: Another reading: ‘appears to stand constructed’]. In its construction my father Tarquinius is known to have spent more than two hundred pounds of gold [Note: Manuscript Rip.: ‘talents’].”

Saint Sebastian said to him: “If you wish to keep this intact, you are breaking yourself.”

Chromatius said: “Why? Are mathematics or an ephemeris worshiped for some sacrificial use, when the courses of the months and years are divided at fixed intervals into a definite number of hours, and the fullness or diminution of the lunar sphere is foreseen by the movement of the fingers, the mastery of reason, and calculation?” [Note: Greek ἐφημερίς properly means a diary, or a record of events and actions arranged by days.]

The presbyter Saint Polycarp said: “There are the signs of Leo, Capricorn, Sagittarius, Scorpio, and Taurus; there are the moon in Aries, the hour in Cancer, a star in Jupiter, a tropical sign in Mercury, Mars in Venus; and in all these monstrous demons an art hostile to God is recognized.

“Christians reject these things so completely that they not only do not possess, worship, believe in, or retain them themselves, but do not even possess those dispositions that allow such trifles to occupy their hearts. For all these things are false and serve deception: they contain a likeness of truth, not truth itself.”

55. Chromatius said to him: “What of the fact that they sometimes foretell the future?”

Saint Sebastian said: “We have learned, through Christ’s revelation, that all these things are exceedingly vain and false. We will now make this clearer to you.

“Order a teacher of mathematics to come to you today. Tell him that at a certain time you were suffering under harsh misfortunes, and ask through which stars this evil happened to you. Without doubt his answers will be such as these: ‘Your time was received by malignant Mars’; or ‘Saturn was apocatasticus’ [Note: Thus most manuscripts. The time when the sun—or another planet—returns to the same part of the zodiac by the same numbers through which it began its course is called by students of heavenly matters ἀποκατάστασις, ‘restoration.’ Columella. Thus the revolution of the planet Saturn to its first position may be intended, or a disturbance of affairs and a κατάστασις, ‘configuration,’ stirred up by its malign star. But manuscript Rip. has apocasticus; Brechtus has apostaticus, that is, retrograde; or rather, contrary, malefic.]; or ‘your year was received in opposition’; or ‘your climacteric years were born at the center’ [Note: Κλιμακτῆρες are called ‘critical’ or ‘climacteric’ years, from κλῖμαξ, meaning ‘step.’ Pliny himself ridicules these exceedingly vain observations in Book VII, chapter 49: ‘Again, there is the school of Asclepiades, which says that fixed periods of life are received from the stars, though it is uncertain how much it assigns to them. They say that longer periods are rare, since at marked moments of hours an immense multitude is born—on the seventh and ninth days of the moon, which are observed by night and day—and by the law of the climacteric years they die, which they call climacteric years; hardly do those so born exceed the age of fifty-four. The inconsistency of the art itself therefore first reveals how uncertain the matter is.’ He then adds examples from the most recent census, which the emperors Vespasian, father and son, conducted as censors within four years. After inserting several examples, he continues: ‘Another inconsistency of mortality: Homer records that Hector and Polydamas were born on the same night, men of very different destinies. In the consulship of Gaius Marius and Gnaeus Carbo for the third time, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, Marcus Caecilius Rufus and Gaius Licinius Calvus were born on the same day—both orators, but with such different outcomes. This also happens daily throughout the world to those born in the same hours: masters and slaves, kings and destitute people, are born alike.’]; or ‘you were bound together with the evil’; or ‘the invisible [influence]’; or ‘the configuration’; or ‘the course in the stars was stationary around you.’

“When he has said these and similar things, he attempts to assign and prove something that appears reasonable. Now question another mathematician, telling him that those very hours and that very time were abundant for you in favorable circumstances. At once you will see him bring forward countless rational configurations by which he can prove that good things ought to have happened to you at those times.

“For he holds a circle gathered together from every side, in which he receives diverse and varied causes and from which he obtains an opportunity to say whatever he wishes.”

56. Since they cannot foresee the future at all, they call things “climacteric”—that is, uncertain refuges of nature. People born at different times have perished in the same shipwreck; born at one hour of the day or night, one is brought down to beggary while another rises to kingship. In one battle an innumerable multitude is struck down; and on one day, indeed at one moment [Note: Another reading: ‘at an atom of a point’], in one house, two women are born—one most chaste, the other becoming unchaste. If the stars have assigned the merit of each, neither is the prostitute to be blamed nor the chaste woman to be praised.

“Certainly, legislators and rulers punish those who violate their sacred laws; and for this reason there is a forum, a judge, and laws: so that the just may rightly be praised and the unjust deservedly punished.

“And I do not want you to regard as pointless the fact that you observe yourself not yet saved. For if you were to cast away completely from yourself the ceremonies of the enemy of the human race, you would learn within yourself what is true.”

57. Hearing this, Chromatius said: “He is the true God, who is proved to have such worshipers as you. For all your speech flows with such reasoning that it inclines even the minds of beasts toward true reason.

“Therefore, let this very thing that I seemed to have acquired for the ornament of my house [Col. 1046C] be destroyed, lest its preservation hinder my salvation. For I believe—and this is my faith—that if I completely separate from myself all the things that the law of Christianity abhors and prohibits, I shall deserve to obtain both present and future salvation.”

58. Hearing this, his son Tiburtius said: “I will not permit this precious, excellent, and incomparable work to be destroyed for any reason. But, lest I seem to oppose my father’s salvation, let two furnaces be brought and kindled before the entrance of the room. If, after it has been destroyed by them, my father does not recover his health, let both of them be thrown into separate burning furnaces.”

When his father heard this, he forbade it to be done. But the saints not only did not fear the promised death; they also steadfastly urged that the furnaces be prepared.

59. Then they approached all the crystal and entirely glass idols and the whole mechanical work. Suddenly, while the saints’ hands were breaking them, a young man appeared before Chromatius’s eyes, his face radiating with a fiery brightness, and said to him: “My Lord Jesus Christ, in whom you have believed, sent me so that you may recover the health of all your limbs.”

At this voice, Chromatius, restored to complete health, began to run after the young man so that he might kiss his feet. But the young man said to him: “Take care not to touch me, because the sanctification of baptism has not yet washed you clean from the filth of idols.”

When his son Tiburtius saw this, he threw himself at the feet of Saint Polycarp. Chromatius himself, the prefect, clasped the feet of Saint Sebastian, and both cried out with one voice: “Christ is the true God, the true and almighty only-begotten Son of God, whom you, his good ministers, proclaim.”

## CHAPTER XVII. The Baptism of Chromatius and Tiburtius

60. Then the blessed Sebastian said to Chromatius:

“As you yourself know, I hold the command of the first cohort; but long ago I resolved not to know, nor did I wish to know, whether it was the military service of a human being [Note: Manuscript Rebdorf: ‘wickedness’]. For this one purpose I wished to remain hidden beneath the military cloak: to instruct wavering minds and make doubters steadfast, lest those whom faith had made warriors yield to the pains of suffering.

“But you, bearing the summit of the highest power, cannot remove yourself from the spectacles or absent yourself from the business of judging. Therefore, pretending to be ill, ask for a successor for yourself, so that, free from the occupations of the world, you may receive the rudiments of the future life and, born again through a second birth, become offspring of eternal parents.”

On that same day, therefore, he sent to his friends who were stationed in the palace. Receiving from them letters of recommendation, he undertook the apprenticeship of divine service before he was baptized.

61. How shall I recall how full of faith he was, and how keen in intellect when he stood against the claims of unbelievers? The continuation makes this clear. For at the beginning, when he was washed in the water of the most sacred font, his faith of mind shone forth unmistakably. Asked whether he believed, he said: “I believe.” Asked again whether he renounced all idols, he replied: “I renounce them.” The priest continued his questioning, asking whether he renounced all sins. But he said: “You ought first to have asked this [Col. 1048A] before I entered these halls [Note: [Col. 1047D] Others: ‘of the kingdom.’] of the King of heaven. But now I shall dress myself again, unbaptized, so that I may first forgive everyone against whom I am angry; restore the written acknowledgements of debt to all my debtors; and, if I have violently taken anything from anyone, order it to be returned intact. I have two concubines after my wife’s death; I shall give them dowries and hand them over to husbands; I shall release myself from every bond arising from my actions, whether servile, freeborn, private, or public. Only then will I promise to renounce all demonic sins and the pleasures of the world.”

The presbyter Polycarp said to him: “The heavenly water will wash you more blessedly when you have hastened to complete in full the things you say you will do by your own choice. For this reason, too, the period of forty days is imposed upon those who are to be baptized, so that during [Note: [Col. 1047D] Others: ‘throughout all the days.’] those days they may themselves learn that they must renounce all the arts of the enemy and the commerce of the world, if they truly wish to become Christians.” [Col. 1048B]

62. Then the most wise young Tiburtius said: “Father, if you ask for time in order to renounce your affairs, I, who was still about to undertake the business of the forum, renounce merely the will to undertake it; and I, who was to become an advocate for conducting the lawsuits of mortals, shall embrace Christianity in order to conduct angelic actions, once I have begun to be one of the number of those who receive eternal life and become advocates of holiness.”

Then Blessed Sebastian embraced him. When Saint Polycarp had baptized him, Sebastian himself became the father of his new undertaking.

63. Therefore, when only a very few days had passed, and Chromatius had duly renounced all the affairs of the world [Col. 1048C], Chromatius received the newness of sacred baptism. With him, from his household, were one thousand four hundred persons of both sexes. First he freed them all from the bond of slavery for the sake of manumission, and furnished them with excellent gifts, saying: “Those who are beginning to have God as their father ought not to be slaves of a human being.”

CHAPTER XVIII. Chromatius, having resigned the prefecture of the City, nourishes Christians during the persecution.

64. At that time the pope of the city of Rome was a man named Caius, of great prudence and great virtue, while Carinus, Diocletian, and Maximian were emperors. [Note: [Col. 1047D] Saint Caius the pope is commemorated on 22 April. He sat from the consulship of Carus II and Carinus, in the chronological year 283, until the consulship of Diocletian VI and Constantius II, in the chronological year 296.] Diocletian, however, was in the City with Maximian; Carinus was stationed with his entire army in the regions of Gaul. Because of Carinus, Diocletian’s persecution of the Christians began to be sluggish, since [Note: [Col. 1048D] Perhaps Vopiscus had this in mind when he wrote of him, “out of hatred for our religion”: “He banished all the best of his friends; he chose or retained the worst,” and below: “He showed the greatest deference to wicked men.” Christians of such character were also regarded as having been in his retinue, although Orosius likewise testifies that Carinus otherwise lived disgracefully. But jealousy was increased by the fact that he had Christians in his entourage, even blood relatives, as is clear from the Life of Saint Julian, 9 January, chapter 18, no. 35.] Carinus had certain friends whom their profession of this title adorned.

65. Therefore, after Carinus had been killed at [Note: [Col. 1048D] Most manuscripts read this way; some have “at Maguntiaca,” one “at Moguntiaco”; Mombricius has “at Montiacum”; Brechtus, “at the Margus”: correctly. Thus Vopiscus: “For he fought against Diocletian in many battles. But he fell in the final battle, fought near the Margus.” Other copies have “at Martium.” Eutropius, Book IX: “Afterward Diocletian defeated Carinus, who was living in universal hatred and detestation, in a great battle at the Margus, betrayed by his own army, which he had considered the stronger—or certainly abandoned—between Viminacium and Mount Aureus.” Aurelius Victor, On the Caesars: “But when Carinus reached Moesia, he immediately engaged Diocletian near the Margus; while eagerly pressing the defeated enemy, he was killed by a blow from one of his own men.” The Margus was a city of Moesia, and also a river, as can be seen on the itinerarium.] Maguntiacum [Col. 1049A], during the consulship of Maximian and Aquilinus [Note: [Col. 1049D] Almost all manuscripts read this. Perhaps one should read “Maximus and Aquilinus,” unless Maximian Herculeus was substituted for him; he is said to have held his second consulship in the following year, A.D. 287. Thus, since Carinus had been killed in the preceding year, during their consulship, a violent persecution arose in the West.], a persecution arose of such a kind that no one could buy or sell anything unless he had offered incense to little statues [Note: [Col. 1049D] Saint Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks, Book I, chapter 5, reads similarly: “This one [Chus] first, at the devil’s instigation, set up a little statue to be worshiped.” Others read statunculum, and staticulum, as here; staticulus is also a term used by Tertullian. Brechtus has statiunculis, that is, “small statues of idols.”] placed at the spot where people had come to make their purchases.

Around the apartment blocks, around the streets, and around the nymphaea as well [Note: [Col. 1050C] In cities, insulae are houses enclosed on every side by streets and separated from other houses, just as sea islands are surrounded on every side by waters. Suetonius, Nero, chapter 16: “and that porticoes should stand in front of the apartment blocks and houses, from whose terraces fires might be kept away”; and Julius, chapter 41: “He conducted the census of the people neither in the customary manner nor in the customary place, but by streets, through the owners of the apartment blocks.” In the ancient description of the City, under each district the number of apartment blocks is given.], there were also enforcers who would neither allow anyone to buy nor permit anyone to draw water unless he had made an offering to the idols. [Note: [Col. 1050D] Others: “nymphs.” In the same description of the City, besides baths and lakes, several nymphaea are also listed.]

66. Then, after taking counsel with Saint Bishop Caius, Chromatius, an illustrious man, received all the Christians into his house and cared for them all in such a way that no one at all succumbed to the necessity of sacrificing. But because the force of the persecution had become so great that the very fact of his Christianity could not be concealed, Chromatius obtained, by an imperial rescript, permission to reside for the sake of healing on the Campanian coast [Col. 1049B], where he was master of a broad tract of land [Note: [Col. 1050D] Others have: “where a stream flows beneath, in which there was a fishpond,” an ineptly corrupted reading]. He also granted permission to every Christian who wished to go with him in order to avoid the persecutor’s rage.

Then a dispute arose between Saint Polycarp and Blessed Sebastian: which of the two should remain in the City, and which should go with Chromatius, who had received so large a Christian population. While they were arguing, the venerable Pope Caius said: “While both of you seek the crown of suffering, you are abandoning the people acquired for the Lord. Therefore it seems to me that you, Brother Polycarp, because you hold to the straight path of the priesthood and are filled with the knowledge of God, should go with him, both to strengthen the minds of the believers and to build up those whose spirits are wavering [Note: [Col. 1050D] Manuscript Rip.: “restore”; others: “confirm.”].”

When he heard this, Polycarp fell silent and accepted the pope’s gentle command with equanimity.

The Lord’s Day came, on which Bishop Caius, carrying out the things of God within Chromatius’s house, addressed them all in these words: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, knowing human frailty, established two degrees for those who believe in him—confession, that is, and martyrdom—so that those who despair of being able to bear the weight of martyrdom may hold fast to the grace of confession and, giving [Note: [Col. 1050D] Others: “providing a place.”] their side to the combatants, may care for Christ’s soldiers who are going to fight for his name. Let those who wish go with our sons Chromatius and Tiburtius; those who wish may remain with me in this city. For no distances of earth will divide us whom the charity of Christ binds together; nor do our eyes feel your absence, because we behold you with the sight of the inner person.” [Col. 1050A]

67. While Pope Caius was saying these and similar things, Tiburtius, a most illustrious man, cried out: “I beg you, father and bishop of bishops, do not allow me to turn my back on the persecutors. For it would be exceedingly joyful and desirable for me if I could be killed a thousand times for the true God, provided only that I might attain the dignity of that life which no successor could take away from me and to which no age could impose an end.”

Then Saint Caius, rejoicing with him in his faith, shed tears and prayed that all who remained might emerge victorious from the contest and receive the triumph of martyrdom.

CHAPTER XIX. The distinguished deeds of Saints Sebastian, Tiburtius, and others in the City.

[Col. 1050B]

68. Those who remained with the venerable Pope Caius were Marcellianus and Marcus, together with their father, the most illustrious man Tranquillinus; also Blessed Sebastian; and the very handsome young man, yet more beautiful in mind, Saint Tiburtius; and Nicostratus, from the first bureau, with his brother Castorius and his wife, named Zoe; likewise Claudius with his brother Victorinus and his son Symphorianus [Note: [Col. 1050D] He seems above to have been called Felicissimus. But all the manuscripts except Ripatorius have Symphorianus here; others call him Symphronianus or Sympronianus. He is entered in the martyrologies on 7 July, while Felicissimus and Felix are entered on the second of that month], who had been freed from dropsy.

These alone, while everyone else departed with Chromatius, remained with Bishop Caius. He consecrated Marcus and Marcellianus with the honor of the diaconate, and made their father Tranquillinus a presbyter. Saint Sebastian, who concealed himself under the guise of military service for the advancement of many, he appointed defender of the Church; the others he made subdeacons.

69. But because no safe place could be found for a hiding place [Note: [Col. 1050D] Manuscript Rip.: “to be guarded.”], they all stayed with a certain Christian, Castulus, the palace zetarius [Note: [Col. 1050D] What zetae or zoetae were, and over whom the zetarius presided, was explained above at chapter 3]. Castulus lived there in the palace, in a high and very lofty place. This lodging was considered suitable because Castulus himself and all his household were most Christian; and although the law concerning sacrifices was raging everywhere in its fury, it was concealed among those attached to the palace, since no suspicion could fall upon them.

Thus, as we have said, all these men stayed with holy Pope Caius at the home of Castulus the zetarius, in the highest parts of the palace. Day and night they were occupied with groans and tears, fasts and prayers, entreating the Lord that they might be considered worthy, through endurance of confession, to be joined to the number of the holy martyrs.

70. Religious men and women secretly went up to them and obtained various graces of healing from the Saints. For once they had been strengthened by firmness in the true faith and had established the foundation of their virtues, the grace of healing followed them. Through their prayers the eyes of the blind were illuminated, the sick were healed, and demons were driven from possessed bodies. [Col. 1051B]

71. Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, Blessed Tiburtius came upon a man who had fallen from a height and shattered his head and all his limbs, so that those who recognized him as their son were concerned only with his burial. Then he said to them as they wept: “Allow me to pray over him [Note: [Col. 1051D] Others: “to enchant him”; others: “to sing over him.”]; perhaps he will recover his health.”

When everyone had given him room, he approached the man and, slowly reciting the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed over his wounds, so restored his bones, head, and all his internal organs that, as though nothing had happened to him, he became completely well.

[Col. 1051C]

72. After he had done this, he began to leave. But the man’s parents held him back, saying: “Come, take him and have him as your slave, and we shall give you all our possessions with him, because you have restored alive to us the only son we had, whom we already regarded as dead.”

He said to them: “If you do what I shall tell you, I shall value highly the reward for this healing.”

His parents said to him: “If you should deem it worthy to have us ourselves as slaves, we cannot oppose you; indeed, we desire it, if you judge it fitting.”

Then he took their hands, separated them from the crowds, and made known to them the power of Christ’s name. When he saw that their minds were firmly fixed in the fear of the Lord, he led them to Pope Caius and said: “Venerable pope and minister of divine law, behold those whom Christ has won today through me. In them my faith, like a young tree [Col. 1051D], has first burst forth into fruit.”

Then Saint Bishop Caius baptized them—the young man together with his parents—and they gave thanks to God.

CHAPTER XX. The martyrdoms of Saints Zoe, Tranquillinus, and others.

73. But since it would be too much if we wished to recount all that Christ did through them, and how much he did, let us explain only how each one came to the palm of martyrdom. Most blessed Zoe, on the feast of the Apostles, while praying at the Confession of the Apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 1051D] The Confession is the part of a church where the bodies of the saints rest, usually beneath the high altar.], was seized by pagans lying in wait. She was taken to the patron of the district of the Naumachia [Note: [Col. 1051D] There were several Naumachiae in the City: one in Diocletian’s ninth district, others in the thirteenth, and two in the fourteenth, across the Tiber. Baronius, in the year 286, no. 13, considers this to have taken place across the Tiber, and that new offices were then assigned in specific places to specific men for the purpose of seeking out Christians; thus several patron-prefects were assigned to one district of the City, each seeking Christians in the portion entrusted to him.], and was forced to burn drops of incense before the little statue of Mars [Note: [Col. 1052D] Others: “the little idol,” as above].

Then she replied: “You force a woman to sacrifice to Mars in order to show that your Mars delights in women. But although he was able to rob the most shameless Venus of her modesty, he will not prevail against me, who bear the trophy of faith upon my forehead. For I am not struggling against him by my own strength; trusting in the power of my Lord Jesus Christ, I despise and ridicule both you and him alike.”

Then the patron of the district sent her into a very dark prison and for five days [Col. 1052B] made her see neither light nor receive food or drink. The only voice heard was that of the man who had confined her there, saying: “There you will die of hunger, thirst, and blindness unless you promise to make an offering to the gods.”

74. But when six days had passed, information about her was given to the savage prefect, who ordered her to be hung by the neck and hair from a tall tree and smoke from a dung heap to be applied beneath her. As soon as she had been hung, she gave up her spirit in confession of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1052D] She is commemorated on 5 July.]

They removed her body, tied it to a stone, and immersed it in the bed of the Tiber, saying: “So that the Christians may not take her body and make her a goddess for themselves.”

75. After her martyrdom had been celebrated, she appeared in a dream to Blessed Sebastian and told him how she had received the martyrdom of the Lord. When Saint Sebastian had recounted this, Saint Tranquillinus rushed forth, saying: “Women are going ahead to the crown—why are we living?”

He too went down on the eighth day after the feast of the Apostles and approached the Confession of Blessed Paul. He likewise suffered an ambush, was seized, and was stoned to death by the people [Note: [Col. 1052D] 6 July]. His body was committed to the waters of the Tiber.

76. Likewise Nicostratus and Claudius, together with Castorius, Victorinus, and Symphorianus, while searching along the banks of the Tiber for the bodies of the Saints, were seized by the persecutors and brought before the prefect of the City. The judge was Fabianus, who urged them to sacrifice. For ten days he tried to move them by threats and blandishments, but could not move them in the slightest.

Then he reported them to the emperors, who ordered them to be tortured three times [Col. 1052D]. When they could not be compelled by any means to yield to the tortures, he ordered them to be thrown headlong into the middle of the sea. Bound with immense weights, they were cast into the waves of the sea, and in a clean place among the waters they celebrated the crown of martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1052D] 7 July.]

Thus the unbelievers plotted against the faithful, and, tormented by wicked fury, could not bear even to hear the Christian name.

CHAPTER XXI. The martyrdom of Saint Tiburtius.

[Col. 1053A]

77. Meanwhile, a certain man joined Bishop Saint Caius under pretended faith, saying that he was a Christian. But he was an apostate, fraudulent in all his speech, and crafty in every undertaking.

Why say more? Blessed Tiburtius, a most learned, noble, and holy man, frequently reproved him because he arranged the hair above the crown of his forehead with a barber’s art; because he continually [Note: [Col. 1053D] Manuscript Rip.: “drank.”] indulged himself and ate while playing; because he presented himself too freely to the gaze of women; because he removed himself from fasts and prayers; and because, devoted to sleep, he did not take part [Note: [Col. 1053D] Others: “in vigils.”] in the all-night vigils spent in hymns to God.

Although Blessed Tiburtius rebuked him sharply for these things, as we have said, he pretended to accept the admonition calmly. By his cunning he arranged for the unbelievers to seize Saint Tiburtius while he was praying. He had himself seized in that arrest and brought with him to the secret chamber of the savage judge.

When they had been brought in, Prefect Fabianus said to the man who had betrayed himself by this device: “What is your name?”

He replied: “Torquatus.” [Note: [Col. 1053D] The Metaphrast has Curtuatus; perhaps one should read Turcuatus.]

Fabianus said: “What do you profess?”

Torquatus said: “I am a Christian.”

Fabianus said: “Do you not know that the invincible princes have ordered that those who refuse to sacrifice to the gods be tormented with various punishments?”

Torquatus said: “This man is my teacher, and he himself has always taught me this: whatever I see him do, I must do.”

78. Fabianus turned to Saint Tiburtius and said: “Have you heard what Torquatus claims? What do you answer to this?”

Saint Tiburtius said: “Torquatus has long been pretending that he is a Christian. For the power of the holy name itself bears heavily and painfully that its name should be appropriated by those who do not love its character [Note: [Col. 1053D] Others: “its morals.”].

Indeed, most illustrious man, this word ‘Christian’ is a title of divine virtue: it belongs to the followers of Christ, who truly practiced philosophy, who were truly called Christians, and who fought bravely to crush their lusts.

Do you believe, most illustrious man, that this man is a Christian—this man who, in the pandering of his own [Note: [Col. 1053D] Others: “softening.”] refinement, arranges the fringes of his head [Note: [Col. 1053D] Some omit fibras; others read “loses the hairs.”], who loves a barber, who carries his shoulders delicately, who stretches his flowing gait [Note: [Col. 1053D] Others: “his bent gait.”] in disgraceful affectation, who treats men carelessly but looks more attentively at women? Christ has never deigned to have such men as servants.

But since he has claimed that he will imitate me, you will now prove in his presence that he has lied. Here he will clearly show what he has always been.”

79. Fabianus said: “You will act more wisely if you look to your own safety and do not despise the decrees of the princes.”

Saint Tiburtius said: “I cannot better look to my safety than by despising your gods and goddesses and confessing that the one Lord Jesus Christ is my God.”

Torquatus [Col. 1054A] said: “Not only is this Christian himself wicked, but he also persuades and deceives many and teaches everyone that all the gods are demons. He himself, with his associates, with whom he practices magical arts [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “disasters.”], spends day and night occupied with incantations.”

Saint Tiburtius said: “A false witness will not go unpunished.”

And he said to the judge: “This man whom you see, most illustrious sir, seething with the cares of his wickedness, has joined himself to the Christians for no other reason than to devise how he might present himself to us as though he were a Christian and how he might pretend to others that he was most faithful. [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “I used to rebuke him.”]

Yet I rebuked in him a Cyclopean gluttony [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “the boundless shame of wine”; Brechtus: “the stench of one submerged in wine.”], modesty drowned in wine, and the sanctity of the divine name buried. Drunk, he suffered thirst, and vomited hunger. Not as a Christian but as some Antonian banqueter, he ate, drank, and vomited; and now he accuses Christians, denounces Christians, incites a gentle judge against us, hands a sword to a judge unwilling to use it, and urges us to bow our necks to demons.

We see your desire; we see your bloody counsels; and by your criminal art of speech we perceive the poisons of your heart. Gird yourself now, most cruel man [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “most Christian.”]; perform the office of executioner; claim for yourself even the judge’s voice; apply the goads; hang Christians; condemn, strike, burn; employ every torture. You have received us well.

If you threaten exile, the whole world belongs to those who practice philosophy. If punishment, we escape the prison of the world. If fires, in our desires we overcome things greater than these. Decree whatever you please; every punishment is cheap to us when a pure conscience accompanies us.”

[Col. 1054C]

80. Prefect Fabianus said: “Return to your family and be what nature has dictated to you. Born noble, you have fallen into such filth that you wish to undergo punishment, disgrace, and death all at once [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “that you may be able to…”].”

Saint Tiburtius said: “O wisest of men, and judge appointed over the Romans! Because I do not wish to worship the harlot Venus, the incestuous Jupiter, deceitful Mercury, and Saturn, the murderer of his children, I incur the disgrace of nobility [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “the disgrace of low birth.”]. And because I adore and venerate the one true God who reigns in heaven, you threaten that I must be tormented with punishments.

We do not assent to your persuasion; we do not deny that Christ, the Son of God, descended from heaven to earth for this purpose: so that a human being might be able to ascend from earth to heaven. Therefore, trampling under my feet all these empty images that you worship without cause [Col. 1054D], I have subjected myself to God almighty.” [Note: [Col. 1054D] Others: “We do not refuse, resist, or deny.”]

81. Then Fabianus ordered burning coals to be poured before his feet and said to him: “Choose one of two things for yourself: either throw incense upon these coals, or walk over them with your bare feet.”

Then Blessed Tiburtius made the sign of the cross and firmly walked over them with his bare sole. He began to say to the prefect: “Lay aside unbelief and learn that this alone is God, whom we confess to rule over all creatures. You, if you can, put your hands in hot water in the name of your god Jupiter; and if your Jupiter is able, let him make you feel no heat from the burning.

For me, in the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, it seems that I am walking over rose-covered flowers, because creation serves the command of its Creator.”

82. Fabianus said: “Who does not know that your Christ taught you magic?”

Saint Tiburtius said: “Be silent, wretched man, and do not inflict this insult upon my ears, so that I must hear you, barking with a rabid mouth, pronounce his holy, honey-sweet name.”

Then Fabianus, angered, dictated the sentence, saying: “As a blasphemer of the gods and guilty of atrocious insults, he shall be punished with the sword.”
