He was led out along the Lavican Way, three miles from the City, and, pouring out a prayer to the Lord [Col. 1055B], he departed after being struck by a single blow of the sword. [Note: [Col. 1055D] Saint Tiburtius is commemorated on 11 August, on which day the memory of Saint Chromatius, his father, is also observed.]

He was buried in the same place by a certain Christian parent. In that place Christ has always bestowed many benefits, to the praise of his name, even to the present day.

CHAPTER XXII. The martyrdoms of Saints Castulus, Marcellianus, and Marcus.

83. After this, Torquatus arranged for Castulus, the palace zetarius and the host of the Saints, to be arrested. When he had been bound, hung up a third time, and questioned a third time, he persevered in confession of the Lord. He was thrown into a pit, and a mass of sand was poured over him. With the palm of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 1055D] 26 March.] he departed to the Lord.

84. After this Marcellianus and Marcus were seized. Both were bound to a stake and had sharp nails driven through their feet [Col. 1055C]. To them the utterly deranged Fabianus said: “You shall stand with your soles fixed there until you render to the gods the service owed to them.”

Then the two brothers, fastened to one piece of wood, sang a psalm, saying: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity.”

Fabianus said to them: “Unhappy and wretched men, abandon your madness and free yourselves from the torments hanging over you.”

Both replied: “We have never feasted so well; only now have we begun to be fixed in the love of Christ. Would that you allow us to remain as we are for as long as we are clothed in this garment of the body.”

When one day and one night had passed and they continued in psalms and hymns, he ordered both of them, where they stood, to be pierced through the sides with spears. Thus, through the glory of martyrdom [Col. 1055D], they departed to the starry realms. [Note: [Col. 1055D] 18 June.]

They too were buried on the Appian Way, two miles from the City, in the place called Ad Arenas, “At the Sands,” because there were sand quarries there from which the walls of the City were built [Note: [Col. 1055D] Others: “constructed.”].

CHAPTER XXIII. The glorious contest of Saint Sebastian.

[Col. 1056A]

85. After these events, Blessed Sebastian was confronted by those lying in wait. Because, as we have said, he seemed to hide beneath a military cloak, although he was a most worthy soldier of Christ, the prefect reported him to the emperor Diocletian.

Diocletian summoned him and said: “I have always counted you among the foremost of my palace. Yet, to the detriment of my safety and as an insult to the gods, you have hidden until now.”

Saint Sebastian said: “For your safety I have always worshiped Christ, and for the stability of the Roman world I have always adored him who is in heaven, considering that it is the mark of a mad and foolish mind to seek help from stones.”

Then Diocletian, angered, ordered him to be led into the middle of the field and tied up like a target for arrows; and he ordered the archers [Col. 1056B] to shoot him [Note: [Col. 1055D] Others: “to seize him”; others: “to sew him”; others: “to throw them at him.”]. The soldiers placed him in the middle of the field and filled him with arrows from every side, so that he was bristling with the blows of arrows like a hedgehog [Note: [Col. 1055D] Others: “stitched together”; others: “inserted.”].

86. Believing him to be dead, they went away. Then Irene, the wife of Castulus the martyr and zetarius, whose name was [Note: [Col. 1055D] Most manuscripts have Hirene; Rabanus, Herene; others, Herena or Aerena.], went out at night to take away his body and bury it.

Finding him alive, she brought him to her house, to the lofty staircase where she lived near the palace [Note: [Col. 1055D] Others: “to the lofty apartment block.”]. There, within a few days, he recovered perfect health in all his limbs.

87. When all the Christians came to him, they urged him to withdraw. But after praying, he went down and, standing upon the steps [Note: [Col. 1055D] The location of these steps of Heliogabalus, or Elagabalus, may be inferred from Lampridius, who writes in his Life of Antoninus Heliogabalus: “He consecrated Heliogabalus on the Palatine Hill, beside the imperial residence, and built a temple for him …, intending that no god except Heliogabalus should be worshiped at Rome.” That Antoninus had been the priest of this god.], said, as the emperors approached:

“By unjust insinuations the priests of the temples besiege the minds of your imperial power, suggesting false accusations against the Christians and saying that they are enemies of the Republic. Yet through their prayers the Republic itself is improved and grows; they do not cease praying for your empire and for the safety of the Roman army.”

As he said these and similar things, Diocletian said: “Are you Sebastian, whom we ordered to be killed by arrows not long ago?”

Saint Sebastian said: “For this purpose my Lord Jesus Christ deigned to raise me again: so that I might confront you and bear witness against you before all the people, because your persecution has boiled over in an unjust judgment against the servants of Christ.”

88. Then he ordered him to be led into the hippodrome of the palace [Note: [Col. 1056D] Some manuscripts have epidromium; others hypodromium; others correctly, hippodromium.] and beaten with clubs until he breathed out his spirit [Note: [Col. 1056D] Rabanus and others: “until he was exhausted”; others: “beaten with clubs.”].

Then they took his body by night and threw it into the Cloaca Maxima, saying: “Lest the Christians make him their martyr.” [Note: [Col. 1056D] On the astonishing sewers of the City, see Baronius in his notes on the Martyrology, 26 August; Andrea Fulvio, Antiquities of Rome, Book III, chapter 30; and Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 15.]

Then Blessed Sebastian appeared in a dream to a certain most religious matron, Saint Lucina, saying: “In that sewer which is beside the circus you will find my body hanging on a [Note: [Col. 1056D] Brechtus and most manuscripts have “on a hook.” Baronius believes that this hook, in relation to the sewer, was drawn through the martyr’s body, as is shown to have been customary by several testimonies of the ancients. Lampridius, in his Life of Commodus: “Let the executioner be dragged by a hook; let the executioner be dragged by a hook, according to the custom of the senate and of our ancestors.” And in his Life of Heliogabalus: “He was dragged most filthily through the streets, led through the sewers, and thrown into the Tiber.” But when the hook had been driven into the body, what was it from which the body hung? Perhaps a compound hook, as is used to pull out objects that have fallen into deep wells; or perhaps one tooth of it had been fixed in the wall. Some manuscripts seem to indicate a more reliable reading, in which gumpho and gonpho are written. It should be read in gompho. Gomphos (γόμφος) means “nail” or “joint.” Thus Statius, Silvae IV, concerning the Via Domitiana:

“Then, with bosses pressed together on either side,

and with frequent joints binding the road.”

That is, the stones were joined so that they would not twist or be torn apart from one another. Tertullian, Apology: “We offer our necks to lead, solder, and joints.” Franciscus Zephyrus the Paraphrast renders it “larger nails.” The same word occurs below in the martyrdom of Saint Thyrsus. Here, then, one should understand a nail projecting somewhere from the wall, or another iron instrument used for fastening stones.] joint. [Col. 1057A] When you have lifted it, carry it to the catacombs [Note: [Col. 1058B] On the catacombs, or catatombs, see Baronius in his notes on the Martyrology, 3 January and 20 January.] and bury it at the beginning of the crypt, near the memorials of the Apostles.”

89. Then Blessed Lucina herself, with her servants, went out in the middle of the night. She lifted him, placed him in her carriage [Note: [Col. 1058B] Others: “tent”; others: “wagon”; the Syriac has “cart”; thus the Monk argues that this should be read. We discussed the pavone, or pabone, on 16 January, in the Life of Saint Marcellus, chapter 5.], and brought him to the place he had indicated. There she buried him with every care. Saint Lucina herself did not leave that holy place for thirty days.

[Col. 1058A]

90. After some years, peace was restored to the Church. As soon as the Church received the glory of peace, she made her house into a church [Note: [Col. 1058B] This matter is discussed in the same Life of Saint Marcellus.]. Leaving all her possessions for the repose of Christians, she made the Church itself her heir in Christ, who, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns equally in the unity of power forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1057]

BOOK ON THE CONFLICT BETWEEN VICES AND VIRTUES, TO SIMPLICIANUS. (G,S)*

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 1057C]

The apostolic voice proclaims throughout the world, dearest brother, and says to those standing in the battle line of faith, lest they grow sluggish through security: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution.” But since at this time Christianity has become religious even in its own rulers, and since for the faithful who live devoutly in Christ Jesus there are now lacking bonds, beatings, scourges, prisons, racks, crosses, and whatever other diverse kinds of torture there may be, how will what sounded forth through the Apostle be true—someone may say—that all who live devoutly suffer persecution? Or perhaps, in a time of peace, no one wishes to live devoutly in Christ Jesus, and that is why these things are absent? Who would say this, even as a deceiver?

Therefore, in this statement of the Apostle, not the particular persecution of certain individuals but the universal persecution of all must be understood. And since there are many within the bosom of Mother Church who, while living devoutly in Christ, are subjected to insults and assailed by bitter reproaches, injuries, and mockery, is this, someone may say, that universal persecution which the Apostle described as being suffered by all who live devoutly in Christ? Yet I would not readily call it that, since there are certain people in the Church so devoted that none of the wicked would dare disparage them to their faces.

Another persecution, therefore, more savage and more harmful, must be understood from the Apostle’s words. It is not inflicted by mortal severity, but produced by the hostility of vices. For while pride rises against humility; empty glory against fear of the Lord; pretense against true religion; arrogance against submission; envy against brotherly affection; hatred against charity; slander against the freedom of just correction; anger against patience; harshness against gentleness; swelling conceit against humble love; worldly sorrow against spiritual joy; torpor or laziness against the practice of virtue; restless wandering against firm stability; despair against confidence in hope; greed against contempt for the world; self-love against love of God; theft and fraud against simplicity; deceit and falsehood against truth; gluttony of the belly against pure frugality and moderation; foolish merriment against measured sorrow; loquacity against prudent silence; bodily impurity and lust against untainted chastity; spiritual fornication against purity of heart; and the appetite for this age against love of the heavenly homeland—when these vices strive to oppose the virtues, what else do they suggest to us than that a cruel persecution rages against the gathered ranks of the virtues of those living devoutly?

O how harsh, how bitter, is the struggle with pride, which cast the angels from heaven and expelled man from paradise (Gen. III), whose army and weapons are the vices that we have briefly touched upon. But let us see how the camps of heaven and hell engage in battle, and how the weapons of Christ and the devil contend.

## CHAPTER II

First, pride says:

Certainly you are better than many—indeed, almost everyone—in speech, knowledge, honors, and riches; and all bodily and spiritual gifts are available to you. Therefore despise everyone and show yourself superior to all.

Humility, on the other hand, replies:

Remember that you are earth (Gen. III), that you are corruption and a worm (Job XXV), and that even if you are something, unless you humble yourself as much as you are great, you utterly lose what you are (Ecclus. III). Are you higher than the first angel (Ezek. XXVIII)? Are you more splendid on earth than Lucifer in heaven (Isa. XIV)? If he fell through pride from such great sublimity, how will you, by pride, climb from the depths to heavenly exaltation? As long as you live here, you are held under the condition of which it is said through the Wise Man: “For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks on many things” (Wis. IX).

How densely, do we suppose, is our clay enveloped on earth in the darkness of pride (Isa. LXIV), if in heaven the star that rose at dawn could lose the spheres of its light (Isa. XIV)? Listen, then, rather to the light of truth saying: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII). Elsewhere he forewarned in what way he should himself be followed, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

Hear, swelling pride; hear still the teacher of humility saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV); and again: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

Hear also what the Apostle says concerning that light of truth, inviting you to follow it. He says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped; rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and appearing in human form. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). If, therefore, the divine majesty lowers itself with such great humility, human weakness ought not to be proud of anything.

## CHAPTER III

Empty glory says:

Come, do whatever good you can; show everyone the good you do, so that everyone may call you good, so that all may proclaim you holy and venerable, so that you may be known as one chosen by God; so that no one may despise or scorn you, but that everyone may pay you the honor due to you.

Fear of the Lord replies:

If you do anything good, do it not for transient honors but for eternal ones. Conceal what you do as far as you can. If you cannot conceal it completely, let there nevertheless be in your heart the will to conceal it; then no guilt of ostentation will be imputed to you. For it cannot be a crime that something is eventually revealed which you always wish to have kept hidden.

Thus you will seem to have fulfilled two sayings of the Redeemer that appear almost contradictory: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing; rather, let your almsgiving be in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI); and: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Take great care lest that saying about hypocrites apply to you: “They do all their works so that they may be praised by men. Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. XXIII)—that is, merely the praises of men, which they loved.

Therefore watch yourself in everything you do, lest, struck by the exaltation of vainglory, you hear, along with those who also gloried in signs of miracles: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X).

But fear, for it is written: “The fear of the Lord is glory, and boasting, joy and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart, and will give gladness, joy, and length of days. It will be well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed” (Ecclus. I). And below: “The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and its branches are long life” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV

Pretense suggests:

Since you do no good in secret, pretend outwardly to be what you do not wish to be inwardly, lest you be detested once everyone knows you.

Religion, on the other hand, replies:

Do nothing of the kind; rather, strive to become good, though you are not. For to show people that you are upright when you are not—what else is that but condemnation? Remember what is said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of plunder and impurity. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may also become clean” (Matt. XXIII).

Likewise, remember that saying repeatedly impressed upon us: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (ibid.).

And there is also what is written about such people: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII).

## CHAPTER V

Arrogance objects:

What sort of person are you, that you should obey those above you and serve those inferior to you? It is more fitting that you command them, for they cannot equal you in intelligence, diligence, or strength. Obey, therefore, God’s command, and trouble yourself no longer about anyone.

Blessed submission replies:

If God’s command is rightly to be obeyed, it is necessary to submit to human authority. For Christ the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me; but whoever despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke X).

But, you will say, this ought indeed to be done if the one who commands were such as the person through whom God ought to command. Since he is not such a person, obedience is not owed to him.

The Apostle, however, says the opposite: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII). Since this ordinance has thus been established by divine right, it must not be obscured by human arguments.

What sort of people those who command ought to be is not for subjects to investigate. For the same Apostle continues: “Those who resist will incur judgment upon themselves” (ibid.).

And to the first shepherds of the Church the Lord himself says: “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority among them are called benefactors. But it must not be so among you; rather, whoever is greater among you shall be the servant of all, just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Luke XXII).

Finally, because he made clear that not all would be such, he assumed the persons of all subjects in the disciples and forewarned them, saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do everything they tell you, but do not do what they do. For they tie up heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matt. XXIII).

## CHAPTER VI

Envy likewise says:

In what way are you less than this man or that? Why, then, should you not be either their equal or their superior? How many abilities do you possess that they do not? Therefore they ought not to be superior to you, or even your equals.

Brotherly affection, however, replies:

If you consider yourself superior to others in virtues, O man, you will keep yourself more safely in the lowest place than in the highest. For a fall from a height is always worse. But if, as you claim, some are superior to you and others your equals, what harm does that do you? What damage does it cause you?

Take great care lest, while you begrudge others a position of eminence, you imitate the one of whom it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. II). Those who belong to his party imitate him.

## CHAPTER VII

Hatred says:

Far be it from you to love the one who is opposed to you in everything, who disparages you, insults you, provokes you with injuries, reproaches you for your sins, and always hastens to surpass you in words, deeds, and honors. If he did not envy you, he would certainly not put himself before you in this way.

But sincere charity replies:

Because these things you describe are hateful in a person, does it follow that God’s image in that person is not to be loved? On the contrary, Christ, who loved his enemies while hanging on the cross and prayed for them, warned his disciples before the torment of the cross, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke XXIII; Matt. V).

This had previously been said through Solomon, for we read: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head, and the Lord will reward you with good” (Prov. XXV).

To this saying the Apostle, speaking from the Spirit of Christ whose meaning he possessed, adds: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (I Cor. I).

On the contrary, John says concerning those known to hate their brothers (Rom. XII): “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (I John III). And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him.

Again: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II).

But you say: “It is enough for me that I love those who love me.” The Lord, however, answers: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” (Matt. V).

What else can you, O man, object to this? Certainly, “whoever hates his brother remains in death, and whoever loves remains in God, and God in him” (I John IV).

Therefore vomit out all the bitterness of gall, and in whatever way you can, take up the sweetness of charity. Nothing is sweeter than it, nothing more blessed in life, as it is written: “Hatred stirs up strife, but friendship covers all who are not contentious” (Prov. X).

Indeed, charity strives to conform us to God. Therefore the evangelist John, affirming this, says: “God is charity” (I John IV). And the distinguished preacher Paul says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

Hence charity is not without reason said to cover the deeds of sins, as it is written: “Charity covers all offenses” (I Pet. IV).

## CHAPTER VIII

Slander says:

Who can endure, or cover in silence, how many wicked things this one or that one commits, except perhaps someone who consents?

But just correction replies:

The evils of one’s neighbor must neither be left unspoken nor consented to; rather, one’s neighbor must be reproved openly with brotherly charity, not secretly slandered.

If someone objects that he is unwilling to rebuke his brother before his eyes because, becoming exasperated, he might not improve but instead take scandal from the correction, divine Scripture responds and, in the opposite direction, declares that slander is even more scandalous, saying: “While sitting, you slandered your brother and placed a stumbling block against the son of your mother” (Ps. XLIX).

For the person who realizes that he is being slandered takes greater scandal than one who sees that he is being corrected.

And because the faults of offenders must sometimes be covered in silence so that they may be corrected at a more suitable time, the passage continues: “You did these things, and I was silent” (ibid.).

Finally, lest slanderers applaud themselves because of this prudent silence—those who always prefer to disparage secretly and never advance to open correction—the passage adds: “You thought that I would be like you” (ibid.).

It is as though he said: “It is wicked to think that I should appear like a slanderer, but I remain silent for a time while awaiting a suitable opportunity for correction.”

Thus it immediately continues: “I will rebuke you and set your sins before your face” (ibid.), as though it said: “Not in secret, as is your custom, but openly, as my concern requires, I will rebuke the sinner, awaiting a suitable time for correction, and set his offenses before his face.”

But you say: “I do not hate him; I love the one whom I judge and reprove in secret.”

The answer is: “On the contrary, you hate him more and do not love him; that is why you slander him and do not correct him.”

How detestable slander of one’s neighbor is, the divine utterances testify in many places. Hence there is the saying: “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, him I pursued” (Ps. C); and this: “Whoever slanders his brother slanders the law” (James IV); and also the words of the Apostle Paul: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal.).

## CHAPTER IX

Anger says:

The things done against you are such that they plainly cannot be endured with equanimity. Indeed, it is a sin to tolerate them patiently; and unless they are resisted with great exasperation, they will thereafter be heaped up against you without measure.

Patience replies:

If the suffering of the Redeemer is brought to mind, nothing is so harsh that it cannot be endured with an even spirit. For Christ, as Peter says, “suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps” (I Pet. II).

The Lord himself also said to us: “If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more the members of his household?” (Matt. X). And elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV).

But how great are the things we suffer in comparison with his sufferings? He endured reproaches, mockery, insults, slaps, spitting, scourges, a crown of thorns, and the cross (John XVIII, XIX); while we wretches—for I say this to our shame—are wearied by a single speech and cast down by a single word. We do not consider what is said: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II).

Therefore the goads of anger must be blunted, and its condemnation must be feared. Hence we read: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V).

Yet a remedy is indicated there when it continues: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” (ibid.).

It is as though it were plainly said: Do not pour forth even a silent prayer in your heart unless you first bring the offended neighbor to gentleness by making satisfaction.

Our gift is our prayer; our altar is our heart. Whoever strives to do this whenever anger has arisen without cause between two people will in no way incur the condemnation stated above.

But there are many who, when forgiveness is requested of them, do not forgive offenses. Against them comes the Lord’s saying: “If you do not each forgive your brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. XVIII).

“You say that he has committed many offenses against me and has offended me repeatedly; and because, without cause, he assails me with many injuries, it is not fitting for me to forgive him so many faults.”

To this it is not I but the Lord who responds. For when Peter said to him, “How often will my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” the Lord answered him: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (ibid.).

How many people are slow to release the injuries done to them, yet quick to forgive those done against God? It sometimes happens that, under the pretext of avenging the Lord’s injuries, angry people avenge their own.

Finally, what should be said about those who are so blinded by the heat of anger that they burst into words of cursing, except what the Apostle says: “Neither the revilers nor the robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI)?

The Apostle James also vehemently condemns this, saying: “No human being can tame the tongue; it is an restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse men, who were made in the image and likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. This ought not to be so, my brothers. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (James III).

For this reason it is also said elsewhere: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII).

## CHAPTER X

Harshness says:

Are mild words to be addressed to these foolish and senseless people, who are just like brute animals, when they offend? Surely the harshest words should be used instead, so that they may learn to revere your dignity.

But gentleness replies:

You must follow not your persuasion in such matters but the instruction of the Apostle Paul, who warned his beloved disciple about this, saying: “Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, with complete purity” (I Tim. V).

And again: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, ready to teach, patient, correcting modestly those who think differently” (II Tim. II).

And again: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke, with complete patience and instruction” (II Tim. IV).

The evil of harshness is plainly pernicious: it harms those under authority and accomplishes less. Indeed, it often happens that those who have been angered reject even a correction offered in charity and hurl arrows of contempt against words that would bring salvation.

The Wise Man warns against this when he says: “Whoever reproves a scoffer brings injury upon himself” (Prov. IX).

Conversely, concerning one who profits from reproof, he says: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (ibid.).

Therefore it is written: “My son, in your gentleness honor your soul” (Ecclus. X). And the Apostle says: “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI).

The same Apostle, teaching bishops, says that they should “show themselves gentle toward all” (II Tim. II).

## CHAPTER XI

Swelling conceit says:

You have God in heaven as your witness; do not concern yourself with what people on earth may suspect about you.

But humble self-abasement replies:

No occasion for slander or suspicion of whispering should be given. If these are present, your deeds should be disclosed to the slanderers so that they may be corrected; or, if they are absent, your deeds should be concealed with a humble protestation.

For the Apostle warns us to give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach (I Tim. V).

He also condemned those who, bearing the Christian name, reclined in an idol temple and, although they themselves considered an idol nothing and ate the sacrificed food as though it were harmless, nevertheless by this act dragged the weak consciences of their brothers toward the abominable rites of idols (I Cor. VIII).

Therefore he says: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and to the Church of God” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XII

Sorrow says:

What do you have over which to rejoice, when you endure such great evils from your neighbor? Consider with what sorrow of heart all those must be regarded who are engaged in such bitter hostility against you.

But spiritual joy replies:

I know that sorrow is twofold; indeed, I have experienced two sorrows of the heart: one that produces salvation (II Cor. VII), and another that contrives destruction; one that leads to repentance, and another that brings to despair.

You seem to recognize one of these, but it is the one that produces death altogether. Therefore you should not be saddened by the things you urge, but rather rejoice in what you do not yet understand.

Hence the Lord, the eternal giver of joy, said: “When people persecute you and speak every evil against you falsely on my account, rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V).

Remember that the apostles, the heights of our religion, went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

Therefore there should be no place for sorrow in afflictions, since such an abundance of joy follows them.

## CHAPTER XIII

Torpor or laziness says:

Are you constantly devoted to reading and to prolonged study of the Scriptures? You will contract ophthalmia or inflammation of the eyes. If you shed tears without ceasing, you will even lose the light of your eyes. If, by extending your vigils, you complete the appointed measure of psalms, you will fall into insanity of the head. If you exhaust yourself by daily labor, when will you rise for spiritual work?

But diligence and tireless virtue reply:

Why, O man, do you set before yourself such long periods of time for accomplishing good? Do you know whether you will live tomorrow—or even whether you will spend a single hour in this life? (James IV.)

Perhaps you have forgotten what the Savior says in the Gospel: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore shake off the sluggishness of torpor, and always remember that the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the lukewarm, the soft, or the idle, but by the violent, those who use force, as the Savior says (Matt. XI).

## CHAPTER XIV

Restless wandering says:

If you believe that God is everywhere, why do you guard one particular place where so many evils are committed, rather than passing on to other places?

Stability replies:

If it is as you say, that you confess God to be everywhere, then this place you desire to flee must not be abandoned, because God is there also.

“But,” you will say, “I seek a better place; I find a better one.”

I answer: Will you find a better place—or even one like that which the devil, his angel, and man lost?

Remember, then, that the first angel fell from heaven, for it is written: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X); and the first man was expelled from paradise and came into the misery of this age (Gen. III).

Consider that Lot, tested by the ordeal of evils, was holy among the Sodomites (Gen. XIX), but, growing sluggish through security on the mountain, he became drunk and sinned with his daughters (ibid.).

This weariness of wandering adds yet another form to itself, when it also draws certain people who persevere in their own discipline away from spiritual matters, entangles them in earthly business, or strives to occupy them with the most worthless concerns. It acts against the Apostle’s saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II); and again: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (I Thess. V).

## CHAPTER XV

Despair says:

Consider how much and how greatly you have committed against God and your own soul: how grave the crimes, how countless the offenses. Yet you have not changed your life for the better, nor corrected your conduct in any useful way until now. For behold, as you see, you remain bound by an evil habit. You try to rise, but weighed down by the burden of sins, you fall back again.

What, then, should you do, when certain condemnation threatens on account of the past and no amendment arises for the present, except not to abandon the pleasures of temporal things while you are delayed from attaining the promises of the age to come?

Confidence in hope replies:

If the matter concerns capital offenses, behold David, guilty at once of adultery and murder, described as delivered from the jaws of hell by the Lord’s mercy (I Reg. XII).

Behold the most shameless Manasseh, the most impure and filthy of all sinners, restored through repentance from death to life (II Chron. XXXIII).

Behold the sinful woman in the city, polluted by countless stains of sin, who anxiously ran to the fountain of mercy, washed the Lord’s feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them with perfume; she deserved to be wholly cleansed (Luke VII).

Finally, she heard: “Your sins are forgiven,” and: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (ibid.).

Behold Peter, bound by the chains of his threefold denial, loosening the knots of his fall through the bitterest tears (Luke XXII).

Behold the robber, liable to condemnation to death for both sedition and the shedding of his brother’s blood, who in a single moment of time and with a single word of confession passed from the cross to paradise. For it was said to him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

What a beautiful example of a conversion to be desired! For the robber is released into forgiveness so quickly that grace appears more abundant than prayer.

Behold Saul, persecuting the Church of God, killing many for the name of Christ, and almost wholly drenched in the blood of the holy martyrs; converted at last by the Lord’s voice, he became an apostle and was called a vessel of election (Acts IX).

When so many and such great examples precede us, therefore, let evil conversations give no place to despair, since it has also been written: “When the sinner has turned from his iniquity and has practiced judgment and righteousness, he will live by them” (Ezek. XXXIII).

And elsewhere: “Do I desire the death of the wicked,” says Adonai, “rather than that he should turn from his evil way and live?” (Ezek. XVIII.)

But concerning a life that has not been changed for the better, what else should I answer except that what someone did not do yesterday, he should do today? Let him not postpone conversion from day to day, since he does not know whether he will have even one day for correction.

And always resisting evil habit in return for the gifts received from above, let him say morning and evening: “Behold, now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI).

## CHAPTER XVI

Greed says:

You are certainly without guilt in desiring to acquire certain things, because you do not seek to multiply them but fear to be in need; and what another holds wrongly, you yourself will spend more properly.

But contempt for the world replies:

The pleasant things of this age are obtained by no one without danger or offense. For the more one has, the more one desires to have; and so one cannot find a measure for possessing while hastening to serve the countless cares of this age.

As Scripture says: “The one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver” (Eccles. V).

This desire to possess, always drinking and always thirsting, never satisfying its longing—how detestable it is, the Apostle Paul indicates when he says: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. III).

Explaining how harmful it is to the soul and opposed to salvation, the same Apostle says: “Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many useless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction” (I Tim. VI).

The Wise Man himself declares how detestable the greedy person is when he says: “Nothing is more wicked than the miser” (Ecclus. X).

The holy James reveals how harmful the accumulation and hoarding of riches are, saying: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire” (James V).

Nor did our Redeemer wish to pass over in silence the evil of this accursed desire. He explains how deadly it is when he says: “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God” (Mark X).

And elsewhere: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX).

If, then, the desire for worldly things is presented as so dangerous for everyone, how much more deadly will it be for those who belong to the Lord’s portion, who have renounced the world, and who have already ceased to be worldly in dress and conduct?

The words of the Redeemer are directed especially toward destroying the destructive disease of greed. He says: “Do not be anxious about your soul, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. For all these things the nations of the world seek” (Luke XII). And elsewhere he adds: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

O how blessed, how secure, how worthy of embrace is this saying! No one in this life is so secure as the one who desires nothing apart from Christ and possesses him. For everything considered necessary for a human being is shown to be possessed under this possession, just as Paul, the richest of the poor, said: “As having nothing, yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI).

“All things,” he says—that is, not what is superfluous, but what is necessary for human life. He confirms and explains this elsewhere when he says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI).

But perhaps you will say: “For this reason those who have been called into the Lord’s portion happen to have more, so that Christ’s poor may receive distributions from them more generously than from ordinary people.”

I agree with this, but only with respect to those placed above, not those subject to authority. The example of Lot’s wife taught this most forcefully: as she went out from Sodom and looked back, she was changed into a pillar of salt and breathed out her spirit (Gen. XIX).

Hence Christ also warns that such a thing must be avoided, saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

Peter says the same: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (II Pet. II).

For what is said in the true proverb happens to them: “The dog returns to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (Prov. XXVI).

This disease of greed is never better restrained than when the day of death is meditated upon without ceasing, and a person considers what he will shortly be in the tomb.

This remained fixed in the memory of the one who said: “Man is corruption, and the son of man a worm” (Job XXV).

It did not depart from the heart of the one who taught: “In all your words remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII).

What good, I ask, will preserved riches do then? (ibid. V.)

Hear what holy Job says about them: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job I).

Hear also the Apostle: “We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away” (I Tim. VI).

## CHAPTER XVII

Self-love says:

If you give what you possess to those in need, from what will you be able to support yourself and those subject to you, without want and with dignity?

But the love of God replies:

“If you observe the apostle’s measure in this matter, you will be able to accomplish both. For he himself says to the Corinthians: ‘If the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. For this is not so that there may be relief for others and affliction for you, but according to equality. At the present time [Col. 1069C] let your abundance supply their want, so that their abundance may also supply your want, so that there may be equality’ (II Cor. VIII), just as it is written: ‘He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not have less’ (Exod. XVI).

“For this reason the righteous Tobias also admonishes his beloved child, saying: ‘As much as you have, according to your means, give alms from it; and if you have little, do not be afraid to give alms according to your little’ (Tob. IV). Likewise the incarnate Truth teaches: ‘Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you’ (Luke XI). Hear also what is written: ‘Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy’ (James II). To the contrary, the prophet admonishes, saying: ‘Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor without shelter into your house; if you see a naked person, cover him, and do not despise those of your own flesh’ (Isa. LVIII).

“Remember what happened to the man clothed in purple: he was not condemned because he had taken what belonged to others, but because he had not given his own possessions to the needy poor man; and, placed in hell, he came to beg for the smallest things, although here he had denied small things to another (Luke XVI).

“Consider also what the Judge of heaven will say to those placed on his left: ‘Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food’ (Matt. XXV), along with the other things terrifyingly enumerated there.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. Theft and fraud, although they differ in the degree expressed by the words, nevertheless say one and the same thing.

Theft says:

[Col. 1069D]

[Col. 1070A]

“If you do not take what belongs to another, you cannot be either rich or adequately provided for from your own possessions.”

Fraud, however, says:

“If you deliver everything entrusted to you unimpaired, and do not think that you ought to reserve even a little for yourself, how will you either provide for your own needs or win the favor of your friends and household?”

But simplicity replies to both:

“It is better to be poor and in need, and to please no one through what has been given, than to injure anyone through theft or fraud. For whoever unjustly seizes what belongs to another by any means closes to himself the entrance to the kingdom of heaven.”

Therefore Paul, that outstanding preacher, rebukes certain people, saying: [Col. 1070B] “But you do injury and defraud—and this to your brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?” (I Cor. VI). And he adds, among other things: “Neither thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

Theft and fraud, therefore, exclude a person from the kingdom of God; for this reason they must be entirely avoided.

## CHAPTER XIX. Deceit and lying also say the same thing.

Deceit is carried out through ingenuity, whereas lying is carried out through a simple word. Deceit therefore says:

“To offer one example among many: when you seek to deceive someone by not giving, you weave delays when he asks, saying, ‘I already have something that I can give you,’ while concealing in your heart what you possess, either so that you may keep it for yourself or, if you wish, give it to someone else.”

Lying says:

“By no means do I have what you ask for”—even though he does have it. Thus lying frustrates the one who asks not by the artful ingenuity of deceit, but by the simple word of denial.

But truth replies to both:

“One must deceive no one either by artful ingenuity or by a simple word, because whoever lies by any kind of contrivance sins. For it is written: ‘The mouth that lies kills the soul’ (Wisdom). Moreover it is said: ‘Their portion will be in the lake of burning fire and sulfur, which is the second death’—for all liars (Rev. XXI).”

## CHAPTER XX. Gluttony of the belly says:

[Col. 1070D]

“God created all things clean for eating; and whoever refuses to be satisfied with food, what else does he do but oppose a gift that has been granted?”

But pure frailty and simple restraint reply:

“Of the things you say, one is true. To prevent human beings from perishing through hunger, God created all things clean for eating; but so that they would not exceed the measure of eating, he commanded abstinence (Gen. I).

“For among its other evils, Sodom perished through satiety, as the Lord himself attests when he speaks through the prophet concerning Jerusalem: ‘This was the iniquity of Sodom, your sister: pride, fullness of bread’ (Ezek. XVI).

“Therefore, just as a sick person approaches medicine, so each person ought to approach food—not seeking pleasure in it, but satisfying necessity. Hence the Truth warned through the Gospel: ‘Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts become weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness’ (Luke XXI).

“On the other hand, concerning the insatiable voracity of some, the Apostle says: ‘For many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame, with minds set on earthly things’ (Phil. III). And elsewhere: ‘Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both it and them’ (I Cor. VI).

“Finally, the man who observes restraint in taking food thoroughly eludes this stain and this gluttony of the belly: that is, he not only completes his refreshment while always remaining hungry, but also, except when bodily necessity or hospitality requires it, rejects more elaborate and more pleasing dishes.”

## CHAPTER XXI. Foolish merriment says:

[Col. 1071A]

“Why do you hide the joy of your spirit within? Go out in public in a cheerful mood; say something outside that will make either you or your neighbors laugh; make them happy through your happiness.”

But wise joy and moderated sorrow reply:

“From where does such great joy come to you? Have you conquered the devil? Have you escaped the punishments of hell? Have you reached your homeland from exile? Have you received any assurance concerning your election? Or perhaps you have forgotten what the Lord says: ‘The world will rejoice, but you will grieve; yet your grief will be turned into joy’ (John XVI).

“Or perhaps you have forgotten what he says elsewhere: ‘Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep’ (Luke VI). And what is said through holy Solomon: ‘Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and the end of joy leads to mourning’ (Prov. XIV). And, conversely, what is taught through the Gospel: ‘Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted’ (Matt. V).

“Again, remember what is said through Solomon: ‘The righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; and no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things remain uncertain for the future’ (Eccl. IX).

“Therefore restrain your empty joy, because you have not yet escaped punitive misery. Is not a person considered insane among human beings if, confined in prison darkness, he tries to rejoice?”

## CHAPTER XXII. Excessive talk says:

“He will not be held guilty of wrongdoing who speaks many things, provided they are good; rather, the one who is proven to speak evil things, even if few, will be held guilty.”

Prudent silence replies:

“What you say is true. Yet while many good things appear to be spoken, it often happens that speech begun with good things turns toward something perverse, as Holy Scripture itself declares: ‘You will not escape sin through much speaking; but he who spares his lips is discerning’ (Prov. X).

“And even if crimes are avoided amid many words, can useless and idle words be avoided—words for which an account will certainly have to be rendered in the future (Matt. XII)? A measure must therefore be maintained in speaking (Ivo, part XI, ch. 55), and sometimes even useful words must be restrained, as the holy Psalmist is read to have done. For he says: ‘I was silent and humbled, and I kept silence even from good things’ (Ps. XXXVIII).”

## CHAPTER XXIII. Lust says:

“Why do you not now indulge in pleasure, since you do not know what will follow you? You ought not to waste the acceptable time in your desires, because you do not know how quickly it will pass. For if God had not wished human beings to unite in the pleasure of the flesh, he surely would not have made male and female at the beginning of the human race.”

But undefiled chastity replies: [Col. 1072B]

“I do not want you to remain ignorant of what you will receive after this life, for either reward or punishment awaits you. If you live piously and chastely, you will rejoice without end in another life; but if you live this life impiously and luxuriously, you will be tormented by eternal fires in the next.

“Therefore you ought to live the more chastely and purely precisely because, as you say, you do not know how quickly the allotted time will pass.

“As for your claim that at the beginning of the human race God created male and female for the purpose that they should unite in mutual embraces (Gen. I), you speak entirely truly in some cases. But after the human race had spread far and wide, permission to marry was left to some—namely, those who had not professed virginity or widow’s chastity—while it was forbidden to others, that is, to those who had decided to remain virgins or continent.

“Fornication, however, is granted to no one with impunity. Perhaps you do not consider, or you think it should be disregarded, what the Apostle says to the sexually impure: ‘Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who fornicates sins against his own body’ (I Cor. VI).

“If you think this of little importance, hear how afterward you will lament and groan over it forever. ‘Neither fornicators,’ the same Apostle says, ‘nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who have intercourse with males will possess the kingdom of God’ (ibid.).

“O how momentary is the pleasure of the flesh, how fleeting the hour of intercourse, through which eternal life is lost. What benefit, I ask, does that bring to the body, or what profit does it confer, which so quickly leads the soul to Tartarus?”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Spiritual fornication says:

[Col. 1072D]

“Is a person doing anything deserving condemnation if he consents to lust in his heart but does not proceed to the act of the lust he has desired? Certainly not, because sin, as the Apostle writes, ‘when it is complete, gives birth to death’ (James I).”

But purity of heart replies:

“Certainly the one who does not preserve purity of heart and chastity of spirit commits sin. Therefore the very author of all purity says in the Gospel: ‘Everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matt. V).

“Hence it is also said through blessed Job: ‘I made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not think upon a virgin’ (Job XXXI). And what portion has God assigned from above, and what inheritance comes from the Almighty on high? For if consent to an evil thought were not displeasing to God our Creator, it would certainly not be said through Isaiah: ‘Take away your wickednesses from your souls before my eyes’ (Isa. I), nor would the Gospel say against the Pharisees: ‘Why do you think evil things in your hearts?’ (Matt. IX).

“Nor would the Apostle Paul write to the Romans: ‘Their thoughts accuse or even defend one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ’ (Rom. II).”

## CHAPTER XXV. Love of the world says:

[Col. 1073B]

“What can be more beautiful, more honorable, more attractive, or more delightful than what we see each day in this present life? O how marvelous is the chamber of heaven—in the pleasant air, in the light of the sun, in the waxing and waning of the moon, in the variety and course of the stars.

“How delightful is the earth—in the flowers of the groves, the sweetness of fruits, the pleasantness of meadows and streams, the luxuriant stalks of crops, the leaves of vineyards and the grape-clusters on their full branches, the shade of forests and green palms, the running of horses and dogs, the leaps of stags and does, the flights of hawks, the feathers and necks of peacocks, doves, and turtledoves, the painted walls and ceilings of houses, the drums and songs of organs and every kind of musical instrument, [Col. 1073C] and the beautiful appearance of women—their eyebrows and hair, their eyes and cheeks, their throat, lips, and hands, together with the other adornments applied externally, especially necklaces adorned with gold and gems, and all the rest of this kind, which the mind cannot now recall individually through the senses.”

But love of the heavenly homeland replies:

“If the things beneath heaven please you so greatly, why do the things in heaven not delight you even more? If you value a prison so highly, what must the homeland and the city be worth? If such are the things cultivated by exiles, what are those possessed by children? If mortals and wretched people are so richly endowed in this life, how will immortals and blessed people be rewarded in the other?

“Therefore the love of the present world, in which no one is born without being destined to die, immediately withdraws, so that love of the future world may take its place—a world in which all are made alive in such a way that thereafter they do not die. There no adversity disturbs, no necessity constrains, no hardship troubles; rather, everlasting joy reigns.

“But you will ask what exists there, where such great and such perfect blessedness endures. No one can say otherwise than that whatever is good is there, and whatever is evil is nowhere there.

“You ask what that good is. Why do you ask me? It has been explained by the Prophet and the Apostle: ‘Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him’ (Isa. LXIV; I Cor. II).

“David, though crowded around by many worldly riches, yearned for this happiness when he said: ‘For what have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired upon earth?’ (Ps. LXXII). He abounded in many royal banquets and other pleasures, and nevertheless cried out: ‘I shall be satisfied when your glory appears to me’ (Ps. XVI), and again: ‘My soul thirsted for the strong and living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?’ (Ps. XLI), and again: ‘Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged’ (Ps. CXIX).

“Hence the Apostle Paul also says: ‘I have the desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better’ (Phil. I).

“Having now passed through these matters, although I have omitted many things, [Col. 1074C] I have nevertheless, as it seems to me, shown in brief the strong camp of our enemy, with which he never ceases to attack those who live piously in Christ.

“Behold, dearest brother, amid my other occupations I dictated and wrote this discourse for you during the nighttime hours, though in an unpolished style. Since I recognized that it exceeded the limits of a letter, I preferred to call it a little book on the conflict between vices and virtues. If you find anything edifying in it, take care to have others read it as well.”

[Col. 1073]

# TWO BOOKS ON THE VOCATION OF THE GENTILES (C, G, S)

## BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE. [Col. 1073D] On the question debated between defenders of free will and preachers of grace, and on the author’s aim and arrangement

For a long time a great and difficult question has been debated between the defenders of free will and the preachers of the grace of God. The question is whether God wills all human beings to be saved. Since this cannot be denied, the inquiry is why the will of the Almighty is not fulfilled. [Col. 1074D] And since this seems to occur according to human wills, grace appears to be excluded (Rom. XI); but if grace is given in return for merits, it is clear that it is not a gift but a debt.

Hence the question arises again: why is this gift, without which no one is saved, not bestowed on everyone by the one who wills all to be saved? Thus no end is found to the opposing arguments, so long as what is manifest is not distinguished from what is hidden (I Tim. II).

Concerning this conflict of opinions, therefore, I shall endeavor to inquire, insofar as the Lord assists me, with what measure and moderation one ought to think. I shall exercise and examine the modest capacity of my understanding in those matters that, as I believe, have settled soberly in my heart, so that if my pen proceeds according to principles containing neither offense nor perversity, it may be useful not only to us but also to others that we have reached some limit which we ought not to exceed.

First, then, we must discuss the movements and degrees of the human will. Between the will and the grace of God some people make an unsound distinction, supposing that the preaching of grace denies free will, and failing to notice that the same rule can be directed against them on the ground that they deny grace when they do not wish it to be the guide of the human will but only its companion.

For if the will is removed, where is the source of true virtues? If grace is removed, where is the cause of meritorious good works?

## CHAPTER II. On the will of the human soul, the various kinds of will, and the fact that God never ceases to care for all human beings

But now, with Christ’s help, let us begin what we have undertaken to discuss.

In every human soul, insofar as it is granted to understand and experience, there is naturally a will of some kind: through it a person either desires what pleases him or avoids what displeases him. As regards the natural movement of this will—which has been weakened by the vice of the first transgression—there are two kinds, according to which the human will is either sensual or animal. But when the grace of God is present, a third kind is added through the gift of the Spirit, so that the will may become spiritual and, through this higher movement, may judge all affections arising from whatever source according to the law of heavenly reason.

The sensual will, which we may also call carnal, does not rise above the movement that arises from the bodily senses, as is seen in the souls of little children. Although they make no use of any judgment of reason, they nevertheless show that they want some things and do not want others: they love what delights them through seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching, and they hate what offends them. But what is loving except willing? And what is hating except not willing?

They therefore have a will of their own, which, although incapable and ignorant of foreseeing and providing, nevertheless loves to do what caresses the bodily senses, until the vigor of rational understanding is awakened through the body’s more mature functions and begins to move the limbs that serve it—not at another’s prompting but according to its own law.

From this sensual appetite, in which those whom we see as senseless and foolish even in more advanced years remain, one rises to the animal will. Before it is moved by the Spirit of God, this will can indeed raise itself above sensual movement, but without participation in supreme love it remains occupied with earthly and perishable things.

Even human intellects, if they do not shamefully serve bodily pleasure and restrain their desires according to the laws of justice and honor, acquire nothing beyond the reward of temporal glory. Although they adorn the present life with propriety, they do not possess the reward of eternal blessedness, because they do not refer their right actions and good pursuits to the praise and honor of the one from whom they received the ability to understand more sublimely within that animal discernment and to shine more brightly than others.

For although some have directed the sharpness of their minds not only toward the institutions of the most useful arts and the teachings of the liberal disciplines, but also toward the investigation of the highest good, and have perceived the invisible things of God through their understanding of the things that have been made, yet, because they did not give thanks to God or acknowledge him as the author of this ability, but said that they were wise—that is, because they gloried not in God but in themselves, as though they had approached the contemplation of truth through their own studies and reasoning—“they became futile in their thoughts” (Rom. I).

What they had found through God’s illuminating grace, they lost through the blindness of pride, falling back from heavenly light into their own darkness—that is, from the immutable and eternal good to mutable and corruptible nature.

When such people therefore fall back into love of themselves and please themselves so greatly that everything they judge praiseworthy in themselves they attribute not to God’s gifts but claim for themselves and ascribe to the effort of their own will, they remain far from that spiritual will. They possess nothing by which they may advance to eternal life, and they even begin within themselves to corrupt those very temporal gifts of God, passing from their good use into the practice of countless vices.

For although it is written (Deut. XXXII) that, when the Most High apportioned the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and that the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob, the lot of his inheritance Israel; and although it is written that the Lord said to Israel: “You shall be holy to me, because I, the Lord your God, am holy, and I separated you from all the nations so that you might be mine” (Lev. XX); and although it is written in the book of Esther, where Mordecai says: “I give you thanks, Lord, because you have performed new signs and wonders such as have not been done among the nations, dividing the whole age into two portions, choosing one for your people and leaving the other to the nations” (Esther X); and although Paul and Barnabas say: “We also are mortal human beings like you, proclaiming that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, who in past generations allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways” (Acts XIV);

although, therefore, the Scripture of truth declares these and many similar things, nevertheless, in accordance with that same Scripture, we believe and most devoutly confess that God’s providential care has never been absent from the whole human race.

Although he directed a people specially chosen for himself toward piety through particular institutions, he nevertheless withheld the gifts of his goodness from no human nation, so that they might be shown to have received the prophetic utterances and legal commandments through the service and testimony of the elements.

Hence they became inexcusable, because they made gods for themselves out of God’s gifts: they worshiped as objects of adoration what had been created for their use.

The nation that the Lord separated for himself from all other nations would also have entirely fallen into this impiety, had he not extended the purpose of his mercy to sustain the falls of the elect. For the pages of the Old Testament are full of accounts of Israel’s defection, so that it may plainly appear that it was always the work of divine grace that not the entire people departed from the Lord.

Thus human nature, corrupted by the transgression of the first human being, even amid God’s benefits, commandments, and assistance, is always inclined toward a worse will; to entrust it to itself is nothing other than to abandon it.

This will is wandering, uncertain, unstable, inexperienced, weak in accomplishing but quick to dare, blind in its desires, puffed up by honors, anxious amid cares, restless through suspicions, more eager for glory than for virtue, more attentive to reputation than to conscience, and, throughout all its experience, more wretched when enjoying what it desires than when deprived of it. Of its own powers it possesses nothing except an ease of falling into danger, because a changeable will that is not governed by an immutable will approaches iniquity more quickly the more intensely it applies itself to action.

As long as a person takes pleasure in what displeases God, his will is animal. For even if he acts with good morals, he still lives badly if he does not live for the glory of God.

This is the distinctive and chief characteristic of the pious: that they glory in the Lord and love themselves only in God. They love themselves properly who love in themselves the works of God. For God loves in us what he himself made, and he hates what he himself did not make (II Cor. X).

If, therefore, we love God’s work in ourselves, we rightly love the good will in ourselves; and if it were not God’s work, it ought not to be loved. What person, unless he has an evil will, does not love the good will in himself, which is the first planting of the heavenly farmer?

For the Truth says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.” Whatever is not to be uprooted was plainly planted by the Father (Matt. XV).

The good will is the first seed of all virtues. Resting upon its origin, it finds repose in that eternal and immutable will, so that it may truly be spiritual, because “the one who clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI). Through the communion of the one who illuminates and the one who is illuminated, of the one who justifies and the one who is justified, of the one who rules and the one who is subject, every action is referred to one. And what is referred to one belongs to both, because what God has given cannot be alienated from God, nor what a human being has received from the human being.

## CHAPTER III. On the treatment of this question: when a person begins to be a person of good will, whether the former will is corrected or another is given to him; and on the fact that in sacred writings “all” is sometimes said for “some”

It seems necessary here to examine whether, when a person begins to possess a good will, the very will that was already in him is corrected, or whether another will is given to him—one that he did not have and that is opposed to the former. To make this clearer, let us not hesitate to investigate the matter more deeply.

All human beings were created without defect in the first human being, and by that same human being’s transgression we all lost the integrity of our nature. From this came mortality; from this, the manifold corruption of body and soul; from this, ignorance and difficulty, useless anxieties, illicit desires, sacrilegious errors, vain fear, harmful love, unjust joys, decisions that must be regretted, and a multitude of miseries no less great than that of crimes. When these and other evils had invaded human nature—faith lost, hope abandoned, understanding blinded, and the will enslaved—no one found within himself the means of restoration. For even if there was someone who attempted, by the natural effort of his understanding, to resist his vices, he arranged only the life of this present age fruitlessly; he did not advance to true virtues [Col. 1078B] or eternal blessedness.

Without the worship of the true God, even what appears to be virtue is sin; and no one can please God without God. But the one who does not please God—whom does he please except himself and the devil? When a human being was stripped by the devil, he was deprived not of his will but of the soundness of his will, since he could not have been cast down from the state of innocence unless he had sinned by his will. Thus the nature that had been good was made evil in quality. And that movement of the soul which can never exist without some love—that is, without some will—did not lose its desire, but changed its affection: it received in longing what it ought to have rejected by judgment.

Therefore, when a human being returns to piety—for this reason it is said, “The spirit goes forth and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII), because unless God converted it, it would not return—he does not become a new formation or a new creation; no other substance is created in him, but the same substance that had been weakened is restored. Nothing else is taken away from him except the vice that nature did not possess. For in Adam there was a nature without vice, but through disobedience of the will he contracted many evils and transmitted them to his descendants, where they were multiplied more and more.

These evils cannot be conquered and reduced to nothing except by the grace of the Savior, who restores his work by his own work. As the apostle John says: “For this purpose the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John III). And just as he breaks the bonds of the captive, so he clothes the nakedness of the one who has been stripped, and so he heals the wounds of the wounded, so that what he accomplishes in him may also be accomplished through him. It is certainly not advantageous for a person to fight his enemy without a protector [Col. 1078D]. For he is engaged in combat with the one by whom he was once overcome.

Let him not therefore trust in his own strength, which did not stand even when it was whole; let him seek victory through the one who alone was not conquered and who conquered all. And if he seeks, let him not doubt that he received from the one whom he seeks the very desire to seek him. Nor, because he is led by the Spirit of God, should he suppose that he does not possess free will—a will that he did not lose even when he voluntarily surrendered himself to the devil. The judgment of the will was corrupted by him, not removed. What was not killed by the one who wounded it is not taken away by the one who heals it. The wound is healed; the nature is not removed.

But what perished in nature is restored only by the author of nature, with whom what nature lost has not perished. For wisdom is eternal, truth is eternal, goodness is eternal, justice is eternal; indeed, the light of every virtue is eternal, and whatever is virtue is God. If he does not work in us, we can share in none of the virtues. Without this goodness nothing is good; without this light nothing is luminous; without this wisdom nothing is sound; without this justice nothing is right.

The Lord says through Isaiah: “I am, I am God, and there is no one besides me who saves” (Isa. XLV). And Jeremiah says: “I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to direct his path” (Jer. X). A mortal human being, born carnally from a lineage condemned in Adam, does not attain the spiritual dignity of a new kind unless guided by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1079B]. Nor does anyone desire this dignity unless he has received the warmth of that desire, concerning which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

This fire is the love of God, which the lover of the world cannot grasp with a captive heart. For he is full of love for vanities. Even if he is able to avoid some of them, and, having passed beyond bodily and visible things, to advance toward understanding eternal and invisible realities; even if he withdraws from the worship of images and ceases to venerate heaven and earth and all the elements of this world—still, being disturbed by Christ’s humility, he will not grasp faith in and love for Christ, nor by his own judgment overcome the scandal of the Lord’s birth and death (1 Cor. I).

Because the wisdom of the world resists the wisdom of God, it pleased God, in order that the pride of those who presume upon themselves might be blinded, to save believers through the foolishness of preaching. Hence those swollen with secular learning consider the cross of Christ more worthy of ridicule than worship; and the more highly someone has ascended toward the structures of human disciplines, the more he disdains the lowliness and weakness of our preaching.

Nor is it surprising that pagan philosophy opposes the gospel of Christ’s cross, since even Jewish learning resists it. Therefore neither the learned nor the unlearned, nor human beings of any lineage or rank, are led to God by human reasoning. Rather, every human being who is converted to God is first moved by God’s grace. For he is not his own light, nor does he kindle the course of his life with the ray of his own light.

If blessed John—than whom no human being was born greater (Matt. XI)—was not the light, because he did not shine by his own brightness, but had received from that true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world what enabled him to be light (John I), who is it that could, by his own judgment alone, break through so many conflicts of opinions, so many bonds of habit, and so many prejudices of antiquity? Who could receive from an external teacher’s merely sounding voice only this much from grace—that he heard—and everything from the will—that he believed?

If this were so, there would be no difference between grace and the law; nor would the Spirit of mercy give life if the letter that kills remained. The law commands what must or must not be done, but does not provide that it be done or not done beforehand, because it is obeyed not through freedom but through fear [Col. 1080A] (2 Cor. III).

But the Lord, so as not to abolish the law but to fulfill it, made the command of the law effective through the assistance of grace. By multiplying mercy, he removed punishment, so that he might not punish sin by exacting vengeance but erase it by forgiveness. Thus he freed the adulterous woman, who according to the provision of the law was to be stoned, both by truth (Matt. V) and by grace. When the executioners, reproved and terrified in their consciences, left the trembling accused woman under the judgment of the one who had come to seek and save what had been lost (John VIII), he stooped—that is, he humbled himself toward humanity and bent down to the work of our restoration—and wrote with his finger upon the ground, so that by the decrees of grace he might render void the law of commandments and show himself to be the one who had said: “I will place my laws in their understanding, and I will write them upon their hearts” (Luke XIX; John VIII; Jer. XXXI).

This he does every day, inserting his will into the hearts of those who are called. With the stylus of the Holy Spirit, whatever the devil in his envy falsified on the pages of the soul, truth rewrites in mercy. When, therefore, the word of God is brought to the ears of the flesh through the ministry of preachers, the operation of divine power is mingled with the sound of the human voice, and the one who aroused the ministry of the evangelist also formed the disposition of the hearer.

The food of the word becomes sweet to the soul; the old darkness is driven away by new light; and the inner vision is stripped of the obscurity of ancient error.
