The mind passes from one will into another. The will that is being expelled lingers for a while, but the will that is born lays claim to all that is better, so that the law of sin and the law of God may have distinct and separate dwelling places in the same person. While the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit resists the desires of the flesh, the tempter may indeed dare to lie in wait through outward things, but the mind, fortified by God’s help, prevails (Rom. VII; Gal. V).

For the material of these struggles has been preserved for the great benefit of the faithful, so that holiness may not grow proud while weakness is being assailed. Hence the Apostle also says: “To prevent me from being exalted by the greatness of the revelations, an angel of Satan was given to me to buffet me. For this reason I pleaded with the Lord three times that he might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Cor. XII).

Let the Lord therefore seek his image, and let the good shepherd find the sheep that has gone astray. Let him not disdain to carry upon his shoulders the sick sheep, long wearied on a trackless path, and to save it not merely by calling it back but also by carrying it (Luke XV). Let the Lord seek his image, and, wiping away the accumulation of all the filth that has fallen upon it, let him clear the mirror of the human heart.

For it is written: “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed?” (Job XIV). “Is it not you alone?” Let the Lord seek his image, so that in its renewal and justification the grace of the one who reforms it may appear, just as the apostle Paul testifies that this happened in himself, saying: “I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; they had only heard that the one who formerly persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy, and they glorified God in me” (Gal. I).

If, therefore, the Christian people at that time had learned this, and if those members of the primitive Church—who were of one heart and one soul (Acts IV)—believed in such a way that, whenever they saw someone converted from error to knowledge of the truth, they glorified God and confessed that the faith of the convert was a divine gift, then the Lord himself was teaching his disciples, the teachers of all nations, in this way when he said: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

With this faith fixed and humbly grounded in our hearts—that we most beneficially believe that all good things, and especially those that advance us toward eternal life, are possessed by God’s gift, increased by God’s gift, and preserved by God’s gift—I think a devout understanding ought not to be disturbed by my question, which arises concerning the conversion of all human beings and not of all human beings, if we do not obscure what is clear by means of what is hidden; if, while we obstinately press against closed things, we are not shut out from what is open. It should be enough for us to walk in that to which we have attained.

For what is surprising if people do not come to the mysteries of life, when many who seemed to have come depart? Of them it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John II). Their likeness is found also in those who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds (Titus I).

For although it is written, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Rom. X), the Lord nevertheless says of some: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII). And again: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will say to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’” (ibid.).

Such people do not call upon the name of the Lord, because they do not possess the spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII). For no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. XII). And all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God (Rom. VIII). They come to God through God; and those who desire to be saved are altogether saved, because they conceive the very desire for salvation through God’s inspiration and come to the knowledge of the truth through the illumination of the one who calls them.

They are children of promise, the reward of faith, the spiritual seed of Abraham, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, foreknown and predestined to eternal life, as the Holy Spirit testifies through the prophet Jeremiah, saying:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not remain in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (1 Pet. II; Jer. XXXI; Heb. VIII) [Col. 1082A].

“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will place my laws in their understanding, and I will write them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And they will not teach each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the least of them to the greatest; for I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more. And I will give them another way and another heart, so that they may fear me all their days, for their good and for the good of their children after them. And I will establish with them an eternal covenant, which I will not turn away from them after them; and I will place my fear in their heart, so that they may not depart from me; and I will visit them in order to make them good” (Jer. XXXII).

Through Isaiah also, the Lord foretells the same things concerning his grace, by which he makes a new creation from all human beings, saying:

“Behold, I am making new things, which will now arise, and you will know them. And I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in dry land” (Isa. XLIII). “The beasts of the field will bless me, the sirens and the daughters of ostriches, because I have given water in the wilderness and rivers in dry land, to give drink to my chosen race, my people whom I acquired for myself, so that they may declare my mighty works.”

And again: “By myself I swear: surely righteousness shall go forth from my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back, because every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess God” (Isa. XLV).

If it is impossible that these things should not come to pass—for God’s foreknowledge is neither uncertain, nor his purpose changeable, nor his will ineffective, nor his promise false—then all those concerning whom these things were foretold (Jer. XXXI) are saved without any exception.

For he gives his laws in their understanding and writes them in their hearts with his finger, so that they receive knowledge of God not through the work of human teaching but through the instruction of the supreme teacher. For “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. III).

All these, from the least to the greatest, know God, because, in order that they might come to Christ, they heard and learned from the Father. All who are led out of error are directed into the way of life. To all, once their heart has been changed, it is granted to think rightly and to will rightly; into all is inserted the fear by which they are instructed in God’s commandments (Jer. VI; John VI; Ps. CXVIII).

A way is made in the wilderness, and dry land is watered by rivers, so that those who previously did not open their mouths to confess God, and who had passed over into the wildness of beasts like mute and irrational animals, may, cleansed by the springs of the divine utterances, bless and praise God (Isa. XLIII), declaring the mighty works and wonders of the mercy of the one who chose them, adopted them as sons, and made them heirs of the new covenant (Eph. I; Gal. III).

But if—as the Apostle says—a humanly confirmed covenant is not rejected or superseded, how can the divine promise be in any respect annulled? What the Lord promised to Abraham without condition and granted without law remains entirely firm and is fulfilled every day. For even if some to whom these things were foretold did not believe, their unbelief did not nullify the faithfulness of God. “God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (Rom. III).

Those who, after hearing the gospel, refused to believe became more inexcusable than they would have been if they had heard no proclamation of the truth. But it is certain that in God’s foreknowledge they were not children of Abraham, nor numbered among those concerning whom it was said: “All the tribes of the earth will be blessed in your seed” (John XV; Gen. XXII).

He promised that they would believe, who said: “And they will not teach each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the least to the greatest.” He promised that they would be reconciled, who said: “I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more” (Jer. XXXI, XXXII; Heb. VIII). He promised that they would obey, who said: “I will give them another way and another heart, so that they may fear me all their days” (Isa. XLV). He promised that they would persevere, who said: “I will place my fear in their heart, so that they may not depart from me; and I will visit them in order to make them good.”

Finally, he promised that all without exception would obey him, who said: “By myself I swear: surely righteousness shall go forth from my mouth, and my words shall not be turned back, because every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess God.”

If we say that what God swore would happen does not happen, we attribute—God forbid—falsehood and lying to God, the truth. But if, as piety and faith persuade us, God’s words do not fail and what he has ordained comes entirely to pass (Matt. XXIV), how will the firmness of his truthful promise appear to us, while many thousands of human beings still serve demons and bow their knees to idols? Only if we understand that such declarations of God were issued according to that unchangeable knowledge in which the whole human race has already been distinguished before him; and whether he speaks of the good or of the wicked, he remembers one part as though he were omitting no human being.

For when the Apostle says: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. V), does he not appear to have said that all human beings have been renewed? Or when he says: “For in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself” (Col. I), does he not speak as though he wished no one to be understood as excluded from this reconciliation? Or when he says: “In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things” (Heb. I), does not the form of the statement sound as though all human beings had been transferred by the Father into Christ’s inheritance, according to the prophecy of David: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II)?

For when the Lord says, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII), does this not seem to promise the conversion of all? Or when it is prophesied of the Church: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and crooked things shall become straight, and rough ways shall become smooth” (Isa. XL), does any human being seem to have been omitted who is not signified as destined to be subjected to Christ?

What of the statement: “And all flesh shall come before me to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord” (Isa. LXVI)? Or: “In those days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II)? Or: “The Lord lifts up all who fall and raises up all who have been crushed” (Ps. XLIV)? Is it not stated as though no one were excluded from this gift of God?

The people of God therefore possess their own fullness. Although a large part of humanity either rejects or neglects the grace of the Savior, among the elect and foreknown, who have been distinguished from the generality of all, a certain special universality is nevertheless counted, so that from the whole world the whole world appears to have been liberated, and from all human beings all human beings appear to have been taken up.

Likewise, when the impious are discussed, divine Scripture orders its language in such a way that what is said of a certain part appears to pertain to all human beings. Such is the statement of John the Baptist: “The one who comes from heaven is above all; what he has seen and heard, he testifies, and no one accepts his testimony” (John III).

Or the Apostle’s statement: “All seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s” (Phil. II). Or what the psalm of David sings: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII).

These and other testimonies, which those who investigate may produce in greater number, clearly demonstrate that sometimes the whole earth is named for a part of the earth, the whole world for a part of the world, and all human beings for a part of humanity. Scripture, however, often quickly makes their distinction clear, so that the reader’s understanding is transferred from the designation of the whole to the part that is meant.

Such is the Apostle’s statement: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. I).

Was Christ power to those for whom he was a stumbling block? Or wisdom to those for whom he was foolishness? But because some of the same people would be justified by faith while others would be hardened by their own impiety, he distinguished one class of believers and unbelievers under the designation “those who are called.” Thus he showed that those whom he signified as alien from the faith, although they had heard the gospel, were outsiders with respect to the calling.

By this rule the divine word promises through Isaiah, saying: “I will lead the blind by a way they do not know, and they shall tread paths they do not know; I will make darkness into light before them and crooked things straight. I will do these things for them, and I will not abandon them” (Isa. XLII).

But what follows—“They themselves turned back”—must be referred to a certain part of their race, not to those of whom he said, “I will not abandon them.”

Again the Lord says to Jacob (Isa. XLIII): “Do not fear, because I am with you. From the east I will bring your seed, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, ‘Give them up,’ and to the south, ‘Do not hinder them any longer’; bring my sons from a distant land and my daughters from the ends of the earth, everyone upon whom my name has been called. For I prepared him for my glory, and I formed him and made him” (ibid.).

But what follows—“I brought out a blind people, and their eyes are blind, and they have deaf ears”—cannot in any way apply to those whom he says he prepared for his glory. In all these statements that are made concerning one human race, the earlier words apply to some persons and the later words to others.

In the Apostle also, what is done in one part of the people is narrated under the name of the whole people, and in the remainder the fullness is counted. When he was discussing the blindness of the Jews and demonstrating that some of them were saved by grace, he says: “I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I myself am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. XI).

The foreknown people, the people not rejected, are those who have been justified in Christ. What appears to be said of all Israel is shown to apply only to those whom the election of grace left for himself, as the following words of the Apostle’s discourse explain (ibid.).

For he adds: “Or do you not know what Scripture says in Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life’” (1 Kings XIX). But what does the divine reply say to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal” (Rom. XI).

“So also,” he says, “at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

Therefore not all Israel was rejected, nor was all Israel chosen. Voluntary blindness turned away one part; gratuitous illumination reserved another part for itself. Yet the discourse concerning them is framed in such a way that no distinction of the whole race appears to have been made between those who perish and those who are saved (2 Cor. II).

For when we read: “According to the gospel, they are enemies for your sake, but according to election, beloved for the sake of the fathers” (Rom. XI), the wording sounds as though it calls the same people beloved whom it had called enemies. But the Apostle himself dispelled this darkness by saying: “Because blindness has happened in part to Israel” (ibid.), so that we should understand one race to have been divided into two classes, and “every human being,” “all fullness,” and “all Israel” to refer not always to the whole but very often to a part.

Among these forms of expression in Scripture, we must also observe the manner of speaking by which what pertains to people of different times is promised as though it were said of one generation of the same age. Thus the holy apostle Peter, writing to the gentiles of his own time and of a future time, says:

“But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition, so that you may proclaim the mighty works of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light; you who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1 Pet. II).

When these things were being proclaimed, were those people still alive who in earlier generations had all been left by God to walk in their own ways (Acts XIV)? Were those very same people who had previously been handed over to their own wills now being called from darkness into marvelous light? Had they not already died, already departed from this world, with no return from error to truth available to those long dead?

And yet, because grace would exist many centuries later among the descendants of the impious, the customary manner of speaking has touched upon the matter in such a way that those who had previously been abandoned appear now to be the ones being chosen. These statements, however, do not pertain to the same individuals but to people of the same nation. The calling that shone forth near the end of the world does not return to the age that had passed.

Thus, in a certain manner, they are both the same and not the same—the people about whom and to whom these things are said—since in one respect they are not divided from the generality, while in another they are separated from what is common.

## CHAPTER IV. He refutes the accusation that, by what has been said above, the author contradicts the Apostle, who declares that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; and that the depth of the divine mysteries and judgments is not to be investigated by us.

But when those who love contentious accusations read or hear these things, they will say that by such discussions we contradict the Apostle, who declares that God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II).

We accept this passage of the Apostle’s words in such a complete and full sense that we subtract nothing from what precedes or follows and pertains to it. For, even if we set aside the other testimonies of the divine utterances, this passage is sufficient both to nullify what they maliciously allege and to defend what they impiously deny.

Writing to Timothy, therefore, the apostle Paul says: “I urge, therefore, first of all that supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity” (ibid.). “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.”

Since this is the rule of apostolic teaching with which the universal Church is instructed, let us not wander into an alternative interpretation according to our own judgment; rather, let us inquire what the universal Church herself believes. For there can be nothing doubtful in the command if obedience agrees in its devotion.

The Apostle therefore commanded—or rather, through the Apostle, the Lord who spoke in the Apostle (2 Cor. XIII)—that supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all human beings, for kings and for those who are in positions of authority. The devotion of all priests and all the faithful holds this law of prayer so harmoniously that there is no part of the world in which such prayers are not celebrated by Christian peoples.

Thus everywhere the Church supplicates God not only for the saints and those already regenerated in Christ, but also for all unbelievers and enemies of the cross of Christ (Phil. III); for all worshipers of idols; for all who persecute Christ in his members; for the Jews, whose blindness prevents the light of the gospel from shining upon them; and for heretics and schismatics who are alienated from the unity of faith and charity.

What does she ask for these people except that, abandoning their errors, they may be converted to God, receive faith, receive charity, and, freed from the darkness of ignorance, come to the knowledge of the truth (2 Cor. IV)?

Because they cannot provide this for themselves, weighed down by the burden of evil habit and bound by the chains of the devil, and because they cannot overcome their deceptions, to which they have clung so obstinately that they love falsehood as much as truth ought to be loved, the merciful and just Lord wills human beings to pray for all of them.

When we see innumerable people rescued from such profound evils, we should not doubt that God has granted what we prayed he would grant. And, giving thanks for those who have been saved, we should also hope that those who have not yet been illuminated will likewise be rescued from the power of darkness by the same work of divine grace and transferred into the kingdom of God before they depart this life (Col. I).

But if the grace that saves has passed over some, as we see happen, and the prayer of the Church offered for them has not been received, this must be referred to the hidden judgments of divine justice. We must recognize that the depth of this secret cannot be laid open to us in this life. “We know in part, and we prophesy in part”; and now “we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. XIII).

Nor are we wiser or more knowledgeable than the blessed Apostle. When he was discussing the power of grace, entering into the secret of great mysteries, he was overcome by matters that could not be expressed.

For after saying: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation: blindness has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters” (Rom. XI), and so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The one who delivers will come from Zion and will turn away impieties from Jacob; and this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isa. LIX), he continued:

“According to the gospel, they are enemies for your sake, but according to election, beloved for the sake of the fathers” (Rom. XI). “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief, so they also now have not believed in your mercy, so that they too may obtain mercy.”

“For God has enclosed all people in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all.”

When he had poured forth these mysteries of divine works—things surpassing the measures of human understanding—in a kind of mental excess, he transferred the whole method of exposition to astonishment. Admiring what he had set forth, he exclaimed:

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

## CHAPTER V. Why in earlier ages all the nations were left to walk in their own ways, with Israel alone excepted; and why God gives grace to one person but denies it to another.

The assertion of the teacher set forth above gave occasion for a multifaceted question, so that the reason for God’s grace being distributed differently among so many peoples and ages might be sought: namely, why in earlier ages all the nations had been allowed to enter upon their own ways (Acts 14), with only Israel—which was to be instructed in the divine utterances and chosen for knowledge of the truth—excepted, and why Israel’s unbelief eventually made room for the nations to be saved—as though, if one people had remained steadfast in the faith of its own race, God’s mercy could not have extended itself to the other nations.

Why, finally, should those whose diminution is salvation for the nations not be delivered from their blindness before the fullness of the nations enters—as though those who are all to be saved, once all the nations have been adopted, could not be illuminated together? Or how will all Israel be saved once its blindness has been removed, when an innumerable multitude of it, failing in its unbelief, did not reach the times promised for those who are to be saved? Or how is it now said that the fullness of the nations, whose calling had not previously occurred, is entering, when so many thousands of people of every age and condition, in all the nations beneath heaven, die without Christ’s justification?

[Col. 1088C] But the pious and learned teacher preferred to suspend the causes of these mysteries and judgments upon the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, rather than rashly investigate the secret of the most just truth and most merciful goodness, which is withdrawn from human understanding: omitting nothing of what ought not to be unknown, and touching upon nothing of what may not be known (Rom. 11). For many things occur in the administration of divine works whose causes remain hidden while only their effects are shown, so that although what happens is evident, why it happens is not: the matter is brought into the open, while its rationale is withdrawn into concealment. Thus, in the same matter, presumption concerning the inscrutable is restrained, and falsehood concerning what is manifest is refuted.

For if I do not know why that man is created a Greek and this one a barbarian; why one is born in wealth and another in poverty; why the one is elevated by the beauty of a strong and lofty body, while another is disfigured by the contracted weakness of feeble limbs; why the one, born of Catholics, is nourished in the cradle of truth, while another, the offspring of heretics, imbibes the poison of error with his mother’s milk; and, finally, if I cannot judge a thousand other differences in bodily appearance, in the qualities of souls, in the circumstances of times, and in the customs of regions—

[Col. 1088D] therefore I do not know that God is the creator and ordainer of all these things. He certainly created the bodies and spirits of individual human beings in such a way that, apart from the voluntary diversity arising afterward from each person’s own choice, he varied the very beginnings of their constitution by a most diverse multiplicity.

Many opinions of empty talkers would disturb us and draw us in different directions—people who have rashly presumed to define what cannot be known, attributing these original inequalities to fates, which are nothing, and to the stars—unless we held with the utmost certainty that God the Creator forms each vessel from the original elements as he wills, and regulates the one nature of souls and the one nature of bodies according to measures pleasing to himself.

These works of God would not have been withheld from human understanding if they ought to have become known, and it would have been revealed why each thing happened in this way, unless it were sufficient to know that it happens in this way. The Lord says to Moses: “Who gave a mouth to man, and who made him mute and deaf, seeing and blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?” (Exod. 4). And through Isaiah: “Is it not I who made fertile and barren?” says the Lord [Col. 1089B] (Isa. 66).

In the book of Ecclesiasticus we read: “Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God” (Ecclus. 11). And Job says: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he himself has placed everything in their hands” (Job 12). The same man, arguing about the advancement and decline of all human affairs and referring every change to the judgments of God, says: “With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding” (ibid.). “If he destroys, no one can build; if he shuts a man in, no one can open; if he withholds the waters, everything will dry up; if he releases them, they will overturn the earth. With him are strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and the one deceived. He brings counselors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment. [Col. 1089C] He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord; he leads priests away without honor and overthrows nobles; he changes the speech of the truthful and removes the instruction of the elders; he pours contempt upon princes and raises up those who had been oppressed. He reveals deep things from darkness and brings the shadow of death into the light; he makes nations great and destroys them, and restores the overthrown to wholeness; he changes the heart of the leaders of the earth and deceives them, so that they walk in vain through a pathless place; they will grope as in darkness and not in light, and he will make them wander like drunkards.”

And again, speaking of the impossibility of frustrating God’s will, the same author says: “For he alone exists, and no one can turn aside his purpose; whatever his soul desires, that he does” (Job 23).

One part of humanity is delivered while another part perishes. And if we wish to attribute this to the merits of their wills, so that grace might seem to have neglected the wicked but chosen the good, the case of innumerable peoples will resist us—peoples for whom, throughout so many ages, no proclamation of heavenly teaching shone forth. Nor can we say that their descendants were better, of whom it is written: “The people of the nations that sat in darkness have seen a great light, and light has risen upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death” (Isa. 9).

And to them the apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his wondrous light: you who once were not a people, but now are God’s people; you who once had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy” (1 Pet. 2).

[Col. 1090A] Therefore what the later generations did not deserve is not attributed to their merits; for equal impiety condemned both fathers and children, and the same blindness of ignorance plunged them all together into the same errors. But why God had no mercy on the former and had mercy on the latter—what knowledge can comprehend it, what wisdom can investigate it?

The reason for this distinction is hidden, but the distinction itself is not hidden. We do not understand the Judge, but we see him at work. Why do we accuse hidden justice, when we owe thanks for manifest mercy? Praise and revere what is being done, because it is safe not to know what is concealed.

Consider also the universal multitude of infants, in whom—apart from that sin through which the human race is born into condemnation—neither past merits nor future merits can be assessed. For all those of whom we are now speaking, before any use of understanding and before any exercise of free will, pass over either to eternal blessedness, having been reborn, or to everlasting misery, not having been reborn.

If you acknowledge original guilt, the whole number is under condemnation; if you seek moral innocence, the entire company is without fault. Human justice finds nothing by which to distinguish them, but God’s inexpressible grace has something to choose. The counsel is hidden, but the gift is not hidden; mercy brings the work forth, while power obscures its cause.

Yet what is not seen is as certain as what is seen, because confession of the unknown equity of the author of a manifest work cannot be denied. And if you turn the gaze of your mind toward those who, having spent a long life in wickedness and crimes, are renewed by the sacrament of Christ’s baptism at the very end of life and, without any support from good works, are transferred into fellowship with the heavenly kingdom, by what understanding will you comprehend the divine judgment unless you recognize without hesitation that God’s gifts are gratuitous?

Just as no crimes are so detestable that they can prevent the gift of grace, so no works can be so excellent that, by way of recompense, they establish a claim to what is granted freely. For the redemption by Christ’s blood would be cheapened, and God’s mercy would yield to the privilege of human works, if the justification that comes through grace were owed to preceding merits, so that it would be not the gift of the giver but the wage of the worker.

[Col. 1090D] How could it be proved that no human effort is sufficient to erase original sin unless both the impious and the criminal were received into the kingdom through Christ’s washing, and those who boast in their own righteousness recognized how incapable they are of doing anything worthy of adoption as God’s sons if they do not reach the sacrament of regeneration? They are held under the same condition as the most wicked sinners: they will be equal in sanctification if regeneration is present, and they will perish together if cleansing is absent.

If, then, even among the most wicked, at the very end of life, grace finds some whom it may adopt, while many who appear less harmful are nevertheless excluded from this gift, who could say that this occurs either without God’s dispensation or without profound equity [Col. 1091A]? It is not unjust because it is hidden; rather, it is equitable because there can be no doubt that it is God’s judgment.

For since it depends upon his decision by what sentence a person is to be judged, that sentence is uncertain before the judgment. But once the matter has reached its conclusion, no one is free to complain about the outcome: it is entirely certain that God ought not to have acted otherwise than he has acted.

He also supported the variety of many kinds of calling, all belonging to one grace, with that evangelical comparison (Matt. 20) in which he shows a householder hiring workers for his vineyard at different times under an agreement for a denarius, by which the equality of eternal life is signified. There is no doubt that those admitted into the vineyard at the eleventh hour, being made equal with the workers of the whole day, set before us the lot of those of whom we are now speaking, whom divine indulgence rewarded at the decline of day and the close of life in order to commend the excellence of grace.

He was not paying a price for labor, but pouring out the riches of his goodness upon those whom he chose without works, so that even those who had labored and sweated much, yet received no more than the last, might understand that they had received the gift of grace, not the recompense of works.

And if we too murmur against the householder because those called last are made equal to the workers of the whole day and deserve no more for their many works than those who have scarcely worked at all, what was said in answer to one of them will be said to us: “Friend, I do you no wrong; did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give to this last one as I give to you. Or am I not permitted to do what I wish with what is mine? Is your eye evil because I am good?” (ibid.).

Certainly this generosity seemed unjust to the one who accused it. And what instruction did he receive? What reason was granted to him? The justice of this dispensation was not revealed to him, nor was he admitted to behold the hidden secret. But so that he might refrain from examining God’s judgments, the goodness of the merciful one and the power of the one who wills were set before him, as though the Apostle were also saying to him: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” (Rom. 9).

Therefore, for all human beings, of whatever race, condition, or age, the will of God is the cause by which grace is received. With him the reason for election is hidden, while merits begin from that grace which they received without merits.

If good things could exist without grace, it would not be said: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3); nor would it be said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6). Rather, it would be said: “Unless someone is just and good, he cannot be eternally blessed.”

Nor would it be necessary to be reborn through water and the Spirit if instruction through a commandment were sufficient. And the faith that believes all sins are forgiven through baptism would be emptied if grace were taught to be bestowed not upon the wicked and impious but upon the good and upright.

The origin, therefore, of true life and true righteousness has been placed in the sacrament of regeneration, so that where a person is reborn, there also the truth of those virtues may arise. Those who could scarcely attain the reward of temporal and empty praise begin, through faith, to advance toward everlasting glory.

For whether it is a Jew, puffed up with knowledge of the Law, or a Greek, inflated by the study of natural wisdom, before being justified by faith in Christ, he is shut up under sin (1 Cor. 1; Rom. 1). And if he persists in his unbelief, the wrath of God remains upon him (John 3)—that wrath, namely, contracted in Adam’s transgression, of which the Apostle speaks:

“And you, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we too once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts; and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2).

And again: “You were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope of the promise, and without God in the world” (ibid.).

And again: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

And again: “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light, who has delivered us from darkness and from the power of darkness, and has transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1).

And again: “We too were once foolish, unbelieving, deceived, serving various desires and pleasures, living in wickedness and envy, hateful and hating one another” (Titus 3).

But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, “not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might be heirs according to the hope of eternal life.”

## CHAPTER VI. What human nature is like without grace

And so that it may be shown as briefly as possible what human nature is like without grace, let the apostle Jude say what is accomplished either by the ignorance of the unlearned or by the teaching of the wise. “But these men,” he says, “blaspheme whatever they do not know; and whatever they know naturally, like mute animals, in that they are corrupted” (Jude 1).

Let the evangelist Luke also speak through the words of Zechariah about the night in which the human race lives before the illumination of grace, and about the darkness of ignorance from which God’s people are rescued:

“And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people for the remission of their sins, because of the tender mercies of our God, by which the rising from on high has visited us, to shine upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace” (Luke 1).

The Lord bestowed these tender mercies not for the redemption of one people alone but for the salvation of all nations, as the Evangelist says: “Because Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God” (John 11).

This is what that voice of the Lord declares—a voice resounding throughout the whole world like a trumpet of compassion, inviting and summoning all human beings. For after he had said, “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones; yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Matt. 11), he added:

“All things have been delivered to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him.”

Then he added:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (ibid.).

John the Baptist, in the Gospel of John, testifies in a prophetic spirit, saying: “He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony. Whoever accepts his testimony has set his seal that God is true” (John 3).

Therefore, as far as concerns the blindness of the human race, contracted through a long night of ignorance and pride, the Creator of the world came into this world, and the world did not know him. “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). “He who is above all bears witness to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony” (John 3).

But because the Son of God did not come into the world without purpose, and gave himself for all, dying not only for the nation but also to gather into one the scattered children of God (Titus 2; John 11), and because he says to all, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11), while reserving to himself the decision of an unknowable election and giving knowledge of himself and of his Father to whomever he wills to reveal it—

all the children of light, children of promise, children of Abraham, children of God, a chosen race, a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2), true Israelites, foreknown and ordained beforehand for the kingdom of God, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the nations, accept the testimony of him who came from heaven (John 3). They set their seal that God is true—that is, they plainly show in their salvation that God is true, fulfilling and completing what he promised to Abraham, the father of all nations.

When God promised that Abraham would become heir of the world, he did not hesitate through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what he had promised he was also able to do (Rom. 4).

Who, then, is so alien to Abraham’s faith, who so degenerate from the father of all nations, as to say that God’s promise is either not fulfilled or is fulfilled by someone other than the one who made the promise? “Let God be true, and every man a liar” (Rom. 3).

And everyone who accepts his testimony (John 3) sets this seal and indicates that, through the illuminating light, he has been made one who sees, one who obeys, and one who understands, as the evangelist John testifies:

“We know that the whole world lies in the evil one, and we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son” (1 John 5).

## CHAPTER VII. Why the Savior of all did not give everyone the knowledge of the true God, and why some infants are saved when reborn while others perish without rebirth

If it is asked why the Savior of all human beings did not give everyone this understanding, so that they might know the true God and be—that is, remain—in his true Son, although we believe that the help of grace was not wholly withdrawn from any human beings, as we shall discuss more fully below, perhaps this too has been veiled in the same way as that other matter was hidden: why, previously passing over all the nations, he set apart one people for himself to instruct in the knowledge of the truth.

If God’s judgment in that matter is not to be complained of, still less should we murmur against this judgment, which is carried out in the election of all the nations. For what God has willed to be hidden must not be investigated, while what he has made manifest must not be denied, lest we be found illicitly curious concerning the former and damnably ungrateful concerning the latter.

We are not unaware that there are some of such thoughtless presumption and arrogant pride that they dare to violate by a false-named doctrine what the outstanding teacher of the nations, divinely instructed “not by men nor through man” (Gal. 1), confessed to be far removed, both high and distant, beyond the measure of his knowledge. They wish nothing to be hidden, nothing to remain secret, where the Apostle did not disclose what ought to be thought, but showed what ought not to be investigated.

For no study and no intellectual power is permitted to discover by what judgment or counsel God—immutably good, immutably just, always foreknowing, always omnipotent—“concluded all in unbelief, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. 11), and yet, during those ages in which he was instructing Israel alone, delayed illuminating innumerable peoples of the impious; and why he now permits that same Israel to remain blinded until the fullness of the nations enters, while it perishes in so many thousands of those being born and dying, and is saved in those whom the end of the world will find.

Through this mystery, extended throughout the whole body of Scripture, it has indeed become known to us what has happened, what is happening, and what must happen; but why it was pleasing that it should happen in this way has been removed from the contemplation of human understanding.

But those who are ashamed to admit that they do not know something and who, under cover of obscurity, set traps of deception, refer every distinction by which God chooses some and does not choose others—“For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20)—to human merits and will. They teach that no one is saved freely but by recompense, because it is naturally implanted in everyone that, if they wish, they can share in the truth, and that grace flows to those by whom it has been sought.

This definition, leaving aside for the moment the truth of grace, seems to display some small measure of reason in the case of those who exercise free will. But regarding infants, who without any merit of good will share with all mortals in the wound of original sin, no explanation can be offered that teaches why these are saved when reborn, while those perish without rebirth, under the providence and omnipotence of him in whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh, and to whom it is said: “The days of man are short; the number of his days is with you” (Job 14).

I do not think that these defenders of human wills will use the simplicity of infants so shamelessly as to say either that these things happen by chance or that those who are not reborn do not perish. For they would plainly be convicted either of agreeing with the pagans concerning fate or of agreeing with the Pelagians in denying that sin was transmitted to Adam’s descendants.

Even the Pelagians could not say that infants fail to be baptized because of fate; but because they dared to profess that infants are free from sin, they deserved condemnation.

When the question concerns the distinction among all human beings, and infants cannot be separated from the rest of humanity, and when Truth has likewise said concerning people of every age, “The Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19), those who place the cause of election in the merits of the chosen try in vain, through free will, to open the depth of inscrutable grace.

Although they have put forward many foolish and false claims about the will and judgment of adults, they fail when it comes to the distinction among infants. They cannot boast of having provided a rational account of a question that concerns all human beings but is not resolved for all.

The variety and greatness of divine grace prove that, even in what they say about the wills of adults, they advance arguments against the truth, and the testimonies of the divine utterances oppose their persuasion. If we wished to attach all of these to our discussion, there would be no end to the exposition. Nevertheless, if they come to mind, they will not be omitted, so that, as far as is sufficient, it may be made clear that every good merit of a human being, from the beginning of faith to the completion of perseverance, is both God’s gift and God’s work.

## CHAPTER VIII. Whence faith arises and how it is acquired

Therefore, let the Apostle Paul explain from what source faith itself arises—faith which is the mother of good will and righteous action. He gives thanks to God for the faith of the Romans, saying: “First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1).

Writing also to the Ephesians, he says: “Therefore I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, so that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, enlightening the eyes of your heart, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints” (Eph. 1).

Similarly giving thanks for the faith of the Colossians, he says: “We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and the love you have for all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven” (Col. 1).

And explaining what he prays they may receive from the same author of all good things, he says: “For this reason, from the day we heard it, we have not ceased praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of the Lord, pleasing him in every good work, bearing fruit and increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened with every power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering with joy” (ibid.).

Likewise, concerning the Thessalonians, who served in the spirit of faith and love, he says: “We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers without ceasing, remembering your work of faith, your labor of love, and your endurance in hope of our Lord Jesus Christ before our God and Father” (1 Thess. 1).

And below: “For this reason we too give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of men but, as it truly is, the word of God, who works in you who have believed” (1 Thess. 2).

Could it have been shown more fully or clearly that the faith of believers is God’s gift than by the fact that thanks were given to God because those to whom the word of God was preached through human beings did not doubt it as though it were merely human speech, but believed as God speaking through human beings—God who worked in them so that they might believe?

In his second Epistle to the same Thessalonians, the Apostle speaks in this way about those whose faith in Christ was advancing: “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith grows exceedingly and the love of each one of you for one another abounds, so that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your patience and faith amid all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure as an example of the just judgment of God, so that you may be deemed worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer” (2 Thess. 1).

The Apostle Peter likewise, proclaiming that faith comes from God, writes: “Knowing that you were not redeemed with perishable things, gold or silver, from your empty way of life inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, foreknown indeed before the foundation of the world but manifested in the last times for you, who through him are faithful in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God” (1 Pet. 1).

The same Apostle speaks in his second Epistle about the reception of faith: “Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have obtained a faith equal to ours through the righteousness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Pet. 1).

The Apostle John most clearly teaches from whom the spirit of faith is received, saying: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God, and this is the antichrist” (1 John 4).

He also says that the Gospel is received from the one in whom the Spirit of truth is present: “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we recognize the spirit of truth and the spirit of error” (ibid.).

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, the apostle Peter declares that faith is through the Lord Jesus: “The name of this man whom you see and know has strengthened him, and the faith that is through him has given him this complete soundness in the presence of you all” (Acts 3).

Concerning the faith of Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened among the other women who were listening together to the Gospel, the same history relates: “On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate beside the river, where there seemed to be a place of prayer; and sitting down, we spoke to the women who had gathered. A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, was listening; the Lord opened her heart to attend to what was being spoken by Paul” (Acts 16).

[Col. 1097B] That faith is not from human wisdom but from divine inspiration is confirmed by the voice of Truth himself. For when the Lord said to his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?”, Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus answered and said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

The Apostle Paul also proclaims that this very faith is given according to the measure determined by the will of the giver: “For I say, through the grace given to me, to everyone among you not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly, just as God has allotted to each one the measure of faith.”

The same Apostle commends the unity of right faith and agreement for the honor of God as coming from God: “Now may the God of patience and consolation grant you to have the same mind toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that with one accord and with one mouth you may honor God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 12).

And below: “Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 15).

This testimony teaches that not only faith but also joy, peace, and an abundance of hope are possessed only through the power of the Holy Spirit (ibid.).

Writing to the Ephesians about the riches of grace that repays good for evil, and about faith that is possessed not from ourselves but from God’s gift, the Apostle says:

“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—by whose grace we have been saved—and raised us up together and seated us in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 2).

“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.”

This, then, is characteristic of the new creation through grace: those who are God’s workmanship, who are fashioned in Christ through a heavenly birth, must not grow sluggish in idleness or be dissolved by laziness, but must advance from virtue to virtue (Ps. 83), walking along the way of good works.

For this is what it means to be fashioned; this is what it means to be made new from the old creation; this is what it means to be reformed from the image of the earthly man into the image of the heavenly man. All of this is begun, increased, and perfected either openly through fellow workers of grace or secretly through the ministry of the Spirit, by him whose building and whose workmanship we are (1 Cor. 3, 15).

## CHAPTER IX. That God is the author of all virtues and of every good thing
Abundantly, so far as I judge, these testimonies have demonstrated—although other proofs might also have been gathered—that the faith by which the ungodly person is justified is possessed only as a gift from God, and is bestowed without any preceding merits; it is given so that it may be the beginning of merits. Thus, once it has itself been given rather than sought, all the other good things are conferred in response to its petitions. Therefore, some testimonies must be selected from among the many, showing the generosity of grace in the diversity of its gifts.

That it is from God that a person chooses God’s way and rises from a fall, the Psalm of David sings, saying:

> The steps of a man shall be directed by the Lord, and he shall will his way. When he falls, he shall not be crushed, because the Lord supports his hand. (Psalm 36)

Likewise, that one comes to God under God’s guidance:

> Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your dwelling places. (Psalm 42)

Likewise, that human strength is in the Lord, and that God’s will goes before the one who is to be delivered:

> I shall keep my strength toward you, because God is my protector, my God; his will shall go before me. (Psalm 58)

In Proverbs, too, we read concerning wisdom and understanding:

> For the Lord gives wisdom, and from his presence come knowledge and understanding. (Proverbs 2)

Again, in the same book, concerning God’s administration of wisdom, without which no actions are upright, it is said:

> My counsel and my protection; my prudence, and my strength. Through me kings reign, and tyrants possess the earth. (Proverbs 8)

Elsewhere, that no one can walk rightly unless the Lord directs him:

> The steps of a man are corrected by the Lord; but how can a mortal understand his own ways? (Proverbs 20)

Again:

> Every man seems righteous to himself, but the Lord directs hearts. (Proverbs 21)

And elsewhere:

> The will is prepared by the Lord. (Proverbs 8)

Likewise, concerning thought and counsel:

> There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the Lord’s counsel prevails. (Proverbs 19)

In the book of Ecclesiastes it is said that both possessing what is necessary and using it well are gifts from God:

> There is no good for a man except to eat and drink and show his soul the good of his labor. And indeed I have seen this myself: it is from the hand of God. For who can eat or who can enjoy anything without him? (Ecclesiastes 2)

In the same book we read that the hearts and works of the righteous are in God’s hand, and that they advance in their pursuits only as much as he grants:

> However much a man labors in seeking, he will not find; and whatever a wise man says in order to know, he will not be able to discover. For I have set all this in my heart, and my heart has seen all this: the righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God. (Ecclesiastes 8–9)

In the book of Wisdom, concerning this same work of grace, it is said:

> For he himself is the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise. (Wisdom 7)

For in his hand are we, and our words, and all wisdom, and the discipline of knowledge of works. Concerning continence also, that it is obtained as a gift from God, the same Scripture speaks thus:

> I knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it; and this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was. (Wisdom 8)

The teaching of the Apostle Paul agrees with this statement when he writes in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that. (1 Corinthians 7)

In the Gospel according to Matthew, the Lord is likewise reported to have indicated that continence is a gift:

> When his disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry,” Jesus said to them, “Not everyone grasps this word, but only those to whom it has been given by my Father.” (Matthew 19)

Concerning the fear of God and wisdom, we read in Ecclesiasticus:

> The fear of the Lord is the crown of wisdom; and both are gifts from God. (Ecclesiasticus 1)

And again concerning the same:

> The fear of the Lord has set itself above everything; blessed is the one to whom it has been given to possess the fear of the Lord. (Ecclesiasticus 25)

Isaiah likewise speaks of spiritual riches, whose author is the Lord:

> In our treasures salvation has come: wisdom, piety, and discipline are from the Lord; these are the treasures of righteousness. (Isaiah 33)

Again, concerning the height of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge (Romans 11), whose goodness is preceded by no one’s merit, he says:

> He who measured the waters in his hand, and the heavens with a span, and the whole earth with a handful; he who established the mountains on a balance and the hills on scales—who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor to instruct him? Or whom did he consult, and who instructed him? Or who showed him judgment, or who showed him the way of understanding? Or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid? (Isaiah 40)

For this reason, in the book of Job, according to the same meaning, the Lord’s words are read:

> Who gave to me first, that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is mine. (Job 41)

Jeremiah declares in this way that sound wisdom in a person comes from God:

> I know, Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to direct his path. (Jeremiah 10)

Likewise, that the turning of the heart toward God comes from God, the Lord himself testifies and says:

> I shall restore them to this land, and I shall rebuild them and not destroy them; I shall plant them and not uproot them; and I shall give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord. They shall be my people, and I shall be their God, because they shall turn to me with their whole heart. (Jeremiah 24)

Again, preaching that the knowledge of God comes from God, he says:

> And they shall know that I am the Lord their God; and I shall give them a heart to know me and ears to hear. (Baruch 2)

That every good word and every holy work is the provision of the Holy Spirit, without whom nothing is done rightly, the Apostle Paul teaches in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, saying:

> Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus”; and no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit. There are distinctions of gifts, but the same Spirit; distinctions of ministries, but the same Lord; distinctions of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of tongues. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills. (1 Corinthians 12)

That each person possesses as much grace as the Lord has granted, the same Apostle says to the Ephesians:

> One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in us all. But to each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” (Ephesians 4; Psalm 67)

Again, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, he says that we are not capable even of thinking what is spiritual except through God’s grace:

> We have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us capable ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. (2 Corinthians 3)

And again, in the same Epistle, teaching that the effectiveness and sufficiency for good works are supplied by God’s grace, he says:

> God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that, having sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work, as it is written: “He distributed; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” (Psalm 111; 2 Corinthians 9) He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that in everything you may be enriched for complete generosity.

Writing to the Ephesians, the Apostle teaches that all good things by which God is pleased are gifts from God, and that he should be asked to grant them to those who do not possess them:

> For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; that, rooted and grounded in love, you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God. To him who is able to do far more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us—to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen. (Ephesians 3)

That God is the author of every good thing, and that his gifts are neither uncertain nor changeable but proceed from an eternal will, the Apostle James speaks thus:

> Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration. (James 1)

For he begot us willingly by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of first-fruits of his creation. The prophet Zechariah also joins in this testimony, saying:

> The Lord will save his people on that day like sheep, because holy stones are rolling upon his land: for if anything is good, it is his; and if anything is best, it is from him. (Zechariah 9)

In the Gospel according to Matthew, that knowledge and understanding are gifts of God, which he bestows on whomever he wills, is said as follows:

> Then his disciples approached him and said, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” But he answered them: “Because it has been given to you to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given.” (Matthew 13)

The Evangelist John likewise declares that no one possesses anything good except what he has received from above, saying:

> A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven. (John 3)

In the same Gospel there is also the teaching of Truth itself that no one comes to the Son unless drawn by the Father, because God makes him come, understand, and obey:

> No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I shall raise him up on the last day. For it is written in the Prophets: “And they shall all be taught by God.” Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me. (Isaiah 54; John 6)

And below:

> For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father. (John 6)

That progress and perseverance in faith and good works unto the end are a divine gift and assistance is confirmed by the authority of the holy Scriptures. For the Apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, says:

> Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus. (Philippians 1)

Someone wishing to turn the force of this testimony toward the perversity of his own understanding interpreted the words “he who began in you” as though they said “he who began from you,” so that both the beginning and the completion of the work might be referred not to God but to the human being, who would supposedly have wished both to begin and to complete it. But in the same Epistle that outstanding preacher of grace strikes down this utterly insane pride, saying:

> In nothing be terrified by your adversaries; this is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation, and this is from God. For it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him. (Philippians 1)

And again:

> Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will. (Philippians 2)

Likewise, in the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, he teaches that the beginning, progress, and completion of virtues are from God, saying:

> May God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus direct our way to you. May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all, just as we do for you, so that he may strengthen your hearts without blame in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints. (1 Thessalonians 3)

Writing also to the Corinthians, and commending the persevering growth of all virtues as a gift from God, he says:

> I give thanks to my God always for you, because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge; just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack no grace, as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. He will also confirm you to the end, without blame, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. (1 Corinthians 1)

Again, to the Romans, concerning the love of Christ by which he makes those whom he loves inseparable—that is, persevering unto the end—for what else is perseverance than not being overcome by temptation?:

> Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter.” But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us. (Romans 8; Psalm 43)

Again, to the Corinthians, concerning the victory that Christ brings to completion:

> The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord. (1 Corinthians 15)

Again, to the Thessalonians, concerning the perseverance that God grants:

> May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved whole and without blame at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Faithful is he who called you; he will also accomplish it. (1 Thessalonians 5)

Again, to the Thessalonians, he proclaims that all our good things, whether in doing or speaking, together with perseverance in them, are gifts from God:

> May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, exhort your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word. Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as it is among you, and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil people. For not all possess faith. But God is faithful; he will also strengthen us and guard us from evil. (2 Thessalonians 2)

Let us also hear how the Apostle Peter teaches that the strength of perseverance comes from God:

> The God of every grace, who called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will himself restore, strengthen, establish, and ground you. To him be power and authority forever and ever. (1 Peter 5)

The Apostle John speaks in this way of the victory of the saints as the work of God dwelling in the saints:

> You are from God, little children, and you have conquered the world, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world. (1 John 4)

Again:

> Everything born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith. (1 John 5)

In the Gospel according to Luke, that God grants perseverance in faith is expressed as follows:

> Jesus said to Peter, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has asked to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers, and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” (Luke 22)

In the Gospel of John, concerning Christ’s sheep, which no one snatches from his hand, we read that Truth says:

> But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them from my hand. (John 10)

Again, in the same Gospel, concerning those whom the Father gives to the Son—who all come to the Son, and none of whom perishes—the following words are spoken by the Lord himself:

> Everything that the Father gives me will come to me; and whoever comes to me I shall not cast out, because I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of the Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day. (John 6)

There are many other passages in the sequence of the canonical Scriptures that, in our desire to avoid excessive length, we pass over. For the passages we have selected are neither few nor obscure nor insignificant. They make it completely clear that all things pertaining to the attainment of eternal life can neither be begun, nor increased, nor brought to completion without the grace of God. Against every election that boasts in free will, there resists with invincible force the Apostle’s statement:

> For who distinguishes you? What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? (1 Corinthians 4)

Therefore, the depth of that question which, in accordance with the Apostle’s wonder, we confess to be impenetrable is not resolved by the willing and refusing of free will. For although the good of refusing may be present in a person, he does not possess the good of willing unless it has been given; the former he contracted through guilt by nature, while the latter nature receives through grace.

But what it is that this same nature—guilty in all human beings before reconciliation and wretched in all, yet not justified in all—is distinguished in some part of itself from those who perish by him who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19): this cannot be investigated at all by human understanding. However much the wickedness of the ungodly is accused for resisting God’s grace, can it be proved that those to whom grace was granted had deserved it? Or could that power of grace, which subjected to itself those whom it willed, not convert those who remained unconvertible? Those who were drawn were of the same kind as those who were left in their hardness. But to the former grace, in its marvelousness, gave what it willed; to the latter truth, in its justice, repaid what was owed. Thus God’s judgment is more inscrutable in the election of grace than in the repayment of justice.
