Nevertheless, lest that part of the faith by which we piously believe that God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2) appear to be weakened by what is clearly demonstrated concerning the effects of grace, we must strive, with Christ’s assistance, to make the stability of this definition evident to us. But since the task of necessary investigation requires no slight labor, let us begin the discussion that follows from the beginning of another volume.

## BOOK TWO

### CHAPTER ONE

That there are three matters to which one must hold in the question discussed above; that God is the just disposer; and how, in accordance with what was commanded by the Lord to the preachers, no distinction was made among nations and no one was excluded, but the Gospel was sent to all people, and God’s saving grace appeared to all people; and concerning the mystery of what was said to the apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles”; and concerning God’s hidden judgments in the calling of human beings.

Once all the disputes produced by the contentiousness of intemperate arguments have been removed and rejected, it is clear that there are three matters to which one must hold in this question with which we begin the second book.

The first is that we must confess that God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2).

The second is that there can be no doubt that no one reaches the knowledge of the truth itself and the attainment of salvation through his own merits, but through the help and action of divine grace.

The third is that we must confess that the height of God’s judgments cannot be penetrated by human understanding; and that one ought not to inquire why he does not save all, since he wills all to be saved. For if what cannot be known is not sought between the first and second definitions, no cause for conflict will remain. Rather, both statements will be proclaimed and both believed with a secure and tranquil faith.

For God, with whom there is no iniquity and whose ways in their entirety are mercy and truth (Romans 9; Psalm 24), the good Creator of all people, is the just disposer: condemning no one undeservedly and liberating no one by obligation; punishing what is ours when he chastises the guilty, and bestowing what is his when he makes people righteous. Thus the mouth of those who speak wickedness is stopped (Psalm 62), and God is justified in his words and conquers when he is judged (Psalm 50).

Neither is the condemned person’s complaint just, nor is the justified person’s arrogance truthful, if the former says that he did not deserve punishment or the latter asserts that he deserved grace.

Just as those things brought forth from the divine utterances for the manifestation of grace cannot by any reasoning or argumentative skill be distorted so that statements clear and harmonious amid such a multitude are dragged into some uncertainty of perverse interpretation, so also what is found in the same body of Scripture concerning the salvation of all people must not be rashly attacked by any contrary argument. Rather, the more difficult this very matter is to understand, the more laudably it must be believed. For great is the strength of agreement when authority is sufficient for following the truth even while the reasoning remains hidden.

Let us therefore consider attentively what the Lord commands the preachers of the Gospel. In Matthew he says:

> All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you; and behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age. (Matthew 28)

In Mark, the same apostles are told:

> Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. (Mark 16)

Was any distinction among nations or among any people made in this command? He excluded no one on the basis of merit, separated no one by race, and distinguished no one by condition. The Gospel of Christ’s cross was sent absolutely to all people. And lest the ministries of the preachers appear to be carried out by human work alone, he says:

> Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age. (Matthew 28)

That is: when you enter among wolves like sheep (Matthew 10), do not tremble because of your weakness, but trust in my power. I shall not abandon you in this work until the consummation of the age—not so that you will suffer nothing, but, what is much greater, so that I shall ensure that you are not overcome by any cruelty of those who rage against you.

In my power you will preach, and through me it will happen that, amid contradiction and fury, children of Abraham will be raised up from stones (Matthew 3). I shall make known what I have taught; I shall accomplish what I have promised.

> They will hand you over to councils; in their synagogues they will scourge you, and you will stand before kings and governors for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations. But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you will speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his child; children will rise against their parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all people because of my name. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. (Matthew 10)

Thus, as the Apostle says, the saving grace of God appeared to all people (Titus 2), and yet the ministers of grace were hated by all people. Although some were those who hated and others those who were oppressed by the hatred of their persecutors, neither group was deprived of the designation “all people”: the rebellious portion indeed suffered the loss of its salvation, while the faithful possessed the full dignity of that title.

For the Apostle John says:

> If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. (1 John 2)

There is a great and unspeakable mystery of the sacrament in the fact that the preachers who were told, “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16), had first been told:

> Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel. (Matthew 10)

Although the Gospel was directed toward the calling of all people, and although the Lord willed all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2), he had not thereby taken away his authority over the administration of his dispensations, so that the order of his counsel might proceed otherwise than he had established by a hidden and just judgment.

Therefore the murmurs and complaints of the obstinate have no place, because it is clear that what God willed to happen could not have happened otherwise than he willed.

At a later time, when the Lord Jesus was already seated in the glory of God the Father and the preachers were serving the task they had undertaken, the apostles wished to preach the word in Asia, but they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit; and when they planned to go into Bithynia, they were prevented by the Spirit of Jesus (Acts 16). Grace was not denied to those peoples, but, so far as appeared, was delayed. For afterward the Christian faith also grew strong among them.

The reason for delaying their calling is not clear. Nevertheless, we are taught by the example of what happened that, among general promises, works, and commands, God orders certain things apart from the common causes by a more hidden rationale. I believe this is so that, through the interposition of certain shadows, those things that shine more secretly may become known more wonderfully; so that the eye may not become less attentive through the ease of seeing, nor in a certain way fall asleep through familiarity, if it is not awakened by unusual things.

We know that these unknowable delays of illumination—during which many certainly fail in unbelief—occur not only among the impious in more remote peoples, but also in the cities of the faithful, throughout many homes and families, while even those who are destined to become Christians resist the Christian faith. For many will love what they hate and preach what they do not accept.

And who could make known to the querulous or the curious why the sun of righteousness has not yet risen for certain nations, and why Truth still withholds its rays from darkened hearts, though it is to be revealed? Why are those who need correction allowed to wander for so long, and why is what is to be granted to the aged at the end not granted through such a long lifetime? Why do parents not yet believe although their children already believe in Christ? And again, why does corrupt offspring disagree with devout parents?

Yet God, who grants the beginnings and the growth of faith, is petitioned daily for all people according to his command: if he hears, the grace of his mercy may be recognized; if he does not hear, the judgment of his truth may be understood.

Nor was this same grace absent from the world in former ages—the grace that after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was diffused everywhere (Acts 14), and of which it is written:

> Your flashes have shone upon the world. (Psalm 76)

Although it is clear that the Israelite people were chosen by God’s special care and indulgence, while all the other nations entered upon their own ways—that is, were permitted to live according to their own will—yet the eternal goodness of the Creator did not so turn away from those people that he failed to admonish them to know and fear him by any signs whatsoever.

For heaven and earth and the sea, and every creature that can be seen and understood, were arranged especially for the benefit of the human race, so that rational nature might be instructed, through contemplation of so many forms, experience of so many good things, and reception of so many gifts, in the worship and love of its author. The Spirit of God fills all things; in him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17). For although salvation is far from sinners (Psalm 118), nothing is empty of the presence and power of salvation itself.

Therefore, as the Prophet says:

> The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord. (Psalm 32)

This mercy has never been absent in any age or generation. He has always devoted to governing and nourishing created natures that providence by which he administers and sustains the universe, having established from the eternity of his unchangeable counsel both the times at which he would distribute each thing and the inscrutable and unsearchable measures of his manifold grace, through which he would vary his gifts and sacraments.

For just as this abundance of grace, which most recently flowed out among all nations, does not nullify the grace that fell like dew upon Israel alone under the law, and just as present riches do not abolish the faithfulness of past frugality, so it must not be inferred from the special care of God that governed the children of the patriarchs that the reins of divine mercy were withdrawn from other people. Although these seem rejected in comparison with the elect, they were never deprived of manifest and hidden benefits.

For we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles Paul and Barnabas said to the Lycaonians:

> Men, why are you doing these things? We also are mortal, human beings like you, announcing to you that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them; who in past generations allowed all nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without testimony, doing good from heaven, giving rains and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness. (Acts 14)

What is this testimony that has always served the Lord and has never been silent concerning his goodness and power, except the ineffable beauty of the whole world itself and the rich and ordered generosity of his ineffable benefits? Through these, certain tablets of the eternal law were offered to human hearts, so that in the pages of the elements and the volumes of the seasons the common and public teaching of divine instruction might be read.

Heaven, therefore, and all heavenly things, the sea and the earth, and everything in them, with the harmonious concord of their beauty and order, proclaimed the glory of God and spoke, in perpetual preaching, of the majesty of their author.

And yet the very great number of people who were permitted to walk in the ways of their own will did not understand this law, nor follow it. The fragrance of life that breathed toward life became for them a fragrance of death toward death, so that even through those visible testimonies it might be learned that the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. (2 Corinthians 2–3)

### CHAPTER TWO

That no one reaches the knowledge of the truth itself and the attainment of salvation through his own merits, but through the help and action of divine grace.

Source/review notes: Raw Terra review retained as complete=false solely for the previously omitted inline source anchors; six substantive review edits and all ten anchors were applied at their corresponding passages.

Therefore, what was carried out in Israel through the establishment of the Law and the prophetic utterances was always carried out among all nations through the testimonies of the whole creation and the miracles of God’s goodness. But since, among that people over whom both forms of instruction presided, no one was justified except by grace through the spirit of faith, who could doubt that those from whatever nations and in whatever ages were able to please God had been distinguished by the spirit of God’s grace? Although that grace was formerly more sparing and more hidden, [Col. 1108B] it nevertheless denied itself to no age: one in power, various in extent, unchanging in purpose, manifold in operation. For even in those days when rivers of ineffable gifts water the whole world, the same manner and measure are not bestowed upon everyone.

Although the same truth is preached to all through the ministers of the word and of God’s grace, and the same exhortation is offered, nevertheless it is God’s field and God’s building, whose power works invisibly so that what is built or cultivated may advance through growth. As the Apostle Paul testifies when he says: “What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers of him in whom you believed, each as the Lord granted. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth. The one who plants and the one who waters are one. But each will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Cor. 3). “For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building.”

Thus, each person is an assistant, laborer, and minister of this field and building to the extent that the Lord has granted to each. And those who are cultivated through the labor of the ministers advance to the degree to which the author of growth has raised them. For the Lord’s field does not contain a uniform or single planting. And although the structure of the whole temple coheres in one beauty, not every stone has the same place or the same function. So too, in one body, all the members do not perform the same action (Rom. 12), as the Apostle says: “But now God has placed the members, each one of them, just as he willed” (1 Cor. 12).

The same teacher explains from where these members derive their fitness, usefulness, and beauty, saying: “Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit. There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; varieties of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Since the teacher of the nations proclaims these things with such great light and clarity, on what grounds or for what reason should there be doubt whether the seed of all our virtues comes from God? Or who but the most foolish would complain about the difference among divine gifts, or suppose that what is not bestowed equally from heavenly liberality ought to be attributed to unequal merits?

For if this distribution arose according to the merits of preceding works, the Apostle would not have concluded his catalogue of the gifts with such words: “But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid.). [Col. 1109B] If he had wished the causes to be understood as merits, he would surely have said, “Distributing to each as they deserve,” just as he promised a reward for devotion to those who plant and water, saying: “Each will receive his own reward according to his labor” (1 Cor. 3).

Therefore each person is given, without merit, that by which he may advance toward merit; and something is given before any labor, by which each may receive a reward according to labor. This is also recognized by the testimony of evangelical truth, where it is said by way of comparison that a man going abroad called his servants and handed over his property to them: “To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one” (Matt. 25), to each according to his own ability—that is, according to his own natural capacity, not according to his own merit. For it is one thing to be able to act and another to act; one thing to be able to possess charity and another to possess charity; one thing to be capable of continence, justice, and wisdom and another to be continent, just, and wise.

Not everyone who can be restored is restored, nor is everyone who can be healed healed; for being restorable and healable belongs to nature, whereas being restored and healed belongs to grace. Accordingly, those servants to whom, according to the measure of their capacity—which the distributor of his property had foreseen in them—a different number of talents was entrusted received not the recompense of merit but the material for work.

The vigilant industry of two servants was not only honored with glorious praise but also commanded to enter into the eternal joys of their master. But the third servant’s sluggish idleness and slothful wickedness was punished in such a way that he was both disgraced by the reproach of censure and stripped of the portion he had received. He was indeed worthy to lose an unprofitable faith, because he had not exercised charity.

Therefore, in the discourse that follows, in which the pattern of the future judgment is most openly declared—when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, after all the nations have first been gathered—some are said to be placed on the right and others on the left (ibid.). To those on the right, praised for works of charity, nothing else is charged against those on the left than the neglect of mercy and benevolence. These people, too, had received faith, but they had not pursued love; they will be condemned not for a gift that was not preserved, but for one that was not increased.

Although all good things are gifts of God, God nevertheless bestows some even when they are not requested, so that through what has been received people may seek what has not yet been granted. For the seed that is sown in the earth is not sown so that it may remain alone, but so that by producing fruit it may become abundant and numerous. Its growth indeed comes from the one who gives the increase (1 Cor. 3); but the living earth, already made fertile by the rain of grace, has something expected from it for the enlargement of what it has received.

## CHAPTER III. On considering the differences by which the works and gifts of divine grace have been varied

Having dealt with these matters correctly, as I believe, insofar as the Lord has granted, let us return to the point from which the discussion digressed: namely, to consideration of the differences [Col. 1110B] by which the works and gifts of divine grace have been varied. For the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable (Rom. 11), has always so tempered his mercy and judgment that, by the most secret will of his eternal purpose, he did not wish the measure of his gifts to be equal for all generations or for all human beings.

He helped some in one way—those whom the testimonies of heaven and earth invited to know him—and others in another way, those for whom he provided counsel not only through the service of the elements but also through the teaching of the Law, the prophetic oracles, the signs of miracles, and the cooperation of angels. And he declared his mercy to all human beings in a much greater way when the Son of God became the son of man, so that he might be found by those who were not seeking him and appear to those who were not asking about him; so that he might not excel in only one people of Israelite descent, but so that in every nation under heaven the multiplied seed of Abraham might arise, and those who entered into the succession of heirs might be not children of the flesh but children of the promise (Isa. 65).

And just as grace had been abundant among the other nations in former ages, so now there would be a sparingness of grace among the Jewish people. Yet when the fullness of the nations has entered (Rom. 11), an inundation of the same showers is promised even to their barrenness.

What, then, are the causes and reasons for these differences under the same grace? With the holy Scriptures silent, who will speak? And when the knowledge of the Apostle Paul passes in them from argument to astonishment, who could be so presumptuous as to think that these matters should be opened by discussion rather than marveled at in silence?

Let this secret, so remote from human knowledge, therefore be endured and patiently and calmly left unknown. Yet because closed things cannot be penetrated, the entrance to what has been opened must not therefore be passed by. For many authorities of the divine utterances have revealed, and the continuous experience of all ages has taught, that God’s just mercy and merciful justice have never been absent either from nourishing human bodies or from teaching and assisting their minds.

For he has always sent rain upon the good and the wicked, always caused his sun to rise upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5), always supplied life-giving breezes, and always provided the alternation of day and night. He has always bestowed abundance upon the fields, increase upon seeds, and fecundity upon human generation. And whenever he diminished any of these things, he chastised the turning away and negligence of those who used them badly through kindly corrections, so that in adversity they might seek his mercies, whose justice they had not feared in prosperity.

Finally, if we return to the very beginnings of the world, we shall find that the Spirit of God was the guide of all the saints who lived before the Flood; for this reason they were also called “sons of God” (Gen. 6), since, as the Apostle says, “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8).

But when these same people, neglecting the observance of their fathers, joined themselves in unlawful marriages to the unions of the reprobate, and were judged worthy [Col. 1111B] of destruction because of their ungodly association, the Lord said: “My Spirit will not remain in these people, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6).

From this it is clear that this people, whose generations are arranged in an ordered sequence together with the number of their years, was previously spiritual, namely in that will over which the Holy Spirit presided. He applied the guidance of his governance in such a way that he did not take away the power to turn aside into vices. If this people had not used that power, it would neither have abandoned God nor been abandoned by God. It would have been the people of whom it is said: “Blessed is the one who could transgress and did not transgress.”

Therefore, as long as it remained with God, it remained with that will which God inspired and directed. For “the will is prepared by the Lord,” as it is written. But the advance of this preparation is not always the same, nor is its measure one; for the works and gifts of grace are varied in many ways and through innumerable differences, and within the individual kinds of gifts there are different degrees and unequal quantities.

Just as among the shoots of plants and trees that the earth produces there is not one species or one kind in all of them, but each is born according to the form of its own seed and the quality of its own stock; and just as they do not receive their full beauty immediately upon appearing, but advance through definite and ordered stages until, by successive growth, they reach the complete measure of their form—so too the seeds of spiritual gifts and the plants of virtues are not born in every field of the human heart with all that they will eventually become. Maturity is rarely found at the beginning, or perfection at the commencement.

Yet the powerful and merciful God frequently brings about these remarkable effects of his working. In some minds, without waiting for the expected delay of progress, he introduces all at once whatever he intends to bestow.

In the loins of Abraham, Levi is sanctified, and with him the house of Aaron and the priestly order are blessed (Heb. 7). In Isaac, conceived according to the promise and born contrary to the hope of barren old age, the calling of all nations and the whole pattern of Christ are prefigured (Gen. 18). Jacob is chosen and loved before he is born, with no merit assisting him (Mal. 1). To Jeremiah it is said: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1). John, filled with the Holy Spirit within the womb of his mother Elizabeth, leaps for joy (Luke 1); and, so that no one born of women might be greater than he, he experiences the beginnings of grace before those of nature (Matt. 11).

Although there are also other examples of similar proofs, which we pass over for the sake of brevity, the far more common and numerous portion of humanity is that to which whatever heavenly generosity grants increases little by little, so that the causes of subsequent gifts arise from those already bestowed.

Some who have received faith are not free from doubt—the doubt that the one who said “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” knew to be present in himself (Mark 9). Nor did those who said “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke 17) sense that it was entirely absent from their souls. Some do not understand what they believe, and many remain for a long time within the measure of their simplicity. [Col. 1112B] Many, however, quickly receive the light of understanding.

But understanding itself does not have the same vigor or a similar capacity in everyone. And very many, although they appear adorned with both faith and understanding, nevertheless suffer from a lack of charity; they cannot cling to what they see through faith and understanding, because one cannot persevere in what is not loved with the whole heart.

The gift of charity itself is not always such that the recipient receives everything pertaining to fullness at once. For there is a love that can be surpassed by another love. And often love of God withers because of love of the world, unless it advances through the kindling of the Holy Spirit to that fervor which no cold can extinguish and no lukewarmness weaken.

Since this ineffable gift is the summit of all gifts from God and, in a certain sense, the life of all virtues, the other gifts are granted for this purpose: so that the faithful soul may possess the means by which it can strive toward perfect charity. Because charity is not only from God but is also God, it makes those whom it fills with the river of its delight steadfast, persevering, and unconquerable.

But those who do not know the sweetness of these waters still drink from the streams of this world. Or, even if they have tasted something of the fountain of life with the tip of their lips, they nevertheless delight in becoming drunk from Babylon’s golden cup (Jer. 51; Rev. 17). They are wholly deceived by their own choice and fall by their own will; and if they persist in this laziness, they themselves strip away what they have received.

For any good things can easily perish without charity, and without charity they cannot be beneficial.

## CHAPTER IV. That turning away from God is not the result of divine determination but of one’s own will

These matters, briefly and summarily touched upon, serve to make us know with complete certainty that no believer who has not turned away is abandoned by God, and that no one’s ruin has been arranged by divine determination. Rather, for many who already use the judgment of reason, freedom to depart exists so that not departing may be their reward; and so that what can happen only with the cooperation of God’s Spirit may be credited as merit to those whose will could have prevented it from happening.

This will can be alone in evil actions, but it cannot be alone in good ones. Although it belongs to human nature to have a good will, the vice that entered nature through an evil will is not overcome by the power of nature but by grace.

That first people of God, therefore, was governed by the Spirit of God and, through the instruction of the Holy Spirit, abstained from the fellowship and practices of the accursed and condemned people, preserving its distinction from the mingling of the carnal. God’s patience endured the wickedness of the latter for as long as the good were able to please him by not imitating them.

But when the good too were corrupted by imitating the wicked, and through the failure of the will the whole community conspired in the same wickedness, those whom one impiety had profaned—except for the household of Noah—were destroyed by one sentence (Gen. 6).

God’s goodness was not absent even from that party which [Col. 1113B] did not remain in charity and which, from its beginning, swelled with the poison of the devil’s envy. For the Lord deigned to calm the leader of the wicked people, who envied the merits of his holy brother and contemplated his murder with a brother-killing heart, by a fatherly admonition, saying to Cain:

“Why are you sad? Why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not rightly divide, have you not sinned? Be still. Its desire will be toward you, and you will rule over it.”

He says: “Lay aside the sadness born of envious rivalry and extinguish the flames of cruel hatred. Abel has done you no harm, nor has he injured you by pleasing me. I rejected your gifts by my own judgment, not at his request. For you performed a good work negligently; your offering would have been right if your discernment had been right. Knowing to whom you were offering, you ought to have known what you were promising. You did not divide rightly between me and yourself, because you kept the better things for yourself.

“Therefore this error is yours, and this sin is yours. Be still, and do not turn against your innocent brother. Let your fault rather call you back to yourself. Do not give sin dominion over you; instead, take dominion over it yourself. For by repentance you will neither advance into a greater crime nor remain defiled by that in which you grieve that you displeased me” (Gen. 4).

When God spoke these words to Cain, is it at all doubtful that he wished, and did all that was sufficient as a remedy, to bring Cain back from that frenzy of wickedness? But his persistent evil became all the more inexcusable because of what should have made him more amendable.

God certainly knew beforehand the end toward which the conception of the madman would proceed. Yet because divine knowledge could not be deceived, the deed of his will was not compelled by any necessity to sin. Abel’s safety could have been preserved unharmed from Cain’s intention and deed, unless God had been pleased, with great praise of his patience, that the wicked man’s temporal fury should become the just man’s perpetual honor.

As for the descendants of this fratricide, although they lived according to the character of their ancestor, who could fail to recognize that God never denied them his goodness, if he considers how much such long patience of God, such an abundance of temporal goods, and such a numerous propagation through multiplied fertility could have benefited them? Although these benefits brought the hardened no remedy or amendment, they nevertheless prove that their turning away was not the result of divine determination but of their own will.

But in the preservation of Noah, his sons, and their wives, in whom the seedbed of all nations was being established (Gen. 7), how many works of divine grace were revealed, Holy Scripture makes clear. In the ark, a receptacle of wondrous capacity that received as many creatures of every kind as were sufficient for restoration, the Church is figured as gathering to herself the whole human race. Through wood and water, the redemption of Christ’s cross and the washing of regeneration are disclosed. In those who were saved from that devastation of the world, the fullness of all nations is blessed. The gift of fruitfulness is renewed, and, with only the prohibition against eating strangled animals and blood, freedom to eat whatever one wishes is increased. The security of salvation is consecrated in the testimony of the many-colored rainbow—that is, in the [Col. 1114B] sign of manifold grace (Gen. 9).

These mysteries and sacraments were then instructing not merely a few people of one family but, in them, all their descendants, so that what was devoted to the instruction of the parents might advance the knowledge of their children.

Then, as the increase of human propagation proceeded, when the very multitude of mortals grew proud of its multiplication and, in proportion to the height of its arrogance, wished to insert into heaven a mass of immoderate construction, how marvelous was the justice of the divine judgment by which this insolence was restrained! It confused the single language of those peoples, consonant through mutually intelligible signs, into the diversity of seventy-two languages (Gen. 11). Thus, while concord among the workers perished through their discordant voices, the machinery of their insane undertaking was dissolved, and a timely dispersion of the evil assembly gave inhabitants to the whole world.

In this work of God’s providence, the miracles of Christian grace were being preordained. That grace would call all this dispersion back into the framework of that building in which every knee bows to God and every tongue confesses that Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2).

The breadth of this grace, to be revealed in the fullness of the appointed times, was already indicated by God’s promise to Abraham through signs that were becoming clearer. His two successions—the children of the flesh and the children of the promise—were compared with the multitude of the sands and of the stars. The old man, already alienated from hope of offspring because of his wife’s long-standing barrenness (Gen. 16; 21), believed with praiseworthy faith that through the offspring of one son he would become the father of the world, looking ahead to him in his seed—indeed, seeing him who said: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John 8).

When Abraham was justified by this faith, he had not yet received the commandment of circumcision. He was still in his natural uncircumcision, and his faith was reckoned as righteousness (Gen. 15; Rom. 4). That same faith received the seal of circumcision in the bodily member through which the seed of procreation would reach the flesh in which, without carnal seed, the Son of God—the Word of God—would become flesh and be born from Abraham’s daughter, the Virgin Mary. All those who, regenerated in Christ through the Holy Spirit, believed what Abraham believed were taken into fellowship with this birth.

## CHAPTER V. That even before Christ’s coming the nations alienated from Israel’s way of life, though they had no hope, are not therefore excusable; and how Christ increased his people through the persecutions of the good

Before this seed came, concerning which it was said to Abraham, “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gal. 3; Gen. 22), this faith was contained within the people of one lineage, while the hope of our redemption remained alive among true Israelites. For although there may have been foreigners whom the truth deigned to enlighten during the times of the Law, they were so few that it can scarcely be recognized whether there were any.

Nor are the nations therefore [Col. 1115B] excusable—those alienated from Israel’s way of life, having no hope and being without God in this world, who perished under the darkness of ignorance (Eph. 2)—because the abundance of grace that now waters the whole world did not previously flow with equal generosity. A certain measure of heavenly teaching was always supplied to all human beings. Although that grace was more sparing and more hidden, it was sufficient, as the Lord judged, for some as a remedy and for all as a testimony. Thus it clearly and unmistakably appears that, unless grace had superabounded where sin abounded (Rom. 5), even now the whole human race would be blinded by a similar impiety.

Or perhaps, as many chatter, better natures than those of the ancients have arisen in our ages, and the final times have produced souls more suited to divine gifts? Even if this were so, it would have to be attributed to the goodness of the Creator, who, in calling peoples to eternal life, would have fashioned hearts that did not resist.

But nothing at all has been changed in carnal generation, nor has a nobler offspring sprung from lesser ancestors. Rather, in the people of that time when the Redeemer of the world came, the slower the offspring had become, the stronger was the wickedness found to be.

The impiety of Jewish fury proved this. How suited that generation was to the Gospel of Christ was shown not only by the people but also by the hearts of the scribes, rulers, and priests. It was not enough for them, against the testimony of the Law, against the oracles of the prophets, and against the evidence of divine powers, to rage against the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1) through seditions, insults, spitting, slaps, blows, stones, scourges, and finally the cruelty of the cross; they also pursued the witnesses of his resurrection with the same madness.

When the apostles were flogged by the high priests, they showed that this had been foretold in David’s psalm, saying (Acts 4):

“Lord, you are God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them, who through the Holy Spirit, by the mouth of our father David, your servant, said:

‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise futile things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ’” (Ps. 2).

“For truly in this city they gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed: Herod and Pontius Pilate, together with the nations and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your purpose had decreed should be done” (Luke 22).

Therefore, to manifest the grace of God, which by his external and unchanging purpose was being prepared for the salvation of all nations, earlier times were not rejected as incapable. Rather, these times were chosen because they produced such peoples, whose fierce and deliberate wickedness persisted in doing what God’s hand and purpose had decreed—not with the intention of offering assistance but with the intention of raging. Thus the grace and power of God would be more wondrous: from such hardened souls, such darkened minds, and such hostile hearts he made for himself a faithful, obedient, and holy people.

This people did not reach the light of God’s wisdom through the wisdom of this world, but through that gift, concerning which the Apostle John [Col. 1116B] testifies, saying: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and be in his true Son” (1 John 5).

The Apostle Paul agrees with this testimony, saying: “Giving thanks to the Father, who made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light; who rescued us from darkness and from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1).

And again the same Apostle says: “For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior appeared, he saved us—not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy—through the washing of regeneration by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3).

Could the merits of the people whom Christ found, the character he subjected to himself, and the hearts he turned toward himself have been explained more fully, more clearly, or more truthfully, when he came to heal not the healthy but those who were ill, and to call not the righteous but sinners (Matt. 9)? For the people of the nations who sat in darkness saw a great light, and for those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death, light arose (Isa. 9).

The nations raged, the peoples grew angry, kings raged, and the powers opposed him; superstitions and the errors of the whole world resisted him. But from those who resisted, raged, and persecuted, Christ increased his people. Through the chains, punishments, and deaths of the saints, faith was strengthened, truth prevailed, and throughout the whole world the abundance of the harvest of the Lord’s field multiplied.

For such constancy of faith, confidence of hope, and strength of endurance were supplied from above that the fire of love, which the Holy Spirit had kindled in the hearts of the faithful, could in no way be extinguished by those who oppressed them. Indeed, those who were tortured burned more fiercely, while those who raged often conceived within themselves the very flame they were persecuting. The blessed Apostle Paul, kindled by this fire, boldly and fervently said:

“Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces testing, and testing produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

And again (Rom. 8):

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter’” (Ps. 43).

“But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor [Col. 1117B] principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither powers nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

This love, poured out through the Holy Spirit, brought it about that the world of the faithful conquered the world of the impious. It confounded the cruelty of Nero, the fury of Domitian, and that of many rulers after them through the glorious and innumerable deaths of martyrs, as Christ granted his imitators, through the persecutions of kings, the insignia of eternal crowns.

## CHAPTER VI. That Christ died for all the impious and sinners
There is therefore no reason to doubt that Jesus Christ [Col. 1117C] our Lord died for the ungodly and sinners; for if anyone is found to have been removed from their number, Christ did not die for all. But he certainly died for all. Therefore, before the reconciliation accomplished through Christ’s blood, there was not a single human being who was not either a sinner or ungodly, as the Apostle says:

> For while we were still weak, at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly. Indeed, scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person; though perhaps for a good person someone might dare even to die. But God demonstrates his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath. For if, while we were enemies [Col. 1117D], we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life (Rom. V).

The same Apostle says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> For the love of Christ urges us on, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them (II Cor. V).

Let us also hear what he declares about himself:

> The saying is trustworthy and worthy of complete acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But for this reason I received mercy, so that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display his complete patience, [Col. 1118A] as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life (I Tim. I).

Whether circumcision or uncircumcision, therefore, all humanity was universally shut up under sin; one guilt bound everyone, and among the ungodly—whether greater or lesser—there was no one who could be saved without Christ’s redemption. This redemption entered the whole world and was made known indiscriminately to all people. For on the fiftieth day after that Passover on which the true Lamb had offered himself as a sacrifice to God, when the apostles and those who were of one mind with them, filled with the Holy Spirit, were speaking in the languages of all nations, a multitude of people of diverse kinds gathered, stirred by the miracle, so that the whole world might hear the Gospel of Christ in those who were present.

They had gathered, as it is written, Parthians and Medes, Elamites and those who inhabit [Col. 1118B] Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya around Cyrene, Roman visitors, Jews also and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs, hearing in their own languages the mighty works of God (Acts II). Their testimony would also extend far and wide among those nations that are more remote.

For the accomplishment of this purpose, we believe that the breadth of the Roman Empire was prepared by God’s providence, so that the nations destined to be called into the unity of Christ’s body might first be joined together under the law of a single empire, although Christian grace is not content to have the same boundaries as Rome, and has already subjected many peoples to the scepter of Christ’s cross whom Rome did not conquer by its arms. [Col. 1118C] Yet through the primacy of the apostolic priesthood, Rome has become greater as a fortress of religion than through the throne of its power.

But if, just as we know that certain peoples have been adopted into the fellowship of God’s children against their will, there are even now nations in the remotest parts of the world upon which the grace of the Savior has not yet shone, we do not doubt that, with regard to them also, the time of their calling has been arranged by God’s hidden judgment, so that they may hear and receive the Gospel which they have not yet seen.

Nevertheless, that general measure of assistance which has always been offered from above to all human beings is not denied to them. Human nature, however, has been wounded by so grievous an injury that spontaneous contemplation cannot fully instruct anyone in the knowledge of God unless the true light disperses the darkness of the heart—though in his inscrutable judgment God, just and good [Col. 1118D], has not poured out that light in past ages as he has in these last days. Hence blessed Paul, writing to the Colossians, says:

> The mystery that was hidden from the ages and from generations has now been manifested to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this sacrament among the nations, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory (Col. I).

# CHAPTER VII. How the mystery of the calling of the nations was known to the prophets and the apostles

Was this mystery unknown even to the prophets? Did those through whom the Holy Spirit spoke not know the things whose announcements were made through them [Col. 1119A]? I do not think it should be understood in precisely that way. Rather, the mystery was hidden from the nations themselves, and the Lord revealed it when he wished and to whom he wished.

For concerning the calling of the nations that were not the people of God, and of those toward whom he had previously shown no mercy but now shows mercy, it is said in Deuteronomy:

> And the Lord saw, and was jealous, and was angered because of the anger of his sons and daughters, and he said: “I will turn my face away from them and show what will happen in the end, because it is a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faith. They provoked me to jealousy with what is not God; they angered me with their idols, and I will provoke them to jealousy with what was not a nation; I will anger them with a foolish nation” (Deut. XXXII).

David also foretold this concerning all the nations [Col. 1119B] that would worship God:

> All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and they shall glorify your name (Ps. LXXXV).

And again:

> All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him (Ps. LXXI).

And again:

> All the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him (ibid.).

Isaiah likewise announces similar things, saying:

> For in the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God on the summit of the mountains; it shall be exalted above the hills, and all the nations shall come to it (Isa. II).

And again he says:

> The Lord of hosts will make for all nations [Col. 1119C] on this mountain a feast; they shall drink wine with joy, they shall be anointed with ointment on that very mountain. He will deliver all these things to the nations, for this is the plan concerning all nations (Isa. XXV).

And again:

> The Lord will reveal his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation that comes from the Lord (Isa. LII).

And again:

> Behold, strangers shall come to you through me, and they shall flee to you (Isa. LIV).

And below:

> Nations that did not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who did not know you shall flee to you (Isa. LV).

Hosea likewise prophesies things of the same kind, saying:

> And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” there they shall be called sons of the living God; and the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be gathered together as one (Hos. I).

And again:

> I will have mercy on her who was not beloved, and I will say to the one who was not my people, “You are my people,” and he shall say, “You are my God” (Hos. II).

In the time of the apostles, however, when those who had believed in Christ from the circumcision [Col. 1119D] thought that those who were Gentiles—also called “the uncircumcision”—could not share in the grace of justification, blessed Peter teaches how indistinguishable the two peoples are before God if they come together in the unity of faith. He says:

> When I had begun to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them, just as upon us in the beginning. Then I remembered the word of the Lord, how he said: “John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” If, therefore, God gave them the same grace as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could forbid God?

When they heard these things, they became silent and glorified God, saying:

> Then God has also granted repentance leading to life to the Gentiles [Col. 1120A] (Acts XI).

The Apostle James also speaks of this calling of the nations (Acts XV):

> Men and brothers, listen to me. Simon has related how God first visited the nations to take from them a people for his name. And the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: “After these things I will return and rebuild the tabernacle of David, which has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins and raise it up” (Amos IX), so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, and all the nations upon whom my name has been invoked, says the Lord who does these things. Known from eternity is his work to the Lord.

Simeon too, to whom the Holy Spirit had revealed that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ, spoke these words concerning the salvation of all the nations that was being revealed in Christ [Col. 1120B]:

> Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations and the glory of your people Israel (Luke II).

By these and other testimonies of Scripture it is clearly demonstrated that this exceedingly rich, powerful, and benevolent grace—by which, at the end of the world, all nations are called into Christ’s kingdom—had been hidden in the counsel of God during earlier ages.

Why this manifestation, by which it is now made known to all nations, was not revealed previously is something no knowledge can comprehend and no understanding penetrate. Yet what is devoutly believed concerning God’s goodness—that he wills all people [Col. 1120C] to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II)—ought to be understood as perpetual and eternal, according to those measures by which God knows how to accumulate general gifts with particular graces: so that those who have been deprived of grace may be convicted of their wickedness, while those who have shone by its light may glory not in their own merit but in the Lord.

Along this narrow but straight path of understanding, however, the case of infants presents no small difficulty. They use no judgment of reason by which, recognizing the benefits of their Creator, they might be able to approach the knowledge of the truth; nor do they seem justly liable to accusation for neglecting assisting grace, since they are naturally established in that ignorance which, unquestionably, receives no knowledge and perceives no instruction.

# CHAPTER VIII. Why so great a multitude of unregenerated infants is excluded from everlasting salvation [Col. 1120D]

Since God wills all people to be saved (ibid.), why is so great a multitude of infants excluded from everlasting salvation, and why are so many thousands of human beings in these early stages of life left outside eternal life—as though they had been created for this alone by him who created no one while hating them, namely, that because they came into this world bearing sinful flesh they should fall into the bonds of an inescapable guilt without any guilt arising from their own action?

What could be deeper or more astonishing than this? Nor is it right to believe that those who have not obtained the sacrament of regeneration belong to any fellowship of the blessed. [Col. 1121A] Yet what is still more astounding and more wondrous is that where action causes no offense, where the will offers no resistance, where the same misery, similar weakness, and a common cause are present, there should not be one judgment concerning so great an equality; and that those whom rejection repudiates should be adopted by election.

Nevertheless, our heart will not be disturbed by this height of God’s discernment if, with firm and steadfast faith, we believe every judgment of God to be just and do not desire to know what he has willed to remain secret. Where it cannot be investigated why he judges in this way, it is enough to know who judges.

This question is not, however, so unknowable that we can acquire no instruction concerning it, if a calm gaze, guided by a sober heart, is directed toward contemplating what can be seen. For when we consider [Col. 1121B] how many infants perish among pagans, Jews, heretics, and even Catholic Christians—infants who, insofar as their own wills are concerned, are known to have done neither good nor evil—we learn that the sentence which the human race incurred through the transgression of its first parent still remains over them. Since the severity of that sentence is not relaxed even in their case, how great that sin was is thereby demonstrated.

No one would think that anyone was not born innocent unless it were also harmful to such persons not to be reborn. As for the premature arrival of death, there is no reason for complaint, since mortality entered our nature through sin and once made every day of our life subject to itself. For in some sense a human being could be called immortal [Col. 1121C] if there were a period during which he could not die at all. But corruption never shares so fully in incorruption that what is destined to decline is not always subject to decay.

The beginning of this life is the beginning of death; our age does not first begin to increase before it begins to diminish. If any span of time is added to it, it is not added so that it may remain, but so that it may pass away. Therefore, what is mortal from the day of its beginning, whenever it dies, falls according to the law of mortality; and it is never nearer to being able to live than to being able to perish.

Although the mortality of all human beings arose from one cause, corruptible nature is not drawn into one single weakness but into many. Whether through diseases, infirmities, or wounds, not only the years, months, or days of human life but also all its hours and moments [Col. 1121D] are subject to them. There is no kind of death, nor any manner of dying, that does not befall some portion of the whole mortal race.

For a grievous yoke remains upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all (Eccl. XL). Yet the burdens of this harshest yoke did not fall upon Adam’s children in such a way that divine justice applied none of its measure to them. That justice subjected them to decline according to the laws of decay, but did not withdraw from them the power of its moderation.

Nor did all people encounter every evil because, by a common condition, all were subject to all things. Rather, by varying general necessity [Col. 1122A], the Lord reserved for himself causes of mercy and correction, so that in the one common debt there might be something which the merciful God would remit and the just God would exact.

Since, therefore, God’s just and omnipotent providence continually judges all things, and no one enters this world or leaves it except by the birth and death which the ruler of all things determines according to his highest knowledge and wisdom, as it is written in the Book of Job:

> Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things? In his hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh (Job XII).

And again:

> The days of a human being are short, and the number of his days is with you. Who would dare investigate the causes of his works and plans? (Job XIV).

For it is inscrutable and deeply secret why the human condition has been varied by such great differences. One person [Col. 1122B] is consumed by prolonged infirmity from infancy to old age, and the span of life assigned to him does not end amid enduring pains. Another, vigorous with unimpaired strength, is sustained by the vigor of extreme old age. One reaches his end in childhood, another in adolescence. One is not permitted to advance beyond youth; another cannot grow even to the beginnings of speech.

Mortal nature would find these variously unequal limits of life less grievous if it suffered only the losses of the present age and those who departed this life without the washing of regeneration did not fall into eternal miseries. But since the cause of both the gifts bestowed by grace and the miseries deserved by nature is inscrutable, the very difficulty of understanding sends us back to our Creator.

When we ask [Col. 1122C] how he wills all people to be saved, although he does not grant everyone the period in which they might become capable of receiving grace through voluntary faith, I think it can be believed without impiety and understood without impropriety that these people of only a few days belong to that portion of grace which has always been bestowed upon all nations. If their parents made good use of it, they too would be helped through the same parents.

For the beginnings of all infants, and that entire first stage of not-yet-rational infancy, lies under the control of another’s will; and there is no way they can be helped except through others. Consequently, they belong to the fellowship of those whose upright or perverse affection governs them. Just as they believe through another’s confession, so through another’s unbelief or dissimulation they do not believe. And since they themselves have desired neither the present life nor the future one, just as their birth was brought about through the agency of others, so their failure to be reborn is brought about through the agency of others.

Just as [Col. 1122D], among adults, beyond that general grace which touches the hearts of all people more sparingly and more secretly, a special calling is manifested through a more excellent work, a more generous gift, and a more powerful force, so among countless infants the same election is also manifested. This election was not absent, with respect to those who were not reborn, from their parents; but with respect to those who were reborn, it was present beyond their parents, so that often the care of strangers served many whom the ungodliness of their own people abandoned, and through outsiders they came to regeneration, though this had not been provided for them through their relatives. [Col. 1123A]

In this work of grace, who but someone supremely arrogant and foolish would complain against divine justice because it does not provide the same care for all infants, and because it does not either remove by its power or forestall by its mercy every danger that can prevent the regeneration of those who are dying? This would certainly happen with respect to all if it ought to happen in that way.

It is not hidden, however, how much laziness would be generated in the hearts of the faithful if, in the baptism of infants, there were nothing to fear either from anyone’s negligence or from their mortality—since it could in no way happen that such children were deprived of baptism. Such an unlosable blessedness of infants would most strongly reinforce that opinion [Col. 1123B] of error which dares to preach, against the Catholic faith, that God’s grace is given according to human merits. It would indeed seem, with complete justice, that this should be owed to blameless innocence, so that adoption would pass over none of those whom no guilt touched. Nor would it have been an impious statement if someone had said concerning the baptism of infants: “Grace has what it may adopt; the water has nothing to wash away.”

But all disciples of the truth understand that this has been proclaimed detestably. It is therefore evident that those who are saved are liberated not by merit but by grace, since there is no doubt that those who die without baptism have perished. They certainly would not perish unless they were participants in a very grave sin.

Now, by God’s hidden yet just discernment, it is shown both what grace bestows and what a transgressing nature deserves, so that pride may not rise up against the gift, nor diligence cease in the face of danger. [Col. 1123C]

Whether, then, we contemplate the final ages, or the first, or those in between, it is reasonably believed that God wills, and has always willed, all people to be saved. This is demonstrated by nothing other than those benefits and that providence of God which he has bestowed commonly and indiscriminately upon every generation.

For gifts of this kind existed and still exist so generally that, through their testimony, human beings could be helped to seek the true God. While these gifts proclaim their author throughout all ages, the abundance of special grace has been poured over them.

Although this grace is now provided more abundantly than before, the Lord has kept the reasons for its distributions within his knowledge [Col. 1123D] and concealed them within the secret of his most powerful will. If it flowed uniformly to all, those reasons would not remain hidden.

And just as there is no ambiguity concerning general benevolence, so there would be nothing astonishing concerning special mercy; consequently, the former would be grace, while the latter would not be. But God was pleased to grant both to many and to withhold the former from no one, so that from both it might be apparent that what was bestowed upon a portion was not denied to the whole; rather, grace prevailed in some, while nature recoiled in others.

For we believe and experience this more abundant grace to be so powerful that we in no way suppose it to be violent, so that whatever is done in the salvation of human beings is accomplished solely by God’s will, even when the infants themselves are assisted through the service of another’s will. [Col. 1124A]

# CHAPTER IX. How grace prepares the will as the servant and receiver of its gifts

The grace of God takes precedence in every justification, chiefly by persuading through exhortations, warning through examples, terrifying through dangers, encouraging through miracles, giving understanding, inspiring counsel, illuminating the heart itself, and filling it with the affections of faith.

But the human will is also joined and united to grace. It has been aroused by the aids just mentioned so that it may cooperate in the divine work within itself, and begin to exercise toward merit what it conceived toward zeal through the heavenly seed: if it fails, it has its mutability to blame; if it makes progress, it has the assistance of grace to thank.

This assistance [Col. 1124B] is applied to everyone through countless means, hidden or manifest. What many reject is attributable to their own wickedness; what many receive belongs both to divine grace and to the human will.

Whether, then, we consider the beginnings of believers, their progress, or the kind of those who persevere to the end, no form of any virtue presents itself that is possessed either without the gift of divine grace or without the consent of our will.

For grace carries out its work through every kind of healing and assistance in such a way that, in the one whom it calls, it prepares the will as the first receiver and servant of its gifts. There is no virtue in those who are unwilling, nor can faith, hope, or love be affirmed to exist in those whose consent is alien to these goods.

This consent [Col. 1124C] is produced not only by the exhortation of preachers and the incitements of instruction, but also by fear. Hence it is written:

> The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov. VI).

However many terrors may be applied, fear does nothing other than make the person whom it has made fearful also willing—and not merely willing, but wise. Hence it is also written:

> Blessed is the one to whom it has been granted to have the fear of God (Eccli. XXV).

For what is so blessed as this fear, which is the parent and teacher of wisdom? In devotion to it, the will too is devoted; and through the author of grace it advances by the same fear with which it began.

Therefore, when this fear is introduced even through a kind of powerful terror, reason is not extinguished there, nor is understanding taken away. Rather, the darkness that had weighed upon the mind is dispelled, so that the will, previously perverted and captive, may become upright and free.

Thus, just as the mind receives no virtue unless it has received a ray of true light, so grace confers nothing upon the one whom it calls unless it has opened the eyes of the will within him.

In many people [Col. 1124D], as was discussed above, the will is enriched from its very beginning with the most ardent and rapid increases; in many others, however, progressing slowly and hesitantly, it scarcely reaches those advances that possess sufficient firmness for perseverance.

The Lord says:

> No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John VI).

But this was said so that we might understand that the faith without which no one comes to Christ is possessed through the Father’s gift, in accordance with what is said to the Apostle:

> Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven (Matt. XVI).

In the hearts of those who are to be drawn [Col. 1125A], he brought about their believing; he brought about their willing. For there would be no means by which they could be drawn if they did not follow in faith and will. Those who do not believe are not drawn at all and do not come; those who dissent do not approach but withdraw.

Those who come, therefore, are led by love: they have been loved, and they have loved; they have been sought, and they have sought; and what God willed them to will, they willed. To those who obey him, he gives the will in such a way that even from those who will persevere he does not remove that mutability which can still refuse.

Otherwise, no believer would ever have withdrawn from the faith. No one would be overcome by desire, no one cast down by sadness, no one defeated by anger, no one’s love grow cold, no one’s patience be broken, and no one neglect the grace bestowed upon him.

But because these things can happen [Col. 1125B], and because the descent into consenting to such temptations is exceedingly easy and inclined, that word of the Lord must never cease to sound in the ears of the faithful, the word addressed to the apostles:

> Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation (Matt. XXVI).

If he had instructed the disciples only to watch, and not also to pray, he would seem to have encouraged merely the powers of free choice. But when he added, “And pray,” he sufficiently taught that it would be a gift from above that, even while watching, they would not be overcome by the storm of temptation.

The same is true of what he said:

> Simon, Simon, behold [Col. 1125C], Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers, and pray that you may not enter into temptation (Luke XXII).

If the faith of so great an apostle was destined to fail unless Christ prayed for him, then he undoubtedly possessed mutability that could waver in temptation; nor had he yet been so firmly established in the power of perseverance that he was immune to every danger.

Indeed, so severe a disturbance shook him even after these things that, terrified by the questioning of a single servant girl in the house of Caiaphas, he was brought to a threefold denial of Christ, though he had promised that he would die for him, as his steadfastness failed (Matt. XXVI).

The one who then observed the apostle’s troubled heart with divine rather than human eyes, and by his powerful gaze aroused him to abundant tears of repentance, was able to grant this firmness of spirit [Col. 1125D] to his foremost disciple. Just as nothing deterred the Lord himself from completing his purpose of suffering, so no fear at that time overcame blessed Peter.

But this stability belonged exclusively to the one who alone truly and powerfully said:

> I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again (John X).

In other human beings, however, so long as the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V), and so long as the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak (Matt. XXVI), the unchangeable firmness of mind cannot be found. Truly perfect and secure happiness belongs not to this life but to another.

In [Col. 1126A] the uncertainty of the present struggle, where all of life is temptation and even victory itself is not safe from lurking pride (Job VII), one is not free from the danger of mutability. Although divine protection grants countless saints the strength to persevere to the end, it nevertheless takes away from none what arises from within them and opposes them, so that in all their pursuits and efforts the will and the refusal to will are always in conflict with one another.

The same most blessed Peter endured this conflict even at the completion of all his victories. For the Lord himself testifies and says:

> Truly, truly, I say to you: when you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.

He said this to signify by what death he would glorify God (John XXI).

Who, then, could doubt or fail to know [Col. 1126B] that this most courageous rock, which received both its fellowship in virtue and its name from that principal Rock, had always desired that the steadfastness to die for Christ be granted to it?

Nevertheless, the struggle of trembling was so unavoidable that a man most eager for martyrdom was indeed promised victory in suffering, but not without the temptation of fear.

It is therefore rightly prayed to the Lord not only by beginners but also uniformly by the most advanced saints:

> Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil (Matt. VI).

For to all who remain in faith and love it is granted by him that they not be overcome in temptation, so that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord. He attributes that very glory to those to whom he grants it (I Cor. I), so that although they stood by God’s assistance, because they possessed within themselves the means of falling, the merit of standing belongs to them.

Therefore, just as [Col. 1126C] those who have believed are helped to remain in faith, so those who have not yet believed are helped to believe. And just as the former have it in their power to depart, so the latter have it in their power not to come.

It is thereby made clear that God wills all people, in diverse and countless ways, to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II). Those who come are directed by God’s assistance; those who do not come resist through their own obstinacy.

Although many, loving their darkness, do not receive the splendor of truth, and many who had been illuminated become darkened, the word of God nevertheless remains forever, and nothing falls away from the truth of his promise (Isa. XL).

Each day the foreknown and promised fullness of the nations [Col. 1126D] enters, and every nation, tribe, and tongue is blessed in Abraham’s offspring (John VI). For what the Father gave the Son, the Son does not lose, nor can anyone snatch from his hand what he has received (John X).

God’s firm foundation stands (II Tim. II), and the building of the temple that will remain forever does not totter, with the truth and mercy of God set before all things. From him, what is neither denied to anyone nor owed to anyone is accomplished in those whom he has promised.

For he himself works all things in all (I Cor. XII). But unquestionably all things are just and good, for all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. XXIV).

Just as he foreknew before the ages [Col. 1127A] how great would be the multitude of human beings throughout the whole world—some using common gifts, others assisted by special aids, yet still turning away from the path of truth and life and entering upon the broad way of error and death—so he always foreknew how great would be the number of the devout who, through the help of grace and the service of obedience, would belong to eternal blessedness.

Thus, with none falling away from the fullness of his promises, he—who would neither be deceived by their progress nor fail them in assistance—would glorify above all others those whom he chose from among all.

For God’s manifold and ineffable goodness has always cared, and continues to care, for the whole human race—as we have abundantly proved—in such a way that none of those who perish has an excuse concerning the light of truth denied to him, while no one may glory in his own righteousness, since their own wickedness plunges some into punishment and God’s grace leads others to glory. [Col. 1127B]

# CHAPTER X. Recapitulation of what was defined in this second book, and conclusion of the work: namely, how God wills all people to be saved
What, then, we indicated at the beginning of this second volume, we now commend once more: when the depth and height of grace are under discussion, let us rely upon those three most salutary and truthful definitions. The first declares that it belongs eternally and properly to the divine goodness to will all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II). The second likewise proclaims that every person [Col. 1127C] who is saved and comes to the knowledge of the truth is helped and governed by God, and is guarded so as to remain in the faith that works through love (Gal. V). The third, with moderation and sobriety, affirms that the whole rationale of God’s will cannot be comprehended, and that many causes of divine works are withdrawn from human understanding. Thus, when certain things are observed to have been done either variously or remarkably in times, nations, families, infants, the unborn, and the born, we should not doubt that they belong among those matters which the just and merciful God did not wish to be known in this passing age.

This must be understood as arranged for our benefit. For since we have been saved in hope (Rom.
