VIII), and since God has prepared what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, [Col. 1127D] nor entered into the human heart (I Cor. II), just as we firmly believe that we shall see what we do not yet see, so let us patiently await understanding of what we do not yet understand. If, therefore, treacherous malice ceases and presumptuous arrogance grows quiet, then, once these matters have been properly examined, as I think, no cause for dispute remains, nor is it any longer necessary for us to occupy ourselves with interminable questions (I Tim. I).

For, insofar as the Lord has helped, it has been demonstrated that God’s grace was present to all human beings not only in the last days but also throughout all the ages that preceded them—indeed, with equal providence and universal goodness, but through manifold activity and in differing measure. For, whether secretly or openly, he himself is, [Col. 1128A] as the Apostle says, “the Savior of all human beings, especially of those who believe” (I Tim. IV). If this sentence, of exceedingly subtle brevity and most powerful force, is considered with a calm gaze, it resolves the whole controversy with which we have been dealing.

By saying, “who is the Savior of all human beings,” he confirmed that God’s goodness toward all human beings is universal. By adding, “especially of those who believe,” he showed that there is a portion of the human race which, by the merit of divinely inspired faith, is advanced toward supreme and eternal salvation through special benefits. This, of course, is done without any injustice by the most just and most merciful God. His judgment in these dispensations must not be examined with arrogance but praised with trembling. For even among the peoples of the faithful [Col. 1128B]—as has already been shown—not the same things, nor equal things, are granted to all; and before any reckoning of human merits there is a very unequal measure of divine gifts.

If we do not dare to complain about the judgments of earthly parents when they embrace some of their children with more indulgent affection before examining any of their character or receiving any services of devotion, then among masters too the arrangement of affairs concerning servants is free, and no one rightly reproaches the man who, from a household of one condition, chooses certain persons whom he will honor more kindly and instruct more freely. Shall we then bring a complaint against the most benevolent equity of the supreme Father and true Lord, because in his great household all things vary in countless differences? Although no one possesses anything good that he has not given, [Col. 1128C], not all shine with the same virtues or are enriched with the same gift of graces.

Nor can we assign this diversity of ranks to causes of merit, since grace is the principal cause of every good merit, and whatever is found worthy of approval in individuals is drawn from its resources. Therefore, just as it is impious to conceive any complaint in one’s heart about the manifold works performed by the Holy Spirit within the Church, so one must in no way murmur against that providence which presides over unbelievers. For the just and good arbiter is neither of unjust will nor of uncertain discernment, so that under the immense mercy and justice of almighty God we should suppose that anyone perishes who ought not to perish.

No part of the world is without the Gospel of Christ. Although that universal [Col. 1128D] calling does not cease, this special calling too has now been made common to all. From every nation, from every social condition, thousands of old people, thousands of young people, and thousands of children are adopted daily; and even the weapons with which the world is battered serve the effects of Christian grace. How many people who had delayed receiving the sacrament of baptism during the tranquility of peace have been driven by fear of imminent danger to flee to the water of regeneration! What quiet exhortation had long failed to persuade sluggish and lukewarm minds, sudden threatening terror extorted from them.

Some sons of the Church, captured by enemies, made their masters subject to the Gospel of Christ; and those whom they had served under the condition of war, they became teachers in the faith. [Col. 1129A] Others, while barbarians were aiding the Romans, learned in our regions what they could not have known in their own lands, and returned to their homes with the instruction of the Christian religion.

Thus nothing can obstruct divine grace from fulfilling what it wills, while even conflicts draw people toward unity and wounds are turned into remedies, so that the Church may receive increase from the very place from which it feared danger. Let us therefore turn our examination toward every possible outcome of human affairs: we shall find that no age, no activity, no generation, no birth, and no death is free from the eternal and inscrutable judgments of God.

All the conflicts among differing circumstances, and all the causes of unequal outcomes which we are unable to investigate and distinguish, are simultaneously known and simultaneously distinguished in that eternal knowledge [Col. 1129B]. Nothing there is disordered, even in the qualities of actions that do not yet exist. For in God there is no accidental movement, no new will, and no temporal deliberation; nor does his thought vary along with the inequality of mutable things. Rather, he comprehends all times and temporal things together in an eternal and stable vision, and already requites all things to everyone—he who has already made those things which are yet to come (Eph. I).

Hence comes that saying of the blessed Apostle Paul in his letter to the Ephesians:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through [Col. 1129C] Jesus Christ our Lord, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace,”

and the other things that he connects under the preaching of the same meaning. He teaches that the gift and work of grace have always remained in God’s eternal plan, and that all the children of adoption were chosen not only at the time when, already existing, they were called, but also before the world was created.

In this election, whatever human beings have not been foreknown in Christ will in no way be joined to it. For all who are to come into the kingdom of God, from whatever age they may be called, have been marked out in this adoption that preceded all the ages. And just as no unbeliever has been numbered in this portion, so no godly person has been separated from it.

For from the fullness of the members of Christ’s body [Col. 1129D] the foreknowledge of God, which cannot be deceived, loses nothing; nor can the foreknown sum, chosen beforehand in Christ before the eternal ages, be diminished by any loss. As the Apostle writes to Timothy (II Tim. VI):

“Work together with the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times.”

Against this splendid light of unconquered truth, some people are accustomed to say, without sobriety, that laboring to acquire the merits of good works is superfluous, and that it is also useless to persist in prayers by which one hopes to entreat God, if the election of Christian grace rests upon his unchangeable purpose [Col. 1130A]; for nothing can proceed otherwise than as the will of almighty God has ordained.

But those who ingeniously suppose that they are bringing this objection do not understand that the knowledge of God, which embraces past, present, and future, is not held within time. Things that are to be done stand before him just as do things that are being done or have been done. Since this is entirely true, that power which sees by perpetual and truthful vision created and future-created things, things that have arisen and will arise, things done and to be done, does not need time in order to perceive and distinguish them. Whatever unfolds throughout the ages according to an order determined beforehand, and is displayed through manifold variations, he already comprehends in the whole order that the end of this world will receive from his supreme and perfect judgment.

This eternal [Col. 1130B] and ever-tranquil knowledge imposes no necessity upon us to sin. Iniquity does not flow from the same source as justice. For since the good God made all things good, and evil has absolutely no nature of its own, transgression arose spontaneously from free wills—which it was good to make free. A mutable nature, whose preservation depended upon the immutable essence, tore itself away from the highest good when it perversely delighted in its own possession; God’s grace now heals the ruin that resulted.

For this reason Jesus Christ came into this world, to destroy the works of the devil. These works are destroyed in such a way that, in their destruction, those who are being helped also labor, since this too is given by the one who saves (I John III).

Therefore the blessed Apostle says: “And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation [Col. 1130C] produces endurance, endurance produces character, character produces hope, and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. VII).

The same Apostle also says to the Ephesians: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. II). “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.”

God therefore gives those whom he chose without merits the means by which they may also be adorned with merits. It is pointless to say that there is no reason for action in the elect, since they also act in order to be elect.

The gifts of the virtues cannot be idle, for, as the Truth says, “To everyone who has, [Col. 1130D] more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Matt. XXV). Continence is not therefore given so that it may fail to resist desires; nor is wisdom and understanding granted to anyone so that he may not meditate day and night on the law of the Lord.

What does the gift of love accomplish if the concern of benevolence does not keep watch? What fruit is there in patience if strength has nothing to endure? Or how is it shown that someone lives piously in Christ if no persecution assails him? Or is the peace that comes from God and exists with God truly at rest if it does not disagree with the world? Or can the love of God be obtained without enmity toward the devil?

God’s grace makes no one wholly incapable of being assailed, nor is the Christian army equipped on the right and on the left [Col. 1131A] with the protection of heavenly weapons so that it may engage no enemy. It is more praiseworthy and more fortunate to have been unable to be defeated while fighting than to have been unable to be tempted while idle.

That the concern devoted to prayers is not dissolved by the purpose of divine election I shall prove clearly by one testimony, omitting the rest for the sake of brevity. In the Book of Tobit, therefore, the angel Raphael says to Tobias, his son:

“Remember the commandments of your father, for he commanded you that you ought to take a wife from your father’s kindred” (Tob. VI). “And now listen to me, brother: do not take account of that demon, but ask for her. And know that a wife will be given to you tonight. When you enter the chamber, take the liver of that fish and place it upon the coals; a smell will arise, and that demon will smell it and [Col. 1131B] flee, and it will never appear around her again. When you begin to wish to be with her, first rise, both of you, and entreat the Lord of heaven to grant you mercy and health. Do not be afraid, for she was destined for you before the ages, and you will heal her.”

Although, therefore, what God has decreed cannot in any way fail to happen, the practice of prayer is not removed, nor is the devotion of free will relaxed by the purpose of election. The effect of fulfilling God’s will [Col. 1132A] has been so preordained that through labor in works, perseverance in supplication, and the exercises of the virtues, increases in merit come about; and those who have done good are crowned not only according to God’s purpose but also according to their own merits.

For this reason the determination of this election has been hidden in a secret most remote from human knowledge, and before anyone’s end it is impossible to pronounce that he will be among the glory of the elect. Thus useful fear may preserve persevering humility, and “the one who stands should take care lest he fall” (I Cor. X). If someone should perhaps fall, overcome by some temptation, let him not be swallowed up by sorrow or despair of the mercy of him who raises all who fall and lifts up all who have been crushed (Ps. CXLIV).

For as long as one lives in this body, the correction of no one should be neglected [Col. 1132B], and the restoration of no one should be despaired of. Let holy Church therefore pray, and, giving thanks for those who have believed, let her ask for their perseverance as they make progress; for those who are outside the faith, let her ask that they may believe. Let her not cease from entreaties merely because she has not been heard on behalf of certain people. For God, who wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth, cannot reject anyone without justice (I Tim. II).

---

[Col. 1131]

# ON THE CUSTOMS OF THE BRAHMANS (C, S)*

This treatise is found in manuscript in three of Italy’s most celebrated libraries—the Vatican, the Ambrosian Library at Milan, and the Medicean Library—under the name of Blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Yet its attribution to him may be questioned on other grounds as well as from the difference in style, which seems to differ greatly from Ambrose’s gravity and from his elegance and verbal acuity joined with gracefulness. Nevertheless, since the work has already acquired his name in ancient books, I have added it in this edition among the other uncertain little works that may or may not be attributed to this holy teacher, leaving the matter to the judgment of the sincere reader. We certainly admit that the work itself is not highly polished. Or perhaps Ambrose—if he is to be considered its author—was writing to the Greek Palladius, a man little educated in the Latin language and still young—for he is thought to be the man who was later ordained bishop of the Irish—and therefore adapted himself to the reader’s capacity by using a more open and ordinary style.

[Col. 1131C] Palladius, the desire of your mind, which, kindled by an immense love of wisdom, always wishes to learn new things, compels us to undertake a new and difficult task as well: namely, to review the ancestral customs and way of life of the Brahmans. Since I have neither seen the men themselves nor their lands—for they are separated from our Europe by a great distance across the earth—I shall attempt to recount to you only what I have heard from others and what I have taken from writers.

The Brahmans are called by some “gymnosophists,” and by others “philosophers” or “wise men of India” (Strabo, Book XV of the *Geography*). They live beside the Ganges, the greatest river of all India (Quintus Curtius, Book VIII). This is the Ganges which the Holy Scriptures call Phison, one of the four rivers said to flow out of paradise (Gen. II).

In the first place, our brother Musaeus, bishop of the Doleni, told me that some years earlier, when he was setting out for India in the desire to see the Brahmans, he traveled through almost the whole region of Serica. He reports that there are trees there which produce not only leaves but also a very fine wool, from [Col. 1132C] which garments are made that are now called silk. He also says that a notable stone pillar was visible there, bearing the name of Alexander and this inscription: “I, Alexander, reached this place.”

After passing through many peoples, nations, and regions, he finally arrived in the province of Ariana near the river Indus. Seeing that it was surrounded by deserts and scorched by heat, because the sun set everything ablaze—so that there was the greatest scarcity of water, and, if water was brought from elsewhere, it could immediately be seen boiling even in its vessels—and being unable to endure the heat of the sun and the burning of the land, he was compelled at once to abandon the journey he had begun, turn back, and return to Europe (Pliny, Book VI of the *Natural History*, chapter 23).

He therefore affirms that he saw certain new things, but not the Brahmans. Nevertheless, he reports that he heard some things about the Brahmans [Col. 1132D] from a certain scholar from Thebes who, as he says, had planned to travel to India for the very purpose of seeing and speaking with the Brahmans, but who ultimately fell into captivity.

This man, then—as the bishop related to me—[Col. 1133A] being of gentle disposition but wearied by the burden of a profession unsuited to him, namely legal advocacy in the courts, decided to see India and learn about the land and customs of the Brahmans. Accordingly, he boarded a ship with some merchants on the Erythraean, or Red, Sea. He first sailed to the Adulic Gulf and saw the city of Adulis; soon afterward he reached the Promontory of Aromata and entered the market of the Troglodytes. From there he reached the territories of the Assumitae. Setting out from there with favorable winds, although the voyage occupied a considerable number of days, he finally arrived at Muziris, the chief emporium of all India on this side of the Ganges. He said that a certain Indian king ruled there.

After remaining there for some time and carefully observing the character of the air, the nature of the place, and the customs of the people for several days, [Col. 1133B], he conceived the idea of crossing to the island called Taprobane. The people there, who are said to bear the name of “blessed,” are reported to live to an extremely advanced age—for they consider a human lifespan of one hundred years moderate—because of the remarkable temperateness of the climate and the incomprehensible arrangement of divine judgment (Pliny, Book VI, chapter 22).

The island is governed by four kings, or satraps, one of whom is supreme; the others are subject and obedient to him, as the scholar related (Ptolemy, Book VII of the *Geography*, chapter 4). He also said—if it is easy to believe him—that a thousand islands of the Arabian and Persian sea, as well as those called the Mammolae, obey that ruler.

There is found there the stone called the magnet, which is said by its force to draw iron toward itself. Thus, when a ship with iron nails [Col. 1133C] has put in there, it is immediately held fast and is not permitted to go anywhere, some hidden force of the stone preventing it. For this reason, he said, ships there are constructed with wooden nails.

The island has five rivers, all of them very large, by which the whole land is watered and made more fertile. Consequently, because of the great mildness of the sky, fruit is never absent from the trees. Indeed, at the same time, on one and the same tree, while one branch is flowering, another is producing fruit, and the remaining branches display ripe fruit.

Moreover, the island has dates; nuts that we call Indian nuts, both large and small, though fragrant; and also nuts that we call hazelnuts. The people of that land are nourished by fruit, rice, and milk. The nobles eat the flesh of sheep and goats on certain days, including festival days.

They say that pigs [Col. 1133D] are not found from Thebes as far as the borders of India and Ethiopia, because of the extreme heat. The peoples of the island wear sheep’s skins, worked with no contemptible skill. The sheep themselves are covered not with wool but with a fleece of bristles. There is no use there of either wool or flax, as the scholar related. He also said that merchants come there from the regions of Ethiopia and Persia and from the territories of the Assumitae for the purpose of buying, selling, and exchanging goods, and that pepper grows there and is collected in great abundance.

The people themselves are a very small and insignificant race, living inside rocky caves and accustomed, by the nature of their homeland, to move about across great precipices. Pepper is gathered together with its small branches; he said that the trees themselves are like low and tiny shrubs. He also asserts that the people themselves are very small men and have rather large heads with smooth, cropped hair. The rest of the Ethiopian and Indian race, however, [Col. 1134A], bristles with naturally curly locks.

At this place, he added, I was immediately seized and detained by the man who possessed the greatest power there. He had at once begun to abuse me harshly because I had dared to set foot upon and touch their land. They would listen neither to my excuses nor to my defense with equanimity, for they could not understand the speech of my language, and I did not know the reason for the charge brought against me, because I did not understand their words. We seemed to understand one another only through gestures.

I could indeed recognize the meaning of their words from the grim expression of their eyes and [Col. 1134B] the savage gnashing of their teeth. They, however, judging from my pallor and fear, supposed that my feelings were more deserving of pity.

Thus, after detaining me, they ordered me for six years to perform my former work, providing from the palace of one of their kings only a single measure of grain each year. After six years, when I had gradually learned their speech, I was able to learn many things about neighboring nations and places.

At last, with God’s favor, I was rescued from captivity in the following manner. Another king, hostile to the king mentioned above, accused him before the supreme emperor of that region of having reduced a nobleman and Roman citizen to the most hideous captivity and the most extreme servitude. When the emperor heard this, he immediately sent an investigator [Col. 1134C] of the case there. Afterward, when he had ascertained the truth of the matter, he ordered that the man who appeared to have been convicted of the aforementioned crime be stripped of the entire skin of his body, because he had committed an injury against a Roman citizen (Pliny, Book VI, chapter 22).

They are said not only to honor the Roman emperor with extraordinary devotion but also to fear him incredibly, as one endowed with a brilliant intellect and magnificent courage. They fear the Romans because they are so powerful in arms and strength that, if they wished, they could reach the destruction of their region.

The very man who related these things added that the Brahman race renounces secular affairs not merely by its own choice but rather as though dependent upon the judgment of God and supported by divine aid. By nature they live naked in the regions adjoining the river. [Col. 1134D]. Among them there are no quadrupeds, no cultivation of the earth, no use of iron, and no kind of tool by which any work might be done. They have, however, delightful and excellent breezes, most healthfully tempered (Quintus Curtius, Book VIII).

They always worship God, and profess that they possess a true and distinct knowledge of him and can discern every aspect of his providence and divinity. They pray continually. When they pray, however, they do not look toward the eastern region from which the sun rises, but rather gaze toward heaven.

They eat what they can find above the earth, like cattle—that is, the leaves of trees and wild vegetables. Grass is very abundant among them, including the plant which we call elecampane, as it is also among the Persians. There is likewise a tree there called acanthus [Col. 1135A]. They also have certain native trees that bear I know not what kind of fruit, which they habitually eat.

The men live beyond the bank of the river Ganges, in the regions of the Ocean into which that river enters. The women, however, remain on this side of the Ganges, near the inland regions. Their husbands customarily cross over to them during July and August. Those months seem colder among them because at that time the sun turns toward us and the force of the sun rises above the north wind, which we call Boreas. At that season the air is said to be more temperate and people more suited to sexual intercourse.

After they have spent forty days with their women, they return to their own places. But when a man’s wife has given birth and produced one or two children, her husband does not cross over to [Col. 1135B] her again and no longer has intercourse with his own wife. For, once each son has been substituted in place of his father, they abstain from their own wives for the rest of their lives.

If it happens that someone obtains a barren wife, her husband crosses to her for up to five years and performs the service of a husband to her. If she has not become pregnant during that period, he is immediately separated from her altogether. For this reason their race does not spread among many peoples, both because of the difficulty of the places and because of their custom of abstinence.

This, then, is the life and society of the Brahmans.

They say that the river itself is crossed only with the greatest difficulty (Quintus Curtius, Book VIII), both because of the tyrant Ondonitus, who infests those regions, and because of fear of a certain [Col. 1135C] animal living in the aforesaid river. They say that it is of such size that it could devour an entire elephant.

At the time when the Brahmans customarily cross the river, they assert that by divine judgment this animal is not seen in the river. They also say that enormous dragons are found there, measuring seventy cubits in length. I remember, therefore, that I saw the skin of one which measured forty-two feet in width.

They say that there are also ants as large as a man’s palm, and scorpions as large as a human cubit. Because of these monsters, passage through those regions is dangerous. These animals, however, are not born everywhere, but only in those parts that are uninhabited by human beings. Very many herds of elephants are also said to be found there.

These are the things that Musaeus affirms [Col. 1135D] he heard about the Brahmans from the scholar from Thebes. I shall now append what I read in the histories concerning the life of Alexander, together with what I have taken from various authors that is relevant to them.

Emperor Alexander, since the rule of Macedonia alone was not sufficient for him, nor could he be content with his father Philip alone, used to say that he was himself the son of Jupiter Ammon. And although the very truth of the matter could easily confirm his origin, he nevertheless asserted by certain false means—which seemed to him invincible—that his nature and lineage were otherwise. Thus, with the solemn equipment of war and with troops of cavalry and infantry drawn up, he rose from the region of Macedonia and traversed almost the whole world. Before he reached the province of Babylon, he passed through Europe and Asia as though they were small districts. At last he came also into the regions of our world, to inspect them; and when he found them in accordance with his own inclinations, he said:

“Wisdom, mother of providence, sharing some communion with virtue herself, who is the head of all virtues, abiding in truth alone, nourishing and producing every nature—whose gift is our speech of words—and searching out and discerning common knowledge and understanding, assigning to the unjust what they deserve but sparing the just: grant me, I beg, your favor, so that by these prayers I may reach what I desire, and here behold the Brachmans, men endowed with goodness and wisdom.

“For I have come to learn something from Calanus, an inhabitant of these regions, who hastened to me; and now, at his urging, I desire to learn and see everything more fully.”

[Col. 1136B] But the Brachmans said the following to Alexander in reply:

“You have come to us,” they said, “desiring to learn wisdom; and we Brachmans have at once gladly welcomed such a disposition. For a desire of this kind is held to be sovereignty in our life and conduct—the very thing that you, the emperor, have now wished to learn. A philosopher does not obey another’s dominion but himself rules; no human being has power over him.

“But since until now you have believed nothing we said—for up to the present time people have spoken badly about us to you—you have now come to us after tasting the truth. Calanus was an utterly wicked man among us. Through him you Greeks did indeed come to know the Brachmans, but you could not know them well. He was not one of us: he fled to riches without offering any excuse for himself. It was not enough for him to draw water of chastity from the river Taberuncus, nor to eat pressed milk, by which a mind worthy of God grows—a mind which he had always kept hostile to God, and with which, wickedly inflamed, he flared up in anger, turning it from the goods of wisdom to the vices of pleasure.

“None of us, however, rolls about on burning coals, nor do pains consume our bodies; rather, our life is a kind of medicine for health. By nature’s gift we are strangers to all riches, and death accompanies our life to its appointed end. Even if from time to time certain mortals, to whom a doctrine of false words has come, try to strike us with empty arrows, they cannot injure or corrupt our freedom.

“To lie and to believe a liar are one and the same thing. For the person who persuades another of falsehood does harm, and he also harms himself, because while he believes a lie he cannot easily reach the truth itself. Malicious accusation is a kind of mother of enmity and conflict; from it anger is born, and from these again quarrels and wars arise.

“Yet there is no virtue in killing a human being: as we know, that is the custom of robbers. We call true virtue, rather, fighting the changes of the air with the naked body, cutting off the desires of the belly, and overcoming all its various battles by abstinence and endurance. Therefore, first conquer these enemies of yours above all, if you seem strong to yourself; thereafter you will have no need to engage in external conflicts against anyone.

“For this reason you stir up wars against those who are outside, so that you may supply nourishment and fuel to those whom you have within. But you see that although you conquer those with whom you fight outside, you are defeated by those whom you know to be within you. Consider, then, how many tyrants dwell in the hearts of fools: eyes, ears, nostrils, the belly, the sexual organs, and the whole human body; and how many desires arise inwardly, to all of which mortal humanity succumbs and serves. Because of all these things, people are both slaughtered and become slaughterers.

“But we Brachmans, because we overcome all the wars that we have within, now rest thereafter unharmed and secure in the highest peace. We see the forests and look up at the sky; we always hear the most delightful voices of eagles and other birds; beneath the open air we cover our bodies with the leaves of trees; we eat their fruits and drink water; we sing hymns to God and desire the life of the age to come; and we listen to nothing that cannot benefit us.

“Content with these ways, we Brachmans live, and after exchanging a few words we soon become silent. You, however, say what ought to be done but do not do it. You consider no one a philosopher unless he knows how to speak. All your understanding is on your tongue, and all your wisdom is on the lips of your mouths.

“You gather gold and silver; you require many servants and great houses; you seek honors and pursue offices; you eat and drink as much as pleases you to be satisfied; you also use garments that are always luxurious and soft; and you do things for which you soon afterward feel remorse. You are accustomed to speak against yourselves as though against your enemies, even though you know that you possess control over your own tongue. Those who have been accustomed to remain silent are certainly far better, for by speaking they do not refute themselves.

“You receive reciprocal payment from everyone; you place gold upon your fingers as a glorious ornament, as you suppose. We also see you adorned as women, although you know that the very thing in which you place such great confidence, as a matter of truth, can benefit you nothing. For gold does not exalt souls, nor nourish bodies; on the contrary, through it both are corrupted.

“But we, who know the truth and nature itself, whenever we begin to thirst, go to the river and, trampling upon gold, drink water. Hunger cannot be appeased by gold, nor can thirst be extinguished by it. Gold brings neither healing for wounds nor medicine for sick limbs, nor any restraint of boundless desire; rather, it provides encouragement and a greater provocation toward some new lust of wanting.

“When that natural thirst occurs, once it has received the water it desired, it soon ceases to thirst. Likewise, when natural hunger has received the food it seeks, it comes to rest. If, then, the human soul desired gold in the same way and according to the same nature, as soon as it had received what it wished to obtain, its desire would undoubtedly cease. But it does not cease; rather, it always desires something new, without any interruption, because such a desire does not proceed from nature’s prompting.

“Finally, what among you is used for adornment and glory is despised among us. Calanus is your friend, but he is despised and trampled upon by you. Thus the person who among you was the author of many evils is honored and worshiped, while the useless person is cast away by us. The things that we do not seek at all pleased Calanus because of the greed he possessed for money.

“But such a man was not one of us. He miserably wounded and destroyed his soul; for this reason he was judged worthy of being neither God’s friend nor ours. Nor did he deserve to have security in this world among the forests, nor could he hope for that glory which is promised in the future.”

[Col. 1138B] When Emperor Alexander came to the forests, he could not see Dandamis himself on the way (Plutarch, *Life of Alexander*). For Dandamis was lying in the forest, reclining securely and peacefully upon leaves of trees, near a spring, which he was accustomed to milk into his mouth as the undefiled and uncorrupted udder of Mother Earth.

Alexander sent him a certain friend named Onesicritus (Q. Curtius, book IX, *On the Deeds of Alexander*), saying to him:

“Onesicritus, hasten to bring the aforesaid Dandamis to me, or report the reason why he refuses to come, so that I myself may go to see him.”

He replied:

“I shall do quickly what you command. For just as it is your office to command, so I recognize that it is mine to obey your orders.”

[Col. 1138C] When the aforementioned messenger came to Dandamis, he addressed him in these words:

“Alexander, son of the great god Jupiter and emperor, who is lord of the human race, has ordered you to hasten to come to him. If you come, he will give you many gifts; but if you refuse to come, he will punish you by beheading you as a despiser of him.”

When these words reached Dandamis’s ears, he did not rise from the leaves on which he was lying supported. Instead, laughing, he gave the following reply while remaining reclined:

“The greatest God does not know how to wrong anyone, but again grants the light of life to those souls whom he has released according to their destiny. Therefore, my only lord is the one who forbids murder and does not incite wars.

“Alexander is not a god, because he too is destined to die. How, then, can he be lord of all, when he has not yet crossed the river Tyberoboas, nor established his seat throughout the whole world; when he has not passed beyond the Gades of the zone, nor seen the course of the sun in the middle of the world? Indeed, many peoples have not yet even been able to learn his name.

“But if the land he possesses cannot contain him, let him cross our river, and he will find a land of the kind that knows how to sustain human beings. Whatever Alexander promises me, even if he fulfills it all, will be useless to me. I have leaves for a house; I eat the grasses that lie near me and drink water. I set aside everything else that is gathered with anxiety and perishes, offering nothing but sadness to those who seek and possess it.

“Now, therefore, I rest secure. With my eyes closed, I guard nothing at all. If I wish to preserve gold, I destroy my sleep. The earth supplies everything to me as a mother supplies milk to an infant. Wherever I wish to go, I go; wherever I do not wish to go, I am compelled by no necessity of anxiety.

“And if he wishes to cut off my head, he will not be able to take away my soul. He will merely lift away my head lying there, while my departing soul will leave the head behind, like a piece of clothing, and return it to the one from whom it had received it—namely, the earth.

“When I have become spirit, I shall ascend to God, who enclosed it within this flesh. By doing this, he wished to test us, to see how we would live in this world after departing from him. Later, when we have returned to him, he demands from us an account of this life. Standing beside him, I shall see my wrong and behold his judgment upon those who wronged me; for the sighs and groans of the injured will begin to be the punishments of those who injured them.

“Let Alexander threaten these things to those who desire riches and fear death, because we despise both. For the Brachmans neither love gold nor fear death.

“Go, therefore, and report this to Alexander: ‘Dandamis seeks nothing of yours. But if you believe that you need anything from his possessions, do not disdain to come to him.’”

[Col. 1139B] When Alexander heard this through the intermediary, he began to desire even more to see such a man, and for himself—who had conquered many nations—to be conquered, alone and naked, by an old man.

He therefore went with five or ten friends to the forests mentioned above. When he had come near him and leapt down from the horse on which he was riding, he removed the crown from his head and, abandoning all the prideful arrogance that surrounded him, entered alone to the aforementioned old man and prostrated himself at his feet, saying:

“Greetings, Dandamis. I have come to you because you did not wish to come to me.”

He replied:

“Why have you come to us? Or what do you wish to take away from our concerns? What you desire, we cannot possess; what we possess, you do not need.

“We honor God and love human beings; we disregard gold and despise death. You, however, fear death, honor gold, hate human beings, and despise God.”

[Col. 1139D] Alexander said to him:

“Teach us something of wisdom. They say that you are filled with divinity and often converse with God himself. I, however, wish to know in what respect you claim to be superior to the Greeks, and in what matter you see better than other human beings or possess greater wisdom.”

He replied:

“I would like to convey to you the understanding I have received from God, but you yourself have no place in which to receive such a gift. For your soul has been filled with greedy and immoderate desires, and I now perceive that they are contending with me, because I am trying to tear you away from them. Yet today they grieve greatly because you have not been stained by the death or blood of any nation, and because they still see human beings dwelling in cities.

“You wish to reach the Ocean, beyond which you desire again to occupy another region of the world. Then you are afflicted with sadness when you cannot find something to conquer. How, then, will you be able to satisfy your desire, when the whole world serving you cannot fill or satisfy your soul?

“You have made yourself far smaller than the world. Even if you wished to conquer everything at once and possess all that human beings hold, in the end you must have only as much as either you see me holding while I lie here or as much as I see you occupying while seated. In this respect, if we turn again to other matters, we also prove to be like you in other things.

“For just as you do, I make use of all the elements—air, water, and earth—and I desire to possess nothing beyond them. Everything I possess I possess justly. Even if you alone should possess all the rivers, you could not draw more water from them than I.

“If, therefore, you learn this wisdom from me, you will lack nothing; you will possess everything if you desire nothing. Desire is the mother of poverty, and it cannot be cured by the bad medicine of anxiety. It is always seeking everything as though it could find nothing, because it does not rest in what it has already been able to attain, but is tormented more and more by what it sees that it does not yet possess.

“You will possess immense riches with the greatest pleasure if you are willing to live with me in this way. If you accept my words, you will possess my riches. God is my friend above all, and with him I speak about these very matters; I do not listen to the words of wicked people.

“I have the sky for a roof, and the whole earth is my bed. Rivers provide me with drink; the forest supplies my table. I do not eat the inward parts of animals like lions; nor do the flesh of quadrupeds or birds enclosed within my breast putrefy there. I am not a tomb for the dead; rather, natural providence pours all fruits into me as a mother pours milk.

“I understand what you are seeking. You see me as wise, and I have become such; therefore I live as I was created, I recognize what God does, and I know what ought to be done. You, however, filled with great vanity, think that you possess foresight, although you do not know how to understand that the very things you see each day are works of God.

“I know everything—whence, when, and how things come to be. I foresee rains, droughts, thunderbolts, and storms. This is what delights and refreshes me: God has made me share in some way in his works and counsels.

“I know how an angel comes to me; and whenever the emperor fears something, I then beseech God to grant him some good when he comes to me, to release him from the fear by which he is troubled, and to inspire him with a certain confidence of mind.

“What do you say is more right: to harm human beings or to protect and preserve them? And what is more fitting for the sons of God: to overthrow everything by fighting, or to restore through peace what has been conquered and destroyed?

“Your enormous weight of gold will not benefit you, emperor, nor the multitude of elephants that you have taken from others. This voice of mine and this speech of mine will benefit you. Even if you should wish to kill me, I will not be afraid; for I shall go more quickly to God, who knows both my cause and my life.

[Col. 1141A] “Nothing can be hidden from God, whose eyes are all the stars, the sun, and the moon. You cannot escape all these, nor evade his judgment upon you. Therefore, do not destroy what he has built. Do not desire to scatter what he who made it desires to adorn. Do not sacrifice the blood of cities, nor walk over the corpses of dead nations.

“You will act far more rightly if you care for your own life than if you desire another’s death, and if, disregarding the losses you pursue, you choose true gains. Why, while pursuing one soul, do you wish to extinguish so many nations all at once? Why do you delight in the evils of the whole world? Why do you laugh while others weep?

“Yet by this very act—by wishing to remember me, who live in these solitudes—you have gained yourself. Now you neither fear conflicts, nor desire to harm anyone, nor exercise your valor in the sufferings of others, as you have always done.

“Therefore, cast from your body the fleeces of dead sheep, and do not wish to cover yourself with the garments of the dead. Rather, when you have made yourself such a person, you will honor yourself, because the soul is disciplined when it lives in deserted places.

“Choose, then, this purpose of our life, whose blessedness you will be able to enjoy more than among the Macedonians. They await you each day so that they may destroy the remaining cities with you and plunder whatever they are able to find in them. I judge that they are sad and grieving today because they still see certain nations unharmed, finding, under the authority of your name, an opportunity for their desires and plundering.

“How secure a life in God you could obtain, and how you could now live for yourself, you who still plan to seize many things and desire to slaughter many people—some of which you have already done, others of which you are doing now, and still others of which you promise that you will do.

“But when I have departed from this world, I shall see you set in the air. Then you will indeed proclaim my words, because no multitude of cavalry or infantry will accompany you. And with the greatest anguish of mind you will lament, saying:

“‘Without purpose I have wasted the life of all the time that has passed, consuming it in the honors of this world and in wars.’

“From this you will understand that you have left yourself nothing except the memory of your evils. For I know what the Divinity contains within itself, although I myself am situated among human beings; and then you will say these things to me:

“‘You once gave me good counsel, Dandamis.’

“Then all the souls whom you attacked without cause will come before your sight. Before them, how will you be able to excuse yourself?”

Alexander willingly heard these things and without any anger, for the spirit of God was in Dandamis. But, under the prompting of an evil demon, Alexander changed even as the conversation began. He therefore addressed Dandamis in these words:

“I know that you speak the truth. For, descended from a divine stock, you have been established in these regions, where you can now live without any trouble and with the greatest pleasure, enjoying natural riches and secure peace. I, however, live amid various disturbances and dangers, and I fear many even of those who guard me. More often, fear of my friends comes upon me than fear of my enemies, and every day I dread their plots more than those of my adversaries. I can neither live without them nor trust them. I live, therefore, in distress; I am guarded by the very men whom I fear.

“All day long I pursue and harass various nations; at night, sleep itself troubles and torments me, lest some unexpected enemy should attack me. If I kill those whom I fear, I become sorrowful; if, on the other hand, I wish to be gentle and mild, I am despised. I do not know how I can rescue myself from so many dangers. For even if I wished to live in these deserts where you dwell, that would be utterly impossible for me, because I can now excuse myself before God: he himself has placed me in such a condition of life and among such a class of people.

“But you, in return for the complaints I have poured out—for you have refreshed me in every respect and briefly freed my thoughts from conflicts and battles—accept my gifts. Do not refuse what I offer you as an insult to me. When you caused me to honor wisdom, you did me no small service.”

When he had finished, Alexander signaled to his servants to bring the gifts he had promised. Immediately they presented the finest kinds of gold and silver, various garments, oil, and bread.

When Dandamis saw these things, he laughed and said:

“Can you persuade these birds, which live in wooded places, to accept gold and silver and sing better than they are accustomed to? Since that is entirely impossible, do you want me to be worse than they are? Why should I accept what I can neither eat nor drink? Why should I accept what can be of no use to me? Or why should I guard something that I cannot use, unless perhaps I wish to bind my entirely free soul with chains of this kind? Why should I needlessly subject my freedom to the yoke of the most shameful slavery? I will never do so.

“Nor do I wish to buy anything, since I live in wildernesses where nothing is sold. God provides me with gifts—that is, with the fruits of these regions. God sells nothing to human beings for gold; rather, he bestows sound wisdom upon the person who knows how to receive it.

“I am clothed with the garment in which my mother’s womb brought me forth. I feed upon this air as food [reading uncertain]; I am glad to be as I am, so long as I burden my body with no chains. When natural thirst comes, the drinking of water from a stream is sweeter to me than all honey.

“But if you say that these loaves too possess some pleasure, why did you burn them in the flames? I do not wish to make the remains of fire my food, nor do I desire to turn into my food what I have taken from another’s mouth. Let the fire that baked these loaves consume them itself.

“Yet, so that you may not think that I have done any injury to you, who honor wisdom, I accept only this oil.”

When Dandamis had said this, he immediately rose, traversed the forest, and gathered wood. From it he made a very great pile. After setting it alight, he spoke these words:

“A Brahman,” he said, “has everything, and in abundance he is nourished by all things according to his desire.”

Then, pouring on the oil, and after the pyre had been fiercely kindled, he sang this hymn to God:

“Immortal God,” he said, “I give you thanks for everything.”

When Alexander saw this, he departed, carrying back with him everything he had brought except the oil, and marveling exceedingly.

Dandamis added these further words to his discourse:

“This is what we all are. Calanus, however, was judged by us to be a very wicked man because he presented himself before your presence and did not imitate our way of life. Since he could not be a lover of God, he fled from us and migrated to the Greeks. Despising our customs, he condemned himself to immortal flames.

“You claim to be lord of the wicked nation of the Macedonians; you disparage the Brahmans and order them all to be killed, believing their lying words—something no good man ought to do. We, however, know that we shall render an account of our own way of life to God when we have gone to him. We all belong to him, and we despise empty glory, which fools cannot do.

“How can you adopt our way of life, you who live so badly and always consign to oblivion the things that are good? We Brahmans, remembering how we were once brought into being and seeing for what purposes we ought to live, follow an unimpeachable course of life. For God formed each person according to the definite end of his purpose, to which that person has been assigned.

“We rejoice in desert places, sitting in the midst of forests, and we occupy our senses only with this: that human speech may never be able to separate our souls from such practices. Blessed is the person who needs no one and desires no one else’s glory; but whoever wishes to please everyone must necessarily be everyone’s slave.

“We have no need of cities, in which a multitude of robbers gathers. God has built great houses for us and granted us mountains and forests as well. From these we take simple fruits, and we drink the gifts of pure nature, its waters. Gladly restoring ourselves after labor, we lie down upon their leaves.

“How can you rule free human beings, when you know that you yourselves are subject to the power of many? You serve your own souls in everything they desire. For if you wish to possess many garments—not in order to tend a few flocks of sheep, nor merely a few people to shear the sheep and weave their wool—you require craftsmen.

“What excuse do you make for not having soft garments? Slavery is shown to be the same in small and in great matters. Whoever admires a little gold will desire much; and whoever has been ruler of a small city will wish to rule a larger one.

“Moreover, you take pride even in a small portion of perpetual ornament that shines upon your garments. When your servants have purple clothing, you arrange for your own garments to shine in another color, thinking yourselves more beautiful. If this is not considered good among you, then you are judged poor, since you admire small things.

“You willingly kill the animals that the earth has produced, although you know that they are of the greatest benefit to you. Some of them are shorn, others are milked; with some you cultivate the fields, with others you wage war. Afterwards you rejoice because you have poured out their blood, repaying in such fashion those who have been extremely useful to you. The animals whose fleeces clothe you externally are the same whose flesh burdens you internally, and you begin to be living tombs of dead bodies.

“With minds burdened by so many, and such unsuitable and contradictory things, can you receive within yourselves the knowledge of God? Leave for a little while the flesh of the animals you kill lying there, and understand what becomes of it. Can you endure their stench without fleeing? How much filth and impurity are brought into human souls and bodies—things which, since you yourselves could not endure them, are enclosed within those who desire such foods and are brought forth from them.

“The soul produces anger; these things produce vomit. But the earth produces fruits and flowers, which please us when they are sent forth with their good scents. God planted and provided such banquets for us; you have utterly lost your human senses.

“Your bodies smell like wild beasts, for you are receptacles of dead cattle. You have begun to be worse than lions and wolves. For wolves, if they could live on earthly nourishment, would certainly never feed on flesh. Bulls, horses, and deer live on the proper food of grasses, and thereby are strengthened with sturdier limbs and stronger sinews.

“Why do you not imitate these animals instead? Why do you not eat wild plants and drink water? But because of fire you prepare such banquets for yourselves; and when you see that these foods do not make you stronger than wild beasts, they are not therefore pressed by your snares. You seek out more citizens, incur the greatest expenses, and labor exceedingly over small matters for the sake of a trifling pleasure—where there is nothing except the evident destruction of those things upon which useless labor has been spent.

“Nothing, therefore, is more wretched than your life. We never drink unwillingly; rather, when thirst requires it, we fulfill nature’s necessary function from springs, which continue to flow even when we do not drink. But you, for the pleasure of your bellies and without being hungry, seek constant food and, by various arts, prepare many different dishes for yourselves. You scour the whole sea with nets; you delight in hunting birds that fly through the air and beasts in the mountains. Admiring the speed of your dogs, you criticize the slowness of wild animals and call them inhabitants of evil solitudes.

“You devote yourselves to tracking down these creatures; once tracked down, you hasten to kill them, or else you carry them alive, shut in cages, to the spectacles of the cities—not to sow crops from which you might relieve hunger, nor to provide some necessary service to human beings from them, but to slaughter, with the greatest disgrace, what is akin to you, of your own blood, and, what is more, the work of God; or to thrust it violently, bound in chains, into the bites of beasts.

“You gladly watch this too: wild animals fighting with human beings and devouring a part of nature akin and similar to yourselves. Afterwards you kill those very wild animals, calling them cruel because they have killed a human being. And what appears still more criminal and worse is that, already glutted with human blood and not yet satisfied with so many and such great evils, you desire to fill the bellies of your fellow citizens.

“Moreover, you live by such disgraceful and perverse customs that you build heated rooms over yourselves, so that the food eaten may be forced to digest more quickly for the satisfaction of your greed. You also stretch and distend the intestines of your own bodies by excessive quantities of food. You choose more luxurious dishes and therefore employ skilled craftsmen to season and arrange your feasts.

“We, on the other hand, pray God never to become thirsty. For it is sometimes only in this way that we are drawn away from the rule of truth: namely, when we give our bodies the drink they require. For this reason afterwards we raise our eyes and hands toward the rays of the sun, as though offering some sacrifice.

“But you rejoice whenever you celebrate banquets beyond measure, and you do not put an end to your feasting before you begin to rave from excessive drunkenness and lose through drinking the very understanding you seemed to possess. You burden the perceptions of your hearts with an excessive weight of wine.

“I should think that those among you who are said to be insane are happier. They are always drunk, although they have not bought wine. You, however, take excessive trouble over the price of wine; once you have bought it, you pollute yourselves with drunkenness and beat one another. At last, when you return to sobriety, you can scarcely recognize how you are able to preserve your drunkenness.

“I also hear that, after eating very large quantities, you cannot digest them; and when at last you have barely withdrawn from the greed of the banquet, you vomit everything that normally fills you. In a perverse fashion you even alter nature itself, evacuating from the same opening through which you take in food, and walking on your head rather than on your feet.

“O most foolish human beings, you fill and distend your entrails with gluttony, only later to empty your bodies again by the art of physicians. Through these things you seek the greatest shame and sickness for yourselves, and you are so insane that you wish to overturn nature itself by such treatment, which feels no pleasure at all. The end you obtain from immoderate greed is punishment, not health. For limbs continually become insatiable through diseases; torments accompany them, so that in the end you possess nothing that can be conferred upon an honorable and upright life by all these luxuries.

“Yet I hear you boast that you possess very much, although, when you give much to others, you provide very little for your own people. We therefore judge you poorer still, because you do not even give bread to your parents, while you desire to possess innumerable riches.

“You are slaves of your bellies. For this reason you have a very great crowd of physicians, who empty you by continual purging. They do this either by fasting or by drugs, so that those who were accustomed to gulp down very much wine suddenly cannot even take a small quantity of water whenever they are afflicted by the necessity of illness. Just as then you drink an excessive amount of unmixed wine beyond nature, so now you desire even less water than nature itself demands.

“We do not seek wine at all; we have water, which alone we desire, in which we take the greatest delight, and with which we wisely care for our thirst. We do not hasten to rave and become insane; we pray for death rather than drunkenness, through which human beings must perish in both body and mind. A drunk person seems to live, but as far as wisdom is concerned is judged dead, for he has lost that sublime mind which God gave to humanity.

“What of those who think themselves great and glorious? How they are deceived by false hope and empty allurements! They injure, rob, and slaughter one another with alternating hands, while they themselves ultimately await the death that is necessarily owed to them.

“What, finally, shall I say about those men—as though they were great and providers for others—who, like shameful women, habitually go out after drenching their limbs externally with oil and various scented pigments, polluting the purity of the very air with their own dissoluteness?

“What shall I say about your Stoic philosophers, who, although they are all held by the love of gold, nevertheless seem worthy of your admiration or praise?

“We also hear that you cut off a part of the bodies of your males and eagerly transform them into the female sex; and that among you there is such a person who can neither beget as a man nor give birth as a woman, and who lives only to his own disgrace and injury. Who could think even of such a transgression against the human race and such a pitiable condition without grieving?

“Moved by pity for you, we desire to benefit you as much as we can. For we detest pride, and we love and cherish the whole nature of the human race. Sitting, as it were, in a lofty place in a magnificent house, naked both in mind and body, we look upon all whom we recognize as spectators of the truth and teach them. In this we think ourselves richer than other human beings.

“Macedonia uses force against everyone, although it first suffered force from others. All who have turned toward worse things are judged shameful servants. But the Brahmans appear free from all the evils we have mentioned. No one can conquer or subdue them, because they are held by no desire or love of anything.

“If you truly wish to become wise, come to India. Live naked in the wilderness, casting away all the dignities you love and by which you think yourself adorned; otherwise you will not be accepted by us. Then you will love all those things that you have just now seen and admired. No one will thereafter fight against you, nor will anyone be able to take anything of yours from you. You will not be nourished by another’s contribution or by another’s labor; for you will be rich in everything.

“And since you write that you desire me to benefit you in some way, we do not envy those who truly imitate God in piety. We wish the whole human race everywhere to become better, insofar as this can be accomplished through us.”

*(Some material appears to be missing.)*

[Col. 1147]

## Letters of Several Philosophers, Whose Interpreter Is Saint Ambrose

Collected long ago, together with letters of many others, through the work of Gilbert, Cognatus, and Nozerenus, for the use of students.

### Thales to Pherecydes

[Col. 1147A]

I hear that you are preparing to be the first of the Ionians to speak publicly among the Greeks about divine matters. Perhaps, however, it would be more prudent for you to read what you have written among friends than to permit it indiscriminately to anyone, since it will bring them no benefit. If I learn that it would please you, I wish to be informed of what you are writing. And if you command it, I shall set out for you promptly.

For surely Solon of Athens and I are not so mad and foolish that, although we sailed to Crete to see it and likewise penetrated into Egypt in order to meet priests and astronomers there, we would not sail to you with equal eagerness. Solon himself will also come, if you agree. Nor are you held back by love of that place, so that you rarely cross over to Ionia, nor are you touched by any longing for foreign people. Rather, as I hope, you are occupied solely with the business of writing.

But we, who write nothing, travel throughout Greece and Asia. Farewell.

### Thales to Solon

If you leave Athens, you will be able to live most comfortably at Miletus, as I believe. It is your colony, and you will suffer no serious hardship. But if you abhor tyranny even among the Milesians—for everywhere you have hostile tyrants—living with us among friends will be most pleasant.

Bias has written to you to go to Priene. If you prefer to live in that city, we ourselves shall hasten there to you.

### Pisistratus to Solon

I have neither seized tyranny alone among the Greeks nor appropriated something that belonged to another, since I trace my descent from Cecrops. I claim for myself by right what the Athenians once confirmed by oath to Codrus and promised to his family, but later took away.

In other respects I commit no offense either against gods or against human beings. I order the laws that you yourself gave the Athenians to be observed and to be lived according to; indeed, they are observed better than they could be if affairs were conducted under the rule of the multitude. I permit no one to suffer injustice. As a tyrant, apart from rank and honor, I differ from the people in nothing; I am content only with the stipends that were owed even to those who ruled before me.

Finally, individual Athenians set aside a tenth of their crops—not to be consumed for our purposes, but for public sacrifices and common benefits, and, if war should ever break out against us, to be assigned to its expenses.

I do not resent you for exposing my mind and plan, since you exposed them out of concern for the commonwealth and the city rather than out of hatred for me. Besides, you did not know what sort of king I would be. If you had learned that, you might perhaps have endured my efforts with equanimity and would not have committed yourself to flight.

Return home, therefore, in good faith, trusting me, who have sworn no oath, that there is no danger from Pisistratus to Solon. You know that no one, even among my enemies, has suffered any harm from me.

Finally, if you wish to enjoy our friendship, you will be among my foremost friends; for I see in you no deceit or treachery. But if you do not wish to live in Athens, you may act according to your own judgment. Only do not leave your homeland because of me. Farewell.

### Solon to Periander

You write that very many are plotting against you. But even if you remove them all, you will still not succeed. Someone among those whom you least suspect will plot against you—partly because he fears for himself, partly because he reproaches you for fearing everything and being afraid of every possibility, and partly because he wishes to oblige the city.

It would therefore be best to abstain from tyranny, so that you might escape all the causes of fear. But if you think you must persist in tyranny, you must obtain foreign forces and auxiliary troops greater than the forces of the city, so that no one may then be hostile to you and you may drive no one into exile. Farewell.

### Solon to Epimenides

My laws were certainly not of much benefit to the Athenians; nor, by abolishing them, were you of any benefit to the city. God and the makers of laws cannot help cities by themselves; rather, those who govern the multitude can direct it toward whatever opinion they wish. For such men, if they administer affairs correctly, God and the laws are useful; but if they act badly, they are of no benefit.

Indeed, neither my laws nor the statutes I wrote accomplished anything. But those who transgressed them brought great harm upon the commonwealth, since they did not resist Pisistratus when he attempted to seize tyranny.

Nor was I believed when I foretold what was going to happen. The Athenians considered the man who flattered them more trustworthy than me, who spoke the truth.

After laying down my arms before the council house, I said that I was wiser than those who did not perceive Pisistratus’s desire for tyranny, but braver than those who feared to defend the freedom of the commonwealth. They, however, interpreted Solon’s conduct as madness.

At last, having appealed to my homeland in these words, I departed:

“O my country, this Solon stands ready and prepared to help you both in word and deed; but in the eyes of these people I seem to be mad. Therefore, abandoning you, I depart, the only one among all to be an enemy of Pisistratus. These others are prepared both to favor and obey him.”

You know how, in a friendly manner, with what cunning, intelligence, and skill he seized the tyranny. First he began by gently enticing the people; then he inflicted wounds upon himself. Going out in public and loudly claiming that he had received them from his enemies, he begged them to give him four hundred of the strongest young men as guards.

Although I resisted and protested, they agreed. These men were armed with stout clubs. Surrounded by them, he overturned the constitution of the commonwealth. While they sought, in their empty hope, to free their poor from serving for wages, all were sent under the yoke together and serve Pisistratus alone.

### Solon to Pisistratus

I believe that I shall suffer no harm from you. Before the tyranny I was your friend, and even now I am no more hostile to you than any other Athenian who does not love tyranny.

Whether it is more useful for them to be ruled by one man’s authority or for the state to be administered publicly, let each person decide according to his own judgment. Certainly I acknowledge that you are the best of all tyrants.

I recognize, however, that it would not be useful for me to return to Athens, lest someone rightly reproach me. Long ago I had entrusted the commonwealth to the Athenians to be administered on equal terms, and I had voluntarily declined the tyranny when it was offered to me. If I returned now, I might seem, through sudden repentance, to approve your action.

### Solon to Croesus

I marvelously embrace your goodwill toward us. By the immortal gods, unless I had long ago resolved to establish my home where the commonwealth is free, I would prefer to live with you in your kingdom rather than at Athens, where Pisistratus exercises tyranny by force.

But we live more agreeably according to our principles wherever equal and common laws exist for all. Nevertheless, I shall come to you, so that for a time I may enjoy your hospitality.

### Chilo to Periander

You order me to abstain from military service and live in exile, as though you yourself were going to be safe. Yet I do not think that even a monarch’s possessions are secure; and I judge that tyrant fortunate who manages to die in his own house without bloodshed.

### Pittacus to Croesus

You order me to come to Lydia to behold your wealth. Although I have not seen it, I have no doubt that the son of Alyattes is the wealthiest of all kings and filled with gold.

Nor shall we possess anything more if we come to you at Sardis. We ourselves have no need of gold, being content with the modest means of life sufficient for me and my friends. Nevertheless, I shall come, so that I may become familiar with you, a most humane and hospitable man. Farewell.

### Cleobulus to Solon

You have many friends, and each has a home. Nevertheless, I think Lindus, a free city, would be most suitable for Solon as a place of residence. It is a maritime island; if you wish to remain there, you will fear no harm from Pisistratus, and friends will flock to you from everywhere. Farewell.

### Periander to the Wise Men

I give immortal thanks to Pythian Apollo, because he has brought you together in response to my letter and, as I trust, will lead you to Corinth. I am therefore awaiting you.

You will certainly see for yourselves how courteously I shall receive you. Just as last year you came to Sardis, in Lydia, so now I ask you not to begrudge coming also to me, the tyrant of Corinth. The Corinthians will see you approaching the house of Periander, and they will not do so without rejoicing.

### Periander to Proclus

Your wife’s crime was certainly not according to our wishes; but if you voluntarily do anything against an ungrateful son, you are at fault. Either restrain your savagery toward your son, or I shall come to his aid, for he has himself suffered punishment long enough.

### Thrasybulus to Periander

I concealed nothing from your herald. I led him into a field and struck the taller ears of grain with a stick, while he followed behind me. If you asked him, he would report to you everything he saw and heard me do.

You should act in the same way if you wish to hold tyranny securely and to strengthen yourself in it: remove the leaders of the city, whether they appear to be friends or enemies. For even friends are often suspect to a tyrant.

### Anacharsis to Croesus

I have come to Greece, O king of the Lydians, in order to learn the customs, pursuits, and institutions of the Greeks. I have no need of gold; it is enough for me to return to the Scythians a better and more learned man.

Nevertheless, I shall come to you at Sardis, placing great value on becoming your intimate and friend.

### Epimenides to Solon

Take courage, my friend. If Pisistratus had been threatening Athenians accustomed either to servitude or to poor instruction, he would certainly have possessed a long-lasting dominion. But he has compelled men who are by no means bad or cowardly to serve him. Those who remember Solon’s admonitions and groan with shame will not endure serving tyranny for long.

Even if Pisistratus has seized the city, I do not expect the rule to pass to his children. It is extremely difficult for free people, governed by excellent institutions and laws, to remain under servitude.

But do not, I beg you, wander about as an exile. Come promptly to us in Crete, where no tyrant troubles anyone. If, however, some of his friends should happen to encounter you on the journey—as can happen—I fear that something unfortunate may befall you.

### Pherecydes to Thales

May you die well when your destined day comes. A disease had attacked me when I received your letter; I was covered with lice and shaken throughout by fever.

Therefore I instructed some of my close companions that, once they had buried me, they should deliver to you what I had written. If you approve it, together with the other wise men, then finally publish it for reading; but if you disapprove, do not publish it.

For my part, I am not yet entirely satisfied with it; there is indeed no certainty about the matters discussed. I have neither accepted them as established nor claimed to know what is true. Perhaps I have reserved certain matters concerning theology; the rest ought to be understood. I judge everything rather than disclose everything.

As the disease grew stronger each day, I admitted neither any physician nor any friend at all. But while they stood outside the door and asked in what condition I was, I thrust a finger through the bars of the door and showed them how pestilential a disease afflicted me. I then warned them to come the following day for the solemn funeral rites of Pherecydes. Farewell.

### Anaximenes to Pythagoras

Thales, carried from the prime of youth through the studies of virtue and humanity into old age, met an illustrious death. As he had been accustomed to do, he went out early in the morning with a little maidservant to observe the stars. Forgetful of the shape of the place, while he examined the heavens without caution, he fell into a hollow beneath him.

The Milesians report this as the end of the observer of the stars. But we, who are held by love of letters, continually remember so great a man and rest above all in his teaching; we always make Thales the beginning of our discourse.

### Anaximenes to Pythagoras

You acted more wisely for us by moving from Samos to Croton so that you might live in peace. For the Aeacids are hostile to some, while tyrants rule over the Milesians. The king of the Medes also presses us harshly unless we are willing to become tributaries.

Although the Ionians seem to be fighting the Medes for the freedom of all, they press us from every side so severely that we have no hope of safety. With what state of mind, then, can Anaximenes investigate the secrets of heaven, when the continual fear either of death or of servitude hangs over him?

But you are welcome and valued among the people of Croton and the other Italians, and all who are devoted to learning come to you even from Sicily.

### Archytas to Dionysius

All of us who are Plato’s intimates have sent Lamiscus and Photidas to recover that man from you by right of our ancient friendship. You will therefore act rightly if you remember how earnestly you implored us to urge Plato to come to you, promising that you would do everything and permit him to come and depart freely.

Remember, then, how highly you valued his arrival and how much more than the others you loved him at that time. If some quarrel has arisen, it is fitting for you to act more humanely and restore him unharmed to us. If you do this, you will practice justice and oblige us.

### Arcesilaus to Thaumasias

I have entrusted my will to Diogenes to bring to you. Since I am often ill and my body is not in good health, I decided to make a will, so that if something unexpected should happen, I might depart from life without wronging you—the one person among all who has shown me the greatest affection.

Since you have always been the most faithful of all those here, take diligent care to preserve it, both on account of age and on account of our close relationship. Remember, therefore, how much I entrust to your fidelity, and ensure that what is entirely deposited with you, insofar as it lies within your power, is honorably arranged.

### King Antigonus to the Philosopher Zeno

I consider that fortune and glory have placed me ahead of you in life; but in liberal studies and pursuits, and in the perfect happiness that you possess, I feel that you are far superior to me.

For this reason I have decided to ask you to come to me, persuading myself that you will not allow my requests to be fruitless. Therefore strive in every way to let us enjoy your companionship, knowing for certain that you will be the teacher not only of me but of all the Macedonians together.

For whoever educates the king of Macedonia and trains him in virtue will certainly instruct his subjects also in courage and uprightness. For subjects must generally become like the sort of leader their ruler has been. Farewell.

### Zeno to King Antigonus

I embrace your very ardent desire for learning, since you have undertaken to acquire true, useful, and necessary education, not the popular kind that tends to corrupt morals.

Whoever is held by love and devotion to philosophy and avoids that celebrated and common pleasure which makes the minds of certain young men effeminate clearly preserves nobility not merely by nature but also through a genuine discipline of virtue.

Moreover, if moderate exercise is added to a liberal and noble intellect, and the availability of a teacher is not lacking, it soon develops into the perfect fruit of virtue.

If old age did not stand in my way—for I am eighty years old—and if my body were not also weak, I myself would come to you as you request. Since that is not possible, I am sending you some of my companions. They are in no way inferior to me in the good qualities of the mind, and they surpass me in the advantages of the body.

If you engage with them earnestly, you will lack nothing that belongs to perfect happiness.

### Pythagoras to Anaximenes
