But you, excellent among men, if you were not superior to Pythagoras both in birth and in glory, you would certainly already have migrated from Miletus to us. But now your paternal and ancestral glory has held you back; it would have held me back too, if I were like Anaximenes.

If you abandon the cities because of an omen, they will indeed be deprived of their adornment, and the Medes will press upon them more hostilely. Nor is it always appropriate to investigate the order of the stars and heaven. At times it is better to turn one’s concerns and thoughts toward one’s homeland.

Although I am not always free from my own studies, I am sometimes also occupied with the wars in which the Italians quarrel among themselves.

### Archytas to Plato

You have acted rightly in informing us that you have recovered from your illness. You have also made us better informed about Damiscus.

As for the Commentaries, we took care of the matter and came to the Lucanians, where we met the grandsons of Occelus. We possess what concerns the kingdom, laws, justice, and the origin of all things, and we have sent some of these materials to you.

The rest cannot presently be found. When they are discovered, they will be brought to you.

### Plato to Archytas

It is impossible to say how gladly we received the Commentaries that you brought us; and we admired above all the man who wrote them. For he has clearly shown himself worthy of those ancestors of his, men of the most ancient and excellent character.

These men are said to have been Myraeans; they were descended from those Trojans who migrated with Laomedon, good men, as the traditions handed down about them indicate.

The Commentaries that are with me, about which you wrote, have not yet been sufficiently worked out, nor will they ever be sufficiently worked out; nevertheless, I have sent them.

As for their safekeeping, we both agree. No further exhortation is therefore necessary. Farewell.

### King Darius, Son of Hystaspes, Greets Heraclitus of Ephesus, a Wise Man.

You have written a book On Nature that is obscure and difficult in many respects. If it is expounded word for word, it seems to contain a certain account of the entire universe and of everything that occurs within it—things that are indeed established in divine motion. Many have become so perplexed by these matters that even those who have read a great deal are uncertain, although your account appears to have been composed correctly.

King Darius, son of Hystaspes, therefore wishes to become your student [Col. 1153B] and to share in Greek learning. Come, then, as soon as possible into my presence and to the royal [Col. 1154A] court. For Greeks, generally not much inclined to honor wise men, disdain what has been properly worked out by them, even though such works are not lacking in learning and dignity. With me, however, you will enjoy every honor and every precedence, attentive care each day, pleasant conversation, and a life suited to your character. Farewell.

Heraclitus of Ephesus to King Darius, son of Hystaspes.

All mortals who live upon the earth abstain from truth and justice, but devote themselves without satisfaction to avarice and empty glory, because of their ruinous madness. As for me, forgetful of every wickedness and avoiding the disgust of all domestic envy, which commonly accompanies distinction, I would never come to Persian soil, [Col. 1154B] content with the few things that accord with my own judgment.

# TWO LETTERS CONCERNING A MONK POSSESSED BY AN EVIL SPIRIT

[Col. 1153]

## Notice

[Col. 1153B] In the copy of Saint-Germain-des-Prés of the Scholastics, these two letters followed the three books On Duties. The subject matter led us to believe that the first was by Ambrose: it concerns Anthony, Hilarion, Macarius, Gervasius, Protasius, and the city of Milan, where it is known to have been written. Only the fact that it mentions Germans, English, and Italians caused us to hesitate. The second contains less that is characteristic of Ambrose; nevertheless, we have printed both, because we judged both to be ancient and useful.

[Col. 1153B]

## TWO LETTERS CONCERNING A MONK POSSESSED BY AN EVIL SPIRIT (C, G, S)

### First Letter

[Col. 1153C] A certain religious man, then wearing the monastic habit, was in our own time assailed by an unheard-of temptation from the ancient enemy. The same evil spirit repeatedly befouled portions of his clothing, and even pieces lying apart from him, with an unclean discharge. It was so horrible, foul, and harmful that whatever part of the clothing it touched became thereafter unfit for any use [perhaps “for the use of anyone,” or “for the use of anything”], even though it had been washed.

When I was asked why almighty God had given the crafty serpent such power over him that it displayed outwardly the uncleanness of his heart—a thing it would never have done in his external appearance unless it had first utterly corrupted his interior—whether through unbelief and blasphemy, or certainly through empty and vain glory, I replied: “The pus within the heart has flowed outward through the clothing.” Since he was far away, I did not see him myself; nevertheless, as I believe, I truly foresaw these things in him.

But if this is not so, is the event nevertheless not thought to have occurred without cause, and to have happened so that in him that filth might preserve purity of heart, and the cunning enemy might not defile it with empty glory—just as Paul received a thorn in the flesh so that he might not become proud because of the greatness of his revelations? If any one of these explanations is true—or even if it is not—will what I am finally about to say nevertheless not be true? It most certainly will. What I say is true: that filth is not harmful to the soul outwardly, if the soul itself strives to preserve purity within its heart.

Meanwhile, as you yourself have taken care to judge, I hear that some people among you say: “No one can be perfect in the land of his birth,” taking as their argument the Lord’s words: “No prophet is acceptable in his own country” (Luke 4). They must first be refuted by an argument from truth, and only then must it be demonstrated how the statement should be understood.

Let those who say this listen patiently, because, by failing to consider the meaning of sacred Scripture prudently, they almost despise all the saints. For if their assertion is true, then all who have been converted from among the Romans and live among Romans, all who have come from the Greeks and live among Greeks, all who have come from Italians and live among Italians, all who have come from Iberians and live among Iberians, all who have come from Germans and live among Germans, all who have come from Aquitanians and live among Aquitanians, and all who have come from Englishmen and live among Englishmen will be imperfect.

Look: Paul and Anthony, Egyptians from Thebes, were perfect among the Thebans. Look: Hilarion, a Palestinian, was perfect among Palestinians. Look: Macarius, an Egyptian, was perfect among Egyptians. Look: the city of Oxyrhynchus, consisting of its own citizens, was entirely perfect. And, to come to those nearest and closest to us, Protasius and Gervasius, remaining in this very city of Milan and in their own home, and practicing the life of monks for ten years, were so perfect that they became martyrs.

Or will our province alone be excepted from this rule, so that it has monks not from among its own people but only from foreign lands [perhaps “from outlying lands”]? We must therefore strive more earnestly to live according to the rule of the perfect wherever we may be, and not to turn aside from the path of perfection because of the allurements of parents, relatives, or in-laws (Matthew 19). In this way, certainly, according to the Savior’s teaching, one will be able to renounce father, mother, brothers, sisters, wives, children, houses, fields, and everything one possesses.

I say this not to deny the highest praise to those who withdraw from kingdom to kingdom and from the public world to the desert, but to show that even those who flee their homeland more through their affections than through their footsteps are blessed and perfect.

I therefore beseech those among you who deny that such things can happen to consider carefully why the Lord did not say, “No prophet is perfect in his own country,” but, “No prophet is acceptable in his own country” (Luke 4). What else should be understood there except that he said “not accepted,” that is, “not received”? He intended this to be understood of the ancient prophets and of himself, who were not accepted among the unbelieving Jews but rather despised, as Stephen said to them: “Which of the prophets did they not persecute?” (Acts 7).

### Second Letter

The apostle Paul, preacher of the almighty Lord, says: “Do not rebuke an elder” (Titus 5). But this statement of his must be observed in a case where the elder’s fault does not, by his example, hand over [perhaps “draw”] the hearts of the young to destruction. When, however, an elder provides the young with an example leading to destruction, he must be struck with severe rebuke, because it is written: “He is a snare to the young—all of you” (Isaiah 42); and again the Prophet says: “And the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed” (ibid., 65).

Such great wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we were still considering it with humaneness, we would already have struck it with a fixed sentence of condemnation. For it has been reported that on the Lord’s day, before you celebrated the solemnities of the Mass, you went to plow the harvest-field of Lator, who is present here; and after plowing it, you celebrated the solemnities of the Mass. After the solemnities of the Mass, you did not hesitate to uproot the boundaries of his property.

We had been uncertain about such great perversity, but when our son Quiriacus, the abbot, was questioned by us while he was at Caralis, he declared that he had learned that this was indeed the case.

Because we still spare your gray hairs, we exhort you: come to your senses sometime, old man, and restrain such perversity of conduct and behavior. The nearer you become to death, the more watchful and fearful you ought to be.

Indeed, the sentence of punishment ought to have been hurled against you; but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, for the present we remain silent. As for those whose counsels led you to do these things, we decree that they be excommunicated for two months, but in such a way that, if anything humanly should happen to them within the space of those two months, they are not deprived of the blessing of the viaticum.

From now on, be cautious about their counsels and carefully guard yourself, lest, if you become their disciple in evil when you ought to have been their teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any longer.

[Col. 1155]

# EXPLANATION OF THE CREED FOR THOSE TO BE INITIATED (C, S)

[Col. 1155C] The mysteries of the scrutinies have thus far been celebrated. It was investigated whether any impurity clung to anyone’s body. Through the exorcism, sanctification was sought and applied not only to the body but also to the soul.

[Note: [Col. 1155D] The exorcism is found in the Maurist edition of Ambrose, vol. II, at the end, being taken from the very ancient Vatican manuscript 82, of the eleventh century. [Col. 1156D]]

Now the time and day have come for us to hand on the creed. The creed is a spiritual seal, the meditation of our heart, and, as it were, an ever-present safeguard—certainly the treasure of our breast.

First, therefore, we must understand the meaning of the name itself. In Greek, *symbolon* is called in Latin *collatio*, “a contribution” or “a joining together.” Merchants especially are accustomed to use the word *symbola* when they contribute their money, which is as though packed together into one sum from the contributions of individuals and preserved intact and inviolate, so that no one may attempt to defraud the contribution or the business. Indeed, among merchants there is this custom: if anyone commits fraud, he is rejected as a fraudster.

Thus the holy apostles, coming together as one, composed a brief summary of faith, so that we might grasp the whole sequence of faith briefly. Brevity is necessary, so that it may always be retained in memory and recollection.

I know that especially in the regions of the East, what was first handed down by our elders has been affected, as it were, by fraud on one side and diligence on the other—the heretics by fraud, the Catholics by diligence. While the former attempt to creep in deceitfully, they have added what is unnecessary; while the latter strive to guard against fraud, they seem, through a kind of piety and carelessness, to have gone beyond the limits set by the elders.

[Note: [Col. 1156D] The same statement occurs in Rufinus, Commentary on the Creed. [Col. 1156C]]

Therefore the holy apostles came together and composed the creed briefly. Sign yourselves. Having done this, and with the creed recited, the divinity of the eternal Trinity is most clearly contained in this creed through one operation: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the venerable Trinity.

Our faith is such that we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit with equal mode and dignity. For where there is no distinction of majesty, there ought to be no distinction of faith.

I have often reminded you that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, alone assumed this flesh in bodily form. He became man through the reality of this body; but he possesses the singular privilege of his generation. For he was not born from male seed, but, as Scripture says, was generated by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary.

You recognize the prerogative of the heavenly author. He became man in order to assume our weaknesses in his flesh, but he came with the privilege of eternal majesty. Let us therefore recite the creed. (After saying this, he completed what follows.)

This is what divine Scripture contains. Should we presumptuously go beyond the limits of the apostles? Are we more cautious than the apostles?

“But,” you say to me, “heresies later emerged.” What of it? Consider the simplicity; consider the purity.

When the Patripassians arose, the Catholics thought that “invisible and impassible” should also be added in this respect, as though the Son of God had been visible and passible. If he was visible in the flesh, that flesh was visible, not the divinity. Finally, listen to what he says: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” He says this in his passion. Our Lord Jesus Christ spoke in this way according to his humanity, as though the flesh were saying to the divinity: “Why have you forsaken me?”

So perhaps our elders were physicians and wished to add health to sickness; but medicine is not needed. If medicine was not necessary at the time when the grave sickness of certain heretics’ souls existed, and if it then had to be sought, it is not needed now. Why? The faith is whole against the Sabellians. The Sabellians were especially excluded from the regions of the West.

From that remedy the Arians invented a kind of accusation against us. Since we hold the creed of the Roman Church, they judged and said that we regarded the almighty Father as visible and passible: “You see that they have the creed in such a form as to designate the Son as visible and passible.”

What, then? Where the faith is whole, the apostles’ commands are sufficient. The safeguards of priests are not required. Why? Because weeds are mixed with the wheat.

[Note: [Col. 1158D] Rufinus, in the passage cited, relates that the Roman creed had not been enlarged by any additions and was customarily recited publicly by those being initiated; nevertheless, he follows his own creed of Aquileia. [Col. 1158D]]

Here begins the creed: “I believe in the one Lord.” Say it this way: “His only Son.” Is he not the one Lord? There is one God and one Lord. But so that they may not slander us and say that there is one person [Note: [Col. 1158D] Manuscript: “one passion”], let us also say, “His only Son, our Lord.”

From the divinity of the Father and the Son we come to his incarnation. He was born and buried; you have his passion and burial. “On the third day from the dead”: you have his resurrection. He ascended and sits at the right hand of the Father.

You see, therefore, that the flesh could diminish nothing of the divinity; rather, from the incarnation a great triumph was won for Christ. For how is it that, having risen from death, he sits at the right hand of the Father? It is as though he had brought back to the Father the fruit of a good will.

You have two things: he rose from death; he sits at the right hand of the Father. Therefore the flesh could bring no detriment to the glory of the divinity. You have two possibilities: either our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the prerogative of his divinity and the substance of his generation, sits at the right hand of the Father and rose from death; or else, as the eternal conqueror who acquired the good kingdom for God the Father, he claimed for himself the prerogative of his victory by sitting at the Father’s right hand.

[Note: [Col. 1158D] The words omitted in the manuscript are enclosed in brackets.]

“[To judge the living] and the dead.” Listen, human being. You ought indeed to believe quickly. Faith itself should proceed from love. Whoever loves takes nothing away; a friend who loves his friend takes nothing away; whoever loves the Lord must much less detract from him.

Why do I say “he sits”? Whoever loves has something to fear. And why “the dead”? He himself is to judge us. Beware, therefore, of detracting from the one whom you will have as judge.

Why this mystery? Is there not one judgment of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Is there not one will? Is there not one majesty? Why are you told that the Son will judge, unless so that you may understand that nothing is to be taken away from the Son?

Therefore, consider: you will believe in the Father, and you will believe in the Son. And what comes third? “And in the Holy Spirit.” Whatever sacraments you receive, you will receive them in this Trinity. Let no one deceive you. You see, therefore, that the venerable Trinity possesses one operation, one sanctification, and one majesty.

Understand carefully how we believe in the author, so that you may not perhaps say: “But it also says ‘in the Church’; it also says ‘in the forgiveness of sins’; it also says ‘in the resurrection.’”

What then? The case is the same. We believe in Christ, and we believe in the Father, just as we believe in the Church, in the forgiveness of sins, and in the resurrection of the flesh.

What is the reason? Whoever believes in the author also believes in the work of the author. Finally, lest you think this is our own invention, receive the testimony: “If you do not believe me, believe at least the works.” So this is what you have.

Now your faith will shine forth more fully if you judge that true and complete faith must be directed toward the work of your author.

“In the holy Church and in the forgiveness of sins.” Believe, therefore, in faith, because all your sins are forgiven. Why have you read in the Gospel, when the Lord says: “Your faith has saved you”?

“Resurrection.” Believe that the flesh also will rise. For what need was there for Christ to assume flesh? What need was there for Christ to taste death, undergo burial, and rise again, unless it was for the sake of your resurrection? The whole of this mystery concerns your resurrection.

If Christ has not risen, our faith is futile; but because he has risen, our faith is therefore firm.

I said, then, that the apostles composed the creed. If merchants and contributors of money have this law, that anyone who violates his contribution is regarded as wicked and disqualified, we must take much greater care lest anything be taken away from the creed of our elders.

For you have in the book of the Apocalypse of John—which is counted among the canonical books and is especially useful for the foundation of faith—an explicit mention of our almighty Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 1158D] Although this occurs in other places as well, in that book itself it says: “If anyone adds to or takes away from it, he brings judgment and punishment upon himself.”

Just as nothing should be taken away from or added to the Scriptures of a single apostle, so we ought to take nothing away from or add anything to the creed that we received as handed down and composed by the apostles.

This is the creed held by the Roman Church, where Peter, the first of the apostles, sat and brought the common judgment.

Thus, just as there are twelve apostles, so there are twelve articles. Sign yourselves. Having done this:

“I believe [in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary].” [Col. 1159A]

You have the almighty Father; you have the only Son; you have the incarnation of the Son, as I said. “He suffered and was buried under Pontius Pilate”: you have his passion and burial. Behold four articles.

Let us examine the others. “On the third day [he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will come to judge the living] and the dead.” Behold another four articles—that is, eight articles.

Let us examine the remaining four articles. “And in the Holy Spirit, [the holy Church, the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh].” Behold: corresponding to the twelve apostles, twelve articles have been included. [Col. 1159B]

[Col. 1160A] I wish you to be warned of this: the creed ought not to be written down, because you must hand it back. Let no one write it down. Why? We received it in such a way that it ought not to be written.

“But what then? It must be retained.”

You say to me: “How can it be retained if it is not written down?”

It can be retained more effectively if it is not written down. Why? Listen. What you write down, you read almost casually and do not begin to review through daily meditation; but what you do not write down, you fear losing, and you begin to review it every day.

This is a great protection. Mental and bodily stupors arise, as does the adversary’s temptation, which never rests; some trembling of the body and weakness of the stomach may occur. Recite the creed within yourself; above all, recite it within your own heart. Make it a habit, so that you may recite it even when alone, and more firmly where the faithful are.

[Col. 1159]

# LETTER ON FAITH TO THE BLESSED PRIEST JEROME (C, S)

[Col. 1159B] Apostolic authority declares that without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God.

We therefore faithfully believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one true and only God in essential substance, and a holy and undivided personal eternity.

The divinity of Christ is equal to the Father in all things and consubstantial with him, and the power of the begetter and the begotten is everlasting and, beyond time, one and the same. For he is the creator of all natures, since all things were made through him and without him nothing was made. He is above all that he created, and what he made was never not subject to its creator. It is proper and eternal to him that he is from no one other than the Father and that he is no other than what the Father is.

If power had been added to him, if his dignity had been illuminated, if his sublimity had been exalted, he would have been lesser than the one who advanced him, and he would not have possessed the riches of the nature whose generosity he required.

In the fullness of time, which had been appointed by the eternal plan and promised through the prophetic meaning of words and deeds, he became the Son of Man—not through a change of his substance, but through the assumption of our nature—and came to seek and save what had perished.

He did not come through a local approach or bodily movement, as though he were to become present from a place where he had been absent or were to withdraw from the place from which he had come. Rather, he came through becoming visible and being revealed to all who saw him.

He assumed human flesh and a human soul in the womb of his virgin mother, so that, while remaining in the form of God, he might assume the form of a servant and come in the likeness of sinful flesh. Through this he did not diminish divine things by human things, but increased human things through divine things.

Such was the condition of all mortals, derived from their first parents, that, since original sin passed down through their descendants, no one could escape the punishment of condemnation unless the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

What belongs to the divinity the flesh did not diminish; what belongs to the flesh the divinity did not destroy. He is both eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; inviolable in his own power, passible in our weakness.

In his divinity alone, and together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, he is of one and the same nature; in the assumption of humanity, however, he is not of one substance but of one and the same person. Thus the same one was rich in poverty, almighty in submission, impassible in punishment, and immortal in death.

For the Word was not changed into flesh or into soul in any part of himself, since the simple and unchangeable nature of the divinity always exists wholly in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase. It thus makes the nature it assumed blessed, so that, glorified, it remains in the one who glorifies it.

Why, then, should it seem inappropriate or impossible that the Word, flesh, and soul should be one man, Christ, and one Son of God and man, if flesh and soul, which belong to dissimilar natures, constitute one person even without the incarnation of the Word?

[Note: [Col. 1159D] Ambrose speaks most correctly of a person, not of a nature. For if “one nature of man” is asserted, as many customarily speak, the Monophysites make remarkable misuse of this example to affirm one nature in Christ. In reality, there are two natures, or substances, in man: the spiritual, namely the soul, and the material, namely the flesh. On this example, see the excellent teaching of Athanasius, Maurist edition, vol. I, p. 1279. [Col. 1160D]]

It is much easier for the power of the divinity to establish this union of itself with humanity than for the weakness of humanity alone to establish it within its own substances.

Therefore the Word was not changed into flesh, nor flesh into the Word; rather, both remain in one, and one is in both: not divided by difference, not confused by mixture. The one is not from the Father and the other from the mother; rather, the same one is from the Father before every beginning, and the same one at the end of the ages, in order to be mediator between God and human beings: the man Jesus Christ, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells.

The Lord’s birth according to the flesh, although it possesses certain distinctive features by which it transcends the beginnings of human condition—whether because he alone was conceived and born from an inviolate virgin without sexual desire, or because he was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that fertility gave birth while virginity remained—nevertheless had flesh of no other nature than ours.

Nor was a soul breathed into him at its beginning that differed from the souls of other human beings; it excelled not through difference of kind but through sublimity of virtue.

He had nothing in his flesh that was hostile to him. No discord of desires generated a conflict of pleasures. His bodily senses were vigorous without the law of sin, and the truth of his affections was governed by divinity and mind. He was not tempted by enticements and did not yield to vices.

He was truly man, truly united to God: not drawn down from heaven according to a soul that had previously existed, nor created out of nothing according to the flesh. He bore the same person in the divinity of the Word and possessed, together with us, a common nature in body and soul.

For he would not be the mediator of God and human beings unless he were one and the same God and one and the same human being—both one and true—in both.

The greatness of the subject invites us to a wide-ranging discussion, but in the presence of your learning there is no need for lengthy labor. Bethlehem is before you, where the life-bringing birth of the Virgin shone forth; wrapped in swaddling clothes and received in the narrow space of an inn, the manger welcomed him.

Before you is the infancy of the Savior, proclaimed by angels and adored by magi, which Herod persecuted after the death of many infants. Before you, I say, is the place where his childhood grew, where his youth matured, and where, through bodily development, the nature of true humanity advanced into a perfect man—not without food to relieve hunger, not without sleep for rest, not without tears of compassion, and not without fear and trembling.

For one and the same person, in the form of God, works miracles of great power.

In order to restore the life of all, he took upon himself the cause of all. By paying on behalf of all the force of the ancient bond, which he alone among all people did not owe, he canceled it, so that, just as through the guilt of one all had become sinners, so through the innocence of one all might become innocent.

Thus justice remained in the human being, in whom human nature had been assumed. For there is no way of understanding this outside the truth of our body.

The original bonds of our captivity could not be loosed unless there existed a human being of our race and nature, whom the sentence against the first parents did not bind, and who would erase the deadly bond with his spotless blood, as had been divinely ordained from the beginning.

Thus, in the fullness of the appointed time, the promise, signified in many ways and long awaited, came to fulfillment; and what had always been announced through continuous signs could not be doubtful.

The diverse impiety of heretics is displayed in a great sacrilege when, under the appearance of honoring the divinity, they deny the truth of Christ’s human flesh. They consider it religious to believe that what saves is not true in our Savior, although, according to the promise that preceded all the ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ in such a way that, unless the Word deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved.

It is yours, excellent father Jerome, to explain the mystery of the faith more clearly and to confound heretical perversity. I ask and entreat only this: remember me frequently, unconquerable soldier of Christ. Amen.

# HYMNS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT AMBROSE

[Col. 1161]

## Preface to the Following Hymns Attributed to Saint Ambrose

[Col. 1161] We found these hymns in a hymnal recently revised at Halle. The distinguished German editor, named Adalbert Daniel, after giving a general account of several matters concerning his edition of the *Thesaurus Hymnologicus*, adds the following. Since it may contribute somewhat to understanding the annotations attached to Ambrose’s hymns, it is useful to reproduce it here.

[Col. 1161C] To say a few words about the annotations as well, in accordance with the purpose of our undertaking we excluded those that concern the author and age of the hymns, as well as those of a lexicographical, metrical, or grammatical nature, because all these matters are treated in the glossary.

The highly revered Nickelius encouraged us to illustrate the hymns with ascetical annotations. We would gladly have undertaken this task if it had been possible for us. But unless we had been obliged to devote ourselves above all to brevity, we would have explained many matters concerning the history and doctrines of the Church more fully and extensively.

It is not yet clear to us what method we shall follow in this respect in the next volume, since we do not yet know how much favor our work will win. [Col. 1162C]

It will not be out of place to relate from which sources we drew and what aids we used. Anyone skilled in these matters will easily understand that access to more sources has been opened to us than we could have expected. This would scarcely, or perhaps not at all, have happened had we not been assisted in a remarkable way by the kindness and generosity of many men.

I do not doubt that there will be some to whom the number of manuscript codices seems insufficient; and I myself am especially sorry that I was not permitted to inspect and handle with careful attention the oldest parchment manuscripts in the libraries of Vienna and Munich.

But, unless I am mistaken, many people give too much weight to manuscripts in establishing the correct text of hymns. For the diocesan breviaries printed around the year 1500 were produced by the most careful comparison with the manuscript codices then existing in the dioceses, so that they seem to me, if not to surpass those manuscripts in authority, at least to equal them.

The same applies to ancient and more recent collections of hymns: Cassander examined many German codices, Clichtoveus French ones, and Thomasius Italian ones.

# I. CODICES

1. In the autumn of 1839, while I was staying in Dresden, I visited the breviaries preserved in the Royal Library, when the most welcome opportunity for this undertaking presented itself.

I first went to the breviary which the manuscript catalogue lists under the title A 147, since I had already learned of it from Falckenstein’s precise account. But it is rather a book of hours, since it contains hours of the Blessed Virgin, of the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

Its age certainly does not exceed the fourteenth or fifteenth century; as for its origin, it seems to derive either from the diocese of Metz itself or from some neighboring diocese. The marginal paintings with which the codex is decorated deserve the attention of anyone skilled in these matters. (D. 1.)

2. In the same library I found another breviary, listed in the catalogue under A 228, from the books of Crusius. This breviary, which was used by the Dominican order, appears from the commemoration of certain saints, such as Saint Athala, to have originated in the upper Rhineland.

Nevertheless, I am persuaded that this codex scarcely goes beyond the beginning of the fifteenth century. (D. 2.)

3. Nearly the same account applies to the paper codex that was once kept in the library of the monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt and is now mine. In this codex there is a *Gloss on the Hymns*, which contributes almost nothing toward explaining the hymns. A commentary on the *Summula* of Raymond has been added to this gloss. (E.)

4. We owe the oldest of the codices we inspected to the generosity of Rambach, a most learned man. He was the first to pave the way in hymnology—a distinction that will always belong to him and endure—and he also rendered us the greatest service by supplying us with materials both exceedingly rare and most desirable for our *Thesaurus*.

The codex in question comes from the library of the illustrious city of Hamburg. Staphorst (*Hamburg Church History*, vol. I, pp. 310 ff.) assigned it to the tenth and even the ninth century.

Rambach, however, in *Anthologia*, I, p. 23, since the codex mentions Saint Catherine, rightly determined that it should not be assigned later than the thirteenth century.

But in breviaries of this kind, two parts seem to require distinction: one primitive, the other containing additions from a later period. The same appears to be true of this codex. For the hymns for the feast of Saint Catherine and for the Conception of Mary were copied in letters indicating a later age; and since it is also noteworthy that hymns for the feast of Corpus Christi are not yet found, I do not know whether what we have mentioned should be assigned specifically to the twelfth or even the eleventh century. (H.)

5. I owe to the generosity of Frejer, a most distinguished man, a paper diocesan breviary from the library of the Reverend Chapter of the cathedral at Merseburg.

Although this manuscript scarcely extends beyond the fourteenth century, it contains many distinctive features. Among them are the small number of hymns and octaves, since even the octaves of Epiphany and the Assumption are entirely absent. (M.)

6. Among the manuscripts possessed by Fr. Junius, well known for his tireless labor, and later acquired by the Bodleian Library at Oxford, there is also an ancient German translation of twenty-six hymns.

Several learned men engaged in the study of the Old German language have used this codex. Hickes had already published the first, fourth, fifth, and last hymns; all the others were brought to light through the care and industry of Jacob Grimm, a man endowed with an extraordinary abundance of learning, in whom our homeland now takes pride (*Interpretation in the German Language of Twenty-Six Hymns of the Ancient Church*, now first published, Göttingen, 1830).

Since both the Latin hymns and the German version contained in that manuscript belong to the eighth century—a point that the very learned editor sufficiently confirmed with suitable arguments in his prolegomena—there is no need to explain how highly we value this book of Grimm’s. (O.)

7. When I heard that the library of the University of Würzburg preserved extremely ancient breviaries, I trusted in the generosity of Ludwig, a most learned man to whose care and protection that library was entrusted, and of Reuss, a most distinguished man whose kindness I cannot praise sufficiently.

With all due respect, I ventured to ask the university senate to permit the oldest of those codices to be sent to me. Since it graciously granted my request, I was able to inspect two very ancient breviaries, one of which comes from the celebrated monastery of Ebrach and, unless I am mistaken, was written in the thirteenth century. (W. 1.)

8. The second is a diocesan breviary from the library of the Benedictines, whose monastery venerated Saint Stephen as its patron. Since several later feast days relating to the cult of Mary are absent from it, and the feast of Corpus Christi contains only one hymn, I have no doubt that the codex was written toward the end of the thirteenth century. (W. 2.)

## II. BREVIARIES

### Diocesan Breviaries

[Col. 1164D]

1. *The Book of Canonical Hours, arranged according to the order of the Rubric of the Church of Halberstadt, most diligently revised, corrected and emended, and collated with the most accurate exemplars. Printed by Georg Stuchs at Nuremberg. In the year 1515 of the Virgin’s childbirth. It happily ends on the Ides of November. It is in my possession.* (III.)

2. *The Book of Canonical Hours according to the order of the rubric of the holy Church of Magdeburg, revised with the greatest care and corrected anew, printed in the workshop of Georg Stuchs, citizen of Nuremberg. It ends on the twenty-first day of October, in the year 1514 from the glorious Virgin’s childbirth.* [Col. 1165A] From the library of the Halle Orphanage. (Mgd.)

3. A Meissen breviary printed about the year 1510. From the library of the University of Halle. (Msn.)

4. *The summer part of the Viaticum according to the rubric of the Church of Merseburg.* At the end of the book: *This summer part of the Merseburg Viaticum has been completed and printed with vigilant care, through the art and skill of the industrious Melchior Lotter, fellow citizen of the ducal town of Leipzig, in the year 1504 of the saving Incarnation, on Thursday, the fifteenth day of August.* From the library of Saint Mary’s in Halle. (Msb.)

5. *The Breviary of the Church of Passau, produced with marvelous skill in its formation and with the most watchful care of the capable man Peter Lichtenstein, at the expense, however, of the booksellers Leonardo and Luca Allantse, brothers, of Vienna.* [Col. 1165B] It was completed at Venice in the saving year 1515, on 25 May, while the divine and ever august Maximilian I was happily holding the imperial scepter. This breviary was kindly supplied by the learned Hertelius from the library of the Zwickau Gymnasium. (Pt.)

6. The Breviary of the Church of Salzburg, which is in my possession. I greatly regret that it is mutilated at the beginning and the end, and that the printer’s name and the year are missing. It is, however, splendidly printed. (Sl.)

7. *This breviary, arranged according to the true rubrics of the sacred Church of Minden, after diligent preliminary labor and with the attentive care of the industrious Georg Stachs of Sulzbach, was splendidly produced and ends in the year 1490, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January.* It was kindly sent to me, together with other books [Col. 1165C] from the library of the University of Göttingen, which is presided over with the greatest kindness and generosity by the learned Beneke, by the learned men Havemann and Ranke, whom I honor with the highest respect. (Md.)

8. A breviary carefully revised according to the rubric of the Church of Havelberg. At the end: *At Leipzig, in the workshop of Melchior Lotter, much more accurately and correctly than before, in the year 1518 from the Christian Nativity.* It is in my possession. (Hv.)

9. A breviary of the Canonical Hours to be recited according to the custom of the Severian College of Erfurt. At the end: *This breviary has been printed and completed in the noble and famous city of Mainz, the first inventor of the art of printing, by the honorable man Johann Schöffer, citizen of Mainz, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, in the year 1518 of the Lord’s Incarnation.* I possess the book myself. (Ef.)

10. I also possess a very rare little book printed in France: *Heures à l’usage de Lengres au long sans rien requerir* [“Hours for the use of Langres, in full, without requiring anything”]. Printed at Troyes by Jean le Coq (without year or folio numbers), which contains hymns for the principal feasts throughout the year. We have chosen to designate the book by the letters Lg., since those hymns were undoubtedly in use in the diocese of Langres. (Lg.)

11. *Hymns of the Church, excerpted from the Roman, Sarum and York Breviaries and from elsewhere.* Oxford, Z. H. Parker, 1838. The hymns from the Roman Breviary, corrected, were outside the scope of our undertaking; but the hymns taken from the Sarum and York Breviaries were most welcome. For just as the little book mentioned above could reveal which hymns had been most commonly used among the French, so this one reveals which were used among the English. (Sb. Eb.)

### Monastic Breviaries

12. We had access to many breviaries belonging to the Order of Saint Francis. The oldest is that in the Halle library of Saint Mary’s, which we designate by the letters Fr. At the end one reads: *The breviary according to the custom of the Roman Curia ends. Printed at Venice by Franciscus Renner of Heilbronn, in the year of the Lord 1481.*

Another (Fr. 2) is in my own library. At the end one reads: *The breviary according to the Roman rite ends. Printed at Venice by the art and expense of Andrea de Torresani of Asola, on 14 March 1495; happily completed.*

In addition, we acquired several others differing scarcely at all from these. The first: *The breviary according to the order of the holy Roman Church, revised with great diligence and corrected with faithful care.* It was printed in the royal German city of Nuremberg, very famous, through the art and expense of Anthony Koberger, a citizen of that city, in the year 1486, on the fourth day before the Ides of December. It is in my possession.

The second: *And thus ends the breviary according to the use of the Roman Curia, executed by the art and type of the honorable man Jacob of Pforzheim, citizen of Basel, and prepared under the direction of Brother Nicholas Vincent, of the Order of Friars Minor. In the year 1493 of the saving Incarnation.* From the library of Saint Mary’s in Halle.

From the same library came a third breviary, perhaps older. But its year and the printer’s name are missing. Its pages have not yet been numbered.

Finally, a recent breviary of the Friars Minor was also at hand, which our very dear friend Diedrich, master of the Latin school in the Halle Orphanage, generously gave us: *The Romano-Seraphic Breviary*, etc., Cologne, 1734.

13. The old breviary of the Dominican Order in the Göttingen library belongs to the Order of Preachers; it was also published at Nuremberg in 1582. (Pd.) We owe a more recent breviary of the same order to the library of the Orphanage. It appeared at Paris in 1643.

14. The library of Saint Mary’s in Halle supplied us with an old breviary of the Order of Saint Benedict: *The winter part of the breviary of the reverend fathers of the Order of the blessed Benedict, of the Bursfeld Union of the Observance throughout Germany, ends.* Printed in Paris by Desiderius Maheu, residing in Saint James Street, under the sign of Saint Nicholas, near the Church of Saint Benedict, at the expense of Godfrey Hector, an honorable bookseller, in the year 1518 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on 15 January. (Bd.)

A recent breviary of the same order is in my possession: *The four-part monastic Benedictine Breviary*, printed at the principal monastery of Einsiedeln, beginning in the year 1743 and following.

15. Of the breviaries of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, we consulted two: one from the library of Saint Mary’s in Halle, without year or title, but undoubtedly very old (Aug.); the other from our own collection: *The Breviary according to the rite of the holy Roman Church, corrected and revised with the greatest diligence, in which many things have also been added that had never before been printed in similar breviaries; it happily ends.* In the noble city of Venice, most accurately printed by Jacob de Leuco, in the year 1509 of the saving Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, on the Nones of October. (Aug. 2.)

16. From the same library of Saint Mary’s comes a very old breviary of the Carthusians: *The Breviary of the sacred religion of the Carthusians.* Printed from a most accurate exemplar at Saluzzo by Master Simon Bevilacqua of Pavia, in the year of the Lord 1506, on 22 April. (Ct.)

17. Among the old breviaries of the Cistercian Order, in which the hymns are arranged in a distinctive and unusual manner, we examined one from the Göttingen library: *The chamber breviary for the use of the Cistercian Order, in the current year 1510, carefully corrected by the same monk who had corrected the preceding breviaries of this order, and reduced to this sufficiently ample form; usefully supplied with the points customarily employed in that order by the obedience of the most reverend father, the lord Abbot of Cîteaux; happily begins.* It is offered for sale in Paris under the sign of the Silver Lion, in Saint James Street. (Cs.)

## III. LITERARY AIDS CONTAINING COLLECTIONS AND EXPLANATIONS OF HYMNS

1. Toward the end of the fifteenth century, an *Exposition of the Hymns* was frequently printed in Germany. I know the following editions of this work:

*Exposition of the hymns with a notable commentary.* Cologne, at the press of Heinrich Quentell, 1492.

*Exposition*, etc. Hagenau, 1493.

*Exposition of the hymns with a notable commentary, incorporating histories with the best citations from Sacred Scripture concerning those saints, male or female, in whose honor such hymns are sung.* Cologne, 1494.

*Exposition of the hymns with a notable commentary.* At the end: Printed at Basel by Michael Furter, in the year 1504 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

*Exposition of the hymns with a familiar commentary, long ago published.* At the end: *The book of hymns, with a literal little interpretation laboriously compiled long ago, has been printed again in the house formerly belonging to Heinrich Quentell at Cologne, 1506, toward the end of May.*

The edition in my possession is older than all the others. It bears the title *A Most Useful and Salutary Exposition of the Hymns*. The year and printer’s name are lacking, but everything indicates that it was printed in the Quentell workshop about the year 1490.

In this collection of hymns, I found the beginning of the book noteworthy: “This book is called the Book of Hymns. A hymn is the praise of God with song. There were four principal authors who composed hymns: Gregory, Prudentius, Ambrose and Sedulius. But when a certain wise man named Hilary saw that these men had composed many hymns, he judged it worthy and pleasing to collect some of them together, to compose a brief and useful treatise in one volume, in which all the hymns were included.”

In this preface I seemed to see traces of an exceptional antiquity. I was therefore especially grateful when the learned Gersdorf, with the generosity for which he is known, sent me from the Paulina Library at Leipzig codex 720, which I had heard also contained an *Exposition of the Hymns*. I soon understood that this codex contains the commentary of our Hilary, which, judging from the age of the codex, may certainly be suspected of having been composed in the thirteenth century. We shall discuss below when that Hilary lived, who he was, and what the character of his work is. (Hil.)

2. *Hymns for the Proper of Time and for the Saints, restored anew to the form in which they were written by their authors, and carefully corrected and interpreted according to the law of verse.* In the year of the Lord 1519.

At the end of the book one reads: *With the hymns occurring throughout the cycle of the year provided with a Latin elucidation and with the meanings of difficult clauses indicated. The final hand has been added. At Strasbourg, in the establishment of Johann Knobloch, printer, in the year of human redemption*, etc.

In the preface, Jacob Wimpheling of Sélestat (+1528) names himself as the author; yet, so far as I know, the learned men who enumerate Wimpheling’s books make no mention of this work. In any event, throughout this book he generally follows Hilary. (Wimpf.)

[Note: [Col. 1167D] The exceedingly rare book by the same author, *On the Authors of Hymns and Sequences and on the Kinds of Verse Found in Hymns*, which we hope will greatly assist us, was most generously sent to us by the distinguished Ullmann from the Palatine Library.]

3. *Book of Hymns Newly Recast in Meter. An Apology and Defense of Poetic and Oratorical Majesty. A Brief Explanation of Difficult Terms in Hymns, Perhaps Interpreted by Others with Insufficient Accuracy and Learning*, published by Heinrich Bebel of Justingen, professor of poetry and humane letters at the public school in Tübingen. *Annotations by the same author on certain interpretations of words in the Mammetractus.* Tübingen, 1501.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] A textbook frequently introduced into instruction, a kind of grammar with the strange title *Mammetrachus* or *Mammotreptes*, had acquired an authority and influence that seemed indestructible. Bebel set himself to eradicate it with all his strength. See Gruber, *Encyclopaedia*, s.v. “Bebel.”]

Rambach most generously sent me this book. (Beb.)

4. *Hymns and Sequences, with a careful interpretation of the most difficult words, necessary for all students, both scholastic and ecclesiastical, by Hermannus Torrentinus, who has deserved exceptionally well of all students of the purity of the Latin language.*

At the end one reads: *Printed at Cologne by Martin of Werden in the year of the Lord 1513, on the eve of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.*

A second edition of this book exists: *Hymns and Ecclesiastical Proses, commonly called Sequences, illustrated by the somewhat brief but highly convenient explanation of Hermannus Torrentinus. Let those who delight in pious and Christian songs delight in these.* Cologne. Printed by Peter Horst, 1536.

I examined both editions; but since in the second that learned man followed Clichtoveus more or less, the first edition seems to us far more worthy of esteem. My library supplied this copy. (Torr.)

5. *A Hymnary for the Proper of Time and for the Saints throughout the Whole Year, in the Meters in Which the Hymns Were Composed by Ambrose, Sedulius, Prudentius and the Other Doctors. Newly Revised at Groningen in Frisia. Happily Begins.* At the end: *And thus the end is reached.* I owe it to Rambach. (Gron.)

6. A book was supplied to me from the library of Saint Mary’s in Halle, mutilated at the beginning, which contains psalms and hymns. At the end one reads: *The Psalter of David, with hymns appended, happily ends, through the work and expense of Melchior Lotter, fellow citizen of the ducal town of Leipzig, in the year 1511, on 18 April.* We have designated this work by the letters Lps.

7. We owe both the first and the second edition of the extremely useful work of Jodocus Clichtoveus to the Reverend Rambach, whose exceptional generosity we cannot fail to praise.

*Ecclesiastical Elucidation, explaining more clearly the matters pertaining to the Church’s service and comprising four books.*

—The first: hymns for the Proper of Time and for the Saints throughout the year.

—The second: various ecclesiastical songs, antiphons and responsories.

—The third: matters pertaining to the service of the Mass, especially the prefaces.

—The fourth: the proses sung in the sacrifice of the holy altar.

The book first appeared at Paris in 1515, then at Basel in 1517 and 1519. An abridged version of Clichtoveus’s work, but enlarged in the hymns, appeared at Venice, in Saint Mary Formosa Street, at the sign of the Hope, in 1555.

Since Clichtoveus used Italian, French and Hungarian breviaries, his work must be held in the highest regard. He is indeed very full in his annotations, but not a few of them are useful. (Clicht.)

8. *Ecclesiastical Hymns, especially those called Ambrosian, revised in many places and enriched by the addition of many hymns, with appropriate scholia added in suitable places and an index of the hymns by Georg Cassander. Bede, on the kinds of meter, from the first book on metrics.* Cologne, 1556.

The hymns were printed again in Cassander’s works, published at Paris in 1616.

Cassander, so to speak, edited the text of the hymns extremely well, collating many breviaries, especially German ones, with due care. The author’s notes are not to be highly valued, for almost all of them are dogmatic or polemical in character. In the Roman Church the book is forbidden. (Cass.)

9. Collections of hymns were indeed compiled by Lutherans around the time of Luther, but they are of little value for establishing the text, since I have found that very many things in them were altered. The following were at hand:

*Psalmodia*, etc., by Lucas Lossius of Lüneburg, with a preface by Philip Melanchthon. Wittenberg, at the press of the heirs of Georg Rhau, 1561. (Loss.)

*Selected Songs from the Old and New Testament, with Hymns and Collects or Prayers of a Purified Kind, Such as Are Customarily Sung in the Orthodox and Catholic Church, with an Arrangement and Familiar Explanation*, by Christoph Cornerus. Leipzig, with privilege, 1568. (Corn.)

*Songs from Sacred Scripture Customarily Sung in the Church, with Hymns and Collects*, etc., revised and enlarged by D. Georg Major, 1570. Wittenberg; printed by Laurentius Schwenck of Eisfeld.

*The Psalter of David*, etc., with headings and notes by Adam Siber. Hymns for the principal feast days have been added. Leipzig; printed by Johann Rhamba, 1577. (Sib.)

In my judgment, the palm must be awarded to Luedec’s work: *Vesperale and Matutinale*, etc., 1589 (Lud.), which will also be of the greatest usefulness to those who wish to learn about the ancient worship of the Lutheran Church.

10. *Three Books of Ecclesiastical Hymns Corrected by the Distinguished Andreas Ellinger*, etc. Frankfurt am Main, 1578. (Ell.)

This is the most extensive of all the collections I have seen. But since in the first two books the hymns were completely altered for metrical reasons, I was able to use only the third book. In the other two, Ellinger’s authority influenced me only where he indicated with a stroke that the old and genuine reading was being presented.

11. *The Christian Works of the Ancient Ecclesiastical Poets, together with the Remains and Fragments of Their Works. A Treasury of the Catholic and Orthodox Church and of Religious Antiquity, Collected, Corrected, Arranged and Also Explained by Commentary for the Benefit of Scholarly Youth*, through the diligence and labor of Georg Fabricius of Chemnitz. Basel, Johann Oporinus, 1564. (Fabr.)

12. I owe to the Reverend Thilo: *Paraphrases and Meditations on the Sunday Gospels by the Holy Fathers and Doctors of the Church Who Wrote in Measured Prose* (in the second part: *on the Gospel narratives explained in public assemblies on the feast days of the Saints*), collected from their various writings by M. Joachim Zehner, pastor and superintendent of the Church of Schleusingen. Leipzig, at the expense of Thomas Schürer, 1602.

This is a most useful book. We cannot fail to acknowledge that its author was thoroughly familiar with the hymns of the ancient Christian Church; and the book makes it entirely clear that even at that time the most learned Lutherans were lovers of the ancient hymns. (Zehn.)

13. *The Complete Works of Joseph Maria Thomasius, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church*, etc. The second volume, containing the Psalter, revised against two editions and manuscript codices and enriched with notes by Antonio Francesco Vezzosi, Cleric Regular. Rome, 1747. (The hymns are contained on pp. 351–434.) (Thom.)

This book is sufficiently rare in Germany, but no editor of sacred hymns can possibly do without it. Thomasius collated the oldest codices of the Vatican and a great many Italian ones; therefore, if anyone undertakes to investigate the hymns of the ancient Church down to the eighth century, he must draw from this book as from a primary source.

14. *Anthology of Christian Songs from All the Centuries of the Church, Arranged in Chronological Order and Accompanied by Historical Remarks*, by August Jacob Rambach, preacher at Saint James’s in Hamburg. Volume One, containing the principal Greek, Latin and Old German hymns of the Church. Altona and Leipzig, Hammerich, 1817.

Our *Thesaurus* shows how often and to what extent we have turned Rambach’s distinguished studies to our own use. (Ramb.)

15. *Garland of Sacred Hymns Serving Public Devotion. Ancient Hymns Selected, Cleansed of the Errors with Which Repeated Editions Had Been Overrun, and Enlarged with Strophes. New Hymns Adopted and Recently Inserted.* Cologne, 1806. Printed by the heirs of Schauberg.

This book of Walraff, which the Reverend August, recently taken from us by death, gave us, is of great benefit to those who have devoted their studies to learning the hymns produced by the Church after the age of Luther.

16. Bjørn’s book: *Selected Hymns of the Ancient Christian Poets of the Latin Church.* Copenhagen, 1818. It assisted us only in a few matters.

17. *Latin Anthology from the Christian Poets of the Middle Ages, Published for Gymnasia and Lyceums and Accompanied by Notes*, by Joseph Kehrein, teacher at the Gymnasium of Mainz. Part One, containing the first eight Christian centuries. Frankfurt am Main, Sauerländer, 1840.

The author follows the purpose of leading the pupils of Catholic gymnasia to an acquaintance with sacred hymns. If this undertaking were successful, we should rejoice exceedingly. It hardly needs to be pointed out that Kehrein’s annotations are intended for students, although we were also permitted here and there to turn some of them to our own use. (Kehr.)

Having now enumerated these aids to our work, it remains for us, with grateful hearts, to commemorate those men who supported our undertaking by their counsel and assisted us in our labors. First among them stands the Reverend Thilo, whose authority was of the greatest value to me in this work as in other matters; the Reverend Tholuck, who was deeply concerned that our labors should prosper; Hermann Dryander, no less skilled in Latin hymns than in German ones; and F. A. Eckstein, a most learned colleague, who assisted me to no small degree with the courtesy that is characteristic of him.

Finally, I cannot fail to give thanks to two men who, from the very beginning of the work and throughout my entire labor, stood by me with counsel and assistance: August Voigt, most closely joined to me by our shared vocation in education, and Christian Diedrich, whom both our shared scholarly career and the bond of an old friendship have intimately united with me. Through the work and industry of these men I was helped greatly in rooting out and correcting errors, although some mistakes escaped both me and my fellow correctors.

May the Lord, the Almighty, of the Christian Church, whose honor all hymns celebrate, whom songs proclaim, and whom sequences and antiphons vie with one another in exalting with praises, grant that the fruit of our studies here too may contribute to the salvation of the Christian Church. We offer our work as a gift to all who reverently honor the name of Christ; we offer it to the most holy Redeemer as a sacrifice for the unity and loving concord of the Church; nor do we pray for anything else from the depths of our hearts than that we too may experience what we read written concerning the most holy patriarch: “The Lord looked upon his offerings.”

I was writing at Halle, in the Royal Pedagogium, on 21 May 1841.

[Col. 1171]

## HYMNS ATTRIBUTED TO ST AMBROSE. (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 1171C] I.—I copied this poem from the hymnary of Thomasius, who, as I shall demonstrate in the appropriate place, deservedly included it in the catalogue of Ambrosian hymns. Only a fragment of the hymn, vv. 13–24, *Fit porta Christi pervia* [“The gate of Christ is made passable”] (sung at the solemnity of the Purification of Mary or at other feasts of the Blessed Virgin), has in fact been received into ecclesiastical use; the Maurist editors maintain that it is a complete poem and proceeds from Ambrose.—1–4. Nearly the same words recur in Sedulius’s alphabetical hymn, *A solis ortus cardine* [“From the region of the rising sun”], in which he undoubtedly imitated our poet. This practice gradually began to spread and gain ground when writers of hymns sought to recommend their offspring to the faithful by means of a better-known tune, weaving the lights and flowers of the ancients into their poems. To give one example: among six hundred hymn openings, Fortunatus’s outstanding *Pange lingua gloriosi* [“Sing, tongue, of the glorious”] occupies first place in its opening verse. 1. Ps. 112:3: “From the rising of the sun unto its setting, the name [of the Lord] is worthy of praise,” etc.—13–16. The poet had regard to Ezek. 44:1–3: “The Lord said to me: This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it; and it shall be shut for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it,” etc.—14. Luke 1:28: “Hail, full of grace.”—15. In hymn 4, which we gave among the others at the end of the preceding volume, verse 10 likewise says: *Claustra pudoris permanent* [“The barriers of chastity remain intact”].—18. In the hymn cited above, verse 13: *Procedens de thalamo* [“Coming forth from the bridal chamber”].—20. There, verse 15: *Gigas geminae substantiae* [“Giant of twofold substance”].—21. Fabr. reads *honor et parentis* [“the honor also of the parent”].—24. H. E. Ct. reads *resolve* [“release”].—25–28. It is sufficiently well known that Christ is compared with a stone in Holy Scripture: Eph. 2:20; 1 Cor. 3:11; 1 Pet. 2:4. Likewise, Isa. 28:16 and Ps. 118:22 are in the New Testament itself referred typologically to Christ the Redeemer (Rom. 9:33; Acts 4:11; Matt. 21:42). Yet the Fathers did not choose to stop within these bounds. In Gregory, 1 Sam. 4:14 and 5:12 seemed to conceal Jesus under the figure of stones; above all, the passage Dan. 2:34, adapted to his use by our poet, pleased mystical interpreters: “You looked until a stone was cut from the mountain without hands.” They do not doubt that the prophet indicated the birth of the undefiled Virgin, whom, they affirm, the Old Testament often calls a mountain. Consult the same Gregory on the words 1 Sam. 1:1, “There was a man from Mount Ephraim”: “By the name of this mountain the Blessed ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, can be signified; for she was a mountain, who by the dignity of her election surpassed every height of the elect creation. [Col. 1172D] Is not Mary a lofty mountain, who, that she might attain the conception of the eternal Word, raised the summit of her merits above all the choirs of angels even to the throne of the Godhead? Hence Isaiah, prophesying the pre-eminent dignity of the mountain, says: ‘In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains.’” [Col. 1173A]—33–36. Isa. 45:8: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior.”—42, 43. Compare the hymn cited above, verse 1: *Veni redemptor gentium* [“Come, Redeemer of the nations”].—44. Sedulius: *ut carne carnem liberans ne perderet quos condidit* [“that by flesh freeing flesh he might not lose those whom he created”].—45–48. Poets, as it were stupefied by wonder at the divine Incarnation, celebrate in similar words that miracle than which nothing more sublime can be imagined. Damasus: “He whom neither the expanses of earth nor the waves of the sea, nor heaven itself, can contain, gathered himself into tiny limbs.” Fortunatus: “Whom the whole world cannot contain, a maiden’s womb bears . . .”; and Luther: “He whom the whole world’s compass never enclosed lies in Mary’s womb.” We scarcely need point out that the song *Gelobet sei’st du, Jesus Christ* [“Praised be thou, Jesus Christ”] echoes nothing but Ambrose, Sedulius, and Fortunatus.]

### Hymn on the Nativity of the Lord

From the region of the rising sun

And to earth’s farthest boundary,

[Col. 1171] Let us sing Christ the prince,

Born of the Virgin Mary.

[5] Rejoice, every nation—

Judaea, Rome, and Greece,

Egyptian, Thracian, Persian, Scythian:

[Col. 1172] One king possesses all.

Praise your prince,

[10] All blessed and lost,

Living, weak, and dead:

Henceforth none is dead.

[Col. 1173] The gate of Christ is made passable,

Filled, full of grace;

[15] The king passes through, and it remains

Closed as it was through the ages.

The offspring of the heavenly Godhead

Came forth from the Virgin’s chamber,

Bridegroom, redeemer, creator,

[20] Giant of his own Church.

The mother’s honor and joy,

The immeasurable hope of believers,

Through the dark draughts of death

Releases us from our crimes.

[25] The stone coming from the mountain,

And filling the world with grace,

Whom the prophets of old proclaim

Cut not by hands.

He who was made the Word made flesh

[30] By angelic proclamation,

Was born, virgin of a virgin,

From the Virgin’s virginal enclosure.

The heavens gave dew,

And the clouds poured forth the Just One;

[35] The opened earth received the Lord,

Bringing forth salvation.

Wondrous conception:

It brought forth Christ as offspring,

So that the virgin might give birth,

[40] And after birth stand a virgin.

[Col. 1173] Let every soul exult

That now the Redeemer of the nations,

The Lord of the world, has come

To redeem those whom he created.

[45] The creator of every race,

Whom the whole world cannot contain,

Has enclosed himself in thy womb,

Holy Mother.

He whom the Father before time,

[50] God, begot as God,

The gracious virginity of his mother

Brought forth in time.

Taking away all crimes

And bestowing holy gifts,

[55] Bringing increase of light,

Inflicting loss upon darkness.

[Note: [Col. 1173A] II.—The Benedictine editors of Ambrose put forward as the sixth hymn the portion, vv. 23–28, of the poem just presented, *Orabo mente Dominum* [“I shall pray to the Lord with my mind”] and what follows: “We present as the sixth hymn, or rather a fragment of a hymn, one supported by the authority of Cassiodorus, for we read his testimony concerning it in the following words (on Psalm 101, p. 537, Rouen edition): ‘Hence too that roseate hymn of St Ambrose for the sixth hour breathed according to the Apostle; for he says: *Orabo mente Dominum*, etc.’ Nor is this hymn unworthy of the senator’s praise if only its sense be considered. Yet it may not without reason be called into doubt whether it was truly composed by Ambrose, since the laws of metre are wholly neglected in it. For from all that has already been said by us, it is clearly shown that the sacred bishop was more skilled in this genre than to stumble so often. But we did not think Cassiodorus’s authority should be denied, and so this most pleasing little poem was admitted among the poems of our Ambrose.” Yet the Benedictine Fathers did not investigate the hymn whose fragment they cite, nor did more recent editors of Cassiodorus. Garetius indeed notes in the margin: “This hymn is wanting”; and we see that this note was repeated by the authors of the Venetian edition of the same Father’s works, even though Thomasius’s hymnary had already been published. That most diligent man found the complete Ambrosian poem in Vatican codex 82; but since Thomasius, alas, is quite unknown among us also, he escaped the notice of very many hymnologists of our age.—4. The reading we have adopted rests on conjecture. The Vatican manuscript reads: *In noctis claudat auditum* [“May he close the hearing of night”]. Since this displeased Thomasius, he wrote: *Innocens claudat auditum* [“May the innocent one close the hearing”]. But I do not understand what suitable sense this conjecture has; moreover, it makes the poem badly turned. This being so, I propose *et noctis claudat aditum* [“and close the entrance of night”]; and there is no need to demonstrate that *et* and *in* are confused a thousand times (Weber on Lucan, *Pharsalia* 6.153; 8.184, and elsewhere).—6–12. Ps. 118:164: “Seven times a day I have praised thee because of the judgments of thy righteousness.”—23, 24. 1 Cor. 14:15: “I shall pray with the spirit, and I shall pray also with the mind; I shall sing with the spirit, and I shall sing also with the mind.”]

### At Sext

Unfolding twice three hours,

The sun enters upon the day,

So that it may complete the sixth

And close the entrance of night.

[5] Therefore now let us, fellow servants,

Mindful of the saying of the prophet,

Loose our mouths in songs,

With prayer mingled with Davidic strains.

That, truly, seven times a day,

[10] [Col. 1174] Praying with the psalter

And singing praises to God,

We may joyfully discharge our obligation.

For thus the grace of Christ

Gives pardon to sinners,

[15] And impious death will not be present

To those who often confess.

Remember, nevertheless, that there must not be lacking

To the servants of God who pray

What the voice of Paul the apostle

[20] Foretold must be observed by us.

His voice merited this:

That he might say likewise to God,

“I shall pray to the Lord with my mind;

I shall pray also with my spirit.

[25] Let not the voice alone sing to God,

While our understanding elsewhere,

Led astray, wanders wavering,

Anticipated by empty chances.

For then the prayer of those who sing

[30] Is acceptable to God,

If the pure mind does the same thing

That the voice of song expresses.”

[Note: [Col. 1174A] III.—Rambach, *Anthology*, p. 116 ff.: “After Bede’s time they (he means the poems *Obduxere polum* and *Squalent arva*) had fallen almost wholly into oblivion, until Cassander made them known from an old manuscript along with several other Latin church songs. Because of their distinctive tone and many poetically beautiful passages, they seem to me to deserve a place in this collection as well.” But this does not compare with Gervinus, who greatly praises our poem and the one that follows (*History of German National Literature*, vol. 3, p. 13): “Hardly have more beautiful songs been made than the Latin ones on excess of water and lack of water.” I willingly concede and grant the poem such merits as it has; but I should not wish to pass over what cannot be denied: that the poet imitated Ovid, Virgil, and Horace.—4. Virgil, *Culex* 373: “I am compelled to approach pools bereft of Phoebus’s light.”—5. Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.94: “the sky flashes with frequent fires.” Horace, *Odes* 1.34.6: “with flashing fire.”—7. Virgil, *Georgics* 3.261: “the gate of heaven thunders.”—8. “the ethereal axis”: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 6.175.—9–24. Kehrein: “The poem seems in stanzas 3–6 to imitate Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1.262 ff.: ‘The crops are laid low and the farmers’ lamented prayers lie fallen; the fruitless labour of the long year perishes. Rivers, overflowing their banks, rush over the open plains and carry off crops, shrubs, cattle, men, houses, and their household shrines together with their fields. One man gains a hill; another sits in a curved boat and rows where he had lately ploughed. One sails over crops or the roofs of a submerged villa . . . Or curved keels grind vineyards beneath them. After long seeking for land on which it can settle, a wandering bird falls upon the mast, its wings wearied.’”—But we may also retrieve what belongs to other poets. I mean Horace, *Odes* 2.2.9–10: “A race of fishes clung to the topmost elm, once the familiar dwelling-place of doves.”—25. Cassander and Kehrein read *eversos* [“overturned”].—34. Bede cited it in his book on metrics.—37. Fabricius reads *ramum* [“branch”].—38. Bede: *pacificae* [“peaceful”].—39. Fabricius: *fulmine* [“by lightning”].]

### Hymn for Seeking Fair Weather, otherwise: in Petition for Fair Weather

Clouds of heaven have covered the sky,

And hide the day, the sun driven away;

For long we endure continuous nights,

Bare of stars and bereft of the moon.

[5] The sky flashes terribly with flashing fire,

And the world trembles, its hinge shaken;

Heaven’s gate thunders, and you would think

The bonds of the ethereal axis had been broken loose.

The waters of the sea swell with rains,

[10] Nor do the straits now know their own bounds;

Water surges amid the lands,

And a wandering keel cuts through the fields.

The sailor seeks his harbours, the sailor his shores,

The sailor seeks his retreats,
[15] The host has become a guest, the sailor a guest among the vines;  
The harvest, a guest, sails above the sailor.  
The weeping farmers abandon their cultivated fields;  
They gaze upon the grievous shipwreck of their labor.  
The joyful harvest floats—seed and wealth;  

[20] Children, houses, livestock, and fields migrate.  
You may see the lofty roofs of houses being carried away,  
And roofs being set down in changed places;  
Fish playing among mournful birds,  
And fish playing upon trembling roofs.  

[25] You may see nests with their trees overturned,  
Being carried across the waters together with their tender young;  
Nor does the mother, in exile, lay aside her cares,  
But compels the older offspring through fear.  
A crowd of men watches; a crowd at the windows  

[30] Watches; a crowd of womanly modesty  
Laments its hunger, a crowd of supplicants;  
The sailor supplies sustenance from the ships.  
Jesus, spare those redeemed by your death.  

The former age endured the Flood,  

[35] [Col. 1175] So that water might cleanse the sins of the earth;  
But the earth has been cleansed by your blood.  
Now let the dove, bringing in its mouth  
The branch—the gift of the peace-bearing olive—  
By descending in joyful flight, signify  

[40] That the lands have been stripped bare by the watery stream.  
Eternal Father, may glory always be yours,  
And to Christ, together with the Begotten One, may glory ever be to you, holy [Father], etc.

[Note: [Col. 1175A] IV.—3. Kehrein is correct: “Beda and Rambach have *nullus roris* (‘no dew’), which I did not wish to adopt because of verse 5; Fabr. has *ruris* (‘of the countryside’). *Rus* is rightly read after *arva*, *agrum*, and *terram*; *ros* (‘dew’) is wrong.—39. Fabr. wrongly reads *Abrami*.”]

### Hymn in Petition for Rain

The fields lie barren under abundant dust;  
The dry land grows pale, the earth cracks;  
There is no dignity of the countryside, no beauty,  
When no grace of flowers grows green.

[5] The hard earth thirsts, unfamiliar with dew;  
The spring now knows no waters, nor the rivers their course;  
The soil knows no grass, nor does it know the plow;  
Broken open, it lies hideous in a great fissure.

The day burns beneath the sun, the heat is fiery;  

[10] It scorches the birds themselves; the leafy branches  
Refuse shelter to the weary; the dust of the sand  
Is spat out from the dry mouth of the traveler.

With their mouths toward the winds, wild beasts; with their mouths toward the winds, cattle;  
And men, catching the breezes of the winds;  

[15] Birds too open their mouths to the winds,  
Wishing by this stratagem to soothe their thirst.

The hind refuses her young, the hind her offspring;  
The hind, weary from thirst, refuses her young;  
The sorrowful hind abandons her faithful offspring,  

[20] Since she cannot carry them the grass she has sought.

The young men have come, seeking the familiar cups  
Of the well, but the water has fled;  
And they return to their empty vessels and homes,  
Alas, drinking their own tears from their mouths.

[25] The ox leaves its empty manger;  
Wishing to crop the grass of the meadows,  
It turns over bare earth; thus every animal,  
Defrauded, dies and collapses upon the grass.

The common country people explore the roots of the woods  
[30] With sorrowful, stooping labor,  
And seek to relieve their hunger with bark;  
But the dry earth provides no tender juices.

Our sins deserve this hunger;  
But, Christ, show favor through your own mercy,  

[35] So that, the heavier the guilt, the greater the grace,  
May it loosen the bonds of just punishment.

Now, we beg you, calmly open the heavens  
And relax the fields with fertile rain.  
For the merits of Elijah you gave rain  

[40] To the impious ages; grant it also to us.

Eternal Father, may glory always be yours,  
And to Christ, together with the Begotten One,  
And to the Spirit, equal in holiness,  
One God, mighty through everlasting ages, illustrious forever.

[Note: [Col. 1175A] V.—This is a hymn proper to Compline, or to feast days, as it appears in Wimpfeling; or to the season of Lent, as many books note. For example, Hl.: “This hymn is to be sung at Compline every day until the Lord’s Supper.” Mgd. gives a different instruction: “This hymn is retained for three weeks and is changed only when the feast of the Annunciation or of the arrival of the relics of Saint Maurice occurs.” In the ancient Breviary of the Carthusians it is sung at Compline throughout the year. The old Italian breviaries, such as Fr., lack our hymn, as does the present usage of the Roman Church [some monastic usages retained it, such as the Breviary of the Order of Preachers printed in 1643].
