The diligence of Luther was therefore the more modest: imitating the ancient poet, he composed the song *Christ, der du bist Tag und Licht* (“Christ, you who are day and light”); nor did pious care for the sacred song fail after his time. I refer to the song of Erasmus Alber, *Christ, der du bist der helle Tag* (“Christ, you who are the bright day”), which Knapp declares to belong to Michael Weisius. And I believe he is right, since John Weitius had already taken his side, prefacing his commentary as follows: “The author of this German ode is said to be Michael Weitius, etc.” Weitius, however, did not illustrate the German hymn, but Joseph Clauder’s translation in *Psalmodia Nova*, century 1, no. 39: *Lux Christe lucidissima* (“Light, Christ, most radiant”). There are also very ancient German translations of the poem; see Hoffmann, *Geschichte des deutschen Kirchenliedes*, pp. 143, 150, 180, 183, 185.—K. E. P. Wackernagel, *Das deutsche Kirchenlied*, p. 333 (translation by Urbanus Regius).—1. Oxford manuscript: *die* (“day”).—2. Th.: *detegens* (“revealing”).—3. Cass.: alternatively, *lux ipse lucis* (“the light itself of light”). Thom.: *Lucifer lucem proferens* (“the light-bearer bringing forth light”), but, with Cassander and here and in all the verses of the poem, manuscripts H., E., and O. have this reading.—4. Thom.: *Vitam beatam tribue* (“grant blessed life”).—6. O.: *nocte et* (“and in the night”).—7. Thom.: *ut sit* (“that it may be”).—10. Thom.: *ne hostis* (“lest the enemy”).—11. Thom., Fabr.: *ne caro* (“lest the flesh”); O., Msn., Lps.: *consentiat* (“consent”). O. omits *caro* (“the flesh”).—12. Thom.: *et ne nos* (“and lest us”); Fabr.: *reos tibi* (“guilty before you”).—14. D. 2: *vigilat* (“keeps watch”), perhaps because of the passage in Scripture, Song of Songs 5:2: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”—22. Thom., Gron.: *in isto gravi* (“in this grievous”).—23. Gron.: *es qui* (“you who are”). The same hymnary adds this verse:

> To you we cry, O Lord;  
> Do not abandon us;  
> Hasten—do not delay;  
> Come to the aid of us wretched ones.

This verse, unquestionably spurious, also occurs in the German translation in Riederer, *Nachrichten zur Kirchen-Gelehrten-und Bücher-Geschichte* II, p. 165:

> We cry to you, we call upon you;  
> Do not leave us in distress;  
> Hurry, and do not delay too long;  
> May your help come to us poor ones.

[The monk of V. Salzburg: “Let the hymn be sung and read at Compline; whoever recites it devoutly at night, the devil cannot deceive him, nor can any grievous dream be pleasing to him.”]]

### Hymn for Compline

Christ, who are light and day,  
You reveal the darkness of night,  
And are believed to be the light of light,  
Proclaiming blessed light.

[5] We beseech you, holy Lord:  
Defend us in this night;  
May there be rest for us in you;  
Grant us a peaceful night.

May heavy sleep not rush upon us,  
[10] Nor may the enemy snatch us away;  
Nor may the flesh, consenting to him,  
Make us guilty before you.

[Col. 1177] May our eyes receive sleep,  
But may our heart always keep watch toward you;  
May your right hand protect  
The servants who love you.

Look upon us, our defender;  
[15] Restrain those lying in wait;  
Guide your servants,  
Whom you purchased with blood.

Remember us, O Lord,  
In this grievous body;  
You who are the defender of the soul,  
Be present with us, O Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1177A] VI.—Breviaries that adorn Matins with hymns assign the preceding poem to Saturday. The Roman Breviary also commands that at Matins on the feast of the Holy Trinity the stanzas printed in larger type be sung. The verse “Give your right hand” belongs to the hymn *Aeterna coeli gloria*.—1. Cass.: *summe ... clementia* (“highest ... mercy”).—6. Cass.: *benignus* (“kind”).—11. Fabr.: *accinctus ut sim* (“that I may be girded”).]

### Hymn for Matins

(From an ancient Book)

God of supreme mercy,  
Creator of the world’s structure,  
One in power,  
And three in person.

[5] In your goodness, receive  
Our tears together with our songs,  
So that with a heart cleansed of filth  
We may enjoy you more fully.

Burn our loins and diseased liver  
[10] With fitting fire,  
So that, girded, they may remain forever,  
With the worst luxury removed.

That all of us who now break  
The hours of night by singing  
May be richly endowed  
With the gifts of the blessed homeland.

#### Another Reading of the Same Hymn

(From the Roman Breviary)

Father of supreme mercy,  
You who rule the world’s structure,  
God of one substance  
And three persons.

[5] In your goodness, receive  
Our tears together with our songs,  
So that with a pure heart, cleansed of filth,  
We may enjoy you more fully.

Burn our loins and diseased liver  
[10] With fitting flames,  
So that our limbs, girded, may keep watch,  
With the worst luxury removed.

That all of us who now break  
The hours of night by singing  
May be richly endowed  
With the gifts of the blessed homeland.

Give your right hand to those rising,  
[Col. 1177] So that the sober mind may rise,  
Burning and returning due thanks  
In praise of God.

Grant this, most loving Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1177A] VII.—According to the Roman Breviary, it is sung on Friday at Matins; the two verses printed in larger type are sung at Lauds on Trinity Sunday. The verse “The morning star rises and shines” is itself taken from the hymn *Aeterna coeli gloria*.—4. Cass.: *concinentes* (“singing together”).—5. We should not forget Wimpfeling’s ingenuity: a bed is said to be made from selected and softer herbs, upon which the ancients rested.—8. Cass.: *ad te* (“to you”); Fabr.: *medelas* (“remedies”).—10. Cass.: *delinquimus* (“we sin”).]

### Morning Hymn

(From an ancient Book)

You, unity of the Trinity,  
Who powerfully rule the world,  
Attend to the songs of praise  
That we sing while keeping watch.

[5] For we rise from our little bed  
At the quiet time of night,  
To ask from you a remedy  
For all our wounds.

So that whatever, through the deceit  
[10] Of demons, we have done wrong at night,  
Your power’s glory  
May wipe it away from heaven.

May no filthy body be present,  
Nor sluggishness beset our hearts;  
May the contagion of sin  
[15] Not cool the ardor of the spirit.

For this, Redeemer, we ask you:  
Fill us with your light,  
Through which, in the circles of our days,  
We may fall into no deeds of evil.

#### Another Reading of the Same Hymn

(From the Roman Breviary)

You, unity of the Trinity,  
Who powerfully rule the world,  
Attend to the song of praise  
That we sing while keeping watch.

[5] For we rise from our little bed  
At the quiet time of night,  
To ask from you a remedy  
For all our wounds.

So that whatever, through the deceit  
[10] Of demons, we have done wrong at night,  
Your power’s glory  
May wipe it away from heaven.

May no filthy body be present,  
Nor sluggishness beset our hearts;  
May the contagion of sin  
[15] Not cool the ardor of the spirit.

For this, Redeemer, we ask you:  
Fill us with your light,  
Through which, in the circles of our days,  
We may fall into no deeds of evil.

The morning star rises and shines,  
[Col. 1178] Going before the sun as its herald;  
The darknesses of night fall away;  
May holy light illuminate us.

Grant this, most loving Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1177B] VIII.—Thomasius: From Saint Ambrose, according to a manuscript of the Queen of Sweden and the Mozarabic Breviary, Friday after the First Sunday of Lent. Codex O. is also included.—2. O.: *solus* (“alone”).—4. O.: *perpete* (“everlasting”).—5. O.: *cedet* (“will yield”).—13, 16, 17. Thom.: *ne* (“lest”).—18. O.: *gulam venter* (“the belly [for] the throat”).—24. O.: *Christo* (“to Christ”).]

### Morning Hymn

Creator of eternal light,  
You who are wholly light and day,  
Who experience no night at all,  
By nature everlasting light.

[5] Now the pale night yields  
To the approaching arrival of day;  
Blunting the light of the stars,  
The bright morning star is present.

Now we rise from our bed,  
Singing thanks to you,  
Because the sun, returning,  
Has brought the day back after the blind night.

May neither the joy of the flesh  
[10] Nor seductive passions secretly creep upon us;  
Nor may our mind yield to the deceits of the world,  
We ask you, holy one.

May anger not provoke quarrels,  
Nor may gluttony incite the belly;  
May hunger for wealth not pervert us,  
Nor shameful luxury seize us.

[20] But, sober with steadfast mind,  
Remaining chaste in body,  
With our whole faithful spirit,  
May we spend this day, O Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1178A] IX.—Thomasius found the hymn in a very ancient manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. It is also mentioned in the rule of Bishop Aurelianus and is not absent from Cassander. Ellinger’s third book, XXI, also identifies it as a hymn for Sext during Lent.—3. Thom.: *aequali* (“equal”).—15. Since the darkening of the sun will be a sign of the final age.—17–29. These verses are absent from Cassander and Ellinger’s books.—18. Thom.: *Abraham*.—19. Thom. alternatively: *reperitus* (“having been discovered”).—19, 20. Pelbartus, *Pomoerium*, Sermon on the Trinity II: “Third, the Mosaic Law showed the Trinity revealed to the patriarchs by manifold prefiguration. First, to Abraham, who saw three angels descending in the person of the Lord: he saw three and worshiped one. Likewise Isaac blessed Jacob three times; Jacob saw a ladder of three steps, etc.”—26. Thom.: “Paul was indicated by another hand in the manuscript, whose earlier letters had been erased; he is the subject here.”—17. Th.: *et nos* (“and us”).—21, 22. Cass.: *unum rogemus cum Patre, Dominum regemque Filium* (“let us ask one [God] with the Father, the Lord and king Son”).—26. Cass.: *peracto* (“having been completed”).—27. The same: *sub isto* (“under this”).]

### Hymn for Sext

Now the sixth hour is gradually passing,  
By twice three courses of the hours;  
And the day, at an equal point,  
Looks toward both nights.

[5] Come, suppliant servants;  
With mind and mouth lift up  
The blessed name of God  
With worthy praises and song.

For this is that time  
[10] When the judgment of the ages  
Was handed over to an unjust death  
By the judgment of mortals.

When the sun, suddenly terrified  
By horror at so great a crime,  
Threatens death to the world  
And flees the impious day.

At this time also blessed Abraham,  
[15] Skilled in the mystery,  
Saw three and believed in one.

The Savior gave this hour  
As fitting for prayer,  
When he told his faithful servants to ask the Father.

[25] At this time also that steadfast one obtained the grace of faith which he preached to the nations.

But we, subject in due love  
And in righteous fear,  
Against all the assaults  
That the savage enemy launches,

Let us ask one God: the Father,  
[30] The king, and the Son,  
And likewise the Holy Spirit,  
The Lord in Trinity.

So that prayer may preserve at that same time those whom the Passion, accomplished at this time, redeemed.

[Note: [Col. 1179A] X.—Thom.: “In another [manuscript], no. 11, it is entitled *Hymn for Vespers on a fasting day*. From the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden and Vatican manuscripts 82 and 83. Bishop Aurelianus prescribes it in his Rule for Easter.”—1–4. Cf. Matthew 20:5.—2. Another [manuscript], no. 11: *quia* (“because”).—3. Vatican 82: *mercedem largus* (“generous with reward”).—9–12. Matthew 27:45.—9. Cass.: *qua* (“by which”).—13–24. Matthew 27:52–53.—13. Thom.: *resuscitans* (“raising”).—21. Cass.: *credere* (“to believe”).—28. Thom.: *quo est* (“by which it is”). Cass.: *hoc est* (“that is”); our reading is supported by another manuscript, no. 11.—29–32. The ancient Christians were accustomed to fast on station days until None.]

### Hymn for None

The third hour three times turns,  
At which Christ is accustomed to return,  
Generous with the reward of the vineyard,  
To hire laborers.

[5] It is fitting for the prepared to stand ready,  
Lest God’s reward pass by;  
For at this hour he is accustomed  
To plant the vine and fasten Christ to the heart.

This is the hour that shone forth  
[10] And dispelled the clouds of the Cross,  
Stripping the world of darkness  
And restoring serene light.

This is the hour when Jesus commanded  
Bodies to rise from the tombs,  
To emerge free from death,  
His spirit being released.

[15] Ash returns to blood,  
And dust restores flesh;  
The dead mingled with the living  
See the glory of Christ.

You might believe that the ages had been renewed,  
[20] The laws of death having been dissolved,  
And that, by the gift of blessed life,  
They were running in an everlasting course.

Let us therefore, as those who draw near,  
Sing praises to God with song:  
The thief confessed his faith,  
By which he was redeemed at that time.

[25] By this grace we are accustomed  
To break our fasts joyfully,  
So that, as a likeness of the future gift,  
Those who have been tested may not know hunger.

[Note: [Col. 1179A] XI.—Thomasius: From the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. Bishop Aurelianus includes it in his Rule under the Lucernarium. See the Mozarabic Breviary, p. 107. Codex O. also contains it.—4. Thom.: *somno relaxet otio* (“may sleep release [the body] into rest”); Mozarabic Breviary: *somnus relaxet otium* (“sleep may release leisure”).—10. Thom.: *cura* (“care”).—12. O.: *blandus in isto corpore* (“gentle in this body”).—16. O.: *visui* (“to sight”).—20. O.: *vigilve* (“or watchful”).]

### Hymn for Night

God, who by fixed laws  
Distinguish night from day,  
So that sleep may relax  
Bodies wearied by cares into rest,

[5] During this dreadful time of night  
We ask you that, while sleep  
Holds the weary mind,  
The light of faith may illuminate it.

Lest the deceitful enemy provoke us  
[10] With wanton cares and pleasures,  
Calling upon the secret things of night  
And the body’s seductive passions.

May no terror of anxious fear  
Steal upon the senses;  
Nor may a deceptive image of the eyes  
Mock the wandering mind.

But when deep sleep has bound us,  
[15] Unaware of cares,  
May faith in no way sleep;  
May the wakeful sense dream of you.

[Note: [Col. 1179A] XII.—Thomasius from the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden and codex O.—1. O.: *tempore* (“at the time”).—10. Thom.: *unius quoque* (“of each one also”).—11. Thom.: *Aegyptum mortem* (“death upon Egypt”).—18. Thom.: *tantorum* (“of such great things”). [Col. 1179B]—21. O.: *vero* (“indeed”).—24. O.: *defensi* (“protected”).—34. Thom.: *quia stinctas* [uncertain reading].—37. Thom.: *quare vigilemus* (“why should we keep watch”).—38. Thom.: *splendidas manus* (“bright hands”).—41. O.: *noctisque mediae* (“and of midnight”).]

### Hymn for Night

It is the time of midnight;  
The prophetic voice admonishes us:  
Let us sing praises to the Lord,  
Always to the Father and the Son,

[5] And also to the Holy Spirit:  
For the Trinity is perfect,  
And of one substance;  
We must always praise it.

This time contains terror,  
[10] For when the destroying angel  
Brought death upon Egypt,  
He destroyed the firstborn.

This hour is salvation for the righteous,  
Because then the angel there  
Dared not punish,  
Fearing the sign of blood.

Egypt wept bitterly  
[15] Over the dreadful funerals of its children;  
Israel alone rejoiced,  
Protected by the blood of the Lamb.

We are the true Israel;  
Let us rejoice in you, O Lord,  
Despising the enemy and evil,  
Redeemed by the blood of Christ.

It is indeed the very time  
[20] When, according to the Gospel voice,  
The bridegroom is believed to be coming,  
The founder of the heavenly kingdom.

The holy virgins come out  
To meet his arrival,  
Carrying bright lamps  
And rejoicing with great joy.

But the foolish remain behind,  
[25] Those whose lamps have been extinguished,  
Knocking at the door in vain,  
The palace of the kingdom already closed.

Let us keep sober watch,  
Carrying minds made bright,  
So that, when Jesus comes,  
We may be worthy to go out to meet him.

At midnight  
[30] Paul and Silas too,  
Bound in prison,  
Were released while praising Christ together.

This world is a prison for us;  
We praise you, Christ God:  
Release the bonds of those who believe  
In you, Christ.

Make us worthy, holy king,  
[35] Of the glory of the coming kingdom,  
So that we may deserve  
To sing your praises forever.

[Note: [Col. 1179B] XIII.—Thom.: “The very ancient manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, and the Mozarabic Breviary for the weekday after the First Sunday of Epiphany. Bishop Aurelianus places this hymn in his Rule at Prime. In the Alexandrian manuscript the heading of the present hymn reads: ‘A hymn to be said on Wednesday.’ You see that Rambach greatly departed from the truth in his *Anthology*, p. 117: ‘The hymn *Fulgentis auctor* is from a codex formerly belonging to Fr. Junius, now in the library at Oxford, containing twenty-six church songs used in the old Frankish or Alemannic Church (Tenzel’s *Monatliche Unterredungen*, 1691, p. 726), from which three [*Mediae noctis tempore*; *Aeternae*, not *Aeterne*, *lucis conditor*; and the hymn repeated here], together with a Frankish translation probably dating from the ninth century, are printed in J. G. ab Eckhart’s *Commentarius de rebus Francicis orient.* I, II, p. 948. These hymns unquestionably belong at least to the seventh century and, quite apart from their distinctive value, are highly remarkable because they prove that the oldest German Church, like the Church in Ireland, possessed an independence in song and liturgy that it subsequently almost entirely lost.’ The learned man was unaware of the authority of Thomasius, by which the chronology is established quite differently. Grimm later published our hymn, together with the others, from the Oxford codex.”]

### Morning Hymn

Author of the shining ether,  
You who established the moon as light in the nights,  
The sun along the courses of the days,  
By a fixed path.

[5] The black night is now driven away;  
The splendor of the world is reborn;  
And new vigor of mind  
Raises us to sweet actions.

The returning day now urges us  
To sound your praises;  
And the gentler face of heaven  
Brings serenity to our hearts.

Let us avoid every slippery path;  
[10] Let the spirit turn away from evil;  
Let deeds not defile our life;  
Let the tongue not become entangled in guilt.

But while the sun completes the day,  
May deep faith burn;  
May hope call us toward the promises;  
May love unite us to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] XIV.—Thomasius: From manuscript no. 1352 of the Queen of Sweden and codex O.—10. O.: *simul et* (“also together”).—15. O.: *perpeti* (“everlasting”).—16. O.: *debita demus gloriae* (“let us give due glory”).]

### Hymn for Lauds

After the morning praises  
That we sing to the Trinity,  
The true head of the household  
Reminds us to sing again.

[5] Let us always be diligent,  
Lest God’s work pass us by;  
But let us pray attentively,  
As the Apostle teaches.

Let us sing to the Lord with the mind;  
Let us sing with the spirit as well,  
Lest a wandering mind, in shameful things,  
Cover our inactive spirits.

But seven times in this day  
[10] Let us sing praises to the Lord,  
And give perpetually  
The glory due to the Divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] XV.—Thomasius: The very ancient manuscript of the Queen of Sweden and the Mozarabic Breviary. It is entitled “A daily hymn for Terce.” Codex O.—10. O.: *splendida* (“splendid”).—12. O.: *praemio* (“reward”).]

### Hymn for Terce

Holding to the appointed order,  
Let us ask with devout heart,  
At the third hour of the day,  
For the glory of the threefold Power.

[5] So that we may be a dwelling place  
For the Holy Spirit,  
Who once at this hour  
Was distributed among the apostles.

[Col. 1181] Following this order,  
[10] The founder of the heavenly kingdom  
Adorned all things splendidly  
With the rewards of eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] XVI.—Thomasius: From the very ancient manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. Codex O.—2. O.: *fervente prompti spiritu* (“with a fervent, ready spirit”); it is likely that the German translator read *prompti*.—14. O.: *tenebricat* (“grows dark”).]

### Hymn for Sext

Let us sing praises to the Lord  
Again with fervent spirit:  
The hour, having turned six times,  
Calls us to prayer.

[5] Because at this hour, for the faithful,  
The grace of true salvation—  
The sacrifice of the blessed Lamb—  
Is granted through the power of the Cross.

By whose most radiant light  
Midday grows dark;  
Let us receive with our whole heart  
The grace of so great a splendor.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] XVII.—Thomasius: From the very ancient manuscript of the Queen of Sweden. This hymn is assigned to None in manuscript Alex. 11, where it begins: *Perfectum Trinum numerum*, etc. Codex O.—Thom.: *perfecto trino numero* (“with the perfect number three”).—5. O.: *regula* (“rule”).—6. O.: *prodita* (“revealed”).—11. O.: *habent* (“they have”).—12. Thom.: *dirigunt* (“guide”).—8. Acts 3:1: “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer.”]

### Hymn for None

With the perfect number three,  
At the boundaries of three hours,  
Singing the praises that are due,  
We sing at None.

[5] Holding the sacred mystery of God  
With a pure heart,  
And the rule of the master Peter,  
Revealed by the sign of salvation.

Let us too sing with the spirit,  
Adhering to the apostles,  
Who, by the power of Christ,  
Guide those whose feet are still weak.

[Note: [Col. 1181A] XVIII.—The very ancient manuscript of Thomasius and codex O.—1. O. omits *rex* (“king”).—3. O. omits *hoc* (“this”). [Col. 1181B]—4. O. has *legibus* (“laws”).—5. Thom.: *te precantes* (“entreating you”).—11. Thom.: *consistens* (“subsisting”).—17. O. omits *et* (“and”).—18. Another manuscript, no. 11: *praesentant* (“present”).—21. O.: *mult. seniorum* (“the multitude of elders”).—24. O.: *adorant* (“adore”).—33. O.: *Davidis* (“of David”).—34. O. omits *es* (“you are”). [Col. 1182A]—38. O. omits *es* (“you are”).—43. O.: *palmis signis* (“marked with palms”).—47. O.: *desonamus* [uncertain reading].—48. Thom.: *unum* (“one”).]

### Hymn to Christ

Christ, King and Lord of heaven,  
Greatest Savior of the world,  
You who by this gift of the Cross  
Freed us from the guilt of death,

[5] We now ask you in prayer:  
Preserve your gifts,  
Which through the catholic law  
You have given to all nations.

You are the Word of the eternal Father,  
[10] Brought forth from the divine mouth,  
God subsisting from God,  
The only-begotten Son.

[Col. 1182] Every creature  
Confesses you as Lord of the world.  
Begun at the Father’s command,  
All things were perfected by your power.

[15] To you all the angels  
Offer heavenly glory;  
The choir of archangels  
Praises you with divine voices.

The multitude of elders,  
Twice twelve in number,  
Carrying bowls full of fragrances,  
Adoringly worships you.

[20] The Cherubim and Seraphim,  
The thrones of the Father’s light,  
With the sixfold clapping of their wings,  
Resound with perpetual shouting.

Holy, holy, holy,  
Lord God of Sabaoth;  
All heaven and earth  
Are full of your glory.

Hosanna, Son of David;  
[25] Blessed are you by the Father,  
Who in the name of God  
Came from on high, O Lord.

You are the spotless Lamb,  
Given as a victim to the earth,  
Who washed the garments of the saints  
In your blood.

The multitude of blessed martyrs  
[30] Placed in heaven,  
Marked with palms and crowns,  
Follow you, the leader of glory.

Add us to their number,  
We ask you, Lord;  
With one voice we proclaim you,  
With one song we praise you.

[Note: [Col. 1182A] XIX.—It occurs in the hymnary of Thomasius, who, to my great regret, passed over in silence where he obtained it. It also appears among the Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, June III, p. 842, copied from an ancient Milanese Breviary. Learned men add that it may unquestionably be believed to be a hymn by Saint Ambrose. Although this judgment has not yet been sufficiently investigated and established, it is supported by many arguments. But more on these below. The discovery of the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius is described by Ambrose in his letters, *Opera*, ed. Bd., II, p. 873 (a spurious letter in the appendix, p. 483). See also Augustine, *City of God* XXII, 8; *Confessions* IX, 7.—1, 2, 11, 12. Ambrose, in the sermon he delivered before the people when the relics were discovered: “Although this is God’s gift, nevertheless I cannot deny the grace that the Lord Jesus granted during my priesthood; and because I myself am not worthy to be a martyr, I have acquired these martyrs for you.”—6. Ambrose: “All the bones were intact, and there was very much blood; the tomb was wet with blood, and the marks of triumphant gore appeared.” Gregory of Tours, *Miracles* I, 48.—8. Ambrose, in the same place: “You have read God saying: ‘The blood of your brother cries out to me.’ And here this blood cries out by the evidence of its color; the blood cries out by the proclamation of its working; it cries out by the triumph of its suffering.”—13. Thom.: *hic* (“here”).—14. Ambrose, in the same place: “They [the Arians] deny the benefit, although they cannot deny the deed.”—15, 16. I know nothing about this miracle.—17ff. Ambrose I, 1: “They [the Arians] deny that the blind man was illuminated, but he does not deny that he was healed. He says: ‘I see, though I did not see’ ... He is a known man, formerly employed in public service when he was well. Severus by name, a butcher by trade. He had laid aside his occupation after the affliction had fallen upon him. He calls as witnesses the men whose services had previously supported him; he summons as judges of his healing those whom he had as witnesses and arbiters of his blindness. He cries out that when he touched the fringe of the martyrs’ garment, in which the sacred relics are clothed, his sight was restored ...” It is not rash to accept the judgment added by the editors: “Nothing is more certain or more attested than this miracle, not only because of the very great authority of Ambrose ... but also because of Augustine’s eyewitness—if I may use that expression—testimony, which may be read in Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, and even more explicitly in the Sermon on the Nativity of the Martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. The same miracle, together with the others mentioned in this letter, is also narrated by Paulinus in the *Life of Ambrose*, who likewise could have been an eyewitness.”—22. *Acta Sanctorum*: *tergit* (“wipes”).—25–28. The poet either means the demoniacs who were freed through the martyrs’ gift, or he is referring to the violence of the Arians against the Catholics, weakened—not to say broken—by this manifestation of the saints.—29–32. Acts 5:15; 19:11–12: “God performed extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick, and diseases left them and evil spirits went out.” In the same way, the poet asserts in these verses that the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius shone with miracles.]

### On the Discovery of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, Martyrs

I sing new thanks to you, Jesus,  
Discoverer of a new gift,  
For the martyrs Protasius  
And Gervasius, newly found.

[5] Pious victims lay hidden,  
But the sacred spring did not lie hidden;  
The blood cannot lie hidden  
That cries out to God the Father.

Grace, shining from heaven,  
[10] Revealed the sacred limbs.  
We cannot be martyrs,  
But we have discovered martyrs.

Tell me who would seek the voices  
Of witnesses where the deed itself has become faith:  
The man restored from mental blindness  
Acknowledges the work of the martyrs.

The blind man, having received his sight,  
[15] Proves the merit of the sacred death.  
Severus is the man’s name;  
His occupation was public service.

When he touched the martyrs’ garment  
And wiped his clouded eyes,  
Light flashed forth immediately,  
And blindness, driven away, fled.

[20] The crowd, freed from its bonds and from the coils of dragons, returns home with grace, released throughout the whole city.

We have seen the ancient ages  
Throwing handkerchiefs,  
And by the touch and shadow of bodies  
Health restored to the sick.

Glory to you, O Lord.  
Glory to the Only-Begotten, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1183B] XX.—It occurs in codex O., in Cassander, in Ellinger III, 35, and in Thomasius. In his Rule, Bishop Aurelianus, as printed by Holstenius in *Codex Regularum* III, p. 57, [Col. 1183C] wishes it to be sung at the Lucernarium and at Matins throughout Easter. Manuscripts Alex. 11 and Vatican 82 also contain the hymn, which we find additionally mentioned by Hincmarus. It is also placed in the ancient Carthusian Breviary for Matins during the Easter season until the Ascension of the Lord.—2. Thom., Carthusian Breviary: *sancto serenus lumine* (“serene with holy light”); O.: *sanctus serenus* (“holy, serene”).—3. Alex. 11: *quod diluit* (“which washes away”).—5. Thom.: *perfidis* (“faithless”).—6. Vatican 82: *visus illuminans* (“illuminating sight”). [Col. 1184A]—7. O.: *solvat* (“may release”).—9. It and the Carthusian Breviary: *cruce* (“cross”).—16. Cass., Vatican 82: *Jesu breve acquisivit fidem* (“Jesus gained faith briefly”); Thom., Carthusian Breviary: *Jesum brevi quaesivit fide* (“he sought Jesus with brief faith”); Ell.: *Jesu brevi acquirit fidem* (“he gains faith in Jesus briefly”).—12. Alex. 11: *praevenit* (“precedes”).—13. O.: *obstupent et* (“and they are astonished”).—14. O.: *corpore* (“body”).—19. O.: *tollat* (“may take away”).—25ff. It is a very well-known opinion of the ancient Fathers that the devil, unaware of Jesus Christ’s divinity, incited the Jewish priests to kill the God-man (*theánthrōpon*), but was most miserably deceived by the Redeemer’s death, which not only did not impede human salvation but became its greatest assistance. The author of the poem holds the same view. Attracted as by bait by Christ’s death, Satan swallowed the hook—that is, he killed himself with his own sword. Perhaps the poet had before his eyes the passage from the Book of Job, chapter 40: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or bind his tongue with a cord?” At least this much is certain: the devil is very often compared with Leviathan. Compare also the ancient German song, probably from the twelfth century, in H. Hoffmann, *Geschichte des deutschen Kirchenliedes bis auf Luthers Zeit*, pp. 23ff., whose fifth stanza is:

> An angelic cord has been woven,  
> From which you were born;  
> That was your lineage,  
> The angel was God’s power,  
> There death was killed without strangling,  
> Which had been hidden from you.  
> Holy Mary!

—28. O. omits *ut* (“so that”); Cass.: *resurgat vita omnium* (“the life of all may rise”); Ell. inserts the little word *et* (“and”).—32. Thom.: *quaerit* (“seeks”); Cass.: *perisse se sola* (“that it alone had perished”); O.: *gemat* (“may lament”).]

### Easter Hymn for Terce

This is the true day of God,  
Holy, serene in its light,  
On which sacred blood washes away  
The shameful sins of the world.

[5] Restoring faith to the lost,  
And illuminating the blind with sight:  
Whom does the acquittal of the thief not free from grievous fear?

Changing the cross into a reward,  
The thief gains Jesus through brief faith;  
And the just man, taking the first step,  
Reaches the kingdom of God.

The angels are astonished at the deed,  
[10] Seeing the punishment of the body,  
And the guilty man clinging to Christ  
Seize blessed life.

A wondrous mystery:  
That flesh should wash away the world’s filth;  
It removes the sins of all,  
Cleansing the flesh’s faults through flesh.

What could be more sublime than this:  
[15] That guilt should seek grace,  
That love should dissolve fear,  
And death should restore new life?

Let death devour its own hook  
And bind itself in its own knots;  
Let the life of all die,  
So that the life of all may rise again.

When death passes through all,  
Let all the dead rise;  
Death, consumed by its own blow,  
Mourns that it alone has perished.

[Note: [Col. 1184B] XXI.—This hymn is assigned chiefly to the Holy Spirit because it is remembered that at this hour he descended upon the apostles in the form of fiery tongues; it is found in all ecclesiastical books. For everyone agrees concerning the hymns of the hours called the lesser hours: even in the very oldest parchments containing songs for Matins and Vespers, these hymns are not absent: *Jam lucis orto* ... *Nunc sancte* ... *Rector potens* ... *Rerum* [Col. 1184C] *Deus*. Codex M. seems to depart from this rule, assigning no hymn even to Terce. But this should be attributed to negligence rather than intention, as is demonstrated by the Breviary of the Church of Merseburg, printed with the hymn in its customary place.—2. Hincmarus and Gottschalk read: *unus Patris cum Filio* (“one with the Father and the Son”); so does Vatican 82. E. Hil.: *unus vel unum* (“one or one thing”). Codex II: *unum cum Patri Filio* [uncertain grammar]. Wimpfeling: *unus cum Patri Filio* [uncertain grammar]. Lud.: *unum cum Patre et Filio* (“one with the Father and the Son”). Cass., Fabr., Hv.: *unum Patri cum Filio* (“one to the Father with the Son”).—4. H.: *infusus* (“poured in”).—6. Vatican 82, H., Ill., Sl., Msb., Pt., Mgd., Torr., Lps.: *confessione* (“confession”). Vatican 82, H., Cass., Fabr.: *personent* (“may resound”).—7. D. 2: *flammascat* (“may flame”). Vatican 82: *flammascat ignis charitas* (“may love, fire, flame”).—8. Fabr., H.: *proximus* (“neighbor”). Hilary: “In the sun there are three things: the sphere, its brightness, and its heat. Just as the sphere of the sun is naturally shining and hot, so the supreme Father is naturally wise and loving. And just as the sun’s sphere, splendor, and heat are not three suns but one sun, so the supreme Father, his wisdom, and his love are not three Gods but one God. In the fiery sphere of the sun we should understand the Father, in its splendor the Son, and in its heat the Spirit.” Among the ancients, the supreme mystery of the Trinity is very often illustrated by the example of the sun. Bartholomew collected examples in *Adversaria* XLV, 10.]

### Hymn for Terce

Now, Holy Spirit,  
One with the Father and the Son,  
Deign readily to enter  
Our breast, poured into it.

[5] Let mouth, tongue, mind, senses, and strength  
Resound with confession;  
Let love flame with fire;  
Let ardor set our neighbors ablaze.

[Grant, most loving Father,  
And you, only one equal to the Father,  
With the Spirit, the Paraclete,  
Now and throughout every age.]

[Note: [Col. 1185A] XXII.—The hymn is placed at Sext throughout the year in all the old Breviaries and in the Roman Breviary. Hilary: “The subject matter of this hymn is taken from the qualities of the air, because the greatest heat usually occurs at midday and is harmful to the body. Therefore we ought to ask God to extinguish in us the flames of vices . . . We ought to pray at the sixth hour, at which Adam was expelled from paradise; let us return there by good works, with Christ consenting, who was placed on the cross at that same hour.” Ludecus adds that the sixth hour is the time for eating, after the example of Saint Peter, Acts 10:9. —3. Ludecus, Fabricius: “by whose splendor.” —4. Fabricius: “and who [is] with fires.” —6. Cassiodorus, relying on I know not what authority: “the greatest.” —8. Ludecus, in the margin: “and firm.”]

## Hymn at Sext

*(From an old book.)*

[Col. 1185]

Powerful and truthful God,  
who regulate the changes of created things,  
who furnish the morning with splendor  
and midday with fires,

[5] Extinguish the flames of strife,  
take away harmful heat,  
grant health to bodies  
and true peace to hearts.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Powerful and truthful God,  
who regulate the changes of created things,  
who illuminate the morning with splendor  
and midday with fires.

[5] Extinguish the flames of strife,  
take away harmful heat,  
grant health to bodies  
and true peace to hearts.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1185B] XXIII.—In the same way, the readings of all the books agree in assigning this hymn to the ninth hour. —1. Ludecus: “who preserve all things firm and intact.” —2. H., Sl., Hv., Ct., Mgd., Gron., Torr.: “remains.” —3. Vat. 82: “daylight.” —7. St.: “of the black [night].” —8. H., Hv.: “presses upon.”]

## Hymn at None

*(From an old book.)*

God, enduring strength of all things,  
remaining unmoved in yourself,  
determining the seasons  
of daylight by their succession,

[5] Grant a bright evening,  
so that life may never fall away,  
but that the reward of holy death—  
everlasting glory—may await us.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

God, enduring strength of all things,  
remaining unmoved in yourself,  
determining the seasons  
of daylight by their succession,

[5] Grant evening light,  
so that life may never fall away,  
but that the reward of holy death—  
everlasting glory—may await us.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1185B] XXIV.—This hymn, in which victory over nocturnal illusions is requested, belongs at Compline in old and more recent books, either throughout the year or on weekdays [Col. 1186A] (compare, however, what we noted concerning Hymn 5). Merati, in Gavantus, *Thesaurus* III, p. 228: “The Psalms [of Compline] are immediately followed by a hymn, which the monks varied according to the season, as Martene reports. Among us Romans the hymn is never changed. It is the same throughout the whole year.” But learned men are mistaken when they mention monks alone. They ought not to have passed over the many churches of Germany, England, and other regions in which, during the Middle Ages—for today they follow the Roman custom—it has been clearly established that on feast days they sang a hymn at Compline (for example, III., Mgd., Hv., Ef., and many others). For the most part they repeat at Compline part of the hymn sung at Vespers, or divide the poem in such a way that it is suitable and appropriate to both hours. —3. Cassiodorus: “The poem will scan if you read *tua*”; this was approved by the correctors. —4. Cassiodorus: “Some read *et custodia*; so do Gron., H., Hl., Clicht., Fabr., and others.”]

## Hymn at Compline

*(From an old book.)*

Before the end of daylight,  
we ask you, Creator of all things,  
that in your accustomed mercy  
you may be our guardian for protection.

[5] Let dreams and phantoms  
of the night depart far away,  
and restrain our enemy,  
lest our bodies be defiled.

Grant this, almighty Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Before the end of daylight,  
we ask you, Creator of all things,  
that in your mercy  
you may be guardian and protection.

[5] Let dreams  
and phantoms of the night depart far away,  
and restrain our enemy,  
lest our bodies be defiled.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1185B] XXV.—All books that assign hymns to Matins attribute this poem to Wednesday at the Nocturn. —6. Fab.: “our crime.” —10. Cassiodorus: “One should read *noctibus*, as the book of Saint Benedict has it, although in all the copies I have seen *novimus* is read, evidently through the fault of scribes. I think this happened because nearly the same verse occurs in another hymn, *Primo dierum omnium*, where it is certainly established that *novimus* is to be read. Moreover, although Clichtoveus reads *novimus* in this edition, he nevertheless appropriately interprets the passage as though he had read *noctibus*. For he cites the passage of the prophet David, Psalm 134: ‘In the nights lift up your hands in the holy places’; and elsewhere, Psalm 119: ‘At midnight I rose to give thanks to your name.’ He also cites Paul, Romans 13: ‘It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep,’ and the example of one who had worked with his hands at night and, imprisoned with Silas, had praised God in the deep of night.” —14. Wimpfeling: “we come forth.”]

## Hymn at Matins

*(From an old book.)*

Best Creator of all things,  
our ruler, look upon us;  
free us, sunk in harmful rest,  
from sleep.

[5] Holy Christ, we ask you:  
forgive our crimes.  
We rise to confess  
and break through the delays of night.

We lift up minds and hands.

[10] The prophet commands us  
to do this in the nights,  
and Paul has approved it by his deeds.

You see the evil we have done;  
we disclose what is hidden within us,

[15] We pour out groaning prayers;  
forgive what we have sinned.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Best Creator of all things,  
our ruler, look upon us;  
free us, sunk in harmful rest,  
from sleep.

[5] Holy Christ, we ask you:  
forgive all sins.  
We rise to confess  
and break through the delays of night.

[Col. 1187] We lift up minds and hands.

[10] The prophet commands us  
to do this in the nights,  
and Paul has approved it by his deeds.

You see the evil we have done;  
we disclose what is hidden within us,

[15] We pour out groaning prayers;  
forgive what we have sinned.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1187A] XXVI.—The more recent Breviaries of the Roman Church have changed nothing in this poem, which is sung everywhere on Thursday at the Nocturn. —2. Clichtoveus: “Some read *calores*”; so Hilary. —Cassiodorus is wrong: “confidentes.” —5. Wimpfeling: “that you may remove.” —8. The same: “that we may ward off.”]

## Hymn at Matins

Black night covers  
all the colors of the earth;  
we who confess ask you,  
just Judge of hearts,

[5] To remove our sins,  
wash away the filth of the mind,  
and grant the grace of Christ,  
so that crimes may be kept at bay.

Behold, the impious mind grows sluggish,  
which harmful guilt gnaws at;

[10] It longs to remove the darkness  
and to seek you, Redeemer.

Drive away the darkness  
as completely as possible from within,

[15] So that it may rejoice  
to be placed in blessed light.

[Note: [Col. 1187A] XXVII.—By the testimony of all the books, this hymn is assigned to Friday at Lauds. —3. Wimpfeling: “of heaven.” —7. Fr.: “and fragrant”; Clichtoveus and others: “in praise.” The learned man himself, for metrical reasons, proposes *Flagrans et in laudem Dei* (“burning and in praise of God”), which did not displease the correctors. —9. Clichtoveus and others: “born”; so Bebius. —15. Fab.: with that boldness to which he is accustomed, changed *diei* (“of the day”) to *temporum* (“of the times”). —18. Wimpfeling: “in our [hearts]”; Hilary: “in the depths.” —20. Thus Clichtoveus, Hilary, Fr., Augustine. Many read: “in which greater charity exists.”]

## Hymn at Lauds

*(From an old book.)*

Eternal glory of heaven,  
blessed hope of mortals,  
only-begotten Son of the Most High Thunderer,  
offspring of the chaste Virgin.

[5] Give your right hand to those rising;  
let the sober mind arise,  
burning and giving due thanks  
in praise of God.

The Morning Star shines forth  
[10] and announces the scattered light;  
the darkness of night falls away;  
may holy light illumine us,

And, remaining in our senses,  
may it drive away the night of the world,

[15] And at every end of the day  
preserve our breasts cleansed.

The faith first sought  
may take root in deep senses;

[Col. 1187] May the second hope rejoice with it,  
in which the greater charity exists.

Glory be to God the Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Eternal glory of heaven,  
blessed hope of mortals,  
only-begotten Son of the Most High Thunderer,  
offspring of the chaste Virgin.

[5] Give your right hand to those rising;  
let the sober mind arise,  
burning and giving due thanks  
in praise of God.

The Morning Star shines forth  
[10] and, as the sun’s herald, goes before it;  
the darknesses of night fall away;  
may holy light illumine us.

And, remaining in our senses,  
may it drive away the night of the world.

[15] And at every end of time

May the faith first sought  
put down roots in the heart;

May the second hope rejoice with it,  
in which the greater charity exists.

Glory be to God the Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1187B] XXVIII.—This is a hymn for Saturday at Lauds. —3. Hilary, Wimpfeling: “mirror.” —10. Hilary: “we await.”]

## Hymn at Lauds

*(From an old book.)*

Dawn now scatters the sky;  
day slips down upon the earth;  
the ray of light leaps forth;  
let every slippery thing depart.

[5] Let the phantom of night fall away;  
let the guilt of the mind collapse;  
whatever dreadful thing  
night has brought through sin, let it fall.

So may that final morning  
which we await with bowed heads

[10] Flow forth for us into light  
while this song resounds.

Glory be to God the Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Dawn now scatters the sky;  
day slips down upon the earth;  
the ray of light leaps forth;  
let every slippery thing depart.

[5] Let the phantom of night flee;  
let the guilt of the mind collapse;  
whatever dreadful thing  
night has brought through sin, let it fall.

So may the morning which we,  
bowed down, pray will be the final one

[10] Flow forth for us together with the light  
while this song resounds.

Glory be to God the Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1187B] XXIX.—Everyone clearly perceives that the author of the poem had in mind a day of fasting. But according to the ancient custom of the Church it is recited daily at Prime, and yields to no other hymn throughout the year. Gavantus, *Thesaurus* III, p. 211 [Col. 1188A]: “Amalarius reports that Prime is to begin with the prayer *Deus in adjutorium*, together with the *Gloria Patri*, but says nothing about the hymn. *Jam lucis orto*, since no hymns were recited at Rome in his time (?), nevertheless Saint Benedict, who was earlier than Amalarius and distinguishes Prime from Lauds in chapter 17 of his Rule, prescribes that this order be observed in it: ‘At the first hour,’ he says, ‘let three psalms be said separately and not under one Gloria; let the hymn of that hour follow the verse *Deus in adjutorium*, before the Psalms are begun.’ I can certainly affirm that I have inspected no book except one that placed the hymn *Jam lucis orto* at Prime. The Roman Breviary changed nothing. —2. Bd.: “we pray.” —5. Torr.: “may restrain.” —14. Torr., Gron.: “sun.”]

## Hymn at Prime

Now that the star of light has risen,  
let us humbly beseech God  
that in the acts of the day  
he may keep us from those who harm.

[5] May he restrain and temper the tongue,  
lest the horror of strife resound;  
may he foster and cover the sight,  
lest it drink in vanities.

May the innermost places of the heart be pure,  
and may folly stand apart;

[10] May temperance in food and drink  
wear down the pride of the flesh.

So that when the day has withdrawn  
and fate has brought back the night,

[15] Through abstinence from the world  
we may sing glory to him.

Glory be to God the Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1188B] XXX.—All churches accustomed to sing hymns at Vespers—some are, so to speak, **ἄμουσοι**, “without song,” and omit them altogether—indicate that this hymn is to be sung on Sunday. A highly unusual custom is found in the English Breviary, by which it is prescribed that *Lucis creator* be recited until the Kalends of August, and thereafter *O lux beata*. —10. Ludecus: “of the gift.”]

## Hymn on the Work of the First Day

*(From an old book.)*

Best Creator of light,  
bringing forth the light of days,  
at the beginnings of new light  
preparing the origin of the world,

[5] You who command that morning joined to evening  
be called a day,  
when dark chaos settles in,  
hear prayers with tears.

Lest the mind weighed down by sin  
be an exile from the gift of life,

[10] While it thinks of nothing lasting  
and binds itself with sins.

May it knock at the innermost place of heaven,  
may it take up the reward of life;

[15] Let us avoid every harmful thing,  
let us cleanse every evil.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

[Col. 1189]

Best Creator of light,  
bringing forth the light of days,  
at the beginnings of new light  
preparing the origin of the world,

[5] You who command that morning joined to evening  
be called a day,  
dark chaos settles upon us:  
hear prayers with tears.

Lest the mind weighed down by sin  
be an exile from the gift of life,

[10] While it thinks of nothing lasting  
and binds itself with sins.

May it knock at the heavenly door,  
may it take up the reward of life;

[15] Let us avoid every harmful thing,  
let us cleanse every evil.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1189A] XXXI.—This hymn belongs to Monday at Vespers. —2. Ill., Mgd.: “you might confound.” Hilary, Fabricius, Wimpfeling: “he might confound.” —8. Thus all the books I have seen. Cassiodorus: “may they scatter,” namely, the flames. But *dissipet* should be joined with *unda*, so that the poet’s meaning is this: water and fire are so regulated under God’s governance that neither can harm the globe of the earth. The wave tempers the flames of the firmament, which would otherwise burn up the fields; the flame restrains the mass of waters, preventing it from destroying and making the earth’s surface disappear by inundation. Clichtoveus: “The author, following the common opinion of many, says that God established waters above the firmament so that they might temper the heat of the stars, lest they themselves burn up the heavens. This idea is not consonant with natural philosophy, since the celestial spheres were not made to grow hot and cannot be consumed by fire. The clause beginning *ut unda*, however, is better referred to the water beneath the firmament, which tempers the flames of the stars lest they burn the earth. Scripture certainly testifies in many places that waters have been placed above the heavens. But we ought not to be too inquisitively concerned about the reason for which they were placed there.” —16. Bebius: “may they restrain.”]

## Hymn on the Work of the Second Day

*(From an old book.)*

Immense Creator of heaven,  
who, dividing the streams of water  
so that mingled things would not be confounded,  
gave the sky as a boundary,

[5] Establishing a place for the heavenly bodies  
and likewise for the streams of earth,  
so that the wave may temper the flames  
and not destroy the earth’s surface.

Pour forth now, most merciful one,  
[10] the gift of everlasting grace,  
lest through the accidents of new deceit  
ancient error wear us down.

May faith find light  
and thus bear the ray of light;

[15] May it terrify all these vain things,  
and let no falsehood repress it.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Immense Creator of heaven,  
who, dividing the streams of water  
so that mingled things would not be confounded,  
gave the sky as a boundary.

[Col. 1189] Establishing a place for the heavenly bodies  
and likewise for the streams of earth,  
so that the wave may temper the flames  
and they may not destroy the earth’s surface.

Pour forth now, most merciful one,  
[10] the gift of everlasting grace,  
lest through the accidents of new deceit  
ancient error wear us down.

May faith increase the light  
and thus bear the ray of light;

[15] May it trample all these vain things,  
and let no falsehood repress it.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1189B] XXXII.—This is the hymn for Tuesday Vespers. —2. Ludecus: “uncovering.” —3. Hilary, Wimpfeling, Bebius: “and.” —6. [Col. 1190A] Augustine: “supported.” —7. Hv., Ludecus: “fruit.” —8. Cassiodorus: “Others read *partumque*.” —10. Fr., Bebius, Ludecus, Cassiodorus: *virore gratia* (“by the green growth of grace”); Augustine, Hv., Sl.: *viroris gratia* (“by the greenness”); Hl., Mgd., Hl., Wimpfeling, Fabricius: *vigoris gratia* (“by the grace of strength”); Clichtoveus: *vigore gratiae* (“by the strength of grace”). We approved the reading placed second, since it is also commended by the others, who otherwise disagree among themselves. —16. Hl., Mgd.: “deeds”; Ludecus, Fabricius: “blow.”]

## Hymn on the Work of the Third Day

*(From an old book.)*

Mighty Creator of the earth,  
who bring forth the earth’s surface,  
after driving away the troubles of water  
gave the earth an unmoving place,

[5] So that, producing suitable growth,  
beautiful with golden flowers,  
it might stand fruitful in its produce  
and offer pleasing nourishment.

Cleanse the wounds of the mind burned up  
[10] by the grace of green growth,  
so that it may wash away its deeds with tears  
and crush perverse impulses.

May it obey your commands,  
draw near to no evils,

[15] Rejoice to be filled with good things,  
and know nothing of the stroke of death.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Nurturing Creator of the earth,  
who separate the earth’s surface,  
after driving away the troubles of water  
gave the earth an unmoving place,

[5] So that, producing suitable growth,  
beautiful with golden flowers,  
it might stand fruitful in its produce  
and offer pleasing nourishment.

Cleanse the wounds of the mind burned up  
by the greenness of grace,

[Col. 1190] So that it may wash away its deeds with tears  
and crush perverse impulses.

May it obey your commands;  
may it draw near to no evils;

[15] May it rejoice to be filled with good things  
and know nothing of the stroke of death.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1190A] XXXIII.—They read this hymn on Wednesday at Vespers. —4. Hilary: “with beauty.” —7. Cassiodorus: “you order the moon to serve.” ‘This seems rather to be the reading than that found in some copies, *lunae ministrans ordinem* (“serving the moon’s order”).’ Clichtoveus likewise testifies that some read it “less aptly and suitably.” But apart from Fabricius and Ludecus I found no book that offered *ministras*, and I do not see why it is less apt and suitable; indeed, it fits the preceding words, *augens* and *constituens*, extremely well. The books’ disagreement over *ordinem* (*ordine*, *ordini*) is of lesser importance. —10. Augustine: “of direction.” In very many copies: “of plunder.” —12. Many: [Col. 1190B] “might give.” —13. Fabricius, Ludecus in the margin: “of all things.”]

## Hymn on the Work of the Fourth Day

Most holy God of heaven,  
who paint the shining center of the sky  
with fiery brightness,  
increasing it with beautiful light;

[5] On the fourth day, establishing  
the flaming wheel of the sun,  
serving the moon’s order,  
and the wandering courses of the stars,

So that for nights and for light  
[10] you might give a most recognizable sign  
of the boundary of division,  
and of the beginnings of months.

Illumine the hearts of human beings,  
wipe away the filth of minds,

[15] Loosen the bond of guilt,  
overturn the burdens of crimes.

Most holy God of heaven,  
who paint the bright regions of the sky  
with fiery brightness,

[20] Increasing them with beautiful light.

On the fourth day, when you kindle  
the flaming wheel of the sun,  
you assign an order to the moon  
and the wandering courses of the stars,

[25] So that for nights and for light  
you might give a most recognizable sign  
of the boundary of division,  
and of the beginnings of months.

Drive away the night from hearts,  
wipe away the filth of minds,

[30] Loosen the bond of guilt,  
overturn the burdens of crimes.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1190B] XXXIV.—This poem is used at Thursday Vespers. —5. Wimpfeling, Mgd.: “different”; Fabricius, Ludecus, Thomas: “submerged.” —6. Cassiodorus, Clichtoveus, and others: “watering”; Hilary and Wimpfeling incorrectly: “pouring onto the neck.” —[Col. 1191A] 10. Kehrein: “*unda sanguinis* (‘wave of blood’) instead of *unda et sanguis* (‘wave and blood’). By the latter the Savior’s death on the cross is to be understood; by the former one could understand baptism. It is better, however, to refer it also to the death on the cross, and specifically to the Savior’s side wound, as in the hymn of Fortunatus.”]

## Hymn on the Work of the Fifth Day

*(From an old book.)*

Great God of power,  
who send back into the deep creatures born from the waters,  
partly  
partly lift them into the air,

[Col. 1191] sending down those submerged in the waters,  
setting on high those borne toward the heavens,  
so that, sprung from one stock,  
they may seize different places.

Grant all your servants,  
[10] whom the wave of blood cleanses,  
to know no falls into sin  
and to bear no weariness of death.

So that guilt may crush no one,  
nor arrogance lift anyone up;

[15] May the humbled mind not collapse,  
nor the exalted mind fall.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Great God of power,  
who leave those born from fertile water  
partly in the deep,  
partly raise them into the air,

[5] Pressing what is submerged into the waters,  
raising what is carried upward to the heavens,  
so that, sprung from one stock,  
they may fill different places.

Grant all your servants,  
[10] whom the wave of blood cleanses,  
to know no falls into sin  
and to bear no weariness of death,

So that guilt may crush no one,  
nor arrogance lift anyone up;

[15] May the humbled mind not collapse,  
nor the exalted mind fall.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1191A] XXXV.—The books present this hymn for Friday at Vespers. —6. Ludecus: “by the spoken word.”]

## Hymn on the Work of the Sixth Day

*(From an old book.)*

God, fashioner of humanity,  
who alone arrange all things,  
command the earth to produce  
the species of creeping things and wild beasts.

[5] You who, by your commanding word, gave  
the great living bodies of created things,  
subjecting them to humanity  
that they might serve in due order.

Drive away from your servants  
[10] whatever through uncleanness  
either insinuates itself into their character  
or inserts itself into their actions.

Grant the rewards of joys,  
grant the gifts of graces;

[15] Dissolve the bonds of strife,  
fasten the treaties of peace.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Heavenly Creator of humanity,  
who alone arrange all things,  
command the earth to produce  
the species of creeping things and wild beasts.

[5] And the great living bodies of created things,  
by your commanding word,  
to obey your servants  
through the appointed cycles of time.

Drive away whatever,  
roused by the force of desire, attacks us,

[10] Or through character insinuates itself  
or through actions inserts itself.

Grant the rewards of joys,  
grant the gifts of graces;

[15] Dissolve the bonds of strife,  
bind fast the treaties of peace.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1191A] XXXVI.—Thomas found this hymn in Codex Vat. 82, marked with the name of Ambrose; and Gallandus, *Bibliotheca Patrum* VII, p. 772, does not doubt that the hymns *Optatus votis omnium*, *Jesu nostra redemptio*, and *Jam Christus astra ascenderat* were truly composed by Saint Ambrose. The first of these, which we have placed first, is exceedingly rare in liturgical books; among ours it is found in Ellinger and in the old Carthusian Breviary. —4. Ephesians 4:8: “Christ ascending on high,” etc. —5. Perhaps one should read *scandens* (“ascending”). —6. Thom., Ct. omit *ad*. —11. Ct.: “presenting.” —13. Acts [Col. 1191B] 1:9: “He was lifted up, and a cloud received him.” —14. Ell.: “and he made.” —16. Thom.: “had closed [it] for the first-created man.” —20. Ell.: “at the Father’s seat.” —22. Ct.: “for judgment.” —24. Ct.: “kingdoms.” In a similar way Arator celebrates the Lord’s Ascension, *History of the Apostles* I, 36 ff.:

The heavenly choirs resound in praise, when the ruler of Olympus  
raises to the heights whatever he received from below,  
and, entering heaven with the trophy of the flesh as his companion,  
places in the citadel of light the spoils snatched from the dark abyss  
and raises earthly limbs aloft.

—31–32. Augustine, Sermon on the Ascension 2: “Let us ascend with Christ in heart; when the day promised by him arrives, we shall follow also in body. Yet we must know that pride, greed, and lust do not ascend with Christ; none of our vices ascends with our physician.”]

## Hymn on the Ascension of the Lord

The day desired by all in their prayers,  
the sacred day, has shone forth,  
on which Christ, God, the hope of the world,  
ascended the lofty heavens.

[5] The Lord ascending on high,  
returning to his own seat,  
the kingdoms of heaven rejoiced  
at the return of the Only-Begotten.

The triumph of the great battle,  
[10] with the ruler of the world destroyed,  
he presents before the Father’s face  
the glory of his victorious flesh.

He was lifted up upon the clouds  
and gave hope to believers,

[15] Opening paradise,  
which the first-created man had closed.

O great joy for all!  
The one born of our Virgin,  
after spitting, scourges, and the cross,

[20] Is joined to the Father’s seat.

Let us therefore give thanks  
to the avenger of our salvation,  
because he has carried our body  
to the sublime royal court of heaven.

[25] May joy remain common to us  
with the heavenly beings:  
for them, because he presented himself to them;  
for us, because he did not withdraw himself from us.

Now, with our actions summoned onward,  
it is fitting for us to await Christ,

[30] And to live such a life  
as can ascend to the heavens.

[Glory to you, Lord,  
who ascend above the stars,

[35] With the Father and the Holy Spirit  
through everlasting ages. Amen.]

[Note: [Col. 1192A] XXXVII.—In very many churches this most melodious hymn adorns Compline on the Ascension of the Lord (in Fr. at Vespers). As it now stands, it is intoned with great solemnity at Vespers and Lauds. Gavantus, *Thesaurus* S. R. III, p. 471: “At the beginning of the hymn *Salutis humanae sator* in those same Vespers of the Ascension, the celebrant or officiant should join, extend, and raise his hands, and incline his head toward the altar; and, as Bauldry notes in the *Episcopal Ceremonial*, book II, the same applies to the hymn sung at Lauds.” [Col. 1192B] —3. Fabr.: “guardian.” —4. Ell.: “and, at the end, human being of the ages.” —6. Lips.: “bearing.” —10. Fab.: “you redeem.” —12. Ell.: “you are seated at the right hand of the Father”; Corn.: “you remain seated.” —16. Psalm 16:15: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” —17–20. Omitted by Hl., Msb. —17. Ell.: “please, may you be.” —18. Clichtoveus and others: “the future”; Ell.: “you who are.” —19. Cor.: “may ours be in you.” —20. Ell.: “through all ages forever.”]

## Hymn on the Ascension of the Lord

*(From an old book.)*

Jesus, our redemption,  
love and desire,  
God, creator of all things,  
human being at the end of time.

[5] What mercy conquered you  
so that you might bear our crimes,  
enduring a cruel death  
so that you might lift us from death?

Entering the prison of hell,  
redeeming your captives,

[10] Victorious in noble triumph,  
you sit at the right hand of the Father.

May that very compassion compel you  
to overcome our evils,

[15] By pardoning and granting us our prayer,  
to satisfy us with your countenance.

Be our joy,  
you who will be our reward;

May our glory be in you  
[20] Through all ages forever.

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Founder of human salvation,  
Jesus, delight of hearts,  
creator of the redeemed world  
and pure light of those who love.

[5] By what mercy were you conquered,  
that you might bear our crimes,  
undergo death innocent,  
so that you might lift us from death?

You burst through the chaos of hell  
and strip the chains from the bound;

[10] Victorious in noble triumph,  
you sit at the right hand of the Father.

May indulgence compel you  
to repair our losses,

[15] And, granting us possession of your countenance,  
enrich us with blessed light.

You are the guide and path to the stars;  
be the goal of our hearts;

Be the joy of our tears,  
[20] Be the sweet reward of life.

[Note: [Col. 1193A] XXXVIII.—This hymn is found in very few older Breviaries and, according to the rule of the Roman Breviary, is assigned to the festive Matins of Pentecost. —3. Pd.: “by the promised gift of the Father”; Hil., Ct., Fabr., Wimpf.: “promised gifts of the Father.” —5. W. 1, Cs.: “was rising.” —6. Beb.: “mystically”; Cassiodorus: “The obscurity of this passage seems to be removed most satisfactorily if you understand *septemplici*, which is naturally an adjective, substantivally, in this sense: the solemn day was now pressing on, on which the rolling and revolving course of the heavens, seven times sevenfold, signifies blessed times—that is, the future rest foreshadowed by the type of the Jubilee, which consisted of seven years seven times over” (compare verses 7 and 13). —7. Beb.: “with the sphere released.” —9. Cassiodorus: “Others read *tum*; W. 1, Thom., Cs.: *cum*.” —11. W. 1, Beb., Ef., Fabr., Thom., Cs.: “to those praying.” —12. Thom., W. 1, Cs.: “announcing”; Fab., Ell.: “announces that God has come.” —14. Beb.: “adorning”; W. 1, Fr., Hil., Cs., Ct.: “the nurturing fire is”; Wimpf., Fab., Pd.: “the fire has been sent.” But since Christian poets usually adapt themselves to the language of Sacred Scripture, it is likely that our poet follows the wording of blessed Luke, Acts 2: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of an approaching wind, and it filled the whole house.” —16. Beb., Ct., Pd.: “filled.” —18. Others: “by the breathing of the Holy Spirit,” or “when the Holy Spirit was breathed upon”; W. 1, Cs.: “with holy light.” —19. W. 1, Thom., Cs.: “they make diverse voices resound”; Fab., Ell.: “they sound articulate voices.” —20. Acts 2:11: “We hear them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God.” —21. W. 1, Cs.: “is gathered from every nation”; Fabr.: “then recognized by every nation” [Col. 1194A]. —22. W. 1, Ct., Cs.: “Greek, Latin, barbarian.” —24. Others: “to all.” —26. W. 1, Cs.: “the mad crowd”; Vat. 82: “the mad crowd of the spirit”; Beb.: “the crowd touched by madness”; Cassiodorus: “Others read *vesana torva spiritu* (‘mad, grim in spirit’). The frenzied spirit, proceeding from the devil, is opposed to the Holy Spirit.” —27. Ct.: “drunkenness”; Acts 2:13: “They are full of new wine.” —29–32. The Groningen Hymnary incorrectly appended this verse to the hymn *Beata nobis gaudia*. —29. Fabr., Ell.: “but by signs.” —31. Hil., Wimpf., Fabr.: “proved false.” —32. W. 1, Thom., Cs.: “confirming it with Joel as witness.” Compare Acts 2:16. —32–36. You will find this in Thom., Beb., Cl. —33. Thom.: “here”; others: “hence.”]

## Hymn for the Day of Pentecost

*(From an old book.)*

Christ had now ascended the stars,  
returning from where he had come,  
about to give the Holy Spirit  
as the Father’s promised gift.

[5] The solemn day was pressing on,  
on which, in mystical sevenfoldness,  
the world, rolled around seven times,  
signifies blessed times.

When the third hour had come for all,  
[10] Suddenly the world thundered  
and announced to the praying apostles  
that God had come.

Therefore from the Father’s light  
a beautiful fire came,

[15] Which should fill the faithful hearts of Christ  
with the warmth of the word.

Their inward parts filled, they rejoiced,  
breathed upon by the Holy Spirit;  
they sounded forth diverse voices,

[20] They proclaimed the mighty works of God.

Known among every nation,  
among Greeks, Latins, and barbarians,  
while all marveled,  
they spoke in the languages of all.

[25] Then unbelieving Judea,  
mad with a grim spirit,  
rebuked Christ’s disciples  
for belching up drunkenness from new wine.

But Peter confronts this with signs and mighty works  
[30] and teaches them,  
proving by Joel’s testimony  
that the faithless were speaking falsely.

[Thus, Christ, may the Paraclete  
in his goodness now visit us through you,  
and, renewing the face of the earth,  
restore those freed from sins.]

### Another reading of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Christ had now ascended the stars,  
returning from where he had come,  
about to give the Holy Spirit  
to be enjoyed as the Father’s gift.

[5] The solemn day was pressing on,  
on which, in mystical sevenfoldness,  
the world, rolled around seven times,  
signifies blessed times.

When the third hour of light had come,  
[10] Suddenly the world thundered  
and announced to the praying apostles  
that God was coming.

[Col. 1194] Therefore from the Father’s light  
the beautiful, nurturing fire is present,

[15] Which should fill the faithful hearts of Christ  
with the warmth of the word.

Their inward parts filled, they rejoiced,  
breathed upon by the Holy Spirit;  
they sounded forth diverse voices,

[20] They proclaimed the mighty works of God.

Known to all nations,  
among Greeks, Latins, and barbarians,  
while all marveled together,  
they spoke in the languages of all.

[25] Then unbelieving Judea,  
mad with a grim spirit,  
rebuked the sober faithful of Christ  
for being wet with new wine.

But Peter confronts this with miracles  
[30] and teaches them,  
proving by Joel as witness  
that the faithless were speaking falsely.

Glory be to God the Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1194A] XXXIX.—From Codex O., Grimmius was the first to publish Hymn 1, as well as the poems *Deus qui claro lumine*, *Meridie orandum est*, and *Tempus noctis surgentibus* (among us, 40 and 48). And rightly so: until something else is shown, this eminent man will consider these hymns newly published by him, since, unless everything deceives me, no one before this time has ever investigated them in any book. [Col. 1194B] Moreover, a suspicion arises in me that the poem has been compounded from two pieces, one of which begins with the stanza *Pater, qui coelos contines*. For the preceding section contains a doxology, with which poets always took care to end their hymns; thus verses 21–24 suitably conclude the first hymn. It is then easy to see that, from there to the end, the poet sings the Lord’s Prayer, adapted to the laws of poetry.]

## Morning Hymn

God, who are the light of heaven  
and creator of light, who unfold with splendid right hand  
the sky upheld  
by the Father’s arm,

[5] Dawn now covers the stars,  
lifting up the red flood;  
for with moist breezes  
it baptizes the earth with dews.

The Morning Star now demands its chariot,  
[10] with rays and flaming wheels,  
which, ascending the summit of heaven,  
has departed, knowing no delay.

Now the shadow of night is left behind;  
darkness abandons the sky;  
and the Morning Star, a figure of Christ,

[15] Awakens the sleeping day.

You are the holy Day of days,  
and you yourself are the light of light,  
the One powerful through all things,  
the Trinity powerful in unity.

[20] [Col. 1195] We now ask you, Savior,  
and bend our knee to you;  
with our whole voice we beseech  
the Father together with the Holy Spirit.

Father, who contain the heavens,  
let us now sing your name;

[25] May your kingdom come,  
and may your will be done.

This, I say, is your will  
which is entrusted to us to perform:

May we be faithful in spirit,  
remaining chaste in body.

[30] Grant us each day  
our daily bread to eat from you;

Forgive us our debts  
as we forgive our debtors.

Do not allow us to be led  
[35] into subtle temptation,  
but, as suppliants with pure heart,  
deliver us from evil.

[Note: [Col. 1195A] XL.—Found only in Codex O.]

## Morning Hymn

The time of night is for those rising,  
for those saying praises to God,  
to Christ Jesus the Lord,  
in the glory of the Trinity.

[5] We, the choir of the saints, sing psalms;  
we bend our necks;  
we prostrate our knees,  
confessing our sins.

Let us pray continually to God;  
[10] let us conquer evil with good,  
and, with the fruit of repentance,  
render an everlasting vow.

Let us ask Christ and the Father,  
and the Holy Spirit of the Father,

[15] To give us help,  
so that we may conquer the envious enemy.

[Note: [Col. 1195A] XLI.—This is found in Codex O. and in the hymnary of Thomas for Saturday. —4. Thom.: “confessing grace.” —10. Thom.: “everlasting.” —11. Thom.: “neither rising nor setting.” —24. 1 Timothy 6:10: “The root of all evils is greed.”]

## Morning Hymn

With the light of day restored,  
with the first words after sleep,  
let us sing the glory of God,  
with the grace of Christ favoring us.

[5] Through him the Creator of all things  
established day and night,  
sanctioning them by eternal law  
so that they should always follow one another.

You are the true light of the faithful,  
whom the eternal law does not bind;

[10] Night does not follow your rising,  
as you shine with eternal light.

Christ, we ask, grant this  
to your servants as they cry out,  
lest the iniquity of this world  
take our faith captive.

[15] Let us not think impiously;  
let us envy no one;  
lest, when harmed, we return the harm,  
let us conquer evil with good.

Let anger, deceit, and pride  
be absent from our hearts;

[20] Let greed stand apart,  
the root of all evils.

Let wine not occupy the mind  
with continual drunkenness,  
but, fitting our understanding,  
let us drink your cup.

[25] Let sincere charity  
preserve the bonds of peace,  
and let unblemished chastity  
remain with lasting faith.

Let the ever-persuading hunger  
not be directed toward adding estates;

[30] If riches overflow,  
let the Psalm of the Prophet guide us.

Grant, unbegotten Father,  
that throughout the whole day

[35] We may live continually pleasing to Christ,  
filled with the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1195A] XLII.—Thomas. Hymn; and Codex O. Another copy, II, has the heading: “Hymn to be sung on Thursday.” Verse 8: O. reads “of the Holy Spirit.” Verse 9: Another copy, II, “powerful”; O., “lofty faith.” Verse 14: O., “you sit upon the seventh [throne].” Verse 17: Another copy, II, reads *homini* (“for man”) instead of *omnipotens* (“almighty”). Verse 18: Thomas, “You are Hosanna.” Verse 20: O., “[Col. 1196A] You are the first resurrection of the king,” but these words belong to Revelation 20:5–6. Verse 21: Thomas, “hearer.” Verse 23: O., “throne of the lofty seat.” Verse 24: O., “and to you.” Verse 25: Thomas, “to God.”]

## Morning Hymn

God of eternal light,  
Ineffable radiance,  
Judge of the coming day,  
You who see the hidden things of the mind;

[5] You hold the kingdom of heaven,  
And you are wholly in the Word;  
Through the Son you rule all things,

You behold the threefold name,  
[10] One almighty power through all things;

## Morning Hymn

[Col. 1196] Let us render praises to the Lord,

[5] Let us drive away everything harmful,

God, ruler of all things,  
Look favorably upon us,  
Your servants who pray.

[10] And to his only Son,

## Hymn at Terce

Now the third hour rises,  
And we hasten with attentive minds;  
We fulfill the work of singing psalms;  
Let us praise Christ the Lord.

[5] Now, at the third hour,  
Christ was also suspended upon the cross;  
He fulfilled the Father’s will,  
He took away the sin of the world.

He ascended his proper seat,  
[10] He sits at the Father’s right hand;  
The thrones praise together the Lord  
Whom the treacherous had denied.

We worship Christ as God,  
And await him as Judge,  
[15] Him whom the prophets sang,  
Whom the apostles followed.

At the third hour the holy master of the household  
Went out  
And hired workers  
For individual denarii.

[20] In your vineyard, Christ,  
Whose reward we now behold,  
We follow the mystical work  
Because of the excellent promise.

Behold, the hour has come  
[Col. 1197] In which the Holy Spirit  
Made the vessels of the apostles  
Drunk with the word.

Pour understanding into us, Lord,  
[30] That we may sing you in praise;  
Christ, Redeemer of all,  
Sanctify our choir.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] XLVI.—Found in Cassander, Thomasius, and Codex O. Verse 2: O. omits *qua* (“by which”). Verse 4: O., “of Christ.” Verse 12: Colossians 2:14, “blotting out the record of debt that stood against us.” The Germanic translator rendered it ineptly: “dea arloste fona luzzi le mu kascribe.”]

## Hymn at Terce, on the Passion of the Lord

By the faith of God, by which we live,  
By the everlasting hope in which we believe,  
Through the grace of charity,  
Let us sing glory to Christ.

[5] He who, led at the third hour  
To the sacrifice of his passion,  
Bearing the burden of the cross,  
Restored the lost sheep.

Let us therefore pray as subjects,  
[10] Freed by redemption,  
That he may rescue from the world  
Those whom he freed from the bond of debt.

Glory to you, Trinity,  
One equal Godhead,  
[15] Both before every age  
And now and forever.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] XLVII.—From Thomas’s Hymnary. Verses 5–6: Acts 10:9ff.]

## Hymn at Sext

Now the course of the sixth hour  
Turns the times of day;  
It reminds us in every respect  
To render the praises that are due.

[5] Now Peter, praying on his knees,  
Foresees the faith that is to come;  
Now Christ presses on  
To give the living seeds to the waters.

At this mystic time of day,  
The patriarch entertains three  
Messengers who foreshadow the flesh,  
Under the sign of the Trinity.

[10] The perfect total of the highest reckoning  
Is established in its first parts;  
That which is given perfects itself  
And holds together the fabric of the world.

These things, Christ, created by you,  
[Col. 1197] Remain through your power,  
Whose power of glory  
Reigns throughout all ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] XLVIII.—Found in one copy of O.]

## Hymn at the Meal

At midday one must pray,  
Christ must be entreated,  
That he may command us to eat  
Of his holy body.

[5] May he be praised  
Among all peoples,  
He himself, the Lord of heaven,  
Who sits in the highest places.

May he give us help  
[10] Through wondrous angels,  
Who may always guard us  
Throughout every life of this world.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] XLIX.—Thomas’s Hymnary; the Mozarabic Breviary, in the Office before Compline during Lent.]

## Hymn after the Meal Has Been Resumed

After suitable food has been taken,  
After the uses of the meal have been completed,  
To you, illustrious Redeemer,  
We come to bring forth praises.

[5] Come quickly to meet us,  
Taking away the heaviness of food,  
Preparing the body for prayer,  
Giving faith for confession.

So that whatever we utter with our mouth  
[10] In your sacred praises,  
You may confer upon us a crown,  
Giving glory to God alone.

Grant this, most merciful Father, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] L.—Thomasius in the Hymnary. Verses 11–12: compare Acts 10:19ff.]

## Hymn at None

The sun’s vaulted orbit,  
Rolled through nine circles,  
When the path of the hour has been completed,  
Completes the ternary three times.

[5] At this time of the Passion  
The author of all things fulfilled it;  
Now he sent the called servants  
To the labor of the vineyard.

At this hour Peter, mystically,  
[10] Loosed the bonds of the lame man;  
Now he considers the vision.  
He brings it to an end at the third recurrence.
