[Col. 1198] Let us sing the glory of the hymns  
With voice and pure minds,  
[15] To God, who creates prosperity  
For the just through the ages.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] LI.—From Thomas’s Hymnary.]

## Hymn at None

Three times three hours disclose  
The number of sacred faith;  
Now, in the name of the Trinity,  
We ask for the gift of forgiveness.

[5] Behold, the confession of the thief  
Earns Christ’s grace;  
Our praise, or our devotion,  
Earns forgiveness.

Death now perishes through the cross,  
[10] And light returns after darkness;  
Let the horror of sins be opened up,  
Let the splendor of minds shine forth.

Glory to you, Trinity,  
One equal Godhead,  
[15] Both before every age  
And now and forever.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] LII.—The hymn is attributed to Codex O. Verse 9: Codex O., incorrectly, “But you, Lord.” Grimmius recommends reading “But do, Lord.” If I see correctly, the manuscript’s reading is unquestionably genuine; since *tu* (“you”) is very often confused with *tunc* (“then”), there is no need to demonstrate this at length.]

## Hymn at Vespers

God, who by clear light  
Made the day, O Lord,  
We ask for your glory  
As the day bends down toward its end.

[5] Now the sun, as evening presses on,  
Moves toward its setting,  
Enclosing the world in darkness,  
Observing its own boundary.

But then, exalted Lord,  
[10] May night receive your servants who pray,  
Wearied by the labor of the day,  
In a state of rest.

So that the day of this world  
May not depart with minds darkened,  
[15] But, sheltered by your grace,  
May we behold the favorable light.

[Note: [Col. 1197A] LIII.—In my opinion, this hymn does not properly concern the Advent of the Lord, but is a Vespers hymn (compare the note at [Col. 1197B], verse 24). Yet we grant that, as you see was done by the Church according to ancient custom, it can very suitably be applied in many places to the sacred season preceding the Nativity. In all the books that I have seen, however, it is placed among the Advent hymns for Vespers.

Verse 2: Kehr, “eternal.” He adds: “I would rather read *aeterna*.” I would like to know where this corrupt reading arose. It is not found even in Fabricius, whom Kehr follows in this hymn.

Verses 5–8: Codex W. I and Codex Cs.:

“Who, grieving for human beings,  
Carried under the laws of death,  
Having become human, restore  
Life through your blood.”

Verse 8: H. and M., “of the king.”

Verse 9: Cassander and Cornelius, “as evening presses on.” Perhaps the poet had before his eyes Zechariah 14:7: “And there shall be one day, which is known to the Lord, neither day nor night, and at evening time there shall be light.” Clichtoveus writes: “Christ is said to have come when the evening of the world was approaching. For, when five ages of the world had already been completed, he came in its sixth age, which will extend to the end of the world.” Among the Fathers, discussion of the world laboring under the burdens of old age is extremely common. Hear only Ambrose, *On the Good of Death*, chapter 10: “As creation grows old, it lays aside the strength of its youth, as the vigor of its powers is already withering.” In the same sense our poet calls the world languishing.

Verse 10: Psalm 17:6.

Verse 11: M., “most blessed.”

Verse 12: Gronovius, “of the virgin mother.” Kehr writes: “The word *clausula*, which here stands in a somewhat unusual meaning, is equivalent to the *claustrum pudoris* (‘enclosure of modesty’) of another hymn (Hymn 4, verse 12, in the preceding volume), and stands for *utero* (‘womb’).” Correctly, if the word is weighed on the scale of pure language: among writers of Late Latin, *clausula* means the same as a chamber or an area enclosed by a barrier; compare Du Cange, s.v. *clausura*.

Verses 13–16: Philippians 2:10: “That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth.” Codex W. I and Codex Cs. come closer to this passage, reading “of those in heaven, on earth, and also in the infernal regions.”

Verse 14: Cassander, “bending”; another copy, “are bent”; in some copies, “knees.” W. I., “the knee of all should bend.”

Verse 16: Fr., Aug., Gron., Lips., Pd., “confess by a nod.”

Verses 17–20: The Roman Breviary rejected the stanza, and not without reason. To say nothing of the fact that in some books it scarcely coheres with the other parts of the hymn, it is even absent from them. Lossius explains the words as follows: “The fixed and perpetual motion of the heavenly bodies teaches the Church two things: first, the omnipotence and wisdom of God; second, the eternal covenant by which God joined the human race to himself through the Son. Jeremiah 33: ‘My covenant with them shall be inviolable, as heaven is everlasting.’”

Verse 19: Beb., “resisting.”

Verse 20: Cassander, “observed.”

Verse 21: We are surprised that Kehr makes this observation: “One could indeed, though contrary to linguistic usage, understand *Agie* as *age* (‘come’); but it is better to take it as the Greek ἅγος.” [Greek: “sacredness,” “holy thing,” or “sanctuary.”]

Verse 22: Aug., “of the one who is to come.”

Verses 23–24: Cassander: “In the book of Saint Benedict it is read thus: ‘Preserve us in the time of night from the arrow of the treacherous one,’ whose meaning is clear. Although nearly all the others give *hostis* (‘enemy’), I too would judge that reading genuine.” W. I. and Cs., “that we may long remain strangers.”

Verse 24: D. 2, incorrectly, “from the arrow of the provident one.”]

## Hymn for the Advent of the Lord

*(From an old book)*

Bountiful creator of the stars,  
Eternal light of believers,  
Christ, Redeemer of all,  
Hear the prayers of your supplicants.

[5] You, grieving over destruction,  
Because the world was perishing through death,  
Saved the languishing world,  
Giving a remedy to the guilty.

As the evening of the world approached,  
[10] Like a bridegroom from his chamber,  
You came forth most honorably  
From the enclosure of the virgin mother.

At whose mighty power  
All things bend the knee;  
[15] Heavenly and earthly things  
Confess by a nod that they are subject.

[The sun, keeping watch over its setting,  
The moon, retaining its pallor;  
The brightness shining back among the stars  
Observes fixed boundaries.]

We entreat you, Hagie [Holy One],  
Judge of the world who is to come:  
Preserve us in the time of night  
From the arrow of the treacherous enemy.

Praise, honor, power, glory, etc.

## Another Reading of the Same Hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

Bountiful creator of the stars,  
Eternal light of believers,  
Jesus, Redeemer of all,  
Attend to the prayers of your supplicants.

[5] You, so that the world might not perish  
Through the deceits of the devil,  
Moved by an impulse of love,  
Became the remedy of the languishing world.

[Col. 1199] To expiate the common sin of the world,  
[10] You came to the cross  
From the sanctuary of the virgin,  
An undefiled victim.

When the power of your glory  
And your name first sound,  
[15] Both the heavenly beings and those below  
Bend the trembling knee.

We entreat you, great Judge  
Of the final day;  
[20] Defend us from our enemies  
With the weapons of heavenly grace.

Power, honor, praise, glory, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1199B] LIV.—Almost everywhere at Lauds during Advent. I would have you not overlook in this hymn that the poet has very skillfully adapted to his own purpose the passages of Sacred Scripture recited in the Church on Sundays and feast days. Compare verses 3–6 with the epistle for the First Sunday of Advent, Romans 13:11ff.; verses 13–16 with the Gospel for the Second Sunday [Col. 1200A] (or, as it is today in the Roman Church, the First), Luke 21:25ff.; and finally the beginning with the passage assigned in the oldest Lectionary to the Fourth Sunday, Mark 1:1ff.

Verse 1: John repeatedly urges repentance and rebukes every vice and sin.

Verse 3: Bd., “far away.”

Verse 4: Cassander and Rambach, “from the ether.”

Verse 5: E. and Msn., “turbulent”; Pd., “will rise again.”

Verse 9: Fabricius, “from above.” The poet improperly mixes in the following stanzas metaphors used of Christ.

Verse 13: Cassander and Rambach, “so that when he comes a second time.”

Verse 14: Hl., “and when terror surrounds the world.”

Verse 16: Hl., “then protect us, the devout”; Cassander and Rambach, “but then may he, merciful, protect us.”]

## Hymn on the Advent of the Lord

*(From an old book)*

Behold, a clear voice resounds,  
Rebuking every dark thing;  
Let dreams be driven far away;  
Christ shines forth from the ether.

[5] Let the sluggish mind now rise,  
The mind that stands wounded by filth;  
Already the new star shines back,  
To take away everything harmful.

The Lamb is sent from above.  
[10] Let us all loosen our debt;  
For forgiveness, let us all  
Give voice with tears.

So that, when he shines a second time  
[15] And terror surrounds the world,  
He may not punish us for guilt,  
But then, merciful, may protect us.

## Another Reading of the Same Hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

Behold, a clear voice reproves,  
Resounding against every dark thing;  
Let dreams be driven far away;  
Jesus shines forth from on high.

[5] Let the sluggish mind now rise,  
No longer lying upon the ground;  
Already the new star shines back,  
To take away everything harmful.

Behold, the Lamb is sent to us  
[10] Freely to loosen our debt;  
Let us all together, with tears,  
Pray for forgiveness.

So that, when he shines a second time  
And surrounds the world with fear,  
[15] He may not punish us for guilt,  
But then, merciful, may protect us.

Power, honor, praise, glory, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1200A] LV.—The hymn above is found throughout older breviaries, either at Vespers or at Matins. Now it is everywhere recited at the nocturnal office during Advent; moreover, together with the two preceding hymns, on the feast of the Expectation of Blessed Mary. Hilary thinks that this hymn ought to be used in answer to heretics who would say that Christ came, but not from the Father.

Verse 2: E. and Cassander, “coming forth.”

Verse 4: Compare Hymn 50, verse 9.

Verse 7: Gronovius, Beb., “when the proclamation has been heard”; Bd., “when the proclamations have been heard.”

Verse 11: Cassander, “you will repay in kind.”

Verse 13: Cassander, “do not give”; he reports that others read “we are not harmed”; Bd., Hilary, Beb., “we are confined”; Wimpfeling, “we may be confined.”

Verse 16: Clichtoveus writes: “By perpetual celibacy the state of the future life and the perpetual dwelling of the heavenly kingdom are sought, since in it there is continual continence and abstinence from carnal intercourse ... There are also those who read *coelites* (‘heavenly beings’). These express the meaning of this passage more openly. Yet whoever read ‘May we be perpetual celibates,’ or ‘heavenly beings,’ would speak much more appropriately. For the pronunciation is gentler and the structure of the sentence better.” Whatever the case, the authority of the books establishes *coelibes* (“celibates”) as the reading, and it should be explained in no other way than Hilary explained it: “living a heavenly life.” For from Matthew 22:30, “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven,” that manner of speaking could have arisen in which *coelebs* (“celibate”) was used for “blessed.”]

## Hymn on the Advent of the Lord

*(From an old book)*

The heavenly Word coming forth,  
Coming forth long ago from the Father,  
You who, born, come to the world’s aid  
As time runs downward toward its end;

[5] Now illumine hearts  
And set them ablaze with your love,  
So that, when the proclamation is heard,  
At last slippery things may be driven away.

And when, as Judge, you come afterward  
[10] To examine the deeds of the heart,  
Repaying what is due for hidden things  
And giving the kingdom to the just for their good,

May we not finally be hemmed in by evils  
[15] According to the measure of our crimes,  
But, sharing with the blessed,  
May we be perpetual celibates.

## Another Reading of the Same Hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

The heavenly Word coming forth,  
From the Father’s eternal bosom,  
You who, born, come to the world’s aid  
As time’s course slips away;

[5] Now illumine hearts  
And set them ablaze with your love,  
So that, as the heart abandons what passes away,  
The delight of heaven may fill it;

So that when the Judge’s tribunal  
[10] Condemns the guilty to the fire,  
And a friendly voice calls the righteous,  
Who have fulfilled their duty, to heaven,

We may not be rolled, blackened as food for flames,  
[15] Among whirling storms,  
But, possessing the face of God,  
May we enjoy the joys of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1201A] LVI.—The hymn is rarely found in old books (Fr., Aug., and others), but is now celebrated in the Church with greater observance. It is sung at both Vespers services of the Nativity, on unobstructed feast days within its Octave, and on the feast of the Circumcision. In addition, the third verse, joined to another verse taken from elsewhere (“Mary, mother of grace, sweet parent of mercy, protect us from the enemy, and receive us at the hour of death”), together with the doxology, serves for the Little Office of Mary at Compline and at all the hours called the minor hours.

Verse 1: Fr., Aug., “of all things.” There exists a hymn of later age, “Christ, Redeemer of all,” concerning all the saints.

Verse 2: Pd., “from.”

Verse 5: Cassander, Rambach (who follows Cassander’s traces in this hymn), and others, *et*. The little words *et ... ut*, as elsewhere (compare the former colleague Unger’s *Theban Paradise*, part 1, p. 31), are very frequently confused by scribes in hymns.

Verse 13: Cassander, “here.”

Verse 15: Clichtoveus: “He is said to have come alone because he alone, through human incarnation, assumed human nature. For neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit was incarnate.” [Col. 1201B]

Verse 19: Aug., “the arrival of his author.”

Verse 20: Aug. and Pd., “he praises, exulting.”

Verse 24: Psalms 95:1; 97:1. Similarly Gellert: “And earth, which sees him today, sing a new song to him, the Lord.”]

## On the Nativity of the Lord

*(From an old book)*

Christ, Redeemer of the nations,  
Only-begotten of the Father,  
Born ineffably, alone  
Before the beginning.

[5] You are the light, you are the splendor of the Father,  
You are the everlasting hope of all;  
Attend to the prayers  
Your servants throughout the world pour forth.

Remember, author of salvation,  
[10] That once, by being born  
From an undefiled virgin, you took on  
The form of our body.

[Col. 1201] Thus the present day bears witness,  
Running through the circle of the year,  
[15] That you alone, from the Father’s seat,  
Have come as the world’s salvation.

Let heaven, earth, and sea,  
And everything that is in them,  
Exult in song, praising  
[20] The author of your coming.

We also, who have been redeemed  
By your holy blood,  
For the day of your birth  
Sing together a new hymn.

## Another Reading of the Same Hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

Jesus, Redeemer of all,  
Whom, before the origin of light,  
The supreme Father brought forth  
Equal to the Father’s glory.

[5] You are the light and splendor of the Father,  
You are the everlasting hope of all;  
Attend to the prayers  
Your servants throughout the world pour forth.

Remember, creator of all things,  
[10] That once, by being born  
From the consecrated womb of a virgin, you took on  
The form of our body.

The present day bears witness,  
Running through the circle of the year,  
[15] That you alone, from the Father’s bosom,  
Have come as the world’s salvation.

The stars, the earth, and the seas,  
And everything subject to heaven,  
Greet you, author of a new salvation,  
[20] With a new song.

And we, blessed ones whom the water  
Of your sacred blood has watered,  
For the day of your birth  
Pay the tribute of a hymn.

Jesus, to you be glory,  
Who were born of the Virgin, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1201A] LVII.—I found the poem in Codex W. 1, in Thomas’s Hymnary (in Vaticanus 82 it is entitled “Hymn of Saint Mary”), in the old breviaries of the Carthusians and Cistercians, at Matins or Vespers on the solemnities and octaves of Blessed Mary the Virgin, and finally in Ellinger (at Epiphany), but completely altered and differing in many other respects.

Verse 4: W., Ct., Cs., “the Son.”

Verse 10: W. 1, “had foretold.”

Verses 11–12: Isaiah 7:14, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.”

Verse 13: Vaticanus 82 omits “is.”

Verse 14: Thomas, “And what was granted to Mary.”

Verse 17: Luke 1:28; the angel said, “Hail, full of grace.”

Verse 19: Another copy omits “for us.”

Verse 22: W. 1, Ct., Cs., “sang to God.”

Verse 23: Luke 2:16, “and they came in haste.”

Verse 28: It is well known that the Magi signify the multitude of the nations to be converted to the Lord. Less well known is that, according to the opinion of the ancients, they undertook this journey not in their own name, but as envoys chosen from the entire choir of the wise men of the East. Hence Juvencus 1.228ff.: “They bore the name of Magi; chosen nobles therefore arrive at Jerusalem over long roads.” Gaudentius of Brescia, in his letter to his brother Paul, writes: “The radiance of the obedient star declares the great God, whom the Magi, envoys of all the nations, humbly adoring, ...”

Verse 28: Ellinger adds two verses in which there is no trace of our poem:

“And they fixed kisses  
[Col. 1202B] Upon the little King as he cried,  
They offered abundant gifts  
Of frankincense, myrrh, and gold leaf.”

Let us praise the Virgin, mother of God,  
Type of the holy Church,  
In whose tender arms  
Little Jesus rests.”]

## On the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 1202]

We offer a hymn to Christ  
On the Church’s mystery—  
Christ whom a woman in childbirth bore,  
The Father’s Word in the Son.

[5] You alone, a woman among women,  
Were chosen in the world,  
And you were worthy to bear the Lord  
In your holy womb.

The ancient prophets  
Had foretold what came to pass:  
That a Virgin would conceive  
And bear Emmanuel.

[10] This mystery is great,  
What was granted to Mary:  
That she should see brought forth from herself  
The God through whom all things exist.

Truly you are full of grace  
[15] And remain glorious,  
Because from you Christ was born for us,  
Through whom all things were made.

The shepherds who heard  
Sang glory to the Lord;  
They ran to Bethlehem  
[20] To see the Lord who had been born.

Thus the Magi, from the rising of the sun,  
By the sign of the star,  
Bearing the figure of the nations,  
First offer gifts.

Let us therefore, as peoples, ask  
[25] The mother and virgin of God  
To obtain for us  
Peace and forgiveness.

Glory to you, Lord,  
Who were born of the Virgin, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1202B] LVIII.—Wimpfeling and Sb.: the Third and Fourth Sundays in Lent. Thomas: placed in an old monastic Hymnary for Saturday Vespers in Lent. Torrentius reasonably remarks: “This hymn is sung around the spring equinox, when the day is equal to the night, namely, twelve hours.” It is certainly extremely rare in breviaries.

Verse 1: O., thus.

Verse 2: Gronovius, “the day by hours.”

Verse 3: O. and Wimpfeling, “foretelling”; Torrentius, “proclaiming”; Clichtoveus and Sb., “proclaims.”

Verse 4: Cassander, Thomas, Clichtoveus, “to come”; O., “for the times to return at night.”

Verse 6: Cassander and Gronovius, “let us protect”; Sb., “let us make safe”; O., “we strike the chaste breasts” (Torrentius and Wimpfeling).

Verse 7: Genesis 3:1, “The serpent was more crafty than any beast of the earth.”

Verse 8: O., “attempt”; another copy, “assail”; Sb., “access.”

Verse 10: O., “freed”; Sb., Torrentius, Wimpfeling, “freely.”

Verse 14: Cassander and Thomas, “stretch out.”

Verse 15: Sb. and Cassander, “Nor by force, through sleep, [let our] souls be deceived”; O., “having glorified.” Hilary: “A belly seething with unmixed wine easily foams over into lust, and the heaviness of sleep that follows drunkenness makes us more heedless and weaker in resisting the devil’s snares.” Sb. adds a fifth verse: “Grant, blessed Trinity,” etc., taken from the hymn “Kind Creator, hear.”]

## Lenten Hymn

Now the day is drawn toward evening  
Through three times four hours;  
At sunset the sun foretells  
The return of night’s hours.

[Col. 1203] Let us therefore, by the Lord’s sign,  
Protect the enclosures of our hearts.  
Let that crafty serpent  
Attempt no entrance.

[5] But, with the mind strengthened  
By the weapons of chastity,  
Free and watchful,  
With sobriety as its companion,  
Let it repel the wicked enemy.

[10] And let no drunken excess of food  
Finally distend our bodies,  
Lest through the force of sleep  
It defile the soul once deceived.

[Note: [Col. 1203A] LIX.—Contained in W. I and the Breviary of Cs. (from Passion Sunday to Easter, except Palm Sunday). Thomas’s Hymnary, from Vaticanus 82; among the others, only Ellinger, who, as usual, conformed the poem to the rules of meter and thus altered it completely.

Verse 5: W. I and Cs., “when it has been completed.”

Verse 6: W. I and Cs., “by which.”

Verses 13ff.: There are many Christian poets who, in recounting and detesting the horrifying crime of Judas, portray how, like the worst of merchants, he handed over his Lord into the hands of the ungodly. Nor is there lacking lamentation born of anger and hatred at such depravity, nor is a gentler feeling of the heart absent. Thus in old German hymns the poets both curse and pity the betrayer. Compare the song called *Das Iudaslied* (Hoffmann, *History of German Church Songs*, p. 140):

“O poor Judas, what have you done,  
That you betrayed our Lord in this way?  
For this you must in hell  
Suffer pain forever;  
Lucifer’s companion  
You must be eternally.”

Verse 29: W. I and Cs., “and.”

Verse 32: W. I, “whom.” In any case, there is scarcely any need to point out that the hymn above is composed almost entirely from the very words of Sacred Scripture.]

## On the Passion of the Lord

Let us sing a hymn to the Lord,  
Praises to God with a song,  
Who redeemed us by the gallows  
Of the cross and by his blood.

[5] When the day had passed into evening,  
On which Christ was handed over to death,  
The impious man came to the meal,  
He who was Christ’s betrayer.

Jesus announces what is to come  
[10] To the disciples at table:  
“One of those reclining here  
Will himself betray me.”

Judas, the worst of merchants,  
Seeks the Lord with a kiss;  
[15] He, like an innocent lamb,  
Does not refuse Judas a kiss.

For a number of denarii  
Christ is handed over to the Jews,  
Innocent and without guilt,  
Whom the impious Judas betrays.

[20] The governor Pilate declares:  
“I find no fault”;  
After washing his hands in water,  
He handed Christ over to the Jews.

The deceitful, impious Jews  
[25] Ask that the robber be allowed to live;  
They accuse Christ severely:  
“He is guilty; let him be crucified.”

Then Barabbas is released,  
He who had been guilty of death;  
[30] The life of the world is suspended,  
Through which the dead rise again.

[Glory to you, Lord.  
Glory to the Only-Begotten,  
Together with the Holy Spirit,  
Throughout the everlasting ages. Amen.]

[Note: [Col. 1204A] LX.—Found throughout old breviaries, but usually mutilated. Some have five stanzas (verses 1–20), as Sb. and Beb. Hv. omits verses 29–40. The Roman Breviary, following ancient custom, decreed that verses 1–16 should be sung during the Easter season at Lauds; the remainder belongs to the Common of Apostles during the Easter season. Pius V divided the hymn “The Apostles Were Sad” into two parts, so that the second could be sung at Lauds with variation (Gavanti, *Sacred Treasury*, III, p. 555).

Verse 1: Beb., “shining.”  
Verse 8: O., “chain.”  
Verse 12: Ellinger and Fabricius, “the dead rises”; Hv., “rises from the grave.”  
Verse 14: Beb., “and of hell.”  
Verse 16: Beb. and Hv., “the shining angel cried”; O., “the shining angel cries.” Perhaps, according to Matthew 27:5, “But the angel answering said ...,” one should read *respondens* (“answering”).  
Verse 20: O. and Hv., “savage.”  

Similarly in a very ancient song in the vernacular:

“With gentle, sweet words  
The angel spoke to them:  
‘Let your fear be put away,  
You tender, beloved women;  
Jesus, the bold champion,  
Has arisen.’”

Verse 22: O., “foretells.” Matthew 27:7, “Behold, I have told you.”  
Verse 25: Cassander, Thomas, Sb., Beb., Fabricius, “hastening.”  
Verse 28: O., “they kiss.”  
Verse 30: O., “Galilee.”  
Verse 37: Clichtoveus: another copy, “after displaying the wounds.” Compare the song “Put Away Mourning, Magdalene,” with the words: “Look upon the five wounds; behold, they shine like pearls, ornaments of the new life.” Hilary: “The Lord displayed the scars of his wounds for four reasons: so that they might be a sign of victory; so that thereafter they would not doubt the resurrection; and so that they might serve as intercession with the Father.”]

## Easter Hymn

*(From an old book)*

The dawn of light gleams,  
Heaven resounds with praises,  
The rejoicing world exults,  
Groaning hell howls,

[5] When that most mighty King,  
Having broken the powers of death,  
Tramples Tartarus beneath his foot  
And frees the wretched from punishment.

He who was shut up by a stone  
[10] And guarded beneath a soldier’s watch,  
Triumphing in noble procession,  
Rises victorious from the grave.

The groans and pains of hell  
Having now been loosed,  
[15] Because the Lord has risen,  
The shining angel cries out.

The apostles were sad  
At the death of their Lord,  
Whom the impious servants  
Had condemned to a most cruel death.

[20] In gentle speech the angel  
Foretold it to the women:  
“The Lord will be seen  
In Galilee very soon.”

As they hurry off  
[25] To tell this to the apostles,  
Seeing him alive,  
They kiss the Lord’s feet.

When the disciples recognized him,  
[30] They hastened to Galilee  
To see the Lord’s desired face.

With the clear joy of Easter  
The sun shines upon the world with its ray,  
[35] When the apostles now see Christ  
With bodily sight.

The wounds shown to them  
Shine upon Christ’s radiant flesh;  
They publicly confess  
[40] In their voices that the Lord has risen.

King Christ, most merciful,  
Possess our hearts,  
So that at all times  
We may render you the praises that are due.

## Another Reading of the Same Hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

Dawn makes the heavens purple,  
The ether resounds with praises,  
The triumphant world rejoices,  
Horrible hell trembles.

[5] When that most mighty King  
Leads forth from death’s infernal cavern  
The free assembly of the fathers  
Into the radiance of life.

The stone had marked his tomb  
[10] With a very numerous guard;  
Victorious, he triumphs, and buries  
Death in his own tomb.

Enough of funeral rites, enough of tears;  
Enough has been given to sorrows:  
[15] The destroyer of death has risen,  
The flashing angel cries out.

The apostles were sad  
At Christ’s bitter burial,  
Whom the impious servants  
[20] Had killed by the most cruel death.

The truthful angel  
Had foretold to the women:  
“Soon Christ will bring joy  
By his word to the faithful flock.”

[25] At once the women, as messengers,  
Run to the anxious apostles;  
Meeting the radiant Christ,  
They hold his footprints.

The apostles go  
[30] To the heights of Galilee’s mountains,  
And, having obtained what they desired,  
Are blessed by Jesus’ gracious light.

The sun announces  
The Easter joy of the world,  
[35] When the apostles see Jesus  
Shining with new light.

They marvel at the wounds  
In Christ’s flesh, sparkling like stars,  
And whatever they see,  
[40] They proclaim as faithful witnesses.

King Christ, most merciful,  
Possess our hearts,  
So that, reborn to life,  
Our tongue may offer due thanks freely.

[Note: [Col. 1205A] LXI.—Cassander writes: “This hymn is not found in the common hymn books now, nor would it have come to my mind if Bede had not reminded me of it in the first book of his work on meter. I was encouraged to seek it out by Bede’s own words, in which he praises it greatly. Under the heading ‘On Rhythm’ he says: ‘Often, by a kind of chance, you will find even a pattern in rhythm, not merely with the artificer’s method preserved, but with sound and the very modulation leading the way. Thus, resembling iambic meter, that famous hymn “Eternal King, O Lord” has been beautifully fashioned.’ Led, therefore, by this praise, I found it in an obsolete book printed fifty-six years ago—very probably in the Cologne Hymnary—and judged that it should be inserted here.”

From this it may properly be inferred only that books from Germany and England were available to Cassander, since the hymn is by no means rare in Italian books. Vezzosi, in Thomas’s collection, suspects that this is the same hymn cited by Bishop Aurelian in his Rule. If one considers the verses that Grimmius first produced from Codex O., one will scarcely believe that the poet celebrated Easter. Everything points to Matins, and the more detailed account of the redemption accomplished through Jesus Christ is not foreign to that office. Nevertheless, we grant this much: already among the ancients the first eight stanzas of the poem had made it an Easter hymn. On this point, not to mention the headings, very little doubt remains because of the Easter doxologies attached to the poem. The Roman Breviary, as it now stands, selected stanzas 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8 and composed an Easter hymn to be recited on Low Sunday at Matins and throughout the Easter season until the Ascension.

Verse 1: Fabricius, “O king”; the others omit the interjection. If you seek the reason for my unusual deference toward Fabricius, let the meter of the poem come to mind. Nor should you object that I have elsewhere very often complained that Christian poets neglected the laws of meter. Bede’s testimony proves that this hymn was “beautifully fashioned in the likeness of iambic meter.” There is another reason as well: scribes were so free in their writing that at the beginnings of clauses they sometimes added letters unnecessarily and sometimes removed them. Santen, in his commentary on Terence, p. 186, supports our view: “I would prefer, with Hieronymus van Alphen, to add the interjection *o rex*, with the accent more correctly preserved and the line made acatalectic.” What he noted above, that catalectic dimeters result by reading *omnium*, *saecula*, and *filius* as two syllables, does not apply at all in our poem, which is undoubtedly acatalectic.

Verse 3: O. omits “who are before the ages”; Cassander and Hilary, “you are, and ...”

Verse 15: O. omits “and.”

Verse 21: Fabricius, “and who [is] for us”; Thomas, “through baptisms”; the others, “through baptism.”

Verses 39–64: Contained only in Codex O.

Verses 29–32: Matthew 26:51–53, “And the veil of the temple was torn ... and the earth was shaken ... and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose.”

Verse 45ff.: Perhaps here the proper hymn for Nocturns begins.

Verse 49: Grimmius wants to read, “because you yourself are the judge,” although the Germanic translator has: “thanta du selbo urchundo inti suanari pist”—“because you yourself are witness and judge”; V. D. wished to remedy the meter. This is entirely unnecessary with the poet’s intact words, since *quia* is very often a monosyllable among poets of the later period. Compare Barth on Corippus, *On the Praise of Justin*, II.109.

Verse 53: The translator has *thu unserero prustio* (“you [of] our breasts”), but instead of *pectorum* the poet seems to have written *peccatorum* (“of sinners”), producing a rather rough verse, though one composed of eight syllables. Compare 21.47.

Verse 59: Perhaps, “then also.”]

## Morning Hymn (Easter)

*(From an old book)*

O eternal King, Lord,  
Creator of all things,  
Who were before the ages,  
Always the Son with the Father.

[5] In the beginning of the world  
You fashioned Adam as a human being;  
To him, in your image,  
You gave a face like yours.

The devil had deceived him,  
[10] The enemy of the human race;  
You deigned to assume  
The form of his body.

So that you might redeem the human being  
Whom you had already fashioned,  
[15] And unite us to God  
Through fellowship in the flesh.

Who, born of a virgin,

is feared by every soul,

through whom we also, with devoted mind,

believe that we shall rise again.

[20] Who through baptisms

granted us forgiveness,

though we were held in bonds,

bound by conscience.

Who for humanity’s sake

[25] deigned to take up the cross,

you gave your blood

as the price of our salvation.

For the veil of the temple was torn

[30] and all the earth trembled;

then you raised up, Lord,

many of those who were sleeping.

[Col. 1206] You crush by the cross of death

the strength of the ancient enemy,

[35] by which, marked upon our foreheads,

we bear the standard of faith.

May you always deign

to drive him away from us,

so that he may never be able to harm

[40] those redeemed by your blood.

Who for our sake

deigned to descend to the underworld,

so that you might give the gifts of life

to those indebted to death.

[45] To you, during the night,

we sing a hymn through our tears;

forgive us, Lord,

forgive us who confess.

For you yourself are witness and judge,

[50] whom no one can deceive,

seeing the traces

of our secret conscience.

You alone are the investigator

of our hearts;

[55] you are the good physician

who attends to hidden wounds.

You are the one who, at the appointed time,

will bring the world to an end;

you are the just rewarder

[60] of the merits of all.

Therefore, holy one, we ask you:

heal our wounds,

you who are the Son with the Father,

always with the Holy Spirit.

## Another version of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

Eternal King of the heavenly ones,

creator of all things,

equal before the ages,

always the Son of the Father.

[5] When the world was coming into being, you, its craftsman,

joined noble spirit

to Adam’s clay,

giving him the image of your face.

When the envy and deceit of the demon

[10] had disfigured the human race,

you, the craftsman, clothed in flesh,

restored the ruined form.

You who were once born of a virgin,

now are born from the tomb,

[15] and you command us,

buried with you among the dead,

to rise.

You, the eternal shepherd,

wash the flock with baptismal water;

this is the washing of minds,

[20] this is the tomb of sins.

For us, long owing a debt,

you, Redeemer, fastened to the cross,

lavishly gave

your blood as the price of salvation.

[Note: LXII.—This hymn is found almost everywhere in the Breviaries during Eastertide. The Roman Breviary likewise prescribes it—from Vespers until the Vigil of the Ascension—which nevertheless, in my opinion, not only customarily removed the rust of antiquity, but was here excessively eager for innovations. Hilary says: “The subject of this hymn is that the author summons us to the supper of that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, namely, to receive the body and blood of the Lord, of which it is said: He who receives the body of Christ unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, but he who receives it worthily has eternal life; … while we, placed at the Lamb’s supper, are watchful.” Since this seems not far from the truth, I shall venture to propose that the hymn *Ad coenam Agni* was customarily sung in the ancient Church while the baptized catechumens were properly fortified with the body and blood of the Lord. Everything certainly suits the sacred supper very well; nor should you overlook the fact that other poets expressed this meaning more explicitly. Thus, for example, in the Easter song no. 14 in Hoffmann, p. 69:

“You should feed yourselves with the Easter lamb  
and take its holy flesh and blood.  
O Satan, you hateful executioner,  
Christ has tamed your wickedness,  
when that night took great spoil from you.  
That night came upon King Pharaoh,  
when the Red Sea engulfed him,” etc.

—1. Revelation 19:9: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” —2. O., “in white stoles”; Fabr., “in stoles and white garments.” All the baptized were clothed in white clothing. Hence Paulinus, *Letter* 12, to Severus: “From the sacred font the priest leads the infants forth, white in body, heart, and dress.” —3. Baptism was typified by the Israelites’ passage through the Red Sea, 1 Corinthians 10:1 ff.; Arator, *History of the Apostles* II, 81 f.; Avitus, book I, *On the Passage of the Red Sea*; Sedulius, *Paschal Work* I, 120. Pharaoh, moreover, is very often interpreted typologically as the devil. —5. O., “the sacred little body.” —5–6. Cornelius: “Roasted and dried on the cross by the fire of God’s anger, as he himself says: ‘My strength has dried up like a potsherd.’” In addition, it is compared with the roasted paschal lamb. Everyone will concede to us how inept this image is—and more likely to arouse disgust than devotion—which was not adopted by the Roman Breviary in its corrected text. Nevertheless, the poets of our Church were strangely satisfied with it, for example Luther in *Christ lag in Todesbanden*: “Here is the true Easter lamb, of which God commanded; it is roasted on the cross-tree in ardent love.” —7. Loss., *rosido*. —9. O., *vesperum*. —13 f. 1 Corinthians 5:7–8: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; let us feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity.” —17. Cassander: Others, “O true and worthy.” —20. O., E., W. 2, Md., Pd., Thomasius, *a nobis stant*; the others, *redit ad*. In my opinion the verse contains three asyndetic clauses, progressing from the lesser to the greater. Not only are Tartarus’s gates broken, but also the people cast into bondage are freed; a third point follows: the gifts of blessed life are restored to them. This is a celebrated passage concerning the glorious descent into hell. —21. Cassander, Langius, Cs., Thomasius, Bebel, Torrentius, *consurgit*; Fr., *dum surgit*. —22. O., by way of explanatory addition, *tartaro*. —23. O., *tradens*; Fabr., *tyranni trahens*; Lud., “dragging the tyrant in chains.” Compare the Easter sequence *Also heilig ist der Tag*: “So holy is the day that overcame hell and bound the hateful devil therein.” —25–28. Om., Fabr. The stanza is joined as a refrain to many Easter hymns. —28. O., Md., *defendas*.]

## Easter hymn

*(From an old book)*

Watchful for the Lamb’s supper,

and radiant in white garments,

after crossing the Red Sea,

let us sing to Christ our King.

[5] His most holy body,

roasted upon the altar of the cross,

by tasting his rosy blood

we live for God.

Protected on the eve of Passover

[10] from the destroying angel,

rescued from the harshest

dominion of Pharaoh,

now Christ is our Passover,

the Lamb who was sacrificed;

[15] his flesh, offered for us,

is the unleavened bread of sincerity.

O truly worthy victim,

through whom Tartarus was shattered,

the captive people redeemed,

[20] the rewards of life restored!

When Christ rises from the tomb,

the victor returns from the abyss,

dragging the tyrant in chains

and unlocking paradise.

[25] We ask you, author of all things,

in this paschal joy:

defend your people

from every assault of death.

## Another version of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

To the royal feasts of the Lamb,

clothed in white garments,

after crossing the Red Sea,

let us sing to Christ our King.

[5] His divine love

offers the sacred blood;

the priest, Love,

sacrifices the nourishing members of his body.

When the blood has been sprinkled on the doorposts,

[10] the destroying angel is terrified;

the divided sea flees,

and the enemies are drowned in the waves.

Now Christ is our Passover,

the same paschal victim,

and the unleavened bread of sincerity

[15] for pure minds.

O true victim of heaven,

to whom Tartarus is subject,

the bonds of death are loosed,

the rewards of life restored!

[20] Victorious over the conquered underworld,

Christ displays his trophies

and openly drags through heaven

the king subjected to darkness.

Grant that you may be everlasting paschal joy

[25] to our hearts, Jesus,

and free those reborn to life

from the dreadful death of sins.

[Note: LXIII.—I did not find this hymn in the Breviaries, except Cs., although I investigated with great diligence. It is indeed very remarkable that among three authors it is transmitted in different forms. Besides those known to us—Cassander, Bebel, Clichtovaeus, and the book of Saint Benedict—Thomasius presents the poem as follows: lines 1–4 as in Cassander; 5–8, “Let us sing this, the disciples; let us praise the martyr, who first after the Redeemer followed Christ’s cross”; 9–16 as in Cassander; 17–20, “That distinguished martyr himself, preaching through love of Christ, is filled with the Holy Spirit, bearing an angelic countenance”; 21–28 as in Cassander; 17–24; 29–32, “This man, prepared in his head, joyfully received the stones, praying for them to the Lord; joyfully he surrendered his spirit.” Cassander’s lines 25–36 are missing. In this disagreement among the books, I find the opinion very attractive that two songs about Saint Stephen were confused and mixed together by scribes; for this is also a common practice among hymn writers, who, attracted by similarities of thought and wording, mingle different poems by different authors. I would arrange the first hymn as follows: 1, “To Stephen, the first martyr”; 2, “Let us sing this, the disciples”; 3, “For through the apostles”; 4, “O glory to be preferred”; 5, “That distinguished martyr himself”; 6, “There, raising his eyes”; 7, “The Jews rage more fiercely”; 8, “This man, prepared in his head.” The second hymn: 1, “Stephen’s martyr’s crown”; 2, “This first one, in blessed blood”; 3, “When this man, with final words”; 4, “But he, gazing upon heaven”; 5, “Then the impious crowd attacks”; 6, “But he immediately to Christ”; 7, “God, creator of all”; 8, “Grant, Father, through the Son.” That we have judged correctly is attested by Cs., which presents the first poem, and by Ellinger, who in his second book gives the hymn I have placed first, though, as usual, with altered words: 1, “You alone, unique protomartyr, I shall sing”; 2, “Let us sing this, brother, today”; 3, “To the apostles this glory”; 4, “O glory to be preferred”; 5, “You, celebrated martyr, with devoted…”; 6, “Raising your eyes with the Father”; 7, “Then the fiery assembly rages”; 8, “That man prepared his head.”

### FIRST HYMN

3. Cassander, Bebel: “how sweet it is.” —9–10. Acts 6:6: “They set them before the apostles, and after praying they laid their hands upon them.” —11. Saint Stephen is the standard-bearer of the martyrs, who carries the banners before the army of martyrs. Likewise in the hymn *Sancte Dei pretiose*: “You, the heavenly first standard-bearer of the army.” —16. “He followed as the first martyr.” —20. Acts 6:15: “And when they looked at him, they all saw his face as though it were the face of an angel.” —21–24. Acts 7:55. —24. Cassander, *gaudebat*. —26. Bebel, *pressant*. —27. Cassander, *conjurant*.

### SECOND HYMN

8. Cassander, “through love of death”; the Book of Saint Benedict, in which Cassander investigated the poem, *contemptum*. —13. Cassander, “but he, gazing upon heaven.” —22. Cassander, *tradit*. —23. Clichtovaeus, for the meter, *persequentum*. —24. Cassander, “the second prayer.” —30. Cassander, *indulge*.]

## On Saint Stephen

*(Cassander, Bebel, Clichtovaeus)*

To Stephen, the first martyr,

let us sing a new song,

which may be sweet to those who sing

and bring help to believers.

[5] This first man, through blessed blood,

having followed Christ’s glory,

offered the way of salvation

to others through love of death.

For through the apostles

[10] he was approved in the praise of God;

he seized the banners of death

so that he might be placed before all.

O glory to be preferred,

O blessed victory,

[15] that Stephen should have deserved

to follow the Lord!

He, raising his eyes,

saw the Father with the Son,

showing that in heaven he lives,

[20] whom the people sought to destroy.

The Jews rage more fiercely,

and grasp stones in their hands;

they ran to kill

the revered soldier of Christ.

[25] But he immediately hands over

his blessed spirit to Christ,

and for the crime of his persecutors

directs a second prayer:

“God, creator of all,

[30] forgive this evil to the blind,

and this crime which you behold;

forgive it at my prayers.

Grant, Father, through the Son;

grant through the blessed Spirit;

[35] with these three, throughout eternity,

one God in name.”

*(Book of Saint Benedict)*

Stephen’s martyr’s crown,

as his name indicates,

let us sing with free praises

the glorious honor of Christ.

To Stephen, the first martyr,

[Col. 1209] let us sing a new song,

which may be sweet to those who sing

and bring help to believers.

This first man, through blessed blood,

[10] having followed Christ’s glory,

offered the eternal way of salvation

through contempt of death.

When he proclaimed

the word of salvation with final words,

[15] the blindness of Judea rejected

the radiant way of truth.

But he, gazing upon heaven,

saw the glory prepared,

and, granting a lesson

[20] for our generations, revealed a sublime example.

Then the impious crowd attacks

the martyr who was teaching,

and, lately bloodied by the Lamb’s blood,

it puts forth bloodstained [hands?].  
*[The transmitted object is uncertain; perhaps “raises [them].”]*

[25] But he immediately, handing over

his blessed spirit to Christ,

for the crime of his persecutors

directs a second prayer:

“God, creator of all,

[30] forgive this evil to the blind,

and this crime which you behold;

forgive it at my prayers.

Grant, Father, through the Son;

grant through the blessed Spirit;

[35] with these three, throughout eternity,

one God in name.”

[Note: LXIV.—The poem is found in Thomasius, Cassander, Ellinger’s third book—where he altered almost nothing in the hymns—and in Breviary Cs. —2. Mark 3:17, *Boanerges*, which means “sons of thunder.” —12. Thomasius, *hominum*, but Vatican 82, *omnium*. —14. Cassander, *salo*. —16. Vatican 82, *locata*. —17–22. Do not be offended by the poorly fashioned verse; recognize the very words of Holy Scripture, John 1:1–3. The sayings of the Holy Spirit are very often inserted into Ambrosian hymns unchanged and intact. —28. In his Gospel and apostolic teaching. —29–32. The Roman Breviary, in the Office of Saint John before the Latin Gate, reports this with remarkable brevity: “Tertullian relates that, when sent into a cauldron of boiling oil at Rome, he came out purer and more vigorous than he had entered.” So that the passage may not remain somewhat obscure on the testimony of others, understand Crato the philosopher as Saint John’s rival. Thus Fr.: “The philosopher C. had proposed in the forum a spectacle concerning contempt for this world, arranging for two very wealthy young brothers, whom he had induced to buy individual gems after selling their patrimony, to break them before everyone in the presence of the people. As the boys were doing this, it happened that the holy apostle passed that way. Calling C. to him, he said: ‘That contempt of the world which is praised by human speech but condemned by divine judgment is foolish.’ After they had disputed for some time, Crato said: ‘Make the gems whole again, so that what I did for human fame you may cause to be done for the glory of the one whom you call your master.’ Then blessed John gathered the fragments of the gems, placed them in his hand, raised his eyes to heaven, and said …” A prayer follows, heard by God. For the fragments of the gems came together.]

## On Saint John the Apostle

Noble through the love of Christ,

and Son of Thunder,

John revealed the hidden things of God

through sacred speech.

[5] He used to nourish his father’s old age

by catching fish;

while the sea was tossed as he swam,

he stood firm in immovable faith.

He had plunged the hook into the deep;

[10] he fished for the word of God;

he cast his nets upon the waves;

he raised up the life of all.

A good fish is devout faith,

floating above the sea of the world,

[15] supported upon Christ’s breast,

speaking through the Holy Spirit.

“In the beginning was the Word,

and the Word was with God,

and God was the Word.

[20] He was in the beginning with God.

“All things were made through him”;

but let him himself resound in praise,

and, crowned with the Spirit,

be crowned by his own writings.

[25] Passion and blood

that washes away sin are common to many;

by death he achieves for martyrs

what made them martyrs.

Yet, bound by the impious,

[30] he is said to have wiped away the world’s dust

in boiling oil,

and to have stood victorious over his rival.

Glory to you, Lord, etc.

[Note: LXV.—Saint Agnes, Virgin and Martyr, shines in the Church through ancient devotion. She holds a place in the canon, a proper office in the Gregorian Sacramentary with a proper preface, and, by the decree of Pius V, a double rite; the psalms are taken from the Common of Holy Men, Martyrs. There is also the singular honor that on the eighth day a second Agnes is celebrated with a simple rite, because Agnes appeared to her parents and to Constantia. The rubricists forbid calling that festival an octave, and rightly so, since no mention of Saint Agnes is made on the intervening days up to January 28. Nevertheless, in very many ancient breviaries it is called the octave of Agnes. Our hymn on the holy Martyr is found in Breviary Cs., in Thomasius, and in Ellinger. —1. The Fathers invent two declensions for the name *Agnes*: *Agnes, Agnetis, Agnis, Agnae*, as with *Agatha, Agathe,* and *Agathae*. See what the Fathers of Saint-Maur have noted passim in their annotations on Gregory’s Sacramentary. —5–6. She was thirteen years old. Compare Ambrose, *On Virgins* I, 2: “Not yet fit for punishment, and already mature for victory.” —13–14. The same author: “Not so did a bride hasten to the bridal chamber as the virgin came with joyful step to the place of punishment.” —13. Vatican 82, Ellinger, Thomasius, *nuptam*. —25. Vatican 82, *pompa*. Thus it is read in the Legend of Saint Agnes: “The prefect ordered her to be stripped and led naked to the brothel. But the Lord gave such thickness to her hair that she was better covered by her hair than by clothing.” Cs., *percussa*. —26. Cs., *tegens*.]

## On Saint Agnes

We celebrate the feast day

of blessed virgin Agnes,

on which she returned

her destined spirit to heaven,

consecrated by devoted blood.

[5] She was mature for martyrdom,

not yet mature for marriage;

men’s faith wavered,

and the weary old man gave way.

Terrified parents, through fear,

[10] had increased the enclosure of her chastity;

faith, which knows no weakness,

opened the guarded doors.

Who would think she was going forth to marriage?

So joyfully is she led in her countenance;

[15] but she bears new wealth,

endowed with the riches of blood.

She is compelled to kindle

the altars of the wicked deity with torches;

she replies: “Christ’s virgins

[20] have not taken up such torches.

This fire extinguishes faith;

this flame robs the light;

strike here, here, so that with my flowing

blood I may extinguish the torches.”

[25] What a spectacle she bore when struck!

For she covered herself completely with her clothing,

showing concern for modesty,

so that no one might see her uncovered.

In death modesty was alive;

[30] she covered her face with her hand,

and, falling with a bashful collapse,

sought the earth on bended knee.

Glory to you, Lord, etc.

[Note: LXVI.—Breviary Cs., Thomasius, from Vatican manuscript 82, and Ellinger in his second book, in which we know that he brought all the hymns into conformity with the laws of poetry. Besides, you see that almost all the verses have been clarified by the notes scattered through hymn 11. —22. Vatican 82, *mammam*. —31. The same manuscript, *praedicans*. —29–32. Fr.: “The Christians placed the body in a new tomb. As it was being laid there, a certain young man came, dressed in silken garments, followed by more than a hundred boys, white-clad and handsome. He entered the place where the body was being buried and placed there a small marble tablet on which was written: ‘A holy mind, a willing sacrifice, honor to God and libation for the homeland.’ The young man remained there until the tomb had been carefully closed. Then, departing, he was not seen again throughout the whole province of the Sicilians; hence there is no doubt that he was an angel of God.”]

## On Saint Agatha

We celebrate the feast day

of the sacred virgin Agatha,

on which, after defeating the tyrant,

she won the palm of martyrdom.

[5] The tyrant Quintianus,

consular governor of Sicily,

hearing the virgin’s fame,

began to rage, envious.

With the passions of his vices

[10] he tormented his envious mind,

so that he might destroy, with rabid speech,

the virgin dedicated to God.

At once there appear wretches

of his who wished to expose

[15] the most holy religion

which she had held from childhood.

He orders the martyr to stand

before his tribunals,

and addresses her in such a way

[20] as to make her bow her neck to the gods.

But when madness could accomplish nothing,

he tortures the virgin’s breast

and applies very sharp potsherds,

heated in the fire.

[25] To heal her limbs

the holy apostle comes,

and by his word cures the wounds

which the tyrant had inflicted.

Then, coming to the tomb,

[30] a most splendid young man

proclaims the holy mind

and abundant salvation for the homeland.

[Note: LXVII.—Very many churches sang this hymn during Lent—up to Passion Sunday—at Matins, and this is still done today in the Roman Church. In certain dioceses, such as Halberstadt and Magdeburg, it was on the lips of singers for only two weeks of Lent. —3–4. A circumlocution for the Church’s Lenten fast. —4. H., Hilary, *novissimo*. —6. Fabr., *pertulerunt*; Hilary, Augustine, *praetulerunt*. —5–8. Cornelius: “He praises this fast on account of the dignity of its authors: he makes Moses, the prophet Elijah, and Christ its authors, for all of them fasted that many days. Exodus 24:3; 1 Kings 19; Matthew 4.” —11. Ludovicus in the margin, *et arctius*. —12. H., *praestemus*. —14. Hilary, Wimpfeling, *quaeque*. —16. Thomasius, Augustine, and the entire Minor Breviary, except *callidi hostis … tyrannidi*. —20. Lipsius, *flectemus*. —21. Wimpfeling, *Deus tuam*. —25. Psalm 113:1. —29. Thomasius, Augustine, and all the Minor Breviaries, *quod fecimus*. —32. Lipsius, *possumus*; Gronovius, *nunc et perpetim*. —33–36. Missing in very many books.]

## Lenten hymn

*(From an old book)*

Following the mystical instruction of tradition,

let us keep this fast,

by the well-known fourfold cycle

of ten-day periods.

[5] The Law and the prophets first

proclaimed it;

afterward Christ consecrated it,

the King and maker of all ages.

Therefore let us use more sparingly

[10] words, food, and drink,

sleep and amusements,

and stand more strictly on guard.

Let us avoid harmful things,

which overthrow wandering minds;

[15] let us give no place

to the crafty enemy’s tyranny.

Let us all speak with bowed heads,

and let each of us cry out;

let us weep before the judge,

[20] let us bend the avenging anger.

By our evils we have offended

your clemency, O God.

Pour down upon us from above

the forgiveness of the Remitter.

[25] Remember that we are yours,

though formed from frail matter;

do not, we beg, give the honor

of your name to another.

Loosen the evil we have done;

[30] increase the good we ask for,

so that at last we may please you

here and forever.

## Another version of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary)*

Following the mystical instruction of tradition,

let us keep this fast,

by the well-known fourfold cycle

of ten-day periods.

[5] The Law and the prophets first

commended it;

afterward Christ consecrated it,

the King and maker of all ages.

Therefore let us use more sparingly

[10] words, food, and drink,

sleep and amusements,

and stand more strictly on guard.

Let us avoid harmful things,

which overthrow wandering minds;

[15] let us give no place

to the crafty enemy’s tyranny.

Let us bend the avenging anger,

let us weep before the judge,

let us cry out with a supplicating voice,

[20] let us all speak with bowed heads:

By our evils we have offended

your clemency, O God.

Pour down upon us from above

the forgiveness of the Remitter.

[25] Remember that we are yours,

though formed from frail matter;

do not, we beg, give the honor

of your name to another.

Loosen the evil we have done;

[30] increase the good we ask for,

so that at last we may please you

here and forever.

[Grant, blessed Trinity,

concede, undivided Unity,

that the gifts of fasting

may be fruitful for your people.]

[Note: LXVIII.—Thomasius found the poem in Vatican manuscript 82; Muratori attributed it to the manuscript of Saint Paulinus (*Anecdota*, vol. 1, p. 170). —25. Vatican 82 omits *tunc*. —34. The same manuscript, *baptismo*. —35. The same manuscript omits *statim*. —37. The same manuscript omits *is*. To say nothing of the Greeks, who honor Saint George above others with the distinctive title *μεγαλομάρτυρος* (“great martyr”), it is sufficiently clear even from that celebrated song of the German people—“Georio fuor ze male mit michilelmo herige,” etc. (Hoffmann, *Fundgruben*, I, p. 10)—that Western Europe also judged Saint George worthy from the beginning of the highest honor, as one whom it considered supremely worthy. And we do not hesitate to declare that this hymn, found only in Thomasius, is perhaps the oldest Latin hymn on Saint George, both for other reasons and because it recounts Saint George’s life with a simplicity wholly remote from the famous battle with the dragon.

Moreover, anyone who either omits or fails to adorn with the praise it deserves the remarkable caution with which most fifteenth-century Italian breviaries proceed in recounting Saint George’s deeds and fate will incur the charge either of negligence or of injustice. For in almost all of them we read: “In the city of Diospolis in Persia, the passion of Saint George, Martyr, whose acts of martyrdom, although they are counted among the apocryphal writings, nevertheless the Church of God venerates his most illustrious martyrdom among the crowns of the martyrs.” What is more, although the ancient German and English breviaries go astonishingly beyond the limits of truth in recounting Saint George’s miracles, the Roman Breviary now in use offers not even the slightest account of these matters. It is altogether pleasing to acknowledge and approve the moderation and—almost I would say—the sobriety proper to the Roman Breviary. This is evident both in its choice of material and in the fact that it employs only very rarely the octaves that occupy space to the point of weariness in diocesan breviaries. As an example, in the calendar of the Church of Meissen, besides the octaves of the Roman Breviary, the following are enumerated: Dorothy, John before the Latin Gate, the Visitation, Anne, Donatus, Wenceslaus, Jerome, Hedwig, Martin, Catherine, Andrew, Barbara.

—9–12. Manuscript: “George, having been made a tribune, governed his military command well. But seeing that no one named Christ, he gave all his substance to the poor and prepared himself for martyrdom.” —13. His name in the legend is Dacianus. —15–16. Pelbartus, *Sermon on Saint George* I: “G., having bent his knees, prayed to Christ, and immediately fire descended from heaven and burned the temple together with the other priests. Then the earth opened and swallowed all their remains.” —20. Pelbartus, book I: “He ordered him to be placed in a frying pan of molten lead; after making the sign of the cross, he began, through God’s power, to be refreshed in it as though in a bath.” —19. Fortunatus, on Saint George: “Through prison, slaughter, hunger, chains, thirst, cold, and flames, confessing Christ, he led his head to the stars.” —25. A., the wife of Dacianus, believed in Christ and was crowned by martyrdom. —29. Thomasius, *ternis*; since this does not at all suit Saint George, it was written incorrectly by the scribe.]

## On the Nativity of Saint Ambrose

Sing, all peoples,

a praiseworthy miracle,

which was given to the Church

as it struggled in the world.

[5] Ambrose, the great prophet,

predestined by God,

at the time when the devil

had defiled the temples of God.

Christ, who never abandons

[10] those whom he redeemed with his blood,

sent the illustrious man

to destroy Arius.

While he wore the insignia of the world,

he acquired those of paradise;

[15] while he bore the authority of the sword,

he undertook that of the Gospel.

An unknown mystery,

which the Most High knew,

before he had been washed in the font,

[20] he was chosen bishop.

He entered the church

to calm the turbulent people;

everyone’s mouths cried out:

“Ambrose, bishop!”

[25] Then the perfidy of Arius

is purged from the Church;

all the crowds resound,

and Christ’s gifts are not lacking.

Let the dreadful night yield to light;

[30] let the heretics be confounded;

the most devout one is present,

who may cleanse faithless minds.

Power from on high

was given to Ambrose in baptism.

[35] For as soon as he was reborn,

he began to drive out demons.

He received the Church

and governed it fearlessly;

he deserved to be a confessor,

[40] since he did not yield to the Arians.

Glory to you, Lord, etc.

## LXIX. On the Nativity of Saint George the Martyr

It is joyful to remember

the deeds of the holy martyrs,

and in their praises

to sing glory to God.

[5] George, the soldier of Christ,

was born in Cappadocia;

rejecting the world’s vanities,

he purchased heavenly things.

The money he had received

[10] for fragile worldly honor,

filled with the Lord’s faith,

he gave as alms to the poor.

Then, compelled by the prince

to fulfill vows with stones,

[15] those stones he cast, through faith in Christ,

into the depths of the abyss.

The tyrant, inflamed with anger,

inflicted punishments upon the martyr:

savage whips, prisons,

[20] and bolts or frying pans.

He did not tremble at them,

strengthened by the Lord.

But he also brought forth

divine fruits among the people.

[25] He summoned Queen Alexandra

to martyrdom;

she despised the treasures of the world

and earned God’s crown.

At twenty-one years

[30] he triumphed over the prince of the world;

his neck cut by the sword,

he departed to heavenly things.

[Note: LXX.—The Breviary of Cs. presents a most elegant poem on Saint John; Thomasius transcribed it from Vatican manuscript 82. —2. His parent was Aaron, his father Zacharias. —3. That is, to enclose the fetus. —5. Cs., *regiam*. —15. Vatican 82, *prophetici*. —18. The poet understood Matthew 11:11 of the angels: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.” —23–24. Matthew 14:4: “It is not lawful for you to have her.”]

## On Saint John the Baptist

A pious offspring of a noble prophet,

famous through his parent and nobler father,

whom his mother’s womb, unable to contain him,

proclaimed as the herald of his lordly birth.

[5] While the royal chamber of a virgin bore,

in the name of the highest Thunderer,

the glorious pledge,

that noble palace, fertile in inviolate chastity

within its innermost enclosure of modesty,

a voice sent to the mother

[10] nurtured the infant prophet’s joys;

the mothers prophesy through the gift of their children,

and the mute man spoke in the name of his son.

His name must be written, that it may increase

the songs of our voice and loose

[15] the harsh bonds of the mouth;

the letters of the name give free rein

to prophetic words.

For he is the voice of the Word,

the voice of Wisdom,

[20] greater than the prophets and lesser than the angels;

he prepared the hearts of the faithful

and laid out the straight paths of justice.

The defender of what is right,

neither through royal power

nor through harsh death forced

[25] to abandon the path of truth,

he says: “It is not lawful for you

to have your brother’s adulterous wife.”

Hence the king’s savage anger

and bloody funerals,

sold as the price of a dance;

the tables of the tyrant and virgin alike

[30] were filled by drunken luxury with sober blood.

This stepfather gives gifts more insane

than if he were offering cups of poison.

It is better to deny than to grant him the name of stepfather;

it is better to hate him, for love of such men does greater harm.

May there be the greatest glory

[35] to the Trinity,

praise, power, and wisdom;

may there be strength and magnificence

to the one God throughout everlasting ages.

[Note: LXXI.—Breviary Cs., Thomasius in the *Hymnary*, Bebel, Cassander, Ellinger’s third book. —2. Cs., Bebel, *saeculi*. —3. Thomasius, *nostrum*. —5. Thomasius, Cs., *aequales*. —7. Cassander, *secuti*; Bebel, Cs., *praesules*. —11. The passage is Acts 9:15: “This man is a chosen vessel for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles.” It caused Paul to be called by poets and in ecclesiastical offices, in a kind of solemn formula, “the vessel of election.” —12. Bebel, *fidei*; Ellinger, *illius ad*. —16 f. John 21:18: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” —19. Cassander, *ibat*. —20. Cassander in the margin: “Perhaps *subivit*.” —21. Cassander, “Rome, lofty with its summit”; Bebel, “Thus Rome.” —24. Cassander, “and with a poet of such a great name”; Bebel, “with such a noble poet.” —25. Cassander, “such great crowds throughout the circuit of the city”; in the margin, “I think *urbis* should be read.” —26. Cassander, incorrectly, *pendent*. —27. Cassander: “I think *binis* should be read, alluding to Prudentius: ‘See, the Roman people divide through the two-forked streets; light glows in both, one amid the festivals.’” —28. Cassander, *celebrantur festa*; Ellinger, *inclytorum*. —29. Vatican 82, *mundo*.]

## On Saints Peter and Paul the Apostles

The passion of the apostles

consecrated this day for the ages,

bringing forward Peter’s noble triumph

and Paul’s crown.

[5] Equal men were joined

by the triumphant blood of death;

faith in Christ crowned

those who followed God as their leader.

First was Peter the apostle,

[10] and Paul was not unequal in grace;

the vessel of sacred election

matched Peter’s faith.

With the orientation of the cross reversed,

Simon, giving honor to God,

hung and ascended,

[15] not forgetting the oracle that had been given.

Bound as it had been said,

and lifted up by another,

he went where he did not wish,

but willingly overcame harsh death.

[20] From this Rome raised high

the summit of its devotion,

noble, founded upon such blood

and upon so great a prophet.

Throughout the circuit of so great a city,

crowds stand arrayed;

[25] along three streets

the feast of the sacred martyrs is celebrated.

One might think the whole world was coming forth,

the people of heaven converging,

the chosen capital of the nations,

the seat of the teacher of the nations.

[Note: LXXII.—Thomasius in the *Hymnary*. —6. Because he was affixed to the cross. —13–14. The emperor Decius and Valerian, prefect of the praetorium. —16. Thus Fr.: “He ordered Abdon and Sennen to be brought before him in the city of Corduba in Persia … four months later Decius came to Rome, bringing with him blessed Abdon and Sennen bound in chains,” etc. —28. Vatican 82, *craticula*. —29–32. In my judgment the verse is spurious.]

## On Saint Sixtus

Unconquered faith bestowed

the palm of the great contest;

for those who fight for Christ,

a pebble is given from heaven.

[5] Thus the brave athlete Sixtus,

following Peter’s martyrdom,

soon adorned the Church

with the title of confession.

Born at Athens and trained

[10] in the studies of the philosophers,

he changed the art of arts

for apostolic teaching.

For the executioner of tyranny,

roaring like a rabid lion,

[15] brought with him the martyrs

Abdon and Sennen and killed them.

Then hastening toward Sixtus,

he threatens chains, fetters, prison,

execution,

[20] and the sentence of the sword.

Then that devout pontiff,

summoning Lawrence,

commended the Church

to the most faithful Levite.

[25] Both attained

the prize of their contest;

martyrdom by sword and gridiron

gave them their crown.

[Let us therefore be joined as companions,

bearing a hymn to the Lord,

so that through their intercession

our sins may be cleansed.]

Glory to you, Lord.

Glory to the Only-Begotten, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1215B] LXXIII.—This hymn, which vividly recounts the martyrdom of Saint Lawrence, is found in Thomasius’s Hymnary and in the *Breviarium Cisterciense*. Lawrence is called the apostles’ equal because of his remarkable steadfastness of spirit and the terrible martyrdom he suffered; hence, in the Church, apart from Saint Stephen, he received the highest honors among all martyrs. Thus there is a vigil, an office proper to him throughout, and an octave distinguished by a special Mass. I cannot forbear to take advantage of this opportunity to note the exceedingly shameful error of Graeser (*Die katholische Liturgie*, etc., p. 282): “The prayers and Masses found in the Common of Saints are suitable at all times and for all saints, and it is only necessary to insert the saint’s name instead of the name in the breviary prayer or the Mass, so that the same form can today be a Mass of Saint Lawrence, tomorrow of Saint Anne, and so forth.” No one could have scribbled such lies (ψεῦδη) except someone who had looked at the Roman Breviary only cursorily—or not even cursorily.]

[7, 8. Vat. 82: “he had completed.” —29, 30. I have nowhere found in the legends that the executioners themselves were burned up in the dreadful fires of the gridiron; I think this entered the history of Saint Lawrence from the martyrdom of the three youths. Daniel 3:47–48: “And the flame streamed forth above the furnace forty-nine cubits, and it burst forth and burned those Chaldeans whom it found near the furnace.” —23. Cs.: “showing.” —26. Cs.: “indeed.” —31, 32. Thus the antiphon in the martyr’s office: “Blessed Lawrence, while he was placed upon the gridiron and burned, said to the most impious tyrant: ‘It is roasted now; turn it over and eat, for the Church’s resources which you seek have been carried by the hands of the poor into the heavenly treasuries.’”]

## Of Saint Lawrence

The Roman faith consecrated  
Lawrence the archdeacon,  
the equal of the apostles,  
with the martyrs’ equal crown.

[5] Following the martyr Sixtus,  
he reported the prophet’s answer:  
“Do not grieve, my son;  
you shall follow me after three days.”

Undeterred by fear of punishment,  
the future heir of blood  
looked with devout gaze  
upon what he himself would soon undergo.

[Col. 1217] Already then, in that martyr,  
he enacted the martyr’s triumph,  
a worthy successor, holding fast  
the written bond of voice and blood.

Nevertheless, ordered after three days  
to surrender the sacred treasures,  
he promises faithfully and does not refuse,  
adding deceit to his victory.

A most beautiful spectacle:  
he gathers the needy crowds  
and, proclaiming, points them out:  
“These are the Church’s riches.”

[25] Truly, the poor are the everlasting wealth  
of the pious; the needy are perfect riches.  
The greedy man, mocked, grieves  
and prepares consuming flames.

The executioner flees, burned,  
and yields to his own fires.  
“Turn me over!” cries the martyr;  
“Eat, if I am cooked,” he commands.

Glory to you, O Lord;  
glory to the Only-Begotten, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1217A] LXXIV.—This is found in the *Breviarium Cisterciense*, in Thomasius’s *Hymnary*, and in corrected form in Ellinger. —5–8. 1 Corinthians 11:10. —16. Vat. 82: “may remain.” —20. The Holy Spirit. —30. Vat. 82: “the crowds.”]

## Of Saint Michael the Archangel

Bearer of the heavenly mysteries,  
O archangel,  
we beseech you as suppliants:  
visit us in mercy.

[5] With the holy angels,  
with the righteous and apostles,  
continually illumine the place  
where we now dwell in prayer.

Devoutly offer to the Lord  
for us abundant prayers  
of all the most chaste  
teachers and pontiffs.

May he drive back the savage enemy  
and direct the aid of peace,  
and may perfect faith  
at the same time fortify our hearts.

[15] May our voices of glory  
straightway ascend to the throne,  
and may he raise our minds—  
he who shines from a radiant seat.

May his power remain here;  
here may steadfast charity burn;  
here may he come to the aid  
of his servants for their salvation.

[25] May he remove all errors,  
correct wandering thoughts,  
and direct our footsteps  
along the path of peace.

In the radiant citadel of light  
may he inscribe these sacred songs,  
and together enter our names  
in the book of life.

Glory to you, O Lord, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1217A] LXXV.—This poem about the miracles of Saint Martin seems not to have been widely known in Germany, England, and elsewhere. Besides the *Breviarium Cisterciense* and Thomasius’s *Hymnary*, it is found in the third book of Ellinger. —6. Ellinger: “covered.” —11, 12. Thus Pelbartus: “Departing for a short while from the monastery and returning, he found a catechumen dead without baptism. Taking him into his cell, he restored him to life by his prayer … He also restored to life another who had ended his life by hanging.” —13, 14. Fortunatus, *On Saint Martin* (Fabr., p. 715): “While a dead robber was falsely honored, Martin’s voice compels the spirit to speak here, declaring that he had been slain for the great burden of his crimes, and that he too was guilty—not innocent, but even more guilty.” —12, 16. Fortunatus, book 1: “The holy man forced the pagan pine to be cut down; the rustic crowd was ordered to stand beneath it. When the tree, cut with an axe, was already bringing down its lofty ruin, at the command of the cross it was forced to turn back.” —17, 18. Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 14: “When he had set fire to a very ancient and famous shrine in a certain village, the wind drove balls of flame toward the nearest house, indeed toward the adjoining house. When Martin noticed this, he climbed rapidly onto the roof … Then you would have seen, wonderfully, the fire driven back against the force of the wind.” —18. Thomasius: “wax.” —19. Thomasius: “by which it was extinguished.” —21. Ellinger: “from flowing paralysis.” Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* III.9: “A woman suffering from a flow of blood touched Martin’s garment, after the example of the woman in the Gospel, and was healed in an instant.” —23, 24. Fortunatus (Fabr., p. 715): “A man swollen from a serpent’s bite, at the point of death: when this finger was placed upon him, the evil disease flowed away … and by his fingers he drew out the poison like a new ointment; by the touch of the healer he thus survived.” —25, 28. Concerning the miracle performed at Paris, see Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 18. Jordan is mentioned in the kiss because, in the time of the Old Testament, Naaman was cleansed of leprosy by the waters of that river (2 Kings 5:14). Fortunatus likewise says: “What the Jordan possesses, the holy man gave from his mouth.” —27. Thus Vat. 82 and Ellinger. Thomasius has “and which.” —32. Ellinger: “reigns.”]

## At the Feast of Saint Martin, Bishop

Let us sing in fitting hymns  
of Martin, renowned as a warrior,  
noble in his deeds,  
and of the miracles he performed.

[5] When, in the season of cold,  
he found a man without a cloak,  
Christ soon revealed himself clothed  
in the very garment Martin had cut.

By holy power  
he raised three pale corpses:  
a catechumen from fever  
and another from hanging.

By the power of prayer  
a buried robber is revealed;  
the pine that could not fall  
is driven back from its violent descent.

[15] While he was burning the profane shrine,  
he drove the flame into the air;  
the fires were extinguished,  
for rain was present.

He cures a helpless girl of paralysis caused by humors,  
and with the ointment of holy liquid  
scrapes away the root of her disease.

[25] Giving peace to a leprous man,  
he drove away the filth of his sores;  
and that which washed the diseased man  
is Jordan upon his lips.

These and the great miracles  
known throughout the world  
show that the possessor of the lofty Spirit  
now reigns in heaven.

Glory to you, O Lord, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1218A] LXXVI.—Only Thomasius has it in the *Hymnary*. —16. Vat. 82: “to adorn.”]

## Of the Dedication of a Church

This sacred temple of God,  
the altar’s renewal:  
returning each year,  
we offer praises to God.

[5] This great altar of God  
was consecrated on this day;  
in whose honor we all  
earnestly bend our knees.

We pray to the Lord,  
who alone is invisible,  
that he may always command  
that we be sanctified in this place.

Here, fulfilling our vows to God  
and to all his saints,  
whose sacred relics  
adorn this temple of God,

[15] may everyone who enters here  
go out sanctified,  
and, always praying to the Lord,  
remain purified.

Offering continually  
the sacrifices of the rites  
upon this altar,  
with ever-devout minds,

may the Lord sanctify us  
in this holy temple,  
in which we solemnly  
offer the sacred gift.

[25] God, dearest brothers,  
and Christ his Son,  
together with the Holy Spirit,  
let us continually praise in hymns.

[Note: [Col. 1218A] LXXVII.—Contained in codex W. 1 and in Cs. I compared the books of Cassander, Thomasius, and Rambach. Bebelius contains the first four stanzas; Ellinger altered the poem in book II. —2. Vat. 82: “eternal.” —4. W. 1, Bebelius: “and likewise.” —5. Bebelius: “which.” —7, 8. W. 1, Cassander: “whose festivals return each year at the appointed season.” —11. W. 1, Cassander: “blessed.” —15. Cassander: “and is created.” —21. W. 1: “savage.” —26. Another reading: “of the immeasurable.” —27. W. 1, Thomasius: “which are of life.” —34. Cassander: “souls with countenance.” —37. Vat. 82: “may troublesome things torment.” —42. Cassander: “hall.”]

## Of the Dedication of a Church

Christ, gracious ruler of all,  
from the mouth of the eternal Father  
toward the nations, kindly behold  
the prayers and hymn of your suppliants.

[5] Behold, O God, how your suppliant people  
resound in the hall in pure honor,  
whose yearly season brings back  
the festival that must be kept.

This house is known to have been  
rightly dedicated to you;  
in it the people receive  
the sacred Body and drink  
a draught of the blessed Blood.

[10] Here the sacred waters  
wash away ancient sins  
and destroy transgressions;  
through chrism, moreover,  
the race of Christ-worshipers  
is brought into being.

Here salvation is brought to the sick,  
medicine to the weary,  
light to the blind,  
pardon for our offenses,  
and every fear and sorrow  
is driven away.

[20] Here the devil’s savage plunder  
perishes; the stubborn monster trembles  
and, abandoning the bodies he had held,  
quickly flees into distant shadows.

This place is rightly called  
the hall of the eternal King  
and the snowy gate of heaven,  
which receives all the saints  
seeking their homeland.

[25] No storm shakes it,  
no wandering winds tear it down,
