no clouds penetrate it,  
and gloomy Tartarus  
does not harm it with its terrible darkness.

Therefore we ask, O God,  
that you favor us with a serene countenance,  
governing the servants  
who celebrate the joys of your temple  
with supreme love.

[35] May no troubles of life torment us.  
May our days be joyful  
and our nights peaceful.  
When the world perishes,  
may none of us feel the fires.

May this day, on which you behold  
the altar consecrated to you,  
grant us everlasting joy,  
and may it grow strong  
through long continuance of time.

[45] Let glory resound to the supreme Father.  
Let us likewise celebrate the Son and the Holy Spirit  
with a sweetly modulated hymn  
through every age.

[Note: [Col. 1219A] LXXVIII.—Almost all the hymns called “of the Common” are longer in the oldest books and contracted into a few verses in more recent ones. Although it seems certain that the ancient breviaries preserve the genuine form of the poems, it is no less clear that the authors of the poems did not celebrate martyrs, confessors, and others in general, but had one particular saint in mind; the directors of ecclesiastical worship, removing verses that seemed less suitable for the Office of the Common, adopted the remainder for public use. As for the hymn “God, the portion and crown of your soldiers,” it is not even possible to conjecture which martyr the poet praised. I found the verses enclosed in brackets in codex W. 1 and in Thomasius. —2. Another reading: “hope and crown.” —5. W. 1: “hence.” —25. W. 1: “hence we, suppliant, beseech you.”]

## Of the Common of One Martyr

*(From an ancient book.)*

God, portion and crown  
of your soldiers, their reward:  
as we sing the martyr’s praises,  
release us from the bond of sin.

[5] [This witness proclaimed with his mouth  
what his heart’s treasury believed;  
following Christ, he found him  
through the shedding of blood.]

Indeed, rightly judging  
the joys of the world  
and its harmful blandishments  
to be fleeting,  
he reached the heavenly realms.

[10] [He despised the tyrant’s bonds,  
dread chains and scourges,  
and with a clear voice proclaimed  
that God created all things.]

He ran bravely through punishments  
and endured them manfully;  
shedding his blood for you,  
he possesses eternal gifts.

[15] [Because of this, the fury of madness  
ordered the martyr to be killed  
and the just man to be buried in the earth,  
whom the kingdoms of heaven contain.]

For this reason, by humble prayer,  
we all ask you, most gracious one:  
in this martyr’s triumph  
forgive your little servants their guilt.

[25] [That we may rightly inherit  
a share in this gift  
and rejoice forever,  
joined in the courts of heaven.]

### Another version of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

God, portion and crown  
of your soldiers: their reward,  
as we sing the martyr’s praises,  
release us from the bond of sin.

[5] He indeed, judging  
the joys of the world  
and the alluring food of deceit,  
steeped in gall, to be fleeting,  
reached the heavenly realms.

He ran bravely through punishments  
and endured them manfully;  
shedding his blood for you,  
he possesses eternal gifts.

[10] For this reason, by humble prayer,  
we beseech you, most gracious one:  
in this martyr’s triumph  
forgive your little servants their guilt.

Praise and everlasting glory, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1219A] LXXIX.—A poem recited in the present rite of the Church at Lauds on the feast of a confessor who is not a pontiff. Since the ancient writers entirely ignore this pious distinction among confessors, it has happened that the hymn is rarely read in old parchment manuscripts. An exception is found in the ancient breviaries of the Order of Saint Benedict, which assign the hymn to Saint Benedict himself. You should not think this an especially bold attribution, if what I noted above concerning hymns adapted to the Common Office of the Saints has led you to my view. —9–12. Gavanti, *Thesaurus Rituum*, III, p. 360: “When feasts are transferred, and the offices of confessors are transferred to another day, a verse in the hymn ‘This Confessor’ is changed, as in the Breviary revised by order of Urban VIII, so that it may not falsely be said that they died on that day. In the hymn of Lauds for confessors who are not pontiffs, that verse, ‘The day shone forth with light,’ might also seem to require alteration, but it is not changed, because we do not say that this is precisely the day on which the office is celebrated.” —14. Cassander and Bebelius: “bright.” —15. Thomasius: “filth.” —17. From this verse Cassander begins the second hymn for confessors, misled by the authority of books that assign one part of the hymn to Matins and the other to Lauds. —25–28. Omitted by the Roman Breviary, since they were composed more gloriously and not without disparagement of the martyrs.]

## Hymn for Confessors

*(From an ancient book.)*

Jesus, higher crown  
and loftier truth,  
who grant an everlasting reward  
to your confessing servant,

[5] grant the suppliant assembly,  
through the intercession of this excellent man,  
remission of sins  
by breaking the bond of guilt.

When the year’s season returns,  
the day shines again with light  
on which this holy man,  
mighty, departed from the body  
and migrated to heaven.

[10] Judging all the vain joys  
and muddy possessions of earth  
to be defiled,  
he triumphantly holds the things of heaven.

Confessing you continually,  
most gracious Christ and King,  
he bravely trampled  
the proud enemy and his minion.

[15] By deeds and faith of virtue,  
in the order of confession,  
carrying his fasting limbs,  
he obtains heavenly banquets.

This confessor runs farther  
in the contest, enduring,  
than a martyr who suffers a blow  
and pours out blood by the sword.

[25] Therefore, most gracious one,  
we all humbly beseech you:  
through the grace of this holy man,  
forgive us our debts.

### Another version of the same hymn

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Jesus, higher crown  
and loftier truth,  
who grant an everlasting reward  
to your confessing servant,

[5] grant the suppliant assembly,  
at his intercession,  
remission of sinful guilt  
by breaking the bond of sin.

When the year returns,  
the day shines forth with light  
on which this holy man  
migrated from the body among the stars.

[10] Judging the vain joys of earth  
and its splendid estates  
to be polluted with filth,  
he triumphantly holds the things of heaven.

Confessing you continually,  
most gracious Christ and King,  
he trampled the devices of demons  
and the savage prince of hell.

[15] Renowned for virtue and faith,  
devoted to confession,  
carrying his fasting limbs,  
he obtains heavenly banquets.

Therefore, most gracious one,  
we all humbly beseech you:  
through the grace of this holy man,  
forgive us the punishments we deserve.

[Note: [Col. 1221A] LXXX.—Sung at Vespers in the Common of Virgins. —1. From Isaiah 28:5: “On that day the Lord of hosts will be a crown of glory and a wreath of exultation for the remnant of his people.” From this comes the title by which Christ is very often called the crown of apostles, martyrs, and so forth. Compare the invitatory for the feast of All Saints: “Come, let us adore the Lord, for he himself is the crown of all the saints.” —2. Cassander: “conceives”; H.: “which.” —4. Ludovicus and Fabricius: “receive.” —5. Song of Songs 2:16: “My beloved is mine and I am his, who feeds among the lilies.” —7. E., M., H., Hl., Hv., Augustine, Bebelius, Magdeburg, Torrentius, Wimpfeling, Hilarius: “the bridegroom adorning the bride with glory,” less suitably, since verse 8 again mentions brides. —13. In many copies: “in their senses.”]

## Of Virgins

*(From an ancient book.)*

Jesus, crown of virgins,  
whom that mother conceived,  
who alone, a virgin, gives birth,  
mercifully accept these prayers.

[5] You who feed among lilies,  
surrounded by choirs of virgins,  
beautiful bridegroom in glory,  
and who grant rewards to brides,

wherever you go, virgins  
follow and run after you,  
singing your praises  
and sounding sweet hymns.

[10] We beseech you more earnestly:  
increase in our minds  
the complete refusal  
to know the wounds of corruption.

*(From the Roman Breviary.)*

Jesus, crown of virgins,  
whom that mother conceives,  
who alone, a virgin, gives birth,  
mercifully accept these prayers.

[5] You who walk among lilies,  
surrounded by choirs of virgins,  
beautiful bridegroom in glory,  
and who grant rewards to brides,

wherever you turn, virgins  
follow and run after you,  
singing in your praise  
and sounding sweet hymns.

We humbly beseech you:  
add to our understanding  
the complete refusal  
to know the wounds of corruption.

[Note: [Col. 1222A] LXXXI.—From Thomasius’s *Hymnary*. —5. Thus Vat. 82 and Thomasius: “fervent in war.” —29. Compare 22, 29: “this.” Our sins deserve this hunger. —35, 36. Exodus 17:9 ff. —41. Compare hymn above, 41: “Jesus, spare those redeemed by your death.”]

## In Time of War

The savage barbarian sows dreadful wars;  
raging fury continually heaps up wars  
and, exulting, sprinkles itself with fresh slaughter,  
breathing with delight over the many dead.

[5] The unrestrained nation, with its vast hordes,  
continually terrifies us with blazing wars;  
sitting upon the innumerable surface of the sea,  
it disturbs the fields with harsh weapons.

Behold, the very company of Christ-worshipers  
turns its back upon its enemies  
and, trembling along steep and trackless paths,  
flees, exhausted, driven on by shameful fear.

[10] The savage nation harasses thousands with impunity,  
cruelly tears them apart, and cuts down thousands;  
bodies washed in sacred waters  
lie naked everywhere, given over to crows.

Then the proud robber, exulting  
in the heat of triumph, advances,  
stripping the sacred houses, dedicated temples,  
altars sanctified to God—all of them.

[15] The devouring barbarian fire burns cities  
and burns the common, gracious homes;  
the robber leads away bound old men,  
young men, married women, widows, and girls.

The consecrated virgin bewails  
her savage downfall; the virgin bewails  
her bitter ruin and mourns  
the loss of her chastity, willing to endure death’s labor.

[20] Truly, holy God, our many sins  
deserve this great evil.  
Yet now we all humbly ask you:  
look mercifully upon your sorrowful servants.

May immense weeping penetrate Olympus,  
and may devout cries ascend to the air,  
for by the merits of Moses  
Jesus, glorious in name, struck down the Amalekites.

[25] Jesus, Son of almighty God,  
true strength, highest salvation through labor,  
peace and certain rest and every honor:  
now be the helper of your foster-children.

Spare those purchased by your death, we ask;  
restore their courage and drive away fear;  
crush the enemies and scatter them in flight;  
grant the gifts of everlasting peace.

[Col. 1222] Praise and perpetual honor and glory  
to the Father; eternal praise and glory to you, Son;  
one glory to the Holy Spirit,  
as it always was, now and forever.

[Note: [Col. 1222A] LXXXII.—From Thomasius’s *Hymnary*. —12. Vat. 82: “grant those affected forgiveness in your love.” —12–16. Genesis 14:13–20; Exodus 14:21–24; Judges 7:7 ff. —23. Vat. 82: “the nation with the sword.” —28. 1 Kings 2:6. —32. Vat. 82: “or humble.” —33. Compare the preceding hymn, 41. —35, 36. Micah 4:3.]

## In Time of War

Christ, redeemer, behold the sorrowful peoples  
now humbly asking for peace;  
behold the lamentations and sighs, behold their grief;  
bring help from above to the afflicted.

[5] For the savage fury of the neighboring nation  
menacingly threatens the fields,  
destroying our lands with barbarous murmuring  
like a wolf slaughtering lambs.

Who will be our defender unless you yourself,  
merciful author of Olympus, come to our aid?  
Spare the human race its crimes;  
in your love grant forgiveness to the afflicted.

Formerly Abraham, by your protection,  
O creator of the ages, defeated five kings,  
restoring a father with only a few boys  
after the dark enemies had been overthrown.

[10] Trusting in the icy waters of the sea,  
Moses led the burning people through;  
the waters flowed back and immediately  
seized and concealed the entire enemy.

Gideon, commanded to attack,  
cast down the Amalekites with three hundred men;  
he freed the oppressed people and nation  
by relying upon your abundant aid.

[15] You alone, Almighty, accomplished all these things,  
in whose hands everything exists.  
Our salvation is in you, our glory in you:  
you kill and again give life.

For your grace, Jesus, is greater  
than the abundance of our wickedness;  
you do not, in your mercy, know how to despise  
contrite and sorrowful hearts, or the humble.

[20] Save those redeemed by your death;  
save those humbly seeking the promises;  
break the swords, shatter the darts,  
smash the shields of those who desire war.

Now may bitter sighs climb to heaven,  
now may the voice of tears penetrate the clouds;  
may the people’s contrition, gasping with longing,  
be their vow. Merciful Savior, now have mercy.

# Analytical Index to This Volume

## A

**AARON**, that is, Christ; Aaron’s rod is the flesh of Christ, 11.

**ABARIM** is in the desert beyond the Arnon, 19.

**ABEL** signified Christ, 521.

**ABRAHAM** sought nothing through circumcision, 47. He believed what seems impossible to the world, 51. According to the flesh he is the father of the Jews, but according to faith of all believers, 49, 50. Believers are Abraham’s children, 41, 219. He too is a type of all believers, ibid. The gift promised to him was fulfilled for his children in Christ, although he himself also attained it, 221. Abraham signifies Christ according to divinity, while Isaac signifies the human being, 622.

The absent are usually despised, 318.

**ABSTINENCE.** The weapons of abstinence and sobriety must be taken up against spiritual wickedness, 250. A belly contracted by abstinence raises human understanding on high, 495. No offense is so grave that abstinence cannot cleanse it and almsgiving extinguish it, 392. Whoever abstains from illicit things has praise; whoever also restrains himself from things permitted has both praise and reward, 273. It is glorious to abstain from permitted things, especially for the salvation of others, 200. Fasting and abstaining from food are of little benefit unless piety is added, 297. A person is not pleasing or displeasing to God because of food, 102, 103. Some have decreed that meat must not be eaten on Wednesday, some on Saturdays, and others that it should be eaten from Easter until Pentecost, 101. See **FASTING**.

**By accident**, 146.

**AHAB.** The repentance of King Ahab is proposed as an example, 597.

**ACTIONS.** Good actions are weapons of light, 100. Progress is present when what must be done is done according to God’s will, 29. It is greatly harmful to know the reason for truth yet affirm it least of all in the deeds that pursue it, 272. Because of our actions, the Lord either sleeps or keeps watch over us, 441. See **WORKS**.

**ADAM.** Adam’s sin is not far removed from idolatry, 55. If the human being had remained in the condition in which he was made, the enemy would have had no power to approach his flesh and whisper things opposed to the soul, 69. Adam propagated his sin to the origin of the future offspring born from him, 437. Unless Adam had fallen bodily, Christ would not have needed to raise us spiritually in this very life, 450. Adam prefigured Christ, 520. In what respect? 54, 57. Comparison of the first and second human beings, 449. See **ORIGINAL SIN**.

**ADOPTION.** The Holy Spirit is the seal of our adoption, 181.

**ADVENT.** The season of the Lord’s Advent is celebrated for good reason, 391. Sermons were delivered to the people during that season, ibid. What works of piety should then be performed, ibid. One should abstain from wives, ibid.

**ADULTERERS.** Roman laws punish adulterers, not fornicators, 214.

**ADVERSITY.** Both adversity and prosperity have always been dangerous when excessive at the beginning, 6. To make tribulation bearable, one must persevere in prayer, 96. To enable us to endure the disasters themselves, Christ supplies strength, 74. What person would not fear hardships? 188. Why does God permit his servants to be humbled by the wicked? 305. See **TRIBULATION**.

**EGYPT** is interpreted as “pursuing,” “afflicting,” and “confining,” 333. How are the Egyptians destroyed? 4. See **APIS**.

**EQUALITY** is the mother of justice, 3.

**AGNES.** Her martyrdom is described and adorned with praises, 455, 479. She is proposed as an example to virgins, ibid. She appears to parents praying at her tomb, 483. Miracles performed at the same tomb, ibid. See **CONSTANCY**.

**AGRICOLA.** See **VITALIS**.

**ALANS** devastated many places, 564.

**ALLELUIA** means “praise the Lord,” 568.

**AMAZONS** subdued all Asia, 273. They made men so savage that they trained them to eat human flesh, ibid.

**A LOVER.** A lover’s charity is more strongly kindled if he is forbidden to love the one whose benefits he has experienced, 78. Whoever does something out of love acts with his whole mind, 273. One who benefits his enemies cannot fail to love his friends, 53. Where there is contention and dissension, there is no love, 169. See **CHARITY**.

**AMBROSE.** See **FATHERS**.

**AMEN** means “truly,” 80, 157; or “faithfully,” 511.

**THE LANGUAGE OF ANGELS**, 154. Angels, because they are full of charity, are called fire, 335. Although evil princes and powers are still in the firmament, their manner of life is nevertheless on earth, 260.

[Col. 1224]

**SOUL.** Although soul and mind are the same, the soul is called soul for one reason and mind for another, 612. Heretics are refuted who wish the human soul to be a portion of God or to have been made before the body, 333. Also those who assert that certain souls are evil by nature and cannot be compelled toward good, 309. How the saints hold their souls in hatred, 548. The stages of a progressing soul, 13. The soul itself is what either sanctifies or pollutes the body, 137. Its perfect health is that by which it cannot sin; this occurs only in the resurrection, 8. While it sins, it is called flesh, 72. When stained with filth and made flesh by carnal desire, it is called flesh; just as a body rightly governed is called spiritual, 127. Whatever withdraws from God its creator commits fornication, 507. Its weakness, 8; and its poison, 424.

**NEW YEAR** is on the Kalends of January, 224.

**ANTICHRIST.** He will adorn himself with various virtues, 550. He will perform miracles by diabolical art, 551. He may pretend to die and rise again, 552. They will think him to be God, ibid. Why will God permit him to deceive the human race? 551. The time of his persecution, 550. He will appear after the fall of the Roman Empire, 286. What his seven heads are, 549.

**ANTIDOTE.** Its taste is bitter, but what is unpleasant to the throat is life-giving and sweet, 599.

**APIS.** The Egyptians worshiped Apis in the likeness of a cow, 33.

**APOCALYPSE.** Some wished to cut the Apocalypse from the catalogue of divine Scriptures, 586. Who is its author? 499. It is entirely structured around the number seven, 479. It is divided into seven visions, 500. The Apocalypse of Elijah is among the apocrypha, 118. It is cited by the Apostle, ibid.

**APOLLINARIS**, 11.

**APOLLO** was learned in the Scriptures, 107.

**APOLLONIUS**, a magician, is said suddenly to have disappeared while standing before the emperor Domitian, 340.

**APOPHORETA**, 27. At great vows the greatest *apophoreta* are given, 238.

**APOSTLE**, that is, one sent by the Lord to carry out his affairs, 26, 87. After his resurrection the Son of God called them apostles, 28. Why was no one from the Gentiles chosen for the apostolate? 233. The Church was born from the apostles, whom it produced first, 521. The Holy Spirit poured himself into them on the day of Pentecost so that they would be wise for founding the Church and strong for governing it, 10. The gift of heavenly power formerly present in Moses and the prophets appeared visibly in them, 10. Their grace was greater than that of the prophets, 26. They spoke in various languages so that devotion of mind might be released through many tongues, 470. All the apostles except John and Paul had wives, 198. They are Christ’s vicars, 121. They are ministers of justice, 200. Christ’s grace and God’s beneficence are recognized through their merit and glory, 183. The apostles’ injuries were temptations of believers, 171. The apostle’s joy is the purification of the people, 173. Christ sent the apostles to us as teachers so that we might imitate them, because we cannot belong to him directly, 147. The twelve springs signify the twelve apostles, 7. Why should the apostles be called springs? 417.

**APPARITION**, used for appearance, 161, 240, 290.

**APPROVAL** is genuine where there is reward and condemnation, 87.

**WATER.** The changing of water into wine is a great sign sufficient for belief in God’s majesty, 401. How does this sign contain the whole mystery of our resurrection? ibid. How was it also performed for us? 402 and following.

**EAGLE.** Hostile to serpents, it exposes its young to the sun, 452.

**AQUILA**, 30c. Priscilla’s husband, 107.

**ARADA** indicates a suitable effect, 13.

**ARAM.** According to Jewish tradition, Aram, Abraham’s brother, died in the fire of the Chaldeans because he refused to worship fire, 525.

**TREE.** Comparison of the tree of knowledge with the tree of the cross, 450.

**ARCHDEACONS.** Their worst crimes are condemned, 566.

**ARISTOBULUS** means “gatherer of brothers in the Lord,” 109.

**ARIUS** said that the Son of God had a beginning, 504, and was less than the Father, 507. He said that the Son of God was *ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων*, “from things that do not exist,” 348. He is the arch-pirate, 453. Equally to be rejected are the mixture of the foolish Sabellius and the separation of the impious Arius, 322. Arians, 113. By what arguments did they deny that the Son is of the Father’s substance? 354. A response is given to them, ibid. Those who say, “There was a time when the Son was not,” are refuted, 321, 327. A book was published against them, 345.

**ARNON**, a river, 19.

**ARSAPHAR** means the blast or blowing of a trumpet, 12.

[Col. 1225]

**ASEROTH** is interpreted as “blessedness,” 11.

**ASIA** is interpreted as “exalted,” 499.

**ASIONGABER** is interpreted as “the counsels of a man,” 16.

**ASPASIUS**, vicar of the city of Rome, orders Agnes to be struck with a sword, 482.

To assent means that, although one is able to criticize, one remains silent; or, while listening, flatters, 36.

**ASTASIUS**, a count, 486.

**AUGUSTINE.** See **FATHERS**.

**AVARICE.** How great an evil is it? 245. What vices does it generate? 494. It is the nurse of luxury, 567. Why is it compared with idolatry? 272. Both deny God by denying what belongs to him, ibid. Every avaricious person is impious and harmful both to himself and to others, 302.

## B
## B

**Babylon:** How did it fall twice? 565. It designates the city of the devil, which consists of all the ungodly, 555. The Babylonians were the first to call God the creation of a certain Bel, who is said to have ruled over them, 33.

**Baneiacham** signifies “cultivation,” 15.

**Baptism:** The Red Sea was a figure of our baptism, which is not to be repeated, 7. It is compared with the crossing of the Jordan, 415. Just as Christ formerly went before the children of Israel through the sea in a pillar of fire, so now through baptism he goes before Christian peoples in the pillar of his body, 407. When Christ was baptized, he both instituted the mystery of the washing and transformed the human race, like worthless water, into the eternal substance of divinity by the savor of divinity, 305. Christ came to the washing in order to purify the streams of water for us, 403, 406. Christ’s consecration is greater than that of the element, 406. The solemn words are those spoken in baptism, 114. “To water” means to baptize with the solemn words, 121. No one can be cleansed through baptism except under invocation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, 528. Those who were baptized before the Passion received only remission of sins; after the Resurrection, however, both those baptized earlier and those baptized later were all justified through the prescribed form of faith in the Trinity, 51. It is not surprising that the mystery of the Trinity was not absent from the Lord’s washing, since our washing fulfills the mystery of the Trinity, 403. The distinction between John’s baptism and Christ’s, 441. The disciples, in an adulterous baptism under the name of John’s baptism, had not been immersed but defiled, 219. “With faith preserved, I would say that the baptism by which we are washed is more gracious than that by which the Savior was baptized,” 441. Baptism is the foundation of evangelical truth, 130. The Holy Spirit is given to the baptized person, 72. Sins are forgiven in baptism without toil or any work, 49. In it the grace of God seeks no groaning, weeping, or any work, but only confession from the heart, 93. It freely grants forgiveness of sins, ibid. It is the death of sin, 59. And of the world, 270. It is the pledge and image of resurrection, ibid. For the sinner it is a flood; for the believer, consecration, 421. It is a very grave lie when we lie about what we promised in baptism, 554. There are people who are baptized while sick almost every day, 295. A living person was baptized in the name of the dead, 163. Why now neither clerics nor laypeople baptize, nor are believers immersed on any day except when they are sick, 24.

**Barbarians:** Who are called barbarians? 30.

**Barnabas** was an apostle, 141.

**Beatitude:** No one can obtain the perfect privilege of blessedness if the infinity of eternity does not surround it, 604. Christ promises the small magnificent, the earthly heavenly, and the temporal everlasting rewards with glory, 74. How is eternal life given freely when it is the reward of good works? 575. How is the kingdom of heaven seized and plundered? 392, 524. See **Eternal Life**.

**Wars:** What do the tumult and preparations of wars teach the Christian? 475. Whom did the Lord command to be counted as fit for battle from among the Israelites? 1. Civil war is a greater evil than external war, 82.

**Benefits:** If benefits are to be bestowed, how much more must they not be taken away? 138.

**Flattery:** Things that cannot be obtained by authority are usually obtained by flattery, 298.

**Blasphemy**, 41, 43.

**The Good:** The philosophers of this world call nothing the highest good except peace, honor, and virtue, and nothing the highest evil except wickedness, dishonor, greed, and disgrace, 342. The highest evil is eternal death; the highest good is eternal life, 341. See **Beatitude**. Good, when done against the will, is bitter and evil, 33. It is not a great achievement to avoid evil unless one clings to the good: the former is done out of fear, the latter out of love, 96. It is customary for someone gradually to pass from evil to good, 211. Just as a human being consists of three things—body, soul, and spirit—so there are three things that lead to good or evil: thought, speech, and action, 333. Good things are provided before God and human beings when what is permitted is done in such a way that it causes no scandal, 97. All good cannot be blotted out in anyone, 81. It is not without merit when someone thinks about good men, 305. The just are always called good, but the good are not always just, 53. What is evil to the evil person is good to the good person, 100. Who is educated in goodness? 110. Every fool is an accuser of the good, 206.

**Burgundians** claimed Gaul for themselves, 564.

## C

**Cain:** His fratricide is condemned, 592, 594. It is shown that seven crimes were present in him, 594. The sevenfold punishment inflicted on him was just, ibid. In his envy he destroyed his own soul before another’s body, 493. He signified the Jewish people, 521.

**Caiaphas** prophesied not by merit but by the dignity of the priestly office, 155.

**Caius:** Who was he? 110.

**Reed:** The ancients were accustomed to write with it, 543.

**Calatha** means in Latin “rod” and “dominion,” 12.

**Calculus:** A small stone, so called from calculating, 507.

**Cantii, Cantiani, and Cantianilla:** Their martyrdom is celebrated, 458.

**Captivity:** Captivity and disturbance possess neither piety nor chastity, 292.

**Head:** Whoever holds the head has the remaining part subject to him, 266.

**Flesh:** What is called by the name “flesh”? 60. What it means to be in the flesh, 63. Whatever is against the law of God is carnal, 72. Everything prohibited by the law is carnal, 187. Whatever is done without Christ is carnal and therefore mortal, 284. All flesh is irrational in its perception, 187. The Holy Spirit abandons a person when he has either a carnal understanding or carnal deeds, 72. All sins arise outwardly from the side of the flesh, not from the side of the spirit, 229. Every sin is called flesh, especially faithlessness, which is the mother of every crime, 234. Our flesh ought to be our servant—and how? 535. How is it crucified? 60. Unless someone buries the desires of the flesh, he cannot attain eternal blessedness, 11. Whoever restrains himself from the desires of the flesh lives according to the law of the mind, 71. Carnal things are subject to spiritual things, 116. The justice of God does not permit the one who has conquered the vices of the flesh not to be crowned, 272. See **Soul**.

**Castimonius**, preacher, 458.

**Cataphrygians**, 39, 113. They defend, with empty presumption, the proposition that women deacons ought to be ordained, 295.

**Catechumens** are invited to baptism, 441. How appropriately may the catechumen be compared to water and the believer to wine? 405.

**Yielding:** One must always yield to those who are loud and hot-tempered, 275.

**Celsus:** The martyrdom of the little boy, 467.

**Candles:** The adornment of candles shines in baptism, 438.

**Cervicosus**, 130, 314.

**Ham:** He deservedly first received the name “servant,” 255. He sinned and was made a servant because of his lack of understanding, 135.

**The beast’s mark:** What is it? 559.

**Charity:** Although it may be called by a single name, it consists of many things, 138. It is the foundation of all virtues and good things, 493. Why did it receive such a name? ibid. It is the mother of all good things, 139. It is the head and foundation of religion, 155. It is like the mother of souls, 101. Charity cannot exist without the other virtues, nor the other virtues without charity, 524. How can equality be attributed to faith, hope, and charity? 581. Charity always carries peace with it, 273. Whoever follows it is humble toward everyone, 309. The saints possess charity, and are possessed by it, 556. Through it the perfection of salvation operates, 228. No tortures overcome it, 78. Why is there nothing that can separate us from it? 78. Things done with charity possess the fear of God and zeal, 169. Delicate charity, 472. Love fulfills all the commandments, 99. Whatever good we may seem to possess is dead if charity is lacking, 509. True charity, content with its own benefit, cares for the one whom it professes to love, 185. This is greater: that it benefits everyone, 156. The person is perfect in understanding who acts so as to benefit someone, especially a brother, 157. What is someone believed to do for others who does not spare his own people? 130. Charity is feigned in those who abandon their brothers in time of need, 185. See **Love**.

**Chloe:** What does it mean? 113.

**Christian:** It is not enough to bear the Christian name if we do not perform Christian works, 423. The Jews were Christians, and we are now Jews, 82. Christians’ actions are in heaven, where Christ is also their hope of salvation, 260. What is it to be Christ’s disciple except to be a disciple of piety, truth, and humility? 431. Paul wants Christians to be better in every respect, 138. In the Christian religion nothing is artificial and nothing is done in darkness, as among the pagans, 158. A Christian’s good life is a sign of eternal salvation, 100. What is as glorious for him as to recount the sufferings inflicted upon him for Christ? 204. Which Christians are compared to foxes? 445.

**Christ:** Why is he called the Son of God? 329. He rightly made himself equal to God, 254. From whom is it held that he ought not to be believed to be God? 41. It is proved that he is God, 54. And that he is one God with the Father, 79. God is Christ’s Father by nature, ours by grace, 329, 256. He teaches concerning himself what he is, how great he must be believed to be, what hope exists in him, and what those who believe ought to be like, 243. God is the God of peace and love, 209. He gave commandments as God, not as a human being, and chose the one whom he chose by divine judgment, 210. Why is he called Lord? 28. He is the power of God, 131. Eternal, 32. Why? 116. He is the wisdom of God, 112. Why? 116. He himself is justice—and why? 86. He spoke to Moses, 144. It was fitting that God should promise him to the world through illustrious men, 27. He was promised to Abraham through the line of Isaac, 80. Before the Incarnation, he may be called either Christ or Jesus, 255.

In Christ the divine and human natures entered into a sacred exchange; what was that exchange? 331. We confess one Christ, the Son of God, composed mystically of two natures, divine and human, 330. True flesh was assumed by him, crucified, buried, and raised again, 330. What does “the likeness of flesh” in him mean? 70. His humanity was not consumed by his divinity, 526. Having become flesh, he was not changed, 184. According to his divinity he is in every respect equal to the Father; according to his humanity he exists as a perfect human being, 512. Christ became human so that he might assume humanity into God, 191. And so that we might receive power over the devil, 331. His Incarnation was the salvation of human beings on earth and of angels in heaven, 433. In Christ the bosom was faith in John the Evangelist, divinity in God the Father, and virginity in Mary his mother, 406. Christ was made from a virgin, without a man, by the Holy Spirit, 86. Just as divinity had produced him as a virgin, so the virgin Mary gave birth to him, 399. His mother is a virgin; the Father knows no woman, 480. Why? 333, 70, 265. Why is he from David’s seed and from a virgin? 27. And from Jesse’s root, 106. Why does his birth not benefit Christ but us? 265. Neither is there diminution in the Father nor increase in the Son when he is born, ibid. He was born in such a body as Adam had before sin, 70. The agreement of Matthew and Luke in his genealogy is demonstrated, 699. How is Christ the firstborn? 77. How secretly and privately was he born? 397. When Christ was born, peace was established throughout the whole world by Octavian Augustus, 536. How was it interrupted by Nero? ibid. Why was he born in a time of peace? 394. When he arrived, the chrism—that is, royal anointing, which signifies power—ceased, 47. The distinction between the birth of Christ and that of John the Baptist, 396. How did Christ grow while John the Baptist diminished? 395. At Christ’s birth the days increase; at John the Baptist’s birth they decrease, 395. At Christ’s birth glory was brought by angels, splendor by the star, religious devotion by the Magi, and simplicity by the shepherds, 396. The flock signified the people, night the age, and the shepherds were priests, 397. The shepherds knew of his birth before the rulers did: simple rural life before proud dominion, 397. He was born at his nativity, reborn at the Epiphany, and the Church was joined to him, 405, 406. Why was he wrapped in swaddling clothes? 394. He was virgin in every respect, 428. He became poor for our sake, not for his own, 191. How is his father said to have been a carpenter? 399. The common people call the day of the Lord’s birth a new sun, 397. How rightly? ibid. How should we prepare ourselves to celebrate it? 392. With what praises should it be celebrated? 396. The length of the divine service on that day, 394.

How was Christ preached to the dead? 86. How just was it that John should baptize him? 442. How did the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit descend upon him? 513. His first temptation in the desert is examined, 428. Why did he board Peter’s boat in haste? 439. How does the one who is appeased benefit, who also shows mercy when angry and heals the withered hand? 411. His medicine adds more to salvation than infirmity takes away from health, 205. Everything he did was not for his own sake but for the sake of our salvation, 403. His charity is ineffable and beyond human knowledge, 239. His miracles are not buried in oblivion but renewed through virtues, 403. Palms are rightly offered to Christ seated on a donkey, and garments are spread before him, 417. Christ is said to have lived in the world for three decades and twice three months, 522. How is he said to have experienced fear? 514. His soul was troubled—not for death but unto death, not for himself but for us, 330. It was human sorrow, 72. Great weakness is victory, 116. Why did he conquer when he was judged? 43. Through the suffering of the cross he dedicated to us from his side the washing and drink of martyrdom, 331. How did God hand him over, or how did he offer himself to God? 245. How can the Lord of majesty be said to have been crucified? 606, 118, 356. He laid down his flesh or soul, leaving it because he willed, where he willed, and when he willed, 330. His blood is the pomegranate, 11. The sins of sinners fell upon him, 104. His death was prefigured from the beginning of the world in the holy Fathers, 551. It is not his death but that of sin, 269. His Passion is our life, death, the justification of sins, and the destruction of death, 218. Why has he benefited everyone? 46. His flesh was poured out for the salvation of the body, and his blood for our soul, just as had previously been prefigured, 149. He was born and died so that what he had first made he might afterward create again, 265. On the cross, with hands extended, he accused the sin of those killing him, 89. He was killed for those who nullify his benefit, 149. Which rulers crucified him? 118. Christians stone, crucify, and kill him by their vices, 432. There could be no complete remission of sins if he had not died for us, 515. What does it mean to suffer with Christ? 74. Why must one suffer for Christ? 74.

Christ is known through the Resurrection as Lord of all, 27. The Savior confirmed everything he had taught when he rose from the dead, 236. After the Resurrection he appeared to Peter alone, 161. He appeared separately to James, as also to Peter, ibid. And he truly ate, 339. Descending into hell, he freed the dead from the underworld, 102. He will come to judge the living and the dead—that is, the just and sinners, Gentiles and Jews, or souls and bodies, 331. Christ taught by the example of himself that what he commanded us in writing should be done, 602. By the steps through which he humbled himself and descended to us, we must also ascend to him, 514. It is God’s good pleasure when one makes progress in him, 277. What does it mean to put on Christ? 101. How is he to be sought? 436. Whoever is more forceful than Christ will be regarded by Christ as more religious, 393. We follow him when we imitate him, 515. The Apostle calls those devoted to Christ “christs,” that is, “anointed ones,” 229. We must love him more than our father, 445. Christ is the first and head of all his elect, 500. As he is the life of the elect, so he is the death of the reprobate, 532. We were made through him and again reformed by his grace, 112. Nothing is complete without him, 112. The whole arrangement of our salvation is from God, but through Christ, 29. In him salvation is perfect, 224. Without him there is no salvation with God, 87. Without invoking him no one lives with God, 87. One cannot live for God except through Christ, 60. Who would not praise Christ, by whose benefit he lives? 40. All hope is in him, 60. He is the one in whom, unless every creature hopes, it will perish, 267. The one whose entire hope is in him glories in his cross, and for that person the world too is crucified, 231. Whoever is in Christ is filled with the abundance of divinity, 268. As a good and lavish giver, Christ seeks an occasion for how to give, whether to the unworthy or the bashful, 74. He loves us so much that he attributes to himself what benefits us, 73. How does he intercede for us? 77. He is lost by all who sleep and found by those who keep watch, 393. Whoever abandons his fountain is immediately weakened and withers, 411. What does it mean to sin in Christ and against Christ? 140. Christ was an eagle—and how? 452, 456. And a pearl, 465. He is signified in the rock, 85. Moses’ rod and the bronze serpent were figures of his body, 452. How is he a ship? 455. He is rightly compared with leaven, 408.

**Food:** Just as a sick person should approach medicine, so one should approach the taking of food, 495. Why is it permitted to eat with an unbeliever but not with a brother defiled by vices? 128. See **Gluttony**.

**Circumcision:** It possesses no dignity in itself but is only a sign, 49. Before the preaching of faith, Gentiles were commanded to be circumcised if they wished to approach the Law, 266. Why should circumcision have ceased? 209, 223. What is circumcision of the heart? 41, 105.

**Circumcordialis:** A secret discourse, 596.

**Clerics** are rebuked when they are displeased at being corrected by their elders, 463. See **Ecclesiastical**.

**Compelled:** Whoever does something under compulsion receives no reward, 191. See **Will**.

**Heaven:** The true land of the living, 3.

**Thoughts:** It is evident that our thoughts are known by no one except our own mind, 119. Good and evil thoughts will accuse one another, 39. Holy thought will preserve you, 16.

**They were slapped:** That is, they were treated with insults, 125.

**Hair:** It is an indication of a veil, 148.

**Drunken revelries:** What are they? 100.

**Those preparing for baptism:** The mystery of the Trinity, still unknown, must be disclosed to them, 435. And the Creed, ibid.

**Desire:** The Law prohibits desire, 65.

**Confessors** received the palms of a longer and hidden martyrdom, 498.

**Sins:** They must be confessed to God and the priest, 424. How necessary and useful confession of sin is for the sinner, 589. Excuses are rejected, 592, 593. You will then be free of all your iniquities when you have become a witness and accuser against yourself, 591. Your penitent confession is a medicine, ibid. When someone confesses before the judges of this age, he is immediately led to punishment; before the Lord, the one who confesses immediately proceeds to pardon, 59. A confession that is not faithless obtains a place of pardon for the faithful person, 594. That confession does not free which is not made with repentance, 425. See **Repentance**.

**Marriage:** It is blessed only once, 299. Although marriages are pure, one must nevertheless abstain even from what is lawful so that prayer may more easily be brought to fulfillment, 132. On which days should one abstain from marital intercourse? 133. See **Advent**. Husbands who take concubines in addition to their wives are rebuked, 462. See **Matrimony**.

**Conscience:** It always convicts and judges its own accused silently and without contradiction, 462. Although it has no use of speech, it nevertheless does not know how to keep silent, 592. How great is its severity? ibid. It does not die when it is judged in the soul after the death of the body, 593. A mind conscious of evil trembles to speak, loses its understanding, and errs in words, 186. The worm of conscience, 343.

**Counsel:** Good counsel will guard you, 16. What counsel is better than a good will? 501.

**Consolations:** There are two kinds, 170. It is a great consolation for one who suffers to have someone suffering with him, 188.

**Constantia**, daughter of Augustus, was wonderfully healed by blessed Agnes, 483. She built a basilica and ordered a residence to be established there for herself, ibid. She persevered in virginity, through which many noble and ordinary virgins received the sacred veils, ibid.

**Habit:** It rules a human being, 68.

**Contemplative life** makes the minds of certain elect people insensitive to the love of the world, 524. See **Life**.

**Contentions** produce quarrels, whose fruit is the wasting of life, 228. Remove a person from contention and boldness, and you will have him subject, 229.

**Conduct:** Our conduct should be so regulated that no one suffers scandal from it, 146. Good conduct produces salvation, 257. It strikes fear into the delinquent, 247. See **Life**. From the conduct and morals of God’s servants, even when they are silent, they should be understood, 246.

**The converted:** God desires the lamentation of those who turn back, not the death of the dying, 591. See **Correction**, **Repentance**.

**Heart:** God regards the merits of the heart, not of the flesh, 42. Whatever each person strives for from the heart follows him, 95. There are thorns of the heart that habitually wound even the Word of God, 471.

**Coracina:** A sacred object, 33.

**Corinthians:** They wanted to be called Pauline, Petrine, and Apollonian, not Christian, 111.

**Body:** It must be governed by the law of the soul, 73. How is the body subjected to servitude? 143.

**Correction:** What is just fraternal correction? 504. Whoever does not rebuke a brother who is sinning in a certain way encourages him to sin, 465. As long as the sinner is not rebuked, he scarcely seems to himself to be sinning, 247. The sin of one person, when known but not rebuked, contaminates many, 127. Religious chastisement is sweeter than indulgent leniency, 449. One cannot consistently rebuke someone from whom one receives something, 131. Those who are rebuked so that they may be corrected are not destroyed but built up for life, 208. When those who are rebuked change, they bear witness to the one who rebuked them, 190. Whoever is ashamed when reproved promises to correct himself; whoever becomes angry shows that he will become worse, 189. No one wants to be rebuked when he is in error, 125. It is pointless to admonish someone whom you know will do what he intends, 193. Let us be held within discipline through the mortification produced by corrections, 14. See **Charity**. Correct your own way with as much care as you observe another’s, 489.

**Creation:** It is in the power of the creator to make whatever kind of creature he wishes, 83. Why does every creature groan? 75.

**Crime:** The name of disorder constitutes a crime, 207.

**Cross:** The Savior’s cross is the sin and curse of the Jews, 220. The sign of the cross, 134. The devil does not dare to hold those marked with the sign of the cross, on which he was defeated, in the second death, 70.

**Crystal:** Its nature is described, and what it signifies mystically, 585.

**Desire:** It is generated from the fervor of the blood, 166.

**Curiosity:** A dangerous presumption, 489.

**Cyprian**, 27. The feast day of Cyprian the martyr falls during the vintage season, 470.

## D

**Damasus** is today ruler of the Church, 296.

**Daniel:** God made him a confessor, 458.

**The damned:** Their torments, 422. The punishment of eternal damnation must be meditated upon continually, 496.

**David:** Choking lions and killing the Philistine, he was a figure of Christ, 529. He killed Goliath not with an iron weapon but with a spiritual sword, 475. How was this done figuratively? 476.

**Tithes:** They are to be distributed each year, 423, 425.

**Defending:** What is defended by only a few usually appears not to have been proved, 90.

**Degenerating:** To depart from one’s creator, 235.

**To lack:** To have nothing, 256.

**Contempt of earthly pleasures** is especially necessary for one hastening toward heaven, 19.

**Delicacies:** Are they the gates of sin? 299. Spiritual delicacies are better than carnal ones, 391.

**Dephcha** is interpreted as “health,” 8. Why is it the ninth encampment of the children of Israel? ibid.

**Desires:** To endure desires without being conquered by them is characteristic of an illustrious and perfect man, 133.

**The despairing:** The confession of the un despairing thief should give the despairing the greatest hope, 596. Just as no one should despair, whatever his age, if he wishes to turn to the Lord, so no one should feel secure on the basis of faith alone, 410.

**You will not detract:** Never do so if you have examined yourself well, 489.

**God:** He is called “God” on account of fear, but “Father” on account of honor and kindness, and because all origin is from him, 262, 280. “God” is the name of nature and power; the very relation of the names teaches that this power remains undivided in the Father and the Son, 222. Nature itself recognizes its creator by its own judgment, 39, 61. When God is defined, he increases by that very definition, 352. He is rightly estimated when he is called inestimable, 351. He is thought of more truly than he is spoken of, 321. First of all, one must believe that there is one who made all things from nothing through his Word and gave them life through the Holy Spirit, 324. Whatever departs from the confession of one God is considered dead, 234. God cannot be understood as composed of parts, 321. It is proper to God not to have begun but always to be the same as he always is, 325. In God all things are equal in the immensity of infinity, 239. He remains immutable and cannot fail to love what he has made, 43. For God all time is today, 403. With God there is nothing that can be called future, 160. God is shown to require providentially the merits of his work, 36. The wisdom of this age considers God unconcerned, 115. God is said to know what is good, 182. Those whom he knows will be saints are already saints before him and remain so, 30. What is God’s foreknowledge? 81. The justice of God’s foreknowledge, 82. He judges according to justice, not according to foreknowledge, 81. He condemns no one before he sins, and crowns no one before he conquers, 81. How did he predestine those who are saved? 306. See **Predestination**. He chose Paul while Paul was persecuting, knowing that he would become good; he condemned Pharaoh before the future judgment, so that he might be believed to be the one who would judge, 82. He wishes all human beings to be saved, if they themselves also wish it, 292. God’s goodness wishes no one to perish, 53. Because there is one God of all, he justified everyone by one principle, 47. Three things in God preserve the order of times—past, present, and future: goodness, by which we have already begun to exist; mercy, by which we are called to repentance; and justice, by which we shall be judged, 605. What is so great in believing that God generated from himself, when it is not doubted that he made all things from nothing? 120. To say is to make, 565, 534. And to swear is also to make, 542. He is often said to have given what he permits, 538. The justice of God belongs to the sacrament of God, 46. Because what he promised, he gave, 31. He is Father to us when we act and judge when we sin, 392. With God there is no distinction of persons except that of morals and life, 222. How does the truthful God prevail when he is judged? 42. God’s utterances cannot be contradictory, 284. How are people said to be purified? 511. How are anger and indignation found in God? 37. The hand of the Lord has many meanings in Scripture, 504. How is he a consuming fire? 335. Everything must be referred back to God, 13. The glory of God is that all things are said to be from him, through him, and in him, 173. How does something come to be for the glory of God? 146. What is not from God cannot stand, 279. From the structure of the world it can be understood that God alone is to be loved, 32. His power and majesty are perceived from this, ibid. The Lord prefers to be loved rather than feared, 273. What service is so acceptable to God as being loved with one’s whole heart and strength? 536. God cannot be served except with a pure heart, 274. In faith one serves God spiritually through devotion of mind and purity of heart, 227. Why did the Apostle command us to serve God with the measure by which we formerly served the Lord? 62. Let a harmonious voice serve God, let a psalm praise him, and let a hymn exalt him, 273. God begot in such a way that those born free are nevertheless his servants, 251. We then give true thanks to God through him if we keep the measure of his commandments, 274. Only those who keep God’s commandments know God’s name, 507. When we call God Father but display a dissimilar life, we do God an injury, 73. To carry God means to display the image of God in well-performed deeds, 132. The work of God demands a people [reading uncertain] hastening prematurely to the feasts, 14. How is God compelled by our works? 392, 393. What way are we commanded to prepare for the Lord? 462. We have God as a physician, who heals by striking and gives life by mortifying, 414. We received God’s mercy for two reasons, 59. Who would not exalt without limit the benefits God has bestowed on humanity—the Lord on the servant, the creator on the creature? 291. God deigned to adopt human beings as sons for himself according to the example of Christ, 77. How can we be heirs of God, who always lives? 74, 223. What does it mean to pray that God’s kingdom may come? 75. Whoever pleases God is approved by human beings, 103. Who would not fear one whom he knows to be God’s friend? 261. Who can accuse one whom God excuses? 216. God’s support is necessary when human help fails, 204. We make God forget us when we sin, 420. The recompense for contempt of God is disgrace and defilement, 34. A nature that abandons God is called the worst seed, 235. When we do not see God, although he is present, we are absent from him, 182. To claim God’s glory for a human name is almost idolatry, 114. It is a kind of unbelief neither to rejoice in prosperity nor to grieve over adversity in divine matters, 447.

**Devotion:** When it is not broken by the weakness of an occurring affliction, it appears proven, 205. What is willingly accepted is that which is done with a devoted and prudent spirit, 263. To win God’s favor one needs no intercessor, but a devoted mind, 33.

**The Devil:** His name is interpreted as “falling downward,” 548. He is called sin, 65. When he desired high things, he apostatized, 97. Demons continually roam through this air like winds, 565. To hand someone over to the devil means to permit, not to incite or send, 33. The devil’s friendship is miserable, 548. He does not fight against the one whom he holds bound by the chains of sins, but against the one who ceases to sin, 514. He attacks us with our own weapons, 60. Who are the seven spirits that the devil takes with him? 549. He loves his children as a glutton loves a piglet: in order to eat it, 432. He stirs up a storm against God’s servants, but suffers shipwreck himself, 249. This is the true victory: that Satan, who conquered immortal, glorious, feasting Adam, should now be conquered by a mortal, humble, and hungry human being, 428. The devil’s city is the entire body of the reprobate, 503.

**Deacons:** There ought now to be seven, together with some presbyters, so that there may be two in each church and one bishop in each city, 295. Evangelists are deacons who can evangelize without a cathedra, 241. See **Teachers**.

**Deaconesses:** See **Cataphrygians**.

**Words:** Words without deeds are of no benefit, 473.

**Dignitosus:** A man of rank, 301. It is worse to have lost rank than never to have had it, 79.

**Digonbad** is near the valley of Zared, 18. Mystically it signifies an apiary of temptations, ibid.

**Diocletian**, emperor, 310.

**Dionysius**, martyr. See **Eusebius**.

**Our discipline:** Its whole substance is mercy and piety, 297.

**The seventy disciples:** Since they are in the second rank after the apostles, they are rightly compared with seventy palm branches, 7, 417. Why does Christ call the disciples brothers? 501.

**The perfection of disciples** is the joy and crown of the teacher, 279. The crown of the disciples is the glory of their teacher, and his truth is the punishment of unbelievers, 285. The authority of the teacher lies in the confidence of the disciples, 285. For disciples victorious in the contest, the teacher will be worthy of a crown, 261. The teacher’s testimony is found in obedient disciples, 197. The disciples’ sadness is the teacher’s joy, 449.

**Discord:** The beginning of injustice, 100. Where there is dissension, nothing is right, 148.

**Rich:** Someone is rightly called rich who, full of every virtue, has grown to the summit of perfection, 511. How rightly is the rich man compared with a camel? 442.

**Riches:** They are not evil in themselves but are evil for those who use them badly, 342. Just as riches produce neglect of salvation, so poverty, while seeking to be satisfied, turns away from justice, 283. They are alien to us, 342. What riches should be acquired? 4. They are nourishment for vices, 567. It is very rare for someone who possesses them to strive toward rest, 490.

**Teacher:** A teacher must be chosen with great care, 307. Teachers ought to strengthen the weak and instruct the unskilled with gentleness, 104. Whoever teaches faithfully cannot have a bad conscience, 291. The teaching of the commandment would become empty if authority did not precede in the teacher’s conduct, 602. If teachers act differently from what they teach, one must dissent from them, so that the law may be more your guide than a human being, 230. The Apostle calls “teachers” those who, following the custom of the Synagogue, instructed children in the Church by retaining letters and readings, 153. Certain teachers of secular laws are rebuked because they do not undertake the cases of the poor in court without receiving a reward, 566. Why do deacons not now preach among the people? 241.

**Teaching:** The first teaching is to do good, 473. Virtue is the witness of teaching: since what is preached is incredible to the world, it becomes credible through deeds, 28, 31. Bad teaching is signified by wood, hay, and straw, 122. Teaching is leaven, 128.

**Sorrow:** Mental sorrow and bodily pain are so closely connected that one cannot exist without the other, 575.

**The Lord’s Day:** The Apostle commanded that a collection be made on the Lord’s Day, 168.

**Domitian**, saint, 471.

**Domitian’s persecution** had disturbed all the churches, 501.

**Donatists**, 39, 113, 114. They reject those baptized by our people, ibid.

**Gift:** In a gift, the greatness of the giver rather than that of the recipient is considered, 51.

## E
## E

**DRUNKENNESS** makes one sober through heavenly grace, 479. **EBRONA** in Latin means “passing over,” 16. **THE CHURCH** took its beginning from Christ, and in name one may participate in Christ, though not in nature, 248. It was formed from Christ’s side on the cross through his passion and the sleep of death, 333, 520. It is joined to Christ daily; but after the resurrection it will be joined to him far more exaltedly and nobly, 587. Christ is the Church’s bridegroom of blood, 527. It snatched Christ away from the Synagogue, 393. Christ rejected the faithless Synagogue and takes up the faithful Church, 439. The prophets made preparations, and the apostles laid the foundations of the Church, 236. It was gathered from all the nations, something certain heretics denied, 519. It is spread throughout the whole world, 326. Whatever exists outside the Catholic Church is contrary to it, 122. The Church of the elect is divided into seven parts—and what are they? 502. The reprobate remain in the Church only in body and soul; in mind, however, they are outside the Church, 522. The interpretation and order of the names of the seven Churches are explained, 501. They point out the way that leads to life, ibid. The Church tramples upon the world by despising it, so that it may strive more freely toward heavenly things, 546. It is a pillar of fire, 541. Noah’s ark was a figure of it, 440, 521. So too was the woman seeking the drachma, 427; and the fig tree, 11; it is called a heap of stones, 18. The two women grinding are the Church and the Synagogue: one will be taken, the other left, 408. It is established that the Church grew through persecutions, 541. It is a ship in whose mast Christ is seated, the Father in the stern, and the Holy Spirit in the prow; its rowers are the twelve apostles and an equal number of prophets, 453. It is battered by storms but never sunk, ibid. In the Church the law is more truly present where the Lord of the law is feared, 129. Why do the writings of the Apostle not agree in every respect with the order that now exists in the Church? 241. The Synagogue, and afterward the Church, had elders, without whose counsel nothing was done, 298. I do not know through what negligence this custom has grown obsolete, ibid. This is the tradition of the Synagogue that the Apostle wishes us to follow: that while seated they should dispute, the elders according to rank in chairs, those following in benches, and the last on the floor upon mats, 159. The Church is twofold, domestic and public, 170. Wherever presbyters celebrate the solemn rites, it is called a church, 170. Whoever can should come every day and night to the church for the morning office, 425. Some come to it not because they are Christians by faith, but lest people should not think them Christians, 443. Those who came to it rarely, even clerics, are reproved, 448. When you proceed to it, you offer the peace to the bishop, 421. A companion who had built a church is praised, 474.

**ECCLESIASTIC** persons ought to be concerned with the things of God and detached from secular business, 307. No one should readily accept an ecclesiastical dignity unless his life has first been examined, 301. He possesses grace, whatever his character may be, but his rank is effective through the power of the Holy Spirit, 151. Nothing is so harmful as for an ecclesiastic—especially one who occupies a high position—to pursue the riches of this age, 302. In the administration of God’s grace, a woman has no place, 109.

**ECTASIS** is a kind of intense astonishment arising from the sight of difficult and unusual things, 13.

Whoever **LACKS** is imperfect, 255.

All the **ELECT** are called priests—and why? 572. The more one is uncertain whether one has been chosen, the humbler one ought to be, 410.

**ALMSGIVING.** Give to everyone; do not choose whom you will pity, 490. Do not show yourself merciful by means of another’s plunder, ibid. This is justice: since God gives, a person should give from what he has to the one who lacks it, 194. Everyone ought to give to the needy according to what he possesses, 425. It contributes to one’s merit when one gives from one’s own possessions to the needy, 244. One must give in such a way that the act does not make the giver poor, 191. It is not only how much is given that is considered, but from what resources and with what intention it is given, 194. What does it mean to give generously in simplicity? 95. How poorly some people excuse themselves from distributing alms, 444. [Col. 1233] Giving alms benefits the very person who gives, 444. Through this he also becomes richer, ibid. How pleasing is the work of almsgiving, since it cleanses every stain and impurity of a person! 262. Almsgiving is a good gift that purifies every filth and defilement, 368, 426. See **ABSTINENCE, FASTING, MERCY**.

**ELIJAH**, speaking to the widow of Zarephath, prefigured Christ, 530. See **APOCALYPSE, ENOCH**.

**ELIM** is interpreted as “rams,” 7.

**ELISHA** prefigured Christ, while Naaman represented the people of the nations, 531.

What does **ELMON-DEBLATHAIM** signify? 18.

**INSCRIPTION OF CONDEMNATION**, 593, 597.

The **COLLECTIONS OF EMERENTIANA**: the martyrdom of Agnes, 483.

**ENOCH AND ELIJAH** will be apostles at the end of time, 125.

Why is **EPIPHANY** so called? 400. It is a most festive day, 443.

**BISHOP** is interpreted as “overseer,” 364. He sits on a more elevated throne in the Church, ibid. The apostles are the head of the Church and ambassadors of Christ, and these are bishops, 153. The apostles are bishops, 241. Episcopal dignity cannot be equaled by any comparisons, 359. The splendor and diadem of kings are far beneath it, ibid. Yet nothing is more wretched if a bishop’s holy life is put at risk, ibid. In Paul’s time, rulers had not yet been appointed over individual churches, 112, 129. The first presbyters were called bishops, so that when one withdrew, the next would succeed him, 241. But the arrangement was changed through the foresight of the Council, so that merit, not rank, would create a bishop, appointed by the priesthood of many, 242. Bishops and presbyters have one ordination: each is a priest, but the bishop is first; for he is a bishop who is first among the presbyters, 295. In the bishop lies the dignity of all ordinations, 114. All the orders are also present in him, 241. He is the Lord’s vicar, 148. There is one bishop in the Church, 154. Individual bishops ought to preside over individual churches, 153. What sort of person ought to be chosen as bishop? 294. From the Apostle’s rules it is taught what his life ought to be, 360, 361. In his person the salvation of the whole people consists, 303. Bishops are the eyes of the Church, 364. A bishop is bound by the commandment of necessity to preach the word of God, 357. He boldly preaches admonitions concerning salvation to priests and pontiffs, 358. He should be recognized as a bishop more by good works than by profession, and as such more by merits than by name, 359, 364. Whatever a bishop possesses that is pleasing, people regard him as all the more praiseworthy for possessing it, 364. He ought to have only one wife—that is, not two churches, but one alone, and that one Catholic, 360. Content only with the stipends of his own church, he should not covet what he understands to be superfluous; rather, from the very poverty of his church he should willingly distribute to the poor, 361. He should rule his own body with authoritative power, 361. He cannot judge the faithless, 128. A simoniac is sharply punished, 362, 363.

**A FEAST**, 90.

Every **ERROR** is attributed to the flesh, 284. A person can easily understand that he is in error if he sees himself reproved by many, 210.

**ESAU** was a figure of the Jewish people, and **JACOB** of Christians, 226.

**ESMONA** is called in Latin “acceleration,” 14.

**TO BE / BEING.** Everything that exists is either unbegotten, begotten, made, or even reborn, 322. To have existed and not to exist is worse than never to have existed, 135.

**ETHAN**, the third encampment of the children of Israel, signifies “strength” to us; and what does it teach us? 5.

The mystery of the **EUCHARIST** was celebrated during the meal; it was not itself a meal, 149. In the Eucharist Christ’s flesh is truly received and his blood truly drunk, 491. It is a sacrifice for the salvation of all, both living and dead, ibid. When we eat Christ’s body, we participate in his divinity and humanity, 8. It is the true manna, not in figure but in reality, ibid. We receive the mystical cup of blood for the protection of our body and soul, 149. All Christians ought to offer and receive communion every Sunday, 426. Let us cleanse our hearts and bodies so that we may be satisfied at the Lord’s altar with his body and blood, 424. One must approach communion with devoted mind and fear, 149. Whoever approaches the Lord’s table thoughtlessly differs in no respect from an unbeliever, 150.

The **ENCOMIUM OF EUSEBIUS**, and how he removed the signature of Dionysius, who had subscribed to the Arians, 467. He deserved to learn by revelation the end of his life, 468. By what kind of martyrdom did he die in exile? ibid. All his disciples were either priests or martyrs, 467. He instituted the same persons as monks whom he had instituted as clerics, ibid., 468.

**EVE** too is Adam, 54.

The **GOSPEL** is God’s good news, 211. Through it sinners are called to forgiveness, 26. The Gospel of the most blessed Paul, 606. The Gospel is represented by the iron rod, the Law by the wooden one, 508. As far as a servant is from his lord, so far is the Gospel from the Law, 29. It is the image of God’s Law, in whose faith and conduct the truth of the Gospel shines, 150. The discipline of Christians is the Gospel, 543. Paul says that his glory lies in this: that the severity of the Gospel should remain, 141. See **SCRIPTURE, TESTAMENT**.

To **EVANGELIZE** is greater than to baptize, 114.

The **GOSPEL READING** recited on the Lord’s birthday, 394.

**EXCOMMUNICATION.** Whoever is expelled from the Church is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, 127.

**EXAMPLES** persuade more easily than words, 145, 156. A person becomes more ready for the matter entrusted to him if he sees many agreeing with it, 30. One is easily inclined if one sees a companion consent, 134.

**EXORCISM**, 613.

How can **EXORCISTS** be called teachers? 241.

**EXSUPERANTIUS**, Eusebius’s assistant in the priesthood, companion in martyrdom, and partner in labor, 468.

**EXALTATION** is pride, 201.

The final vision of **EZEKIEL** agrees with the seventh vision of John, 578.

## F

Good and sober **STORIES** give grace and example to those who hear them, 244.

The **FANATICS** are without God, 119.

The pagans do not assert that **FATE** is contrary to everyone, 269.

**HAPPINESS** is generally subject to dangers, 602.

**WOMAN** was not made in the image of God, 147, 159. It was inappropriate that a woman, made subject to man, should be called the image of God, 273. She is commanded to fear her husband, 248. A woman who conquers the devil and strives to please God through good works is not improperly called a man, 547.

**FESTIVALS.** The visitation of the one God gives us more than the superstitious presumption of the pagans concerning many gods gives them, 400. We ought to preserve chastity throughout all festivals, 424.

**FAITH** is a gift of God’s mercy, 49. Christ grants us the very thing that we believe, 113. Believers are called that because they believe, 222. Faith is in the mind, 64. It is practiced not in years but in understanding, 480. It is a matter not of necessity but of will, 173. To believe or not to believe is a matter of will, 48. God’s faithfulness consists in what he promised concerning himself, 31. There is no ambiguity in our faith, 242. Our faith is the seal of God’s promise, confirming God’s words, 308. The gentile who believes in Christ, guided by nature, condemns the Jew, 41. The more impossible what is believed seems, the more honorable the believer will be, 51. Faith is an eternal reality, 176. It must be fortified by fraternal love in order to be the believer’s perfection, 227. There are certain degrees of faith, and whoever believes more devoutly confesses more religiously, 449. Faith removes the cloud of error and grants perfect knowledge of God in the mystery of the Trinity, 42. It creates dignity and merit, 47. To the extent that a person has inwardly savored faith, to that extent he will progress, 70. Faith is greater than the Law, 45, 52. Faith justifies those who flee to it, 70. For salvation God’s grace asks faith alone, 48. Whoever believes in Christ receives remission of sins freely through faith alone, 112. Why? 93. He also attains salvation, 84. Faith makes God favorable when it is approved by good works, 135. The hope of the person who has only a profession of faith without good works is vain, 315. Not all who have faith are saved, but only those who persevere in good works, 409. Those are wise and perfect who possess faith not more in words than in deeds, 118. Faith first obtains pardon; continuing holy conduct, together with faith, earns the crown, 233. Whoever loves faith keeps the commandments, 309. The law of faith is the law of security—and why? 73. Where faith is intact, the Savior teaches, watches, and rejoices, 441. It is praise of God’s glory if many are won to the faith, 233. In the believer God appears righteous, 31. Why should believers receive rewards? 76. The stable faith by which Satan alone has always been defeated is God’s armor, 250. Faith is the spiritual armor of incorrupt preaching, 195. Christian faith cuts off all pride, 318. Faith’s victory occurs when all vices and crimes are subdued, 303. Whoever joins himself to the Christian faith becomes a citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household, 236. God could give believers nothing greater than to be called sons of God, while the faithless are disowned, 51. Just as those who do not believe have already been judged, so those who believe are already called heavenly, 166. We shall see God’s glory in proportion to our belief, 177. How can faith and hope be said to remain in blessedness? 579. No one who keeps faith with God can be faithless toward human beings, 315. The life that comes from faith is not this present life but the future one, 32. Just as unbelievers have three punishments, so believers have three glorious things, 38. Nothing drives a person to death more than violating faith under the pretext of faith, 347. Those who appear to restrain themselves from vices without professing Christ are sanctified according to the world but, according to the Spirit of God, are unclean, 187.

The **SON OF GOD** is the divine Reason, called in Greek *logos* (λόγος), a reason that is called by many names, 352. These names are explained, ibid. The saints know the name of Christ, namely that he is the Son of God, partly and partly do not know it, 569. True faith holds that the Son was not born or made externally, as heretics falsely claim, but was generated from the Father’s own substance, 329. We do not say that the Son of God is an extension of some part of the Father, as some have thought, nor do we understand him as a word without a reality, as though he were merely the sound of a voice, 347. He alone was born from God the Father, from the unbegotten substance of God, 265. Through generation he received everything belonging to the Father, so that in power, substance, and name he differs in nothing from the Father, 234. Whoever denies that the perfect Son of God was born from God the Father is an Arian, 255. The Son of God possesses the name “God” by nature, not by adoption, 234. The Father is understood to be in the Son because they have one substance, 184. The Son said, “I and the Father are one,” because of the nature of divinity; “we are,” because of the distinct properties of the persons, 327. He cannot be inferior to the Father, 328. How is he the wisdom of the Father, whether begotten or created? 349. Because he is called the image of the Father, he is to be believed to differ nothing from him, 264. How wrongly do heretics say that the Son is light from light (*ex lumine*), not from the Light (*de lumine*)? 350, 352. We believe that he was born without beginning from the Father’s breast—or, so to speak, from the womb of God’s heart, 348. The deeds of the Son are the deeds of the Father, from whom all things come, 210. Everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son, 72. Why is the Son of God called both Angel and God? 87. By nature he is the envoy of God the Father, 184. The Son of God always appeared to the patriarchs, 40. How was he formerly seen by the Fathers in the Old Testament? 354. In him, through an image, the arrangements of future events that had to be fulfilled in their respective times were perceived, 355. Thus he is understood to have appeared to the ancient Fathers, when, by assuming the arrangement of some visible material, he seemed to be seen, 355. He appeared to Moses, 264. When he assumed a human being, he brought no stain upon eternity by changing spirit into flesh, 355. Rather, in the human being he remained the same as he had been before the world in the Father, 356. We must give thanks to God through no other than his Son, 62. See **CHRIST, TRINITY, WORD**.

We are called **SONS OF GOD** through the grace of Christ, 105. This is the testimony of sons: that the paternal sign should be seen in them through the Spirit, 74. What father would not rejoice in sons who act well? 207. In the glory of his sons lies the glory of the father, 240. The father’s dearest son is the one who imitates his good qualities, 245.

Why is **FORNICATION** the gravest sin? 131. Roman laws excuse fornication, 35. The Apostle does not, ibid. See **ADULTERY**.

The **FRANKS** claimed Germany for themselves, 564.

Who are called **BROTHERS**? 113. Why are they called by this name? 30. Those who sow discord among brothers are poisoners, 576. Whoever does not grieve with his brother insults him, 173. See **CHARITY**.

## G

**GADGAD** is interpreted as “temptation,” 15.

**GAUL.** See **BURGUNDIANS**.

**JOY.** One reaches rest only through labor, and joys only through sorrows, 7.

**KIND / LINEAGE.** To glory according to the flesh means to claim nobility for oneself on the basis of the flesh and the privilege of one’s lineage, 200.

The discovery of the bodies of **GERVASIUS AND PROTASIUS** is described, 484 ff.

**GLORY** is read in the sense of authority, 196. It is good not to conceal the glory of one’s merits, so that believers may be invited, 204. Vain glory is wishing to win where there is no reward, 229. Vain glory produces seven vices, 493.

The **GLUTTONOUS AND DRUNKEN** are servants of the belly and of lust, 333.

**GOG** is interpreted as “straight,” 572.

The **GOTHS** claimed Spain for themselves, 546.

**GRACE** is twofold, 89. Grace is God’s gift, not a due payment for works, but something granted freely through mercy, 89, 232. Human nature is such that people can possess nothing good from themselves unless they receive it from the one who is supremely good, 518, 179. The things of God cannot be learned without the Spirit of God, 119. Whatever good the faithful do, they do through God’s activity, 535. Paul always refers all grace back to God, so that willing is ours, but bringing to completion belongs to God, 257. The Holy Spirit fills with his grace whom he wills, as many as he wills, and as much as he wills, 323. Communication with the Holy Spirit enables us to possess the grace of salvation, 210. The Holy Spirit assists good efforts, 159. Every gift of God’s grace is in Christ, 231—and from Christ, 59. Grace bestows life through Christ, 57. How has Christ’s grace restored a human being to his former state of innocence? 69. God helps the person whom he sees striving with his whole mind, 133. God grants each person grace so that he may draw as much as he thirsts for, [Col. 1236] 240. God wished no one to be excluded from his gift, 180. How does grace abound? 58. The person who remains in God’s grace acquires God, 63.

Who are called **GREEKS**? 30, 31. See **LATINS**.

**GREGORY** is cited, 544, 582, 586. He posited six ages of humanity, 538. See **FATHERS**.
